-> I also testify that this book belongs <-
-> to the Torah-learned leader, the Honorable Nettel, may his Rock preserve him, <-
<note>original: *Ha-Katzin Ha-Torani*. While *Katzin* literally means "officer," in this period it was a title of respect for a community leader or a person of high social and financial standing. The abbreviation *Y"V* (translated here as "may his Rock preserve him") is a traditional blessing for a living person.</note>
-> of Wörlitz. <-
<note>Wörlitz is a town in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, Germany. During the 18th century, it was part of the Principality of Anhalt-Dessau, which had a significant Jewish community.</note>

-> As evidence, I have signed my humble name, Wolf, son of the scholar, <term>our teacher and rabbi</term> Joseph. <-
<note>original: *Ha-Katan* (the small/humble). It was standard practice for a person to refer to themselves as "the small" when signing their name as a sign of religious humility. The term <term>Ma-H-V</term> (an abbreviation for *Morenu Ha-Rav*) is a high-level rabbinic honorific used here for Wolf's father, Joseph.</note>

# The Book
# Two Tablets of the Covenant

-> Pure words · more precious than pearls · a composition on the two Laws · in writing <-
<note>original: "two Laws." This refers to the Jewish belief that Moses received two Torahs at Mount Sinai: the Written Torah (the Pentateuch) and the Oral Torah (the traditions and explanations later recorded in the Talmud).</note>
-> and by mouth, handed down from Sinai · set in order and arranged · by a hero among heroes · <-
-> A man of God, a <term>Holy Lamp</term>, master of the Land of Israel · the scholar <-
<note>original: *Boizina Kadisha* (Aramaic). A title of supreme honor for a mystic or great sage, suggesting he illuminates the world with his spiritual wisdom.</note>
-> complete in every virtue and wisdom, both revealed and hidden · the <term>Gaon</term> <-
<note>original: *Gaon*. A title used for an exceptionally brilliant rabbinic scholar who has mastered the depths of Jewish law.</note>
-> whose radiant light of Torah · shone through all <-
-> the Diaspora · from one end to the other · the honorable our teacher and rabbi <-
-> Isaiah, son of our teacher and rabbi Abraham HaLevi, of blessed memory · <-
-> of the Horowitz family · who is hidden and tucked away <-
-> in his resting place in the Holy Land <-
<note>Isaiah Horowitz (c. 1565–1630), known as the "Shelah" after the initials of this book, moved from Europe to Ottoman Palestine in 1621 and is buried in Tiberias.</note>
-> and whose soul is in the heavenly treasures beneath the Throne of the Ancient Holy One : <-
<note>original: *Atika Kadisha* (Aramaic). A mystical reference to God as "the Ancient Holy One," commonly found in the Zohar.</note>

And a blessing to the head of the provider · enlightened and great · the son of the author · a branch from ancestral trees, the "great eagle with wings" who spreads his wings toward the south, where wisdom, knowledge, and understanding reside; the chief cornerstone, the pious and humble, the great <term>Gaon</term>, the wonder of our generation, our teacher and rabbi Sheftel <term>Segal</term>, may his light shine · Head of the Rabbinical Court and Head of the Academy of the holy community of Poznań and the district, may his Rock protect him · who gave his heart and soul to bring this honored book to print, to illuminate the eyes of the wise with a precious light · our teacher and rabbi, who makes clear and shines, this holy book as the eyes of the upright shall behold · in Israel, a man of <term>Thummim and Urim</term> :
<note>original: *Segal*. A Hebrew acronym for *Se-gan Le-viyah* (Assistant to the Levites), indicating his status as a Levite. *Thummim and Urim* refers to the oracular breastplate of the High Priest, used here to describe the son's perfect clarity in judgment.</note>

Brought to the printing house a second time by men of Torah from the land of Poland, the Torah-learned leaders: the honorable teacher and rabbi Ze'ev Wolf, son of the leader, the honorable teacher and rabbi Samuel Rabbi Kaplish, of blessed memory, from Jarosław · and the honorable teacher and rabbi Shneur Zalman, son of our teacher and rabbi Jonathan Katz, of blessed memory, from Polonne · and our teacher and rabbi Isaac, son of the rabbi Meir Ashkenazi, of blessed memory, from the land of Friesland · and our teacher and rabbi Zvi Hirsch, son of the rabbi Abraham, of blessed memory, from Wronke · and it was edited with intense focus to purify and refine it, and to remove the stumbling blocks of errors that fell into the first editions · with the ultimate beauty of black ink and white paper, and new and fine letters. This book is pleasant to look at and a desire to the eyes, as your own eyes shall behold the uprightness · and these men added to the first editions indices to open the "gates of righteousness," the gates distinguished in Law which are scattered here and there throughout this book · so that the reader may easily find his topic and desire, and so that this book will not be like a "sealed book," closed off to all who seek it · and from now on, each man shall come to his place in peace and fulfill all his desires, with the help of God, may He be blessed :

May he be remembered for good and for a blessing, his name is the exalted leader, the honorable teacher and rabbi Meshel, son of the teacher and rabbi Joseph Emden of Amsterdam, who scattered his silver and gold and poured it from his pocket to strengthen the printing and to assist in this great commandment · because of this, he shall be blessed with thousands for good · and may his reward be from the Lord, and may He bless him with His strength and wisdom :

# **All** you owners of treasures of precious things, of silver and gold, of onyx, topaz, and emerald, of myrrh and aloes; remember the second row: carbuncle, sapphire, and diamond. Search with candles and see
if what is found in your granaries is like what is found in my treasures, which have a "measure longer than the earth" <note>A reference to Job 11:9, describing the vastness of divine wisdom</note>, providing for all the inhabitants of the world. Generation to generation shall praise their works,
and their mighty deeds they shall tell—the actions of praise, the preciousness of the levels of their piety and abstinence. Their witnesses shall testify and be justified through the beauty of the words in the books they authored. Due to their great humility, for
they were men of wonder with exceeding modesty, they did not allow their wisdom to be fully revealed. Instead, they spoke words of blessing, words of the Fathers, and excellent words concerning piety and abstinence.
They merited life by achieving the ultimate good in the world for which they labored. The smoke of their incense rose to the Supernal Bliss, to cleave to the <term>Active Intellect</term><note>In medieval philosophy, the "Active Intellect" is the bridge between the human mind and the divine</note>, the True Worker
whose work is Truth. He who weaves a crown of glory for those borne from the womb, and established a foundation stone, looking upon "seven eyes" with many "sevens" in the various facets of the Torah. He is
the great turtle-dove, outstanding in wisdom and piety, whose deeds are awesome and wondrous—the Lamp of Israel and the "Faithful Shepherd," my grandfather, the eminent genius, our teacher and rabbi, **Isaiah Segal**, of blessed and holy memory,
whose heart saw wisdom in a great and deep understanding. "No secret was hidden from him" <note>original: "la anas leh kol raz"</note>; he knew how to interpret all the voids of the world, with hidden and concealed secrets,
what is above and below, behind and before. Now, I have begun to tell even a fraction of the glory of his praise; I put my hand to my mouth to remain silent, lest I spoil my speech with vanity
that contains sin. They might call me a debtor... also, there is no need to tell of his greatness, for his friend and his history are well known. He did not leave behind Scripture,
Mishna, Talmud, Laws, <term>Aggadah</term><note>Non-legalistic exegetical texts</note>, or <term>Pesikta</term>. Whether a "great matter" <note>Mysticism</note> or a "small matter" <note>Legal debates</note>, the Work of the Chariot or the debates of Abaye and Rava—from that wellspring all the flocks are watered,
the flocks of the holy sheep. Every wise-hearted person will gain further insight into the original legal rulings which our ancestors never imagined... And who would believe a man who possesses such things
and would be so great as to make them known? The staff of his strength and his glorious rod were established in his hand for many generations of peoples who were redeemed by his discipline. He left all honor behind and chose to dwell
in the "Land of the Living" <note>Referring to the Land of Israel</note>, all of it a secret of freedom... and to establish a burial place there for his holy soul at the place of its source, in the House of God, without hindrance from the accusers
who lie in wait on the path to heaven. As I mention him, I am filled with grief and sighing that I did not merit to see him face to face, nor even from behind, to fulfill for me the saying of the wise man:
"Wisdom is good with an inheritance, and an advantage to those who see the sun." Even though I have no benefit from it now, for the flame of the Torah rises of its own accord, and the Torah seeks its lodging...
and the promise to Isaiah: "They shall not depart etc." <note>Isaiah 59:21</note>—and these three shall be for him a "threefold cord" that is not quickly broken. This is my comfort: that his fledgling replaces him like a flame breaking forth
from the spark of his wisdom and his Torah—the child is like the father. All the "generations" in the Bible are written defectively, except for two... a parable of a golden pomegranate and its setting
is a pearl. He is the father of my father, the "Chariot of Israel and its Horsemen," the spirit of the Torah in its truth. "The lip of truth shall be established forever." He bestows the flow of his honor,
showering the people of God with a "Torah of Kindness," a fallen fruit from the wisdom on high. All voices are valid in the Shofar of his praise, his pure words more precious than pearls. The pillars of
the House of Study will testify—those who stand there... on foundations of pure gold, with lattice-work and wreaths, and likewise below, sweet groups.
All his father's house is discerning and leans upon them. Out of his great piety to fulfill the commandment of honoring his father after his death, he fixed them at the end of the book and called them by the holy name: "The Pillars."
These are a book unto themselves, not merely a preface. Truly, it is a great book, and like a bridegroom, his name shall be pleasant, erasing bitterness with many sweet and
sharp matters. A man of understanding and wisdom will see its quality, its essence, and the order of study in his <term>Yeshiva</term><note>An academy for Torah study</note>, in the watering of the thirsty flocks who gather to him to hear his original insights
which are renewed every single day. Happy is the people for whom this is so! For who can tell all the praises of his glory? And in... he entreated me, "Hearken to me," for it is written "to my mother"...
I did not move from my love until I called her "my mother." To the high thrones of greatness, there is the name of my lord, my grandfather, the great and eminent genius, a prince of God, our teacher and rabbi, **Moses Harif**, of blessed memory,
whose name and splendor suit him, for he was sharp (*Harif*), keen, and expert... he would not forget, but would review and return to it. That family was known for its sharpness and acumen,
and he raised many disciples and established a firm foundation which is famous from one end of the earth to the other. May it be the will of the One who dwells in the Bush that their students
should be like them; that they shall not cease or stop the words of the Torah, until the generation of the future.
<meta>catchword: be like them</meta>

# For the commandment is a lamp and the Torah is light; and reproofs of instruction are the way of life <note>original: "כי נר מצוה ותורה אור ודרך חיים תוכחת מוסר" — a verse from Proverbs 6:23, used here as a title and a thematic framework for the book.</note>
->The Book of the Way of Life<-
->and the Book of the Tablets of the Covenant<-

<margin>With all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might, and to walk in all His ways which the Lord your God commanded you, and you shall walk in His awe all the days.</margin>
<margin>And you shall love the Lord your God, to walk in His ways and to keep His commandments, His statutes, and His ordinances, that you may live.</margin>

->**I** am the one speaking, the son of the author: Shabbetai, known as Sheftel, son of the Great Rabbi, the Man of God, our teacher and rabbi <term>Isaiah Ha-Levi</term><note>Isaiah Horowitz (c. 1565–1630), known as the "Shelah HaKadosh" after the title of his most famous work.</note>, may his Rock and Redeemer protect him, Master of the Land of Israel.<-
->Known and famous among all Israel is the high eminence of my father and teacher, may his Rock and Redeemer protect him, for he is great among the Jews, great in Talmud study,<-

and in great deeds. Through great Talmud study, he learned Torah and spread Torah among Israel. He increased the number of academies and increased wisdom, and established many hundreds and thousands of students throughout all the dispersions of Israel. This is the "Torah of Man"—by which I mean the "revealed" part of the Torah, namely the study of analytical debate and legal rulings. However, his desire was also in the Torah of the Lord, which is the "hidden" part of the Torah <note>Referring to Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition.</note>, delving into the secret of secrets. His soul yearned for them, yet he would only transmit them to the modest ones, the unique and chosen individuals. Through great action—for his actions were great and his Talmud study was great because it led to action—he would learn and teach in order to observe, to do, and to fulfill. He was a "Master of Deed," a leader of his generation, holding the staff and the lash and the rod of instruction in his hand to guide them to the path they should walk and the deeds they should do. Also in the excellence of character traits, and in all virtues of ethical instruction, he never turned away. He was a great rebuker in his generation, and with a wonderful awakening of love, he turned many back from iniquity. He brought merit to the public, and if he was good to others, how much more so—by a <term>Kal Va-Chomer</term><note>A logical argument "from minor to major," similar to *a fortiori*.</note>—was he good to his "beloved ones," namely his children and his offspring after him. He was always rebuking his children and his household to keep the way of the Lord and to be cleaved to your Creator. Therefore, when it arose in his mind to ascend to the Land of Israel, his spirit urged him to compose a work for his children and their descendants forever, so they would have a "book of remembrance" encompassing the fulfillment of the commandments and their fine details, as well as understanding their performance through the knowledge of their secrets. For this matter brings an inflammation of the heart to serve the Lord with joy and goodness of heart, and to be careful and diligent, acting out of love. Through the hints of the Torah, "so that you may understand that which you do," one may understand the reason for the action of the commandment performed and know the "Secret of the Lord." Afterward, this merit includes all the laws of character traits, the conduct of piety, and all the paths of repentance in length, breadth, and height. And behold, regarding the fulfillment of commandments, etc., there are many practical commandments which a person performs from the beginning of the year to the end of the year, and they return in a cycle: daily conduct, the Sabbath in its time, the laws of Passover on Passover, Shavuot on Shavuot, the Festival of Sukkot, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Hanukkah, and Purim, as well as the matters of the fasts and their observance, and the like. Regarding everything he mentioned for practical action—"behold, this is new!"—for he innovated many laws from his own intellect. There are many hundreds of innovated laws, for the most part; only a few were mentioned by earlier or later legal decisors. They were only written here to join them all together because people have stumbled in them, either because they lacked knowledge and it was hidden from them, or due to some negligence. This is the matter of "Fulfilling the Commandments." And in explaining the secrets of the commandments according to the truth <note>In this context, "Truth" (Emet) often refers to Kabbalistic interpretation.</note>, he revealed the conduct of his Torah for all the commandments, totaling the numerical value of **Light** <note>The Hebrew word for "Light" (Or) has a Gematria value of 207.</note>. For he enlightened the eyes of the wise who take hold of the "Brightness of the Firmament." Finally, there emerged the section on the paths of repentance along with ethical instructions and the conduct of character traits, and matters of piety. Happy is the eye that sees all this! My teacher and father, may the memory of the righteous be a blessing, had the primary intention in this composition to rebuke and guide in a good and straight path. But when he entered into these matters, the "end of the deed was first in thought." Therefore, he called the work **The Way of Life** <note>original: "דרך החיים" — Derekh HaHayyim.</note>, named after "the reproofs of instruction are the way of life," as seen in his introduction. This instruction comes in the "Repetition of the Torah" <note>A reference to Deuteronomy or a systematic review of the law.</note>, meaning he came to explain everything according to the plain meanings and the juxtaposed verses in the Written Torah and the Oral Torah. The Torah of his mouth is better than a double or manifold goodness. We have moved from matter to matter like an increasing spring, increasing knowledge. Because of the abundance of ethical instruction hidden in this work—his sermons where he would seek the goodness of the commandments, in times of repentance, in times of piety, on Rosh Hashanah, on Yom Kippur, during the Three Weeks of Mourning, and the like—they are sought out by all who desire them. What he preached for Simchat Torah and other occasions, they are all equally good. All his sermons are true "plain meanings" in the truth of the Torah, not in the way of mere homiletics, but rather the words of the Living God. From all of them emerges ethical instruction and awakening. Happy is the eye that saw all this! The general rule is that this composition is a "threefold cord": **Part 1: The Lamp of the Commandment** <note>Ner Mitzvah</note>, which is the fulfillment of the commandments and their innovated laws. **Part 2: The Torah is Light** <note>Torah Or</note>, which is the secrets of the commandments. **Part 3: Ethical Reproof** <note>Tokhehat Musar</note>. As my father and teacher elaborated in his introduction, from the strength of this work he entered into a second work that is similar to it, making an explanation on the entire Torah, also divided into these parts. **The Lamp of the Commandment** consists of the 613 commandments found in all their places. In a Torah portion where none of the 613 commandments were found, he nonetheless found a commandment that is a "branch" of one of the 613. **The Torah is Light**: he revealed the secrets of the ways of the commandments, even those not practiced today. Afterward, **Ethical Reproof**: he extracted from every single portion the explanation of the Written Torah and created a work on the Oral Torah, explaining the Sugyot <note>Complex units of Talmudic discussion.</note> and the methods of the Talmud. The eye sees and the heart rejoices. For both of them together, he called the name **The Tablets of the Covenant** <note>original: "לוחות הברית" — Luhot HaBerit.</note>, and the two Torahs are companions to each other and are one Torah. Thus there are two: the work **The Way of Life** and the work **The Tablets of the Covenant**. And they shall become one, for they are connected to each other; they are joined together and have become lights. Happy is the eye that sees them and the heart that covets them. The practical tools of their bodies were sanctified in holiness, holy and a strength to their God. And since the benefit emerging from these wonderful compositions is immense and great, both in theoretical intellect and in practical intellect, and my eyes have seen all this preciousness, I, the one who sees, said that it is proper and obligatory to bring these matters to print so they may be in the midst of Israel. Happy is the generation that merits this! When this thought first occurred to me, fear entered my heart to approach the holy to do this without the command of my father and teacher, of blessed memory. Since his intention in this work was only for his children and his offspring after him, as mentioned in his introduction—which is the reason he was stringent with us regarding certain restrictions, especially in matters of what is forbidden and permitted, for such was his way to be stringent upon himself and his household and to sanctify himself even in that which is permitted to him—however, after seeing in his introduction that he commanded his children not to withhold good from his students and to let them copy as much as they desired, I said in my heart: since it was permitted to some, it is permitted in its entirety to all Israel. For his students are found throughout almost the entire Diaspora, and the vast majority of the Diaspora yearned for his Torah and his conduct and accepted him upon themselves as a father, a judge, and a head of the academy. All of them sought "the Rabbi" to hear his wisdom and chose his teaching. They accepted him over themselves in many great communities. Most recently, he was accepted in four communities which are the pillars of Torah for all communities: the holy community of **Frankfurt**, the holy community of **Prague**, the holy community of **Posen**, and the holy community of **Krakow**. After this strength, the departure of the righteous one was from the holy community of Prague, for there he was the head of the rabbinical court for seven years before departing from the region for the Land of Israel, to Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt and established speedily in our days. He merited there to be the "Master of the Land of Israel," and thus all the congregation of Israel are generally considered his students.

->And so, with the help of God, I have lifted my hand with all my heart and soul and might to engage in this work. Happy is the people for whom it is so, and this is the blessing.<-

# Introduction

<margin>See the gathering of scholars regarding the matter of whether "study is greater" or "action is greater." This is decided according to the conclusion <note>original: "be-lukha ke-asa"</note> later in Tractate Shevuot, first chapter. This is the end of the note.</margin>

**The plain meaning** <note>original: "peshat"</note> of the verse is that the commandment acts as a lamp to shine before you, as it is written: "The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes" <note>Psalm 19:9</note>. The Torah serves as light for those who study it, while the fool walks in darkness. Now, there are two interpretations for "lamp" <note>original: "ner"</note> and "light" <note>original: "or"</note>. First, a single candle is called a "lamp," while a "light" refers to a great bonfire. This agrees with the conclusion of our Sages, of blessed memory: "Great is study, for it leads to action" <note>Kiddushin 40b</note>. The commandment, which is the physical action, is called a lamp; the Torah, which is the study, is called light. A second interpretation refers to the lamp itself: the "lamp" is the vessel that receives the light—that is, the candle <note>original: "candela"</note> or the wick in the oil—and the "light" is what takes hold of it. They are attached to one another and need one another, for the light of the lamp can only take hold within the lamp. Indeed, if light exists without something to hold onto, it returns to its source and element. Similarly, the lamp has no illumination except through the light that has taken hold of it. Thus, the commandment and study are the cause of 

action, as we have learned in the Mishnah: "Hillel says, an empty person cannot be a sin-fearing person" <note>Pirkei Avot 2:5</note>. However, study has no hold without action, as we have learned: "Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa says: Anyone whose fear of sin precedes his wisdom, his wisdom will endure" <note>Pirkei Avot 3:9</note>. At first glance, these two ideas seem to conflict, but when you investigate carefully, you will see that both are true. A person cannot reach the "Crown of Torah" unless he has the preparation of fearing sin, so that he spreads through the radiance of the Blessed Name with a pure heart, desiring and longing for attachment to Him. If this is not the case, regarding such a person it is said: "But to the wicked, God says: What right have you to recite my laws?" <note>Psalm 50:16</note>. Therefore, one must first clothe himself in the fear of the Lord. Nevertheless, the details of fearing sin, the commandments, and the laws—in their generalities and specifics—remain hidden from him until he merits the Crown of Torah. Then, he proceeds from study to action in every possible way. There is another, more internal way to understand this: the Torah consists of action and contemplation, both the "revealed" and the "hidden" <note>referring to Nigleh (exoteric law) and Nistar (esoteric/Kabbalistic secrets)</note>. The revealed part of the Torah is the fulfillment of its commandments, which are the 248 positive commandments and the guarding of its warnings, which are the 365 prohibitions. For both of these, there are hidden reasons and Divine secrets, all of which are attached to His Great Name. Regarding those who know them, it is said: "I will set him on high, because he has known My name" <note>Psalm 91:14</note>, and "But you who did cleave unto the Lord your God are alive every one of you this day" <note>Deuteronomy 4:4</note>. The order of the levels is thus: one cannot be a "sin-fearing empty person," so one must study first. Thus, study will lead him to action, and he will become a "fearer of sin." Afterward, when he reaches this level, then all of his actions become a ladder to ascend to contemplation, which is the "hidden" part. He will then merit "to behold the graciousness of the Lord" <note>Psalm 27:4</note>. This is the true wisdom—the knowledge of the secrets of the commandments, which are Divine secrets. For this wisdom, the fear of sin must come first, as it is written: "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom" <note>Job 28:28</note>. Furthermore, "his wisdom will endure," and the secrets of the Torah will be revealed to him. Perhaps this was the intent of Moses our Teacher, peace be upon him. This is also the matter we have seen and heard from the group of holy, pious men <note>original: "chassidim"</note> whose occupation was with Divine secrets; they would scrutinize their own actions, repent for their sins, and clothe themselves in the fear of the Lord.

**The text says** afterward: "And reproofs of instruction are the way of life." Initially, the verse spoke of the perfection of the self—that one should be complete through the "lamp of commandment" and the "light of Torah." Afterward, one must perfect others as well. This is the "way to eternal life," for a life of merit is one that brings merit to others: to learn and to teach, to observe and to do. One should never refrain from rebuking others and telling them words of wisdom and instruction to "understand the words of insight." Therefore, the verse uses the term "way" <note>original: "derekh"</note>, just as Jethro said to Moses: "And you shall teach them the statutes and the laws, and show them the way in which they must walk and the work that they must do" <note>Exodus 18:20</note>.

**The verse mentions** "reproofs of instruction" <note>original: "tokhechot musar"</note>, which is a double expression. "Reproof" refers to the past; one must surely rebuke <note>original: "hocheach yochiach"</note> if others have turned away from the good and straight path. "Instruction" <note>musar</note> refers to teaching the way they should walk in the future, as it is written: "Hear instruction and be wise, and refuse it not" <note>Proverbs 8:33</note>. **Reproof** is what is mentioned in the Mishnah: "You shall surely rebuke your neighbor" <note>Leviticus 19:17</note>, which is an exceedingly great commandment. In Tractate Shabbat, in the chapter "All Sacred Writings," Rav Amram the son of Rabbi Shimon bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Hanina: Jerusalem was destroyed only because they did not rebuke one another, as it is said: "Her princes are become like harts that find no pasture" <note>Lamentations 1:6</note>. Just as with a hart, the head of one is beside the tail of the other <note>meaning they walk in single file, looking away from each other</note>, so too the people of Israel in that generation buried their faces in the ground and did not look at one another to offer rebuke. In the chapter "With what [burden] may a beast [go out]," it says: Anyone who has the power to protest the conduct of his household and does not, is held accountable for his household. If he can protest his city and does not, he is held accountable for his city. If he can protest the whole world and does not, he is held accountable for the whole world. It says further there: Rabbi Aha bar Hanina said, never did a favorable word go forth from the mouth of the Holy One, Blessed be He, which He later turned into a decree for evil, except for this matter. For it is written: "And the Lord said to him: Go through the midst of the city... and set a mark <note>the Hebrew letter Tav</note> upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and cry for all the abominations that are done" <note>Ezekiel 9:4</note>. The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Gabriel: Go and mark the foreheads of the righteous with a mark of ink, so that the angels of destruction shall not have power over them; and mark the foreheads of the wicked with a mark of blood, so that the angels of destruction shall have power over them. The Attribute of Justice said before the Holy One, Blessed be He: Master of the Universe, how are these different from those? He replied: These are completely righteous, and those are completely wicked. Justice replied: Master of the Universe, it was in their power to protest, and they did not protest! God said: It is revealed and known before Me that even had they protested, the others would not have accepted it from them. Justice replied: Master of the Universe, if it is revealed to You, was it revealed to them? And this is what is written: "Slay utterly the old man, the young man and the maiden, and little children and women; but come not near any man upon whom is the mark; and begin at My sanctuary" <note>Ezekiel 9:6</note>. (And Rashi explains: At first He said "do not touch," but in the end He said "begin at My sanctuary"). It is further written: "Then they began at the elders who were before the house." Rav Joseph taught: Do not read it as "My sanctuary" <note>mikdashi</note> but as "My sanctified ones" <note>mekuddashai</note>—these are the people who fulfilled the entire Torah from Aleph to Tav. And [it is written] "because of"... And in the *Hagahot Maimoniyot* <note>a commentary on Maimonides' code</note> in the sixth chapter of the "Laws of Ethical Character" <note>Hilkhot De'ot</note>, it is written: However, if it is certain to him that they will not accept the rebuke, it appears that he is exempt, for the Attribute of Justice said before the Holy One: "If it is revealed to You, was it revealed to them?" This implies that if it *had* been revealed to them that the wicked would not listen, they would have been exempt. This is also the implication of the *Tosafot* in the chapter "One who holds a property" <note>Tractate Bava Batra</note>, and so wrote the *Sefer HaMitzvot*, saying it is better for him to be silent, for "it is better for Israel to be inadvertent sinners [than intentional ones]." But the *Ra'am* <note>Rabbi Eliezer of Metz</note> wrote that while he is exempt from punishment, he is not exempt from the actual deed of "You shall surely rebuke." However, the *Hagahot Maimoniyot* quoted the *Sefer Yere'im* explicitly: Just as it is a commandment to say something that will be heard, so is it a commandment *not* to say something that will not be heard, as it is said: "Do not rebuke a scorner, lest he hate you" <note>Proverbs 9:8</note>. Thus ends the quote from the *Hagahot Maimoniyot*. But it seems to me that I can bring proof for the teacher, the *Ra'am*, that one is not exempt from "You shall surely rebuke" from that which is found in the chapter "There are [valuations]" in Tractate Erachin: How far does the obligation of rebuke go? Rav says: Until hitting. Shmuel says: Until cursing. And Rabbi 

<meta>catchword: Yochanan</meta>

<summary>This preface explores the metaphorical relationship between religious action (lamp) and Torah study (light), arguing that while study is superior, it requires the foundation of action and fear of God. It also discusses the communal obligation to rebuke others for their sins, weighing different legal opinions on when one is exempt from this duty.</summary>

# Preface of the Printers and the Proofreaders

**Blessed** be the Rock and praised be the Source! He who conceived the heights of the heavens and who built and founded the earth. From Mount Sinai, He taught His people judgment, law, and statutes. For they are life to those who find them, sweeter than honey and the drippings of the honeycomb <note>original: "devash ve-nofet tzufim"</note>. The thirsty drink His words and draw water from deep wells. They are more beautiful than fine gold and silver. These words of beloved ones are as dear to them as spiced wine. Even the innovations that veteran students <note>term: "talmidim vatikim" - a traditional phrase referring to exceptionally diligent and insightful scholars</note> were destined to produce were already engraved and carved upon the two tablets of the covenant. Each generation and its seekers, those who seek the Torah through its forty-nine facets <note>A traditional concept that there are 49 ways to interpret or "face" the Torah</note>, shine like the light of the seven days. It is like a hammer that shatters the rocks <note>A reference to Jeremiah 23:29, meaning the Torah's words can be interpreted in many ways</note>. The voice of the Lord is in strength, each person according to their capacity, both the revealed and the hidden, as far as their hand can reach to search in the holes and cracks. They left a merit for the generations in the memory of a book; they spread their hands in it... to be a beautiful word for them in this world and the world to come, so that every person’s hand may merit them... as the Rabbis said, "fittingly spoken," <note>original: "shapir ka-amri rabanan"</note> and golden crowns for their heads and necklaces for their generations. 

If we were to tell of them, we would not know how to count them, for of the making of many books there is no end. One cannot explain the concealment of the mysteries of wisdom—the commentaries on the Bible, the Talmud, and the legal codes; the true legal rulings of the Torah; and words of ethics and human conduct, teaching a person to "turn from evil and do good" <note>Psalm 34:14</note> and to cleave to the Lord God. Yet, not every man's hand can reach the attainment... where there is a loss of money, and one who speaks much is, God forbid, praised for this thing; many are deprived and naked of much wisdom and knowledge, and the empty pits cannot be filled. 

This continued until we merited the light of the worlds, the wisdom of the Land of Israel <note>original: "avirah de-eretz Yisrael"</note>. We see here a "tender blessing" whose name testifies to him: *The Two Tablets of the Covenant* <note>original: "Shney Luchot HaBerit"</note>. It is a crown for his lips, and by the lips of the discerning, wisdom is found. He knew his lips... hidden things that emerge from the revealed, just as on the two tablets of the testimony things were engraved and carved. 

This was printed long ago by the "son who is the leg of his father," the Great Genius, our teacher Rabbi Sheftel <note>Rabbi Sabbatai Sheftel Horowitz, the author's son</note>, of blessed memory, with the addition of the "Sapphire and Diamond" <note>Metaphors for beauty</note>, the book *Vavei HaAmudim* <note>term: "The Hooks of the Pillars" - a famous ethical work usually printed with the Shney Luchot HaBerit</note>. Its pillars he made of silver and its base of gold for the "Master of Glory." The glory of fathers is their children, and the glory of children is their fathers. The common side between them is that they are all full of Torah and uphold the fear of heaven. 

Due to its beloved nature, it was lost <note>Meaning the books were sold out or worn out</note>, and only "one from a city and two from a family" <note>Jeremiah 3:14</note> could be found, scattered here and there. Its place of glory was unknown, while many were thirsty, longing, and desiring it. Everyone wants to enjoy the "Table of the Most High" <note>A metaphor for studying holy texts</note>. It is a wondrous, hidden, and concealed thing. Even though it was stated and repeated, it was not repeated for the sake of anything new being added, for that might diminish it. It was appropriate for them to be "hidden in the vessels" among various different vessels... full of errors and mistakes... until merit was brought about through the meritorious, like us, the undersigned at the bottom of the sheet. 

I, Joseph Athias, who long ago was known at the gates of the many, in the streets and markets... because in the lodge of the hotel "righteousness shall lodge in it" <note>Isaiah 1:21</note> to do much that we vowed, we denied sleep from our eyes to bring the book *Shney Luchot HaBerit* from potential to reality—an act of truth and justice. We have come to the "rest and the inheritance," the heritage of beauty, here in the Holy Community of Amsterdam, at the praised printing press of the elder Joseph Athias. He has long been known at the gates of the many in the streets and markets, for he has brought explanation to the many. In his beautiful and praised press, which has many levels of excellence, we presented our words before him, for our desire is to write for a third time the things that were on the first tablets. 

Immediately, he nodded his head to us, and the craftsmen took hold of the work—the work of his labor in the Torah—to hasten to send them out from the "expression of his lips" <note>original: "oreshet sefatav"</note>. Now, you, the observer, let not this thing be a stumbling block or an obstacle to you, to judge us unfavorably and say: "Who is this, and where is he, who presumed in his heart to do so?" <note>Esther 7:5</note>... "In that which is concealed from you, do not investigate" <note>A quote from Ben Sira</note>... "What has straw to do with grain?" <note>Jeremiah 23:28</note>. Let no one accuse us of a trespass in changing the sacred text. For as far as our intellect could reach in simple matters and clear paths, we "cleared the highway" to prepare the way and straighten the path. In places that were wondrous, hidden, or concealed from us, we came to the house of assembly for the wise. There we found that which our soul loved, to return to us the path in which we should walk, so that nothing unrefined should leave our hands, God forbid. Rather, it should be complete in total perfection, as every eye shall look directly at this great sight, in the "visions of the hosts," with black ink upon white paper... by the light of his countenance, without any obstacle or error. We did not need to remove the "thorns of the yods" <note>term: "thorns of the yods" - a calligraphic term meaning even the smallest stroke of the smallest Hebrew letter, the Yod, was perfectly placed</note>, whether lacking or extra... 

Surely every soul will long for it, to "provide prey for his household" <note>Proverbs 31:15</note>. And if you happen to find some small gathering or gleaning in one or two places, it is but a trifle. May your souls live by judging us favorably. And so that it may be complete in total perfection, we have set "markers and ears" <note>term: "tziyunim ve-oznayim" - refers to cross-references and indices</note> for the Torah at the end of the book. Let everyone who seeks go out to the "Tent of Meeting," like tents planted as trees of the garden. Their names are at the beginning. It shall rise upon the table of kings and nobles. This book shall not be like "sealed springs," but rather like an "open alleyway" from both sides. We have done this so that people will not need to search through drawers and hidden places... for "The commandment is a lamp and the Torah is light" <note>Proverbs 6:23</note> and the "way of life is moral instruction." 

What can we say or tell of the praise of the splendor of this book? Surely all who see it will testify and declare that it was made with a full and overflowing purse, with great and doubled expenses. Therefore, do not spare your money! Take money from your acquaintances so that this book may be a treasure in your bags, to meditate on them with beautiful words. May our good memory always come before you, for surely it will be pleasing to you. These are the words of those who pray today, on the day that was twice called "Good" <note>note: Tuesday, the third day of creation, is traditionally called "the day on which 'it was good' was said twice."</note>. 

The first of the month of Adar, [5]457 <note>February 1697 CE</note>.

The words of the small one, Zeev, known as Wolf, son of the Honorable Master Samuel R. Kopels, of blessed memory, from Jarosław.

Schneur Zalman, son of the Honorable Master Jonathan HaKohen from Poznań.

Isaac, son of the Honorable Master Meir Ashkenazi, of blessed memory, son-in-law of the Honorable Master Perli Shillo from the land of Friedland.

Zvi Hirsch, son of the Honorable Master Abraham, of blessed memory, from Wranik.

And a blessing <note>original: "apiryon nimti"</note> is extended to the great Rabbi, whose name is praised, our teacher Hirsch Apter, the distinguished Judge <note>term: "Dayan" - a judge in a Jewish religious court</note> and head of the court of the Holy Community of Kalish, a great city in the land of Greater Poland. He frequently entered the printing house, weighing and searching with all investigations and inquiries, so that nothing unrefined or flawed should leave the hands of the proofreaders. May the Lord spread a peace from on high over him and illuminate his days and years in pleasantness. Amen. Selah.

->**Blessed**<-

<meta>This page transitions from the printers' legal protections and formal introductions into the author's personal preface. The author, Rabbi Isaiah Horowitz (known as the Shelah), begins by addressing his family and explaining his motivation for writing this ethical and mystical guide as he prepares to depart for the Land of Israel.</meta>

# The Generations of Man

**Words** of understanding to bless me: May the Lord bless my sons, my daughters, my sons-in-law, my grandchildren, and their offspring forever. May they all stand for a blessing, and may the Lord increase you a thousandfold. I have composed for them a work of ethical rebuke <note>original: "tochechat musar" — a traditional genre of Jewish literature focused on moral improvement and character development</note>, just as a father disciplines his son. For now is the time for me to speak, as I am uprooting myself from them to settle, with the help of the Blessed Name, in the Holy Land. It is stated in the Talmud <note>original: "Perek Eilu Menalan," referring to a chapter in Tractate Moed Katan</note> that Rabbi Levi asked Elijah: "Is he alive?" since it is written "and he saw him no more" regarding him. Regarding myself, I read this verse with which I began: "The Way of Life" <note>original: "Derech Chayim"</note>, for "the reproofs of discipline are the way of life" (Proverbs 6:23). This is the path before the Lord, the "Land of the Living," for there the Lord commanded the blessing: "Life forevermore."

Through words of Torah, one remembers Him. The intention is to speak pleasant, straightforward words of Torah that are matters of ethics which penetrate the innermost heart. This is why the sages were precise in saying "from within words of Torah," for I have already mentioned the obligation to engage in ethical words when parting from a companion. When the ethics are adorned and beautified with words of Torah, they enter even more deeply into the heart. Similarly, we say in the prayer *Ahava Rabba* <note>The "Great Love" prayer preceding the Shema</note>: "Put into our hearts to understand, to discern, to listen, to learn, and to teach, to observe..." and then "the Torah of his God is in his heart," fulfilling the verse "within my heart is Your faithfulness." These words of Torah, which are ethical teachings, bear fruit and leave an impression once they enter the heart. This study leads to action; thus, when an opportunity for action arises, one remembers the friend who taught him this matter. This is why the passage concludes, "through this, remember him." These things are "remembered and performed," meaning from the moment of the action, the law is remembered—specifically the straightforward Torah teaching given on the matter—and one remembers the speaker. This "brings redemption," as we have learned: "Whoever says a matter in the name of the one who said it brings redemption to the world." And if the speaker has died, it "causes the lips of those who sleep to speak" <note>A Talmudic concept (Yevamot 97a) suggesting that when a scholar's teachings are quoted after their death, their soul experiences a form of speech in the afterlife</note>. Thus, remembrance occurs in two ways: the action causes one to remember the law (Torah), and one remembers his friend. Both are good together. Then the verse is fulfilled: "For the commandment is a lamp..." in its fullness and goodness. When there is a "Way of Life," one will merit to live, departing with ethical rebukes; through ethical rebuke, there will be "Torah is Light," and then one will merit the "Lamp of Commandment," for study leads to action.

Since my intention is to benefit you—my children (may their Rock and Redeemer protect them) and those joined with you—to merit the World to Come, I have reflected that it is impossible to reach the goal of "clinging" <note>term: "deveikut" — mystical attachment or communion with the Divine</note> except through the body of "Torah is Light." By this, I mean standing upon the reasons for the commandments and being careful regarding the "thou shalt nots" and "thou shalts," for many are not careful. This stems from one of three causes: First, sometimes it is because "if a person commits a sin and repeats it, it becomes to him as if permitted." There are many, due to our many sins, who are sunken in disparagement. As our Sages of blessed memory noted regarding theft, forbidden relations, and evil speech: most stumble in theft, a minority in forbidden relations, and everyone in the "dust" of evil speech. I give a sign: there is no charge that does not involve the "Dust of the Three" <note>original: "A"L" (Ayin-Lamed), an acronym for Arat (forbidden relations), Gezel (theft), and Lashon Hara (evil speech)</note>. Therefore, these are placed together in the order of the Confession (*Viduy*): "We have robbed, we have spoken slander..." <note>The author here engages in complex wordplay/Gematria involving the Hebrew letters and the number 248 (the number of positive commandments/limbs of the body), suggesting that these three sins affect the entire spiritual stature of a person.</note> Our Sages noted that these three are extremely grave sins found in every generation. The second cause: sometimes it is due to a lack of knowledge, where the matter was not known to the public or the community was not fluent in a particular commandment. Therefore, it is fitting for me to make known some of the "New Laws" <note>original: "chiddushim" — innovative legal insights or clarifications</note> which I have innovated with the help of the Blessed Name, which were not mentioned in the words of the earlier authorities. All this is within the "Lamp of Commandment."

Our Sages of blessed memory asked: "Why do Israel pray and are not answered? Because they do not know how to pray with the Name, as it is said: 'I will set him on high, because he has known My name. He shall call upon Me, and I will answer him.'" I have already mentioned in my introduction that study leads to action, and from there and above, one reaches "answering." This is the content of the liturgy arranged in the *Ahava Rabba* blessing. It says: "Put into our hearts to discern, to listen, to learn and to teach, to observe and to perform and to fulfill..." This is our request for study to lead us to action ("to perform and fulfill"). Afterward, we ask: "Enlighten our eyes in Your Torah, and make our hearts cling to Your commandments, and unite our hearts to love Your Name." This is a request that the Holy One, blessed be He, enlighten our eyes in the secrets of the commandments, as King David (peace be upon him) said: "Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of Your Torah." Through this, we shall be clinging to His Name, may He be blessed, in love and fear. It is explained in the *Zohar* and by the Sages of Truth <note>term: "Kabbalists"</note> that from the physical aspects of Torah and prayer—that is, action and speech—garments are created for the soul from the atmosphere of the Lower Garden of Eden. However, those unifications and "clinging" in the Upper Garden of Eden, which are subtle spiritual levels, come only from the secret of the "Intentions" <note>term: "kavanot" — mystical meditations on the Hebrew names of God during prayer or performance of commandments</note>, which are within the secret of knowing His names, may He be blessed. Now, I have not come to compose a full treatise on this noble subject here, but rather later in its small place; here I answer as one mentioning the "chapter headings" of what is necessary. Know, my children, let it not enter your thoughts that what I arrange in these pamphlets regarding the secrets of the commandments and prayers means I have reached the depth of the matter. It is not even like a drop in the great sea, for those secrets have no end or limit. Even if a man lives a thousand years twice over, he would not reach the end of a single commandment, its depth, its root, and the root of its root. Only Rabbi Shimon <note>Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, traditional author of the Zohar</note> and his companions, who were not merely flesh and blood, saw this. Also, the knowledge of the great ones among our pious ones and the disciples of the sages of the generations comes from his great light. However, "not every brain can bear this." I have come only to reveal a small bit of the little I have received from the mouths of scribes and from books that follow the *Zohar*, specifically from the latter holy books of **Rabbi Be'er Sheva** <note>original: "Ba'er Navai," likely referring to Rabbi Issachar Baer Braunthal</note> of blessed memory, the divine **Rabbi Moshe Cordovero** <note>A major 16th-century Kabbalist in Safed</note> of blessed memory, and the greatest of the latter ones, the holy man of God, the **ARI** <note>Rabbi Isaac Luria, the foundational figure of modern Kabbalah</note> of blessed memory. I will add a small touch of my own to provide wisdom and understanding in the explanation of these matters. It is known that holiness is like a spring that joins; if a man sanctifies himself a little from below, they sanctify him much from above. May the Holy One, blessed be He, grant us wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, and then we shall merit to enter the innermost chambers, through many thousands of levels of goodness, to the Place of the Blessed One.

<column-break/>

**Happy** are those whose way is perfect, who walk in the Torah of the Lord. For behold, I have reflected on creating for every ethical teaching a support from the words of Torah—in length, breadth, and depth—so that it enters the heart more deeply and one fulfills "to learn and to teach, to observe and to perform and to fulfill."

**And** in order to fulfill this verse, "For the commandment is a lamp," I thought in my humble estimation <note>original: "be-tziyurei d"l" — likely "dal," meaning 'poor/humble'</note> of what the Sages said: "To one who begins a commandment, they say: Finish it." A whole thing, not a half thing. Since my intention is to benefit you...

**And Torah is Light** shall be fulfilled through the knowledge of the reasons for the commandments and their secrets. Regarding this it is said: "Which if a man does them, he shall live by them." As it is written, "which he shall do" refers to the actual performance of the commandment. And "he shall live by them" refers to the clinging to the hints of the commandment, which is the life and vitality of the commandment. From this spiritual side, which is "Thought," one has clinging to His Name, may He be blessed. The intention of the commandment is the secret of His Name, may He be blessed. Without this, there is no clinging in the physical action to the Spirituality, which is the goal of all spirituality: He, may His Name be blessed.

**Also**, the "service of our heart," which is prayer in place of the sacrifice that brings us closer to Him, must be prayer with intention. Then it is a "body with a soul." The physicality of the prayer is its order as arranged for us by the Sages of blessed memory, in awe and fear. And the soul is the intention of the secrets of the prayer.

---

**Behold**, these pamphlets which I am bequeathing to you are a "triple-threaded cord": **Ethical Rebuke**, **Torah is Light**, and **Lamp of Commandment**. Their sign is: *The Lord is the portion of my inheritance* <note>original: "H' MeNAT chelki" — a play on the word Menat, using the first letters of Musar (Ethics), Ner (Lamp), and Torah</note>.

**Since** students are also called "sons," and I have merited, thank God, to raise many students, I hereby command you: any student whose soul desires to copy these pamphlets, do not withhold good from its owners. And you, my sons, hear the instruction of your father. Let it be a memorial between your eyes, and pass them on to your children, for it is your life and the length of your days. Even more so, my sons, I command you to review them with added holiness, purity, and clinging, for it is double for salvation—many times over what I have mentioned within my work. Now, as I depart for the journey prepared for me to the Holy Land, to cling to the "Lands of the Living," I call these pamphlets by the name:

**Way of Life** <note>original: "Derech Chayim"</note>, based on the aforementioned verse: "For the commandment is a lamp, and Torah is light; and reproofs of discipline are the way of life." This is the path to eternal life. And since for the "tread of a foot" there are three joints (as mentioned regarding the laws of kosher and non-kosher legs), so I shall arrange three chapters for the upright body that walks on the path of the Tree of Life. **Chapter 1** is called the "Ten Utterances." **Chapter 2** is called the "Ten Commandments." **Chapter 3** is called the "Ten Praises." These three chapters bring a person—who is the goal of creation—to his true purpose. Corresponding to these, the Men of the Great Assembly established the prayer... Adam the First, who was the goal of creation, as we say in Tractate Rosh Hashanah: "According to whom do we pray now? This day is the beginning..."

He introduces his work as a guide combining ethics (Musar), law, and Kabbalistic secrets (Torah Or), emphasizing that spiritual intention is the "soul" that brings the "body" of physical commandments to life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's introduction, focusing on the biblical and legal obligation of "rebuke" or "moral correction" (tochecha). He transitions from his personal departure to the Land of Israel to the philosophical and religious justification for writing this ethical guide for his children.</meta>

<page-num>51</page-num>
<header>The Generations of Man</header>

<margin>
<note>original: "סנ"ס" — likely a reference to a specific legal authority or shorthand</note> || In any case, the *Nimukei Yosef* <note>A 14th-century commentary on the Talmud</note> at the end of the chapter "He who comes upon his sister-in-law" <note>Tractate Yevamot</note> says: One might say that we only speak to someone who will accept it from us; otherwise, the verse "you shall surely rebuke" <note>Leviticus 19:17</note> would imply that even if one is struck, one must continue. According to the first interpretation there, a person is obligated to receive the commandment. It is proven that this applies even if they do not want to listen. Our Sages taught in Tractate *Eruvin* that one is obligated to rebuke until they are hit or cursed. There, it refers to an individual, but for the public, no. Our Sages taught in Tractate *Shabbat* regarding rebuking the members of the Exilarch’s household: "They will not accept it from me," yet the Talmud replies that one must rebuke them anyway. In the chapter "A person should not stand," <note>Tractate Berakhot</note> it says one should not rebuke unless they know the person will listen; but if they won't listen, one is still obligated to rebuke at least once. This is the conclusion of the words cited there.
</margin>

Rabbi Yochanan said: until scolding. This means he holds that even if one has already reached the point of scolding and even cursing, and if he knows for certain that the person will not accept it despite all this, he is still not exempt from the positive commandment of "you shall surely rebuke" until he is struck. Maimonides <note>The Rambam, a preeminent 12th-century scholar</note>, in the sixth chapter of the *Laws of Ethical Character*, ruled like Rav, even though the *Smag* <note>Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, a 13th-century legal code</note> wondered at him and ruled like Rabbi Yochanan. Since the law generally follows Rabbi Yochanan over Rav, and certainly over Shmuel in matters of forbidden acts, why did Maimonides rule this way? However, the *Hagahot Maimoniyot* <note>A commentary on Maimonides</note> wrote as follows: In the *Midrash Tanchuma* on the portion *Ki Tisa*, it implies the words of our Master the author <note>Maimonides</note>, who said that the Attribute of Justice asked the Master of the Universe: "How are these different from those?" etc., until: "Even so, they should have been stirred by the holiness of Your Name and accepted upon themselves being struck by Israel, just as the prophets suffered. For Jeremiah and Isaiah suffered many troubles from Israel, as it is written: 'I gave my back to the smiters' (Isaiah 50:6)." Immediately, the Holy One, Blessed be He, was filled with wrath and said to the angels of destruction: "Slay utterly old and young, maids and little children" (Ezekiel 9:6). This is the language of the Midrash and the language of Maimonides. And even according to the words of the *Smag*, who ruled like Rabbi Yochanan—"until scolding" and no more—nonetheless, it is proven from Rav and Shmuel that even if one knows they will not accept it, one is obligated to rebuke. For even Shmuel, who is more lenient than Rav, still holds that even after scolding, when one knows for certain they will not accept it, one is obligated to rebuke. And in this reasoning, Rabbi Yochanan does not disagree with Rav and Shmuel. Furthermore, he holds that there is no commandment to derive benefit, and one should not say that Rabbi Yochanan disagrees; in this matter, he does not disagree that one was obligated to rebuke before the scolding, even if it was established in his mind that they would not accept the rebuke. And even if we say that Rabbi Yochanan disagrees with them, and this itself is his reason—that he holds "until scolding" and no more because then it is revealed to him that they will not accept the ethical instruction—if so, it would not have been appropriate to rule like Rabbi Yochanan, who is a lone opinion in this reasoning against Rav and Shmuel, who hold the commandment of rebuke applies even after scolding, which is the same as "knowing for certain they will not accept." Since the words of Rabbi Yochanan are nullified against his colleagues, so it is.

<margin>
That which is said in the chapter "He who comes upon his sister-in-law" <note>Tractate Yevamot</note>, where Rabbi Ila’a said in the name of Rabbi Eleazar son of Rabbi Simeon: "Just as it is a duty for a person to say a word that will be heard, so is it a duty for a person not to say a word that will not be heard." Rabbi <note>Judah the Prince</note> says it is an obligation, as it is said: "Do not rebuke a scorner, lest he hate you" (Proverbs 9:8). And he is not exempt, for this is a separate matter. This applies to a case where the sins are not known, where it is forbidden [to rebuke] because they will mock the one rebuking and will sin regardless. Therefore, "It is better that they be unintentional [sinners] and not intentional [sinners]" <note>original: "mutav she-yiyu shogegin ve-al yiyu mezidin"</note>. This is like the case found in Tractate *Shabbat* in the chapter "One who asks" and in Tractate *Beitzah* in the chapter "One who brings" regarding the "addition to Yom Kippur" <note>The practice of starting the fast early</note>. We see people eating and drinking until dark, and we do not say anything to them because "it is better they be unintentional and not intentional." Maimonides wrote in chapter one of the *Laws of the Tenth Day Rest*: "Women who eat and drink until dark and do not know that it is a commandment to add from the weekday to the holy day—we do not protest against them, so that they do not come to do so intentionally. For it is impossible to have a guard in every single house to warn them. Leave them be, so they are unintentional and not intentional." And so too with similar matters. These are his words. And the *Rosh* <note>Rabbeinu Asher, 13th-century scholar</note> in Tractate *Beitzah* wrote that the author of the *Itur* said this only applies to something not explicitly clear in the Scripture, such as the "addition of affliction on Yom Kippur." But in a case of a protest written explicitly in the Torah, we do protest and humble them until they cease. These are his words. And this is the reason: since the prohibition is not explicitly clear, we fear they will not believe and will not submit, and regarding this, it is an obligation not to say something that will not be heard, because it is better they be unintentional. But regarding a matter where the prohibition is publicized, known, and clear—then "you shall surely rebuke," even a hundred times. Furthermore, one can explain the words of Rabbi Eleazar son of Shamuah <note>or Simeon</note> that "one should not say a thing that will not be heard" as referring to rebuking a scorner, for a scorner mocks the words of the rebuker and laughs at him. For even if they were sinners who did not listen to the voice of their prophets, that was not categorized as "scorn," but rather the false prophets misled them into thinking their words were true. So too, if one rebukes his fellow and the fellow answers the rebuke by saying "I did not do this," or "I did it, and I acted according to the law," then one is obligated to rebuke until striking, each according to his view. However, if he laughs at the words of the rebuker and mocks him, then it is an obligation for the rebuker not to speak. Furthermore, Rabbi Eleazar son of Shamuah is speaking of someone who wants to be stringent with himself and rebuke beyond the measure one is obligated to rebuke. To this he says: do not do so, and "it is better not to say a thing that is not heard" because of "do not rebuke a scorner," and mark this.
</margin>

---

### And Because
of Maimonides' ruling "until striking," it seems to me that this refers to inviting him <note>to change</note> and being steadfast with him, following Rashi's view. The rebuker should be like an "iron pillar," not showing favoritism even to a great person. In the chapter "Helek" <note>Tractate Sanhedrin</note>, Jeroboam merited kingship because he rebuked Solomon, etc. And in the final chapter of *Ketubot*: "This Torah scholar whom the people of his town love—it is not because he is so superior, but because he does not rebuke them," etc.

<margin>
Behold, regarding the fulfillment of the commandment of rebuke, he is exempt after this from "guaranty" <note>Arvut — the shared spiritual responsibility Jews have for one another</note>.
</margin>

---

### And Just As
it is a great commandment for the rebuker to rebuke, so is it a great commandment for the one rebuked to accept the rebuke. As it is taught in Tractate *Tamid*, first chapter: Rabbi said, "Which is the straight path a person should choose for himself? He should love rebuke." For as long as rebuke is in the world, contentment comes to the world, and goodness and blessing come to the world, and evil departs from the world, as it is said: "But to those who rebuke, it shall be pleasant, and a good blessing shall come upon them" (Proverbs 24:25). And in the chapter "There are in Arachin" <note>Tractate Arachin</note>, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri said: "I call heaven and earth to witness that many times Akiva was punished because of me, because I used to complain about him before Rabban Simeon son of Rabbi; and all the more so, it increased his love for me," to fulfill what is written: "Do not rebuke a scorner lest he hate you; rebuke a wise man and he will love you" (Proverbs 9:8).

<margin>
<note>original: "כנ"ק" — likely shorthand</note> And Rashi explained that the words of the rebuker are like sufferings <note>original: "yisurin"</note>, and a person must choose them to be elevated.
</margin>

Behold, the greatness of the commandment of rebuke is explained. Therefore, it is fitting for everyone to speak at length with words of rebuke according to his ability. Even though all the aforementioned matters refer to rebuking for a sin already committed, nevertheless, we also learn from this to stand and warn about the future, to make known the "good and straight path." A God-fearing person will fulfill both obligations, for rebuke for the past and teaching ethics and conduct for the future are all placed in one "bag" <note>original: "hada machta" — an Aramaic idiom meaning they are considered a single unit</note>. There is one virtuous reason for both: "so that they may hear and so that they may learn" and "be careful to do all the words of the Torah." And so Moses our teacher did both. After he taught the Torah and the commandments to all of Israel, when he was about to depart to the paths of eternal life near his death, he fulfilled the "rebuke of discipline." "These are the words" (Deuteronomy 1:1) are words of rebuke; he rebuked them for the past, for how they had sinned since leaving Egypt, and he taught them ethics for the future, both in the fulfillment of the Torah and its commandments—study and action—and in the internalizing of character traits <note>original: "middot"</note> in a way that leads to cleaving to the Blessed One <note>original: "deveikut"</note> and walking in His ways and His attributes, as is explained in many verses in the book of Deuteronomy. And see, my sons, may your Rock and Redeemer protect you, that all the ethical teachings mentioned in the words of our Sages in the Talmud and the Midrashim, and what the authors of the books of Repentance, Character, and Ethics wrote at length afterward—as well as those who speak according to the Secret <note>original: "Sod" — Jewish mysticism/Kabbalah</note>, the secret of cleaving, like the holy Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai in the *Zohar* and the *Tikunim* and those who followed him in early and later generations—the words of all of them are elevated in the ethical words of Moses our teacher, for him who has eyes to see. Then he will see everything with the eye of the intellect, well-explained. Happy is the eye that saw all these.

---

### And These
are the words which Moses spoke near his death, as he was going on the Way of Life. And just as the Master of the Prophets did, so did all the prophets after them. They rebuked Israel and warned them for the future, and they did this most especially near their departure from the world. So did Joshua and his disciple, and so did Samuel and David. And so did the elder of Samuel, and even earlier in Israel, Jacob our forefather, before his departure, called his sons, etc. It is the way of all the righteous: at the time of their departure, they occupy themselves with the rebuke of discipline with even greater strength.

I know that my soul is not righteous enough to be counted among the righteous; nevertheless, "Go out by the footsteps of the sheep and graze your young goats" (Song of Songs 1:8) is written. Therefore, I will follow in the footsteps of the early ones to graze on wisdom and ethics, to understand...
