<meta>This page continues the discussion of "Awe" and "Fear of God," transitioning from the psychological state of the individual to a grand cosmological survey of the created world. It draws heavily from the Zohar and Midrash to describe the structure of the heavens and the earth, including early mystical descriptions of a spherical world.</meta>

If you were before such a great man, you would feel fear and shame in his presence, even if that great man were from a distant land, was not your teacher or the sage of the city, and you did not expect a reward from him or fear a punishment he might inflict. Despite all this, it would be a great insolence for a youth to act otherwise. And even though that great man is molded from matter <note>original: "krotz mechomer"</note> just like the youth, the distance between the human and the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah: the indwelling presence of God in the world</term> is thousands upon thousands of myriads of times greater. This is an infinite *a fortiori* <note>original: "kal va-chomer," a logical argument from minor to major</note> deduction. When a person remembers that he is but a putrid drop, dust of the earth, a maggot and a worm, he should not even be able to steady his face before the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, the Master of all worlds, who is elevated to the ultimate height. By the very nature of shame and fear, one is compelled to fulfill all His commands, may He be blessed—whether refraining from what He forbade or performing what He commanded—even if no punishment or reward were involved. This is as stated in the Zohar: "Because He is Great and Ruler, the essence and root of all worlds." <note>original: "begin de-ihu rav ve-shalit, ikra ve-shorsha de-khol almin"</note> And now I will explain "Great and Ruler" according to my strength, as I introduced in my words, praising the ability to discern His creatures; then the matter of His loftiness, may He be blessed, will sink into our hearts. I will begin to discern the matter of the chain of existence from bottom to top:

## The Earth
This is the final point, the matter of this world, and there is no matter as coarse, murky, and dark as the earth. It is the lowest of the world of the elements, which are, from bottom to top: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire. Nevertheless, how many wonders upon wonders of the Creator did the blessed Creator make in this earth! As revealed in the Zohar: Rabbi Judah opened and said, "'And God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters' <note>Genesis 1:6</note>... The Holy One, blessed be He, created the world, created six heavens above, and created seven earths below..." <note>original: "Kudosha Berikh Hu bara alma, bara shesh shekhakim le-ela, bara sheva aratzot le-tata"</note> All of them have stars and constellations that serve in every firmament, and they are all in harmony and established one upon the other to accept the kingdom of their Master. From all the firmaments, there are various chariots and servants, differing from one another—some have six wings, some have four wings, some have four faces, some have two faces, some have eight. Some are flaming fire, some are water, and some are wind. So it is with the seven earths below; all of them are inhabited, except for those that are upper or lower <note>this likely refers to the mystical realms of the earth such as Arka or Gehenna</note>. The Land of Israel is the highest of them all, and Jerusalem is the highest of all inhabited land. And our colleagues taught, as hinted in the ancient books and the Book of Adam, that all these lands are found below just like the firmaments above, one upon the other. Between each land is a firmament that separates them. Therefore, all the lands are distinguished by their names, and in them are various creatures, differing from one another like the chariots above—some with two faces, some with four, some with one, and their appearances are not alike. And if you say that all people descended from Adam, it is not so; for Adam did not descend to all those lands to father children, nor did he have many wives. Rather, Adam is found only in this world, the highest of them all, which is called *Tevel* <note>the Hebrew word for the inhabited world</note>, as it is written: "He commanded His earth, Tevel" <note>Job 37:12</note>. This *Tevel* is attached to the upper firmament and is connected to the Higher Name, as it is written: "He will judge Tevel in righteousness" <note>Psalms 9:9</note>. Therefore, the children of Adam are found in this highest realm called *Tevel*, and they are superior to all, just as it is above. For just as above there is a firmament higher than all others, and upon it is found the Throne of Glory, as it is written: "like the appearance of a sapphire stone was the likeness of a throne, and upon the throne was a likeness like the appearance of a man upon it from above," <note>Ezekiel 1:26</note> so too in this *Tevel* is found the king of all, which is Man... etc. And in the book of Rav Hamnuna Saba <note>A legendary scholar mentioned in the Zohar</note>, it is explained further: that the entire inhabited world rolls in a circle like a ball <note>original: "mitgalgela k-igula k-khadura"</note>. Some are above and some are below, and all these creatures differ in their appearance due to the difference in the air. Therefore, there is a place in the world where, when it is light for some, it is dark for others; for these it is day, and for those it is night. And there is a place that is entirely day, where night is not found except for one small hour... etc. See there at length. The *Pardes* <note>The classic work "Pardes Rimmonim" by Moshe Cordovero</note> transcribed this in the "Gate of the Order of their Standing." Behold, here you have the creation of the globe of the Earth. And it is found in the Midrash: "The Earth stands forever." Rabbi Levi said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in Man, He created in the Earth. Man has a head, and the Earth has a head, as it is written: 'the beginning of the dust of the world [Tevel]' <note>Proverbs 8:26, where the Hebrew 'rosh' means both head and beginning</note>. Man has eyes, and the Earth has eyes, as it is written: 'and it shall cover the eye of the earth' <note>Exodus 10:5</note>. Man eats, and the Earth eats, as it is written: 'a land that eats its inhabitants' <note>Numbers 13:32</note>. Man drinks, and the Earth drinks, as it is written: 'it drinks water from the rain of heaven' <note>Deuteronomy 11:11</note>. Man becomes agitated, and the Earth becomes agitated, as it is written: 'the earth shook and trembled' <note>Psalms 18:8</note>. Man gets drunk, and the Earth gets drunk, as it is written: 'the earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard' <note>Isaiah 24:20</note>. Man vomits, and the Earth vomits, as it is written: 'and the land vomited out its inhabitants' <note>Leviticus 18:25</note>. Man has hands, and the Earth has hands, as it is written: 'and the land, behold, it is wide of hands' <note>Genesis 34:21, meaning spacious</note>. Man has a navel, and the Earth has a navel, as it is written: 'who dwell at the navel of the earth' <note>Ezekiel 38:12</note>. Man has thighs, and the Earth has thighs, as it is written: 'and gather them from the thighs of the earth' <note>Jeremiah 31:7, meaning its remote parts</note>. Man has feet, and the Earth has feet, as it is written: 'the earth stands forever' and supports its duties." Thus far. Behold the wonders of creation in the earth! And how much one should observe the life and the high and lofty souls; and further to observe how many hidden matters of the Exalted One are in the earth—gold, silver, copper, iron, all metals, treasures, and virtues that have no limit or measure. And so it is today for one who knows how to discern the vegetation that grows from the earth—all kinds of seeds, grains, legumes, vegetables, and all kinds of fruit trees. Afterward, the types of herbs that have fragrance, and thousands upon thousands of myriads of types of herbs whose utility and virtue we do not understand, except for King Solomon—may peace be upon him—who knew them, for the wisdom of God was within him. And even more wondrous is the form of the plants and their colors; there is no artist like our God, blessed be He.

<column-break/>

"And he looked at the image." <note>This refers to a famous teaching that Joseph saw an image of his father Jacob, which prevented him from sinning with Potiphar's wife.</note> Rabbi Isaac said: When they show it to him, it is written to teach you that Joseph was occupied with a mitzvah <term>mitzvah: a commandment or good deed</term>. If Joseph had known that the Holy One, blessed be He, would record him for praise, and that his father would hear of it and rebuke him... as it is written, his father would lead him to all the judges, and then he would be willing... the Holy One, blessed be He, writes of him, "Behold, he goes out to meet you." In simplicity and in change, he was going out to meet him. If he had known his strength, that the Holy One, blessed be He, writes of him "And he looked at the image" and praise, he would have prevented the public revelation... thus far. This is difficult from beginning to end. At the beginning, it says he did not do it for the sake of heaven <note>meaning he only resisted because he saw his father's image</note>, as our Sages said: "The deeds of the ancestors are a sign for the children," and even so... and at the end it says "if he had known..." My explanation of this is as I have said: if he had known that through this he would be praised, he would have done it with even more enthusiasm. It is an *a fortiori* argument: if not for this, then how much more so? But the point is: if he had known this, he would have realized that he was being given a great trial, much more intense than he could bear from his own faith, and he would have been even more careful. From this, the Zohar’s intention is that one must know the reward and the punishment; for then one knows how great they are, and will be more diligent. One should not refrain from a sin only because of the punishment, or do a mitzvah only because of the reward, even though by nature and through habits one refrains from sin and is diligent in mitzvot. This is also found in *Reshit Chokhmah* <note>A 16th-century Kabbalistic ethical work by Eliyahu de Vidas</note>, Chapter 1, and the essence of the matter is as follows: It is possible to explain that even though a person fears the punishment, this is not the main thing. Rather, one should fear the sin itself and be distant from punishment... but what he explains is the punishment that will happen to his soul, which will cause it to be bitter and trapped... as our early sages taught: "Do not be like servants who serve the master for the sake of receiving a reward." Rather, it should be for the sake of Heaven... For if a person knew the great evil that rules over him through sin, he would fear for the honor of his Creator and place it under his feet... like a slave who rules over a king... In this manner, we find that the early ones were careful. When he remembers that he is a sign for others, and even for his children after him, through his sins... and so for his descendants... he will not allow his soul to be sold for nothing... as explained in the portion of *Mishpatim*... One can say that the purification of the soul is according to the size of the sin; so one must purify the soul... and according to what the Rashba <note>Rabbi Shlomo ben Aderet</note> explained... the uprightness of the mitzvah. And so in the Midrash: "Woe to the person whose sin is forgotten..." The reason is that according to the darkness and the stain on his soul, so he needs a remedy to wipe away that bitterness. And let him be careful to distance himself from the sin because it is a source of evil... until he is upright in the mitzvah... and at the end of the fear of sin, he will attain the fear of the Elevated One. Thus far.

---

## More
One can see from the earth the living creatures, as it is written: "Let the earth bring forth living souls," etc. <note>Genesis 1:24</note> and beasts, etc. Who is it and where is he who can know the number of the wisdom concerning the impure and the pure, and the impure and pure beasts, and so too the impure and pure birds, and their legs in their quality and quantity? Particularly the large beasts such as the elephant and the *re'em* <note>a giant ox-like creature or unicorn in Jewish legend</note> and their like, and the signs of resourcefulness seen in them, and their food and sustenance. All of this the earth includes.

## Now
Let us speak of the element of Water, which surrounds the element of Earth. For all the earth is like a mustard seed compared to the Great Sea that surrounds it. This sea is very great. Everything that exists on dry land exists in the sea, and the sea is thousands of thousands of thousands of levels greater than the earth, according to the secret of "the paths of the sea" and its companions—the awesome, great fish of which our Sages spoke in the chapter "One who sells a ship" <note>Baba Batra, chapter 5</note>, and the secret of the Leviathan, with which the Blessed Name prides Himself in His words to Job. In such a way, the existence of the earth and all its host are considered as nothing against the element of Water, whether in quantity or in quality; for the earth is in the ultimate state of density and murkiness, while the element of water is a clear and pure mirror.

## Afterward
We will go from the element of Water to the element of Air, which surrounds the element of Water. See the great difference in the matter of the thinness and purity of the air compared to the element of water. For air is spiritual in relation to water, as it cannot be grasped by the hand like water. And who is he who can have knowledge of the matter of the secret of the spirit and the blowing of
the winds...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and mystical exploration of the motivations behind divine service. Having established the greatness of the Creator on the previous page, the author now distinguishes between "External Fear" (fear of punishment) and "Internal Awe" (shame before God's majesty), drawing heavily from the Zohar and the teachings of Medieval Jewish philosophers.</meta>

# Essay 3 and Essay 4

We perform the commandments in order that we may merit the World to Come <term>Olam Ha-Ba: the spiritual afterlife or the era of resurrection</term>. However, it is not fitting that God should grant us merit solely based on our service if our goal is merely the result that reaches us. Rather, the perfection of service is that He does not need us, and this service reaches us as an eternal legacy. When we serve in this manner—out of our love for Him, may He be blessed—the matter is changed entirely. These are the words of the Rabbi, of blessed memory <note>likely referring to Rabbi Yosef Albo in his *Sefer Ha-Ikkarim*</note>; see there. In every way, one should serve. This was his view regarding the nature of service and the commandments. However, the author of the *Etz Chaim* <note>Rabbi Isaac Luria, the "Ari"</note> attained a higher understanding, asserting that there is no "inner" fear or service except in the way that will be explained later, God willing.

Now, I say that even though the path mentioned by the aforementioned Rabbi Yosef is "inner," even if it were not fully inner, it is not entirely "external" either. It falls into the first category I mentioned: "The one who serves in order to receive a reward." <note>original: "Ha-oved al menat lekabel peras"</note> For there are two types of "serving for reward." First, I am moved to note that the Sages said: "Be not like servants who serve the master in order to receive a reward" <note>Mishnah Avot 1:3</note>. This is difficult, for the promises of the Torah are always calling man to the service of the commandments for the sake of reward! As it says, "so that it may go well with you and you may lengthen your days," and "so that it may go well with you and your children after you." Furthermore, the Holy One, blessed be He, Himself said: "Who would give that their hearts would remain like this, to fear Me and keep all My commandments all the days, so that it may go well with them..." <note>Deuteronomy 5:26</note>. The *Midrash Shmuel* answers this (derived from Rashi's commentary) that the Sages meant one should not work for reward in *this* world, for "the reward for a commandment does not exist in this world" <note>original: "S'char mitzvah be-hai alma leka"</note>. However, the Sages were not speaking of the spiritual reward and recompense of the soul.

**Behold**, regarding Awe and Love, there are two types that are external—namely, the "Back" and "External" aspects—where a person sees only themselves; they fear for themselves and love themselves. 
**And there are two** that are "Inner," characterized by "Face-to-Face" Awe and Love. This is the inner service, "Before and Within." In this state, one fears God and not oneself, and similarly loves God and not oneself. What is the nature of this "Inner Awe"? The Zohar explains this on the portion of *Bereshit* <note>Genesis</note>: "The fear of Awe is the essence: that a man should fear his Master because He is Great and Ruler, the root and essence of all worlds, and everything before Him is considered as nothing... and he should place his will in that place called Awe." These are the Zohar's words. His words are divine, wise, and profound, and they require much explanation. As the Rabbi <note>the Ari</note> elaborated in the explanation of the "Gate of Awe," happy is the eye that sees his words! I, too, will not refrain from discussing this matter of "Great and Ruler" to awaken hearts to fear God and not to fear for one's own sake.

I will reveal a bit of what is hinted at: the meaning of "His power" is not like human power, for "Great is our Lord, and of His understanding there is no number." When a man contemplates even a little of His greatness and loftiness, he will fear before Him and be ashamed. For Awe comes from Shame <term>Boshet: a mix of modesty, humility, and existential embarrassment before God's presence</term>. Thus Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai <note>the traditional author of the Zohar</note> explained in the *Tikunim* regarding Awe stemming from shame. He said: "One who possesses shame will not easily sin... for 'In the beginning' <note>Hebrew: *Bereshit*</note> contains the letters of 'Fear' <note>Hebrew: *Yira*</note>, for Awe and Shame are one." He further stated that those who commit sins have no shame before the Holy One, blessed be He, of whom it is said, "the whole earth is full of His glory," and "He sees the kidneys and the heart." This is linked to the verse "The reward of humility is the fear of God." One who has the fear of God is led to humility, which is the "Higher Divine Presence" <note>Shekhinah</note>. Regarding this, the Sages said: "Awe was a small thing for Moses." Consequently, one must fear and be ashamed before the Divine Presence that is before him, for "the whole earth is full of His glory," and he should not transgress any of His commandments. The author of *Duties of the Heart* <note>Rabbi Bahya ibn Paquda</note> wrote: "The pious one says: Do not rebel against your Master while He is watching you." This is the level of Awe of which the verse says, "that His fear may be upon your faces, so that you do not sin." The Sages explained in the *Mechilta*: "'Upon your faces'—this refers to shame." This teaches that shame leads to the fear of sin. From here they said: it is a good sign for a person to be bashful. Anyone who feels shame will not quickly sin, and one who has no shame, it is known that his ancestors did not stand at Mount Sinai. They proved that Awe is Shame because the verse says "upon your faces"—and Awe is usually in the heart. Why "upon your faces"? Because the shame visible on the face leads to the fear of sin. A person who is ashamed of doing something wrong before other people and is modest in his actions, and who becomes embarrassed when spoken to and cannot look another in the face due to the dread of the King's majesty—this leads him to the fear of sin.

**Now**, to explain my words, I will bring a parable regarding fear and shame before flesh and blood. Suppose there is a man distinguished in Torah and piety, exceedingly lofty in his virtues. He meets a youth and says to him, "Do this thing for me," or "Go on this mission for me." The youth would rush to perform any service possible. Now, if that youth were to refuse or act insolently, the whole world would spit in his face and say, "How brazen are you to refuse such a man?"

<meta>catchword: man</meta>

<column-break/>

...for a long time, and everything according to the value of the speakers, each according to their level of excellence, as mentioned. This is the secret of their intention... the twelve constellations and their actions, as is known from the pious ones. Conversely, this is the secret of "all the dust stands" <note>referring to the lower physical world</note>, involving the life-force of animals and birds, dogs and pigs, which are symbols of folly and base thoughts. All of them are waiting for their sustenance, existing in cycles in a world that is "hidden." All the names are according to the value of those who occupy themselves with them. 

One might ask: why did the Sages write in the portion of *Bereshit* that "When the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world, a 'Bad Child' was born—a prosecutor and accuser?" This refers to the "Evil Fear" <note>original: "Yira Ra'ah"</note>. The question is: why would there be such a thing as "Evil Fear"? Is not the "Fear of the Lord" always good? The explanation provided later is that "Evil Fear" refers to the fear of punishment—the four deaths of the court <note>stoning, burning, slaying, and strangling</note> which stem from the four "husks" <term>Kelippot: shells or forces of impurity that conceal the divine light</term>: "Unformed, Void, Darkness, and Deep."

Similarly, in the *Tikunim*, it says: "There is Awe and there is Awe." There is the "Holy Shame," and there is the "Evil Fear" which is the fear of being struck or punished for one's sins. Regarding this "Evil Fear," the Sages said: "One who transgresses is punished by the prosecutor." But the "Fear of the Lord" is the "Fear of Shame" <note>Awe of Majesty</note> which is the beginning of all commandments. This Awe is a pillar for one's dwelling and faith. The Masters of the Mishnah said: "The fear of sin is the beginning of wisdom." One who has this fear will then know the Torah and say, "These are my commandments and these are my obligations," and he will fear to transgress them. 

But one who does not fear—what is his faith? One who sits in the Sanctuary and acts as if he does not see the King—how is he viewed? This is why King David said to his son Solomon: "Know the God of your father and serve Him." If a man is in a place where the Torah is given to him, and he still acts as if he is hidden and transgresses the commandments, he is like one who has no faith. As the Rabbis said: "An ignorant person cannot be pious" <note>original: "Lo am ha'aretz chasid"</note>. And why? Because the Torah and the commandments come from two levels: Love (from the side of Kindness/Chesed) and Awe (from the side of Strength/Gevurah). Since the whole Torah and its commandments come from these two divine attributes, one must serve through both. Therefore, the Sages concluded: "An ignorant person cannot be pious, nor a bashful person learn."

**And now**, the question returns to its place: if the "shame of punishment" is also called a type of fear, why is it dismissed? For we see in the portion of *Bereshit* that the threat of punishment is used to return people to the good path. Furthermore, the text says that when a man knows the Torah and its commandments, he should fear the punishment for transgressing them. This will be explained further based on the Midrash...

<meta>catchword: and he will understand</meta>

It draws on the Zohar to contrast "Holy Awe" with "Evil Fear" (fear of punishment), emphasizing that true piety requires an inner transformation where one is ashamed to sin in the presence of the Infinite.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the motivations for serving God, shifting from the abstract concepts of fear and awe to a visceral, anatomical argument for gratitude. It transitions from the philosophical "Ten Essays" into a section titled "The History of Man," emphasizing that the physical construction of the human body is the primary evidence of God's benevolence.</meta>

# Ten Essays

The benevolent acts that the Holy One, Blessed be He, performed for man began when He created him from a putrid drop <term>tipah s'ruchah: a humble reference to human biological origins</term> and established him with wisdom. He created in him various orifices and cavities. He made the openings of the eyes to look and see; He made the eyelids to close his eyes to sleep and to avoid looking at evil, as it is written: "He who shuts his eyes from seeing evil" <note>Isaiah 33:15</note>. He made the openings of the ears for hearing. He made the openings of the nose to smell and to drain the excess fluids of the head. He made the mouth for eating and speaking. He made the teeth to grind food. He made the tongue to knead the food within the mouth and to articulate speech. He made the throat and the esophagus to swallow food and drink. He made the windpipe to raise and lower the breath of life, which travels through the lungs to the <unclear>nostrils</unclear> and the mouth, and to produce the sound of speech which emerges from the lobes of the lungs through the breath of life. He made the heart to be a dwelling place for the spirit of life and to think thoughts.

He made the upper belly—which is the stomach—to receive food and drink within it and to sustain the entire body through the nourishment of that food and drink, giving it life. He made the liver on the right side with <unclear>the vascular system</unclear> and blood in the walls of the liver to heat the upper belly; through the heat of this "cooker" and the red and yellow bile, the food and drink are cooked within the upper belly. He made the intestines to receive the waste of the food and drink, which rolls through their twists slowly until it reaches the place where waste is expelled. He made the two kidneys and <unclear>the ducts</unclear> to warm the lower region so it may function and expel the body's needs. Regarding these, our Sages said: "The heart understands and the kidneys advise" <note>A Talmudic concept from Berakhot 61a regarding the intuitive functions of organs</note>. He made the spleen on the left side over the black bile to cool the heat of the innards, the intestines, and the belly so they do not dry out or scorch from the intense heat of the warming organs—the blood, the liver, and the red bile. Our Sages also said: "The spleen laughs" <note>Berakhot 61a</note>.

He made the bones of the spine and the rest of the bones to be a strong structure for the body. He placed flesh upon the bones to warm the coldness of the bones. He made the tendons and blood; these are his life-lines to sustain the body, running from side to side and mouth to mouth. He made the navel, which holds the connection of the bones and limbs. He made the joints of the fingers, hands, feet, arms, thighs, knees, legs, ankles, the soles of the feet, the vertebrae of the neck, the shoulder blades, and the vertebrae of the spine so they can stretch, reach, fold, bend, stand, and sit. He placed skin over them from above to cover the bones, tendons, and flesh, covering the body so it is protected from cold and to shield the moisture of the body and internal organs.

He made the skull of the head to be king over all the limbs, housing the brain where the settled mind, the soul, and wisdom dwell. He made the jawbones around the brain so the brain and eyes would not be jolted by the <unclear>impact</unclear> that rises from below to the head. He made the hair of the head to warm the head so it does not grow cold, as there is no flesh between the skin and the bone of the skull. He made the hair of the beard to give grace to the face and to distinguish the appearance of men from women.

He provided for the male and female all the requirements for life while they were still in their mother's womb until emerging into the air of the world; for the fetus cannot receive nourishment through the mouth while it is closed until it emerges. He made hands to feel, grasp, take, hold, and perform work to sustain the person. He made feet to stand the body upon them and to carry it everywhere. After the person emerges into the world, God raises him and makes him beautiful in every way. Can a person then use his wisdom and understanding to perform commandments enough to repay the goodness the Holy One, Blessed be He, has already done for him? These are the words of the sage.

Furthermore, I say: Look, O man! If you were being helped by a fellow human who was merely a <unclear>servant</unclear> or a lowly person, and a specialist doctor came and healed you, you would love him as your own soul, even beyond the payment you would give him. So too, if you were walking on a path of transgression—the Holy One, Blessed be He, gave you eyes to see, ears to hear, hands, feet, a brain, and a heart to understand and be wise. All this He gave you as a free gift! How could you not love Him with all your world, for His love and humility are toward you? He brought you into existence and did good for you without you having any prior merit. Even if He were not to give you a reward for the commandment you perform, you still could not repay Him one-thousandth of the goodness He gave you first. This is especially true for us, the nation of Israel, whom He chose as His holy people. While the portions of other nations are placed under the hands of heavenly ministers, we are the portion of the Lord; His people, the Assembly of Israel, is His. He is our Father. How could we not love Him with the love of our very souls? Our hearts and souls should be devoted to the holiness of His names all the time we live. His love should be fixed in our hearts to do His will with a whole heart, great joy, and an awakening of the heart.

For this is the matter of "Higher Love," which stands above "Fear." Fear consists of being afraid and ashamed before Him, lest we rebel, Heaven forbid, against anything He commanded—whether a positive commandment or a negative one, from the Torah or from the Sages. But Love means that everything should be done with the flaming of the heart, serving Him with joy. One should not worry about any pain or damage that might befall him because of his service. All the money in the world, and even his body and soul, should be as nothing compared to the love of His service. See and contemplate the love for a woman: when a man is united with her at the peak of his pleasure, he would not separate from her even if he knew it would cause great loss. How much more so, out of love for the Holy One, Blessed be He, should one be careful and diligent in His service! He should not give sleep to his eyes or any rest, but dedicate everything to serving Him, may He be blessed.

Regarding this, the verse says: "Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy and a good heart, out of the abundance of everything" <note>Deuteronomy 28:47</note>. The Divine Rabbi Isaac Luria <note>original: "Ha-Elohi Ha-Ari zal"</note> explained: Your service should be with such joy that it exceeds the joy you would have over the "abundance of everything" that might come your way. The students of the Divine Ari testified that he said whatever merit he achieved of the Holy Spirit was because he was exceedingly happy, with great joy, in the performance of a commandment.

Regarding this matter of love, our Sages said in the Midrash Rabbah: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: With three languages of affection did the Holy One, Blessed be He, love Israel: with "attachment" <term>devikah</term>, with "longing" <term>chashikah</term>, and with "desire" <term>chafitzah</term>.
- From where do we know "attachment"? As it is said: "And you who are attached to the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 4:4</note>.
- From where do we know "longing"? As it is said: "The Lord longed for you" <note>Deuteronomy 7:7</note>.
- From where do we know "desire"? As it is said: "And all the nations shall praise you, for you shall be a land of desire" <note>Malachi 3:12</note>.
And we learn this from the passage of that wicked man <note>Shechem son of Hamor in Genesis 34</note>: with attachment, "his soul was attached to Dinah"; with longing, "Shechem my son longs for your daughter"; with desire, "for he desired the daughter of Jacob."
Rabbi Abba ben Elisha adds: also with "love" and with "speech."
- With love: "I loved you, said the Lord" <note>Malachi 1:2</note>.
- With speech: "Speak to the heart of Jerusalem" <note>Isaiah 40:2</note>.
And we learn this from the passage of that wicked man: with love, "and he loved the girl"; and with speech, "and he spoke to the heart of the girl"—words that comfort the heart. Thus far his words. I have already spoken at length previously in the introduction...

<column-break/>

...in His Torah and in His commandments. The end of my giving <note>referring to divine service</note> is for wisdom, and not for the sake of any worldly thing. Then one will recognize the ultimate purpose of the intellect. And it is not to fear the "goodness" that is given to the soul, because He is Truth, and the end of the goodness is found in its creation, etc.

Observe that this was the high level of our father Abraham; he was warned and cautioned not to serve except out of love. This is the "Higher Level" mentioned, attained through the three "Awakenings" and the love for Truth itself. This is proven from the words of the Sages who said elsewhere: "Perhaps one might say, 'I will study Torah so that I may become rich...'" No, the law is "out of love," etc. And it says: "Who greatly desires His commandments" <note>Psalm 112:1</note>—one desires His *commandments*, not the reward of His commandments.

This was the intention of the Sages when they said: "The Holy One, Blessed be He, wanted to merit Israel..." <note>Mishnah Makkot 3:16</note>. That is, serve out of love. And it says that the "fear" mentioned here is a metaphor for this matter, because its awe is... for it says "the fear of the rod" <note>fear of punishment</note>. He who does His words out of fear is discussed in the Chapter "He Who Hired Workers" <note>Talmud tractate Bava Metzia</note>. His opinion was recorded in the Chapter "The Soul" and in the Chapter "Chelek" <note>Sanhedrin 90a</note>. His words there are praiseworthy, for there are seven types of "Fearers," but the essence is the one who serves out of love, like the words of our Sages. All the sages have elaborated on this. We find ourselves returning to the root: I say that whatever you intend in the words "to love Him" is included before the two types of fear that precede love.

<margin>As it is written in the Midrash</margin>
In the Midrash <note>Leviticus Rabbah 27:2 on Job 41:3</note>: "Who has preceded Me, that I should repay him?"
Who praised Me before I gave him a soul?
Who circumcised his son before I gave him a male child?
Who made a ritual fringe <term>tzitzit</term> before I gave him a garment?
Who made a mezuzah before I gave him a house?
Who made a parapet before I gave him a roof?
Who made a sukkah before I gave him a place?
Who separated the "forgotten sheaf" and the corner of the field <term>pe'ah</term> before I gave him a field?
Who separated the priestly gift <term>terumah</term> and tithes before I gave him a granary?
Who brought an offering before I gave him livestock?
It is upon Me to pay his reward! "Whatever is under the whole heaven is Mine" <note>Job 41:3</note>. For He is the one who gives me everything; it is upon Me to pay his reward. Thus far his words.

From this, one can bring to mind all the parts of our service:
Regarding the commandments of the body, the Holy One, Blessed be He, gave him the life of the body before the existence of the commandment.
Regarding the commandments of the intellect, such as faith and unity, He gave him the source of intellect and speech.
Thus, for all of them, the awakening of the heart includes all these generalities and details. Therefore, the obligation is upon every person to move toward the love that precedes the commandment.

---

One should not perform the "commandments of action"—which are the 248 positive commandments—by saying, "I will do and think this because it is hard on my body or my money and the like." Rather, I perform this thing with alacrity for the sake of my Creator<-

# Ten Essays

The great and powerful winds <note>original: *ruach* - can mean wind, spirit, or breath</note>, both those that are manifest and those that are not, their origins, their entries, and their essence are such that the element of Water is considered as nothing compared to the element of Wind.

**Afterward**
**And just as** the element of Wind is considered as nothing—as if it were naught—compared to the element of Fire that surrounds it; the foundational Fire is so exceedingly subtle that the Wind is considered "physical" by comparison. Here you have the elements, which exist in degrees one above the other.
We shall say: what can we speak of the immense greatness of the Sphere of the Moon, which surrounds the world of the elements? Its brightness and splendor are such that what we see is not the essence of the firmament’s radiance, but rather a thin appearance <note>the text uses a metaphor of a thin membrane or "tunic"</note> clothed in light. Indeed, there is no comparison between the world of the elements and the Sphere of the Moon, neither in its quantity nor in the quality of its subtlety.

And likewise, there is no comparison between the Sphere of the Moon and the Sphere of Mercury <term>Kokhav: literally "Star," but traditionally refers to Mercury in this context</term>, neither in its quantity nor in the quality of its subtlety.
And likewise, there is no comparison between the Sphere of Mercury and the Sphere of Venus <term>Nogah</term>, neither in its quantity nor in its subtlety.
And likewise, there is no comparison between the Sphere of Venus and the Sphere of the Sun <term>Chamah</term>, neither in its quantity nor in its subtlety.
And likewise, there is no comparison between the Sphere of the Sun and the Sphere of Mars <term>Ma’adim</term>, neither in its quantity nor in its subtlety.
And likewise, there is no comparison between the Sphere of Mars and the Sphere of Jupiter <term>Tzedek</term>, neither in its quantity nor in its subtlety.
And likewise, there is no comparison between the Sphere of Jupiter and the Sphere of Saturn <term>Shabbetai</term>, neither in its quantity nor in its subtlety.
And likewise, there is no comparison between the Sphere of Saturn and the Sphere of the Zodiac <term>Galgal ha-Mazalot: the sphere of the constellations</term>, in which are fixed <note>The text contains a string of acronyms likely referring to stellar counts or classifications</note>, neither in its quantity nor in its subtlety.
<margin>Which surrounds all of them every 24 hours every single day</margin>
And likewise, there is no comparison between the Sphere of the Zodiac and the Encompassing Sphere <note>the *Primum Mobile*</note>, the "Right-hand Sphere," which surrounds everything every single day, perpetually, and compels all the other spheres to rotate around the world in a direction opposite to their natural motion, by the will and power of the Creator imbued within it.

Who can measure the clarity, the purity, the subtlety, and the matters of the hidden worlds in their entirety? "Who can express the mighty acts of the Lord?" <note>Psalm 106:2</note>. As it is written in the blessings of the section "We do not wrap ourselves," and it is said, "Zion said: The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me" <note>Isaiah 49:14</note>. For regarding this, the Holy One said to her in His love: "I created twelve constellations in the firmament; and for every constellation, I created thirty cohorts <term>karton: from the Latin *cohors*</term>; and for every cohort, I created thirty camps <term>gistra: from the Latin *castra*</term>; and for every camp thirty..." and so on, totaling 365,000 myriad stars corresponding to the days of the solar year. "And all of them I created only for your sake, yet you say I have forsaken and forgotten you?" <note>Paraphrasing the Talmud, Berakhot 32b</note>. Each sphere is like a soul compared to the sphere above it, and above all is the Sphere of Intellect, the Tenth Sphere, "Holy to the Lord." This entire chain of existence is called by the Sages of Truth <term>Chachmei ha-Emet: a traditional term for Kabbalists</term> the "World of Action" <term>Asiyah</term>. Know that there is a Physical Action and a Spiritual Action. Spiritual Action refers to the angels, the powers of the spheres, and the inner essences of which it is said, "The heavens declare the glory of God" <note>Psalm 19:2</note>. They are the Intellectual Spheres, for they are the inner essence of the spheres like the soul is to the body. Know that all which the early philosophers investigated—dividing existence into three parts: the Lower World, the World of Spheres, and the World of Angels—is all included by the Sages of Truth under the single name "World of Action," for the philosophers' intellects did not merit to grasp more than that. Now we have spoken of the World of Action; yet who can grasp even one-thousandth of a millionth of the greatness and height of the "Palm Tree" <note>likely a reference to a specific spiritual structure</note>, the secrets of its governance? Its name is Sandalphon, and he is the "one wheel <term>Ofan</term> upon the earth." How much more so, then, who can know the height of the World of Formation <term>Yetzirah</term>? There is no number to the legions of the heavenly host there, the holy angels, Cherubim, Living Creatures <term>Chayot</term>, and Seraphim. Regarding their height above one another, I will mention one mentioned in the Zohar: Hadargiel is his name, and he is higher than all other angels by 1,060,000 parasangs <term>a Persian unit of distance</term>. His voice travels through 200,000 firmaments surrounded by black fire. This was the second angel Moses encountered when he ascended to receive the Torah, and Moses was afraid of him until he mentioned the Seventy-Two-Letter Name. When the angel heard this, he trembled and approached him, walking with him until they reached the river of fire and the pit of "Snatchers" <note>angelic beings of destruction</note>. He was lower—I cannot say—higher than all his fellows by a journey of 500 years. He stands behind the Curtain <term>Pargod</term> of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and weaves crowns from the prayers of Israel. When the crown reaches the head of the Holy King, He receives the prayer of Israel, and all the heavenly host tremble and say: "Blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place." Hadargiel said to Moses: "I cannot go further with you, lest the fire of Sandalphon burn me." At that moment, Moses trembled until the Holy One held onto him, as it says, "And he spread His cloud over him." The collective name for the World of Formation is <margin>Metatron</margin>. In Tractate Chagigah, the section "One does not expound," it says: from the earth to the firmament is a journey of 500 years, and the thickness of the firmament is a 500-year journey, and so between each firmament. Above them are the Holy Living Creatures <term>Chayot ha-Kodesh</term>: their feet are equal to all [the distances below] combined, their ankles are equal to all combined, their legs, their knees, their thighs, their bodies, their necks, their heads, and their horns—each segment equal to all that is below it combined. Above them is the Throne of Glory; the legs of the Throne are equal to all combined. The King, the Living and Eternal God, dwells upon them.

<margin>And who</margin> **And who** can even bring to mind a single secret out of the millions of hidden mysteries in the World of Creation <term>Beriyah</term>, whose collective name is <margin>Akhatriel</margin>? How much more so is it impossible to grasp even a tiny fraction of a fraction of the World of Emanation <term>Atzilut</term>, where the Unique Master, who has no second, unites with them in a perfect union. The collective name of Emanation is the Unique Name, the Tetragrammaton <term>Y-H-V-H</term>, may He be blessed. The secret of Emanation is hidden from the eyes of all living things; even Moses our teacher did not grasp Emanation directly, for his prophecy came through the union of the attributes of Beauty <term>Tiferet</term> and Sovereignty <term>Malkhut</term> via the Chamber of Will, as explained in the *Pardes* in the "Gate of Jubilees," which I cited above. Now, O son of man, travel with your intellect from below to above, to the height of the degrees of the worlds. Do not wonder, but see through your contemplation that there is no beginning and no end to the height of this exaltation. Afterward, travel with your intellect from above to below, and contemplate how the Unique Master, called the Infinite <term>Ein Sof</term>, spreads through all of them, to the point where it would be incorrect to say "This is Sovereignty" and "This is the Infinite," God forbid. Rather, Sovereignty also contains the light of the Infinite. Not only this, but within the spirit and the life of the Living Creatures, and the life of the angels, and the life of all the work of Creation from the first point to the last—it is all "And You give life to them all" <note>Nehemiah 9:6</note>. Our Sages explained: "You bring them all into being." This means that since He is their life-force and brings them forth from nothingness, they must necessarily be influenced by Him and draw their vitality from Him. Since He gives them life, it follows that He is their very existence, and that their existence and life are renewed every moment and every hour. He brings into being and gives life to everything, a matter that is renewed every day, perpetually—the work of Creation. It is an overflowing flow that gives life, sustains them, and sets them in their form. If, God forbid, one were to imagine the withdrawal of the "branches" <note>the emanations</note> which are renewed, they would cease; they exist only through the renewal of His light and His vitality, like a river that never ceases but is renewed, like the waters of a river that are new at every moment. For the Infinite, the King of Kings, rules over all, for His essence pierces and descends through the *Sefirot* <term>the ten divine attributes</term>, and within the *Sefirot*, and within the Chariots, and between the Chariots, and within the angels, and between the angels, and within the spheres, and between the spheres, and between the lower elements, and within the elements, and between the earth and its offspring, down to the final point in the depths—"The whole earth is full of His glory" <note>Isaiah 6:3</note>. These are the words of the *Pardes*. <margin>And who</margin> And who is he, and where is he, who was formed from matter, a putrid drop, who would withdraw his shame and not fear the Great and Exalted One, blessed be He? Who would refrain from doing what He forbade or fail to fulfill what He commanded?

<margin>This is</margin> **This is** the "Inner Awe"—that a person should fear the Lord because of His exaltedness, and not out of fear of punishment or for the sake of reward. Rather, out of awe and shame, he should fulfill all His words and with honor uphold the Torah. He should set his heart to study and learn, to keep and to do and to uphold all the words of the study of Torah, whether from the Written Law or the Rabbinic laws. For the words of the Sages were also commanded by Him, may He be blessed: "You shall not turn aside from the things they tell you" <note>Deuteronomy 17:11</note>.
Furthermore, through this Inner Awe, a man will come to Inner Love. For when he contemplates His Lordship and the exaltedness of the Exalted One, and then contemplates how, despite His immense greatness, how great is His humility and His goodness and His great kindness—that He brought the worlds into existence out of a generous will to do good for us, so that we might know and recognize His divinity—and that He constantly influences us with His abundant kindness, both in the existence of man as a whole, whom He created with the wisdom of his limbs in total perfection... thus says the *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* <term>SMaG: a 13th-century legal code</term> regarding the commandment of Love: "And he should think in his heart of the goodness..."

<meta>The previous page discussed the hierarchy of the celestial spheres (Moon, Mercury, Venus) and the subtlety of the elements, transitioning from physical cosmology to the spiritual disposition required to perceive the Creator. This page continues the "Ten Essays" by defining the ten attributes of a "Lover of God," using Abraham as the primary exemplar, and concludes with a philosophical extract from Rabbeinu Tam's *Book of Righteousness* on the nature of love and the soul.</meta>

# Ten Essays

...that the third pleasure <note>This continues a list of spiritual pleasures or attributes from the previous page.</note> is to despise those who despise His company and to love those who love Him, may He be blessed. This is because his love for the goodness of this world is considered as nothing compared to the service of the Creator, may He be blessed. Seventh: that all toil, lack, and affliction should be sweet to him in the face of the love of God, may He be blessed. Eighth: that no personal business of his should take precedence over the business of God, may He be blessed. Ninth: to make known to all people the love of God, may He be blessed, and to glory in it. Tenth: <note>The text repeats numbers or lists them slightly out of sequence in the original manuscript.</note> that he shall not listen to the voice of inciters or those who would lead him astray from the service of the Lord, may He be blessed. Ninth: if events should befall him, whether good or bad, he will not abandon anything for the sake of the service of God, may He be blessed. Tenth: that he should not perform his service for the sake of receiving a reward, for then his service would be "dependent on a thing" <note>A reference to the Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 5:16: "Love that is dependent on a [temporary] thing."</note>. When these ten attributes are gathered in a person, he is called a "Lover of God, may He be blessed," and he is a Chassid <term>Chassid: a term for a "pious one" who goes beyond the letter of the law</term> in the ultimate sense. Regarding this, the Creator, may He be blessed, said of Abraham our Father, peace be upon him, "Abraham My friend" <note>Isaiah 41:8. The text uses "friend/lover" interchangeably.</note>, for only at the time when all these attributes were seen in him did he earn this title.

I shall now explain these attributes to you from the Scriptures. **The First Attribute:** Know that the love of Abraham our Father, peace be upon him, was to teach all who came the service of the Creator, may He be blessed, and to call out His name constantly, as it says, "And he called there upon the name of the Lord" <note>Genesis 12:8</note>. It says in another place, "And he built there an altar to the Lord and called upon the name of the Lord" <note>Genesis 13:4</note>. And it says, "And he planted an *Eshel* <term>Eshel: interpreted by sages as an orchard or an inn for travelers</term> in Beersheba and called there on the name of the Lord" <note>Genesis 21:33</note>. This is to inform you that in every place he went, he would call upon the name of the Lord and engage in His service, and he was not deterred by the fears or terrors of this world.

**The Second Attribute:** That the pious one is more attached to Divine love than he is attached to any worldly pleasure. For it is well known that there is no pleasure or joy for a man like that found in children, as it is said, "Let your father be glad and let her who bore you rejoice" <note>Proverbs 23:25</note>. Yet Abraham our Father, peace be upon him, was more attached to the service of God than to the love of his children; he distanced his son Ishmael from him out of his great love for God.

**The Third Attribute:** That the pious one despises all who despise His company, may He be blessed, and loves those who love Him. For the Creator, may He be blessed, said to Abraham: "Go forth from your land, from your birthplace, and from your father’s house" <note>Genesis 12:1</note>. And he despised his family and his father’s house because they despised God, as it is said: "And Abram went, as the Lord had spoken to him" <note>Genesis 12:4</note>.

**The Fourth Attribute:** That the pious one’s love for all the goodness of the world is considered as nothing compared to the love of God, may He be blessed. Behold, the Creator said to Abraham, "Take now your son, your only son, whom you love—Isaac" <note>Genesis 22:2</note>. It specifies "whom you love" to show all people that even though he loved him with the ultimate love, he set it aside and distanced him for the sake of the love of the Creator.

**The Fifth Attribute:** That the pious one considers all toil and burden as a pleasure and a delight in the service of God, may He be blessed. For Abraham our Father was accustomed to comfort and rest in his house, yet when his trials came, he did not loathe them. He received everything with a pleasant countenance. From his youth, the Creator tested him with journeys, then with the taking of Sarah to Pharaoh’s house, then with the Covenant of Circumcision, then the trial of driving out Ishmael, and then the binding of Isaac. Had his service been out of fear and not love, he could not have endured all these trials. But through his great love for God, everything was sweet in his eyes, as it is said: "Many waters cannot quench love" <note>Song of Songs 8:7</note>.

**The Sixth Attribute:** That he does not let any of his own affairs precede the affairs commanded by the Creator, may He be blessed. We find that in everything the Creator commanded him, he did not delay with any other action until he had fulfilled God's command. Regarding the Covenant of Circumcision, it is written: "In the selfsame day was Abraham circumcised" <note>Genesis 17:26</note>; he did not put any business first until he completed the commandment. Regarding Ishmael, it said: "Whatever Sarah tells you, listen to her voice... for through Isaac shall your offspring be named" <note>Genesis 21:12</note>, and it is written immediately after: "And Abraham rose early in the morning, took bread and a skin of water, and placed it on her shoulder..." <note>Genesis 21:14</note>. We learn from this that the matter was told to him during the night, and therefore he rose early in the morning before doing anything else to complete the command of God.

**The Seventh Attribute:** That the pious one shall make known to every person his love for the Creator and His ways. For so God said of Abraham, that out of his humility, he would remind the people of his generation and make known to every person his love for God, as the scripture says: "For I have known him, so that he may command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the Lord" <note>Genesis 18:19</note>. That is to say, he would inform them so they would be lovers of God through his love. He did not mention "his children" alone, but "his children and his household"—meaning all who were joined to him and over whom he had authority.

**The Eighth Attribute:** The pious one shall not worry over evil, poverty, or the insults of scoffers. It is said that from his youth, Abraham began to seek the service of God, and the people of his generation mocked him, but he did not heed any man until they cast him into the Fiery Furnace and the Creator saved him, as it is written: "I am the Lord who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans" <term>Ur: literally "Fire." Jewish tradition teaches Abraham was thrown into a furnace for his faith in Ur.</term>.

**The Ninth Attribute:** That when events occur to the pious one, whether good or bad, he will not nullify his service. So did Abraham do, for in everything that happened to him, whether good or bad, his heart remained faithful, as it is said: "And You found his heart faithful before You" <note>Nehemiah 9:8</note>.

**The Tenth Attribute:** That the pious one’s love for God is not dependent on anything, nor is it for the sake of receiving a reward. Because Abraham did not seek reward for his service, the Creator said to him: "Your reward is very great" <note>Genesis 15:1</note>. For it is the way of God with His pious ones: when they do not serve for the sake of reward, He gives them their reward and grants them double goodness. As He said to King Solomon, peace be upon him: "Because you have not asked for riches..." and it is written afterward, "I have also given you that which you have not asked: both riches and honor" <note>1 Kings 3:11-13</note>. These are the attributes of love. Whoever possesses these ten attributes, his love is called "Perfect Love." Of these attributes it is said: "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might" <note>Deuteronomy 6:5</note>. Thus far are the words of Rabbeinu Tam <note>Rabbeinu Tam (c. 1100–1171) was a premier French Tosafist; *Sefer HaYashar* is an ethical work attributed to him.</note>.

# More
Rabbeinu Tam wrote in the *Book of Righteousness* (*Sefer HaYashar*), in the fifth gate, as follows: Love is joined from two parts—the first from the side of the Lover, and the second from the side of the Beloved. According to the nature of the Lover's attributes, so will be the strength of his love for the beloved attributes found in the one he loves. I say that the attributes of the Lover are: a Good Intellect, a Pure Soul, and Humility. If a person possesses even a few of these, he will be drawn to love all in whom these attributes are found, because "kind follows kind" <note>A philosophical principle that similar natures are attracted to one another.</note>. The pious one, by the strength of his intellect, will not fail to love the Creator, for the Creator has bestowed upon him the treasures of uprightness and universal truths. Therefore, when a person is drawn [to God], it is a sign that he possesses something of the Creator’s attributes. He follows after Him just as the intelligent man is drawn to the company of the intelligent, the wise to the wise, the fool to the company of fools, the youth to the company of youths, the pious to the company of elders, and every man to the company of those like him.

Therefore, when you see a person distancing himself from the service of God, know that he possesses none of the Creator’s attributes, but rather their opposite. Perhaps if there is in him intellect, holiness, integrity, or uprightness, we know that these attributes belong to the Creator, and when a man has even a trace of them, they draw his heart toward God. Just as the soul is drawn upward toward that which is superior... because it is drawn to the "Place of Intellect" from which its temperament was derived. But when [the soul] is weighed down to the earth until it is bent over, it walks with a stooped posture because of the [animal] soul which is from the dust and is drawn to the physical chain.

Thus we know that the "Good Intellect" within a man speaks to him to seek out its own kind. The "Pure Soul," which is like a "molten mirror" <note>Job 37:18</note>, reveals to him what is hidden of the secrets of God. When the soul is refined and pure, a man can see through it the Creator, His light, His integrity, His beauty, and His other powers, perceiving them with the intellect—just as a man sees in a polished mirror that which was hidden from him. But if the soul is not pure and clear, he cannot see the hidden things, for it is clouded with "ashes." A viewer cannot see what is behind him if the mirror is not clear and fine enough for the sight to pass through. When it is pure, the sight of the intellect and its illumination pass through to what lies beyond. Then, the soul follows the Creator.

Therefore I say: when a man possesses these two attributes—Good Intellect and a Pure Soul—there is awakened within him a perfect love for the Creator, may He be blessed. And when perfect love for God flourishes, Awe (Fear) grows from that love. For we see that anyone who loves another person because of the good qualities found in them, that love sits upon his neck and humbles him to seek the will of the beloved. He finds no rest except in the time of his toil for the sake of the beloved, and that toil is more pleasant to his heart than rest. When he does something that is good in the eyes of the beloved, then the lover's own soul becomes precious in his own eyes, because he was able to find favor in the eyes of his beloved. And if he should happen to sin or err, or do something not good in the beloved's eyes, the lover is desolate and ashamed, slinking away like ashamed people do. This is the power of love, which doubles his submission to the beloved, as the scripture says: "For love is as strong as death" <note>Song of Songs 8:6</note>.

After love has humbled him with a "double will," we must explain why love has this power. We say: the lover's love for the beloved is due to the perceived treasures in the beloved. Because the lover also has some good attributes, that small portion of choice attributes within him draws him toward the Source, just as every kind is drawn to its own kind. This is a sign of a "noble soul"—that it is drawn to all that is honorable. This is Love. But the "submission" <note>Referring to the awe or fear that accompanies love.</note> of the lover to the beloved is because of the beloved’s superiority and greatness. When a student recognizes the excellence of his master and his wisdom, he prepares his love to be in accordance with the master's will. Thus, he fears and loves the beloved, just as a servant fears his master and a student his teacher because of the advantage the master has over him, and because he always hopes to learn from his discipline. These attributes are necessary—that the lover be in awe of his beloved. Thus it is clarified that from Love comes Awe.

<summary>This page outlines the ten spiritual attributes defining a "Lover of God," using the life and trials of Abraham as the ultimate model of piety. It then presents a philosophical argument from Rabbeinu Tam's Sefer HaYashar, explaining that true love for God arises from a pure soul and intellect, and that this love naturally produces a sense of awe and submission.</summary>

<meta>The previous page concluded a list of ten attributes of a "Lover of God" and began a discussion on the soul's delight in divine service. This page transitions into a deeper analysis of the psychological and mystical nature of desire, using the Talmudic figure Yalta and her husband Rav Nachman as a starting point to explore how human passions can be redirected toward the Creator.</meta>

# Ten Essays

...that we are commanded to do such and such. Regarding a prohibitive commandment <note>Hebrew: *Lo Ta'aseh*</note>, a person should think and say: "How much I desired to eat pork," and so on; "but what can I do? My Father in Heaven has decreed it upon me." Our Sages, of blessed memory, explained the verse "With all your heart" as meaning "with both your inclinations" <note>The *Yetzer HaTov* (Good Inclination) and the *Yetzer HaRa* (Evil Inclination)</note>. This means that in a positive commandment, or in the Evil Inclination regarding a prohibitive commandment, one subdues it. Thus, the commandment is fulfilled doubly: he fulfills the positive act through the counsel of the Good Inclination, and he subdues the Evil Inclination. 

Regarding this matter, I received from the mouth of the "Holy One of God," my father and teacher—may his memory be for a blessing in the life of the world to come—an explanation of the passage in the Talmud, Tractate Chullin, in the chapter "All Meat" <note>Chullin 109b</note>. There, Yalta <note>The wife of the sage Rav Nachman</note> said to Rav Nachman: "Consider that for everything the Merciful One [God] forbade us, He permitted us something similar. He forbade us blood, but He permitted us liver. He forbade menstrual blood, but He permitted the blood of purity. He forbade the fat of domestic animals, but permitted the fat of wild beasts. He forbade pork, but permitted the brain of the *Shibbuta* fish <note>A fish traditionally identified as having a taste similar to pork</note>. He forbade the forbidden fat of the 'large-tailed sheep,' but permitted the tongue of the male. He forbade a married woman, but permitted a divorcee during her husband's lifetime. He forbade a brother’s wife, but permitted the brother’s widow in a Levirate marriage. He forbade the beautiful captive woman <note>A non-Jewish woman taken in war</note> except under specific conditions, but permitted a beautiful woman in marriage. I now desire to eat meat cooked in milk <note>A forbidden mixture in Jewish law</note>." Rav Nachman said to his butchers: "Prepare for her a roasted udder <note>An udder contains milk but is permitted to be eaten if prepared correctly, providing the taste of meat and milk together</note>." 

This is difficult to understand: would a distinguished woman like Yalta speak with her husband Rav Nachman about such matters which, at first glance, seem like idle talk? Not only that, but our Sages saw fit to record these words in the Talmud! One might say the Talmud gathered these things to teach the law that he permitted the roasted udder, which resulted in a practical legal ruling discussed at length by the *Tosafot* and the Codifiers. But if that were the only reason, the Talmud should have shortened the account and just brought the ruling.

My father and teacher, of blessed memory, explained that from these words a great concept emerges. It relates to what I said: that in every prohibitive commandment, one should think in his heart of the desire he has to do it, and yet he refrains and does not do it for the sake of the glory of Heaven. This is like the teaching of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: "A person should not say, 'I do not want to eat pork,' but rather he should say, 'I would like to, but what can I do? My Father in Heaven has decreed it upon me.'" 

This is the matter Yalta was addressing: for every forbidden thing, the Merciful One provided a corresponding permitted thing so that we might taste it and know that the taste of the forbidden thing is good, and we will desire it, yet we will leave the forbidden act for the sake of the Creator’s glory. Thus, the taste of the *Shibbuta* fish is like the taste of pork; therefore we know the taste of pork is good, we desire it, and we refrain for the glory of the Creator. Behold, the Torah forbade us meat and milk in combination, and we would have a desire for it; therefore he said: "Prepare the udder for her." 

From this, a sweet light shines upon the words of my father, of blessed memory. This is the plain meaning. Now we shall come to the explanation of the matter regarding the inner power of the soul's desire. I will first quote what is written in the *Reshit Chochma* <term>Reshit Chochma: "The Beginning of Wisdom," a famous 16th-century Kabbalistic ethical work by Eliyahu de Vidas</term>, in the "Gate of Love," Chapter 3: 

"Cleaving <note>Hebrew: *Dveikut*</note> occurs when a person attaches his soul to the soul of his fellow in a way that they have a complete bond of love, etc., as it says: 'And Ruth cleaved to her,' meaning the cleaving of her will. This cleaving does not indicate total unity, for it is possible for the attachment to separate. The proof is from the verse: 'As a belt cleaves to the loins of a man, so have I caused the House of Israel to cleave to Me.' A belt is sometimes attached to a person and sometimes not, for he unties it from himself. However, the word 'Desire' <note>Hebrew: *Cheshak*</note> indicates a bond of love that is greater, for it implies that even when he leaves her, she remains bound in his mind, in a state of connection and union." 

He further explains that "Longing" <note>Hebrew: *Shikika*</note> is like being tightly bound or pressured, as one does with ropes around wood to tighten them. The root of "Delight/Will" <note>Hebrew: *Chafetz*</note> is even greater, indicating the total aim of a person's face toward the beloved, not moving from her for even a moment, as it says: "with a perfect heart and a willing soul." We find this regarding the prince Shchem: "He did not delay doing the thing, for he delighted in Jacob’s daughter" <note>Genesis 34:19</note>. It was as if he had no other will in the world but this one will alone. We also find the term "Delight" used for physical intimacy, as the Zohar explains on the verse "as I have delighted." 

<insert>And he [the author's father], of blessed memory, explained this matter</insert> regarding the levels of the soul—*Nefesh*, *Ruach*, and *Neshamah*—but according to our subject, it will be explained based on what I wrote above. I will also add a "touch of my own" regarding these three words: **Cleaving** (*Dveika*), **Desiring** (*Chishuka*), and **Delighting** (*Chafitza*). They are three ascending levels, and I will explain them in two ways that converge.

**First Way:** **Cleaving** is the awakening of a person to serve the Creator that comes to him from the side of the Good Inclination. But it is as the Creator said regarding the "light" [of the belt], that sometimes the "light" is loosened—meaning the Evil Inclination fights with him and makes the matter heavy for him. Even though he overcomes it, he does not do the act with enthusiasm or joy. For the enthusiasm of the soul in joy—in its speech, its thoughts, its generalities, its details, and the precision of the commandment’s intentions—this is what is called a person "cleaving" to God. 

However, when he adds holiness and completely nullifies the influence of the Evil Inclination—meaning the service of the commandment gives joy to his heart from the abundance of everything—this state is called **Desiring** (*Cheshak*). It is an awakening from the Holy One, as it says: "The Lord desired you." This is a superior connection. 

The pious and holy sage [Rabbeinu Tam] wrote in his commentary on the prayers regarding the "Additional Prayer" for the New Moon: "A person must serve God with 'both hearts'—with the Good Inclination and the Evil Inclination." This means doing it out of love so that both hearts are equal in the action. One who performs a commandment as a "burden" is not working with the Evil Inclination, for it is against his will. 

**The Second Way** is even more inward. It is not enough for the Evil Inclination to be set aside; rather, one takes from its energy to serve God. From the side of the Evil Inclination, he creates an even greater closeness. Specifically, in a positive commandment, he takes the awakening of the Evil Inclination's counsel and "rises like a lion" to overpower it. He turns the very action suggested by the Evil Inclination into the service of the Sanctuary. Regarding this, the Tanna <note>A teacher of the Mishnaic period</note> said: "Who is a hero? He who subdues his inclination." He did not say "he who kills" or "he who nullifies," but "subdues," meaning he takes it and conquers it. This is precise: "With all your heart—with both your inclinations." 

Behold, if one fulfills commandments without this awakening, it is called **Cleaving**, for he is attached to God. But when he is awakened to the desire, and despite all this, he overpowers it like a lion for the sake of the service of the Holy One, this is called **Desiring** (*Cheshak*). His soul desires the bad, but he transforms that passion to desire the Holy One. This is service out of "Great Love."

The concept of **Delighting/Will** (*Chafetz*) is a higher level. We call it "Eternal Love." For "Delight" is the ultimate will that chooses continuously without pause. I will offer a parable: a man's love for a woman. He desires her and is intimate with her, and at the time of union, he would not separate from her for any reason in the world. Nevertheless, after the union is finished, his delight and will are completed, and his desire is satisfied. However, in the service of the love of God, it is an "Eternal Love." The delight and will do not cease. Even when the commandment is finished in its fullness and goodness, he desires and wants even more to cleave. This is the concept of "One commandment leads to another." For the more a truly perfect person performs and serves, the more he desires to do more. He moves from perfection to perfection, toward the Divine Desire. Even if he cannot perform it, he still longs for it, like Moses who longed to enter the Land of Israel just to fulfill its unique commandments. This love is "Eternal Love."

Returning to the Talmudic passage, it says: "And all of them are learned from the section of that wicked man [Shchem]." It is difficult: what benefit is there in learning from the section of a wicked man? "Who can produce a pure thing from an impure one?" But according to what I wrote above, it is clear: he subdues his inclination, which is "the wicked one," and transforms the desire. 

(The words of Rabbi Abba bar Isha, who added two levels—Love and Speech—will be explained later.)

I will now clarify the words of Rabbi Menachem Recanati <note>A 13th-century Italian Kabbalist</note>, of blessed memory. He wrote that Shchem ben Chamor the Hivite, who came upon Dinah, is a mystery of the Serpent who came upon Eve and cast filth into her. Dinah's soul was already planted from the mystery of the "Queen" <note>The *Shekhinah*</note>. (The name Dinah contains the letters of *Adonai* <note>A name of God associated with the *Shekhinah*</note>). Leah, the Higher Mother, gave birth to six sons and one daughter, and this daughter is the *Shekhinah*, which is "Judgment" (*Din*). Because of sin, that wicked man's soul cleaved to Dinah. He was "attached, desiring, and delighting" in her. So too, it is proper for a man to attach his soul to the *Shekhinah* with these three levels. 

The matter of inner love is now explained. To complete the subject, I will bring the words of our Master [Rabbeinu Tam] in the *Sefer HaYashar* <term>Sefer HaYashar: "The Book of the Upright," an ethical treatise often attributed to Rabbeinu Tam</term>, regarding what he wrote about love in the second gate: 

"Love is tested by ten things in the lover. First: that he loves the Torah of God. Second: that he takes pleasure in the delight of serving God, etc."

<summary>This page explores the concept of transforming physical desire into spiritual passion, using the Talmudic story of Yalta and the Kabbalistic levels of Cleaving, Desiring, and Delighting. It argues that the highest form of worship involves subduing the Evil Inclination and redirecting its intensity toward the love of God.</summary>
