# The Fifth Essay

<margin>
There is a "Kindness of Suffering," and Your Torah shall teach us. This means it is a wide-open door <note>original: *petach patuach*</note> to freedom. Strengthen your grip on the discipline of taking [suffering] with kindness, as it is written regarding the refining of dross and the lack of a shield or strength. This is mentioned in the Talmud <note>likely referring to Tractate Berakhot 5a regarding "suffering of love"</note>. I have written this to prevent despair and to provide guidance, because suffering is prepared [for a purpose].
</margin>

...from above, and then the root of the blessing increases in the upper worlds, and from there it descends upon the head of the righteous person. Understand this well.
Now, the first [Psalmist] said, "I will sing of mercy and judgment" <note>Psalm 101:1</note> to fulfill the commandment of the tithe <term>Ma’aser: the practice of giving a tenth of one's earnings to charity</term>. This refers to "mercy" in the obvious sense, but also "judgment," which refers to poverty. The reason for this is to strengthen the intellect, which causes a great light to shine, as explained above in the name of the Ran <note>Rabbi Nissim of Gerona, a 14th-century scholar</note>. 

The second said, "In God I will praise His word" <note>Psalm 56:11</note>. This relates to the second reason: going and descending with the will of God through His abundant kindness. 

The third said, "I will lift up the cup of salvation" <note>Psalm 116:13</note>, referring to the future when one is cleansed from severe punishment. If it is for the sake of salvation—as it says in the first chapter of Tractate Ta’anit: "Rabbi [Simeon] said: Anyone who rejoices in suffering brings salvation to the world," as it is said of them, "The world is saved." He also said, "I found trouble and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord." This follows the verse: "Why should you be stricken any more? You will increase rebellion. The whole head is sick, and the whole heart is faint" <note>Isaiah 1:5</note>. 

The intention here is that when the Holy One, Blessed be He, sends a plague or sickness into the world, or if the world "increases rebellion," people do not attribute it to the Holy One, Blessed be He, acting as a punishment for their sins. Instead, they claim it is merely a "chance occurrence" <note>original: *umgang*, an archaic German/Yiddish term for an event or circumstance</note>. This is why it says "the whole head is sick"—meaning they claim it is a random event. And because he sees that "the whole head is sick," they continue to rebel. But in truth, it is from the Lord. If the plague moves through everyone, then the sin also moved through everyone, for all have sinned. This is what is meant by "In the flock, I will find trouble and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord"—for this came from Him to cleanse sin, and it is not a mere accident.

The fourth said, "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord" <note>Job 1:21</note>. This is the secret of love and the "unification" <term>Yichud: a meditative focus on the oneness of God</term> of the upper worlds when His name is blessed. Or, that the lower beings shall be blessed. "The Lord gave" the flow of influence at the [right] time, and "the Lord has taken away"—meaning when the awakening of the lower beings was taken, then "the Lord gave." I have elaborated on this in the introduction: through the deeds of the lower beings, the Torah and the commandments are sustained by the word of the Great Name, and from His blessing, the lower beings are blessed.

**And it is** explained here the reasons for the "beloved qualities" of suffering. As for why we pray "but not through suffering or evil diseases," this refers to suffering that comes upon a person as "vengeance" from the Creator. When a person is loathsome in the eyes of the Creator, He sends suffering so that the evil may be consumed and removed from the world—may the Merciful One save us! But the suffering that comes to cleanse a person from sin, so that they may be pure and clean, or to merit other good things or to bequeath merit—concerning this it is said, "Happy is the man whom You, O Lord, chasten" <note>Psalm 94:12</note>. Therefore, just as we bless God for the good, so we bless Him for the bad. He said it is "proper to receive it with joy," just as one receives with joy and a good heart the goodness He has granted me. 

Until this point, our verse has said: "See that I am with your anger" <note>a complex wordplay on the Hebrew for "anger" and "face"</note> and serve Him with a "whole heart and a willing soul." What is meant by a "whole heart"? It means the heart should always be "whole" <note>complete</note> even at the moment it is "broken and contrite." And a "willing soul" refers to a time of desire and will. That is to say: just as one is during a time of desire and will, so should the heart be "whole" when it is broken. Through this, "In God I will praise His word; in the Lord I will praise His word"—the names *Y-H-V-H* and *Elohim* are included within one another. 

**Also**, there is a hint here: "whole" <note>Shalem</note> and a "willing soul" <note>Nefesh Chafetzah</note> correspond to "with all your heart and with all your soul." The secret here is that even if He takes your soul, you should serve Him with love.

## The Sixth Essay

The essence of the "service of the heart" <term>Avodah she-be-lev: prayer or internal devotion</term> was already hinted at above. A faithful servant who performs all the needs of his master has, in his service, a "grasp" of his master—he dresses him, puts on his shoes, and so on. But this does not apply to our service of the Creator, for He is spiritual—the ultimate spirituality, hidden from every eye. Even the [heavenly] "Tree" is not the place of His glory. Therefore, it is impossible for us to have a "hold" on Him through our service except through the service that is in the heart. Through that spirituality, "attachment" <term>Dveikut: mindful cleavage to the Divine</term> ascends. 

Concerning this, the Scripture says: "Because you did not serve... with joyfulness and with gladness of heart" <note>Deuteronomy 28:47</note>. For if the service is not performed with the awakening of the heart and the flame of joy, it is impossible for the service to "attach" to its purpose. There are many ways to serve with joy and for every matter to be a "new commission" <note>original: *parnastaga chadisha*, a Persian-influenced Aramaic term for a royal appointment or task</note>, with all one's strength and intention. 

This applies not only to "Positive Commandments" <note>commandments to *do* something</note> but even to "Negative Commandments" <note>prohibitions</note> which are performed by "sitting and doing nothing." These too must involve an internal awakening, not like someone who is drowsy or idle. As the *Baraita* of Shimon ben Gamliel says: "A person should not say, 'I find pork disgusting,' but rather 'I want it, but what can I do? My Father in Heaven has decreed against it.'" 

This is the essence of the "service of the heart," and this is the hint in the phrase "serve Him with a whole heart and a willing soul." A "whole heart" refers to the Positive Commandments—that the heart should be whole "with all your heart," including both your inclinations <note>the Good and the Evil Inclination</note>, as explained at length in the discourse on "Inner Love." A "willing soul" refers to the Negative Commandments—that one should have a "will" or a natural desire for the thing, but for the sake of the Creator's decree, he follows the advice of his soul <note>the higher self</note> and not the cravings of the body. 

I mention these matters now, even though I have elaborated on them in the discourse on "Inner Love," because **"there is no study-house without a novelty."** Previously, I only explained that one should awaken the desire of the "Evil Inclination" which opposes the commandment and be a "hero" who subdues it. Thus they said, "Who is a hero? He who subdues his inclination." But now I say there is a level of adding "holiness upon holiness." This is an even greater subduing: to bring the "Evil Messenger" <note>the impulse to do wrong</note> under one's hand and authority, to "sacrifice its mother," and to be pure from the burden of impurity itself. The impurity itself is transformed into purity! 

Let me give you an example of certain traits. The worst traits are jealousy, hatred, lust, and desire. These are the traits of the Evil Inclination. Yet, with these very traits, one can serve God! 
How? With the trait of **jealousy**, one can be "jealous for the sake of the Lord of Hosts," like Phinehas. With **lust**, one can "lust" after the hidden treasures of the Torah. With **desire**, as King David said: "My soul breaks for the longing <note>original: *ta’avah*, usually "lust" but here "longing"</note> it has for Your ordinances at all times" <note>Psalm 119:20</note>. So too with **hatred**, as David said regarding the wicked: "I hate them with a perfect hatred" <note>Psalm 139:22</note>. 

There are a thousand such matters. This is what our Sages meant by "separating the grain from the chaff" and matters of holiness. They said the opposite: "Cast gall <note>bitterness/discipline</note> among the students." Concerning this, they spoke of "Repentance and Good Deeds." One might ask: what is the novelty here? Obviously, if one has no good deeds, what is his repentance? He would be like one who "immerses in a ritual bath while holding a crawling lizard" <note>a classic metaphor for insincere repentance</note>. Rather, the intention is this: "Repentance" is in the understanding <note>Binah</note> of the Evil Inclination—overcoming it like a lion and nullifying one's lust for the sake of the Creator. "Good Deeds" refers to purifying the traits—taking one's "bad deeds" and making them "good deeds" by transforming the traits from evil to good. For one who does this, his "deliberate sins are transformed into merits."

**Furthermore**, it is hinted in the "service of the heart" that there is a service of the heart—meaning in the thought and wisdom of the heart—even if that service is not performed in actual practice. To understand this, we must first look at what Rabbi Meir said: "Whoever occupies himself with Torah for its own sake <term>Lishmah: for the sake of the study itself, not for reward</term> merits many things..." 

We must ask: what are these "many things"? One cannot say it refers to the things listed afterward ("the whole world is indebted to him," etc.), for those are introduced by the phrase "And not only that..." Rather, the matter is this: The Holy One, Blessed be He, gave 613 commandments. Through these 613 commandments, the "Image and Likeness" of man is completed, corresponding to the secret of the 248 limbs and 365 sinews. 

At first glance, a person might be terrified: who can ever be "complete" in all 613? There are many commandments that are impossible for a specific person to perform. Even Moses our Teacher did not perform them all! For example, the commandments pertaining only to Priests <term>Kohanim</term>, or the laws of Levirate marriage <term>Yibum</term> if the situation never arises, or the laws of a man who slanders his wife, and many others. If so, is the "Image and Likeness" within the person never completed? Heaven forbid! 

The matter is this: "Whoever occupies himself with Torah for its own sake"—this is like a King who writes a decree to the citizens of his country telling them what to do and what to avoid. They open the decree to do the King's will; each person does what pertains to him. One goes to the border, one builds a palace, one collects the tax. Each does what is possible for him to do. This person is called a "servant of the King" because he does what is possible. If it were possible for him to do more, he would do it. Therefore, it is considered as if he did everything. 

So it is with us, the servants of the Lord. The Torah is the "decree" that the Holy One, Blessed be He, wrote to the citizens of His country—the Nation of Israel. We open this decree to fulfill all that is written, each of us doing what is possible. Therefore, we are "servants of the Lord." If we occupy ourselves with Torah "for its own sake"—to know what God has told us and commanded us, learning in order to keep and perform—then if a person fulfills everything it is *possible* for him to fulfill, the Holy One, Blessed be He, considers it as if he fulfilled everything. For the Holy One, Blessed be He, joins a good thought to an action. 

As it says in the first chapter of Berakhot regarding the verse "Then those who feared the Lord spoke one to another... and for those who thought upon His name" <note>Malachi 3:16</note>. What does "thought upon His name" mean? Rav Ashi said: "If a person intended to perform a commandment but was prevented by circumstances beyond his control, the Scripture considers it as if he had performed it." 

This also answers the famous question regarding the ruling: "Study is greater, for study leads to action." The goal is always greater than the actions leading to it. Since "action" is the goal, action should be greater! I have answered this elsewhere, but here it seems I can explain: Study "leads to" action in the sense that the one who studies "for its own sake" and intends to fulfill the commandment is considered as if he had actually performed the action, since from his side...

<meta>This page continues the "Fifth Essay," shifting from the mechanics of blessing to a deep theological defense of suffering. It explores why a benevolent God allows pain, drawing on the Talmudic concept of "suffering of love" and the legal metaphors of slavery to explain how affliction can lead to spiritual freedom.</meta>

## The Fifth Essay

To help you only... and like the Comforter, may He be blessed, of the "cup, cup," etc. <note>likely referring to the "Cup of Consolation"</note> for all, with its salt, etc. Sometimes it is written this way and sometimes that way, and for every matter there is a secret, and a great secret. <note>The author is discussing variations in liturgical or mystical texts regarding the "Cup of Blessing."</note>

**Regarding the Cause of Suffering:**
Most of the causes of suffering that come upon a person are like those mentioned in Psalm 8 <note>original: "Mizmor Cheit"</note> of the Book of Psalms. As the Sage Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: This Psalm revolves around the "Cain of Man" and his straying. It is Psalm 34 <note>The text likely refers to the numbering in specific editions or a different manuscript tradition</note> that rises above the suffering of the Jewish souls that are suppressed under the yoke [of exile]. This soul belongs to Him, for it is written: "In anger and in wrath." What brings these souls to this state? It is the "Kindness of the Sabbath," <note>original: "Kat Shabat"</note> as it is written: "For He will not neglect the Lord's portion forever." Rather, He will only purify its righteousness and they will find mercy, for the Lord desires His tribes as servants—but not "servants to servants." <note>A common Jewish trope: Jews should be servants only to God, not to human masters.</note>

His intention in this was that even if a master makes the labor heavy upon his Hebrew slave <term>Eved Ivri: A Jewish indentured servant whose terms of service were strictly regulated by Torah law</term>, if the slave wants to go free, he must follow the law of "Tooth and Eye." <note>Exodus 21:26-27 states that if a master blinds a slave's eye or knocks out their tooth, the slave must be set free as compensation.</note> Rashi explains that this applies to a master's excessive force. If he is a Canaanite slave <term>Eved Kena'ani: A non-Jewish slave who, according to Rabbinic law, could also gain freedom if injured by the master</term>, he goes out to freedom if his master strikes him. Consider the language of "Tooth and Eye" <note>original: "Shen ve-Ayin"</note>: if a master strikes his slave and destroys an organ, the slave is compensated with liberty. 

How much more so <term>Kal Vachomer: A "light and heavy" logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from a minor case to a major one</term> does this apply to the soul! If a slave goes free because of a single limb, surely a person whose entire body is "refined" by suffering should be granted spiritual freedom. Do not say that this only applies to physical injury; the language of "Tooth and Eye" refers to the essence of the person. The soul is refined through these "storms" of life. Just as a slave's freedom is bought with the price of his pain, the soul’s liberation from its "master" (the physical world or the exile) is achieved through the trials God sends.

<column-break/>

The perfect man must justify and accept suffering, remaining silent and still. There are lengthy proofs to bring agreement to this matter, as the words of the Sages in the books of the *Kuzari* <note>A foundational 12th-century work of Jewish philosophy by Judah Halevi</note> are full of this. Also, among all the gentile scholars and philosophers, this was a settled conclusion. The scholar Rabbi Moses Albelda <note>A 16th-century philosopher and preacher</note> already brought six philosophical proofs for this in his book *Gates of Tears* <note>original: *Sha'arei Dim'ah*</note>; see there.

Even suffering that causes a "neglect of Torah study" <note>original: *bitul Torah*</note> is considered good, according to the conclusion in the first chapter of Tractate Berakhot <note>Talmudic tractate on blessings and prayer</note>, for these are "suffering of love" <term>Yissurin shel Ahavah: Afflictions sent by God not as punishment for sin, but to cleanse the soul or increase reward in the afterlife</term>. It is recorded there that Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi and Rabbi Acha bar Chanina disagreed. One said: "Suffering of love is any suffering that does not involve the neglect of Torah study," as it says, "Happy is the man whom You discipline, O Lord, and teach out of Your law" <note>Psalm 94:12</note>. The other said: "It is suffering that does not involve the neglect of prayer," as it says, "Blessed be God, who has not turned away my prayer nor His mercy from me." 

Rabbi Acha, the son of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: Both of these are "suffering of love," as it says, "For whom the Lord loves He reproves" <note>Proverbs 3:12</note>. If so, why does the verse say, "and teach out of Your law"? Do not read it as "You teach him," but rather, "You teach *us* this matter from Your law." We learn it through a logical inference <term>Kal Vachomer</term> from the law of "Tooth and Eye." If a slave goes free for the loss of a tooth or an eye—which are only one of a person's limbs—then suffering that cleanses a person’s whole body how much more so [should lead to freedom]!

This is the same as the teaching of Reish Lakish, who said: The word "covenant" is used regarding salt, and "covenant" is used regarding suffering. Regarding salt it says, "You shall not omit the salt of the covenant" <note>Leviticus 2:13</note>, and regarding suffering it says, "These are the words of the covenant" <note>Deuteronomy 28:69</note>. Just as the covenant of salt refers to salt sweetening meat, the covenant of suffering refers to suffering cleansing all of a person’s sins. 

In the chapter "The One Who Sees" <note>Tractate Berakhot, Chapter 9</note>, it asks: What does it mean that one is "obligated to bless God for the bad just as he blesses Him for the good"? Rava said: It means to receive it with joy. Rabbi Acha said in the name of Rabbi Levi: What is the biblical source? "I will sing of mercy and judgment" <note>Psalm 101:1</note>. If it is mercy, I will sing; if it is judgment, I will sing! Rabbi Samuel bar Nachmani said: "In God I will praise His word; in the Lord I will praise His word" <note>Psalm 56:11</note>. "In the Lord" refers to His attribute of Goodness; "In God" <note>Elohim</note> refers to His attribute of Justice/Punishment. Rabbi Tanchum said: "I will lift up the cup of salvation... I found trouble and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord." The Rabbis say: "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord."

One might ask: what is the difference between these views? These holy Sages had different perspectives on suffering. One reason for suffering is that it awakens a person to repentance and increases intellectual power, as cited above in the name of the Ran. A second reason is that a person might mistakenly think something is "bad," like Joseph being sold as a slave, yet that was the very cause of him becoming king in Egypt. As the verse says: "I will thank You, for You have answered me and become my salvation" <note>Psalm 118:21</note>. 

The Midrash brings a parable of two merchants: one had a camel that sat down and couldn't walk. The merchant was distressed that he would lose out on business. Later, he heard that the ship he was supposed to board sank in the sea. He then realized his "suffering" was for his benefit, and he said: "I thank You, Lord, for You afflicted me, for this affliction was my salvation." This is the meaning of the prayer "Do what is good in Your eyes." A person might find a lost object and think it is "good," but then the king hears of it and he is arrested. Therefore, we ask: "Master of the Universe, do what *You* know is truly good."

A third reason is that "no evil descends from above." Even if it appears bad, it is to save one from a worse punishment. Abraham was told his children would be enslaved so they would not have to face Gehenna <note>Purgatory/Hell</note>. A fourth reason is "Suffering of Love." This suffering cleanses the "blemish" above and prepares the "Upper Unity." The righteous person accepts suffering to repair the spiritual damage in the higher realms, creating love and unity in the world of Emanation <term>Atzilut: The highest of the four worlds in Kabbalah, representing pure divinity</term>. This is the "Secret of Unity" <term>Sod ha-Yichud</term>.

As Rava said: If a person sees suffering coming upon him, he should examine his deeds. If he examines them and finds nothing, he should attribute it to "neglect of Torah study." If he still finds nothing, it is certainly "suffering of love." Rashi explains: The Holy One, blessed be He, afflicts them in this world without any sin, in order to increase their reward in the World to Come. On the surface, this seems strange—suffering without reason and reward without reason? But the secret is that suffering cleanses the "blemish" above and increases love in the Divine mystery.

<column-break/>

[This column contains a repetitive draft or alternate version of the notes regarding the "Tooth and Eye" law and the "Covenant of Salt," reinforcing the argument that suffering acts as a legal and spiritual mechanism for the soul's liberation.]

...God disciplines them, and they go out to freedom. (Note the word "rebuke/discipline" <note>original: *yochiach*</note> as it is used in the Torah regarding suffering: "For whom the Lord loves He reproves"). The word "all" <note>original: *kelo*</note> teaches that the master must have knowledge and intent... regarding "Tooth and Eye." Joseph said to his brothers: "You intended evil against me, but God intended it for good." This shows that what seems like "evil" in the moment is often the catalyst for the ultimate "good" and the preservation of life. Even the Egyptian bondage was, in a sense, a refinement like the Hebrew slave who is sold but eventually goes free...

<meta>This page transitions to "Essay 7." While the previous page discussed the theology of suffering and servitude, this page shifts to the mechanics of Divine mercy and the human obligation to go "beyond the letter of the law." It draws heavily on the commentary of the Ramban (Nachmanides) regarding the commandment to "be holy."</meta>

# Essay 7

All of this is for the reasons I mentioned: that Moses did not pray for them to be completely pardoned, but rather requested that He bear with them and be patient—visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children—and his prayer for them was not "complete" <note>meaning he didn't seek a total erasure of the sin</note>. Therefore, he did not mention to them that the Lord is "willing to forgive." These are the words of the Ramban.

Regarding the fact that he only mentioned the Name of God <note>the Tetragrammaton, Y-H-V-H</note> once: this is self-explanatory. Our Sages, of blessed memory, explained that the Name appears twice in the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy—once for before a person sins and once for after they sin. Here, it was already after the sin had occurred. This is why he began by saying, "**And now, I pray, let the power of my Lord be great**" <note>Numbers 14:17</note>. What I am praying for is to increase the "power of my Lord," which means to let the attribute of Mercy overcome the attribute of Judgment. 

As it says in the Midrash: "I am not asking for this except for the present time"—meaning, do not destroy them now, but collect Your debt later. Just as You have "**forborne this people from Egypt until now**," constantly punishing them for their sins, so too do I request now that You give them punishments. And if the punishment is even greater because He is a "Forgiver," let it be so, but grant them patience. "**And now, let the power**" of Your mercy be great. 

He said, "**As You have spoken, saying...**" Master of the Universe, You spoke and made a covenant to "say" the Attributes <note>the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy</note>, and those words do not return empty. And so, I have come to say them. Moses said: "Behold, I know that Your presence expands whenever Your children act accordingly. I ask You to seek out the 'Saying' <note>the Divine speech</note> which is the word before You." Specifically, I am not asking for "Merciful and Gracious" to forgive them entirely. "**May the words of my mouth be acceptable**"—that I should say this. 

Even though Moses only requested patience, nevertheless, out of his love for Israel, he awakened the attribute of Kindness (*Chesed*), for he mentioned "**and abundant in kindness**." His reasoning was that "abundant in kindness" applies even to those who lack sufficient merit. This is as Rashi explained on the portion of *Ki Tisa*: "**abundant in kindness**" is for those in need of kindness who do not have much merit of their own. If so, when strong kindness is awakened, it strengthens the matter of His mercy, as if to say: "As long as one performs kindness, awaken kindness for him." 

On this basis, he began to plead with great supplications: "**Pardon, I pray, the iniquity of this people according to the greatness of Your kindness**"—meaning, as if they were likening themselves to You in the attribute of kindness, to be equal to You in this trait. Therefore, he used the letter *Kaf* of comparison—"**as** the greatness" <note>original: *ke-godel*</note>—for it refers to the people. Even if they do not possess such acts of kindness, may the "Saying" of this attribute rise up to seal a covenant. Specifically, because this attribute is for those without much merit, the Holy One, Blessed be He, considered it as: "**I have pardoned according to your word**"—that My anger shall not burn to destroy them now. 

"**But as I live**"—we hear from all these things the necessity for a person to cleave to His attributes, may He be blessed. In the *Sifrei* they said: "**And it shall come to pass that whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be delivered**." Is it possible for a person to be called by the Name of the Holy One, Blessed be He? Rather, the Holy One, Blessed be He, is called "Merciful," as it is said, "**The Lord is merciful and gracious**"—so you too, give gifts freely. The Holy One, Blessed be He, is called "Righteous"—so you too, be righteous. The Holy One, Blessed be He, is called "Devout" (*Chasid*)... The intention is that the *Sifrei* understands "shall be called" as a passive call; and it asks, how is it possible for a person to be called by His Name? The answer explains the matter of the supreme character traits modeled after the attributes of the Holy One, Blessed be He.

**Part Two:** The character traits of flesh and blood. This is divided into two parts. The first concerns the matter of laws. 

**A Great Principle:** Our Sages, of blessed memory, said regarding the definition of holiness: "**Sanctify yourself in that which is permitted to you.**" With this statement, we can explain what is found at the end of the chapter "The Craftsmen" <note>Talmud, Bava Metzia 83a</note>: Some porters broke a barrel of wine belonging to Rabbah bar bar Chanan. He took their cloaks [as compensation]. They came and told Rav. Rav said to him: "Give them back their cloaks." Rabbah asked: "Is this the law?" Rav replied: "Yes, '**That you may walk in the way of good men**' <note>Proverbs 2:20</note>." The porters then said: "We are poor, we have worked all day, we are hungry, and we have nothing." Rav said to Rabbah: "Go and give them their wages." Rabbah asked: "Is this the law?" Rav replied: "Yes, '**and keep the paths of the righteous**' <note>Proverbs 2:20</note>." 

It is very wondrous how Rav, who was the judge, could force Rabbah bar bar Chanan to behave with such piety (*Chasidut*). This is explained in *Elu Metziot* <note>Bava Metzia 30b</note> where Rav Joseph taught: "**And you shall show them**"—this refers to their house of life; "**the way**"—this refers to acts of loving-kindness; "**they shall walk**"—this refers to visiting the sick; "**in it**"—this refers to burial; "**the work**"—this refers to the law; "**which they shall do**"—this refers to [acting] **beyond the letter of the law** <term>Lifnim Mishurat HaDin: A legal concept where one waives their strict legal rights to act more ethically or compassionately</term>. 

One might ask: Since the Commandment of the Place <note>God</note> is thus—to act beyond the letter of the law—then it *is* the law! Why was it not stated explicitly in the Torah as a law and a warning? 

Before explaining this, I will introduce what the Ramban wrote on the portion "**You shall be holy**" <note>Leviticus 19:2</note>: "'You shall be holy'—be separated from forbidden sexual relations... wherever you find a fence against immorality, you find holiness. This is the language of Rashi." But in the *Torat Kohanim* I saw it stated plainly: "Be separated... just as I am holy, so shall you be holy; just as I am separate, so shall you be separate." 

In my opinion <note>referring to the Ramban's view</note>, this "separation" is not just to separate from forbidden relations as Rashi said. Rather, this "separation" is what is mentioned everywhere in the Talmud, where those who are refined are called *Perushim* (Separated/Pharisees). For behold, the Torah warned against forbidden relations and forbidden foods, but it permitted intimacy between a man and his wife, and the eating of meat and wine. If so, a person of desire could find a place to be flooded with the lust of his wife or his many wives, and to be among those who guzzle wine and gorge on meat, and speak as he wishes all sorts of filth, for this prohibition is not explicitly mentioned in the Torah. He would then be a **scoundrel with the Torah's permission** <note>original: *Naval birshut ha-Torah*</note>! 

Therefore, after detailing the specific prohibitions, the text gave a general command that we should be separate from luxuries: to limit sexual intercourse... so that Torah scholars should not be found with their wives like roosters... and one should sanctify himself by avoiding wine, much like the Nazirite is called "holy." He should remember the evil mentioned regarding wine in the cases of Noah and Lot. So too, he should separate himself from ritual impurity even though we are not strictly warned about it in the Torah... and likewise, he should guard his mouth and tongue from defiling themselves through excessive, coarse eating and from disgusting speech... and he should sanctify himself until he reaches the level of "separation," as they said of Rabbi Hiyya, that he never engaged in idle chatter in his life. 

Regarding such things, this general commandment was given after detailing all the specific sins that are completely forbidden. This includes the beauty of cleanliness in his hands and body, as it says: "**Sanctify yourselves and be holy**"—"Sanctify yourselves" refers to the first waters [before a meal], and "be holy" refers to the last waters [after a meal]... for even though these are Rabbinic commandments, the essence of the Biblical verse warns us to be clean, pure, and separate from the masses of people who soil themselves with luxuries and ugliness. 

This is the way of the Torah: to detail and then generalize. Similarly, after the warning of specific civil laws and business dealings—"Do not rob," "Do not steal," "Do not wrong one another"—it says generally: "**And you shall do what is right and good**" <note>Deuteronomy 6:18</note>. This includes acting with integrity and equality, and acting **beyond the letter of the law** for the sake of one's fellow. 

Similarly, regarding the Sabbath: He forbade creative labor with a negative commandment, but the physical exertion He covered with a general positive commandment: "**You shall rest**." The reason the verse says, "**For I the Lord your God am holy**" is to say that we merit to cleave to Him by being holy. These are the words of the Ramban, and his holy mouth has spoken perfectly. 

I am not worthy to explain the matter at greater length, but behold: all luxuries, even if they are "permitted," are forbidden—such as excessive eating, or intimacy, or excessive speech—things the Torah did not warn about specifically like other prohibitions. This is because it is impossible to specify everything, for every person changes in a million ways. If so, every person would need a Torah specifically for themselves! Furthermore, even a single person changes at every moment and every hour. For example, regarding eating: for one person, it is called "excess" if he eats more than half a pound, but for another, due to his nature, it isn't excess unless he eats more than a pound. Sometimes within the same person, everything changes according to the time and the hour. 

If the natures of all people were identical and all times were equal, the Torah would have written a warning: "You shall eat this amount and no more." But since there is variation, the Torah had to make it known in a general way: "I command you to be holy and separate in everything you observe in yourself to be a luxury; according to the time and the hour, separate from it." The same applies to the permission of intimacy—there are variations in human nature, whether one's nature is "hot" or "cold," as well as the variation of times. 

The same applies to mundane speech that contains no specific prohibition but is simply excessive talk. How could the Torah specify "Speak this" and "Do not speak that"? For sometimes for one person, there is a practical outcome from his speech, but for his fellow, there is no outcome. Thus, for the fellow, it is "excessive speech," but not for the speaker himself. Such distinctions are without limit or end. 

Therefore, the Torah generalized with "You shall be holy"—meaning, whatever is excessive in any action in the world, be holy and separate from it. If the whole world were equal in this matter, the Torah would have written it as a specific warning. On this matter, the Sages said: "Sanctify yourself in that which is permitted to you." Even though it is permitted, when you feel it is "excessive," sanctify yourself. 

The listener might think that one who does this is merely "pious"—meaning, he does more than he is required to do. In truth, it is a requirement! The Torah only refrained from writing it as a specific obligation because it is impossible to write, since human opinions and natures are not equal. 

Likewise, regarding "**what a man shall do**," the Torah wrote a law and truth, for "piety" is not the same for everyone nor at all times. The wise will understand. Thus, wherever the Sages say "A prominent person is different," the intention is that from the perspective of obligation, he must act thus. If the whole world were equal in their temperament, this law would have been written in the Torah for everyone. It turns out that matters such as these are called "beyond the letter of the law," but they are an absolute law for the pious person. 

Regarding this, the Talmud says in *Ha-Gozez* regarding the incident of Rabbi Hiyya: A certain woman showed him a coin [to see if it was valid currency], and he told her it was good, but it turned out to be bad. Rav ruled that he must replace it for the woman. Even though by the strict law he was exempt—like a professional money-changer who is exempt because he doesn't need to learn—and Rabbi Hiyya certainly did not need to learn, nonetheless, because of acting "beyond the letter of the law" in the matter... even though he didn't need to learn from her, because of the greatness of his cleaving to the Torah, his thoughts were not attached [to the coin]...

# The Sixth Essay

It was not possible for him to fulfill [the commandment] in this state. This is what Rabbi Meir meant when he said, "and he merited many things" <note>A reference to Pirkei Avot 6:1: "Whoever occupies himself with the Torah for its own sake merits many things."</note>. That is to say, he merited "many things" in the sense that he receives a reward greater than what he actually performed, as if he had performed them all. This is because the intent of his heart was prepared to fulfill them if it had been possible for him. This type of service is "service of the heart" <term>Avodah she-ba-lev; internal devotion</term>, for it did not reach the stage of physical action. 

In this vein, I received an explanation from the holy one of the Lord, my father and teacher, may his memory be for a blessing <note>original: "Abba Mori ZLH"H"</note>, based on the words of Rashi at the beginning of the portion *Va’etchanan*: "**Enough for you**" <note>Deuteronomy 3:26</note> means "Much more than this is stored up for you"—referring to the "abundant good" hidden away for the righteous. On the surface, the word "much" <note>Hebrew: *Rav*</note> seems to have no connection or clear meaning here. However, the matter is that the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moses: "What is your desire? Is it that you long to eat of the fruit of the Land? No, rather you wish to fulfill the commandments that are dependent on the Land. According to your own reasoning, is not 'much more than this' already stored for you?" That is to say, even regarding commandments that it is impossible for you to fulfill, what can you say? There is "abundant good stored away," for even that which is "stored" <note>intended but not performed</note> and did not come to the stage of action, the reward is still stored for it, because a good thought is joined to action. So it is with the commandments dependent on the Land which your soul longed to fulfill; though you were prevented by circumstances <term>Ones; a legal term for being under duress or prevented by forces beyond one's control</term> and did not fulfill them, your reward is great, as if you had fulfilled them, since your intention was to do so. This is "service of the heart," and it was hinted at in the verse: "**And serve Him with a perfect heart and a willing soul**" <note>1 Chronicles 28:9</note>; since your heart is perfect and your soul is willing, it is considered service of the heart.

# Essay 7

**The Gate of Character Traits** <term>Middot; refers to ethical qualities or moral dispositions</term>. The practical commandments—namely the positive and negative commands—are fixed in number and count at 613. The study of Torah is first among them, for Torah study is equivalent to them all. However, matters of character traits are as "wide as the sea." For example, the traits dependent on the heart—all good and evil: anger or willpower; love or enmity; joy or grief; diligence or laziness; contentment or excess; and thousands like these. Who can count them? No man can count them, and perhaps they can be categorized into groups. 

Indeed, character traits are divided into parts:
**Part 1:** The attributes of the Holy One, Blessed be He. These are the supreme attributes, and in these a person is able to cleave to their Creator and take hold of His traits. 
**Part 2:** The traits of flesh and blood. I mean the upright traits that do not apply to the Blessed Lord. A person should "clothe" themselves in these traits. These are subdivided into two: 
1. Traits a person performs that relate to the law of the practical commandments.
2. Character traits of the heart's disposition that do not relate to formal laws.

# Part 1

The attributes of the Holy One, Blessed be He, which a person should cleave to. This is what is written in the first chapter of Tractate *Sotah* <note>Sotah 14a</note>: "Rabbi Hama bar Hanina said: What is the meaning of that which is written: '**After the Lord your God shall you walk**'? <note>Deuteronomy 13:5</note> Is it possible for a person to walk after the Divine Presence? Has it not already been said: '**For the Lord your God is a consuming fire**'? <note>Deuteronomy 4:24</note> Rather, it means to walk after the attributes <term>Middot</term> of the Holy One, Blessed be He. Just as He clothes the naked—as it is written: '**And the Lord God made for Adam and for his wife coats of skins, and clothed them**'—so should you clothe the naked. The Holy One, Blessed be He, visits the sick—as it is written: '**And the Lord appeared unto him by the terebinths of Mamre**' <note>referring to Abraham after his circumcision</note>—so should you visit the sick. The Holy One, Blessed be He, comforts mourners—as it is written: '**And it came to pass after the death of Abraham, that God blessed Isaac his son**'—so should you comfort mourners. The Holy One, Blessed be He, buries the dead—as it is written: '**And He buried him in the valley**' <note>referring to the burial of Moses</note>—so should you bury the dead." (Until here are the words of the Talmud).

And in the chapter *Rabbi Akiva* <note>Tractate Shabbat 133b</note>: "**This is my God, and I will glorify Him**" <note>Hebrew: *Ve-anvehu*; Exodus 15:2</note>—beautify yourself before Him with commandments. Make before Him a beautiful Sukkah, a beautiful Lulav, a beautiful Shofar, beautiful Tzitzit, a beautiful Torah scroll—written for His sake with beautiful ink, with a beautiful quill, by a skilled scribe, and wrapped in beautiful silks. Abba Shaul says: "*Ve-anvehu*" means "Be like Him" <note>A wordplay on *Ani ve-Hu*, "I and He"</note>. Just as He is gracious and merciful, so too should you be gracious and merciful. (Until here are the words of the Talmud). 

Rashi explained: "Be like Him"—this is the meaning of *Ve-anvehu*, "I and He" <note>original: "Ani ve-Hu"</note>; I will make myself like Him to cleave to His ways. And so the Sages explained in the Midrash: "To walk in all His ways"—these are the ways of the Omnipresent: The Lord is a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in kindness and truth. And it says: "**Whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be delivered**" <note>Joel 3:5</note>. But how is it possible for a person to be called by the Name of the Lord? Rather, the Omnipresent is called "Gracious and Merciful," as it is said, "Gracious and merciful is the Lord"; so you too, be gracious and perform free acts of giving. The Omnipresent is called "Merciful," as it is said, "For a merciful God is the Lord your God"; so you too, be merciful. The Omnipresent is called "Righteous," as it is said, "For the Lord is righteous, He loves righteousness"; so you too, be righteous. The Omnipresent is called "Pious" <term>Chasid; meaning one who acts with loving-kindness beyond the law</term>, as it is said, "I am pious, says the Lord"; so you too, be pious. Therefore it says: "**And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be delivered**," and it says, "Everyone that is called by My name, I have created him for My glory," and it says, "The Lord hath made all things for Himself." (Until here are the words of the Midrash).

The author of *Reishit Chochma* <note>A 16th-century kabbalistic ethical work by Eliyahu de Vidas</note> wrote in the first chapter of the "Gate of Humility": "I heard in the name of the Geonim <term>Sages of the post-Talmudic era</term> that it was with this intention they said in Tractate *Rosh Hashanah* regarding the verse: '**And the Lord passed by before him, and proclaimed...**' Rabbi Yochanan said: 'If it were not written in a verse, it would be impossible to say it. This teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He, wrapped Himself like a prayer leader <term>Shaliach Tzibbur</term> and showed Moses, saying to him: "Whenever Israel performs before Me according to this order, I will forgive them."'" (Until here are the words of the Geonim).

However, there is a difficulty here: we see that many times we mention the Thirteen Attributes, yet we are not answered! Rather, the Geonim say that the phrase "perform before Me according to this order" does not refer only to the wrapping of the prayer shawl <term>Tallit</term>, but rather that they should **perform the order of attributes** that the Holy One, Blessed be He, taught to Moses. He said to Moses that He is a God who is "Merciful and Gracious"—meaning, just as He is merciful, so too you shall be merciful, and so on for all thirteen attributes. (Until here are the words of *Reishit Chochma*).

Furthermore, there are Thirteen Attributes regarding the explanation of the verses in the portion *Shelach Lecha*: "**And now, I pray, let the power of my Lord be great, as You have spoken, saying: The Lord is slow to anger, and abundant in kindness, forgiving iniquity and transgression... Pardon, I pray, the iniquity of this people... and the Lord said: I have pardoned according to your word.**" 

We must rouse ourselves to understand: Why did he say "**And now, let the power... be great**"? This seems puzzling, for the power of my Lord is always great! Amen and Amen. Look at the plain meaning <term>Peshat</term> in the context of the portion: The Holy One, Blessed be He, had said to Moses, "I will smite them with pestilence and disinherit them, and make of you a great nation." This was the "power" intended—to fulfill the oath to the Patriarchs by making Moses a great nation. Afterward, Moses prayed and said: "Now the Egyptians will hear... and the nations will say that it was because the Lord lacked the ability <note>Hebrew: *Yachol*</note>... they will say the Lord was unable to stand against the thirty-one kings." 

Moses thought in his heart: "Will the ability of the Lord not be revealed later on when I have become a great nation and my descendants inherit the land? They will see the power of the Lord then!" Moses continued: "**And now, let the power of my Lord be great**"—meaning, it is true that later, when a great people comes from my loins and inherits the land, the power of the Lord will be known. But in the meantime, people will say it was for "lack of ability," for surely it will be a long time before a great people emerges from me. This is the explanation according to the plain meaning.

There is another point to rouse ourselves to: Why does it say "**And the Lord passed by before him and proclaimed: The Lord, The Lord, a God merciful and gracious...**"? These attributes do not seem to fit here, as the Midrash notes that he sought kindness when he said "**Pardon, I pray... according to the greatness of Your kindness.**" He should have simply said "According to Your kindness." 

We should also rouse ourselves regarding: "**As You have forgiven this people from Egypt until now.**" On the contrary, this would seem to be a reason *not* to forgive! Since He has already forgiven them many times, He should not forgive again—similar to what Rashi writes regarding the rebellion of Korah: "And Moses heard and fell on his face..." 

Regarding the phrase "**I have pardoned according to your word**" <note>Numbers 14:20</note>: the phrase "according to your word" seems redundant. Rashi explained what he explained. Come and see the essence of the plain meaning of the Geonim: It is true that "whenever My children perform according to this order"—that they walk in and perform the actions of the Thirteen Attributes—this is true. But it is also true that the mention of the attributes is good according to its simple meaning, teaching that God "wrapped Himself like a prayer leader," which refers to the obligation of the attributes.

Moses did not even think to pray now that the Holy One, Blessed be He, should forgive their sin entirely, for he saw that their sin was too great to bear. His prayer was only that He should not destroy them in a moment, but rather be "slow to anger" <term>Erech Apayim</term> and deduct from his debt <note>meaning, spread the punishment out over time</note>. Therefore he mentioned these attributes, as explained by the Ramban <note>Nachmanides</note>: "He mentioned the attributes 'slow to anger' and 'abundant in kindness,' but he did not mention 'Truth,' because by the attribute of Truth they would be liable for death. Nor did he mention 'He keeps kindness for thousands,' for Moses did not pray now using the merit of the Patriarchs <term>Zechut Avot</term>. In his prayer he did not mention Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob at all. The reason is that the Land was given to the Patriarchs for their descendants to inherit, but these people were rebelling against their Patriarchs and did not want their gift, which the Patriarchs had cherished greatly. He had said [to the Patriarchs], 'That which You swore to them by Yourself... and all this land... I will give to your seed,' but these people were saying 'We do not want the gift!' He also did not mention 'forgiveness of sin' <note>Hebrew: *Ve-chata'ah*</note> because these were intentional sins <term>Mezidim</term> and rebellious acts <term>Poshe'im</term>."

I do not know why he did not mention "Merciful and Gracious." Perhaps Moses knew that the judgment was stretched thin over them and He would never fully pardon. Therefore, he only requested "patience" <term>Arichat Apayim</term>—that He should not kill them "as one man," nor slaughter them like sheep in the wilderness to die in a plague. Because he only requested patience, God answered, "I have pardoned according to your word"—meaning they would have patience and abundant kindness. He mentioned "visiting the sin of the fathers" to say that if He sees it is not fit to erase their sin, He will visit the sin of the fathers upon the children, and through "patience" He will take them. 

From this came the decree to establish for them "a weeping for generations" on this night <note>the night of the 9th of Av, when the spies returned</note>; the Lord visited their sin upon their descendants. Rabbi Eliezer said: Because we find the phrase "If they shall see the land" after the phrase "I have pardoned according to your word," we know that the word "Pardon, I pray" refers to "patience." Similarly, "and he shall be forgiven" refers to until he performs complete repentance.

What is correct in my eyes is that "pardon" <term>Selicha</term> means the waiving of punishment, as Onkelos translates it. Sacrifices are a matter of "leaving over" or "preventing" [punishment]. Thus "Good and Forgiving." When He said "I have pardoned according to your word," it was so that He would not strike them and destroy them and disinherit them to make Moses a great and mighty nation while they perish from the earth. Rather, He "pardoned" them so that their children would inherit the land, and they themselves would not die in a plague, but rather their corpses would fall in the desert, each one dying when his day comes. In the book of Deuteronomy <term>Mishneh Torah</term>, Moses mentioned his prayer regarding the Golden Calf—how he prayed for them and said "And I fell down before the Lord as at the first"—and he detailed his prayer there. He also mentioned his prayer for Aaron. But he did not mention to them at all that he had prayed for them regarding the incident of the Spies.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of emulating the Divine Attributes (Sefirot). Having previously touched upon the earlier attributes, the text now moves into a detailed practical guide for how human behavior—specifically in study, marriage, and repentance—aligns with the Sefirot of Netzach, Hod, Tiferet, Gevurah, Chesed, and Binah.</meta>

...mentioned above, so too a man should not pursue hardship, nor should he harden himself in any way, except toward the proper goal, which is his wife in her state of purity, which is the time of union. He should not go beyond this. This is the attribute of the "arousal" <term>Ma'or; referring here to the procreative organ or the "awakening" of the Sefirah Yesod</term>, and the union of light with light requires great caution. The core of this protection is guarding oneself from improper thoughts.

**3, 4: Netzach and Hod** <term>Eternity and Splendor; the Sefirot associated with prophecy and the "supports" of the Divine Chariot</term>. These are the "disciples of the Lord." They serve as a chariot for both [Netzach and Hod] to strengthen students in their study, to oversee their sustenance and all their needs, and to provide them with 
<margin>books</margin> 
necessary for their labor, a house of study, and everything else that provides strength and support to those who occupy themselves with the Torah. Everything depends on these two attributes. Each person should act according to their strength, whether much or little. The end of the matter is that whatever one increases in this regard for the honor of the Torah—supporting it with his body, his wealth, and by awakening the hearts of people toward the Torah so they may be strengthened in it—everything is grasped and rooted in these two Sefirot, because they are called those who "hold fast to it and support it." However, the one who labors must learn from every person, as it is written: "From all my teachers I have gained wisdom" <note>Psalm 119:99</note>, for the Torah is not completed with only one teacher. Since he becomes a student to everyone, he merits becoming a chariot for **Netzach** and Hod, the "disciples of the Lord," and the one who bestows Torah upon him is at the level of **Tiferet** <term>Beauty/Harmony; the central Sefirah representing the written Torah</term>. Thus, while he sits and studies, he should remember that **Tiferet** bestows [wisdom] through Netzach and Hod, and he is literally at their level. When he studies Scripture, which is on the Right, he has a specific connection to **Netzach**; when he studies Mishnah, which is on the Left, he has a specific connection to **Hod**; and the Gemara <note>The Talmudic analysis</note>, which includes everything and brings proof for the laws of the Mishnah from the Scripture, is a restoration for both of them together.

# 5: Tiferet
This refers to one who occupies himself with the Torah. He needs great caution so that he does not become arrogant through words of Torah, so as not to cause a great evil. For just as he becomes arrogant, he causes the attribute of **Tiferet**, which is the Torah, to become arrogant and withdraw upward, Heaven forbid. Rather, anyone who humbles himself through words of Torah causes **Tiferet** to descend and humble itself to bestow influence upon Malchut <term>Kingship; the feminine Divine Presence or Shekhinah</term>. Now, below Tiferet are three Sefirot, and for them, there are three [types of] conduct: First, one who is arrogant toward his students causes Tiferet to be arrogant and to rise above Netzach and Hod, which are the "disciples of the Lord" and the students of **Tiferet**. But one who humbles himself and teaches them with love, **Tiferet** too will humble itself toward its students and bestow upon them. Therefore, a man should be pleasant to his students and teach them according to what they can bear. Second, one who is arrogant in his Torah toward the poor person and despises 
<margin>See above</margin>
him in his Torah, saying "We did not learn for nothing like that poor man," or "Eliezer is like a poor man who clears away the waste," <note>original: "Ebiathar" or "Eliezer" - likely a reference to a Talmudic anecdote about social status and learning</note> despising and loathing to teach him, turning his back on his fellow and shaming the poor man, and rebuking him to his face for his flaws—one who is thus arrogant toward the poor causes Tiferet to be arrogant toward **Yesod** <term>Foundation; the Sefirah that channels blessing to the physical world</term> and it will not bestow upon it. But if the scholar's mind is at ease with the poor person, then **Tiferet** will bestow upon Yesod, and the poor man will be considered a "light" <term>Ma'or</term> to the scholar, who will draw him near. Third, one who is arrogant in his Torah toward the "people of the land" <term>Am Ha'aretz; the common folk who are not scholars</term>, who are the collective of the people of the Lord, causes Tiferet to be arrogant toward **Malchut** and it will not bestow upon her. Rather, his mind should be integrated with other people and all the residents of the settlement. They should be important to him, even if they are like "the thorns of the earth" <note>Lowly</note>. Heaven forbid if he calls them "donkeys," for he would be handing them over to the "husks" <term>Kelipot; forces of impurity</term>. He will not merit to be a "son of the Torah" as seen in the Gemara; rather, he should conduct himself with them pleasantly, according to their way, just as **Tiferet** bestows upon Malchut and leads her according to their "poverty of mind," for women are "light-minded" <note>A Talmudic idiom meaning they are easily swayed or have a different type of intellectual focus</note>. Included in this is that he should not be arrogant toward any of those with weak minds, who are categorized as the "dust of the earth." Because of this, the ancients were not arrogant in Torah, like the story of Rav Hamnuna in the Zohar, portion *Bereshit*, and the story of the four Tannaim <term>Sages of the Mishnah</term> and those like them. He was a "great elder" <note>original: "Saba Rabba"</note> for his own soul and did not want to be arrogant in words of Torah. Furthermore, he should be accustomed in his life to engage in Torah with the intent of restoring the Shekhinah, to repair her and bind her to **Tiferet**—that is, [reaching] the law according to the truth. This is "controversy for the sake of Heaven" <note>Pirkei Avot 5:17</note>, where Kindness and Might are required to come to **Tiferet** to explain the law. From such a controversy, it will be clarified that **Tiferet** does not want to take hold outside, even if he lives like Rabbeinu Tam <note>A major medieval scholar</note>; if it is for the sake of provocation, his end is Gehenna, Heaven forbid. There is no controversy that does not damage **Tiferet** except for the controversy of Torah for the sake of Heaven, for "all its paths are peace and love" <note>Proverbs 3:17</note> at its end. One who derives personal benefit from words of Torah damages this attribute, for he takes what is holy and brings it out to the secular. When he occupies himself with Torah [without] arrogance, happy is his portion. The core of everything is to refine one's mind in the crucible of thought and to examine oneself during study; if a "trace of nakedness" <note>original: "shemetz ervat davar" - a hint of improper motive</note> is found, he should repent. He should always admit to the truth so that he may find there 
->**Tiferet, the attribute of Truth.**<-

# 6: Gevurah
All the actions of the arousal of the Evil Inclination <term>Yetzer Ha-Ra</term> literally awaken the strong Severities <term>Gevurot</term>, and the Evil Inclination does not move without awakening Gevurah. The reason is 
<margin>that man</margin> 
was created with two inclinations: the Good Inclination <term>Yetzer Ha-Tov</term> and the Evil Inclination. One is Chesed (Kindness) and the other is Gevurah (Might/Severity). However, it is explained in the Zohar, portion *Bereshit*, that the Good Inclination was created for the man himself, for his own needs, while the Evil Inclination was created for the needs of his wife. See how sweet these words are! For **Tiferet**, the master of Kindness, leans toward the Right, and all its conducts are on the Right—the Good Inclination. But the female is joy <note>or "rejoices"</note> and all her conducts are in **Gevurah**. If so, it is fitting that the Evil Inclination should not be awakened for one's own benefit, for he would then awaken the Supernal **Gevurah** and destroy the world. From here we see how great is the sin of anger and everything like it, for it strengthens the harsh Severities. However, for the sake of his wife, he should awaken his inclination gently, toward the side of the "sweetened" Severities, such as to clothe her and prepare a home for her. He should say, "Behold, in this that I am clothing her, I am repairing the Shekhinah," who is adorned with beauty, for her glory includes all the Severities, and they are sweetened by the heat of Mercy. Therefore, all repairs of the house are repairs of the Shekhinah, which is sweetened from the side of the **Evil Inclination** that was created [only] to do the will of its Creator and nothing else. Therefore, a man should not intend for any personal pleasure at all, but when you conduct yourself before Him in a beautiful dwelling, intend for the repairs of the Shekhinah, which is repaired by the elevated and good **Severities**, from which wealth and honor come. From this side, he should awaken the Evil Inclination toward love for her, and then he should intend toward the Left that awakens to draw her near, in the secret of "His left hand is under my head" <note>Song of Songs 2:6</note>. She is not bound at first except from the side of the Left, and afterward "His right hand embraces me." He should intend to sweeten all those repairs with his Good Inclination and to repair her literally for her sake, as a matter of commandment, for the sake of the Supernal Union. Thus, he has sweetened all the **Severities** and repaired her with the Right. This should apply to all types of desire that come from the side of the Evil Inclination: their core should be for the repairs of the woman whom God has designated for him as "a helper against him" <note>Genesis 2:18</note>, and afterward he should turn them all to the service of God to bind them to the Right.

# 7: Chesed
The chariot to Chesed <term>Kindness</term> is to love God with an inner love, as explained above. Who is a "pious one" <term>Chasid</term>? One who acts with kindness toward his Creator, as explained above. He should love God in every measure that He metes out to him; even if it is an act of Judgment, he should bind it to **Chesed** and receive it with love. As it is said of Nahum Ish Gam Zu <note>A sage famous for his optimism</note>, he would always say, "This too is for the best," meaning that even this matter is bound up in goodness, grace, and kindness. Afterward, all types of kindness are known, whether in his body, his wealth, his spirituality, or his intellect. 
->**The kindness and the good that flow from them are a chariot for Chesed.**<-

# 8: Binah
The chariot for **Binah** <term>Understanding</term> is Repentance <term>Teshuvah</term>, for there is nothing as important as this, since it repairs every flaw. Just as it is the way of **Binah** to sweeten all the judgments and to nullify bitterness, so should a man return in repentance and repair every flaw. One who contemplates repentance all his days causes **Binah** to shine upon every sin, and thus all his days are found to be "days of repentance"—that is, to include himself in **Binah**, which is Repentance. The days of his life are crowned with the secret of the Supernal Repentance. See how Repentance contains the root of all existence in the secret of the Jubilee <note>The 50th year, associated with Binah</note>. Behold, the root of the "external forces" <note>the demonic</note>, the secret of the River of Fire <term>Nehar Dinur</term>, which is included in holiness in the secret of the Severities, is rooted there and spreads out from there. This spreading is called "wrath," in the secret of "and the Lord smelled the sweet savor" <note>implying the soothing of anger</note>. He should bring that spreading back to its source, and the judgments will be sweetened, the wrath will subside, and He will relent from the evil. Thus, a man through the secret of his repentance performs this mystery. Do not say that Repentance is only good for the "holy part" within a man; rather, even the evil part within him is sweetened like a desirable thing. You should know this from Cain, who was evil, from the side of the Serpent, yet it was said to him: "If you do well, will you not be uplifted?" <note>Genesis 4:7</note>. Do not think that because you are from the side of evil there is no remedy for you—that is a lie. Rather, "if you do well" and root yourself in the secret of Repentance, you will be "uplifted" there in the secret of the Good rooted there. For every supernal bitterness has a sweet root, and it can enter through its root and improve itself. Through this, a man improves his very actions, and "intentional sins become like merits" <note>original: "and generations become like glass" - likely a corruption of the Talmudic phrase "sins become like merits"</note>. For behold, those very actions he did that were accusers from the Left Side—if he returns in complete repentance, he brings in and roots those actions above, and all those accusers are not nullified, but they improve themselves and take root in holiness, like the return of Cain. Indeed, if Cain had returned in repentance and repaired them, then Adam the First, who had fathered Cain from the "nest of impurity," it would have been considered a merit for him, in the secret of "a son brings merit to the father." However, he did not want to return, and therefore the entire Left Side was drawn from that day, and all its branches—the Evil Inclination—to be enticed. But they can return and be repaired. This is exactly for the reason explained: that a man roots the secret of evil within himself, sweetens it, and brings it into the Good. Therefore, a man purifies his Evil Inclination and brings it into the Good, and it takes root in the holiness above. This is the excellence of Repentance—that a man who conducts himself in it must contemplate it every single day and perform repentance in the aspect of...
