# Discourse 7

In other matters, he should not have looked <note>Refers to a person of high standing not engaging in undignified labor</note>, but it was considered in his view as a matter of "the law of the penny," as one who needs to learn, and similar to the case of Rabbi Ishmael son of Rabbi Yose in the chapter "These Found Objects" <note>Talmud, Bava Metzia 30b</note>. It is told that while Rabbi Yose was traveling on the road, he met a man carrying a bundle of wood. The man set it down to rest, and then said to the Rabbi, "Help me lift it." The Rabbi asked, "How much is it worth?" The man replied, "Half a zuz." The Rabbi gave him the half-zuz and declared the wood ownerless (*hefker*). The man then claimed it again, and the Rabbi gave him another half-zuz and declared it ownerless again, and so on. The Talmud asks: Was not Rabbi Yose an elder, and this labor was beneath his dignity? The answer is that Rabbi Yose was acting **beyond the letter of the law** <term>Lifnim mishurat hadin; acting with more compassion or self-sacrifice than the law strictly requires</term>. For certainly, if one were always weighed down by the mundane matters of existence, like this incident with Rabbi Ishmael, he could surely fulfill the commandment of the Torah—especially a man as devoted to the Torah as he was. For the Torah writes, "And you shall hide yourself from them" <note>Deuteronomy 22:1</note>, which the Sages explain means there are times you *should* hide, such as when an elder finds an object but returning it is beneath his dignity. However, the Torah spoke of this in a different context, and regarding this specific matter, it is called "beyond the letter of the law." This "beyond the law" is an extension of what the Torah commanded; it essentially becomes the law itself, but only in such specific circumstances.

Furthermore, there is a matter where even if the whole world were equal in this regard, and the law dictated a certain path, one should still act close to the law as in the ruling of Rav Chanan <note>Likely referring to Rabbah bar bar Chanan in Bava Metzia 83a</note> regarding those workers. He told the man: "Be a compassionate overseer and have pity on the poor, and out of compassion, you should forgive such a loss caused by poor workers." Forgiving in the heart is true forgiveness. "Therefore, return their cloaks to them and pay them their wages." Even though it was revealed that he had not truly forgiven them in his heart (since he had seized their cloaks), Rav said: "I am your teacher, teaching you for your own benefit, **so that you may walk in the way of the good** <note>Proverbs 2:20</note>." This means: since your nature is such, do not change your nature now. In this case, we do not say "beyond the letter of the law," but rather we speak of something where if the nature of all men were such, the Torah law would be so. Yet here, it applies because Rabbah did not forgive in his heart, and the phrase "so that you may walk in the way of the good" applies as explained. The Torah calls that "good path" by various names. The Tosafot <note>Medieval Talmudic commentators</note> ask why sometimes it says "beyond the letter of the law" and other times "so that you may walk in the way of the good," and they wrote what they wrote, though they questioned their own answer. In my view, it is settled as I have written.

Behold, we see that it is a great thing to clothe oneself in holiness and conduct oneself with as much abstinence as possible. One is obligated by the Torah, even under pressure, to be "strong as a lion" in alacrity regarding positive commandments. My proof for this is close to what is found in the *Sefer HaPardes* attributed to Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, the preeminent 11th-century commentator</note> regarding the fifty fasts. He said it would be proper to conduct oneself in all of them as one does on the Ninth of Av, but we do not decree a restriction on the community unless they can withstand it. He wrote: "Therefore, whoever is able to withstand it is obligated to conduct himself thus." And I have shown this to you.

**The second** area concerns matters not related to legal rulings, but rather the levels of character traits <term>Middot; ethical qualities or dispositions</term> of flesh and blood. These include: distancing oneself from brazenness, hatred, jealousy, lust, and pride; and the virtues of compassion, grace, and trust in the Blessed One—casting one's burden upon God, fearing the honored and awesome Name, and having a broken and humbled heart when remembering one's iniquities and sins. One should keep these before his eyes always, maintaining a vitality full of regret, pain, and concern. There are thousands of such traits.

<margin>
Regarding these matters, the Gateway of Character Traits has no limit or number.
</margin>

**Furthermore**, there is a matter that enters the secret of the character traits called **Derech Eretz** <term>Proper Conduct; literally "the way of the land," referring to etiquette, social ethics, and worldliness</term>. How a person should conduct himself in all his ways: guarding his body while sitting, walking, leaving, entering, eating, and dressing. This includes the conduct of youths and maidens, the elderly with the young, and the conduct of Torah scholars and the common people. Everything is beloved in the words of our Sages and the authors. I will dedicate a specific section to this, called the "Section of Proper Conduct," so that these matters may be clarified.

**Now** let us examine and reflect, saying: "Blessed be the Merciful One who gave us a three-fold Torah." By this, I mean that true perfection is comprised of three parts:

## Study | Deed | Traits

**Deed** refers to the 613 commandments, their generalities, details, and minutiae. **Study** is Torah study, which "is equivalent to them all," as the Sages said: "Study is great because it leads to action." **Traits** refers to the Gateway of Character Traits and its divisions which I mentioned. A hint to this is found in the verse: "You shall be wholehearted (*Tamim*) with the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 18:13</note>. The word **Tamim** (תמים) serves as an acronym for **T**almud (Study), **M**a'aseh (Deed), and **M**iddot (Traits). The letter *Tav* of *Tamim* is large to hint at what was said: "Study (*Talmud*) is great." The *Tav* also hints at mercy, which relates to study. The explanation of the verse "You shall be wholehearted" is that you shall be whole—you and the Lord your God—in His presence. The letter *Yod* in *Tamim* is internal and hidden.

Beyond what I have mentioned regarding dwelling in the presence of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and His mercy and grace, there is an internal dimension to human conduct through the **Ten Sefirot** <term>Divine Emanations; the ten attributes through which God interacts with the world</term>. These are the most internal traits of the Holy One, Blessed be He. This is the "hidden internal" within the word *Tamim*. When a person aligns his conduct with them, he is on high and becomes a "Chariot" <note>A vehicle for Divine presence in the world</note> for the Divine, following the order from bottom to top. The "Perfect Man" organizes himself according to what the Divine Sage [Rabbi Moshe Cordovero] arranged in the book *Tomer Devorah* <note>"The Palm Tree of Deborah," a 16th-century classic of Kabbalistic ethics</note>.

<term>1. Malkhut (Sovereignty)</term>: The essence of the **Shekhinah** <term>The Divine Presence; the feminine aspect of God</term> for a man is through the female. A man stands between two "females": the lower female [his wife] and the spiritual female, which is the soul that provides "sustenance, clothing, and intimacy" <note>The three biblical obligations of a husband to a wife</note>. The Shekhinah stands over him to bless him through everything he gives and does for his wife in his home. This is like the attribute of **Tiferet** <term>Beauty/Harmony; the central Sefirah</term>, which stands between two females: the Higher Mother <term>Binah; Understanding</term> to influence him with all he needs, and the Lower Mother <term>Malkhut</term> to receive from him sustenance, clothing, and intimacy.

The Shekhinah will not come to him unless he resembles the Supernal reality. A man separates from his wife for one of three reasons: 1) During her menstrual impurity; 2) When he is a scholar occupied with Torah all the days of the week; 3) When he is traveling and guarding himself from sin. During these times, the Shekhinah clings to him and does not leave him, so that he is never without a "spouse," but rather remains a "complete man," male and female. The Shekhinah pairs with him. A man must be careful that the Shekhinah does not depart from him when he goes on a journey; he must be careful with his soul, praying the "Traveler's Prayer" and holding fast to the Torah. Because of this, the Shekhinah—who is the "Guard of the Way"—constantly stands by him. When he occupies himself with the Torah, she stands with him. When he is careful to avoid sin and occupies himself with Torah while his wife is in her impurity, the Shekhinah stands with him. Afterward, through the immersion of purity, or on the Sabbath, or upon returning from a journey, it is the time for the "commanded intimacy" <note>Marital relations</note>. At that time, the Shekhinah is always open above to receive holy souls, and it is proper for him to "visit" his wife. In this way, the Shekhinah is always with him, as explained in the Zohar, portion *Bereshit*.

The "visitation" of his wife is necessary specifically at the time when the Shekhinah is in her place—namely, on the Sabbath. However, in a time of communal distress, when the Shekhinah is not "between the two arms," it is forbidden. As explained in the *Tikunim* on *Bereshit*: one who goes out to unite with the "King's Daughter" so she never separates from him must first sanctify himself with all the "ornaments" and fine garments, which are the refinements of the character traits mentioned above. After he has refined himself and intended to accept her yoke upon himself by occupying himself with Torah and bearing the yoke of the commandments, she is immediately "married" to him and does not depart—on the condition that he sanctifies and purifies himself.

Once he is holy and pure, he should intend to fulfill for her "sustenance, clothing, and intimacy," which are the three things a man owes his wife. 1) To influence her with all his deeds from the "Right" <note>Chesed; Kindness</note>—this is **Sustenance**. 2) To **Cover** her from the side of *Gevurah* <term>Strength/Judgment</term> so that the "External Forces" <note>Evil or chaotic spiritual forces</note> do not rule over her. There should be no "Evil Inclination" in his performance of commandments, such as doing them for physical gratification or imagined honor; for the Evil Inclination is present in such a commandment, and she [the Shekhinah] flees from it because it is "uncovering nakedness." Thus, one must always cover the "nakedness" and hide it so it does not rule. All his deeds should be for the sake of Heaven, with no portion for the Evil Inclination. Similarly, Tefillin and Tzitzit are great shields for her against the External Forces; one should be accustomed to wearing them all day. 3) To unite her with *Tiferet* through the **Intimacy** of the *Shema* prayer and by setting fixed times for Torah study. When he sets a "time" (an *Onah*) for everything, he should intend that this is the "time" of the Shekhinah, the King's Daughter. There is a hint to this in the *Tikunim*.

<term>2. Yesod (Foundation)</term>: A man must be careful of any "joining" that leads to improper thoughts, so that he does not come to a "nocturnal emission" <term>Keri; accidental wasting of seed</term>. He must not speak obscenities; even pure speech that leads to improper thoughts must be avoided. This is the precise meaning of the verse: "Do not let your mouth bring your flesh into sin" <note>Ecclesiastes 5:5</note>. The Zohar warns that one should not be seduced by speech that brings the "holy flesh"—the sign of the Covenant—into the sin of emission. For if the speech itself were the sin, why say "to bring into sin"? It means that even if the speech is not a sin, if it *leads* to improper thoughts, one must be careful of it. "Why should God be angry at your voice?" even if the voice was permitted, if it leads to a bad action, the voice and the speech become evil. Great care is needed for the "Sign of the Covenant" <term>Brit; circumcision/procreative purity</term> not to have improper thoughts and not to destroy [seed].

Furthermore, one must be careful because **Yesod** is the "Sign of the Covenant of the Bow" <term>Keshet; referring to the Rainbow and the procreative organ</term>. The "Bow" is not drawn above to shoot arrows except toward the attribute of *Malkhut*, which is the "Target" for the arrow that guards the drop [of seed] and is meant to create a "branch" and "fruit." Just as the Supernal Bow never descends except for the sake of the "Target"...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the transformation of the mundane into the holy. It follows the previous page's focus on the ethical conduct of the righteous (specifically the "Elder" and the "pious ones"), transitioning here into a famous Rabbinic teaching about King David and the purification of intent.</meta>

...and to the study halls. I would return the <unclear>unclear word</unclear> to its city, and it should be counted. It is found that this <note>referring to the soul's orientation</note> and the custom of going to synagogues and study halls was not a matter of a specific generation’s choice, but an essential necessity. Furthermore, regarding the idea that every single day it is renewed—and even currently—that his legs would "overturn" his desires: because King David saw many times that even when he had a specific business or residence in mind, his legs would forcibly bring him to synagogues and study halls specifically. 

Rather, the matter is this: King David went to every place he desired to go to conduct his affairs, and he did what his heart desired, for he had great business dealings, especially as a great and mighty king. However, he said that **the entirety of his business** was for the sake of maintaining synagogues and study halls, to fight the "wars of the Lord" for His people Israel and to occupy himself with their needs. This is what is meant by "my legs brought me to synagogues and study halls." It does not mean he was turned away from where he intended to go, but rather that the *reason* for his going was for the sake of these holy institutions.

The general principle that emerges is: **all his handiwork was for the sake of Heaven.** This applies not only to the fulfillment of the Torah and the commandments—where it is obvious that the act should be for the sake of Heaven, meaning that no external motivation like fear of punishment or love of reward should be mixed into the good deed, but rather from beginning to end it should be entirely for the Name of God—but even in mundane, secular matters. That is to say, in his business, his eating, his drinking, and his physical relationships, and many things like them: they should all be for the sake of Heaven. They then become "mundane matters performed in the purity of holiness" <note>original: *chullin she-na'asu al taharat ha-kodesh*; a legal concept applied here to ethics, where everyday acts are treated with the sanctity of Temple offerings</note>. Thus, all the deeds a person performs for himself are actually for the sake of Heaven.

### Article Nine
The labor of thought in the heart: for the fulfillment of the aforementioned statement, "In all your ways, know Him" <note>Proverbs 3:6</note>, or the labor of thought in the heart, so that "he sees no iniquity in his heart" <note>Psalm 66:18</note> and it does not even arise in his thought.

### In Thought
It is written: "He has not beheld iniquity in Jacob, nor has He seen perverseness in Israel; the Lord his God is with him, and the shout of a King is in him" <note>Numbers 23:21</note>. This is difficult, because the matter seems redundant in the verse. Furthermore, there are three changing terms in the verse. First, the verse says the language of "beholding" <note>original: *habtabah*</note> and at the end the language of "seeing" <note>original: *re'iyah*</note>. At first, it says "iniquity" <note>original: *aven*</note> and at the end "perverseness" <note>original: *amal*</note>. Also, at the beginning, it mentions the name "Jacob," and at the end, the name "Israel." There is further redundancy and change: in one place it says "with him" and in the other "in him."

To explain this, I will provide brief introductions:
1. There is a difference between **beholding** and **seeing**. Beholding is a more intense scrutiny than ordinary seeing, as Rashi explains in the portion of *Chukat* regarding the Copper Serpent: "he looked and saw," and it is written "and he beheld."
2. **Iniquity** (*Aven*) refers to the thought in the heart, as in the phrase "workers of iniquity," or "If I have seen iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear." **Perverseness** (*Amal*) refers to the sin committed in actual deed, such as neglecting a positive commandment or violating a negative one, as it says "his soul was shortened by the perverseness of Israel" <note>Judges 10:16</note>. And do not be surprised that "Man is born to perverseness" refers to the fulfillment of positive commandments.
3. The name **Israel** is higher in level and degree than the name **Jacob**, as is well known.
4. There is a difference between **"with him"** and **"in him."** "In him" is more internal than "with him." This is similar to the liturgy of "The soul You have given **within me**" <note>original: *Elohai Neshamah*</note>: You created it **in me**, You formed it **in me**, You breathed it **in me**; afterward it says "and You preserve it **inside me**" <note>original: *be-kirbi*</note>, and then returns to the word "**in me**" and says "and You are destined to return it **to me**" <note>original: *bi*</note>. The matter of spirituality and the soul and its cleaving to the body: according to the intention of creation, if Adam had not sinned, the soul would have been "in him" essentially, and in the future, He will return it "to him" because the world will return to its original perfection. But now, it is "inside him" and not literally "in him," but only in proximity—it is "with him," meaning alongside him. This is what is written: "The Lord is **with him**," and "Jacob is the lot of His inheritance." The Kabbalists have already written: do not read "with him" (*immo*) with a *patah* vowel, but rather "His people" (*ammo*) with a *hireq*. And it is written, "Israel, in whom (*be-cha*) I will be glorified." Thus, for Jacob it says "with him," and for Israel it says "in him."

Now I will explain the verse according to the teaching of our Sages: For Israel, the Holy One, blessed be He, does **not** join a bad thought to a deed, but a good thought He **does** join to a deed. For the nations, it is the opposite: a good thought is not joined to a deed, but a bad thought is joined to a deed. 

This is the matter in the portion of Balak: "And behold, one of the Children of Israel came and brought his brethren the Midianite woman," etc., and his name is not mentioned until later in the portion of Phinehas, where it says "And the name of the man..." etc. The Satan cries out that when he committed the sin in practice, He did not mention him, even though he intended to sin; only after he actually sinned did He mention him. Similarly, regarding Elimelech, it says "A certain man went from Bethlehem in Judah," but did not mention his name since he had not yet fully departed to dwell in the fields of Moab; only afterward does the text specify "And the name of the man was Elimelech."

However, one must always pray, "The Rock, His work is perfect, for all His ways are justice." Is there, God forbid, favoritism in this matter? That for the wicked person, it is "twice good"—bad thought is not joined to deed and good thought is? And for the non-Jew the opposite—"twice bad"? 

Rather, Blessed is He and Blessed is His Name, He is righteous in all His ways. Regarding a member of Israel, his soul is emanated from a holy place, and its legal presumption <term>Chazakah; a legal status based on most likely probability</term> is one of purity. Therefore, even if he thinks a bad thought, we say he will certainly wake up before it comes to action and will regret it. Thus, if he was prevented by circumstances beyond his control (*ones*) and the sin was not committed, the presumption is that even if he hadn't been prevented, he would have retracted on his own. And conversely, with a good thought: if he thinks to do a commandment but is prevented from doing so, the presumption is that if he hadn't been prevented, he would have done it and not retracted. Regarding this, the verse says: "And to You, O Lord, is kindness, for You reward a man **according to** his work" <note>Psalm 62:13</note>. It does not say You reward him for "his work," but *according to* his work—meaning even if he didn't do it, he receives a reward as if he had. This is the presumption of the good thought.

This is the meaning of our prayer: "Act for the sake of Your right hand." This refers to the merit of the fathers to be saved through them. It is as if one were to say: Act for the sake of wood and stone, for even though there was sin, there is still merit in them—namely, the power of understanding within them toward holiness and purity from the power of their souls. But the non-Jew, whose soul is from the side of impurity, is called "unclean, unclean," and the presumption is the opposite; therefore, his judgment is also the opposite.

Now, even though for Israel the Holy One does not join a bad thought to a deed, this is not the standard for the "Pious Ones" (*Chasidim*). The verse says: "If I have seen iniquity (*Aven*) in my heart, the Lord will not hear." "Will not hear" here means He does not "accept" it—meaning God does not judge this thought as if it were a deed. Nevertheless, the Holy One **sees** it, though in a passing way, not with a "complete beholding." This is what is meant by "Iniquity, if I have **seen** it in my heart"—meaning a thought that is in the manner of "seeing" but not "beholding." For if a person were to occupy his mind in the manner of "beholding," deepening how to commit the sin, exerting himself in this thought, and becoming inflamed and clever in thinking of schemes...

<column-break/>

...to the members of his household. It was not easy for Rabbi Chisda regarding the money for his household. This is a forced change, and it is difficult. Why was Rabbi Chisda's table not stopped from... etc. For all of this, the principle is that he did not focus on the pleasure of the body, but acted only to strengthen the body so that it would be strong for the service of the Creator. And this is correct, as written in *Ketubot*, where he said: "I have not benefited even with my small finger." That is, even though I ate, I did not derive physical pleasure at all. These are the words of the Tosafot there in *Ketubot* regarding "I have not benefited...": "Before a person prays that the Torah should enter his body, he should pray that delicacies should not enter his body." This was the conduct of the Rabbi, end of quote.

Now I will explain the words of my heart regarding what the Sages said: "It is revealed and known before You that our will is to do Your will," etc. "You know..." etc. This matter belongs to the concept of the "House of the Heart," that a person should focus his eyes and heart on his words and hold onto them to prevent the Accuser. For it is possible that even if his intention is for the sake of health, it could be for the sake of the pleasure of the body. The main thing is to treat it with disdain, to say that even though he feels pleasure, his intent is not for the physical delight, but to strengthen his limbs. Regarding this, he said: "He is our strength and our shield and our refuge..." In all your ways, as mentioned in *Ketubot*, "Your heart knows... bitterness." Therefore, he said the language "It is revealed and known before You," meaning that the good intent is revealed before You, even the hidden thoughts... and the fear of God lengthens days...

Furthermore, this passage can be explained according to what is mentioned in *Berakhot*: "If a person sees that afflictions are coming upon him, let him examine his deeds." If he examines and finds nothing, let him attribute it to the neglect of Torah study. On this, he warned not to stop... for David said "I have searched my ways," meaning I searched through all my ways and all my deeds and found no "iniquity" (*aven*). That is, no bad thought or "perverseness" (*amal*)—meaning the neglect of Torah. Regarding this, he mentioned that every day he would be involved in various affairs, being in such-and-such a place, and "I found no thought of sin, and I searched and was forced to conclude that it was because of the study halls"—meaning the neglect of Torah. He also mentioned "synagogues," meaning the neglect of prayer, even though in *Berakhot* they only mentioned Torah... but here the Midrash is more inclined to include all matters...

<meta>This page continues the ethical and mystical instruction regarding the "ways of the upright." It focuses on how the divine attributes (Sefirot) of Wisdom and the Crown serve as models for human behavior, leading into a lengthy legal and philosophical discussion on the necessity of directing every mundane action—from eating to sleeping—toward the service of the Creator.</meta>

<header>Article 1</header>

->So that all his days might be spent in repentance:<-

### 9. Wisdom
Behold, the <term>Supernal Wisdom</term><note>Hebrew: Chochmah. In Kabbalah, this is the first point of divine revelation or "insight."</note> is spread over all existing things, despite being hidden and very exalted. Concerning it, it is said: "How many are Your works, O Lord! In wisdom You made them all" <note>Psalm 104:24</note>. In this way, it is fitting for a person that his wisdom should be available to all, and he should be patient and do good to every single person according to his strength. Whatever he can influence others with from his wisdom, he should influence them.

Behold, the attribute of Wisdom has two aspects: the "Upper Face" which turns toward the <term>Crown</term><note>Keter, the highest Sefirah</note>—this aspect does not look downward but rather receives from above—and the "Lower Face" which turns downward to supervise the <term>Sefirot</term><note>The ten divine emanations/attributes</note> as Wisdom spreads its influence toward them. So too should a man have two faces: the first face is his solitude with his Creator in order to increase his wisdom, and the second is to teach others from that same wisdom which was influenced upon him.

Furthermore, it is the way of Wisdom to supervise all of existence, to think deeply about all created things, as it is said: "He devises means so that no outcast be banished from Him" <note>2 Samuel 14:14</note>. It is also written: "For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, says the Lord, thoughts of peace and not of evil, to give you a future and a hope" <note>Jeremiah 29:11</note>. Thus, a person must keep his eye open to the conduct of God's people to be of benefit. His thoughts should be aimed at bringing back the outcasts, thinking good thoughts about them and giving good counsel. He should guide them with good conduct toward an upright path, serving as their intellect and guiding thought to lead them toward good and integrity.

Just as Wisdom is called "Father"—for it is the father of all existence, as it is said, "In wisdom You made them all"—so should a person be a father to all the Holy One's creatures, and particularly to Israel. He should seek mercy and blessing for the world. He should be a <term>Chasid</term><note>A pious person</note> who prays for those in distress as if he were their father, having mercy on Israel and bearing their burden with a pleasant countenance like the Merciful Father Above, who carries everything.

### 10. Crown
The <term>Chariot</term><note>A mystical structure or vehicle for divine presence</note> for this level is the attribute of humility, which includes all other attributes. For according to the greatness of the Holy One, so is His humility; for in the <term>Crown</term><note>Keter</note>, which is high and exalted, He crowns all of the Emanation, and He crowns them, as it were, by lowering His eyes to supervise them constantly. Furthermore, therein are all the "beginnings of the Head" <note>A mystical reference to the parts of the Divine "Face"</note>—the eyes, ears, the removal of anger, and the holiness of the mouth, as will be explained later at length under the letter <term>Kadesh</term><note>Holy</note>.

Thus, the secret of "You shall be <term>Tamim</term><note>Wholehearted/Simple/Perfect</note> with the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 18:13</note> is clarified. Concerning being "wholehearted" and seeking mercy, it says: "Let my heart be wholehearted in Your statutes." For all attributes and behaviors depend on the awakening of the heart, for "Many are the thoughts in the heart of man." The Torah says: "Circumcise the foreskin of your hearts," for one must have a pure and complete heart like light, to awaken will and thought to draw near to the divine attributes and the <term>Tav</term><note>The final letter of the Hebrew alphabet, here symbolizing the completion of a spiritual task</note> of the Name.

**With a whole heart and a willing soul, for the Lord searches all hearts: Article 8—The cleaving of the heart in all ways to the service of God, may He be blessed.**

<term>Maimonides</term><note>Rambam, the great 12th-century philosopher and jurist</note> wrote in the eighth of his *Eight Chapters* (which he set as an introduction to the Tractate *Avot*): "A person must subjugate all the powers of his soul and always keep one goal before his eyes: the attainment of God, may He be blessed, insofar as it is within human power to know Him. He should make all his actions, his movements, his rest, and all his words lead toward this goal, so that none of his actions are 'actions of vanity'—meaning, an action that does not lead to this goal. 

For example: he should set his intention when eating, drinking, having marital relations, sleeping, waking, moving, or resting, solely for the health of his body. And the intention behind the health of his body should be that the soul finds its instruments healthy and complete to acquire wisdom and to acquire the virtues of character and the intellectual virtues, until he reaches his goal. One's intention should not be for pleasure alone, choosing only the most pleasant food and drink, but rather he should intend for what is beneficial. If it happens to be pleasant, so be it. 

If he intends for pleasure, it should be according to the wisdom of medicine. For instance, if his appetite for food has weakened, he may stimulate it with desirable, pleasant foods. Or if one's 'black bile' <note>melancholy/depression</note> is aroused, he should remove it by listening to melodies and music, by strolling through gardens and beautiful buildings, and by the company of beautiful forms, and similar things that expand the soul and remove the sickness of black bile. The intention in all this is that he should heal his body, and the ultimate goal of healing his body is to acquire wisdom. 

Similarly, when he occupies himself with acquiring wealth, his ultimate intention in spending what he finds through his labor should be for his physical senses and to sustain his existence until he attains such knowledge of God as is possible." 

Maimonides continues: "The art of medicine has a great role in the moral and intellectual virtues and in the knowledge of God." These are his words. See how he explains that one should use all the powers of his soul so that the ultimate goal is the knowledge of God alone. One should not do any deed, small or great, nor speak any word, unless that act or word leads to a virtue or to that which leads to a virtue. He should look at every act and movement and see if it leads to that goal or not; only then should he do it. This is what the Torah asks of us when it says: "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might"—meaning, with all parts of your soul, making the goal of every part a single goal: to love God. 

Concerning this, the prophet warned: "In all your ways know Him" <note>Proverbs 3:6</note>. Our Sages explained this to mean: "Even in a matter of transgression"<note>A provocative Rabbinic phrase suggesting that even in difficult or complex situations, the goal remains the Truth/God</note>—meaning that one should place that action before him as a goal for the sake of Truth, even if it has an aspect of transgression from another side. The Sages summarized this entire matter briefly in words so precise they cannot be improved upon: "Let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven." There is no doubt about this great and awesome matter, about which entire books have been written without completing it. Know that everything is said according to one's capacity. These are the words of the great Master, Maimonides.

Along these lines, the *Tur* <note>The seminal law code by Jacob ben Asher</note> wrote in Section 231: "His intention should not be for his bodily pleasure, but to strengthen his body for the service of God. Likewise, in everything he does in this world, he should not intend for his own pleasure but for the service of the Creator, as it is written: 'In all your ways know Him,' and the Sages said: 'Let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven.'" 

<term>Rabbeinu Yonah</term> organized this matter in his commentary on *Ethics of the Fathers*: "Let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven, even optional matters like eating, drinking, walking, sitting, rising, marital relations, and conversation. All your physical needs should be for the service of your Creator or for something that leads to His service. 

*Eating and drinking:* How so? It goes without saying that one should not eat forbidden things. But even when eating permitted things while hungry and thirsty—if he does so for bodily pleasure, it is not praiseworthy. Rather, he should intend to fulfill his physical needs to live so that he may serve his Creator. 

*Sitting, rising, and walking:* How so? It goes without saying that he should not sit in the company of scoffers, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor walk in the counsel of the wicked. But even sitting in the counsel of the upright, standing in the place of the righteous, and walking in the counsel of the wholehearted—if he does so for his own pleasure and to fulfill his own desires, it is not praiseworthy, unless he does it for the sake of Heaven. 

*Sleeping:* How so? It goes without saying that one should not sleep at a time when he could be occupying himself with Torah and commandments to indulge himself. But even when he is weary and needs to sleep to rest from his exhaustion—if he does it for bodily pleasure, it is not praiseworthy, unless he intends to fulfill his physical needs so that he can serve his Creator, so that sleep provides rest for his eyes and body for health, and so his mind is not confused in Torah study due to exhaustion. 

*Marital relations:* How so? It goes without saying he should not commit a sin. But even regarding the obligation mentioned in the Torah—if he does it for bodily pleasure or to fulfill his desire, it is disgraceful. Even if he intends to have children to serve him and take his place, it is not praiseworthy, unless he intends to have children for the service of his Creator or to fulfill the obligation of the Torah, like a man paying a debt. 

*Conversation:* How so? It goes without saying he should not speak slander or obscenity. But even when speaking words of wisdom, his intention must be for the service of his Creator or for something leading to His service. The general rule is: a man is obligated to set his eyes and heart upon his ways and weigh all his actions in the scales of his intellect. When he sees something that will lead to the service of the Exalted Creator, he should do it; if not, he should not do it. Whoever possesses these traits will find himself serving his Creator all his days, even when sitting, rising, walking, and during business, even in eating, drinking, and intimacy, and all his needs." 

In this manner, our Holy Rabbi <note>Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, the editor of the Mishnah</note> raised 

->his fingers upward at the time of his death and said: 'It is revealed and known before You that I did not benefit from them except for the sake of Heaven.' These are the words of the Tur:<-

**And according to** this, we should also interpret the Mishnah in *Berakhot*: "'And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart'—with both your inclinations, the Good Inclination and the Evil Inclination." This means that even in material affairs that stem from the "Evil Inclination"—such as eating, drinking, intimacy, and the pursuit of wealth—one's goal should be the love of God. This is how Maimonides explained the verse "In all your ways know Him," even in a matter of transgression.

<meta>This page concludes the author's "Ten Utterances," a series of mystical and ethical discourses. It transitions from a discussion on the alignment of the human heart and liver with the Divine Presence into a new section regarding the Hebrew alphabet and the foundations of creation.</meta>

<page-num>58</page-num>
<header>Ten Utterances</header>

Esau is Edom <note>The traditional association of Esau with the nation of Edom and, later, the Roman/Western world</note>, and the heart is the place of understanding, for if a person is insightful and wise, he will understand his ultimate end. Behold, the liver is placed on the right side of the body, while the heart leans toward the left. It is proper to make the heart prevail over the liver. Therefore, this is the counsel advised to him: he should place the Name of the Lord before him and visualize the <term>Shekhinah</term><note>The Divine Presence, often viewed as the feminine or immanent aspect of God</note> directly opposite him. In doing so, his left side corresponds to the "Right Hand" of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and his right side corresponds to the "Left Hand" of the Divine. Thus, the "heart of the wise" is found at his right <note>Referencing Ecclesiastes 10:2, "A wise man’s heart is at his right hand, but a fool’s heart is at his left"</note>, and not in the "heart of the fool" which is on the left. In this way, the heart is remembered over the liver. This is the meaning of the verse: "I have set the Lord always before me; because He is at my right hand, I shall not be moved" <note>Psalm 16:8</note>. This implies that even though the liver is on my physical right, I place the Lord before me so that the heart comes to the right—the "Exalted Right Hand of the Lord." This is what it means to "place his heart there."

**Furthermore**, I have an explanation for this verse, "I have set the Lord always before me," alongside our verse, "Know the God of your father" <note>1 Chronicles 28:9</note>. Behold, according to the verse "I have set the Lord," it seems to contradict the words of our Sages of blessed memory, who said: "Anyone who walks with an erect posture is as if he pushes against the feet of the Divine Presence," because the Divine Presence is above his head. Thus, they said a person should visualize the Divine Presence *above* his head. In that case, his right hand would be <term>as it were</term><note>Original Hebrew: *kivyakhol*. A term used to qualify human descriptions of God, meaning "as if it were possible to say."</note> beneath the right hand of the Holy One, Blessed be He—hand under hand and foot under foot. For man is in the image of the Supernal Form in all his limbs, and he is a "supernal shadow" that has expanded into a form and a supernal appearance seen in the "shining mirror." His right-side shadow corresponds to the right side of its Root. Truly, in the realms above there is neither right nor left; rather, the matter is that the fear of Heaven should be upon him, and he should consider that the Lord is standing over him. Yet, King David said, "I have set the Lord *before* me." Similarly, our Sages said that after the <term>Amidah</term><note>The standing prayer, the central part of the Jewish liturgy</note> prayer, one gives the greeting of peace first to his left, which corresponds to the "Right" of the Holy One, and then to his right, which is the "Left" of the Holy One.

The matter is this: one who is a <term>Perfectly Righteous person</term><note>Tzadik Gamur; one who has never succumbed to sin</note>, who has never tasted the flavor of sin, is a "supernal shadow" walking in God's ways—blessed is he. The Divine Presence is literally above his head, clinging to him hand under hand, foot under foot, eye under eye, and surrounding every limb of his life with the corresponding limb from the realm below, as mentioned in the introduction to the book *Toldot Adam*. This is the one who walks in the "secret of the likeness." But one who has sinned, and whose deeds and attributes

<margin>S.G.S. explained in the small dust regarding the order of their standing, learned in the matter of the end of the 10th utterance.</margin>are opposite to the attributes of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and who has clung to the "Left Side" <note>The Sitra Achra or the realm of impurity/judgment</note>—as our Sages said: "For those who go to the left, it [the Torah] is a potion of death"—such a person must visualize and place the Divine Presence *before* him. This turns his left toward the Right of the Holy One through "Repentance out of Love," about which our Sages said that "intentional sins are transformed into merits." Regarding this, it is said: "I have set the Lord before me always," and it is also written: "And my sin is before me always" <note>Psalm 51:5</note>. We learn the "always" of "I have set" from the "always" of "my sin," so that the Lord is always opposite the sin. It turns out that this verse of "I have set" is a temporary motivator for the <term>Penitent</term><note>Ba'al Teshuvah; one who has returned to the path of righteousness</note>, and he should never move this thought from his mind all the days of his life. 

So too, we in the *Amidah* prayer—the "Prayer of the Afflicted when he faints"—state most of our requests so that our hearts may understand how to understand the evil of sin, and that He may return us in complete repentance and forgive our iniquities. Because we act as penitents, therefore after the prayer, we fulfill "I have set the Lord before me always" and give the greeting of peace to the left. This matter is hinted at in the verse in Malachi: "'I have loved you,' says the Lord. 'But you ask, "How have You loved us?"' 'Was not Esau Jacob’s brother?' declares the Lord. 'Yet I have loved Jacob, but Esau I have hated.'" <note>Malachi 1:2-3</note>

Behold, the love of lovers comes in two forms. Sometimes love is due to similarity—they are similar to each other in nature, attributes, and affairs. Sometimes it is the opposite: the love and union come from opposing natures. As the philosophers said, it is impossible for a woman to conceive from a man when their temperaments are identical, unless her nature is the opposite of his nature. This is what the verse means: "I will make him a helper against him" <note>Genesis 2:18; Hebrew: *ezer kenegdo*, literally "a helper opposite him"</note>—meaning when there is an opposition in their natures, then there is "help" and the memory to give birth. This is what is meant by "How have You loved us?"—is the love based on "likeness," when we resemble Your attributes and walk in Your ways, or is it a love where there is "opposition"? To this He answered: "Was not Esau Jacob's brother?" Jacob resembles his Creator, while the "Opposer" (Esau) I have hated. 

You might ask: is this not obvious? Naturally, one who opposes the Blessed Name is loathsome in His eyes. But there is a dispute among the Sages of Israel whether a "Perfectly Righteous person" is superior or if a "Penitent" is superior. In truth, the law follows both views, for there is a distinction between different types of repentance. Our Sages in Tractate Yoma distinguished between "Repentance out of Fear" and "Repentance out of Love." In repentance out of fear, intentional sins are treated as accidents; in repentance out of love, intentional sins are transformed into merits. These words are expanded upon in the Zohar and will be explained later, with God's help, in the section on Repentance. With God's help, most people's repentance is out of fear; in that category, the "Perfectly Righteous" is superior. But I have seen "Elevated People" whose repentance is of the highest quality, and they are few; regarding these, they said "The Penitent is superior." 

This verse "How have You loved us?" speaks of the distinguished people and the whole world, as if debating: "How have You loved us? Is it from the side of similarity (the Perfectly Righteous) or the side of opposition (the Penitent)?" To this, He replied: "I loved Jacob," for he was a "simple man" and was always wholehearted with his God, even in his mother's womb—when she passed by houses of study, he struggled to emerge. "But Esau I hated"—even though the literal meaning refers to the generations, it hints that repentance is not loved quite as much [as original righteousness], for even though intentional sins are treated as accidents, even an accident requires atonement.

<margin>P.N.S. and liver around books; this matter is in the storm of blows and *skinas* [unclear]... as it is in the supernal secrets.</margin>**But** regarding King David, who said "my sin is before me," our Sages explained that he "established the yoke of repentance." As it is written, "my sin is before me always"—he did not move for a moment from his inner regret. Thus, "I have set the Lord before me always" was fulfilled in him through the secret of how that which was a "potion of death" for those on the left was turned to the Right of the Holy One, because the intentional sins were turned into merits. Regarding this it is written: "Know the God of your father and serve Him with a whole heart and a willing soul." David said to his son Solomon: "the God of your father," because David had fulfilled all the above. He warned him that service must be with a whole heart and a willing soul, so that the cleaving to and knowledge of God should not depart for a moment—whether in the aspect of the "Perfectly Righteous" whose understanding is above his head, or in the "Correction of Iniquity" where one sets the Lord before him always. For "the Lord searches all hearts," and the cleaving should be through the "awakening of the heart," whether through the Presence above the head or the Presence set before him. Only let the knowledge and remembrance of the Blessed Name not cease for a single moment, as the verse says: "But you who clung to the Lord your God are all alive today" <note>Deuteronomy 4:4</note>.

### The Commandment of the Lord is Pure

Behold, I have seen that these Ten Utterances are great roots for the Unity of the Name and the Unity of the People of Israel. They have made the Blessed Lord "one unique entity" [in the world], and He has made them one unique entity. Therefore, we are His servants, the faithful of His house, to serve Him with inner awe and love and with a whole heart, and to cling to His attributes and to the many matters of the "awakening of the heart." For these great roots of ours, there are many branches, especially the "Gate of Character Traits" which is "longer than the earth in measure" <note>Job 11:9</note>. Therefore, I said in my heart that there should be a functional pause, to record a "Gate" in its own right to mention the branches, even if they are but hints—though these things have no set measure, you shall see a small portion of them. I will mention some of them in this Gate, through which "the righteous shall enter," and it shall be called the **Gate of Letters**, arranged according to the Alphabet. It is said that our God is exalted in His initial state and His crown. Your sign is: "With ten utterances the world was created," and the world was created with the letters of the Torah. As we learned in the Sifrei: "It shall be a sign upon your hand and a memorial between your eyes, so that the Torah of the Lord shall be upon your face."

<meta>This page continues the "Ten Utterances," moving from the Ninth Discourse, which deals with the power of thought and the performance of commandments, into the Tenth Discourse, which focuses on the practice of "Shiviti"—placing the Divine Presence constantly before one's consciousness.</meta>

# The Ninth Discourse

Regarding this, our Sages of blessed memory said: <note>original: "Arzal" - acronym for "Adoneinu Rabboteinu Zichronam Livracha"</note> **"Sinful thoughts are harder to bear than the sin itself."** The reason for this is that the action of a sin is performed with physical "vessels" (the body), whereas sinful thoughts <note>original: "hirhur’ei aveirah"</note> exist in the spiritual realm, within the mystery of thought. It is only when thought is directed through the eye or the ear that one gazes upon it. However, even then, one sees it only through the "way of seeing," for the ear does not truly "hear" the thought—meaning, there is no literal hearing, only a protective layer. This is hinted at in the verse: "And the Lord heard, and His anger was kindled." <note>Numbers 11:1</note> It is also said: "The Lord knows the thoughts of man, that they are vanity." <note>Psalm 94:11</note> This means that even though He does not punish for the thought alone, the Lord nonetheless knows it even before it is translated into action. It is called "vanity" <note>original: "hevel," literally "breath" or "vapor"</note> because anything that is not completed is called "hevel," just as the Sages referred to unfinished wooden vessels as a *golem* <note>a raw, unshaped form</note>. Similarly, they hinted at this in the verse: "Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile." <note>Psalm 32:2</note> This means: Happy is he whose sinful thoughts the Holy One, Blessed be He, does not "count" against him; even more so, happy is the one in whose spirit no guile ever arose.

Let us return to the matter: The Holy One, Blessed be He, does not "look" at a bad thought to focus on it, because "the Lord his God is with him" <note>Numbers 23:21</note>, since his soul stems from the side of holiness, within the mystery of the <term>Yod-He-Vav-He</term> <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter Name of God</note> and the union of the attributes of Tiferet (Beauty/Harmony) and Malkhut (Sovereignty), as explained in the introduction to *Toledot Adam*. This is the meaning of "The Lord his God is with him," similar to the verse: "For the Lord's portion is His people; Jacob is the lot of His inheritance." <note>Deuteronomy 32:9</note> The phrase "The Lord his God is with him" refers to the idea that "He has not beheld iniquity in Jacob." For even though He did not "behold" it, He nonetheless saw it; therefore, the verse mentions the name "Jacob" <note>representing the Jewish people in a lower spiritual state</note>.

However, regarding a **good thought**, the verse mentions "Israel" <note>the people in their higher spiritual state</note>, hinting at the commandments. The explanation of the verse is that there is much "toil" <note>performance of deeds</note> that people are happy to fulfill, and their entire prayer and existence is centered on not being prevented from doing so by force. The Holy One, Blessed be He, "contracts" His thought above concerning those who are "engrossed" in study but cannot physically perform the deeds—such as now, during the destruction of the Temple, when we cannot perform the service of the Sanctuary, the sacrifices, or the laws of ritual purity and impurity. There are many such examples. The Holy One knows the will of Israel is so great that He not only "beholds no toil," but it is as if He does not even see the lack of action.

There are many of the **613 commandments** <note>original: "taryag mitzvot"</note> that are impossible to fulfill individually. I have already written at length about this above regarding the discourse: "Anyone who engages in the Torah for its own sake merits many things." The Torah was given to the entire congregation of Israel collectively, like a king who writes a decree to his servants, warning them and commanding the whole community what to do and what not to do. Now, when the servants read the script, each one is careful and diligent in the king's service to the best of his ability, for this specific command might apply to one servant and that command to another. Sometimes they all share in certain commands equally. If they fulfill the king's letter, they are all considered "faithful servants," as if each one of them had fulfilled the entire decree.

So too, the Torah is a script from the Holy One, Blessed be He, and we, Israel, are His servants. When we engage in the Torah for its own sake—meaning, with the intent to fulfill the King’s decree by doing whatever is possible—and one's thought is focused on the fulfillment of the entire text, even the parts one cannot physically perform (because it was not possible for him), the Scripture considers it as if he had fulfilled it. This is the meaning of: "The shout of a King is among them." <note>Numbers 23:21</note> This refers to "not seeing toil in Israel," because the knowledge and connection to the King's script is within them, and their soul longs to fulfill it. This is a wondrously high level. Therefore, the verse specifies "Israel."

The general rule is this: A person should purify his thoughts and let no "abominable thought" enter his mind, even distantly. He should always cling in thought to the fulfillment of the Torah and its commandments, yearning and desiring them. If he is prevented from performing something, he should grieve and reveal his thought before the "Knower of Thoughts," saying: "Master of the Universe, it is revealed and known before You that if it were possible for me to fulfill this, I would do so." This is what our father **Abraham** did when he offered the ram in place of his son Isaac; he spoke as if his son were the one slaughtered, as if his blood were sprinkled, and as if he were flayed, etc. Since his *intention* was to do so, it is considered as if it were actually done.

Regarding this, the verse says: "For the Lord searches all hearts, and understands every intent of the thoughts; if you seek Him, He will be found by you; but if you forsake Him, He will cast you off forever." <note>1 Chronicles 28:9</note> The phrase "The Lord searches all hearts" refers to the **good thought** in the heart; He searches for it to reward it. Therefore, it says afterward: "If you seek Him, He will be found by you," for "one who comes to purify himself is assisted." But the phrase "He understands every intent of the thoughts" refers to the **bad thought**; even though He does not "search" for it (to punish immediately), He nonetheless understands and knows it, and evil is drawn from it, for "one who comes to defile himself, the way is opened for him." Therefore, one must sanctify himself in deed, in speech, and in thought.

-> **The Tenth Discourse** <-

The Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah</term> dwells in the heart after the fulfillment of the nine previous levels. Then, the number ten represents the "Gate of Entry" to this Tenth Discourse, which is the "Holy of Holies." This is the principle of: **"I have set the Lord always before me."** <note>Psalm 16:8; original: "Shiviti Hashem lenegdi tamid"</note> A person should remember this "always" and not move his thought from his Creator, whether in mundane matters or specifically during prayer.

In the *Tur* <note>a foundational code of Jewish law</note>, it is written: "I have set the Lord always before me"—this verse is a great principle in the Torah and in the virtues of the righteous who walk before God. For a person's sitting, movements, and business while he is alone in his house are not the same as his sitting, movements, and business while he is before a great king. Nor is his speech or the opening of his mouth as he pleases while with his family the same as his speech in the king's presence. How much more so when a person takes to heart that the Great King, the Holy One, Blessed be He, whose glory fills the entire earth, stands over him and sees his deeds, as it is said: "If a man hides in secret places, shall I not see him? says the Lord. Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord." <note>Jeremiah 23:24</note> Immediately, fear, humility, and dread of God will come upon him, and he will feel shame before Him always. He will not feel ashamed before people who mock him for his service to God, even when acting privately. When he lies down on his bed, he should know before whom he lies, and as soon as he wakes from his sleep, he should rise with zeal for the service of his Creator, blessed and exalted be He. These are the Tur's words.

And this is the meaning of "Know the God of your father," for He always stands over you and within your innermost parts; "He searches all hearts," and "no man can hide in secret places." Therefore, his "setting" <note>from "Shiviti," setting or placing</note> should be constant, and he should be filled with fear, humility, and shame.

---

<margin>Furthermore</margin>
This verse, **"I have set the Lord always before me,"** is also hinted at as an awakening for another matter, in addition to the first awakening. This stems from a person's remembrance that the Creator stands over him, sees, and knows his thoughts. It is a moral lesson mentioned by one of the ethical sages: A person should consider, when his Evil Inclination <note>original: "Yetzer HaRa"</note> tries to entice him to violate a negative commandment or neglect a positive one—what should he think? He should ask himself: "Do I believe that the Blessed Name knows, sees, and watches at every moment, or do I not believe?" If he does not believe, then he is a denier of the very essence of God's existence. And who among Israel is such a denier? Heaven forbid! For every Jew is ready and prepared to suffer stoning, burning, beheading, and strangulation—all cruel deaths—rather than deny God. Rather, he is among the believers that the King of Kings, the Holy One, Blessed be He, sees, gazes, looks, and understands, and even tests the heart, as it is said: "I the Lord search the heart and test the kidneys." <note>Jeremiah 17:10</note>

How, then, could he have the audacity <note>original: "azut panim"</note> to sin before the King, right in His presence while His eyes are watching? This is "I have set the Lord always before me." This thought will remove him from sin and stir him to be righteous and pious, for he will say: "I will do the will of my Maker, who is gazing and looking at me." Regarding this, we say in the confession: **"Our Father, our King, we have sinned before You"**—meaning, how much audacity did we have to sin *before* You, knowing that Your eyes see! And this is simple to understand.

When a person remembers this, then even a "light" sin will be in his eyes like a "grave" one. For how can one rebel in the presence of the King, even in a small matter, while the King’s eyes are watching? This is what the prophet Samuel said: "For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry." <note>1 Samuel 15:23</note> Rabbi David Kimchi <note>Radak</note> explains that the word "as" is missing in the Hebrew, meaning all rebellion against God's word is *like* the sin of witchcraft, and "stubbornness" <note>original: "hafzar"</note> is a great and heavy thing, like iniquity and idolatry.

As it says in *Midrash Tanhuma*: "If a man hides in secret places..." This is like a minor lord who built a province and made hidden chambers within it. So the Holy One, Blessed be He, says to adulterers: "Are you hidden from Me?" as it is said: "The eye of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, 'No eye shall see me'; and he puts a veil on his face." <note>Job 24:15</note> The adulterer says, "No creature knows of me," but "My eyes roam throughout the whole earth." What is the way of sinners? They wait for the hour of darkness. Likewise, thieves "dig through houses in the dark." So the verse says: "Woe to those who seek deep to hide their counsel from the Lord, and their works are in the dark, and they say, 'Who sees us? and who knows us?'" <note>Isaiah 29:15</note>

The adulterer is particularly harsh because he "pushes away the Divine Presence," so to speak. God fills the upper and lower worlds, as it is said: "Do I not fill heaven and earth?" In what place, then, does this man commit adultery? When he comes to commit the act, he says to the Omnipresent: "Remove Yourself and give me one hour." And, so to speak, because God is "slow to anger," He gives him space, as it is said: "For He knows false men; He sees iniquity also; will He not then consider it?" <note>Job 11:11</note> And "he puts a veil on his face"—meaning He who dwells in the "secret place of the Most High" puts a face <note>on the resulting child</note> that is transformed from Him, so that the child's face resembles the adulterer. These are the words of the Midrash.

And in *Reshith Chochmah*, in the "Gate of Fear," Chapter 10, it is explained that there are two types of ugliness and disgrace in the sinner:
1. He despises the King by saying He does not watch him, while he hides himself. This is: "If a man hides in secret places, shall I not see him? says the Lord." (And here there is a pause in the verse's meaning).
2. "Do I not fill heaven and earth?"—this is the second flaw: he "pushes away" the Divine Presence, for the Holy One fills all.

In a similar vein, they said: "Anyone who does not have pity on the honor of his Creator, it would have been better for him had he not come into the world." And they said in the Gemara regarding Joseph: This refers to one who commits a sin in secret. Rabbi Isaac said: "Anyone who commits a sin in secret is as if he pushes the feet of the Divine Presence," for it is said: "The heaven is My throne, and the earth is My footstool." <note>Isaiah 66:1</note> These are his words.

I also heard in my youth an explanation of the verse from the great Genius, our teacher Rabbi Ephraim, may his memory be a blessing: It is known that all physical desires come from the liver, for the liver is entirely made of blood...

# The Gate of Letters

## The Gate of Letters

Regarding our antiquity: I have found it written in the holy writings of the Ari, of blessed memory <note>original: "Ha-Ar"i zal" – Rabbi Isaac Luria (1534–1572), the father of modern Kabbalah</note>, when he spoke of the loftiness, height, and concealment of *Adam Kadmon* <note>original: "A"K" – Primordial Man, the first and highest realm of emanation</note> and the Hidden Light <note>original: "S"K" – likely referring to "Saba de-Kaltin" or a similar level of hidden emanation</note>. He said as follows: In these supreme contemplations, at the ultimate level of loftiness and concealment, began the description common among the Sages to call God by the name *Ein Sof* <note>The Infinite</note>, which refers to the "Hidden Light." Thus, wherever we expound upon the concealment and revelation within the world of *Atzilut* <note>The World of Emanation, the highest of the four spiritual worlds</note>, it is appropriate—according to the proper order of study regarding the heights of the universe—to apply the term *Ein Sof* to the concealment of the "Supreme Crown" <note>Keter Elyon</note>. This is to exclude this title of *Ein Sof* (and other such titles) from being applied to the "Master of Will," may His name be blessed and exalted above all blessing and praise. Regarding the Master of Will Himself, we are not permitted to contemplate Him at all, but rather must simply accept the necessity of His existence. I also found in the "Scroll of Secrets" of the Maharam’e <note>original: "Maharam"e" – Rabbi Menahem Azariah da Fano (1548–1260), an Italian Kabbalist</note> as follows: The Great Master, the Ramak <note>original: "Rehamach"em" – Rabbi Moshe Cordovero (1522–1570), a leading Kabbalist of Safed</note>, wrote: "Blessed is He, and evil shall not dwell with Him; our Primordial One is exalted..." until the end of the passage stating that "sustenance <note>original: "hashefa'ah"</note> comes only from Him." Based on this, we shall interpret the phrase "He exists, and there is no time for His existence" <note>A line from the *Yigdal* prayer</note> as meaning that His "Will" exists, but there is no "time" for His existence, for He is above time and even above the "order of times." He is uniquely one with the world of *Atzilut*, and He preceded everything. Here, the author is speaking of the absolute, primordial Master of Will.

## The Fifth Principle
That one must not worship or pray to any other besides Him. For to Him alone, may He be blessed, is worship and greatness due, and not to any other, for all others are created beings and have no power apart from Him. He, may He be blessed, is omnipotent, and nothing is withheld from Him. This is what the aforementioned prayer says: "Lord of the universe, who reigned before any creature was created," which indicates His greatness and His kingship.

## The Sixth Principle
The flow of His prophecy was given to the people of His treasure and His glory. For in His goodness, He bestows the flow of His prophecy upon an individual or individuals of the human species who are worthy and upright in His eyes, in order to guide the human species in the path they should walk and the deeds they should do.

## The Seventh Principle
"None has arisen like Moses." This man, Moses, was exceedingly great in prophecy, above all the prophets who existed from the beginning of the world to its end. All other prophets who preceded him, and even those who arose after them, were all below him in level. He was the chosen of God, and it was through him that the "Torah of Truth" was given to Israel, which restores the soul. He attained a level of knowledge of the Creator that no other human attained. Maimonides wrote that his prophecy was distinguished from all other prophets in four ways:
1. **First:** No other prophet was spoken to by God except through an angel or a metaphor, but Moses was spoken to by God "mouth to mouth," as it is said: "Mouth to mouth I speak with him." <note>Numbers 12:8</note>
2. **Second:** All other prophets received prophecy only through a dream or a night vision, or during the day in a manner where all their senses were nullified, as it is written: "In a vision I make Myself known to him, in a dream I speak with him." But of Moses it is said: "Not so is My servant Moses... mouth to mouth," etc.
3. **Third:** When the flow of prophecy came to all other prophets, their strengths would fail and they would become weak. With Moses, no trembling or weakness overtook him in any way; rather, he spoke "as a man speaks to his fellow."
4. **Fourth:** Prophecy did not rest upon other prophets whenever they desired, but only by the Will of God and after preparation. But Moses was prepared at all times; whenever he wished for the Spirit of God to rest upon him, it did so, as it is said: "Stand, and let me hear what the Lord will command you." <note>Numbers 9:8</note>

## The Eighth Principle
"A Torah of Truth He gave," etc. This is the Torah of God from Heaven, which is now in our hands. It is entirely from the Holy One, Blessed be He; it reached Moses our Teacher through the process called "speech." Moses, in the manner of a scribe, wrote and engraved it from the mouth of the Holy One, from the word *Bereshit* <note>In the beginning</note> until the words "before the eyes of all Israel."

<margin>
Moses wrote it from the mouth of the Almighty. There is no difference between the verse "I am the Lord your God" and the verses "Timna was a concubine" <note>Genesis 36:12</note> or "And the name of his wife was Mehetabel." It is all equal, the speech of God; all its verses and words are His utterances. So too is its Oral explanation; the manner of performing the commandments was also a Law given to Moses from God at Sinai. Moses told us, and he is faithful in his mission, as it is written: "In all My house, he is faithful."
</margin>

## The Ninth Principle
"God will not exchange nor change His law." He has not changed the Torah of Moses, and no other Torah shall ever come from God. There shall be no addition or subtraction from it, neither in the Written Law nor the Oral Law. Regarding God's Torah, it is said: "Do not add to it and do not subtract from it." <note>Deuteronomy 13:1</note> As for what is said in Jeremiah, Chapter 31: "Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah; not like the covenant that I made with their fathers..." the Radak <note>original: "Rada"k" – Rabbi David Kimhi (1160–1235), a leading medieval commentator</note> wrote as follows: "The 'New Covenant' means it will be permanent and never broken, unlike the covenant God made at Sinai which was broken..." Alternatively, the prophet was not predicting a *new* Torah, but rather that the covenant with the ancestors would be renewed. This "new" Torah is simply their own repentance. He explains the phrase "not like the covenant I made with their ancestors" to mean that they broke the first one, but this one they will not break, for "I will place My Torah in their hearts." It will not be forgotten. The entire matter is that the "new" covenant is not a replacement, but a fulfillment. Even Malachi, the seal of the prophets, says in his concluding words: "Remember the Torah of Moses My servant, which I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel, statutes and ordinances." This entire passage refers to the future. You see, then, that there will never be a new Torah, only the one given at Horeb. These are the words of the aforementioned Sage. However, there are "seventy faces" <note>multiple layers of interpretation</note> to this matter. It is known that just as man became physical, the Torah became physical. If man had remained in the "garments of light," the Torah would have been understood in a much more spiritual sense. As the *Pardes* <note>The classic work *Pardes Rimonim* by Rabbi Moshe Cordovero</note> writes in the "Gate of the Soul": the commandment "Do not plow with an ox and a donkey" wouldn't apply literally in the Garden of Eden—how could there be literal plowing there? Rather, it would be understood in the spiritual sense of what are called "Ox" and "Donkey." So too in the future, when the world returns to its spiritual state, the Torah will shed its physicality, and the commandments will be understood according to the comprehension of that era. But it is all this same Torah itself; only its light will shine more brightly, just as man himself will shine.

## The Tenth Principle
"He watches and knows our secrets." This means the Holy One, Blessed be He, supervises and knows the deeds of men, and does not hide His eyes from them, as it is said: "Great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are open to all the ways of the sons of men." <note>Jeremiah 32:19</note> It is also said: "He tells a man what his thought is." As for the phrase "He sees the end of a matter at its beginning," this explains the secret of Knowledge and Free Will—that they do not contradict one another. I have already explained this at length in the introduction to *Toldot Adam*; look there and you will understand how He "sees the end of a matter at its beginning."

<margin>
*Toldot Adam* <note>Likely the author's own work or a reference to a specific commentary of that name</note>
</margin>

## The Eleventh Principle
Reward and punishment. The text says "according to his deed and according to his wickedness." This points to what I elaborated on above in the introduction to *Toldot Adam*: that reward and punishment are not arbitrary agreements but natural consequences. The "reward of a commandment" is the commandment itself <note>meaning the spiritual light created by the act</note>, and the "punishment for a transgression" is the transgression itself. This is why the Sages were precise in their language, saying: "In the World to Come, the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads." They did not say "with crowns," but "with *their* crowns"—meaning the crowns they themselves created through their deeds. As a man's conduct is during the "weekday" <note>this life</note>, so is his conduct on the "Sabbath" <note>the afterlife</note>.

## The Twelfth Principle
"He will send at the end of days our Messiah," the Offshoot of David, to redeem His people Israel from the hand of the nations. The kingdom shall return to Israel, they shall no longer serve strangers, and the House of Israel shall return to their land for a good name and for praise, even more than their initial successes. Also, the nations shall serve the Messiah of God who will reign then; they will enter his covenant. He will establish righteous judgment in the land, and the City of God shall be holy to the Lord, never to be uprooted or destroyed. "A ruler shall come out of Jacob," and then "saviors shall ascend Mount Zion to judge Mount Esau." He shall rule over every tongue and nation, as it is written: "The Lord your God will gather you from all the peoples where the Lord your God has scattered you." Then the Name of the Lord shall be One, and all the House of Israel shall know Him and give Him thanks. Blessed be the Lord, the Savior, who dwells in Jerusalem. Hallelujah!

## The Thirteenth Principle
The Resurrection of the Dead. Even if they have already rotted and returned to the four elements, just as God brought man into existence from a tiny drop, so will He bring him forth from the "remnant of the element" that remains. All this will be for those who occupied themselves with Torah and commandments. The Lord shall rejoice in His works and grant a good reward even to the body for the good deeds it performed while bound in the world. "And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake." For You are a True Judge; blessed be the True Judge who gives life and sustains from generation to generation; He was, He is, and He will be.

# These are the Thirteen Principles, corresponding to the numerical value of "One" <note>original: "Echad" = 13</note>. For in truth, they are unified in the existence and unity of the Lord, like a flame bound to a coal.
->As the secret is explained in the Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer:<-
->He is Great, and before the world was created, He and His Name were alone. Afterward, the Name was revealed. These matters are ancient, and I have explained them at length in the introduction to *Toldot Adam*.<-
