<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on the sanctity of thought and the heights of "Adam Kadmon," this page begins a new alphabetical encyclopedia of virtues and concepts titled the "Gate of Letters." The author starts with "Aleph" and "Emunah" (Faith), framing the work through Maimonides' Thirteen Principles of Faith, but immediately infusing them with Kabbalistic terminology from the Zohar and later mystics.</meta>

# The Gate of Letters

-> Truth and Faith — Creatures — Sinews — Etiquette — Praise — Generosity — Alacrity — A Good Companion — Purity — The Good Inclination — Seriousness — A Good Heart — Moderation — A Faithful Spirit — Satisfaction — Humility — Prudence — Modesty — Holy — Will — Silence — Repentance <-

**Truth and Faith:** The foundations of the religion are the thirteen principles recorded by Maimonides <note>original: "Ha-Rambam" – Rabbi Moses ben Maimon (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note> in the Mishnah, in the chapter "Chelek" <note>The tenth chapter of Tractate Sanhedrin</note>. They are: the existence of God, His unity, the removal of corporeality (that He has no body), that He is primordial (eternal), that it is proper to worship Him and no other, and prophecy (the prophets of truth and justice), the prophecy of Moses our Teacher (peace be upon him), that the Torah is from Heaven, that the Torah shall not be changed, God’s knowledge of deeds, reward and punishment, the Messiah, and the resurrection of the dead. Regarding these, the praised song "Yigdal Elohim Chai" <note>Magnified be the Living God – a liturgical hymn based on these 13 principles</note> was established. Now, I shall explain them one by one. You shall recite the praised song of *Yigdal*, and afterward, I will record how the thirteen principles are hinted at in the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy. I will explain the matter according to its root and the truth found in the secrets of the Kabbalah.

**The First Principle:** He exists, and there is no time limit to His existence. He is called **The Necessary Existence** <note>original: "Mechuyav Ha-Metziut" – a philosophical term for a being whose non-existence is impossible</note> and, according to the strength of the Kabbalists, **The Infinite** (*Ein Sof*). He is the Cause of all Causes and the Reason for all Reasons. From His existence comes the existence of everything living, both spiritual and physical, the unfolding of the Emanation (*Atzilut*), the creation of the Creation (*Beriyah*), the formation of the Formation (*Yetzirah*), and the making of all that is Made (*Asiyah*). In Him is the endurance of their existence. If we were to imagine the nullification of all beings other than Him, His existence would not be nullified because of them, for He has no need for any other, yet all beings need Him. He lives with them and gives them life according to His simple will, like the magnitude of His power, desire, and will.

**The Second Principle:** He is One, and there is no unity like His unity; it is hidden. Even the Infinite (*Ein Sof*) is One in His unity—the True Unity. This is not like a "General Species" which includes many types, nor like a "Specific Individual" in a count, nor like a "Composite Unity" which can be divided into parts, nor like a "Simple Body" that can be physically divided, nor like the number one in a sequence. This is why it is said, "He is One and there is no unity like His unity." The secret of this unity, as we are occupied with it, lies in the secret of His Blessed Names, which represent Judgment and Mercy; they are in a state of True Unity. As it is said: "Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One." It is only the actions that result from them that appear divided to the world according to the weakness of those who receive them.

<margin>
<gloss>Explanation: A "General Species" is like the concept of "Clothing" which includes all types of garments, or "Animal" which includes all living creatures. A "Specific Individual" is like a specific king from a line of kings. A "Composite" is like a person made of various elements. A "Simple Body" refers to the four elements (fire, air, water, earth) which, though simple, can still be divided or broken down. The "Unity of Number" refers to the number one in a series (1, 2, 3...). None of these apply to God, for His unity is absolute and indivisible.</gloss>
</margin>

From the side of the recipients, according to their capacity, a division is perceived; but from the side of their power in their Source, they are without end (*Ein Sof*) and without limit. It is almost inappropriate to even use the word "One" for Him, as we find in *Sefer Yetzirah* <note>The Book of Formation, an ancient mystical text</note>: "Before 'One,' what can you count?" For the secret of Emanation is the secret of "One, Unique, and Unified," where connection applies but not separation. However, in their Root, even the term "connection" does not apply due to the extreme concealment of the Simple Essence. This is why it concludes, "And also Infinite (*Ein Sof*) to His unity," for He is the "Soul of the Soul" to their Mastership. That is, His Names are the souls of the worlds, and He is the Soul to them. The comparison is like the relationship of the body to the soul, used only to satisfy the human ear.

**The Third Principle:** He has no likeness of a body, and He is not a body, as it is said: "For you saw no form." This principle proceeds to say that even though we have used the secret of His Names to describe His Necessary Existence in the relationship of "Body to Soul," the parable is not identical to the reality. God forbid, He has no likeness of a body and is not a body, and the properties of a body do not affect Him, such as movement, rest, or other changes. The Torah speaks in the language of man, but we must clarify a secret that many ask: after saying "He has no likeness of a body," why must it also say "He is not a body"? Is that not obvious by logic? We explain: He has no likeness of a body—meaning He has no likeness even to things that are *not* bodies, such as the angels. He has no likeness to them. I say there is a deep matter here, and I will preface with the words of the Sage in the book *Elim* <note>likely referring to "Sefer Elim" by Joseph Solomon Delmedigo</note>. He wrote: If the superiority of Matter over Form is difficult for you, as we have analyzed in our generation... some say Matter always yearns and longs to change its current form for another form... they do not look at the acts of God. Form changes in the soul... but the Supernal Soul has no change or substitute at all... even in the heights of the heavens where the light is exalted beyond measure, He is the Generator of the world.

Even in mistaken thoughts, there is no doubt that between the stripping of the first Form and the dressing of the second Form—because of the waste and decay between them—there exists a very honorable reality that is unattainable. This is called "Dust," as in Tractate *Temurah* regarding the idea that "everything was from dust and everything returns to dust." It is said there regarding the ash of a burnt egg that it is permitted to be eaten, and we do not say "that which comes from the impure is impure," why? Because it has become mere dust. This reality is what our Rabbis called "Hyle" <note>original: "Yuly" – a Greek philosophical term for primordial matter</note>; it is the true carrier of the second Form in the specific absence prior to its existence... it is the "Simple Law." 

<note>The author is using a complex philosophical argument here: Form (the shape or identity of a thing) is temporary, but Matter (the underlying substance) is more enduring. God is compared to the ultimate "Matter" or "Substance" that remains even when all "Forms" (worlds/shapes) change or vanish.</note>

To refine what the Sage mentions: the physical build of an embryo or a person is temporary, flesh and bone and sinews. The sinews are formed from the white... all are formed in the womb... the main matter is from the mother and the form is from the father. This deep matter of "Right and Left" forces is the "Holy Principle" of Matter over Form even in physical beings, for it is the carrier of existence that sustains the changing forms that come and go. All forms have nullification and substitution except for Him. He merits the entire "table" of awakening; the actions do not limit Him. His power then is as His power now—to receive forms one after another while they all perish, yet He stands. This is the truth itself without doubt, and from here the secret of the Resurrection of the Dead is understood, and the eternity of the pious who are close to the Supreme King. Know that even in the lowest matter of existence—the "impression" in which no other impression remains after forms change—we say in the chapter "Ha-Gozel" <note>Bava Kamma 96a</note> regarding a silver bar (*Naska*) made into coins (*Zuzi*): he hasn't acquired it. Why? Because he can turn them back into a bar. This is a "change that returns to its original state." But if coins are made into a bar, he *has* acquired it. Why? Because if he turns it back into coins, they are "different coins." From this we learn the advantage of that which perishes, which is the Matter, over the changing Forms (the coins). This completes the acquisition. The wise person who understands the depth of this matter will know that this is the root: the substance and center of existence is superior to the Form, and the Body [of existence] is superior to the many physical forms.

<columns>2</columns>

**The Fourth Principle:** He is primordial to everything. "The eternal God is a dwelling place." Absolute primality, as it says: "I am the first and I am the last." It says there is no beginning to His beginning. For something can be a "beginning" but still have a beginning prior to it. For example, the New Moon of Nisan is the first of the months that follow it, but the year that passed was a "beginning to its beginning." So too, year before year, week before week. This is not the case for Him. He has a beginning like Jacob was the first of the tribes, and there is one above Jacob... however, God is First and there is no beginning to His beginning. Furthermore, I have come to provide insight: there are two principles here—the first, which was mentioned above, that He exists and there is no time limit to His existence, and what is mentioned here, His Primality.

<column-break/>

**Therefore**
<gloss>Therefore, let the wise among Israel begin to reflect on your doubts... for your foundation is an enduring existence... our taste for your commandments is according to the secret of the worlds... the roots of the changing beginnings... and all the foundations... for they are like those longing for gold... and all the languages and lips... and they sought the House of Jacob... for it is secondary to the Thought which is the essence.</gloss>

<meta>This page continues the "Gate of Letters" from the previous page, specifically focusing on the intersection between the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy (from Exodus 34) and the Thirteen Principles of Faith (as defined by Maimonides). The previous page introduced the concept, and this page provides the detailed mapping and a concluding prayer.</meta>

# **Abounding in Kindness**
The seventh attribute <note>The author is listing the "Thirteen Attributes of Mercy" revealed to Moses at Sinai</note>. Our Sages of blessed memory said that God "leans toward kindness." This means that if a person's merits and iniquities are perfectly balanced against one another, the Holy One, blessed be He, tilts the scale with His hand to make the merits outweigh the sins, as if they were more numerous. He shows pity as long as the person’s sins do not include those that characterize the "willful sinners of Israel who sin with their bodies," such as a "skull that never donned phylacteries" <note>Hebrew: *Karkafta de-la manach tefillin*. This is a Talmudic term (Tractate Rosh Hashanah 17a) referring to someone who has never performed the core commandment of wearing Tefillin (leather prayer boxes), symbolizing a total rejection of Jewish practice</note> due to mockery and disdain for the commandments, or those who commit forbidden sexual acts and similar transgressions.

# **And Truth**
The eighth attribute. This means He makes His word and His promise true; His truth shall not return empty. Furthermore, the Sages said in the first chapter of Tractate Berakhot: "The Holy One, blessed be He, never retracted a favorable word."

# **Preserver of Kindness for Thousands**
The ninth attribute. Even for many generations, He guards the love of the righteous person to perform kindness for their descendants, as it is written: "And God remembered His covenant with Abraham, etc."

# **Forgiver of Iniquity**
# **and Transgression**
# **and Sin**
**The tenth attribute** <note>Forgiver of Iniquity</note> refers to a sin committed intentionally, but driven only by physical desire <note>Hebrew: *Letayavon*—sinning for the "appetite" rather than out of rebellion</note>. Proof of this is the verse: "That soul shall be utterly cut off, its iniquity (*avona*) is upon it."

**The eleventh attribute** <note>and Transgression</note> refers to rebellion, where the sinner acts specifically to provoke Heaven. As it is said: "The King of Moab transgressed (*pasha*) against me."

**The twelfth attribute** <note>and Sin</note> refers to an accidental error, as it is said: "If a soul shall sin (*techeta*) through error." These three types of sins are mentioned in His attributes. The first two follow the logic of "not only this, but also that" <note>A legal reasoning style: if God forgives intentional rebellion, how much more so an accident</note>, ending with the accidental sin. There is a homiletic interpretation (*Derash*) that the reason "Sin" (the accident) is mentioned last is to teach that if one performs Repentance, all intentional iniquities and rebellions are considered by God as if they were merely accidental errors. It says "Forgiver of Iniquity and Transgression" to say that through Repentance, He carries them away until no trace of them remains. As it is said: "They become like glass" <note>A metaphor for being wiped clean or becoming transparent/pure</note>. In the place where Penitents stand, even the perfectly righteous cannot stand.

**"He will by no means clear the guilty"** is called the thirteenth attribute. Our Sages of blessed memory taught that this refers to "clearing" through suffering for those who repent, to polish away the sin, but "not clearing" for those who do not repent.

***

Now, regarding the explanation of the first two Names: **"The Lord, the Lord"** <note>Hebrew: *YHVH, YHVH*—the Tetragrammaton repeated twice at the start of the Attributes</note>. The Sages say: "I am the Lord before a person sins, and I am the Lord after a person sins." Why does He need the Attribute of Mercy *before* one sins? The intention of the words above is that He is exceedingly merciful, like a father’s mercy for a son. It can also be explained that "before he sins" means that even if a person *thinks* of sinning, the Holy One does not join a bad thought to an action <note>In Jewish thought, God generally does not punish for bad thoughts alone, only for actions</note>; this is from the Attribute of Mercy. 

However, I have a deeper secret regarding this, which I hinted at in the introduction to my work **The Generations of Adam** (*Toldot Adam*). It is the secret of Rabbi Eliezer the Great’s statement: "Before the world was created, there was only He and His Name alone." Therefore, these two Names—the Lord, the Lord—contain a hidden meaning: The first Name indicates the Hidden Existence and the Beginning of this Name, which points to the truth of His Being and His Necessary Existence. The second Name indicates the second principle, the secret of "Let there be Light," including the unification of the Names in His oneness. This is the secret of "The Lord before he sinned" and "The Lord after he sinned." "Before he sinned" refers to before the existence of sin—that is, before the world was created. "After he sinned" refers to after He brought the world into existence. I do not mean "before the world was created" in a literal sense (for then the term "attribute" would not apply), but rather that He conducts Himself with the mercy of a father to a son. The root of this attribute was revealed from the very essence of Existence itself. Understand this.

# **God (*El*)**
This hints at the strength and power of Mercy. From this emerges the principle that **He is not a body**; for a body is weak and always requires a vehicle or something external to it. But He who is in the Heavens and the Earth made them... the intention is that He is not like flesh-and-blood kings who require advisors.

# **Merciful (*Rachum*)**
This attribute points to the principle that He is **Primordial**—the first and the cause of all. He brings things out of absolute non-existence. By His goodness, He brought into being that which was not.

# **And Gracious (*Chanun*)**
The fifth attribute. Moses said: "And I besought (*Va-etchanan*) the Lord at that time," for this refers to the One who gives "gratis gifts" (*matnat chinam*). Therefore, one should not pray to or serve any other, for He is the One who bestows and influences His creatures with a generous eye.

# **Slow to Anger (*Erech Apayim*)**
This attribute points to the principle of **Prophecy**. The matter of prophecy depends on a person's closeness to God. Sins act as "screens" or "veils." Since there is no man so righteous on earth who does not sin, even a tiny veil should act as a barrier. However, the attribute of "Slow to Anger" causes the veil to be overlooked, for if God is patient with the wicked, how much more so with the righteous.

# **Abounding in Kindness (*Rav Chesed*)**
He leans toward kindness. This means that according to the natural order of things, one might not be worthy of kindness, but He "leans" toward it beyond what is naturally prepared. This relates to the **Prophecy of Moses**, which was above human nature.

# **And Truth (*Emet*)**
This is the principle of the **Torah of Truth** which was given to us.

# **Preserver of Kindness for Thousands**
This is His nature, desiring the preservation of the Torah and that it should not change. This is the principle that **The Torah is eternal and shall not be changed**. He added "for thousands" to show that time will continue, for the Torah is "length of days." In this finite world, the reward of the kindness also continues for a set time—this is the "fruit" a person eats in this world, while the "principal" remains for the World to Come, which is eternally long without end.

# **Forgiver of Iniquity and Transgression**
From here emerges the principle of **Knowledge**—that He supervises human beings and their actions. If He supervises and does not close His eyes to see evil, how much more so does He supervise and see the good deeds they perform. From this also comes the principle of **Reward and Punishment**—to give to each man according to his ways. "Iniquity" is a sin done intentionally out of desire, while "Transgression" is rebellion against the Creator without the urge of desire. God examines the heart and the kidneys <note>A biblical idiom for the innermost thoughts and emotions</note> and punishes accordingly. Yet, if one returns in complete Repentance, He "forgives iniquity and transgression."

# **Forgiver of Sin**
From here emerges the principle of the **Coming of the Messiah**, for then the "filth of the serpent" <note>The spiritual impurity brought into the world by the Fall of Adam</note> will cease. God will consider intentional sins as if they were mere errors (*chata'ah*).

# **And Clears (*Ve-nakeh*)**
This refers to the **Resurrection of the Dead** for those who repent. For suffering purifies and cleanses, and certainly death completes the cleansing of filth. Then they shall be clear and pure.

***

# Thus, the 13 Principles emerge from the 13 Attributes.
I found an ancient prayer established in the name of *Tuvyomi* <note>Likely a reference to a specific sage or a liturgical tradition</note>; this is its version: "May it be Your will, the Sacred Name, thirteen [Attributes] for the sake of Abraham and Isaac, the first ones in the thirteen covenants <note>Circumcision is associated with thirteen covenants in the Talmud</note>; for the sake of Jacob the 'simple man' and his offspring, the thirteen [tribes]; grant us understanding with those who fulfill Your Torah which is interpreted through the thirteen rules <note>The thirteen hermeneutical principles of Rabbi Ishmael used to interpret the Torah</note>; and bless me... and do not withhold from me Your thirteen attributes; shine Your face upon me... and establish peace for me from my enemies through these thirteen."

***

**Explanation of the prayer:** "Abraham and Isaac, the first ones in the covenant" refers to the end of the chapter "He who circumcises" <note>Tractate Shabbat, chapter 19</note>, where it says thirteen covenants were made with Abraham... and through our ancestor Jacob and his sons, there were thirteen including the two sons of Joseph <note>Ephraim and Manasseh</note>, corresponding to the thirteen attributes... and the phrases "Bless me," "Shine Your face," and "Establish peace" correspond to the verses of the Priestly Blessing <note>Numbers 6:24-26: "The Lord bless you... The Lord make His face shine... The Lord lift His countenance... and give you peace."</note>.

It concludes with an ancient prayer that ties these thirteen-fold concepts to the Patriarchs and the Priestly Blessing.</summary>

# The Gate of Letters

---

And look there, regarding the power of connection and unification: it is explained that He has no physical form and is not a body, and that He is primordial <term>Ancient (Kedem); the Hebrew word for "ancient" or "before," which the author links to the Divine Name</term> according to the verse "The eternal God is a dwelling place" <note>original: מעונה אלוהי קדם, Deuteronomy 33:27</note>. For the combinations of the letters of the Name, along with the count of their letters and words, equals the numerical value of *Kedem* [144]. That is to say: *Yod-Vav-Dalet*, *He-Aleph*, *Vav-Aleph-Vav*, *He-Aleph* <note>The author is using a method called *Milui* (filling), where each letter of the Four-Letter Name (YHVH) is spelled out as a word. Different spellings yield different numerical totals used in Kabbalistic meditation</note>. There are thirty-four letters and six words, which total the value of *Kedem*. Its inner essence is *Chesed* (Kindness), for the inner essence of the Name is "Ancient," just as "The Lord is He and His Name is He," as I explained above. This is sufficient for the wise.

And since He is "Ancient," He is therefore the "mold" of all created beings and their root, and He alone has the power. Therefore, one must serve and pray to Him and not to any other. And since the root of all existing things in our time—from the formative to the abstract—is close to them through the flow of prophecy, they all saw evidence like a flash of lightning. This is the "beholding of the branches in their root." It is only our iniquities that create a barrier and a wall. But for those who are worthy, the flow of prophecy pours out. He poured the flow of prophecy upon the six hundred thousand of Israel at once by changing the laws of nature, and the prophecy of Moses our Teacher (peace be upon him) was exalted above them all for the sake of the Torah of Truth. 

The Torah is the revelation of His blessed Godhead. To instill eternal faith, all of Israel needed to reach this level of prophecy—to see with their own eyes the receiving of the Torah and that Moses was a "trusted servant of the house" <note>A reference to Numbers 12:7, meaning a perfectly reliable messenger</note>, so that they would believe in the Lord and in Moses His servant. This follows what the **Smag** <term>Sefer Mitzvot Gadol; a 13th-century legal code by Rabbi Moses of Coucy</term> wrote in his introduction: This positive commandment [to believe] is that the Holy One, blessed be He, created His world and gave the Torah to His people Israel through Moses His chosen one, the "trusted servant of his house." He enriched them with 613 commandments and first took them out of Egypt with signs and great wonders. He split the sea for them and brought down the Manna for them, renewed every morning for forty years. This is the wondrous sign in the eyes of all the scholars of the nations. 

And when the Master of All wished to give the Torah from the highest heavens upon Mount Sinai with terrifying voices and torches, He called to Moses, His chosen one, and said to him: "Behold, I come to you in a thick cloud, so that the people may hear when I speak with you, and may also believe in you forever" <note>Exodus 19:9</note>. Why was this necessary? Is it not already written at the Red Sea, "And they believed in the Lord and in Moses His servant"? Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: I want Israel to believe that you are a prophet through the signs and wonders you have performed; but regarding the Torah I wish to give, I do not want them to believe in you through any sign or wonder, but rather by hearing with their own ears that I am speaking with you. 

The Holy One, blessed be He, did this so that if Israel is in exile and a person comes—whether a Gentile or an Ishmaelite <note>The author refers here to other world religions, specifically Christianity and Islam, which claim to succeed or replace the Torah</note>—to tell them to leave the Torah and follow other gods, even if he performs a sign or a wonder, Israel can answer him: "Even if you multiply signs or wonders like the son of Amoz <note>Referring to the prophet Isaiah</note>, we will not believe you to change His Torah, unless we hear with our own ears God speaking with you as He spoke with Moses." For even with Moses, His chosen one, they did not want to believe in the Torah except through what we heard—that He spoke with him. After giving the Torah, He said: "You have seen that I have spoken with you from heaven" <note>Exodus 20:19</note>. This means: you are never to believe any person who says I have changed this Torah, unless you see that I speak with you from heaven to change it. 

And because we know we are not to believe any Gentile or Ishmaelite regarding a sign or wonder they might perform to change our Torah, the Torah explains how such a person has the power to perform a sign: "If there arise among you a prophet or a dreamer of dreams and gives you a sign or a wonder... and the sign or wonder comes to pass... you shall not listen to the words of that prophet... for the Lord your God is testing you" <note>Deuteronomy 13:1-4</note>. This explains to you that the power of the sign or wonder is not from his own high power; rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, brought about this sign to test Israel. 

After the passing of Moses our Teacher, prophets arose for Israel and spoke in metaphors and parables, hidden things. Thus the festivals were established. For the prophets prophesied through the Holy Spirit, serving as instruments for the Holy One. This concluded with Malachi, who was the last of all the prophets. He said at the end of his words, sealing all prophecies: "Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome day of the Lord" <note>Malachi 3:23</note>. This means: I am the last prophet, and from me until Elijah comes, no prophet shall arise. And I command you in the name of the Holy One, blessed be He: "Remember the Torah of Moses my servant, which I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel, laws and statutes" <note>Malachi 3:22</note>. This means: let it not enter your hearts that the prophets who stood before me prophesied to change the Torah of Moses, for they all came to strengthen the law of the Torah of Moses. These are the words of the **Smag**, and may his lips be kissed <note>A Hebrew idiom meaning "his words are perfectly correct"</note>.

I have already explained the Torah of the *Yod-Dalet* <note>Likely referring to the 14 Principles or a specific Kabbalistic configuration</note>, proving that the Torah is the very spirit of His Godhead, all of it His names. Just as He is eternal, so the Torah is eternal; He will not change it nor exchange it. Through the Torah, we are attached to Him through Individual Providence <term>Hashgacha Pratit; the belief that God actively supervises the lives of individuals</term>, in the secret of "the vision seen in the mirror," where He watches and knows our secrets. Through the Torah, there is reward and punishment, as it is said that they are seven: "The reward of a commandment is a commandment, and the recompense for a transgression is a transgression" <note>Ethics of the Fathers 4:2</note>.

## And He Answered
Because it is impossible for the letter of the Torah to be revealed now in this "murky garment" <note>The physical body/material world</note>, for man is... <unclear>piqar</unclear>... like faith. For when our righteous Messiah is sent, then one will forget... like his deeds... the Messiah will gladden... like wine. And the dead will awaken—as the Aramaic translation says—from the "resting of the serpent" and from the transgression of matter, and they will be purified to accompany:
->A new covenant to receive a new light.<-

### The Thirteen Principles
These are derived from the Thirteen Attributes [of Mercy]. From each and every attribute, one principle emerges. Before explaining this matter, I must first introduce the explanation of the Thirteen Attributes. For **Rashi** <term>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, the primary medieval commentator</term> spoke briefly in his explanation, and the **Tosafot** <term>Medieval glosses on the Talmud</term> in Tractate Rosh Hashanah established thirteen attributes... they are lengthy in their explanation, but still do not cover everything necessary. 

I found in the *Hora'ah Kodesh* <note>A reference to a specific source or "Holy Instruction"</note> an expansion on the intent of the Tosafot. I have copied his language: The first name [Hashem] is not counted among the thirteen attributes, but is adjacent to the call, as in "The Lord calls: The Lord, God, merciful, etc." There is no major pause between "and He called" and the first Name. Rather, both are attributes of mercy: one before a person sins, and one after he sins and repents. This appears to be Rashi’s view. 

This is proven from the Tosafot there: "Zion said: The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me." The Congregation of Israel said before the Holy One, blessed be He: "Master of the Universe, those two good attributes You gave me at Sinai, how could You forsake them and how could You forget them?" Thus it appears they are two distinct attributes. The explanation of how this is prepared from the Name *Hashem* is that it is the attribute of mercy, because the Four-Letter Name is the name of *Havayah* (Existence/Being), and this "Existence" brings forth and gives being to all that exists. Thus, He is Father and Mother to the blessed ones... and He is the Living One, Long-lived, etc., and His mercies are supreme over all His children, the blessed offspring. This is "The Lord" before one sins. 

But when one sins and becomes a "wayward and rebellious son," and He removes him because he does not listen to them... his father takes him out, etc., and He turns into "cruel" toward him. Yet if he listens to his parents' chastisement and repents, He will surely have mercy on him and he will be saved. This is "The Lord" after one has sinned and repented. Thus, the two names are two attributes of mercy.

**El (God)**
The third attribute. This indicates a language of "strength" within this attribute of mercy. As I wrote first, it follows the first two attributes to say that for one who has not sinned, or who sinned and repented, He is a fortress and a strong redeemer in times of trouble, even against the laws of nature. This is why the Psalm says "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?" <note>Psalm 22:2</note> regarding Queen Esther, who said it in a time of trouble due to the plot of Haman.

## Rachum (Merciful)
This is the fourth attribute. We must understand what this attribute adds to the Name, and why the attribute of *El* was placed in between. It would seem more logical to place "Merciful" directly after the two names of mercy rather than placing the name *El*—which does not explicitly mean mercy—between them. I heard that this Name is the attribute of mercy... between the first two Names mentioned. Even for a person who has sinned and not yet repented of his sin, His mercies are still upon him; He does not hurry to punish him and does not arouse all His wrath. 

Scripture supports us: "For the Lord your God is a merciful God; He will not fail you nor destroy you" <note>Deuteronomy 4:31</note> and "He, being merciful, forgives iniquity and does not destroy." "He will not destroy you" and "does not destroy" implies that the person *deserved* destruction, but the attribute of His name "Merciful" shields him so that He does not arouse all His wrath. Therefore, the third attribute, *El*, comes first to say that He is a fortress and strong to have mercy even by changing nature. But He only acts with that specific [miraculous] attribute for one who has not sinned or who sinned and repented—the first two attributes—for both of those are worthy of a miracle and a change in nature. But He does not act so for one who has sinned and not yet repented; such a person is dealt with by the fourth attribute, which is "Merciful" [meaning patience].

## Ve-Chanun (And Gracious)
This is the fifth attribute, which indicates a "free gift" <term>Matnat Chinam; a gift given without the recipient having earned it</term>. Thus they interpreted the word *Va'etchanan* ("And I implored"): that the righteous do not want to receive the reward for their commandments in this world; rather, whatever they receive, they want it to be a free gift. Furthermore, their own righteousness is small in their eyes, as Jacob said: "I am too small for all the kindnesses" <note>Genesis 32:11</note>. 

Furthermore, they said in Tractate Hagigah: The Holy One, blessed be He, opens three treasuries: one for those who study Torah and perform commandments, one for those who perform acts of kindness, and one for those who have merit in neither this nor that. From this last one, He gives a free gift. This is what is meant by "I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious"—meaning, even if he is not worthy.

## Erech Apayim (Slow to Anger)
The sixth attribute. He is long-suffering with His anger and wrath toward both the innocent and the wicked, hoping the latter will take it to heart and repent. The word *Apayim* (Faces/Anger) is in the plural because it is composed of the attribute of Kindness and this one [Judgment]. *Arichut* (length) refers to this, and *Racham* (mercy) refers to that. As it is written: "And He many times turned His anger away." Furthermore, He does this for the wicked just as He does for the righteous. According to this, the plural "two angers" refers to two countenances: the "Countenance of Intellect" for the righteous, and the "Countenance of Punishment" for the wicked. He is patient with the wicked according to their wickedness, to "feed" them their few merits here in this world so that they are not lost in the World to Come... or rather, he pays them here so they are destroyed in the World to Come. He is patient with the wicked so as to pay him for his small merits here, so he does not have a portion in the world that is entirely good.

<meta>This page continues the "Gate of Letters," moving from the mystical configurations of the Divine Name to the laws and spiritual significance of martyrdom—Sanctifying the Name of God (Kiddush HaShem)—and whether a specific blessing should be recited before such an act.</meta>

# The Gate of Letters

Whoever is [in a situation where the law dictates] that they should be killed rather than transgress, yet they transgress and are not killed, may God preserve us, they have desecrated the Name. If ten Jews were present, it is a public desecration of the Name and a nullification of the positive commandment of <term>Sanctifying the Name (Kiddush HaShem); the act of making God's holiness manifest in the world, often through martyrdom</term>, as well as a violation of the negative commandment against <term>Desecrating the Name (Chilul HaShem); an act that brings shame or dishonor to God's presence</term>, and so on. In my opinion, one who has the opportunity to sanctify the Name and fulfill the positive commandment of "And I shall be sanctified in the midst of the children of Israel" <note>original: ונקדשתי בתוך בני ישראל, Leviticus 22:32</note>, when it is publicized to the children of Israel or just before they kill him, should recite a blessing with joy:

-> **Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to sanctify His name in public** <-

This is the law, for we recite a blessing over the fulfillment of positive commandments, as stated in the <term>Tosefta (Additions); a legal supplement to the Mishnah</term> in the tractate of Blessings: "One who performs a commandment must bless before it." Although there are many positive commandments for which we do not recite a blessing, reasons have already been given for them, and those reasons do not apply to the commandment of "And I shall be sanctified." See the <term>Abudarham; a 14th-century Spanish rabbi famous for his commentary on Jewish liturgy</term>, who finds the reason that sometimes we do not bless over a commandment when there is doubt whether the act will be completed. For example, "And you shall judge righteously" <note>original: ושפטתם צדק, Deuteronomy 1:16</note> is a positive commandment, but we do not bless over the execution of judgment because perhaps the litigants will not accept the ruling. If so, they might forgive each other for what was claimed, and the essence of the "act" of the commandment would be upended. Similarly, we do not bless over acts that depend on the will of others, such as giving charity, the tithe for the poor, the gleanings, the forgotten sheaves, the gifts to the convert, orphan, and widow during the festivals, the gifts given to a departing slave, or giving a boundary to a convert. Since it is possible that they might refuse or waive the gift, the commandment would be upended. Some commandments do not receive a blessing because they are "a commandment that comes through a transgression" <note>original: מצוה הבאה בעבירה</note>; for example, we do not bless over <term>Chalitzah; a ceremony that releases a widow from the obligation to marry her brother-in-law</term>, because it is a commandment that comes through a transgression, as he is bypassing the commandment of the levirate marriage. The same applies to returning stolen goods, interest, and similar cases. See the aforementioned book where he elaborates. Therefore, there is no reason not to bless over the sanctification of the Name. One cannot say that we shouldn't bless because perhaps the persecutor will change his mind and release him—as the Abudarham said regarding "judging righteously"—because that logic does not apply here. Even if the Holy One, Blessed be He, performs a miracle and the person is saved, just as Daniel and his companions were saved, has he not fulfilled the commandment of "And I shall be sanctified"? For the moment he surrendered his body to be killed, he sanctified the Name in the midst of the children of Israel. Regardless, the temporary suffering of life is not a desecration; on the contrary, like the gleanings and forgotten sheaves, many commandments are praised for this reason. Perhaps they do not bless for this reason on commandments of abundance and kindness, and that is why we only bless on positive commandments that a person is obligated to pursue and perform, such as <term>Tefillin (phylacteries)</term>, <term>Mezuzah (doorpost scroll)</term>, <term>Sukkah (tabernacle)</term>, <term>Lulav (palm branch)</term>, <term>Matzah (unleavened bread)</term>, and <term>Maror (bitter herbs)</term>, and the like. This is not the case for commandments one is not obligated to pursue, such as gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner of the field (*pe'ah*). One is not obligated to buy a field just to give gleanings, unless he already has a field and a harvest. Likewise, one is not obligated to pursue being a judge; if he is a judge, he is commanded to judge righteously, but he is not obligated to bring himself to that position. According to this, one might think we shouldn't bless over the sanctification of the Name because one is not obligated to bring himself into such a situation—on the contrary, if he can flee, he should flee, using all his resources, "giving all the wealth of his house" <note>Song of Songs 8:7</note> so as not to be killed. However, I have reconsidered, as one can counter this logic with the cases of charity and merit, which are commandments one *should* pursue, as it is written, "Happy is he who considers the poor" <note>Psalm 41:2</note>, meaning he doesn't wait for the poor man to come to him. There are three reasons why we don't bless regarding "righteousness" and other cases in Abudarham: perhaps the poor person will refuse, and as for other commandments, there is a third reason: a researcher in the Jerusalem [Talmud] notes that regarding the choice in the commandment of sanctifying the Name, one should pursue this commandment, as Rabbi Akiva said: "All my days I was troubled by this verse, 'with all your soul'—even if He takes your soul—when will it come to my hand that I might fulfill it?" <note>Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 61b</note>. Even if one says this isn't the literal meaning or the law to pursue death for the sanctification of the Name, for the Sages already wrote that as long as there is an extra commandment through which generations can live and his soul remains alive... but when the commander brings it to his hand in a way that he is forced to fulfill it, it is clear to me that he should bless. There is another version from the Tosefta in the third chapter of *Berakhot* and at the end of *Pesachim*, and according to the custom of <term>Ashkenaz (German/Eastern European Jewry)</term> where they bless during the prayer "It was You before the world was created," saying: "Blessed are You... who sanctifies His name in public."

---

<margin>
It is written in <term>Sefer Hasidim (Book of the Pious); a 12th-13th century foundational text of German-Jewish pietism</term>: Why do we bless over the Hanukkah [candles]? [Similar logic to] the obligation... in section 9, sign 7, as the <term>Smak (Sefer Mitzvot Katan); a popular 13th-century code of laws</term> ruled... and it is not in the book... he is obligated in the commandments... for the covering [of the blood]... in the absence... therefore... as if he were taking [it] in the tractate of *Menachot*... [this marginal note is highly abbreviated and difficult to decipher, but it compares the requirements for blessings across various physical commandments like ritual slaughter and Hanukkah].
</margin>

And this was established according to the Jerusalem Talmud... that one should take care that His name is not called in vain... and this is the decree of the Scripture for us, that we bless over it even if it hasn't happened to us today, being here. Nevertheless, whoever actually sanctifies the Name [should bless]. Even according to <term>Maimonides (Rambam); the preeminent 12th-century philosopher and codifier</term>, who did not write a concluding signature for the blessing "It was You," and as is the custom of the <term>Sephardim (Jews of Spanish/Middle Eastern descent)</term>, nonetheless, in his opinion, if the opportunity for sanctifying the Name comes to one's hand, he should certainly bless, especially since this commandment is more precious than all the positive commandments in the world. All blessings are dependent on holiness (*Kedushah*), for the formula of all blessings includes "Who has sanctified us," so how could we not bless over holiness itself? After I wrote this in my sermon, I found that the accepted authority, our teacher Rabbi <term>Menahem Recanati; a 13th-century Italian kabbalist and halakhist</term>, wrote in section 76: "One who sanctifies the Name is obligated to bless over the sanctification of the Name... since it is a positive commandment from the Torah, as it is written, 'And I shall be sanctified in the midst of the children of Israel.'" I rejoiced that I had reached the same conclusion as this great authority. However, regarding the wording of the blessing, it seems clear to bless "to sanctify His name in public." For the Sages of Israel have already disagreed on the logic of the wording of blessings—sometimes we bless using the prefix "on" (*al*) and sometimes using the prefix "to" (*le*). One cannot learn from one to the other. Commandments performed immediately should be blessed with "on," such as "on the reading of the Megillah," "on the immersion," "on the washing of hands," "on the eating of Matzah," "on the eating of bitter herbs." But for those commandments like wrapping oneself in *Tzitzit* (fringes) or sitting in a *Sukkah*, the language should indicate a continuing state: to be wrapped in *Tzitzit*, to sit in the *Sukkah*, to eat, to travel, and to sleep there. The holiness shall rest upon him from several blessings... afterward they brought the opinion of the RI"V <note>Rabbi Isaac ben Judah</note>, who distinguished that for commandments that can be performed by a messenger, one blesses using "on" (*al*), but for a commandment that one must perform personally, one must bless using "to" (*le*). Just as the <term>Rosh (Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel); a major 13th-century legal authority</term> wrote... it seems from their words that they agree... and I find this a very good reason despite the questions they raised against it... therefore, one must bless here with "to" (*le*), for is there any commandment more personal than this, which cannot be done by a messenger? Do not misunderstand the language of Rabbi Recanati who wrote "to bless *on* the sanctification of the Name" to mean that this is the specific formula; rather, the RI"V said a person is obligated to bless *regarding* the sanctification of the awesome and revered Name, but the formula is as I said. Perhaps he [Recanati] intended his own formula, but according to the understanding of the Rosh and other Sages... or like Hanukkah as I wrote, and it should not be changed.

---

<margin>
In *Sefer Hasidim*: why do we bless over the Hanukkah candle? ... one might extinguish it... and I have found a better reason... the language is... because the lighting... if one blessed "on the lighting of the Hanukkah candle," it would imply [the act was already done]... therefore we bless "to kindle the Hanukkah light," for we are obligated to kindle it for the sake of Hanukkah.
</margin>

## And Know
That this blessing is because we bless over the positive commandment of "And I shall be sanctified in the midst of the children of Israel." This commandment is to sanctify His name in a public forum (*parhesia*) among Israel. But when it is not in public, even though one should be killed rather than transgress—such as in cases of [avoiding] idolatry, murder, and forbidden sexual relations, or any transgression during a time of religious persecution—even though he cherishes himself, it is not for the sake of "And I shall be sanctified," or it is not the place for a blessing. Likewise, for those holy and pure ones of Israel who are tortured so that they will recant something that would harm Israel, and they suffer tortures worse than death—even if it is in public and known to many in Israel—there is no place for this blessing for two reasons. First, the commandment of "And I shall be sanctified" only applies when the Gentile wants to make him deviate from the religion of the Torah or the religion of Israel... and he wants to make him violate the religion in public; it is to this that "And I shall be sanctified" refers. But tortures that are not intended to make him violate the religion... as explained in the tractate of *Ta'anit*... this is not included in "And I shall be sanctified." How could he bless? Perhaps, God forbid, he will not withstand the test. For our Sages of blessed memory said, "Had they [the torturers] beaten Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah [as severely as others], they would have [succumbed]..." But for the positive commandment of the other letters... the blessing and the strength and holiness... he shall say to him and wrap him in honor...

---

## It is Written
In the Zohar: One who surrenders himself to death for the sanctification of the Name and makes a firm resolution in his mind during the acceptance of the Yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven [the *Shema* prayer] and "Love [the Lord your God]... with all your soul," even if He takes your soul—it is as if the thing was done in practice. It is considered like the Binding of Isaac, on the condition that he is righteous in all his ways, for "a sacrifice with a blemish will not be accepted." I have been graced with a beautiful prayer for this, that a person should pray that the Holy One, Blessed be He, should help him toward the sanctification of His Name, and it is arranged among the other prayers.

<meta>This page continues the "Gate of Letters," a section of the manuscript focused on the practical application of faith and mystical intentions. While the previous page discussed the legal aspects of martyrdom, this section begins with daily spiritual mindfulness and returns to the laws of Sanctifying the Name toward the end.</meta>

# The Gate of Letters

**To Receive Faith:** When a person rises from their bed or engages in any business in the world, before speaking even a single word, they should turn, wash their face, and think of the Creator of the universe, may He be blessed. One should hold a steady thought that He is One, Unique, and Individual. Reflect that He is the King of Kings, the Holy One, Blessed be He; He is the Great One and Ruler, the root and essence of all worlds. One should gaze at the heavens and the earth and contemplate in their heart the verse: "Lift up your eyes on high and see: who created these?" <note>original: "שאו עיניכם וראו מי ברא אלה", Isaiah 40:26</note> Reflect that He, may He be blessed, created existence out of absolute nothingness. Think: "How manifold are Your works, O Lord!" <note>original: "מה רבו מעשיך ה'", Psalm 104:24</note> and contemplate the limits of His handiwork in the creation of the earth and all its hosts—the inanimate, the vegetable, the animal, and the speaking <note>The "speaking" refers to human beings, the fourth level of creation in medieval philosophy</note>—as well as great creatures, wondrous wisdoms, great mysteries, all that is within it, and the wonders of the Leviathan. He forms mountains and creates the wind and flaming fire. All of this is considered like a mustard seed compared to the world of the celestial spheres, and each sphere is naught compared to the sphere above it. All of them are considered as nothing compared to an angel, and one angel compared to another is "high above the high" <note>original: "גבוה מעל גבוה", Ecclesiastes 5:7</note>, by the thousands and tens of thousands, with no number to His legions. All of them are as if they were not when compared to the Throne, high and lifted up, and the Throne is as nothing compared to His Glory. He is the Cause of all causes and the Reason for all reasons, and there is none beside Him. Then, one will be filled with awe to fear His Presence, may He be blessed, and love will also enter the heart to cleave to Him. After this meditation, one should begin with the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord..." etc.

**Generally**, part of "cleaving in faith" is that for every action one wishes to do—even in the near future—one should say: "I will do this if God wills," whether it is a great matter or a small matter. The sign for this is the verse: "The counsel of the Lord, it shall stand" <note>original: "עצת ה' היא תקום", Proverbs 19:21</note>. The word *hi* ("it" or "she") <note>original: היא</note> is an acronym for "If the Name Desires" <note>original: אם יחפוץ השם</note>, for then their desire will be aligned with the "Place of His Glory." Similarly, if one wishes to engage in commerce, such as buying or selling merchandise, they should say: "I trust in the Lord and hope in the Lord; may His kindness protect me, and may the Name, blessed be He, send me my sustenance and my needs." For salvation belongs to the Lord. Do not think He must open the windows of heaven to drop down a sack full of coins; rather, the Name, blessed be He, prepares it through His good will via nature, as our Sages of blessed memory said: "'The Lord your God will bless you'—one might think even if they sit idle? Therefore, the verse says: 'in all that you do.'" One should trust that this business is the means sent by the Name, blessed be He, to decree for them. This is also written in the *Duties of the Heart* <term>Duties of the Heart; (Chovot HaLevavot) an 11th-century work of Jewish philosophy by Bahya ibn Paquda focused on the internal spiritual life</term>. If one profits, they should say: "I profited with the help of the Name," as it is written: "And you shall know that it is the Lord who gives you the strength to achieve wealth." Conversely, if some misfortune occurs, God forbid, one should say: "This was from the Lord." If it happened because of some sin, they should examine their deeds "measure for measure" and correct the wrong. Do not be like those people without knowledge who are like animals; when the Name brings a loss of money, they respond by reducing their charity or the like. This is like "extinguishing a fire with straw"—the fire is quenched for a moment, but afterward, it blazes even more. It is also like a thirsty person who slakes their thirst with salt water; for a moment the thirst departs, but afterward, they become even thirstier. Rather, one should examine if they perhaps sinned regarding money and return it to its owner, or perhaps withheld charity; let them give, and give again, and thank the Lord, may He be blessed, for "he who confesses and abandons [sin] shall find mercy." When going to perform any matter, one should say: "I am going to do this with the permission of the Name, blessed be He, and for the sake of His Name," and pray a short prayer in this version: "Master of the Universe, in Your holy words it is written, 'He who trusts in the Lord, kindness shall surround him.' It is also written, 'And You give life to them all.' Apportion to me from Your kindness to place a blessing in the work of my hands in this Your world."

**And all** that happens to a person, they should believe it is from Him, may He be blessed. For example, if a wicked person meets them and insults or shames them, they should accept it with love, saying: "The Lord told him to curse" <note>A reference to King David's reaction to Shimei ben Gera in 2 Samuel 16:10</note>. He is a messenger of the Omnipresent because of sins. One should behave this way with all occurrences, whether good or bad, believing and saying: "This was from the Lord." Likewise, in every action or craft one does, whether it is a commandment or a mundane matter, the Name of Heaven should be "regular in their mouth." For example, if building a structure, buying a vessel, or making a new garment. Thus writes the *Beginning of Wisdom* <term>Beginning of Wisdom; (Reshit Chochma) a 16th-century kabbalistic moral manual by Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas</term> in the "Gate of Love," chapter 9: Before performing an act, one should repeat and say with their mouth and express with their lips: "This thing, or this commandment, I am doing to unify the <term>Shekhinah; the Divine Presence represented as feminine</term> with the <term>Holy One, Blessed be He; the masculine aspect of the Divine</term>," and they should focus on this unification.

**Let the Lord be mentioned** and intended so that every conduct is directed toward the Creator. For the Morning Prayer, one should say: "Behold, I am going to unify the Shekhinah with the Holy One, Blessed be He, with the 'Right Arm,'" and similarly for other prayers and commandments. This matter is explained in the Zohar, and these are the words of Rabbi Eliezer, of blessed memory: "Rabbi Eliezer said: In all of a person’s deeds, they should be for the Holy Name, and they should mention with their mouth the Holy Name over everything they do, so that all is for His service. Then the <term>Other Side; (Sitra Achra) the realm of evil or impurity</term> will not rest upon them, because they have invited the Holy Name, and then holiness will dwell upon that work." Although he began by speaking of what a person does—meaning their physical actions—it might be that even in a commandment there is some flaw, for God "tests the hearts" and knows all. But when at the start of the action one explicitly says it is for His service for the sake of the Lord, with the intention for unification, etc., then all "external forces" are removed so that the commandment does not become spoiled. This is also evident from his words saying "In *all* of a person’s deeds"—what does "all" include? Certainly, it means not only holy blessings, which must be mentioned (since the "husk" of impurity wants to grasp onto the spiritual commandments even more than onto physical things of no substance), but even in worldly matters, one should say "For the sake of the Lord," so that no influence of filth dwells on any of their deeds. If the ancients, peace be upon them, behaved this way, it was because before performing a commandment, they would express the intention with their mouths. Regarding Rabbi Abba, peace be upon him, at the three Shabbat meals, the Zohar says: "When Rabbi Abba would sit at the Shabbat meal, he would rejoice in each one and say, 'This is the holy meal...'" and so too for the other meals. Likewise, one pious man said in the Zohar: "Come and see, it is written: 'And all the women whose hearts stirred them in wisdom spun the goats' hair' <note>Exodus 35:26</note>. This means that while they were doing the work, they would say: 'This is for the Sanctuary,' 'This is for the Tabernacle,' 'This is for the Veil.' Thus the craftsmen of Israel brought holiness upon their hands, and the work was sanctified, and when it ascended to its place, it ascended in holiness." It says further later on that even in worldly matters one must mention God: "One who builds a building, when they begin to build, they must mention that it is for His service—such as building a synagogue—and then they merit heavenly assistance and the Holy One, Blessed be He, invites holiness upon it and calls it 'Peace.'" What is the meaning of "And you shall visit your habitation [and not sin]" <note>Job 5:24</note>? This means expressing the word with the mouth when it is for the sake of heaven, and then they merit assistance and "shall not sin." From this, we can derive the rule for all other worldly matters. (Thus far from *Beginning of Wisdom*). In my opinion, it is not enough to simply say "In the name of the Lord I do this" as if it were a physical task; rather, one should use the phrasing used for a commandment: "For the sake of the unification of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and His Shekhinah, through that Hidden and Concealed One." One should say this for every craft and action. The reason is as I wrote above: all deeds should be for the sake of heaven. Even a physical act, like building a house, one should say: "I am building it so it may be a place and a house of assembly for those who study Torah." In this way, even the profane becomes holy, and everything becomes a commandment. This explains what is said: "The Lord was with him"—meaning the Name of Heaven was "regular in his mouth." A difficulty arises regarding the wife of Samson; it is written, "She saw that he had told her all his heart," and our Sages explained that this means he mentioned the Name of God, saying, "I am a Nazirite of God." She knew that this righteous man would not mention the Name in vain. Rather, the "regularity of the Name" in one's mouth is as I explained: in every matter in the world, saying "If the Lord wills" or "With the help of the Lord" or "For the sake of the Lord I am doing this," and the like. However, to explicitly mention the Name of God [the Tetragrammaton] in such a way—God forbid.

**Also** belonging to the principle of Faith is the positive commandment of **Sanctifying the Name** (Kiddush HaShem). This means a person must surrender their soul, body, and resources for the sanctity of His Name, may He be blessed, as it is said: "And I shall be sanctified in the midst of the children of Israel." Sanctifying the Name occurs when a non-Jew intends to make a Jew transgress their religion and the matter is "in public." "In public" means in the presence of ten Israelites; in such a case, one must be killed rather than transgress. This applies to any of the transgressions if the non-Jew intends to make them abandon the religion, even for a "shoelace strap" <note>original: ארכר שרוח (likely a corruption of 'arka d'msana'), referring to a minor Jewish custom or distinct way of dressing</note> which is merely a general custom in Israel—if the non-Jew comes to make them change it, they must be killed rather than transgress. If it is during a "time of decree" <note>A period of government-led religious persecution</note>, one must be killed rather than transgress even in private. These laws are explained well in the Talmud and the legal Codes. Regarding what was said about "in public," this does not necessarily mean ten people must be physically standing there. Rather, even if they are not watching—if the matter takes place in a hidden spot where those ten are not present—if the matter is publicized to ten, it is called "in the midst of the children of Israel." Proof for this comes from the Talmud: "Was not Esther [acting] in public?" <note>Sanhedrin 74b</note> The difficulty there is: perhaps when she was taken, they took her at a time when ten Israelites were not present? However, since the matter was public knowledge, even if not seen, it is called "in the midst of the children of Israel." Thus it was taught: Rabbi Yohanan said in the name of Rabbi Simeon ben Jehozadak: They voted and concluded in the upper chamber of the house of Nitezeh in Lydda: Regarding all transgressions in the Torah, if a person is told "Transgress and you will not be killed," they should transgress and not be killed, except for idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and murder. Regarding idolatry, we do not distinguish between a time of decree and a time of no decree, nor between private and public, nor between whether the non-Jew acts for his own pleasure or intends to make the Jew abandon the religion. The *Knesset Yosef* wrote that the reason for this is not because of the prohibition of Desecrating the Name, but because of the inherent severity of those specific sins; therefore, they are forbidden in every circumstance. Maimonides wrote in the *Book of Commandments* and the *Foundations of the Torah*: Any-

To bless and to shine light upon a fellow man with blessings—from where do we learn this? From Moses, as it is written: "Behold, you are this day as the stars of heaven for multitude." <note>Deuteronomy 1:10</note> What is written afterward? "May the Lord God of your fathers add to you a thousand times so many more as you are," etc. <note>Deuteronomy 1:11</note> These were two blessings: one was "The Lord God of your fathers..." which is one, and afterward "and bless you, as He has promised you," to acknowledge and add blessings upon blessings. And if a person counts the praise of his friend but does not radiate blessings upon him, he is seized first from Above <note>Meaning he is held spiritually accountable for his stinginess of spirit</note>. But if he blesses him, he himself is blessed from Above. And when a person seeks to bless another, he must do so with a **good eye** <note>Meaning with genuine generosity and without jealousy</note> and not with an **evil eye**. In everything, the Holy One, Blessed be He, desires the love of the heart. Now, if the Holy One, Blessed be He, requires one who blesses his friend to do so with a good eye and a good heart, how much more so does one who blesses the Holy One, Blessed be He, require a good eye, a good heart, and the love of the heart? For this reason, it says: "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart," etc. This ends his words.

<margin>Source: Sefer Chasidim</margin>
**A**nd your fellow’s money shall be as dear to you as your own. If a loss reaches your fellow, you are obligated to seek mercy for him—that the Holy One, Blessed be He, should fill his lack, as is found in the blessings in the chapter "One who Recites" <note>A chapter in Tractate Berakhot</note>, where they say to a man concerning his ox or donkey that died: "May the Place <term>The Place (HaMakom): a traditional name for God, suggesting His presence fills every 'place'</term> fill your lack." The general rule that arises: one must always see to it that they are beloved below and pleasant Above, as it is written: "Good with God and with men," and it says, "And find favor and good understanding in the sight of God and man." We have learned: "Anyone with whom the spirit of creatures is pleased, the Spirit of the Place is pleased with him." <note>Pirkei Avot 3:10</note> One should always look to increase love, as seen in the first chapter of *Shabbat*: Rava bar Machasiah said in the name of Rav Chama bar Guria in the name of Rav: "One who gives a gift to his fellow must inform him," as it is said, "to know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you." <note>Exodus 31:13</note> It was also taught this way: From here Rabbi Simeon ben Gamliel said: "One who gives a piece of bread to a child must inform the mother." What should he do to the child? <note>To show the mother he was fed</note> Abaye said: He should rub him with oil and put blue kohl around his eyes. And nowadays, when we worry about sorcery <note>The original text notes "Kishuf," or magic, fearing such marks might be misinterpreted</note>, what should he do? Rav Papa said: He should rub him with a bit of that same food. This ends the quote.

**And if** one knows any good news to tell a man or woman of Israel, he should run to them to tell the news, as it is written: "He is a good man and comes with good news." <note>2 Samuel 18:27</note> And he should inform them of any stumbling block. One should also look out for his fellow on the road or in any business, and give him guidance, saying to him: "My brother, be careful in this matter." For the great principle of "Love your neighbor as yourself" means he should take the other's well-being into his own soul. It is said in the book *Orchot Tzaddikim* <note>The Ways of the Righteous, a 15th-century ethical work</note> in the Gate of Love, and it was copied 
<margin>Source: Sefer Chasidim. One who gives a gift to his fellow needs his assistance... regarding buying and selling... and he should not withhold money from him... etc.</margin> 
greatly because behaving with affection and friendship with people brings other benefits in this world. When one behaves with love toward everyone and helps them, if he should fall, many will help and support him. If a man stands against him to quarrel with him, many will silence those who speak evil and will counsel them otherwise. If trouble comes upon him, everyone grieves for him and gives him a hand. If he comes to poverty and want, many will have mercy on him by giving gifts. And the benefit for the World to Come: because he is beloved by all, his words are heard, and he will have the power to rebuke people so they improve their ways. Also, through love, he will live in peace with the world, and through love he is quiet, tranquil, and free for discipline and to do good deeds. Also, through love, they will help him and do his work... and he will find extra relief to serve the Creator, may He be blessed, with perfect service. On account of love, he finds favor in the eyes of all who see him, and his good deeds will be accepted by all, and each one will desire to do as he does. And what is the path for a person to reach love? Let every person be remembered by him in this way: that he should help with his soul and his money according to his ability. Helping with the soul means he should serve every person, whether poor or rich...
<margin>Be careful not to visit your fellow's house too often... as it says "Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor’s house, lest he be weary of you and hate you." <note>Proverbs 25:17</note></margin>
...the work of the city. With his money, it means he should lend to the rich in their time of need... and similarly, he should bestow gifts according to his strength... sending portions and presents even to the wealthy. And he should be generous with his own: if he has business with people, all his dealings should be in good faith. He should not be fastidious over a small matter with his fellow. He should always desire that his fellow benefit from him, and he should not strive to benefit from his fellow. His words should be gentle with people; if they shame him, he should not shame them; if a man errs, he should not mislead him. He should carry the yoke of the world on his own neck, but he should not be a burden upon them. He should not quarrel with people, but should receive every person with joy and a pleasant countenance, for a pleasant countenance strengthens love. He should deal with his fellow for his fellow's benefit and comfort every person in their sadness and anxiety. If a man reveals a secret to him, he must not reveal it, even if the man makes him angry. He should not speak evil of a man, nor should he listen to evil spoken of a man. He should always strive to find merit for people wherever possible. He should be even more careful than this, and then he will be beloved by all. He should tolerate every person and overlook things, not exalting himself over anyone, but humbling himself before everyone. In everything, he should aim for the sake of Heaven. This ends his words.

And if, Heaven forbid, your fellow has done you some evil, forgive him immediately, for you are required to love him as yourself. <note>The author now transitions to the dangers of conflict</note>... For the greatest evil in the world is **strife** <term>Machloket: communal division or bitter argument</term>, which is harder than **idolatry**. As our Sages of blessed memory said: The generation of Ahab were victorious in their wars even though they were idolaters, because there was connection and peace among them. But the generation of Saul were defeated in their wars, even though they had no sin, because there were informers and stirrers of strife among them. The secret of the matter is as explained above: we, the Assembly of Israel, are unified in the secret of the "True One." When there is strife, then, Heaven forbid, there is division and separation Above, "a cutting of the plantings" <note>A Kabbalistic metaphor for causing a rupture in the divine unity</note>. The prohibition of strife is from Moses. When one spark of fire is lit, the bonfire grows—God save us—a fire that consumes unto destruction. As Rav Ashi said in Sanhedrin: "Strife is like a leak in a water pipe; once it starts, it widens." 

I heard from my relative, the wondrous Sage, our teacher Rabbi Pinchas Segal, of blessed memory, that this thing is hinted at in the letters of the word **Machloket** <note>מחלוקת</note>. How so?
*   **M** <note>מ</note>: It has only a small opening at the bottom; such is the beginning of a quarrel. 
*   **Ch** <note>ח</note>: Afterward it increases and becomes a wide-open gate.
*   **L** <note>ל</note>: Then the fire of strife flares up to the heights; this is the letter Lamed, a tower flying in the air. 
*   **V** <note>ו</note>: Afterward it descends below to the abyss; this is the letter Vav <note>A vertical line</note>, reaching the height of the firmament and the depth of the earth. 
*   **K** <note>ק</note>: Then it lasts for a long time and has a standing position; this is the shape of the Kof, which has two legs. 
*   **T** <note>ת</note>: And the letter Vav that separates is the "staff of the tribe" <note>The letter Tav is sometimes described as a Vav with a foot, or here associated with the staff of judgment</note> in his hand to maintain the strife. 

But this staff turns into a snake! Therefore, whoever hopes to live and merit seeing the face of the Divine Presence should run from the venom of the snake and distance himself from strife, even from the smallest beginning. Why should I elaborate on the disgrace of strife when all the books are full of it? Take this rule in your hand: the sin of strife is harder than the sin of idolatry, as we found with Ahab and Saul. Furthermore, our Sages said in three places: The Holy One, Blessed be He, overlooked idolatry but did not overlook strife. First, in the days of the generation of Enosh, when they began to worship idols... but because they were among themselves robbers and oppressors, He did not overlook them, as it says, "for the earth was filled with violence." Second, in the generation of the wilderness, when Israel came to the incident of the Calf, the Holy One, Blessed be He, forgave them; but when they came to strife, He did not overlook it, for everywhere you find the desecration of strife, you find a great plague—as we know from the strife of Korah. Third, the idol of Micah: because there was peace among them, He gave them a delay... but when the tribes divided against the tribes of Judah and Benjamin and there was no peace, they brought these calamities upon those... five hundred thousand chosen men of Israel fell slain... and Pekah in Judah killed one hundred and twenty thousand in one day. Surely the lowest of Israel would suffer all four deaths before he would commit idolatry; how then should he not restrain himself from creating strife, which is harder than idolatry? Rava said: "Anyone who passes over his traits <note>Meaning one who is not fastidious about his own honor and forgives easily</note>, they pass over all his transgressions." One should not only not grieve over a thing done to him that might strengthen strife, but on the contrary, he should rejoice that this opportunity came to him to fulfill the trait of "passing over his traits." He is a "pious man among the pious." When he went to his bed, he would say: "I forgive and pardon anyone who has distressed me." Come and see how great is the power of peace, for even to enemies the Holy One, Blessed be He, said: "Offer them peace," and even in this time our Sages said we ask after the welfare of the heathens for the sake of the paths of peace. They said of Rabban Yochanan...

It uses Hebrew letter shapes as an allegory for how arguments escalate from small openings to destructive fires that damage the divine unity.</summary>
