# The Gate of Letters

## The Letter Aleph is concluded

### **The Letter Bet: Fellow Creatures** <note>Hebrew: *Beriyot*, referring to all created beings, but specifically used here for human relationships.</note>
It is written, "And you shall love the Lord your God," <note>Deuteronomy 6:5</note> and it is also written, "And you shall love your neighbor as yourself." <note>Leviticus 19:18</note> Behold, these two loves are joined together and become one through the unity of the Creator, may He be blessed. For this is how we conclude the blessing: "Who chooses His people Israel with love," and "Who loves His people Israel." We then recite the verse of Divine Unity <note>The Shema: "Hear O Israel..."</note> followed by the commandment of loving God: "And you shall love the Lord your God." Furthermore, the Ten Commandments conclude with the words "which belongs to your neighbor." <note>Exodus 20:14, concluding the prohibition against coveting.</note>

The commentators have written that there are 620 letters in the Ten Commandments, corresponding to the numerical value of *Keter* <note>original: "כתר" meaning Crown, which equals 620 in Gematria</note>, the Crown of the Torah. 613 of these letters hint at the 613 commandments <note>known as the *Taryag* mitzvot</note>, with each letter representing one commandment. In this case, what purpose do the remaining letters serve? The ancient sages discussed this. Some say they correspond to the seven Rabbinic commandments, while others suggest different matters. However, the clearest explanation is one I observed in the words of *The Zioni* <note>Menachem Zioni, a 14th-century Italian Kabbalist</note>, who says the remaining letters are those in the phrase "which belongs to your neighbor" <note>original: "אשר לרעך" — *asher l're'echa*</note>. This is the "foot" upon which the entire Torah stands. This accounts for the 7 letters <note>which, added to 613, reach the 620 of the Crown</note>.

This is similar to what is taught in the section "With what may we light?" <note>a chapter of the Mishnah, Shabbat 31a</note> regarding Hillel the Elder's instruction to the prospective convert who wanted to learn the whole Torah while standing on one foot. Hillel told him: "That which is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. This is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary—go and learn it." The explanation of "your fellow" is: "That which is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow," and "Your friend and your father’s friend, do not forsake" <note>Proverbs 27:10</note>. This refers to the Holy One, Blessed be He—do not transgress His words, for it is surely hateful to you when a friend transgresses your own words. It also refers to your literal fellow, regarding matters like theft, robbery, adultery, and the majority of the commandments. These are his words.

Indeed, if you examine this closely, you will find that the majority of commandments depend on loving one's fellow as oneself: all the laws of charity, the forgotten sheaf, the corners of the field, priestly gifts and tithes, and honest business dealings. It includes the prohibition against interest and many similar laws. Furthermore, it encompasses almost all character traits: avoiding resentment and enmity, loving kindness and showing mercy, judging others favorably, not standing idly by your neighbor's blood, and distancing oneself from gossip, slander, libel, mockery, jealousy, hatred, and grudges. It touches on anger, theft, the pursuit of honor, and thousands upon thousands of similar traits. One will fulfill most "positive" commandments and avoid most "negative" ones, becoming perfect in all character traits, if they love their fellow as themselves. Even matters that seem unrelated to human relations, such as forbidden foods or the prohibition of leaven on Passover, can be fulfilled through this principle. If one loves their fellow as themselves, they will surely love the Holy One, Blessed be He, whose providence and "unfathomable kindness" <note>original: *chesed chinam*</note> sustain the world.

Behold, "love your neighbor as yourself" is the leg upon which the world stands. Loving your neighbor is the catalyst for "loving the Lord your God." This is the secret of the Patriarchs, as it is said, "Abraham who loved Me" <note>Isaiah 41:8</note>. These Patriarchs are the two pillars of the Torah, and it is fitting that they resemble one another. Just as the love of the Omnipresent must be "with all your heart, soul, and might"—meaning to fulfill God's commands with the heart and soul, distancing oneself from evil and base desires, and inflaming the soul with divine thought until one would sacrifice their life rather than transgress—so too in the love of fellow creatures, one must be perfect.

**How so?**
"With all your heart" means not hating any person in your heart, as it is written, "Do not hate your brother in your heart" <note>Leviticus 19:17</note>. Hatred in the heart mostly stems from envy. Hatred born of envy is far greater than hatred born of insult or pride, for the latter may have a remedy through reason or apology. However, hatred born of envy has no remedy, for every time the envied person succeeds, the "smoke" of that fire rises again. This is what destroyed the Second Temple; though they did not commit idolatry, sexual immorality, or murder like in the First Temple period, it was this hatred that cast my people into exile and scattered them. This remains the cause of all the expulsions, killings, and troubles we have ever faced in this exile; the stench of this smoke still rises to destroy us. This hatred in the heart is called "unfounded hatred" <note>term: *sinat chinam* — hatred without a practical cause, purely internal and spiteful</note>, and it is the most difficult of all because it involves both the malice of envy—which removes a person from the world—and the hatred within the heart. Regarding this, it is said "with all your heart," for a person is obligated not only to avoid speaking evil, but to love the person in their heart and remove any trace of envy or competition. This is "love of the heart."

### **Furthermore**
There is another type of hatred: when a person hates his fellow not out of envy or competition, but because of the "evil of the traits" in the soul that are stirred within him. Just as nature dictates that one loves those who are similar to them, so when people differ in their traits and temperaments, hatred may fall between them. This is not as severe as the first type, but it is difficult to correct. Therefore, we are warned to be careful of it, as it is said, "with all your soul." This means even if your fellow's temperament is not equal to your own "soul," you are obligated to bear with him and love him for the sake of the Creator who made him.

The third type of hatred is that which arises from "monetary matters" <note>original: *dara d'mamona*</note>. This is what is meant by "with all your might" <note>In Hebrew, *me'odecha* (might) is often interpreted as *mamonecha* (money)</note>. Similarly, this hatred often falls between people of the same profession, for "every craftsman hates the members of his own craft." We are warned against this as well. If a craftsman considers that everything—wealth and honor—comes from God, and that no man can touch what is prepared for his fellow, he will not hate his professional rival. On the contrary, he should love him because of their similarity.

Likewise, if a dispute and a commandment <note>likely referring to a legal obligation or a lawsuit</note> fall between people, and they "approach the judgment and are judged," most will quarrel over the matter of the dispute. But truth must take its course—why should they hate one another afterward? For all of the community is like a single body made of different limbs. Just as if a man's hand were to strike his leg, the leg would not strike the hand back to take revenge, so too if a man sins against another, it is a commandment not to take revenge or bear a grudge, but to forgive him immediately and pray to God to forgive him. This is what our forefather Abraham did: "And Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech." <note>Genesis 20:17</note>

One should also consider: how much do we ourselves sin every single day before the Creator, and He forgives our iniquities and transgressions? If we are "children of the Lord your God," we are commanded to walk in His ways. We are therefore obligated to forgive as He does and to overcome our natural traits. For whoever "overcomes his traits" <note>original: *ma'avir al midotav* — meaning to let go of personal grievances and anger</note>, Heaven passes over his sins, measure for measure. "You shall surely rebuke your fellow" in ways that settle upon the heart, so as not to bear a sin because of him—not in thought, speech, or action. Instead, in these three ways, we should benefit him. This is "love your neighbor as yourself." All things that are loved and desired by you, you must strive through action and speech to do for your fellow, to seek peace between a man and his wife and between a person and their fellow, as it is written, "Seek peace and pursue it." And in thought, you should desire in your heart that good should come to him, and you should pray to God for him as you pray for your own well-being. These are his words.

### **And the Worst**
The worst and most difficult types of hatred include those who hate the ones who rebuke and discipline them to show them the straight path, as it is said, "They hate him who rebukes in the gate." <note>Amos 5:10</note> There is a hatred even worse than this: those who hate the doers of good and the pursuers of justice, as it says, "They are my adversaries because I follow the thing that is good." <note>Psalms 38:21</note> Those who walk in the way of hatred are "haters of God," for they hate those He loves, and they hate the Torah and the commandments; since they loathe and despise the laws, they hate those who fulfill them.

### **In the Zohar**
At the beginning of the section *Pekudei*, Rabbi Isaac opened with: "The Lord has been mindful of us; He will bless—He will bless the house of Israel," etc. <note>Psalms 115:12</note> "The Lord has been mindful of us and will bless"—these are the men who entered the darkness of the wilderness, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, blessed them and added to them at all times. Come and see: he who speaks of the praise of his fellow among other people must also bless him...

<column-break/>

In the verse "Be attentive, O Israel" there are 30 letters, and so too in the verse "Love your neighbor as yourself" there are 13 letters... <note>The text here appears to be a Kabbalistic analysis of the numerical values of verses related to social harmony.</note>
...all the blessings of a Torah scholar... 60 parts...
...Your neighbor as yourself... and in the eye of salvation, the strength and the blessing...
And your sign: "Length of days is in her right hand; in her left hand are riches and honor." <note>Proverbs 3:16</note>

# The Gate of Letters

-> **The Letter Bet: Fellow Creatures (continued)** <-

...to bless him and to bestow blessings upon him. From where do we learn this? From the Mishnah, as it is written: "Behold, you are this day as the stars of heaven for multitude." <note>Deuteronomy 1:10</note> What is written immediately after? "May the Lord, the God of your fathers, add to you a thousand times as many as you are..." <note>Deuteronomy 1:11</note> These are two blessings: one is "The Lord, the God of your fathers," and the second is "and bless you as He has promised you," to acknowledge that blessings should be added upon blessings. If a person sees the success of his fellow and does not bestow a blessing upon him, he is held accountable first by the Heavens. But if he blesses him, he himself is blessed from above. A blessing intended for one's fellow must be given with a "good eye" <note>original: *ayin tova*; meaning with true generosity of spirit and without jealousy</note> and not with an "evil eye." In all things, the Holy One, Blessed be He, desires the love of the heart. Just as one who blesses his friend must do so with a good eye and a good heart, how much more so one who blesses the Holy One, Blessed be He! One must have a good eye, a good heart, and the love of the heart; as it is said: "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart..." <note>Deuteronomy 6:5</note> This concludes the quote.

**And let the money** of your fellow be as dear to you as your own. If your fellow suffers a loss, you are obligated to seek mercy for him, that the Holy One, Blessed be He, may fill his deficiency, as is stated

<margin>In the Talmud, Tractate Berakhot, in the chapter "He who recites" <note>Berakhot 14a</note>, where they say to a man whose wealth or donkey has perished: "May the Omnipresent fill your lack."</margin>

always to be beloved below and pleasant above. As it is written: "Good with God and with men," <note>1 Samuel 2:26</note> and it is said: "So shalt thou find favor and good understanding in the sight of God and man." <note>Proverbs 3:4</note> We have also learned: "Whoever the spirit of humanity is pleased with, the Spirit of the Omnipresent <note>original: *HaMakom*; a Rabbinic name for God</note> is pleased with him." <note>Pirkei Avot 3:10</note> One should always seek to increase love, as stated in the first chapter of Tractate Shabbat: Rava bar Machsi said in the name of Rav Chama bar Guria in the name of Rav: "One who gives a gift to his fellow must inform him," as it is said: "That you may know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you." <note>Exodus 31:13; referring to the Sabbath as a gift</note> It was also taught: "From here Rabbi Simeon ben Gamliel said: One who gives bread to a child must inform his mother." How does he do so? Abaye said: He rubs oil on him or puts blue shadow <note>term: *kouchla*; antimony or eye paint used to mark the child so the mother sees they were cared for</note> on his eyes. Nowadays, when we fear witchcraft, what does he do? Rav Papa said: He rubs a bit of that same food on him.

**And if** any good news occurs for all of Israel or for a daughter of Israel, one should run to him to bring the news, as it is written: "He is a good man and comes with good news." <note>2 Samuel 18:27</note> Also, if one knows of an obstacle in his fellow's path or in some business matter, he should run and warn him, saying: "My brother, guard your spirit in this matter." For the great principle of "Love your neighbor as yourself" <note>Leviticus 19:18</note> means one should love him as his own soul. The book *Orchot Tzaddikim* <note>term: *Orchot Tzaddikim*; "The Ways of the Righteous," an anonymous 15th-century ethical work</note> in the "Gate of Love" says: "Great benefit comes from acting with affection and friendship toward people. One benefit in this world is that he lives in joy and love with everyone, and all will help him if he falls or comes to need assistance. If a man stands against him to quarrel or shame him, there will be many who speak up for him and hide his flaws.

<margin>
Note: To learn for himself and to be a person who turns to others always... [The rest of this marginal note is written in a highly abbreviated cursive script, likely a citation to a specific legal code regarding financial damages].
</margin>

<margin>
Note from the *Tosafot*: Regarding "one who gives a gift must inform him"—this applies specifically to a gift given in secret where the recipient wouldn't know the source. But if one gives publicly, it is not necessary. See Tractate Shabbat, page 10.
</margin>

If a trouble comes upon him, everyone grieves for him and gives to him. If he comes to hardship or poverty, many will have mercy on him by giving gifts. The benefit for the World to Come is that because he is beloved by all, his words will be heard, and he will have the power to rebuke people so they may improve their ways. Also, through love, he will live in peace with the world, and through love, he will be quiet and tranquil, free to study and perform good deeds. Through love, they will help him and do his work, and he will find extra relief to serve the Creator, may He be blessed, with perfect service. Because of this love, he finds favor in the eyes of all who see him, and his good deeds will be acceptable to all, and everyone will desire to act as he does. The way for a person to reach the love of all people—I will enlighten you and show you the way—is to help with his soul and his money according to his ability. He should have a "good eye" <note>generosity</note> for every person—favor for the poor, favor for the rich, and integrity. Helping with money means lending to the rich in their time of need to prevent loss, and as much as possible helping the poor in their time of distress. Similarly, he should provide gifts according to his ability; at times sending portions and presents even to the wealthy. He should be generous with his own property. If he has business with people, all his dealings should be in good faith. He should not be petty with his fellow over small matters. He should always desire that his fellow benefit from him, and he should not strive to benefit from his fellow. His words should be gentle with people. In his social gatherings, he should not take advantage of the hour. Let him not err, but rather bear the yoke of the world on his own shoulders while not being a burden on others. He should not quarrel with people, and should receive every person with joy and a pleasant countenance, for a pleasant face strengthens love. He should deal with his fellow for his fellow's benefit and comfort every person in their sadness and worry. If a man reveals a secret to him, he must not reveal it, even if they anger him. He should not speak evil of any person, nor listen to evil spoken of others. He should always strive to find merit in people wherever possible. Through this care, he will be beloved by all and blessed by all. He should not be prideful toward any man, but humble himself before everyone, and in everything, he should intend his actions for the sake of Heaven." This concludes the quote.

And if, Heaven forbid, your fellow has done you some evil, forgive him immediately, for you are required to love him as yourself. Any other loss will be temporary, but strife is like "the shedding of iron" <note>an idiom for a permanent or deep scar</note>... the hand returns and takes vengeance, as stated in the ethics above. Say in your heart: "What is this to you?" For everything that happens to a man is a payment from God for his sins; it is not a matter of chance. Therefore, do not quarrel, for the greatest evil in the world is strife (*Machloket*), which is harsher than idolatry. As our Sages of blessed memory said: The generation of King Ahab was victorious in their wars even though they were idol worshippers, because there was fellowship and peace among them. But the generation of King Saul was defeated in their wars, even though they had no sin, because there were informers among them. The secret of the matter is as explained above: we, the Assembly of Israel, are unified in the secret of the True One. When there is strife, there is, Heaven forbid, division and separation above, "cutting the plantings" <note>term: *kitzutz baneti'ot*; a Kabbalistic metaphor for heresy or causing cosmic disunity</note>. The prohibition of strife is equal [to all others]. Just as a single spark of fire can spread a conflagration—may we be saved—strife is a fire that consumes unto destruction. As stated in Sanhedrin: strife is like a breach in a dam; once it starts, it rushes through.

I heard from my light, the Great Gaon, our teacher Rabbi Pinchas Segal <note>The author's father or primary teacher</note>, of blessed memory, that this is hinted at in the letters of the word **Machloket** (Strife):
How so?
The letter **Mem** (מ) has only a small opening at the bottom; so is the beginning of a quarrel.
Afterward, it grows and becomes a wide-open entrance like the letter **Chet** (ח).
Afterward, the fire of strife blazes upward; this is the letter **Lamed** (ל), which is like a tower flying in the air.
Afterward, it descends to the depths; this is the letter **Kuf** (ק), which reaches both the high heavens and the depths of the earth.
Afterward, it persists for a long time and gains a foothold; this is the shape of the letter **Tav** (ת), which has two legs.
The letter **Vav** (ו) that separates [the letters] is like the staff in a man's hand to maintain the strife, but this staff turns into a snake. Therefore, whoever hopes for life and merits to see the Divine Presence should run from the breath of the "snake" and distance himself from strife, even from the smallest beginning. Why should I elaborate on the disgrace of strife when all the books are full of it? Take this rule in your hand: the sin of strife is harder than the sin of idolatry, as we found with Ahab and Saul.

Furthermore, our Sages said in three places that the Holy One, Blessed be He, overlooked idolatry but did not overlook strife:
1. First, in the generation of Enosh, when they began to worship idols, as it is said: "Then began men to call upon the name of the Lord." <note>Genesis 4:26, interpreted by Sages as the start of idolatry</note>. But when it came to the Generation of the Flood, who were robbers and oppressors of one another, He did not overlook them, as it is said: "For the earth is filled with violence." <note>Genesis 6:13</note>
2. Second, in the generation of the Wilderness: when Israel committed the act of the Golden Calf, the Holy One, Blessed be He, forgave them. But when they came to strife, He did not overlook it; for wherever you find the "curtain" of strife, you find a great plague, as with the rebellion of Korah.
3. Third, the idol of Micah: as long as there was peace among them, He gave them a reprieve, as it is said: "And the children of Dan set up for themselves the graven image..." <note>Judges 18:30</note>. But when the tribes were divided against the tribes of Judah and Benjamin and there was no peace between them—these attacking those and those attacking these—then the Holy One, Blessed be He, brought account and punished them, as it is said: "And our fathers were smitten with a very great slaughter," and "there fell of Israel five hundred thousand chosen men." <note>2 Chronicles 13:17</note> And when the tribes of Judah and Benjamin came against the ten tribes, they punished them, as it is said: "For Pekah the son of Remaliah slew in Judah a hundred and twenty thousand in one day." <note>2 Chronicles 28:6</note>

Certainly, even the least among Israel would think of the four types of court-ordered execution before he would commit idolatry; how then can he not restrain himself from creating strife, which is harsher than idolatry? Rava said: "Whoever passes over his own tendencies <note>meaning: ignores an insult or yields in a dispute</note>, Heaven passes over all his transgressions." Therefore, not only should one not grieve over a matter that harms him by holding onto strife, but on the contrary, he should exult and rejoice that this opportunity came to his hand to fulfill the act of "passing over his tendencies." This is an act of kindness. Every time Mar Zutra went to his bed, he would say: "I forgive and pardon anyone who has troubled me." Come and see how great is the power of peace, for even to enemies the Holy One, Blessed be He, said: "Offer them peace," as it is written: "When you approach a city..." <note>Deuteronomy 20:10</note> Even in this time, our Sages said we should greet the non-Jews with "Shalom" for the sake of the ways of peace. It was said of Rabban Yochanan [ben Zakkai]...

# The Letter Bet: **Fellow Creatures**

<margin>
Note: The verse "And you shall love the Lord your God" <note>original: *Ve-ahavta et Hashem Elokecha*</note> contains 30 letters, and similarly, the verse "And you shall love your neighbor as yourself" contains 30 letters. This indicates their equality. Furthermore, the word "to your neighbor" <note>original: *le-re'acha*</note> is not found in the verse regarding the love of God. Look closely at the secret of the 500, as the words "the Lord your God" <note>original: *Hashem Elokecha*</note> signify the growth of the 500. There are hidden meanings here involving three parts... to add to his success and help him sit among the great. There are four categories to investigate: the labor of loving the Holy One, Blessed be He, and the labor of loving your neighbor as yourself. Consider how Jacob supported his right hand... it is known that the Second Temple was destroyed because of this <note>meaning: the lack of interpersonal love</note>. This is the secret of the holiness of the Blessed One. From here we learn that loving a friend does not require sacrificing one's own life, as the Sages said, "Your own life takes precedence." Nevertheless, you should treat your neighbor as your own soul. The essence of the connection between people is the foundation of the Temple, and when this was lost, the Temple was destroyed. Therefore, a person should rejoice in the success of others and the honor of the Creator.
</margin>

It is written: "And you shall love the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 6:5</note> and it is written: "And you shall love your neighbor as yourself" <note>Leviticus 19:18</note>. Behold, these two loves are joined and opened through His Unity, may He be blessed. For this reason, we conclude the blessing before the *Shema* with: "Who chooses His people Israel with love," and "Who loves His people Israel." Then we recite the verse of Unity <note>the *Shema*</note> followed by the commandment to love God: "And you shall love the Lord your God." Furthermore, the Ten Commandments conclude with the words "which is to your neighbor" <note>Exodus 20:14, in the prohibition against coveting</note>. 

The Sages have written that in the Ten Commandments, there are 620 letters, corresponding to the numerical value of *Keter Torah* <note>original: *Keter* = 620, meaning "The Crown of Torah"</note>. Of these, 613 letters correspond to the 613 commandments <note>term: *Taryag Mitzvot*; the total number of biblical laws</note>, with each letter hinting at one commandment. What do the remaining seven letters serve? The early sages spoke of this, saying they correspond to the seven Rabbinic commandments, or to eleven other matters. 

However, the clearest explanation is what I understood from the words of the *Tzioni* <note>Menachem Zioni, a 14th-century Italian Kabbalist</note>, who says: what are the remaining letters? They are the letters of the phrase "which is to your neighbor" <note>original: *asher l're'acha*</note>. This is the "foot" upon which the entire Torah stands. This refers to the famous story of the convert who came before Hillel and asked to be taught the whole Torah while standing on one foot. Hillel told him: "That which is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. This is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary; go and study." <note>Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a</note> 

The explanation of "That which is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor" is linked to the verse "Your neighbor and your father’s neighbor, do not forsake" <note>Proverbs 27:10</note>. This "neighbor" refers to the Holy One, Blessed be He—do not transgress His words. For just as it is hateful to you when a friend defies your words, do not defy God's. It also refers to literal neighbors: do not commit theft, robbery, or adultery. Most commandments depend on this. 

Indeed, if you examine closely, you will find the majority of commandments are dependent on loving one's fellow as oneself: all the laws of charity, the agricultural gifts to the poor <note>term: *Leket, Shikcha, and Pe'ah*</note>, tithes, honest business dealings, the prohibition against interest, and many others. Furthermore, almost all noble character traits depend on this: grace, patience, kindness, judging others favorably, not standing idly by the blood of your neighbor, distancing oneself from gossip, slander, tale-bearing, mockery, jealousy, hatred, and grudges. It also includes controlling anger and the pursuit of honor. 

Through these thousands of traits, a person fulfills most positive commandments and avoids most negative ones. Even matters that do not seemingly involve interpersonal relations—such as forbidden foods or leaven on Passover—can be fulfilled through an *a fortiori* <note>term: *Kal VaChomer*; a logical inference from a minor premise to a major one</note> argument: if a person loves his fellow human as himself, how much more so should he love the Holy One, Blessed be He, who bestows free kindness upon him? This is the "eternal love." Thus, "Love your neighbor as yourself" is the leg upon which the world stands; it is the catalyst that leads to "And you shall love the Lord your God."

The pious sage Rabbi Abraham Saba <note>15th-century author of *Tzeror HaMor*</note>, may his memory be for a blessing, wrote that these two loves are the two pillars of the Torah and should resemble one another. Just as the love of the Omnipresent is "with all your heart, soul, and might," so too should be the love of fellow creatures. 

**With all your heart:** This means not to hate any person in one's heart, as it is said: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart" <note>Leviticus 19:17</note>. Hatred in the heart usually stems from jealousy. Hatred born of jealousy is much greater than hatred born of an insult or a dispute over a specific matter. A dispute over a matter can be resolved and healed, but hatred from jealousy has no remedy, for every time the jealous person sees his fellow’s success, his grief is renewed. This is the trait that destroyed the Second Temple, which otherwise had Torah and good deeds. It is what has lengthened our exile and scattered the remnant of Israel. It caused all the expulsions and troubles of this long exile. This hatred is called "baseless hatred" <note>original: *sinat chinam*</note> because it enters a man's heart for no practical reason other than envy. It is the most difficult of all, as it "removes a person from the world." Therefore, "with all your heart" means one must not only avoid harming a friend but must actively remove any speck of jealousy or rivalry from the heart.

There is another type of hatred: when one dislikes a person not out of jealousy, but because of a clash of temperaments. Just as nature dictates that like-minded people love one another, those with different dispositions may feel a natural dislike. This is not as severe as the first type, but it must be mitigated. We are commanded to tolerate others, as implied by **"with all your soul."** Even if your friend's character does not align with your soul, you are obligated to bear with him and love him for the sake of the Creator who made him.

The third type of hatred arises from financial matters <note>original: *drara d'mamona*</note>. This is addressed by **"with all your might"** <note>Hebrew *me'odecha* also means "wealth"</note>. This type of hatred is often found between people of the same profession. A person should realize that all wealth and honor come from God, and no man can touch what is prepared for his fellow. Instead of hating a competitor, he should love him because of their shared craft. If a legal dispute arises, let the judge decide and let the truth take its course; there is no reason to hate the other afterward. All of Israel should be like a single body; if a man's hand accidentally strikes his leg, the leg does not strike the hand back in revenge. So too, if a person wrongs you, do not take revenge or bear a grudge. Forgive him immediately and pray for him, as the elder Abunash did, or as Abraham prayed for Abimelech. Consider how much we sin against God every day, yet He forgives us. If we are "children of the Lord your God," we must follow His ways and be "one who passes over his retaliations" <note>original: *ma'avir al middotav*; meaning one who overlooks personal slights</note>. If you overlook the wrongs done to you, Heaven will overlook your transgressions—measure for measure. Reprove your fellow with words that sit well on the heart, and do not bear sin because of him in thought, speech, or deed. This is the true meaning of "Love your neighbor as yourself." You must strive in action and speech to bring peace between a man and his wife and between a person and his fellow. In your thoughts, you should desire that good comes to them, and pray for their welfare as you pray for your own.

# Additionally
Regarding the types of hatred: the most difficult is when people hate those who rebuke them or try to guide them on the right path, as it is said: "They hate him who reproves in the gate" <note>Amos 5:10</note>. Even worse is when the wicked hate those who do good and pursue justice, as it is said: "They are my adversaries because I follow the thing that is good" <note>Psalms 38:21</note>. Those who walk in the way of hatred are effectively haters of God, for they hate those who love Him and they hate the Torah and the commandments. Since they loathe the laws, they hate those who fulfill them.

There is a story of a wise man who saw a person who was worrying. He said to him: "If your worry is for this world, may the Name <note>a common Jewish way to refer to God, *HaShem*</note> remove your worry. But if your worry is for the World to Come, may the Name, may He be blessed, add worry upon your worry." And behold, to the power... <unclear>support him</unclear>. Furthermore, I found a story of a wise man who lived in a bitter place where the people were in great distress. He would speak and increase his words, yet he did not feel the distress. They said to him: "Do you not feel pain since we are all in pain?" He said to them: "No." They asked: "Why?" He replied: "If I were to see this distress in my dream, I would not feel it when I was awake. Therefore, I do not grieve over this, for I see it as it is. When I return to the True Intellect, all matters of this world <note>original: *Ha-Olam Ha-Zeh*</note> are like a dream, and clear counsel is only found when one is truly awake." Thus it is fulfilled:

# The Letter Dalet: Proper Conduct
**"In all your ways acknowledge Him, and He shall direct your paths."** <note>Proverbs 3:6</note> In the Tractate *Berakhot* <note>the Talmudic volume on Blessings</note>, the sage Bar Kappara taught: "Which is the small scriptural portion upon which all the essentials of the Torah depend? You must say: 'In all your ways acknowledge Him, and He shall direct your paths.'"
And in the first chapter of Tractate *Sotah*, it is said: "Anyone who straightens his paths merits and sees the salvation of the Holy One, Blessed be He, as it is said: 'To him who orders his way I will show the salvation of God.'" And we learn in the *Chapters of Rabbi Nathan*: Rabbi Eleazar says, "Let you have two hands in the Torah and one hand in **proper conduct** <note>original: *Derech Eretz*, literally 'The Way of the Land,' referring to ethics, manners, and worldly occupation</note>. Anyone who has neither Scripture nor proper conduct is not part of civilized society."
Rabbi Shimon bar Nachmani said: "For twenty-six generations, **proper conduct** preceded the Torah <note>this refers to the 26 generations from the creation of Adam until the giving of the Torah at Sinai</note>. This is what is written: 'To guard the way to the Tree of Life.' 'The way' refers to **proper conduct**, while 'the Tree of Life' refers to the Torah." Anyone who is careful with proper conduct merits to see consolation, as it is said: "To him who orders his way I will show the salvation of God."

## The Subject of Proper Conduct
This refers to upright behavior, excessive modesty, the excellence of character traits, and all desirable qualities. It is to be beloved by all creatures and to love all creatures. A person of peace sustains the existence of the world in its generalities and its details, both in matters of Heaven and matters of this world.
Conduct yourself with **proper conduct** in all your ways. There are three perfections of conduct: 1. A person's conduct with themselves. 2. A person's conduct in their home. 3. A person's conduct with others.

**And in every** one of these ways, one should conduct themselves with the three "perfections" that encompass all wholeness: the perfection of wealth, the perfection of the body, and the perfection of the soul. Our Sages, of blessed memory, hinted at this in the verse: "And Jacob arrived whole" <note>Genesis 33:18</note>, explaining that he was "whole in his wealth, whole in his Torah." These are also hinted at in the love of the Blessed God: "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might." "Your might" refers to the perfection of wealth. "Your heart"—the heart being the primary life-force of the body—refers to the body. "Your soul" refers to the perfection of the soul.

And I shall explain the way of a person's perfection with themselves through three things. A person should contemplate that the Holy One, Blessed be He, elevated them above all existing things according to the order of the levels: **Inanimate, Plant, Animal, and Speaker** <note>the "Speaking" level refers to humans</note>. As it is written: "Yet You have made him a little lower than the angels, and crowned him with glory and honor. You made him to have dominion over the works of Your hands; You have put all things under his feet: all sheep and oxen..." etc. Behold, the plant draws nourishment and "eats" from the minerals of the inanimate world. The animal eats the plant. And the human, who is the "speaker," eats the animal. Know that everything the Holy One, Blessed be He, created in His world was created only for His praise. Every creature yearns and longs to rise from its current level until it reaches the level of that which consumes it. When the animal eats the plant, the plant is transformed into animal matter. When the human eats the animal, the animal flesh is transformed into human flesh. 
Therefore, an unlearned person <note>original: *Am Ha-aretz*, literally 'person of the land'</note> is forbidden to eat meat, for "woe to the flesh because of the flesh." Since the unlearned person lacks wisdom, he is like a beast eating another beast; the animal could argue: "What makes your blood redder than mine?" <note>a Talmudic logic used to question the superiority of one life over another</note>. But the wise person who eats the animal—or the animal that merits to become human flesh—is then elevated through the human's intellect and the soul given by the Blessed Name. He rises to the level of an angel until he cleaves to the Blessed Name by adopting the attributes of the Holy One, Blessed be He, as much as it is possible for a human to resemble his Creator.

Even if the Torah had not been given, God forbid, the entirety of "Proper Conduct"—that is, the ways of ethics and upright behavior—would still require that at all times and moments, the fear of Heaven be upon a person. He should love God, cleave to Him, and think of His greatness always, for the whole earth is full of His glory. He sees both the revealed and the hidden. One should accept the yoke of His kingdom, be in awe and ashamed before Him, and always act with modesty, whether at home or outside, keeping his head bowed. As our Sages said: "One who walks with a stiff, upright posture is as if he is pushing away the feet of the Divine Presence." One should be humble <note>literally "poor of eyes"</note> and not engage in laughter or mockery—all because of the fear of the Kingdom of Heaven upon him. He should never move his thoughts from the greatness of the Blessed Creator and His conduct with His creatures. He should not distract his mind while sitting in his house, walking on the way, lying down, or rising. He should pray to Him and trust in Him always.

Furthermore, it is part of **proper conduct** to give honor to one's soul, which is a "portion of God from above." It is his duty to ensure his thoughts do not embitter the soul, but rather he should do its will and nullify the will of the body in favor of the soul's will. He should do everything according to the nature of the soul, not the nature of the body, which chases after desires, luxuries, jealousy, and honor. Rather, he should follow the nature of the soul, which opposes all of this. He should consider that through the soul, he merits the great honor of having a connection with his Creator. Therefore, he must exalt the soul over the body. 

He should learn from the body itself: just as in **proper conduct** one exalts certain limbs over others—giving honor to the right hand over the left, and the head over the rest of the body—so too should he exalt the soul. As the Sages taught in the chapter "With what may a woman go out?": "When one puts on shoes, put on the right first... when one washes, wash the right and then the left... when one anoints with oil, anoint the right and then the left." And one who wishes to anoint his whole body should anoint his head first, because the head is the king over all the limbs. 
And it is not only in this matter that they spoke, but in every single action. So too with other limbs: one exalts the heart over other organs because the heart understands, and the power of the brain where thought resides governs the movement of his work, his clothing, and his efforts. The reason the limbs are ranked one above the other is due to the spread of the soul within them; some limbs show more of the soul's power than others. If so, is it not **proper conduct** to exalt the soul over the entire body and make it king? The body should be humbled under the soul, following its ways so that one's actions are done with holy purity. The body should be drawn after the soul, and the body should be considered a "case" or "receptacle" for the soul. It is fitting to compare this to the law: "We save the case of a holy book along with the book itself." 

A person should consider that God raised him above all animals so that he would be exalted over them, and not be "like a horse or a mule which have no understanding." Even in physical and necessary matters, the exaltation of the soul should be before his eyes. He should have the **proper conduct** to lean away from the animal side and toward the intellectual side in all his deeds: in his eating, his drinking, his labor, the tending to his needs, his speech, his walking, his clothing, and his business dealings. All these deeds should be pleasant, refined, and highly ordered. 

I will mention briefly what Maimonides <note>original: *Ha-Rambam*</note> wrote in the *Laws of Character Traits* regarding this, with some of my own additions: One should not eat or drink what is merely pleasant or sweet to the body, but rather what is beneficial to the body. And even that which is beneficial, he should not fill his belly like an animal, but only according to what is necessary for his sustenance. This little that he eats and drinks should be done in cleanliness and purity. He should only eat in his home, at his own table, which should be set with a clean cloth. He should eat and drink calmly, not like a glutton. He should not eat anything in a shop or in the marketplace. He should not eat or drink while standing. He should not wipe the bowl or lick his fingers. He should not eat every bit of food in the bowl, but should leave over a little so as not to appear gluttonous. 
He should not eat with an unlearned person. It is only fitting for him to eat at a "meal of a commandment" <note>original: *Seudat Mitzvah*</note>, such as an engagement or wedding feast, provided it is a scholar marrying the daughter of a scholar. The righteous and pious ones of old would not eat from any meal that was not their own. 

"When the Lord your God expands your border... and you desire to eat meat..." Resh Lakish said: "The Torah is teaching **proper conduct**: that a person should not eat meat unless he is in a state of financial abundance." Maimonides wrote in the fourth chapter of *Laws of Character Traits*: "The Sages commanded as a matter of **proper conduct** that a person should only eat meat when he has a craving for it... a healthy person should eat meat only from one Sabbath eve to the next. But if he is wealthy and it is appropriate for him to eat meat every day, he may eat it."
One should not eat or drink dangerous things, just as the Sages warned against drinking water from rivers at night or drinking "uncovered" water <note>water left out, which might have been poisoned by a snake</note>. One should not go out alone at night. They also mentioned dangerous foods in the Tractate *Pesachim* (page 110), in Tractate *Niddah* (page 17), and in Tractate *Ketubot*. They mentioned things that are bad for the lungs and for health. Furthermore, the Sages mentioned many foods that are dangerous in Tractate *Berakhot* (page 39), *Pesachim* (page 44), and *Bava Kamma* (page 82). The great master Maimonides, who was an expert physician in his wisdom, wrote at great length about harmful and healthy foods in the *Laws of Character Traits* (Chapter 4). He also mentioned the order of eating, the matter of the bathhouse, the order of washing, and the conduct of marital intimacy <note>original: *be'ilah*</note> and its proper times.

<summary>This page defines the concept of Derech Eretz (Proper Conduct) as a prerequisite for Torah study, outlining a hierarchy where the soul must govern the body. It provides practical ethical and hygienic guidelines for daily life, heavily citing Maimonides and Talmudic wisdom on eating, health, and social behavior.</summary>

# The Gate of Letters

<note>Rabbi Yochanan</note> ben Zakkai was such that no man ever preceded him in offering a greeting of peace <note>original: "Shalom"</note> in the world, not even a non-Jew in the marketplace. Our Sages of blessed memory said: "Be first to greet every person" and "Be a tail to lions," etc. What does it mean to greet "every person"? Even if you see that his heart is against you, be the first to greet him with peace. For if you do so, you will cause him to love you. Furthermore, even if he does not submit to making peace, the Holy One, Blessed be He, will discipline him and subdue him beneath you, as it is said: "And if it will not make peace with you... then the Lord your God will deliver it into your hands" <note>Deuteronomy 20:12-13</note>. 

And so we find with King David, peace be upon him, who pursued peace with Saul, as it is written: "I am for peace; but when I speak, they are for war" <note>Psalms 120:7</note>. Regarding Saul, it was not enough that he would not be reconciled with David; he pursued him to kill him. Yet, the Holy One, Blessed be He, delivered Saul into David’s hand in the cave, as is known. Nevertheless, it did not enter David’s heart to harm him, for a person must be a "lover of peace and a pursuer of peace," as it is written: "Seek peace and pursue it" <note>Psalms 34:15</note>. 

The Sages explain this: Seek your friend and pursue your enemy. Seek peace in your own place and pursue it in other places. Seek it with your body and pursue it with your money. Seek it for yourself and pursue it for others. Seek it today and pursue it tomorrow. Do not despair and say, "I cannot make peace," but rather pursue peace until you attain it. 

Why should I elaborate further on the greatness of peace? For it is well-known and famous even in this world. Later, in the section on the <term>Sukkat Shalom: "Shelter of Peace," a liturgical reference to God's protection</term>, I will expand on this. I have only come now to conclude this discourse on loving peace, to fulfill that which is said: "Therefore love truth and peace" <note>Zechariah 8:19</note>. One should cleave to peace and fulfill the command "Love your neighbor as yourself" <note>Leviticus 19:18</note>. 

Indeed, the righteous are called by the Name of God, as it says in the <term>Sifrei: an ancient legal commentary on the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy</term>, that in the future the righteous will be called by the Name of the Holy One, Blessed be He. For "You shall love the Lord your God" is aligned with "Love your neighbor as yourself"; one who fulfills this fulfills that. When the love and cleaving to the Name is upon a person, they are called by His Name. For the Name of the Holy One, Blessed be He, is "Peace" <note>original: "Shalom"</note>, as found in the first chapter of Tractate Shabbat: Rav Hamnuna said in the name of Ulla that it is forbidden for a person to greet his friend with the word "Peace" in a bathhouse, because it is said: "And he called Him: The Lord is Peace" <note>Judges 6:24; a bathhouse is considered an undignified place to use a Name of God</note>.

# The Letter Bet is Completed

# Letter Gimel: Sojourning
**"I am a stranger in the earth; hide not Your commandments from me."** <note>Psalms 119:19</note> The Torah says: "For you are strangers and sojourners with Me" <note>Leviticus 25:23</note>. This presents a difficulty: if one is a "stranger" <note>original: "Ger"</note>, they are not a "sojourner/resident" <note>original: "Toshav"</note>, and if they are a resident, they are not a stranger. This is the same question Rashi asked in the Torah portion *Chayei Sarah* regarding the words of our forefather Abraham, who said: "I am a stranger and a resident with you." 

The explanation of this verse is as follows: If you are "strangers"—meaning you always keep it before your eyes that you are mere temporary travelers in this world—then you will be "residents with Me" in the World to Come, in His eternity. The matter of always remembering one's "strangerhood" <note>original: "Gerut"</note> in this world includes the fulfillment of the Torah and commandments. It should be a constant reminder that a person’s dwelling is not in this world; rather, their dwelling is above, from the source of the soul, which is a "portion of God from above." 

The soul <note>original: "Neshamah"</note> is placed within a person, and its life in this world—which is far from its place of origin—is for the sake of service and guarding, namely the study of Torah and the fulfillment of commandments. In this world, the soul is a foreigner, like a stranger in another land, for it is a resident of the upper world. 

It is exactly like an envoy sent by a King from among his faithful household to a foreign land. The King commands him what to occupy himself with on this mission and urges him: "Be strong and diligent in the work of your mission, for suddenly and without warning I will send for you and take you back to me. If you betray your mission, woe to you! I will strip you of the honor of your house, remove your head, and you will become a disgrace and a proverb. But if you are faithful in your mission, then I will build for you a faithful house, and the glory of your house now with me in my presence will be greater than it was before, with additional splendor and greatness." 

So it is: the King is the King of kings, the Holy One, Blessed be He. He takes the soul from the upper dwelling, from the unique place of the <term>Shekhinah: the Divine Presence</term>, and sends it to this world, placing it within a human being. The purpose of this mission is the occupation with Torah and commandments. Throughout one's days in this foreign land, one must not divert their mind for even a moment from the mission. For this occupation with Torah and commandments is directed toward the sparks of the light of the *Shekhinah* that shine in the palace of the Holy One, Blessed be He. 

He commanded him through the words of Isaiah: one should not go after the affairs of this world at all—neither much nor little. Especially since this world is a foreign land, the opposite of the upper world. Here, good is seen as bad and bad as good. This world loathes the good and chooses the bad, lusting for food, drink, and all physical pleasures. A person should only take the minimum required to live so that he may fulfill his mission. All excess should be shunned, especially traits like jealousy, lust, and the pursuit of honor. Since he is not of this world but merely an envoy and a stranger in the land, what has he to do with the affairs of this world? He should be preoccupied only with his mission. Day and night he should not cease from cleaving to the mission, worrying greatly: "Perhaps in the middle of my work, the Holy One, Blessed be He, will suddenly take me and return me to the place where I was at first, and I have not yet finished the mission." 

Therefore, let the holy service be heavy upon him at every time and every moment, to do his work—the work of Heaven. Regarding this, David prayed: "I am a stranger in the earth"—because I am an envoy to a foreign land. Master of the Universe, You are the one who assists the soul <note>source has a typo "Hanimah" for "Neshamah"</note>; let not Your commandments, which are the orders of my mission, be hidden from me. But a person who makes for himself a permanent dwelling in this world and behaves according to its customs betrays his mission. When the Holy One, Blessed be He, returns him to his place and says to him, "You, the envoy, show me your mission," and he has forgotten the mission and instead settled in, fell in love with vanity, and did the opposite of his mission—woe to him for that shame! 

A person should take this to heart all the days of his life, every day, every night, every hour, and every moment. Even if he is occupied with the mission, he should be full of trembling: "Perhaps I am falling short of what is necessary." For perhaps suddenly, "As a bird that wanders from her nest, so is a man that wanders from his place" <note>Proverbs 27:8</note>, since his dwelling is not here. 

And so says the *Midrash Shmuel* on the Mishnah: "If not now, when?" <note>Ethics of the Fathers 1:14</note>. It says that one should not wait to see what the day will bring. It does not say "If not today," but "If not *now*," to teach that even today itself is in doubt whether one will live or not. At every moment one is prepared for death, for in a moment one may die. A person has nothing but his current hour. Therefore it says, "If not now, when?"

> And so says the book *Even Bohan* <note>original: "The Touchstone," an ethical work</note>, presenting a parable about those who forsake the Lord: The world is like level ground, but at its edge is a deep pit, a den of lions, or a pit with no water but full of snakes and scorpions that cannot be charmed. Many people bustle about, digging and seeking gain, while the person lacks sense. He looks into the pit, laughs, and falls.
> 
> By the mercy of God, perhaps he might repent. It happens that as he falls, he catches hold of the roots of bushes growing in the walls of the pit. He clings to the thicket of roots so as not to go down further and be swallowed. Meanwhile, he lifts his eyes and sees a small window where honey flows. He stretches out his hand to nourish himself from it constantly. One hand clings to the root while the other brings honey to his mouth. Sometimes he eats, and sometimes he stops.
> 
> And behold, there are two rats—one white and one black—constantly eating away at the root of the bush. But he is enticed by the honey he found and does not feel the rats eating it. He does not know until the bush is uprooted from its source, and he falls suddenly into the depths. His dwelling is among the snakes and lions; they eat him and finish him, and there is no one to say, "Return."
> 
> You who lack understanding, be silent and I will teach you wisdom. The meaning of this wonderful parable is intended to hint at the fate of the wicked, and conversely, the reward for those who keep the way of the Lord. Although the world appears as level ground to the eyes of sinners—a floor without bumps or pits—at the edge of life, the end of man is an open grave, a deep pit at the bottom of which the angels of destruction roar like lion cubs, longing to prey upon the soul of the wicked. 
> 
> While the cursed wicked have their faces turned downward, falling close to the floor of this pit—for in their lives they are called "dead"—they are entangled in the thicket of the "Tree of Life" (the soul). They find around them the sweets of time, like honey for sweetness, and they eat in quiet and security, forgetting the terrors of the earth beneath them. The world has not placed fear in their hearts that they might fall into the pit where there is a heavy mixture of rulers and shepherds tearing at their pieces.
> 
> And behold, the two rats—the white and the black—they are the Day and the Night, which gnaw away at the threads of their lives. They begin with the morning and end with the evening, until they fall entirely. This is for the day of the "black hour." Together with that which they ate of the nectar of honey, they shall eat the fruit of their deeds, a fruit that is wretched to the eyes.
> 
> Therefore, in all greatness, a person is a stranger in the earth. Will you set your eyes upon it? It is gone. Our days are like a passing shadow. The Sages explained: Not like the shadow of a tree, nor like the shadow of a wall, but like the shadow of a bird passing by.

The holy and upright Patriarchs in the land: Abraham said, "I am a stranger and a resident with you." Regarding Isaac it was said, "Sojourn in this land." Jacob said, "The days of my sojourning." David—the "fourth leg of the Chariot"—said, "I am a stranger in the earth." Therefore, let this strangerhood in the earth be a reminder between your eyes always. One should not occupy himself with matters pertaining to establishing a permanent dwelling in this land, for his home is in the upper dwelling. Then he will not worry about a world that is not his; he will only worry constantly that perhaps he is falling short in the service of the Blessed Name. He will be fearful and anxious to guard and to do, fulfilling the principle: "Do not rest or be still for even a moment from the service of the Blessed Name." As it is brought in the book *Orchot Tzaddikim* <note>original: "The Ways of the Righteous," a famous ethical work</note>...

<meta>This page continues the "Gate of Letters," moving from the discussion of greeting others with peace to the essential duties of parents in raising and disciplining their children. It emphasizes that a child's spiritual success is the primary responsibility of the parents.</meta>

<page-num>64</page-num>
# The Gate of Letters

If, Heaven forbid, one sleeps through the morning <note>original: "Shacharit"</note> and lets the crown of the day pass without returning, every diligent person should instead rise early, morning after morning; then, happy is he and happy are his children after him. Any father who is concerned for his child [and avoids disciplining him] is like one who causes his son’s death, as it is written: "Chasten your son while there is hope, and let not your soul be moved to his destruction" <note>Proverbs 19:18</note>. For if you do not discipline him, you are effectively setting him on a path to death, as he may go out to bad culture or a bad life, and his death would be better than his life. The punishment for the father is very great in the World to Come <note>original: "Olam Ha-Ba"</note>, as seen in the words of our Sages of blessed memory. Conversely, happy is the father in this world and the next if he disciplines his son in his youth and guides him on a good and straight path. He will live in comfort, quiet, and tranquility, not grieving over a son who turns to bad culture or commits transgressions. Instead, the son will walk in the way of the Blessed Name, his source will be blessed, and he will find favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man. It will be good for the father in the World to Come, as we learn in the Midrash: "Chasten your son, and he will give you rest" <note>Proverbs 29:17</note>—meaning your son will give you rest from the judgment of Gehenna <note>Hell</note> and will provide delights for your soul by bringing you into the Garden of Eden with the righteous. This is also found in the Zohar at the end of the portion of *Bechukotai*: "A son brings merit to the father" <note>original: "Bera mezakeh abba"</note>. They said that the rescue of fathers by their sons is greater than the rescue of sons by their fathers. For fathers only save their sons from the sufferings of this world—securing them wealth, strength, or life—but on the Day of Judgment, they cannot save them from the judgment of Gehenna. As it is said: "None can deliver from My hand" <note>Deuteronomy 32:39</note>—Abraham cannot save his son Ishmael, nor can Isaac save his son Esau. But sons *can* save their fathers from the judgment of Gehenna. Thus, the power of the son is greater than the power of the father. The father's merit does not avail the son regarding the World to Come, and the son's merit does not avail the father regarding this world, but only regarding the World to Come, which is the eternal and pure world. The reason the son’s power is so "beautiful" <note>meaning effective</note> is that his existence and the extra nature of his soul come from the strength of his father who guided him. Therefore, happy is the father who rebukes his children at all times, at every moment, and in every step, word, sight, movement, and action. 

Women are also commanded to rebuke their children, just as the father is, and perhaps even more so because they are home more often. Regardless of whether the father is a Torah scholar or very busy with earning a livelihood, he cannot watch the youth's actions every hour. If he is busy with business, travel, or the marketplace, the mother is the one in the home. In Tractate *Berakhot*, in the chapter "One who Recites," it says: "Greater is the promise given by the Holy One, Blessed be He, to women than to men," as it is written: "Rise up, you women who are at ease; hear my voice, you confident daughters" <note>Isaiah 32:9</note>. Rav said to Rabbi Hiyya: "By what merit do women earn [the World to Come]?" By bringing their children to the synagogue to learn Scripture, and their husbands to the study hall <note>original: "Beit Rabban"</note> to learn Mishnah, and by waiting for their husbands to return from the study hall. Since the nature of women is often more compassionate, an obligation is placed upon them to "clothe themselves in the tools of a man"—meaning, not to have a cruel heart, but to be firm enough to rebuke the child with discipline and moral correction. They should not listen to the child's complaints until he turns from the evil way and walks in the good and straight path. I say that those mothers who [overly] pity their children by refusing to strike or discipline them are actually "slaughtering" them. It is as if they have killed them, cooked them, and fed them to the wild beasts.

### Parents should always have a prayer ready in their mouths
They must pray for their offspring to be students of the Torah, righteous, and possessors of good traits. They should focus on this during the "Illumination of the Torah" in the Morning Blessings <note>original: "Birkat HaTorah"</note>, specifically at the words: "May we and our descendants..." and similarly in the blessing "Great Love" <note>original: "Ahava Rabba"</note>: "Our Father, Merciful Father... have mercy on us and put into our hearts..." One should also think of their children and their children’s children forever. Likewise, in the prayer "So that we do not labor in vain nor give birth to terror," in all such places, one should make their prayer permanent, with all their heart and soul. It is found in the *Yalkut* on the verse "Trust in the Lord": Elijah related a story of a certain priest who was exceedingly God-fearing. He had ten sons and four daughters from one wife. Every day he would pray, prostrate himself, and even lick the dust with his tongue so that not one of them would fall into transgression or anything unseemly. It was said that a full year did not pass before Ezra came and the Holy One, Blessed be He, brought Israel up from Babylon. That priest was brought up as well, and he did not leave this world until he saw High Priests and young priests among his sons and grandsons for fifty years. Afterward, he entered his eternal world, and of him it is said: "Trust in the Lord and do good" <note>Psalms 37:3</note>.

### It is written in *Reshit Chochma*:
"A person must be exceedingly careful to guard his mouth and tongue from speaking anything unseemly in front of his children, and certainly from doing such things." Even if an action is unseemly whether done in front of the son or not, it is much more disgraceful if the father does it in front of the son, lest the son learn from him. If the father hears of something unseemly done by others, he should show great distress in front of his son and speak at length about its disgrace. He might say, "May a curse come upon so-and-so who did this," and emphasize its ugliness so the matter becomes loathsome in the son's eyes and he distances himself from it. Conversely, if he hears of something praiseworthy done by others—such as diligent study or fine writing—he should praise it highly in his son's eyes. He should say, "How much satisfaction this person has brought, and in the end, he will inherit a high level." He should exaggerate the praise so the son hears and desires to do the same. In short, he should strive mightily to distance his son from ugliness and anything resembling it, and draw him close to the traits of the pious and the upright. When the father performs a commandment <note>original: "Mitzvah"</note>, such as binding the *Lulav* <note>palm branch used on Sukkot</note> or similar acts, he should do it in front of his son to train him, so that the commandments become beloved to him.

### A great principle for a father who disciplines his son:
His intention should be that the son walks in the straight path even in secret, when not in the father's presence. He should see to it with all his strength that he guides him in the attribute of Truth, as it is written: "They have taught their tongue to speak truth" <note>Jeremiah 9:4</note>. He should emphasize the great punishment for lying, even in idle conversation, and glorify the great reward for one who speaks the truth. He should cast a great fear upon the child regarding the utterance of even a single lie. If the habit of truth is fixed in the son's heart, then the son will fulfill all his father's commands. He will be afraid that if his father asks, "Did you do such-and-such?" he would have to answer truthfully out of fear, lest he be caught in a lie and his punishment be doubled. Because he is forced to tell the truth, he is effectively forced to turn from evil and do good. Here in Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt soon, I was close with a great pious man <note>original: "Chasid"</note> from the Sephardic community. Even if they had given him all the riches of the world, he would not, Heaven forbid, let a word that was not clearly true leave his mouth. He told me of his father's custom when he and his brothers were youths: if a complaint came that something improper had been done, the father would say, "Whoever confesses his sin and tells the truth, I will forgive him, provided he is careful from this day on not to repeat his folly. But whoever denies it—and I will investigate and search—if I find he lied and denied it, I will punish him manifold." And so he did; he forgave the one who confessed and even gave him a gift of coins for telling the truth, while the one who lied was punished severely. Thus he raised his children in the attribute of Truth, "buying" the truth with coins to fulfill "Buy the truth" <note>Proverbs 23:23</note>. His son became the pious man mentioned above, with the nature of truth fixed in him forever. Every clever person should act with knowledge on how to raise his children in good deeds, charity, piety, and all upright traits.

### Now I will speak of the attribute of Hope for fulfillment:
A father should always be promising his children [rewards]. For this, a father should give over his soul, body, and resources, spending much on his children's Torah study, considering it as nothing. He should lead the child in the way of discipline and scribe-craft <note>original: "Safrut"</note>, and also through persuasion and uprightness. He should praise the hidden rewards of learning Torah according to the youth's strength and as his intellect grows. How so? When he first learns to speak the Holy Tongue and verses like "The Torah that Moses commanded us" and "Hear O Israel," he should use the things a child loves to persuade him to go to the teacher to learn. When he grows older and despises the small gifts, give him things according to his new desires. If he grows and despises those, say to him, "Learn Torah and I will marry you to an important woman." Later, when he is more accustomed, say, "Learn Torah so that you will be a leader and a 'Rabbi' and be called by that title." Later still, tell him that in the merit of the Torah he will merit the Garden of Eden. Finally, when he becomes wiser, he will learn Torah for its own sake <note>original: "Lishmah"</note>, and not for any worldly thing. As it is said: "From doing it not for its own sake, one comes to do it for its own sake." Regarding the nature and order of study, I shall remember to record it, God willing, in the "Pillar of Torah."

<column-break/>

<gloss>S.G.H.</gloss>
The *Reshit Chochma* says: "Train a lad [according to his way]" <note>Proverbs 22:6</note>. If you train a lad according to the way of a youth, helping and teaching him according to his strength—how much to study and how much to pray—even a thousand times... [The text suggests that if a child is allowed to follow a bad path in youth, it becomes his nature]. If you let him go bad from his youth, do not leave him to his evil way or his youthful nature, for if he is not disciplined by your hand to return to the good, even when he grows old he will not depart from it. This is because it becomes like a natural foolishness to him, and he will not be able to change. Conversely, if you discipline him toward the good, those traits will become his nature, and he will not be able to depart from them. (See the words of the Sages of blessed memory on "Train a lad according to his way"). It is like saying: "Now, my son, in your youth..." meaning if you set a young man in his youth to a certain action, know that for all these things [God will bring you to judgment]. Similarly, "Train a lad," etc.—even when he grows old, he will not depart from that first path to which he was accustomed.

It highlights the importance of honesty, the power of prayer for one's descendants, and the use of progressive incentives to encourage Torah study.</summary>
