-># The Gate of Letters<-

->From the perspective of holiness and from the perspective of health—to transcribe all these matters would be a great length. I shall mention some of them in the sections concerning the order of eating in the Laws of Eating,<-
->and the order of intimacy in the Laws of Intimacy. Whoever wishes to understand them all should look in all the places I have marked.<-

## **M**oreover
Our Sages of blessed memory warned that a person should guard himself against dangers, bandits, evil creatures, a shaky wall, and a damaged bridge. "In every place, the Lord has established them." <note>A variation of Psalms 103:19</note> Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: "A person should always enter [a city] when it is good <note>original: "be-ki tov," meaning after sunrise</note> and leave when it is good <note>before sunset</note>," as it is said, "And none of you shall go out of the door of his house until morning." <note>Exodus 12:22</note> In the chapter on the "Order of Fasts," Rabbi Yannai said: "A person should never stand in a place of danger and say, 'A miracle will be performed for me,' for perhaps a miracle will not be performed; and if a miracle is performed, they deduct it from his merits." <note>Talmud, Ta'anit 20b</note> This is also mentioned in the chapter "With what may one light" <note>Talmud, Shabbat 32a</note>. They also warned about the danger of sorcery <note>witchcraft</note> regarding purchases made in haste, and one who cracks a louse... and one who pulls greens from a garden bed and eats them <note>The text refers to various folk beliefs and superstitions found in the Talmud regarding activities that invite demons or sorcery</note>, as found in the chapter "One who carries out wine" <note>Talmud, Shabbat 81b</note> and in Tractate Chullin, chapter "All flesh" <note>page 105</note>. They further mentioned at length many things that are difficult because of "damaging spirits" <note>original: "mazikin"</note> in the chapter "Evenings of Passover" <note>Talmud, Pesachim 111a</note>; see there at length. And they warned of many things because of an "evil spirit" <note>original: "ruach ra'ah"</note> as found in Chullin and in the chapter "He who brings sheep into the fold." They warned of a plague in the city and a famine in the city, etc. The Rama <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles, 16th-century legal authority</note> wrote in the *Tur*, section 116, that one should flee from the city when there is a plague in the city, and one should leave at the beginning of the plague and not at the end. All these things are due to danger, and "he who guards his soul will keep far from them." This is the common practice. Do not wonder at this: regarding the illness of smallpox <note>original: "blattern" in Yiddish/German</note> among children—if people are not careful to move the children and take them out of the city, the fathers will certainly be held accountable in judgment for the deaths of these nursing infants who did not sin, and the weaned children who did not transgress, who died of this sickness because their fathers did not care to help them escape. Therefore, every God-fearing man should be afraid and tremble at any trouble that might come. All these matters of guarding the body are included in the warning "Take heed to yourself and keep your soul diligently" <note>Deuteronomy 4:9</note>. It is also part of "proper conduct" <term>Derech Eretz (the way of the land/social etiquette)</term> to guard the body, for it is the case and the sheath for the soul, so that it may be a throne for the soul. It is also proper conduct to see that one's body is always clean—his fingers, his nostrils—from all dirt and filth. As it was taught in the chapter "With what may one hide": "A person washes his face, hands, and feet every day for the sake of his Creator," as it is said, "The Lord has made all for His purpose." <note>Proverbs 16:4</note> Aside from this reason, it is natural that physical cleanliness leads to an awakening of the soul's purity. When one is not clean, the power of the soul is dulled, and he acts like animals and beasts. One should not eat food that produces a foul odor from his mouth... and he should strive to appear in a good temperament so that he is not repulsive to other people. His whole body should be clean, and he should trim his hair and beard so that he is not unsightly to others; even more so, he must ensure no bad odor comes from his mouth and that he does not soil his clothes. He should also be careful with the dignity of his garments; he should wear a handsome and clean garment. It is forbidden for a stain or grease to be found on his garment, as it says in the chapter "These are the knots," that if a scholar <term>Talmid Chacham</term> is found with a grease stain on his garment, he is liable for death <note>a hyperbolic Talmudic expression of the disgrace such a person brings to the Torah</note>. He should not wear the garments of kings, such as gold and purple, at which everyone stares, nor the garments of the poor which shame the wearer, but rather average, handsome clothes according to his means. His flesh should not be visible through his clothes, like the very light linen garments found in Egypt. Also, by a person's gait, it is recognizable whether he is a wise man of understanding or a fool; so Solomon said in his wisdom: "Even as the fool walks on the way, his heart fails him, and he tells everyone that he is a fool." <note>Ecclesiastes 10:3</note> Behold, some aspects of proper conduct regarding physical perfection have been explained. To detail all matters of proper conduct is impossible; "let the wise man hear and increase his learning." This proper conduct is the path and the gateway to reach the perfection of the soul, which a person ought to enlarge and heal as mentioned above in the "Intellectual Treatise." However, the "proper conduct of the intellect" is that one should not try to be wiser than his ability and the level of his wisdom allows, as King Solomon, peace be upon him, said: "Do not be overly wise, lest you be confounded." <note>Ecclesiastes 7:16</note> And as our Sages of blessed memory said: "Do not seek out what is too wondrous for you." <note>Ben Sira 3:21</note> Rather, one should go upward in understanding step by step, adding to his wisdom and insight in a gradual manner; and "you shall remember wisdom."

## **P**roper Conduct
Regarding the perfection of one's wealth: One should always ensure that what the Blessed Name has given him is guarded and not lost. In the chapter "All who swear" <note>Talmud, Shevuot 45a</note>, Shmuel said: "I will tell you something... my father used to inspect his property twice a day, and I do not go up but once a day." Shmuel followed his own reasoning, for Shmuel said: "He who inspects his property every day finds a coin." Abbaye used to inspect his property every day; he found a gardener <unclear>carrying out</unclear> bundles of wood. He said to him, "Where are these going?" He replied, "To the master's house." He said, "The Sages have already preceded you" <note>meaning, your vigilance saved you from theft</note>. We can learn from this that a person should look over everything he has; if not every day, he should at least set one day every month. And he should establish his expenditures and how much they amount to. If he wants his expenses to be more profitable, he should reflect on how to economize so as not to collapse. The wife should be the overseer of the house, always looking after everything they have—vessels and clothes—to keep them whole, clean, and organized. Likewise, with the food in the house. My father and teacher, the pious one, wrote... "I have an old tradition from my ancestors not to throw away any old account <note>receipt or ledger</note> even though it has been calculated and paid in full and nothing currently comes of it. Nevertheless, do not throw it away; let it be placed in a hidden spot, for who knows what the day will bring? Perhaps a time will come when something must be proven from it." Thus far his words. They taught: "Any Torah that is not accompanied by work will eventually be nullified." Therefore, a man must see to and find for himself, with God's help, a craft or some business from which he can provide for himself and his household. He should not rely on the gifts of flesh and blood, nor on their loans. "Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord."

## **P**roper Conduct
Regarding the perfection of these three—wealth, body, and soul—which one should practice with his wife, his children, and his household. For the perfection of the soul, he must lead them and rebuke them in matters of Heaven, generally and specifically, and in the ways of morality <note>original: "mussar"</note>. If he does not do so, he is held accountable for their sins, as our Sages said in the chapter "With what may a beast": "Anyone who could have protested the behavior of his household and did not, is held accountable."

## **T**he Principal
The great foundation is raising children for the study of Torah and "teaching them to your children," for this is the purpose of procreation—to have children and grandchildren forever occupied with Torah and commandments. It is known that "man is born as a wild donkey's colt" <note>Job 11:12</note> and "the inclination of a man's heart is evil from his youth." Therefore, one must habituate and train him in good and upright traits from the time he can speak, as our Sages said: "A child who knows how to speak, his father teaches him 'Hear O Israel' and 'The Torah that Moses commanded us,'" and similar things. The verse says: "Train a child according to his way; even when he is old, he will not depart from it." <note>Proverbs 22:6</note> The father and mother should not withhold discipline; train him from his youth and add to it day by day as much as he can bear according to his understanding. One should not spare the "rod of discipline," as it is written: "He who spares his rod hates his son, but he who loves him seeks him with discipline." <note>Proverbs 13:24</note> All the bad traits that a person should distance himself from—such as oaths, curses, anger, cruelty, pride, impudence, envy, hatred, lust, gossip, mockery, evil speech <term>Lashon Hara</term>, and the like—are many. Likewise, the good traits with which a perfect man should be clothed are the opposite of these: fear, shame <note>modesty/conscience</note>, silence, and many others. Above all is the knowledge of the Blessed Name according to his strength, and that words of holiness and fear should always be in his mouth. In all these "Gates of Character Traits," one must discipline his body to acquire them in his soul. One should rebuke [his children] every single day—rebuke even a hundred times—speaking gently, not resting or being quiet until they are acquired in his soul. This should begin from the age of three or four years to guide him. One should start from childhood for two reasons: First, because our Sages said: "Childhood is a crown of roses" <note>Aramaic: "Yankuta klula de-varda," meaning what is learned in youth is preserved</note>; whatever one acquires in his soul in childhood remains naturally established all his days. This is "Train a child according to his way"—while he is a young lad, he should practice good traits, and then "even when he is old, he will not depart from it." Second, when a father begins to discipline his son with the "rod of discipline" and with great awe while the lad is small, he will have "open rebuke and hidden love." The son will always stand in awe of the father, trembling when he hears his father's discipline, even when he grows old. But if in his youth the father showed him excessive affection and never grieved him, then later when he grows up, he will turn his ear away from listening to the voice of his father and mother. They compared this to a sapling: while it is young, a person can bend it and straighten it according to his will. But if it grows into a crooked tree, it is impossible to straighten it afterward. So it is with a lad. Regarding this, King David said: "That our sons may be like saplings grown up in their youth" <note>Psalms 144:12</note>—this is the parable of the sapling. Therefore, "he who loves him seeks him with discipline" <note>Proverbs 13:24</note>, meaning he should stand in the "morning" <note>a play on the Hebrew word "shicharo," which means both to seek and refers to the morning/dawn</note>, meaning while he is small. Therefore, the discipline should be in the morning. Regarding this "morning," the Rabbis hinted: "The sleep of the morning removes a man from the world." But this is also true: a father must be careful not to "sleep through the morning"—that is, the child's youth. Likewise, every person should habituate himself in his youth and wake with an awakening...

Having concluded the previous section on physical and familial responsibilities, it now focuses on the letter "He" for Hillel (Praise) and begins the letter "Vav" for Vatranut (Generosity).</meta>

# Letter He: Praise
This letter of praise <note>Hebrew: *Hillel*</note> should serve as a reminder for you of the praise due to the greatness of the Lord, who is praised—blessed is He and blessed is His name. It also encompasses the great works of the Lord which He, blessed is He, brought into existence to be lauded and praised, as it is written: "Let every soul praise the Lord." <note>Psalm 150:6</note> Our Sages said in *Genesis Rabbah* 70: "For every single breath <note>Hebrew: *neshimah*, playing on the similarity to *neshamah*, soul</note> that a person breathes, they must offer praise." These are the words of Rabbeinu Bahya on the Torah portion *Kedoshim*, regarding the verse where King David says, "The Lord blessed my times" <note>This refers to a non-canonical or interpretative reading often cited in homiletic literature</note>. It hints that the Great Name <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH</note>—about which it is written, "This is My name forever" <note>Exodus 3:15</note>, but written as "to be hidden" <note>The word *le-olam* (forever) is written without a *vav*, allowing it to be read as *le-alem* (to hide)</note>—includes in its permutations the twenty-four hours of the day (twelve by day and twelve by night). It also includes the moments, symbolized by the number 864 <note>The text uses a Gematria/cipher system to reach this number</note>. For in the rotation of the first letter of the Name, we find fourteen hours and moments. Therefore, the verse concludes, "I am the Lord," meaning that the "I" of the Infinite opens at all hours and moments through the Great Name that encompasses them all. These are his words, though his meaning is cryptic and has many interpretations—"all of which the wind shall carry away." <note>A phrase meaning they are secondary or less certain</note>

In my youth, I received a beautiful explanation of this: that in the "rotation of the first letter"—referring to the first letter of the Name—we find fourteen hours in its "fullness" <note>*Millui*: spelling out the letter name</note>. If you rotate it through the four letters of the Name, you find 864. <note>The math here involves Kabbalistic permutations of the letters of God's name with their spelled-out forms</note>. However, this interpretation also seems distant from the plain language. Furthermore, the relationship between these "fillings" is inconsistent.

But then, the Lord enlightened my eyes through what the Rabbi wrote in *Pardes Rimonim* <note>A seminal Kabbalistic work by Moshe Cordovero</note>, in the "Gate of Specific Names," Chapter Two. He wrote that when you join the letter *Aleph* with the name *Yod-He-Vav-He*, and combine each letter of the Name with the six vocalization marks <note>Vowels</note>—which are the five phonetic movements symbolized by <insert>Dew and Rose</insert> <note>Hebrew: *Tal ve-Rod*, a mnemonic for the Hebrew vowels</note> plus the *Sheva*, which is the intermediate movement—the result is as follows: Rotate the six vowels of the *Aleph* with the *Yod* ten times, and likewise with the *He* thirty-six times, and with the *Vav* thirty-six times, and with the second *He* thirty-six times. The total equals 864. Specifically: the rotation of *Aleph* with *Yod* equals 396; *Aleph* with *He* equals 210; *Aleph* with *Vav* equals 252; and the final *Aleph* with *He* equals 210. The sum is 864. He elaborated on this because one finds wonders in it. This is the secret of the twelve hours of the day and twelve of the night.

Through this, the words of Rabbeinu Bahya are clarified, as is what is written in *Reshit Chochma* <note>"The Beginning of Wisdom," a 16th-century ethical-kabbalistic book</note> at the end of the tenth chapter of the "Gate of Awe": "There are 864 parts in an hour, and corresponding to them, the four-letter Name rotates in its vowel permutations... these are the 864 breaths that a person breathes [in an hour]. For every single breath, there is a letter from the four-letter Name that gives it the vitality of that breath." This is the meaning of "Man lives by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord." <note>Deuteronomy 8:3</note> Since the Blessed Name gives the breath and life, it is fitting that all one's breaths be dedicated to the service of the Creator. When a person contemplates this, he will fear sin and find within himself humility and lowliness. For how can he sin or act lightheadedly with the very life that the Blessed Name sustains and flows into him? 

My master, of blessed memory, would say that because of this, the Books of the Palaces <note>*Heichalot* literature, early Jewish mystical texts</note> refer to the Blessed Name as a "Humble King" <note>original: *Melech Aluv*</note>. For there is no greater "insult" than this: that with the very life that He, may He be blessed, flows into a person and their limbs—which He prepared for the person to serve Him—the person rebels. This is like a king who gave his servant money to sustain himself, and the servant took that money to buy a stick to strike the king. Is there any worse servant than that? Yet, the Blessed Name is "humble," overlooking transgression and acting with patience. How much more so should a creature formed from a "foul drop" <note>A common Rabbinic reference to human humble biological origins</note> overlook his own impulses and pride?

---

## Further General Rules of Praise
One must praise and thank the Blessed Name for everything He bestows, whether good or bad, for our Sages of blessed memory established blessings for all things. In truth, everything the Blessed Name does is for the good. Therefore, just as one blesses for the good, one must bless for the bad. One should offer praise and thanks for every single benefit that comes to him: whether spiritual—such as an increase in intellectual insight—or physical, or financial. Even if it is a small amount, it should be great in his eyes. He should think, "Who am I and what is my life, that I should have more than this or that person?" Certainly, if the Blessed Name bestows great and abundant bounty upon him, he should glorify and praise Him. Likewise, if the Blessed Name sends him some suffering, he should consider that "in God, the darkness is for the good," <note>A common idiom in Jewish thought that even hidden darkness has a divine purpose</note> and he should glorify and exalt Him. He is obligated to praise, as the Sages learned from the verse: "In the Lord <note>referring to mercy</note> I praise the word; in God <note>referring to judgment</note> I praise the word." <note>Psalm 56:11</note> I have already elaborated on this in the fifth discourse.

### Further
Within this general rule is a specific matter: a person is obligated to praise the Lord for his **sneezes**. This is mentioned in the *Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer*: From the day heaven and earth were created, no man ever became ill and survived. Rather, wherever he was—on the road or in the market—if he sneezed <note>Hebrew: *atas*</note>, his soul would depart. This continued until Jacob came and sought mercy for this. He said before the Holy One, Blessed be He: "Master of the Universe, do not take my soul from me until I have commanded my house, my children, and my household." He was answered, as it is said, "And it came to pass after these things, that it was said to Joseph [that his father was sick]." <note>Genesis 48:1</note> All the kings of the earth heard this and trembled, for no one had been safe [from sudden death] since the world was created. Therefore, a person is obligated at the time of his sneezing to thank the Holy One, Blessed be He, for turning him from death to life, as it is written: "His sneezings flash forth light." <note>Job 41:10</note> I have heard that some people say when they sneeze, "For Your salvation I hope, O Lord," <note>Genesis 49:18</note> which is beautiful. The intent of this praise to God is: "Just as I was saved just now, so too I hope for Your ultimate salvation," similar to the Blessing of Deliverance <note>The *Gomail* blessing</note> said by those who owed a debt [of gratitude] and were granted good.

### Further
Included in this is the duty to praise and laud everything that the Holy One, Blessed be He, created, for this is His glory. The actions of the Craftsman testify to the wisdom of the Craftsman, as it is said, "How manifold are Your works, O Lord!" and "Great are the works of the Lord." One should examine the entire chain of existence and contemplate as much as possible. Even that which appears "ugly," the Lord made all of it with wisdom. Therefore, the Sages established blessings for seeing unusual creatures, just as they did for beautiful ones. For the greatest Craftsman in the world knows why He made them so. 

This is seen in the story of Rabbi Shimon ben Eleazar, who was coming from Migdal Eder, riding on a donkey, and his heart was haughty because he had studied much Torah. He encountered a man who was very ugly. He said to him, "How ugly is this man!" The man replied, "Go to the Craftsman who made me and say to Him, 'How ugly is this vessel You have made!'" Immediately, Rabbi Shimon descended from his donkey and prostrated himself before him, saying, "I have sinned against you, forgive me." The man said, "I will not forgive you until you go to the Craftsman who made me." When the people of the city came out to meet the Rabbi, saying "Peace be upon you, our Rabbi," the man asked them, "Who are you calling 'Rabbi'?" They said, "The one walking behind you." He replied, "If this is a Rabbi, may there not be many like him in Israel." They asked what he had done, and he told them. They said, "Even so, forgive him." He replied, "I forgive him, provided he does not make a habit of this." 

This applies not only to human form, but to everything created in the world—one should not speak disparagingly of it. The *Duties of the Heart* <note>Bahya ibn Paquda</note> tells of a pious man walking with others who found a stinking carcass on the path. One person said, "How this carcass stinks!" The pious man replied, "How white its teeth are!" <note>Finding something to praise even in a carcass</note> This was to say: "Why do you speak of its shame? Contemplate the praise within it." He certainly did not praise it because he enjoyed the smell, but to counter the disparagement. 

Our Sages also derived the prohibition of treating food with contempt, for it is a plant that grows from the Exalted One. Therefore, it is forbidden to harm anything in the world unless it is for His glory. Rabbi Moses Cordovero wrote similarly in *Tomer Devorah*: "One should not despise any existing thing, for all were created with wisdom. One should not uproot a plant unless it is needed, nor kill a living creature unless it is needed, and should have mercy upon them." This is the general rule: compassion for all existing things, not to destroy them, is rooted in wisdom. One only elevates them from level to level—from plant to animal, and from animal to human—at which point it is permitted to uproot a plant or slaughter an animal in order to grant it merit <note>By using its energy for human service of God</note>.

### And the Praise
The most excellent praise of all, which rises above all others regarding created things, is the praise of the excellence of the Torah—both its hidden and revealed aspects—and the praise of the righteous, the pious, and people of good deeds, in order to provoke "scribal envy" <note>Positive competition in learning</note> so that wisdom may increase.

->The Letter He is Completed<-

# Letter Vav: Generosity
In Tractate Megillah, Rabbi Nechunya the Great was asked, "By what merit have you lived so long?" He replied, "In all my days, I never accepted gifts," as it is written, "He who hates gifts shall live," <note>Proverbs 15:27</note> "nor did I insist on my rights <note>original: *lo amadeti al midotai*, meaning he was forbearant and didn't hold grudges or demand strict justice</note>, and I was generous with my money." This does not mean one should be a spendthrift or wasteful, for Rabbi Chiya said in the name of Ulla: "A Torah scholar should be exacting even about less than a penny's value." Rather, the matter is to be generous in the place where it is appropriate to be generous, weighing his words in the scales of the Torah. Let him learn from Jacob our father, who was...

<meta>This page continues the ethical instructions within the "Gate of Letters," specifically concluding the section on the letter Dalet (representing *Derech Eretz* or "Proper Conduct"). It follows the previous discussion on spiritual and family life, moving now into the practicalities of household peace, financial wisdom, and social humility.</meta>

# The Gate of Letters
**Truth**

**A father and mother** should be careful not to instill fear in a child using "impure" things—for example, saying "the cat," "the dog," or "the non-Jew" will take the child. For "a covenant is made with the lips" <note>Hebrew: *berit karuta lisfatayim*—a traditional belief that spoken words, especially warnings of harm, have the power to come true</note>. God forbid <note>Hebrew: *Bar minan*</note>, this gives strength to the "Shells" <note>Hebrew: *Klippah*—in Kabbalah, these are the forces of impurity</note> associated with those names, and there is a fear the child may be harmed by them. One should also avoid such speech regarding their servants. One who guards their soul will stay far from this. This matter is well-known to the "Sages of the Secrets" <note>The Kabbalists</note>. It is said of such a person that they are "holy," and "in His palace, all say 'Glory.'" <note>Psalm 29:9</note> Here I have explained the "Way of the Land" <note>Hebrew: *Derech Eretz*—referring here to ethical behavior and social etiquette</note> that brings perfection to the soul within one's home.

## Proper Conduct
Regarding the perfection and purity of the body: This is one of the four "Tractates of Ethics." The explanation is based on the verse "as the waters cover the sea" <note>Isaiah 11:9</note>, which Rav Azira taught in the name of Rabbi H. regarding how one manages their home.

**It is taught** in the name of Rav Assi: "What does the verse mean, 'A good man is gracious and lends; he conducts his affairs with justice'? <note>Psalm 112:5</note> It means a person should always eat and drink less than what his means allow, dress and cover himself according to what his means allow, but honor his wife and children *more* than what his means allow. For they are dependent on him, but he is dependent on the One who spoke and the world came into being." Rashi <note>The preeminent medieval commentator</note> explains: "A good man is gracious" refers to one who lends to others, and "conducts his affairs with justice" means he is balanced in his spending. Furthermore, a person must always be careful not to wrong his wife <note>Hebrew: *ona'at isha*—referring to verbal or emotional distress</note>, for since her tears are frequent, the punishment for wronging her is quick to come. Rashi glosses this as: <gloss>punishment</gloss> for wronging her comes quickly. One should not cast excessive fear upon his household, but rather conduct everything with gentleness. Regarding the laws of lighting Shabbat lamps, Rabba bar Rav Huna said: even though the Sages said a man must say three things in his home on the eve of Shabbat as it gets dark <note>"Have you tithed? Have you prepared the Eruv? Light the lamp."</note>, he must say them gently so that the family will accept them from him. Rav Ashi said: "I had not heard this teaching from Rabba bar Rav Huna, yet I fulfilled it through my own common sense." In the chapter "The One Who Casts" in Tractate Gittin, Rav Hisda said: "A person should never cast excessive fear within his house, for the 'Concubine of Gibeah' <note>A tragic biblical story in Judges 19 where a man's harshness led to a national catastrophe</note> had excessive fear cast upon her, and it led to the fall of tens of thousands in Israel." Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: "Anyone who casts excessive fear in his home will eventually stumble into three sins: sexual immorality, bloodshed, and the desecration of the Sabbath." They further said: "Always be careful to honor your wife, for blessing is only found in a man's house because of his wife," as it says, "And he treated Abram well for her sake." <note>Genesis 12:16</note> It is told that Rabbi Hiyya's wife used to trouble him. Yet when he would find a particularly nice piece of silk, he would wrap it up and bring it to her as a gift. Rav said to him, "But she troubles you, Master!" He replied, "It is enough for us that they raise our children and save us from sin." This is a matter of kindness, and it was a common saying in the mouth of Abaye: "Peace in the home enriches it." It is written in the name of Rabbi Simcha: "One who strikes his wife violates the prohibition 'Why do you strike your fellow?'" <note>Exodus 2:13</note>

## Proper Conduct
For a woman, it is to be humble toward her husband, listening to his voice. Her words with her husband should be with grace, supplication, honor, fitness, and humility. She should listen to his words and do his will, always showing him a joyful face. She should be mindful of his mealtimes and prepare delicacies that he loves. She should set aside her will for his <insert>even if his words seem strange in her eyes</insert>. It is brought in the chapter "The One Who Casts" in Tractate Nedarim: There was a certain Babylonian man who went up to the Land of Israel and married a woman. He said to her, "Bring me two *butzini*." <gloss>meaning: melons</gloss> She brought him two *shragin*. <gloss>meaning: lamps; based on Nachmanides' explanation of the word 'butzinia'</gloss> He said to her [in frustration], "Go break them on the *bava*!" <gloss>meaning: he meant for her to break them on the gate, but she thought he meant on the head of the Sage Baba ben Buta</gloss>. Baba ben Buta was sitting and judging a case. She went and broke them on his head. He asked her, "Why did you do this?" She replied, "So my husband commanded me." He said to her, "You have done the will of your husband; may the Omnipresent bring forth from you two sons like Baba ben Buta."

## The Woman
At the time of her husband's anger, she should be calm. In his time of trouble, she should comfort him. In his time of joy, she should rejoice with him. In those moments, she should not allow any hidden grief in her heart to show, so as not to sadden him. She should always adorn herself before him with humility, grace, and modesty. Her clothes should be according to their means. In their life of love and in their poverty, she should be happy with his gifts and show that they are plenty, even if they are few. She should pray every day for her husband to succeed in his work and for her children to succeed in Torah and commandments.

## And Let There Be
Great peace between a man and his wife, for the Name of God dwells between them. As our Sages of blessed memory said: "If a man and woman are worthy, the Divine Presence rests between them." <note>The Hebrew words for man (Ish) and woman (Isha) both contain letters from God's name (Yud and He). If those letters are removed, only the word 'Esh' (Fire) remains</note>. But if they stray into conflict, God forbid, the Name is erased and what remains is "Fire and Fire." It is well known how great the commandment is to bring peace between a person and their fellow, and how much more so between a man and his wife. If the Sages spoke of the wife of another, how much more so for one's own wife. He and she should see to it that peace lives between them; then they are fortunate in this world and it will be good for them in the World to Come.

## Proper Conduct
Regarding the perfection of wealth in the management of one's home: I have already mentioned the words of our Sages—that one should honor his wife and children more than his means. Many who watch over women's affairs say their words are meant to guard their bodies, their ways, their behavior, and their intentions.

## Regarding
The expenses for his children: Our Sages have warned in many places that a person should be careful not to show favoritism between children. It is proper for a man to give his children as much as he can to make a distinguished and worthy marriage match (*Shidduch*), to support Torah scholars, and to connect with a great and well-born family. The main "principal" <note>Hebrew: *keren*—referring to the core character of the person</note> is the person himself, that he should be established in all high virtues and traits. However, it is seen among some fathers that when they have wealth, as they grow older, they give each of their children a large sum after they are married, keeping for themselves only what they estimate to be enough for their daily needs. This is a great foolishness. It brings a person into a state of great poverty and leads to great sin. For the "wheel of fortune" turns quickly; perhaps one day the wheel will turn against the father. It is a bitter thing for a father to have to rely on his children's table, for it is something against nature. Though children may support their father, he becomes a heavy burden upon them. Even if they are wealthy, all his past goodness is forgotten, and because of this, the children fall into great poverty of spirit. Therefore, any wise person who "sees what is being born" <note>An idiom for anticipating consequences</note> will not do this. Only regarding the dowry for a worthy marriage should he give, for that is a great purpose. But to distribute large gifts afterward—he should not do this at all during his lifetime. For there is no evil in the world like the evil of a father or mother being dependent on their children's table. Of such a person it is said, "It is like death." I have heard people say jokingly that when Jacob came to Egypt, he merited being supported by his righteous son who provided for everyone, yet he said, "Now I can die, after I have seen your face" <note>Genesis 46:30</note>—meaning, it was as difficult as death in his eyes to be forced to rely on him. There is a folk proverb: "One father supports ten sons with love and will, but ten sons cannot support one father with love and will." Therefore, no wise father should cause himself to fall into this trait by his own choice. If it happens from Heaven, that is another matter, for "sufficient is the trouble in its time," and may the Merciful One save us.

## Proper Conduct
For the perfection of body, soul, and wealth in one's conduct toward others: How is "Perfection of the Soul" achieved? By always associating with the wise and people of beauty, learning from their deeds and their devotion. From every person in whom he sees something good, or some lesson or behavior, he should learn. As Ben Zoma said: "Who is wise? He who learns from every person." <note>Ethics of the Fathers 4:1</note> Likewise, if he knows his words will be heard, he should teach others from his Torah and instruct them in commandments, good deeds, and traits. He should fulfill the verse "You shall surely rebuke your fellow" <note>Leviticus 19:17</note> to return people to what is good in every way possible, so that he is both meritorious himself and brings merit to others.

## Perfection
Of the body: One should perform acts of kindness with his physical self for everyone, being of service to each person and fulfilling "Love your neighbor as yourself." He should be humble and lowly before all the world. When he thinks of himself and his fellow, he should remember his fellow's good traits and remember his own anger and flaws. He should give honor to his fellow, walking to his fellow's left, and possess a "shamefaced" <note>meaning: modest or bashful</note> countenance. He should not lift his eyes haughtily. His speech with people should be gentle, without raising his voice, and in humility. Nachmanides wrote in the letter he sent to his son: "My son, conduct yourself with the trait of humility to walk in it always. All your words should be gentle, your head bowed, your eyes looking down toward the earth but your heart upward. Do not look a person in the face when speaking with them. Every person should be greater than you in your eyes. If he is wealthy or wise, you must honor him. If he is poor and you are wealthier or wiser than him, consider in your heart that you are more guilty than he and he is more innocent than you—for if he sins, it is an accident, but your sins are intentional. In all your deeds, words, and thoughts, consider yourself as standing before the Omnipresent, with His Presence over you, for His glory fills the world. Your words and speech should be with awe and fear, like a servant before his master. Be ashamed before every person. If someone calls you, do not answer with a loud voice, but gently, like one standing before his master." These are his words.

## Perfection of Wealth
One's business dealings should be in good faith. His "no" should be "no" and his "yes" should be "yes." He should not change his word; he should guard the utterance of his lips. He should perform acts of kindness with his money as much as possible, and "the noble man stands by noble deeds." <note>Isaiah 32:8</note>

---

->The Letter Dalet is completed<-

<header>The Gate of Letters</header>

<margin>
<note>original: "ספ"ק דנזיר" - end of the first chapter of Tractate Nazir</note>
At the end of the first chapter of Nazir: "And not hidden and hidden," <note>Referring to the complexities of vows and awareness</note> which is to say, beneath the investigation of every transgression. It is known that one section is at the end of the Torah portion *Masei* <note>Numbers 33:1–36:13</note>. He mentioned zeal through the verse: "She rises while it is yet night..." [Proverbs 31:15] until "she shall not eat of the bread of idleness" [Proverbs 31:27]. This "bread" is the sustenance of the Torah, as explained in the Zohar. It becomes "tasty dishes" for me, as I heard regarding the positive commandments. Since the Torah says, "Come, eat of my bread," and when one brings in "sharp" spices <note>meaning deep or difficult insights</note> they are eaten with the "perfume" of heaven. Therefore, one requires the secret of zeal, as written in the book *The Beginning of Wisdom* <note>Hebrew: Reshit Chochmah, a famous 16th-century kabbalistic ethical work</note>.
</margin>

to any prohibition, God forbid, nor to any bad character trait. Instead, "turn toward the good" <note>Psalm 34:15</note> through some commandment or good action. Let his character be good so that he may serve as a dwelling for the Divine Presence (*Shekhinah*). 
He should be zealous and early to bring himself to this good, performing the act with alacrity and joy. Concerning this, Ben Tema said: "Be bold as a leopard... and strong as a lion" [Ethics of the Fathers 5:20]. One should not give even a moment's rest for the Evil Inclination to find shelter or lead him astray. "Strong as a lion" refers to the idea of: "Who is strong? He who conquers his [evil] inclination," as mentioned by Ben Zoma. 

In the book *The Ascent of Traits*, it is written: "Know, my son, that the quality of zeal is a precious trait. From the very beginning of man's creation, he was only created to be zealous in his actions and his ways, as it is written: 'And man became a living soul' [Genesis 2:7]. What is the meaning of 'living'? It means 'zeal' <note>The author links the Hebrew word for "living" (*chaya*) with vitality and quickness</note>." 
Our Sages of blessed memory said in the *Aggadah* <note>homiletic traditions</note>: God made man an "expert worker" for himself, for if he does not toil, he does not eat. See what is written regarding man's placement in the Garden of Eden: "to work it and to guard it" [Genesis 2:15]. Did it really need "working" and "guarding"? Rather, it was to make him zealous... (until here are his words).

One can also interpret the verse "which a man shall do, and live by them" [Leviticus 18:5] to mean "living" in the sense of the "living soul" mentioned above. This means a person should perform commandments with vitality and zeal, and not like a lazy person. When a spirit of laziness or sadness resides in a man, it is an external force <note>a "shell" or unholy energy</note> that makes all his limbs heavy, so that he lacks the strength to rise from his bed for Torah study or prayer, or for other commandments. In such a state, his limbs are as if they were dead. But a man should do them and "overpower like a lion" through his cleaving to the "Living God," and then he truly "lives by them." 

This is also close to the meaning of Rashi's commentary in Tractate Berakhot regarding the requirements for a cup used for a blessing; one requirement is that it must be "living" <note>Hebrew: *chai*</note>. Rashi explains this in the old language as *fresco* <note>original: "פרישק"ו" (fresco) - French/Italian for fresh</note>, meaning it is healthy and its flavor has not faded. It is all the same concept.

### Completed the Letter Zayin [Zeal]

# The Letter Chet: A Good Friend
We learned in the first chapter of *Ethics of the Fathers*: "Acquire for yourself a companion (*chaver*)." Our Sages also said: "Either a companion or death" <note>Taanit 23a—emphasizing that human connection is vital for survival and sanity</note>. The Sage said: "A man without a friend is like a left hand without a right hand." 
The pious Rabbi Yonah wrote that among the paths of repentance, a person must have a friend to speak with. If he should violate the resolutions of his repentance, the friend can rebuke him, wake him up, and save him from sin. Regarding such people it is said: "Then those who feared the Lord spoke to one another..." [Malachi 3:16]. 

So too, regarding the study of Torah, our Sages said: "A sword is upon the lonely [scholars]..." <note>Taanit 7a—warning against solitary study which can lead to error or foolishness</note>. Friends must review their learning together and explain it. How good and how pleasant! 

This is the meaning of the "change" <note>the benefit</note> that comes from the association of friends for study:
1. If they are both wise and have served their teachers sufficiently, they join together to "sharpen" one another. They must fulfill the words of our Sages in Tractate Shabbat: Rabbi Jeremiah said in the name of Rabbi Eleazar: "Two Torah scholars who sharpen one another in Jewish law (*halacha*), the Holy One, Blessed be He, grants them success." Do not read the verse as "and your glory (*hod’cha*)" but "and your sharpening." Not only that, but they rise to greatness. If they do so, they merit the Torah which was given with the "right hand." Rav Nachman bar Isaac said: "These are the Torah scholars who are referred to as being at the right hand of the Torah." One must be careful that this study is done "for its own sake" (*lishma*), without pride or thinking, "When will I get my turn to show how my words drip with grace and the depths of Torah?" 

Rabbi Jeremiah said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: "Two Torah scholars who are gentle with one another in Jewish law, the Holy One, Blessed be He, listens to them." Rashi explains "gentle" to mean they discuss the matter with a pleasant spirit so they can learn from one another. "He will speak to nations under us"—He will humble them <note>The author uses a play on words between "speaking" and "leading"</note>. All humility comes through gentleness. To "speak" is like "he led," as in the Aramaic translation of "He shall lead." According to the first explanation, the debate should be gentle and not with shouting, so that one understands his friend's words and then admits to the truth. According to the second explanation, they should help one another if a difficulty arises in their analysis. We see this often in the Talmud: "This works well for Abaye according to Raba..." even though they were usually disputants.

**Furthermore**, there is a second type of friendship: a group of students where each one lacks knowledge, but through joining together, their understanding and knowledge increases. Regarding this they said: Rabbi Abba said in the name of Resh Lakish: "Two Torah scholars who listen to one another in Jewish law, the Holy One, Blessed be He, listens to their voice." Rashi explains "listening" as teaching and explaining things to each other. "The one who sits in the gardens, companions listen for your voice" [Song of Songs 8:13]—the "gardens" are the study halls. 

Rabbi Abba also said: "Two Torah scholars who form a group (*madgilim*) for one another in Jewish law, the Holy One, Blessed be He, loves them." Raba said: "This applies when they [at least] know the general form of the topic, and when there is no great teacher in the city to learn from." Rashi explains "forming a group" as gathering together to say, "Let us learn this here together, since we have no rabbi to teach us the 'form' that a rabbi passes down to his student." The concept of *madgilim* is that they gather and toil until they understand the plain meaning, and then they continue to add to it. 

Also included in the category of a "Good Friend" is what Rabbenu Tam wrote in *The Book of Uprightness* (*Sefer HaYashar*) at the beginning of the fourth gate. He lists it as one of the modes of Divine service: a person should be strict with himself and associate with those like himself—the pious with the pious, the humble with the humble. In times of trouble or distress, he should avoid the opposite of these: people of luxury, the [arrogant] rich, the wicked, fools, the tyrant, the lowly, the contemptible, and the heretics. For the company of all these will destroy his faith, and Divine service cannot be maintained among them. 

One should always associate with a pious person and "dust oneself in the dust of his feet." Do not associate with an unlearned person (*Am Ha'aretz*), even if he appears pious. As we see in Tractate Shabbat: Rabbi Abba said in the name of Resh Lakish: "If an unlearned person is 'pious,' do not dwell in his neighborhood." Rashi explains: because he does not know the fine details of the commandments, his piety is not complete enough to learn from him.

**When** a person has a good friend and they join together for the sake of Torah and good deeds, in faith and with a whole heart for the service of God, happy are they! Each will help the other to awaken. Beyond their regular study, they should set aside one hour every day to examine their deeds and increase their spiritual awakening and repentance. They should love each other as their own souls, like the love of David and Jonathan. The Sage said: "No distance is too narrow for two lovers, and the whole world is not wide enough for two enemies." 

**Also** included in "friend" is what the Sages said: "A friend whom you see"—meaning wherever a person sees a "holy society" (*chavurah kadisha*), he should join them. For example: a society for visiting the sick, a burial society, a Psalms-recitation society, or a society that maintains a specific commandment, such as providing clothes for the needy or oil for synagogue lamps.
**Furthermore**, regarding a good friend, the Sage said: "A man's friend is his intellect; his enemy is his desire." A person should join himself to his intellect and his soul.

### Completed the Letter Chet

# The Letter Tet: Purity
Impurity that requires purity is found in three categories: spiritual impurity, physical impurity, and an intermediate type that is both spiritual and physical.
Spiritual impurity refers to the "Spirit of Impurity" that rests upon the hands. It is removed only through washing. It says in *Sefer HaKavanot*:
The following things require washing with water: one who rises from bed, one who leaves the bathroom or the bathhouse, one who trims his nails, one who removes his shoes, one who touches his feet, or one who scratches his head. Some say even one who walks among graves, one who touches a corpse, one who cleans his clothes of lice, one who has marital relations, one who touches a louse, or one who touches his body with his hand. 

If one did any of these and did not wash: if he is a scholar, his learning is forgotten from him; if he is not a scholar, he may lose his mind. One who lets blood and does not wash will be in fear for seven days. One who shaves and does not wash will be in fear for three days. One who trims his nails and does not wash will be in fear for one day—and he will not even know what he is afraid of! (Until here are his words). One must be careful to wash properly three times. However, one only recites the blessing over the washing of the hands in the morning... [Text cuts off]

<meta>This page continues the "Gate of Letters," moving through the alphabet of ethical traits. The previous page discussed the letter Dalet and began the letter Vav (Generosity/Vatranut). This page concludes the letter Vav and transitions into the letter Zayin (Zeal/Caution).</meta>

# The Gate of Letters

Our Rock <note>A poetic title for God</note> said, "And Jacob was left alone" [Genesis 32:25], and our Sages of blessed memory said that he remained because he forgot "small jars." This teaches that the righteous hold their property dear; above all, this is because they do not stretch out their hands to steal <note>original: "pachim ktanim"—the small jars Jacob retrieved, showing he valued even small items earned honestly</note>.
Yet we find elsewhere that he was generous even with his money, as our Sages of blessed memory interpreted the verse "in the grave which I dug for myself" [Genesis 50:5]. This teaches that Jacob took all the gold and silver he brought from the house of Laban and made it into a pile, saying to Esau: "Take this pile in exchange for your share in the Cave of Machpelah." Therefore, a person should learn from him not to scatter money for vanity or without need, but in the place of a commandment (*mitzvah*), he should give righteously. Regarding other
commandments that depend on funds—such as hiring a teacher, buying books, a *Tallit*, *Tefillin*, or a Torah scroll—any commandment that one buys at a high price, God forbid, is considered an ascent in holiness and is warned <note>meaning, it is highly valued in heaven</note>. He gave a sign and gave it 
without a commandment, for the "husk" <note>term: "Kelipah" - in Kabbalah, the shell of impurity or evil that thrives on lawlessness</note> finds comfort in abandonment. Therefore, one should spend freely for the sake of a commandment, and one should not abandon any commandment because of its cost. After all, Rabban Gamliel took an *etrog* <note>the citron used on Sukkot</note>
for a thousand *zuz* <note>an ancient currency; a thousand was an exorbitant sum</note>, provided that he did not spend more than a fifth of his wealth, as our Sages of blessed memory said: "He who spends freely should not spend more than a fifth." And even though the words of [the Talmudic tractate] Bava Kamma
imply that a person does not need to spend great wealth for a single commandment, even if it is a passing opportunity, this is why it was considered a great deed of Rabban Gamliel that he bought the *etrog* for a thousand *zuz*
in his wisdom. Even if it is not a passing commandment, when there are more available to sell, our Sages of blessed memory said in the first chapter of Bava Kamma: "For the beautification of a commandment (*hiddur mitzvah*), one spends up to a third." Rashi explains that if one finds
two Torah scrolls to buy, one more beautiful than the other, he should add a third of the price and take the beautiful one. For it is written: "This is my God and I will glorify Him" <note>original: "Zeh Eli ve’anvehu" (Exodus 15:2)</note>—beautify yourself before Him with commandments. Make for yourself a beautiful Torah scroll,
a beautiful *Lulav*, a beautiful *Tallit*, and beautiful *Tzitzit*. This is also the language of the Tosafot: "Up to a third of the commandment, that he should add a third to take the beautiful one," etc. Therefore, it clearly implies the opinion of the Rif in the chapter
"The Great Rabbi." The Rashal <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria, a 16th-century legal authority</note> in the book *Yam Shel Shlomo* on Rashi’s commentary regarding the "third for a commandment"—that he should add a third to take the beautiful one, etc.—it clearly implies the opinion of the Rif in the chapter
"The Stolen Lulav," who brought this teaching of beautifying the commandment, etc., on this Braita <note>an ancient oral tradition</note>: "Make for yourself a beautiful Torah scroll," etc. And so the Rosh explained there: that if one bought a *Lulav* and then happened upon another
finer one, he should add up to a third of the first one's price to exchange it for the finer one. This is "beautification" according to Rashi. But this is difficult for me: if so, there is no end to the matter! If twenty finer ones happen upon him,
each more beautiful than the last, should he give for all of them? <note>original: "v’chi litaiv l’chula" - should he give for all of them?</note> And this is the language of the Pnei Yehoshua regarding the price as found in the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (Smag). Its language in the first chapter of Bava Kamma is: "For beautifying a commandment, up to a third." Our teacher Jacob <note>The Tur</note> explains
that this does not mean that if he sees a beautiful Torah or a beautiful *etrog* he must add a third—for it is always possible to find something more and more beautiful. Rather, if he bought an *etrog* of the minimum size (a *ladum* or
an egg according to Rabbi Yehuda) and found a beautiful one, he should give up to a third more. But if it is larger than an egg, he does not need to add more. These are the words of my teacher and rabbi, etc. And so too
is the opinion of the Rosh in Bava Kamma. This is not such a great wonder regarding the Rosh, whose words seem to contradict themselves; for in "The Stolen Lulav" he brought the words of Rabbi Isaac of Orbe, that beautifying the commandment is based on "This is my God and I will glorify Him."
Therefore, he explained according to the Rif. But here, where it is the core of the statement, he explained the matter according to the reconciliation found in the Tur at the end of section 650, which is based on the Smag. These are the words of the Rashal, of blessed memory. But to me, it seems
that Rashi’s words are the most accurate. As for the objection against Rashi—that there would be no end to the matter because one could always find something more beautiful—it seems to me they were not precise with Rashi’s language. For in the Tosafot and the Chiddushim <note>analytical Torah commentaries</note>,
it is specifically when he *wants* to buy an *etrog* and there are several beautiful ones here, all of which are valid—then he should buy the most beautiful, even if he must add a third over the
price of the basic, valid one that is not so beautiful. But if he has already bought a valid *etrog* and acquired it—meaning he paid for it—and after some time a more beautiful *etrog* becomes available,
Rashi would agree that he does not need to buy it. This is implied by Rashi’s language, as he wrote: "If he found two Torah scrolls to buy," implying at the time he wants to buy, he found them so. And so, we can say
that the logic of both Rashi and the Tosafot is good: that at the start of the purchase, he should buy the most beautiful one found, even if it is more expensive by a third. But if he has already
bought an *etrog* and acquired it, then he does not need to add a third for beautification. He only needs to add a third even afterward for the sake of its size—that is, if what he bought was only
the exact minimum size, he should buy a larger one and add a third. But if what he already bought was large and not limited to the minimum size, then he does not need to add afterward for
the sake of beauty, but specifically at the start of the purchase before he acquires it, he should buy the beautiful one. And thus the words of the Rosh in the chapter "The Stolen Lulav" and in Bava Kamma are settled, for they agree with one another.
The words of both Rashi and the Tosafot are the "words of the Living God," and one who fears Heaven fulfills both. It is stated further in the Gemara <note>The Talmud</note>: Rav Ashi asked, "Is the 'third' calculated from the inside or
from the outside?" <note>meaning: is it 33% of the base price or 25% of the total?</note>. This remained an unsolved query (*teiku*). In the West <note>The Land of Israel</note>, they said in the name of Rabbi Zera: "Up to a third is from his own; from then on, it is from the Holy One, Blessed be He."
Rashi explains: Up to a third is from his own—meaning that third which he adds for the beautification of the commandment comes from his own pocket and he is not reimbursed in his lifetime, as we say "Today is for doing [the commandments] and not for receiving their reward." But from that point on, whatever he adds for beautification beyond
a third, the Holy One, Blessed be He, will repay him in his lifetime. The Yad Ramah <note>Rabbi Meir Abulafia</note> says: Up to a third, he reduces his own wealth, and it will be a merit for him in the World to Come. And what he adds beyond the third—
the addition will not be a loss to his wealth, for the Holy One, Blessed be He, will repay him, as it is said, "it is upon Me and I shall repay." And the principal remains for the World to Come. The legal decisors wrote that one is not obligated
to squander great wealth for a passing commandment, nor more than a fifth; this applies to the fulfillment of a positive commandment. But to avoid a negative commandment—which is "rise and do not act"—he should give
all the wealth of his house and not transgress.

## More

Regarding the trait of generosity between a man and his fellow: Maimonides wrote at the end of the chapter in the "Laws of Ethical Conduct," as follows: His business dealings should be in truth. Our Sages of blessed memory say: his "no" should be "no" and his
"yes" should be "yes." He should be exacting with himself in his accounting, but when he gives, he should be generous to others. When he takes from them, he should not be exacting with them. He should pay the price of a purchase immediately.
He should obligate himself in matters of buying and selling even in places where the Torah does not obligate him, so that he may stand by his word and not change it. If others become obligated to him in judgment, he should be forgiving
and permit it to them. He should be a lender and a gracer. He should not infringe upon the profession of his fellow. Thus far his words. One should also see that a person does not enter into a quarrel that is not his, as our Sages of blessed memory said: "He who did not do good"
is he who comes with a power of attorney <note>to sue on behalf of another</note>. Our father Suria <note>likely a reference to a specific ethical teacher or ancestor</note>, of blessed memory, said regarding expenses: "Some are hollowed out." "That which you shall do"—this is "beyond the letter of the law." Do not go to quarrel quickly with your creditors.
"And judges and officers you shall appoint for you"—meaning for yourselves; judge yourselves before you come to trial. Do not enter into lawsuits even if you are in the right, for
it is a disgrace for a scholar to degrade himself before judges. For regarding the two litigants, our Sages of blessed memory said: "They should be in your eyes like wicked men," and they did not distinguish between man and man. Thus far. His intent
is bad as a man who is lustful after the attribute of Justice. Even if his fellow is found liable to him in judgment, it is proper to waive something, unless it is a matter of absolute necessity or freedom.
"Let the law pierce the mountain" <note>term: "Yikov ha-din et ha-har" - a phrase for strict, unyielding justice</note>, but even then, not with haste, but with deliberation. Then a person cleaves to the Attribute of Mercy from Above. And toward the gentiles, it is a great commandment to sanctify the Name
with money—to return [lost items] to them so that they might say, "Blessed is the Lord, God of Israel." And although the trait of generosity is good, concerning the "generosity" of being a guarantor, which our Sages warned against:
A person should always guard himself against being a guarantor. I also am commanded and sworn by my ancestors, of blessed memory, that I should not be a guarantor for any man. So I command you with the strength of
->a command, and you shall guard yourselves exceedingly!<-

## Commandment

<margin>A humble person, as follows</margin>
It is a great and boundless commandment to have pity on the poor regarding their pledges <note>collateral</note>. Therefore, hold onto this commandment with love. In general, see to it that you perform all charity and acts of kindness.
To the distinguished poor, the distinguished person comes first. Do not stumble, God forbid, with poor people who are not worthy. "Your own poor come first." In any case, let no
humble person return ashamed. In the book *Orchot Tzaddikim* <note>The Ways of the Righteous, a classic ethical work</note>, it says: Let him be generous with his wealth to write and buy books and lend them to those who cannot afford them; his righteousness stands forever. Let him be generous,
taking care not to worry if the books are damaged because people are studying from them. And with his household vessels, let him be generous to lend to his neighbors and acquaintances. Let him be generous
to lend his money to the poor, and if he can afford it, lend to the rich as well. Let him be generous in his business dealings; he should never be exacting over a small matter, whether it is a rebel, wine,
oil, or anything else that might be scattered and not found. Let him be generous with his body, to toil for every person, to bear his yoke and burden, to feel pain in their distress, to pray
for them, to rejoice in their joy, to visit the sick, and to perform kindness with the dead. Above all, he must be generous with the wisdom of his Torah—to teach every person knowledge and to draw them
->toward Heaven. This is the greatest generosity of all types of generosity: one who volunteers to bring a person to the life of the World to Come. Thus far.<-

# The Gate of Letters

**There is also** a spiritual impurity which is the "great-grandfather" <note>original: "avi avi avot ha-tum'ah"—a technical term for the highest level of ritual impurity</note> of all impurities; this is the impurity caused by transgressions, as is written explicitly regarding forbidden relationships and forbidden foods. 
In the synagogue, one must be exceedingly careful to avoid contact <note>likely referring to touching one's body or unclean surfaces during prayer</note>, and if this occurs during a meal, one must purify their fingers.
The term "impurity" applies to every transgression a person commits. When one purifies themselves from all sin and guilt, they are called "pure," as it is written: "And I will sprinkle **clean water** upon you, and you shall be clean; from all your filthiness and from all your idols will I cleanse you" [Ezekiel 36:25]. King David, peace be upon him, also said: "And cleanse me from my sin" [Psalms 51:4]. We find purification through water, as it is written: "He shall wash his flesh in water and be clean," and we find purification through fire, as it is written: "Everything that can withstand fire, you shall pass through fire and it shall be clean" [Numbers 31:23]. This is how the purification of sins works: Water and Fire represent <term>Chesed</term> <note>Kindness/Mercy</note> and <term>Gevurah</term> <note>Strength/Judgment</note>. The concept of purification by fire is the "Strength" of repentance; it should burn within him like a flaming fire, and he should endure great ascetic practices according to the weight of the sins he committed—even corresponding to the four types of capital punishment, of which burning is the most severe. Corresponding to the "Waters of Higher Kindness" is the secret of the <term>Mikveh</term> <note>a ritual immersion pool</note>. How great is the matter of the ritual bath, both for ritual impurity and for the impurity of transgressions! Therefore, it is indispensable. 

Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas <note>original: "R"H," referring to the author of Reshit Chochma</note> wrote in the "Gate of Love" regarding the secret of the Mikveh: It is already known what Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explained in the *Zohar* and the *Tikunim* <note>foundational works of Kabbalah</note>, that it relates to the "Higher Secret" of the nine points on every side. The secret of the Mikveh is the secret of the letter *Yod*, which is satisfied by 40 <term>se'ah</term> <note>a unit of volume; a Mikveh must hold at least 40 se'ah of water</note>. So too, the name of God [YHWH] spelled out contains four letters, each comprising ten <note>4x10=40</note>. This is the secret of "The Mikveh of Israel is the Lord" [Jeremiah 17:13]. Our Sages said: "Just as a Mikveh purifies the impure, so does the Holy One, Blessed be He, purify Israel"—meaning the purification of their souls which are attached to His Name. Thus, one who immerses is truly clinging to the Name of God to purify their body and soul: the body through the physical water, and the soul through the spirituality of the Name that dwells there. Elsewhere, I will explain the secret of the Mikveh's structure and the mystery of immersion. For now, I have only come to inform you of the great virtue of the Mikveh. Happy is the one who habituates themselves to this purity constantly; it helps for all impurities and even for the impurity of sins. It leads to "Purity of Heart," as King David said: "A **pure heart** create for me, O God" [Psalms 51:12]. The first letters of the Hebrew phrase "**L**ev **T**ahor **B**ara" <note>Create a pure heart</note> can be rearranged to spell **Tevila** <note>Immersion/T-B-L</note>. From purity of the heart's desires comes purity of thought, which resides in the brain. One will then have pure thoughts, and the "Open Eye" <note>a Kabbalistic reference to divine providence</note> will dwell upon him. His eyes will be too pure to look upon evil. Afterward, this purity extends to all his limbs <note>original: "HGT HGM," referring to the emotional and physical attributes</note> and his "sinews" which correspond to the 613 commandments. It is written in *Reshit Chochma* that one who separates from ritual impurity is called "pure," as it says "and he shall wash his flesh in water." But one who separates from the impurity of sin is called both "pure" and "holy." "Pure," as it is written, "And you shall be purified from all your impurities," and "Holy," as it is written regarding forbidden relationships, "Do not defile yourselves with any of these," and similarly with forbidden foods, "Do not make yourselves impure with them," followed by "Sanctify yourselves and you shall be **holy**." 

**Another general rule:** A hint of purity is found in garments, for the removal of "invalid" clothing leads to purity, as it is written: "Purify yourselves and change your garments" [Genesis 35:2]. One is obligated to ensure their clothes are pure from filth and impurity, and that they are not stained with oil or grease. Our Sages said that a scholar who is found with a stain <note>original: "revav"—a grease or oil stain</note> on his garment is liable for a great punishment. The matter of clothing is this: the garments clothe the body, and the body clothes the soul. By purifying the garments, one awakens the purity of the body; and the purity of the body awakens the purity of the soul. Likewise, all of a person’s utensils—such as cups, bowls, and spoons—should be seen to be clean without any grime, only pure and clean. A woman should also ensure that cooking vessels are very clean from all grime. All these matters bring about purity of the soul, for one causes the other. This adds extra purity, so that his hands are clean and overflowing with abundance, all to increase holiness.

**Furthermore,** there is purity in eating, as the ancients used to practice eating "mundane foods in a state of sacred purity." However, this is a very difficult thing to maintain since we are all [ritually] impure nowadays. Therefore, one must at least ensure that the food items are not "prepared to receive impurity." This means the bread one eats should be kept "pure" by ensuring no water touched the grain from the time of harvest <note>in Jewish law, grain only becomes susceptible to ritual impurity after it has been intentionally wetted</note>. One would then knead the dough with fruit juice (which does not make food susceptible to impurity). One would only eat eggs and fruits that have not been "prepared" to receive impurity. When wanting to drink, one should go to the river so as not to touch the water [in a vessel]. The holy <term>Ari Zal</term> <note>Rabbi Isaac Luria, the great 16th-century mystic</note> used to practice this from Rosh Hashanah until after Yom Kippur. In the *Tur* <note>a classic code of Jewish law</note>, it is written in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud: "Rabbi Chiya said: If you can eat your food in purity all year, do so; if not, do so for seven days [a year]." The *Avi HaEzri* wrote that these are the seven days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. Therefore, it is the custom in Germany <note>Ashkenaz</note> that even someone who is not careful about "Bread of Gentiles" <note>term: "Pat Shel Goyim"—bread baked by a non-Jew without Jewish participation</note> all year is careful during these Ten Days of Repentance. 

The *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo's commentary</note> cites the *Tashbetz* regarding this: Rabbi Samuel of Joinville says that this is not precise; the custom is specifically about eating "mundane food in purity" which has no inherent prohibition. But regarding "Bread of Gentiles," which involves a prohibition, if one treats it as prohibited for these seven days, they should not be able to eat it all year either <note>due to the laws of vows</note>. However, the holy Ari Zal said the truth is that it only refers to "mundane food in purity." Rabbi Samuel did not understand the plain meaning; "Bread of Gentiles" here does not mean there is a forbidden element in the bread itself, but refers to bread brought from outside the city from those gentiles who sell it. Those who avoided "Bread of Gentiles" during these days did so because such bread had certainly been "prepared to receive impurity" <note>by being wetted with water</note>. They would instead bake their own bread and guard it from water so it remained "pure." Thus, the "Bread of Gentiles" mentioned here is avoided for the sake of eating "mundane food in purity."

**The Letter Yod: The Good Inclination** <note>original: "Yetzer Tov"</note>. Philosophers divided human desires into three categories: The Good, the Beneficial, and the Pleasant. The "Pleasant" refers to the body's desire for sweet and delightful things, such as the craving for food, physical intimacy, and all passions. Even if these are harmful to the body in excess, the coarse physical body still lusts for them. The "Beneficial" refers to one who acts wisely and abandons the "Pleasant" when it is bad for their health; they choose what benefits the body. This is of a higher level, yet it is not eternal, for eventually, when the time of passing comes, the body is gone. The third way is the desire of the perfectly righteous: to cling to the Torah and the Commandments all the days of their lives and to do what is "Good" in the eyes of God. This is called "**Good**." 

Thus, the "Evil Inclination" <note>Yetzer Hara</note> is the lowest extreme, likened to an animal, following the "Pleasant," and this evil eventually destroys itself. The "Good Inclination" is the highest extreme, clinging to the "Good." The "Beneficial" part is the middle ground. If a person follows the "Beneficial" only to be healthy and live a long life, this leans toward the "Evil Inclination." But if they follow the "Beneficial" so that they may be healthy and able to perform sacred service, this leans toward the "Good Inclination." Let a person choose wisely!

**Furthermore,** I say that the term "Good Inclination" can be explained in three ways. Happy is the man who walks, stands, and sits in its shadow. The Holy One, Blessed be He, gave the Torah and the Commandments "to perform them today" in this world and "to receive their reward tomorrow" in the World to Come. There are two aspects: the performance "today" and the reward "tomorrow." 
Regarding the "performance today," it is called "Good Inclination" <note>Yetzer Tov</note>, where "Good" means "Radiance," as in "when he dresses [improves] the lamps" <note>original: "be-heitivo et ha-nerot"—using the root for 'Good' to mean 'to clean/light'</note>, or "And God saw the light that it was **good**." Our Sages explained that when Moses was born, "she saw him that he was **good**," meaning the house was filled with light. The wise man has his eyes in his head; he does not walk in darkness. One who rebels against the King of Kings, the Holy One, Blessed be He, the Master of Worlds, is a fool, for there is no greater sin than this. It is a matter of shame. One who is intellectually sound is happy to do the will of his Creator, even if he receives no reward. As Rashi explained regarding the Heavens: Look at the Heavens—have they ever changed their nature? And they receive no reward! A wise man sees and looks and "sees that the light is good." "The wise man's eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness" [Ecclesiastes 2:14]. The fool does not understand, as our Sages said: "A person does not commit a transgression unless a spirit of folly enters him." I give this sign: every sinner is a fool. Therefore, a person should awaken their intellect and walk with the wise to become wise.

It is also called "Good Inclination" in terms of the reward to be received "tomorrow." That is a world that is "entirely Good." Regarding this "Good," it was the first thing in [God's] thought and the end of
