# The Gate of Letters

At night, if one must wash their hands; similarly, if one is in doubt—having risen early to study and washed their hands, then returned to sleep before daybreak—whether they must wash again when the day brightens. The <term>Rema</term><note>Rabbi Moshe Isserles, a major 16th-century legal authority</note> wrote in the <term>Shulchan Aruch</term><note>The Code of Jewish Law</note> that one should wash their hands without a blessing. Therefore, one must warn the common people when they rise for <term>Selichot</term><note>Penitential prayers recited before the New Year</note> before and after Rosh Hashanah, that they should wash their hands again when the day brightens. There is a further doubt regarding whether washing is required after sleeping during the day; due to this doubt, one should wash their hands at least three times even after a nap to maintain oneself in a state of purity. This is a "spiritual impurity," meaning it is not felt by touch, and its purification is achieved through washing.

<margin>Furthermore</margin> **There is** a tangible impurity, which is an impurity that exits the body itself, such as <term>Zav</term><note>a specific type of bodily discharge</note>, a seminal emission, or leprosy.

<margin>Furthermore</margin> **There is** an intermediate impurity, such as touching animal carcasses, reptiles, or the impurity of a corpse. In these cases, one becomes impure because they touched something tangible, but the tangibility did not stick to them; for this reason, I called it "intermediate." It is proper for a person to be pure and to distance themselves from becoming impure by any means possible. Even though, due to our many sins, we do not currently have the Holy Temple—and thus there is no concern regarding the "Awe of the Temple" <note>the fear of entering the Temple while impure</note>—nevertheless, why should a person draw impurity upon themselves? This is true unless it is for a commandment, such as attending to the needs of the deceased. Aside from that, one should separate from all impurity. Even though we are all currently impure <note>referring to the halakhic status of "impurity of the dead" in the absence of the Red Heifer rituals</note>, why should one add and draw more impurity upon themselves? Praiseworthy is the person who regularly immerses in a <term>Mikvah</term><note>a ritual bath</note>, for then they are purified from many impurities. Even regarding the immersion of a <term>Ba’al Keri</term><note>one who has had a seminal emission</note> for the sake of Torah study and prayer—regarding this, opinions multiplied in the Talmud and among the legal authorities as to whether the requirement was abolished. It is found in a letter of the <term>Rambam</term><note>Maimonides</note> that the heads of the academies in Babylon were astonished by him, asking why he was so lenient regarding the immersion of a *Ba'al Keri*. He, of blessed memory, replied to them that in all his days he never neglected it, but he could only write in his legal code that which is the strict law. I say: "He who comes to purify himself is assisted." Whoever resolves to remain in purity, surely the Holy One, Blessed be He, will assist him in making purity available. However, if it is not available, he should not neglect Torah study or prayer for this reason, since the law is that the requirement is abolished and one is not strictly liable. Nevertheless, one should clothe themselves in holiness at times of spiritual awakening. I testify by the One Name that there was a person who used to immerse himself at his designated times, and sometimes in a spirit of awakening. He also used to immerse on the day his wife immersed following her days of menstruation, for he said in his heart: "Perhaps there will be some stray thought in my heart when separating from my wife." A person should strive to sanctify themselves during the time of intimacy, lingering so as to draw down holiness from above during the union.

<margin>Furthermore</margin> **There is**, in addition to the three types of impurity mentioned above, a "clinging foot" of the "Unclean Chariot" <note>a mystical reference to the forces of spiritual impurity</note> which a person should guard against. This is something that does not technically make one impure, but it is dirty and offensive, and it causes the removal of spiritual light. It is forbidden by law to recite the <term>Shema</term> or to pray or study Torah in a place of filth. These laws are explained in the Talmud and the legal codes, and I will mention only two things as a reminder and an awakening: First, a person should always be careful that their anus is clean, wiping themselves well so that not even a speck of excrement remains, even if it is covered. For the law rules that excrement in its place, even if covered and not visible while standing, is forbidden. Second, semen is treated like excrement regarding filth, in addition to the fact that it is technically impure. Therefore, one who is clean and pure should wipe themselves with a white cloth <note>original: "lulav," likely a transcription error for "blai" (rags/cloth)</note> when separating from his wife after union. If there is semen on his shirt for any reason, he should not wear that shirt unless it is washed well. My father and teacher, of blessed memory, wrote in his will: "At all times let your garments be white" [Ecclesiastes 9:8]—meaning literal garments, that they should not be soiled with stains of excrement or drops of urine. This is based on the verse "Guard your foot when you go to the house of God" [Ecclesiastes 4:17]—"guard" means to be careful when you stand in prayer before the Omnipresent. This includes many things, such as ensuring that the shoes on your feet are not soiled with mud or filth when you go to the house of God, for the ground is holy. In *Sefer Hasidim* <note>The Book of the Pious, a 12th-13th century ethical work</note>, it is written that one should have two pairs of shoes, one specifically for prayer. This is the meaning of "coming to the King's gate in soiled clothing." The *Rokeach* <note>Rabbi Eleazar of Worms</note> wrote that a person who cannot immerse should scrub their hands, arms, and body with water to cleanse themselves of any clinging semen, to fulfill "Prepare to meet your God, O Israel" [Amos 4:12]. *Sefer Hasidim* also says: a man should keep water near him at night so that if he sees a seminal emission and cannot pour <term>nine kavim</term><note>approx. 12-13 liters of water, a specific measure for purification</note> over himself, he can at least scrub the area where the semen touched. He should also check his trousers to ensure there is no trace of excrement. A person should also be accustomed to having bran in a vessel, so that if they touch fat, blood, or anything forbidden, they can remove the residue with the bran. Nothing cleans the hands like bran, as it is not harsh. There is a story of a certain pious man who, even when he slept with his wife, had a specific white shirt for it, saying: "Perhaps semen will stick to the shirt I usually wear... and how could I wear <term>Tefillin</term>?" It is good to have garments designated for prayer if possible, as the Sages learned from the verse "Prepare to meet your God."

<margin>Our Teacher Jonah wrote</margin> in the chapter "One who recites" <note>a chapter in Tractate Berakhot</note>: One who is obligated in a blessing but cannot say it because their hands are not clean, or because they are in an unclean place—such as a sick person whose bed is not clean and who cannot endure the time it takes to clean it—should meditate on the blessing or prayer in their heart. Even though one does not fulfill their obligation except through speech, he should meditate in his heart, and God will see the heart and reward the thought. We find this in the Midrash: "Hearken to my words, O Lord" [Psalms 5:2]—the Master of the World says: at the time I can speak, "hearken to my words," and at the time I cannot speak, "consider my meditation." "Meditation" refers to thought. This is also apparent from the verse "Examine me, O Lord, and prove me; try my reins and my heart" [Psalms 26:2]. Thus far his words. However, in section 85, the <term>Beit Yosef</term><note>Rabbi Yosef Karo</note> wondered about this, for if one cannot articulate with the lips, meditation is also forbidden, as stated in the chapter "The Stove" [Tractate Shabbat]: "In every place it is permitted to meditate on words of Torah except for the bathhouse and the latrine." The *Beit Yosef* wrote that perhaps this does not refer to literal filth, but to cases where the hands or the place are not "clean" but not necessarily "filthy." In such a case, one cannot speak, but one may meditate. But the *Beit Yosef* himself noted that this explanation is forced. However, it seems to me that the plain meaning of Rabbi Jonah’s words is not that one should meditate on the *text* of the blessing—for then there would be no difference between speech and thought—but rather, Rabbi Jonah means to meditate on the *obligation* of the blessing and to feel sorrow that he cannot perform it due to the lack of cleanliness. Then the Holy One, Blessed be He, accepts this meditation as if he were in a clean place and had prayed. This is based on the Sages' principle: "If one intended to perform a commandment but was prevented by circumstances, the Scripture credits it to him as if he had performed it."

<margin>Regarding the night</margin> when it is common for people to stand and urinate: a person should accustom themselves to having a urinal made of metal or glass, which do not absorb, as written by the <term>Tosafot</term> and the <term>Rosh</term>. He should pour a <term>revi'it</term><note>approx. 3-5 fluid ounces</note> of water into it each time he urinates, and the vessel itself should be washed and clean. Then he is permitted to recite the blessing "Who formed man" and to study Torah. It seems to me that if the vessel is clean and no smell emanates from it, it is sufficient to wash the vessel from Sabbath eve to Sabbath eve.

<margin>And it is forbidden</margin> to walk in filthy alleys, for it is forbidden to walk four cubits without meditating on Torah; how then can one walk in filthy alleys where it is forbidden to meditate on Torah? <margin>Regarding</margin> what is called a "place of filth," the *Beit Yosef* brought a response from the <term>Rashba</term><note>Rabbi Shlomo ben Aderet, 13th-century Spain</note>: We must be careful during prayer or eating not to touch a "place of filth." What is called a "place of filth"? He replied that it is not just literal filth, but even the covered parts of a person's body, like the thigh, because of the sweat there. This also applies to scratching one's head. However, uncovered places like the face and arms are not considered "filthy" because there is no sweat there. This is our custom. In *Shevet Yisrael*, it is written that the common people are not careful about this and touch covered parts of the body while in the synagogue or while studying or eating. They must be warned not to do so, and if they do, they require immediate washing of the hands. I have heard that pious men used to place a vessel full of water where they studied because...

# The Gate of Letters

Everything is included within each other, and this is the secret of how every commandment contains within it all other commandments. This is also found in the *Raya Mehemna* <note>The "Faithful Shepherd," a mystical section of the Zohar</note>, which states: "One who fulfills a single commandment properly, it is as if he has fulfilled all 248 positive commandments," for there is no commandment that does not include all 248. Thus, in every single commandment and in every single limb <note>Jewish tradition counts 248 positive commandments corresponding to 248 limbs of the human body</note>, all are included. What is in one is in the other. On an inner level, if one performs a commandment according to its law, they create a complete angel out of its 248 spiritual limbs to advocate on their behalf. Since every commandment is composed of 248 parts, this is what the Mishnah means: "He who performs one commandment acquires for himself one advocate" <note>Hebrew: *Peraklit*, a legal term for a defending attorney</note>. Rabbi Zeira said in the first chapter of *Sotah* <note>A tractate of the Talmud</note> in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: "For anyone who performs a single commandment in this world, it precedes him and goes before him to the World to Come, as it is said: *'Your righteousness shall go before you; the glory of the Lord shall be your rear guard'* (Isaiah 58:8)." This "righteousness" is the angel created from that commandment, who serves as the advocate. However, a difficulty arises: if every angel has 248 spiritual limbs reflecting the spiritual pattern of the 248

limbs of the "Supernal Man" <note>Adam Kadmon, a kabbalistic concept of the primordial divine structure</note>, how can a single commandment create a whole angel of 248 limbs? It is because every commandment is inherently composed of all 248. Let us return to the matter: "And your loins shall be holy." A person's 248 limbs and 365 sinews serve as a garment for their soul (*Nefesh*, *Ruach*, and *Neshamah*), which contains 613 spiritual lights made in the image and likeness of the 613 spiritual elements in the secret of the "Measurement of the Stature" <term>Shiur Komah</term><note>A mystical concept describing the "dimensions" of the Divine</note> of the Supernal Man, as explained at length previously in the introduction to *Toldot Adam*. Thus, "your loins" refers to the "house of your friend" <note>Playing on a Hebrew pun between *Re'acha* (your friend) and the loins/body</note>. The investigator says that from there comes the "boiling" of the Evil Inclination, and one must not defile it, for it is the House of God. The Evil Inclination is also hinted at in the feet, for "her feet go down to death" (Proverbs 5:5). There is also a hint that the heat of the Evil Inclination affects the intellect through the feet, as we learned in the first chapter of *Yoma* <note>Regarding the High Priest on Yom Kippur</note>: "If he sought to doze off... they would say to him: 'My Lord High Priest, stand and cool your feet once on the stone floor,'" for the warmth of the feet awakens sleep and cancels out holy thoughts. This applies to all desires. Regarding this, people say jokingly

that Ruth "uncovered the feet" of Boaz so he would cool down and not listen to the voice of the Evil Inclination, which was enticing him: "Go to her, you are a young man and she is available." This is the meaning of "investigating your feet" in the "house of your friend"—to guard against lust and desire, hinting at the commandment: "Do not covet your neighbor's house."

## Note that from the perspective of the Good Inclination, man is a "friend" to the Holy One, Blessed be He. Therefore, it is called the "Good Inclination" after the Holy One, Blessed be He, who is the True Good; no evil descends from Above. By this matter, pride shall be moved from its heights.

It is a great secret to know what I mean by the connection to the Good Inclination, and why it is named after God. From the Holy One, Blessed be He, no evil descends, only good. Even that which appears evil is for the sake of an ultimate good. This is explained at length in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah) and cited in the *Pardes* <note>A kabbalistic work by Rabbi Moshe Cordovero</note> in the Gate of Names: Since the Holy One created nothing in His world except for His glory, how did He create the Evil Inclination, which is like a rebellious servant in the palace? The conclusion of that discussion is that the intention of the Evil Inclination is for a "double good." It entices a person to desire, and if the person does not listen to it—saying, "The Master says one thing and the student another; whom should I obey?"—then his reward is doubled and quadrupled, for "according to the pain is the reward." This is what the Sages meant by "And behold, it was *very* good" (Genesis 1:31)—"Good" refers to the Good Inclination, while "*Very* good" refers to the Evil Inclination. Thus, even the inclination for "evil" is for the purpose of good and is "very good." This is the meaning of the verse "In all your heart"—meaning with both your inclinations. The Zohar and the *Tikunim* explain that the heart has two chambers: one for the Good Inclination and one for the Evil. "A wise man's heart is to his right" (the Good) and "a fool's heart is to his left" (the Evil). If a person follows the "revealed" intent of the Evil Inclination, he goes to the left side, the "Side of Death." However, if he follows the "hidden" intent of the Evil Inclination—which is "very good," meaning it exists so that he may struggle and overcome it—then he fulfills "I have set the Lord before me always." Then the "left" is aligned with the "right" of God, and everything becomes the Good Inclination. In fact, the ultimate purpose of evil is the greatest good. Therefore, a person should say to his heart when a desire for a sin or a bad trait arises: "How can I obey this? For its very essence and inner intent is the opposite [of what it suggests]!" This is the meaning of "My flesh trembles for fear of Your judgments"—even the "good" judgments. We confess that we did not listen to the "hidden" voice that intended for our good. We did not even act "equally" <note>Hebrew: *Shaveh*</note>, meaning we did not pursue the Good Inclination as much as we pursued the Evil. We acknowledge: "You are righteous in all that has come upon us, for You have acted in truth." "Truth" <note>Emet</note> refers to eternity. The purpose of both inclinations is for man's eternal existence. Truth is also a seal of the One. If you ask what a thing is, and you want to tell the truth, there is only one answer (e.g., "This is a cup"). But if you want to lie, you can tell ten thousand lies. Unity is Truth. Thus, the "Truth" of creating two inclinations is for one single purpose: the hidden purpose of the Evil Inclination is the True Good. We only "acted wickedly" because we followed its revealed surface. A person should realize that the Good Inclination's revealed side is its truth, but the Evil Inclination's *inner* truth is even "better." Therefore, if I sin, I am following neither the Master nor the student's inner intent. We confess "for the sin we sinned before You with the Evil Inclination." Why specify the Evil Inclination when all sins come from it? We are saying: we shouldn't use the excuse that "the leaven in the dough <note>the Evil Inclination</note> prevents us," for we now admit that the inner reason for the Evil Inclination is actually the opposite—to help us achieve greatness. **The Good Inclination** also means a person's *desire* should always be good, even when not actively performing a deed. When a sin comes to hand, he should push it away, and when a commandment comes, he should do it with zeal. But even when he is "idle," his heart should think of good things and loathe evil. He should constantly desire to do commandments he cannot currently do, thinking: "If I could, I would do this." God joins such a good thought to a deed, for He examines the heart. This is explained in *Keli Chemdah* regarding the building of the Tabernacle: "From every man whose heart moves him, you shall take My offering." They didn't actually have enough pure gold, but because their hearts truly *wanted* to give more than they had, God sent a blessing so that the little they had became much. This is the power of the **Good Inclination**.

## But for the wicked, it is the opposite. They have an "evil thought," saying: "If I had the power to take revenge, I would do such and such; if I had the money, I would follow my desires..."

It emphasizes that a sincere desire to do good is credited by God as a completed action.</summary>

# The Gate of Letters

Everything is included <note>original: "כלול" (klalul) - matching the catchword from the previous page</note>. Regarding the act, meaning the beginning of Creation, you will always find the phrase: *"And God saw, and behold, it was very good."* This is because the intention is focused on the ultimate goal—the end of the action—which is the world that exists after the five <note>Likely referring to the five millennia or the five levels of the soul</note>, which is the World to Come, a world that is entirely good. Since this is the ultimate goal, it was the first thing in [God's] thought. The precedence of *this* world <note>the physical world</note> is only like the natural precedence of the **shell** before the **fruit**; the fruit grows from within it. Likewise, through the good deeds of this world, the "fruit of the righteous" grows into a "tree of eternal life" in the world that is entirely good. Who is so mad that they would not grasp onto the true goal, which was the very first thought of Creation?

Know that the matter of the **Good Inclination** <term>Yetzer HaTov</term> and the **Evil Inclination** <term>Yetzer HaRa</term> is modeled after Jacob and Esau. According to the literal appearance, Esau is the firstborn because he emerged first. But in truth, Jacob is the firstborn, as he was first in thought <note>original: "המחשבה ראשונה", correcting the OCR "השפה"</note>, as explained regarding the generations. Esau, who emerged first, is the **shell** that precedes the fruit, which is Jacob. Similarly, in truth, the soul precedes the body, for souls were already created at the creation of the world. Furthermore, before a person is born, they are made to take an oath to follow the path of good, as our Sages of blessed memory said regarding the verse, *"To Me every tongue shall swear"* (Isaiah 45:23). Also, while the infant is in its mother’s womb, a candle burns above its head, and it gazes and looks from one end of the world to the other, as stated in the chapter *HaMaplet* <note>Tractate Niddah 30b</note>. The "candle" is a metaphor for the light of education that spreads through one's intellect and the inclusion of all things within it; through this, one gazes and looks, which is the attainment and knowledge of the Unity of the Light from one end of the world to the other—the beginning of the thought and its end. Through this, one stands upon the secrets of the Torah and its wondrous reasons. As is said there: "They teach him the entire Torah," as it is written: *"He taught me and said to me..."* (Proverbs 4:4), and it says, *"When God’s company [secret] was over my tent"* (Job 29:4). 

By gazing from the womb, all that the child saw, knew, and attained is sought from him. This is what they meant when they said: "As soon as he emerges into the atmosphere of the world, an angel comes and strikes him upon his mouth, causing him to forget the entire Torah." The reason for this is so that his actions will not be compelled, allowing him to have **free choice** and to choose the good. Then, as he enters his life, the Evil Inclination comes first, following the way of the shell preceding the fruit; *"man is born a wild donkey's colt"* (Job 11:12), and *"the inclination of man's heart is evil from his youth"* (Genesis 8:21). Only later, when he reaches maturity <note>age 13</note>, does the Good Inclination become active within him.

Thus, to the eyes, it appears as though the Evil Inclination is more "senior" than the Good Inclination and possesses the right of the firstborn. But in truth, it is the opposite. Through this, we can understand the verse: *"There was a little city with few men in it, and a great king came against it... and there was found in it a poor wise man"* (Ecclesiastes 9:14-15). Our Sages of blessed memory explained this regarding the Evil Inclination, as Rashi brings in his commentary on Ecclesiastes: the "little city" is the body; the "great king" is the Evil Inclination, whom many obey; and the "poor wise man" is the Good Inclination, for the "children of the upper chamber" <note>spiritually elevated people</note> are few. 

One might ask: according to the common perception that the Evil Inclination precedes the Good Inclination in a person, how can it say that the "great king" (the Evil Inclination) besieged the city and *then* the poor man (the Good Inclination) was "found" there? It should be the opposite: the Good Inclination arrives last and finds the great king already in the city, and must then distance, pursue, and separate himself. But according to what we have said—that in the power of true reality, the existence of the Good Inclination comes first and holds the right of the firstborn because it was the "first in thought" for the "end of the action"—the verse is understood. When it says *"and man did not remember that same poor man,"* it means that because of the joy one takes in their physical actions, they forget the truth. This answers Rashi's difficulty: even though we see the "great king" arrived first, in truth the "poor man" preceded him. The proof is that in the mother's womb, there was a "burning candle," but the angel struck the mouth and caused him to forget. This is the meaning of *"he did not remember the poor man."* Understand this well. Therefore, the essence of the firstborn belongs to the Good Inclination, and it takes a "double portion"—in this world and the World to Come. The Evil Inclination, which thinks itself the firstborn, is a "cunning wicked one" who presents his argument first. 

As stated in the Zohar (Vayeshev): <note>original Aramaic: "ת"ח על דא אקדים..."</note> "Come and see: because of this, [the Evil Inclination] comes early to a person on the day he is born, so that people will believe him. For when the Good Inclination arrives <note>at age 13</note>, the person is no longer able to believe it, for the Evil Inclination lies upon him like a heavy burden. Who is this 'cunning wicked one'? It is the Evil Inclination, who arrives first to state his words before the Judge <note>the person</note> until his fellow litigant arrives, as it is said: *'The first to plead his case seems right'* (Proverbs 18:17). This 'cunning wicked one' denies the truth and was 'cunning' <note>referring to the serpent in Eden</note>. He precedes his fellow, the Good Inclination, and ruins the person entirely so that he cannot lift his head, as if he carries all the burdens of the world on his shoulders." See there. In truth, the Good Inclination is the beginning and has the right of firstborn. These are matters of importance.

->Furthermore<-

Thirdly, why is the Good Inclination called by the name "Good"? It is after the verse *"The Lord is good to all"* (Psalms 145:9). The Blessed One is the essence of Good, and He imprinted "a portion of God from above" <note>the soul</note> within man. The Good Inclination is the guardian of the soul; therefore, it is called "Good" after the name of the Truly Good One, blessed be He. From this perspective, the Holy One, blessed be He, calls Israel His "friends" and "neighbors," as in the verse *"Your own friend and your father's friend, do not forsake"* (Proverbs 27:10). In the path of kindness, it says *"the child from your neighbor's house."* See the Zohar (Beshalach) on the verse *"A friend loves at all times"* (Proverbs 17:17). Regarding the verse *"Keep your foot from your neighbor's house,"* our Sages wrote: "Your friend and your father's friend" refers to the Holy One; do not forsake the service of Him and cleaving to Him. "Keep your foot" means to cool your [Evil] Inclination so that it does not incite you or rule over you, and do not have "other thoughts" against your "Friend." Who is "your neighbor's house"? It is the holy soul that entered you, which He gave within you. 

The Zohar explains "Keep your foot" <note>Hebrew: *Hoker*, interpreted as *Kar*, "cold"</note> as a language of cooling—to cool the heat of the Evil Inclination so it does not heat up the power of evil. The "house" is the body, as it says *"Before the keepers of the house tremble"* (Ecclesiastes 12:3). Why does it call the soul a "city" or "house"? As our Sages said: "If a person sanctifies himself a little below, they sanctify him much from above." Likewise, if one defiles themselves a little below, they are defiled much from above. Thus, what one does at the "bottom" of the house is felt "above" in the city. 

In *Reshit Chokhmah* <note>a 16th-century Kabbalistic ethical work</note>, at the end of the fourth chapter on Tithes: "Due to the sin of Adam and the sin of the Golden Calf, the Torah became materialized. Now, when a person performs a physical commandment, it may seem like a small thing in the eyes of the Blessed Name, but he sins greatly [if he neglects it], for by performing the physical commandment, he awakens its spiritual root above. Spirituality above has no measure or end. Therefore, it said 'sanctifies himself a little below, they sanctify him much from above'—without measure." Similarly, it is explained in *Charedim*: "Let no good deed you do for His Name's sake seem small in your eyes, even a single word or look, for the act from you is great to us." Likewise regarding a disgraceful transgression: a shift of one cubit on the earth results in a shift of many miles in the celestial spheres. As explained in the *Tikunim* regarding the vowel points: below they appear small, but above they are infinite. We can then understand that the Blessed Name gives reward to man by appointing many thousands of angels over every commandment. The reason is that the spiritual essence of that commandment is drawn from the highest spiritual source through those "small" breaths [of speech or action]. Since it is impossible for the Supernal Light to be contained in a single angel, there is one primary angel who is the essence of the commandment's light, and under him are thousands of angels who receive the sparks of the light. From this, we understand the matter of impurity: below it may be a "piece of fat the size of an olive," but above it is impurity without measure. 

The body is the "house of your Friend"—the house of the Holy One, blessed be He, through the soul. This is the meaning of "First in thought, last in action," and the matter of *"For the Lord your God walks in the midst of your camp... therefore your camp shall be holy"* (Deuteronomy 23:15). In the Zohar (Acharei Mot), Rabbi Shimon opened: *"For the Lord your God walks in the midst of your camp to save you..."* "The Lord your God" refers to the Shekhinah <note>the Divine Presence</note> whose power is found within Israel. We learned there are 248 limbs in the body, and all of them become defiled when a person is defiled. "Your camp shall be holy"—who is your "camp"? These are the limbs of the body. *"That He see no unseemly thing in you and turn away from you."* It says "in you"—no blemish or nakedness should be seen in your body, rather "your camp shall be holy," meaning all 248 limbs should be holy. *Reshit Chokhmah* explains that they must all be unified. 

Thus we understand: "A person defiles himself a little, they defile him much." Even if he only sinned with one limb, they defile him "much"—all 248 limbs. Likewise regarding holiness: "Your camp shall be holy"—even if he only sanctifies one limb, all 248 limbs (the "camp," plural) are sanctified with a supernal holiness ("holy," singular). As our Sages said: "One who performs a single commandment properly merits the life of the World to Come." 

The intention until here is to be careful of defilement <note>original: "סיאב" (si'av)</note>, for "one commandment leads to another," and then the entire "stature" <note>the spiritual form of the person</note> is sanctified. The opposite is also true, Heaven forbid, for by committing one transgression, one violates the principle of all commandments. There is further power and secret in this, as previously explained in *Tikunei Toldot Adam*: the root of the 248 positive commandments and their spirituality is the secret of the **Supernal Man** <term>Adam HaElyon</term>. Included in the 248 positive commandments are the 365 sinews which correspond to the negative commandments. From the perspective of their root in the Supernal Light, number and count do not apply, Heaven forbid, except in the way of circles within circles, as explained regarding the secret of the number Ten in *Atzilut* <note>the highest of the four worlds in Kabbalah</note>, which are an absolute unity. Number only exists in the way of "chain of descent" <term>Hishtalshelut</term>, cause and effect, but all is one absolute unity.

<summary>This page explores the mystical origins of the human soul and the two inclinations, arguing that while the Evil Inclination appears first in life, the Good Inclination is the true "firstborn" in God's thought. It emphasizes how physical actions and the 248 limbs of the body have infinite spiritual consequences in the upper worlds.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Gate of Letters," moving from the conclusion of the letter Yud into the letters Kaf and Lamed. It maintains the theme of ethical self-improvement and the spiritual anatomy of the soul. The catchword from the previous page was "sins" (avannot).</meta>

And this is possible, that this is the explanation of the "Tree of Life" <note>Hebrew: Etz Chaim</note>, that one should purify the sparks of evil and the "husks" <term>Klippot; spiritual shells that conceal divine light</term> from which all transgressions arise, God forbid. This means that all transgressions occur at the moment of the act, whereas a sin in the "writing of thought" <note>The internal mental state</note> exists even in a matter where there is no speech or thought of coming to the sin itself. This is a law and a fixed limit for him, and he has no permission to change it. Thus he concludes in other ways for one who merits to see the letters as they truly are. Study this well.

## The Literal Meaning
The literal meaning <term>Pshat</term> of the "Tree of Life" through the "Master of the Will" <note>A reference to God or the spiritual leader</note> means that a person should bring himself to a state of "Fear" <note>Awe of Heaven</note>. The explanation of another way <term>Da'at Acheret</term> is that one who binds himself to Fear will find the letter *Yud* emerges for him. They call this a sign for "law and judgment," and a "scourge for the wicked." Furthermore, one who clarifies himself for matters of Fear [attains] the Name of God <note>represented by the letters Yud-He-Vav</note>. Regarding this, they hinted in the verse: *"Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin"* <note>Ecclesiastes 5:5</note>. Even permitted speech that might cause one to come to wickedness is forbidden. Then they will merit to avoid the forbidden. What does "to cause to sin" mean? It does not mean the speech itself is the sin, but rather speech that *leads* to sin.

## Further Interpretation
There is another way to explain this through the numerical values <term>Gematria</term> and combinations of the Name. [The text discusses various letter combinations and biblical references like Noah and Joseph]. For all these explanations, the Torah triumphs over them: that we have sinned by not loving the Lord even with our "Good Inclination" <term>Yetzer HaTov</term>. In all things, one should guard his soul and his spirit from the "Evil Inclination" <term>Yetzer HaRa</term> and its offspring. Let the good come and receive the good from the "Good Creator" who leads him on the good path, and then he will merit the world that is entirely good.

->The Letter Yud is completed<-

## The Letter Kaf: The Scale of Merit
The letter *Kaf* stands for *Kaf Zechut* <term>the scale of merit; judging others favorably</term>. As it says in the first chapter of *Ethics of the Fathers*: *"Judge every person toward the scale of merit."* This trait is superior and precious; it subdues envy and hatred and brings "peace in the land." As our Sages of blessed memory said: "He who judges his fellow favorably, they [Heaven] judge him favorably." This is a high and lofty level, reaching the level of Issachar. Through this, one finds "Grace" <note>Hebrew: Chen</note> in the eyes of God. The Jerusalem Talmud explains that "Grace" <note>Chen</note> is found in the land and in the heavens. [The text interprets "Grace" through the stories of Joseph, Benjamin, and the kindness shown to others]. I said, perhaps he did this for the honor of his Creator, to love Benjamin who was given grace. Even when things look bad, I said it is "grace," perhaps because God desires the Jewish people. By the power of thought, one should judge favorably, for this is the correct way. Note the sign: "My son, do not act with him like a cruel person." This is the secret of Yom Kippur, where one merits to have their sins removed. If a person returns in repentance to his essence, even a completely wicked person <note>Hebrew: Rasha Gamur</note>, they will advocate for him to be judged favorably at the time of the act. Whoever reaches this conclusion takes upon himself all the conducts of humility. This is our explanation: to judge favorably in any way possible, even in a distant way. Initially, when we are foolish, judgment is difficult, but the Creator assists in every deed. Through the merit of the Torah, we learn this dwelling. Even with the Hanukkah [lights] and the education <note>Hebrew: Chinuch</note> of a youth, one finds every kind of merit possible. This is the "society that assists God" to bring merit. He wanted to bring everything to the unity of God. This grace is found deep in the heart of one who loves and succeeds in clinging to God. All the Midrashic interpretations suggest that our love for the level of Sinai will be given for righteousness. This is the justification and grace for every merit.

## From the Book "Choice of Pearls"
In the book *Mivchar HaPeninim* <note>An 11th-century ethical work</note>, it says: See the Book of Virtues, which explains: "Do not make it a guilt upon us." Be careful to find merit for a servant. One who does not possess this trait will not be like Simeon and his descendants, who should be judged favorably even if he has fallen in a simple view. [The text references the faith of Israel]. They are "believers, the children of believers." It is known that before Me, they are believers. As it is written: *"And in her faith,"* and *"to make you believe."* It is as if they said His face is to believe, and if one looks deeply, they will find faith in his heart. Study this well.

## And it is written
It is written in *Midrash Shmuel* <note>A commentary on Pirkei Avot</note> in the name of the sages: "Judging favorably" was only said regarding an "average person" <term>Beinoni</term> whose deeds are balanced. But for a completely wicked and famous sinner, even if he appears to do good, it is distant from the scale of merit. One should not justify him, lest he be held as a good man while doing wrong. However, the moral sages said that a "transgression for its own sake" <note>Done with a pure motive</note> is greater than a "commandment not for its own sake." If one does not merit, even if the act is not beautiful now, we should pass over it properly. A person may commit a transgression against his fellow or his brother, but on that day, he performs repentance.

## And what is it
Even though the obligation is to judge one's fellow favorably, nevertheless, if one can clarify the matter for the sake of Heaven, he should do so. If he finds that the person is twisted, he must fulfill the obligation to *"surely rebuke your fellow"* and speak with him gently, with justice, peace, and grace. Grace <note>Chen</note> is a matter between man and his fellow, and it is also a matter between man and God, or a commandment in a matter where one can compel judgment for the sake of Heaven.

->The Letter Kaf is completed<-

---

## The Letter Lamed: A Good Heart
The letter *Lamed* stands for *Lev Tov* <note>A Good Heart</note>. *"Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me"* <note>Psalm 51:12</note>. For the heart is the source of life, placed in the center of the body. It is the body of the "Holy of Holies," which is the central point of the world. Our Sages of blessed memory explained that a "pure heart" in the world is established like the supernal vision. One should return to God, and the heart humbles the body where the spirit of life dwells. All the nourishment of the body depends on it. Then we will understand that the structure of the body is repaired. It is established like the supernal light, the spirit of life that dwells above and takes hold of it. This is connected to the matter of the Cherubim. [The text discusses the holiness of Jerusalem and the Temple]. Jerusalem is in the center, and it is forbidden for the House of God to be destroyed while Israel remains. And then, sins...

<column-break/>

Sins are removed from the three levels of the spirit, and his soul is purified. This is the aspect of "Knowledge" <term>Da'at</term>, the Holy Temple. This is to teach his generations not to forget the exile, but to have faith to come to the Eternal House. A person should hold a true resolve to bring his soul to the "Hidden Light" <term>Or HaGanuz</term> and the life of God's abundance, which is connected through prayer and the festivals. One who fears sin will come to all the King's matters. This is the thought: that the heart should hear and take hold of the "spirit of life." This is the light of the King of Glory. The Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah</term> should not be far from the house. When peace is established, the spirit of life and songs are mixed. The middle part of the heavens provides strength to reject all worldly settling. The "Heart of the Divine Presence" is like a spark of the first spirit, connected to life and the brain for all limbs. It protects the life of the universe. See the writings of Maimonides <note>Rambam</note> (Part 3, Chapter 6) regarding the soul. The soul is like the "Ark Cover" <term>Kaporet</term> before the Holy of Holies. This fire of the Cherub's wings shines. To this, the heart honors the entire body. It blows through the veins of the spirit. It is written that the "form of the creatures" <term>Chayyot</term> leads the heart and all souls and all the limbs below. Through the "Wings of a Dove" <note>The soul</note> covered in silver, the soul joins the higher spirit. There are five ways of life that dwell on guard. The heart must be like the Torah of the Holy of Holies. It says: *"And they shall make for Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them"* <note>Exodus 25:8</note>. It does not say "in it," but "in *them*"—within the heart of every individual. This is the awakening of the heart to bring in piety and life. This is humility. One should live for the Torah, the commandments, and piety. Then the Holy Spirit <term>Ruach HaKodesh</term> enters him, and the mercy of kindness is stirred. It is said: *"Do not stray after your heart."* From here, Rabbi Yitzhak said: "The eye sees..." A person looks with grace and humility. Even if one finds a wicked person, do not stray after your heart and your eyes. The power of the eyes follows the heart. The heart hears the destruction within it and then returns it to God. The heart should not be "foreign" to holiness. Do not stray after your heart—this refers to the "agent of sin." Give your heart to the "Good Inclination." Abraham's heart was a loving heart, a wise heart. The heart exists to do good. [The text references Jacob and the holiday of Hanukkah]. The heart is the main thing, as it is explained that the heart and the soul are the light of the heart. The "Upper Heart" is what our Sages meant: one should take the heart toward the good. Repentance must come from the power of thought. All that follows from the thought of the heart—the thoughts of the Children of Israel with God—is holiness. The word "Heart" <note>Lev/Levav</note> points toward holiness. One should not return to the heart of a wicked person. From Heaven, a heart of stone is a danger. A person should rebuke his own thoughts with repentance and trembling. In the depth of thought, there is healing and humility. One should speak with all his might. If his soul does not merit, the heart will not be awakened.

## And one
One who is at such a level enters the innermost holiness with life; he is always pure. It is written in the book *Orchot Tzaddikim* <note>Ways of the Righteous</note>: They should depict in their hearts the forms of everything and guard them. They should engrave it upon the heart and not turn to thoughts of vanity and emptiness. The wise shall write upon their hearts the "Writing of God," so the foundation of Torah, commandments, and piety will be firm. The soul will be refined. Of this, it is said: *"Write them on the tablet of your heart."*

## And I found
I found a manuscript of the godly Rabbi Moshe Cordovero <note>The Ramak, a famous 16th-century Kabbalist</note> of blessed memory, who wrote as follows: "Collect the deeds of your heart." He explained this verse as inner guidance: "A fire shall be kept burning on the altar; it shall not go out." This "action" nourishes the life of the law. The spirit of Elijah the Prophet, of blessed memory, is to the heart. Therefore, there shall be light in this. Upon every thought of the heart, one should say the aforementioned verse. He will see the Divine Presence. The heart and the soul act together, guided by the love and fear of God.

## And since
Since it has been clarified that the heart is the "Lamp of God" in which is the Holy of Holies, the Torah and commandments should be placed in it, corresponding to the Tablets. It is fitting that his heart be a foundation for the Holy of Holies. He should have a steadfast life and grace. Sins should not be mentioned. If he thinks in his heart or neglects the Torah, let him make a strong resolve in his heart never to return to that way. Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Yose: "One measure of piety in the heart is great." One should not be heavy-hearted lest he be pursued, God forbid, by the love of eating and drinking or other pleasures, for these guard evil in the heart and do not find favor. One should merit the commandments. Our Sages said: The Divine Presence dwells with the heart. He should build humility for the honor of his Creator, with trust. The heart should not feel [false] joy, but should desire forgiveness. Then he will have "Grace." This is seen in the deed of Hillel, who gave [merit] for the sake of God. Until here is what we have written regarding the heart and the conduct of the past. One should straighten his heart and then he will see a "Good Heart." A "broken and contrite heart" <note>Psalm 51:17</note> is called the trust of humility. He will be desired by God. Through all these, he will attain humility and a straight world.

->The Letter Lamed is completed<-

<meta>This page concludes the discussion on the letter *Samekh*, focusing on the virtues of contentment and trust in God, and begins the letter *Ayin*, which discusses the profound importance of humility.</meta>

# The Gate of Letters

One who has half of his desire in his hand already wants double; if he has a hundred, he desires two hundred. Therefore, "increasing possessions increases anxiety" <note>A quote from Pirkei Avot 2:7</note>, for the more one amasses, the more worry he invites. How so? Because what he already holds is always only half of his desire, and he constantly craves as much again. Thus, when he has a hundred, his only worry is how to obtain another hundred; when he has two hundred, he worries about getting another two hundred, and so it goes forever. It follows that the neck of the one who increases possessions also increases anxiety. But one who is "happy with his portion" <note>Pirkei Avot 4:1</note> and with what the Blessed Name has graciously given him—even a little will be sweet and sufficient for him. Such a person is truly wealthy forever. **Regarding** the World to Come, many good virtues flow from the quality of contentment: he will not lust or covet, and certainly, he will not steal or cheat his fellow. His business dealings will be in good faith, and he will not fulfill the will of the Evil Inclination <term>Yetzer Ha-Ra; the internal impulse toward selfishness or sin</term>, which always wants "more"—though this "more" is actually "less," as we explained regarding increased anxiety. Our father Jacob asked the Holy One, Blessed be He, for nothing more than basic contentment: "bread to eat and clothes to wear." Similarly, King Solomon prayed, "Give me neither poverty nor riches" <note>Proverbs 30:8</note>. Therefore, a person should not be rushed after money, seeking schemes to gather it, lest he separate himself from the life of the World to Come—which is the occupation of the Torah. The Torah of truth is "eternal life planted within us," and we are commanded to meditate upon it day and night. Indeed, "Torah combined with a worldly occupation is good," but the Torah must be the primary focus. If God expands one's borders and grants wealth without great toil, one must ensure that this "wealth is not kept by its owner to his own harm," God forbid. Instead, he should always strive to perform charity and kindness according to the blessing God gave him. He must not become arrogant because of his wealth, God forbid, for pride is "a fire that consumes unto destruction." May the Merciful One grant long life before the Blessed Name; a person should say, "I am unworthy of all the kindnesses" <note>Genesis 32:11</note>, and do the will of his Creator.

# There is another great and wondrous virtue that flows from the quality of contentment: attaining the high and lofty level of Cleaving <term>Dveikut; spiritual attachment to the Divine</term> through the virtue of Faith.
This is the virtue of Trust <term>Bitachon</term>. For one who amasses vast wealth until he stops counting where it came from—trust is not relevant to him. He cannot truly say he trusts in the Blessed Name to give him this abundance, for what room is there for trust when he already has it? Trust is only truly applicable for one’s basic satisfaction and the needs of his soul and household. According to the blessing, it is appropriate to trust in the Blessed Name who created him to provide bread; for He, Blessed be He, sustains all from the "horns of the wild oxen to the eggs of lice" <note>A Talmudic idiom for the entirety of the animal kingdom</note>. But to say "I trust in the Blessed Name to give me treasures and the hidden wealth of kings"—such a man has stepped outside the bounds of proper counsel. In reality, his situation is not one of trust. It is already known what has been written extensively about the virtue of Trust: that it is "the faith of the craftsman." As the verse says: "Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord" <note>Jeremiah 17:7</note>. For the one who trusts has handed himself and all he owns over to the hand of the Creator, relying on Him with total assurance. He accepts with love whatever the Holy One, Blessed be He, sends upon him, whether good or bad, for he trusts that even the seemingly bad is for the good. Even if it appears otherwise, "God intended it for good." One who places his affairs truly upon trust in the Blessed Name cleaves to Him. Of such a person the verse says: "But you who cleave to the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 4:4</note>, for he cleaves to His Great Name. He recognizes that God "burns everything and gives life to everything" from the Life that is from Him. As the sages interpreted: "You give life to them all"—You, the *Milui* <term>the "filling" or expanded spelling of a Divine Name</term>, give life to them all. This is why it is written: "He who trusts in the Lord, kindness (*Chesed*) shall surround him." One might ask: should it not have said "*His* kindness" or "*His* kindnesses"? Rather, it says *Chesed* because the word's numerical value is 72 <note>Hebrew: חסד = 8+60+4=72</note>, which matches the "filling" of the Name YHVH <note>The Name spelled out: Yod-Vav-Dalet (20), He-Yod (15), Vav-Yod-Vav (22), He-Yod (15) = 72</note>, which is the essence of Kindness. Happy is the one who makes the Name of the Lord his trust, for he is a true believer and cleaves to the Blessed One, on the condition that he fulfills the Torah, the commandments, and ethical traits; then he is secure.

->The letter Samekh is completed<-

# The Letter Ayin: Humility

<margin>
The Generations of Man <note>original: *Toldot Adam*</note>
To the furthest extreme
</margin>

**Who can glorify** the greatness and splendor of this trait of Humility and lowliness of spirit? Even Moses our Teacher, in whom all the perfections of character and intellect were completed more than any other human—and who additionally reached the levels of prophecy such that "none like him has arisen," being the "father of Torah, father of wisdom, and father of prophecy"—despite all this, the Holy One, Blessed be He, did not praise him for any quality other than Humility. This trait encompasses all others, as it says: "And the man Moses was very humble, more than any man" <note>Numbers 12:3</note>. Therefore, it says "more than any man," which includes even the First Man <note>Adam HaRishon</note>. This will be explained according to what is written in the introduction to **The Generations of Man** <note>original: *Toldot Adam*</note>. The trait of Humility is unique; while in most traits the "middle path" is best, in Humility one must lean toward the furthest extreme. One must be humble to the ultimate degree, as is known from the *Laws of Character* <note>A reference to Maimonides' Mishneh Torah</note>. So too the Mishnah explains: "Be *very, very* humble of spirit," using the word "very" twice to indicate this trait must exceed all other virtues. While the middle path is generally praiseworthy, here one must go to the final extreme. This is like what Rav Nachman said: "Neither it [pride] nor even a bit of it." Furthermore, it is a prohibition from the Torah, one of the many negative commandments, as the Ramban <note>Nachmanides</note> wrote. The Talmud in *Sotah* asks: "Where is the warning against the haughty of heart?" Rav Nachman bar Isaac says it is written: "Lest your heart be lifted up and you forget the Lord your God." And "Before destruction comes pride." Rabbi Abin said in the name of Rabbi Elazar: Not in every place where it says "dwelling" does the Divine Presence dwell below on earth; rather, the "mountain" which was chosen <note>Sinai</note> was made so because it was low. The Divine Presence dwells with the lowly of spirit. One who is haughty violates a negative commandment. In addition to this, our Sages of blessed memory and all the masters of ethics and character were very stringent. I have written the reason for this previously: because Pride and the pursuit of Honor drove the First Man from the world, as he placed "envy" in Eve. Understand the internal meaning: the desire of the "lust to the eyes" and honor—"you shall be like gods." It is known that the first sin of our first father brought the Evil Inclination into the world. From him, all sins spread, for once he introduced the Evil Inclination, it became the "father of all sins." In that initial state, the trait of Humility was lacking. Sin is the opposite of these virtues; one who is not humble pursues honor and is never satisfied, whereas the humble man is satisfied with bread, salt, and measured water because of his lowliness. He is not "perfumed" by the praise of men, for he always considers himself as low as the earth compared to the virtue of his fellow. Therefore, the trait of Humility is the repair <term>Tikkun</term> for all the sins in the world. Once the comprehensive sin of Adam is repaired, all are repaired. This is what was hinted at regarding Moses our Teacher: he was "more humble than any man" <note>Adam</note>—specifically the first Adam. This is also why our holy master Rabbi Isaac Luria <note>The Ari</note> spoke of the "Garments of Light" <note>original: *Kotnot Or*</note> that spread from Adam who sinned. I need not elaborate further on this introduction or copy the words of our Sages and the masters of ethics, for my desire is to summarize them. I will mention a few, and they will suffice for anyone who has a portion in the God of Israel and His Torah. The Sages spoke at length in the first chapter of Tractate *Sotah* regarding the abomination of the haughty spirit. It says there: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: "Any person who has within him pride is as if he worships idols." It is written here: "Every proud heart is an abomination to the Lord," and it is written there regarding idols: "And you shall not bring an abomination into your house." Rabbi Yochanan himself said: "It is as if he denied the Fundamental Principle <note>God</note>," as it says: "Lest your heart be lifted up and you forget the Lord your God." R. Chama bar Hanina said: "It is as if he committed all the forbidden sexual relations," for "abomination" is used in both contexts. Further there, Rabbi Elazar said: "A person with pride is worthy of being cut down like an Asherah tree <note>A tree used for idolatry</note>." It is written: "The high of stature shall be hewn down," and of idols it says: "And their Asherah trees you shall cut down." Rabbi Elazar also said: "The dust of a proud person will not be stirred [in the Resurrection of the Dead]," as it says: "Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust." It does not say "those in the dust," but "you who dwell in the dust"—meaning those who made themselves like a neighbor to the dust [through humility] during their lives. Thus, pride is like denying God, like the most severe forbidden relations, and it prevents one from rising in the Resurrection. Woe to him that he was created! For the purpose of man is to return in the Resurrection. Therefore, this is the "law of man": dust, blood, salt—his soul should be like dust to all. As our father Abraham said: "I am but dust and ashes." He should consider himself as the "worm of the earth," as David said: "I am a worm and not a man." And Moses our Teacher was the most humble of all, as he said: "And we are what?" <note>Exodus 16:8</note>—meaning he felt he had no independent existence in the world compared to his Creator. In Tractate *Chullin*, in the chapter "The Covering of the Blood," it says he was more humble than all, for the initials of these humble men—**A**braham, **D**avid, **M**oses—spell **ADAM** <note>Man</note>. Moses was the humblest of all. At the very least, a person should not value himself more than a worm or the dust of the earth; he should be a treading-place for all. "My soul shall be as dust to everyone." As the verse says: "I gave my back to the smiters and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair; I hid not my face from shame." And it says: "Let him give his cheek to him that smites him; let him be filled with reproach" <note>Lamentations 3:30</note>. This is the trait of the "Long-Suffering" <note>original: *Savlan*</note>, which is a great trait of humility from the kindness and mercy of the Blessed Name. One who has no power and simply suffers is not called "long-suffering," for he is forced. But one who has the power to act and yet suffers [insult]—that is called true long-suffering. We must learn this from the King of Kings, the Holy One, Blessed be He, who suffers and has mercy on His creatures even though He has all power, Blessed be He.

# A person should take to heart the words of our Sages in the first chapter of *Sotah*: Rav Chisda said in the name of Mar Ukva: "Any person who has pride within him, the Holy One, Blessed be He, says: I and he cannot dwell together in the world."
As it says: "Whoso is haughty of eye and proud of heart, him (*Oto*) I cannot [suffer]." Do not read it as *Oto* (him), but *Itto* (with him). But with the contrite, He dwells, as it is written: "I dwell with the contrite and lowly," and "He restores the contrite and the lowly of spirit." Rav Huna and Rav Chisda—one says "The contrite is with Me," and one says "I am with the contrite."

# The Gate of Letters

# The Letter Mem: Deliberation

The language of the Talmud in the tractate *Berakhot* <note>original: *Berachot* 20a; a foundational text of Jewish law and ethics</note>, in the chapter "One whose dead [lies before him]," states: "Deliberation, deliberation is worth four hundred *zuz*" <note>A *zuz* was a silver coin; the phrase emphasizes that patience is incredibly valuable</note>. This ethical instruction was a frequent saying in the mouth of my holy father and teacher, may his memory be a blessing for the life of the world to come: that a person should not praise any deed, whether great or small, until they have taken counsel in their heart and acted as a "wise person who foresees the outcome." For anyone who acts in haste will, for the most part, find their work ruined. The sign of this is the verse: "I said in my haste, 'All men are liars'" <note>Psalms 116:11</note>, meaning that when one acts in haste without deliberation, the result is a failure <note>The author puns on the word "liar" (kozev) and "failing/disappointing" (achzav)</note>, like a spring whose waters do not fail. And the Scripture says: "When I reach the appointed time, I will judge with equity" <note>Psalms 75:3</note>. This does not apply only to legal judgment, but to all things a person does; they should take an "appointed time" and a season for every desire, to contemplate it before doing it. My father and teacher gave a mnemonic: "Repentance (*Teshuvah*) brings Salvation (*Teshuah*)" when one performs their affairs calmly and thinks before acting. This applies not only to action but also to speech; no word should leave one's mouth, for bad or even for good, until they have first stirred it around to see its ultimate end and what will be born from it.

**The Sage said:** Deliberation is a tower of strength, while haste is the gateway to regret. **The Sage said:** He who rides with haste is never safe from stumbling. **The Sage said:** You have more power over what you have not yet done than over what you have already done. This means that if one acts in haste, they cannot fix it afterward; but the deed one wishes to do but has not yet rushed into—that can still be performed if it is good. Therefore, let no one hurry.

**The Sage said:** Wait, and you will be saved from regret. **King David, may peace be upon him,** said: "I considered my ways and turned my feet to Your testimonies" <note>Psalms 119:59</note>. Thus said David: "Every path I desired to walk and every thing I wanted to do, I would contemplate before acting. If it was good and upright in the eyes of the Place <term>Ha-Makom; a traditional name for God implying He is everywhere</term> and in the eyes of people, I would proceed. But if it seemed not good to me, I would leave it." For every matter has two paths and perspectives. This is the meaning of "I turned my feet to Your testimonies" forever. Therefore, a person should cling to this trait until it becomes second nature: never to perform any action in the world, great or small, nor speak any word—even when hearing one's own insult—without first taking it to heart, consulting with the intellect according to the law, remembering the Creator and His holy Torah, and placing the attribute of mercy before one's eyes. Then you shall walk in safety and not stumble.

<margin>
S.G.S.
My teacher wrote in the *Book of Intentions* <note>Likely the *Sefer Ha-Kavanot*, a mystical work</note> regarding Yom Kippur: I received a reason why one should not hurry to do any deed with haste, even if some people urge it or mock the delay. Except in a matter of a *Mitzvah* <term>a religious duty or good deed</term> that is clearly good, where one should be swift. But in all other things, sit and do nothing; that is better.
</margin>

And not only in optional matters should one act thus, but even in the performance of a commandment (*Mitzvah*), one should act with deliberation. This is the essence of the passage in *Berakhot* which says "Deliberation is worth four hundred *zuz*." It was told of the holy Rav Adda bar Ahavah that he once saw a woman wearing a garment he thought was immodest and forbidden for a Jewish woman, so he tore it from her in the marketplace. It turned out she was not Jewish <note>Talmud Berakhot 20a; the story warns that even "pious" zeal can lead to embarrassment if one doesn't deliberate first</note>. Now, you might ask: do we not say "the zealous are early to perform commandments"? This applies only to a *Mitzvah* whose path is clear and understood, such as going to the Synagogue or the Study Hall, or fulfilling the practical commandments of the Torah. But in a matter requiring contemplation—for example, if one intends to give charity and meets many poor people—one should not hurry, but first consider which poor person's need is greater, for the most pressing need comes first. How much more so in optional, mundane matters: one should not act or speak until taking the proper time to be wise. Even in matters of prohibition, such as a dispute or a quarrel, act with calmness and do not hurry. Then peace will come, and you will rest and be quiet all your days from pain, finding favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man.

## The Letter Mem is completed.

# The Letter Nun: Faithful in Spirit

**Faithful in Spirit** is a great and beloved virtue before the Holy One, Blessed be He. His eyes are upon such people, as it is written: "My eyes are upon the faithful of the land" <note>Psalms 101:6</note>, and "O Lord, are not Your eyes toward faithfulness?" Through this virtue, the Holy One, Blessed be He, is described, as it is said: "A God of faithfulness without iniquity." Moses, the choice of all creatures, was praised with this trait, as God testified: "In all My house, he is faithful" <note>Numbers 12:7</note>. And what is faithfulness? It is that a person trusts in their God, fears nothing else, accepts the Creator's decree, and commits their body, soul, and wealth to Him. All their business dealings and words should be in good faith and integrity, letting their "yes" be yes and their "no" be no. A faithful person does not rush to get rich but trusts in God in all matters, as it is written: "Trust in the Lord and do good... and cherish faithfulness."

**And now,** regarding this letter of **Faithful in Spirit**, we are not dealing with business honesty or the matter of truth versus lies—for that will come later, God willing, under the Pillar of Truth. Rather, the discussion here is about being "faithful in spirit," as in the verse: "A faithful spirit conceals a matter" <note>Proverbs 11:13</note>. Let a person be a "master of secrets" in all their affairs. Do not reveal your own secrets to anyone, and do not reveal the secrets of others that have been disclosed to you. As the Sage said: "Your secret is your prisoner; if you reveal it, you become its prisoner." He also said: "Do not reveal to your friend what you would hide from your enemy, unless you have tested him many times to be a faithful lover, lest he turn into an enemy and reveal your secret." Sadly, in our generations, faithful people have ceased to exist. Do not even desire to know the secrets of others. It is written in *The Choice of Pearls* <note>original: *Mivchar HaPeninim*; a famous medieval book of ethical maxims</note> that a man once revealed a matter to his friend and asked, "Do you understand?" The friend replied, "Yes, I understood, but I have already forgotten it." Therefore, a person should act as if they have forgotten the secret of their fellow; in this, they are faithful.

Sometimes being "faithful in spirit" means reporting a matter correctly. See how faithfulness stands against every spirit <note>a pun on the word *ruach*, meaning both spirit and wind</note> and does not hide the truth. For example, if one is appointed as a communal leader (*Parnas*) to spend money according to the will of the people: even if he knows himself to be honest, and the world considers him a man of faith and does not demand an accounting from him, it is still the proper way to provide a meticulous accounting, even down to the smallest coin. For we have no one greater or more faithful than Moses, yet the Midrash tells us that when the work of the Tabernacle was finished, Moses said to Israel: "Come, let us make an account before you." He sat and calculated, but he forgot about one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five shekels that he had used for the hooks of the pillars <note>Exodus 38:28</note>. He began to worry, thinking, "Now Israel will say Moses took them for himself!" But the Holy One, Blessed be He, enlightened his eyes, and he saw they were the hooks for the pillars. He then told them: "You are witnesses for me through this account." If Moses did this, how much more should you, my friend, search your own heart.

**Also, if a person** is given a deposit to guard, they should try to avoid accepting deposits whenever possible. But if it is impossible, and by accepting it they are performing a great act of kindness—for instance, if the owner is going on a dangerous journey and there is no other trustworthy person—then they should only take it if they write down exactly what the deposit is, every large and small thing. Or, they should place it all in a bag and have the depositor seal it with their own seal. All this is so that no suspicion of theft shall arise, God forbid, and everyone will know he is faithful. It is not enough that the Holy One knows the truth; in matters like this, one must be careful to be beyond reproach.

## The Letter Nun is completed.

# The Letter Samekh: Contentment

The trait of contentment (*Sippuk*) is a precious stone, a crown and a diadem. Happy is he in this world, and it shall be well with him in the World to Come. A "good heart" in this world makes one happy, for such a person is truly wealthy, as we have learned: "Who is rich? He who is happy with his portion." Conversely, one who is never content is always lacking, as our Sages of blessed memory said: "No man dies with [even] half...

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical ethical treatise, completing the section on the letter Ayin (Anavah - Humility) and beginning the letter Pe (Pidyon/Pe - Redemption/Grace). The previous page concluded the letter Nun.</meta>

# The Gate of Letters

**Also**, one should conduct oneself with the trait of humility regarding their clothing, for this is a great principle. So it is written in the Zohar, portion of *Vayeshev* <note>original: *Vayeshev* 184b; a foundational work of Jewish mysticism</note>: "And they stripped him of his coat" <note>Genesis 37:23</note>—this means to say that if my people strip themselves of their [prideful] garments, then the Evil Inclination, which rules over a person when they adorn and beautify their clothes and curl their hair, will have no power. This is the meaning of "they stripped him of his coat"—meaning "remove from me that which is prideful." He who is righteous strengthens himself against the Evil Inclination and wages war against it. What is written? "He left his garment in her hand and fled, and got him out" <note>Genesis 39:12, referring to Joseph and Potiphar's wife</note>. One should leave [the prideful garment] and strengthen himself against the inclination, fleeing from it to be saved so that it does not rule over him.

**It is written** in the book *The Menorah of Light* <note>original: *Menorat HaMaor*, a popular 14th-century ethical work by Isaac Aboab</note>: One who holds onto the trait of humility should be separate and removed from all human filth, and should be diligent in every matter of holiness, purity, and abstinence. For humility is recognized through eight things:
**First**, that he should forgive anyone who has done him evil, even if he has the power to pay him back, as it is said: "Say not, 'I will do to him as he has done to me; I will render to the man according to his work'" <note>Proverbs 24:29</note>. (And this is what I said above: being patient even when one has power). The sage said: "He who cannot suffer one word will hear many words."
**Second**, if troubles come upon his body, his wealth, or the death of his children or relatives, he should justify the Divine Decree and accept the judgments of God with love. For it is the way of humility to accept suffering, as we find with Aaron <note>the High Priest</note> when Nadab and Abihu died; he justified the decree upon himself because of his humility and did not complain about his trouble, as it is said: "And Aaron held his peace" <note>Leviticus 10:3</note>. It is also written: "Be silent before the Lord and wait patiently for Him" <note>Psalms 37:7</note>, for in times of trouble, the humble and the wise accept them with love and remain silent, as it is said: "Therefore the prudent shall keep silence in that time" <note>Amos 5:13</note>.
**Third**, if people praise him, he should not become arrogant, but rather lower himself in the way of humility and not let his heart become haughty. We find this with our forefather Abraham, whom Ephron honored and called "My lord, a prince of God," yet he humbled himself even before commoners, as it is said: "And Abraham bowed down before the people of the land" <note>Genesis 23:12</note>.
**[Fourth]**, if God provides him with wisdom, understanding, great wealth, authority, or favor in the eyes of the king, or other things people usually use to aggrandize themselves, he should not raise his heart over his fellows. Rather, he should be humble and modest, conducting himself as he did before attaining authority, as it is said: "If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place" <note>Ecclesiastes 10:4</note>—meaning your original place [of humility].
**Fifth**, when he sees suffering coming upon him, he should repent immediately lest he has sinned, and he should not refrain from doing so out of pride. We find this with the people of Huldah <note>The text likely refers to the returnees in the time of Ezra</note> when Ezra rebuked them; they returned and repented immediately, as it is said: "We have trespassed against our God, and have taken strange wives... yet now there is hope" <note>Ezra 10:2</note>, and they repented for their sins and made their actions right.

<margin>Humility</margin> A person needs to examine themselves during their studies so as not to become arrogant because of their Torah knowledge. One should open their eyes and admit to the truth; likewise, one should not be ashamed to learn from any person and to accept the truth from whoever says it. Regarding a matter he does not know, he should not be ashamed to ask, even of those lesser than him, and certainly of those greater. The sage said:
->The question of a wise man is half of wisdom.<-

**And included** in humility is this: if a fellow person has wronged him in matters where it is proper, good, and right to sue him and seek judgment, he should not "hand over his judgment to Heaven" <note>meaning, calling for divine punishment instead of human court</note> when there is a judge on earth. As we learn at the end of the chapter "The Injurer" <note>Tractate *Bava Kamma* 93a</note>: Rabbi Yohanan said that one who hands over judgment against his fellow to Heaven is punished first, as it is said: "And Sarah said to Abraham: 'My wrong be upon thee'" <note>Genesis 16:5</note>, and later it is written: "And Abraham came to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her" <note>Genesis 23:2</note> [showing she died first]. This applies when he has a legal remedy on earth. Rabbi Isaac said: "Woe to the one who cries out more than the one against whom he cries." The author of the *Hah* <note>likely referring to a specific rabbinic authority or codifier</note> wrote the reason in the name of his teacher: that it is not proper to stir up judgment Above, for the King [God] should always be approached with will and kindness. When one stirs up judgment, it creates an accusation Above and the King becomes angry while executing judgment; it is written, "The wrath of a king is as messengers of death" <note>Proverbs 16:14</note>. Therefore, the one who cries out is removed first because he stirred up the judgment that was quiet. This is like "one who digs a pit falls into it." For this reason, Mar Zutra would say every night before he slept: "May the Master [God] forgive anyone who distressed me."

And for this reason, even though he did not hand over judgment, he did not want the hand of Esau to be the one to stir the judgment, and every matter should stir the attribute of Mercy. Rava said: "He who passes over his retaliatory feelings <note>term: *Ma'avir al midotav* - letting go of one's grievances</note>, all his transgressions are passed over." Also, his prayer is heard, as it is found in the tractate *Ta'anit*: It happened that Rabbi Eliezer went down before the Ark and said twenty-four blessings but was not answered. Rabbi Akiva went down and said "Our Father, our King" and was answered. A Heavenly Voice went out and said: "It is not because this one is greater than the other, but because this one [Akiva] passes over his grievances and the other does not." See how great is the level of humility and forgiveness—his prayer is heard, his sins are forgiven, and he merits to be in the presence of the Divine Glory, as it says: "I dwell with him that is of a contrite and humble spirit" <note>Isaiah 57:15</note>. He also merits the Torah, for one who is arrogant <note>original: *ADL ASTH* - likely a mnemonic or shorthand</note> forgets his Torah, but the humble and pure merit it. Just as the Torah was given on Mount Sinai, the lowliest of mountains, so the spirit of the Lord—which is the Divine Presence—rests upon him, as it says: "And the spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him" <note>Isaiah 11:2</note>.
