# The Letter Ayin is Completed
---

**The Letter Pe: Redemption (*Pidyon*)** Its meaning is "strength," as Rashi explains on the portion *Vayechi*: "The son of *Pud*, Joseph" <note>Genesis 49:22; the author is playing with the root P-D-H/P-D-T</note>, a son of grace. In the Aramaic language, *Aphiryon* <note>A term for a palanquin or canopy; Song of Songs 3:9</note> suggests beauty and favor, as in *Bava Metzia* 72b.
**The intention of Redemption** is that a person should always find favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man, and should be good with God and with people.

**Graciousness (*Chanan*)**: Anyone with whom the spirit of his fellow creatures is pleased, the spirit of the Omnipresent is pleased with him <margin>in Ethics of the Fathers</margin> <note>original: *Pirkei Avot* 3:10</note>. This was a regular saying in the mouth of Abaye: A person should always be clever in the fear of God, giving a soft answer that turns away wrath, increasing peace with his brothers, his relatives, and with every person—even a stranger in the market—so that he may be beloved Above and pleasant Below, and acceptable to all creatures. It was said of Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai that no man ever preceded him in greeting, even a stranger in the market. This is the meaning of "receiving every person with a beautiful face"—with a bright and smiling countenance. **A good man** brings good news, while an evil man covers and hides it.

**My father and teacher, peace be upon him, wrote** in the ethical will *Yesh Nachalin*: Do not benefit from any gift in any place you visit, lest you disgrace yourselves. Act according to the custom of that place, and then you will be beloved to them. But "comfort them in their ways"—a person should never deviate from the local custom. For Moses went up to the heights and did not eat bread <note>Exodus 34:28</note>, while the ministering angels came down below and did eat bread <note>Genesis 18:8</note>. Furthermore, they said: "When you enter a city, follow its laws." **The sage said**: Do not stand in your poverty as an enemy <margin>1</margin>, and do not let a thousand friends seem too many in your eyes. The Sages of the Mishnah said regarding this path: "There is no man who does not have his hour" <note>*Pirkei Avot* 4:3</note>.

**"And you shall be clean before the Lord and before Israel"** <note>Numbers 32:22</note>. Our Sages learned from here that a person must distance himself from suspicion. As we learned in the tractate *Shekalim*: The one who takes up the chamber-offering does not enter with a hemmed garment, nor with shoes, nor with sandals <note>so they couldn't hide coins in them</note>, lest he become poor and people say he was impoverished as a punishment for the chamber-offering, or lest he become rich and they say he grew rich from the chamber-offering. A person must fulfill his obligations to people just as he must fulfill them to the Omnipresent, as proven from the Torah, the Prophets, and the Writings. From the Torah: "And you shall be clean before the Lord and before Israel." From the Prophets: "The Lord God of gods, He knows, and Israel he shall know" <note>Joshua 22:22</note>. From the Writings: "So shalt thou find favor and good understanding in the sight of God and man" <note>Proverbs 3:4</note>. Similarly, our Sages said: Hannah said to Eli, "No, my lord" <note>1 Samuel 1:15</note>—"You are not a lord in this matter, for the Divine Presence and the Holy Spirit are not with you, since you judged me guilty and did not speak merit of me. Do you not know that I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit, and have drunk neither wine nor strong drink?" Rabbi Eleazar said: From here we learn that one who is suspected of something he did not do must inform [the suspecter]. And Eli answered: "Go in peace." Rabbi Eleazar said: From here we learn that one who suspects his fellow of something they did not do must appease them, and not only that, but must bless them, as it is said: "And the God of Israel grant thee thy petition." And so we find many things in the Talmud that were forbidden solely because of suspicion <note>term: *Marit Ayin* - the appearance of the eye</note>.

**There are two reasons** for this matter: First, so that the glory of Heaven is increased. For if a person is suspected of a transgression, then Heaven forbid the glory of Heaven is diminished, because people will say, "This certain person rebelled against God and did such-and-forth," and perhaps others will learn from him to act likewise. Therefore, one must inform and clarify, as the children of Gad and Reuben said: "God knows, and Israel shall know, that it was not in rebellion or in trespass." The second reason is that God desires that we love each man his brother, and one who hates violates a negative commandment: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart" <note>Leviticus 19:17</note>. Love is the commandment upon which the whole Torah stands: "Love thy neighbor as thyself." If one believes his fellow has committed a sin, then it is permitted to hate him, as explained in the chapter "Arvei Pesachim" <note>Tractate *Pesachim* 113b</note> regarding the verse "If you see the donkey of him that hates you lying [under its burden]"—which refers to a case where one saw him commit a sin. In such a case, it is permitted and even a commandment to hate him, as it is said: "The fear of the Lord is to hate evil" <note>Proverbs 8:13</note>, and "Do I not hate them, O Lord, that hate Thee? And am I not grieved with those that rise up against Thee? I hate them with perfect hatred" <note>Psalms 139:21</note>.

It then begins the section on the letter Pe, focusing on "Redemption" interpreted as finding favor with others and avoiding suspicion to maintain communal peace and God's honor.</summary>

<meta>The previous page concluded the discussion on the letter *Mem* (Deliberation) and *Nun* (Faithfulness), and likely began the letter *Ayin* (Humility/Anavah). This page continues the detailed exploration of Humility before transitioning to the letter *Pe*.</meta>

# The Gate of Letters

**Also,** one should conduct oneself with the trait of humility regarding their clothing; this is a great general principle. So it is written in the *Zohar* <note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah)</note> on the portion of *Vayishev* <note>Genesis 37–40</note>, of blessed memory: "And she caught him by his garment, saying..." <note>Genesis 39:12</note>. This teaches that the Evil Inclination <term>Yetzer HaRa: the innate human drive toward selfish or base desires</term> has power over a person when they fix themselves up, adorn their clothes, and curl their hair. Thus it is written: "She caught him by his garment," meaning the Inclination seizes the person. But one who is righteous gathers strength against it and wages war. What is written? "He left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got himself out." He should leave the "garment" <note>Metaphorically, the external focus on vanity</note> in the Inclination's hand, strengthen himself against it, and flee from it to be saved so that it does not rule over him. These are the words of the *Zohar*.

**It is written** in the book *Menorat HaMaor* <note>original: "The Candelabra of Light," a popular 14th-century ethical manual by Isaac Aboab</note>: One who grasps the trait of humility should be separate and removed from all human filth, and should be diligent in every matter of holiness, purity, and abstinence. For humility is recognized through eight things:
1. That he forgives anyone who has done him evil, even if he has the power to pay them back. As it is said: "Do not say, 'As he did to me, so I will do to him; I will repay the man according to his work'" <note>Proverbs 24:29</note>. (This is what I mentioned above regarding being "forbearing after reaching capability"). The sage said: "He who cannot suffer one word will hear many words."
2. If troubles come upon his body, his wealth, or the death of his children or relatives, he should justify the Divine decree <term>Tzidduk HaDin: accepting God's judgment as just even in tragedy</term> and receive the judgments of God with love. For it is the way of humility to accept suffering. We find this with Aaron the Priest, peace be upon him: when his sons Nadab and Abihu died, he justified the decree because of his humility and did not loathe his trouble, as it says: "And Aaron was silent" <note>Leviticus 10:3</note>. And it is written: "Be silent before the Lord and wait patiently for Him" <note>Psalms 37:7</note>, for in times of trouble, the humble and the wise accept them with love and remain silent, as it says: "Therefore the prudent man shall keep silence in that time" <note>Amos 5:13</note>.
3. If people praise him, he should not become arrogant, but rather lower himself in the way of humility and not let his heart become haughty. We find this with our father Abraham, peace be upon him, whom Ephron honored and called "My lord, a prince of God," yet he humbled himself and even prostrated before the common people, as it says: "And Abraham bowed down before the people of the land" <note>Genesis 23:12</note>.
4. If God grants him wisdom, understanding, great wealth, authority, or favor in the eyes of the king, or other things people usually use to aggrandize themselves, he should not raise his heart over his fellows. Rather, he should be humble and modest, conducting himself as he did before attaining authority, as it says: "If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place" <note>Ecclesiastes 10:4</note>—meaning, do not leave your "original place" of humility.
5. When he sees suffering coming upon him, he should repent immediately lest he has sinned, and he should not refrain from doing so out of pride. Just as we find with the people in the time of Hulda <note>Likely referring to the era of Ezra, as the text mentions him next</note>, when Ezra, peace be upon him, rebuked them, they returned and repented immediately, as it says: "We have trespassed against our God, and have taken foreign wives... yet now there is hope" <note>Ezra 10:2</note>. Their repentance atoned for their sins and straightened their actions. These are the words of the *Menorat HaMaor*.

**Humility** is something a person must build within their learning, so they do not take pride in their Torah knowledge. They should live humbly and admit the truth. Also, one should not be ashamed to learn from any person, receiving the truth from whoever speaks it. Regarding something he does not know, he should not be ashamed to ask, even of one smaller than himself—certainly from one greater. The sage said:
->The question of a wise man is half of wisdom.<-

**In general,** humility means that if a fellow man sins against him in matters where it is right and good to sue him or seek judgment, he should not "hand over the judgment to Heaven" <note>Meaning, asking God to punish the offender</note> when there is a human judge available on earth. For we learn at the end of the chapter "The Injurer" <note>Tractate *Bava Kamma* 93a</note>: "Whoever hands over judgment against his fellow is punished first." This is seen when Sarah said to Abraham: "My wrong be upon you" <note>Genesis 16:5</note>, and later it is written: "And Abraham came to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her" <note>Genesis 23:2; he outlived her because she invoked divine judgment</note>. If there is a judge on earth, Isaac said: "Woe to the one who cries out more than the one cried against." Rabbi He-Hasid <note>Likely Judah the Pious</note> wrote in the name of his teacher that it is not proper to stir up judgment Above, for the King <note>God</note> should always be approached with will and kindness. When one stirs up judgment and an accuser Above, the King becomes angry to enact the judgment, and it is written: "The wrath of a king is as messengers of death" <note>Proverbs 16:14</note>. Therefore, the one who cries out is settled with first because he disturbed the quiet judgment. This is like "he who digs a pit shall fall into it." For this reason, Mar Zutra <note>A Talmudic sage known for his piety</note> would say every night before he slept: "I forgive anyone who has vexed me." His reason was that even though he did not hand over judgment to an earthly court, by not stirring up judgment at all, he awakens the Attribute of Mercy. Rava said: "Whoever passes over his feelings <note>original: *Ma'avir al Midotav*; meaning one who is not litigious or easily offended</note>, God passes over all his transgressions." Also, such a person's prayer is heard, as found in the tractate *Ta'anit* <note>25b</note>: It happened that Rabbi Eliezer went before the Ark and said twenty-four blessings but was not answered. Rabbi Akiva went and said "Our Father, Our King" (*Avinu Malkeinu*) and was answered. A Heavenly Voice went out and said: "It is not because this one is greater than that one, but because this one [Akiva] passes over his feelings and this one [Eliezer] does not." See how great the level of humility is—their prayer is heard, their sins are forgiven, and they merit to be in the partition of the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah: the indwelling presence of God in the world</term>, as it is written: "I dwell with the contrite and humble spirit" <note>Isaiah 57:15</note>. Such a person also merits Torah, for one who is arrogant forgets his learning, but the humble merit Torah just as it was given on Mount Sinai, the lowest of mountains. Thus the spirit of the Lord—the *Shekhinah*—rests upon him, as does the spirit of wisdom and understanding.

->### The Letter Ayin is Completed<-

**The Letter Pe: Redemption (*Pidyon*)** Its meaning is explained by our Sages... <note>The text here uses complex abbreviations referring to Aramaic translations</note> Joseph was a "son of grace" (*Ben Chen*). The Aramaic expression for this is: "Let us bring a canopy (*apiryon*) to you."

**The intention of Redemption** is that a person should always find grace and good understanding in the eyes of God and man, being good with both the Divine and with people.
**Education (*Chinukh*):** Anyone with whom the spirit of his fellow creatures is pleased, the spirit of the Omnipresent is pleased with him. In the chapter "One who Recites," it was a common saying in the mouth of Abaye: "A person should always be cunning in the fear of God, giving a soft answer that turns away wrath, increasing peace with his brothers, his relatives, and every person—even a non-Jew in the marketplace—so that he may be beloved Above and cherished below, and accepted by all creatures." It was said of Rabbi Jochanan ben Zakkai that no man ever preceded him in greeting, not even a non-Jew in the marketplace. This is what it means to "receive every person with a beautiful face" <note>Pirkei Avot 1:15</note>—with a bright and smiling countenance. **A good man** brings good tidings, while the evil man covers and hides them.

**My father and teacher,** peace be upon him, wrote in his ethical will *Yesh Nachalati*: "Do not change from the local custom. Wherever you are, conduct yourselves according to the custom of that place, and then you will be beloved by them." This follows Tanchum bar Chanilai's teaching: "A person should never deviate from the custom." For Moses went up to the Heavens and did not eat bread <note>acting like an angel</note>, while the ministering angels came down to earth and did eat bread <note>acting like humans</note>. Furthermore, the Sages said: "When you enter a town, follow its customs." The sage said: "Do not let even one enemy stand in your eyes, and let even a thousand friends not seem like too many." The Sages of the Mishnah said regarding this: "Pursue [peace], for there is no person who does not have his hour."

**"And you shall be clean before the Lord and before Israel"** <note>Numbers 32:22</note>. Our Sages learned from here that a person must distance himself from suspicion. As we learned in the tractate *Shekalim* <note>3:2</note>: The one who took the contribution from the Temple treasury would not enter wearing a hemmed garment, nor shoes, nor sandals <note>so they couldn't hide coins in them</note>. Lest if he became poor, people would say he was punished for a sin against the treasury, or if he became rich, they would say he stole from the treasury. A person must satisfy the expectations of people just as he must satisfy the Omnipresent, as proven from the Torah, the Prophets, and the Writings. From the Torah: "And you shall be clean before the Lord and before Israel." From the Prophets: "The Lord God of gods, He knows, and Israel, he shall know" <note>Joshua 22:22</note>. From the Writings: "And find grace and good favor in the eyes of God and man" <note>Proverbs 3:4</note>. Similarly, the Sages said: "Distance yourself from what is ugly and from anything that resembles it." In tractate *Berakhot*, the chapter "One who Recites": "And Hannah answered and said, 'No, my lord...'" <note>1 Samuel 1:15</note>. Ulla (or some say Rabbi Jose bar Hanina) said: She said to him, "You are not a 'lord' in this matter <note>referring to Eli the Priest wrongly suspecting her of being drunk</note>; for the Divine Presence and the Holy Spirit are not with you if you have judged me unfavorably rather than favorably. Do you not know I am a woman of troubled spirit?" Rabbi Eleazar said: From here we learn that one who is suspected of something they did not do must inform the accuser [of the truth]. And Eli said: "Go in peace." Rabbi Eleazar said: From here we learn that one who suspects his fellow of something they did not do must appease them, and not only that, but must bless them, as it says: "And the God of Israel grant your petition." We find many things in the Talmud that were forbidden solely because of the appearance of suspicion.

**There are two reasons** for this matter:
1. So that the honor of Heaven is magnified. If a person is suspected of a transgression, the honor of Heaven is diminished, for people will say, "This person rebelled against God and did such-and-such." Perhaps others will learn from him to do the same, God forbid. Therefore, like a group, one must make it known [that they are innocent], as the sons of Gad and Reuben said: "God knows, and Israel shall know, that it was not in rebellion or trespass."
2. Because God desires that we love one another. One who hates violates a negative commandment: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart" <note>Leviticus 19:17</note>. Love is the commandment upon which the entire Torah stands: "Love your neighbor as yourself." If one believes his fellow has committed a sin, it might be permitted to hate him, as it says: "The fear of the Lord is to hate evil" and "Do I not hate those who hate You, O Lord?" and "I hate them with a perfect hatred" <note>Psalms 139:21-22</note>.

<summary>This page concludes the section on the letter Ayin (Humility), emphasizing silence under suffering and avoiding divine judgment against others, then begins the letter Pe, focusing on social grace, avoiding suspicion, and maintaining a good reputation before both God and man.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Gate of Letters," focusing on the letter Ayin for Anavah (Humility). It follows the previous discussion regarding how humility should manifest in one's physical appearance and clothing.</meta>

# The Gate of Letters

**Behold**, the entirety of our Torah, our actions, and our fulfillment of the positive and negative commandments—and all the levels of holiness through which we sanctify ourselves—exist solely so that we may merit "cleaving" <term>deveikut: a state of intense spiritual attachment</term> to the Blessed One. As it is written: "But you who cleave to the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 4:4</note>, meaning to be with Him in His presence and within the shelter of the "Spirit of Spirits." One who removes himself from the dwelling of the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah: the localized, feminine aspect of God's presence in the world</term>—woe to him and woe to his destiny! Woe to the day he was born, for any good deed he performs is as if he cast it into the depths of the sea, and all that good is forgotten. Even if he is "satisfied" with commandments, the reason the Divine Presence cannot dwell with him is that he does not consider the Divine Presence at all.

For example: if a wise man comes among unlearned people, even if he is not the greatest sage or an expert in his wisdom, he is still considered "wise" relative to them. But if this wise man comes to a group of truly great and distinguished sages, where even the smallest among them is "thicker than his loins" <note>an idiom meaning far superior; see 1 Kings 12:10</note>, he is certainly considered nothing compared to them. This is similar to what the woman of Zarephath said to the prophet Elijah: "Why have you come to remind me of my sin?" <note>1 Kings 17:18</note>. Until you arrived, my deeds were weighed against the deeds of my city-dwellers [and I seemed righteous], but now [compared to you, I am a sinner]. We find that even if a person has some merit relative to those lower than him, if he does not constantly place the Blessed Name before him—failing to fulfill "I have set the Lord before me always" <note>Psalm 16:8</note>—he will never achieve true humility. For if he did so, he would think: "What am I? What is my life worth compared to the glory of the Divine Presence? He is holy and His ministers are holy, while I am soiled and filthy, a murky, despicable, and loathsome piece of matter." Therefore, because he removes the Divine Presence from before his eyes [by being proud], the Divine Presence also removes Itself from him.

One who is worthy of the Spirit of the Divine Presence finds that It rests upon him, just as It rested upon Mount Sinai because it was the lowest of the mountains. In the book *Reshit Chochmah* <note>original: *Rachash*; "The Beginning of Wisdom," a famous 16th-century kabbalistic ethical work by Eliyahu de Vidas</note>, in the section "The Gate of Humility," it is brought that Rabbi Isaac of Akko <note>a 13th-14th century Kabbalist</note> wrote what he heard from the mouth of Rabbi Meir, a student of Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla. Rabbi Gikatilla said: "The man who directs his heart to refine his traits, to straighten his ways and deeds, and to pursue humility as the ultimate perfection—being one who is insulted but does not insult, who hears his shame and does not respond—immediately the Divine Presence rests upon him. He will not need to learn from flesh and blood, for the Spirit of God will teach him."

He thus becomes a "chariot" <note>a vehicle for divine manifestation</note> for the Holy One. Rabbi Moshe Cordovero, in the book *Tomer Devorah* <note>The Palm Tree of Deborah</note>, Chapter 2, writes: "A person must resemble his Creator through the secret of the attribute of *Keter* <term>Keter: 'Crown', the highest and most hidden of the ten Sefirot (divine emanations)</term>. He must possess the behaviors and actions that are its primary conduct. The first, which encompasses all, is the trait of humility. This is because *Keter* depends on humility; it is the highest of all attributes, yet it does not count its own height or pride itself upward. On the contrary, it always looks downward." This is for two reasons: First, it is "ashamed" to look at its Cause [the Infinite]; rather, its Emanator always looks upon it to bestow good, and it looks toward those below it. So too, a man should be ashamed to look upward to act pridefully; instead, he should constantly look downward to bestow upon his subordinates. This trait is generally associated with the "head," for a man only shows pride by lifting his head upward, while the humble man bows his head downward. Behold, there is none so patient and humble as our God in the attribute of *Keter*, which is the ultimate Mercy. No flaw or sin enters before Him, and no restrictive attribute prevents Him from bestowing and bestowing and bestowing and constantly doing good. So must a man be: no cause in the world should prevent him from doing good, and no sin or improper deed of others should stop him from providing for those who need his goodness. Just as God sits and provides "from the horns of wild oxen to the eggs of lice" and does not despise any creature—for to despise a creature is to despise the Creator—and as their existence would not last a moment without His mercy, so must a man do good to all. He should not despise any creature because of its flaws; even the smallest of the small should be precious in his eyes. He should set his mind upon them and do good to all who require his help. This trait is tied to *Keter* through the secret of the "Head." Thus far are his words.

And behold, regarding the trait of *Keter*, which is a crown and wreath to all other traits, our Sages of blessed memory hinted at this in the teachings of the Mishnah: "Wherever you find the greatness of the Holy One, blessed be He, there you also find His humility."

<margin>
It is so written in Tractate Shabbat, the chapter of "Rabbi Akiva" <note>Shabbat 88b</note>: "Those who are insulted but do not insult, who hear their shame and do not respond, who act out of love and rejoice in suffering—of them the Verse says: 'But those who love Him shall be as the sun when it goes forth in its might'" <note>Judges 5:31</note>. Initially, the matter of poverty <unclear>afflicts</unclear> because it is proper to receive all suffering from man as a kindness to him. One should rejoice in suffering, as our Sages said <unclear>in the Jerusalem Talmud</unclear>... even if it is a lie... and not only this, but regarding everyone who insults him... he should say it is merely "wind" <note>ephemeral/meaningless</note>...
</margin>

The trait of humility must exist in thought, in speech, and in action.

**In thought:** How? He should think of himself as if he were nothing, and that non-existence would be better than his existence. He should view himself as the lowliest of all creatures in the world. He should remember that he originated from a "putrid drop" and from murkiness, and that his body is a place of filth. How can he be prideful when he is prone to pain and when his body produces excrement? He is full of filth, waste, and earwax. Afterward, he should remember the "filth" of his sins, iniquities, and transgressions. He should not distance them from his sight like a putrid waste; rather, it is proper to distance them from the entire earth. He should remember how little he knows of the depth of the Torah and its secrets. If so, what is he worth? Is not a stillborn better than he? It would have been better had he not been created. How then can he be proud?

The divine and pious Cordovero writes in *Tomer Devorah*: "I have found a remedy to habituate a person to the trait of humility using a bandage of three 'medications':
1. He should habituate himself to flee from honor as much as he can. For if he conducts himself so that people honor him, he will learn the side of pride.
2. He should train his thoughts to see his own lowliness. He should say: 'Even though people do not know my flaws, what does that matter to me? Do I not recognize myself? I am despicable in this and that...' whether in his lack of knowledge, weakness of ability, or the waste that leaves his body. He should always be loathsome and rejected in his own eyes.
3. He should always think of his sins and desire purification, rebuke, and suffering. He should ask: 'What is the best suffering in the world that will not distract me from the service of God?' There is none more beloved than those who shame, despise, and insult him. For insults do not drain his strength, do not make him ill, do not take away his food or clothing, and do not harm the life of his children. If so, a little shame is better than fasting or self-affliction with sackcloth and lashes, which weaken the strength for divine service."

Therefore, when insults come upon him, he should rejoice in them and actually desire them. This is what King David meant regarding Shimei ben Gera: "The Lord said to him: Curse" <note>2 Samuel 16:10</note>. Meaning, it was all sent from God because of my sins. This is an act of kindness—that these sufferings, which do not diminish my life or vitality, should atone for the punishment of my sins. How could I not receive them with love from the Blessed One? Therefore, even though David was a great and holy king, he accepted it with love. How much more so should a commoner like me accept every insult, hear his shame, and thank the Lord.

It is written in the eighth section of the "Gate of Humility" in the name of Rabbi Isaac of Akko: "It is written in the books of the Kabbalists... that one of the greatest repairs for one who seeks the knowledge of God is to be among the 'insulted ones,' even by his wife and household, of whom he is not afraid and before whom he is not embarrassed. He should not be an 'insulter.' If he must rebuke his household to remove them from the 'path of death'—where they transgress the will of the Place <note>God</note>—and to guide them on the 'path of life,' he should rebuke them in a way that he does not feel anger in his heart, but his heart should always be happy in the Holy One."

Similarly, Rabbi Eliyahu [de Vidas] wrote, as copied in the *Yalkut* on the portion of *Ki Tissa*: "The Sages taught: Be humble toward every person, and toward the people of your household more than anyone else."

## It should further be seen
That there is submission and humility in his **speech**: let his words be gentle with people, as Maimonides <note>original: *Rambam*</note> wrote. His heart and his preparation for the [divine] yoke should be such that he speaks gently. He should not stare into the face of a person while speaking with them; his head should be bowed, and his speech should be truthful. Like the Gemara says: out of "fear of man," one should not answer in a loud voice, but with soft, gentle words. If he hears his shame, he should be silent and endure it.

**Submission in his deeds:** This means a "lowly soul" regarding all matters of desire. He should not pursue the fulfillment of lusts in matters of food or immorality. This is called "soul," as it says: "In all the desire of your soul" or "whatever your soul asks of you." A "broad soul" <note>greedy</note> is one that pursues desire, as it says: "The soul is never satisfied." One who pursues the desires of food and other cravings of the heart becomes proud, as it is written: "Lest you eat and be satisfied, and build good houses and dwell in them... and your heart be lifted up, and you forget the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 8:12–14</note>.

**Also**, his walking should be with submission, with a bowed head and eyes cast down. He should not look beyond four cubits, and should always remember the "four cubits" that belong to every man—the grave. This is what the Sages of the Mishnah hinted at: "And be lowly on the earth," meaning he should always remember [what is] inside the earth, for "dust he is, and to dust he shall return."

It provides practical methods for achieving this state through thought, speech, and action, drawing heavily on the kabbalistic ethics of Rabbi Moshe Cordovero and Rabbi Isaac of Akko.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical ethical treatise, focusing on the letter Ayin (Anavah - Humility) and transitioning into practical applications of this trait in speech and action.</meta>

# The Gate of Letters

<margin>
It is written in the Talmud, Tractate Shabbat, chapter "Rabbi Akiva," that the Sages taught: Those who are insulted but do not insult in return, who hear their shame and do not respond, who act out of love and are happy in their sufferings—of them the verse says: "And those who love Him shall be as the sun going forth in its might." <note>original: Judges 5:31</note> For it is fitting to receive all sufferings with love. This is the third path I mentioned: that just as a person’s name grows through sufferings, it is also a path to the fear of Heaven. As the Sages said: "Those who are insulted..." <note>original: *shome'im cherpatam*</note> and the commentators explain that even if people are tearing at them or arguing with them, one should say, "This is my judgment," even if it is false. Not only that, but even if they are physically harmed, one should not respond. This is like the story of Tamar who was led out to be burned and did not shame Judah. <note>original: Genesis 38:25</note>
</margin>

Behold, our entire Torah, our deeds, and the fulfillment of the positive and negative commandments <term>mitzvot; religious duties</term>, and all the holiness with which we sanctify ourselves—it is all for the sake of meriting attachment <term>deveikut; spiritual cleaving</term> to Him, may He be blessed, as it is written: "And you who cleave to the Lord your God are all alive today." <note>Deuteronomy 4:4</note> This means to live with Him in His domain and in the shelter of the Spirit. One must guard oneself against being cast out from the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah; the indwelling presence of God</term>. Woe to the person and woe to their fate on the day they were born, for every sinner who dwells [in sin] is as if they have cast away the Divine Presence. Furthermore, all satisfaction is forgotten, even if one is satisfied with commandments. The reason the Divine Presence cannot dwell with a person is that they do not think of the Divine Presence at all. For example, if a wise man comes among common folk, even if he is not the greatest sage or an expert in his wisdom, he is still wise relative to them. But if this wise man comes to a group of great, distinguished sages, whose smallest [student] is "thicker than his loins," <note>an idiom for being far superior</note> he is certainly considered nothing compared to them. This is like what the woman of Zarephath said to Elijah the Prophet: "Why have you come to remind me of my sin?" <note>1 Kings 17:18</note>—meaning that before you arrived, my deeds were weighed against the deeds of my townspeople [and I seemed righteous], etc. Thus, even if a person has some merit relative to those lower than them, they must realize that they are not setting the Lord before them always. If they did, they would think: "What am I? What is my life worth compared to the glory of the Divine Presence?" He is holy and His ministers are holy, whereas I am defiled and soiled, a murky, despised, and loathsome material body. Therefore, since such a person removes the Divine Presence from before their eyes, the Divine Presence also departs from them. But the one who is crushed and humble of spirit, the Divine Presence dwells upon them, just as the Divine Presence dwelt on Mount Sinai because it was the lowest of the mountains.

In the book *The Beginning of Wisdom* <note>original: *Reshit Chochmah*, a 16th-century Kabbalistic ethical work</note>, in the "Gate of Humility," it is brought that Rabbi Isaac of Acre (peace be upon him) heard from the mouth of Rabbi Moshe, the student of Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla <note>a famous 13th-century Spanish Kabbalist</note>, that Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla said: A man who prepares his heart to refine his character traits, to straighten his ways and deeds, and to pursue humility as the ultimate perfection—to be "insulted but not insulting," to hear his shame and not respond—immediately the Divine Presence will rest upon him. He will not even need to learn from flesh and blood, for the Spirit of God will teach him. Such a person becomes a "Chariot" <term>Merkavah; a vehicle for Divine revelation</term>.

And the godly Rabbi <insert>author of</insert> *Abundant Kindness to Abraham* <note>original: *Chesed Le-Avraham*, by Abraham Azulai</note> wrote: The secret of the "Palm Tree" <note>referring to the book *Tomer Devorah* (The Palm Tree of Deborah) by Moses Cordovero</note> in the second chapter is that a person should be like a "thorn" <note>original: *kotz*; likely referring to the *kotzo shel yod*, the humble point at the top of the Hebrew letter Yod</note> in the secret of the attribute of the Crown <term>Keter; the highest Divine attribute</term>. One must embody the conduct of the Eleven [Attributes] that give birth to everything, which is the trait of Humility. This is because it is dependent on the Crown, which is above all other attributes, yet it does not act proudly or exalt itself upward. Rather, it descends and looks downward. This is for two reasons: First, because it is ashamed to look at its Cause [the Infinite], but rather its Emanator gazes at it constantly to do it good, and it in turn gazes at the lower realms. So too, a person should be ashamed to look upward in pride, but should constantly look downward to lower themselves as much as possible. This attribute is generally associated with the head, for a person only acts proudly by lifting their head upward, while the humble person bows their head down.

Behold, there is no one more patient and humble than our God in the attribute of the Crown, which is the ultimate Mercy. No blemish, sin, or emptiness enters before Him, nor any attribute that prevents Him from watching over, influencing, and doing good constantly. So too must a man act: no cause in the world should prevent him from doing good, and no sin or unworthy deed of people should enter before him to hinder him from doing good to those who need his kindness. Just as God sits and feeds everyone from the "horns of the wild oxen to the eggs of lice" <note>a Talmudic idiom for the greatest to the smallest creatures</note> and does not despise any creature—for if He despised them because of their lowliness, they would not survive in the world for even a moment, but He watches over them and grants His mercy to them all—so must a man do good to everyone. No creature should be despised before him; even the smallest of the small should be very precious in his eyes. He should set his mind on them and do good to all who require his help. This trait is dependent on the Crown in the secret of the "Head."

Regarding our subject: concerning the attribute of the Crown, which is a crown and diadem to all character traits, it seems our Sages hinted: "In every place you find the greatness of the Holy One, Blessed be He, there you find His humility." Humility must exist in thought, in speech, and in action.

**In thought:** How? One should think of themselves as nothing <note>original: *ayin*</note>, as if their existence were a void of goodness. They should see themselves as the lowliest of all creatures in the world, remembering they branched out from a "foul drop" <note>referring to human conception</note> and their gestation was through a place of filth. How can one be proud when they are full of pain, with the ugliness of waste exiting their body, their belly full of filth, and foulness in the nose and ears? Furthermore, one should remember their sins, iniquities, and transgressions; it is not enough to distance oneself from them as far as the eye can see, like foul excrement, but rather one should distance themselves as far as the earth is wide. One should remember the littleness of their knowledge and understanding in the depths of the Torah and its secrets. If so, what is he worth? A carcass is better than he, and it would have been better had he not been created. How then can he be proud?

The godly sage Cordovero <note>Moses Cordovero, 1522–1570, a leading Kabbalist in Safed</note> wrote in *The Palm Tree of Deborah*: I have found a remedy to habituate a person to the trait of humility through a "bandage of three medicines."
1.  **First:** Habituate oneself to flee from honor as much as possible. For if one conducts themselves so that people honor them, they will train themselves in pride, and their nature will always desire it, making it difficult to break the habit.
2.  **Second:** Habituate one's thoughts to be in self-reflection of their own lowliness. One should say: "Even though people do not know my deficiencies, what does that matter to me? Do I not recognize in myself that I am despised in this and that?" Whether it is through a lack of knowledge, weakness of power, or the repulsiveness of food and the waste that exits from it, until humility becomes repulsive in his own eyes <note>meaning he truly feels his lowliness</note>.
3.  **Third:** Think of one's sins always and desire purity, repentance, and sufferings. One should say: "What are the best sufferings in the world that will not distract me from the service of God? None are dearer than those who insult, despise, and blaspheme me." For these do not take away one's strength, they do not cause illness, they do not take away food or clothing, and they do not take away one's life or the lives of one's children. Therefore, one should almost desire them and say: "Why should I fast or afflict myself with sackcloth and lashes which weaken my strength for God's service? It is better that I am 'lashed' by the hands of people—let me be absorbed in the contempt and shame they give me, and my strength will not depart." When insults come upon him, he should rejoice in them and indeed desire them.

One should make a bandage for the heart from these three medicines and train in them all their days. The essence of the matter is what King David said regarding Shimei ben Gera: "The Lord told him: Curse" <note>2 Samuel 16:11</note>—meaning, the Blessed Name sent him to me because of my sins. This is from the trait of His kindness toward me: that these sufferings, which do not diminish my life or my health, should cleanse the punishment of my sins. How could I not receive them with love from the Blessed Name? Therefore, even though David was a great and holy king, he accepted it with love. How much more so should a commoner like me receive every insult, hear his shame, and thank God.

Rabbi Chaim wrote in the "Gate of Humility" in the name of Rabbi Isaac of Acre: It is written in the books of the Kabbalists that one of the great rectifications for seeking the knowledge of God is that a person should be humble even before his wife and household, of whom he is not afraid and before whom he is not ashamed. He should not be an oppressor, etc. If he must rebuke his household to remove them from the path of death—where they transgress the will of the Omnipresent—and to straighten them and guide them in the path of life, which is the path of doing God's will, he should rebuke them in a way that he does not feel anger in his heart. His heart should always be happy in the Creator. So it is written in *Tanna Debei Eliyahu* <note>an ancient Midrashic work</note>, as copied in the *Yalkut* on the portion *Ki Tissa*: The Sages taught: Be humble to every person, and to the members of your household more than to anyone else.

---

## Further Insights
One should show submission and humility in their **speech**, speaking gently with other people, as Maimonides <term>Rambam; 12th-century philosopher and jurist</term> wrote to his son: "Accustom yourself to speak gently, and do not look into the face of a person when speaking with them. Your head should be bowed, and your eyes should look toward the ground with awe." If a person calls him, he should not answer with a loud voice, but gently, and should greet them as one does for many people, and the like. If he hears himself being shamed, he should remain silent and endure it.

**Submission** in one's deeds: One should have a lowly soul regarding all matters of desire. Do not pursue the fulfillment of desires regarding food and physical pleasures. We find that desire is called "soul" <note>original: *nefesh*</note>, as it says: "Whatever your soul desires" and "whatever your soul asks of you." A "wide soul" is one that pursues its desires, as it is written: "And the soul is not filled." One who pursues the desire for food and other heart's desires becomes prideful, as it is written: "Lest you eat and are satisfied, and build good houses and dwell in them... and your heart becomes haughty and you forget the Lord your God, etc." <note>Deuteronomy 8:12-14</note>

**Also**, one's walk should be with submission, with a bowed head and a slouching posture, and the eyes should not look beyond one's four cubits. One should always remember the four cubits that belong to every person: the grave. This is what the Sages of the Mishnah hinted at: "And be lowly on the earth," meaning one should always remember the earth, for "dust you are, and to dust you shall return."

# The Gate of Letters

...to his mouth, and he longs and desires to fill his mouth. <insert>(A marginal note: The sage said, "Nothing stands as a barrier before desire like closing one's eyes.")</insert> He has much power; therefore, a person should be "closed off" during the six days of action—by which I mean the time of existence in this world, where a "day" is considered a thousand years. It is not the "good way" to be closed off [from God] during these days of action, for these are the days to perform deeds, while tomorrow <note>meaning the World to Come</note> is the time to receive their reward. On the day of the Sabbath, he will then "open an inheritance without boundaries" <note>original: *nachalah bli meitzarim*, a Talmudic expression for boundless spiritual reward</note>. For now, it is enough for him to occupy the "four cubits of the Law" <term>halakha: Jewish law and practice</term>. It is said, "The Lord is with him," meaning the law follows his view. Who can measure the intensity of the virtue of seclusion <term>hitbodedut: a practice of spiritual isolation and internal meditation</term>, which causes the "secret of the friend" <note>possibly referring to divine intimacy or prophetic insight</note> to rest upon him? And if he goes out for the sake of a commandment, he should go as the verse hints: "Walk humbly with your God" <note>Micah 6:8</note>. Immediately afterward, he should return to his enclosure.

This practice also brings him to the light of the Torah, for seclusion is a wondrous "remedy" <term>segulah: a spiritual property or charm</term> that opens a great gateway in the Torah for him, as that is where his "home" is. Furthermore, seclusion is a great act of submission by man before the Blessed Name; it shows he is a subjugated servant who has no permission to leave his master's chest <note>metaphor for God’s domain</note>. He does not seek "ownerless freedom" <term>hefker: lawlessness or being without a master</term>, for he finds no pleasure in such freedom—that is, in wandering the length and breadth of the land. Thus, all his days are spent in repentance. One who merits the level of seclusion, reflecting every day on repentance, regretting the past with complete remorse and abandoning sin entirely—certainly all his sins are forgiven. He merits an extra measure of holiness and can reach the level of Divine Inspiration <term>Ruach HaKodesh</term>. The sign for this is "Pure and Holy" <note>original Aramaic: *bar qaddish*</note>, meaning he shall "wear purity"—referring to seclusion.

Behold, it is known that the pious man <term>chasid</term> secludes himself with his Creator by rising at midnight, as it is written: "At midnight I will rise to give thanks to You" <note>Psalm 119:62</note>, and as our Sages of blessed memory explained at the beginning of the tractate *Berakhot*, and as the *Zohar* discusses at length. Therefore, he merits a "greater calling" and becomes the fourth leg of the [Divine] Chariot <note>The Chariot usually consists of the Patriarchs; the fourth leg is often King David or the Pious individual</note>. The sign for this is "a furnace of fire, a son of the embers" <note>original: *tanur aphur bar*, likely a mystical mnemonic</note>, hinting that he was in the "embers" <note>ash/humility</note> and rose in the level of "the son" <note>purity/seclusion</note>.

### And this is
The matter of Noah, of whom the Scripture says: "Noah walked with God" <note>Genesis 6:9</note>. This means he walked in places of seclusion where only the Blessed Name was present. For he required a "storm-hedge" <note>original: *sa'ar*, playing on words for storm, hair, or boundary</note> for his inner self; had he walked among the people, it is possible he might have learned from their [evil] deeds. But Abraham knew the great power of "cleaving" <term>deveikut</term> to the Blessed Name and did not need such a hedge. He would walk among the people in order to convert them, as our Sages said: "Abraham would convert the men and Sarah would convert the women." 

However, one who does not possess such great power as Abraham and yet desires seclusion for himself—if a commandment to be performed or a merit to benefit the public presents itself, he should go and attend to that business and then return to his seclusion. In such a case, sin will certainly not come to his hand, since he is occupied with the business of a commandment. But to be among people just for the sake of it, without the business of a commandment, there is reason to fear he might learn from their deeds. 

From this concept, my father and teacher (peace be upon him) explained a passage in the Talmud <note>Sanhedrin 11a</note> regarding Samuel the Small. It says there: "He was worthy of having the Divine Presence rest upon him, but his generation was not worthy of it." This is difficult: if the generation is unworthy, why should the individual be withheld from what he deserves? My father and teacher explained that because his generation was unworthy, they "prevented the qualities" from his body. It is possible that this righteous man had within him some quality that acted as a barrier between him and prophecy—not because of himself, but because of his involvement with his generation. Even though he kept the entire Torah and was a righteous and pious man <note>original: *tzaddik ve-chasid*</note>, this small quality acted as a partition against prophecy. The "call from heaven" that he heard did not come from his own essence, but was affected by his generation. 

This also explains what our Sages said: "A righteous person is seized for the sin of the generation." One might ask: "If Tuvia sinned, should Zigud be lashed?" <note>A Talmudic idiom for unfair punishment</note>. Why should the sinners perish while the righteous man remains? Many interpretations have been said on this, but this is not their place. According to what we have mentioned, the "clarification" of the righteous man's suffering is due to some sin he committed—but the sin was only committed because of the generation, as he learned from their deeds. On his own, he would never have come to this sin. This is the meaning of being "seized for the sin of the generation." Therefore, the level of seclusion is high and exalted. Through this virtue, one will merit many holy and pure levels and will see hidden things.

## The Letter Qof: Holiness [Kedushah]
"And God created man in His image, in the image of God He created him" <note>Genesis 1:27</note>. This refers even to the structure of the body, its limbs, its sinews, and all that is within it—all of them hint at supernal matters. Therefore, "He breathed into him the breath of life." If I were to explain this, many notebooks would not suffice to explain even one-thousandth of what is hinted at in the *Book of Splendor* <note>Zohar</note>, the *Tikkunim*, the *Book of Concealment* <note>Sifra DeTzniuta</note>, the *Elder on Judgments* <note>Saba DeMishpatim</note>, and other places. I have come only to bring down, in a general way, one or two secrets regarding the general structure, though the details are beyond my strength <note>original: *cheili tarli*</note>.

### Behold,
The "Lower Man" <note>humanity</note> exists in the secret of the "Measure of the Stature" <term>Shiur Komah: the mystical concept of the Divine 'body'</term> of the "Great Supernal Man," etc. Take the analogy of curtains, and as they said in the Midrash of Rabbi Nehuniah ben HaKanah <note>The Bahir</note>: To what is this compared? To a man who has arms with which he protects his head. The arms are a metaphor for the Body. This rises to the "White World" <note>Olam HaLavan</note> via the metaphor of a "strand of hair" extending from the head, representing Endurance <term>Netzach</term> and Kindness <term>Chesed</term>. This is the metaphor for the White World above his head [at the moment of] birth, and within it is the secret of generations, the "Hands," and the "Watchers" <note>mystical terms for divine forces</note>. This is the "gleaning" and the sowing of the seed that is drawn from all the limbs and raises his kidneys. The power of man is complete in perfect unity; he "cleaves to his wife and they become one flesh," and He "blessed them and called their name Adam."

The head corresponds to the three highest [emanations], which are considered as one. Kabbalists have written that the brain, the grace [of the face], and the tongue correspond to Crown <term>Keter</term>, Wisdom <term>Chokhmah</term>, and Understanding <term>Binah</term>. They have written at length on this. The language of the book *Avodat HaKodesh* <note>Service of the Holy, by Meir ibn Gabbai</note> is as follows: "The First Chariot, which is a chariot for His knowledge that is excluded from all comprehension, is hinted at in the head according to the secret of the *Sections of the Chariot*. These are Wisdom, Understanding, and Knowledge <term>Chokhmah, Binah, Da'at</term>. In the creation of man, these are the brain, the skull, and the tongue." 

Afterward, in the "Chariot of the Building" <note>the lower seven emanations</note>, corresponding to Greatness and Power, the metaphor of the arms is used. The book *Gate of Heaven* <note>Sha'ar HaShamayim</note> elaborates on the section of "Formation" <term>Yetzirah</term> which the Sages described. In the head, the three highest emanations are hinted at: the membrane of the brain, the bone that covers it, and the skin upon it. This is a hint to the "Supernal Crown" <term>Keter Elyon</term>. Therefore, it has hair to hint at the "Supernal Root"; these are worlds and channels that spread out from the power of the Infinite <term>Ein Sof</term> hidden within it. 

The skull elevates its status and its power to each individual hair of the head; each exists as its own entity with its own nourishment to show the "strength and power" and the supernal influence from which all emanated beings draw—the source of "Infinite Investigations" <note>original: *Ein Sof*</note> that "no eye has seen, O God, beside You" <note>Isaiah 64:3</note>. The Infinite, which is before and outside everything, rises for each [hair] individually, and one does not need its neighbor. This is unique to the hair of the head, unlike other hair on the body. It is known that every single hair is a world unto itself. There is a hidden root that attaches to our skin; as the "life of the hair," everything that enters its source within the skin approaches the reality of the nature of flesh and brain. 

Under the membrane, it divides into three brains to show the three realities within Wisdom <term>Chokhmah</term>: "The Writing," "The Intention," and "Knowledge," as we explained in previous gates. Similarly, the bone that covers the brain has many hollows and many chambers to show hidden worlds, such as the "370 Columns of Light" that are in the Crown <term>Keter</term>, as explained in the Gate of the Qualities of Conduct. From these depend the senses, which are seven: Sight, Hearing, Smell, and Speech, as explained in the *Tikkunim*, though this is not the place for it. 

The masters of anatomy said: "Thirty-two paths extend from the brain to the body," to hint at the "Thirty-Two Paths of Wisdom." Similarly, thirty-two sources flow from the head to the thirty-two teeth that a person has in his mouth, to hint at the thirty-two paths and the thirty-two [mentions of the name] "God" <term>Elohim</term> in the creation story. These thirty-two teeth are divided in a spiritual form: four upper incisors and four lower incisors, and two upper canines and two lower—that is eight. Then five molars on the right and five on the left—that is ten in the upper jaw, and ten corresponding to them in the lower jaw. Here is hinted a great matter: there are eight from this side and eight from that side, with the tongue placed in the middle between the canines and the incisors. Thus we have two fives <note>the letter Hei = 5</note> and a six <note>the letter Vav = 6</note> in the middle to represent the Four-Letter Name <term>Y-H-V-H</term>. The "Yod" is the brain above all, serving and influencing all thirty-two. This is the secret of the Name [Y-H-V-H] rising in the upper teeth, and the [second] H-Y-H below in the lower teeth—meaning male and female, "seven and seven pipes" <note>Zechariah 4:2</note> like this:

### And this is
The Name. And behold, they are the seven branches of the "Upper Menorah" <term>Menorah: the temple candelabrum</term> in the secret of the Giver, and the secret of the ten branches of the "Lower Menorah" which is the Receiver. These are the qualities of Beauty <term>Tiferet</term> and Sovereignty <term>Malkhut</term>, and the generations whose faces turn toward the "Unique Center" that emerges through the power of speech. In this, the reason is established why the children of Israel "shall not speak lies," for the punishment for lying is great, as it turns the "Source of Living Waters" into... <note>sentence continues on next page</note>. He also elaborated on the form of the face and the eyes, and in another place on the appearance of the entire body: the shoulders, the fingers, the feet, the belly, and the intestines. It is a wondrous matter; see there. 

Just as the hand <note>original: *yad*, also meaning power or the number 14</note> is hinted at in the teeth, so it is hinted at in the features of the face: the two eyes are in the form of two "Yods," and the nose is in the form of a "Vav," hinting at the letter "Dalet" and "Dalet" which equals "Chet" <note>8</note>. This would be the secret of "Dalet," which is Mercy <term>Rachamim</term>. But when you look directly, or when two or three [features] are joined, the upper canines are neutralized and only the nose remains—then there is "burning anger" <note>original: *charon af*, literally 'burning of the nose'</note>. If speech is corrupted, God forbid, the "hand" is with you. "And your eyes shall behold your Teacher" <note>Isaiah 30:20</note>. 

Similarly, the "hand" and "hand" <note>14 and 14, making 28</note> are hinted at in the form of the body: The head is the "Yod" <note>10</note>; there are ten fingers of the hands, five against five representing the two "Heis" <note>5 and 5</note>; and the body is like the line of the "Vav" <note>6</note>. # The Gate of Letters

...I hated my lovers. But when the darkness is removed, then the glory of Heaven remains in its place, as does the love of fellow creatures. **Therefore**, a person should see to it that all their actions are for the sake of Heaven, to increase the glory of "The Place" <term>Makom: a traditional name for God, implying He is the 'place' of the world</term>. Let him be good with God and with people, so that the "spirit of the creatures" <note>original: *ruach ha-beriyot*, meaning the general public or society</note> is pleased with him. Do not be misled by a different interpretation: do not desire the counsel of the Evil Inclination, which incites you and flips your perspective according to your own intellect. It might tell you that there is a commandment and a reward in glorifying and beautifying yourself by revealing your wisdom and piety to others so they will love you, so you find favor in their eyes, and so their spirit is pleased with you—for this is merely a branch of arrogance.

Rather, the true test is if a person fears Heaven in secret. If, in the open, he performs the commandments of the Name <note>God</note> and removes all lordship from himself, a person like this—within whom God has placed a "spirit of grace"—even if they do not display outward piety or reveal their private affairs to others, a "thread of grace" <term>chut shel chesed: a divine aura of favor</term> is naturally drawn over them. When the spirit of the creatures is pleased with him, it is a clear sign that the spirit of the Omnipresent is pleased with him. This is the meaning of the verse: "When the Lord is pleased with a man’s ways, He makes even his enemies to be at peace with him."

Sometimes, there are people who are loved by others because they flatter them or provide them with pleasures; such people are hated by God if they do not uphold the Torah and the commandments. This is why the sages were precise in saying, "Anyone with whom the spirit of the creatures is pleased..." and they did not say, "Anyone who is loved by the creatures." Love that depends on a specific thing <note>like a bribe or flattery</note> is nothing. It only counts when the interaction comes from the "inner spirit"—when people are naturally pleased by the man's inner grace without flattery or the hope of receiving greatness from him, but simply because his traits are upright in their eyes and they consider him "good with God and with people." Then, the spirit of the Omnipresent is pleased with him. In any case, in addition to his righteousness and piety toward God, he should see to it that he is pleasant "below" as well, as was said of Abbaye <note>a famous Talmudic sage</note>, for this itself is the will of the Name.

We learned in the Tractate Eduyot, at the end of Chapter 5: "At the time of Akavia ben Mahalalel's death, his son said to him, 'Father, commend me to your colleagues.' He replied, 'I will not commend you.' The son asked, 'Perhaps you have found some wrong in me?' He replied, 'No; your own deeds will bring you near, and your own deeds will distance you.'" **In general**, we learn from this trait the moral rebuke of my father and teacher (peace be upon him) in the testament of *Yesh Nochalin* <term>Yesh Nochalin: an ethical work by Abraham Horowitz, the author's father</term>, who said: "Truly, you must never quarrel with the community—not for money, not for authority, and not for anything in the world. Even if it seems to you that the community is doing you a great injustice, speak your matters before them gently. Let your lips answer, and let your voice not be heard crying out before them in the manner of men of strife and contention. Afterward, whatever decision they make regarding you, do not turn from the word they tell you, right or left." This means that even if their words seem to you as sharp as vinegar in oil, nevertheless, do as they command. For you must consider that they are calling "right" what is truly right, because the spirit of the Lord is upon the heads of the people and its leaders, and He will never forsake His pious ones.

Guard yourselves from oaths and from stumbling. Afterward, one must fear the Holy One, Blessed be He, who provides for every generation and its seekers, every generation and its leaders. Regarding "the one who rises above every head," even the "head of the water-trench" <note>a low-level official</note> is appointed from Heaven. The sign of this is "Help," for the daughter of the many <note>the majority</note> is preferable, and the words of individuals are voided in the presence of the many. This applies even in a dispute for the sake of Heaven, and even if the truth is with the individuals. We find this with Rabbi Eliezer the Great, whom the sages excommunicated because he disagreed with the majority, and they paid no heed to all the signs and wonders he performed before them—such as saying "let this carob tree prove it," or "let the stream of water prove it." Therefore, I command you and warn you with an extra warning to distance yourselves from this thing and anything like it very, very much. These are the words of my father and teacher, may he rest in peace.

## The Letter Tzadi: Modesty (*Tzniut*)

The trait of modesty is a great and wonderful virtue. A person should be modest in all their ways: in their eating and drinking, in their speech and their walking, and in their clothing. He should be modest with his wife; in general, all his affairs should be conducted with modesty and a "shamefaced" quality. For the virtue of shame is great. Rabbi Yose used to pride himself on his modesty, saying that the walls of his house never saw the hem of his shirt; thus he was modest even in his bedchamber, even in the dark.

We are obligated to learn the ways of modesty from our father Abraham. When he went down to Egypt, he said, "Behold, now I know that you are a woman of beautiful appearance." Our sages explained that until that moment, he had not truly "known" her <note>meaning he had not stared at her beauty</note> because of the great modesty of them both. In the Tractate Shabbat, the chapter "With what may a beast go out," our Rabbis taught: "It happened that a man married a woman with a stumped hand, and he did not realize it until the day of her death." Rabbi Kasa said, "How modest this woman was, that her husband did not recognize her defect!" Rabbi Hiyya replied to him, "That is her natural way; rather, see how modest this man was, that he did not recognize his wife's defect!"

Go and learn from the modesty of Joseph the Righteous, as it is said, "And his master's wife cast her eyes upon him..." She raised her eyes to look at him, but he did not raise his eyes to look at her. It is said in the *Aggadah* <term>Aggadah: Jewish homiletic and narrative traditions</term> that an iron band was placed under his neck so that his eyes would be forced to look at her, yet he still did not look, as it is written, "His feet they hurt with fetters; his soul came into iron."

**And all the more so**, a woman is obligated to be exceedingly modest. "All the glory of the king's daughter is within" <note>Psalm 45:14</note>. She should hide and modest herself from every man in the world as much as possible. This matter is severe throughout the generations for daughters: no part of her body, even the smallest amount, should be seen or found or revealed, so that she does not cause any man to stumble by her appearance. See Maimonides (may his memory be a blessing). It says in Tractate Shabbat, "Outward ornaments are counted with inward ornaments," to tell you that one who gazes at a woman's small finger is like one who gazes at her "place of vulnerability" <note>a euphemism for nakedness</note>. One should not even hear her voice, for "a voice in a woman is nakedness," nor see a single hair of her head. The Zohar is very emphatic about the sin of seeing [immodesty]. Even in the innermost chambers, one must be careful. Rabbi Yochanan (?) said in Tractate Yoma: "Kimchit had seven sons, and all of them served in the High Priesthood. The Sages asked her: 'What good deeds do you have in your hand?' She replied, 'The walls of my house never saw the hairs of my head.'"

**And so**, they spoke at great length about modesty in eating and drinking. I will write a bit more on this later in the section on the "Holiness of Eating." Let one be awake and understand the virtue of modesty. For it is not only that one must be modest in the bathroom, etc., for "the whole earth is full of His glory" (as the Targum translates it), and as it is written, "Walk modestly with your God." Even in the "place of the husks" <term>klipot: 'shells' or spiritual forces of impurity</term>, in the filthy place of the bathroom, there are several laws of modesty regarding how a person is obligated to behave, as mentioned in the Talmud and the Codes of Law. One is obligated to be modest at night just as in the day, in the presence of the Lord who sees. A certain story describes a man who descended before Rav Nachman; Rav Nachman said, "This one is modest in his ways." How did Rav Nachman know? Did he enter the bathroom with him to know if he was modest or not? For we have learned: "One is not called 'modest' unless he is modest in the bathroom." The secret of the matter is that he should not give an "opening of the mouth" to the *klipot* that camp there to prosecute him. Therefore, he should clothe himself in the holiness of modesty. By the power of the modesty he practices there, he remains attached to holiness even though he is in a place of impurity. How much more so in pure places! All his affairs should be in modesty, whether revealed or in secret, for everything is revealed before Him, may He be blessed, and "the whole earth is full of His glory."

**They asked a Sage**, "What is modesty?" He replied, "That a person should be ashamed before himself." This matter is hinted at in the words of the Prophet: "He has told you, O man, what is good and what the Lord requires of you: only to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk modestly with your God." It says "with your God" because it is not enough to be modest in front of people, but even in secret, in a place where no one sees. For with the Name, you should be modest in all your senses: touch, taste, smell, hearing, and sight. Keep this rule in your hand: anything that you would not do—for example, if you were standing before a king of flesh and blood and seven elders—do not do it in secret. Except for necessary matters like intimacy and the bathroom, which one must do; even so, let them be done with extra and increased modesty.

**Furthermore**, a great, wonderful, high, and lofty virtue included in the trait of "walking modestly with your God" is the virtue of Seclusion <term>Hitbodedut: spiritual isolation for meditation</term>. A person should hide himself and sit alone within his "four cubits of Law," closed off and sequestered from chance occurrences. He should not "go out"—meaning he should not leave his "House of Holiness"—and he should not mix among people. This is based on what Jeremiah said: "O that I had in the desert a lodging place..." For then a person is saved from all sins that occur between a person and his fellow. He also guards the "Holy of Holies" in his thoughts and actions, and is saved from sin and from vanity. He can then increase in Torah because there are no distractions before him, and he does not learn from the deeds of the generation. He becomes secluded with his Maker; this is "walking modestly with your God," being hidden and closed away with no one but the Name. Even when he leaves his seclusion, he should only go "with your God"—meaning to the Synagogue and the House of Study, which are the House of God. Upon returning from there, he should immediately return to his seclusion.

My father and teacher (may he rest in peace) gave an interpretation of the text regarding a child: While a fetus is in its mother's womb, a lamp burns over its head, and it looks and sees from one end of the world to the other. As soon as it comes out into the air of the world, an angel comes and strikes it on its mouth <note>making it forget the Torah it learned in the womb</note>. So too the child—the youth of Israel whom God loves—as long as he is in the "chamber of his Torah," the "lamp of the commandment and the light of the Torah" are with him. As soon as he goes out into the air of the world, the angel comes—that is the Evil Inclination, the Satan, the Angel of Death, far be it from us—and strikes him on his mouth. The "strike" occurs when he mixes with people and opens his mouth for evil speech, gossip, mockery, and many such things. All the toil of man is for his mouth.

It concludes by framing modesty as an internal state of being alone with God through seclusion (Hitbodedut).</summary>
