It draws heavily from the *Sefer Charedim* (The Book of the Devout) by Rabbi Eleazar Azikri (16th century).</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

And I shall mention the reminders listed in the *Sefer Charedim* <note>A classic 16th-century work on the commandments and ethics</note> which are still customary even now, and I shall add a touch of my own; however, there is much, much more than these.

### Thought in the Mind and the Heart
"You shall have no other gods," "You shall not covet," and "Take care, lest you forget the Lord your God." Our master, Rabbeinu Yonah <note>Rabbi Jonah Gerondi, a 13th-century ethicist</note>, of blessed memory, wrote: everywhere it says "Take care" <note>Hebrew: *Hishamer*</note>, "Lest" <note>Hebrew: *Pen*</note>, or "Do not," it is nothing other than a negative commandment. Behold, we are warned with these prohibitions to remember the Blessed Name at all times. A person is obligated to constantly acquire for their soul the behaviors necessitated by this memory, such as awe, modesty, the refinement of thoughts, and the correction of character traits <term>Middot: internal qualities or ethical virtues</term>, as it is said, "In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified, and shall glory." Until here are his words.

We are also commanded not to forget the standing at Mount Sinai, as it is said, "Take heed to yourself, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget the things which your eyes have seen... the day that you stood before the Lord your God in Horeb." This is also included among the prohibitions. From the language of the Sages <note>literally "the language of the Tosefta"</note> in Tractate [blank], we learn: that we should not forget the deeds of Amalek <note>The biblical arch-enemy of Israel</note>; that we should not forget how we provoked the Blessed Name to anger, as it is said, "Remember, and do not forget, how you provoked the Lord your God to wrath." Included in this prohibition is that one should not forget their own sins. 

Also: not to forget the leprosy of Miriam <note>To remember the punishment for gossip</note> in order to be careful of "evil speech" <term>Loshon Hara: derogatory speech or gossip</term>; not to become arrogant, as it is said, "Lest you eat and are full... and your heart be lifted up"; not to become angry, for one who is angry is like one who worships idols, as it is said, "There shall no strange god be in you"; not to test the Lord; not to take revenge or bear a grudge; and not to follow after idolatry. 

It is written in the Talmud: "You shall not take [the name of the Lord in vain]," which implies one should not "take" (accept) a false report or listen to gossip. "You shall not harden your heart," which is said regarding charity. "Do not seek after your own heart." "You shall keep yourself from every evil thing," meaning one should not have [sinful] thoughts by day that lead to impurity at night. "You shall not be afraid of any man." "You shall not consent to him, nor listen to him, nor shall your eye pity him"—referring to an enticer to idolatry. One must also distance themselves from jealousy, lust, and the pursuit of honor. 

All of these are negative commandments situated in the mind and heart, and there are many more. There are also matters from the "Words of Tradition" <note>The Prophets and Writings</note> and the "Words of the Sages" <note>Rabbinic law</note> that depend on thought and heart: Do not trust in yourself until the day of your death; do not be wise in your own eyes; do not be scornful of any person; do not judge your fellow until you have reached his place; when your enemy falls, do not rejoice; do not make your prayer a fixed routine; do not be like servants who serve the master for the sake of receiving a reward; if you have learned much Torah, do not take credit for yourself; do not rejoice, O Israel, unto exultation; do not despair of retribution; do not worry about tomorrow's trouble, for you do not know what a day may bring. There are many more.

### And There Are
Positive commandments that depend on the mind and heart: to believe with true faith and the Thirteen Principles <note>Maimonides' Thirteen Principles of Faith</note>, and they should be fixed in one's heart; the commandment of love; the commandment of awe; to cleave to Him; to fear the Lord; to love the Lord in order to act according to a world-law established in one's heart. 

When one recites the *Shema* and accepts the Kingdom of Heaven, saying "And you shall love [the Lord your God] with all your heart," they should be prepared to give up themselves and all they possess for the Sanctification of the Name <term>Kiddush HaShem: martyrdom or acting in a way that brings honor to God</term>. As it says in the Zohar: "Service in the heart—this is prayer." 

With intention, the attributes of the Holy One, Blessed be He, should be rooted in one's heart: "Merciful and gracious, long-suffering, etc." One must have "Awe of the Sanctuary," and now, in our sins, since we have no Temple, one should engrave in their heart the awe of the Synagogue. One should not speak any [idle] conversation in the synagogue, even when it is not the time for the *Pesukei D'Zimra* <note>Verses of Praise</note>, the *Shema* and its blessings, or the *Amidah* prayer. 

The virtue of Choice resides in the heart: "And you shall choose life." The virtue of Trust: "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God." "And you shall know this day, and lay it to your heart, that the Lord He is God." Remembering the kindnesses of the Lord: "And you shall remember all the way which the Lord your God led you these forty years." To remember the Exodus from Egypt. Fearing one’s father and mother. Loving your neighbor as yourself. Loving the stranger. "In righteousness shall you judge your fellow." To take to heart every sin of your youth. To take to heart every occurrence, as it is said, "You shall consider in your heart, that, as a man chastens his son, so the Lord your God chastens you." 

Remember and Observe <note>The two aspects of the Sabbath</note>. The commandment of Repentance <term>Teshuvah: literally 'returning' to God</term>, the essence of which is in the heart. "Lay these My words upon your heart," which is the acceptance of the yoke of the commandments. "Circumcise the foreskin of your heart." "And you shall remember all the commandments of the Lord and do them." There are many more. 

There are also matters from the "Words of Tradition" and the Sages: in Tractate *Berakhot*, "A person should always incite the Good Inclination against the Evil Inclination," as it is said, "Tremble, and sin not." A person should always be "cunning in fear" <note>meaning: wise and resourceful in practicing the fear of God</note>. One should be "despised in his own eyes" and "lowly of spirit before every person." To grieve over the destruction of Jerusalem: "If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." Do not be afraid [of God] except through "heaviness of head" <note>serious-mindedness and humility</note>, and not out of laziness or sadness, but out of the joy of a commandment. To rejoice in suffering, as it is said, "Joy to the righteous is to do justice." I shall sing of mercy and justice. Just as one blesses God for the good, so too [for the bad]. 

Deliver to the generation: [unclear phrase regarding a neighbor]. Your fellow's property should be as dear to you as your own; the honor of your fellow like the awe of your teacher; and the awe of your teacher like the awe of Heaven. Be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, and brave as a lion to do the will of your Father in Heaven. Remember two things: know from where you came, where you are going, and before whom you are destined to give an account. Other things: know what is above you—a seeing eye, a hearing ear, and all your deeds are written in a book. Be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and bringing them closer to the Torah. To contemplate the fulfillment of the commandments and the fear of the Lord, and not like those of whom it is said, "Their fear of Me is a commandment of men learned by rote." To be zealous for the fear of the Lord and to covet wisdom and humility. One should look forward to salvation speedily in our days. There are many more things, but a "good heart" is a great rule that includes everything.

### In the Eyes
**Turn from evil:** "Do not seek after your own eyes," meaning one should not gaze at a woman or other forbidden relations. One should not look at idols, as it is written, "Turn not unto idols." 

From the Words of Tradition and the Sages: It is forbidden to gaze even at an unmarried woman, as Job said, "I made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze upon a maiden?"—unless he is looking to see if she is right in his eyes for the purpose of marriage. It is forbidden to look at the colorful garments of a woman when he knows who she is, even if they are spread out on a wall. One should not look at domesticated animals, wild beasts, or birds when they are mating. It is forbidden to look even at the head of one's own [unclear]. It is forbidden to look at a rainbow. It is forbidden to look at the moon <note>specifically during the blessing of the New Moon</note>; so wrote Rabbeinu Meir HaLevi in the name of the Scribes. It is known that it is forbidden to look at the "lifting of the hands" <note>the Priestly Blessing</note> of the *Kohanim*. It is forbidden to look at the face of a wicked person. One does not look at the face of someone who is eating, nor at their portion, so as not to embarrass them (Maimonides, Chapter 7 of the Laws of Blessings). It is forbidden to look [at the Hanukkah lights] for personal use. It is forbidden to read poetic phrases, parables of idle chatter, or words of lust because of the "seat of the scornful" (The Rosh, in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah).

**And do good:** This depends on the eyes: To look at the *Tzitzit* <term>Tzitzit: ritual fringes on a four-cornered garment</term>, as it is written, "And you shall look upon it..." To weep over the death of a virtuous person, as it is said, "And let their brethren, the whole house of Israel, bewail [the burning]."

### In the Ears
**Turn from evil:** Not to listen to an enticer [to idolatry]; not to listen to a false prophet. 

From the Words of Tradition: "You shall not carry a false report," meaning one should not listen to a master of "evil speech" <note>a gossip</note> before his fellow arrives. From the Words of Tradition and the Sages: Our Sages said, "Do not let your ears hear idle things, for they are the first of all the organs to be scorched." 

In the synagogue: A woman's voice is "nakedness" <note>meaning: it is a sensual distraction during prayer or study</note>. Since the destruction of the Temple, it is forbidden to listen to or rejoice in the sound of melody and musical instruments. From the Words of the Sages: When you are in prayer, your eyes should be directed downward and your heart upward. One's eyes should be closed during the time of prayer, as seen in the Zohar. A person must be "lowly of eyes," as it is said, "The lowly of eyes He shall save."

### Do Good
To hear Torah; to hear moral rebuke; to hear the sound of the Shofar; to listen to the judge of those days. One must let his own ears hear all the blessings, and many of them are from the Torah, such as prayer <note>according to some opinions</note>, the Grace after Meals, and the Blessing over the Torah. To incline an ear to the Torah [reading] and the prayer of the Prayer Leader. One should not answer an "orphan Amen" <note>an Amen said without hearing the blessing or knowing which blessing it follows</note>. One must incline an ear to the Reading of the Torah.

### In the Mouth and the Throat
(Since the virtue of man is speech, and he is thus called a "speaking living being," and as the verse says, "And man became a living soul," which the Targum <note>Aramaic translation</note> renders as "a speaking spirit"—therefore, it is fitting to give this its own honor. Because the account is long, it will be included under the letter "S" for Silence <note>Hebrew: *Shetika*</note>. I will mention here only a few words related to the mouth and throat.) 

"You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor." "You shall not revile God." "Do not curse a prince among your people"—you shall not curse a king of Israel, a prince, or a Head of the Yeshiva. There is an additional prohibition against cursing any other Jew. Regarding cursing oneself, the prohibition is doubled in the Torah, as it is written, "Take heed to yourself, and keep your soul diligently" and "Take good heed to your souls," and "Take heed" <note>Hishamer</note> is a negative commandment. It is said in the Zohar that many thousands and myriads of evil angels answer "Amen" after his curse to fulfill it; therefore, every man should be careful. 

"You shall not afflict any widow or fatherless child"—included in this "affliction" is even speaking harshly to them. "You shall not wrong one another," and it is written, "You shall not wrong one another" <note>referring to two different verses</note>. Our Sages explained this as "wronging with words" <term>Ona'at Devarim: causing emotional pain through speech</term>. Where it says "You shall not wrong your brother," we establish that as "monetary wronging" <note>overcharging or fraud</note>. 

I heard in the name of the preacher, our teacher Rabbi David Feivush, of blessed memory, that the words of our Sages are very precise. In one verse it says "his brother" and in the other "his fellow." This is because monetary wronging applies even between a man and his brother, as it says, "Just judgment between a man and his brother and his stranger." Rashi explains "his stranger" even regarding matters of residence or the division of property between brothers. Thus, in monetary matters, there is sometimes wronging even between a man and his brother. But "wronging with words"—that is, words of provocation and belittling—this is not found between a man and his brother, for if his brother is belittled, he himself is also belittled. Therefore, it is written "you shall not wrong your fellow." 

Behold, I have recorded a few things that are under "turning from evil" regarding speech, and they will appear at length under the letter Silence.

### Speaking
Tradition and the Words of the Sages: In the first chapter of Tractate *Nedarim*, it is taught: anyone who does not say a thing in the name of the one who said it violates a prohibition, as it is said, "Do not rob the poor because he is poor." "Go not forth hastily to strive." "Do not answer a fool according to his folly." It is forbidden to interrupt [the study of] the words of the Torah with idle words, as it is written, "The Holy One, Blessed be He, makes the wind"... [text cuts off].

<meta>This page continues the "Gate of the Letters," specifically focusing on the mystical anatomy of the human being as a reflection of the Divine. It connects the physical body to the structure of the Tabernacle, the Menorah, and the 613 commandments. The catchword "And I shall remember" (ואזכור) from the previous page transitions into this systematic comparison.</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

In the likeness of a shadow <note>Hebrew: *Tzel*</note> of that which is above, it hints that everything comes from Him, may He be blessed. Therefore, man exists in the "Supernal Shadow." Behold, the crown <note>The *Atarah*</note> upon the holy covenant <note>A term for the sign of circumcision</note> is like a head and a cantor, the secret of "a crown for the head." The surface of the covenant, which is like a line, is in the likeness of the letter *Vav* (ו). The five toes of the feet correspond to the two letter *Hehs* (ה) <note>Together, *Yod-Heh-Vav-Heh* forms the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter Name of God</note>. These are the secret of the "shadow," as it is written: *He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty* <note>Psalm 91:1. The Hebrew word for shadow, *Tzel* (צל), is numerically 120, but here it is used to link man to the Name *Shaddai* (Almighty)</note>. *Shaddai* (שדי) is the Name used when God said to His world, "Enough!" <note>The Talmud explains *Shaddai* as *She-amar l'olamo dai*—He who said to His world, "Enough!"</note>. Since man is a "microcosm" <term>Olam Katan: "Small World," a philosophical concept that the human body reflects the entire universe</term>, the Name *Shaddai* is hinted within him. How so? Under the nose, the letter **Shin** (ש) is engraved <note>original: <image-desc>calligraphic Hebrew letter Shin (ש) with three distinct decorative points on its heads</image-desc></note>; when the arm is spread out in its width, it is like the letter **Dalet** (ד); and the crown of the covenant is the letter **Yod** (י). These matters were already explained at length above in the introduction.

## The Generations of Man

There it is also explained that the ten fingers of the hands—five corresponding to five—hint at the Ten Sephirot <term>Sephirot: The ten creative powers or attributes of God in Kabbalah</term>. Regarding these, King David said: *When I see Your heavens, the work of Your fingers...* <note>Psalm 8:4</note>. It is also written: *My hand founded the earth, and My right hand spanned the heavens* <note>Isaiah 48:13</note>. The right hand represents the heights, and the left hand encompasses all. There are fourteen joints in the five fingers of each hand: three joints in each finger, except for the thumb which has only two. All of this hints at the "filling" <note>A Kabbalistic method of spelling out the names of letters</note> of the letters of the Divine Name. The right hand corresponds to the letters *Yod* and *Heh*, and the left hand to *Vav* and *Heh*. The "filling" of the letters *Yod* (יו"ד) and *Heh* (ה"א) consists of five letters, like the five fingers of the right hand, and their joints total fourteen, the numerical value of "Hand" <note>Hebrew: *Yad* (יד) = 14</note>. Similarly, the "filling" of *Vav* (וא"ו) and *Heh* (ה"א) corresponds to the five fingers of the left hand, and their joints also total fourteen.

**Furthermore**, the verse *He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty* refers to the Tabernacle and the Temple, which are the image of the "Supernal Man." The Temple and its vessels were all made "by the hand of the Lord," as the lower world was designed to correspond to the upper world. As the Midrash says regarding the Tabernacle and Temple: *Lord, I love the habitation of Your house,* and afterward it says, *the place where Your glory dwells* <note>Psalm 26:8</note>, which refers to the world. Therefore, man, who is called a "microcosm," is also called a "sanctuary," as it is written: *And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them* <note>Exodus 25:8</note>. It does not say "within it" <note>singular</note>, but "among them" <note>plural</note>—meaning within the inner heart of every individual. The heart of man corresponds to the Holy of Holies. The "walls" <note>or "veins/coverings"</note> of the heart have five "eyes" or openings, containing two "pupils" like the two Cherubim. Therefore, a heart that "plots wicked schemes" is like one who brings an idol into the Holy of Holies. The eyes, which see beyond the "four cubits" allotted to a person, are compared to the eyes of Moab, who caused the Cherubim to be removed to the outside. When a person flees from the fence of modesty, they distance themselves from holiness. 

The Menorah <note>The seven-branched candelabrum</note> that was in the Temple to shine before God corresponds to "the soul of man, which is the lamp of the Lord, searching all the inner depths" <note>Proverbs 20:27</note>. First, I will explain how man is depicted in the structure of the Menorah. The Menorah had three projections from each side, with cups on the branches. There were branches of the Menorah on each side, and the upper projections were smaller than those below them. So it is in man: the three projections of the body are the arms, then the two legs (which are smaller in terms of their "projections"), and finally the two ears, which are even smaller. The height of the Menorah was eighteen handbreadths, which is three cubits—exactly the height of an average person. Thus, the physical form of man points to the holiness of the Menorah that stood in the Holy Place of the Tent of Meeting. His internal parts—the heart and its extensions—correspond to the Holy of Holies and the Ark-cover <note>the *Kaporet*</note>. This is why it says, *The soul of man is the lamp of the Lord*. The "mold" of the soul, which is the body, is like the vessel of the Menorah, and then it "searches all the inner depths," which is the Holy of Holies, a chamber within a chamber. Regarding this it is said, *The King has brought me into His chambers* <note>Song of Songs 1:4</note>. This is the hint in the verse: *For the commandment is a lamp, and the Torah is light* <note>Proverbs 6:23</note>. This means the revealed part—the holiness of the body—points to the commandments which a man performs and by which he lives; this is the "lamp of the commandment" located in the Holy Place. "Torah is light" refers to the secret spiritual essence, which is the light of the Torah, corresponding to the Holy of Holies where the Tablets and the Torah scroll were placed. Furthermore, the total structure of man—248 limbs and 365 sinews—corresponds to the 248 positive commandments and 365 negative commandments, as I have elaborated in the introduction.

## The Generations of Man

These correspond to the 613 spiritual "limbs" of the soul, hinted at in the first and last letters of the words *Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah* <note>The three levels of the soul: Vitality, Spirit, and Breath</note>, which total 613. The root of the soul is above in the secret of His Blessed Name, which contains 32 paths of wisdom; together with the letters from the Name of 72, they equal 248. The 365 sinews emerge from the attribute of *Gevurah* <term>Gevurah: Strength or Judgment</term>, as I explained at length in the introduction. From this, the secret of the "stature of man" <term>Shiur Komah: A mystical concept describing the "dimensions" of the Divine manifestation</term> corresponding to the supernal stature becomes clear to you.

**Know** that God has made "one against the other" <note>Ecclesiastes 7:14</note>. Just as there is a stature of holiness on the "Right Side" called the "Supernal Man," so too against it He made a stature on the "Left Side" called the "Man of Belial" <note>A personification of evil/worthlessness</note>, which is like a "monkey in the face of a man." Choice is given to man to lean toward the "scale of merit" or the "scale of guilt." The 248 commandments are the stature of the Supernal Man and the holy limbs. Every commandment contains a secret hint, as explained in the *Tikunim* and the *Raya Mehemna* <note>Sections of the Zohar</note>, for the word "Mitzvah" (Commandment), when transformed through the *Atbash* cipher <note>A system where the first letter of the alphabet is replaced by the last, etc.</note>, becomes the letters of the Name of God (*Y-H-V-H*). Thus, the commandments encompass the entire stature. This is what the Sages said in Tractate Sotah: "Whoever performs one commandment in this world, it precedes him and goes before him," for from that commandment, a complete angel is created with 248 limbs to serve as his advocate. The book *Reishit Chochma* <note>The Beginning of Wisdom, a 16th-century work of Kabbalistic ethics</note> writes that within the first man, Adam, who included all souls, some souls hung from the hair of his head, some from his nose, some from his torso, and some from his feet. Thus, every soul is comprised of 248 limbs. Similarly, every "accuser" created by man's sins takes the power of the 248 limbs and becomes a limb of the stature of Samael <note>The principal angel of evil</note>. This is the meaning of "Do not say I will repay evil" <note>Proverbs 20:22</note>. The Zohar (Parashat Miketz) explains: do not say "I will complete the evil"—meaning Samael—through my sins, by giving him a full stature. One should not labor in theft or sin, for by doing so, one "completes" the Evil Inclination while the Good Inclination is diminished. Therefore, "Wait for the Lord, and He will save you." Thus, the "stature" of evil is completed through many bad deeds. Every single sin is a part of a limb, comprised of 248 parts. This is the secret of what is said in Parashat Kedoshim: anyone who commits a transgression, Heaven forbid, it pushes him down and goes before him to the Day of Judgment. The soul becomes "clothed" in "filthy garments" <note>Zechariah 3:3</note>. This is why the verse says, *You shall be holy, for I am holy* <note>Leviticus 19:2</note>. This implies that a person must sanctify their entire stature from head to toe.

First, this is done in a general way, and then in a specific way. In a general way, as the Sages said: "Learn and collect." For every sense and feeling, the Holy One, blessed be He, gave a command of what to do and what not to do. 
- For the **heart**: "Do not follow your own heart." 
- For the **eyes**: "And after your own eyes." 
- For the **ears**: "Do not bear a false report." 
- For the **mouth**: "You shall not eat any abominable thing." 
- For the **tongue**: "Do not take the Name of the Lord in vain," "Do not swear falsely," and "Do not bear false witness." 
- For the **hands**: "Do not join hands with the wicked." 
- For **prohibited unions**: "Do not commit adultery," "Do not be a harlot." 
- For the **feet**: "Do not walk after other gods." 
These are the prohibitions. As for what *to do*: 
- For the **heart**: "And you shall keep these words upon your heart." 
- For the **eyes**: "Lest you forget the things your eyes have seen." 
- For the **ears**: "Hear, O Israel, the statutes." 
- For the **tongue**: "And you shall teach them diligently to your children." 
- For the **hands**: "You shall open your hand." 
- For **prohibited unions** <note>meaning the sanctification of intimacy</note>: "Be fruitful and multiply," and "Take wives and father children." 
- For the **feet**: "In all the way that the Lord your God commanded you, you shall walk." 

In a specific way, I have already elaborated above that perfection is divided into three parts: 1. Study (Talmud), 2. Action (Ma'aseh), and 3. Character Traits (Middot). I shall now record the perfection of the human stature—how one should be sanctified in these three holinesses.

**Regarding Study (Talmud):** One should enslave their entire stature to the Torah. The wisdom in the brain, which is thought, and the heart should be given over to the Torah to be wise, understanding, and clear. One's 248 limbs should be open to hear the words of Torah. One's eyes should "behold uprightness" within the holy books. One should not remove their ears from hearing the Torah. In the nose, it should be a "sweet savor" <note>metaphorically</note>. One's mouth should speak words of Torah. The throat <note>the *Kaneh*</note> should be the secret of "Acquire <note>*K'neh*</note> wisdom, acquire understanding." The voice should go out from the throat through the mouth to study aloud, as the Sages said: "Do not read 'to those who find them' but 'to those who bring them out with their mouths'." The esophagus <note>the *Veshet*</note>, which is for eating, should fulfill the "way of the Torah": "A morsel of bread with salt you shall eat..." <note>Pirkei Avot 6:4</note>. Then the belly will be clean. The orifices of the body should be kept pure so that one may study Torah in purity. With the hands, one should carry holy books. One's hands should also indicate the "accents" of the Torah <note>the *Ta'amei HaMikra*</note>, the melodies of the Torah, Prophets, and Writings, whether in the vocalization of the book or in the raising of the voice and the sweetness of the melody—the *Pashta*, *Darga*, and *Shofar Mehu pach*. These musical accents should be shown with the hands as was done by those who read the Prophets in the Land of Israel. Also with the hands, one should form the shapes of the complex subjects mentioned in the Talmud, such as in Tractates Eruvin and Sukkah. One's feet should run to the Torah and the House of Study, going "from strength to strength." Thus, one becomes a "chariot" and a full "stature" for the study of Torah.

**Regarding Action (Ma'aseh):** One should "turn from evil and do good" in everything pertaining to every limb, both external and internal, from head to foot, whether from the written Torah or from the tradition of the Sages...

<header>The Gate of the Letters 74</header>

Regarding money worth a *perutah* <note>The smallest denomination of currency in rabbinic law, roughly the value of a grain of silver</note> or more, one who takes it violates the prohibition "You shall not steal." Even for the smallest amount, it is a Torah prohibition. These are his words. It was taught: "You shall not steal" in order to provoke; "You shall not steal" in order to pay back fourfold or fivefold <note>original: *tashlumei daled v'he*. This refers to a person who steals with the intent of being caught so they can "charitably" pay back the fine</note>. One who borrows without the owner's knowledge is called a robber, and a borrower is not permitted to lend the item to another; if he does lend it, he is considered a robber.

<margin>And do good</margin> **And do good**: There are many positive commandments that depend on speech which are clear and well-known. I will mention one thing from the *Book of the Devout* <note>original: *Sefer HaCharedim*, a 16th-century work by Elazar Azikri on the commandments</note>, and these are its words: Prayer is a positive commandment from the Torah, and it is the "Service of the Heart." It is written: *And you shall serve the Lord your God* <note>Exodus 23:25</note>. Since the language of "service" <note>work/labor</note> is used, the Sages learned that a person’s hands during prayer should be placed one over the other upon the heart, like a servant before his master. Our Master Abraham, the son of Maimonides <note>Maimonides' son and successor as leader of Egyptian Jewry</note>, wrote that this applies during the first three and last three blessings of the *Amidah* <note>The standing prayer</note>; however, during the middle blessings, which are requests, one’s hands should be spread out like a beggar. We find this in Abraham’s prayer: *I have lifted my hand to the Lord* <note>Genesis 14:22</note>, which the Targum <note>The Aramaic translation</note> renders as "I have raised my hand in prayer." Similarly, with Moses’ prayer: *I will spread my palms to the Lord*; and when *Moses raised his hand*; and in Solomon’s prayer: *And he spread his palms toward the Heavens*. There is also the commandment of the "Lifting of the Hands" for the Priests to bless the people, where the right hand is raised above the left, and this is correct according to the Kabbalah <note>Jewish mystical tradition</note>.

<margin>Regarding the legs</margin> **Regarding the legs**: Simple prohibitions were said regarding them, known to all, such as not bowing to idols, etc. Also, one must not bow upon a stone floor even to the Name <note>God</note>. If one bows in a "simple" manner <note>meaning full prostration with arms and legs spread out</note>, he receives lashes by Torah law. If it is not "simple," it is forbidden by the decree of the Sages. Therefore, one should spread out mats or types of straw in the synagogue to create a separation between the face of the congregation and the stones. If there are none, he should spread the corner of his *tallit* <note>prayer shawl</note> to make a separation between his face and the stones when bowing. Also forbidden by the Sages regarding the legs is going outside the "Sabbath boundary" <note>The limit one can walk on the Sabbath, usually 2,000 cubits from the city</note> on the Sabbath or Festivals. One should also not take "a large stride" when leaving the synagogue, as it is forbidden. Even without this, they warned against taking a large stride because it takes away one five-hundredth of the light of a person's eyes <note>their eyesight</note>. A large stride on the Sabbath is a severe prohibition by the words of the Scribes <note>the Sages</note> because of the verse: *If you restrain your foot because of the Sabbath...* <note>Isaiah 58:13</note>, meaning your walking on the Sabbath should not be like your walking on a weekday. However, it is permitted to run for the sake of a commandment, even on the Sabbath, as it says: *Let us know, let us run to know the Lord* <note>Hosea 6:3</note>. Examples include running to the synagogue or the House of Study. The question was asked: one who goes from the synagogue to the House of Study, what should he do? Should he run or not? It seems that for the study of Torah it is better, for Torah study is greater than prayer. We learned in the first chapter of *Shabbat* that one does not interrupt Torah for prayer. The Ran <note>Rabbi Nissim of Gerona</note> wrote that this applies even if there is no time left <note>to pray later</note>. Even though it is written in the *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* <note>the Great Book of Commandments</note> that Jonathan <note>unclear reference, likely a printer's error for "They said to him," referring to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai</note> said this only for those like Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his colleagues whose Torah was their sole occupation—whereas people like us *do* interrupt for the Shema and Prayer—this is not because prayer is higher than Torah, but because of our weakness, for we eventually stop anyway; therefore it is proper to interrupt. Furthermore, the holiness of the House of Study is greater than the holiness of the synagogue, as stated in the first chapter of *Megillah*: one may sell a synagogue to buy a House of Study, but not a House of Study to buy a synagogue, for we "elevate in holiness and do not downgrade." There is no reason to forbid running for fear of onlookers who do not know he is running to the House of Study. Evidence can be brought from the language of the Gemara in *Berakhot*: Rabbi Helbo said in the name of Rav Huna, "One who leaves the synagogue should not take a large stride." Abaye said: "We only said this regarding leaving, but regarding entering, it is a commandment to run," as it is said: *Let us run to know the Lord.* This is difficult: what is Abaye coming to teach us? It is obvious since the first statement said "one who leaves." One must explain that Abaye comes to teach us that not only is it *permitted* to run to the synagogue and it is not considered a "large stride" that damages the eyesight, but it is actually a *mitzvah* <note>good deed/commandment</note>. Abaye teaches us: do not interpret "one who leaves should not stride" to mean "but one who enters *may* stride but it isn't a mitzvah"; rather, he teaches that it is a positive act. Some explain: "only regarding leaving" means leaving the synagogue to not return now; but if he leaves to do his business and return immediately, he should hurry and run. Thus he teaches us to run to the House of Study. We have an established rule in *Niddah*: "The Holy One, Blessed be He, hates one who enters his own house suddenly," and how much more so the house of his fellow.

<margin>And do good</margin> **And do good**: Positive commandments depending on the legs include rising and showing honor before one's father and mother with awe and fear; and rising and showing honor before a scholar, even if he is not one's primary teacher; and rising and showing honor before an elderly person—meaning seventy years old—even if he is an unlearned person. See the innovative explanation of the commentators that "legs" includes speaking to such a person in language of honor, lordship, and humility, and bowing the head before him. The law of "standing" is that when the person enters within four cubits <note>about 6-8 feet</note>, one must stand to his full height. One should go with his legs to visit the sick, to accompany the dead, and to escort guests who are departing on a journey. Likewise, the Scribes said it is a mitzvah to walk to be among the first ten in the synagogue. A person is obligated to greet his teacher on a Festival, as it is said: *Why are you going to him today? It is neither the New Moon nor the Sabbath* <note>2 Kings 4:23</note>. From this we learn that on the New Moon and Sabbath, one *must* go to greet their teacher. Regarding a friend returning from a journey, the tractate *Berakhot* says it is a mitzvah to run toward the kings of the nations, so that if one merits the World to Come, he will see the even greater glory of Israel and recognize how great it is.

<margin>And there is</margin> **And there is** a commandment that depends on the mouth, the eyes, and the legs, and that is the Sanctification of the Moon <note>original: *Kiddush Levanah*, the monthly outdoor prayer over the New Moon</note>. Rav Yehuda said: "One who sees the moon in its renewal says: 'Blessed are You, Lord... who by His word [created the heavens]...'" I already wrote above in the name of Rabbi Meir HaLevi that it is forbidden to gaze directly at the moon, and there is a secret <note>Kabbalistic reason</note> to this matter; one only looks at it with a "valid glance" in order to bless, and once he begins the blessing, he does not gaze at it.

<margin>And a custom</margin> **And a custom**: A beautiful custom we practice here in Jerusalem, may it be built and established speedily in our days, is to say a Psalm after the conclusion of the blessing. We say the Psalm of ten "Hallelujahs": *Hallelujah, praise God in His sanctuary...* <note>Psalm 150</note>. This is very correct to awaken the light of the Moon above, which is the Kingdom of the House of David, to which we hint when saying, "David, King of Israel, lives and endures." Afterward, we say the teaching of the school of Rabbi Ishmael: "Had Israel only merited to greet the face of their Father in Heaven once a month [through this blessing], it would be enough for them." Abaye said: "Therefore, we must say it standing." Afterward, the *Kaddish d'Rabbanan* <note>the Scholars' Kaddish</note> is said. How very good and beautiful this matter is, for in the future, the "blemish of the moon" will be removed, and the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and then *Great and sanctified will be His great Name...* and the Name and the Throne will be complete. To those who know the hidden wisdom <note>original: *yodei chen*, Kabbalists</note>, it appears to me that the reason women distance themselves from this commandment—even though it is like other time-bound positive commandments such as the *Shofar* and *Lulav* [which women may perform]—yet we have never seen women performing the Sanctification of the Moon, even though they are careful with all other prayers. This is because the "blemish of the moon" was caused by the first woman, namely the sin of Eve, and they distance themselves out of shame. Even though they found a rectification afterward—for the New Moon was given to them because they did not sin or listen to the Ancient Serpent, who is the Satan and the Evil Inclination—and therefore the New Moon was given to women so they would observe it more than men, as seen in *Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer* and cited in *Tur Orach Chaim* section 417. Nevertheless, woman was the first cause of death <note>original: *hamasiach* - likely meaning "The Destroyer" or death</note> coming to the world, and afterward the men strengthened this [impurity] through the Golden Calf, and we are not yet purified. Sometimes it is diminished and sometimes full. <margin>With the legs</margin> With the legs, one leaps three times and says: "Just as I leap [toward you and cannot touch you]..." I received from my teacher, the pious Gaon, Rabbi S. <note>likely Rabbi Shimon or Shmuel</note>, of blessed memory, to be very careful when leaping not to bend the knees, for then it would look, Heaven forbid, as if he were bowing to the moon. Rather, he should stay on his tiptoes and leap. Evidence can be brought for my teacher's words from the first chapter of *Sanhedrin*: Rabbi Yochanan said, "Whoever sees a rainbow in the clouds should fall on his face," as it says: *Like the appearance of the rainbow... I saw and fell on my face* <note>Ezekiel 1:28</note>. But in the West <note>the Land of Israel</note>, they cursed this practice because it looks like one is bowing to the rainbow. However, he certainly recites the blessing.

<margin>Regarding pleasure</margin> **Regarding pleasure**: There is "turning from evil" and "doing good" from the Torah, the Prophets, and the Scribes. We will elaborate on this later in the Laws of Forbidden Relations and the Holiness of Marriage, and in the holy Laws of Forbidden and Permitted Foods. As I wrote above, even though this depends on a specific organ—namely the mouth and the esophagus—nevertheless, it sustains the entire body. Therefore, I will remember it now.

<margin>The Torah</margin> **The Torah** mentioned regarding forbidden and permitted foods: *Sanctify yourselves and be holy* and *Do not make your souls detestable*. It is explained in the *Zohar* regarding this matter that impure foods—which the Torah [forbids]—an external and impure spirit dwells upon them. Therefore, one who eats those things defiles his soul and shows that he has no holiness or part in the God of Israel. For the speech found in a person's limbs is the essence of the person, and the soul is clothed there; thus, he defiles his own soul and the spirit that dwells within the body, and the spirit of impurity rests upon him, may God save us. The author of *The Beginning of Wisdom* <note>original: *Reshit Chochma*, by Eliyahu de Vidas</note> wrote that one who eats permitted things for the sake of Heaven, the spirit of holiness and purity rests upon him, and the soul enjoys that eating from the side of the holiness within it. This is the meaning of: *The righteous man eats to satisfy his soul* <note>Proverbs 13:25</note>. According to the plain meaning, this is difficult: does the soul need satisfaction? The body is what is hungry! Rather, the matter is that in the eating itself, there is a side of holiness, and from that holiness, the soul derives pleasure. This is explained even more clearly in the name of the Divine Rabbi Isaac Luria <note>original: *Ha-Ari zal*</note>, who explained the verse: *For not by bread alone does man live, but by everything that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord does man live* <note>Deuteronomy 8:3</note>. Philosophers have already investigated the cause of the soul's connection to the body through eating—does the soul eat? Rather, it is a structural necessity...

<meta>This page continues the "Gate of the Letters," transitioning from the laws of physical theft discussed on the previous page to the ethical and spiritual laws governing the use of the senses and limbs: the mouth (speech and food), the nose (smell), and the hands (action and creation).</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

The explanation of a loan from the "Words of the Living God" <note>original: *MD"CH* - likely referring to a specific homiletical work or a name for the Torah</note> that was given on the Tablets: One should not speak during a meal because of the danger <note>Refers to a Talmudic health warning</note>, lest the windpipe <note>original: *kaneh*</note> precede the esophagus <note>original: *weshet*</note>. One should not speak in a washroom because of the danger of the wicked <note>likely referring to spiritual impurities</note>, as they should rest [from speech] there; one requires modesty and silence to be saved from it. One who walks on the road and reviews his studies, but interrupts his study and says: "How beautiful is this plowed field! How beautiful is this tree!"—it is as if he is liable for his own soul <note>A quote from *Pirkei Avot* (Ethics of the Fathers) warning against distracting oneself from Torah study for mundane aesthetics</note>. One does not interrupt between the blessing "He Who Redeemed Israel" and the Silent Prayer <note>The *Amidah*</note>, nor between the head-tefillin and the arm-tefillin, even to answer "Kaddish" or "Kedushah" <note>communal prayers</note>. One should pray in a whisper so that their fellow cannot hear them. Do not despise any person—neither great nor small, neither Gentile nor Jew—rather, keep your eyes lowered to guard yourself from [harming] him, and honor him according to his will. Do not increase conversation with women; the Sages said this even about one’s own wife, and all the more so regarding the wife of his fellow. About one's wife, they said this when she is ritually impure, and all the more so regarding another's wife. A person should never open their mouth to the Accuser <note>original: *Satan*</note>, as it is written: *We would have been almost like Sodom* <note>Isaiah 1:9</note>, and immediately it is written: *Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom* <note>Isaiah 1:10; the Sages teach that by comparing themselves to Sodom, the people invited that label upon themselves</note>. And Jehu son of Nimshi spoke as if he would worship idols, and in the end, he actually worshipped them. Do not quarrel with a person for no reason if they have done you no evil. The Sages said: "Evil refers to nothing but the serpent," meaning one who caused you to sin. But "for no reason" means that if they caused damage to your body or property, do not quarrel with them, for all is vanity. Do not slander a servant to his master. "A generation that curses its father" <note>Proverbs 30:11</note>—the eighth chapter of the tractate *Pesachim* explains this to mean that one should not act as a prosecutor <note>original: *kategor*</note> against Israel even if the generation is wicked. We see this from Joshua, who was punished because he slandered them, even though they had acted wickedly. The wise man Rabbi Abraham HaLevi <note>A 16th-century kabbalist and scholar</note> said that he saw in a manuscript Midrash in the Western Lands <note>North Africa/Morocco</note> that the officer who was punished—who said, "Even if the Lord made windows in the heavens" <note>2 Kings 7:2</note>—did not mean to say God couldn't do it, but rather that this generation was like the generation of the Flood, who deserved to have windows opened in the heavens [for destruction] as it is written: *and the windows of heaven were opened*. He wondered how such an evil generation could merit such a great miracle. Isaiah the Prophet was also punished because he acted as a prosecutor against Israel. Do not say to your neighbor, "Go and return, and tomorrow I will give," when you have it with you. Regarding talk of business on the Sabbath, it is written: *from pursuing your own affairs* <note>Isaiah 58:13</note>, meaning there should be no idle chatter on it. And it says in the Jerusalem Talmud that they barely permitted asking after someone's peace <note>greeting them</note> on the Sabbath; these are the words of the *Tosafot* <note>Medieval commentators</note>. In the *Zohar*, it calls this the "blessing of the frivolous." On the Sabbath, it is forbidden to give a greeting of peace to a wicked person, but for the sake of the "ways of peace," one should intend the greeting for his Creator or change the wording. And you shall say "May you live thus," <note>original: *ko le-chai*</note> and "You are peace." He said to them: A generation that directs its heart to the Living One of the Worlds, etc. It is forbidden to "steal the mind" <note>term: *Gneivat Da'at* — deception or misleading someone</note> of any person, even the mind of a Gentile.

## And Do Good
The positive commandments related to speech will be explained in their proper places, such as "Remember the Sabbath day," which will be explained in the tractate *Shabbat*, and the additions and the *Kiddush* <note>Sanctification of the day over wine</note> which are found in the tractate *Pesachim*. I will mention a few things here. Regarding joy: one must say, "I am a person of judgment," and even if his fellow says otherwise, he should accept it from him. Similarly, regarding a firstborn: if a firstborn of a clean animal is born to him, it is a commandment to sanctify the firstborn according to the explanation in the *Midrash Rabbah*. In the *Book of Ethics*, it says: "Every person who mentions a righteous man and does not bless him violates a positive commandment: *The memory of the righteous is a blessing* <note>Proverbs 10:7</note>. And one who mentions a wicked man and does not curse him, as it says: *but the name of the wicked shall rot*." One should appease the poor with soft words, and "offer your soul to the hungry." To eulogize the destruction of the Temple and the exile of the Divine Presence <note>original: *Shekhinah*</note>, as it says: *If I forget you, O Jerusalem* from the heart, *let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth* if I do not mention you with the mouth. And one should raise his voice, as it says: *The voice of your watchmen—they lift up their voice, together they sing*. As it is found in the *Zohar*: it is forbidden for a person to fill his mouth with laughter until the Temple is rebuilt, as it says: *Then [only then] will our mouths be filled with laughter*. One should not sleep until he engages in Torah, as it says: *and he who is satisfied shall lodge, he shall not be visited by evil* <note>Proverbs 19:23</note>—meaning he should be satisfied with words of Torah. One should sleep while reciting the *Shema* or words of Torah, and should not interrupt with mundane speech, as it says: *Speak in your hearts upon your beds*—which refers to the *Shema*—*and be still, Selah*. See, there are many more, and they will be explained in their places.

## In the Mouth and Shame
"Turn from evil" includes many appropriate things and their ways, such as forbidden foods, and also disgusting things. Also, "danger is more serious than a prohibition." Also regarding "And Do Good," such as "in the evening you shall eat matzah" and the meal for the conclusion of the Sabbath. There is an opinion that continues the narrative in this way. Having seen that the matter of eating is both general and specific—meaning specifically regarding one of the limbs, which is the mouth and shame <note>Euphemism for the reproductive organs</note>—it includes the master of the whole body. Similar to this, the matter of procreation depends specifically on the limb that is the head of the body, and it forms the whole body from which it is born. In my choice, I studied Torah with the great Rabbi, the distinguished and pious Gaon, our teacher Rabbi Shlomo, of blessed memory <note>Referencing the Maharshal, Solomon Luria</note>. When I took leave of him to go to my wedding, I said to him: "Rabbi, bless me and command me what to do." He said to me in these words: "Sanctify yourself in these two matters: in the sanctity of food and in the sanctity of procreation. Be very careful to distance yourself a thousand cubits from anything that touches upon a prohibition. Sanctify yourself greatly in their holiness, for the other commandments of the Torah do not leave a physical impression, but these two things—eating sustains the body, and procreation forms the body and renews it, and this stands forever." These were his words, a holy mouth, and let it be for a life [of the world to come]. Therefore, I chose to mention at the end, after the sanctity of the specific limbs, these two which are general. I will mention them by the names: "Laws of Forbidden and Permitted Foods" and "Laws of Forbidden and Permitted Procreation."

## In the Nose
"You shall not commit adultery" <note>original: *Lo Tinfaf*</note> includes the prohibition of all forbidden sexual relations. But they also interpreted it as an acronym <note>original: *notarikon*</note>: *Lo Tehaneh L'Af*—"Do not give pleasure to the nose." The commentators explain that this means it is forbidden to smell the scent of a married woman's perfume. Similarly, they interpreted other forbidden relations regarding the nose <note>original: *chotem*</note>. There is a hint in the eighth [law] of idolatry: it is forbidden to smell the incense of idolaters from the banned items. It is a commandment to smell spices on the Sabbath <note>referring to the *Havdalah* ceremony or Sabbath pleasure</note>, and "they shall blow through the nostrils" on the Sabbath, as will be explained in tractate *Shabbat*.

## In the Hands
There are many prohibitions regarding the making of an idol or image: not to make them and not to keep them. We learned in the chapter "All Images": One who finds vessels upon which is the form of the sun, the form of the moon, or the form of a dragon, should cast them into the Dead Sea. Maimonides <note>original: *Rambam*</note> wrote in his Commentary on the Mishnah, and these are his words: "The form of the sun and moon does not mean that one finds a simple circle and it is forbidden; for that would be just a sun or a round arch that one calls a moon. Rather, the masters of images, called *talasms* <note>term: *talasms* — Talismans or astrological charms believed to draw down celestial power</note>, attribute forms to the stars, until they say the form of Saturn is a black old man, and a beautiful form is a pretty young girl with gold jewelry, and half of the sun is the form of a crowned king sitting on a chariot with four goats. And when they said 'the form of the sun and moon,' they meant the form attributed to the sun and the form attributed to the moon." These are his words. And so wrote the Rema <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles</note> in his glosses on the *Tur*, section 141. There is a great wonder in this matter, for we find two prohibitions regarding the form of the sun and moon: 1) The law of one who finds them, where it is forbidden to benefit because we fear they were worshipped. 2) The law regarding the maker, where the Torah forbade making the likeness of the "attendants" <note>celestial bodies</note> that are in the heights, whether in the upper dwelling or the lower dwelling. Even if one does not make it for the sake of idolatry, the verse forbade the making itself. If so, where does the talisman explanation fit? Rather, the explanation is that one makes a form that is like the example of the sun and the example of the moon, as the Gentiles do—making a circle like a face and making rays around it, for that is the sun, as the power of the rays are the sparks of the sun. And similarly, they make the form of the moon. For if not, and we explain it as talismans, then it is difficult to understand the question the Talmud asks in the chapter "All Images" regarding the Mishnah: "Rabban Gamaliel had forms of the moon on a tablet on his wall, which he would show to the unlearned and say to them, 'Did you see it like this, or like this?'" Is this permitted? Does it not say: "You shall not make with Me" <note>Exodus 20:23</note>—meaning the likeness of My attendants who serve before Me in the heights, like the sun and the moon? The Talmud answers that it was different for Rabban Gamaliel because it was for instruction. But regardless, on Rabban Gamaliel's tablet, there were no talismans, for there is no "talisman" in the moon above that he would ask "did you see it like this?" Rather, it must be the forms of the moon in their simple sense as they appear. And humans have the power to make forms from types of arches that are like the white arch [of the moon], and the Torah forbade doing so, except it was permitted for Rabban Gamaliel as explained there with three answers. So too regarding idolatry: we say the Gentiles make their likenesses of the sun and moon as they are and worship them. Therefore, one who finds them is forbidden to benefit from them. And so I have seen with my own eyes in the great places of Germany <note>original: *Ashkenaz*</note> that they draw the likeness of the sun and moon, and it is immediately recognizable to the viewer that this is the sun and this is the moon; they are so skilled at making their likenesses. Thus, the Mishnah's "likeness of sun and moon" is meant literally. To say otherwise is far-fetched—that the Tanna <note>Mishnah sage</note> spoke generally but meant talismans. Even though I am not worthy to disagree even with the smallest of the students of Maimonides, nevertheless, it is proper to be concerned for my words as well. But in any case, one who finds a talisman is certainly forbidden, for it is clearly an idol. One is also forbidden to make a protruding form of a human. There is a dispute among the Deciders <note>original: *Poskim*</note> whether the prohibition is specifically a complete form with all limbs, or even just the form of a head. The *Shulchan Aruch* (section 141) does not decide clearly, but writes in the name of "some who say" that only a complete form is forbidden. But the Rema decides and writes that such is the custom. Nevertheless, it seems to me a proper thing not to follow this [leniency], since the *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* <note>original: *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* (SMG) - a 13th-century halakhic work</note> quotes his teacher that one should not be lenient in this. Regarding this, it is said: "Sanctify yourself [by abstaining from that which is permitted]." "You shall not steal, and you shall not deal falsely, and you shall not lie to one another"—stealing money is a prohibition regarding a Gentile just as it is for a Jew. And even "stealing the mind" <note>deception</note> is forbidden toward a Gentile as it is toward a Jew, as found in the third chapter of *Zevachim* <note>actually *Chullin* 94a</note>. In the book *Levush* <note>Rabbi Mordecai Jaffe</note>, section 155, it says as follows: There is a reason, even though it is written "to one another" <note>original: *be-amito*—usually meaning "your fellow Jew"*</note>. "You shall not steal" does not rely on "to one another" in the flow of the language; for if so, it should have said "from one another." Furthermore, the cantillation marks <note>original: *ginun t'vir*—the *tevir* mark</note> separate them, as we say in tractate *Nedarim*: "the placement of the logic... these are the divisions of the cantillation marks." This implies the cantillation marks are from the Torah. Therefore, anyone who steals money...

# The Gate of the Letters

## The Spleen
In a case where a puncture was found in its thick head, in the thin area where the membranes are—for even in the edge of the spleen that is thin and thick, it has a fatty layer at its edge that surrounds it at its thin head—whether it is red like a beet or like a thin rod <note>original: *kolsha*</note>, this question has come before me several times. I have deliberated with the masters of the law after reviewing all the decisors, and we found no explicit permission [to eat it]. On the contrary, the language of the *Tur* <note>The *Arba'ah Turim*, a foundational code of Jewish law</note> tends toward declaring it unfit <term>treif|unfit for consumption according to Jewish dietary law</term>, as he wrote in section 43: "If the spleen is removed, it is kosher, but if it is punctured, there is a distinction between its first head and its counterpart, for the spleen's first head is thick, etc." From this, it appears there is no distinction except between one head and the other; however, regarding the first head itself, there is no distinction between its thin part and its fatty part. If it were true that any puncture in the thin part—wherever it may be—is kosher, why did he write that regarding a puncture there is a distinction specifically between one head and the other? Even in the first head, there is a difference between its fatty part and the thin part within it! Therefore, who has seen this and can testify? Only one whose heart emboldens him would permit it. Indeed, I found in a new responsa <note>A written legal decision</note> that ruled this way, and wrote at the end: "In conclusion, here in Lifenshto <note>Likely a place name, possibly Liepstadt or similar</note> and throughout the region of our Master <note>referring to the Rema, Rabbi Moses Isserles</term>, the custom is to declare it unfit wherever the puncture is on the thick side, making no distinction at all for any thinness within it; but on the thin side, we declare it kosher along that entire side."

## Now
I shall record some of the differences between the later Geniuses <term>Geonim Batrai|Great rabbinic authorities of the early modern period</term>: the Maharshal <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria, 1510–1573</note>, the Maharam, the Mahara, and the Maharam, may their memory be a blessing. I will not record instances where the Maharshal permits and the Rema forbids, for there is no practical outcome from this, as we follow the rulings of our Master [the Rema] in this generation, and who would be so reckless as to be lenient for themselves while being strict for others? However, I will record a few places where the Maharshal is strict; even one who is normally lenient and follows the Rema should personally be strict like the Maharshal, for in most cases his reasoning and logic are sound.

**He wrote** in *Torat Chattat* <note>The Rema's book on dietary laws</note> Rule 1, Section 1: Meat that was not rinsed a final time [after salting] and was cooked: if there is sixty times the volume <note>The standard ratio for neutralizing a prohibited substance</note> in the pot against the blood and salt upon it, everything is permitted. The Maharshal forbids that specific piece of meat.

**Rule 2:** Meat that was rinsed but not salted and then cooked: one requires sixty times the volume against the entire piece, and that piece is forbidden. But if it is a time of great need or involves a significant financial loss, one may permit it. The Maharshal forbids it.

**Rule 3:** Meat that sat for three days without rinsing and salting is forbidden unless there is sixty times the volume in the water against it. But if there is sixty, we are lenient even regarding that piece. The Maharshal forbids it.

**Rule 4:** Meat that sat for three days without rinsing and salting and was then roasted and cooked: in the case of roasting, it is permitted, but it is forbidden to cook it after roasting. If one cooked it after the fact <term>bedi'avad|an action already performed</term>, it is permitted. The Maharshal made no distinction and forbade it entirely.

**Rule 5:** A piece of meat that was salted but was not rinsed beforehand is forbidden even after the fact, even for roasting. Even if it is a time of great need or significant financial loss, one should be lenient. The Maharshal, may his memory be a blessing, made no distinction and forbade it entirely.

**Rule 6:** He brought the opinion of the Maharshal that the principle "as it [the meat] expels [blood], it does not absorb [it]" <note>original: *agav d'palit*</note> only applies if it was salted near other meat. But if it fell into the brine <term>tzir|the salty liquid extracted from meat during salting</term> or the brine fell on it, it is forbidden immediately after the duration of the salting process. The author [the Rema] disagrees and holds that they are the same whether it was salted near meat or fell into brine. Afterward, the author wrote: "However, to be strict..." until "even though..." and these are his words in *Amudei Shlomo*: "What I wrote is the opinion of the Rema, that by the letter of the law one need not be strict, yet in a place of need one should be lenient as written in the sections. But the Maharshal wrote that by the letter of the law it is forbidden, so do not pay attention to what is written in *Torat Chattat*." End of quote.

**See there:** He wrote in the Glosses that in a case of significant loss or for the sake of a commandment meal <term>seudat mitzvah|a celebratory feast for a religious occasion</term>, we say that brine does not flow until after the duration of salting and is not considered "boiling" and thus does not forbid. But if it is not for a commandment or a significant loss, even the brine that comes out of the meat after its salting period is considered boiling and forbids if it falls on meat or if meat falls into it. It must be said that it only forbids to the depth of a peel <term>k'dei klipah|a thin outer layer</term>, for in the glosses of section 6 and in *Torat Chattat*, he compares it to meat that was salted and brine was found on it later, and he permits it with peeling, as will be explained later in Section 10. And this is the law here. End of quote. Regarding the words of *Torat Chattat*, the Maharshal wrote: "In my books, I have written that one should not rely on this even in a time of great need." And regarding the Rema's ruling that it only forbids a peel's depth—bringing proof from meat salted and then found with brine—the Maharshal ruled that peeling is not enough for the part that was inside the brine.

**Rule 12:** If one salted even in a perforated vessel, it is forbidden to eat boiling hot food in it at the outset; after the fact, it is permitted even in an earthenware vessel. The Maharshal ruled that if it is forbidden, it implies it is forbidden even after the fact.

**See there:** The *Agur* wrote that specifically boiling food is forbidden to eat from it, but it is permitted to return and salt in it, etc. So wrote the *Bet Yosef*. He also wrote that if it is not perforated, it is permitted to salt meat in it that has already stayed the duration of salting and has been rinsed like water according to the law. Thus it seems to me that this is only when one does not want to leave it there a whole day. But if one wants to leave it there a whole day, even if it isn't "salting," it is considered "soaking is like cooking" <term>kavush kemevushal|the principle that items soaked for 24 hours are legally considered cooked together</term>, and it is considered soaked in a forbidden vessel.

**Rule 14:** In *Sha'arei Dura*: Meat that stayed the duration of salting in a perforated vessel and was then moved to a non-perforated vessel and brine was found, the custom is to permit it via peeling. This is the custom. End of quote. The Maharshal ruled that the action follows the vessel, and peeling does not help, just like meat found inside brine is not permitted with peeling except for what is above and outside the brine.

**Rule 15:** It is written in the *Agur* that it is forbidden to use a vessel that one soaks [meat] in, even if one only soaked in it for one hour, for we fear that blood might still be stuck to it. However, after the fact, it is permitted because the rinsing is valid. End of quote. Even if one did not soak in it, etc., because we fear. But in a perforated vessel that was used for salting, it is permitted to salt meat in it, for "salting" is not relevant here. Some say even a vessel used for soaking, if it was washed well so that no blood is stuck to it, it is permitted to salt kosher meat in it. This is specifically if one does not intend to leave the kosher meat there for a whole day; but if one wants to leave it there a whole day, it is forbidden due to "soaking."

**Rule 17:** Cold meat in a cold non-kosher vessel requires rinsing. The Maharshal wrote: "Since it requires rinsing... it seems to me that travelers do not act correctly when they place cooked fish in non-kosher bowls... and all the more so the gherkins <note>original: *kishuvin*</note> that are called *ugerkes* in the language of the land <note>Yiddish/German: *Gurken*</note>, which are forbidden to eat in a non-kosher bowl, and especially their brine. Likewise, salted cabbage and the turnip-water which is liquid—even if not salted—it is forbidden, and all the more so if salted. He who comes to be purified from Heaven, they shall assist him." End of quote.

**Rule 18:** The Rashba permitted salting meat in a vessel [previously used for] Gentile wine. It appears this is also when one does not intend to leave it there for a whole day, for otherwise, "soaking is like cooking."

**Rule 4:** He ruled there regarding salted fish bought from Gentiles: if one sees non-kosher fish among them, it is forbidden to buy from them even if they are not soaking together. But if one already bought them, they are permitted, for a doubt regarding Rabbinic law is ruled leniently. We say that perhaps they were mixed together only after they had finished expelling [their juices]. But if they are fatty, then it is a doubt regarding Torah law and they are forbidden. If it is a doubt whether they are fatty or not, they are permitted because it is a "double doubt" <term>s'fek s'feka|a legal situation where two distinct uncertainties exist, often leading to a lenient ruling</term>: perhaps they were mixed after expelling juices, and perhaps they aren't fatty. However, according to the Maharshal in his book, section 78, there is no permission to buy salted fish from Gentiles, and even if already bought, they are forbidden. For this is not called a doubt—rather, the fish are pressed and absorb each other's salt and juices. This is forbidden unless one sees the non-kosher and kosher fish lying on the table salted without touching each other; then it may be permitted after the fact. Even so, "cursed be the man" who buys them at the outset, because fish are prone to this. According to the Maharshal, even in this law where there is a doubt about a doubt regarding fatness, we do not go for the lenient ruling of a double doubt; to the Maharshal, it is only a single doubt, and thus it remains a doubt regarding Torah law [and is forbidden].

**See there:** The *Agur* wrote: However, if there were sixty parts of the kosher fish against the non-kosher, one may buy them at the outset, and we do not worry about the prohibition that perhaps the non-kosher were more numerous [before]. End of quote. The Maharshal made a distinction in his book: specifically if it is lying in the middle, then certainly it was salted with them, and if there is sixty, they are permitted. The kosher fish, excluding a peel's depth from each one—and if there is sixty in the peels of all of them against the non-kosher—the peels are also permitted. But if the non-kosher is not found in the middle, all the fish touching it are forbidden at the outset, for perhaps he placed them together after the salting period, at which point the salt has the power to diffuse the prohibition through them all. After the fact, they are permitted with peeling if there is sixty, since it is a doubt regarding Rabbinic law.

<summary>This page discusses complex laws regarding the kashrut of the spleen and provides a detailed comparison of ritual stringencies between the Rema and the Maharshal regarding meat salting and fish. The author emphasizes personal stringency in following the Maharshal's stricter rulings even when the common practice follows the Rema.</summary>
