<meta>This page continues the "Gate of the Letters," specifically focusing on the spiritual and legal dimensions of the letter Tet (ט), which the author connects to the concept of Tov (Goodness) and the purity of food. It shifts from technical discussions of the spleen to the broader philosophy of dietary holiness and specific controversies in ritual slaughter.</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

But the Rabbi <note>referring to the Arizal, a foundational 16th-century Kabbalist</note> of blessed memory, mentioned above, said: there is nothing in existence that does not contain an element of holiness. As our Sages of blessed memory said: "There is not a single blade of grass below that does not have a constellation <note>original: *mazal*</note> above that strikes it and says to it, 'Grow!'" The meaning behind this is the power of spiritual influence flowing from above. As it is written: "The soul of man is the lamp of the Lord" and "I will answer the heavens and they shall answer the earth." Thus, every food in the world is a mixture of "body" and "soul." The visible food is the "body," and the holiness of the spiritual influence from on high—which draws into it, telling it to grow—is its "soul." When a person eats, the body and soul are kept joined through that act of eating; for the person's soul derives pleasure from the "soul" of the food, and the physical body from the "body" of the food. 

This is the meaning of the verse: "Not by bread alone [does man live]"—meaning, man cannot exist on the physical bread alone which is visible to the body. For if that were so, what benefit would the soul receive? Rather, "but by everything that comes from the mouth of the Lord"—meaning that within the source of the bread is the "mouth of the Lord," which is the spiritual influence drawn into it, telling it to emerge and grow, through which "man lives." This interpretation is a wondrous one. 

The author of the *Reshit Chochma* <note>An influential 16th-century ethical work by Elijah de Vidas</note> wrote the following: "Therefore, it is proper for a man to be stringent with himself regarding his own food, ensuring it contains no side of prohibition at all. For behold, Ezekiel the Prophet would praise himself that he never ate from an animal about which a scholar had to give a ruling <note>original: *horeh bah chacham*</note>, even if it was eventually permitted, simply because a doubt regarding its status had arisen." This is as our Sages said in the chapter *Elu Terefot* regarding the verse "No offensive flesh entered my mouth." How much more so, then, if there is an actual side of prohibition in the food itself, that one should keep far from it! Indeed, there are many matters where a dispute has fallen among the later legal decisors as to whose ruling the law follows—one forbids while the other permits. Certainly, Ezekiel the Prophet (peace be upon him) would not have eaten according to the one who permits, for the one who forbids views that piece of meat as prohibited, which is a weightier matter than a simple scholarly inquiry. The author of *Duties of the Heart* <note>original: *Chovot HaLevavot*</note> wrote that the pious would avoid seventy gates of the permitted out of fear of entering a single gate of the prohibited. Thus far are the words of the *Reshit Chochma*. See how far the holiness of food extends! Now, I have seen "men of ascent" <note>spiritually elite individuals</note>, and they are few—perhaps not even two in a generation—who will not eat anything subject to a legal dispute, even if the world acts according to the lenient ruling and the law was decided as such.

**M**y sons, the children of Israel (may their Rock and Redeemer preserve them), I will record for you several matters to warn you to be stringent in areas where the general public is not careful. Do not "follow the majority to do evil," since these matters are based on the core law, as will be explained.

**Furthermore**, I am informing you: Behold our great masters among the later authorities, the Genius <term>Gaon|an eminent rabbinic scholar</term> Maharal <note>Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague</note> of blessed memory, the Gaon Maharash <note>Rabbi Shmuel Eidels, the Maharsha</note> of blessed memory, and the Maharal <note>likely a reference to another contemporary authority</note> of blessed memory—each of them composed and organized works on the Laws of the Forbidden and Permitted <note>original: *Issur v'Heter*</note>. They wrote that they occasionally disagree. It has already become the established custom to follow the rulings of the Gaon Rema <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles, whose glosses on the Shulchan Aruch are the standard for Ashkenazi Jews</note> of blessed memory to be lenient in the end, and the law was decided according to him. By Heaven's grace, he merited this, much like the law follows the House of Hillel even though the House of Shammai were sharper of mind. 

In a case such as this, I must inform you that the Gaon Maharshal <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria, a contemporary and critic of the Rema</note> of blessed memory is considered a "later authority" <note>original: *batrai*</note> regarding his composition on the Laws of the Forbidden and Permitted, for he wrote it after the Rema had already composed his work *Torat Chatat*. This was the sequence of events: the students of the Gaon Maharshal (peace be upon him) transcribed his rulings and brought them to the Rema while he was composing *Torat Chatat*. Therefore, the Rema several times cites the Maharshal's prohibitions, and the Maharshal responds to him. Afterward, the *Torat Chatat* reached the hands of the Gaon Maharshal, and he wrote his own work based on it. Thus, the Maharshal is the later authority. However, as I have said, the custom has already spread throughout the Jewish lands—in the Kingdom of Poland, Bohemia, Moravia, and Germany—to rule like the Gaon Rema. Nevertheless, it is proper for every man to be "a prince in his own home," to sanctify himself and be stringent upon himself regarding what this authority or that authority forbids. Even if the later authority is lenient in a public ruling based on custom, one should be strict for oneself. Certainly, one should not be lenient for oneself while being strict for others. I will record several instances, and let the wise man hear and increase his learning.

**And behold**, the acts of piety that are required by the core law are these: First and foremost is a great matter regarding the checking of the slaughtering knife <term>shechita|ritual slaughter</term>. Rabbenu Yonah wrote in his *Gates of Repentance* <note>original: *Shaarei Teshuva*</note>, as cited in the *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo's commentary on the Tur</note> at the end of section 18: "It shall be pleasant for those who rebuke, and a blessing of good shall come upon them; let them be meticulous regarding the laws of slaughter and its inspections. They should choose a slaughterer who fears sin, for a great multitude of Israel depends on him for the commandments of slaughter and inspection." Truly, although most people involved in slaughter are experts, there are places where oversight is lacking and there is no rebuke; there, many people involved in slaughter are not experts. Furthermore, we have seen in some scandals that many experts are far from the fear of sin. One who is not fearful in his heart will not understand how to be precise in checking the knife, for one must focus his heart intensely during the check. Do you not see that a person may check a knife two or three times and not feel a fine nick <note>original: *pegimah*</note>, only to find it afterward because his heart finally understood through the sense of touch? Without the intention of the heart and the fear of God, a man will fail in checking the signs and other matters. Thus far are his words. 

And I, the man, add to this words that should be sealed upon the heart: regarding the fact that people eat meat brought from the settlements and the outskirts of the city. Even if a slaughterer was appointed there whom the residents accepted, sometimes they accept anyone they choose, even if he is not exceptionally pious or of great faith. Even in a great city, a "mother city in Israel," it is proper for every God-fearing person to tell the head of the Rabbinical Court to investigate and inquire: how is the knife of the local slaughterer? Even if he is God-fearing, in addition to piety, he needs exceptional skill. I saw one of the true ascetics who would not eat meat unless he slaughtered it himself. He once came to a city that was great before God, conducted with piety and holiness, and the scholars of the city asked him why he would not eat the meat slaughtered by their expert slaughterer. He went once to the slaughterer's knife, checked it, and said to the slaughterer: "Tell me, how do you perceive this knife?" The slaughterer said: "It is kosher." He told the slaughterer: "Check it again." He checked it again and said it was kosher. The ascetic then showed it to the scholars and said: "See, there is a nick right here." They investigated, and indeed it was so, and the scholars of the city were amazed. See how far this matter reaches! One must be exceptional in the fear of Heaven and exceptional in his sense of touch. It was not for nothing that the Sages of the Talmud had the custom of checking the knife themselves and with their own honor, not trusting any butcher even if he were God-fearing. For the checking of the knife requires great composure and fear of Heaven. And behold, when we merited (may we not be put to shame) to come to Jerusalem, the Holy City (may it be rebuilt and established speedily in our days), I saw the conduct of knife checking here with great awe, and it is shown to the scholars of the city. Such is the custom in this entire kingdom; my eyes saw it and my heart rejoiced.

**Second**, regarding the "massaging of an adhesion" <term>sircha|an abnormal adhesion on the lung</term>: According to our custom—due to our many sins which are far from the path of the Torah—a custom has spread in many lands and communities to rub and squeeze even an adhesion that is not in its natural order (which is considered a terminal defect <term>terefah|unfit</term> mentioned in the Talmud). The Rashba <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Aderet</note> already wrote that those who do this are as if they are feeding *terefah* meat to Israel. Rabbenu Yonah and Rabbenu Tam wrote similarly, as did the great later authorities. Although the Rema <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles</note> wrote in the *Shulchan Aruch* (Yoreh Deah, section 39) in a way that implies it is not proper to do so, he nevertheless did not protest it, as was his way—not to overturn an established custom whenever it was possible to uphold it. However, the "zeal of the Lord of Hosts" should ensure that this evil custom is not listened to. Even regarding the "shaking of the lung" permitted by Mar Jacob Gaon, his own teacher disagreed with him. And you, my sons, I command you: do not eat meat that was declared kosher through the power of "massaging" in a place where the adhesion was legally a terminal defect. Do not buy meat from a butcher until you have inquired about this. All the residents of the Land of Israel and all the Jewish dispersions living in the Ottoman Empire declare such cases *terefah*.

**Regarding a gall bladder adhesion:** The Gaon Rema wrote in his *Torat Chatat* (Rule 8, end of chapter 8): "The glosses of the *Mordechai* <note>Rabbi Mordechai ben Hillel</note> wrote that there is a doubt if the gall bladder is adhered to another place, whether it is *terefah*." But in the *Mordechai* (Chapter *Elu Terefot*), he ruled it permitted. The same was written in the "Long" version of the *Issur v'Heter* (Rule 52). This is also the opinion of the *Beit Yosef* regarding an adhesion on the liver's lobe—that we do not declare it *terefah* unless it is on the lung. Maharish also wrote in his inspections that such a liver adhesion is kosher. It seems the same would apply to the gall bladder, for they share the same reasoning. This is contrary to the words of the *Terumat HaDeshen* <note>Rabbi Israel Isserlein</note> who wrote (Section 163) that any place where a puncture disqualifies the animal, an adhesion also disqualifies it. It seems to me that the Gaon Rema did not see the full words of the *Terumat HaDeshen*, for there he refuted with good reason the proof from the liver lobe. Furthermore, what the Gaon wrote—that the *Mordechai* ruled it permitted—is not the case. The *Mordechai* only wrote that regarding the liver lobe. On the contrary, the *Terumat HaDeshen* proves from the *Mordechai* that an adhesion is *terefah* in any place where a puncture is *terefah*. This is simple in my eyes—that the Gaon Rema did not see the *Terumat HaDeshen* inside the book itself, but only saw the beginning of his words as cited in the *Knesset HaGedolah*. Had he read the whole response, he would have seen that there is no proof from the liver lobe. Therefore, one should not permit what was written there in the *Orchot Chaim* to permit it—Heaven forbid one should act so! For all the Rema's proofs are refuted. I saw another book of Responsa called *Sefer Mishpatei Shmuel* which ruled it *terefah*, according to my words and the Gaon in the *Ma'or*.

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual necessity of dietary stringency, arguing that food contains a "soul" of holiness. It covers specific controversies in Jewish law, particularly focusing on the integrity of slaughterers, the checking of knives, and disagreements between the Rema and Maharshal regarding lung and gall bladder adhesions.</summary>

# The Gate of the Letters

...that is the "head of the Kaf" <note>The shape of the Hebrew letter Kaf resembles a curved palm or a vessel</note>, and in any case, regarding the residual fat on a knife, we do not measure it against the handle. End of quote.

**See there** <note>Hebrew: *Ayin Sham*, a standard cross-reference</note> where he brings the words of the *Beit Yosef* <note>The foundational 16th-century legal code by Joseph Karo</note>, who wrote in the name of the *Shibbolei HaLeket* regarding lemons of "Nahripi Romi" <note>Likely a specific geographic variety or trade-name for lemons</note> that even though they were cut with a non-kosher knife, since their sharp juices are abundant and many of them were cut with a single knife, the absorbed flavor of the forbidden fat on the knife is nullified among them. While the first lemon cut should technically be forbidden, since we cannot identify which one it was, it is nullified by the majority of the others cut afterward with that same knife. Thus he wrote. And so wrote the *Arukh* in Section 38. End of quote. 

I found it written concerning this: It is difficult to understand why the author brings this ruling of the *Beit Yosef*—that the flavor of the knife is nullified—as if it were the final law. This is not so. It makes sense according to the *Beit Yosef* because he ruled like Rabbi Ephraim, who held that we do not say "the piece itself becomes forbidden" <term>Chaticha Na’asit Neveilah: the principle that a permitted food item entirely transforms into a forbidden substance once it absorbs a prohibited flavor</term> except in the case of meat and milk. Therefore, if one cut sharp vegetables with a non-kosher knife, one only needs to nullify the specific flavor absorbed in the vegetable. However, we follow the strict Torah law that "the piece itself becomes forbidden" regarding all prohibitions in the Torah. Therefore, if one cut a sharp vegetable with a non-kosher knife, we require sixty times the volume of the entire vegetable <note>The standard ratio for nullifying forbidden flavors in Jewish law is 1:60</note>. The *Beit Yosef* himself wrote this in Section 96. But if one cut with a non-kosher knife, one needs sixty against the entire radish because its sharp smell makes it like a Torah-level prohibition. 

One can further bring proof from the *Tur* <note>An early 14th-century legal code</note> in the Laws of Passover regarding wheat stalks that were split during the rest of the year <note>referring to wheat that might have come into contact with leaven</note>... and nullification does not apply because we measure by the entire knife's capacity, and if so, the stalks become entirely leavened <note>Hebrew: *Chametz*</note>. End of quote. Even though this ruling is a wonder in my eyes and I cannot fully reconcile it—for why would the stalks become entirely leavened? We only say "the piece itself becomes forbidden" when it absorbs something prohibited, but when it absorbs something permitted—leaven during the year is permitted—the rule should not apply. It is like a piece of vegetable that absorbed meat and was then cooked in milk; if we know how much meat was absorbed in the onion or vegetable, we do not need sixty times the whole vegetable, only sixty against the absorbed meat, because the vegetable itself hasn't become a "forbidden piece" yet while it is still entirely permitted. Therefore, I wonder at the *Tur* as to why the stalks become entirely leavened. I will not settle this matter now. Regardless, in a case of actual prohibition, as here with the lemons cut by a non-kosher knife, the whole piece becomes forbidden.

**See there** regarding the law of hot meat cut with a "day-old" dairy knife <note>A knife used for dairy within the last 24 hours</note>, which requires sixty times the volume of the knife's absorbed flavor. It seems to me this only applies if he cut the meat while it was still on the fire, or just removed from the fire but still in the "first vessel" <term>Kli Rishon: the original pot in which food was cooked, which retains the highest heat and legal power to transfer flavors</term>. But if he already placed it in a "second vessel," the intensity of its heat has passed, and it only requires a thin peeling of the surface. This implies that even if the meat is as hot as "the hand recoils from it" <term>Yad Soledet Bo: the halakhic threshold of heat (approx. 110-120°F) at which cooking and flavor transfer occur</term>, once it is out of the fire, it is treated more leniently. However, the *Maharshal* <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria, a 16th-century authority known for his rigorous analysis</note> disagrees in his work *Issur V’Heiter*. He says the concept of a "second vessel" only applies to soup or liquid which cools quickly, but not to a "solid mass" <term>Gush: a solid hot item like meat or fish, which retains its internal heat even in a second vessel</term>. As long as the hand recoils from it, it retains its heat and transfers flavor effectively. Therefore, it seems that if meat or fish were moved from the pot to a bowl, as long as they are still scalding, they are treated as a "first vessel" regarding the laws of meat and milk.

### Rule 62
Regarding the law of blood in eggs: if there is a doubt whether the blood was on the white or the yolk, it is a "Rabbinic doubt" and we are lenient, because we hold that blood in eggs is only a Rabbinic prohibition. However, the *Maharshal* wrote that he found in the *Tosafot* <note>Medieval commentaries on the Talmud</note> that there is a view that blood in eggs is a Torah-level prohibition. Thus I found it, and it seems to be the core view since the great sages were in doubt whether it is from the Torah. End of quote.

### Rule 70
Regarding the law of one who slaughters a hen and finds fully formed eggs inside: it is customary to salt them even if the outer shell is hard, but one must not salt them together with meat. So wrote the *Maharshal*. He wrote that if one salted them with meat, the egg becomes "forbidden" <note>like a carcass</note>, and if it was then cooked with other eggs, they would require sixty times its volume to be permitted.

**See there** regarding a case where the yolk of such an egg got mixed with milk; one should be strict. Even though it appears from the *Maharshal* that there is no concern for the prohibition of meat and milk here, the *Maharshal* ultimately ruled like the *Rashbam* <note>Grandson of Rashi and major commentator</note> that as long as the shell has not hardened in the way eggs sold in the market have, it has the status of meat in every regard. He wrote that this was also the opinion of Mahara of Yom Tov, who wrote that for this reason we have the custom that even if the shell is completely finished, we do not eat them with milk, lest it was not actually fully hardened. End of quote.

### Rule 71
Regarding the law of milk from an animal that was slaughtered and found to be a *treifah* <term>Treifah: an animal with a physical defect that would cause it to die within a year, making it non-kosher</term>. He ruled that if it is a defect that might have just happened—such as a hole in the brain membrane—it is permitted. But the *Maharshal* ruled like Mahara to forbid any *treifah* found within three days of its milk being taken.

### Rule 74
The *Davar Zeh* <note>referring to a specific author or section</note> wrote: a "thing that will eventually be permitted" <term>Davar Sheyesh Lo Mattirin: a forbidden item that will naturally become permitted later, such as food on the Sabbath or leaven after Passover; such items are never nullified even in a ratio of 1:1000</term> that fell into broth, or that broth itself fell into another broth, it is forbidden even in a thousand parts. According to the explanation that the *Maharshal's* reasoning follows Rabbi Yochanan... it follows that a prohibition that is not inherent to the object itself, but rather because it absorbed another forbidden substance, still qualifies as a "thing that will eventually be permitted." This disagrees with the view of Mahara-i <note>Rabbi Israel Isserlein</note> in Section 110, who wrote regarding a piece of meat that absorbed blood that it is *not* called a "thing that will eventually be permitted," because the meat itself isn't the source of the prohibition; the absorbed blood is. The Rema <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles</note> relied on Mahara-i's words that since it is a Rabbinic prohibition, we are lenient. This same logic is applied to the law of a "piece fit to be served to guests" <term>Chaticha HaReuyah L’Hitkabed: a prestigious piece of food that is too important to be nullified in a mixture</term>. End of quote. However, the *Maharshal* in his notes on the *Agudah* <note>A legal work by Rabbi Alexander Suslin</note> wrote: I found it written that meat that sat for three days without salting <note>making the blood "set" and unremovable by salt</note> and then got mixed with other pieces is nullified by a majority. The reason seems to be that it isn't considered a "thing that will eventually be permitted," since it could have been roasted previously, and the specific thing that is now forbidden (cooking it) remains forbidden forever. It seems that even if it were a "piece fit to be served to guests," it is still nullified because the meat isn't the root of the prohibition, only the blood absorbed within it. Mahara-i's words here prove that according to the *Maharshal*, it is not nullified even in a thousand if it is an inherent prohibition.

**See there** that an item that will spoil before it becomes permitted is not called a "thing that will eventually be permitted," and is thus nullified. The *Maharshal* disagrees.
**See there** that an item forbidden on Passover is not called a "thing that will eventually be permitted" <note>since it's only permitted after the holiday</note>. The *Maharshal* disagrees.

### Rule 75
Regarding the matter of food cooked by non-Jews <term>Bishul Akum: food cooked by a non-Jew is generally forbidden to Rabbinic law to prevent social assimilation</term>. He ruled that if an Israelite stirred the coals, even after the food was already partially cooked <term>Ma’achal Ben Drusai: food cooked to the point of being edible in an emergency, usually 1/3 or 1/2 cooked</term> by a non-Jew, it is permitted. This is unlike other authorities who wrote that the Jew must stir the coals *before* it reaches that level of cooking. The *Maharshal* ruled that the Jew's involvement must be earlier.

**See there** where he ruled that lighting the fire or heating the oven helps avoid the prohibition of non-Jewish cooking. But the *Maharshal* proves from Mahara-i that it is not permitted even if a Jew stirs the coals once the cooking is near completion. Only regarding bread is it permitted, which is proof that "tossing a wood chip" into the fire only helps with non-Jewish baking, not general cooking.

### In the Chapter "Ein Ma'amidin"
Rav Assi said in the name of Rav: small salted fish are not subject to the prohibition of non-Jewish cooking. The *Tosafot* explain: Rabbi Yochanan says that since the text specifies "salted," it implies that if they were *not* salted, they would be forbidden. Therefore, we must be speaking of fish that are somewhat large and sometimes "ascend to a king's table" <term>Oleh Al Shulchan Melachim: a criterion for the prohibition of non-Jewish cooking; if a food is prestigious enough for a royal feast, it is forbidden if cooked by a non-Jew</term>. If not for this, there is a difficulty... The law follows the lenient view on both counts: if it can be eaten raw, or if it doesn't go on a king's table, it is permitted. If so, why did Rav mention "salted"? Even unsalted fish should be permitted! The *Beit Yosef* in Section 113 also raised this difficulty and answered: small fish, when cooked, *do* ascend to a king's table, but are permitted because they can be eaten raw. When not salted, they are permitted because they are too small for a king's table. The *Beit Yosef* derived this from the *Rashba*. However, our aforementioned Rabbis left room to be strict regarding small fish. Some fish that are small now but will grow large are not served to kings while small. But there is a second type: fish that remain small forever. If these are served to kings, they are forbidden. Regarding these, Rav Yosef said: when salted, they are permitted; but if not salted, they are forbidden. It is proper to be concerned about this.

### Rule 76
Regarding the custom, Mahara-i wrote that many are accustomed to be lenient and wait only one hour after a meat meal, then they clear the table, recite the blessing after meals, and then eat dairy. However, those who are scrupulous distance themselves for six hours. The *Maharshal* wrote: in any case, it seems that even if one waited six hours, it is still forbidden to eat...

The Maharshal brought the Mahra'i's view plainly and did not distinguish at all between the outset and after the fact. Also, in his book Section 78, he brought it and did not bring the opinion of those who permit it.

**See there**: Regarding the law of fish and poultry that were salted together: they are forbidden. The "Or Zarua" and the *Arukh* wrote that the fish are forbidden only when they are placed next to the poultry or beneath them; but if they are placed on top of the poultry, they are permitted. The Maharshal wrote similarly in the chapter "Gid HaNasheh" <note>The chapter in the Talmud concerning the sciatic nerve and dietary laws</note> but wrote that they require a "peeling" <term>Klipah: the removal of a thin surface layer where flavor might have been absorbed</term> from the place of contact. This applies only when it is known that from beginning to end the fish were on top; but in a case of doubt, it is forbidden, as the standard practice is to cover them, since they require salting. End of quote.

**See there**: The *Beit Yosef* wrote that if the poultry was salted and becomes "secondary" <note>incidental contact</note>, it is also non-kosher <note>original: "treif"</note>. But his words are not correct. The Maharshal ruled according to the *Beit Yosef*.

**Principle 23**: Regarding the matter of "the bottom prevails" <term>Tathaa Gavar: the principle that if a hot item and a cold item meet, the temperature of the bottom one determines the heat transfer</term>. He wrote as follows: In the glosses of the *Sha'arei Dura* in the name of *Torat HaBayit* <note>by Rabbi Shlomo ben Aderet, the Rashba</note>, it says that if they are placed side by side, they are treated as if they only require "peeling." The Maharshal wrote that it seems to him that if the forbidden item is hot and the permitted item is cold and they are side by side, the whole thing is forbidden. If the forbidden item is cold and the permitted item is hot, it seems proper to be strict like the words of the Rashba, requiring a "peeling." End of quote.

<margin>Requires sixty-fold nullification; if there is no sixty, the whole thing is forbidden. Similarly, regarding salting in Section 38, see there. In the second part of the *Tur* Yoreh De'ah Section 93, he wrote that the whole thing becomes forbidden. But in Section 105, he ruled that it only becomes forbidden up to the thickness of a "finger-breadth" <note>original: "k'dei netilah"</note>, and one must be careful with the surface of milk that falls, as it is thin and easily spreads through the whole piece—likewise for a forbidden solid that falls on a permitted piece. But the Maharshal ruled explicitly that even for a forbidden solid, one needs sixty-fold nullification.</margin>

**See there**: He brought the words of the *Tur* regarding roasting: even if the bottom item is hot, it is sufficient to remove a "finger-breadth." The Maharshal wrote as follows: "We do not hold like this, but rather like the words of the *Sha'arim* <note>The Sha'arei Dura</note>, and we do not distinguish between boiling and roasting; even for roasting, it is insufficient." End of quote. In Chapter 27 he wrote that the whole thing is forbidden, and in Section 100 [and] 93 he wrote that the whole thing is forbidden, yet in Section 105 he ruled that only a "finger-breadth" is forbidden, and one must be careful with a drop of milk that falls, for it is fluid and spreads easily through the whole piece, even if a solid forbidden item falls on a permitted piece. But the Maharshal ruled explicitly that even for a forbidden solid, one needs sixty-fold nullification.

**See there**: In a case where meat fell into cold milk, or vice versa: the meat requires a "peeling," and the milk—because it is impossible to "peel" it—[is a matter of debate]. Rabbi Isaac <note>Riva</note> ruled strictly against the peeling, and Rabbi Isaac wrote... and the Mahra'i wrote that one should cut it away like the Riva. The [author] ruled that the milk is permitted. In Section 41 he ruled thus, but wrote that one should only be lenient in a case of great need since the Mahra'i wrote to be strict. The Maharshal did not distinguish even in a case of need. Rabbi Meir [of Rothenburg] himself in *Tur* Yoreh De'ah Section 81, Law 40, ruled that we require sixty against the "peeling," and likewise in... 137 regarding the law of "Libation Wine" <note>Wine handled by non-Jews</note>.

**See there**: He ruled that if one placed hot forbidden food into a cold bowl, it is "hot into cold," and the bowl requires "peeling." If one placed meat into a dairy bowl, both require "peeling." These are the words of the Maharshal: "This is not so, for I have proven here and in my other books from all these laws... that in a bowl that was used that day, a hot item without broth is forbidden. Since there is no broth, there is only a small amount of emission [of flavor], and it is irrelevant to say 'the bottom prevails' or 'the top prevails.' Therefore, as long as it is hot, the heat of the vessel causes it to absorb and forbid. It also becomes forbidden whenever there is no sixty-fold nullification, for the heat of roasting and the heat of boiling both require sixty."

<margin>A forbidden item with other pieces: they are forbidden according to what was said that salting and roasting are like boiling. However, if they were not salted together, but rather a salted piece merely touches the meat, even if both are salted, it is certainly not forbidden.</margin>

**Principle 28**: The rule that one piece forbids its neighbor through contact <term>Negiah</term> applies specifically if the piece itself is forbidden. But a piece that became forbidden only by absorbing flavor from a forbidden source does not forbid another through contact, even if they were roasted or salted together. The Maharshal wrote: "But if a piece that was forbidden due to absorbing flavor from other forbidden pieces was roasted or salted, it follows the rule that salting and roasting are like boiling. However, if they were not salted together, but a salted piece touches the meat, even if both are salted, it is certainly not forbidden."

**Principle 33**: He ruled that there is no difference regarding a "secondary vessel" <term>Kli Sheni: a vessel that was not on the fire but contains hot liquid</term> between wood, metal, or clay. The Maharshal ruled like the *Agudah* <note>Rabbi Alexander Suslin</note> and the *Asheri* <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note> that a clay vessel absorbs even in a secondary vessel.

<margin>A perforated vessel forbids other meat that was roasted or cooked with it in an oven because of the "aroma" <term>Reicha</term>, even though it does not spread and is like something thick that does not saturate; nevertheless, the fattiness saturates it and carries the aroma and the taste of the blood with it.</margin>

**Principle 35**: He ruled regarding the law of "aroma" <term>Reicha Milta: whether aroma is legally significant</term> that for us, one should be strict in every case, especially in large quantities. The Maharshal further wrote regarding "aroma": where meat was forbidden because of blood—such as if it was salted in a vessel that is not perforated—it forbids other meat roasted or cooked with it in an oven because of the aroma. Even though blood does not spread and is thick, the fattiness carries the aroma and the taste of the blood with it.

# The Gate of the Letters

Like the example of a judge who guards his children, so too Israel drinks the wine of Israel which is produced in holiness. This mirrors the "Supernal Israel" <note>A mystical reference to a higher spiritual state or the sefira of Tiferet</note> which is changed, rooted, and blessed by that holy, supernal wine. They do not drink wine produced in impurity or from the side of defilement, for within it dwells the beginning of impurity, and it does not belong to the portion of Israel. Anyone who drinks with them <note>non-Jews</note> becomes defiled in his spirit and is himself made impure, having no portion in the World to Come. For that World to Come is "guarded wine" <note>original: "yayin de-netara," referring to the wine stored in its grapes since the six days of creation</note>. Therefore, the holy people of Israel must guard this above all else, so they may be bound to the place of the World to Come; for this reason, we bless the Holy One, Blessed be He, over wine. End of quote.

Understand the concept of Binah <note>The Sefirah of "Understanding"</note>, which is the World to Come. There, the "Preserved Wine" is found, for within Binah, the "Six Supernal Extremities" <note>The six emotional attributes of the divine</note> are hidden, and the *Kelipot* <term>Kelipot: "shells" or spiritual forces of evil/impurity</term> have no grasp there. They only have a grasp when the Six Extremities expand into their place in this world. This is what the Sages, of blessed memory, meant regarding the World to Come when they cited the verse: "No eye has seen, O God, besides You" <note>Isaiah 64:3</note>, which refers to the wine preserved from the six days of Creation. This means that the secret of the six days of Creation is guarded there.

Through the sin where [Adam] squeezed a cluster of grapes, the power of the *Kelipot* grew strong, and there the intoxicating wine is found. But we, the People of Israel, whose souls are from the side of holiness, and all our yearning is for the World to Come—as we have learned: "All Israel has a portion in the World to Come"—we, the Israel below, intend to align ourselves with the Israel above, the secret of the "Glory of Israel" <note>Tiferet Yisrael</note>, which desires the life of the aforementioned world. When the holy Israel sanctifies itself below by refraining from drinking the wine touched by a non-Jew, it awakens the "Preserved Wine" in Binah to flow down through the "Israel Above." Therefore, we recite blessings and sanctify <note>Kiddush</note> over wine. One who drinks from the touch of a non-Jew becomes defiled and shall be called "unclean, unclean," and does not merit the life of the World to Come. The Zohar states that this is not only true for wine, but for all forbidden foods—one defiles oneself through them—but wine is of a higher degree than them all. Who is the man who would not take these warm words to heart, to be careful with the utmost caution and to sanctify himself with the "Ten Sanctities"?

**And I found** in the book *Reasons for the Commandments* authored by the Rabbi, Master Menachem of Babylon, who wrote regarding the negative commandment not to drink libation wine <note>original: "yayin nesech"</note>: "In the days of my youth, I saw men of great deeds who were stringent upon themselves. Even when they desired wine, they would not drink it even if the uncircumcised <note>non-Jew</note> had not touched it, simply because he had cast his eyes upon it. In such a case, there is no sign of blessing in it. This is a custom of piety, for once the uncircumcised sees the color of the wine or its scent and desires it in his thought—and the general thought of a non-Jew is toward idolatry—even though it is in the hand of a Jew, he has already formed an image of it in his mind. God will reckon even the smallest detail of stringency, and he who guards himself from this merits the wine preserved in its grapes after the filth is forgotten." Even for those who are lenient in the lands of the uncircumcised, etc., they saw the great need to be sanctified in this, as it says, "You shall be holy," and to be stringent with all stringencies. Regarding this, it is said: "Sanctify yourself even in that which is permitted to you."

### Now
I have come to the matter of "New Grain" <note>The OCR reads "Cheresh" (earthenware/deaf), but the context of "Masechet Challah" and the Torah prohibition indicates "Chadosh" (New Grain), which cannot be eaten until the second day of Passover</note>. See and consider: this prohibition applies whether the Temple stands or not, whether in the Land of Israel or abroad, whether it belongs to a Jew or a non-Jew. It is forbidden by the Torah, as written in the verse, and the law follows Rabbi Eleazar at the end of the tractate *Kiddushin*, for the author of the Mishnah summarized the law according to him in the end of tractate *Challah*: "New Grain" is forbidden by the Torah in every place. It is proper to be very grieved over this commandment, for only the "elevated souls" <note>original: "bnei aliyah," refers to the spiritually elite</note> are careful with it. Even though there are lenient views mentioned in the *Tur* <note>The Code of Law</note> Section 193 that rely on the majority of grain being "old" <note>ripened before the cutoff</note>, and other doubts, know, my children (may God protect you), that in these times when Torah is increased in almost every province, I have seen great disputes. In the lands where the Rosh and the Mordechai lived, those are "hot lands" where most grain indeed falls before the prohibition cutoff. But in the land of Poland, and especially Russia, Volhynia, and Lithuania, the vast majority of grain falls *after* the cutoff. To apply the leniencies of hot lands to these regions is a public falsehood; on the contrary, from these lands, grain is transported to other places. Therefore, my children, do not follow the majority to do evil, but strengthen yourselves in this commandment, you and your descendants for generations. The words of the Lord are pure words; may they be as lights.

### Now
I shall record the warnings of abstinence from forbidden things which my father and teacher, of blessed memory, commanded in his ethical will *Yesh Nochalim*. May they not depart from our mouths or the mouths of our children forever. These are they:

### Do Not
Eat frequently at feasts in any place unless you are among modest and worthy people who are known to you as people of truth, good and upright in their hearts. Our Sages said: "The refined people of Jerusalem [would not join a meal unless they knew who their companions were]." In the general sense of their words are many matters.

<margin>Beer</margin>
### Do Not
Drink in the house of a non-Jew, even the ale they call "Beer," and certainly not the honey-drink they call "Mez'd" <note>Mead</note> which is more intoxicating, except for incidental drinking or while traveling at an inn. But do not establish a fixed meal, as some people of the province do, for fixing a meal in the house of a non-Jew is forbidden by the Rabbis to prevent intermarriage, as stated in the *Shulchan Aruch*. Even though my teacher, the Rama, wrote that the custom is to be lenient in these provinces, it is proper and correct that you be among the stringent.

<margin>Do not</margin>
### Do Not
Eat the "fatty tail" <note>original: "yid ha-behemah," referring to specific hindquarter fats</note> of the animal unless you know they have been slaughtered and porged <note>purged of forbidden veins and fats</note> with great heat, so they are entirely removed. For they are forbidden because of the "suet" <term>Chelev: forbidden fats that were offered on the altar in the Temple</term>. Therefore, I warn you about them because the common practice has spread without reason. Regardless, it is proper for a pious person to abstain from the meat of the hindquarters of an animal unless an expert has porged it precisely and reliably. Even though most porgers are experts, it is good for a pious person to say he will not eat hindquarter meat at all, so he does not come to eat other meat of animals and birds that even a great master cannot clarify from a book.

<margin>Do not</margin>
### Do Not
Eat those dried "blobs" and mushrooms called *Shwamen* <note>Yiddish/German: Schwämme</note>, for they tend to develop worms while still attached to the ground and are then dried with the worms inside. The *Tur* Section 74 states that any fruit that tends to develop worms while attached may not be eaten until checked internally. Based on this, it would seem that beans <note>original: "polin"</note> and dried peas are also forbidden unless checked well before drying. However, since the Rama in *Torat HaChatat* was pressed to permit them when cooked based on certain reasons, we shall also permit them since the public has adopted this. Regardless, the mushrooms remain in their forbidden state. If you wish to cook fresh beans, cut each one in half first to check for worms. As for the legumes called *Arviss* <note>Chickpeas/Peas</note>, since they usually only develop worms after being detached, there is a remedy: scatter them on a table to check for holes, then instruct your household to put the legumes into cold water. The worms and the holed beans will float to the top; throw them out and pour out that water. Then put the remaining legumes into a pot of boiling water so that if any worm remains, it will die instantly. This remedy is written in Section 11 regarding fruits that develop worms while attached. I am amazed at the majority of the world who are not careful to do this when cooking legumes, and are also not careful with the aforementioned mushrooms. It is already known what the Tosafot wrote regarding the act of Rabbi Ishmael, that the prohibition of forbidden foods is more severe than other transgressions. The Midrash says: "All the labor of man is for his mouth"—all the labor a man faces in the World to Come is because of his mouth, because he was not careful.

<margin>Do not</margin>
### Do Not
Eat those whole nuts called *Steils-nissen* <note>likely "Stahl-nüssen" or stone-nuts/hazelnuts</note> when they have been cooked in the vessels of non-Jews. Even though most non-Jewish vessels have not been used that day <note>rendering the absorbed flavor "stale" and less prohibited</note>, it is good to be stringent in such a case. It is also possible they are forbidden as "food cooked by non-Jews" <note>Bishul Akum</note>, for they might be served at a king's table and are not eaten raw. End of the words of my father and teacher, of blessed memory.

<margin>Further</margin>
### Further
I inform you, my children, that while I was in the holy community of Frankfurt, I saw every single year that the cherries called *Kirshnish* have worms in them, just as is common in beans. They are careful there not to eat a cherry without opening it to check for worms. They told me this is a constant thing, and worms are usually found in the sweet ones. But the sour ones called *Weichseln* <note>Morello or sour cherries</note> are not so prone. When I came to increase Torah in the holy community of Prague, I checked there and found the same. Therefore, my children, pay attention to this, for I do not know if it is the same everywhere in the world or specifically in these warm lands. Regardless, it requires clarification.

<margin>155</margin>
->To eat cheese after [meat] only until they have cleared the table and recited the blessing, to avoid the appearance of impropriety; <note>original: "mar'it ayin"</note> this is what I have received. End of quote.<-

<margin>(See the children of Y. 17... the Rambam and the Rashba ruled to wait six hours, and the Beit Yosef in section 173 wrote that this is the world's custom, and so ruled the Rama. The Rambam and Rashba wrote that this amount of time is necessary even after eating poultry...)</margin>

**The Beit Yosef** <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo (1488–1575), author of the Shulchan Aruch</note> wrote in the section on the Laws of Blessings (173) in the name of the *Zohar* <note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism</note> that one should be strict regarding meat after cheese, even poultry, just as one is strict regarding cheese after meat. The *Zohar* states there that one who is not careful in this matter will be under a spirit of impurity for forty days; if a son is born to him during those forty days, the child is given a soul from the "Other Side" <note>original: "Sitra Achra," the realm of spiritual evil</note> which is not holy—may God protect us. Therefore, one who guards his soul should keep his distance and sanctify himself even in matters permitted by strict law; regardless, a blessing shall come upon the one who is stringent. In the Talmudic chapter *Kol HaBasar*, Mar Ukva said: "In this matter, I am like vinegar, the son of wine <note>A metaphor meaning he was less pious than his father</note>; for if my father ate meat now, he would not eat cheese until tomorrow at this time. But as for me, I will not eat it in this meal, but I will eat it in the next meal." This "next meal" is understood as a six-hour wait according to the Rambam, the Rosh, and the Rashba. Mar Ukva called himself "vinegar" [for only waiting until the next meal]; therefore, one who sanctifies himself even more shall be called holy, and happy are his children after him.

**Rule 85:** Regarding a meat spoon used for milk (or vice versa) which requires "sixty" <term>Sixty (Shishim): The legal requirement that kosher food be sixty times the volume of the forbidden substance to neutralize it</term> to be nullified. The ruling is that there is no difference whether the spoon was dipped once or twice. However, the Rashal <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria (1510–1573)</note> wrote in his books: "I wrote that sixty is required, and I have a tradition that one need not be so strict as to require sixty for every single dip if it was dipped three times. Only if it was dipped four times must one provide sixty, for the first sixty nullifies the prohibition, and the second sixty is in case the flavor was 'reawakened,' but beyond that, we do not worry."

**On the same subject:** It is written in the "Gates" of Rabbi Isaac of Düren in the name of the *Or Zarua*: if a pot becomes forbidden due to meat and milk (which is an "Isur Hana'ah" <note>a prohibition against deriving any benefit</note>) and food was cooked in it—even if the pot was not used within the last twenty-four hours and thus did not forbid the food—one must still "throw the value of the pot into the river" so as not to benefit from something forbidden. It seems to me that according to our custom of being lenient with hot water, there is no need for concern... The Rosh discussed this regarding a knife used for idolatry. The Rashal also cited the *Or Zarua* and wrote that we have not merited the custom of being lenient with hot water... and I ruled like the Rashba that one must discard the value.

**On the same subject:** To praise the wise man who permits a prohibited substance that fell into a pot by measuring it against sixty: it is written in the *Sefer Mitzvot* that one must investigate if water was added to the pot after the forbidden item fell in. The *Tur* disagrees, holding that even if it was added unintentionally <note>original: "b'shogeg"</note>, we hold that all prohibitions in the Torah that require sixty are permitted if the addition was unintentional. The Rashal ruled that the Sage must investigate this, following the *Sefer Mitzvot*, as do the *Smak*, Maharam, and the author of *Sha'arei Dura*. This rule of "unintentional addition" applies only to dry items that do not mix; but with liquids, the piece itself becomes "nevelah" <note>un-slaughtered carrion</note> in the case of meat and milk according to everyone. The Rama also wrote that it is good to be strict and investigate. Therefore, every God-fearing person should remember this and not forget.

**On the same subject:** Regarding the law that if a forbidden item is soiled, it still joins the prohibition. It is written that this applies only if the addition is of the same type as the first prohibition; but if the second is a different type, they do not join together, and the second nullifies the first. The Rashal wrote that this is only if both fell in at once. But if they did not fall at once, the first piece already became forbidden like carrion, and it can never be permitted.

**On the same subject:** He wrote regarding the Rashba that if a forbidden item was mixed with its own kind and a different kind, and the mixture was spilled, we view the different kind as if it were not there... The Rashal and the Rashba ruled this as law, but it does not seem correct to me at all. For there, Rabbi Mani holds that the forbidden item of the same kind is also prohibited because it imparts flavor, but the Torah decreed it is not nullified. But here, where the different kind is forbidden by Torah law due to "imparting flavor," if the mixture is spilled, even if there was some of the same kind present, it remains a doubt, and a doubt regarding a Torah law is ruled stringently.

**Rule 89:** If the kidneys were removed, the animal is kosher. The Ra'ah wrote that even if they were perforated or diminished—even if the hole reaches the "white part"—it is kosher. The Rashal wrote: "That which he declared kosher regarding a defect in the kidney up to the 'cleft' does not seem right to me." See the book regarding the chapter *Elu Terefot* <note>The chapter of the Talmud dealing with terminal organic defects</note>.

<margin>On the same</margin>
**Rule 94:** The *Hagahot Ashiri* wrote that if blood is found in the kidney, it is kosher. The Rashal wrote: "In my books, I wrote that one should hesitate to permit blood in the kidney." The Rashba wrote in a Responsum regarding a needle found in the gizzard: if it was entirely swallowed into the thickness of the flesh, with an inch sticking out toward the pouch and toward the outside, but the needle did not push through and there was no visible hole on the inside or outside, we tend toward leniency. We assume it came from the inside, through the esophagus with the food. At that time, the Maharam <note>Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg (1215–1293)</note> ruled to forbid such a case. I heard from a great scholar that the Rashba and the Maharam do not actually disagree: the Rashba speaks of the needle resting in the thickness of the flesh, while the Maharam speaks of it being swallowed along the length of the gizzard. This is a beautiful reconciliation of their words. However, one should not be lenient, as the Rashal implies the Maharam forbids it in all cases, because flesh in that area cannot heal since the inner lining is tough... if a hole isn't visible from the inside, it must have come from the outside.

**I have come to remind and warn** those who keep chickens and cats in their homes: one must fear "darisah" <term>Darisah: A predatory attack where a cat or predator injects venom through its claws, making the prey non-kosher (treifah)</term> if the cat is seen entering the chickens' area. The *Tur* (Section 50) mentions the Rashba's view that perhaps our domestic cats are "civilized" with chickens and we need not fear unless we see them chasing. However, it is proper to be concerned. If one sees the cat chasing and striking, it has certainly made the bird a *treifah*, even if the cat is house-raised. When we haven't seen it chase but only enter the area, people are generally not concerned; but it is proper to be wary. The *Beit Yosef* says this is because the Talmud was concerned about *darisah*, and the cats of their time were as familiar with chickens as ours are now. Even if the *Shulchan Aruch* doesn't explicitly say one must be concerned, it is proper to be so, as the Talmud is concerned. Every "master of his soul" should be wary.

**Now I have come to speak and warn** with great warnings regarding the drinking of wine, for you, my children (may God protect you). This warning is very grave: do not drink wine in any place or setting, even among Israelites, unless it is certain to you that the wine was made with proper supervision and great care to avoid contact with a non-Jew. This stumbling block is common among our people, who are lax in supervision. The great spiritual blemish that comes from "ordinary wine" <note>original: "stam yeinam," wine handled by a non-Jew</note> is immense. The Zohar on the portion of *Shemini* warns: "Come and see, the holy Israelites... everything depends on the Life of the World to Come, for that is the life of all, above and below. It is the place where 'Guarded Wine' dwells... and from that time, life and holiness flow to all. The wine of Israel is like the 'Other Israel' <note>Supernal Israel/Tiferet</note>... for Israel below is like the Tree of Life... and for this reason, we bless the Holy One over it. Because the Israelites below are worthy, they merit this. But 'Ordinary Wine' is defiled, and whoever draws near to it becomes defiled... certainly the wine that a non-Jew produces." Therefore, do not say this is a small thing, for everything an Israelite does below is a mirror of the example above, especially wine, which stands in a supernal place.

<meta>The previous page concluded a discussion on the laws of meat and milk, specifically the requirement to wait between eating them to avoid spiritual impurity and the influence of the "Other Side." # The Gate of the Letters

**And regarding what is written** in the fifth chapter of the Laws of First Fruits <note>original: "Bikkurim"</note>: "In this time, when no dough is ritually pure because of the impurity of the dead, one separates one portion of Challah <note>The portion of dough gifted to the priest</note> for every [batch], one part in forty-eight, and burns it; and another portion is separated due to doubt that it might be impure," end of quote. Do not learn from this that one must initially separate a measure of one in forty-eight. For in that very same chapter, [Maimonides] wrote that Challah is also called *Terumah* <note>A generic term for a priestly gift or heave-offering</note> and all its laws are like the laws of *Terumah*, except for one law in which Challah differs: namely, that a drunkard or a blind person may separate Challah initially, which is not the case with *Terumah*. The Master <note>Maimonides</note> gave a reason for this distinction: because in dough, there is no "bad" or "good" quality that would require a discerning heart and eye to separate from the better portion. 

If so, the Master’s words seem to contradict themselves. For he wrote in the third chapter of the Laws of *Terumah* as follows: "In this time, when [the gift] is destined to be burned because of ritual impurity, one may separate any amount <note>original: "kol she'hu"</note> initially," end of quote. Here, the Master explained the reason for this: because we do not have pure *Terumah*. This same reason applies to Challah as well. Even if one were a master builder <note>original: "bar nagar," a Talmudic idiom for a scholar</note>, how could he distinguish between *Terumah* and Challah in this law? If Maimonides, in his great wisdom, knew of a logical reason to distinguish them, he should have explained it and informed us, just as he explained the reason for the distinction he made between Challah and *Terumah* regarding the separation by a blind or drunk person—which is easy to understand even without him explaining it.

**Rather**, it must be the Master's opinion that regarding Challah, too, one has the permission to separate "any amount" initially. However, in the Laws of First Fruits, he wrote the "letter of the law"—that the rule for Challah even in this time is to separate a measure of one in forty-eight, and such is the rule for *Terumah* as well. But permission is granted to a person to separate any amount because we lack ritually pure *Terumah* and Challah. This is why the Master was precise in his language, writing in the Laws of *Terumah*: "and in this time... he *has the right* <note>original: "yesh lo"</note> to separate any amount," and he did not write "he *separates* any amount." This implies that although the letter of the law is to separate a specific measure, one need not be exacting in the matter; rather, a person has the right to separate any amount if he wishes. This is also the language of the legal deciders <note>original: "Poskim"</note>, and most of the early authorities <note>original: "Geonim"</note> ruled that in this time, when the *Terumah* is destined for burning because it is impure, a person is permitted to separate any amount. Maimonides did not need to repeat this permission regarding Challah, since he had already written there that Challah is also called *Terumah*. Having noted the one law in which they differ and explained its reason, you may learn from this that in all other matters, their laws are equal. The Master wrote similarly in the Laws of Prayer, Chapter 3, regarding the Evening Prayer <note>original: "Arvit"</note>: "One who prays the prayer before its time has not fulfilled his obligation and must repeat it; however, one *has the right* to pray the Friday night Evening Prayer on the eve of the Sabbath before the sun sets, because the Evening Prayer is optional and we are not exacting about its time," end of quote. The author of the *Migdal Oz* <note>A commentator on Maimonides</note> was also precise there, noting that whenever Maimonides uses the expression "he has the right," it means it is permitted only in a case of pressing need.

**And such is the custom in the Land of Israel.** Once, close to Passover, we saw some people counting the matzahs after baking in order to separate one in forty-eight. We said to them: "Behold, all year long we separate only a tiny amount!" and they did not respond because they did not know and did not understand. I and my colleague, the distinguished sage, a "welling spring" <note>A metaphor for an ever-increasing scholar</note>, the late Rabbi Eliyahu Sasson, went and asked one of the giants of the generation, the late Rabbi Moshe di Trani <note>Known as the Mabit (1500–1580), a major legal authority in Safed</note>, according to the law, what should be done regarding the separation of Challah, and if there is a reason to distinguish between the Challah of Passover and the Challah of the rest of the year. He told us that our rabbis did not want there to be any "memory" of leaven <note>original: "chametz"</note> in Safed, and that the practical law is to separate any amount initially, and there is no difference between Challah all year round [and Passover]. There is nothing more to it. Therefore, the custom has spread throughout the Land of Israel that we only separate a tiny amount for the Great *Terumah*.

**Afterwards**, one separates the First Tithe <note>original: "Ma'aser Rishon"</note> and gives it to the Levite. The Levite then separates a tenth part of his own—this is the Tithe of the Tithe <note>original: "Terumat Ma'aser"</note>—and gives it to the priest. Now, in our many sins, since we are all ritually impure, it is forbidden for the priest to eat the *Terumah*. However, he is permitted to benefit from it at the time of its destruction—namely, to use it as fuel for heating, or if it is oil, to light his lamp, or if it is wine, to sprinkle it [for its scent].

**And afterwards**, one separates the Second Tithe <note>original: "Ma'aser Sheni"</note>. Its law is that it must be eaten in Jerusalem in a state of ritual purity. Now, if the tithe is pure—for example, if it never became susceptible to impurity—is it possible to eat it in Jerusalem? We do not eat the Second Tithe when there is no Altar, as written in the first chapter of *Hanizakin*. Throughout the Land of Israel, outside of Jerusalem, we redeem it for the value of a small coin <note>original: "perutah"</note> and throw that coin into the river. This is because in this time, when there is no Temple, we may initially redeem it for a small coin. But in Jerusalem, it is forbidden to redeem it when it is pure. Instead, they cook it so that it becomes impure through the touch of a person—for we are all impure today since there are no ashes of the Red Heifer—and then one can redeem it even in Jerusalem. For the rule that one does not redeem in Jerusalem applies only when the tithe is pure; but when it is impure, one may redeem it, and one redeems it for the value of a small coin.

**In the third and sixth years** of the Sabbatical cycle <note>original: "Shmita"</note>, in place of the Second Tithe, one gives the Tithe for the Poor <note>original: "Ma'aser Ani"</note>, and it must be distributed among the poor. It has become the custom in the Land of Israel, when they separate the Poor Tithe, to say: "I hereby declare my property ownerless <note>original: "hefker"</note>, for I am [now] a poor man," and then he re-acquires it. I have complained about this practice from the day I arrived here, for their "ownerless" declarations are not truly ownerless. It is established for us that property does not become ownerless unless declared before three people. I also found in the book *Sefer HaCharedim* <note>Written by Elazar Azikri (1533–1600)</note> that they rule like me, writing: "This is a delusion." Its source is in the *Tur* <note>A code of Jewish law</note>: if someone has debts owed by others, whether by verbal agreement or by a contract, let your soul be certain that he has not acted properly. Whether at the time of declaring the property ownerless he forgave the debts or not—if he forgives them, truly and legally he can forgive even in their presence, even a pledge, and the forgiveness is valid, as the *Mordechai* wrote at the beginning of *Sanhedrin* and as the Rama cited in the *Tur*, *Choshen Mishpat* section 241. Thus, it is considered a forgiveness when he promised it. However, if he intends to be paid later, it is considered stolen in his hand. A thing is only forgiven if it is sincere; if not, he is found not to be a poor man. One cannot say that since it is not yet the time for repayment, he is poor at that moment; for even if he has declared what is in his hand ownerless, while the debts are not yet due, this means nothing. For would one who has bags of gold coins <note>original: "haraki dinarim"</note> in debts be considered poor? This only applies to one who is on a journey and cannot access funds, as we learned in the tractate *Pe'ah*: "A homeowner who was traveling from place to place and needs to take the Gleanings, Forgotten Sheaves, and the Corner of the field... let him take and eat." But someone who is in his home and can obtain money based on what he has, or sell his debts for less than their value, is considered wealthy. This is clear. I discussed this with the great scholars of legal ruling, and they agreed with my words. 

There is also another group that has the custom of estimating how much the tithe is worth, and then throughout the year, when they give charity, they credit it against the Poor Tithe. This, too, does not seem right to me for two reasons. First, this charity is given every year, even when the Poor Tithe does not apply. Second, if one does this, he will need to inform the poor person every time that what he is giving him is from the Poor Tithe, so that the poor person does not come to steal from him <note>The sense here is about the psychological impact on the poor person's dignity or the donor's intent</note>—heaven forbid—if the poor person thinks the donor is sending it from his own [personal] funds, as explained in Maimonides, Chapter 10 of the Laws of Gifts to the Poor. Therefore, one who has the fear of Heaven in him should perform the commandment properly. Let it be for God according to its value to fulfill His commandment. Do not seek justifications to spare your soul, for one will not become poor from this; on the contrary, he will be blessed. As they said in the chapter *Bameh Madlikin*: "For the sin of [neglecting] *Terumah* and Tithes, the heavens are closed... but if they give, they are blessed," as it is said: "Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in My house. Test me in this, says the Lord of Hosts, and see if I will not throw open the floodgates of heaven and pour out so much blessing that there will not be room enough to store it" <note>Malachi 3:10</note>. What is the meaning of "until there is no room enough"? Rami bar Rav said in the name of Rav: "Until your lips wear out from saying 'Enough!'" It is forbidden to test God by saying, "I will do such-and-forth commandment and see if I am blessed," except regarding the tithe. As Rabbi Yochanan said: "Tithe, so that you may become wealthy" <note>original: "Asser bishvil she-titasser," a pun on the Hebrew words for tithe and wealth</note>. And it was said in the first chapter of *Ta'anit*: In the entire Torah it is forbidden to test, except for the tithe, as it says: "Test me in this." The matter is that regarding the tithe, the Holy One, blessed be He, promised that He would certainly send the blessing. This is not the case with other commandments, where He did not promise to certainly send a blessing to the living person when he performs the commandment; if he were to test and see that there is no blessing, he might again refrain from serving the Name, may He be blessed. Therefore, all whose hearts are touched by the fear of God should take these things to heart.

**And there** is yet another bad custom added to what I wrote regarding the declaration of property as ownerless. They act as if they are in doubt regarding the knowledge of the Sabbatical years. They say: "If this year is a year of the Second Tithe, let the tithe be in such-and-forth a portion of my produce and be redeemed for a small coin; and if it is a year of the Poor Tithe, I hereby declare my property ownerless, etc." The author of *Sefer HaCharedim* has already excommunicated people for this, writing that this is a custom of the ignorant. The time of the Sabbatical year is not hidden from the eyes of the wise, for all Israel follows Maimonides regarding the release of debts <note>original: "Shmitat Kesafim"</note> and the agricultural work of the seventh year. Therefore, one should not do this. Rebuffing a commandment in its time is wrong; everything is beautiful in its season.

**And regarding** the start of the year: we have already learned at the beginning of Tractate *Rosh Hashanah*: "On the first of Tishrei is the New Year for vegetables." It says in the Gemara that this is when their vitality emerges, which is a Rabbinic law. How much more so for grain, whose tithing measure is from the Torah. And "In Shevat is the New Year for trees"—namely, regarding the tithe of fruits, for we do not tithe the fruit of a tree that blossomed before the 15th of Shevat together with fruit that blossomed after the 15th of Shevat. A practical difference also arises regarding the third year of the Sabbatical cycle, in which the Poor Tithe applies: we do not redeem fruit that blossomed from the New Year of the third year until the 15th of Shevat; we judge it as fruit of the second year that has passed and separate Second Tithe from it; but from the 15th of Shevat onwards, it is Poor Tithe. And so too for the 15th of Shevat that will come. This is the language of Maimonides in Chapter 4 of the Laws of Second Tithe: "On the first of Tishrei is the New Year for the tithe of grain, legumes, and vegetables, and wherever 'New Year' is said, it means the first of Tishrei... and in Shevat is the New Year for the tithe of trees. How so? Grain and legumes that reached the stage of obligation for tithes before the New Year of the seventh year, even if they were completed..."

# ->The Gate of the Letters<-

I also inform you regarding the small infestations called "mites" <note>original: "milben"</note> and "maggots" <note>original: "regenzilchiot"</note> found during the summer days <note>The Hebrew "Kain" is likely a transcription error for "Kayitz" (summer).</note> in all fruits and dried goods, such as plums and raisins, whether large or small, as well as in types of legumes, rice, and millet. We are not normally accustomed to seeing these, but it is a common occurrence. Many times in the Pelag market <note>original: "S.K. Plag"</note>, I prohibited the entire market that sells these items, because the inspector must have very keen and fine vision. Many times people inspected them and said they were clean, but another observer came and showed everyone how they were filled with countless moving and wriggling insects. Therefore, there is an obligation to look into this, as it is a prohibition from the Torah <note>Eating insects is a severe biblical violation.</note>.

**Now** I have come to serve as a reminder regarding the laws practiced in the Land of Israel, should you be privileged in your hearts to come to the Holy Land to dwell, so that you may know what to do. I urge you to be very meticulous with them so that you do not sin, God forbid. One year after my arrival in Jerusalem (may it be rebuilt and established soon), it was the Sabbatical Year <term>Shmita: the seventh year of the agricultural cycle where the land must rest</term>. Many of the inhabitants of the Holy Land sought to exempt themselves because of the great hardship, for the eve of the seventh year was a time of famine, and they did not even have enough to eat day by day, let alone prepare their homes for the seventh year. They offered distant excuses, but I judged for myself and thought in my heart: I am more obligated to fulfill this than they are, even if I must sell the cloak off my shoulders. For God might say to me: "Why did you come from a place where you were exempt from these commandments to a place of obligation, only to abandon the commandment here? Why did you come to defile My land?" It is one thing for those already living there; their punishment is not as great. But anyone who travels to the Holy Land does so to sanctify themselves and fulfill the commandments tied to the land. As our Sages said at the end of the chapter "The Accused Wife" <note>original: "Sotah"</note>, Rabbi Shamlai taught: "Why did Moses our Teacher long to enter the Land of Israel? Did he need to eat its fruit? Rather, he said: 'Many commandments were commanded to Israel that can only be fulfilled in the Land of Israel; let me enter the land so they may all be fulfilled through me.'" The point is that a person should bring themselves into the obligation of a commandment in order to fulfill it. Even if one is not strictly required, they should seek the obligation. One who does not do so is sometimes punished in times of trouble, for the Heavenly court observes this. As seen in the chapter "The Piercing" <note>original: "HaMakat"</note>, an angel said to Rav Katina, who was wearing a cloak that did not require ritual fringes <term>Tzitzit</term>: "In a time of Divine wrath, one is punished even for failing to pursue an optional commandment." And in the chapter "With what may we light," one Tanna <term>Sage of the Mishnah</term> holds that children die for the sin of neglecting the Mezuzah <note>The scroll placed on doorposts</note>. This is because they should have sought to live in a house that requires a Mezuzah to fulfill the mitzvah. Therefore, one should desire to bring themselves into the obligation of the commandments in the Land of Israel. If one comes to the Land and fails to perform the commandment that comes to hand, God forbid! Some time after I took these things to heart, I found the same sentiment in the "Book of the Devout" <note>original: "Sefer HaCharedim"</note> by the pious Rabbi Eliezer Azikri, who wrote: "All who come to dwell in the Land of Israel must be very careful with the Sabbatical Year and all commandments dependent on the Land, just as the Amoraim <term>Sages of the Talmud</term> who dwelt in the Land were careful. This is so that the merit of dwelling in the Land is not marred by the sin of neglecting its unique commandments, which would result in a loss greater than the gain. May the God of Israel help us fulfill them. Amen."

-># And these are: The Great Offering, the Tithes, and the Poor Man’s Gifts (Gleanings, Forgotten Sheaves, and Corners) <-

All of these are mandated by the Torah <term>De-orayta</term> in the Land of Israel even in this current time. The book "Ramosh" <note>likely a reference to a specific commentary</note> mentions that according to Maimonides <note>Rambam</note>, these laws are only Rabbinic <term>De-rabbanan</term> today in Israel. The Rema <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles</note> wrote that some disagree and hold they are still Torah mandates today, though the common practice did not follow this. However, "accept the truth from whoever speaks it" <note>A famous maxim of Maimonides</note>; the final law is that they are Torah mandates. The root of the matter is found in the chapter "The Uncircumcised." Rabbi Yochanan said that the sanctity with which Ezra sanctified the land stayed holy forever. All our Rabbis in the Land of Israel behaved as if the laws were from the Torah even after the destruction of the Temple. The "Book of the Devout" notes that the authors of the *Ka-ka-m*, *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol*, and *Ba'al HaTerumah* all ruled this way, as did Rashi, the Tosafot, and Rabbi Shimshon. This was also the ruling of the Gaon, Rabbi Joseph Tov-Elem, and others. The laws of these offerings are explained in Maimonides and the *Semag*, and some are mentioned in the *Shulchan Aruch*. However, many major works on the *Tur* and *Shulchan Aruch* omitted the laws of the Sabbatical Year because they mistakenly thought it was only a Rabbinic law. But in truth, they are Torah mandates! Regarding the gifts of the poor <note>Gleanings, Forgotten Sheaves, etc.</note>, only a tiny minority observes them properly. Regarding the Great Offering <note>Terumah</note>, the laws are complex—such as when the tithe is due, and the difference between a "snack" and a "fixed meal," which involves many details. My children, if you merit coming to the Land, these laws are explained in Maimonides. What is not clear there, I will clarify for you. I will write out the laws of the Sabbatical Year more clearly for you, and the poor man’s gifts are well-explained in Maimonides and the *Semag*. I do not need to record them all here, especially since those gifts only apply to someone who owns a field or vineyard, which is not so common.

## Regarding
The order of separating the Great Offering and tithes: one must know which year of the Sabbatical cycle it is, as the order changes. The law follows the consensus of Maimonides. Rabbi Joseph Karo <note>Beit Yosef</note> wrote that the year 350 <note>1590 CE</note> was a Sabbatical year. Based on this, the current year 383 <note>1623 CE</note> is a full Sabbatical year. About ninety years ago, a scholar arose to challenge the calculation of the Sabbatical year based on his understanding of Maimonides. The Rabbis of Jerusalem and Safed stood against him and investigated the matter thoroughly. They sent a scholar to Safed and concluded that the traditional custom was correct according to Maimonides. Thirty years after that, in the days of Rabbi Levi ibn Habib, someone else tried to dispute the ancient custom, but all the sages of Jerusalem and Safed gathered and agreed on a single view. They sent word to the communities in Thessaloniki and Constantinople, and all agreed with the earlier Rabbis. This custom spread to all Jewish communities near and far. According to that calculation, the Sabbatical year is now the year 383 <note>1623 CE</note>, and the next will be 390 <note>1630 CE</note>, and so on.

## And the Order
of separation is as follows: In the **first year**, one separates the Great Offering <note>Terumah Gedolah</note>, the First Tithe <note>Ma'aser Rishon</note>, the Offering of the Tithe <note>Terumat Ma'aser</note>, and the Second Tithe <note>Ma'aser Sheni</note>. The **second year** is the same. In the **third year**, one gives the Poor Man's Tithe <note>Ma'aser Ani</note> instead of the Second Tithe. The same pattern follows for years four, five, and six. In the **seventh year**, no offerings or tithes are separated at all. This cycle repeats forever. Now I will explain: the first portion separated is the Great Offering. A "generous eye" gives one-fortieth, an average person one-fiftieth, and a "grudging eye" one-sixtieth. However, according to the Torah, there is no set amount; even a single grain of wheat exempts the entire pile. This is why it is called "Great," similar to how the morning Kiddush of Shabbat is called the "Great Kiddush" <note>Kiddusha Raba</note> even though it is shorter than the evening one. Rabbinically, one should not give less than one-sixtieth. If it is ritually pure, the Priest eats it; if impure, the Priest burns it under his cooking pot like wood. This was in the time when ritual purity existed in Israel. But after the time of the Gemara, when the ashes of the Red Heifer were no longer available, everyone is presumed to have "impurity of the dead." Therefore, the Gaonim established that one may separate any small amount for the Great Offering, as it must be burned anyway. This is also the rule for the dough-offering <note>Challah</note>. Since it cannot be eaten by the Priest today and must be burned, one may separate any amount from the start.
