<meta>This page continues the author's instructions regarding agricultural laws in the Land of Israel, specifically focusing on the point at which produce becomes liable for tithes and the complexities of the Sabbatical Year (Shmita).</meta>

->### The Gate of the Letters ###<-

Regarding one who pickles <note>The Hebrew "Kovesh" refers to preserving food in salt or vinegar.</note>: the act of pickling is considered the "completion of the work" <term>Gmar Melacha: the final stage of processing that makes produce legally liable for tithes</term> since the food is not normally eaten that way <note>i.e., raw</note>, and this processing is done by the hand of an Israelite. However, in the *Book of the Devout* <note>Sefer Charedim, a 16th-century work on Jewish law and ethics</note>, he ruled that one is exempt from tithing in this case, and his reasoning is sound. As for drying with salt, this occurs after the stage where it is normally set aside for tithing to be eaten as a snack. None of these actions establish a requirement for tithing until the processing is fully complete, as stated at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Tractate Ma'aserot. Thus, we find that you cannot say the act of pickling itself is the completion of the work; rather, the pickling does not make it a "completion," but the work was already finished previously. Just as the completion of wild fruits is like the completion of all wild growth, therefore even when he pickles them, he is exempt. Some are also concerned regarding the priestly dues <term>Terumot</term> because since they are bitter <note>The text likely refers to certain fruits like olives or citrons before processing.</note> and not fit for eating, perhaps their sweetening is the "completion of the work." However, it was ruled in the *Book of the Devout* that this idea is vanity. He wrote that our teacher Rabbi Yosef Karo <note>The famous author of the Shulchan Aruch</note> instructed that the "completion of work" does not depend on the fruit being ready to eat; for many vegetables are not fit for eating until they are cooked, and yet we have a Mishnaic rule that "a vegetable that is bundled is liable from the moment it is bundled."

# Fruits
Fruits purchased from common folk <term>Am Ha'aretz: those not trusted to be meticulous with tithing</term> are called *Demai* <note>original: "Demai" (doubtful produce)</note>. They are treated as a matter of doubt; even though the seller says they have been tithed, he is not trusted. The presumption is that one is obligated to separate the "Great Offering" <term>Terumah</term> and the tithe, because eating untithed produce is a capital offense <note>in the eyes of Heaven</note>. So wrote Maimonides <note>Rambam</note>. The *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher</note> wrote that since it is a doubt, one may sell the "tithe of the tithe" to a priest at the price of non-sacred fruit. Likewise, one separates the Second Tithe, and there is no loss in this, as it belongs to the owner himself after he redeems it with money. But the nine parts of the First Tithe <note>given to the Levite</note> and the five parts of the Poor Tithe in its designated years, one is not obligated to actually give away from *Demai* because it is a doubt, and the rule is: "the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to take from his fellow." One can say to the Levite or the poor person: "Bring proof that this was not already tithed, and then take the tithes." And even though we do not physically give the Poor Tithe from *Demai*, one must still "designate it by name" <note>verbally declare which part of the produce is the tithe</note> without physically separating it, saying: "the tithe of what is here shall be Poor Tithe." See the second chapter of the ninth section of the Laws of Tithes <note>referring to Maimonides' Mishneh Torah</note>.

# Now
**Now**, you, my children (may God protect and sustain you), I shall record some conduct for the Seventh Year <term>Shmita</term>, should you be privileged to come and dwell in the Land of Israel—may the Name, Blessed be He, save you quickly, Amen. From the start of the New Year of the seventh year, which is the Sabbatical year, whoever owns a field or a vineyard is obligated to rest from working the land. Which labors are forbidden are explained by Maimonides in the *Laws of the Sabbatical and Jubilee Years*. Just as there is "rest" on the Sabbath, the Sabbatical year is a time without labor. There are two matters: first, regarding trees that produce fruit every year and also herbs that are not sown. Most people rely on these in the Sabbatical year even though they were not newly planted, having grown from seeds that fell in the field or from roots that were cut previously and grew back. These are called "aftergrowth" <term>Sefichin</term>. According to the Torah, all these are permitted, provided one does not harvest them in the same manner he harvests every other year, as explained in Maimonides, Chapter 4 of the *Laws of the Sabbatical Year*. However, the Sages forbade gathering them because of "transgressors"—so that a person would not go and secretly plant watermelons, cucumbers, and garden greens in his field, and when they grow, eat them and claim "they are merely aftergrowth." Therefore, they forbade all aftergrowth that grows in the seventh year, even to eat them with "Seventh Year Sanctity" <term>Kedushat Shevi'it</term>. Only the aftergrowth of trees and herbs that are not normally sown are permitted to be eaten in the seventh year, even if they grew then, provided they are eaten with "Seventh Year Sanctity"—meaning they must not be wasted and must not be used for commerce, as the laws are explained in Maimonides, Chapters 5 and 6.

# And Since
**And since** a non-Jew has no legal power of acquisition in the Land of Israel to remove its "Seventh Year Sanctity," even produce from a non-Jew's field must be eaten with that sanctity. However, whatever a non-Jew has is treated as "aftergrowth" <note>Sefichin</note>; even if he planted it by hand, I am not commanded over his Sabbatical year. For an Israelite, it is like aftergrowth that rose up on its own, which is permitted to eat with Seventh Year Sanctity. Even though the Sages decreed that an Israelite's aftergrowth is completely forbidden, that is only because the decree against "transgressors" applies there—those who might plant and claim it grew on its own. But in the fields of non-Jews, this decree does not apply, as the Israelite's involvement is known there. Therefore, everything grown by non-Jews, even if planted by hand, is called "aftergrowth" in the hands of an Israelite. These aftergrowths were left under the original Torah law because the Rabbinic decree does not apply. So wrote Maimonides at the end of Chapter 4: "If a non-Jew purchased land in the Land of Israel and sowed it in the seventh year, its fruits are permitted, for the decree against aftergrowth was only because of transgressors, and non-Jews are not commanded regarding the Sabbatical year for us to decree against them." Nevertheless, one is obligated to eat them with "Seventh Year Sanctity."

# And it Seems
**And it seems** to me that when Maimonides wrote "its fruits are permitted," he meant when the non-Jew gives them for free or sells them for a piece of meat and the like. But if there is a concern that money will come into the hands of an Israelite <note>i.e., if an Israelite buys them with money</note>, it is forbidden to buy from him with coins, since the Seventh Year "seizes its value" <note>The sanctity of the fruit transfers to the money used to buy it</note>, and both the fruit and the money remain with Seventh Year Sanctity, as explained in Maimonides, Chapter 6. Consequently, the coin given to the non-Jew for the fruit he bought is sanctified, and one would be obligated to spend that coin only on food to be eaten with Seventh Year Sanctity. If this coin then reaches the hand of another Israelite, he will stumble by using it improperly. This is similar to the law of "cracked wheat" <note>grains that might have become leavened</note> which is forbidden to be sold to non-Jews if there is a concern they might sell it back to an Israelite for Passover, as explained in the *Tur* (Orach Chaim, section 467). This concern applies even if the Sabbatical year in our time is only a Rabbinic obligation <term>D'Rabbanan</term> rather than a Torah one <term>D'Oraita</term>. Even for the one who holds it is Rabbinic, one should not be lenient. We cannot say we only worry about Torah prohibitions like Leaven <note>Chametz</note>, for even with wheat we are concerned even when they are not certainly Leaven by Torah law. It was argued that one could permit it based on a "double doubt" <note>Sfek Sfeika</note>: perhaps they didn't become leavened, and even if they did, perhaps the non-Jew won't sell them to an Israelite. However, since the stringent view is based on a common occurrence, all the more so with the Sabbatical year, which is a "wheel that turns in the world" <note>a cycle that affects everyone</note>. Furthermore, there is no reason to say that the Rabbinic view of Sabbatical sanctity doesn't include the rule that the money "seizes the sanctity." Therefore, the law is simple: it is forbidden to buy vineyards from a non-Jew. I have heard that the "men of action" <note>pious individuals</note> here in Jerusalem (may it be rebuilt) are careful not to buy from them.

# Further
**Further**, I must make known the laws of "Removal" <term>Bi'ur: the obligation to remove Sabbatical produce from one's home once that species is no longer available for animals to eat in the field</term>. One may eat as long as that species is found in the field. To be stringent, the verse says "for the beast that is in your land shall all its increase be for food"—as long as the beast eats this species from the field, you may eat from what is in the house. Once it is gone for the beast in the field, you are obligated to "remove" it. Maimonides wrote in Chapter 7: "When the time for Removal arrives, if he has much fruit, he distributes three meals' worth of food to every person. It is forbidden to eat after the Removal, whether for the poor or the rich. If he did not find people to eat it at the time of Removal, he burns it in fire or throws it into the Dead Sea." However, the *SeMaG* <note>Sefer Mitzvot Gadol</note> wrote that if one declares them ownerless <term>Hefker</term> before three people when the time for Removal arrives, he may re-acquire them and they are permitted. Here is the language of the *Book of the Devout* regarding Maimonides' words: "Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote: 'If he had much fruit, he distributes three meals' worth...' This is from the Mishnah (Shevi'it, Chapter 9). Rabbi Yehuda says the poor may eat after the Removal but not the rich. Rabbi Yose says both poor and rich may eat after the Removal. This is also taught in the *Torat Kohanim* and the Jerusalem Talmud. This is the version of Rabbeinu Shimshon and Maimonides. Maimonides explained: 'Poor' refers to those who gathered fruits from the fields of others as ownerless property; 'Rich' refers to the field owners themselves who gathered from their own fields while they were ownerless." It is known that the law follows Rabbi Yose. They wrote according to this version that wherever it implies eating is forbidden after Removal, it means when one "holds onto them" without declaring them ownerless. But if he removes them from his domain and then re-acquires them, he may keep eating until they are finished. So it says in the Tosefta: "One who has Sabbatical fruits when the time for Removal arrives distributes them to his neighbors, relatives, and acquaintances, and takes them out and places them at the entrance of his house and says: 'Our brothers of the House of Israel, anyone who needs to take, let him come and take.' Then he may bring them back into his house and continue eating until they are finished." The *SeMaG* also cited this Tosefta and wrote: "Thus you have learned that the Sabbatical Year requirement is that a man should not hold onto the fruits as his own, but must declare everything ownerless." In the Jerusalem Talmud, it is told that Rabbi Isaac had some produce, and when the time for Removal arrived, he asked Rabbi Yoshiya, who told him: "Go out and declare it ownerless before others." This is a great remedy for the inhabitants of the Land in this time; even though it is permitted to buy fruit from a non-Jew, since the non-Jew's ownership does not exempt it, the Seventh Year sanctity applies, and one must "remove" them at the proper time. They are like aftergrowths that grow in a fallow field, which are permitted, but still carry the sanctity and the obligation of Removal.

<meta>This page continues the author's instructions for his children regarding agricultural laws in the Land of Israel. While the previous page focused on insects and general purity, this page dives into the complexities of the Sabbatical year (Shmita) and the laws of tithes for produce of doubtful origin (Demai). It draws heavily on Maimonides and Rabbi Yosef Karo.</meta>

# ->The Gate of the Letters<-

If one was pickling <note>original: "Horesh" - here likely referring to a preserving process like pickling or salting</note> and the pickling constitutes the <term>completion of work: the stage of processing when produce becomes legally liable for tithes</term>, since the items are not eaten as they are, then that work is considered finished if done by the hand of an Israelite. However, in the *Book of the Devout* <note>original: "Sefer Charedim" by Rabbi Eliezer Azikri</note>, it was ruled that one is exempt, and his reasoning is sound. The rule that pickling in salt is one of the six things that establish produce for tithes <note>preventing one from eating it as a casual snack without tithing first</note> only applies after the work is finished, as seen at the beginning of the first chapter of the tractate on Tithes. Thus, you cannot say that the act of pickling itself is the "completion"; rather, the completion was already done by a non-Jew, and this is like the completion of all fruits—therefore, even when he pickles them, he is exempt. There are also those who are concerned about lupines <note>original: "Turmusim," a type of legume that is naturally bitter</note>, which are bitter and unfit for eating, wondering if their sweetening constitutes the "completion of work." But it was ruled in the *Book of the Devout* that this is also vanity. He wrote that our Master, Rabbi Yosef Karo <note>the author of the Shulchan Aruch</note>, of blessed memory, instructed that the "completion of work" does not depend on making the fruit fit for eating, for many vegetables are not fit for eating until they are cooked, and yet the Mishnah states: "A vegetable that is bundled is liable from the moment it is bundled."

### **Fruits**

Fruits purchased from a "common person" <term>Am Ha'aretz: a person not trusted to be meticulous with tithing laws</term> are called *Demai* <term>Demai: produce that is "doubtful" as to whether it was properly tithed</term>. They are treated as a doubt; even if the seller says they are tithed, he is not believed. Since the presumption is that they are untithed, one is obligated to separate the Priestly Portion (*Terumah*) and the Tithe (*Ma'aser*), because eating untithed produce is a sin punishable by spiritual excision <note>original: "Koret"</note>. So Maimonides wrote in his composition: since it is a doubt, the Tithe of the Tithe <note>the portion the Levite gives to the Priest</note> is sold to a priest, and this also applies to the tithes of produce from non-Jews. One also separates the Second Tithe, and there is no loss in this, as it remains his own after he redeems it with money. However, regarding the nine parts of the First Tithe <note>given to the Levite</note> and the Poor Man’s Tithe, one is not obligated to actually give them away from *Demai* produce. This is because of the legal principle: "The burden of proof rests on the claimant" <note>original: "Ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-reayah"</note>. One can say to the Levite or the poor person: "Bring proof that this was not already tithed, and then take the tithes." Nevertheless, even though we do not give away the Poor Man’s Tithe from *Demai*, one must still designate it by name, saying: "The tithe of what is here shall be the Poor Man’s Tithe," as Maimonides wrote in the ninth chapter of the Laws of Tithes.

**Now**, you, my children—may the Rock guard you and keep you alive—I shall record some of the conduct for the Seventh Year <term>Shmita: the Sabbatical year occurring every seven years</term>, should you merit to come and dwell in the Land of Israel (may it be rebuilt and may He save you, Amen). Once the New Year of the seventh year begins, which is the Sabbatical year, anyone who has a field or vineyard is obligated to cease working the land. The specific forbidden labors are explained in Maimonides’ *Laws of the Sabbatical and Jubilee Years*. Crops that grow "on their own" during the Sabbatical year without labor are of two types. The first type includes trees that produce fruit every year and wild herbs that most people do not sow. These "on their own" plants in the Sabbatical year come from seeds that fell previously or from roots that were cut and grew back; these are called "aftergrowth" <term>Sefichin: plants that grow from spilled seeds or roots during the Sabbatical year</term. From the perspective of the Torah, all these are permitted, provided one does not harvest them in the usual annual manner. However, the Sages prohibited "aftergrowth" because of transgressors—so that a person would not secretly sow grain, legumes, or vegetables in his field and then, when they grow, claim "they are just aftergrowth." Therefore, they prohibited all aftergrowth of grains and herbs, even for eating with the "sanctity of the seventh year." Only the fruit of trees and wild herbs that are not typically sown are permitted to be eaten in the seventh year, even if they grew in the seventh year. However, one must eat them with the "sanctity of the seventh year" <note>original: "Kedushat Shevi'it"</note>, meaning they must not be wasted and must not be used for business/commerce.

**Since** a non-Jew's ownership in the Land of Israel does not exempt the land from the sanctity of the seventh year, everything belonging to a non-Jew is treated as "aftergrowth." Even though it grew by the hand of a non-Jew, the non-Jew is not commanded regarding the Sabbatical, but for an Israelite, it is like aftergrowth that rose on its own. The law is that they are permitted to be eaten with Sabbatical sanctity. Although the Sages prohibited the aftergrowth of an Israelite's field entirely to prevent people from sowing and lying about it, this decree does not apply to what grows for a non-Jew. This is because the Israelite knows that everything grown by a non-Jew, even if sown by hand, is called "aftergrowth" for the Israelite, and these were left under the original Torah law because the Rabbinic decree does not apply there. So wrote Maimonides at the end of the fourth chapter of *Laws of Sabbatical and Jubilee*: "A non-Jew who bought land in Israel and sowed it in the seventh year—its fruits are permitted, for the decree on aftergrowth was only because of transgressors, and non-Jews are not commanded." But one is still obligated to eat them with the sanctity of the seventh year.

**In my opinion**, these fruits are only permitted when the non-Jew trades them—for example, if he sells them for a piece of meat or similar, where there is no concern it will reach another Israelite. But to buy them from him with money is forbidden, because the money "catches" the Sabbatical status, and both the money and the fruit remain sanctified. This is explained in Maimonides, chapter six. Thus, the coin given to the non-Jew for the fruit becomes sanctified, and it must be spent only on food to be eaten with Sabbatical sanctity. If that coin then reaches an Israelite, he will stumble by using sanctified money for mundane things. This is similar to the law of "wine among wheat" <note>referring to a mix-up where items become forbidden for use, especially regarding Passover</note> mentioned in the *Tur, Orach Chaim* section 467. Even if the Sabbatical year today is only a Rabbinic obligation, we do not permit it by saying the decree of "money catching sanctity" only applies to Torah laws. Furthermore, I have heard that "men of action" <note>pious individuals</note> here in Jerusalem are careful not to buy from non-Jews with money for this reason.

**Additionally**, I must inform you of the laws of "Removal" <term>Biur: the requirement to remove Sabbatical produce from one's home once it is no longer available to animals in the wild</term>. One may not eat the produce once that species is no longer found in the field. As long as a wild animal can eat that species from the field, you may eat what is in your house. Once it is gone for the animal in the field, you must "remove" it. Maimonides wrote that when the time for removal arrives, if one has much fruit, he distributes three meals' worth to every person. It is forbidden to eat it after the removal time, whether for the poor or the rich. If he finds no one to eat it at the time of removal, he must burn it or throw it into the Dead Sea. However, the *Great Book of Commandments* <note>original: "Sefer Mitzvot Gadol" or SMaG</note> wrote that if one renounces ownership <note>original: "Mafkir"</note> in front of three people at the time of removal, it remains permitted. Here is the language of the *Book of the Devout* regarding Maimonides' words: Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote that the Mishnah says one distributes three meals' worth to each person, and the poor may eat after the removal, but not the rich—these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda. But Rabbi Yosesi says both the poor and the rich may eat after removal <note>if it was properly renounced</note>. This is the version found in the *Sifra* and the Jerusalem Talmud. Rabbi Shimshon and Nachmanides also agree. This means the prohibition only applies if one continues to hold onto the produce as his own; but if he renounces it and takes it out of his possession so that any person or animal could eat it, and then happens to acquire it again, he may continue eating it until it is finished. The *Tosefta* says: one who has Sabbatical fruit at the time of removal should distribute it to neighbors and relatives, place it on his doorstep, and say: "Our brothers of the House of Israel, anyone who needs to take, let him come and take." Then he can bring it back in and eat. This is a great remedy for those living in the Land today. Even for the fruits of non-Jews, which have Sabbatical sanctity, they must be "removed" at the proper time.

# The Gate of the Letters

And those gathered in the third year: one separates from them the **Poor Man’s Tithe** <term>Ma’aser Ani: a tithe given to the poor in the 3rd and 6th years of the seven-year agricultural cycle</term>. If they did not reach the stage of tithing until after the New Year <note>Rosh Hashanah</note> of the third year, one separates the Poor Man’s Tithe from them. Similarly, for fruit of the tree that reached the stage of tithing before the 15th of Shevat <note>Tu BiShvat, the New Year for Trees</note> of the third year, even if they ripened and were gathered afterward at the end of the third year, they are tithed according to the past year, and one separates the **Second Tithe** <term>Ma’aser Sheni: a tithe eaten by the owner in Jerusalem</term> from them. Likewise, if they reached the stage of tithing before the 15th of Shevat of the fourth year, even if they ripened and were gathered in the fourth year, one separates the Poor Man’s Tithe from them. But if they reached the stage of tithing after the 15th of Shevat, they are tithed according to the coming year. These are his words. He further wrote there: Regarding vegetables, their tithing follows the time of their picking. How so? If they were picked on the 15th day of the third year, even if they reached the stage of tithing and ripened in the second year, one separates the Poor Man's Tithe from them. If they were picked in the fourth year, the Second Tithe is separated. The citron <note>Etrog</note> alone among other tree fruits is treated like a vegetable, following the time of its picking for both tithes and the Sabbatical year. How so? If it was picked... etc. See there. **And what is the stage of tithing, and what is the "threshing floor" stage that forbids even a snack, and which things establish the requirement for tithes?** All of these are explained in Maimonides' <note>Rambam</note> *Laws of Tithes* in Chapter 3.

**And all this** obligation to separate priestly gifts <term>Terumot</term> and tithes <term>Ma'aserot</term> applies when the produce belongs to an Israelite. However, regarding one who buys from a non-Jew, where the laws have been set: it is not that a non-Jew has a legal acquisition in the Land of Israel to exempt the land from tithes. For Maimonides clearly ruled that a non-Jew has no acquisition in the Land of Israel to exempt it from tithes. Some explain that the distinction of whether there is acquisition or not applies only to Torah law, but regarding Rabbinic law, everyone agrees there is no such acquisition. Thus, whether it is according to the law of the Land or according to Torah law—and even in this present time, according to what I concluded above to rule like Rabbi Yochanan—the sanctity established by Ezra remains holy forever.

**But** there is this distinction: there are fruits that one purchased from a non-Jew while in the possession of the non-Jew in the Land of Israel. After they were finished by the non-Jew, the Israelite is exempt from all priestly gifts and tithes. The obligation is because of the "leveling" <term>Miruach: the smoothing of the pile of grain which signals the completion of processing</term>; a non-Jew is exempt, not because he has acquisition to exempt the land, but because the Torah says "your grain" <note>Deuteronomy 14:23</note> and not the grain of a non-Jew, and the Merciful One did not impose the obligation upon him. But if the non-Jew hired an Israelite to finish his fruits, or if the Israelite finished them for him under duress, since they were finished by an Israelite, they are liable for priestly gifts and tithes. For a non-Jew has no acquisition to exempt the land except when he himself performs the leveling. This is also implied in the *Sefer HaCharedim* in the first chapter of the *Laws of Terumot*, where he wrote: The fruits of a non-Jew that were finished in the ground he bought in the Land of Israel—if their work was completed by the non-Jew and the non-Jew performed the leveling, they are exempt. This implies that only if the non-Jew finished them himself are they exempt, but if an Israelite finished them, they are liable.

**And even** what grows in the field or vineyard of an Israelite—if the work was completed by a non-Jew, they are exempt by Torah law, as Maimonides wrote in the aforementioned chapter. We do not say "a non-Jew is merely a watchman for the Israelite's fruit"; since its legal status is that of being in the non-Jew's hand, they are only liable for priestly gifts and tithes by Rabbinic decree. The general rule of the matter is that everything depends on the act of leveling: if the one who levels is a non-Jew, even if the fruits belong to an Israelite, they are exempt by Torah law. If the one who levels is an Israelite, even if the fruits belong to a non-Jew, they are liable for priestly gifts and tithes. If the one who levels is a non-Jew and the fruits belong to a non-Jew, then they are exempt by Torah law and even exempt from Rabbinic decree—except for the grain and wine of an Israelite, or an Israelite who sells his fruit to a non-Jew after they reached the stage of tithing and the non-Jew completes the work. Even though the non-Jew is the one leveling and the produce should be exempt, the Sages nevertheless made him liable by Rabbinic decree. This was concluded in the *Sefer HaCharedim*, and he explained why the Sages made him liable in these cases and not when the fruits belong to a non-Jew and the finisher is a non-Jew. He said: In these cases, it is a decree because of the "wealthy men" <note>Hebrew: Ba'alei Kissin</note>, as explained in Tractate Menachot in the chapter of Rabbi Ishmael. This refers to wealthy people who own many fields and are stingy with their money, wanting to avoid separating so many priestly gifts and tithes; they would sell the crop to non-Jews before the leveling to be exempt, and thus hire non-Jews to level it. Therefore, the Sages decreed that their cunning would not avail them. But regarding the fruit of a non-Jew grown in his own land, this decree does not apply at all, as stated in the Tosafot <note>Medieval commentaries on the Talmud</note> in the chapter of Rabbi Ishmael. The same law applies to an Israelite who sells his fruits to a non-Jew before they finish ripening—that is, before they reach the stage of tithing; the Sages did not decree here, for surely he would not sell just to be exempt from tithes, since the non-Jew would only buy unripened fruit at a great discount, losing the owner more than the cost of the tithes.

**And there was already** a great controversy in the time of the K.Y. <note>original: "הכ"י", likely referring to the author of the Knesset HaGedolah</note>, for there were those who wanted to tithe the fruit of a non-Jew even if the non-Jew performed the leveling. Most of the Sages gathered and grew numerous, and they decreed with a strict ban <note>Hebrew: Nachash, an acronym for a type of excommunication</note> for all time that no man should tithe what he buys from a non-Jew after the non-Jew has finished and leveled it. This is based on the ruling of Maimonides in the first chapter of the *Laws of Terumot*.

**And if** an Israelite bought them from a non-Jew before their work was completed, there is a distinction: if he bought them while they were still attached to the ground, then their status is as if they belonged to an Israelite and grew on an Israelite's land. He must separate priestly gifts—even a small amount—and give the **First Tithe** <term>Ma'aser Rishon</term> to the Levite, and the **Tithe of the Tithe** <term>Terumat Ma’aser: the portion the Levite gives to the Priest</term> to the Priest. In the years of the Second Tithe, he must redeem it according to the law, and in the years of the Poor Man's Tithe, he must give the Poor Man's Tithe to the poor.

**And if** the Israelite bought them from the non-Jew after they were detached but before the work was completed, and the Israelite finished them, Maimonides wrote in the first chapter of *Laws of Terumot* as follows: "They are liable for everything by Torah law. He separates the **Great Offering** <term>Terumah Gedolah: the first portion given to the Priest</term> and gives it to the Priest. He separates the Tithe of the Tithe and sells it to the Priest. The First Tithe remains his own, because he can say to the Levite regarding the tithe, and to the Priest regarding the Tithe of the Tithe: 'I come with the power of a man <note>the non-Jew</note> from whom you could take nothing.'" And they asked: Why did they say he should not give the Tithe of the Tithe to the Priest like the Great Offering? Because it says regarding the Tithe of the Tithe, "When you take from the Children of Israel the tithe" <note>Numbers 18:26</note>—meaning that whatever you take from an Israelite, you separate from it the Tithe of the Tithe and give it to the Priest. But whatever you take from a non-Jew, you do not give the separated Tithe of the Tithe to the Priest; rather, you sell it to the Priest and take the payment for it. These are his words. Nowadays, we follow the practice of taking the separated Great Offering and Tithe of the Tithe and destroying them by throwing them out in a hidden place. I asked them: "Why do you do this and not give them to the Priest? Granted, in this time it is forbidden to eat or drink the Terumah <note>due to ritual impurity</note>, but one could still benefit from it—if it is oil, he could light his lamp with it!" They answered me that this practice <note>giving to the Priest for fuel</note> is not widespread among everyone, and it is better that it be destroyed so the Priest does not come to a stumbling block <note>accidentally eating it while impure</note>. I said that regarding the Great Offering it is a small matter, as a single grain can exempt the whole pile, and they act correctly. But regarding the Tithe of the Tithe, when it is a large amount, they should not do so; rather, they should give it to the Priest as a gift or for a double payment as the aforementioned Gaon did, so that the Priest has it and will not stumble by it.

**I will return** to the body of the law. Behold, regarding what to do with the Poor Man's Tithe, Maimonides did not mention it, nor did the author of the *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher</note>. However, it is simple to me that it follows the rule of the First Tithe: just as the Israelite says to the Levite, "I come with the power of a man from whom you could take nothing, so from me too you shall not take," he says the same to the poor person. It is the same logic. Only the priestly gifts <note>Terumot</note>, which are themselves forbidden for non-priests to eat, must be given to the Priest (though he takes payment for them). But regarding the First Tithe and the Poor Man’s Tithe, which are not forbidden for an Israelite to eat—the issue is merely a monetary claim—he keeps them for himself. Similarly, he redeems the Second Tithe for a small coin. This is also what he wrote in the *Book of the Devout*, that one keeps the Poor Man’s Tithe for himself in its year. This is also implied in the responsa of Maimonides brought in the *Sefer HaCharedim* (page 52), where Maimonides considers that one only needs to separate and give the Terumot and sell them to the Priest, and also to redeem the Second Tithe, and nothing more. Perhaps just as he does not give the First Tithe to the Levite, so too he does not give the Poor Man's Tithe to the poor. Nevertheless, one must designate them by name for all the tithes because they render the produce "untithed" <term>Tevil: produce from which tithes have not yet been taken and is thus forbidden to eat</term>; even the Poor Man's Tithe renders it untithed, as stated at the end of Tractate Makkot. After that, he keeps the First Tithe and Poor Man's Tithe for himself.

**And if** one buys from a non-Jew after the work was completed by the non-Jew, then he is exempt from everything, as we explained above. There are three categories: 1. Buying from a non-Jew and the Israelite finishes them: then the law is as if it grew for an Israelite and was finished by an Israelite, and he must give the priestly gifts to the Priest without taking payment, and likewise the tithes to the Levite and the poor. 2. When he buys from a non-Jew detached fruit before the completion of work, and afterward the Israelite finishes them: then he gives the Terumah to the Priest but takes payment, redeems the Second Tithe, and keeps the First Tithe and Poor Man's Tithe for himself. 3. When he buys from a non-Jew after the work was completed by the non-Jew: then the Israelite is exempt from everything. Let me repeat: we buy vegetables, legumes, oil, and other fruits from non-Jews because their work was finished by the non-Jew. When we buy them to eat, the work is already finished, and all the fruits are done. But as for servants who buy grapes to make wine, the work of the wine is finished by the Israelite. Similarly, if an Israelite bought olives from a non-Jew to produce oil, and the Israelite produced the oil, then the completion was done by the Israelite; the Israelite is obligated in them and should act according to what I wrote in law #2.

**If** he bought olives from a non-Jew with the intention to eat them and not to produce oil, then their completion was already done by the non-Jew and he is exempt. But when he wants to pickle them in salt, there is...

It also explains the rationale behind the current practice of destroying certain tithes to prevent ritual mishaps.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of agricultural laws in the Land of Israel, specifically focusing on the timing of tithes across the seven-year Sabbatical cycle and the status of produce grown or processed by non-Jews. It refers back to the definitions of "completion of work" mentioned on the previous page.</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

If they were gathered in the third year, one separates the **Poor Man's Tithe** <term>Ma'aser Ani: a tithe given to the poor in the 3rd and 6th years of the seven-year cycle</term> from them. Even if they only reached the "season of tithes" <term>Onat HaMa'asrot: the stage of growth at which produce becomes liable for tithing</term> after the New Year <note>Rosh Hashanah</note> of the third year, one separates the Poor Man's Tithe. Similarly, regarding the fruit of the tree: if they reached the season of tithes before the 15th of Shevat <note>Tu B'Shvat, the New Year for Trees</note> of the third year, even if they were finished and gathered afterward at the end of the third year, they are tithed based on the past year, and one separates the **Second Tithe** <term>Ma'aser Sheni: a tithe eaten by the owner in Jerusalem during the 1st, 2nd, 4th, and 5th years</term> from them. Likewise, if they reached the season of tithes before the 15th of Shevat of the fourth year, even if they were finished and gathered in the fourth year, one separates the Poor Man's Tithe from them. But if they reached the season of tithes after the 15th of Shevat, they are tithed based on the coming year. Thus far are his words. He further wrote there: Regarding vegetables, the time of their picking determines their tithing year. How so? If a vegetable was picked on the first day of the third year, even if it reached the season of tithes and was finished in the third year, the Poor Man's Tithe is taken from it; and if it was picked in the fourth year, the Second Tithe is taken. The Citron <note>Etrog</note> alone among the fruits of the tree is treated like a vegetable, following the time of its picking for both tithes and the Sabbatical year <note>Shmita</note>. How so? If it was picked, etc.—see there for more. **And what constitutes the "season of tithes," what is the "threshing floor" stage that forbids even a snack, and what actions establish a requirement for tithing to forbid snacking?** All of these are explained in Maimonides' *Laws of Tithes*, Chapter 3.

**And all of this** obligation to separate the Great Offering <term>Terumah Gedolah: the first portion given to the Priest</term> and tithes applies to land that was a Jewish conquest. However, regarding one who buys from a non-Jew <note>Hebrew: Goy</note>, the law is as follows: Ownership by a non-Jew in the Land of Israel does not exempt the land from tithes. Maimonides <note>Rambam</note> already ruled as law that a non-Jew's acquisition in the Land of Israel does not uproot the obligation of tithes. Some explain that there is no disagreement over whether there is "acquisition" or not according to Torah law, but according to Rabbinic law, everyone agrees there is no such acquisition <note>meaning the land remains "holy" and liable for tithes</note>. Regarding the Great Offering and tithes, since we hold that nowadays they are Rabbinic, it is as if the non-Jew has no acquisition to exempt them. This is true even if the obligation were from the Torah even in this age, according to what I concluded above to rule like Rabbi Yochanan, that the holiness established by Ezra <note>upon the return from Babylon</note> sanctified the land forever.

**However**, there is a distinction: there are fruits purchased from a non-Jew's field or vineyard in the Land of Israel after they were finished by the non-Jew. In this case, the Israelite is exempt from all Great Offerings and tithes. This is a scriptural decree: the "smoothing of the pile" <term>Miruach: the final processing of grain</term> by a non-Jew grants an exemption. This is not because his ownership uproots the holiness, but because the verse says "your threshing floor" and "your grain" <note>Numbers 18:27; the "your" implies grain finished by a Jew</note>. It seems that even though the Merciful One wrote this, if a non-Jew hires an Israelite to finish his fruits, or if they were handed over to him by force, and they were finished by the hand of an Israelite, they are liable for the Great Offering and tithes. For a non-Jew's ownership does not exempt the produce except when the non-Jew "smooths" it with his own hands. This is also implied in Maimonides' novel insights in Chapter 8 of *The Laws of the Great Offering*, where he wrote: Fruits of a non-Jew that grew in soil he purchased in the Land of Israel—if their work was finished by a non-Jew and the non-Jew smoothed the pile, they are exempt, because specifically the non-Jew finished them with his hands. But if an Israelite finished them, they are liable.

**And even** in a field or vineyard leased from an Israelite, if the work was finished by a non-Jew, it is exempt by Torah law, as Maimonides wrote in the aforementioned chapter: "A non-Jew who finishes the fruits of an Israelite—since their 'smoothing' was done by a non-Jew, they are not liable for the Great Offering and tithe except by Rabbinic decree." The whole matter follows the act of smoothing: if the one smoothing is a non-Jew, even if the fruits belong to an Israelite, they are exempt by Torah law. If the one smoothing is an Israelite, even if the fruits belong to a non-Jew, they are liable for the Great Offering and tithes. If the one smoothing is a non-Jew and the fruits belong to a non-Jew, they stand on their Torah status and are exempt even by Rabbinic decree. This is what Maimonides wrote regarding an Israelite who sells his fruits to a non-Jew after they reached the season of tithes and the non-Jew finishes the work: he is also exempt since the non-Jew is the one smoothing. Nonetheless, the Sages obligated him by Rabbinic decree. This was the conclusion in the *Book of the Devout* <note>Sefer Charedim</note>, and he explained why the Sages obligated him in this case but did not obligate him when the fruits belong to a non-Jew and a non-Jew smoothed them. He said: In the first case, it is because of a decree against "wealthy men" <term>Ba'alei Kissin: literally 'owners of purses'</term> as mentioned in Tractate Menachot, in the chapter of Rabbi Ishmael. This refers to wealthy landowners who have many fields and, wishing to spare their money from separating so much Great Offering and tithe, sell the grain to non-Jews before the "smoothing" stage to be exempt; alternatively, they hire non-Jews to smooth it. Therefore, the Sages decreed that their cunning should not be effective. But regarding the fruits of a non-Jew grown in his own land, this decree does not apply at all, as written in the *Tosafot* <note>medieval commentaries on the Talmud</note> in the chapter of Rabbi Ishmael.

**The same** law applies to an Israelite who sells his fruits to a non-Jew before they finish ripening—that is, before they reach the season of tithes. The Sages did not make a decree here, for he certainly would not sell them just to be exempt from the Great Offering and tithes; since they are not fully ripened, the non-Jew would only buy them cheaply, and the landowner's loss from the low price would be greater than the cost of the Great Offering and tithes.

**And already** there was a great controversy in the time of the holy ones <note>likely referring to the 16th-century scholars of Safed</note>. There were those who wanted to tithe the fruits of a non-Jew even when the non-Jew smoothed the grain. But most of the Sages prevailed and issued a strict decree that for all time, no person should tithe produce purchased from a non-Jew after the non-Jew finished and gathered it. This matter is discussed in the *Kessef Mishneh* <note>commentary on Maimonides by Joseph Karo</note> in Chapter 1 of *The Laws of the Great Offering*.

**And if** the Israelite purchased them from the non-Jew before their work was finished, there is a distinction. If he purchased them while they were still attached to the ground, the law is as if they were the Israelite's own. Even if the non-Jew owned the land, the Israelite must separate the Great Offering—even if only a small amount <note>original: "Reved Mu'at"</note>—and give the **First Tithe** <term>Ma'aser Rishon: 10% given to the Levite</term> to the Levite, and the **Tithe of the Tithe** <term>Terumat Ma'aser: 10% of the tithe given by the Levite to the Priest</term> to the Priest. In the years of the Poor Man's Tithe, he should redeem it according to the law, and in the years of the Second Tithe, he gives it to the poor <note>The text here seems to conflate the years or terms slightly; usually Ma'aser Ani is given to the poor directly</note>.

**And if** the Israelite purchased them from the non-Jew after they were detached but before their work was finished, and the Israelite finished them, Maimonides wrote in Chapter 1 of *The Laws of the Great Offering*: "They are liable for everything by Torah law. He separates the Great Offering and gives it to the Priest. He separates the Tithe of the Tithe and sells it to the Priest, but the First Tithe is his <note>the Israelite's</note>." This is because he can say to the Levite regarding the tithe, and to the Priest regarding the Tithe of the Tithe: "I come by the power of a man <note>the non-Jew</note> from whom you could take nothing. Why then did the Sages say he should not give the Tithe of the Tithe to the Priest like the Great Offering? Because it is said regarding the Tithe of the Tithe: 'When you take from the Children of Israel the tithe' <note>Numbers 18:26</note>. This means untithed produce <term>Tevel</term> that you take from an **Israelite** requires you to separate the Tithe of the Tithe and give it to the Priest. But untithed produce that you take from a **non-Jew**, you do not give the Tithe of the Tithe to the Priest; rather, you sell it to the Priest and keep the proceeds." Thus far are his words. Nowadays, the custom in the Land of Israel is that the one separating the Great Offering and the Tithe of the Tithe takes them and destroys them—he pours them out in a hidden place. I asked them: "Why do you do this and not give them to the Priest? Even though nowadays it is forbidden to eat or drink the Offering <note>due to ritual impurity</note>, one could still use it for sprinkling, or if it is oil, for lighting, or wine for sprinkling on clothes." They answered me that this is no longer considered a service to the Priest, and it is better that it be destroyed so it does not lead to a stumbling block <note>accidental consumption of holy items</note>. I said that regarding the Great Offering, which is a tiny amount nowadays—one grain of wheat exempts the whole pile—they act well. But regarding the Tithe of the Tithe, which is a large amount, they should not do this; they should give it to the Priest for free, or for a cheap payment according to the value of its aforementioned use, and the Priest will be grateful to them so that he does not stumble by it.

**I will return** to the body of the law. Behold, Maimonides did not mention what to do with the Poor Man's Tithe, nor did the *Tur* <note>the legal code Arba'ah Turim</note>. However, it is plain to me that it is the same as the law of the First Tithe: the Israelite says to the Levite, "I come by the power of a man from whom you could take nothing, so you shall take nothing from me either." He should say the same to the poor man, for the reason is one and the same. Only the Offerings <term>Terumot</term>, which are themselves forbidden to non-priests for eating, must be given to the Priest (though he may take payment for them). But regarding the First Tithe and the Poor Man's Tithe, which an Israelite is not forbidden from eating—it is merely a matter of monetary value—he keeps them for himself. Similarly, regarding the Second Tithe, he redeems it for a small coin. This is written explicitly in the *Book of the Devout*: he keeps the Poor Man's Tithe for himself in its year. This is also implied in a Responsum of Maimonides cited in the *Book of the Devout* on page 52. There, Maimonides considers that one only needs to separate and give the Offerings, or sell them to the Priest, and redeem the Second Tithe. Perhaps just as he does not give the First Tithe to the Levite, so too he does not give the Poor Man's Tithe to the poor. Nevertheless, one must "call the name" <note>verbally designate</note> for all the tithes, because they are currently "untithed" <term>Tevel</term>, and even the Poor Man's Tithe causes the produce to be *Tevel*, as seen at the end of Tractate Makkot. Afterward, he himself keeps the First Tithe and the Poor Man's Tithe.

**And if** he buys from a non-Jew after the work was finished by the non-Jew, he is exempt from tithing, as I explained above. Thus, there are three laws: 1) When buying from a non-Jew while the crop is attached and the Israelite harvests it, the law is as if it grew for an Israelite; the Israelite finishes it, gives the tithes to the Levites, and the Offerings to the Priests (taking payment for them), and both the tithes for the Levites and the poor must be given. 2) When he buys from a non-Jew after it is detached but before the work is finished, and the Israelite finishes it, he gives the Offering to the Priest but takes payment for it; he redeems the Second Tithe, and he keeps the First Tithe and the Poor Man's Tithe for himself. 3) When he buys from a non-Jew after the work was finished by the non-Jew, the Israelite is exempt from everything. This is the case for most things we buy from non-Jews, such as wheat, legumes, oil, and other fruits, because their work was finished by the non-Jew. Likewise, when grapes are bought to eat, their work is already finished, as is the case for all fruits. But grapes bought to make wine—the completion of the wine-making happens by the hand of the Israelite. Similarly, if he buys olives from a non-Jew to produce oil, and the Israelite extracts the oil, the completion happens by the hand of the Israelite; the Israelite is then obligated in them and should act according to what I wrote in the second law.

**If** he bought olives from a non-Jew with the intent to eat them and not to produce oil, then they were already finished by the non-Jew and are exempt. But if he wants to pickle them in salt, there is one who...

# The Gate of the Letters

<gloss>
So says Rav Papa regarding the twenty-seven letters <note>original: "כפתח כ"ז", referring to the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet plus the 5 final forms</note>, and the general rule of "MNBPCh" <note>An acronym for the letters pronounced with the lips: Mem, Nun, Vav, Peh, Het—referring to phonetic or mystical groupings</note> was interrupted... until the ruling was made for him as a "petaḥ" <note>A Hebrew vowel mark</note>... like "Lo," "Li," "La," etc., until "And he shall not establish it." See there, for these are types of great dangers, see there. And look at what was discussed regarding several protections in the tractate of Bava Kama, the chapter titled "Ha-Koneh" <note>The Purchaser</note>, see there.
</gloss>

<margin>Furthermore</margin> It was said: Bread baked in the evening <note>original: "mizvach me-apanya"</note> is hard on the belly; bread that is still "breathing" <note>blowing steam</note> is hard on the head; bread that is still "trembling" <note>soft and fresh from the oven</note> is hard on the eyes. What is their remedy? Let it be submerged <note>perhaps in wine or soup</note>. And I heard that this refers to the foam that rises on the barrels when they ferment, but when making a "pouring spout" <note>apopa</note>, when one pours liquid into a vessel, this foam is merely liquid. Nevertheless, it is proper to be careful even there, for **danger is treated more strictly than ritual prohibition** <term>Chamira sakanta me-issura: a legal principle stating that health risks require more caution than religious law</term>.
<margin>Furthermore</margin> It was said: One who eats something that fell from the table to the ground, it is hard on the breath of the mouth.

<margin>Furthermore</margin> It is found in the words of our Sages of blessed memory <note>Chazal</note> that they decreed a third category in the conduct of eating that does not pertain to "forbidden or permitted" <note>Kosher laws</note>, nor is it a matter of great danger; rather, it is **excellent conduct**. As it was taught in the first chapter of Shabbat (page 10a): The first hour is the meal of the Lydians <note>cannibals or gluttons</note>; the second is the meal of heirs <note>who do not work</note>; the third is the meal of heirs; the fourth is the meal of all people; the fifth is the meal of laborers; the sixth is the meal of Torah scholars. From that point onward, eating is like **throwing a stone into a leather wineskin** <note>meaning it is harmful or provides no benefit to the body</note>. Abaye said: We only said this if he tasted nothing in the morning, but if he tasted something in the morning, it does not matter. And it is written in the book *Paths of Faith* <note>original: "Shevilei Emunah," a 14th-century work by Meir Aldabi</note>: The Tanna <note>Sage</note> likens one who eats after six hours to a leather bottle full of wine but lacking a little; if one shakes it, it stays strong, and if one puts a stone in it, the wine will rise because of the stone and will not be so damaged. But the wine will not be as good as if the bottle were full of wine to begin with. So it is for one who eats after six hours; while it will benefit him so that he does not die of hunger, it will not benefit him as much as if he had eaten before six hours. The reason is that before six hours, the stomach seeks its nourishment, and if it does not find it, the "bad humors" <note>unhealthy bodily fluids</note> take over and harm him. This is what he wrote. And it seems to me that Rashi, in his brief words, hinted at what the *Paths of Faith* said. For Rashi’s words "like throwing a stone into a leather wineskin" mean it is hard on the body. But to me, it seems it is neither harmful nor beneficial. Look closely at his words and you will find them in *Paths of Faith*. See how great is the power of Rashi, for every single word is a path from his mouth encompassing great matters.

<margin>In Tractate Bava Metzia</margin> in the chapter "Ha-Mekabel" (page 107b), things were said regarding **morning bread** <term>Pat Shacharit: the morning meal, traditionally bread and salt</term>: It protects against the heat and the cold, and from demons, and makes the simple-minded wise, and makes one successful in legal judgment, and successful in learning and teaching, his words are heard, and his study remains in his hand; his flesh does not produce sweat <note>meaning he stays healthy</note>, he is attentive to his wife and does not desire another woman; and it kills the parasite <note>original: "kinah," perhaps a tapeworm</note> in his intestines. Some say it brings in love and removes jealousy. See there. And also in the chapter "Ha-Chovel": "Better is a small piece of salt than sixty runners who run and cannot catch a man who has eaten his morning meal." And the Rabbis said: Rise early and eat in the summer because of the heat, and in the winter because of the cold. As it is written: "They shall not hunger nor thirst, neither shall the heat nor sun smite them" (Isaiah 49:10). Since they shall not hunger nor thirst, it follows that the heat and sun shall not smite them. One Sage said to another: You tell me this from the Prophets, but I tell it to you from the Torah: "And you shall serve the Lord your God" (Exodus 23:25)—this refers to the Reading of the Shema and Prayer; "and He shall bless your bread and your water"—this refers to bread with salt and a pitcher of water in the morning. From that point onward: "And I will take sickness away from the midst of thee" (Exodus 23:25).

<margin>Furthermore</margin> Many foods are beneficial, as found in Tractate Berakhot, the chapter "How do we Bless" (page 39a). Rav Hisda said: A cooked dish of beets <note>or chard</note> is good for the heart and good for the eyes, and all the more so for the intestines. See there. Rabbah bar Shmuel said in the name of Rabbi Hiyya: After every food you eat, eat salt; and after every drink you drink, drink water, and you will not be harmed. See there. And he who concludes his meal with water will not suffer from intestinal illness. How much? Rav Hisda said: A pitcherful for the bread. Rav Mari said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: One who is accustomed to lentils once every thirty days prevents croup <note>original: "askara," a fatal throat infection</note> from his house; but not every day, because it is hard on the heart's weakness. Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi said in the name of Rav: One who is accustomed to fish does not suffer from intestinal illness. Not only that, but small fish make a person's whole body fruitful and multiply. And it appears to me that "small fish" refers to a species of fish that remains small, as I wrote above regarding "that which rises on a king's table." See there. Rabbi Yannai said: Anything the size of an egg—an actual egg is better than it. Rav Dimi said: One soft-boiled egg is better than six "log" <note>measures</note> of fine flour. Rabbi Zera said: One soft-boiled egg is better than four "shlikata" <note>fully boiled eggs</note>. Anything the size of an egg—an egg is better than it. The Rabbis taught: Cabbage is for nourishment but is hard on the intestines; leeks are hard on the teeth but good for the intestines. Every green vegetable makes one pale; everything small makes one small; every "soul" <note>living creature/meat</note> restores the soul; anything close to the "soul" <note>organs near the heart</note> restores the soul, etc. See there at length.

<margin>See there</margin> Rabbi Isaac said: It is forbidden to eat raw vegetables before the fourth hour <note>approximately 10:00 AM</note>. Rava said to his servant: When you bring me a piece of meat, bring it to me from where it is close to the blessing <note>meaning near where the blessing over slaughter was made, or a choice cut</note>... <note>The text here becomes very technical regarding cuts of meat and their health effects</note>.

<margin>Further</margin> There are many more things there. And also in the chapter "Three who Ate" regarding asparagus, etc. In the chapter "One does not Stand," two things were mentioned: in large amounts they are hard, and in small amounts they are good: the spleen and the diaphragm.

<margin>In Pesachim</margin> in the chapter "These Pass By," the Rabbis taught: Three things increase waste, bend the posture, and take away one five-hundredth of a person's eyesight: coarse bread <note>kibar</note>, new beer, and raw vegetables. This only applies if forty days have not passed, but if it is like other vegetables... if one eats hot food and leeks, it is fine. And in Tractate Bava Kama, the chapter "Mutiple," the Rabbis taught: Five things were said regarding garlic: it satisfies, it warms, it makes the face shine, it increases seed <note>fertility</note>, and it kills parasites in the intestines. Some say it brings love and removes jealousy. I have heard this applies specifically when it is cooked, but raw it is not healthy.

<margin>In Tractate Niddah</margin> in the chapter "Every Hand," and also on page 17, it says: Four things—one who does them is liable for his life and his blood is on his head: One who eats peeled garlic, a peeled onion, or a peeled egg; one who drinks diluted liquids that have stayed overnight; one who sleeps in a cemetery; one who trims his nails and throws them into the public domain; and one who lets blood and then has marital relations. Regarding the one who eats garlic, etc.—even if they are placed in a basket or wrapped and sealed, an **evil spirit** <term>Ruach Ra'ah: a harmful spiritual influence or impurity</term> rests upon them. They only said this if one did not leave a bit of their root or peel on them, but if he left some, there is no concern.

<margin>In Ketubot</margin> in the chapter "Even Though," they mentioned certain things that are hard for pregnant women and harmful; see there. There are many things scattered throughout the Talmud, and I have not recorded them all, but you will see a small portion.

<margin>Now</margin> the time has come to speak of things that point to the concept of **"mundane matters done in the purity of holiness."** It was not for nothing that the Torah mentioned the language of holiness regarding eating: "Sanctify yourselves and you shall be holy." For we find the first commandment given to Man was: "Of every tree of the garden you may surely eat; but of the tree of knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat of it." At first glance, this is difficult; it should have only said "From the tree of knowledge do not eat." But there is a hint here: sometimes eating is a commandment <note>Mitzvah</note>, and sometimes abstaining from eating is a commandment—namely, fasting. Both are essentially the same, for fasts, which diminish one's fat and blood, are like the atonement of a sacrifice. As we say in the prayer: "May it be Your will that my fat and blood which were diminished today be like the fat placed upon the Altar." This matter will be discussed at length later in Tractate Ta'anit, God willing. And sometimes eating is in the mystery of the sacrifice, as our Sages said: "Now, a man's table atones for him," and it stands in place of the Altar. The matter is that eating has both a physical and spiritual aspect, as mentioned above in the name of the divine AriZal <note>Rabbi Isaac Luria, the great 16th-century Kabbalist</note>. The verse says: "Man lives by everything that proceeds out of the mouth of the Lord." Therefore, the connection of the soul with the body is through food; the spirituality of the food strengthens the power of the soul, and the physicality of the food strengthens the power of the body. Both are joined like the hidden soul within the body, whereby the body is sanctified and the soul is refined as a chariot <note>Merkavah</note>. This is hinted at in the verse "Ein Ashnah" <note>The source is unclear, likely a mystical acronym or reference to a text</note>... and this is on the condition that "The righteous eats to satisfy his soul." This means he sanctifies himself through eating that which is permitted, where there is no doubt or fear of prohibition, and he eats only for his sustenance and life-force in order to serve his Creator, to engage in Torah and Commandments, and also gives of his bread to the poor. As will be explained later at length, this is then called a "Commandment Meal" <note>Seudat Mitzvah</note>. On this level, there is a commandment to eat, for all his eating is an altar of atonement like a sacrifice. But for the "evil" of good and evil, the secret is "lusting to eat" all that is forbidden. But the ultimate pleasure of man, who was made in the Image and Likeness, was to resemble the form of his Creator, to be like Him in all His ways, as it says "You are gods." And the food he eats shall be in the mystery of a sacrifice, and his eating shall be sanctified. Through this, we can explain the statement in Midrash Bereshit Rabbah: Rabbi Huna in the name of Rabbi Matna says, "The world was created for the sake of three things: for the sake of the Dough Offering <note>Challah</note>..."

<summary>This page lists various Talmudic health tips and dietary warnings, emphasizing that "danger is stricter than religious law." It concludes by explaining that eating, when done with holy intent and for the sake of serving God, transforms a person's table into an altar of atonement.</summary>

# The Gate of the Letters

<margin>
155. It is good to be stringent and purchase celery <note>original: "karpas"</note> for oneself in... 180. So that it comes from a Jewish hand, as in the Mishnah in the book, etc., and as I wrote above.
</margin>

Regarding the aforementioned: since a non-Jew does not have the power of legal "acquisition" <note>to remove the sanctity of the land</note>, these are like "silver" that grew in the soil of the Land of Israel, which are subject to the law of Removal <term>Bi'ur: the requirement to remove Sabbatical produce from one's home once that crop is no longer available for animals to eat in the fields</term>. For our Sages, of blessed memory, were numerous and powerful, and like the conclusion of the Sabbatical year, they could fulfill the commandment of Removal without a formal declaration, meaning by making it ownerless <term>Hefker: renouncing ownership so anyone may take it</term> as mentioned above. Even though in the opinion of our Teacher <note>likely Maimonides</note> one must burn them—and so wrote Rashi in the chapter "Where They Were Accustomed"—that the Removal happens in a place where the feet of wild and domestic animals tread, nevertheless, the aforementioned Geonim <note>early medieval sages</note> and their proofs are sufficient to rely upon in a time of great need.

We have thus learned that any fruit a Jew buys in the seventh year is subject to all the sanctity of the Sabbatical year. When the time for Removal arrives, he should fulfill the commandment of Removal, which means making them ownerless in the presence of three of his friends, and afterward, he may re-acquire them and eat them forever. Even after the time of Removal, it is permitted to buy them from a non-Jew. For it is proven explicitly from all the great authorities we mentioned above that the fruits of an Israelite were not forbidden after Removal except because he kept them in his house and did not make them ownerless to fulfill the commandment. But for a non-Jew, who was not commanded in this, it is not relevant to forbid them, just as we did not forbid them before the time of Removal. He did not sin by keeping them since he was not commanded. However, once the Jew buys the fruit from the non-Jew, even immediately after the time of Removal, the obligation of Removal falls upon him; he makes them ownerless before three friends and then re-acquires them.

This can also be learned from the words of Nachmanides <note>Ramban</note>, who wrote that if a Jew withheld the fruits in order to eat them <note>without declaring them ownerless</note>, they are forbidden to be eaten. This implies that if we know he did not withhold them to eat them but rather to make them ownerless at the time of their Removal, or after their Removal, they are not forbidden. Likewise, if he was under duress and did not make them ownerless at the time of Removal, when he informs the Rabbinical Court, they should instruct him to make them ownerless or to destroy them... or when his duress passes, he should make them ownerless and then re-acquire them.

### And Know
That in every place where "Removal" is mentioned as "when the crop is gone for the beast from the field," etc., and similarly where the Sages specifically set times—such as: one may eat dried figs until Hanukkah, dates until Purim, grapes until Passover, and olives until Shavuot <note>original: "Atzeret"</note>, as found in the chapter "Where They Were Accustomed"—all these things refer to the eighth year, which follows the Sabbatical year.

### Further
I am here informing the reader to prevent error when studying Maimonides <note>Rambam</note> in the Laws of the Sabbatical Year, Law 9, where he wrote: "On the first of Tishrei is the New Year for the Sabbatical year regarding the eating of sixth-year fruits that entered the seventh." If they were grain, legumes, or fruit of the tree and reached the "season of tithes" before the New Year, they are permitted. The meaning of "New Year" here is the New Year that falls on the 15th of Shevat for trees, and for grain, the literal New Year <note>1st of Tishrei</note>, as written in Law 13. And regarding Sabbatical fruits that go out into the year following the Sabbatical: for grain, legumes, and trees, we follow the "season of tithes." This is the explanation: tree fruits that reached the season of tithes before the 15th of Shevat of the eighth year, even if they ripened and were gathered afterward at the end of the eighth year, they are considered Sabbatical fruits.

## And You Shall Surely Know
That the entire Sabbatical year is ownerless; there are no priestly gifts <note>Terumot</note> nor tithes <note>Ma'aserot</note>, neither First Tithe, Second Tithe, nor the Poor Man's Tithe. It is written in the book *Sefer Charedim*: even fruits that grew on the land of a non-Jew in the seventh year... are like those grown on Jewish land and are exempt from tithes. This is the practice and the ruling of the giant of the generation, Moshe di Trani <note>the Mabit</note>, of blessed memory.

## Since You Are Sons
My children, I have revealed to you some of the matters of tithes and the Sabbatical year, as you will soon arrive at the land. When the Sabbatical year comes, be careful regarding the "Cancellation of Debts" <term>Shmitat Kesafim: the Torah's requirement to forgive outstanding loans at the end of the Sabbatical year</term>, which applies even outside the Land of Israel. The *Ya'abetz* cried out like a crane <note>a metaphor for loud, persistent protesting</note>—why is this not observed? As explained in the *Tur*, *Choshen Mishpat* section 67. The matter is easily fixed by means of a *Pruzbul* <term>Pruzbul: a legal document that transfers private debts to a rabbinic court, allowing them to be collected after the Sabbatical year ends</term>. Do this while you are healthy and well. While I was still outside the Land, I saw some of my sons who were careful in this, for how could a person neglect the commandment of his Creator, especially a commandment that comes only once every seven years? You can know which year is the Sabbatical according to what I wrote above; the Sabbatical year will be the year 370 [1610 CE]... may you run to the commandment and may God be with you.

## The Prohibition of Uncovered Liquids

<margin>
How much did our Sages, of blessed memory, debate these prohibitions in the Mishnah and Gemara, and how many laws there are, as explained in the *Tur*, *Yoreh De'ah*, and the *Beit Yosef*, section 116. They were more stringent regarding a doubt of danger than a doubt of ritual law. It says in the Gemara that Shmuel would not drink water from the house of a widow, for she has no fear of a husband and might not be careful, and he feared perhaps the water had been left uncovered <note>where a snake might have drunk and left venom</note>. Truly, the *Tur* and the *Or Zarua* wrote that people are now lenient even in apartments with uncovered liquids, as snakes are not commonly found now, etc. This is from the words of the Tosafot in the chapter "One May Not Stand." Nevertheless, "he who guards his soul will keep far from them," and "holy shall he be called." Regarding those who are lenient, we say "The Lord preserves the simple," since many have trodden this path. But this custom... you should know that if you do not say this, it is a great virtue to guard oneself and act according to all the laws explained in the Mishnah and Talmud. Why else would the *Tur* have written all the laws if nothing remained of them? It must be as explained.
</margin>
How much did our Sages, of blessed memory, debate these prohibitions in the Mishnah and Gemara... <note>The main text repeats the content of the margin note regarding uncovered liquids and the risk of snake venom.</note>

### Further
It is explained there in the *Tur* that several things are forbidden, as in the first chapter of *Avodah Zarah*: "Our Rabbis taught: A person should not drink from rivers, nor from streams, nor from ponds because of the danger." What is the danger? Leeches.

## In Tractate Shabbat
In the chapter "One Who Takes Out Wine," and in Tractate *Chullin*, the chapter "All Flesh": It says there that one who pulls a vegetable from a bundle that was tied in a garden—it is difficult <note>dangerous</note> regarding witchcraft. Three things are considered difficult regarding witchcraft: 1. Pulling a vegetable from a bundle; 2. Killing a louse on one's clothes; 3. Wiping oneself with a potsherd. Therefore, "he who guards his soul will keep far."

## And in the Chapter 'Arvei Pesachim'
Rabbi [X] said: Four things, he who does them, his blood is on his own head <note>he is responsible for his own demise</note>, and one of them is drinking "diluted" water <note>original: "mayim she-chalin," likely meaning water left out or of questionable source</note>. And it was said: We only said this if a child asked for them, but if an adult asked for them, we have no concern.

## And in Tractate Chullin

<margin>
Section 69.
According to the chapter "One Who Sells Fruit," which discusses great dangers. Sometimes one is smitten... for one who enters between a palm tree and a wall... and one who passes over spilled water, etc. And see there... that one does not fast or suffer... and there are those who say...
</margin>
In the chapter "All Flesh," he mentioned several things regarding eating that lead to danger: One should not pour the "final waters" <term>Mayim Acharonim: the ritual washing of fingers after a meal</term> onto the ground. He said the reason is not just because of filth, but because an "evil spirit" rests upon them.

### Further
He said: One should not remove anything from the table while a person is holding a cup in his hand, not because something might go wrong with the meal, but because it is "difficult" <note>leads to</note> for "tzareda" <note>likely a type of seizure or trembling</note>. This applies to taking it and not returning it, but taking it and returning it is fine.

He said: Regarding the sweeping of crumbs—it is not only for the sake of cleanliness, but because it is "difficult"...

### A Good Custom

It is for a person to habituate himself to take a "quarter-log" <term>Revi'it: a Talmudic liquid measure, roughly 3-4 ounces</term> in one pouring on his hands: once on his right and once on his left.
