<meta>This page continues the discussion of the table as a spiritual altar, moving into the mystical significance of the "First" offerings—Challah, First Fruits, and Tithes—and how the act of eating can be transformed from a physical necessity into a sacrificial act of atonement and holiness.</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

<margin>
Sign 60
As a general rule regarding tithes, it also hints at the holiness of eating grain <note>original: "טבכר", likely a corruption of "תבואה" (produce) or a reference to a specific crop</note>, for tithes are indeed applied to spelt <note>original: "בכסמס", likely "כוסמין" (spelt)</note>.
</margin>

**Challah** <term>Challah: the portion of dough set aside for the priests</term>, **First Fruits**, and **Tithes**: it is in the merit of the **First Fruits** that the world was created. Why does the verse say, "*In the beginning* <note>original: "Bereshit"</note> God created the heavens and the earth"? For there is no "beginning" <note>Reshit</note> except for **Challah**, as it is said, "The *first* <note>Reshit</note> of your dough-kneading"; and there is no "beginning" except for **Tithes**, as it is said, "The *first* <note>Reshit</note> of your grain"; and there is no "beginning" except for **First Fruits**, as it is said, "The *first* <note>Reshit</note> of the fruits of your land." This concludes the Midrash.

We must ask: what is the great power of these three commandments that the world was created for their sake? It is understandable when our Sages said elsewhere that the world was created for the sake of the **Torah** and **Israel**, as that includes everything—the world exists for Israel so they may receive the Torah. But here it is difficult. Furthermore, the Midrash uses the language of exclusion: "There is *no* beginning except Challah," implying that nothing else can be called "beginning" but Challah. Then it says the exact opposite for Tithes and a third time for First Fruits. Thus, these three statements seem to contradict one another. 

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the first of your grain," this refers to the **Great Contribution** <term>Terumah Gedolah: the first gift given from the harvest to the priest</term>, yet the Midrash applies it to Tithes? Why did it change the language? 

The matter is this: the ultimate purpose of creation was for the sake of the Torah, which man fulfills. Just as the Torah has a "body" and a "soul"—meaning the revealed and the hidden aspects—which are bound together, so too is man. He has 248 limbs and 365 sinews corresponding to the 613 commandments. He is "holy" and "holy of holies," meaning holy from the side of the soul, while the body is also worthy of being holy. 

But how is this possible? Does man not have animalistic traits, such as drinking and eating? He eats like an animal; how then can he maintain a connection to the Torah, which is holy in its revealed sense and the "holy of holies" in its hidden sense? To solve this, the Holy One, Blessed be He, sanctified the food that man eats. He commanded that the "beginning" <note>Reshit</note> of the food be taken for His Name and given to the Priest. Only then is the remainder permitted. This is explained in the *Gates of Light* <note>Sha'arei Orah, a foundational 13th-century Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla</note> regarding the secret of the "Hundred Blessings," and the secret of Priest, Levite, and Israelite, and the secret of the Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah <note>the three levels of the soul: the vital, the emotional, and the intellectual</note>. 

The Israelite gives ten percent to the Levite, and the Levite gives one-tenth of that to the Priest. Furthermore, when the grain is ground and becomes dough—and bread is the most important part of the meal, for a meal is named after the bread—it is called "the first of your dough-kneading." Since the fruits of the tree still remained unsanctified, the Holy One, Blessed be He, commanded to take from the Seven Species <note>the seven agricultural products special to the Land of Israel</note>, which are the "kings" over all fruits, the **First Fruits** <note>Bikkurim</note>. Then everything becomes sanctified.

This is the meaning of the Midrash: "There is no beginning except Challah." This means that when it becomes dough, the previous sanctifications are not enough; it specifically requires the "first of your dough." Similarly with Tithes, the "first beginning" <note>the Terumah</note> is not enough on its own.

<margin>
Sign 25
Know that at every level of this process, the **Tzadik** <term>Tzadik: a righteous, spiritually refined person</term> brings down the spirituality of the food during his eating. One brings down the holiness from the spiritual source, for "soul toils for soul." There are levels of "soul of the soul." Similarly, for all sacrifices, there is a different essence that causes a "pleasing aroma" to rise to God from above. This is explained in the *Gate of Holiness* <note>Sha'ar HaKedushah by Hayyim Vital</note>, Part 3. Regarding the order of the levels of eating for Israel, this is mentioned in the Zohar, portion *Beshalach*. Evidence is found in the name of our Righteous Messiah... it is explained that one who is worthy receives the **Manna**, which is from the upper world. "I will rain down bread for you from heaven"—this is the generation of Moses. Indeed, they ate the "tastes of the Lord" before the higher pleasure that spreads to all worlds. It was in the secret of holiness, for "The table which is before the Lord" is the secret of the **Showbread Table**, which was always before Him. 
</margin>

Only when the Tithes are given does the holiness descend. Then, a person is prepared in body and soul to receive the Torah in its revealed and hidden aspects. The general rule is: a person who is a **Tzadik** and eats only what is permitted to him, his eating is in the place of a sacrifice. He directs the "attribute of formation" toward the Creator, as it were. His eating is like the holiness of the altar's consumption, for he eats only so that his soul may remain attached to the service of his Creator. 

But one who has distanced himself from the Holy One, Blessed be He, and blemished his soul, must bring a literal sacrifice for himself to restore peace and spiritual vitality. He must bring himself as an offering, for he has become like an animal. Since he distanced himself, "he is compared to the silenced animals." This is the secret of the verse: "When a man <note>Adam</note> among you brings an offering to the Lord; from the animals, from the cattle or the sheep, you shall bring your offering." The hint is: a man who has become distant needs to bring *himself* near—that is the meaning of "brings an offering *from among you*." But one who is already close and attached to the Name <note>original: "Y-W-D-A", likely a cipher for the Tetragrammaton Y-H-V-H</note>, then the Name of the Lord is upon him, and "from the animals... you shall bring your offering" means that what you *eat* is your sacrifice.

The text uses the word **Adam** rather than **Ish** <note>two different Hebrew words for "man"</note> to hint at the "Man" in the vision of Ezekiel. According to his spiritual path, if Adam had not sinned, he would have been commanded to eat from every tree of the garden, for he would have brought down the spiritual influence of the food from above. As mentioned, every food has a spiritual essence. But when Adam sinned, the repair was **Fasting** <note>Ta'anit</note>. In the book *Ten Utterances*, it is written that Adam fasted all the days of his life—the 130 years mentioned by the Sages—as part of the repentance he performed. He fasted for the number of years equal to the numerical value of **Ta'anit** <note>Ta'anit (תענית) = 580. The text notes "480" or "580" and mentions this will be explained at length later</note>.

In the tractate *Ta'anit*, it explains that since he sinned through eating, and eating brought death to the world, the repair is fasting. However, this "death" is also very "good" <note>referencing a Midrash on Genesis 1:31</note>, and in the future, eating will return to a spiritual state that sustains, such as the Manna hidden for the righteous. This is hinted at in the name of **Eve** <note>Chaya</note>, for she was "the mother of all living" <note>Chai</note>. Eve caused death through eating, but in the future, she will return to life. This is the secret of "Mother of All" <note>Em Kol</note>: the letters of "Mother of All" <note>A-M-K-L</note> are the same as **Food** <note>Ma'akal: M-A-K-L</note>. 

The word **Food** <note>Ma'akal</note> has the numerical value of **91**, which is the same as the union of the two Names of God <note>Y-H-V-H (26) + A-D-N-Y (65) = 91</note>. Before the repair, man lives through fasting or his food is a sacrifice for him. Even now, one who is a Tzadik, through his righteousness and pure thought, brings down the spiritual flow of food from the highest heights. In his eating and drinking, he should have this intention: for example, if he drinks water for his thirst, he should think that water is "Kindness" <note>Chesed</note> emerging from the "Fire of Strength" <note>Gevurah</note>. When he drinks wine, he should think of the "Wine Preserved in its Grapes" from the six days of creation.

There is a hint in the verse: "For the tree of the field is man's [life]... do not cut it down." Behold, the tree from which Adam ate caused a "cutting off." But the "Food Tree" is the secret of the holy festivals. Also, the Name of God <note>Y-H-V-H</note> is hinted at in the word "Tree" <note>Etz</note>... this is the aspect of "This is my God," and "This is the table which is before the Lord." In the secret of the beginning, the **Snake** <note>Nachash</note> was involved with the tree of Adam, and the letters of the **Table** <note>Shulchan</note> were given over to the Snake. However, the **Pure Table** has the letters of **His Whisper** <note>Lachashan</note>, which is the upper holiness carried by the High Priest. The table is an altar of atonement. Our Sages said: "The Priests eat, and the owners are atoned for." This hints at the souls reincarnated in pure foods; the one who eats in the aforementioned way is like the Priest, and through this, the "owners" (the souls within the food) are atoned for. This will be explained further, God willing.

<column-break/>

Behold, through the order of the spiritual levels of food, it is explained in the Zohar... that everything he ate was through the Name of God. As it is written in the verse, one who eats with holy intention receives nourishment from the Divine Splendor. Abraham used to ask the travelers about the spirituality of the nourishment, as we say in the Grace After Meals: "Who feeds the whole world in His goodness, with grace and with kindness."

Anyone who sanctifies himself more draws a more internal spiritual flow through his eating. This fits well with what is written in the *Gate of Holiness*, that the table is like an altar. So too wrote Rabbeinu Yonah in the *Book of Fear*: a penitent must confess before eating and examine his deeds up to that moment. Then his body becomes a vehicle for holiness... a person is not worthy of holy food except through great kindness. 

Behold, every person of flesh should fulfill "You shall slaughter... and you shall eat" before the Lord your God, in the place of a sacrifice. In every sacrifice, there was a confession <note>Viduy</note> to atone for sins. Therefore, before the "Table of Wisdom," one should confess for his wickedness so that he may be worthy. On the Sabbath and Festivals, when we do not say the standard confession, one should instead say the verse: "And you shall direct your heart to the Lord... to love the Lord your God with all your heart and all your soul, for the sake of your life," and arouse oneself to general repentance.

# The Gate of the Letters

Kingship <note>original: "Malchut"</note> stands around Foundation <note>original: "Yesod"</note> and is subjected from the opening <note>original: "pstat semi" - likely a Kabbalistic shorthand for a specific permutation of divine names</note> and *Zeir Anpin* <note>The emotive divine attributes</note>... and it is like "from my name" and *Zeir Anpin* or the "Other Side" <note>original: "ss," likely referring to Samael</note> to seal them, sweetened judgments, and they rectify them.

It includes because it is a "New Moon," there Kingship is rectified from the left into the right, and the foundation of the right, and those are "Goodness and Kindness," and the foundation and those are "the 70 names." And "Goodness and Kindness" of the days are plucked in the 36 [attributes] in Understanding and spread over the six [directions]... all the days of my life... And the secret that was rectified from the right: "I shall dwell in the House of the Lord," which is the Kingship called the "House of the Lord," there is Beauty for the "length of days" to the Crown <note>Keter</note> which is above it... "for length of days." And after the spheres were included through the rectification of the table, there is a prayer in the way of a request: "May it be Your will, Lord my God and God of my fathers, that I have intended my intentions, and provide my sustenance and the sustenance of the people of my household with the sustenance and provision of all Your people Israel by Your hand. Do not make me dependent on the gifts of flesh and blood, nor on their loans, but only on Your hand... The eyes of all look to You in hope, and You give them their food in its proper time; You open Your hand and satisfy the desire of every living thing." One should be careful to pray this immediately after their prayer so that it serves as the rectification for the food in the "House" as explained in the Zohar, until here. And the words of the holy teacher <note>the Arizal</note> explained the words of Rabbi Yiba the Elder etc. that if he did not rectify the table, he would not be provided for.

**Regarding the law** mentioned in *Orach Chayim* section 168: that one places a broken piece of bread under a whole loaf and breaks from both together (see there), the Great Genius Rabbi Solomon Luria <note>the Maharshal</note> wrote that if there is another person with him, it is proper to divide them, so that one makes the blessing over the whole loaf and one over the broken piece.

**Gloss:** The *Sefer Mitzvot Katan* <note>The "Small Book of Commandments" by Rabbi Isaac of Corbeil</note> wrote in the laws of prayer that regarding what we say—that it is forbidden to pray without a belt—this only applies to the "Standing Prayer" <note>the Amidah</note>. But regarding the *Shema* and other blessings, there is no concern about the belt, provided that "his heart does not see his nakedness" <note>meaning there is a physical barrier, like trousers, between the upper body/heart and the genitals</note>, as implied in the chapter "One who stands" in the tractate *Shabbat*, where they wanted to remove their belts during the meal, even though they were reciting the blessing over the bread and the Grace after Meals. However, if his heart "sees" the nakedness, it is forbidden even for other blessings, contrary to Rashi's commentary who says it is permitted. So wrote the Ran in the 104th chapter of *Shabbat*.

**Ethical Words** <note>original: "Divrei Musar"</note> that a person should practice at the meal are explained in the *Tur Orach Chayim* and in the glosses of section 170. Regarding what is written: "One should not drink his cup in one gulp, and if he does, he is a glutton." Know that every "cup" mentioned by the Sages without qualification refers to a *revi'it* <note>a "quarter-measure," approximately 3–5 ounces</note>... and anyone who shames his fellow through a matter of law etc. should guard against these things, and his heart should be free for his Creator, and the table should be clean and pure. A person should seat the poor and the unlearned <note>original: "Ammei Ha-aretz"</note> at his table to teach them words of Torah. He should be humble and lowly upon seeing the goodness of the Holy One, blessed be He, and his heart should be humbled before Him. After the meal, he should bless the man, his household, his children, and all that is his with a blessing. A *revi'it* is the volume of an egg and a half. Give to a manservant or maidservant from every type of food and drink, as explained in the *Tur Orach Chayim* section 169.

<margin>
to give
And it seems to me
</margin>
**And it seems to me** that if he gave to him at the start, during the breaking of the bread, he is not obligated to give him exactly the same foods he eats, but only to give him food like the rest of the household members. Or perhaps, as a matter of pious conduct, he should give him from every type that is a luxury or that the servant craves, just as we find regarding a Hebrew slave—where the Torah says one should not make him perform "slave labor," like carrying his clothes after him to the bathhouse. Yet we see everyone uses our servants for such things; the reason is that from the start, we hire the servant on the condition that he will perform these tasks.

**H.B.Y.** <note>likely an abbreviation for a specific commentator</note> in the aforementioned section brings the words of Rabbenu Yonah... who wrote regarding a servant who has not washed his hands: "It is forbidden to place a piece of bread into his mouth." Some say we can learn from here that it is not proper to give food except to one whom you know will recite a blessing. But it seems that since one intends to perform a commandment by giving as charity <note>original: "Torat Tzedakah"</note>, it is permitted. However, his words do not seem correct, for giving to a servant is also a commandment, and even so, one should not give to him unless he knows he has washed his hands. In truth, the *Keneset HaGedolah* rejected the words of Rabbenu Yonah, for at the time he is performing the "breaking of the bread" <note>HaMotzi</note>, it is part of his wages, a portion of his work for which the employer is obligated to provide sustenance. Therefore, it seems that in the context of charity, it is proper to give even to someone whose habits are unknown—provided you do not know *for certain* that he will *not* bless, which would violate "Do not place a stumbling block before the blind." However, it is a good thing when giving to a poor person whom you do not know for certain will bless, to say to him: "Take this, wash your hands, and recite a blessing before and after eating." Furthermore, it seems that even if you know he has committed some other sins, do not refrain from giving to him for that reason, unless he is a wicked person in all matters. Perhaps this was the intention of Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram in the chapter "The Partners," when Rabbi [Judah the Prince] opened his storehouses [during a famine] and forbade the unlearned from entering. Rabbi Yonatan did not want to reveal his identity, so he said: "Feed me like a dog or a raven." Rashi and the Tosafot explained what they explained, but it can be explained that he meant: "Behold, the dog and the raven sinned, as the Sages said: Three mated in the Ark [against the rules]: Ham, the dog, and the raven... yet despite this, Noah fed them. So you should feed me." Rabbi fed him, and though he was pained later [thinking he fed an unlearned person], nevertheless, when dealing with a person, it is a great good. This is the proper conduct even if he is lowly in other matters: give to him as charity and warn him to wash his hands and bless before and after eating; this is good and upright. When giving a piece of bread to a poor person, give it with honor and a pleasant countenance. As the Zohar says: Rabbi Pinhas would spread a tablecloth for the hungry... a person's portion is such that if a poor person happens upon him, whoever receives him with a pleasant face, fortunate is his portion... it is as if he created the soul for himself. For this reason, Abraham was kind to all the world, and the Holy One, blessed be He, considered it as if he made them, as it is written: "And the souls they made in Haran." And even though we established "do not spread"—what is "do not spread"? To spread a tablecloth over the bread and food for the wise... Rabbi A. would spread a cloth, as it is said "break" <note>peros</note> a piece, and we must spread a cloth and offer comfort before his children so he is not shamed. And "break" it before him with a good eye. Thus, the matter of spreading a cloth for him is a way of showing honor, like inviting a guest and rejoicing with him.

**In the Zohar**, portion *Terumah*: "He who awakens at the table and enjoys those foods must remember and grieve over the holiness of the Holy Land and the Palace of the King which is destroyed. Because of that sadness he shows, he may remain at his table with the joy he has, and there the Holy One, blessed be He, considers it as if he built His House and rebuilt all those ruins of the Temple; fortunate is his portion." Therefore, we are accustomed to say the Psalm "By the Rivers of Babylon" (137) before the Grace after Meals. Specifically because the table is in place of the Altar, but due to our many sins, we do not have the Altar itself. One should remember: "Woe to the children who were exiled from their Father's table," and the exile of the table is because the Temple was burned... as the Zohar says on *Lamentations*: the acronym of "How" <note>Eikhah</note> is "How <note>Eikhah</note> does the City <note>Ha-Ir</note> sit <note>Yashva</note> solitary <note>Badad</note>." But on Sabbath and Festivals, we say the Psalm "When the Lord returns the captives of Zion" (126).

**And one should not bless** over an empty table, as it says in the chapter *Chelek*: "Anyone who does not leave bread on his table will never see a sign of blessing." And in the Zohar, portion *Terumah*, the reason is given: the supernal blessing does not rest upon "nothingness" but only upon "something." This is the secret of "The Table which is before the Lord," which was always set with the Showbread <note>Lechem HaPanim</note>, through which blessing spread to the sustenance of the world in the manner of "something from something." Just as with the jar of flour and the cruse of oil [of Elijah], everything was "something from something." In the chapter *Chelek*, it says this specifically when there is no whole loaf with him, but if there is a whole loaf, he is like one who serves idols, who "set a table for Luck" <note>referring to Gad, a pagan deity</note>. Rashi explains this as one who brings a whole loaf after he has eaten so it remains on the table... implying the prohibition is only to *bring* a whole loaf, but if it was already there, he need not remove it. So it is in the *Shulchan Aruch*. But the general language implies it is forbidden whenever a whole loaf is present with him. So wrote Maharil section 40: "From here it seems one should remove the whole loaf from the table when reciting Grace after Meals." Furthermore, it is proper to prepare a clean, whole table, for it is like the word in the Medrash that blessing is not found [on emptiness]. The Rosh wrote in *Berakhot*: "In some places, they have the custom to extend meat and bread and give it to a poor person before the one reciting the blessing."

**And one must** remove the knife from the table during the blessing because the table is an Altar, and it is written: "You shall not build it of hewn stone," for iron shortens life and the Altar lengthens it. No iron tool was heard in the House [the Temple] while it was being built. Furthermore, the *Beit Yosef* brings reasons in section 180 and wrote that he did not know how to distinguish between Sabbath and weekdays; however, the custom of Israel is the law <note>meaning they only remove it on weekdays</note>. In *Tola'at Yaakov*, a reason is given: that it is forbidden to lift iron over the Altar because iron represents the power of Esau <note>war/sword</note>, therefore it should be removed from the Sanctuary. But on Sabbath, when there is peace in everything and no Accuser or evil occurrence, and iron is the "sword of the Sabbaths," one should not remove it, for we do not stir up judgment at all. Therefore, on Sabbath, we do not remember the destruction of the Temple, but only the building of the Temple in our consolation. Then you shall establish them according to the words of Rabbi Simcha brought by the *Beit Yosef*.

After the final washing of the hands <note>Mayim Acharonim</note>, when he is ready to recite Grace after Meals, he should say: "Behold I am prepared and ready to fulfill the positive commandment of Grace after Meals, as it is said: 'And you shall eat and be satisfied and bless the Lord your God for the good land He has given you,' for the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shekhinah <note>Divine Presence</note> through that which is hidden and concealed." And let it be...

# The Gate of the Letters

I have received a tradition that it is good to break the bread—especially on Sabbaths and Festivals—from a loaf made in a long shape, which resembles the letter *Vav* (ו).
Then, the Name of God <note>YHVH</note> is hinted at, which includes all ten "beings." Specifically: the breaking of the *Hamotzi* bread is in the shape of the letter *Yod* (י).
The two hands that hold the bread (as mentioned above) have five fingers on each hand; these represent the two *Hehs* (ה)
of the Name. The bread itself is in the shape of the *Vav* (ו). Thus the Name is completed.
Behold, how many sanctities are there in the breaking of the bread and in every piece he breaks from it! It is written
in the *Sefer Chasidim*: "The bread over which he recited the *Hamotzi* blessing, he would not give any of it to a servant [first]." And from
the *Hamotzi* bread he would leave a little and eat it after the meal... so that
the taste of the blessing remains in his mouth. And it is written: "He shall leave a blessing behind him" <note>Joel 2:14</note>. And thus says the *Kolbo* in Chapter 24:
"All Israel is accustomed not to feed domestic animals, wild beasts, or birds from the piece of bread that touches
the piece used for the blessing." So wrote Rabbi Asher <note>The Rosh, a 13th-century legalist</note>. And so too in the *Abudraham*. The *Agur* wrote in the name of Rabbi
Avigdor, who wrote in the name of Rabbi Simcha: "A person must eat the bread he broke at the start [of the meal]
before he eats any other bread, so that he eats it with appetite." This is from the words of *Shibbolei HaLeket*. Nevertheless,
one should leave a little to eat at the end of the meal, as mentioned above in the name of *Sefer Chasidim*.

Since the blessing over bread and the washing of hands are connected to each other, one should not interrupt between them, as I wrote above.
Even an interruption without speaking—if he delayed for the time it takes to walk 22 cubits <note>approx. 33 feet or 10-11 meters</note>—it is considered an interruption,
according to the *Rema* in the *Tur*, Orach Chaim, Chapter 166.

Regarding one who relieves himself and then wishes to eat: there is a debate among the legal authorities as to how he should proceed with the blessings of
"Who formed man" <note>Asher Yatzar</note> and "On the washing of hands" <note>Al Netilat Yadayim</note>. Opinions are many. In the book *Birkat Avraham*, he wrote at length
that every known opinion has a flaw. Therefore, a person should wash twice: on the first, he blesses "Who formed man,"
and on the second, "On the washing of hands." Nevertheless, he should be careful to touch a covered place on his body [between washings] so that he brings
himself into a definite obligation to wash; for if his hands remained clean and he simply washed them, how could he bless "On the washing of hands"
afterwards? This is simple to understand.

## And it seems to me
Regarding the "Prayer for Sustenance" which the *Zohar* says a person should pray for his food: it is written in the book *Kitzur Reishit Chochmah* <note>An influential 16th-century Kabbalistic ethical manual</note>:
"Furthermore, he should pray for his sustenance every day after his [standard] prayer before he eats...
and each one should pray according to his strength." Men of [pious] action have provided a version to say before washing: "You are the God
who feeds, sustains, and provides for all creatures in Your kindness, from the horns of wild oxen to the eggs of lice. The eyes of all
look to You... You open Your hand..." <note>Referencing Psalm 145</note>. It seems to me that if he forgot and did not pray until he had already washed his hands,
he may pray it between the washing and the *Hamotzi* blessing, and it is not an interruption. Just as they said that even between
the blessing and the eating, saying "Bring salt" or "Bring food for the oxen" is not an interruption since it is for the needs of the meal—
so too this prayer is for the needs of the meal. For even if one has all the food ready, he must pray for it, as it says
in the *Zohar* regarding Rav Yeiva the Elder: even though he had food to eat, he would not prepare it until he had requested it from the "House of the King" in prayer. The reason is that the intention of the prayer is for the Holy One to bestow upon him the spiritual sustenance
which is the root of the physical food, so that his eating may be in holiness.

...into his mouth, the piece of the *Hamotzi*, and he speaks at the time of tasting before swallowing, it is considered an interruption. And from this law, there is an additional prohibition not to bless at the time of tasting, for we have learned that
one may taste [during a fast] for the sake of the taste... <note>This gloss clarifies the technicalities of "tasting" versus "eating" and the danger of making an "interruption" (hefsek) between a blessing and its fulfillment.</note>

## And even though
I said it is an interruption if he speaks at the time of tasting, nevertheless, I do not say this without reason. Even after the fact, if he wrote and spoke at the time of tasting, he should
return and bless, just as one who interrupts between the blessing and the eating. Since we do not want to be in a state of doubt regarding a blessing, he should remove himself from the doubt and calculate his words with thought.
He should not speak from the beginning of the blessing until the swallowing of the food... there is a time to speak and a time for commandments.

And my custom was formerly: before the washing and outside [the dining area], to recite *Asher Yatzar*, to confess, and to pray the sustenance prayer. Then to touch the body so that

# The Gate of the Letters

<margin>
Let us return
to the first
matter
</margin>
Let us return to the first matter, such as the initial washing and the raising of the ten fingers, based on the secret of the verse: "Lift up your hands in holiness and bless the Lord" <note>Psalm 134:2</note>. Just as the blessing over bread <note>HaMotzi</note> involves taking it with ten fingers, so too are ten things said regarding the **Cup of Blessing**, hinting at the secret of the ten Divine emanations <note>original: "Havayot," referring to the ten Sefirot</note>. Many explanations based on the attribute of Kindness <note>Chesed</note> are said about them in the Zohar in its place, and similarly in the *Tikkunim*. The upshot of what is written there is as follows:

**Crowning** <note>Atara</note> is the secret of the "Higher Crown" which crowns all the luminaries beneath it, serving as a crown for the head of the Righteous One. **Enwrapped** <note>Atuf</note> is the secret of "wrapping in light as a garment" <note>Psalm 104:2</note>, the secret of the higher letter *Yod* which was enwrapped in light and became "Air" <note>original: "Avir," a Kabbalistic wordplay where the letter *Yod* enters the word "Or" (Light) to create "Avir"</note>; thus we have the triad of Crown, Wisdom, and Understanding. **Rinsing and Washing** are the secrets of "And they shall be purified and sanctified." **Purification** comes from the right side, the secret of the Priest <note>Kohen</note> about whom we learned: "He immersed and ascended, he may eat of the Terumah" <note>Priestly tithes</note>. **Sanctification** comes from the side of the Levites, the secret of the left, as it is said: "And you shall sanctify the Levites."

**Full** <note>Malei</note> refers to the attribute of Beauty <note>Tiferet</note>, as in "full of the blessing of the Lord." One receives the cup with both hands, and within it is the flow of the Right and the Left, which fill the Beauty. "And may He fill your longing from Your blessings." It is then placed in the **Right hand**, for "The right hand of the Lord is exalted." One **places his eyes upon it**, as in "The eyes of all look to You in hope" <note>Psalm 145:15</note>; these are the "daughter of the right eye" and "daughter of the left eye," which are the attributes of Victory <note>Netzach</note> and Splendor <note>Hod</note>, known as "the eyes of all."

This corresponds to the **Foundation** <note>Yesod</note>, as is known. **Life** <note>Chai</note> hints at the Foundation, the "Life of the Worlds," which includes eight blessings. "Life" continues until the blessing for the Land, where its sustenance is found, to make known that in the Land, its rest is established by laws. One must mix "many waters" into them, and then the influence is designated for the Kingdom <note>Malkhut</note>, which is the "Land," providing sustenance with great mercy. This mercy is revealed in the attribute of "Good." The Foundation is called "Good," and that Land is moistened by the "Right hand of Moses" and his "Glorious Arm" <note>Tiferet</note>.

The **Table** stands in place of the **Altar**. On the Altar, they would also pour wine with water every day of the Festival. One **raises it a handbreadth**; the cup is the "Cup of Salvations," the "Cup of the Children of God." The Attribute of Judgment below, which is the Kingdom, is raised upward. One **sends it to the members of his household**; this refers to the **Higher Mother** <note>original: "Ima Ila'ah," the Sefirah of Binah</note>, who raises the "Building." We have only four [requirements], and your sign is "Five." This hints at the final *Heh* of the Divine Name, which is the letter *Dalet* <note>the fourth letter, numerically 4</note> and is also five <note>numerically 5</note>. The matter is that, as it were, in exile she is "impoverished" <note>original: "Dalah," a pun on the letter Dalet</note>, due to the removal of the letter *Vav* from her, as explained in the introduction to *Toldot Adam*. The matter of *Vav* and *Heh* being "five" is because the Name is not currently whole. Nonetheless, one must take hold of the four legs of the Higher Chariot: Kindness, Strength, and Beauty, bound and unified in the Kingdom through the Foundation, the pillar upon which the world stands. For "Rinsing" and "Washing" refer to Kindness and Strength, "Full" is Beauty, and they are bound together in the Cup of Blessing, which is the Kingdom, through the "Life of the Worlds." When we emerge from exile through these four, we shall emerge to receive all the rest. This is the meaning of "For with joy you shall go forth" <note>Isaiah 55:12</note>.

<margin>
And all
the time
he blesses
</margin>
**And the Cup** he holds in his right hand. He should place the cup on the palm of the right hand with the fingers held upright. The sign for this is: "And I placed the cup on the palm of Pharaoh" <note>Genesis 40:11</note>. One should not follow those who have the custom of holding the cup in the right hand such that the fingers surround the cup, though there is some evidence for this in the Zohar.

And all the time he blesses, he holds the cup in the right hand, and the left hand should not assist it. This is the secret of the **Grace After Meals** <note>Birkat HaMazon</note> according to the mystical tradition explained in the Zohar: Sustenance flows from the Right side to the *Tzaddi* <note>the Righteous One/Yesod</note>, and the "Righteous One" <note>Itzadik</note> bestows it upon "Justice" <note>Tzedek/Malkhut</note>. We say: "And his cup is that of a Torah scholar." One who says "From His goodness" <note>mi-tuvo</note> is an ignoramus. The Foundation is called "Good" when it includes all the blessings coming to it from above. Between those that spread to descend below, unless it is filled with Kindness from the secret of the food and the great flow coming to it from above, from the Source of Blessings without interruption, given without withheld, since there is no Judgment there at all—this is "In His great goodness." But "From His goodness" implies only *part* of His goodness.

Even though that attribute is called "Good" and includes all blessings, it also flows down to those who are unworthy. But when the flow comes from the Source above, it becomes [infinite], and then He gives to all who are fitting, for "His kindness is forever." This is why we say, "Who feeds the whole world... and in His great goodness, continually," etc. He feeds and sustains everyone, meaning both the good and the evil. He concludes the blessing with "Blessed art Thou, Lord, for the land and for the food." "The Land" is the Land of Life, and "The Food" is the Kindness of Abraham. This blessing is the awakening and cleavage to the Higher Right, and one must not awaken any Left; therefore, the cup is in the Right. Through the second blessing, which is the Blessing for the Land—for the first blessing was established by Moses our Teacher when the Manna descended, which is "Bread from Heaven" <note>Tiferet</note>, and it is said to be "with kindness"—and the second blessing is the "Face of Joshua," which is like the "Face of the Moon" <note>the secret of the Higher Land</note>. Therefore, Moses brought them in to inherit it. Now, the Blessing of the Land, the "Moon," shines from the "Sun," which is the "Face of Moses," from the side of the Right, from the Source of Sustenance, in the secret of "He who caused His glorious arm to go at the right hand of Moses." One must mention the **Covenant** <note>Brit</note> and the **Torah** in this blessing, which are the Foundation and the Beauty. One must mention the Covenant before the Torah, for such is the order from below to above. "A desirable, good, and spacious land."

<margin>
And know
And between
blessing
Behold I
</margin>
**And know** that the spreading of the Good to the lower beings is the secret of the **Torah**, the secret of the "thighs" of the divine structure. Regarding this, we say, "We thank Thee, Lord our God." All of this is because the Good is drawn down for the preservation of the worlds and to perform miracles and wonders for Israel; therefore, one mentions the miracle of the Exodus from Egypt.

**And between** the fact that the "Land of Life" is blessed from the secret of the Right and receives the flow and light of life from there, one must ask for mercy in the third blessing: "Have mercy, Lord our God, upon us," etc., through the power of the Holy Temple. For now, due to our many sins, the Kingdom of the House of David is distanced from her Beloved in exile with her children. When the Temple is built and the "Dew" descends, the holiness will be complete. "At His presence, all the earth shall tremble." Solomon established this, for Bathsheba was fitting for David. "The Tower of David, on which hang a thousand shields" <note>Song of Songs 4:4</note>. The matter of the "Thousand" is that each one is comprised of all, and the general whole is comprised of the sub-wholes. In this way, the Higher Crown <note>Keter</note> is called the "Large Aleph," and the Kingdom <note>Malkhut</note> is the "Small Aleph."

**The Fourth Blessing**, "The Good and the One who does Good," is the secret of the light of their eyes. "Say of the Righteous that it is Good," for he poured out the "Good Oil" that comes from the Higher Right, the secret of Kindness and Mercy. It is entirely from the side of the Right; there is no Left there at all.

**Behold I** will mention a few grammatical nuances in the Grace After Meals, even though most of the congregation [knows them]. When there are three, we are obligated to **Invite** <note>Zimmun</note>. Rashi explains "to invite" means to prepare together for the blessing, like the language of "appointed times." The *Kolbo* says the matter of the *Zimmun* is the multiplication of praise and greatness to the Creator, as they warn one another and gather together to thank Him, praise Him, and glorify Him for His abundant goodness, as it is written: "Exalt the Lord with me, and let us extol His name together" <note>Psalm 34:4</note>. I have seen a stumbling block where many diners, when sitting together in a group of three, one will get up and leave, saying, "There will be a *Zimmun* without me." But the fool walks in darkness and separates himself, for while the other two and the newcomer fulfill the obligation, he himself has not fulfilled it, for he was obligated in the *Zimmun* to thank, praise, and laud.

**When the leader repeats** and says "Blessed be He of whose bounty we have eaten," the diners should say "Amen" before the leader starts the following "Blessed..." because here the Blessing of Invitation <note>Zimmun</note> is completed, and afterward the Grace After Meals begins. I have seen great men conduct themselves this way. So it is found in Chapter 3 of *Berakhot*. And in the *Tur* (Section 198): If someone enters and hears them inviting, if he hears the leader say "Let us bless He of whose bounty we have eaten," he should say "Blessed be His Name always, forever and ever." If he enters when they respond "Blessed be He of whose bounty we have eaten," he should respond "Amen."

**"We have not lacked"** <note>lo chaser lanu</note> and **"May we never lack"** <note>v'al yechsar lanu</note>. Some have the custom to say the word *chaser* with a *Kamatz* under the *Chet* and a *Patach* under the *Samekh*, like the simple verb form <note>Pa'al</note> such as *pakad*. Others say it with a *Chirik* under the *Chet*, like the heavy verb form <note>Pi'el</note>. Those who use the heavy form for "lacked" should also say "may we never be deprived" <note>v'al yechasser</note> with a *Sheva* under the *Yod* so that both come from the same grammatical root.

**And I** have chosen to say it according to the first way, for then the vowel points add up to the numerical value of **Bread** <note>Lechem = 78</note>. For every dot is 6, and every line is 6, and a *Kamatz* is 16. Similarly, Jacob asked for "Bread to eat," and he should not lack it. There are many nuances in the versions of the Grace After Meals, and they are explained in the commentary on Grace After Meals by the Genius, Rabbi Z. Shapiro, of blessed memory. Every God-fearing person should learn from him and do likewise.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the spiritual and practical laws surrounding a meal. # The Gate of the Letters

In my thoughts, when I say this teaching of our Sages of blessed memory regarding the verse found in the third chapter of *Berakhot* <note>original: "Tanya b'Perek 3," referring to the Talmudic tractate Berakhot 48b</note>: From where do we derive the requirement for Grace After Meals from the Torah? As it is said: "And you shall eat, and be satisfied, and you shall bless the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 8:10</note>. "And you shall bless"—this refers to the Blessing of the Provider <note>Hazan</note>; "The Lord your God"—this refers to the invitation to bless as a group <note>Zimun</note>; "For the land"—this refers to the Blessing of the Land; "The good"—this refers to the blessing for the rebuilding of Jerusalem; and likewise it says: "This good mountain and the Lebanon." "Which He gave to you"—this refers to the blessing of "He who is good and does good" <note>HaTov veHaMeitiv</note>. Ravina says, etc. See there.

**And I have seen** in the *Order of Holiness* <note>likely referring to the book *Seder HaYom* or a similar ethical-liturgical manual</note> that one should place the text before their eyes at the time of the Grace After Meals, just as one does during the Prayer <note>the Amidah</note>. This is a good custom, especially when there is a formal quorum <note>term: Zimun - a quorum of three or more who have eaten bread together</note>, that the one leading the blessing should wrap himself in an upper garment, so that the awe of Heaven is upon him. All this is done so that he does not become arrogant when he has eaten, is satisfied, and feels fat and prosperous.

**And these are the words of my father, my teacher, of blessed memory** in *Emek Berakha* <note>A work on the laws of blessings by Rabbi Abraham Horwitz</note>, page 66, side B: Since the Grace After Meals is a <term>Mitzvat Aseh</term> <note>a positive commandment</note> from the Torah, it is proper to focus on it intensely and with precision in its words, so that he does not "swallow" them <note>speak them too quickly or unclearly</note>, and to say it in a loud voice, for the voice awakens the intention of the heart.

**And these are the words** of *Reshit Chochma* <note>The Beginning of Wisdom, a 16th-century Kabbalistic ethical work</note> in the Gate of Holiness, Chapter 15: Regarding the matter of Grace After Meals, it is proper that he thinks when he blesses that he is fulfilling a positive commandment. Therefore, he must not bless with lightheadedness or while drowsy without intention; rather, he should prepare himself to "meet his God" and bless with awe and love, as is the way of all commandments that require awe and love. For through "love," he will remember the great kindness that God has done for him, bestowing upon him and preparing his sustenance even though he was not worthy of it due to his sins. This is the meaning of saying "Who feeds the world in His goodness, with grace, with kindness, and with mercy," meaning: in His kindness, He feeds everyone, whether they are wicked or good. And he should take to heart the secret of "Ishmael my son, bless Me" <note>A famous passage in Berakhot 7a where God asks the High Priest for a blessing</note>. For they <note>the Sages</note> thought that He is blessed through the "lower ones" <note>humanity</note> so that there may be the power of preparation to bestow His goodness upon us. We are His children, doing the will of our Father in Heaven with passion and love, blessing word by word, calmly and moderately, giving Him praise, as in the phrase "For You have given our ancestors a heritage of a desirable land, a covenant, and the Torah," etc. And he should bless in a loud voice—meaning, so that the members of his household hear his voice—and not bless in a whisper. For saying the blessings out loud awakens the focus of those who have eaten. If it is the New Moon, he should remember <note>the prayer</note> *Ya’aleh VeYavo*; if it is the Sabbath, *Retzei*, and the like. One who speaks in a whisper forgets everything, following what our Sages said regarding the study of Torah: that it must be expressed through the mouth, as it is said: "For they are life to those who utter them" <note>Proverbs 4:22</note>... "ordered in all things and secure" <note>2 Samuel 23:5</note>, as they interpreted in the tractate *Eruvin*. The same applies to the matter of blessings. End of quote.

**In the blessing** over His existence, one should say "Blessed is He and blessed is His name," but not when blessing alone; rather, he should simply begin "Blessed are You, Lord," etc. This is implied in *Orach Chaim* <note>The section of the Code of Jewish Law dealing with daily life</note> chapter 192 and 200, and also in *Abudarham*, and in *Kol Bo* chapter 25. My teacher and master, may his memory be a blessing, wrote this explicitly in my commentary on the Grace After Meals.
**It was written** in *Shibbolei HaLeket* and its explanation, and also in the book *P.G. K.B.*: Each person sitting at the table is obligated to say every single blessing in a whisper along with the leader, even the closing formulas of the blessings. This is also found in the *Shulchan Aruch*. My teacher, of blessed memory, wrote on this: one should finish slightly before the leader so that he can answer "Amen."
**The legal authorities wrote** that one should not mention the "Mighty Acts of Rain" or the "Kingdom of Heaven" in the Grace After Meals, for it is not fitting to mention the "Kingdom of the World" next to the "Kingdom of the House of David." For this reason, my teacher wrote in his *Shulchan Aruch* chapter 188: when saying *Ya’aleh VeYavo* on a Festival or New Moon, one should not say "For You are a King, Gracious and Merciful," but rather "For You are God, Gracious and Merciful." And so it is in *Abudarham*. One should not say "Retzeinu" with a *cholam* <note>a vowel sound like 'oh'</note> but rather "Ratzinu" with a *sheva* <note>a short 'eh' or 'ih' sound</note>. One should not say "That on every day," but rather "At every time and every moment." One says "Amen" after the "Merciful One" <note>HaRachaman</note> petitions in the Grace After Meals, even though they do not contain the Name of God, and similarly after any supplication or request, even if there is no formal blessing or Name of God. We find this with the Prophet Jeremiah, who said "Amen" after a request, as it is said: "Amen, so may the Lord do" <note>Jeremiah 28:6</note>. And we say "Amen" after the *Kadosh* <note>Sanctification</note>, as written in the *Levush* in chapter 99. It is written in the *Shulchan Aruch* chapter 188: If one was eating and the Sabbath ended, he still mentions the Sabbath in the Grace After Meals, for we follow the start of the meal. The same applies to the New Moon, Purim, and Hanukkah.

->Sn"l<- <note>Likely the initials of a student or the author's name, Solomon Luria or similar</note>
> (Levi, my teacher the Maharam of Lublin <note>Rabbi Meir Lublin</note> of blessed memory said: for this reason the *Magen Avraham* ruled... he ruled for the Master... and ruled that for a Sabbath meal, one should ideally intend his meal <note>to end</note> because it is close to the end of the Sabbath... and since the signs are not according to the words of our teacher... and as long as it is Sabbath... if he forgets the mention of the New Moon... a weekday in the middle of the week... and if his meal continues into the night of the New Moon... he should mention the New Moon... and if the meal is on Saturday night at the conclusion of the Sabbath, he should mention the New Moon... it all depends on the end of his meal... and one should not say *Mizmor LeDavid* and also *Ya'aleh VeYavo*... for that would be like a weekday and Sabbath mixed together... since if he says *Ya'aleh VeYavo* it makes it look like today is the New Moon, etc.)

**And it is good** to say after "Fear the Lord, His holy ones," the verse "Give thanks to the Lord for He is good," etc., and the verse "The youth who trusts in the Lord," etc. After the Grace After Meals, close to the blessing recited over the cup <note>of wine</note>, my teacher wrote in his commentary on the Grace After Meals that it is proper to say the verse: "I will lift the cup of salvations and call upon the name of the Lord" <note>Psalm 116:13</note>, as a desire for the future feast that the Holy One, Blessed be He, will make for the righteous. And this is why <unclear>one</unclear> blesses and says: "I will lift the cup of salvations and call upon the name of the Lord." In *Shibbolei HaLeket*, it says that by law, one who eats only to "satiate the throat" (meaning, an olive’s bulk or an egg’s bulk) has not fulfilled "satiety of the stomach." Therefore, a rabbinic obligation does not override a Torah obligation. It is written "And you shall eat"—this is eating, "and be satisfied"—this is drinking. If so, one is not obligated to recite the Torah-mandated blessing unless he drinks, if he needs to drink. But if he does not need to drink, he is not <note>obligated</note>. The Torah’s approach is only when there is an appetite. Therefore, one who eats with others who ate and drank, while he only ate and needs to drink but has not yet drunk, he cannot fulfill the obligation for the others who ate and drank; for his obligation is Rabbinic, while theirs is from the Torah, and a Rabbinic obligation cannot override a Torah one. This is the end of his words. And these are the words of the Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Yechiel</note> in the chapter "Three who Ate": From this we see that the best way is that if all know how to bless, the one who ate enough to be "satisfied" should lead. But if they do not know, even one who ate only an olive's bulk may bless to fulfill the obligation even for those who ate until they were satisfied. See the *Tur Orach Chaim* and the *Beit Yosef* in chapter 197 regarding these laws.

->Sn"l<-
I have heard from some of the scholars who study during large feasts, at the time of drinking honey-water called "Mead," that they recite the Grace After Meals over a cup of beer in a place where wine is not common. <gloss>The reason is because beer is a 'drink of the land' and a staple of the meal; and since it is from the five species of grain, it takes precedence over the honey-water called 'Mead,' as is written in the laws of precedence.</gloss>
**It appears** that if they know and do not know... what they know is that this species precedes the more beloved one... as written in the *Tur* chapter 211... and he has the status of the five species... but here we do not bless over it the blessing for bread, etc. But for those who ate... and for the reason written by the Rama <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles</note> and quoted in the *Beit Yosef* chapter 209: "one does not follow the majority for the five species of grain."... The main point is that since the drink's primary purpose is for the sake of the water and not to provide nourishment, it does not have the rule of the five species, for there is only a mere flavor here... just like the "letter-shaped cookies" mentioned later, where one blesses "by whose word all things exist" <note>Shehakol</note>... and also Rabbeinu Yonah wrote this regarding water...
**Here** you have it clearly, that for beer, it does not have the status of the five species because there is only a mere flavor here. And it is permitted... as I found written in the *Tur* chapter 211 and thus the *Shulchan Aruch* ruled. And it is known that beer is more common to people than wine.
Furthermore, it was ruled that we do not follow the majority but rather the designated purpose... therefore one should not recite Grace After Meals except over the drink set before him... and also grain used for drinking... it is presumed that at large feasts, if there is no beer before him on the table, but it was in his mind to drink it, it is considered as if it is before him... and beer and food at the time of drinking is considered early and preferred... and furthermore as we ruled... if it was brought to him specifically... as written in *Terumat HaDeshen* chapter 32 and quoted in *Beit Yosef* chapter 210. But if he does not want to eat but rather... then what is brought to him is considered the time of drinking... as ruled in *Tosafot*... chapter 168 and 210. If so, what we have written regarding our case, since he intended to drink beer and it is not before him, it is very clear that he should not wait for the beer but should bless over the mead if he has no wine.
->Exposition<-

<meta>This page continues the ethical and spiritual guidance regarding meals. While the previous page discussed the liturgical requirements of the Grace After Meals, this page shifts focus toward the physical and moral discipline required during the act of eating itself, warning against gluttony and explaining the spiritual benefits of moderation.</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

They did not decree <note>referring to Rabbinic rulings on the times for prayer and tefillin</note> that one should engage in gluttony <note>original: "achila gasa," literally a "coarse eating"</note> like a horse or a mule that has no understanding. Such behavior brings on sleep or flatulence, and this causes them to be unable to don tefillin, as mentioned above. Even though they are later "coerced" by sleep or flatulence <note>meaning they cannot help it once it starts</note>, they are still called "transgressors of Israel," because they are punished in the end for the thing they did willfully at the beginning. For they should have eaten only to satisfy their hunger and to maintain their life alone—to stand before the Lord, to serve Him, and to bless His name—and not to fill the "twin" <note>a metaphorical term for the appetite or the stomach</note> excessively.

**Furthermore**, gluttony leads to a "nightly occurrence" <note>term: Keri - an involuntary nocturnal emission, rendering one ritually impure</note>. This is similar to what we say in the beginning of the first chapter of *Kiddushin*: excessive eating leads to physical discharge, and excessive drinking leads to physical discharge. This naturally applies to the matter of ritual impurity as well, for both are an abomination to the Lord.

**The wise man** <note>original: "maskil"</note> will take this matter to heart and separate himself from his desires. He will not fill his belly and fulfill his lust like a beast. For "who is a hero? He who subdues his inclination" <note>referring to the *Yetzer Hara*, the internal drive toward selfishness or excess</note>. If his inclination entices him to eat, he should break its strength and subdue his desire. Then, awe and holiness will rest upon him, as it is written: "Fear the Lord, you His holy ones" <note>Psalm 34:10</note>. Our Master Yonah <note>Rabbi Yonah of Gerona, a 13th-century moralist</note> wrote that while one still craves food, he should withdraw from his desire for the honor of the Creator. Such a person is meritorious, subdues his inclination, and is atoned for, because his Creator has refined his physical desires. The author of *The Beginning of Wisdom* <note>term: Reshit Chochmah - a major 16th-century Kabbalistic ethical work by Eliyahu de Vidas</note> elaborated on this at length in the "Gate of Holiness." The conclusion of his words is that on this path, our Sages said: "From a meal that you enjoy, pull your hand back." There are two great remedies in this: first, that he does not ruin his eating, and second, the humbling of the inclination and the breaking of desire. It is written in the book *Table of Four* <note>original: "Shulchan Arba," by Rabbi Bahya ben Asher</note> on the verse "Take for the hunger of your houses and go": this comes to instruct and teach human knowledge that it is not proper to eat except to break one's hunger alone, not to fill their bellies and follow after the sense of taste and the animalistic soul. For this is a disgrace to us, utter vanity, and a thing with no substance. Furthermore, it says in the tractate *Gittin*: "From a meal that you enjoy, pull back your hand." Regarding this, it is promised: "You shall be holy"—you shall be "separated," as Rashi explains—as is fitting for you. Furthermore, our Sages said in tractate *Berakhot*: "He [the Prophet Elijah] said to Rav Yehuda, the brother of Rav Salla the Pious: Do not be angry and you will not sin; do not become drunk and you will not sin." The students of Rabbeinu Yonah explained: "Do not become drunk and you will not sin" means do not eat to total satiation, so that you do not come to sin. For when a person is full and well-fed, he forgets the matters of the Creator, may He be blessed.

The *Book of the Pious* <note>Sefer Hasidim, 12th-century German-Jewish ethical text</note> says in Section 3: "The righteous man eats to satisfy his soul." Just as a wise man is recognized by his wisdom and his views, and is distinguished by them from the rest of the people, so too must he be recognized in his deeds: in his eating, his drinking, his physical relations, his sleep, his gait, his speech, and his business dealings. All these deeds should be pleasant and highly refined. He should not be a glutton, but should eat food appropriate to maintain the health of his body, and he should not engage in gluttony. He should not be eager to fill his belly like those who fill their stomachs with food and drink until their bodies and bellies nearly burst. Regarding them, it was said in the tradition: "I will spread dung upon your faces... the dung of your festivals" <note>Malachi 2:3</note>. These are the people who eat and drink and spend all their days as if they were festivals. (In the chapter "One who Asks," they compared the "wheel" to the Creator; this refers to dung, as it is written: "I will spread dung on your faces, the dung of your festivals." Rav Huna said: these are the people who abandon the study of Torah and spend all their days as if they were festivals. Rabbi Levi said: after three days, the belly bursts and falls upon his face, saying to him: "Take what you put in me!") They say to one another: "Let us eat and drink much, for tomorrow we die." This is the food of the wicked. But the wise man eats only one or two dishes, eating enough for his survival, not until his belly is full. This is what King Solomon, peace be upon him, said: "The righteous eats to satisfy his soul" <note>Proverbs 13:25</note>. This is also found in the *Maimonides* in Chapter 5 of the "Laws of Temperament" <note>Hilkhot Deot</note>; see there.

We learn from all this that one must be careful about excessive eating. Our Sages likewise said in the chapter "One may not stand": "Filling the belly... is bad." This means filling the stomach causes many types of evils. **And if** his inclination entices him to eat to fill his belly and his lust, he should reply to it: "What advantage is there for a man in excessive eating and drinking? Does not the vomit and excrement increase according to the amount of food and drink?" If he fills his body like rain falling on the earth, the waste will quickly be expelled, whether upwards or downwards, as flatulence before the bed. Then his inclination will be humbled, and the evil of the discharge will prevent the man from deviating from the path.

**This moral rebuke** was hinted at by our Sages in their statement (in the chapter "How do we bless"): "Who is rich? He who has a bathroom near his table." This means: who is "rich" in the quality of their character and virtues? One who has a bathroom "near his table"—meaning, near his thought when he sits to eat. He should have the bathroom in his mind and say to his heart: "Why do I need many sacrifices, to kill cattle and slaughter sheep? Even if I had all the wealth of Joseph, what would it profit me, since all food ends up in the bathroom?" There is no difference between the eating of cattle, beasts, and birds—everything returns to the place of filth.

**And our Sages expounded** on the verse: "I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tested you in the furnace of affliction." Just as this furnace, even if you give it all the wood in the world, it burns it and casts it out, so too is the throat of a man; even if you give it all the foods in the world, it casts them out. The "wise man has his eyes in his head" <note>Ecclesiastes 2:14</note> and will remember this when he sits to eat, and then he will certainly not be drawn after his desire.

**He should also remember** at the time of eating that all that he adds in food, he adds flesh for the worms at his end. As our Sages said in *Tractate Avot*: "The more flesh, the more worms." When a person remembers these two things at the time of eating—first, that the end of eating is the bathroom; and second, that increasing flesh increases worms—then he will certainly pull his hand back from excessive eating and eat only enough for his survival. All of this is hinted at in the portion of the Manna, which was the food of the generation in the desert. It says: "They gathered it, every man according to his eating" <note>Exodus 16:16</note>. This means: "according to his eating"—exactly the measure of food for each man, which is to say, for survival, no more and no less. As it says afterward: "And they measured it with an omer; he that gathered much had nothing over, etc." This wonder was meant to awaken the hearts of men and to teach the people knowledge: that there is no benefit for the person who eats more than is necessary for life, for it all goes to waste, as mentioned above in the name of the Midrash ("the throat of a man... casts it out"). "And he that gathered little had no lack"—meaning, even the one who ate little lacked nothing, since he sustained his soul until its appointed time.

It says afterward: "But they did not listen to Moses"—meaning they pursued luxuries and intended only to fill their bellies, which results in waste expelled upwards or downwards, as mentioned before. What is written after that? "It bred worms and stank." This comes to teach for that hour and for all generations that anyone who does this has not remembered his end, for the abundance of food increases flesh for worms after his death.

**It says further**, "and it stank," even during his lifetime, for an abundance of food increases vomit and excrement in summer and winter. A person should remember all this and vow to limit his eating and drinking. He should not fill his belly until he achieves his lust. This will be his peace and his good—that he eats according to his benefit <note>original: "to'alato"</note> and not for his worms <note>original: "tola'ato," a wordplay on "benefit" and "worm"</note>. Especially for scholars, who are more separated from the rest of the people, it is proper that they also conduct themselves with this separation, so as not to be defiled by the "delicacies of the king" and permitted pleasures, but only that which is for the maintenance of their soul and body. This is health for them and nothing more, as hinted in the portion of the Manna. Therefore our Sages said: "The Torah was given only to the eaters of the Manna." This means it is proper for every master of Torah to be like the "eaters of the Manna"—conduct himself with the separation described regarding them: they had exactly what they needed, no less and no more, all measured out for their survival. It is possible that for this purpose, they said in the first chapters of *Shabbat* and *Pesachim*: "The meal of a Torah scholar is at the sixth hour." As you already know, the sixth hour is midday. So should a scholar conduct himself: eating at the "midday," meaning a middle, moderate meal. Not that he should engage in gluttony, nor should he deprive his soul of all good; rather, he should intend in his eating for the maintenance of his soul and the health of his body, so that he may be healthy and strong for the service of the Name, may He be blessed.

**The end of the matter:** A wise man should grasp the middle line. His eating should be like the "half-shekel" of the sanctuary; his bread should be eaten by weight and his water drunk by measure. This is for his health and for his survival. Even on Shabbat, he should not eat excessively, as written in the *Shulchan Aruch* (Section 291). There are many sayings of our Sages that support this and distance Torah scholars from pleasures. The primary one is the Baraita of the "Acquisition of Torah" <note>Pirkei Avot, chapter 6</note>: "This is the way of the Torah: a morsel of bread with salt you shall eat... and do not crave the table of kings." King David said: "It was good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn Your statutes" <note>Psalm 119:71</note>. (Also in the book *Results of Life* <note>original: "Totzaot Chaim"</note> it is written in the name of Rabbi Solomon HaLevi Alkabetz, the teacher of the author of *The Orchard* <note>Moses Cordovero</note>, that wherever gluttony and nightly gorging are found, the 'Other Side' <note>evil spiritual forces</note> is present. Therefore, one who guards his soul should stay far away.) Other authors and speakers on this subject hint at what is common knowledge, but bringing them all would be a burden; let them be studied in their respective places. They are life to those who find them.

It encourages a "middle path" of moderation, using the biblical Manna and the habits of Torah scholars as models for eating for health rather than pleasure.</summary>
