It introduces "The Gate of the Letters," focusing on how the physical act of eating must be elevated into a service of God through "kavanah" (directed intention) and self-discipline.</meta>

<header>The Gate of the Letters</header>

->One should focus on the Table Blessings with complete intention; then he shall eat in holiness and purity.<-

# Section 1: One Should Focus
on the table blessings more than other blessings, because food and drink bring a person toward a coarse nature and haughtiness of heart. From this, one may come to forget the Holy One, Blessed be He, as it is written: *Lest you eat and be satisfied... and your heart be lifted up and you forget [the Lord]* <note>original: "פן תאכל ושבעת... ורם לבבך ושכחת"</note>. Therefore, a person must contemplate and apply extra intention to the table blessings so that his table becomes "the table which is before the Lord." He should pull his heart toward a desire for the Blessed Creator and not toward the side of desiring food and drink. He must remember the Essential One <note>God</note> specifically in the place that is the cause for forgetting Him. This has been discussed at length in the work *The Four-Fold Table* <note>original: "Shulchan Arba," an ethical work by Bahya ben Asher</note>, and I have not copied his full language here so as not to be overly lengthy.

<margin>**And in the *Book of the Pious*** <note>original: "Sefer Hasidim," a 12th-century German Pietist work</note> it is written: There was a story of a man who died several years before his time. After many years, he appeared in a dream to one of his relatives. The relative asked him, "How are things conducted in the world where you are?" He replied, "Every day they judge me because I was not meticulous in the blessing over bread <note>Hamotzi</note>, the blessing over fruits, and the Grace After Meals with the heart's intention. They say to me: 'You intended only for your own pleasure!'" The relative asked him, "Is there not a judgment for the wicked for only twelve months? You have been there much longer and they are still judging you!" He replied, "They are not judging me with harsh punishments like the completely wicked <note>original: "Rasha'im"</note>, [but the scrutiny continues]." Therefore, one must focus his heart at the beginning of his opening words on what he is blessing: whether over bread, or fruit, or wine, or ale. The general rule is that at the time of eating, a person's heart should be attached to the Blessed Creator more than any other time during the day. This is the meaning of *And they saw God and they ate and drank* <note>Exodus 24:11</note>; the explanation is that they were contemplating and "seeing" the Divine Glory in their hearts while they were eating and drinking. This was discussed at length by the author of *The Four-Fold Table* (Gate 2) and the author of *The Worm of Jacob* <note>original: "Tola'at Yaakov," a Kabbalistic commentary on the liturgy</note> in the order of the blessings of enjoyment.</margin>

---

->### It shall be holy • For not by bread alone does man live<-

# Section 2: A Person Must
sanctify himself at his table, as it is said, *You shall be holy for I am holy* <note>Leviticus 19:2</note>—sanctify yourself even with that which is permitted to you. Therefore, one should not be a glutton <note>original: "gargeran"</note> or a swallower, but rather like one eating before the King of Glory, for the Lord of Hosts is the King of Glory, Sela. Your mnemonic is "RL" <note>the Hebrew letters Resh and Lamed</note>, which signifies thinking during the time of eating that you are eating "Before the Lord" <note>original: "Lifnei HaShem"</note> and that there is no partition separating you from the Blessed God. Creating such a thought brings a person to holiness and purity and clothes them in humility and awe. Let the fear of Heaven be upon him, and let his eating not be merely to fulfill his lust—for one who eats to fulfill his lust is like one who is cursed—rather, *that which every soul must eat, that alone shall be done* <note>Exodus 12:16</note> for the Lord. One should be extra careful with the phrase "for every soul" <note>original: "le-chol nefesh"</note>, for man has two souls: the Vital Soul and the Intellectual Soul. The Vital Soul is nourished and sustained by physical food and drink; however, the Intellectual Soul derives no pleasure from physical foods, but only from spiritual blessings and intellectual thoughts, for these are its "bread." As it is explained regarding the soul of our teacher Moses, peace be upon him: for forty days he ate no bread and drank no water—this refers to the three pilgrimage festivals <note>meaning he was sustained by the spiritual light</note>. When one intends to fulfill the commandments practiced during a meal, the soul is sustained within the body. In everything one eats and drinks, there should be a beautiful and specific intention. For if it is a "commandment meal" <note>original: "Se'udat Mitzvah"</note>, that mitzvah becomes the portion of the soul by which it is sustained. Even more so, one should focus on the commandments dependent on that meal: the kosher status of the foods and the distancing from forbidden things according to the ways of the Torah. One should also focus on their blessings, or on strengthening and healing the body to stand and serve before God in the service of Torah and worship, and to engage in all holy matters. In truth, these noble and spiritual intentions sustain the noble soul and keep it alive, for it is holy and *shall eat of the holy things*. This is the meaning of *For not by bread alone... but by everything that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord does man live* <note>Deut 8:3</note>. This means that through the commandments <note>the "word of God"</note> associated with the meal, man lives—meaning, the soul is sustained within the body in the manner mentioned above. Similar to this, the author of *The Worm of Jacob* wrote regarding the verse *And may [God] give to you*, that it is holy to internalize this matter within the context of the meal. He informed us that their intention in eating should be to sustain the body to serve its Creator. You should know that the soul's existence in the body and its actions are only revealed through eating and drinking. We have already written in the definition of this book that food and drink do not directly benefit the soul, but through the medium of eating, the Creator maintains the soul in the body so it can perform its actions with the body. It is a great necessity to provide for the soul's state and perfection. Therefore, when a person sits to eat at his table, he must intend that his body be healthy so the soul can perform its actions... until his soul is bound above and his thought wanders among the upper, eternal realms so that his soul may endure through their endurance. This is the end of his words for our purposes. Although these words are beloved, I must be brief. Such matters were discussed at length by the author of the *Akedah* <note>Isaac Arama</note> in the portion of "Kedoshim" (Gate 64), in "Vayeira" (Gate 7), and in "Vayechi" (Gate 20).

<margin>**And he ate before God**</margin>

<margin>**The wise man**, the wise of heart, treats every day's meal as a commandment meal. His intention is not for the bread he eats, but only to heal and maintain his body to be sound and ready for the service of the wise soul. This is the language of the *Tur* (Orach Chaim 231): "In everything from which he derives benefit in this world, he should not intend for his own pleasure but for the service of the Blessed Creator, as it is written: *In all your ways, know Him*." Our Sages said: "Let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven," to the point that even if one were thirsty or hungry, if he ate and drank for his own pleasure, it is not praiseworthy; rather, he should intend to eat for his sustenance in order to serve his Creator. Similarly, the *Kuzari* <note>by Judah Halevi</note> wrote on the verse *Happy is the man who fears always*, that the level desired by the text is that of a person who is always in fear in all his matters and actions, and his intellect contemplates their purpose. He mentions "Adam" <note>man</note> and not "Ish" <note>man/person</note> because the term *Adam* is derived from *Adamah* <note>earth/ground</note>. It is as if it says: "Happy is he who is careful of the 'earthly' qualities rooted in matter, who leaves the material and is drawn toward the intellect." One who does this will never sin in the matter of food and drink, for it is not fitting for a human to focus on the sense of taste to fulfill a lust, for in this matter he is no different from a beast. Rather, he should focus on the purpose: that his body be healthy and strong so he can serve God. Anything beyond this purpose is a sin.</margin>

<margin>**And in the chapter** written by the author of *The Beginning of Wisdom* <note>original: "Reshit Chochma"</note> in the Gate of Holiness, citing the Ra'avyah: "A person should always withdraw when he has finished a third of his meal..." One who wants to be holy should not eat except as a medicine, so that he does not become ill and be idle from Torah and commandments. Therefore, he should not fill his soul with coarse foods, and even with good things he should not complete his desire, even on the Sabbath. For excessive eating causes excessive sleep, as our Sages said: "They would not feed [the High Priest] much, for food brings on sleep." When one trains himself to be satisfied with a little, he finds rest for his soul and is sanctified by the Torah.</margin>

<margin>**It appears to me** that this is what our Sages meant when they said (Talmud, Berakhot 5a): "Who are the 'transgressors of Israel with their bodies'? Rav said: A skull <note>original: "Karkafta"</note> that does not put on tefillin." This is difficult at first glance—how do we know that a person who doesn't wear tefillin is a "transgressor with his body"? Perhaps it refers to someone who committed a physical sin like murder, theft, or adultery, which are done with the hands or the body?</margin>

Rather, it seems to me: regarding any sin in the world that one might suggest as the meaning of "transgressor with the body," this one is the most difficult. Why did the Tanna <note>Sage</note> specify "with their body"? He should have just said "transgressors of Israel" generally. Because of this, he had to explain that "transgressors of Israel with their body" refers to a "skull that does not wear tefillin." This explanation clarifies "with the body," for when a person fills his belly with coarse eating, he is a transgressor with his body—meaning his transgression was committed *using* his body, by putting more than is proper into his body. It is known that a full stomach causes excessive sleep or brings about flatulence <note>making one ritually unfit to wear tefillin</note>, as mentioned above. Because of this, he will be unable to wear tefillin, as we say: "Tefillin require a clean body." Abaye and Rav Yehuda explained this to mean that one must not pass gas in them or sleep in them. Therefore, they called those people who "sin against their own souls" "transgressors of Israel with their bodies." Because they transgressed with their bodies through the food and drink they inserted into themselves, it becomes impossible for them to eat a moderate meal and the day passes and they have not [donned tefillin]...

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual necessity of moderation and intention (kavanah) during meals, arguing that gluttony distances a person from God. It interprets the Talmudic phrase "transgressors of Israel with their bodies" as referring to gluttons whose overeating prevents them from wearing tefillin due to sleep or physical impurity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the ethics of the table, moving from the specific blessings over food to the physical and spiritual manner in which one should eat. It emphasizes that maintaining physical health is a religious obligation, as a sick body cannot effectively serve God or study Torah.</meta>

<page-num>85</page-num>
<header>The Gate of the Letters</header>

**It is written** in the book of *Ibn Shu’eib* <note>Joshua ibn Shu'eib, a 14th-century Spanish scholar</note> in the sermons for the festival of Sukkot, regarding the verse: *Go, eat your bread with joy and drink your wine with a merry heart...* <note>Ecclesiastes 9:7</note>, and these are his words: A verse never loses its literal meaning <note>original: "אין המקרא יוצא מידי פשוטו" — a principle that the plain meaning of the Bible remains valid even when deeper interpretations are added</note>. King Solomon was warning man to rejoice in what God has graciously given him—that he should eat his bread and drink his wine with joy. This involves both the cultivation of the body and the soul. Cultivating the body means—as is known in the way of medicine—that when a person eats in a state of joy, the food is digested well; but if he eats in a state of worry, the opposite occurs. Cultivating the soul means for a person to rejoice in what the Name, Blessed be He, has granted him, as it is said: *Who is rich? He who is happy with his portion* <note>Pirkei Avot 4:1</note>. This is the way of the wise, who are satisfied with their necessities and give thanks and praise to Him who granted them. The wicked are the opposite; they are in pain even in the evening because they are hungry, and they are not satisfied with necessities alone but seek excesses. This way of theirs is their folly. The verse says *your* bread and *your* wine—meaning from what is one's own, reached by the labor of one's hands from what is permitted, and not from theft. Furthermore, one should not establish his meal just anywhere, like the manner of the crude, as noted regarding Rabbi Phinehas ben Jair and his colleagues. One who does this finds favor with God in his actions, for *God has already accepted your deeds* <note>referencing the end of Ecclesiastes 9:7</note>. Thus far his words.

**I have written** this to serve as a reminder for all people, both common folk and men of rank, rich and poor alike. One who enters to dine should rejoice in his portion, whether it be a little or a lot, and he should eat with joy, following the principle: *The precepts of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart* <note>Psalm 19:8</note>. Even if he has only a little to eat, he should arrange his table in a manner that is pleasant to him, as if he were eating many delicacies and all sorts of treats.

## A person should eat according to virtue, not according to desire

<margin>Section 5. Already</margin> it has been mentioned in several books that a person should intend for his eating to be according to what is beneficial and not according to what is tasty. This means a person should eat what is beneficial for his bodily health so that he may be healthy and strong for the service of the Name, Blessed be He. He should not eat according to what is tasty—meaning what is sweet to the palate or has a good aroma that the human soul craves for its own pleasure—for it may be that it harms him and causes a difficult illness. The Rambam <note>Maimonides, the preeminent 12th-century Jewish philosopher and physician</note> discussed this at length in the *Book of Knowledge* <note>original: "Sefer HaMada"</note>, in the *Laws of Temperament* <note>original: "Hilchot De'ot"</note>, chapter 3, and in the *Eight Chapters*, chapter 4; see there. The author of *Paths of Faith* <note>original: "Shevilei Emunah" by Meir ibn Aldabi</note> wrote in the introduction to the eighth path as follows: It is clear to every person of intellect that the holy and pure Torah, given to us from the mouth of the Almighty through Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, was given to us for our perfection. Although its parts vary—some being the 365 negative commandments <note>corresponding to the days of the solar year</note> and 248 positive commandments <note>corresponding to the limbs of a person</note>, totaling 613 commandments—all of them are included in two intentions: the management of physical health and the management of spiritual health. That is, the cultivation of the body and the cultivation of the soul. The cultivation of the soul depends on the cultivation of the physical temperament and bodily conduct—conducting oneself in health and striving so that one does not fall into illness. However, the cultivation of the soul is to serve its Creator, Blessed be He, and to engage in intellectual wisdom so that it may perceive intellectual concepts in actuality and be helped by its faith, for this is why the soul was placed within. The cultivation of the body precedes the cultivation of the soul in time, for it is impossible for a person to conceive of intellectual concepts—even if they are taught to him, and certainly not on his own—while he is in pain, or in great lack, or hungry, or thirsty. But after reaching the first perfection <note>physical health</note>, it is then possible for him to reach the final perfection <note>spiritual/intellectual growth</note>, which is undoubtedly more honorable... Therefore, a person must be understanding in his actions, in his food and drink, and in the management of his nutrition and all his movements, to maintain the health of the body for the service of his Creator. He should think that the survival of the body is the survival of the soul through healthy conduct, for through it the vessels of the body will be healthy and able to do their work. When the soul finds itself healthy and strong, it can then perform its deeds and labor to acquire good traits, as I have explained. When the enlightened person strives in this matter, his path is one of Divine will, for a person is meant to keep the laws of physical health and the ways of medicine just as he keeps the laws of spiritual health, which are the commandments and all the laws of the Creator, Blessed be He. For the Torah and the commandments cannot be fulfilled except through the health of the body... In conclusion: know that the focus on the body and perfection from illnesses is a form of service to the Creator, Blessed be He, for through the peace of the body, the soul is strengthened to do its work and acquire honorable traits. All this is not possible without physical health. (And these are the words of Maimonides in *Laws of Temperament*, chapter 3: A person must direct his heart and all his deeds solely to know the Name, Blessed be He... and so on until what he wrote at the end of that chapter: Rather, he should set it upon his heart that his body be whole and strong so that his soul may be upright to know the Lord, Blessed be He, for it is impossible to understand and contemplate wisdom while hungry and sick or when one of his limbs is in pain...) He also wrote in the seventh path: And his conduct in eating according to health I have explained in the fifth path, and there I explained in the introduction that it is a commandment to conduct oneself in the management of health and not to eat everything for one's pleasure. Similarly, the house of study said to a servant: eat for appetite, swallow for medicine; let not your eating be for taste, nor for the pleasure the palate finds in it. Thus far his words. The author of *The Beginning of Wisdom* <note>original: "Reshit Chochma," a 16th-century kabbalistic work by Eliyahu de Vidas</note> discussed this at length in the "Gate of Holiness." This is a summary of his language: We shall explain that whoever wishes to be sanctified should not eat his food except for medicine, so that he does not become ill and be deterred from Torah and commandments. Therefore, it is proper that he not fill his soul with coarse foods, and even of good things, he should not completely fulfill his desire.

<margin>And already</margin> we have brought previously (in section 43) in the name of the *Tur* <note>Jacob ben Asher's code of law</note> that it is a commandment to conduct oneself well to guard one's health so that one will be healthy and strong for the service of the Name, Blessed be He. Therefore, I saw fit to mention here some of those ways which, if a person does them, he shall live according to the laws of health. The chief of physicians <note>referring again to Maimonides</note> wrote in the *Book of Knowledge*, *Laws of Temperament*, chapter 4: Since maintaining a healthy and whole body is among the ways of God—for it is impossible to understand or know anything of the knowledge of the Creator if one is sick—a person must distance himself from things that destroy the body and conduct himself with things that make the body healthy and sound. And these are they:

<margin>Never</margin> should a person eat except when he is hungry... A person should not eat until his belly is filled, but should rather decrease by about a quarter... A person should not eat until he walks before the meal until his body begins to warm... Whenever a person eats, he should sit in his place... and anyone who moves about after eating brings upon himself bad and difficult illnesses. One should sleep at the beginning of the night on his left side and at the end of the night on his right side. One should not sleep immediately after eating, but should wait after eating about three or four hours... Things that loosen the bowels, such as grapes, figs, mulberries, pears, and watermelons, a person should eat them before the meal... Things that bind the bowels, such as pomegranates and apples, a person should eat them immediately after his food and should not eat much of them. When a person wants to eat poultry and meat together, he should eat the poultry first. Similarly, with eggs and poultry, he eats the eggs first. With small livestock <note>like sheep/goats</note> and large cattle <note>like beef</note>, he eats the small livestock first. A person should always prioritize light things and afterwards the heavy.

<margin>In the summer</margin> days, one should eat cold foods and not use many spices, and should eat vinegar. In the rainy days <note>winter</note>, one should eat warm foods and use many spices, and eat a little mustard. One follows this pattern in cold places and warm places, in every single place according to what is appropriate for it.

<margin>Always</margin> should a person strive that his bowels be loose all the days of his life, and be close to a slight diarrhea. This is a great principle in medicine: as long as waste is expelled with difficulty, many illnesses follow. How much should a person loosen his bowels... And they said another principle for bodily health: as long as a person exercises and exerts himself greatly, and is not over-sated, and his bowels are loose, no illness will come upon him and his strength will increase, even if he eats bad foods. But for anyone who sits securely and does not exercise, or one who delays his bodily needs, or one whose bowels are hard—even if he eats good foods and guards himself according to medicine—all his days will be full of pain and his strength will fail him.

<margin>Gluttonous eating</margin> is like a deadly poison to a person's body and is the root of all illnesses. Most illnesses that come upon a person are only because of bad foods or because he fills his stomach and eats gluttonously, even of good foods. This is what Solomon said in his wisdom: *He who guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from troubles* <note>Proverbs 21:23</note>—guarding his mouth from eating bad things or from over-satiation, and his tongue from speaking except for his needs... See there. There are foods that are extremely bad, and it is proper for a person never to eat them, such as: large salted and dried fish, old salted cheese, truffles and mushrooms, old salted meat, wine from the vat <note>newly pressed wine</note>, and cooked food that has sat until its aroma has faded, or any food with a foul, pungent, or bitter smell. These are like deadly poison to the body. A person should always restrain himself from tree fruits and not eat much of them, even dried ones, and certainly not fresh ones. But before they have ripened fully, they are like swords to the body, and all carobs are always bad.

# The Gate of the Letters
## Warning against excessive drinking, lest it lead to ruin and degradation

<margin>Section 3</margin> Just as one must be cautious regarding excessive eating, as mentioned previously, so too must one be cautious regarding excessive drinking. For drunkenness destroys a person’s body and ruins his intellect, causing all the evils in the world to befall him. We see this in the case of Noah, for whom drunkenness caused evil and disgrace, and became the reason he cursed his descendants. Our Sages of blessed memory said <note>in Tractate Sanhedrin 70a</note>: "Three 'Vavs' <note>The Hebrew letter 'Vav' is also the word for 'hook' and can phonetically represent a cry of woe</note> were stated in the context of wine: *And Noah began* [Vayachel], *and he planted a vineyard* [Vayita], *and he drank of the wine and became drunk* [Vayesht]." The intention here—as written in the book *The Beginning of Wisdom* <note>original: *Reshit Chochmah*, a 16th-century kabbalistic ethical work</note> in the "Gate of Holiness"—is that all these letters come to teach "Oy" and "Woe." They are three 'Vavs' to indicate that he damaged the [divine] unity, for the word 'One' [Echad] is numerically linked to three <note>This refers to complex kabbalistic associations between the letters and divine attributes</note>.

**And in the Midrash** on the portion of the Nazirite: *Look not upon the wine when it is red* <note>Proverbs 23:31</note>. The Holy Spirit warns regarding wine that a person should not become intoxicated. Why? *When it is red* <note>original: "כי יתאדם" (ki yit’adem)</note>—because its end is "blood" <note>original: "דם" (dam), a play on the word for red</note>, for he will commit a transgression that carries the penalty of death. Another interpretation: *When it is red* refers to the blood of menstruation and the blood of a discharge. *When he puts his eye in the cup*—the word for "cup" [Kos] is written such that through the "cup," he puts his "eye" [the Hebrew *Ayin*] in the "cup" <note>This is a play on words suggesting that drunkenness leads to looking at forbidden women</note>. The Torah uses clean language to say that he will come to engage in forbidden sexual relations. *It goes down smoothly* <note>original: "יתהלך במישרים" (yit’halech be-meisharim)</note>—eventually, his wife will tell him "I have seen a red spot" <note>indicating she is ritually impure</note> and he will not desist from her. Rabbi Assi said: If he is a Torah scholar, he will eventually declare the impure to be pure and the pure to be impure. Another interpretation: *It goes down smoothly*—eventually he will permit transgressions and treat them as "smooth" and ownerless like a plain. He will speak with a woman and eventually defile his mouth with evil words in his drunkenness and feel no shame.

We have learned that nothing is as good or clear as wine, yet it is the head of all other drinks that a person consumes to the point of intoxication. Specifically, those who study Torah must be even more careful of drunkenness, for intoxication leads to excessive sleep, which causes them to be idle from the words of Torah. Furthermore, it is a disgrace for a Torah scholar to be drunk, more so than for the rest of the people. Our Sages of blessed memory said in the *Hidden Midrash* <note>original: *Midrash HaNe'elam*, part of the Zohar</note>: Rabbi Isaac said that the Evil Inclination only entices a person through eating and drinking, and through the joy of wine, it gains dominion over man through mockery. What is written of the righteous? *The righteous eats to satisfy his soul* <note>Proverbs 13:25</note>, and he never becomes intoxicated. For it was said to Judah: "This young scholar who is bitter <note>likely meaning acting inappropriately or smelling of wine</note>—about him I read the verse: *As a ring of gold in a swine's snout* <note>Proverbs 11:22</note>." Moreover, he desecrates the Name of Heaven <note>term: *Chillul Hashem* — an act that brings shame upon God or the Jewish community</note>, as the Evil Inclination is only awakened through wine, for "wine makes one forget their stones" <note>A play on a verse suggesting loss of foundations/principles</note>. I have already cited above in the previous section in the name of *The Book of the Pious* <note>original: *Sefer Hasidim*</note>, which are the words of Maimonides in the "Book of Knowledge" <note>original: *Sefer HaMada*</note>: Just as a wise man is recognized through his wisdom and his views, and is distinguished by them from the rest of the people, so too must he be recognized in his actions—in his eating and his drinking.

And thus wrote Maimonides in *The Laws of Ethics*, Chapter 5: "When a wise man drinks wine, he drinks only enough to soak the food in his stomach. Anyone who becomes intoxicated is a sinner, is disgraceful, and loses his wisdom; and if he becomes intoxicated in front of the unlearned, it is a Desecration of the Name." Regardless, a person of understanding should distance himself from intoxication as far as "the shot of a bow," so that he does not come to disgrace and shame. For sometimes a person might consider a thing during his intoxication, or say something, that even if a man were given a house full of silver and gold, he would not have done it [if sober]. Rabbi Eleazar said: Be careful with the power of weight <note>meaning the gravity of the situation</note> when a person is drunk; all great transgressions appear to him as a plain <note>insignificant</note>, and he sins with the "vessel of knowledge" and prayer, and his time is wasted, and his intellect is ruined, and even his prayer becomes an abomination. Happy is he who has never been drunk in his days!

However, I seek to find merit for the "holy ones in the land"—those young men, men of renown and servants of God—who sometimes drink more than is appropriate at large feasts, particularly "Mitzvah Feasts" <note>term: *Se'udat Mitzvah* — a celebratory meal accompanying a religious commandment, like a wedding or circumcision</note>. Surely their intention in this was for the sake of Heaven. From such drinking, many fellowships were formed, and through this, our Sages said that there were many [scholars] at the table, debating with sharp wisdom. We find in the chapter "HaMotzi" <note>A chapter in the Talmud</note> that Rabbi Yochanan found his heart [strengthened] and his wisdom returned to him [after drinking], and he asked about all the "voids of the world." From this, we see that through joy, the wise man reveals the secrets of wisdom. The reason is that the blessings of wisdom and wine [share a connection] with the intellectual soul. Then, it is more prepared to reveal the hidden things of wisdom, as our Sages said <note>in the chapter "All are Forbidden"</note>: "Give them more wine so they will say something [of Torah]." This is the secret of the phrase: "When wine enters, the secret comes out" <note>original: "נכנס יין יצא סוד" (Nichnas yayin yatza sod). In Gematria (Hebrew numerology), the word for wine (Yayin) and secret (Sod) both equal 70</note>. By this, they meant that through the drinking of wine, words of Torah—which are called "secrets"—should emerge. This is why they said it was given between two letters <note>A reference to the 70 "faces" or interpretations of the Torah</note>. Rashi explains on the word "given to you" that its numerical value hints at the strength of the giving of the Torah, which was given according to this number, for the Torah has seventy faces.

It seems to me that this was also the intention of Rabbi Akiva at his son’s feast, as mentioned in the chapter "With what may a woman [go out]": It happened that Rabbi Akiva made a feast for his son, and over every single cup he brought, he would say: "Wine and life to the mouths of the Rabbis! Life and wine to the mouths of the Rabbis and their students!" One might ask: Why did he say this over the cup and not over the food? Furthermore, why did he say "to the mouths of the Rabbis"—do not all of Israel require life? Rather, Rabbi Akiva’s intention was to awaken the hearts of the Rabbis and their students during the wine-feast, so they would not intend their drinking for the pleasure of intoxication or to fill their bellies. Instead, their primary intention should be for the good purpose that follows—that the thought of the joy of the wine-feast should open their minds so they might speak words of Torah through the power of the cups. This is why he said "to the mouths of the Rabbis," to indicate to them that this wine is only worthy when the Rabbis and their students are reclining together. But if commoners who are not students of Torah are mixed among them, who learn from them to drink like "masters of writing" <note>likely meaning those who drink habitually or without higher purpose</note>, they think only of the cup of intoxication and drink their cup all at once—these are like "confused grains" and not "of the type of Torah." Unlike the scholars who drink and break [their habits], the commoners' whole intention in drinking is to fill the throat. In such a case, one should instead sing the "Psalm of Afflictions." A deaf man does not hear and does not speak holy words of Torah; this is not the way.

And this is what our Sages said <note>in the fifth chapter of Nazir</note>: "The pure-minded of Jerusalem were refined; they would not join a feast unless they knew who was reclining with them." This is clear. For this purpose, some of the sages would appoint a group of Torah scholars, showing that their intention was to generate joy in the soul. For through the joy of the soul, the Holy Spirit may rest upon them, as our Sages said <note>in the chapter "One may not stand"</note>: "The Divine Presence [Shekhinah] does not rest upon a person through laziness... but through the joy of a commandment." The intention of the great ones, even when they drink to a state of intoxication, is desirable because their intent is not to fill the belly or to "draw their flesh with wine," but toward the good thing that results from it. As I wrote above, their main intent is to inquire and search for wisdom. For when the physical powers are strengthened, the spiritual powers are also strengthened, and they become as two spirits within them. This is as Rabbi Bahya wrote in the portion of *Toledot* regarding the "tasty foods" of Isaac. On this and similar matters, our Sages said in the chapter "The One who Sees": "What is a small passage upon which all the bodies of the Torah depend? *In all your ways, know Him, and He will straighten your paths* <note>Proverbs 3:6</note>." Rava said: "Even for a matter of transgression." Rashi explains: "In all your ways—even when performing a transgression, set your heart to it if it is for the need of a commandment." Thus we said in the chapter "Nazir": "A transgression performed for a holy sake is greater than a commandment performed not for its own sake." Nevertheless, I say: drink, but do not lose your mind; that is not the way.

->Let no man eat the bread of sorrows<-
->Let him rejoice in his freedom, He who satisfies the hungry<-

<margin>Section 4: One must</margin> A person must rejoice in his portion and trust in his Creator, who provides his sustenance. He should not constrain himself with the minutiae of poverty, but should conduct himself at his meal in a pleasant manner. Thus they said in the Midrash: "All the days of the poor are evil"—this refers to one who is "poor" in his faith and "harsh" in his faith. If sustenance happens to come to him, it seems to him as if it is more than his property [warrants] and he will need to rely on others; thus all his days are in sorrow and anxiety. But he who rejoices in his portion and believes in the Holy One, Blessed be He—that He provides his sustenance at every time he needs it—his heart is forever joyful and good, as if a set table and a feast are always before him. Furthermore, we learn in the Midrash: "Better a dry morsel with quietness" <note>Proverbs 17:1</note>—this refers to the one who rejoices in his portion and is always quiet and tranquil. Since he is happy with what the Holy One, Blessed be He, has provided for him, he will never steal or act despicably. Thus he is quiet and trusting. "...than a house full of feasting with strife"—this refers to one who does not rejoice in his portion, but pursues coarse foods and will steal and rob in order to satisfy his desires all his days. Consequently, all his days are in strife and quarrel, and he is pursued by other people. He who desires but a little to satisfy his soul, and does not intend for the pleasure of his body—he truly knows his Creator.

<meta>The text transitions from the dangers of wine to the virtue of contentment (rejoicing in one's portion) and trusting in Divine Providence for sustenance.</meta>

<summary>This page warns against the physical and spiritual ruin caused by drunkenness, particularly for Torah scholars, while offering a nuanced defense of drinking for the purpose of uncovering "Torah secrets" through joy. It concludes by praising the virtue of being content with one's portion and trusting in God for livelihood.</summary>

<meta>The previous page discussed the dangers of excess, specifically cautioning against drunkenness using the example of Noah and the symbolic meaning of wine. This page transitions to a more positive instruction: how to transform the act of eating into a sacred ritual, comparing the dining table to the Altar in the Temple.</meta>

<header>The Gate of the Letters 86</header>

<margin>
The upright ones and words of Torah at the table
</margin>

...the earth, for nothing is as praised as building the Altar. This acts as the likeness of a "Peace Offering" <note>original: *Zevach Shelamim*, a type of sacrifice in the Temple shared between the altar, the priest, and the owner</note> brought as a pleasing aroma to the Lord. Arranging words of Torah at the table is in the likeness of the "Men of the Stand" <note>original: *Anshei Ma’amad*, representatives of the public who stood by during Temple sacrifices</note> who would occupy themselves with the Story of Creation, and so on. The Grace After Meals corresponds to the song that the Levites would sing on the platform, along with the prayers they would pray. Behold, three things are included here which are the sustenance of the world: The first is Words of Torah; the second is the Divine Service, which is represented by the Grace After Meals; and the third is Acts of Kindness, which is the kindness one performs for the poor at his table. These are the three "mothers" <note>original: *amot*, usually meaning "cubits" or "mothers/foundations"</note> that stand before the Altar. Do not read it as "cubits" [*amot*] but as "nations" [*umot*] or "foundations." These three things that a person must fulfill at his table are the foundations of all the commandments. Thus you have come to know how a person's table is an Altar of atonement for him and for the whole world in this time [when the Temple is destroyed]. This concludes the quote for our purposes; we have shortened the language to fit our intent and skipped what was not essential.

**And what appears** to us, according to what is included in the words of these two aforementioned commentators—Rabbi Joseph Ya’avetz and the author of *The Worm of Jacob* <note>original: *Tola'at Ya’akov*, a mystical commentary on the prayer book by Meir ibn Gabbai</note>—is that both intended the same thing: to inform us how a person’s table is an altar of atonement in this era. **And even though** the aforementioned authors differ in some of the implications of the discussion: the author of *The Worm of Jacob* considers three things a person must fulfill at his table—feeding the poor, Torah study, and Grace After Meals—paralleling the Table on High [the Altar], which was chosen with three crowns: the Priests occupied with the service; the Levites singing on the platform;

<margin>
Feeding the poor in any case
</margin>

and the "Men of the Stand" who would read the Story of Creation. Feeding the poor at one's table is the likeness of the Service, which is the sacrifice. [Torah study] is the likeness of the Men of the Stand who would read the Story of Creation every day. And Grace After Meals corresponds to the song that the Levites would sing on the platform. However, in the book *The Beginning of Wisdom* <note>original: *Reshit Chochmah*</note> in the name of Rabbi Joseph Ya’avetz, he mentions only two things a person must fulfill at his table: [feeding the poor] in place of the sacrifice, and Torah study in place of the song the Levites would sing. Regarding the third, the Grace After Meals, he mentions nothing.

Nevertheless, there is no difference between them regarding the core intent at all; "these and those are the words of the Living God." One master said one thing and the other said another, but they do not disagree. It is only that the author of *The Worm of Jacob* descends into the specific count of what a person must fulfill to make his table worthy of being offered before the Lord—meaning, literally like an Altar. Since the Altar was one cubit [*amah*] by one cubit to find the sum, these three things correspond to the Altar being chosen with three "crowns" as mentioned above. God also made one corresponding to the other, matching the three things upon which the world stands. But Rabbi Ya’avetz does not descend into the count; he simply lists one by one what must be fulfilled so that the table becomes an Altar of atonement. These are feeding the poor and Torah study, and through this, his sin is atoned for as if he brought a sacrifice. As for the Grace After Meals, since it is a biblical obligation <note>original: *de-oraita*</note> and one is required to bless regardless, he does not count it among the others. **Furthermore**, Rabbi Ya’avetz is speaking of the table of kings—and "who are the kings? The Rabbis"—meaning he is only speaking of the table of a Torah Scholar <term>Talmid Chacham<gloss>a person extensively learned in Jewish law and tradition</gloss></term>, whose table is greater than the table of the rest of the people. For the lesson is "In all your ways, know Him" <note>Proverbs 3:6</note>; in all his deeds and all he does, the Lord makes him successful, for he intends everything for the sake of a commandment. Even the bread he eats is not intended for physical pleasure, but for the sustenance of the soul, as it is written: "The righteous eats to satisfy his soul" <note>Proverbs 13:25</note>—meaning the literal soul, the thing the spirit depends upon. He intends it for the sake of a commandment so that his body will be healthy for the service of the Blessed Creator, as mentioned at the beginning of this section. Automatically, he intends for his table to be an Altar of atonement to the best of his ability. **But** the common people, who are not as meticulous in the commandments, are also not as careful to ensure their table is an altar of atonement. Therefore, he speaks only of the table of a Torah Scholar. He says that a person should make his table atone for him now that the Temple is not standing, as if he offered a sacrifice on the Altar. He says that in place of the sacrifice, he should feed the poor, and in place of the song, he should speak words of Torah. Because he is speaking here only of the table of a Torah Scholar who is careful in all matters, he is naturally careful with his table. Therefore, he does not count Grace After Meals here, because all the people participate in this, as there is no one so poor in Torah knowledge among Israel that they would not recite the Grace After Meals.

---

<margin>
And perhaps...
until here
</margin>

**And perhaps** this is what our Sages of blessed memory intended when they said <note>in the Talmud, Tractate Bava Batra, and cited by the *Tur* in the laws of meals</note>: "What is the table of a Torah Scholar like? Two-thirds covered [*gadil*] and one-third exposed [*galai*], upon which the cups and bowls are placed." (The explanation is: "Two-thirds covered" means the width of the table is covered with a cloth on the side of the eaters to wipe their mouths and place the bread, and the outer third is exposed to place the bowls and cups so they do not soil the cloth and disgrace the eaters). This concludes the language of the statement.

<margin>side b</margin>

**From here** it implies that some good deed or good character trait comes to them when the table is "two-thirds covered," and so on. Therefore, they specifically said "the table of a Torah scholar," because they must possess more good traits than the rest of the people, as mentioned above. In many places in the Talmud, they say, "A person of distinction is different." Who are they? Those whose path is a good way or a good trait, compared here to a Torah scholar. When his table is as described—with a cloth over two-thirds and one-third exposed—**therefore**, why say "What is the table of a Torah scholar like?" and so on? Are we not all sons of one man? Whether wise, simple, or one who does not know, we all spread a cloth on the table for the sake of modesty and cleanliness in a measure that suffices for all of us. **Therefore**, why were they specific about this measure of two-thirds covered and one-third exposed—no less and no more? **And furthermore**, why did they use the word *gadil* <note>usually meaning "braid" or "fringe"</note> instead of *mapah* [cloth]? **And furthermore**, why does it say "two-thirds *gadil*" without explaining that the bread and meal items are placed upon it, as it explains regarding the "one-third exposed" that the bowls and cups are placed upon it?

<margin>
The purpose of sustenance...
and ate... he made...
at his table... that is...
the rest of the people
</margin>

**Side B:** It seems to me that our Sages hinted here at what we mentioned regarding the words of Rabbi Ya’avetz. Because it is the way of a Torah scholar to be separate and careful in his deeds more than the rest of the people—as they said: "Whatever he does, he does for a good purpose"—the question is asked: "What is the table of a Torah scholar like?" For surely the table of a scholar is greater than the table of the rest of the people in its excellence and the strength of Torah and commandments. They do nothing, small or large, unless some good purpose follows from it. So he asks: In what way is their table greater than the rest of the people? (Meaning, what good purpose is derived from the table of a scholar?) **He answered:** "Two-thirds *gadil*." The word *gadil* is from the language of "greatness" [*gedulah*] and "exaltation." It means the Torah scholar performs two types of commandments at his table—meaning during the time of eating—which are called "greatness" [*gadil*]. These are Torah and feeding the poor, for these two are good for the forgiveness of sin and the pardon of iniquity, as mentioned above. **Torah** is called *gadil* because its status and exaltation are above all other deeds.

<margin>He who feeds</margin>

the poor at his table—which is the highest form of charity, as mentioned above—is also called *gadil*, based on the verse: "Righteousness exalts a nation" <note>Proverbs 14:34</note>, which our Sages interpreted as referring to Israel. And it is written: "And who is like Your people Israel, one nation in the land?" **As for what it says**, "one-third exposed" [*galai*], this is according to its plain meaning. That is to say, since he made his table an altar of atonement through the poor and the Torah, his meal is considered like a sacrifice on the Altar, and he is forgiven. Then he may eat and drink as he wishes, for it is holy, and he eats from the sacred things just enough for his life, so that his body is healthy for the service of God.

<margin>The word *galai*</margin>

indicates eating and drinking with brokenness and mindfulness. For the word *galai* [exposed/revealed] and the word "famous" [public/manifest] have the same meaning and also refer to "knowledge" [*da’at*]. The philosophers called physical pleasures "manifest things" [*mefursamot*] because they utilize the manifest—the body, which is revealed and manifest—while the soul, "the King's daughter, is all glorious within" <note>Psalm 45:14</note> and has no pleasure from this at all. **As for what it says** "one-third," no more and no less, it comes to teach us a moral lesson: when a person engages in "manifest" things, namely eating and drinking like the rest of the world, he should not eat to satisfy himself by filling his belly and his lust like an animal. Rather, he should eat a third, drink a third, and leave the remaining third empty. As Elijah said to Rav Yehuda: "Eat a third, drink a third, and leave a third," etc. This is the meaning of "one-third exposed" [*galai*]—meaning empty. This is easy to understand. **With this**, the questions we asked regarding the statement are answered, and everything works out beautifully, agreeing from every side with what we mentioned.

<margin>
And there is no difference...
so that you may dwell...
when you sit...
to dine with a ruler etc.
</margin>

Happy is the one who prepares these two things at his table: Torah study and distribution to the poor. Then his table becomes "the table that is before the Lord," and it is accepted to atone for him as stated. It seems that the Scripture also hinted at this in saying: "When you sit to dine with a ruler..." <note>Proverbs 23:1</note>. This means that when a person sits to dine with the "Honorable Ruler"—which is the soul that resides within him and rules over his spirit to keep it from speaking [nonsense]—the "Intellectual Soul" **will surely understand...** internally. One [third] for the Torah, which is called "bread," and one for the poor man to eat...

<meta>The text cuts off at the catchword "with him" [atô]. It continues the allegorical interpretation of Proverbs 23:1, linking the "ruler" to the soul and the meal to spiritual activities.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the table of a person serving as an altar of atonement. It compares the acts performed at a meal—specifically sharing food with the poor and speaking words of Torah—to the sacrificial service in the Holy Temple, drawing on the works of Rabbi Joseph Ya’avetz and the kabbalistic commentary Tola’at Ya’akov.</meta>

<header>The Gate of the Letters 86</header>

<margin>And their standing</margin>
<margin>Words of Torah on the table</margin>
<margin>Literally feeding the poor</margin>
...the land, for there is nothing as praised as the altar for offering a sacrifice. This is comparable to the peace-offering <term>Zevach Shelamim; a type of voluntary sacrifice shared by the altar, the priest, and the owner</term> that is brought as a pleasing aroma to the Lord. Arranging words of Torah at the table is like the "Men of the Standing" <term>Anshei Ma’amad; lay representatives of the Israelites who stood by during Temple sacrifices</term> who were occupied with the story of creation, and so on. Furthermore, the Grace After Meals <note>original: "Birkat HaMazon"</note> corresponds to the song the Levites would sing on the platform, as well as the prayers we pray. Behold, three things are included here which are the foundation of the world: the first is words of Torah; the second is Service <note>original: "Avodah"</note>, represented by the Grace After Meals; and the third is Acts of Lovingkindness, which is the kindness one performs with the poor at his table. These are the "three cubits" <note>original: "amot"</note> that comprise the height of the altar; do not read it as "cubits" <note>amot</note> but as "mothers" <note>imot</note>, meaning these three things a person must fulfill at his table are the "mothers" <note>sources/foundations</note> of all the commandments. Thus far, you have been shown how a person's table is an altar of atonement for him and for the whole world in this time <note>the era after the Temple's destruction</note>. This concludes his words for our purposes; we have shortened his phrasing to suit our intent, though we were compelled to bring what we did. 

It appears to us, based on what is included in the words of these two aforementioned commentators—Rabbi Joseph Ya’avetz and the author of *The Worm of Jacob* <note>original: "Tola’at Ya’akov," a 16th-century kabbalistic work by Meir ibn Gabbai</note>—that both intended one thing: to inform us how a person’s table is an altar of atonement in this time. Even though these authors differ slightly in the implication of the lesson: The author of *Tola’at Ya’akov* counts three things a person must fulfill at his table—feeding the poor, Torah study, and Grace After Meals—paralleling the "High Table" <note>the Altar</note> which was crowned with three crowns: the Priests engaged in the service, the Levites singing on the platform, and the Israelites in their standing <note>Ma’amad</note> who would read from the story of creation. Feeding the poor at one’s table is like the Service, which is the sacrifice. Torah study is like the "Men of the Standing" who would read from the story of creation every day. And the Grace After Meals corresponds to the song the Levites would sing on the platform. 

However, the author of *The Beginning of Wisdom* <note>original: "Reshit Chochmah"</note> in the name of Rabbi Joseph Ya’avetz, mentioned only two things a person must fulfill at his table in place of a sacrifice: [Charity] and Torah in place of the song the Levites sang. Regarding the third—the Grace After Meals—he mentioned nothing. There is no real difference between them in terms of their core intention; both are "the words of the Living God." One master said one thing and the other master said another, and they do not actually disagree. It is simply that the author of *Tola’at Ya’akov* followed a numerical count, reckoning what a person must do for his table to be fit to be "sanctified before the Lord"—meaning exactly like the altar—and from this he derived the count and timing of the three crowns the altar wears, as mentioned above. He also set this up against the "three things upon which the world stands." 

Rabbi Joseph Ya’avetz, however, did not follow a numerical count; he only listed specific items one must fulfill so that his table becomes an altar of atonement, namely: feeding the poor and Torah study. Through these, his sin is atoned for as if he offered a sacrifice. But Grace After Meals, which is a Torah-mandated obligation <note>original: "De-Oraita"</note>—and since one is already obligated by the Torah to bless over food—he did not include it among those [voluntary] spiritual acts. Furthermore, Rabbi Joseph Ya’avetz was referring to the "Table of Kings"—and who are the kings? The scholars <note>original: "Rabbanan"</note>. That is to say, he was speaking only of the table of a Torah scholar, whose table is greater than the table of common people. For a pious person is distinct in all his actions, and in everything he does, the Lord grants him success because he intends it for the sake of a commandment. Even the bread he eats is not intended for bodily pleasure, but for the sustenance of his soul, as it is written: "The righteous man eats to satisfy his soul" <note>Proverbs 13:25</note>. This means that because of his concern for the thing upon which the soul depends, his intention is for the sake of a commandment, so that his body may be healthy for the service of the Blessed Name, as mentioned at the beginning of this chapter. Consequently, he also intends for his table to be an altar of atonement to the best of his ability. 

But the common masses, who are not so meticulous in the commandments, are not careful to ensure their table is an altar of atonement. Therefore, he speaks only of the table of the Torah scholar. He says that in this way, his table will atone for him now in the time when the Temple is no longer standing, as if he offered a sacrifice upon the altar. He said that in place of the sacrifice, he should feed the poor, and in place of the song, he should speak words of Torah, and it will be considered as if he offered a sacrifice. Because he is speaking here only of the table of a Torah scholar—who follows all the ways of piety and is careful at the table—he does not count the Grace After Meals here. For in the Grace After Meals, even the common people fulfill it perfectly; you will not find even the most "impoverished" in Israel <note>meaning impoverished in Torah knowledge</note> who does not recite the Grace After Meals.

---

<margin>Page Side B</margin>
**And it is possible** that this is what our Sages of blessed memory intended when they said <note>in Tractate Bava Batra, Chapter 'Chazkat HaBatim,' and in the Orach Chaim section 165</note>: "What is the table of a Torah scholar like? Two-thirds covered and one-third exposed, upon which the cups and bowls are placed." (Rashi explains: "Two-thirds covered"—the width of the table is covered with a cloth on the side of the diners to wipe their mouths and to set the bread upon; and the outer third is exposed to set the bowls and cups upon so they do not soil the cloth or the food of the diners). Thus far is the language of the statement. 

It implies that they would achieve some good deed or character trait from the table being two-thirds covered, etc. Therefore they specifically said "the table of a Torah scholar," because they must live as masters of good character more than the rest of the people, as mentioned above and in many places in the Talmud where it says "an important person is different." Now, consider: what good character trait is derived—God forbid—from the table being covered as mentioned, two-thirds covered and one-third exposed? Furthermore, why did they ask "What is the table of a Torah scholar like?" etc. Are we not all the children of one man? God forbid [to suggest otherwise]! If he is lacking because he does not know to spread a cloth on the table for the sake of modesty and cleanliness, the measure should be equal for all of us. Furthermore, why were they meticulous about this specific measure: two-thirds covered and one-third exposed—no more and no less? Furthermore, why did they say "braided/covered" <note>original: "gadil"</note> rather than "cloth" <note>original: "mapah"</note>? Furthermore, why does it say "two-thirds covered" without explaining that the bread and meal items are placed upon it, while it does explain regarding the "one-third exposed" that the bowls and cups are placed upon it?

---

<margin>Page Side B</margin>
**Page Side B:** It seems to me that our Sages of blessed memory hinted here at what we mentioned nearby in the words of Rabbi Joseph Ya’avetz. That is, in the life of a scholar, it is the way of the pious to be distinct and measured in his actions more than the rest of the people, as mentioned. Everything he does is done for a good purpose or because it is a path toward that purpose. Therefore, regarding the statement "What is the table of a Torah scholar like?" etc., surely the table of a Torah scholar is greater than the table of other people in the excellence and strength of Torah and commandments. They would not do a small thing or a large thing unless some good purpose could be drawn from it. The Sages were asking: In what way is their table "greater" than the table of others? (Meaning, what good purpose is drawn from the scholar's table?) 

They answered: "Two-thirds *gadil*." The word *gadil* <note>meaning braided or covered</note> comes from the language of *gedulah*—greatness and loftiness. It means that the Torah scholar should perform two types of commandments at his table (that is, during the time of eating) which are called "greatness" <note>gadil</note>. These are Torah and the poor, for "two are better than one" for the forgiveness of sin and the pardoning of iniquity, as mentioned. Torah is called "greatness" <note>gadil</note> because it makes one great and elevates him above all other actions.

<margin>And the one who feeds</margin>
**And the one who feeds** a poor person at his table—which is the most excellent form of charity as mentioned—is also called "greatness" <note>gadil</note> based on the verse: "Righteousness [Charity] exalts a nation" <note>Proverbs 14:34</note>, which our Sages interpreted <note>in the chapter 'HaMocher Et HaSefinah'</note> as referring to Israel, as it is written: "And who is like Your people Israel, one nation on the earth?" 

As for what it says, "one-third exposed" <note>original: "galai"</note>, etc.—this is according to its simple meaning. That is, since he has made his table an altar of atonement through the poor and the Torah, his meal is considered like a sacrifice and an altar. Therefore, let him eat and drink as he wishes, for it is holy. <margin>And so his holy portion shall be eaten</margin> And so his holy portion shall be eaten for the sake of his life's sustenance, so that his body is healthy for the service of the Blessed Name. <margin>And the word 'galai'</margin> And the word *galai* <note>exposed/revealed</note> refers to eating and drinking with clarity and knowledge, for the word "revealed" <note>galuy</note> and the word "famous/public" <note>mefursam</note> share the same meaning. You also know that the philosophers called physical pleasures "the famous/public things" <note>mefursamot</note>, because one uses the "famous" part, which is the body that is exposed and public, whereas the soul—"all the glory of the king's daughter is within"—derives no pleasure from this at all. 

And as for the "one-third"—no more and no less—the number three is a moral lesson: when a person engages in "public/physical things," namely eating and drinking in the way of the world, he should not eat just for his own intent. Rather, he should eat [to fill] one-third [of his stomach], drink [to fill] one-third, and leave the remaining third empty. As Elijah said to Rav Yehudah <note>in the chapters 'Erev Pesachim' and 'Gittin'</note>: "Eat a third, drink a third, etc." This is the meaning of "one-third exposed" <note>galai</note>, meaning empty. This is easy to understand. 

With this, the questions we raised regarding the statement "and the breath..." are answered, which are those we mentioned nearby. <margin>Torah and a portion for the poor</margin> The person who fulfills these two things at his table—namely Torah and kindness to the poor—then his table will be "the table which is before the Lord," as explained. It appears they hinted at this in the verse that says: "When you sit to dine with a ruler, etc." <note>Proverbs 23:1</note>. This means when a wise person sits with the "Noble Ruler"—of whom it is said "he who rules his spirit is better than he who captures a city," which is the intellectual soul—then "you shall surely understand" <note>the verse repeats the word 'understand'</note>... twice. Once for the Torah, which is called understanding <note>Binah</note>, and once for the poor, so that his eating may be...

# The Gate of the Letters

**All** sour and bad fruits should not be eaten, except for a tiny amount during the summer in hot climates. However, figs, grapes, and almonds are always good, whether fresh or dried, and a person may eat as much of them as they need; nevertheless, one should not make them a dietary staple <note>original: "shomer achilatan," implying one shouldn't rely on them as primary sustenance</note> even though they are the best of all tree fruits.

**Honey** and wine are bad for children but good for the elderly, especially during the rainy season <note>the winter months</note>. A person should eat in the summer only two-thirds of what they eat in the rainy season. This is the summary of his words, as we have skipped what was not absolutely necessary to write here. While a person is eating, they should not drink even water; if one drinks a great deal during the meal, it causes the food not to "cook" <note>An ancient medical concept where digestion was viewed as a "cooking" process in the stomach</note> properly. It is like a cooking pot: if you put in a little water, the food cooks thoroughly, but if there is too much, it will not cook for a very long time. So says the author of *Provision for the Way* in the third section <note>original: *Tzedah LaDerech*, a 14th-century work by Menachem ibn Zerach</note>. (The same is found in *Paths of Faith* in the fifth path. This applies specifically *during* the meal, but after the meal, one should drink a large amount at once so that it "rinses" the food in the stomach, as our Sages of blessed memory said in the chapter "All the Meat": "The one who follows his meal with water will not suffer from intestinal illness." Rashi <note>the preeminent medieval commentator</note> explains this as drinking enough water after the meal so that the food floats in it.)

**The rest** of the matters regarding foods that are healthy for the body or harmful to the body, and their quantities—here a person must be daring until they are close to a slight diarrhea. This is a great principle in medicine: as long as one's waste is expelled with difficulty, many illnesses arise. One should also consider which foods are good to eat in the summer and which are good in the rainy season; there are some foods that are unfit to eat in either summer or winter. See *Shimoni* in the place mentioned, and *Paths of Faith*, and *Provision for the Way* (Article 1, Section 3). Also, see *The Candelabrum of Light* (Section 4, Chapter 3) and it will be well for him.

**One should** seek out "thin" <note>light or refined</note> foods, for in accordance with their digestion, the intellect descends and the heart is opened, as our Sages of blessed memory said: "Wine and fragrances make one wise" (Tractate *Yoma*).

**One should be careful** of "coarse" <note>heavy or unrefined</note> foods as much as possible, for the intellect is thickened by them and loses its clarity and purity (for the food belongs to the physical body while the intellect is separate). This matter is proven and tested by city dwellers whose delicacies and drinks are light and pure—are they not more successful in every wisdom and understanding of science than the villagers who eat barley, onions, and other foul foods? Three things were said: One who eats and does not walk [afterward], his food becomes blood <note>original: "dam," here meaning congested or unhealthy</note> and this is the beginning of intestinal illness. But they only said this regarding the morning meal. Resh Lakish said in the first chapter of *Kira*: One who eats and drinks and does not walk four cubits <note>about 6–8 feet</note>, his innards rot, and this is the beginning of a "bad spirit" <note>likely referring to foul gas or metabolic waste</note>. But they only said this regarding the evening meal. If one needs to relieve himself but holds it back, this is the beginning of bad breath. **Our Sages said:** A Torah scholar should not eat or drink while standing. The *Tur* (Section 173) wrote: "The Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, 13th century</note> was accustomed to washing his hands between meat and fish, for danger is more serious than a ritual prohibition." (And it is written in the *Tur*, Section 4, and in the *Torah of the Sin Offering* in the name of the *Long Prohibition and Permission*: "Fish that were salted with poultry need not be forbidden due to danger, for there is no danger in salting.") It is also good to pause between them with a drink so that they do not mix together in the stomach while "cooking." The summary of the matter: The best of all physicians is "necessary prevention," which is for a person to distance themselves from coarse, heavy foods and drinks that cause dangerous illnesses, and also from overeating even light foods, for they increase "excess humors" <note>original: "sam paprish," referring to waste fluids or phlegm in medieval medicine</note> and cause illnesses. When one is careful in these things, they will not need a doctor, even if they have a weak constitution. If they do need one, even though it is permitted to seek advice (as the Sages said: "And he shall surely heal—from here we learn that the physician is given permission to heal"), one should first pray before the Holy One, Blessed be He, and cry out and plead for relief, and He will hear the prayer. One should also go to a wise man to pray on their behalf, as Rabbi Pinchas bar Chama taught: "Anyone who has a sick person in his house should go to a wise man to seek mercy for him." Above all, a person should place his trust in the Creator of the world, in whose hand it is to preserve health and heal illnesses, as it is written: "I am the Lord, your Healer."

---

## One should linger at his table to do the will of his Creator

**Section 6:** A Torah scholar must linger and stay a long time at his table, as we learned in the chapter *He-hedaya*: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: "Three things lengthen a person's days and years: one who prolongs his prayer, one who prolongs his stay at his table (Rashi explains: because through this, the poor come and are fed), and one who prolongs his stay in the bathroom." It is explained there that this is appropriate for every single person. And what is the reason for lingering at the table? Perhaps a poor person will come and he will give to him. For it is written: "The Altar was of wood, three cubits high," and it is then written: "And he spoke to me: This is the table that is before the Lord." The verse begins with "Altar" and ends with "Table." Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Eleazar both said: "As long as the Temple stood, the Altar atoned for Israel; now, a person's table atones for him."

**Behold,** according to the plain meaning of the statement, if one feeds a poor person at his table (or sends portions to the poor), it is considered like a sacrifice. We now stand in a time where it is possible to merit this before eating. But if a person is traveling and there is no poor person with him, or if he is alone, or at night when there are not many poor people wandering about, or in a place where the poor are not common—what is his remedy so that his table becomes an Altar of atonement? **It is possible** to say that he should have in his mind the value of the food that a poor person could have eaten at his table, and give that sum of money so the poor person can buy his own meal. However, the Talmud does not say this; it says "perhaps a poor person will come," implying that the main thing is to give from his own bread to the poor, as it is written: "Is it not to share your bread with the hungry?" This implies giving from what you yourself are eating. The reason is that it provides immediate gratification to the poor person. Furthermore, for the poor person himself who has no one to give to him, how shall his table atone for him? It is possible for us to say that if he is accustomed to giving, or intends to give during his meal to atone for him, that is one way; another way is through Words of Torah spoken during the meal, for the Torah atones more than sacrifices. As our Sages said: "Sacrifice and meal-offering do not atone, but Words of Torah do atone." If he is eating alone and has no companion to speak with, let him study. If there is no one else in the house he can speak with, perhaps he should speak to himself during the meal. The Sages said: "From where do we know that even one who sits and occupies himself with Torah has the Divine Presence with him?"

**In the Midrash** on Ruth, the Sages said: "'And Boaz ate and drank and his heart was good'—because he occupied himself with Words of Torah, as it is said: 'The Torah of Your mouth is better for me than thousands [of gold and silver].'" **Thus we find** that in any place where there are no poor people, or if he is poor himself, his table becomes an Altar of atonement through his occupation with Torah. It is fitting that it be called an "Altar" [*mizbe'ach*] because an Altar is so called because one slaughters [*zovchin*] sacrifices upon it; similarly, through the study of Torah, a person slaughters his Evil Inclination, as they said: "If this repulsive one [the inclination] meets you, drag him to the Study Hall."

**The wise person** will take this to heart, and from the beginning of his meal, he will direct his focus so that he eats in order that his table becomes an Altar of atonement, as mentioned above.

**If he does not have** enough for himself alone, or if he has enough but is in a place without poor people, let him occupy himself with Torah at his table with those eating his bread or by himself, for it atones for sin like a sacrifice, or more than a sacrifice. **Better are the two together:** meaning, he should give of his bread to the poor and also study Torah at his table. Through this, his table will truly be an Altar of atonement, as if he offered a sacrifice upon the Altar. The author of *Reshit Chokhmah* wrote in the name of the pious Rabbi Yosef Yaavetz: "When eating at a table... it begins with the Altar and ends with the Table to say that when the Temple stood, a person was atoned for by sacrifices and the singing of the Levites; now, in place of sacrifices, one feeds the poor, and in place of the song, one speaks Words of Torah." Some have the custom to sing songs, hymns, or psalms after the meal, and this is a beautiful custom to be saved from punishment. But the main "speech" should be a law, a new insight into a verse, or a legend <note>original: *Aggadah*, homiletical teachings</note>. The author of *The Worm of Jacob* <note>original: *Tola'at Yaakov*, a 16th-century kabbalistic work by Meir ibn Gabbai</note> wrote in *The Secrets of Blessings*: "It is fitting for us to make known the straight path a person should choose while at his table so it becomes an Altar of atonement... for when a person feeds the poor at his table, his sacrifice is a Peace Offering to the Lord. Therefore, one must feed them from the best of the table, just as the fat and the blood were offered to the Most High, as it is written: 'When you set aside the fat from it'—meaning the choice part."
