## The Gate of the Letters

**All** sour fruits and grapes should only be eaten in small amounts during the summer in hot climates. Figs, grapes, and almonds are always good, whether fresh or dried, and a person may eat as much of them as they need, though one should not eat them constantly, even though they are the best of all tree fruits. Honey and wine are bad for children but good for the elderly, especially during the rainy season <note>the winter months in the Land of Israel</note>. A person should eat two-thirds as much in the summer as they eat in the winter. This is the summary of the words of our Sages <note>original: *rabboteinu zichronam livracha* (R'Z'L)</note> regarding food, and to broaden one's understanding, it is written: while a person eats, they should not drink at all; for if one drinks heavily while eating, it causes the food not to digest <note>original: *titbashel*, literally "to cook," reflecting the ancient view of digestion as a heat-based process</note> properly. It is like a cooking pot: if you put a little water in it, the food cooks thoroughly, but if there is too much water, it will not cook for a long time. So writes the author of *Provision for the Way* <note>original: *Tzedah LaDerekh*, a 14th-century halakhic work</note> in another place, Chapter 3. (It says the same in *Paths of Faith* <note>original: *Shevilei Emuna*</note> in the fifth path: specifically *during* the meal one should not drink, but *after* the meal, one should drink a large amount at once so that it rinses the food in the stomach. As it says in the Talmud: "One who clears his meal with water will not suffer from intestinal illness." Rashi <note>the preeminent medieval commentator</note> explains this to mean drinking enough water after a meal so that the food "floats" in the water).

**Further** matters concerning foods that are healthy for the body or harmful to it: how much a person should soften their bowels until they are close to a mild laxative state—this is a great principle in medicine, for as long as one's waste is expelled with difficulty, many illnesses come. Also, which foods are good to eat in the summer and which in the winter, and which foods should not be eaten in either season. See Maimonides <note>original: *Maimoni*, referring to the 12th-century physician and philosopher Moses Maimonides</note> in the aforementioned place, and *Paths of Faith*, and *Provision for the Way*, Discourse 1, Chapter 3. Also see *The Candelabrum of Light* <note>original: *Menorat HaMaor*</note>, page 83, for his own good.

One should be careful after eating "thin" <note>easily digestible</note> foods, lest the food remains linger and cause heart palpitations <note>original: *yitkapeach ha-lev*</note>, as mentioned before by Rav Chisda regarding those with a spiritual sensitivity (Tractate Yoma).

**One should be careful** of "heavy" <note>difficult to digest</note> foods according to their strength, so that their intellect may rise during the day and they may be happy and successful in their time and intention. (For food returns to the body and to the intellect, and becomes a "different" intellect). This matter is a law and a virtue of people of high standing, whose food for their dwellings and their drinks are thin and pure; they are the ones who are wise in every science and understand knowledge more than those who eat rich, heavy foods that cause anger and other "smoky" foods. As the many say, Resh Lakish said: "One who eats and does not drink, his eating is blood, and this is the beginning of intestinal illness." This was said only regarding the morning meal. Resh Lakish also said in the chapter *Kira*: "One who eats and drinks but does not walk four cubits <note>about 6 feet</note>, his entrails rot, and this is the beginning of a 'bad spirit'." This was only said regarding the evening meal, where one would need to cleanse their body after "vomiting it upon the dust," which is the beginning of a "bad spirit." Our Sages said: A Torah scholar should not eat or drink while standing. The *Tur* <note>a major code of Jewish law</note> wrote in Section 173: "My father, the Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note>, was accustomed to wash his hands between eating meat and fish, for danger is more serious than a ritual prohibition" <note>original: *chamira sakanta mei-issura*, a legal principle stating that health risks are treated more strictly than religious bans</note>. (It is similarly written in the *Tur*, section Yoreh De’ah 116. And the *Torat Chattat* wrote in Rule 2 in the name of the *Long Issur V’Heter* that bread that became moist from contact with poultry need not be forbidden due to danger, for there is no danger in salting). It is also good to separate meat and fish with a drink so that the flavors do not mix excessively in the stomach. The summary of the matter: the best medicine is essential caution, which means distancing oneself from heavy, burdensome foods and drinks that bring on illness, and also from eating too much, even of light foods, because they expand in the belly and cause illnesses. When one is careful in these things, they will not need a doctor, unless they have a naturally weak constitution—then they will need advice. As our Sages said: "'And he shall surely heal'—from here we learn that permission is given to a doctor to heal." One should pray before the Blessed Lord that He should counsel and prepare the cure for him and hear his prayer. One should also go to a wise person to pray for him, as it is said (in the chapter *Yesh Nochalim*): Rabbi Phinehas bar Chama taught: "Anyone who has a sick person in their house should go to a wise person and ask for mercy for them, as it says: 'The king’s wrath is as messengers of death; but a wise man will pacify it.'" Above all, a person should place their trust in the Creator of the universe, in whose hand it is to preserve health and heal illnesses, as it is written: "I am the Lord, your healer."

## One should linger at his table to do the will of his Creator

**Section 6: It is necessary** for a Torah scholar to linger and spend time at his table, as we study in the chapter *HaRoeh*. Rav Zera said in the name of Rav: Three things prolong a person's days and years: lingering in prayer, lingering at one's table, and lingering in the bathroom. Rashi explains there: "Lingering at the table—perhaps poor people will come and he can feed them." It says there that the table is like the Altar. It is written: "The altar was of wood, three cubits high... and he said to me, 'This is the table that is before the Lord'." Rabbi Eleazar and Rabbi Yochanan both said: "As long as the Temple stood, the Altar atoned for Israel; now, a person's table atones for him."

According to the simple meaning of the statement: if one feeds the poor at their table (or sends portions to the poor), it is considered like a sacrifice on the Altar. This is fine when it is possible to have them present, but if a person is traveling and there is no poor person with him, or if it is night when poor people are not wandering about, or in a place where the poor are not common—what is the remedy so that the table becomes an Altar of atonement? One might say he should intend in his mind that the food he eats is shared with the poor by giving money later for them to buy a meal. But the Talmud does not say this; it says "perhaps a poor person will come," implying the main thing is giving from one's own sustenance. This is like the story of Mar Ukva. Furthermore, even a poor person who has no one else to give to—his own table atones for him. It is possible to say that if he has no poor person to give to, he should have another person in the house with whom he can speak words of Torah, or he should study by himself while eating. For the Torah atones more than sacrifices, as our Sages said (in Tractate Rosh Hashanah and Yevamot) on the verse: "If it shall be atoned... with sacrifice and offering"—it is not atoned by sacrifice, but it *is* atoned by words of Torah. Even if he eats alone and has no poor person to give to or anyone to speak words of Torah with, he should study by himself. As our Sages said (in *Ethics of the Fathers*): "From where do we know that even if one person sits and occupies himself with Torah, the Divine Presence is with him?" Regarding Boaz, it is said: "Boaz ate and drank and his heart was merry"—because he occupied himself with words of Torah, as it says: "The Torah of Your mouth is better for me [than thousands of gold and silver]." It follows that in any place where there are no poor people, or if he himself is poor, his table becomes an Altar of atonement through the study of Torah. It is fitting to call it an "Altar" (*Mizbeach*) because just as an Altar is where sacrifices are slaughtered (*zovichin*), through the study of Torah a person "slaughters" their evil inclination. As our Sages said: "If this repulsive one [the evil inclination] meets you, drag him to the Study Hall."

**The wise person** will take this to heart, and from the beginning of their meal, they should intend to set aside a portion of their bread for the poor, so that their table may be an Altar of atonement as mentioned above.

**If he does not have** enough for himself, or if he has enough but is in a place without poor people, let him occupy himself with Torah at his table with his fellow eaters or alone, for it atones for sin like a sacrifice—and more than a sacrifice. It is best to do both: to give of his bread to the poor and also to study Torah at his table. In this way, his table becomes a true Altar of atonement, as if he offered a sacrifice upon the Altar. As the author of *Charedim* wrote in the name of the pious Rabbi Joseph Yaavetz regarding the "Third Meal" <note>the mystical Saturday afternoon meal</note> where people ate at one table: "It seems to me that the beginning of the house is the Altar and the conclusion is the table." This means that just as the Altar in the Sanctuary provided atonement through sacrifices and the song of the Levites, now, in place of the sacrifice, one feeds the poor, and in place of the song, one speaks words of Torah. Some are accustomed to sing hymns or psalms after the meal to be saved from punishment, but the main thing is the actual speech—saying some law, a new insight into a verse, or an ethical teaching (*Aggadah*). For there are three categories: the completely righteous who speak of these things, the intermediate, and the wicked who speak of nothing [holy] at all. The author of *The Dew of Jacob* <note>original: *Tola'at Ya'akov*, a Kabbalistic work on prayer</note> wrote in the "Secrets of the Blessings" regarding the aforementioned statement: "It begins with the Altar and ends with the table... it is proper for us to make known the upright path a person should choose while at his table, so that it will be an Altar of atonement... and thus the table will atone for the person in this time just as the Altar did in the time of the Temple." For when a person feeds the poor at his table, it is as if he is offering "Peace Offerings" to the Lord. Therefore, one must feed them the best of what is on the table—the "fat, the milk, and the blood" which were offered to the Most High. As it is written: "When you set aside the fat thereof from it"—the "fat" means the best part, as in "the fat <note>the best</note> of the land."

# The Gate of the Letters

Those mentioned <note>Referring to the poor and scholars mentioned on the previous page</note>, namely the portion for the poor and words of Torah at one's table. For through the power of the four-letter Name <note>The Tetragrammaton, the holy four-letter name of God</note>, which contains two aspects: for a plain young man is solitary and poor, and also the Holy One, Blessed be He, can speak with him... and my teacher changed it <note>This likely refers to a specific pedagogical tradition or a correction in the manuscript's lineage</note> because the young man studies a law every day. 

(The *Zohar* writes in the portion of *Vayechi* regarding the matter of Zebulun and Issachar: "From here we learn that whoever supports a master of Torah receives blessings from above and below, and not only that, but he merits two tables <note>original Aramaic: 'tari patora'</note> which no other person merits... for the wealth with which he is blessed in this world, and he merits to see his portion in the World to Come... all of them shall dwell for the law of the seas, and he for the law of the ships; the law of the seas in this world, and the law of the ships in the World to Come." End of quote.)

And certainly, what is eaten upon the table—which occurs twice a day, evening and morning—is considered like the "continual offerings" <note>The *Tamid* sacrifice</note> that were offered every day upon the Altar as a pleasing aroma to the Lord. As mentioned above, nowadays a person's table atones for them. **And especially** when a person is good with God and good with people, and honors the Torah at his table—meaning the student who studies Torah—placing the Mishnah <note>The foundational work of Rabbinic law</note> before him while he eats. It is then considered as if he offered a sacrifice upon the actual Altar, for thus the fat and blood are offered to the Most High. This is the praised path mentioned above in the name of the author of *The Worm of Jacob* <note>original: *Tola'at Yaakov*, a Kabbalistic work by Meir ibn Gabbai</note>.

**Behold**, I have elaborated somewhat on the table to let you know that "man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of the Lord"—these are the commandments dependent upon it by which a man shall live the True Life. **And now** I have come to return to the first matters and to turn through the sections <note>original: "bharrat," likely an abbreviation for 'be-vayar ha-devarim,' explaining the matters</note> and to mention all the things which are the necessities of the meal in a brief way with a few notes:

**Section 1: One should focus** during the Blessing over the Table <note>Grace After Meals</note> more than other blessings, and say them in a loud voice and with full intention.

**Section 2: When a person sits** to eat, it should be a holy act. He should sanctify himself even in what is permitted to him. During his eating and drinking, his heart should be focused on his needs <note>original: "le-pharesh mahauto," to clarify his essential needs</note>; he should not fill his throat greedily. While he still desires to eat, he should leave his meal for the sake of the honor of the Creator, may He be blessed. The general rule is that he should think at the time of eating that he is eating before the King, the Lord, according to the saying of our Sages: "It is as if they ate from the table of the Omnipresent, Blessed be He." Through this, the poor shall also take hold and benefit from them, and the "faith of his times shall be his strength" <note>A reference to Isaiah 33:6</note>.

**Section 3: Just as** one must be careful of excessive eating, so must one be careful of excessive drinking. For there is no drink more loathsome than strong drink <note>Likely referring to beer or grain alcohol</note>, for every drunkard has no substance, only triviality; he abandons the life of his soul and falls.

**Section 4: Let his heart be good** during his meal, whether it be a little or a lot, and let him eat his bread with joy, and let sighing and groaning flee <note>A play on Isaiah 35:10</note>.

**Section 5: A person should eat** what is good and beneficial for health, and not just what is sweet to his mouth at the moment.

**Section 6: A pious person should** linger at his table so that his table may become an atoning altar. The poor should eat at his table, and he should speak words of Torah over it. When the poor person eats, give him the best of the table. He should speak actual words of Torah at his table and not rely solely on the Grace After Meals; even if he is alone, he should say some Psalm or Mishnah or the like. Then his table will truly resemble an altar, "a fire-offering of pleasing aroma."

---

->A supplement at the end of my composition for the book *Valley of Blessing* <note>original: *Emek Beracha*</note> written in my youth regarding the mystical intentions of the table mentioned there, branching into sections:<-

**The Annotator says:** After seeing that six virtues regarding the table were brought by my father and teacher (may his Rock and Redeemer protect him), speaking of matters of eating and elaborating on them for our eternal good, I said in my heart that I too am on his foundations. I will not withhold my mouth from speaking, and I will add a "gem of my own" to clarify and explain the words of my father and teacher through hints and secrets that I happened to innovate—words sweeter than honey and the drippings of the honeycomb.

**Since** it is written in the *Zohar* in the portion of *Bereshit*: "Rabbi Simeon said to him: 'Open your mouth and I shall place my words in it.' How much must a man labor in the Torah day and night! For the Holy One, Blessed be He, listens to the voices of those who occupy themselves with Torah, and with every new insight discovered in the Torah by one who labors in it, a new heaven is made." (End of quote.) Behold, it is heard from this statement that he who innovates words of Torah creates new heavens. Therefore, I said to myself that those things God has graced me to seek from my heart, I shall mark them upon the matter of the vision of the Ladder that Jacob saw, "its top reaching the heavens." Perhaps I too will be built up by the merit of words of Torah to create new heavens with this innovation I shall innovate for you.

**It is written** in the portion of *Vayetze*: "And Jacob vowed a vow, saying: 'If God will be with me, and guard me on this way that I am going, and give me bread to eat and a garment to wear, and I return in peace to my father's house, then the Lord shall be my God...'"

**It is difficult:** Why did Jacob not vow immediately when he left his father's house, before he saw this great and awesome vision of the dream of the Ladder? Is it not an "all the more so" argument <note>original: *Kal v'chomer*</note>? If Jacob feared that "sin might cause a hindrance" even after the Holy One promised him "Behold, I am with you and I will guard you wherever you go," how much more so should he have feared beforehand! Some commentators who felt this difficulty wrote according to their way what they wrote. But I, in my integrity, shall go in the path of the labor which is with me; with my pen I shall hold it for those who know the hidden wisdom <note>original: "yode'ei chen," practitioners of Kabbalah</note> and understand insight.

**Another difficulty:** Why did Jacob our forefather vow with the language "Then the Lord shall be my God"? This seems like an "unreliable promise" <note>term: *Asmakhta* - a legal term for a conditional commitment where the person doesn't truly intend to follow through, making it non-binding</note>. Even though many on the "right side" have written in the name of Rabbi Immanuel of Fano <note>A prominent 16th-century Italian Kabbalist</note> that vows, oaths, and "hand-clasping" agreements do not fall under the rule of *asmakhta*, nevertheless, it would have been better for Jacob to be more zealous for the commandment and to vow in a language that is more firm and established.

And even if one can resolve this difficulty well—that on the contrary, Jacob our forefather did this to show a practical ruling that for a vow there is no law of *asmakhta*, as our Sages said: "And Jacob vowed a vow *to say*—to say for future generations who vow in times of distress"—so too we can say that he vowed in the language of a condition to show generations that in a vow there is no *asmakhta*. Nevertheless, another difficulty arises: Since he wanted to vow, he should not have made his vow dependent on a condition, but should have vowed whether the condition was fulfilled or not!

**Furthermore**, why did Jacob use the expression of "I" <note>original: *Anokhi*</note> when he said "which *I* am going," and why did he not use the shorter "I" <note>original: *Ani*</note>? It is agreed upon by all Kabbalists that the word *Anokhi* refers more to the internal essence than the word *Ani*. Therefore, the Holy One began the Ten Commandments with "I <note>*Anokhi*</note> am the Lord your God," and not "*Ani* the Lord your God." Would that I knew why Jacob spoke with the language of the internal!

**The difficulty** that rises above them all is what is written: "Then the Lord shall be my God"—that he made the acceptance of God's divinity dependent on a condition. Heaven forbid that our forefather Jacob would do such a thing! Even though Rashi settled this according to the plain meaning <note>original: *pshat*</note>, writing that the vow actually refers to "And this stone... [shall be a house of God]," nevertheless, according to the flow of the text, it does not seem so. Therefore, I too shall answer my part, and may God be with me.

**It is known** that Jacob and Esau were two opposites in one subject—namely, in the womb of their holy mother Rebecca. They are a hint to the unfolding of existences descending from the Lord, which are grasped and tied to the "Side of Holiness," yet they are separate in levels... even if they change equally, if one rises the other falls. Nevertheless, they are tied in one knot... for He gives life to all and brings all into being. They are exactly like the image of Jacob and Esau who were in one body. Their names are fitting for them to hint at this: Esau from the language of "action" <note>original: *Asiyah*</note>, which is the World of Action, and Jacob from the language of "heel" <note>original: *Ekev*</note> and "end," which is the World to Come, as it is the end of all man.

The letter *Yod* <note>the 'y' sound</note> at the beginning of Jacob's name, which is added to the word "heel" <note>*Ekev*</note>, hints at the ultimate purpose that brings man to the World to Come, which is called the "end" <note>also *Ekev*</note>. This *Yod* hints at the Ten Commandments, which include the entire Torah. Regarding this *Yod*, the hint comes in the verse: "He shall crush your head, and you shall crush his heel" <note>Genesis 3:15, the prophecy regarding the serpent/Satan and humanity</note>.

**For it is already known** to anyone who has entered slightly into the gates of Kabbalah that the secret of the soul, the Angel of Death, and the Evil Inclination <note>original: *Yetzer Hara*</note> are all one. Therefore, the Lord said to the serpent, "He shall crush your head," meaning: through the Evil Inclination, man shall clarify your nature and rule over you with the "head"—that is, the letter *Yod*, which is the "head" of the letters of Jacob's name. (It is also the head of all the letters of the Alphabet, as mentioned in the *Pardes* <note>original: *Pardes Rimonim* by Moses Cordovero</note>... for the *Yod* is the head of all because the letter *Aleph* is first, but the *Yod* sits upon the *Aleph* like this: א <note>A reference to the scribal shape of the letter Aleph, composed of two Yods and a Vav</note>).

The *Yod* hints at the Ten Commandments, which are the totality of the Torah, as it is written that the Torah is a "healing stone" for the Evil Inclination. And it says, "and you shall strike his heel"—meaning that when the *Yod* is removed—that is, when he removes himself from the Torah and only the "heel" <note>*Ekev*</note> of Jacob remains—then you, the serpent, can strike him... and the "breaking of the yoke" refers to Esau, who is under the rule of Samael <note>The name of the accuser/Satan in Kabbalah</note>. Perhaps this is also what the verse hinted at by saying "and his hand was holding the heel of Esau," meaning that when the *Yod* is removed and only the heel remains, then Esau—who is the secret of the Evil Inclination—has dominion over that heel. Therefore, the heel is attributed to Esau, but Jacob the Righteous is grasped by the *Yod*—that is, the...

Catchword: **Yod**

# The Gate of the Letters

...him at his table, yet his heart did not know his daughter was with him, even if he prepares what is before him, it is destined to come upon him. This is according to what our Sages, of blessed memory, said <note>original: "Sazal" (Sichronam Livracha)</note> in the chapter "One who asks" <note>Babylonian Talmud, Tractate Shabbat 151b</note>: A person should always ask for mercy regarding this trait <note>poverty</note>, so that he does not come to poverty. For it is something destined to come upon him, or his son, or his grandson. For if it does not come to him, it comes to his son, and if not to his son, to his grandson, as it is said: "For because of <note>Hebrew: "Biglal"</note> this thing" <note>Deuteronomy 15:10</note>. The school of Rabbi Ishmael taught: It is a wheel <note>Hebrew: "Galgal," playing on the word "Biglal"</note> that revolves in the world. See there. Another interpretation: Rabbi Hiyya said to his wife: "When a poor person comes, bring him bread quickly, so that others will bring it quickly to your children." She said to him: "Are you cursing them <note>by implying they will be poor?</note>?" He replied: "No, the verse is written: 'For because of this thing.'" Thus far. This is the meaning of "Understand our haste" mentioned in the verse, meaning one should prepare for his future, for if it does not come to him, it comes to his son, etc.

**Furthermore**, it shall be our task to write and explain the words of the Sages mentioned nearby, where they said that a person's table becomes an Altar of Atonement through the portion given to the poor and <term>Divrei Torah</term> <note>literally "words of Torah"; discussing sacred texts or laws during the meal</note>. Their intent here is literal Torah—to say during the meal some law, a new insight on a verse, or a legendary tale <note>Agadah</note>, as the Rabbis and Rabbi Jacob Emden <note>the "Ya'avetz"</note> explicitly wrote in the words cited above. This excludes the opinion of those who wrote that by reciting the Grace After Meals <note>Birkat HaMazon</note>, one fulfills the obligation of speaking Torah at the table. This is also explicitly implied by the author of *Tola'at Yaakov* <note>a 16th-century Kabbalistic work by Meir ibn Gabbai</note> cited above, who considers Torah at the table to correspond to the "Men of the Watch" <note>Temple participants</note> and Grace After Meals to correspond to the Song of the Levites. From this, we see that Torah is one thing and Grace is another, and one does not exempt the other. 

Here, three things are included which sustain the world: The first is **Torah**; the second is **Service** (represented by Grace After Meals); and the third is **Acts of Kindness** (the mercy shown to the poor at one's table). It is explicitly understood that all three—the portion for the poor, Torah study, and Grace After Meals—must be performed at his table so that his table becomes an Altar of Atonement. 

The book *Reshit Chochma* <note>"The Beginning of Wisdom" by Eliyahu de Vidas</note> in the "Gate of Holiness," chapter 17, elaborates on this in the name of the *Zohar*: that a person should speak Torah at his table before reciting Grace After Meals, in order to unify the "Table" with "Torah." See there. Additionally, the Torah is compared to bread, as it is said: "Come, eat of my bread" <note>Proverbs 9:5</note>. The intent is that just as bread is the primary nourishment for the body, so Torah is the primary nourishment for the soul. This teaches us that it is proper for every wise person to eat "two breads" <note>original: "Lechem Mishneh"</note>: The first is the bread God gave us to eat, which benefits the body but not the soul (material bread); the second is spiritual bread which benefits the soul, namely the words of Torah that a person speaks or thinks during the time of eating, as mentioned two or three times.

**And it is possible** that this is also the intent of our Sages in what they said regarding the verse: "A land of wheat and barley..." <note>Deuteronomy 8:8</note>—that this entire verse was stated for the sake of <term>Shi'urin</term> <note>legal measurements</note>. It is known that wheat and barley relate to the vessels of the Tabernacle. As we learned regarding food vessels: a "loaf of wheat" and "sides of barley." Wine is measured by a "fourth of a log" to bring joy to creatures. On the Sabbath, a "pomegranate" is the measure for a hole in a householder's vessel. "Olive oil and honey" provide measures for dates—honey being like a large date. 

You already know that we have no food or drink more praiseworthy than these Seven Species with which the Land of Israel was blessed. In all of them, the Sages measured things that are the "bodies of the Torah," hinting that when a person eats of these seven species—wheat, barley, etc., which encompass all food and drink—he should not intend his eating merely to fill the belly with material wheat and barley (which benefit the body but not the soul). Rather, he should aim for spiritual wheat and barley (which benefit the soul). He should apply his words to "measurements," meaning he should think with every single swallow about the laws of measurements derived from these species. By doing so, he will also come to remember the rest of the Torah, and the subject will expand, for "one commandment leads to another" <note>original: "Mitzvah goreret mitzvah"</note>. This is the meaning of: "For not by bread alone does man live" <note>Deuteronomy 8:3</note>—meaning material bread alone—"but by everything that comes from the mouth of the Lord"—that is, the words of Torah spoken or thought during the meal while swallowing the food; by this, a man shall truly live.

And let "his hands be faith," meaning he should also remember the four fingers which hold the food and drink. They hint at the Torah and the Service, as the Sages said in Tractate *Ketubot*: each of these fingers was designated for a specific commandment. This one for the measurements of the Breastplate; the ring finger for the Priest’s meal-offering; the middle finger for the vessels of the Tabernacle; the index finger for the Sin-offering; and the thumb for Aaron the Priest and the leper.

->Beyond this, the ten fingers hint at the two Tablets of the Testimony<-
->Five fingers on each hand, corresponding to the five commandments written opposite five<-

<note>The following lines in Rashi script are fragmentary or include mystical abbreviations</note>
Just as one lifts the cup for a blessing at the time of his passing <margin>referring to a deathbed or ritual cup</margin>... and for wine... it is revealed and known before You... my fingers... small... as our fathers... for he never intended for the enjoyment of eating... and this eating for the sake of Heaven... with his fingers... those who bring the food from the fingers... and there is another matter... with the ten fingers... and there is a hint to great principles known to the early wise men... and not only the wise men of Israel... and also the washing of hands and feet... and behold the fourteen joints... he will understand... and may the wise man hear and increase his learning.

<column-break/>

Thus, let it be for him and his son at the time of the meal, which possesses an extra grace like that of the Temple. From all that has been mentioned here, we conclude that a person must bless his table with actual words of Torah, following the style of the Grace After Meals.

**And if** he is not "a son of this"—meaning he is not a scholar who can study Torah at his table—they teach him to say every single time some Psalm during the meal that is somewhat related to the matter of the meal, so that he may be exempt from punishment, as brought above in the name of the author of *Tola'at Yaakov* and *Reshit Chochma*.

**For those who are scholars**, they should not rely primarily on a Psalm, but rather on actual words of Torah, a complete study <note>original: "Gitya Gemura"</note>. Nevertheless, it is good and proper to say the Psalm "A Song of David, the Lord is my shepherd" <note>Psalm 23</note> at the table every single time, immediately after eating the bread over which the "HaMotzi" blessing was said. This is because it speaks of trust in God for one's sustenance and other general matters. By this, he is permitted [to trust] that he will not go to Gehenna <note>Hell</note>, as it says there: "Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil." One who fears Heaven fulfills all these. 

See also in the letter *Zayin* <note>indicating a cross-reference in the book</note>, to remember what was mentioned in the book *Meshal HaKadmoni* <note>"The Ancient Proverb," a 13th-century work of fables and ethics</note> in the 28th gate. He wrote that one who feeds the poor at his table should feed them the choicest items on the table, just as "the fat and the blood" were offered to the Most High. For there is nothing as praiseworthy as that which is raised up to God. And so it should be, that he gives the poor the best of the table, especially if it is a distinguished poor person, for then it shows he received him with a "shining countenance" and treated him with honor.

Proof for this is found in the precise language of the verse which says: "For he gave **of his bread** <note>Hebrew: "Mi-lachmo"</note> to the poor." It does not simply say "bread," but "his bread," hinting at what was mentioned nearby: that when one feeds a poor person food and provisions—which is the highest level of charity because the benefit is immediate—one should give him the choicest part of the table. This is hinted at by "his bread," meaning that which he himself desires for his own sustenance because of its quality, because it is good to eat and more pleasant to him than all other food on the table. That very item he should give to the poor, and then it is as if he offered an actual sacrifice.

Proof also comes from Abraham our father, peace be upon him, who thought the angels were [human] guests and slaughtered three oxen for them to feed them three tongues in mustard. Rashi explains <note>Babylonian Talmud, Tractate Bava Metzia 86b</note> that this is the manner of kings and princes. He presumably gave each one a whole tongue to treat them equally, like Manoah, so as not to cause jealousy between them. Since he had only three tongues, nothing remained for him or his household except the rest of the ox meat, which is not as good. Presumably, he ate with them, as it is a matter of ethics to bring guests into one's home and then join them in eating and drinking. Or, even if he did not eat with them during the meal, he gave them alone the three tongues, which were the choicest items on the table, and for himself, he left no tongue and ate the other meat which is not so choice. It is fitting that every disciple of Abraham our father follow this custom—to see and do likewise with those who eat at his table, and thus his sins and iniquities will be atoned.

**And he should choose** to give his bread to a poor person who possesses some Torah knowledge, who knows how to recite the Grace After Meals and other blessings over food, for then it is pleasing. He should not give his bread to an "Am Ha'aretz" <note>an unlearned or boorish person</note>, as we find in Tractate Bava Kamma (page 104) that Rabbi [Judah the Prince] was distressed by this and said: "Woe to me that I gave my bread to an Am Ha'aretz." See in the book *Shelah HaKadosh* <note>"The Two Tablets of the Covenant" by Isaiah Horowitz</note> regarding those in these lands who support the hands of students by taking them from all that is in their house to feed them from the food of their table, Sabbath and weekday, the entire year. Goodness shall not depart from them, for it is good for the guests to be with them, eating and drinking together like one of the householder's own children.

God shall reward their actions, and may their wage be complete from the Lord, the God of Israel. Through this, the hosts fulfill their obligation on their table regarding the two things mentioned...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the spiritual significance of the dining table, moving from the physical act of eating to the anatomical and mystical symbolism of the throat. It specifically contrasts the "windpipe" (source of voice and Torah) with the "esophagus" (source of physical desire), using the biblical figures of Jacob and Esau to illustrate these concepts.</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

And these are his words: most deaths occur because of eating. This is the meaning of the verse, "Behold, I am going to die, so why do I need a birthright?" <note>Genesis 25:32</note> Since the birthright <term>Bechorah; the spiritual primacy given to the firstborn</term> is the secret of the windpipe <note>original: "Kaneh"</note>, and "I" <note>Esau</note> am opposed to this, for I am a master of passion, which is the attribute of the esophagus <note>original: "Veshet"</note>. This is why he said, "Behold, I am going to die"—if so, why do I need the birthright? It also hints, as it is written, "Behold, I am going to die," as if to say the esophagus is the Satan <note>a wordplay in Hebrew where "Veshet" (esophagus) and "Satan" share similar phonetic qualities or spiritual themes</note>, the prince of Esau. Therefore, you will find in the word **Ha-Satania** <note>the Satanic/accusatory force</note> the first letters of "Haman," to hint that Haman also drew the Satan upon himself because of his feast, and through its power, he went to his death. This was Esther's intention in the feast she prepared for him. Behold, I have explained well the secret of the birthright that Jacob bought from Esau, etc., through the revolving secret of the blessings that Jacob took from Esau.

->(The secret of section 80, from the 46 levels of the script, 80 goodnesses in the blessing of the table and the rest of the number of blessings.)<-

For the blessings also flow from the secret of the World to Come, which is <term>Binah; Understanding, the third sphere of the Sephirot</term>, as it is found in the *Tikunim* <note>The Tikunei Zohar</note>, and as the verse says: "The blessing of the Lord, it makes one rich" <note>Proverbs 10:22</note>, hinting at *Binah*. I brought this passage in the introduction to the first part. The word "blessing" is found to be a "threefold cord" <note>Ecclesiastes 4:12</note>, hinting at one matter: the windpipe, the *Yud* of Jacob, and the secret of the blessings. They all drink from the waters of the Upper Well, the secret of the World to Come, which is *Binah*. Therefore, when Esau cried out over the blessings, he also cried over the birthright, for they are one and the same matter. Since the blessings come from the secret of the windpipe, a person must be very careful with them, especially the blessing over eating, so that he does not, God forbid, cause death to follow there, and this is sufficient for the wise.

<margin>See regarding one's table, for charity <note>original: "Tzedakah"</note> is hinted at by the letters *He* and *Aleph*. How so? Our Rabbis said: One who gives charity to a poor person from your friend's [table] in six [measures], he has six (*Vav*). And they said: One who appeases him is blessed with eleven blessings—this is *He* (5) and *Vav* (6), which together equal eleven. The intention in all this is the secret of the windpipe, which is hinted at, etc., so that one does not follow "another name" <note>idolatry or impurity</note> during the time of eating. Furthermore, there is a secret in this matter: five times the letter *Vav* in its full spelling equals the numerical value of *Adonai* <note>The Name of God</note>, which is the name of the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah; the indwelling presence of God</term> as is known. The Divine Presence is also hinted at in the number "Chai" (18). As it says in the *Tikunim* (Tikun 26)... it rises to eight... 1x1, 2x2, 3x2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9x9... all together it equals the number of the "310 worlds" <note>Hebrew: "Shai Olamot," a traditional concept of the reward for the righteous</note>. This is why it says "and to Jerusalem," for then the *Shekhinah* descended below ten. This is the reason why no holy matter is performed with fewer than ten men, for the *Shekhinah* does not dwell there. Up to this point, there is a hint to the letter *Vav* and *Adonai*, which is the name of the *Shekhinah*, which is *Vav*. Thus it is hinted at in the *Vav* of Jacob and the *Yud* of Jacob, to hint that the *Vav* of Jacob, which is the windpipe (*Vav*), and the essence of Jacob are all one matter.</margin>

**Based on** these words that I have written—that Jacob (the secret of section 6, from the 46 levels of the script, 80: Torah study at his table, and he shall be wise to the eyes) is the secret of the windpipe—I say that this is the hint found in the five times Jacob's name is written "full" with a *Vav* <note>as in Leviticus 26:42</note>. For the secret of *Vav* is the windpipe, which is six handbreadths <note>the numerical value of Vav is 6</note>. Five times *Vav* equals thirty, which is the letter *Lamed*, from the language of "learning" <note>Hebrew: "Limud"</note> Torah. This hints that one should not follow "another name" even during the time of eating, but rather follow the windpipe, meaning he should study at his table. As I have seen many of our Rabbis do, they all come through the power of the *Vav*, so that it is expounded as *He* and *Aleph*, and then he will rise from this to be...

**And my father**, my teacher, of blessed memory, wrote in the name of Rabbi Hai: In the book *Sod Ha-Zahav* <note>The Secret of Gold</note>, the completely righteous study Torah at the table; average people say a Psalm; the wicked say nothing at all. Make your ear like a funnel to hear my words regarding this secret: for whoever does not study Torah at the table follows "another name" and not the windpipe. Then the *Yud* is removed from Jacob <note>Hebrew: Y-A-K-V</note>, and when he brings skin <note>physicality</note> over his table, he sins. If he does not even say Psalm 114 <note>"When Israel went out of Egypt"</note>, then the *Yud* of Jacob that was removed enters into the windpipe <note>original: "Kaneh"</note>, and then the word "Windpipe" (*Kaneh*) becomes "Lamentation" (*Kinah*). The cause of the lamentation is because the *Yud* was removed and only the "Heel" (*Akev*) remained, and then the serpent is coiled around the heel and pursues him. Also, the Satan that is in the esophagus becomes a literal Satan, as mentioned above.

**Or** in this way, that man will find many opinions, for their words are like a monument. There will be a plain *Zayin*, as it says in the *Pardes* in the "Gate of the Letters," chapter 17, and these are his words: the shape of a plain *Zayin* is a *Vav* with a *Vav* on its back, and my intention in this is that the *Vav* of Jacob that was removed will go and return to Jacob, and then he will return from the letter *Zayin* to be plain, and the letters of the names will be as mentioned above.

**And regarding** this secret, they hinted at what is written: "And he was drunk," as was said regarding Noah (the secret of section 50, from the 46 levels of script, of blessed memory, to say [he was drunk] from much drinking). The explanation is "the beginning of wisdom," and my father brought it—that it is the language of "Woe." "And his wine was..." when he followed the esophagus and not the windpipe, then the *Vav* of Jacob departed... and they went there... and he became a *Vav* and *Chai* (18)... it is all names... and the esophagus became Satan. He goes because the esophagus was seized by much eating and drinking and became "cursed" <note>Hebrew: "Arur"</note> from the *Vav* or the *Nun*. Just as it spreads to its length, which is names, it becomes a *Nun*, and so it spreads to its width... and they were all seized. And then *Vav* and "it was" and "my father" equals 20, and it hints to God... and I told you that he who follows the esophagus joins that *Vav* and is cast out. And the letter *Zayin* in its full spelling equals 203... behold, six times *Vav* that was created during Noah's drinking, for there too the Satan came and poked among them, for Noah was strong through Ham the father of Canaan. And Canaan is the secret of "and the Canaanite was then in the land," which is the secret of impurity and profanation as the Kabbalists said. It is possible that it hints to "the Canaanite king of Arad" <note>Numbers 21:1</note>... not the blind man kills, but the sin kills... and the conclusion is that the Canaanite is the cause of sin, he is king, for the skin is the messenger of sin.

**And regarding** this it is said: "He who guards his mouth and his tongue, guards his soul from troubles" <note>Proverbs 21:23</note>. Behold, the mouth is the gateway to the windpipe and the esophagus. They said that he who guards properly is saved from "trouble" <note>Hebrew: "Tzarah," which sounds like "Zarah," the "other" or "foreign" side</note>, which is the *Vav* mentioned above that spreads from the *Zayin* and the esophagus.

**But** the *Vav* of Jacob, which hints at the windpipe when it is in its full spelling, equals the numerical value of *Ehyeh* <note>The Divine Name "I Will Be"</note>. The verse said: "How beautiful and how pleasant you are, O love, with your delights" <note>Song of Songs 7:7</note>. The verse praises Israel—how very beautiful and pleasant they are in the eyes of God when they cause love through the power of a commandment that is a delight. This refers to the delights of the Sabbaths and Festivals. When one fulfills the commandment of being fruitful and multiplying, for each one he receives a good reward, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, loves him for this. And this is "behold in the nations," for the good reward a person receives for the commandments of the Torah and labor is not a wonder; but for that which we add love through the power of a commandment that is a delight, that is the beauty. See elsewhere the opposite: "How beautiful and how pleasant" in that you love the Holy One, Blessed be He, and cease from delights—for example, one stops in the middle of a feast and goes to the Synagogue. The reason we receive reward for these is because the intention in all of them is for the sake of the commandment and not for the sake of the body. Regarding those who delight for the sake of the body, it is said: "Your new moons and your appointed feasts My soul hates" <note>Isaiah 1:14</note>. Furthermore, I say that the *Vav* of Jacob equals the value of "Another" <note>Hebrew: "Achar"</note> to hint that he who follows this path, all his deeds go to "another place"—to the intention of the Creator, as it is said: "Let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven" <note>Pirkei Avot 2:12</note>, and as Maimonides and the *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher</note> wrote in *Orach Chaim*, section 231. But one whose intention is for the body, who follows his excesses, then his thought is stuck from the cleaving to the Creator and clings to his materiality. For the soul, sufficiency is enough, and it does not need excesses. Regarding this, the verse hints "after" <note>Achar</note>...

For we also find by Abraham that he did not want to follow excesses, but only what God had graciously given him, as in the matter he replied to the King of Sodom. And the verse says: "Because <note>Hebrew: "Ekev"</note> Abraham obeyed My voice" <note>Genesis 26:5</note>. And behold, you find in Abraham the entire word "Jacob" <note>Yaakov</note>... and Jacob was revealed in him, for it is found that he was tested with ten trials. Regarding this, it said "Ekev" <note>heel/because</note> which Abraham heard, etc. And it is the "heel" (*Akev*) from Jacob, which hints at humility and lowliness, the opposite of "your heart becomes haughty" <note>Deuteronomy 8:14</note> from much eating and drinking. For this, the hint comes in the portion of *Pekudei*: "A *Beka* for every head, half a shekel" <note>Exodus 38:26</note>. For it is already known that the half-shekel hints at the conduct of man—that his deeds should be by weight, measure, and rule, and he should not follow excesses. So wrote Rabbeinu Bahya. Therefore they called it a *Beka*, for the letters of *Beka* are the letters of *Akev* from Jacob. And it said "a Beka for every head," similar to what was said regarding Haman... which also hints that one should not follow excesses, as my father elaborated there. This is what it said: "Because (*Ekev*) Abraham obeyed My voice." And this is enough. In my humble opinion, this verse means that Abraham kept the "Eruv of Foods" <note>Eruv Tavshilin; a legal mechanism to allow cooking on a festival for the Sabbath</note>. Hear now the secret of their words, for they hinted in these short words at everything I have written. It is impossible to understand their words without this introduction. Come and see: On the Sabbath, there is an "extra soul" <term>Neshamah Yeterah; the additional spiritual capacity granted on the Sabbath</term> and an addition of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, it is a commandment to delight in it, because eating—all eating—is for the secret of the reason of Isaac... so that the body will be alive, strong, and happy to receive the Holy Spirit, as the commentators explained there. It turns out that Sabbath eating is on the side of the windpipe and not the side of the esophagus. This secret is hinted at in the *Tikunim*, Tikun 17... a closed *Samekh* hints at the [letter] *Zayin*... and it is said "it shall be joy"... and like the Sabbath day it shall open... and the Sabbath is a building that shall not be... "close the door before borrowers," as it was said "borrow on My account and I shall repay." What is the "opening" for their children? These are the souls... His entire intention is that the closed *Samekh* hints at the diminishment of the flow which is closed from every side. When you take the "nest" <note>Hebrew: "Ken," wordplay on "Kaneh"</note> from it, and a *Bet* remains, then the entrance is open for the flow to descend from above. And that nest is the *Vav*, and all...

<meta>This page continues the anatomical and mystical comparison between Jacob and Esau, focusing on the throat's two tubes: the windpipe (Kaneh) and the esophagus (Veshet). # The Gate of the Letters

The letter **Vav** (the letters of "Judge" are like the letters of "Judge") <note>original: "Dayan". This likely refers to a mystical equivalence or a specific scribal tradition regarding the shape or numerical value of the letters in Jacob's name</note> in the name of Jacob signifies that Jacob was "complete." Therefore, it is written immediately, "And he called his name Jacob." <note>Genesis 25:26</note> Our tradition explains that the Holy One, Blessed be He, called him Jacob, for then he became "the portion of Jacob, the lot of His inheritance." <note>Deuteronomy 32:9</note> Regarding this matter, and in contrast to the World to Come, the scripture says: "And Esau was a man who knew hunting, a man of the field, but Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in tents." <note>Genesis 25:27</note> As it is written, "I have lived <note>original: "Garti"</note> with Laban," which hints at the 613 <note>The Hebrew word "Garti" has the numerical value of 613</note> commandments. Alternatively, this "complete Jacob" consists of the letter **Yud** <note>representing the divine</note> joined with the **Ekev** <note>the "heel," representing the physical or lower world</note>; understand this well.

**To instruct** upon their natures—that one represents This World and the other represents the World to Come—the scripture says: "And Esau was a man who knew hunting, a man of the field, but Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in tents." This hints that This World is the portion of Esau. His entire essence is to chase after excesses, to "hunt the hunt," bringing it in day and night without ceasing, to be a "man of the field" always—sitting at the corners <note>of the streets/markets</note>, wandering far and wide, never quieting the heat of desire and greed. The cause of this is "the belly of the wicked that always lacks," <note>Proverbs 13:25</note> and they always say, "Peace be upon you, my soul," because the "eye of This World" <note>the material perspective</note> equals the numerical value of **Shalom** (Peace). <note>The author is playing on the idea that the wicked seek a false peace through material accumulation</note> About this, the scripture hints, "Esau is Edom" <note>Edom means "Red"</note>, for the dwelling of desire and greed is in the liver, which is entirely blood. Therefore, the bile <note>original: "Marah," also meaning bitterness</note> is suspended from it, for "bitterness shall be the end" <note>2 Samuel 2:26</note> for one who pursues honor. Since the word "Edom" hints at the liver <note>Kaved</note>, as explained, it says Esau is Edom. But "Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in tents," meaning he dwells in tranquility in "two tents"—namely, This World and the Next. For regarding Jacob, it is said "I have plenty," <note>Genesis 33:11</note> emphasizing the trait of contentment. Then he dwells in quiet and security, resting and still. This is not the case for one who pursues desires, who will never rest or be still; of them it is said, "The wicked are like the driven sea." <note>Isaiah 57:20</note> All their food is "sorrow" to them, for they are always in fear, saying "What shall I eat tomorrow?" Such a person eats only like "Ben Drusai" <note>A Talmudic reference to a thief who ate food only partially cooked because he was in a hurry</note>, rushing to put his hand to the hunt, trusting only in what he can grab for his portion.

> (The secret of section 4, from the 46 levels written by my lord, my father, of blessed memory: He shall eat for blood <unclear>a spider's web</unclear> and how the <term>SMC</term> <note>Samael, the prince of Esau</note> humbles the wicked.)

He says, "Blessed be the Lord day by day," <note>Psalms 68:20</note> and eats his bread with joy, for he does not desire excesses, only what he must eat to sustain the soul—that is, to live and be strengthened in the Torah, to rejoice in it, for it "gladdens the heart," as it is written, "The precepts of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart." <note>Psalms 19:9</note> Concerning this, the scripture says, "A man has joy in the answer of his mouth, and a word in its season, how good it is!" <note>Proverbs 15:23</note> It means that a "Man"—a title for one who is important—is one who serves in two things: Torah and being happy with his portion. "The answer of his mouth" hints at the Torah, and "a word in its season, how good it is" means that when there is a "good word" <note>spiritual success</note> at that time, even if his last penny is gone from his pocket and he has nothing for tomorrow, it is still "good" in his eyes. For he knows that "the Lord will not withhold good from those who walk uprightly." From what I have written, Jacob is the "heel" <note>Ekev</note>, a term for humility, lowliness, and treading down the blood of the firstborn <note>overcoming animalistic drives</note>. While the forgetfulness and impulse that come from excessive desire lead to unrest, Jacob dwells in quiet in both This World and the World to Come—where there is neither eating nor drinking. This is Jacob's attribute: he did not seek to fill his belly to excess, but said only, "Bread to eat [and clothing to wear]." <note>Genesis 28:20</note> But in Esau, we find the attribute of gluttony, as seen in the Midrash on Proverbs: "The belly of the wicked shall want"—this is Esau, who said to Jacob, "Let me swallow <note>original: "Hal'iteini"</note> some of that red, red stuff." This wicked man opened his mouth like a camel and said, "Open my mouth and pour it in!" Perhaps he even finished the whole pot and swallowed it greedily, as we have learned: "One does not stuff a camel, nor force-feed it, nor make it swallow." Just as Jacob and Esau were in one womb, it hints at the unfolding of the worlds—for everything found in the human body, which is called a "small world," contains two primary matters upon which our life depends: Jacob and Esau. These are the **Windpipe** <note>Kaneh</note> and the **Esophagus** <note>Veshet</note>. The Windpipe is the secret of speech, which emanates from the soul whose dwelling is <unclear>...</unclear> corresponding to the World to Come. The Esophagus, which is for eating and drinking, is the secret of Esau. Also, when the Esophagus <note>Veshet</note> is expanded, the letter **Zayin** of *Veshet* becomes a long **Nun**, hinting at the "Satan" <note>original: "Satania"</note>, the prince of Esau. This matter is explained in the *Faithful Shepherd* <note>original: "Ra'aya Meheimna," a section of the Zohar</note> on the commandment of the holy Shofar. It says: "The Faithful Shepherd said: Certainly, the limbs and the arteries of the heart are in distress, like Israel. They need to be awakened by the Windpipe, which is the Shofar. This Windpipe <note>Kaneh</note> is like a Shofar, and through it, the breath emerges to remove the anger of the bile which overpowers the heart and the limbs. That spirit which blows ascends through the Windpipe... and there is the model of This World, where there is eating and drinking, and afterwards the wicked Esophagus <note>Veshet</note> dominates... eating and drinking... until the Satan spreads through eating and drinking and overpowers all limbs... but on Yom Kippur, there is no eating or drinking, and it is like the Windpipe." This is the meaning of that passage.

> (The secret of section 20, from the 46 levels written by my lord, my father: That a person should not fill his belly like a beast, for it brings him to shame.)

Because the Esophagus corresponds to This World, and it is the way of the wicked to prepare and place much food and drink in its expansion... and it becomes a long **Nun**, and then the word "Veshet" <note>Esophagus</note> becomes "Shaton" <note>Satan</note>. This is his "folly" <note>original: "Shtut"</note>, for "Shto" is a term for folly. But the "wise man's eyes are in his head," <note>Ecclesiastes 2:14</note> meaning he always looks to keep the letter **Zayin** of "Veshet" at the beginning <note>maintaining balance</note>. For those who put eating at the front, they push the Spirit <note>the letter Yud</note> to the back, and the letter **Nun** becomes a "stretched-out Nun" <note>final Nun</note>, forming the word "Shetin" <note>demons/follies</note>. This is when the Satan is complete and causes the person to sin, as seen in the verse: "Jeshurun waxed fat and kicked." <note>Deuteronomy 32:15</note> Because of satiety, they rebel. So you find with the Generation of the Flood, they only rebelled against G-d because of food and drink. So you find with the people of the Generation of the Wilderness, as it is said, "The people sat down to eat [and drink and rose up to play]." What is said of them? "They have turned aside quickly from the way." <note>Exodus 32:8</note> And so the scripture says: "When I bring them into the land... a land flowing with milk and honey, and they eat and are sated and grow fat, then they will turn to other gods." <note>Deuteronomy 31:20</note> After the Satan causes them to sin, he ascends and accuses, then descends and kills. This is found regarding the "fools" <note>original: "Shatu"</note> of the people who gathered the meat—"while the meat was still between their teeth, the anger of the Lord burned against the people." <note>Numbers 11:33</note> But the Windpipe, which is the secret of the Shofar and the secret of the World to Come—where there is neither eating nor drinking—of it they said: "Acquire <note>original: "K'neh," a pun on Kaneh/Windpipe</note> wisdom, acquire <note>K'neh</note> understanding." <note>Proverbs 4:5</note> This means the Windpipe hints at that which contains only the voice—the "Voice of Jacob," which is the speech carved from the soul, as it is said: "And man became a living soul," which the Aramaic translates as "a speaking spirit."

**And behold**, there are six rings in the windpipe. The author of *Well of Living Water* <note>original: "Be'er Mayim Chayim"</note> wrote that they mystically correspond to the verse: "And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord." <note>Isaiah 11:2</note> And in the book *Orchard of Pomegranates* <note>original: "Pardes Rimonim"</note> in the Gate of Appellations: In the windpipe there are six rings, and they correspond to the six Sephirot <note>divine emanations</note> and the "stairs to the Upper Throne." To this I will add my own touch: the windpipe hints at the seven extremities and the "Holy Palace" situated in the center, as mentioned in the *Book of Creation* <note>original: "Sefer Yetzirah"</note>. Thus, in the windpipe, there are seven rings, and the voice that emerges from between them is the "Holy Palace." It is already known to the wise among the children of Israel that the secret of the Holy Palace in the center is the secret of Jacob, who is the "Middle Line." And perhaps we can say that the six rings hint at the six things my lord, my father, wrote regarding the meal—to hint that one should not be drawn during his meal after excesses, but only after the Windpipe <note>the spiritual</note>. As I have explained, Jacob is the Windpipe and Esau is the Esophagus, and they are in one body, just as Jacob and Esau were in one womb. It is also clear that the secret of Jacob and the secret of the Windpipe both lead to one point: they both hint at the World to Come. Therefore, you find in this portion that Jacob bought the birthright from Esau, which hints at his entire life-force. For the secret of the birthright <note>Bechorah</note> is the letter **Yud** of Jacob, as stated in the *Corrections of the Zohar* <note>original: "Tikunei Zohar"</note>, Correction 71: "For the drop [of life] is the Yud of Jacob, and it flew away from Adam when he sinned, leaving him alone without help. Therefore, Jacob bought the birthright from Esau to return it to its place." It is known to the masters of hidden wisdom that Adam's sin was in the "Kingship" <note>Malchut</note>, which is the Yud, the secret of the Tithe and the birthright. Then the Serpent became coiled around the "Heel" <note>Ekev</note>, as it is said: "And you shall strike his heel." Jacob "restored the crown to its former glory" and bought this Yud, which is the birthright. For Jacob corresponds to the World to Come, and this Sephirah is the "Gate through which the righteous shall enter" to behold the upper pleasantness in the Garden of Eden. Then "Esau went away from before Jacob his brother," for he removed the idols from the Upper Land. Thus, Jacob bought the secret of the Yud and brought out the secret of the Windpipe. But Esau's portion fell to the Esophagus. Therefore, Onkelos translates "And Esau sold the birthright" using a term related to the Esophagus <note>The author sees a linguistic link in the Aramaic "Vazbin" or the Hebrew "Vayivez" (despised) to the physical throat</note>. Every mention of the Esophagus hints at all we have written—that he took the Esophagus as his portion and sold the Windpipe (the secret of the Yud) to Jacob. Therefore, the scripture mentions how Esau said "Let me swallow," for he only ate for the Esophagus. Thus he said, "Behold, I am going to die," because Jacob's eating was only to be strong and healthy for the service of G-d.

> (The secret of section 60, from the 46 levels written by my lord, my father: That the air should emerge for the Will, and not just after the pleasure of the taste.)

Therefore, he eats what is beneficial for the body and strengthens its health, and does not eat what is merely pleasant and sweet to him. His intention in eating is not for the sake of desire. This is not the case for the glutton and the drunkard; their intention in eating is only for desire, and their ear does not listen to what is beneficial, only to what is pleasant, even if it is harmful. This is the reason for the intention we mentioned.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Jacob’s spiritual perfection and the mystical significance of his name, transitioning into the "Gate of the Letters" which explores the mystical mechanics of blessings, the union of Divine names, and the consequences of benefiting from the physical world without acknowledging its spiritual source.</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

The concept of the "end being entwined with the beginning" <note>A classic Kabbalistic principle from the Sefer Yetzirah and Sefer HaBahir suggesting that the final result of creation is rooted in its first thought</note> and its meaning being "closed" is explained in the *Book of Bahir*. It is clarified through the introduction regarding the "living beings" and the "thorn" <note>likely referring to the decorative "crowns" or "tits" on Hebrew letters</note>. It is well known that anyone who recites a blessing over fruit or any food in the world has, through that blessing, acknowledged His Blessed Name. This is because He is the one who brings everything into existence and gives life to all. According to our introduction regarding the "neighborhoods" and the Holy of Holies, our Sages of blessed memory said: "There is no blade of grass below that does not have a constellation <note>original: "mazal"</note> above that strikes it and says to it, 'Grow!'" According to this law, one only blesses because of the abundance flowed upon them from the Supernal Authority that supervises everything. This is as our Master, the *Bachya* <note>Rabbi Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century commentator</note>, explained in the portion of *Bereshit* <note>Genesis</note> regarding the verse "to divide between the light and the dark." One should look there.

He adds to this that one is blessed with a successful blessing when they realize that anyone who does not bless is a denier of all this. This is the secret of the saying "it is as if he steals from the Holy One, Blessed be He." For one who plucks the "wings" <note>metaphor for the spiritual essence or sparks within food</note> without a blessing steals and misappropriates His influence. They remove the "wings" from receiving the fullness of the stars—like a fool who removes a friend's garment. This causes the "Megalnim" <note>likely a reference to specific destructive spiritual forces or angels of judgment</note> to pay back with gold and pleasantness, while their spirits block the soul of all angels. These are the conducts of the "Name" regarding sustenance; the Lord has made all. Therefore, one who does not bless is called a "robber of the Holy One, Blessed be He." This is the secret of the "Faraway Name," as it is written regarding Phinehas, who was a "son of" <note>unclear/illegible</note> and stole from this, closing off the Hashgacha <note>Divine Providence</note> of the Thought we began with, as remembered.

When the Community of Israel <note>Knesset Yisrael</note> says that one who denies Him causes food to be withheld from the table, it is as explained there. By opening the "gates" for the created word to reach the spiritual forces, I will return and take "My grain in its time and My wine in its season." One who is not grateful for the goodness of the "Returner of the Spirit" <note>God</note> will have that goodness withheld from him, as it says, "Your sins have turned these away." <note>Jeremiah 5:25</note> This is the simple meaning of the Unity of the Life-Giver.

However, there is another way to explain the words of our Sages and the secret of the "Order of Issachar" <note>Referencing Rabbi Issachar Baer, author of the Kabbalistic work *Ba'er Hetev* or similar mystical traditions</note>. In it is the secret of Kabbalah: the secret of the "Refinement" and the "Virtue" <note>term: Segulah</note> of the Complete Mountain to return to the Holy One, Blessed be He. One who steals from Him is explained through the foundation of "Virtue" explained by the Sages of Truth <note>Kabbalists</note>. This is the secret of "blessed" <note>Baruch</note> being entwined in the end, and the end being entwined in the beginning, through the power of the attachment of the Foundation <note>Sefirah of Yesod</note> in many places and verses.

Now it will be explained how the power of the letter *Nun* is magnified. The verse says, "You neglected the Rock who begot you" <note>Deuteronomy 32:18</note>. Our Sages interpreted this: "Whenever Israel does the will of the Omnipresent, they add strength to the Power Above." This is the secret of "You shall have..." <note>illegible</note> and the secret of being uplifted through blessings. This is the matter of the "desire" the Holy One has for the prayers of the righteous. This is the secret of "every man whose heart makes him willing" <note>Exodus 25:2</note>. Aside from these verses and sayings, the simple and the received traditions help to stand upon the essence of these words. If our Sages had the ability—or if one does not distance their mind from knowing the additions that oppose this—then the "Holy Service" <note>Avodat HaKodesh</note> would be preserved in its portion. In the introductions to the *Book of Charedim* <note>by Elazar Azikri</note>, the genius of our generation wrote about the "sweetness of the words." With the agreement of the Sages, one will find rest for his soul and sweetness for his bread. The "Holy Sweetness" is for the one who has the intellect to mend, for his words are the words of the Living God.

According to the secret of his words from the famous discourse regarding "stealing from the Holy One and the Community of Israel," this refers to "Blessed be He" and the "New Wine" <note>Tirosh</note> from the abundance that flows to the "Crown" <note>Atarah/Malchut</note>. From the "Gift of the World" <note>Migad Olam</note>, which is the Community of Israel, comes the "Blessing of the Lord." For there the Cup of Blessing <note>the Sefirah of Malchut</note> is found in the secret of the letters *Bet* and *He* <note>Numerical value 7</note>, as stated in the *Tikunim* <note>Tikunei Zohar</note>. They gave a sign for this: "The blessing of the Lord—it makes rich" <note>Proverbs 10:22</note>, for it enriches the "Vessel of Reception" with its abundance. One who does not bless is a thief and a robber, separating the "Union" through his withdrawal, thereby trespassing against the Holy things of Heaven. He becomes a "companion to a destroyer" <note>Proverbs 28:24</note>—namely, Jeroboam son of Nebat, who separated those who were joined, made the golden calves, and set up a false system.

And behold, to add to the perfection of the blessing, the general rule of all blessings is: "Blessed are You, Lord our God..." We mention two names: the Tetragrammaton <note>YHVH - the Attribute of Mercy</note> and the name "Our God" <note>Eloheinu/Elohim - the Attribute of Judgment</note>. This is the vitality of the Attribute of Mercy with the Attribute of Judgment. For *Elohim* acts like the spring of Nature in the rising of the sun; this is the Attribute of Judgment, to provide life according to the natural order of things. But the name *YHVH* is the Attribute of Mercy, the body of the flow, the revelation of the "Light of the Face of the King is Life." Then, an additional blessing is found in the world, changing nature (which is the name *Elohim*). This is because the one who brings news of the Attribute of Judgment does so through Mercy. This is the meaning of "The Lord is greater than all gods <note>Elohim</note>." Therefore, in our blessings, when we wish to draw abundance upon them, we must connect these two names.

The secret of these two names, with the assistance of the Tetragrammaton, maintains the world in the numerical value of *Y-K-K* which is 140. <note>Translator's note: This involves complex Gematria/letter substitutions</note>. "The Holy Lord" is the sign that provides sustenance, as it is the "Sign of Life" that includes all the holy letters. This is explained in the *Zohar* and the *Pardes* <note>Pardes Rimonim by Moshe Cordovero</note>. In the "Wrappings of the Highest Place," the "Highest God" <note>Elohim Elyon</note> and the "Paths of Judgment" represent the letters of *Elohim*. This means our abundance in everything is the "Word riding upon the Chair," which is the Chair of Mercy, serving the Supernal Chariot.

When Israel sinned with the Calf, they caused a separation. What was once joined as "Life" <note>Chai</note> and "These" <note>Eleh</note> in the "Path of the Truth of God" <note>Elohim</note> became divided. This is why it says, "These <note>Eleh</note> are your gods, O Israel" <note>Exodus 32:4</note>—they took the *Eleh* out of *Elohim* and left it in the realm of the husks <note>term: Klipot</note>. This is the secret of "Who <note>Mi</note> are these <note>Eleh</note>?" <note>Genesis 48:8</note>—Jacob saw that they were worthy of blessing because the light of the "Who" (*Mi*) was still joined to "These" (*Eleh*), forming the name *Elohim*. One who blesses on anything acknowledges the Supernal Source and establishes the name *YHVH* with *Elohim*, connecting *Chai* with *Eleh*, reversing the damage of Jeroboam. May the wise man hear and increase his learning.

---

**You have been shown** <note>Atah Hareita</note> through the words of our Sages mentioned here the greatness of the punishment for one who enjoys this world without a blessing. This is the discourse mentioned above in the name of Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa: "Anyone who enjoys this world [without a blessing] is as if he steals from the Holy One, Blessed be He, and the Community of Israel." How awesome is this statement! How great is the power of the hint our Sages gave. You already know their saying: "Anyone who robs his fellow even the value of a penny, it is as if he takes his soul." How much more so one who robs the public, and how infinitely more so one who robs the Divine Presence <note>term: Shekhinah</note>. Worse than this, they compared him to Jeroboam son of Nebat, who sinned and caused Israel to sin. This is harder than the first, for "anyone who causes the public to sin, no opportunity is given to him [to repent]." Thus, the great obligation of the "Blessings of Pleasure" <note>Birkhot HaNehenin</note> is established.

The versions of the blessings are also based on the Secret, as in the book *Tola'at Yaakov* <note>The Worm of Jacob</note>. The blessing "That all exists by His word" <note>Shehakol Nihyah Bidvaro</note> includes all blessings, for "All" is the foundation of everything. Therefore, if one said this over anything, they have fulfilled their obligation. The blessing "Creator of Souls" <note>Borei Nefashot</note> is from its own kind, for He is the "Treasury of Souls," in whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and He is the "Life of the Worlds." Therefore, we conclude it with "Blessed is the Life of the Worlds."

Over anything that grows from the ground, one blesses "Who creates the fruit of the ground" <note>Boray Peri Ha-Adama</note>. This refers to the "Holy Ground" that is constantly worked to grow everything to nourish every living soul, for from there all types of sustenance and spices emerge. This is the model of the "earthy dust" below. Over the fruit of the tree, one blesses "Who creates the fruit of the tree" <note>Boray Peri Ha-Etz</note>. This refers to the Tree of Life which bears fruit, for it is a "fruit tree making fruit of its kind" in the Supernal Land. In this model, we bless over the fruits of the tree below. After them, we bless "Creator of many souls," except for the fruits for which the Land of Israel is praised, over which we bless the "One Blessing that is like Three" <note>term: Me'ein Shalosh</note>. The reason for a distinct blessing for the Land of Israel is that it is the source of all blessings. This blessing is of the "Three" kind because everything is contained within it; although it is like four <note>referring to the four species or foundations</note>, it is called "like three" because these are from the Torah. It is the "fourth leg" <note>of the Divine Throne</note> and the secret of the Oral Torah, the "Woman of Valor."

Also, the fruit of the vine... <note>illegible</note>. In this order, they established a unique blessing for wine due to its importance: "Who creates the fruit of the vine" <note>Boray Peri Ha-Gafen</note>. For "wine gladdens God and men," coming from the Supernal Wine preserved in its grapes. You already know the Sages' saying: "The Vine is the Community of Israel."

You already know that for anything over which one recites a blessing—whether to eat it or to smell it—the blesser must hold it **in his right hand** when he blesses, for the blessing...
