<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Gate of the Letters," moving from the general concept of blessings into the mystical relationship between the Patriarchs, the Hebrew alphabet, and the specific laws of enjoying the physical world (Berakhot). It bridges the gap between Jacob’s spiritual ladder and the mundane act of eating.</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

Recall the seven days of the week: the six days of work are "closed" <note>In Kabbalistic thought, the six weekdays represent a more concealed or restricted state of divine light compared to the openness of the Sabbath.</note>, but on the Sabbath, that restriction—which is represented by the letter *Vav* (ו)—is removed. It becomes "Peace" <note>original: "Shalom"</note>, for there remains a "daughter" <note>original: "Bat," often a reference to the Shekhinah or the final letter He of the Divine Name</note> from the "closed Mem" (ם), while the "open Mem" (מ) is left open to provide life and allow the divine flow to descend. This is a deep mystery, revealed only to those who understand the true nature of the six workdays and the Sabbath. Only then will one know why there is an "additional soul" on the Sabbath. One who wishes to understand the core of these matters should study the book *Pardes Rimonim* in the "Gate of the Colors" <note>original: "Gate of A-B-Y," likely referring to the four worlds: Atziluth, Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah</note>, and there they will find rest for their soul.

According to my own approach, I say that the "six" refers to their completion, represented by the "closed Mem." This is the *Vav* of the "windpipe" <term>Kaneh: The windpipe, which in this mystical anatomy represents the passage of breath and spiritual voice, as opposed to the esophagus which represents material consumption.</term> which follows the breath and draws the *Vav* unto itself to open the gate. But for one who does not rule over themselves, the gate of the windpipe will remain closed forever. Our Sages hinted at this regarding the commandment of the *Eruv Tavshilin* <note>A legal ritual—literally "blending of cooked foods"—that allows one to prepare food on a Holiday for the following Sabbath.</note>. The Talmud gives two reasons for this: Rabbah said it is so one may choose a "fine portion" <note>original: "Maneh Yafeh"</note> for the Sabbath and a fine portion for the Holiday. Rav Ashi said it is so people will say, "If we cannot bake from a Holiday to a Sabbath without a ritual, how much more so from a Holiday to a weekday!" This is a partial obligation for Israel for the sake of their own enjoyment. Regarding the Sabbath, everyone agrees we need "for you" <note>referring to physical enjoyment of the day</note>, but on a Holiday, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua disagree. Therefore, Rabbah said the commandment of *Eruv* comes to teach that just as his eating on the Holiday is from the side of the "windpipe"—turning away from the "tasty treats of Isaac" <note>referring to the physical appetites Isaac enjoyed in the Bible</note>—it is a "fine portion." This relates to the verse I cited earlier: "How beautiful and how pleasant you are..." <note>Song of Songs 7:7</note>. This is why he used the word *Maneh* (portion), which contains the same letters as *Man* (Manna), which came from the initials of "Please let me swallow..." <note>referring to Esau’s demand for the red lentil stew in Genesis 25:30</note>. This means our eating should not be like the Manna <note>which was purely spiritual</note> but rather a "fine portion" <note>sanctified physical eating</note>. 

Rav Ashi, however, said the reason is to show that they should restrain the "destruction" within the spreading attributes and trust in God’s promise, so one cannot say "What will I eat tomorrow?" This is the meaning of "one may not bake from a Holiday to the Sabbath," etc. It was necessary to establish this to hint at the "hollow space" when a Holiday and Sabbath occur consecutively. At such times, one increases their meals over several days, and time is prepared <note>original: "hazai"</note> to drag a person after physical pleasures. 

And this is the secret: One who hears and guards the *Eruv Tavshilin* (blending of cooked foods) in the evening <note>original: "Erev"</note>—this is a hint to what is missing. Thus, when the Sabbath and a Holiday are adjacent, they established the *Yaknehaz* ritual <note>An acronym for the order of blessings: Wine (Yayin), Kiddush, Candle (Ner), Havdalah, and Time (Zman)</note>. They hinted at this secret: the *Vav* of the "measure," the *Vav* of Jacob, and the *Koph* of the "windpipe" <note>original: "Kaneh"</note> which stands against the windpipe. Heaven forbid, it hints at what is written: "Seven lamps shall give light toward the one center shaft" <note>referring to the Menorah</note>. The intention is as I explained above: the "windpipe" (Kaneh) and the name *Y-A-K-O-V* (Jacob) are all one matter. The "seven lamps" are the seven spiritual directions, and the Holy Voice aimed at the center—which is clothed in "Peace"—is the "seven powers of holiness" discussed in the "Chapter of Power." These belong to the secret of the World of Formation <note>original: "Olam HaYetzirah"</note>. Therefore, they are called the "World of Intellects," just as the intellects are a garment for the inner sun, so too are they a garment for the spirituality of the "Directions" and the "Upper Holy Palace."

**And to return** to the first matter: regarding Abraham, it is written: "Because [Ekev] Abraham heard My voice." This "Ekev" <note>meaning 'because' but literally 'heel'</note> is the "Ekev" of Jacob (Ya'akov). You will also find in him the letter *Yod* of Jacob, which represents his ten trials. It is possible that this is the *Yod* that was divided between Abraham and Sarah <note>According to Midrash, the Yod from Sarai's name was split into two Hehs—one for Abraham and one for Sarah</note>. For I have already written that the *Yod* hints at the "seven words of their spirit." Therefore, a *Heh* (5) was given to Abraham and a *Heh* (5) to Sarah. He merited even more, as our Sages said: the *Yod* of Sarah complained until it was placed at the head of Joshua <note>from Hoshea to Yehoshua</note>. One might ask: why specifically Joshua? According to my path, it is known that Joshua "did not depart from within the tent" <note>Exodus 33:11</note>, meaning he ruled over his physical ways. Thus his appearance was the light of the esophagus and the breath following the windpipe, for he did not eat for forty days. It is possible that the "portion" (*maneh*) is equal to the "staff" (vav), for the staff is shaped like the letter *Vav*. This is the secret that God showed Moses: that the staff—which is the secret of the letter *Heh* of Jacob—turned into a snake. This means that the power of evil was "en-snaked" <note>wordplay on 'Nachash' (snake) and 'Nitchabesh' (bound)</note> upon the "heel" (Ekev). Afterward, when he returned in repentance, it turned back from a snake into a staff. You find this in the phrase "like a Cushite" and "take in your hand." And Moses "rested his hand upon Joshua" <note>Numbers 27:23</note>, hinting at all the above. For "his hand" <note>original: "Yado"</note> contains the letters of *Yod*, which is the *Yod* of Jacob. The word "rested" <note>original: "Samakh"</note> has the numerical value of "plague" <note>original: "Negep"</note>, hinting that Joshua did not eat. All of this he transmitted to Joshua; therefore, the *Yod* came to Joshua. 

Since we have placed all of Jacob within Abraham, it is written of him: "Blessed be Abraham by God Most High, Possessor [Koneh] of Heaven and Earth." It appears that "Possessor [Koneh] of Heaven" and the letter *Koph* refer to Abraham, and not just to "God Most High." The word "Koneh" (Possessor) shares the letters of "Kaneh" (windpipe) and *Vav*. He said "Possessor of Heaven and Earth" because it is known that the matter of "types of Heaven and Earth" is as explained in the *Zohar* and the *Pardes*. There is the spiritual Heaven and Earth—about which it says "The Heavens shall be glad and the Earth shall rejoice"—and there is the physical Heaven and Earth, which are from the side of the "Husks" <note>original: "Kelipot," or forces of impurity</note>. Regarding the latter, it is said: "For the earth shall wear out like a garment and the heavens shall vanish like smoke." This is the secret of Esau, the secret of the esophagus, the secret of This World. These are the physical Heaven and Earth. Thus, their initials are *A-S-H*—"He made [Oseh] Heaven [Shamayim] and Earth [Aretz]"—meaning the Heaven and Earth of the "Wicked" [Rasha]. The *Zohar* writes in the portion of *Toldot* that what is mentioned in the blessing of Esau—"the fatness of the earth... and the dew of heaven"—refers to the heaven and earth of the World of Action <note>Asiyah</note>. But what is mentioned in the blessing of Jacob—"May God give you of the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth"—refers to the Upper Heaven and Earth. This is the meaning of "Possessor of Heaven and Earth."

**And according** to these words, a difficulty in the portion of *Vayetze* is resolved. The verse says: "I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac..." Regarding Isaac, who was his actual father, it does not say "your father," but regarding Abraham, who was his grandfather, it does say "your father." The intention is that Abraham was like a father in a different way, as explained. Whereas with Isaac, it might have seemed inappropriate since Isaac loved Esau, so God called Jacob the "son of Abraham" specifically. Particularly in this vision, where the "ladder set on the ground with its top reaching to heaven" hints that even though a man walks upon the physical earth—meaning eating, drinking, and existing—it is proper for his "head" to reach the heavens. His intention should be for the sake of Heaven.

**And when** Jacob saw that God promised him this, he clarified the vision of the ladder. When he understood that God called Abraham "your father" for the sake of the "correction," he strengthened himself to add to the previous levels. He took hold of the spreading attributes and made this vow. He said: "If God [Y-H-V-E] will be with me..." meaning if there will be "being" <note>original: "Havayah," a play on the Divine Name</note> in everything I do. "I will always see that my intention is for the sake of Heaven, for the sake of God [Elohim]. All my deeds shall be for His name and not for mine." For this is the ultimate request: that He place me on the path I am walking—hinting at the *Yod* of Jacob, the "seven words of their spirit." I ask of Him to place me on that path, which is the secret of the "windpipe." I do not ask for luxuries, but "bread to eat and clothing to wear." And it continues: "then the Lord [Y-H-V-E] shall be my God [Elohim]." It is known that the Good Inclination (the side of Jacob) flows from the Attribute of Mercy (the name *YHVH*), and the Evil Inclination (the side of Judgment) flows from the Attribute of Justice (the name *Elohim*). This is the meaning of "The Lord shall be my God"—meaning, I will always see to connect the Good Inclination to the actions of the physical world. When I follow the matters of the Evil Inclination—meaning eating and drinking—I must elevate them <unclear>illegible</unclear>. My entire intention will be for the sake of the soul, which is the side of the Good Inclination. This is the meaning of the "six steps to the Throne" which equals the numerical value of "I" <note>original: "Anokhi"</note>, the secret of the *Yod* of Jacob. These are the "six reasons" my father of blessed memory wrote regarding the matters of eating. "May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before You, O Lord, my Rock and my Redeemer."

-> You, my children, may you be comforted. Now is the time to speak of the "Blessings of Enjoyment," for everything depends on the holiness of eating. This is an essential matter that our Sages emphasized greatly. <-
-> See Tractate Berakhot, page 35b, regarding "It is the Lord's..." <-

---

**We have learned** at the beginning of the chapter "How do we bless?": The Rabbis taught: It is forbidden for a person to enjoy anything of this world without a blessing. Anyone who enjoys this world without a blessing has committed sacrilege <note>original: "Me'ilah," the sin of misappropriating sacred property</note>. Rashi explains: It is as if he enjoyed something consecrated to the Temple, for it is written, "The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof." What is his remedy? Rava said: He should go to a scholar from the beginning so the scholar may teach him the blessings, so he will not come to commit sacrilege. Rav Judah said in the name of Shmuel: Anyone who enjoys this world without a blessing is as if he enjoyed the holy things of Heaven. Rabbi Levi raised a contradiction: It is written, "The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof," but it is also written, "The heavens are the Lord's, but the earth He gave to the children of man." This is not a difficulty: one verse refers to *before* the blessing, and the other to *after* the blessing. (Meaning: before the blessing, "the earth is the Lord's"; after the blessing, "the earth He gave to man.") 

Our Sages and Rabbis established this. Consider the story of the wealthy man of Laodicea. They used to bring before him a golden table... upon which were all kinds of food and delicacies. When they would set it down, they would say: "The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof." When they would remove it, they would say: "The heavens are the Lord's, but the earth He gave to the children of man." This was for the same reason: at first, before they blessed, it belonged to the Holy One, Blessed be He. We have no right to enjoy it until we bless His Name with the blessings of eating. Once they had blessed, they would say, "the earth He gave to man," for they had already eaten what they ate after blessing the Almighty.

Rabbi Hanina bar Papa said: Anyone who enjoys this world without a blessing is as if he steals from the Holy One, Blessed be He, and the Community of Israel, as it is said: "Whoso robbeth his father or his mother, and saith: 'It is no transgression', the same is the companion of a destroyer." "His father" is none other than the Holy One, Blessed be He... What is "a companion of a destroyer"? He is a companion to Jeroboam son of Nebat, who destroyed Israel. (Rashi explains: He steals from God His blessing, and from the Community of Israel because when people sin, the fruits are cursed.)

<meta>This page continues the "Gate of the Letters," transitioning from the mystical properties of the Hebrew alphabet to the practical and spiritual necessity of the "Blessings of Enjoyment" (Berakhot HaNehenin). It connects the act of reciting a blessing over food to the maintenance of the divine flow between the upper and lower worlds.</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

<margin>Assembly of the Great</margin>
The one who conceals the end of the word "Blessed" <note>original: "Baruch"</note> within the Unity <note>A reference to the meditative intention (Kavanah) of unifying the various aspects of the Divine Name during prayer.</note> ... [esoteric letter permutations] ... The explanation regarding the blessing is clarified through a single introduction. It is known that anyone who blesses the Emanations <note>original: "Sefirot," the ten attributes of God through which He interacts with the world.</note> or the Master of the World does so because, in his mind, he recognizes that the Blessed One is the source of all things; He is the Cause of all causes and the Reason for all reasons. Even though the Senses may attempt to argue and distance us from this truth, our Sages of blessed memory said: "There is not a single blade of grass below that does not have a 'Constellation' <note>original: "Mazal," here referring to a spiritual source of influence</note> above that strikes it and tells it: 'Grow!'" Consequently, the power of a thing comes only from the flow of influence bestowed upon it from the Upper Hand, which supervises every creature. This is as our teacher, Rabbenu Bahya, explained in the *Book of Duties* regarding the verse "to distinguish between the holy and the profane"—one should look there. From this, we understand that whoever does not recite a blessing is essentially a denier of all this. Our Sages said: "It is as if he steals from the Holy One, Blessed be He." For the wicked believe that everything comes to them without a blessing, like thieves, and they imagine their success comes solely from the 'Beginning' <note>referring to physical causes</note>, attributing power to the sun, moon, and stars... they say these are the masters of the earth and provide their food, forgetting the One who performs all this. Therefore, one who does not bless is called a "thief" from the Holy One, for he takes from the corrected Order of things... and it is written that the flow will be withheld from him.

Regarding the phrase "**and the Assembly of Israel**" <note>original: "Knesset Yisrael," a mystical term for the collective soul of Israel and the Shekhinah (the Divine Presence)</note>, this means that whoever is ungrateful causes the flow to be withheld from his own "Constellation." It is fitting that the goodness be withheld from him, as explained in the Gate of Repentance... there is another way to explain this through the "Path of Wonders" and the "Path of the End." Therefore, God says: "I will take back My grain in its time and My wine in its season" <note>Hosea 2:11</note>. This is explained through the mystery of the "Path of the Sages," that the Assembly of Israel is a "High Path." When they were as one, as explained in many places in the Zohar... this matter is very near to us. This is the mystery of the verse "He will surely go, weeping..." <note>Psalm 126:6</note>. As long as the children of Israel were in exile, the Holiness of His Kingdom was hidden... and the mystery of Ishmael... this is the matter of the "Tephillin of the Master of the World" <note>A famous Talmudic concept suggesting that God, as it were, wears tephillin containing verses about the uniqueness of the Jewish people.</note>. This is the mystery of the Holy One, Blessed be He... and one should stand upon the root of these matters. If a person has the ability, they should not let these words leave their mouth. These verses are explained in the *Sefer Ha-Kodesh* <note>likely "Shelah HaKadosh" by Rabbi Isaiah Horowitz</note> in the section on Service, and in the *Pardes Rimonim* by our teacher Rabbi Moses Cordovero... [specific chapter references: 7, 10, 11, 14, 17, 4, 19...] One who finds this path for his soul will find life and the strength of the Torah. These are the words of the Living God; they are life to those who find them.

One should connect the end of "Blessed" to the one who hides the light in the "Years," meaning the Holy One, Blessed be He, and His Presence <note>original: "Shekhinah"</note>. By not blessing, one prevents the flow from descending from the "King of the World." This is discussed in the *Tikunim*... The blessing is the "Hand" that supports the Assembly of Israel... and whoever does not bless steals from his Father and Mother <note>Metaphorically, the "Father" is the Holy One and the "Mother" is the Shekhinah</note>. He is a companion to a "man who destroys," for he separates the "Branches" and makes a "Blemish." This is the simple meaning of the twenty-two letters mentioned above.

Now, adding to the previous points, the formula of all blessings is: "**Blessed are You, L-rd our G-d, King of the Universe.**" The name "**L-rd**" <note>The Tetragrammaton (Y-H-V-H), representing the attribute of Mercy.</note> and the name "**G-d**" <note>original: "Elohim," representing the attribute of Judgment.</note> are combined. This unites Mercy with the Attribute of Judgment, because He created the world with both, as explained in the Zohar. The name "**G-d**" corresponds to the natural order, but the Name of Mercy (the Tetragrammaton) is the "Body of the Tree." The word "**King**" <note>original: "Melekh"</note> connects the two. This brings an "additional blessing" to the world, drawing nature into the spiritual, transforming Judgment into Mercy. For "Great is the L-rd above all gods." Therefore, in our blessings, we strive to constantly draw down this flow. We must accept these two Names together. The five letters of the name *Elohim* represent the five "Strengths" <note>original: "Gevurot"</note> that descend to the "Upper Kingdom" (Malchut)... as explained in the *Pardes*... through this, His kindness is spread. This is the mystery of the phrase "**G-d of your fathers, the G-d of Israel.**" If one separates the Name of Mercy from the Name of Judgment, they cause the attribute of Judgment to act alone. Our intent in the blessing is to unite them, so that the "Image" <note>original: "Temunah"</note> is complete. When one blesses with wisdom and focus, the "Three Vessels" of the soul receive their life-force.

This is also the explanation of why Joseph's soul was reunited with his brothers and his father Jacob... that the flow from the Divine Names should be united. This is why Jacob found the attribute of Judgment to be a source of blessing... for when the "Who" and the "These" <note>original: "Mi" and "Eleh," which together form the letters of "Elohim"</note> are joined, it is a complete blessing. Therefore, one who blesses is himself blessed by the Holiness that God placed in those days... for now, they are in the state of "Elohim." And the blessing of the soul is one... may God establish His Name in all the world. For anyone who argues against this or distances himself from it—know that these words are supreme. The union of the Name of Mercy with the Name of Judgment... may the one who understands this be wise, and may it add strength to them.

---

->**You have been shown**<-
to know, through the words of our Sages mentioned here, the great punishment for one who enjoys this world without a blessing. The "father" of all these teachings is the statement mentioned nearby in the name of Rabbi Hanina bar Papa: "Anyone who enjoys this world [without a blessing]... is as if he steals from the Holy One, Blessed be He, and the Assembly of Israel." From this statement, we see how great the "deception" is—for our Sages used the term "stealing." You already know their teaching: "Whoever robs his fellow even of the value of a penny, it is as if he takes his soul." How much more so one who robs the Public and the Presence of God! Worse still, they compare such a person to Jeroboam son of Nebat, who sinned and caused Israel to sin. This is even more severe, for you know the teaching in the *Ethics of the Fathers*: "Whoever causes the public to sin, no opportunity is given to him to repent." Thus, the obligation of the "Blessings of Enjoyment" is of the highest priority.

The versions of the blessings were also established according to the esoteric "Secret." The book *Tola'at Yaakov* <note>A 16th-century Kabbalistic commentary on the liturgy by Meir ibn Gabbai.</note> says: The blessing "**...by whose word all things came to be**" <note>original: "Shehakol"</note> includes all blessings, for "All" is the foundation of everything, and everything is within it. Therefore, if one says this blessing over any food, they have fulfilled their obligation. The blessing for "Souls" <note>original: "Borei Nefashot," the blessing after eating simple foods</note> is of the same kind, for He is the "Storehouse of Souls" in whose hand is the soul of every living thing. This refers to the Upper World. The signature of this blessing is "**Blessed is the Life of the Worlds.**"

**Over every** thing that grows from the ground, one recites a specific blessing. This refers to the "Holy Land" <note>The spiritual archetype of the Land of Israel</note> which is constantly worked to nourish every living soul, for from there all types of sustenance emerge for all worlds. The physical earth below is a reflection of this. Over the fruit of the tree, one blesses "**...who creates the fruit of the tree.**" This refers to the "**Tree of Life**" <note>original: "Etz Chaim"</note> which bears fruit of its kind in the Upper Land. The physical trees below are grafted onto this spiritual source. Finally, we bless "**...who creates many souls**" <note>Borei Nefashot</note>, except for those fruits for which the Land of Israel is praised, over which we recite the "Three-faceted Blessing" <note>original: "Me'ein Shalosh," a condensed version of the Grace After Meals.</note>.

**The reason** for this is to give honor to the "Upper Land of Israel," for she is the source of all blessings. They established this blessing corresponding to her and for her honor. It is "three-faceted" because everything is contained within her. Even though it contains four themes, it is called "three" because three are from the Torah and the fourth is from the Sages, corresponding to her as the "Fourth Leg" of the Divine Throne, and she is the mystery of the "Oral Torah," the "Woman of Valor."

**The Vine:** It is written, "You moved a vine from Egypt" <note>Psalm 80:9</note>. Because of this mystery, they established a unique blessing for wine due to its importance. It is "wine that gladdens God and men," coming from the "Upper Wine" that is preserved within it. You know the teaching: "This vine is the Assembly of Israel."

You also know that for anything one blesses over—whether to eat it or to smell it—the one blessing must hold it in his **right hand**, for the act of holding is part of the blessing...

### The Gate of the Letters

Throughout the six days of work, that "line" <note>The author is referring to the letter **Vav** (ו), which looks like a vertical line and represents the flow of divine energy into the six days of the week.</note> is closed. However, on the Sabbath, that line—which is the letter **Vav** or represents "Peace"—expands. This is because the "Peace" <note>original: "Shalom," ending in a closed Mem (**ם**)</note> remains from the "closed Mem," but the opening is made wide to provide life, and the divine abundance <note>original: "Shefa"</note> descends. This is a deep secret, revealed only to those who understand the difference between the six days of work and the Sabbath. Then one will understand why there is an "additional soul" <note>original: "Neshama Yeteira"</note> on the Sabbath. Anyone who wishes to stand upon the essence of these matters should study the *Book of the Orchard* <note>original: "Sefer HaPardes," the classic Kabbalistic work by Rabbi Moses Cordovero</note> in the section on the "Gate of the Alphabet," and there they will find rest for their soul.

In his way, I say that the **Vav** is hidden within the "closed Mem." This refers to the **Vav** of the "Pipe" <note>term: <term>Kaneh</term> — literally a "reed" or "pipe," used in Kabbalah to describe a conduit for divine light</note> that follows the pipe and draws the **Vav** upon itself to open the gate. But for one who does not draw the **Vav** of the "Pipe" upon themselves, the gate will remain closed forever, for this **Vav** seals it. 

Our Sages hinted at this through the commandment of the "Mixing of Cooked Dishes" <note>term: <term>Eruv Tavshilin</term> — a ritual that allows one to cook on a Festival for the following Sabbath</note>. They asked in the Talmud: "What does this suggest?" Rabbah said it is so that one may choose a fine portion for the Sabbath and a fine portion for the Festival. Rav Ashi said it is so people will say: "We may not bake on a Festival for the Sabbath, and certainly not from a Festival for a weekday." <note>This is a legal safeguard to preserve the sanctity of the holy days.</note> 

Behold, one is warned on the Sabbath to take more pleasure in their own cooking for their own enjoyment. This is because on the Sabbath, everyone agrees we require "for you" <note>A reference to the Talmudic principle that half of a holiday should be spent in spiritual pursuit and half "for you"—meaning physical enjoyment like eating.</note>. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua disagree on this. Rabbah said that the commandment of the "Mixing" <note>Eruv</note> comes to say that one’s eating on a Festival is like that which is "acquired" <note>A pun on the word "Koneh," meaning "acquired" or "creator," and "Kaneh," meaning "pipe."</note> through the secret of Isaac's delicacies. As my father and teacher <note>original: "A"A," abbreviating "Adoni Avi"</note> explained regarding the laws of Festivals, this "fine portion" refers to the verse I cited above: "How beautiful and how pleasant..." <note>Song of Songs 7:7</note>. 

Therefore, they used the language of a "portion" <note>original: "Manah"</note>, which contains the letters of "Manna" <note>original: "Man"</note> found in the acronym of the verse "Feed me, I pray thee..." <note>Genesis 25:30</note>. This means that our eating should not be like the Manna, but rather a "fine portion." Rav Ashi said the reason is to show the "Eye of Peace," so that a person eats with a sense of sufficiency and does not worry, "What will I eat tomorrow?" 

They found it necessary to establish this to hint at these paths. When a Festival and Sabbath are adjacent to one another, one increases their meals on consecutive days. One might, God forbid, get swept away by physical pleasures. <unclear>Therefore</unclear>, one must remember the "Mixing of Dishes" as a hint to remove excess. Similarly, when a Festival and Sabbath are adjacent, they established the "Y-K-N-H-V" <note>term: <term>Yaknehaz</term> — a mnemonic for the order of blessings (Wine, Sanctification, Candle, Havdalah, Time) when a Festival begins Saturday night</note> as a hint. The letter **Yod** is from Jacob, and then **K-N-H** <note>Kaneh/Pipe</note> which refers to the verse: "Seven stalks of grain coming up on one stalk" <note>Genesis 41:5</note>. The intention is that the "Pipe" is the **Vav**, which is the **Yod** and **Vav** of Jacob in its fullness. The "seven stalks" are the seven extremities <note>Sefirot</note> and the Holy Palace in the center. Their "clothing" is the six holy palaces that shine in the secret of Sovereignty <note>original: "Malchut"</note> when they enter the World of Formation <note>original: "Olam HaYetzirah"</note>. Therefore, they are called the "World of Separated Intelligences," for these intelligences are the clothing for the inner life-force and the spirituality of the "Extremities."

**I shall return** to the first matter: regarding Abraham, it is written "Because [**Ekev**] Abraham obeyed My voice" <note>Genesis 26:5</note>. This word "Ekev" <note>meaning "heel" or "because"</note> is part of "Jacob" <note>Ya-akov</note>. You also find the **Yod** of Jacob in the ten trials of Abraham. It is possible that this is the letter **He** that was divided between Abraham and Sarah. For I have already written that this is the "Secret of the Hand" <note>The letter He has the numerical value of 5, representing five fingers.</note>, five against five. Therefore, He gave a **He** to Abraham and a **He** to Sarah. 

This answers the question: why did the **Yod** of Sarah's original name [Sarai] complain until it was placed at the head of Joshua's name? <note>A famous Midrash: the Yod was removed from Sarai to make her Sarah; that "displaced" Yod was later added to Hoshea to make him Joshua (Yehoshua).</note> Why specifically Joshua? According to my path, it is because it is known that Joshua "did not depart from the tent of Moses." In Moses, you find that he drew the "S" out of the "Shaddai" <note>A mystical permutation of divine names</note>. Moses followed the "Pipe," for he did not eat for three periods of forty days. 

It is possible that the Staff of Moses was made in the shape of the letter **Vav**. This is the secret of what God showed Moses: sometimes the staff—which was the secret of the **Vav** of Jacob—turned into a snake. This means the snake is coiled at the "heel" <note>Ekev</note>. When it is a snake, it is a literal snake. And when Moses leaned his hand upon Joshua, it hinted at all the above, for "His Hand" <note>original: "Yado"</note> contains the letters for **Yod**, which is the **Yod** of Jacob. He "leaned" <note>original: "Sa-mach"</note> upon him, which also contains the letter **Mem** <note>representing the 40 days Moses fasted</note>. This was handed over to Joshua, and thus the **Yod** came to Joshua. 

Since our eyes are on Abraham, all of "Jacob" is written regarding him: "Blessed be Abram of God Most High, Creator [**Koneh**] of heaven and earth" <note>Genesis 14:19</note>. It appears that "Creator of heaven etc." refers to Abraham himself, not just to God Most High. The word "Koneh" <note>Creator/Owner</note> uses the same letters as "Kaneh" <note>Pipe/Reed</note>. It says "Creator of heaven and earth" because the matter of the transformation of heaven and earth is explained in the *Zohar* and the *Pardes*. There is a "Spiritual Earth" over which the heavens rejoice, and there is a "Material Earth" from the side of the "Husks" <note>term: <term>Kelipot</term> — spiritual shards or shells that conceal divine light</note>, about which it is said "the earth shall wear out like a garment." 

This is why the acronym for "Heaven and Earth" <note>original: **Sh**amayim **V**'**A**retz</note> spells "S-V-A," which relates to the "Prince of Darkness." The *Zohar* writes (Portion of Toldot) that Esau's blessing—"the fatness of the earth and the dew of heaven"—refers to this physical, material earth. But Jacob's blessing—"May God give you of the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth"—refers to the Upper Heaven and Earth, which are "acquired" through the "Pipe" <note>Kaneh</note>. This is the meaning of "Koneh [Acquirer/Creator] of heaven and earth."

**And** according to these words, one difficult question in the Portion of Vayetze is resolved. The verse says: "I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac..." Regarding Isaac, who was his actual father, it does not say "your father," but regarding Abraham, his grandfather, it does. The intention is that Jacob and Abraham were unified in one matter, whereas with Isaac, it was seemingly not so, for he loved Esau <note>who represents the "Side of Judgement"</note>. Jacob saw that this matter was very good in the eyes of God through the vision of the Ladder. Its "foot was set on the earth and its top reached to heaven," hinting that even though a person walks in the "earthly" material world—eating and drinking—his intention in these actions should be "for the sake of Heaven" <note>original: "L'shem Shamayim"</note>.

When Jacob saw this, he strengthened himself to follow this path of sufficiency and made a vow: "If God will be with me..." He asked that in everything he does, his intention be for the sake of the Name of God, and not for his own name. He did not ask for luxuries, but only "bread to eat and a garment to wear." Then "the Lord shall be my God." This means: I will always ensure the connection is good. Even when I follow the matters of the "Evil Inclination"—eating and drinking—I will bind them to the Divine Name, for my primary intention will be for the soul. 

Up to here is what I have been moved to innovate regarding the "Six Steps to the Throne," which numerically equal "I" <note>original: "Anochi" = 81</note>, the secret of Jacob's hand. These are the six branches that my father wrote concerning the matters of eating. "May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before You, O Lord, my Rock and my Redeemer."

->Now, my children, it is time to speak<-
->of the Blessings of Enjoyment, which conclude with the holiness of eating<-
->a necessary matter that our Sages emphasized greatly<-
->See Tractate Berakhot, page 35a to 35b<-

**We learn** at the beginning of the chapter "How do we bless?": The Sages taught that it is forbidden for a person to enjoy anything of this world without a blessing. Anyone who enjoys this world without a blessing has committed "sacrilege" <note>term: <term>Me'ilah</term> — the sin of misappropriating property that belongs to the Temple</note>. Rashi explains: It is like enjoying things consecrated to God, for it is written, "The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof." What is the remedy? Let him go to a scholar from the start, and they will teach him the blessings so that he does not come to commit sacrilege.

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: "Anyone who enjoys this world without a blessing is as if he enjoyed the holy things of Heaven." Rabbi Levi raised a contradiction: It is written, "The earth is the Lord's," but it is also written, "The heavens are the Lord's, but the earth He has given to the children of man." There is no difficulty: one verse refers to *before* a blessing, and the other *after* a blessing. <note>Before you bless, the food belongs to God; after you bless, He gives you permission to eat it.</note>

The Tosafot and Rabbenu Yonah wrote: This is like the story of the householder of Ludkia who had a golden table brought before him, laden with all kinds of food and delicacies. When they set it down, they would say, "The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof." When they removed it, they would say, "The heavens are the Lord's... but the earth He has given to the children of man." They wanted to show that before they blessed, the food belonged to the Holy One, Blessed be He, and we have no right to enjoy it until we bless His Name. After eating, they said "the earth He has given to man," because they had already blessed God and were permitted to eat.

Rabbi Hanina bar Papa said: "Anyone who enjoys this world without a blessing is as if he robs the Holy One, Blessed be He, and the Community of Israel." For it is said: "Whoso robbeth his father or his mother, and saith: 'It is no transgression,' the same is the companion of a destroyer" <note>Proverbs 28:24</note>. "Father" is the Holy One, Blessed be He... "Companion of a destroyer" refers to Jeroboam son of Nebat, who destroyed Israel's relationship with their Father in Heaven. (Rashi explains: He robs God of His blessing, and the Community of Israel because that sin causes the fruits to be cursed and ruined.)

### The Gate of the Letters
-> Signature: 23b 2 <-

<margin>
At the conclusion of the Gemara regarding the status of custom, etc.: the expression "opened with a jug and ended with a barrel" <note>This is a common Talmudic idiom for a shifting argument.</note>. Rav Papa explains this as a matter of "appeasement" so that they might merit <unclear>business</unclear> for buying and selling, etc.
</margin>

From the abundance [of caution], one should also be careful regarding the **bread of a non-Jew** <note>original: "Pat shel Goy"</note>, and should only break bread from the **bread of an Israelite** <note>original: "Pat shel Yisrael"</note>, even if it is coarse bread <note>term: <term>Kibar</term> — a cheaper, bran-heavy bread</note>. However, the *Hashar* <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria</note> objects and cries out that one should remove the "clean" <note>refined white</note> bread of a non-Jew from the table until after the blessing of "Who brings forth bread" <note>original: "HaMotzi"</note> is recited. The reason is so that one does not appear as a glutton <note>original: "koshtan"</note>. These are the words of the *Mordechai* <note>a 13th-century legal authority</note> there, and they are derived from the words of the *Tosafot* <note>medieval commentaries on the Talmud</note> at the beginning of the chapter "All the Images," on the heading "But a piece of wheat," etc.

**B** The Mahara"i <note>Rabbi Israel Isserlein</note> wrote in *Terumat HaDeshen*, section 80 and section 2, in a responsa quoted by the *Beit Yosef* in the aforementioned section: "Blessed is He. If one is not careful about the bread of a non-Jew and does not intend to eat for the entire meal anything but the 'clean' bread [of the non-Jew], it is considered 'refined,' even if the members of his household are eating bread that is not refined but is 'kosher' <note>meaning Jewish-baked bread of lower quality</note>. When both loaves are placed on the table, he must break the refined bread of the non-Jew, since he is the one breaking bread and he only intends to eat from that bread and not from the 'kosher' [Jewish-baked] one." For when we say that what appears first in the Torah's verse takes precedence, or that the "important" or "beloved" item takes precedence, this only applies if one wishes to eat from both of them. But if he only wishes to eat from the other, he is not obligated to eat from the "first," "important," or "beloved" item just to give it precedence, even if it is sitting right in front of him. This is also what the *Shulchan Aruch* wrote (on Principle 5, Section 9).

**C** He also wrote in the *Choshen Mishpat* in the aforementioned section in the name of the *Mordechai* (regarding the Sabbath, in the chapter "One may not place"), in the name of the Ra'avyah <note>Rabbi Eliezer ben Joel HaLevi of Bonn</note>: "If one is careful about the bread of a non-Jew, but an Israelite who is *not* careful about it is reclining with him at the table (and two loaves are before them: a 'beautiful' non-Jewish loaf and a 'coarse' Jewish loaf), since the obligation of the meal falls upon the host, he should break the 'beautiful' refined bread of the non-Jew."

**Specifically**, this applies if an Israelite who is not careful is reclining with him, or if he himself is not careful. In that case, he should break the "beautiful" bread of the non-Jew. This is the meaning of the aforementioned words of the Ra'avyah, who specified in his words: "and an Israelite who is not careful is reclining with him at the table," etc. This is unlike the interpretation of the Mahara"i in *Terumat HaDeshen* (Section 154) regarding the words of the Ra'avyah. There he wrote: "Ra'avyah did not specifically mean that an Israelite who eats non-Jewish bread must be reclining with him; even without him, it would be permitted if he took it [the non-Jewish bread] first." Do not say that it is more stringent because it is on the table while the host is normally careful about it. According to his interpretation of Ra'avyah, even though they did not testify that one should break the "beautiful" non-Jewish loaf if two loaves are placed before him by mere chance—even if he is eating alone—the *Shulchan Aruch* ruled (in *Orach Chayim* and *Yoreh De'ah*) that it is not considered "strict" for a host who is usually careful to break the beautiful non-Jewish bread when an Israelite who is not careful is reclining with him. Therefore, this is the opinion of the *Mordechai* as we brought above in Section A.

And in my humble opinion, the reason to distinguish in the aforementioned case of non-Jewish bread is that when he eats alone, or when someone who is not careful sits with him at the table, he might come to eat it [the non-Jewish bread] before him, as I have written... <note>The text here becomes highly abbreviated and refers to specific legal citations regarding mixtures and the appearance of the bread on the table.</note>

<column-break/>

...And it appears that this reason is said regarding the prohibition of the bread of non-Jews. It is a light prohibition, as it was only forbidden because of the concern that one might come to marry their daughters <note>original: "Chitun," the classic Rabbinic reason for the decree against Gentile bread, intended to prevent social mingling that leads to intermarriage</note>. But if there is no concern of social intimacy or if it is a case of great necessity, there are significant leniencies that permitted non-Jewish bread, especially when traveling. And because of "enmity" <note>term: <term>Eivah</term> — the legal principle of avoiding friction or hatred between Jews and non-Jews</note>, and if the oven was lit by an Israelite, etc., the Sages permitted it. Thus, when both loaves are placed before him on the table, he should break the "beautiful" non-Jewish loaf, for it is more "honorable" for the blessing <note>original: "Kavod HaBerakhah"</note> of "Who brings forth bread." And since it is permitted to be eaten, it is permitted for the entire meal. (And the *Mordechai* wrote in the name of others that this is for the honor of the Name, etc.)

## Principle 2: Discussing which bread we bless "Who brings forth" and which bread we bless "Sustenance," containing 7 sections:

**A** The *Tur* <note>The foundational legal code by Rabbi Jacob ben Asher</note> wrote in Section 168 as follows: "**Bread that comes as a snack** <note>term: <term>Pat Haba B'kisnin</term> — dough that is either filled with sweets, made with juices/spices, or baked into a hard cracker</note>—which is bread made like pockets filled with sugar, almonds, walnuts, and varieties of spices—one recites over it 'Who creates varieties of sustenance' <note>original: "Borei Minei Mezonot"</note>, and after eating it, the 'Blessing after Sustenance' <note>The shortened version of the Grace after Meals</note>. However, if he ate an amount of it that others would normally 'establish a meal' upon, even if he personally is not full, he must recite 'Who brings forth' <note>HaMotzi</note> and the three blessings [of the full Grace After Meals]. (And he requires the ritual washing of hands, though some say one does not need washing at all except for actual bread; therefore, he should wash his hands to avoid doubt but not recite the blessing over the washing, for the blessings do not hinder the act. See the *Beit Yosef*, Section 158). If, at the start, he intended to eat only a little and blessed 'Sustenance,' but afterward ate the amount that others establish a meal upon, he must recite the three blessings of the Grace After Meals, even though he did not recite 'Who brings forth' at the start. But if he ate an amount that others do *not* establish a meal upon, even if *he* personally establishes a meal on it, he does not recite 'Who brings forth' or the Grace After Meals, for his opinion is nullified by the standard of all other people. These are the words of Rav Alfas <note>The Rif, an 11th-century Moroccan scholar</note>." Anything made for snacking is called by this name.

**B** If one mixed honey, oil, milk, or varieties of spices into the dough (and the liquids in the dough are the majority) and baked it, even if he did not fill the dough with anything, it is called **snack-bread**, provided that the taste of the mixed fruit or spices is recognizable in the dough. This is according to the Mahar"i in his *Shulchan Aruch*. However, the Rav [Isserles] wrote in his *Shulchan Aruch* that some say this is "actual bread" unless there are *many* spices or honey, like the sweet treats called **Honey Cake** <note>original: "Lekach"</note>, where the little bit of honey or spices are the primary ingredient.

**C** And the pious <note>original: "Yere Shamayim" — one who fears Heaven</note> should satisfy all opinions and should not eat snack-bread initially except in the middle of a meal, so that it is covered by the blessing of the bread of the meal.
<margin>
As noted in the manuscript: he wrote there that "the majority and the essence" is the determining factor.
</margin>

# Gate of the Letters

->Do not turn to the right or to the left:<-

**The blessing** of the Lord is what enriches the earth, causing it to bear and sprout, giving "seed to the sower and bread to the eater." <note>Isaiah 55:10</note> From there it branches out; the food becomes three "heads," representing the three worlds <note>Kabbalistic concept of the worlds of Creation, Formation, and Action</note> which provide life and sustenance to every living soul, from the highest of heights to the lowliest of beings. For the blessing of the Lord fills the earth, and without it, nothing would endure for even a moment. Therefore, one is obligated to recite a blessing over every thing from which one derives pleasure <note>term: <term>Birkhot HaNehenin</term> — blessings recited before enjoying food, fragrance, or sights</note>, in order to awaken the blessing from the highest Source down to the final end, for everything depends on this. When the "Upper Earth" is watered, the "Lower Earth" also drinks and sprouts, yielding its produce and the fruit of the field—as it says: "If you walk in My statutes... the land shall yield its produce and the trees of the field their fruit." <note>Leviticus 26:3-4</note> If you bless, you bless Me as well; these are his words.

After seeing how the matter of the "Blessings of Pleasure" is determined, so that it may be arranged before you in complete perfection, I have copied here the first part of a deep composition titled **Berakhah** (Blessing) by my late honored father and teacher, along with my own annotations. In this work, all the laws of blessings are clarified. Fortunate is the one who is expert in them and in their names for the House of Israel through their blessings.

## Principle 1: Discussing which bread is preferred for the blessing of "Who brings forth bread" <note>original: "HaMotzi"</note>. It contains three sections, concluding the laws of foods and their sanctity.

<margin>Translator's Note: This discusses the priority if one wishes to eat from two types of bread. If one only wants the refined bread, even if a whole loaf of coarse bread <note>term: <term>Kibar</term> — bread made with bran or unsifted flour</note> is present, one should not necessarily prefer the coarse loaf unless they are equal in one's eyes. However, if the refined bread is more desirable, follow the rules below. In sections 330 and 52, the *Yere’im* writes that one blesses over a piece of wheat bread rather than a whole loaf of barley, because the species of wheat takes precedence. Most legal authorities order the blessings as explained in section 200. This is explicitly decided in the chapter "How do we bless" <note>a chapter in the Talmudic tractate Berakhot</note> regarding the question: "Is a whole loaf always preferred?" The conclusion is that everyone agrees that if they are of the same type (e.g., two pieces of wheat), the whole loaf is better. But if one is wheat and the other barley, the wheat takes precedence even if it is just a piece. This is recorded in the *Shulchan Aruch* <note>The Code of Jewish Law</note> at the end of section 168. It is a matter of the "honor of the King" to choose the wheat, which is a superior grain. There is much to say regarding the dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yohanan here, but I will not lengthen the discussion.</margin>

**1.** The *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, author of a major 14th-century legal code</note> wrote in section 168: If a person has before them pieces of fine bread and a whole loaf, and they are both of the same grain, one blesses over the whole loaf—even if the whole loaf is coarse bread and the piece is refined, and even if the whole loaf is smaller than the piece. However, if the whole loaf is made of barley and the piece is made of wheat, even if the wheat piece is small, one places the piece under the whole loaf and breaks them both together.

Regarding barley bread and spelt bread <note>original: "Kosemin"</note> (if one intends to eat both), one blesses over the barley because it is one of the Seven Species <note>The seven agricultural products praised in the Bible as special to the Land of Israel</note>, even though the spelt might be finer. Between refined bread and coarse bread of the same grain, one blesses over the refined. Regarding the refined bread of a non-Jew and the coarse bread of an Israelite, one may bless over whichever one prefers. Thus far are his words. **And from his words** we have learned the four categories of priority regarding bread for the blessing of "Who brings forth," which we can remember by the acronym **CHM"SH** (חמ"ש). These stand for: **Ch**aviv (Preferred), **M**in (Species - the seven), **Sh**alem (Whole), and **H**aleh <note>a play on the letter Heh</note>, substituting the "H" for a "Ch" <note>note: This refers to Jewish-baked bread, known as Pat Yisrael. The author notes that the letters Chet and Heh are interchangeable in Hebrew grammar.</note>. (It does not literally mean the *Challah* loaf, but rather bread of an Israelite, or bread where a Jew assisted in the baking, as will be explained later). I will now explain the quality of these four priorities according to the *Tur* and his reasoning.

**Preferred (Chaviv):** How so? If one has two loaves of the same grain, and both are whole or both are pieces, and both are either Jewish-baked or both are non-Jewish-baked: if one is finer/cleaner than the other, one simply blesses over the refined one. As the *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo's commentary on the Tur</note> wrote: "It is a simple matter that it is more appropriate to bless over that which is more important." The *Tosafot* <note>Medieval French/German commentators</note> also wrote that if one is whiter than the other, one blesses on the whiter one because it is more desirable.

**The Reason** is self-evident: all blessings over pleasure depend on "belovedness" <note>original: "chavivut"</note>. It is for the belovedness of the pleasure that one blesses and praises God. Therefore, one should seek out the most desirable item to fulfill the "belovedness of the commandment," since the same blessing applies to both. **Seven Species:** How so? If one has two breads, one from wheat or barley and one from other grains like spelt (called *Spelt* <note>note: original text uses the phonetic Yiddish/German "Spelt"</note>) or rye (called *Korn* <note>note: original text uses "Korn"</note>), the *Tur* holds the importance of barley is greater—even if the other is more desirable to him—because barley is one of the Seven Species. This is certainly true if the choice is between wheat and rye; one blesses on the wheat because it has two advantages: it is both more desirable and one of the Seven Species.

**Whole (Shalem):** How so? If one has two loaves of the same grain, the *Tur* rules one blesses on the whole loaf even if it is coarse and small, while the broken piece is refined and large.

**Jewish-Baked (Halah/Pat Yisrael):** How so? If one has two loaves, one baked by a non-Jew and one by an Israelite, and both are of the same grain and equally fine, the *Tur* holds that one must prioritize the bread of the Israelite. We learn this from his statement: "Between the fine bread of a non-Jew and the coarse bread of an Israelite, one may bless on whichever he wants." From this we infer that it is only when the non-Jewish bread is superior (refined) that it is an equal choice. This is because each has an advantage the other lacks: one is refined, the other is Jewish-made. (This assumes both are either whole or both are pieces; but if one is whole, the whole loaf takes precedence). If both were equally refined, the choice would not be equal; one would have to bless on the Jewish-baked bread.

<margin>This refers specifically to bread made from the dough of an Israelite. However, bread from the dough of a non-Jew where the oven was stoked or the fire was handled by an Israelite <note>term: <term>Hemshech</term> — a Jew's participation in the baking process that renders the bread "Pat Yisrael"</note> is treated as bread of an Israelite regarding the blessing. We can learn this from the *Tosafot* and *Mordechai* in the chapter "How do we bless." They say that if one has the bread of a villager <note>coarse</note> and the bread of an Israelite, one blesses on the bread of the Israelite. If the non-Jewish bread is cleaner and more desirable, and the Jewish bread is not, he may choose. This only applies to one who is not strict about avoiding non-Jewish bread entirely <note>term: <term>Pat Palter</term> — bread from a commercial non-Jewish baker, which some are lenient to eat</note>. This is discussed in the *Beit Yosef*.</margin>

Otherwise, he should have stated the greater novelty <note>an academic point about the text's structure</note>. With this, we have completed the four categories of priority in bread, which are signaled by the acronym **CHM"SH**, as we mentioned in the name of the *Tur*. To ensure the matter is complete, I am bringing further words from the *Mordechai* <note>Rabbi Mordechai ben Hillel, 13th-century authority</note> on this subject, so that the laws of bread priority are whole and harmonious. He writes: "Regarding a piece of wheat and a whole loaf of barley, our Rabbi says one blesses on the piece of wheat because wheat is superior, as it is mentioned first in the Biblical verse. But with pieces and whole loaves of the same grain—even if the pieces are refined and the whole is coarse—one blesses on the whole." The Jerusalem Talmud <note>original: "Yerushalmi"</note> says: if one has a piece of *gluska* <note>term: <term>Gluska</term> — a fine, high-quality white bread</note> and a whole loaf of coarse bread, one blesses on the whole coarse loaf. But if one has a piece of *gluska* and a whole loaf of *ben-chanan* <note>another type of coarse bread</note>, one blesses on the whole one. It is also taught: between impure bread and pure bread, bless on the pure. Between refined-but-impure bread and coarse-but-pure bread, one may bless on whichever he desires. The same applies to non-Jewish bread; if they are equal, bless on the Jewish bread. If the non-Jewish bread is cleaner and more desirable, bless on whichever you prefer (if you are not strict about non-Jewish bread). The *Beit Yosef* quotes this and notes...

# And what seems correct to me:
-> From what the Tur wrote: "And those rolls, etc., and if he established [a meal] on them, etc., and if he ate them during the meal, etc." as was cited inside in Section 3. <-

The blessing "Who brings forth" is better; there are two paths for these rolls and pastries <note>original: כיסנין - kisnin</note>. **Path One:** if he eats them not as part of the meal, then we bless "by whose word all things exist" <note>original: כמ"מ - likely meaning the general blessing for snacks</note> over them. But if he established his meal on them, or ate an amount that others usually use for a meal, it becomes his meal. **Path Two:** if the ruling of the *Tur* regarding these during a meal is that he ate them "not for the sake of the meal"—meaning he does not establish a meal on them to eat for the sake of a meal to fill his stomach, but rather eats them during the meal for pleasure and dessert—then their law is like fruit, which requires a blessing before it. This is as I wrote in the words of my teachers, which I proved above: he wrote concerning meat and fish, and then regarding rolls, etc., until the "First Path" mentioned in the name of the Rama <note>Rabbi Meir Abulafia</note>. If his eating is "for the sake of the meal"—meaning he does not eat for pleasure and dessert but with the intent to be full, such as when he hasn't filled his stomach yet and seeks food to satisfy his soul—then it is considered "for the sake of the meal." It is regarded like meat and fish; even if they come after the main course, if they are "for the sake of the meal," one does not bless over them even if he eats only a little. **These two paths** were mentioned and simplified in the words of the *Tur* cited nearby in that paragraph beginning "and those rolls whose batter... and they are filled..." etc. And if he established a meal on them, he blesses 'Who brings forth' even if he did not bless over other bread first. This is the First Path I mentioned. And as he wrote afterward: "And if he ate them during the meal not for the sake of the meal, they require a blessing before them," meaning specifically not for the sake of the meal, as above—not for satiation but for pleasure. Then they require a blessing before them, for they are like fruit brought during a meal. But if they come "for the sake of the meal"—meaning to eat and be satisfied—the *Tur* holds they do not require a blessing and are considered like meat, fish, and other things that are the core of the meal. This is the Second Path I mentioned. With this, the term "not for the sake of the meal" used by the *Tur* is explained. **And in this**, the laws of rolls and pastries differ from the law of fruit and meat, fish, and vegetables mentioned in Rabbi Pappa's statement. For those—fruit, meat, fish, and vegetables—do not depend on the intent of the eater. Over fruit, one must always say a first blessing during the meal if eating them for dessert, even if he says he eats them for sustenance. Meat, fish, and vegetables never require a blessing during the meal, even if he eats them for dessert and pleasure alone and not to be full. But all these rolls and pastries mentioned above depend on the intent of the eater. If he eats them as "pastries" for dessert, he must bless over them even during the meal, like fruit. But if he eats them as sustenance, he does not need to bless over them during the meal. **In this way**, what we questioned above regarding the *Tur's* language is settled—why regarding rolls he said "and if he ate them during the meal," making it dependent on the person. In Section 157, the *Tur* brought Rabbi Pappa's words: "The law is that things brought... do not require [a blessing]..." in the name of the sages, not making it dependent on the person but rather teaching which items brought during a meal are "for the sake of the meal," like meat and fish, and which are "not for the sake of the meal," like figs and grapes. These do not depend on the person's intent; as soon as they are on the table, it is known whether they are for the meal or not. Meat and fish are always brought for the needs of the meal, and therefore the Sages called them "for the sake of the meal," and one never blesses over them during the meal because the bread exempts them. Figs and grapes are always for dessert and require a blessing even during the meal. These two types—meat/fish and fruit—do not depend on the eater's intent. But rolls and pastries are not defined by their nature; they depend on the intent of the eater: whether he eats them as sustenance or as dessert. Therefore, the *Tur* used the language "if he ate," to show it depends on his intent.

this, what we questioned above is also settled: why the commentators did not mention rolls and "bread brought in baskets" alongside other foods in Rabbi Pappa's statement. This also resolves the difficulties we raised earlier regarding the *Tur's* words on this matter. This is sufficient for the understanding person. <summary>This page analyzes the legal requirements for blessings over rolls, wafers, and filled pastries (pashtida) during a meal. It distinguishes between eating for satiety (sustenance) and eating for pleasure (dessert), noting that unlike fruits or meat, the blessing for these dough products depends on the consumer's intent.</summary>

# Gate of the Letters

<margin>
Just as [the law states] "did not give a blemish, not even a little," and as if it were possible to say, "as if God is angry," everyone agrees that one must judge these as "pocket-bread" <note>original: כיסנין - Kisnin</note>. Since it is written that one does not "knead the dough" because this [type] is primarily based on liquids and contains no water at all. However, according to the aforementioned definition of snack-bread, they differed over bread made from dough mixed with honey or other types of liquids where the flavor of the mixture is dominant. The Mahar"k <note>Rabbi Yosef Colon, a 15th-century Italian scholar</note> holds that this is also called <term>Pat HaBa'ah BeKisnin</term> <note>literally "bread that comes in pockets/envelopes," referring to grain-based snacks that are not eaten as a main meal</note> since the taste of the mixture is noticeable in the dough. However, the author of the *Masoret* holds that this is called "complete bread" as long as the water in the dough is the majority, even if other liquids were added. Since they are treated as secondary or as a flavor-enhancer, they are nullified by the water, and one must concern himself that its law is that of complete bread in all respects. Thus far his words.
</margin>
...the flavor of fruit or spices is noticeable in the dough. [One should not eat them] except within a meal—that is, after having first recited the <term>HaMotzi</term> <note>the blessing over bread: "Who brings forth bread from the earth"</note> over complete bread. (Alternatively, one may eat a quantity of it that others usually establish as a full meal, or eat it even outside of a meal and recite *HaMotzi* and the three blessings [of Grace After Meals] over it, similar to the snack-bread mentioned above). Nor should one eat those cakes called *Stral-Kuchen* <note>likely a type of Streusel or Striezel cake</note> which have fat mixed into their kneading and the taste of the fat is noticeable in the dough, except within a meal (unless one eats a quantity that people establish as a meal, like the snack-bread above). This means he first blesses *HaMotzi* over complete bread and afterward eats these aforementioned items as he wishes, whether a little or a lot. (The *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo's commentary on the Tur</note> wrote a similar compromise in Section 168 regarding the law of rolls that were boiled in water or fried in oil but still have the "form of bread"; this will appear later in Sections 50 and nearby). However, that bread which is kneaded with milk and contains no water at all, only actual milk, and the taste of the milk is clearly noticeable in it—all agree that it has the status of snack-bread, and one does not recite *HaMotzi* or the three blessings over it, but only <term>Mezonot</term> <note>the blessing for grain-based snacks: "Who creates varieties of nourishment"</note> (when eating it outside of a meal), unless he eats a quantity that people usually establish as a meal. This certainly applies to those pastries we are accustomed to making for **Purim** <note>the Jewish festival of lots</note> called *Purim-Kreplach*, where the dough is kneaded with honey and various spices and filled with sweets; their blessing follows the law of snack-bread in all their rulings and regulations according to everyone.

**3.** The *Tur* <note>the Arba'ah Turim, a foundational code of Jewish law</note> wrote in the aforementioned section: **Rolls** (meaning small, thin breads) whose batter is thick (meaning when they were mixed with water and flour they were made thick) are considered complete bread, and one recites *HaMotzi* and Grace After Meals over them. But if one mixed them with water or fried them in oil (meaning they were not baked in an oven) but they still have the "form of bread" (meaning after boiling or frying they did not dissolve completely and it is recognizable that it was bread), the *Tur* writes in the aforementioned place that some say one recites *HaMotzi* and the three blessings, but he brings other authorities there who say one recites only *Mezonot*. Even if the batter was thick and it has the appearance of bread, since it was boiled in water or fried in honey, one does not recite *HaMotzi* according to those authorities. This applies even if the dough was obligated in the <term>Challah</term> <note>the requirement to set aside a portion of dough for the Priest</note> gift, for the blessing of *HaMotzi* is not like the law of Challah. Challah follows the kneading of the dough, but the blessing of *HaMotzi* follows the time of baking. The *Shulchan Aruch* adds that a "God-fearing person" should only eat them by first blessing over other [actual] bread. My teacher <note>original: מורי' עז</note> wrote: "All this refers only to that which has the appearance of baking...". After boiling or frying, if it has the form of bread [it is debated], but if it does not have the form of bread—such as *Lokshen* <note>noodles</note> as they are called in German, or *Rimzlech*—everyone agrees one does not recite *HaMotzi* or the three blessings because it is not called bread. However, *Pshuda* <note>pastry or pie</note> and *Kreplach* <note>filled dumplings</note> are considered to have the form of bread, and one should not eat them unless they are within a meal [after] other bread. Thus far his words.

<margin>
[Regarding] the difference: And if you say, according to the truth of what they wrote, these salted and... their batter is soft and they are thin. Why? Since the wafers made in [the region of] Neubrunn are very thin and light, they therefore lose the status of bread and one never blesses over them... The *Mordechai* <note>13th-century German scholar</note> at the beginning of the chapter "All the Hand-Flour" regarding rolls... he recites *HaMotzi*... Rabbeinu Yerucham wrote... it is possible to establish a meal... thus it is for rolls... one must distinguish and say... they are different than the *Wafllotk* mentioned above...
</margin>
<margin>
Afterward, the thinness is not exempt.
</margin>

The *Tur* further wrote in Section 168: Those whose batter is soft, meaning very [liquid], one recites *Mezonot* over them, but if one establishes a meal on them, one recites *HaMotzi* and the three blessings. And if one eats them within a meal for a purpose other than the meal, they require a blessing before them but not after them. Thus far his words.

It seems to me that I have not seen in these provinces dough whose batter is as soft as the pastries our women make, adding flour to them. Even that dough from which they make thin wafers fried in oil called *Hoiz-Blasen* <note>literally "house-bubbles," likely a very light, crispy fried pastry</note> in German—even so, its kneading is thick, it is just rolled out [thinly]. However, I have heard that some women in the **province of Russia** sometimes make dough that is very soft and thin; they put flour and water in a pot or bowl and mix the flour and water together with a spoon. Their way is to pour that dough with a spoon onto a wide baking tool so it does not spill out, and they are baked in the oven without any kneading or rolling at all, for it is impossible to knead or roll that dough by hand or with a rolling pin because it is very soft like porridge, or even more so, for it has much water and pours like water onto the leaves they are baked on in the oven. They call these wafers *Nizhen* in the Russian language because they are baked on leaves <note>original: עלין</note>. Regarding this dough and its like, the *Tur* wrote: "And those whose batter is soft... one recites *Mezonot*... and if he establishes a meal, he recites *HaMotzi*." One should not say that the "soft batter and thin" items the *Tur* wrote about also include those cakes made in the city of **Prague** from fine flour where the batter is also very soft; it flows from a spoon out of the vessel and one pours it into an iron mold called a *Porben*. There is another iron above it like it, and the dough is poured between the two irons, and when it is pressed together with the iron like a pair of tongs called a *Zwang*, the wafer is inside and is baked immediately on the iron which is very hot. There are shapes and images on those wafers called *Nigort* in German, in the form and likeness of... and the wafer is inside. These wafers are called *Waflotke* <note>waffles</note> in the language of their mouths. These have no status of bread at all because they are spread very thin. Even if one establishes his meal on them, he only recites *Mezonot*. This is similar to the *Tarita* mentioned by the *Tur* in the aforementioned section: "But *Tarita* which has a soft batter, where one takes flour and water and mixes them and pours it on the stove and it spreads and bakes—it has no status of bread and one recites *Mezonot*." The *Beit Yosef* explained his words to mean that even establishing a meal does not help [to make it bread]. In my opinion, these thin *Waflotke* mentioned in the books, made with the two irons, are the very wafers Rabbeinu Yonah mentioned in the chapter "How does one bless" regarding "Ground *Tarita*." He said there that one blesses *Mezonot*, and if one establishes a meal on them, one recites *HaMotzi*. [However], he wrote: "Rabbi Yochanan said: Specifically... for those very thin wafers made with two irons, establishing a meal on them is not considered 'establishing,' and one only blesses *Mezonot*, for a 'meal' is never established on this." Thus far his words. The reason the *Tur* did not explicitly write this law as Rabbeinu Yonah did in the name of Rabbi Yochanan is that he relied on the law of *Tarita* written in the aforementioned section, following the language of the Talmud.

The *Shibbolei HaLeket* <note>13th-century Italian halakhic work</note> wrote: "Regarding *Kuba DeAr'a* <note>Aramaic: bread of the ground</note>: this is when they make a hollow in the stove and put water and flour in it, mixing and baking rolls there. These are the ones with soft and very thin batter mentioned above in Section 3 in the name of the *Tur*." Regarding snack-bread: if one established a meal on [actual] bread, and at the end they brought him these for dessert—meaning he ate them for a reason other than the meal—one blesses *Mezonot* over them, like *Pshuda*, even though it is within the meal. They require a blessing before them but not after them, for the Grace After Meals exempts them. Thus far his words. From the sum of the things explained in this principle, you learn that if snack-bread filled with fruit or sweets comes during the meal—such as those we usually make for Purim called *Purim-Kreplach*, or if sweets called *Lekach* <note>honey cake</note> come during the meal, or if those rolls with soft and very thin batter mentioned in the *Tur* come during the meal (which are those baked in the oven on leaves... and are called *Nalisniki* <note>crepes/blintzes</note> in the Russian language), or if those very thin wafers made with two irons called *Waflotke* come—all of these and their like, if one eats them during the meal, require a blessing before them. But other types of dough foods that come during the meal, other than these four types mentioned here—even those thin cakes called *Hoiz-Blasen* which are very thin and fried in oil or other fats—one does not bless over them.
