<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Gate of the Letters," specifically the laws of blessings on various types of bread and pastries, expanding on the definitions of snacks versus meal-anchoring bread.</meta>

# Gate of the Letters

Fruit juices or spices are not clearly recognized in the dough except during a meal—that is, when one has first recited the blessing "Who brings forth" <note>original: המוציא - *Hamotzi*, the blessing over bread</note> over actual bread. (Unless one eats an amount of it that others usually consider a full meal, or if he eats it even outside of a meal, he must bless "Who brings forth" and the three blessings of Grace After Meals, similar to the "pocket-bread" mentioned above). One should also not eat those cakes called *Schmalzkuchen* <note>original: שמל"ץ קוכ"ן - Yiddish/German: fat-kneaded cakes</note>, where fat was mixed into the kneading and the taste of the fat is recognizable in the dough, except during a meal (unless he eats the amount others set for a meal, like the "pocket-bread" above). This means he first blessed "Who brings forth" over actual bread and then eats these aforementioned items as he pleases, whether a little or a lot. (A similar compromise was written by the *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo’s commentary on the Tur, the foundation of the Shulchan Aruch</note> in Section 168 regarding the law of rolls that were boiled in water or fried in oil but still have the "form of bread"; this will be discussed further in that section). However, bread that is kneaded with milk and contains no water at all—only actual milk—and the taste of the milk is clearly recognizable, is considered "bread brought as a snack" <note>term: <term>Pat HaBa'ah BeKisnin</term> — dough that is either filled with sweets, kneaded with fruit juice/fat, or baked into a hard cracker</note> according to the *Beit Yosef*. One does not bless "Who brings forth" or the three blessings of Grace After Meals, but only "Creator of types of sustenance" <note>original: במ"מ - *Borei Minei Mezonot*</note> (when eating them outside of a meal), unless one eats the amount people usually set for a meal. This applies even more so to those "pocket-pastries" we are accustomed to making on Purim called *Prymkeplekh* <note>original: פרימ"קלע"פליך - likely a regional variation of filled dumplings or Hamentashen</note>, where the dough is kneaded with honey and cumin spices and filled with preserves; these have the status of "bread brought as a snack" in all their laws and rulings according to everyone.

**3.** The *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, author of the primary code of Jewish law used in the Middle Ages</note> wrote in the aforementioned section: "Regarding rolls (meaning small, thin breads, etc.) whose batter is thick (meaning when mixed with water and flour the dough is thick), they are actual bread, and one blesses 'Who brings forth' and Grace After Meals. But if one boiled them in water or fried them in oil (meaning they were not baked in an oven) and they still have the 'form of bread' (after the boiling and frying, meaning they did not dissolve completely but are still recognizable as bread)," the *Tur* wrote that one blesses "Who brings forth" and Grace After Meals. However, in the *Agudah* <note>A 14th-century halakhic work</note>, some authorities are cited who say one only blesses "Sustenance" even if the batter was thick, because as long as it is boiled in water or fried in honey, it lacks the status of bread according to those authorities. Even if it has the "form of bread" regarding the law of *Challah* <note>the requirement to set aside a portion of dough for the Priest</note>, it is not the same as the blessing of "Who brings forth," because for *Challah* we look at the kneading of the dough, but for the blessing of "Who brings forth" we look at the time of baking. The *Shulchan Aruch* concludes that a God-fearing person should not eat them unless they first bless over other bread. My teacher and uncle wrote: "All this only refers to where there is the 'form of bread' after baking (and for the one who says the word 'baking' is a scribal error, it should say: after boiling or frying). But if there is no form of bread, such as *Lakshin* <note>original: לאקש"ין - noodles</note> which are called *Biyya* and *Rimzlich* <note>original: ורימז"ליך - likely fried fritters or pancakes</note>, everyone agrees one does not bless 'Who brings forth' but only the three-fold blessing <note>The shortened grace after meals for grain products</note> because it is not called bread. However, *Pashtida* and *Kreplach* <note>original: וקרעפליך - dough pockets filled with meat or cheese</note> are considered to have the 'form of bread,' and one should not eat them unless he blessed over other bread first."

**The *Tur*** also wrote in the aforementioned book: "And those whose batter is thin (meaning the other type), one blesses 'Sustenance' over them. But if one established his meal on them, one blesses 'Who brings forth' and Grace After Meals. And if one ate them during a meal but not as part of the meal, they require a blessing before them but not after them."

**And it seems** to me that I have not seen in these lands dough with a thin batter, for all the doughs our women make are thick and hard. Even that dough from which they make thin wafers and fry them in oil, called in the common language *Choyn-Blasen* <note>original: חו"יין בלאזן - likely 'Hohlblasen,' hollow fried pastries</note>, even so, the kneading is thick; it is only rolled out very thin afterward. However, I have heard that some women in the lands of Russia sometimes make a very thin and soft batter—meaning they put flour and water in a pot or bowl and mix them together. Their custom is to pour that dough onto wide vegetable leaves so it does not spill out, and they are baked in the oven without any kneading or rolling at all, for it is impossible to knead or roll that dough by hand or with a rolling pin because it is very soft like porridge, or even more so, for it has much water. It is poured like water onto the leaves they are baked on in the oven. They are called wafers in the Russian language, *Panatshni* <note>original: פאנאטשני' - likely from 'ponyat,' related to leaves or pans</note>, named for the leaves they are baked on. Regarding this dough and similar types, the *Tur* wrote: "And those whose batter is soft and very thin, one blesses 'Sustenance,' and if he established a meal on it, he blesses 'Who brings forth' and Grace After Meals." One should not say that the "thin and soft batter" the *Tur* wrote about refers also to those cakes made in the city of Prague from fine flour, whose batter is also very soft. One takes a spoonful of that batter and pours it into an iron mold called a *Poiyben*, and there is another iron like it on top. The dough is poured between the two irons, and when he presses the irons together, various shapes are formed between them. That wafer is inside and is baked immediately by the iron which was very hot, and those wafers come out with shapes and images called in the common language *Niazorit* <note>original: ניאזורי"ט - likely referring to figured or decorative designs</note>, like the image and likeness engraved in the iron. These wafers are called in the common language *Waffelstoch* <note>original: וואפלשטו"כ - Waffles/Waffle-wafers</note>. These do not have the law of bread at all, since they are spread so very thin. Even if one established a meal on them, he only blesses "Sustenance." This is similar to the *Tritta* <note>A thin, poured batter pancake</note> mentioned by the *Tur* in the aforementioned section: "But *Tritta* whose batter is soft—where one mixes flour and water and pours them onto the stove and it spreads and bakes—has no law of bread, and one blesses 'Sustenance'." The *Beit Yosef* explained his words to mean that even establishing a meal does not help for them. In my opinion, these *Waffelstoch* wafers I mentioned, made with iron plates, are the *Niazorit* themselves mentioned by Rabbeinu Jonah. Regarding the *Tritta* of the earth, he said one blesses "Sustenance," but if he established a meal, he blesses "Who brings forth" and Grace After Meals. He wrote: "Rabbi Isaac the Elder said that a wafer brought in these [molds] and similar things, establishing a meal is effective. But regarding these thin wafers made between two irons, establishing a meal is not considered a meal, and one only blesses 'Sustenance,' for one never truly 'establishes a meal' on such a thing." The *Tur* did not write this law regarding the two irons explicitly, as Rabbeinu Jonah did in the name of the Elder, because he relied on the law of *Tritta* which he wrote at the end of the section, following the language of the Talmud.

The *Shivilei HaLeket* <note>A 13th-century halakhic work by Rabbi Zedekiah ben Abraham Anav</note> wrote: "Regarding *Kuba de-Arka*, this means they make a hole in the stove and put water and flour in it, mixing it and baking rolls there. These are the ones with the soft batter and very thin size mentioned above in Section 3 in the name of the *Tur*." If one established a meal on bread, and at the end they brought him these as a dessert—meaning he ate them not as part of the meal—one blesses "Sustenance" over them. They are like fruit brought during a meal; they require a blessing before them but not after them, as the Grace After Meals for the bread covers them. From all the things explained in this principle, you learn that if "pocket-bread" filled with fruit or preserves comes during the meal—such as those usually made on Purim called *Poiy-Kreplach*—or if sweets called *Lechakzin* <note>original: לעק"זן - likely Lekach/Honey cake</note> come during the meal, or if those rolls with soft and very thin batter mentioned in the *Tur* (baked on leaves, called in Russian *Panatshni*) come during the meal, or if those very thin wafers made between two irons called *Waffelstoch* come during the meal—all these and their like are not "bread" when eaten during the meal and require a blessing before them. But other types of dough foods brought during the meal, besides these four types mentioned here—and even those thin cakes called *Choyn-Blasen* which are even thinner wafers fried in oil or other liquids—one does not bless over them...

<column-break/>

...was not little and they are nullified by their minority. Everyone agrees they have the status of "pocket-bread." The practical difference is if all the taste in the dough comes from honey or other liquids and there is no water at all, then according to the first opinion—that is, the "pocket-bread" mentioned above—it is not bread. But if he mixed in a little honey or other liquids, and the water in the dough is the majority, the *Mahari* <note>Rabbi Israel Isserlein</note> holds that this is called "bread brought as a snack," but the *Maharshal* <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria</note> holds that this is considered actual, complete bread since the water in the dough is the majority. Even though he also put in other liquids, since they are the minority, they are nullified by the water, and the dough has the law of actual bread for all matters. This is the conclusion in the *Knesset HaGedolah*.

# Face and Back
One should learn from here the law regarding those pieces of bread that are cooked with beets <note>original: תחלים - tachlim; likely referring to a vegetable pottage</note>, which are called in the German language *Pannin* <note>original: פענ"ין; likely related to "Pfanne" (pan) or bread-dumplings</note>, and are afterwards soaked in beer. One should recite the <term>HaMotzi</term> <note>the blessing over bread</note> and the three blessings of the <term>Grace After Meals</term> over them if there is a piece the size of a <term>k’zayit</term> <note>the volume of an olive, approx. 1 ounce</note>—even if the beer becomes white because of that bread and even if the bread loses its "bread-like appearance" <note>original: תוריתא דנחמא - torita de-nahma; the visual status of bread</note> due to the soaking. Even so, we recite *HaMotzi* over it, provided that there is a full *k’zayit* in a single piece without needing to combine it with other pieces. However, if there is not a full *k’zayit* in a single piece—even if there is a *k’zayit* total by combining small slices—and it has also lost its bread-like appearance, one only recites the blessing "Who creates varieties of sustenance" <note>original: במ"מ - Borei Minei Mezonot</note>. This is because it has two defects: the loss of its form and the lack of a *k’zayit* volume.

### General Rule 3: Regarding the laws of blessings for the five species of grain, rice, and millet, and the dessert of a meal made from them as a cooked dish; containing 20 sections:

<margin>1</margin> The *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher's 14th-century code of law</note> wrote in section 208: Regarding the five species of grain <note>wheat, barley, spelt, oats, and rye</note> from which a cooked dish was made, such as a pot-dish or porridge <note>original: דייסא - daisa</note>—even if one mixed into them honey and many other ingredients in greater quantity than the grain—one recites over them the blessing "Who creates varieties of sustenance" <note>Mezonot</note> and afterwards a single blessing summarizing the three <note>original: מעין ג' - Me'ein Shalosh, specifically the 'Al HaMichyah' prayer</note> (see General Rule 12, section 1). However, if one only added the grain to the dish to thicken or bind it, such as in pancakes <note>original: פאניק"וקן - Panikuken</note> or *Maharni* <note>a type of flour-thickened dish</note>, the grain is nullified by the dish; the dish is considered the primary ingredient, and one blesses over the primary ingredient, which exempts the secondary ingredient (the grain). These rules apply to a dish where the grains were mashed or crushed during cooking, like porridge. But if one eats them as whole grains <note>original: כעיני"ל - ke-einil; whole kernels</note>, whether they are wheat or husked grains, they are not considered significant enough to warrant a [sustenance] blessing; rather, one recites "Who creates the fruit of the ground" <note>HaAdama</note>, unless they are the main part of the meal. The significance of the five species of grain is found when they are baked into bread or made into a dish that nourishes and sustains a person. In those cases, they establish a blessing for themselves (<term>Al HaMichyah</term> or <term>Mezonot</term>). If they are cooked whole, they are treated like any other fruit of the ground. Regarding the final blessing, the *Tosafot* <note>medieval commentators on the Talmud</note> were in doubt whether it should be "Creator of many souls" <note>Borei Nefashot</note> or the "Summary of Three." Therefore, they wrote that one should be careful not to eat raw or cooked whole wheat kernels except within a bread meal. If a person is in doubt about the first blessing, they should recite "By whose word all things exist" <note>Shehakol</note>, for that covers everything; but for the final blessing, one must only say what was specifically enacted. Thus far are the words of the *Tur*. Know that the five grains the *Tur* mentions are: wheat, barley, spelt, oats, and rye. Included in barley is what is called *Gortz* <note>barley groats</note>; oats are what is called *Groits* <note>grits</note>. One must be careful with those *Grupitz* <note>pearl barley</note> made from barley and *Mertz* made from oats, that they should only be eaten during a meal when the kernels are whole, for the reason the *Tosafot* wrote regarding wheat.

<margin>2</margin> The *Tur* also wrote in the same place: For a dish of rice, one first blesses "Who creates varieties of sustenance" <note>Mezonot</note> because it is nourishing, and afterwards "Creator of many souls" <note>Borei Nefashot</note> (see General Rule 12, section 1 for the text of the blessing). This applies when it was cooked until it was well-mashed like porridge. But if it is whole, whether raw or boiled, and the grains are intact, one blesses "Who creates the fruit of the ground" <note>HaAdama</note>. If one mixed rice into another dish and the other dish is the majority, one recites the blessing of the other dish, as rice is not important enough to define the dish if it is not one of the five [primary] grains.

<margin>General Rule</margin> Anything that requires the blessing "sustenance" <note>Mezonot</note> at the beginning requires the "Summary of Three" <note>Al HaMichyah</note> at the end, provided one ate a *k’zayit*, except for rice. Even though one says "sustenance" for rice at the start, one says "Creator of many souls" at the end. A dish of millet <note>original: דוחן - dochan</note> and other legumes is not considered [primary] food; one recites "By whose word all things exist" <note>Shehakol</note> if they are mashed, and "Creator of many souls" afterwards. So it is written in the *Shulchan Aruch*.

**One who makes** a dish from legumes called *Arveiz* <note>peas</note> or split peas, blesses "Who creates the fruit of the ground." If they are very mashed, such as what is called *Duki Arveiz* <note>pea soup/puree</note>, one should bless "By whose word all things exist." We can learn this from what my master and teacher wrote in his *Shulchan Aruch* (see General Rule 5, section 8). Rice is what is called in German *Reizo* <note>Reis</note> and millet is what is called *Reiz* and *Dochan*. There is a dispute in the commentary: some say rice is *Mil* <note>millet</note> and millet is *Panni* <note>panic-grass/millet</note>, while the *Tosafot* wrote that rice is *Rizo*. Because of this confusion, it is best for every person to only eat them during a bread meal after the *HaMotzi* blessing. In that case, they require no blessing at all according to all opinions. This stringency only applies if they were well-mashed in a dish; but if they were not mashed and the grains remain whole, whether rice or millet, one may eat them outside a meal and bless "Fruit of the Ground" at the start and "Creator of many souls" at the end. — Jacob Levi.

**And if** a person needs to eat rice or millet outside of a meal, it seems to me they should bless "By whose word all things exist" <note>Shehakol</note> out of doubt, as the authorities have ruled in many places that wherever there is a doubt about a blessing, one says *Shehakol*, for that covers everything. This logic is also written in the *Terumat HaDeshen*, section 29.

---

### General Rule 4: Regarding the laws of blessings over pleasures during a meal, after a meal, and after Grace After Meals; and one who eats fruit in a friend's house or his own house one after another; containing 7 sections:

<margin>1</margin> We learn in the chapter "How do we Bless" <note>Berakhot 41b</note>: Rav Pappa said the law is that things brought during a meal that are part of the meal <note>original: מחמת הסעודה - machmat ha-se'udah; e.g., bread-staples</note> do not require a blessing before or after. Things brought during a meal that are *not* part of the meal require a blessing before but not after. After the meal <note>but before Grace after Meals</note>, they require a blessing both before and after. There are many interpretations of this teaching. It seems to me that the clearest is the explanation of Rabbenu Yonah, who wrote in the name of Rabbi Yitzhak HeChazzan: Things that come because of the meal—such as meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, porridge, and cheese—which are not usually eaten except at mealtime, are considered part of the essence of the meal. Since they are satiating and one’s intent from the start was to be satiated by them, even if one eats them without bread, one does not bless over them at all, for they are included with the bread itself. The *HaMotzi* said at the start and the *Grace After Meals* said at the end exempt them. This is the language of the *Riaz* in his commentary on the *Alfasi*: Things that come because of the meal, like meat and fish, which people use to eat with their bread, do not require a blessing even if they weren't specifically in mind at the start.

But things that do *not* come because of the meal—meaning things eaten all day even outside of meal times, like figs, grapes, and all other fruits—if they are brought during the meal and eaten without bread, they are not part of the essence of the meal. They require a blessing before eating because the *HaMotzi* does not cover them. However, they do not require a blessing after eating, because one will eventually recite the *Grace After Meals*, which covers everything one ate. "After the meal" refers to the time when people have finished eating and are no longer occupied with the main food—specifically after they have "removed their hands" from the bread but before reciting *Grace After Meals*. Anything brought then, whether part of the meal or not, requires a blessing both before and after. The bread blessings only exempt what is eaten during the core of the meal. This is the general explanation of the *Chayei Adam* in the name of Rabbi Yochanan of the *Tosafot*. This same explanation was written by the *Tur* regarding Rav Pappa’s statement in section 177, and the *Kol Bo* and *Abudarham* also bring it.

**From the words** of all of them: one who eats fruit during a meal without bread should bless over them. This means someone who established his meal on things that come because of the meal, and then they brought...

# The Gate of Letters

He did not establish a formal meal upon them. For if the law dealt specifically with one who established a formal meal, but if he did not establish a formal meal he would recite the blessing for "varieties of sustenance" <note>original: במ"מ - Borei Minei Mezonot</note>, then the author should have specified this. Behold, he explained and wrote generally that one recites "Who brings forth bread from the earth" <note>original: המוציא - HaMotzi</note> over them, implying that in any case one recites the blessing for bread, even if he did not establish a formal meal upon them. And as long as this does not contradict what I wrote in this general rule, Section 1, in the name of the *Tur* <note>a foundational 14th-century legal code</note> regarding "bread that comes in pouches" <note>original: פת הבאה בכיסנין - Pat HaBa'ah BeKisnin; often referring to pastries, crackers, or filled doughs</note> which are filled with sugar, almonds, and nuts—where one recites the blessing for sustenance if he did not establish a formal meal—we can clearly distinguish between a *pasty* <note>original: פוליטא - polita; likely a local term for a savory turnover</note> made with meat, fish, or cheese, and a *pasty* made with sugar, almonds, and nuts. For regarding the savory one, we judge that since meat, fish, or cheese are things that "accompany the bread" <note>original: מלפתין בהן את הפת - melafetin; items eaten to flavor the bread</note> and usually come during the main meal, they do not require a separate blessing before or after them when they appear during a meal. The reason is that they themselves are nourishment and do not come as a dessert but to satisfy hunger. Therefore, the blessing for bread recited at the start and the Grace After Meals recited at the end exempts them, as I will explain later in Rule 4, Section 1, with God's help. If so, it is proper to explain that when they are filled with these savory items—which are called *pashtida* <note>original: פשטיר"א - meat pie/pasty</note>—one should recite the blessing for bread over them, as they are intended for a fixed meal.

However, when the dough-pockets are made with sugar, almonds, nuts, and similar things that do not "accompany the bread," since they require their own blessing when eaten during a meal—as they are eaten for dessert and personal pleasure rather than to satisfy hunger—it is proper for this reason that even when they are filled within dough, one should not recite the blessing for bread over them unless a full meal is established. This seems correct to me from logical reasoning. We can learn this logic from what the "R"I" <note>Rabbi Isaac of Dampierre, a 12th-century Tosafist</note> wrote regarding the "Second Meal," which was quoted in the *Beit Yosef* <note>commentary by Joseph Karo</note> in Section 291: "Even if we said that one fulfills the requirement for the three Sabbath meals with appetizers <note>original: מיני תרגימא - minei targima</note>, one does not fulfill it with fruit." The *Tosafot* <note>medieval commentaries on the Talmud</note> explained there that "appetizers" are like meat and fish and similar items that accompany bread. The *Shulchan Aruch* wrote similarly regarding the laws of the Sabbath meal: "Some say one can fulfill the requirement with things that accompany bread, like meat and fish, but not with fruit."

The author of the *Tagnat Ha-Shulchan* <note>likely referring to a specific commentary on the Shulchan Aruch</note> wrote regarding the law that fruit does not require a Sukkah <note>the ritual booth for the holiday of Tabernacles</note>: "Specifically fruit does not require a Sukkah, but meat, fish, cheese, and other things besides fruit do require a Sukkah even though they are not bread. If one completed his meal with appetizers, he has fulfilled his obligation." We see from this that there is a distinction between meat or fish and fruit regarding the three Sabbath meals, the completion of a meal, and the requirement of a Sukkah. Even those who hold that one cannot fulfill the Sabbath meal or the Sukkah requirement with fruit agree that one can do so with meat and fish, and that they require a Sukkah. The reason for all of them is because they are similar to bread in another way: they provide nourishment just like bread, even though they do not satisfy as much as bread. We can likewise distinguish between them in our case. Simply put: meat, fish, cheese, and vegetables are considered essential to the meal. Therefore, when they are filled in a *pashtida* pie, it is proper to recite the blessing for bread and the three blessings of the Grace After Meals, even if one’s primary intention is for the meat or fish filling. This is because the meat, fish, and vegetables do not strip the dough of its status as true bread, as their essence is to accompany bread and they are categorized as bread. After all, the blessing for bread recited over a small piece exempts everything else in the meal even if eaten separately. This is not the case when dough is filled with fruit, because fruit is not essential to the meal. One’s primary intention is for the fruit—meaning, for the dough to be a vessel for that fruit—and therefore it loses its status as true bread, and one does not recite the blessing for bread or the Grace After Meals unless a full meal is established. Even though it is a filled pastry, we always follow the primary ingredient, which exempts the secondary one, as will be discussed at the end of this section. If so, one should really recite the blessing "Who creates the fruit of the tree" over the fruit, and this filled pastry would be covered by the blessing of the fruit inside it. Yet, the law is that we recite the blessing for sustenance <note>Mezonot</note> or the blessing for bread (if a meal is fixed), because it is considered similar to a "cooked grain dish" <note>original: מעשה קדירה - ma'aseh kederah</note> where the five species of grain are always the primary ingredient, and we recite the blessing for sustenance over them even if one mixed many other types into them. So too here, it is considered like a baked good, and we recite the blessing for sustenance or the blessing for bread if a meal is established.

The *Beit Yosef* wrote in the name of the *Tosafot* and the *Mordechai* <note>13th-century German authority</note>: when one puts crumbs into water and the water becomes white because of the crumbs, the crumbs lose their "bread-like status" <gloss>meaning the appearance of bread</gloss>. Rabbi David Mo"itz used to regularly send bread crumbs at night to be eaten in the morning without the blessing for bread and without the Grace After Meals, so as not to be delayed, so that he could strengthen his head and be able to teach the law. This means there was not a single crumb among them the size of an olive <note>term: כזית - k'zayit; a legal volume measurement roughly equal to one ounce</note> in one piece. Even though all together they equaled the volume of an olive, he still did not recite the blessing for bread or the Grace After Meals, but rather the blessing for sustenance and the "Summary of the Three Blessings," because they no longer had the visual status of bread. But if there is a single crumb among them the size of an olive in one piece, one recites the blessing for bread and the full Grace After Meals, even if the bread has lost its visual appearance. This is explained clearly in the *Beit Yosef* where he cites the *Mordechai*: "It appears this applies specifically to crumbs or a slice that does not have the volume of an olive, but a slice that has the volume of an olive does not lose its status." This is simple. When the *Beit Yosef* says "does not have the volume of an olive," he means that no single crumb or slice contains a full *k'zayit* in one place. And when he says "a slice that has the volume of an olive," it seems to me his meaning is that there is a full *k'zayit* in a single slice without needing to combine other slices. The *Mordechai* also wrote: "Similarly, one who soaks his bread in wine does not recite the blessing for bread over it, for it has left the status of bread since it has reddened <note>original: סמוק - samuk; blushed or turned red</note> and is similar to "pocket bread" <note>snacks</note>, so he recites the blessing for sustenance over the bread and the wine." This is the end of the *Beit Yosef*'s quote.

However, this applies only when there is no other crumb there that has the volume of an olive, as mentioned above in the gloss of the *Mordechai*. Note that regarding the word "reddened" (*samuk*) written inside in the name of the *Mordechai*: check most copies of the *Mordechai* and you will find it written "dissolved/mushy" <note>original: ונמוק - namuk</note> instead of "reddened" (*samuk*). But what can I do? The *Beit Yosef* and Rabbi Meir Tiku-sh <note>Maharam Tikochin</note> accepted the primary version as "red wine and reddened."

<margin>And this is the distinction</margin> between the reading of "dissolved" and "reddened": according to the "reddened" reading, the reason we do not recite the blessing for bread over these crumbs is because they changed from their appearance and took on the red color of the wine, making them resemble snack-bread. Therefore, we recite the blessing for sustenance over them. But if the wine were not red, we would recite the blessing for bread over them. However, according to the "dissolved" reading, even if the wine were not red, we would not recite the blessing for bread over them since they have dissolved and turned to mush.

<margin>It appears</margin> that the *Beit Yosef* and the *Maharam* of blessed memory chose the reading "reddened" as primary because if we followed the "dissolved" reading, the *Mordechai* would be talking about soaking bread in white wine. If so, it would be difficult based on what he wrote elsewhere: "One who soaks his bread in white wine is like one who soaks his bread in water." Regarding water, the *Mordechai* wrote that only when the water turns white from the crumbs do we say the status of bread is gone. So too with white wine, we should say the status of bread is gone only if the wine turned the color of the bread because of the crumbs. One cannot argue that the *Mordechai*'s intent was to say "dissolved" is just like "turned white" in water—meaning that since it dissolved, the wine already turned white from the bread and the bread status is gone. For if so, he should have combined the laws and said: "When one puts crumbs in water or wine and the liquid turns white because of the crumbs, the bread status is gone." Furthermore, why say "since it is dissolved it is similar to pocket-bread"? The reason for "dissolved" is simply that the visual status of bread is gone. Why do I need the extra reason of "similar to pocket-bread" if the bread status is already gone? Rather, this certainly proves that the reading of our masters, the authors of the *Shulchan Aruch*, is the correct one. First, the *Mordechai* comes to teach us that when soaking bread in water, we do not say the bread status is gone unless the water turned white from the crumbs. The same applies to white wine—the bread status is only gone if it turns white from the crumbs, as the same logic applies to both. Then he comes to teach us that if one soaks bread in **red** wine, even if the wine did not turn white from the crumbs, the bread still loses its status because it has "reddened" and resembles snack-bread. Even though the word "red" is not in any copy of the *Mordechai*, but only "soaking bread in wine," it is understood from the context that he refers to red wine, as the *Beit Yosef* explained later: "since it has reddened."

<margin>And if you say</margin> that the reason for red wine is because the crumbs changed their appearance and no longer have the form of bread, making them like snack-bread, then even if the pieces were the size of an olive, one should recite the blessing for sustenance and not the blessing for bread! Just as we do for snack-bread. The answer is: if the pieces have the volume of an olive, they are considered significant and their status is not nullified. Even if they lack the "visual appearance of bread," they never leave the category of bread. As the *Ran* <note>Rabbi Nissim of Gerona, 14th century</note> wrote in the chapter "All are Eaten" regarding a bread-mash, and the *Tur* quotes him: even if crumbs were cooked and no longer look like bread, if there is a piece the size of an olive, it is significant, and one recites the blessing for bread and the Grace After Meals. The reason is because they are...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of dietary laws and blessings, moving from grain-based products to the specific rituals surrounding wine, mead, and the consumption of fruits—particularly those cooked in liquids or requiring inspection for ripeness.</meta>

<page-num>93</page-num>
<header>The Gate of Letters 93</header>

The *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, a 14th-century legal authority</note> wrote in Section 170: after one drinks the cup used for the Grace After Meals and recites the "Three-faceted Blessing" <note>original: "ברכה אחת מעין ג'" - an abbreviated form of the Grace After Meals</note> covering all twelve items in Section 1, the blessing over wine is the Three-faceted Blessing. If he intends to drink more, he should not recite the final blessing until the very end, and he should drink a full *revi'it* <note>a liquid measure, approximately 3-4 ounces</note>. This was also written in the *Shulchan Aruch* <note>the "Set Table," the standard code of Jewish Law</note>. The *Tur* explained the reason in the section on Hanukkah regarding ten things said about the vessels used for blessings. Regarding what he said about reciting the Three-faceted Blessing, this applies even if he blessed mead or honey-water—which they call *mead* <note>original: "מי"ד שנ"ב" - likely a phonetic rendering of "Met" or "Mead"</note>—he is obligated to recite the final blessing afterward, which is "Creator of Many Souls" <note>original: "נפשות רבות" - a shorter after-blessing for general foods</note>, provided he drank the mentioned amount. There is no reason to distinguish in this matter between wine and other drinks.

# ## General Rule 5: Regarding the laws of blessings for fruits, wine, and cooked items; and one who eats cooked fruits that have broth, whether he must wash his hands for this; and if many varieties are before him, which of them takes precedence for the blessing; and over which fruit one recites "Who creates the fruit of the tree" or "Who creates the fruit of the earth"; and after the fact, which blessing is valid; and regarding vegetables, legumes, turnips, wine, and cooked items. It contains 13 sections:

<margin>
**Note:**
Regarding wine and legumes in general, according to the *Tur* Section 220, if the fruit is nullified or if the flavor of the fruit is absorbed into the water, the Rashba <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Aderet, 13th-century Spanish scholar</note> wrote that one recites "Through whose word everything came to be" <note>original: "שהכל" - a general blessing</note>. However, the Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note> wrote that if the flavor is distinct, even if it is in water, one recites the blessing of that species. Thus, we see that water mixed with fruit juice follows the status of the fruit. See the "Blessing of the Kneaded" regarding this, for with the blessing over mixtures, the matter depends on reason; since the substance of the fruit is slightly integrated into the water through cooking, the fruit's essence remains, and one recites the blessing of the fruit because the flavor of the fruit entered the water, as mentioned above. But for other things, it is simple that they remain in their original state.
</margin>
<margin>
On Passover, we wash our hands before the dipping of the vegetable for this reason, as written in *Orach Chayim* Section 473. Regarding the blessing for this washing: since there is a dispute among the Great Rabbis as to whether one must recite "Concerning the washing of the hands" when washing to dip food, he wrote that if one does not wash, he should not bless... and one should be scrupulous. It is proper to act this way in any matter where there is a dispute or doubt regarding blessings: one should not bless, for the lack of a blessing does not invalidate the act, and perhaps he might recite a blessing in vain. See later at the end of this part in Rule 7... This was also written in the *Olat Shabbat* at the beginning of the chapter on "Covering the Blood." The *Tur* also wrote this in Section 473 regarding the law of the blessing over the Hallel prayer. The *Shulchan Aruch* likewise ruled in Section 158 and Section 473 that one does not recite a blessing over this washing—neither during the Passover Seder when washing for the dipping of the *Karpas* <note>the spring vegetable</note> in salt water, nor during the rest of the year when washing to dip food in liquid. **2.** The term *Yana*, called in the German language *Pavidl* <note>original: "פאוי"דלא" - fruit butter or jam</note>, which they make from mandarins/tangerines that they call *Weinklitz* <note>original: "וויין"קליץ" - possibly a local dialect term for small citrus</note>: my teacher taught in his *Shulchan Aruch* to recite over it "Through whose word everything came to be" <note>Shehakol</note>. It is not considered fruit juice because the form has completely changed. But if one recited "Who creates the fruit of the tree," he has fulfilled the obligation. This was also the decision of the author of *Terumat HaDeshen* in Section 29. **3.** Over sesame seeds, one recites "Who creates the fruit of the earth." If they are ground up, one recites "Through whose word everything came to be." So wrote the *Beit Yosef* in Section 204 in the name of Abudarham, and he brought it also in Section 202. I do not know why the *Tur* omitted this law, and the *Shulchan Aruch* did not mention it either.
</margin>

**O**ne who eats cooked dried fruits, such as *Plumen* <note>original: "פלו"מן" - plums or prunes</note> and other varieties that have broth, should not eat them without ritual hand washing <note>original: "נטילה" - Netilat Yadayim</note>, for they are "items whose dipping is in liquid" <note>original: "טיבולן במשקין" - food wet with specific liquids requires hand washing in Jewish law</note>. All things whose dipping is in liquid require washing, as they are taught in Tractate *Machshirin* <note>a section of the Mishnah dealing with liquids and ritual purity</note>. One of the primary liquids is water, and this broth from plums or other dried fruits is included in the category of water. One should not challenge my words from what Rabbi Obadiah of Bartenura said in his commentary on the Mishnah... that fruit juices like mulberry juice or pomegranate juice are excluded... for there it deals with liquid that emerges from the fruit itself... whereas in our case, the broth of the plums consists primarily of water, and it is not called "fruit juice" at all. Fruit juice in every context refers to the liquids drawn from the fruit itself, not that which is cooked and boiled in water. This is not called fruit juice, but "broth." Because it is cooked with the fruit and does not have the appearance of water, it does not exit the category of water for that reason.
Therefore, it is proper that a person wash his hands, as one should not eat dried fruits or other things that have broth without ritual hand washing. And since this is the practice in our time, there is proof...

---

**2.** It is written in the *Sefer Hasidim* <note>The "Book of the Pious," a 12th/13th-century ethical-legal work</note> in Section 852: A person who has a single nut in his hand should not recite the blessing "Who creates the fruit of the tree" and then break the nut, lest the kernel be wormy or rotten until it is unfit for eating, resulting in a "blessing said in vain" <note>original: "ברכה לבטלה" - taking God's name for no purpose</note>. It seems to me he specified a nut because if it is spoiled and its smell is bad, it is unfit for anything and is a blessing in vain. This is unlike other fruits; even if they are spoiled or wormy on the inside, the blessing is not in vain because of the outer shell/peel, upon which the blessing takes effect. Therefore, it is better to bless the fruit while it is whole rather than when it is cut, for in all matters of blessings, a whole item is preferable. Jacob Levi <note>perhaps referring to the Maharil</note> added another reason: breaking the nut creates a "pause" <note>original: "הפסק" - a forbidden interruption</note> between the blessing and the eating, similar to how slicing bread is considered a pause between the blessing and the eating according to the opinion of the Tosafot and the Rosh.

**3.** The author of *Tzedah LaDerekh* <note>a 14th-century halakhic work</note> wrote in Treatise 1, Rule 3: If many varieties were before him and their blessings are the same, and none of them are from the "Seven Species" <note>the seven agricultural products praised in the Torah: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, and dates</note>, he should bless over the one he likes best <note>original: "חביב" - the "favorite"</note>. "Favorite" refers to the species that is usually his favorite, even if he desires the second species right now; he must bless over the species that is his favorite most of the time, eat a bit of it, and then eat the second species if he wishes. This is how the *Tur* and *Shulchan Aruch* explained it in Section 140. If there is a species from the Seven Species among them, he should bless over the Seven Species even if the other is his favorite. Whatever appears first in the biblical verse takes precedence: thus dates come before grapes, because dates are the second mention of "land" in the verse (being fourth in the list), while the vine is the third mention of "land" <note>a technical calculation of proximity to the word "Eretz/Land" in Deuteronomy 8:8</note>. Between a specific blessing ("Fruit of the Tree/Earth") and a general blessing ("Through whose word..."), the specific blessing takes precedence because a specific blessing is more significant than a general one. So wrote Abudarham... following the opinion of the Rosh... Thus, if two varieties were brought before him whose blessings are identical and neither is of the Seven Species, such as apples and nuts, or nuts and citrons, he gives precedence to his favorite... as the *Terumat HaDeshen* replied in Section 32: all blessings of enjoyment depend on the "favoriteness" of the pleasure. Even if he only wants to eat it last, since it is more dear to him, he should give it precedence to bless it first, eat a little, then eat the other species, and then return to eat the first fruit. He does not need to bless a second time, for the fruit he ate in between is not an interruption since his intention was always to eat this.

**And if** there is one of the Seven Species among them, such as figs and apples, he gives precedence to the Seven Species even if it is not as much of a favorite as the other, because it is more distinguished since the Land of Israel was praised through them. And if their blessings are not identical, even if there is one of the Seven Species, such as wine and a radish, he may give precedence to whichever he wants...

I will say my own words and what I found written in the book *Midrash Shmuel* in the name of Rabbi M. Almosnino <note>a 16th-century philosopher and rabbi</note>: Who is honored in this year? He who honors his companions. For one who has a species from the Seven Species, the definition of being "honored" that truly applies to him is that he should be the one to recite the blessing first for that...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the order and necessity of blessings over food, specifically focusing on fruits served during a meal and how the blessing over bread (HaMotzi) interacts with them. It builds on the principles of primary and secondary foods established on the previous page.</meta>

<page-num>26</page-num>
<header>The Gate of Letters</header>

If fruits were brought to someone during his meal: if he eats them by themselves without bread, he must recite the blessing over them. However, if he eats the fruit together with bread, there is a doubt in this matter whether he should bless the fruit or not. Therefore, one who wishes to remove himself from doubt should eat a small amount of them first without bread, recite the blessing over them, and then continue eating them either with or without bread. This was explicitly written by the *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, 1269–1343, author of the Arba'ah Turim</note> at the end of the aforementioned section. The *Mordechai* <note>Rabbi Mordechai ben Hillel, a 13th-century German legalist</note> also wrote this in the chapter "How do we bless," citing the words of Rav Pappa <note>A 4th-century Babylonian sage</note>, and it is brought nowadays in Sivan, page 32. Its language is: "A God-fearing person who eats fruits during a meal should eat a little of them first without bread, bless them, and afterward eat them either with or without bread."

**2** Regarding cooked fruits brought during a meal: it appears to me that they also require a blessing before eating them. Since it is not customary for them to come as part of the "main meal" <note>the filling, savory part of the meal</note>, they are considered as items not brought for the sake of the meal, provided one eats a bit of them first without bread as mentioned above. 
**It is written** in the *Terumat HaDeshen* <note>A 15th-century collection of legal responsa</note> in the *Tashbetz* <note>Rabbi Samson ben Tzadok's rulings</note> regarding the laws of the meal: "If one eats apple *mulyot* <note>original: "מולייאת" - filled pastries or turnovers</note> during the meal after reciting the blessing over bread, he does not need to bless the apples inside the *torta* <note>original: "טורט"א" - a tart or pie</note> at all. This is because the bread <note>the pastry crust</note> exempts everything, and these are considered things brought during the meal as part of the meal, and they require no blessing before or after." This is not comparable to plain fruits brought during the meal, which require a blessing because it is not customary to use them as a "dip" or accompaniment to bread. But for this filled pastry, even if one were eating it outside of a meal, he would not need to bless the apples because the flour is the "primary" <note>original: "עיקר" (ikkar) - the most important component of the dish that dictates the blessing</note> ingredient. 
**This is contrary** to what is written there internally—that one should take a bit of the fruit before eating and bless it "Who creates the fruit of the tree"—for that would lead to a trivialization of blessings <note>original: "קולא" (kula) - a leniency or, in this context, a potentially unnecessary blessing</note>. Since the fruit has now become a cooked dish and is subsumed within the filled pastry where the flour is primary, the blessing recited would surely be in vain. If a person wants to be stringent with himself and remove all doubt, he should take a separate fruit, either raw or cooked, bless "Who creates the fruit of the tree" over it, and then eat those filled pastries as he pleases.

**3** Regarding what was written above—that fruits eaten after the meal <note>meaning after the main meal is finished but before the final Grace after Meals</note> require a blessing both before and after: the *Tosafot* <note>Medieval French and German commentators</note> wrote there and in the chapter "Eve of Passover" that this last law is not common among us today. Our custom is not to "withdraw our hands" from the bread at all until after the Grace after Meals; at any time we are eating fruits or anything else before the Grace after Meals, our intention is still to eat more bread.

**4** It was written at the end of the aforementioned section: "However, if after one blessed the bread, a gift was sent to him from another house, such that he was not relying on them and did not have them in mind—even if they are types of relish <note>original: "מבריס" - possibly a corruption of 'legumes' or 'savories'</note> usually brought to accompany bread—it appears he must bless before eating them. This is a case of 'changing one's mind' <note>original: "נמלך" (nimlach)</note> where he establishes a new blessing for it." I found this also in *Sefer HaPardes* <note>A work attributed to the school of Rashi</note>. But he does not need to bless after eating it, as the Grace after Meals exempts it. My teacher <note>likely referring to Rabbi Moses Isserles, the Rema</note> wrote on this in his *Shulchan Aruch*: "I have not seen people being careful about this, and perhaps the reason is that a person’s general intent is for whatever they might bring him during the meal."

**And it appears to me** that even the author of *Sefer HaPardes* only said one must bless over a gift sent during a meal specifically on a weekday, when it is not so common to send portions. But on Sabbaths and Festivals, when it is common for people to send portions to one another, when one blesses at the start, his mind is naturally on everything they might bring him from other houses. Therefore, he does not need to repeat the blessing over portions sent to him on Sabbaths and Festivals, even according to the opinion of the *Pardes*. This is what logic suggests.
**It is proper** for every God-fearing person to remove himself from doubt: when he recites the blessing over the bread, he should have in mind everything they might send him from other houses, whether on a weekday or on Sabbath, and it will be well for him.

**5** The *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo's commentary on the Tur</note> wrote in Section 179 in the name of the *Kol Bo*: "When a person eats at his friend's house and they are accustomed to eating various types of fruit, and they bring them to him one after another, one blessing is enough for all of them. Even if one type was finished before they brought another, since it depends on the host's intent, there is no 'distraction of the mind' <note>original: "היסח הדעת" (hesech hadaat) - a mental break that would require a new blessing</note>." As we say in the Talmud <note>Berachot 42a</note>: "We, the guests of the Exilarch <note>original: "אנן אחנא דרישי גלותן" - referring to the Jewish leader in Babylon</note>, rely on him." One does not need to bless over each individual item. The *Shulchan Aruch* wrote the same.

**6** The *Tur* wrote in Section 216: "One who blessed over fruits before him, and afterward they brought him more of that same kind, he does not need to bless again even though they were not before him when he blessed." The *Beit Yosef* wrote on this: "It appears we do not require it to be of the exact same species; even if it is a different species whose blessing is the same as the first <note>e.g., both are 'fruit of the tree'</note>, it is covered."

**It appears** that the *Tur* is speaking even when one eats in his own home. If so, he holds that it is not necessary to bless again when they bring him more of that kind in his own home (and even if the first kind was finished before the second was brought, as will follow, for if he were concerned, he would have specified that this only applies when eating at a friend's house where we rely on the host, as mentioned in Section 5). But when one eats at home, where he depends on his own intent, it should have been explained that even an Amora <note>a Talmudic sage</note> needs to explain his words clearly, and certainly the *Tur*, whose way is always to explain his words well and clearly and not in riddles. Since he did not specify here that it refers to a friend's house, we learn that he holds one does not need to bless even in one's own house. One should also not interpret the *Tur*'s words here to mean that it only applies if he had no specific intent at the start to eat only what was before him, for it is simple in all the legal authorities that "changing one's mind" constitutes a distraction of the mind, and he would obviously need to bless again.
**Furthermore**, one should not interpret the *Tur* as speaking only when he specifically intended at the start to eat whatever they would bring. 
The *Tur* himself wrote regarding the laws of ritual slaughter <note>Yoreh De'ah 19</note>: "If at the start when he blessed, many animals were before him to slaughter, and afterward they brought him others... anything that was not before him when he blessed, he must bless over it, unless his intent was for whatever they would bring him." If so, he should have explained it here explicitly as he did there. Since he wrote here "he does not need to bless" plainly, and did not specify "only when his intent was on whatever they would bring," it implies he is speaking of all cases. Even if he didn't specifically have in mind everything they would bring, as long as he is just eating normally at home, he doesn't have to bless again when his family or he himself brings more, as long as he hasn't clearly decided to stop eating at the time of the blessing. And if you ask: what is the difference between eating and slaughtering? One can answer: a meal has a "set nature" <note>original: "קבע" (keva)</note>, but slaughtering does not. This means a person establishes a formal setting for eating; he tastes and eats sweets that are pleasant to his mouth. Therefore, regarding eating, it is assumed that whatever is brought to him is included, and he doesn't distract his mind from eating as long as he is reclining at the table. This is unlike slaughtering, which has no set nature; the assumption is that what is not before him is not on his mind. Therefore, he must have specific and clear intent for whatever they will bring him. This very reason was written by the *Tanya* in his notes on the *Tur*, and you will find it if you seek it. Nevertheless, it is good to be careful at the outset to have in mind at the time of the blessing over fruits everything they might bring, whether eating at home or at a friend's house. My teacher wrote this in his *Shulchan Aruch*.
**Besides** this aforementioned reason, there is another good reason to have intent for whatever they bring later: perhaps he will desire to eat another species whose blessing is the same as the first. In that case, the law states that if the first species was more "dear" <note>original: "חביב" (haviv) - preferred or more beloved</note> to him, it exempts the second species from a blessing. But if it is not the preferred one, it does not exempt it. If he did not intend for it at the start, he may find himself in a doubt if he cannot remember which species he prefers more. To avoid this doubt of whether to bless on the second species or not, it is best to intend for everything they will bring. This is simple to understand.

<column-break/>

And the *Hagahot* wrote above in Rule 20, Section 7: We bless over fruits during a meal near its conclusion, for these require a "doorway" <note>an introduction</note> for eating, and since the meal is almost over, it is like they are separate. The *Mordechai* wrote about what they call "Apples" <note>original: "עפ"ל" - phonetic for the German/Yiddish 'Apfel'</note>. According to this, whether it is "Lamala" or "Demutzia" <note>likely local names for specific cooked fruit dishes or pastries</note>, they are all considered as being brought during the meal for the sake of the meal.
But "snack-bread" <note>original: "פת הבאה בכיסנין" (Pas HaBa'ah B'Kisnin) - such as crackers, cakes, or filled pastries</note> during a meal, as mentioned above and on Festivals, unless one establishes a full meal on them, it is called merely "bread of a bite." Sometimes it is used for a set meal. In the Babylonian Talmud, "bread of a bite" during a meal is considered not for the sake of the meal and requires a blessing before, as mentioned in Rule 19, Section 60. I have already written nearby that there are three laws for this: regarding snack-bread throughout the meal, I have established that one blesses on it during the meal... see there.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of food-related blessings, specifically transitioning from the Grace After Meals to the specific order of precedence when multiple types of food—like fruits, wine, and cooked dishes—are served together.</meta>

<sig>24 I</sig>

The *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher</note> wrote in section 170: after one drinks the cup for the Grace After Meals and recites the "One Blessing that Summarizes Three" <note>Hebrew: *Me'ein Shalosh*, a specific prayer recited after wine, grains, or the Seven Species of Israel</note>—this refers to the 12th rule, section 1, regarding the blessing on wine—if he intends to drink more, he should not recite the final blessing until the very end, provided he drinks a full *revi'it* <note>a liquid measure, approximately 3–4 ounces</note>. This is also what the *Shulchan Aruch* <note>the standard Code of Jewish Law</note> says. The reason is explained by the *Tur* in the laws of Chanukah regarding the ten things mentioned in the general rules of blessings. When he says one should recite the "One Blessing that Summarizes Three," this applies to one who blessed over beer or honey-mead, which they call *Meid*. He is obligated to recite the final blessing after it, which is the "Creator of Numerous Souls" <note>Hebrew: *Borei Nefashot*, a short generic after-blessing</note>, if he drank the aforementioned amount. There is no logical reason to distinguish in this matter between wine and other drinks.

---

->**Rule 5: On the laws of blessings for fruits, wine, and cooked items. Also regarding one who eats cooked fruits served in their broth—does he need to**<-
->**wash his hands for this? If many types of food were before him, which takes precedence for the blessing? And over which fruit does one bless**<-
->**"Who creates the fruit of the tree" or "Who creates the fruit of the ground"? Signs to know which is which, as well as greens, legumes, and turnips, whether raw or cooked. Containing 13 sections:**<-

**1** One who eats cooked dried fruits, such as plums <note>original: *pflumen*</note> and other types that have a broth, should not eat them without ritual hand washing <note>Hebrew: *Netilat Yadayim*</note>. This is because they are items "dipped in liquid," and anything dipped in liquid requires hand washing. This is explained in the laws of ritual fitness, chapter 6. One of the primary liquids is water, and the broth of these plums or other dried fruits is categorized as water. One should not challenge my words from what Rabbi Akiva said in the commentary on the Mishnah regarding the verse: "From where do we include water, honey, and oil? The text says 'water.' Just as water is unique in that it has no descriptive name <note>it is just 'water'</note>, so too wine, oil, and milk have no descriptive name." This excludes mulberry juice and pomegranate juice and all other fruit juices that have a descriptive name <note>e.g., we call it "pomegranate juice," not just "juice"</note>. However, that discussion refers to juice that comes *out* of the fruit itself, as it explicitly says there "mulberry juice" and "pomegranate juice," meaning the essence of the fruit. This applies to any liquid extracted from them or squeezed from them—they are not considered primary "liquids" except for the seven specific liquids <note>Wine, honey, oil, milk, dew, blood, water—often remembered by the Hebrew acronym *Yad Shachat Dam*</note>. But in our case of plum broth, the base is water, and it is not considered "fruit juice" at all. Fruit juice everywhere refers to the liquid that flows from the fruit itself, not fruit that was boiled and cooked in water. That is called broth <note>original: *di-mitsch*</note> because it is absorbed with the fruit. Even if it does not look like water, it is not removed from the category of water.

<columns>2</columns>

Therefore, it is proper for a person to be careful in this: one should not eat dried fruits or other things served in broth without ritual hand washing. This is the practice nowadays in our times. We have a proof from Passover, where we wash our hands before the "dipping" <note>the *Karpas* vegetable dipped in salt water</note> for this very reason. This was also written in the *Orach Chaim* in section 473; see there. Regarding the blessing for this washing: since there is a dispute among the great rabbis as to whether one must recite a blessing over it, we hold that for anything "dipped in liquid," [one does not bless]. See the end of this part in Rule 7 of the Ten Rules; look it up there. See there regarding any matter where there is a dispute or doubt concerning blessings: one should not bless, for blessings are not indispensable <note>the meal remains valid without them</note> and one might recite a blessing in vain. See the end of this part in Rule 7 of the Ten Rules. This was also written by the *Asheri* <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, the Rosh</note> at the beginning of the chapter "Covering the Blood." The *Tur* wrote similarly in section 473 regarding the law of the blessing on this. This was also the ruling of the *Shulchan Aruch* in sections 158 and 473: that one does not recite a blessing on this washing, whether during the Passover Seder when washing for the dipping of the *Karpas* in salt water, or during the rest of the year when washing to eat something [dipped] in liquid. **2** Regarding the drink called in the German language *Paur-shlaa* <note>likely a fruit punch or compote bowl</note> which is made from sour cherries <note>original: *weichseln*</note>: my teacher concludes in his *Shulchan Aruch* that one should bless "By Whose word all things exist" <note>Hebrew: *Shehakol*</note> over it. This is because they do not retain their original substance; since they are completely dissolved, even if one blessed "Who creates the fruit of the tree" over them, he has fulfilled the obligation. This was also the decision of the author of *Terumat HaDeshen* in section 29. See Rule 6, section 2. **3** On sesame seeds, one blesses "Who creates the fruit of the ground." If they are ground up, one blesses *Shehakol*. So wrote the *Beit Yosef* in section 204 in the name of *Abudarham*. This law was also brought in section 203, and I do not know why the *Tur* omitted it.

<column-break/>

**Annotation**
And regarding the sections, I should write what the *Tur* says in section 209. My book also explains the reason for my book regarding water. The *Rashba* wrote that one blesses *Shehakol* over it. For this reason, the *Rosh* of blessed memory wrote that they did not wash. In all his reasoning, as mentioned, one blesses over it according to the type it was. Fruit juice, since it has the law of water according to the opinion of the *Rosh*, is not difficult. Regarding the matter of the blessing of enjoyment: if they did not wash, the blessing of enjoyment is void. The reason is that the water is absorbed into the essence of the fruit, so one blesses over them a version of the blessing for the fruit, because the taste of the fruit entered the water properly. Everything depends on whether they retain their original substance.

<columns>1</columns>

**4** It is written in *Sefer Hasidim* <note>The Book of the Pious, 12th–13th century</note> (in section 852): A person who has a nut in his hand should not recite the blessing "Who creates the fruit of the tree" and then break the nut, lest the kernel be wormy or rotten to the point it is inedible. He would then have recited a blessing in vain. It seems to me that this only applies to a nut, for if it is foul, nothing is fit for anything and it is a blessing in vain. This is unlike other fruit; even if it is foul or wormy inside, he did not bless in vain because of its outer peel, upon which the blessing takes effect. Similarly, for a good fruit, it is better to bless on the fruit while it is whole rather than sliced, for in all matters of blessings, a whole item is preferred. And I will add another reason of my own: breaking the nut constitutes an "interruption" <note>Hebrew: *hefsek*</note> before eating. This is similar to slicing bread, which is considered an interruption if done between the blessing of *HaMotzi* and the eating, according to the opinion of the *Tosafot* and the *Rosh*.

**5** The author of *Tzedah LaDerech* wrote in Article 1, Rule 6: If many types of food were before him and their blessings are identical, but none of them are from the Seven Species <note>the seven agricultural products of Israel listed in the Bible: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, and dates</note>, he should bless over the "beloved" one. "Beloved" refers to the type that is usually his favorite, even if he currently desires the other type. He must bless over the type he likes most often, eat a little of it, and then eat the second type if he wishes. (So the *Tur* and *Shulchan Aruch* explained in section 170). However, if one of them is from the Seven Species, he blesses over the Seven Species even if the other is more beloved to him. Whichever appears first in the biblical verse <note>Deuteronomy 8:8</note> takes precedence for the blessing. Dates take precedence over olives because dates are the second mention of "land" in the verse, and grapes are the third after the first "land." Regarding the hierarchy of blessings: "Fruit of the Tree" comes before "Fruit of the Ground," and "Fruit of the Ground" comes before *Shehakol*, because a specific blessing is more significant than a general one. So wrote *Abudarham* in the laws of blessings. See section five. They follow the opinion of the *Rosh* in the chapter "How do we bless," which the *Tur* brought in section 201. Thus, according to them and the *Rosh*, if two types whose blessings are identical are brought before him, and neither is of the Seven Species—such as apples and nuts, or nuts and citron—he gives precedence to the "beloved" one. Since the blessing on one exempts its companion, it is a commandment to prioritize the beloved. As the *Terumat HaDeshen* replied in a responsa (section 32): all blessings of enjoyment depend on "belovedness," for it is upon the belovedness of his pleasure that he blesses and praises. Even if he only wants to eat it last, since it is more beloved to him, he should prioritize it so that he blesses over it first, eats a little, and then eats the other type, then returns and eats the first fruit he started. He does not need to bless a second time, for the fact that he ate the other fruit in between is not an interruption since his intent was to eat this.

**6** If one of them is from the Seven Species—such as figs and apples—the Seven Species takes precedence, even if it is not as beloved as the other fruit, because it is more significant since the Land of Israel was praised with it. If their blessings are not identical, even if one is from the Seven Species—such as an olive <note>Tree</note> and a radish <note>Ground</note>—he may prioritize whichever he wishes, even if the other is more beloved to him. He can bless over the second one because he must bless over the second anyway after eating the first. In this case, there is no inherent superiority for the "beloved" or the "significant." The Seven Species are called significant because the Land of Israel was praised with them.

<columns>2</columns>

**This is from me:** I say what I found written in the book *Midrash Shmuel* in the name of Rabbi Moshe Almosnino <note>16th-century philosopher and rabbi</note> of blessed memory: regarding what our Sages said about "honoring," he who honors his fellow is truly honored. There is a greatness in the one who honors others; he is the one who is justified in being honored.

<column-break/>

**Annotation**
As mentioned above, all are equal except for water, as mentioned soon after: whichever comes first in the verse comes first in the blessing.
