<meta>This page continues the discussion on the laws of blessings over food, specifically focusing on whether fruits and pastries served during a meal require their own individual blessings or are covered by the initial blessing over the bread.</meta>

# The Gate of Letters

...and they brought him fruits during his meal. If he eats them first without bread, he must recite a blessing over them. However, if he eats the fruit first with bread, there are different opinions on this—whether he should bless over the fruit or not. Therefore, one who wishes to remove himself from doubt should eat a small amount of them first without bread and recite the blessing over them, and afterward, he may eat them either with bread or without bread. This was stated explicitly by the *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, author of the *Arba’ah Turim*</note> at the end of the aforementioned section. Likewise, the *Mordechai* <note>Rabbi Mordechai ben Hillel</note> wrote in the chapter "How does one bless?" regarding the statement of Rav Pappa <note>A 4th-century Babylonian scholar</note> when they brought figs in the month of Sivan <note>Late spring/early summer</note> and so on: "A God-fearing person who eats fruits during a meal should eat a small amount of them first without bread and bless over them, and afterward eat them either with bread or without bread," end of quote.

**2** Regarding cooked fruits brought during a meal, it seems to me that they also require a blessing before eating them. Since it is not customary for them to be part of the main meal, they are considered as things brought not because of the meal itself. However, he should eat a little of them first without bread, as mentioned above.

**It was written** in a gloss: I wrote in the laws of the meal <note>Hebrew: *Hilkhot Se'udah*</note> as follows: If one eats apple-filled pastries <note>Hebrew: *Molyat*, likely related to 'mille-feuille' or a similar filled dumpling/pastry</note> during the meal after reciting the *HaMotzi* blessing <note>The blessing over bread</note>, he does not need to bless at all over the apples inside the tart <note>Original: *Torta*</note>. This is because the bread exempts everything, as these are items brought during the meal for the sake of the meal, and they do not require a blessing before or after. This is not similar to fruits brought during a meal, over which we bless because it is not customary to use them as a side dish for bread. However, with these filled pastries, even if he were eating them outside of a meal, he would not need to bless over the apples because the flour is the primary component <note>term: *Ikkar* — the legal principle that one blesses only over the main ingredient of a dish</note>, end of quote.

<margin>
Section 150.
And so he wrote above in Rule 20, Section 3 and Section 4, that we bless over "pocket bread" <note>term: *Pat Kisnin* — a category of bread-like snacks, such as crackers or pastries, whose blessing status is debated</note> during a meal. We rely on the *Tur* who wrote that the rule is to give it for "sweetening" and "intention" during the meal. His language is: "to eat it during the meal to draw the heart, like *pach patrin* <note>a type of thin wafer</note> etc." According to this, it applies also to *levavim* <note>heart-shaped cookies?</note>, *romil*, *romis*, and *khalas* <note>regional names for various biscuits or pastries</note> during the meal; for the sake of the meal, they are without fruit. But regarding "pocket bread" written during the meal, it seems to me there is reason to be concerned about establishing a fixed meal on them <note>which would change their blessing status</note>. One only says they are a "doubt." Sometimes they are also used to establish a meal. Therefore, they fall under the category of things brought during a meal not for the sake of the meal, which require a blessing before them, as mentioned above in Rule 8. I have already written nearby in Rule 4 the law of rolls and *khalas* bread during a meal... one blesses over them during the meal... and the bread exempts them like the crackers of the *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo</note>, see there.
</margin>

This is unlike what is written there in the main text, that he should take a little fruit before eating and bless over it "Who creates the fruit of the tree" <note>Hebrew: *Borei Peri Ha'etz*</note> etc. For such stringency leads to a leniency <note>i.e., a potential mistake</note>, since the fruit has now become a cooked dish and is nullified within the filled pastry where the flour is the primary part, as mentioned above. Therefore, the blessing he recited over it would be in vain. If he wants to be stringent with himself and remove all doubt, he should take one fruit, either raw or cooked <note>that is not part of a pastry</note>, bless "Who creates the fruit of the tree," and then eat those filled pastries as he wishes.

**3** Regarding what was written above—that items served after the meal require a blessing both before and after—the *Tosafot* <note>Medieval commentators on the Talmud</note> wrote there in the chapter "The Eve of Passover" <note>Hebrew: *Arvei Pesachim*</note> that this law is not found among us now. Our custom is not to withdraw our hands from the bread at all until after the Grace After Meals <note>Hebrew: *Birkat HaMazon*</note>. Any time we eat fruit or anything else before the Grace After Meals, our intention is to continue eating bread at any time.

**4** The *Beit Yosef* wrote at the end of the aforementioned section: "However, if after he blessed over the bread, they sent him a gift <note>Hebrew: *Mincha*</note> that he was not counting on, and he did not have his mind on gifts—even for things that are customary to use as a side dish for bread—it seems he must bless before them. This is considered a 'change of mind' <note>Hebrew: *Nimlach*</note> which establishes the need for a blessing before it. I found this also in the *Sefer HaPardes* <note>A work attributed to Rashi's school</note>. But for the blessing after it, it is not necessary, as the Grace After Meals exempts them," end of quote. My teacher wrote on this in his *Shulchan Aruch*: "I have not seen people being careful about this. Perhaps the reason is that normally a person's mind is set on whatever they might bring him during the meal," end of quote.

And it seems to me that even the *Sefer HaPardes* only said one must bless over a gift of food during the meal specifically on a weekday, when it is not customary to send such gifts. But on Sabbaths and Festivals, when it is customary for a man to send portions to his neighbor, when he blesses at the start, his mind is presumably set on everything they might bring before him from other houses. Therefore, he does not need to go back and bless over the portions sent to him on Sabbaths and Festivals, even according to the opinion of the *Pardes*. This is what seems correct to me through logical reasoning.

It is proper for every God-fearing person to remove himself from doubt and accustom himself, when reciting the *HaMotzi* blessing, to have his mind also on whatever they might send him from other houses, whether on a weekday or on Sabbath, and it will be good for him.

**5** The *Beit Yosef* wrote in Section 179 in the name of the *Kol Bo*: When a person eats at his friend's house, and they are accustomed to eating various types of fruits, and they bring them to him one after another, one blessing is enough for all of them. Even if he finished one type before they brought the other, since he is dependent on the host's mind, it does not constitute a "distraction of the mind" <note>Hebrew: *Hesech HaDa'at*</note>. As we say in the Talmud <note>Tractate Berakhot</note>: "We rely on the table of the Exilarch," so too here we rely on the host's table, and there is no need to bless over each and every one. The *Shulchan Aruch* wrote the same.

**6** The *Tur* wrote in Section 200: One who blessed over fruits before him, and afterward they brought him more of that same type, does not need to bless again, even though they were not before him when he blessed. The *Beit Yosef* wrote on this: "It seems we do not require it to be of the first type; even if it is of another type that is covered by the first blessing <note>e.g., both are 'Fruit of the Tree'</note>," end of quote.

It seems the *Tur* is speaking even when one eats in his own home. Even if we say he does not need to bless when his family members (or he himself) bring more of this type later (even if he finished the first type before they brought the second, as will follow; for if the *Tur* meant specifically when eating at a friend's house, then one blessing would be enough because he relies on the host's table as mentioned). If he meant only at a friend's house, he would have had to specify that. Even an Amora <note>Talmudic sage</note> must clarify his words, and certainly the legal decisors and commentators, and especially the *Tur*, whose way is always to explain his words clearly like a vision and not in riddles. Since he did not specify here that it refers to a friend's house, it shows he holds that even in one's own house, he does not need to bless again.

One should also not interpret the *Tur's* words here—that if they bring him more he does not need to bless—as referring to a case where he did not originally intend to eat anything but the fruits before him and then changed his mind to eat more. Even so, he would not need to bless again? No, for it is simple across all the decisors that "changing one's mind" constitutes a distraction of the mind, and it is obvious he would need to bless again.

Furthermore, one should not interpret that the *Tur* refers specifically to when he intended from the start to eat whatever they would bring. In that case, one blessing would certainly suffice. But what about an unspecified case? The *Tur* himself wrote regarding the laws of ritual slaughter <note>Hebrew: *Yoreh De'ah* Section 19</note> as follows: "If at the beginning when he blessed, there were many animals before him to slaughter, and afterward they brought him others... anything that was not before him when he blessed requires a new blessing, unless his mind was set on whatever they would bring him." If the law here were the same, he should have explained it explicitly here as he did there. Since he wrote here simply "he does not need to bless" and did not specify "only when his mind was set on it," it implies that here it applies to all cases. Even if his mind was not specifically set on whatever they would bring, if he blessed without specific intent and is eating in his own home, he still does not need to bless again when his family or he himself brings more, as long as he did not clearly decide to stop eating at the time of the blessing.

If so, according to what has been said, what is the difference between eating and slaughtering? One can say that there is a "fixity" <note>Hebrew: *Keva*</note> to a meal, but there is no "fixity" to slaughtering. Meaning: a person establishes a firm fixed status for eating because the palate and taste of food are sweet to him, and therefore regarding eating, we assume that when they bring him food, he does not distract his mind from eating as long as he is reclining at the table. This is not the case for slaughtering, where there is no "fixity"; presumably, whatever is not before him is not on his mind. Therefore, his intent must be certain and clear for everything they bring him. This very reason was mentioned in the glosses on the aforementioned words of the *Tur*, and you will find it if you search for it. Nevertheless, initially, it is good to be careful to have in mind at the time of the blessing over fruits everything they might bring him, whether eating in his own home or a friend's home. My teacher wrote the same in his *Shulchan Aruch*.

Besides this reason, there is another reason why it is good to have in mind all that they might bring later: perhaps they will bring him another type of fruit whose blessing is the same as the first. Then, if the first type was more "dear" to him <note>term: *Chaviv* — the principle that a more preferred food takes precedence in blessings</note>, it exempts the second type from a blessing. But if it is not more "dear," it does not exempt it unless he intended for it from the start, as will be explained in the following rule. Since a person cannot always trust himself to know if the first fruit he blessed on was more "dear" than the one brought later, he would be left in doubt whether to bless on the second type or not. Therefore, it is good to intend during the blessing for everything they will bring, so he does not enter into a state of doubt. This is easy to understand.

<meta>This page continues the detailed exploration of the laws regarding the order of blessings (Berakhot), specifically addressing the hierarchy of importance between different types of food and drink, and the botanical definitions that determine which blessing is recited over a plant.</meta>

# The Gate of Letters

Even though a person may prefer the type of food that requires the blessing "By Whose word all things exist" <note>Hebrew: *Shehakol*</note> over others, the *Beit Yosef* <note>The seminal commentary on the *Tur* by Rabbi Joseph Karo</note> wrote in Section 211, and so it is ruled in the *Shulchan Aruch*: It emerges for us <note>original: *yatza l'gumma*, likely a transcription variant of "it emerges for us"</note> that if one has spirits <note>Hebrew: *yayin saraf*, literally "burnt wine," referring to brandy or schnapps</note> and various preserves <note>Hebrew: *mirkahat*</note> containing fruit of the tree or fruit of the ground brought before him, the law dictates that he should first recite the blessing over the preserves—whatever their blessing may be, whether "Who creates the fruit of the tree" or "Who creates the fruit of the ground." This excludes other types of preserves whose blessing is "By Whose word all things exist," for in that case, he would recite one "By Whose word all things exist" for everything. Afterward, he should recite the blessing over the spirits, which is also "By Whose word all things exist," even though the drink might be more desired. Since he is required to give precedence to something that requires the specific blessing of "Fruit of the Tree" or "Fruit of the Ground" over the general blessing of "By Whose word all things exist," he must first bless over the preserves, taste them, and then bless over the spirits and drink; afterward, he may return to eating the preserves if he wishes. One should not act like the common people who first bless over the spirits and only afterward bless over the preserves when they are served, simply because their soul's desire is to drink the spirits first. This should not be done for the reason stated above.

**It was written** by my teacher in his commentary on the *Shulchan Aruch* <note>Referring to the author's primary halakhic authority</note> that the rule stating one blessing takes precedence over another applies only when one intends to eat from both. In such a case, one should prioritize the "favorite" or the more "important" species. However, if one does not wish to eat from both, he only recites a blessing over what he intends to eat, even if the second item is sitting before him and would otherwise take precedence. (See above, Principle 1, Section 2).

**And** according to another answer written by the *Beit Yosef* in his glosses to Section 201 regarding the question of when fruits and wine are distributed at a betrothal house or a house of birth: we bless over the fruits and sweets first and then over the wine. From this, we learn that even if a person intends to eat several types of fruit, if they are brought out one by one, he blesses over whichever is brought first, even if the subsequent fruit would have been more "worthy" of receiving the blessing first. The rules of precedence were only said for when both species are sitting before him simultaneously. I have scrutinized this in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the chapter "One who ate and does not remember" <note>Tractate Berakhot, Chapter 6</note>, where it says "one places the item..." see there.

Regarding the rule that anything appearing earlier in the biblical verse <note>The verse in Deuteronomy 8:8 listing the seven species of the Land of Israel: Wheat, Barley, Grapes, Figs, Pomegranates, Olives, and Dates</note> takes precedence in blessing: The *Tur* wrote in Section 211 that the Sages of *Zaroka* <note>Likely a geographical reference or specific group of scholars</note> would eat grapes as they are. But if one made wine from them, which establishes its own special blessing—"Who creates the fruit of the vine"—it takes precedence. However, a cooked dish made from the five species of grain <note>Wheat, barley, spelt, rye, and oats</note>, whose blessing is "Who creates various kinds of sustenance" <note>Hebrew: *Borei Minei Mezonot*</note>, is more important than the blessing over wine because grains are explicitly mentioned [first] in the verse. My teacher wrote there: The blessing over bread <note>Hebrew: *Hamotzi*</note> precedes the blessing over "sustenance," just as it does all other blessings, even if the other item is more preferred by the person. It seems that these words as written here require some clarification. It is difficult to say that the blessing over bread precedes "sustenance" and certainly other blessings, for what "precedence" is there to speak of regarding bread compared to other foods? Bread always comes first! Rather, the discussion concerns whether one should bless over wine or something else when bread is present. Does one recite the blessing over bread and not the others? For Rabbi Joel, Alfasi, and their colleagues only disagreed regarding the custom of *Rovish* <note>Likely a local custom or specific food item</note> as to whether it constitutes an interruption between washing the hands and the blessing over bread, as the *Tur* cited in Section 166. They were *Zaroka* who "covered their knees" <note>an idiom for humility or a specific group</note>. But to recite another blessing between washing and the bread is certainly forbidden by all because of the "interruption," except for the *Kiddush* of Shabbat, where we sanctify even over beer first at the morning meal. The reason for this is written in the *Tur*, Section 272; see there. Unless we say that my teacher is speaking here of a person who does not wish to eat a full meal's worth of bread <note>Hebrew: *Kezayit*, the size of an olive</note>, in which case he does not need to wash his hands, as the *Beit Yosef* wrote in the name of the *Rokeach* in Section 158. If he has other items before him, such as porridge or "pocket-bread" <note>Hebrew: *Kisnin*, referring to crackers or filled pastries</note>, or things blessed as "Fruit of the Tree" or "Fruit of the Ground," and he wants to eat some bread as well as the other foods—if the law were that he could bless on whichever he wanted because the blessings are not identical (as in Principle 9), then my teacher wrote that the blessing over bread still takes precedence. This is not because of "interruption" (since there was no washing), but because bread is of such high status that it "establishes a blessing for itself," just as the logic was mentioned regarding wine. Furthermore, it seems we can explain my teacher's words cited above as referring to a case where the table was set before him with bread and other important, favorite items, but he had not yet washed his hands for the meal. In this case, when both are present, he should wash his hands and bless over the bread first, and then the bread exempts all other types of food (except for wine and fruit, which do not "sustain" in the same way). This comes to exclude what was written in the *Kol Bo*, Section 104: "One of the students of our French Rabbi <note>referring to the Tosafists</note> wrote of his master: many times I saw my teacher, when they brought before him on the table a new meat dish or cooked meat or eggs fried in honey—things he particularly loved—he would take that item and bless over it before blessing over the bread, saying: 'This is more beloved to me than the bread, and it is more pleasant for me to bless over it first to praise my Creator with what I love.'" It seems to me this also refers to a case where the table was set but he had not yet washed his hands; for if it were after washing but before the bread, it would be an interruption, and one would have to recite a second blessing for the washing <note>to compensate for the improper break</note>.

**8** The *Shulchan Aruch* ruled in Section 203: Berries that grow on a bush receive the blessing "Fruit of the Ground." My teacher wrote on this in his code: The reason it is not called a "tree" is that a tree is only something that produces leaves from its own wood. That is, when the new year begins, even though in the winter months its roots and trunk were preserved in the ground, and its branches remain on the tree, it returns year after year and produces leaves and fruit—this is "Fruit of the Tree." But that which grows its leaves from its roots is not called a tree. For when the winter days arrive, neither branch nor trunk remains in the ground; only the root "nests" in the earth, and the following year the root returns and sends out a new sprout, growing branches, leaves, and fruit. This is not called "Fruit of the Tree." And here, since the wood perishes completely in the winter and then reproduces from the roots, we bless over it "Fruit of the Ground."

**And thus wrote** the *Rokeach*: Every tree that sheds its leaves in the autumn but the wood remains and produces leaves from its own wood is "Fruit of the Tree." But if the leaves dry up and it grows anew from the roots like sesame, it is "Fruit of the Ground." And thus wrote Rabbi Ovadiah <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro</note> in his commentary on the Mishnah: Whenever you take the fruit and the branch remains, and that same branch returns and produces fruit the next year, it is called a tree and we bless "Fruit of the Tree." But where the branch does not remain to produce fruit the next year, we only bless "Fruit of the Ground." And this is the language of the Gemara <note>The Talmud</note> in the commentary on "How does one bless," which says: Where do we bless "Fruit of the Tree"? Where, when you take the fruit, the *guza* <note>trunk/stump</note> remains. It explains that the branch of the tree remains and then puts out other fruit. But where the *guza* does not remain, we do not bless "Fruit of the Tree" but rather "Fruit of the Ground."

**9** The *Mordechai* wrote in the chapter "How does one bless": If one is in doubt whether a fruit is "Fruit of the Tree" or "Fruit of the Ground," he should bless "Fruit of the Ground." For we hold that if one blessed "Fruit of the Ground" over a fruit of the tree, he has fulfilled his obligation, because the blessing "Fruit of the Ground" is a general category that includes both, as even the tree draws its sustenance from the ground. Therefore, he has fulfilled the requirement. However, ideally, it is a "mitzvah of the highest sort" to bless over each species with its specific, appropriate blessing, for the praise is greater that way. It demonstrates "Specific Providence" <note>Hebrew: *Hashgacha Pratit*</note>—that God watches over His creatures to give every man what he needs. This is what is called "according to the nature of the blessings." If one blessed "Fruit of the Tree" over a fruit of the ground, he has *not* fulfilled his obligation, as there is no tree involved at all. (See above, Principle 30, Section 2 and 4). And if one does not know what a thing is, he blesses "By Whose word all things exist," for we hold that this blessing covers everything. Even though the *Mishnah* implies this is only after the fact, since he is in a state of doubt, it is considered as an "after the fact" situation. So wrote the *Tur* in Sections 202 and 206.

**20** All types of vegetables and legumes that are good both raw and cooked—meaning they are just as good cooked as they are raw—one recites the same blessing after cooking as before. But if they are better cooked than raw, such as the vegetable called *gren* <note>likely horseradish or a similar root</note> and the like, and one eats them raw outside of a meal, he blesses "By Whose word all things exist" because their growth is not complete. But after cooking, they are "Fruit of the Ground" because they have been improved. This follows the general way they are eaten, for from the beginning, they were planted with this intent. However, those vegetables that are typically eaten raw with olive oil and vinegar, which are called *salads* <note>Hebrew: *salat-in*</note>, receive the blessing "Fruit of the Ground" even when raw, if eaten outside a meal in the aforementioned prepared state, because it is the way of people to eat them raw and that is why they are planted. But if they are good raw and cooking degrades them, such as the vegetable called in the common tongue *arab shuto* <note>possibly a bitter herb or wild green</note> or what is called *tara'an*...

It emphasizes that specific blessings are preferred over general ones to acknowledge Divine Providence over individual creations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical and ethical discussion regarding the laws of blessings (Berakhot), transitioning from the precedence of specific drinks and preserves to a broader philosophical look at honor, followed by a detailed analysis of the Tur (Section 211) regarding the priority of the Seven Species of Israel when blessings are not identical.</meta>

# The Gate of Letters

<margin>
Regarding the hearing of the five [species] and the action... preceded before them and from their friction, etc. And even though their blessings are equal, I have already awakened to this difficulty and resolved it in its place in the *Tur*, *Choshen Mishpat* <note>The author likely means *Orach Chaim* given the context of blessings, or is referring to his own commentary on the *Tur*</note>, Section 211, in the words I explained with Heaven's help on the *Tur*. And these are my words there, in my humble opinion: For we learned that when their blessings are equal, whichever one he desires, he precedes—this is when neither is from the Seven Species, such as a radish and an olive. But when they are from the Seven Species, such as grapes and an olive, or two from the Seven Species, the one mentioned first [in the biblical verse] precedes. And if you say: the words are an *a fortiori* argument <note>A logical inference: if the rule applies in a minor case, it must apply in a major one</note>—if [the order] is not preferred when the blessings are not equal, surely when they are both from the Seven Species and mentioned in the verse, the one mentioned earlier should be prioritized?
And it may be answered: For the *Rosh* <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, 13th-century commentator</note> already wrote in Chapter *Kol HaMevarkhin* and the *Beit Yosef* brought it, as follows: "In any case, when their blessings are equal, one must precede the Seven Species; and when they are not equal, one must precede..." It is certain that when the blessings are equal, where one blessing exempts the other, he precedes the Seven Species to exempt his companion. But when one must bless over each one individually, then since he must bless regardless, he should bless over whichever he prefers. Therefore, for grapes and an olive, where the blessings are equal, according to what he wrote in Section 212, he should bless over the Seven Species and exempt the other... but when there is no requirement to exempt with a blessing, but rather to bless each individually, the law of precedence does not apply. Thus it is clear according to the *Rosh* in Section 211. Whether we say that since wine is required before the meal, it follows that there is no obligation to prioritize... each blessing stands on its own. This is like the *etrog* <note>citron</note> and the olive... as the *Beit Yosef* wrote... they are completely separate matters. Therefore, from the perspective of the blessing, all rankings are equal... and the Seven Species are listed at the end of the verse... since they are completely separate, the law of precedence does not apply. However, there is a reason for the heart to understand... the case of wine, for they are separate... and this is sufficient.
</margin>

From God they are asked of their honor, and this is what is meant by "He who honors creatures" <note>Referencing Pirkei Avot 4:1</note>; that is to say, it is right to call someone a "honorer of creatures" only if he is a man of lower status who performs an act of honor for a superior. For if a superior man honors an inferior, it would be a disgrace to that superior. If so, the definition of "one who is honored" is when that superior person says his honor is confirmed by the one honoring him. Without doubt, the one who is honored is defined by those who honor him. Therefore, one who honors his fellow, of whom it can truly be said he honors them, such a man is undoubtedly honored, for he receives honor through the very fact that the recipient accepts honor from him. It turns out that while he is the *actor* of honor, he is also the *recipient* of the honor itself; through the fact that he is honored by his own submission to them, it is a great honor for him and a sign of his high stature. According to the definition of "the honored one," which is given according to the superior, he is giving him great honor and a sign of his excellence by being honored through his submission more than through the submission of others. This is a correct and precise point. **End of his words.**

Behold, I offer a parable of my own: "For man is a tree of the field" <note>original: *ki ha'adam etz hasadeh*, Deuteronomy 20:19</note>, and the tree of the field refers to the olive mentioned nearby in our case. As it is said by way of a parable, its precedence is to the north; since it has no name that he should write at all, the honor of its precedence was considered as nothing in his eyes. And this is simple to understand.

One should not ask: What did the *Tur* see, and what forced him to hide this reasoning? And why did he not rule regarding "when their blessings are not equal" that whichever one he wants he should precede always, even among the Seven Species? Why did he write in Section 211: "Barley, bitter herbs, etc., he precedes before the blessing," and this is difficult to estimate, for "first for the land" is last, etc., and "second for the land" is first? <note>Referring to the proximity of the species to the word 'Land' in Deuteronomy 8:8</note>. And he wrote further on this: "Wheat precedes the olive, etc., because it appears earlier in the verse."

And if it is because of Rav Yosef, or some say Rabbi Yitzhak, who said in the Talmud (Chapter *Kol HaMevarkhin*) and the *Tur* brought it in his section: "Whatever is earlier in the verse is earlier for the blessing, etc." We would have established this specifically for things whose blessings are equal, such as wheat compared to barley, or grapes compared to figs. But where the blessings are not equal, whichever comes first—even if it is a lesser species—he may choose whichever he wants always, even when both are from the Seven Species.

And the reason the *Tur* preferred this interpretation is so that the statement of Rav Yosef (or Rabbi Yitzhak) above follows its plain meaning—that he said "Whatever is earlier in the verse is earlier for the blessing" implies in all cases. We would not need to press the text and say that what was said about "whatever is earlier in the verse" was not said about all Seven Species, but only about "Fruit of the Ground" on its own and "Fruit of the Tree" on its own. For example, wheat and barley, where one must precede wheat over barley; or grapes and figs, where one must precede grapes over figs. But in a case where the blessings are not equal, such as barley compared to an olive, it is not so. For among all Seven Species, the one earlier in the verse is earlier for the blessing. But according to what the *Tur* wrote, the statement of the Rabbi above follows its plain meaning, and it will always be the priority, even though the blessings are not equal... and this is the "Desire of the Land," he blessed over its fruit... whereas in the chapter "These are the things that go out," etc., until "this applies to a single species and taste," and he blessed over it "Who creates the fruit of the tree." But for a radish and an olive, etc., if he blessed over the radish, he did not exempt the olive... and look closely there, for that is specifically when at the time he blessed "Who creates the fruit of the ground" he did not intend to exempt the "Fruit of the Tree." But if he *intended* to exempt the "Fruit of the Tree," he does not need to go back and bless. However, initially one should not do this, for perhaps the blessing of "By Whose word" <note>Shehakol</note> is preferable to losing a blessing, since one must give each species its appropriate blessing when the blessings are not equal. As our Sages of blessed memory expounded on the verse, "Blessed be the Lord day by day," etc. <note>Psalm 68:20</note>. And the *Shivah Einayim* <note>Rabbinic work</note> wrote there that if he had before him an etrog and an olive, and he went ahead and blessed over the etrog, even though he is not permitted to precede the blessing, he must...

...he does not need to go back and bless over the wine, since with this blessing he drinks, provided that he intended to exempt the wine with the blessing over the etrog. But if he did not intend to, it is not right that he who is not important should exempt he who is important by way of a blessing, but only by way of intention. According to this explanation, if he was eating apples in abundance and blessed over them, and afterward they brought walnuts before him: if the apples are more beloved to him, he exempts the walnuts with the blessing over the apples. But if they are not more beloved, they do not exempt the walnuts unless he intended for them from the beginning. **End of the words of the *Beit Yosef* in the mentioned place.**

And it seems to me that this is not only when they *afterward* brought walnuts before him, but even if the apples and walnuts were lying before him together. If he blessed over the apples and they are not beloved to him, they do not exempt the walnuts from their blessing unless he intended for them from the beginning, as with the etrog and olive mentioned in the first part of the matter, which deals with them being laid out before him. And even so, he wrote that without intention he does not exempt, for since the olive is of the Seven Species, he is not permitted to precede the other over it; therefore, he needs explicit intention to exempt it. The same law applies if both are not of the Seven Species, but the other is more beloved to him. For what is the difference? One must also establish the priority of the "beloved" over the "non-beloved," just as one must precede the Seven Species over those that are not. He only used the example "and afterward they brought him walnuts" to show the novelty of the latter case: that intention is effective to exempt them with the first blessing even if it is not the beloved one and even if they are not laid out before him. It is an "it goes without saying" argument: it goes without saying that where they are laid out before him at the start, intention would help even if it's not the beloved species. But even if they were not laid out before him at the time he blessed over the apples, and the apples are also not beloved to him, if he intended for the walnuts from the start, he exempts the walnuts that come afterward with the blessing of the apples, for everything follows the intention. And this is simple to understand.

The *Tur* wrote in Section 211, as follows: "And if they brought before him something whose blessing is 'Who creates the fruit of the ground' and something whose blessing is 'By Whose word all things exist,' the blessing 'Who creates the fruit of the ground' precedes, for it is more important, as it only exempts one type of thing, while 'By Whose word' includes all things, etc." So too, "Fruit of the ground" precedes "By Whose word." And the author of the *Halakhot Gedolot* <note>Early medieval legal code</note> wrote that the blessing "Who creates the fruit of the tree" precedes the blessing "Who creates the fruit of the ground." But my master, my father, the *Rosh* of blessed memory, wrote that they are equal, and he may bless over whichever he desires first. Even if one of them is from the Seven Species, he can precede the second to it. **End of his words.**

One should not ask regarding what the *Tur* wrote—that "Fruit of the tree" and "Fruit of the ground" precede "By Whose word"—for the law was already decided: when their blessings are not equal, whichever he wants he may precede, even if one of them is from the Seven Species, as was brought above in this section. The *Rosh* already resolved this, and the *Beit Yosef* brought it in the mentioned section, saying: this rule—that when blessings are not equal he may precede whichever he wants—was only said specifically when one of them is "Fruit of the tree" and the other is "Fruit of the ground," such as a radish and an olive; then he may precede whichever he wants. But when one of them is "Fruit of the ground" or "Fruit of the tree," and the second is "By Whose word," he is obligated to precede the specific blessing of the tree or ground before the general "By Whose word." The reason for the matter is that a general blessing is not considered as important as a specific one like "Fruit of the tree" or "Fruit of the ground," because "By Whose word" includes every thing in the world; it is the "category of categories," as we mentioned. And so it is said: "And over everything, if he said 'By Whose word,' he has fulfilled his obligation."

And this law of precedence mentioned here—that the fruit of the tree and fruit of the ground precede "By Whose word"—applies even when the "By Whose word" item is not of the Seven Species but is more beloved to him than the second species of the tree or ground. This is clearly implied to any who look closely at the *Tur* in the mentioned section, for all laws of precedence mentioned in that section deal with this manner. And so the *Tosafot* <note>Medieval commentators on the Talmud</note> wrote explicitly in the chapter "How do we bless" regarding "the beloved is preferable," as follows: "The specific blessing is much better, even though the species that requires 'By Whose word' is more beloved to him." And so wrote the *Mordechai* in the chapter "How do we bless" on this, even though...

It emphasizes that specific blessings (like Fruit of the Tree) generally outweigh general ones (like Shehakol), and highlights the role of intention (Kavanah) in fulfilling religious obligations.</summary>

# The Gate of Letters

The preserve <note>original: "HaMerkachet"</note> is the primary element and not the spices within it; therefore, one does not bless over the spices. <margin>L</margin> Regarding what we said in the previous section—that one blesses over the mixed confection called *surkakh*—it refers to large pieces that are changed by the honey. The spices are merely for fragrance. Alternatively, some say that the spices are set aside and finely ground into another preserve just to give it flavor; therefore, one does not bless over them individually, as they are nullified by their minority status.

<margin>M</margin> The *Rif* <note>Rabbi Isaac Alfasi, an 11th-century legal authority</note> wrote in the chapter "How do we bless" concerning ground musk-fruits <note>original: "masmukaot"</note>—and no man knows exactly how they are made—see the explanation in the *Arukh* <note>A classic dictionary of Talmudic terms</note> regarding spreads and bundles of fragrance that are meant for a pleasant scent. Regarding fruit of the tree, if one recited the general blessing, he has fulfilled his obligation. This is taught in the *Baraita* in Principle 5, Section 10, and in the *Kol Bo* <note>A medieval collection of Jewish laws</note> on the laws of blessings, Section 69.

**And regarding** what we say in Section 209 regarding honey that was cooked with various types of spices: he wrote that one does not recite a blessing over the preserve because the primary intention is for eating. The initial blessing is "by Whose word all things exist" <note>original: "Shehakol"</note> and after cooking, it remains so. Regarding something that is eaten while raw but is diminished by cooking—such as mustard—if he cooked it, he recites a blessing over it individually. Initially, he recites "Creator of the fruit of the earth," but after cooking, it becomes "by Whose word all things exist." Even if he cooked them with meat or other things that improve them, he only recites "by Whose word all things exist" since the item is only important because of the other ingredient. Some say that if they were originally intended to be cooked, his intention is nullified. Rava said: for something eaten raw, if cooking improves it—such as quinces <note>original: "chavashim"</note> or *adarmos*—the initial blessing is "Fruit of the tree," and after cooking it remains "Fruit of the tree." These are the words of Rabbeinu Yerucham.

<margin>H</margin> The *Beit Yosef* <note>The commentary by Rabbi Joseph Karo</note> wrote in Section 167 and Section 209 in the name of the *Kol Bo* regarding a preserve made from the heart of a palm tree, called *coria*. For all fruits in a preserve, it must be clear that the intention is not to eat the pieces alone, but the preserve as a whole. Regarding the item called *papula* in the *Kol Bo*, the preserve's blessing exempts it. Therefore, one should say that regarding those preserves we are accustomed to making on Purim called *gazie*, and those made on honey-wafers called *lekuch* <note>likely honey cake or gingerbread</note>, one recites the blessing appropriate for the preserve and exempts the wafers, as they are secondary to the preserve. So wrote the Geonim in the *Kol Bo*, Principle 6, Section 52.

### Principle 7: On the laws of the blessing "The Good and the Beneficent" and it contains 9 sections:

**1** Rabbeinu Yerucham wrote in Path 15: even if the second item is better than the first, if the first is already finished, one does not recite "The Good and the Beneficent" <note>a blessing recited when sharing good news or drinking a new wine with others</note> because there is no "increase" of good here. So I found in the name of the *Ra'ah*. **2** This is brought in the *Tur* in Section 19, but there is no clear reason given for it. **3** One should be concerned about the words of Rabbeinu Yerucham who wrote in the name of "his brothers" that we do recite "The Good and the Beneficent" even if the first is finished, though this requires further study. In the end, he leans toward being lenient.

### Principle 10: On the laws of the blessing "Who has kept us alive" and it contains 20 sections:

**1** The *Tur* wrote in Section 223: before the blessing over eating, if one smells the scent of a fragrant wood, he blesses "Creator of fragrant trees"; if it is a herb, he blesses "fragrant herbs." If it is neither wood nor herb—such as musk—he blesses "Creator of various types of fragrance." If he said "various types of fragrance" over any of them, he has fulfilled his obligation. **Our custom** is to bless "various types of fragrance" over any general mixture of spices to avoid doubt.

<margin>2</margin> Regarding a scent that has no physical substance—such as clothes that were perfumed with incense—Maimonides wrote that one does not bless over it. The *Tur* wrote in Section 207: "I did not understand his words," but this is the law. Regarding a scent from a bathhouse <note>original: "banai"</note> that comes from scented oil, one does not bless even if the scent is strong. It seems that if the cinnamon scent is not distinct, or if the vessel was merely used for spices and the scent clung to it, one does not bless "Creator of spices." One only blesses when the spices were made specifically to provide scent.

### Principle 10 [Repeated]: On the laws of the blessing "Who has kept us alive" and it contains 2 sections:

**1** The *Tur* wrote in Section 204: anything that does not grow from the ground—such as meat, fish, milk, cheese, or honey—receives the blessing "by Whose word all things exist." <margin>Regarding the essence: the *Shulchan Aruch* wrote in Section 202 that if they are the primary part of the preserve, one blesses "by Whose word all things exist." The custom is that they must be good. If the food is harmful, the *Tur* says one should not bless at all. There are fruits called "sloes" <note>original: "ba-al sho-an"</note> over which we recite "by Whose word all things exist."</margin>

### Principle 11: On the laws of "Who has kept us alive" and it contains 2 sections:

**1** The author of *Terumat HaDeshen* wrote: concerning grape seeds called *sar-gelenu*, if one drinks the wine afterward, this is serious and requires the "Who has kept us alive" <note>original: "Shehecheyanu"</note> blessing. For new fruits, one blesses before eating them. He brought proof regarding those called *knabel* or *apf-ey*. The *Beit Yosef* wrote that for new grapes, it is better not to bless if there is a dispute, but rather to find another new fruit or a new garment to exempt the doubt.

**2** The *Tur* ruled: if a fruit does not change from year to year, one does not recite "Who has kept us alive." We do not recite this blessing over new vegetables or legumes <margin>because they are stored all year and it is not recognizable that they are new. However, some say one should bless over new wine. The *Rashba* and *Rosh* imply that the world's custom is to bless "Who has kept us alive" even over vegetables that are not seasonal. But because they can be preserved in the ground all year, the strict law is not to bless over them, and this is the better path.</margin>

**And this** is the language of Rabbeinu Yonah: for something not eaten raw but made edible through cooking, one recites "by Whose word all things exist" initially and "Fruit of the earth" after cooking. For something eaten raw but diminished by cooking, such as mustard, he recites "Fruit of the earth" and after cooking "by Whose word all things exist." These are often called "dolls" <note>original: "bubot"</note> in the common tongue. Even if they were changed slightly, they do not lose their initial blessing. Regarding dried legumes, one blesses "by Whose word all things exist."

## Principle 7: On the laws of things over which we bless "various types of fragrance"

**1** Our custom regarding honey called *ba-a*: even if very crushed, one blesses "Fruit of the tree." The *Tur* and Rabbeinu Yerucham discuss this. One is exempted by the primary blessing even if they are finely ground.

**2** <margin>Specifically</margin> Note that for all confections, even if not fit for eating raw or cooked, if the scent is changed, one blesses "by Whose word all things exist." This applies to items like *clampus*, *pinta*, or those called *dolce* or *zogbil* <note>likely ginger</note>. Others write that if they are mixed with oil, the blessing changes. Regarding roses <note>original: "vardinal"</note>, if they are the primary ingredient, one blesses "Fruit of the earth."

**3** Regarding the *lotus* mentioned by Isaac: even if it is hanging on the fruit, it follows the law of the fruit. Some say that since it is intended for sweetness but can be harmful, the blessing is "by Whose word all things exist."

The primary fruit intended for eating, called *kors* (black or red), is the one mentioned by some. I have heard that Jewish merchants make a wine with roses, and it is called *alzamora*. I have also heard of those who soak raisins or "Zovisky" <note>possibly a regional spirit or fruit</note>.

**Finally**, the essence of these fruits follows the majority. One does not bless "Who has kept us alive" over the *lotus* even if it is a new fruit. Regarding roses, we bless "Fruit of the earth" even though our intention is for the scent, because the flower is the essence. As the sages said: God created different types of fruits for eating, and the primary part is called the "stone" <note>original: "avnot"</note>. One does not bless "Fruit of the tree" over the stones/pits, but over the flesh.

**It appears** that for the many preserves we use, even if they are crushed, the blessing is "Fruit of the earth" or "by Whose word all things exist" as explained before. Regarding the preserves called *vardinal*, because they are cooked and changed, the blessing is "by Whose word all things exist."

**L** The *Beit Yosef* wrote: if the item is significantly changed in the preserve, even if it provides the taste, we do not bless over it individually, but rather the blessing on the preserve exempts it.

The preserve <note>original: "HaMerkachet"</note> is the primary element and not the spices within it; therefore, one does not bless over the spices. And regarding what we say in the previous section—that one who blesses over ginger <note>original: "Nagybel"</note> preserved in honey recites "the fruit of the earth"—this refers to large pieces that are not crushed. But for the ginger itself, when it is crushed and pressed into honey or added to another preserve just for flavor, one does not bless over them individually, as they are nullified by their minority status.

<margin>L</margin> Rabbi Isaac <note>likely Rabbi Isaac of Vienna, author of the Or Zarua</note> wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah that he found "Muskapot" <note>musk-scented treats</note> made by an Arab man, and it is unclear if they are the fruit of the earth or fruit of the tree. Therefore, out of doubt, one blesses "fruit of the earth," for even if it were truly from a tree, the blessing of the earth fulfills the obligation. This follows the rule regarding rice and other fruits mentioned in Section 13 and Principle 8, Section 2.

<margin>Ch</margin> It is written in the "Small Sign" for my master and teacher: just as any type of fruit, some of which come from a tree... and they call them *surder* <note>perhaps a regional name for a specific preserve</note>... it is known that they are not eaten alone but only in the preserve. One blesses "fruit of the earth" over them. Rashi <note>the preeminent medieval commentator</note> wrote that if they are placed in white honey, one recites "by Whose word all things exist" <note>original: "Shehakol"</note>, but after cooking, the preserve covers the fruit. From this, we learn the law for those preserves we are accustomed to making for Purim, called *Gazoli* <note>Gozinalli, a nut and honey confection</note>, and those made dry called *Lekach* <note>Honey cake</note>: one recites the blessing appropriate for the preserve, which exempts the secondary ingredients. See the words of our Rabbis on this in Principle 7.

# Principle 6: The Laws of the Blessing "The Good and He Who Does Good" <note>original: "HaTov VeHaMeitiv"</note> – Section 1

**K** The *Tur* <note>the foundational code of Jewish law by Rabbi Jacob ben Asher</note> wrote in Section 222: "A companion for life"—even if one already drank from the first wine and recited the blessing over it, one must bless "The Good and He Who Does Good" upon being served a second, better wine, as there is a change in the wine's quality. This is what I found in the name of the sages of Vienna and Rabbi Yerucham. Just as one remembers the first wine, one must conclude with the second. There is no mystery in this; it is a matter of the master of the house and the sanctification <note>Kiddush</note> of the meal, and one must bless. It seems to me we should be concerned with the words of Rabbi Yerucham, who wrote in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that if one drank the first and the second is needed, he should bless, though he himself suggests being lenient.

# Principle 8: Section 1 – The Blessing over Cinnamon

**A** Over cinnamon called *Zukarda* <note>candied cinnamon</note>, which is a fruit of the ground <note>referring here to the bark/shrub</note>, and not as written in the *Tur* in Section 203. One blesses "fruit of the earth" because it is the custom to eat it dry. Even though the *Tur* says otherwise, we bless as stated.

# Principle 9: The Laws of the Proper Blessing for Fragrances – 2 Sections

**A** The *Tur* wrote in Section 206 that one should bless before smelling, just as one blesses over bread. If the scent comes from a wood or a sap from a tree, one blesses "Creator of fragrant trees." If it is an herb, one blesses "Creator of fragrant herbs." If it is neither wood nor herb—such as musk <note>original: "moshk"</note> or any other good scent—one blesses "Creator of various types of spices." In all cases, if one said "various types of spices," he has fulfilled the obligation. Even though it is written in Section 216 that anything derived from a fruit, like *Turig* <note>perhaps a citron-based perfume</note>, gets "fruit of the tree," we generally bless over blended spice mixtures with the general "various types of spices" to avoid doubt.

**B** This applies only when there is no physical substance to the scent—for example, if one merely inhales the scent in a spice shop. In that case, one does not bless at all, as there is no wood or herb present as a source. This is the reasoning of Rashi and the *Mordechai*. However, if one grinds the wood and enjoys the scent while grinding, he has changed its state and should bless "various spices." This applies whether the fragrance is in a wooden or metal vessel specially designated for it.

### Principle 10: The Laws of the Blessing "By Whose Word All Things Exist" <note>original: "Shehakol"</note> – Section 1

**A** The *Tur* wrote in Section 204: For anything whose primary source is not from the ground—such as meat of domestic and wild animals, fowl, fish, eggs, milk, cheese, and bee honey or water—the blessing is "by Whose word all things exist." Regarding sugar, it is written in Section 202 that one blesses "Shehakol" if the flavor and scent are not primarily from the source. This also applies to lemons <note>original: "limoni"</note> and dates. Regarding new wine and things that might be harmful, there is a doubt, but generally, we bless "Shehakol."

# Principle 11: The Laws of the Blessing "Who Has Kept Us Alive" <note>original: "Shehecheyanu"</note> – 2 Sections

**A** The author of *Terumat HaDeshen* wrote (and it is cited in the *Beit Yosef*): one recites *Shehecheyanu* when drinking new wine or seeing new fruit. Regarding sugar, some say one should bless *Shehecheyanu*, but the custom is to be lenient. Some say one may bless over myrtle <note>original: "hadas"</note> or grapes. It is best not to bless if there is a dispute, but rather to bless over a new fruit or a new garment and have the new wine in mind as well.

**B** The *Tur* ruled in Section 225 that one recites this blessing for something that renews joy from year to year. If a fruit lasts all year, one does not bless. If a fruit grows twice a year, one does not bless. There is a dispute regarding new wine since it stays in the barrel all year, but the custom is often to bless because the harvest is a new event. However, some argue that since the source is the ground and it is a consistent product, one should not bless.

---

**It appears** that the methods we discussed regarding confections—even if they are not pressed—apply here. If it is wood-based, bless "fragrant trees"; if herb-based, "fragrant herbs." If neither, such as musk, bless "various spices."

<column-break/>

**And even if** there is only a bit of scent or color, and one eats it outside of a meal, one blesses "fruit of the earth." Regarding boiled items, it is written in the *Kol Bo* that even for the lemons mentioned by the *Tur* and Rabbi Joseph <note>Karo</note>, one should praise the Creator.

**Here is** the language of Rabbenu Yonah in Chapter 2: A distinction is made between raw things and those improved by cooking. If something is edible raw but better cooked, the blessing changes from "Shehakol" to "fruit of the earth." But for something like dates, which are worse when cooked, the blessing remains "fruit of the earth." If a fruit is cooked with meat solely to flavor the meat, the fruit becomes secondary and the blessing is "Shehakol." This follows the logic of the Exilarch's house <note>original: "Bei Nasi'a"</note> regarding quinces <note>original: "chovashim"</note> and crust-fruits. After cooking, they become "fruit of the earth."

**11.** Regarding quinces <note>original: "chovash"</note>: even though they are improved by cooking, since they are not normally eaten raw, some say the blessing is "Shehakol" when raw and "fruit of the earth" after cooking.

**12.** For fruits preserved in vinegar, mustard, or salt—such as the mustard called *Knekh* in German—one blesses "fruit of the earth" whether raw or cooked.

**13.** Legumes and beans when eaten fresh—called *Chummis* <note>Chickpeas</note> in Arabic and *Mutzini* <note>Lupins</note> in Greek—one blesses "fruit of the earth."

**14.** Regarding legumes cooked in water to be eaten in soup—called *Polia*—if one eats them after cooking without the soup, and the water has been drained so only the legumes remain in the pot, one blesses "fruit of the earth." This is especially true if oil, salt, and pepper are added.

**15.** For those not cooked in water but dried in the sun and then placed on coals to soften, even if they are not normally eaten that way, one blesses "fruit of the earth." This includes the small *Chilo* beans and those placed in baths without oil. All these legumes require "fruit of the earth," except for dry legumes which are not improved by such processes, for which one blesses "Shehakol."

**1.** Rabbi Yerucham wrote in Path 15: If a companion brings a second wine, one blesses "The Good and He Who Does Good." I found this also in the name of the sages of Vienna. But one should be mindful of Rabbi Yerucham's warning that if the first wine was sufficient, one might be lenient.

**1.** Regarding cinnamon called *Zukarda*: it is a fruit of the earth. One should bless "fruit of the earth" because it is usually eaten dry.

**1.** The *Tur* wrote in Section 206: Bless before the scent. For wood, "fragrant trees"; for herbs, "fragrant herbs." For musk, "various spices." We are accustomed to blessing "various spices" on mixed fragrances to exit the doubt.

<margin>Specifically</margin> for a scent without substance, like in a shop, no blessing is made. But if one grinds the spices and enjoys the physical substance, then a blessing is required. This applies even if the fragrance is in a special vessel of wood or metal.

**2.** The *Tur* wrote in Section 204: For meat, fish, eggs, milk, and bee honey, the blessing is "Shehakol." For sugar, if the scent and taste are not primary, it is "Shehakol." This applies to many things that are potentially harmful or processed.

### Principle 10: Laws of Items Glazed in Honey – 3 Sections

**1.** Legumes cooked in honey for Passover: one blesses "fruit of the earth," as the legume is the primary part of the blessing. Even if the water remains in the pot, once they are cooked and seasoned with oil and pepper, they are the main element.

**The same** applies to any fruit whose form is changed by cooking. If it is eaten raw but improved by cooking—like quinces—the blessing becomes "fruit of the earth." But if it is only there to spice another dish, it is nullified.

**Regarding Lemons:** Even though they are a "living fruit," their status depends on whether they are cooked with meat or fish, or eaten alone.

**In the end**, the essence of the fruit is what matters—whether it be quinces, carobs, or dates. One should be careful with the *Shehecheyanu* blessing on these, as there is a dispute; it is better to bless over a different new fruit or a new garment to cover the requirement.

---

**The general rule** is that a person's intention matters. If one is unsure, the blessing "by Whose word all things exist" <note>Shehakol</note> generally covers all foods if they were not strictly required to have a more specific blessing. However, according to the later authorities, one should strive to recite the proper blessing, "fruit of the earth," whenever appropriate.

And I wrote:</margin> One who sees a rainbow says: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, Who remembers the covenant, is faithful to His covenant, and fulfills His word." <note>original: "Zocher ha-berit ve-ne'eman bi-verito ve-kayam be-ma'amaro"</note> This is as stated in the Talmud in the chapter "The One Who Sees" <note>Berakhot 59a</note>, where Rav Pappa said: "Therefore, let us say both [versions]: 'Blessed... Who remembers the covenant, and is faithful to His covenant, and fulfills His word.'" This is also the ruling in the works of the Alfasi and the Rosh <note>major medieval legal authorities</note>. This serves to exclude the opinion of certain confused individuals who reversed the blessing, saying "faithful to His covenant and fulfills His word" first and only afterward saying "Blessed are You... Who remembers the covenant." According to everyone, this blessing does not have a formal concluding signature <note>a "signature" is a repeating of the blessing formula at the end, like "Blessed are You, Lord, Who remembers the covenant"</note>.

->**The thirteen general rules are finished and complete.**<-

# I have now come to write ten things that are said regarding the general rules of blessings. You must know them, for they are the principles and foundations upon which all blessings depend.

<margin>The 1st Principle</margin> is what the *Tur* <note>The Arba'ah Turim, a 14th-century legal code</note> writes in Section 206: every blessing that does not include the mention of the Name [of God] and Sovereignty <note>original: "Shem u-Malkhut" – referring to the phrase "Lord our God, King of the Universe"</note> is not considered a valid blessing. The *Shulchan Aruch* <note>the standard Code of Jewish Law</note> writes that even if one only omitted the word "Universe" <note>original: "Ha-Olam"</note>, they must repeat the blessing—though the scholar Rabbeinu Yerucham disagrees. Note that those people who bless over any tragedy that may come by saying "Blessed is the True Judge" <note>original: "Dayan Emet"</note> but do not say "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, the True Judge," or those who bless over lightning and thunder saying "Blessed is He Who performs the work of creation" or "Blessed is He Whose strength and might [fill the world]" without the full formula, have not fulfilled their obligation for these blessings.

<margin>The 2nd Principle</margin> is what the *Tur* writes: the person reciting the blessing must hear it with their own ears. However, if they did not hear it but articulated the words clearly with their lips, they have fulfilled the obligation. This is also stated in Section 185.

<margin>The 3rd Principle</margin> is what the *Tur* writes: one must hold the item they are blessing over in their right hand. The *Mordechai* <note>a 13th-century German authority</note> writes: "Every blessing over a commandment should be performed while holding the object in the right hand." Similarly, for the *Havdalah* ceremony <note>separating the Sabbath from the weekday</note>, one holds the wine in the right hand. In Section 214, it explains that one should hold the myrtle branch <note>spice</note> in the right hand and the wine in the left, bless over the myrtle, and then move the wine back to the right hand.

<margin>The 4th Principle</margin> is what the *Tur* writes: if one takes a fruit in hand to eat it and recites the blessing, but it then falls from their hand, or becomes loathsome or lost, they must repeat the blessing. This applies even if there were more fruits of that same type in front of them when they blessed the first one, provided they did not specifically intend to eat the others. This is the opinion of many great authorities. In such a case, one should say: "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever" <note>original: "Baruch shem kavod malkhuto le-olam va-ed"</note> because they uttered God's name in vain.

<margin>And if,</margin> when the fruit fell, they had only said "Blessed are You, Lord" <note>original: "Baruch Ata Hashem"</note> and had not yet said "our God," they should finish by saying "...teach me Your statutes" <note>original: "Lamedeni chukecha" — Psalm 119:12</note>. This makes it appear as if they are simply reciting a verse from the Bible, and thus there is no "taking the Name in vain."

<margin>The 5th Principle</margin> is what the *Tur* writes: for all blessings, one must not allow any interruption between the blessing and the eating or drinking.

<margin>The 6th Principle</margin> is what the *Shulchan Aruch* writes: one who eats less than the size of an olive <note>term: <term>Ke-Zayit</term> — approximately 1 fluid ounce or 28 grams</note> of bread or other food, or drinks less than a "quarter-log" <note>term: <term>Revi'it</term> — approximately 3–4 fluid ounces</note> of wine or other liquids, recites the initial blessing but does not recite the after-blessing at all. Some are uncertain if the after-blessing for wine is recited over an "olive-size" or a "quarter-log." Therefore, it is good to be careful to drink either less than an "olive-size" or a full "quarter-log" to avoid the doubt. The *Tur* and *Shulchan Aruch* rule that after tasting the cup used for Grace After Meals, one must drink at least a "cheekful" <note>approx. 2 ounces</note>, which is the majority of a "quarter-log." <insert>The *Tur* and *Shulchan Aruch* write in Section 184 that the amount of food required to necessitate the Grace After Meals is an "olive-size."</insert>

<margin>Know</margin> that Rabbi Isaac of Corbeil <note>the "Maharaq"</note> wrote that the size of an "olive" is half an egg. This is also the view of the *Maharil* <note>Rabbi Jacob Moelin</note> in the laws of Challah.

<insert>
**P.N.S.** <note>Translator note: likely an abbreviation for a specific glossator or "additional note"</note>
This was said regarding the "olive-size" for eating. However, regarding the "olive-size" for the Chanukah oil... <note>The text here enters a complex technical debate about displaced volume in liquids vs. dry measurements</note>. If the "olive-size" mentioned here for the after-blessing were exactly the same as the "quarter-log" mentioned here, why would the *Shulchan Aruch* say there is a doubt? Clearly, they are different measurements. Note that the "quarter-log" is described by the *Maharil* as being nearly the volume of two chicken eggshells. When we say a "quarter-log" is an egg and a half, we mean when measuring by displacing water in a vessel. But when filling the shells, it is two shells. Rabbi Isaac of Prague wrote: "A quarter-log is the volume of an egg and a half." Every soulful person should keep these measurements before their eyes when eating and drinking to ensure they recite blessings according to the required amounts.
</insert>

<margin>The 7th Principle</margin> is based on what the Sages said in the Mishnah: if salt and bread are brought before someone, they bless over the salty food <note>the "primary" part of the snack</note> and it exempts the bread, for the bread is "secondary" <note>term: <term>Tafel</term></note> to it. This is the rule: whenever there is a primary food <note>term: <term>Ikar</term></note> and a secondary food with it, one blesses over the primary and exempts the secondary, even if their blessings are not usually the same. The *Beit Yosef* <note>commentary by Joseph Karo</note> adds that this exemption also applies to the after-blessing. Even bread, which is usually the most important food, can be secondary—for example, if one eats salty fish and eats bread only to soothe the throat from the saltiness, they bless on the fish and the bread is exempted.

<margin>And do not</margin> <insert>
**P.N.S.**
Try to be too clever and say that this rule only applies when the secondary food is strictly medicinal, like the bread for the salty fish. You might think that if you eat the secondary food for pleasure or to be full, it shouldn't be exempted by the primary food's blessing. However, this is not so. It appears clearly from the *Asheri* <note>the Rosh</note> that the primary always exempts the secondary, even if one could have eaten the primary alone. He proves this from the case of radishes and olives—where the radish is the primary and exempts the olive—showing that "secondary" status is determined by the intent of the meal, not just physical necessity.
</insert>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the laws of blessings, specifically concluding the rules regarding the blessing of "Who has kept us alive" (Shehecheyanu) on seasonal items and moving into the detailed laws of after-blessings (Berakhot Acharonot). It bridges the transition from Rule 11 to Rules 12 and 13.</meta>

<page-num>201</page-num>
<header>The Gate of Letters</header>

[Regarding the blessing over seasonal produce:] ...not to say it over any vegetable, even if it is new. For there are vegetables of which one might say, "See, this is new" (meaning it grew this year), yet it has "already been in the world" <note>Ecclesiastes 1:10</note>—meaning this "new" produce actually grew last year and remained delayed in the ground until now. What the world calls "new" is based on the judgment of their eyes, for they see a green appearance and assume it arrived recently and sprouted this year. However, it is possible the truth is otherwise, and it grew last year; because it was only recently plucked from the ground, it appears to people as if it is truly new. Since people cannot be certain if it is truly new or not, Mahari V. <note>likely Rabbi Isaac ibn Ghiyyat or Mahari Weil</note> and my teacher <note>likely referring to the author’s primary instructor</note> agreed that one should not recite the blessing "Who has kept us alive" <note>original: Shehecheyanu</note> over any vegetable, even if it is presumed to be new, lest people be mistaken and come to recite a blessing in vain.

**T**his is how it appears to me to explain the words of Mahari V., so that his words do not contradict each other—specifically the implications of the beginning and end of his statement. At the **beginning** of his words, he opened by saying that one does not recite the blessing "Who has kept us alive" over "vegetables" in general, implying even if it is clearly new, he holds one does not bless. But look at the **end** of his words: "because it stands in the ground... and is not distinguishable between new growth from this year and growth from last year." This implies that the reason is only because it is *not* distinguishable; if its newness *were* recognizable, one would recite the blessing. Thus, the parts contradict! However, it must be as I explained above: even though it *appears* new to people, one cannot rely on this to recite the blessing, as they cannot determine the true essence of the matter. This is why Mahari V. concluded by saying "it is not distinguishable," meaning that when one buys a new vegetable from the market, it is not clearly known if it grew this year or last year. Since we cannot know the matter clearly, we remain in a state of doubt. Therefore, we do not recite "Who has kept us alive" over any vegetable, even if it is new, for we must not enter into the doubt of a blessing said in vain. With this, the sharp words of Mahari V. are well explained. It is possible that for this same reason, the world is not accustomed to reciting "Who has kept us alive" over new bread, because it is not easily distinguished from old bread, and bread is often switched for other bread, just as one vegetable is switched for another.

---

## Rule 12: Regarding the Laws of After-Blessings, their Formulas, and what they Cover, and when one exempts the other. This contains two sections.

**1** The *Tur* <note>The Arba'ah Turim, the 14th-century legal code</note> wrote in Section 210 and Section 208: the variation in blessings between "Who creates the fruit of the tree," "Who creates the fruit of the earth," and things that do not grow from the ground applies specifically to the *first* blessing. However, regarding the *after-blessing*, which is "Who creates many souls..." <note>original: Borei Nefashot</note>, it is the same for all of them. The exceptions are grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, and dates <note>The "Five Species" of fruit associated with the Land of Israel</note>, after which one recites the "One Blessing Reflecting the Three" <note>original: Me-ein Shalosh / Al Ha-Etz</note>. Likewise, if one made a cooked dish from the five species of grain (see Rule 3, Section 1), one recites the "One Blessing Reflecting the Three" <note>original: Al Ha-Michya</note>. I shall now write for you the text of the after-blessings:

**The text of "Who creates many souls":** "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, Who creates many souls and their deficiencies, for all that You have created to sustain the soul of every living thing. Blessed be the Life of the worlds." (The explanation of the blessing: **"and their deficiencies"** refers to essential things like bread and water, without which one cannot survive. **"for all that You have created to sustain the soul of every living thing"** refers to all other things created that are not essential for survival but were created for pleasure and added goodness, such as fruit and the like. The word "deficiencies" is linked to the beginning of the blessing).

**And these are the texts of the "One Blessing Reflecting the Three":**
**For wine:** "Blessed are You... for the vine and the fruit of the vine, and for the desirable, good, and spacious land... have mercy, Lord our God, on Israel Your people and on Jerusalem Your city... and build Jerusalem the holy city quickly in our days... for You, Lord, are good and do good to all. [Blessed are You] for the land and for the fruit of the vine." In this text, it appears it is intentionally not according to Samuel <note>a Talmudic sage</note>, who said in the chapter *Arvei Pesachim* that all blessings must mention the theme of the conclusion just before the end. This is also found in the *Tur*, Section 208.

**For fruit** such as olives, grapes, figs, pomegranates, and dates: one says "Blessed are You... for the tree and the fruit of the tree, and for the desirable land..." until the end, "for the land and for the fruits." Those who live in the Land of Israel conclude: "for the land and for *its* fruits."

**For the five species of grain** (wheat, barley, spelt, oats, and rye): one says "Blessed are You... for the sustenance and the nourishment, and for the produce of the field, and for the desirable land..." until "for the land and for the sustenance and the nourishment." (See Rule 3, Section 1. One must also mention the specific occasion, such as on the Holy Sabbath: "For You are good and do good, and may You comfort us on this Sabbath day," or "rejoice us on this Festival of [Name]," or on the New Moon: "remember us for good on this New Moon day," and then "For You are good and do good.")

**2** The *Tur* further wrote in the aforementioned Section 60: "And my brother, Rabbi Yechiel, wrote in the name of our father, the Rosh <note>Rabbeinu Asher, 13th-century legal giant</note>, that if one drank wine and then water (and not specifically water, but also beer or honey-mead, and other drinks), one does not bless 'Who creates many souls' over the water, because the 'One Blessing Reflecting the Three' said over wine exempts them. Even though the drinks did not come because of the wine—and we hold that wine exempts all other drinks regarding the *first* blessing because of its importance—nevertheless, even if they are not included in the 'fruit of the vine' formula, the after-blessing covers them."

<gloss>This means: even if at the time one blessed over the wine, they only intended to drink that single cup and no more, but afterward found they wanted to drink another cup of water or another beverage. In such a case, the wine requires you to go back and bless 'By Whose word all things exist' <note>Shehakol</note> over the water, because the first blessing over the wine no longer exempts it due to the 'interruption of intent' (as seen in Tur section 174). Nevertheless, when you later bless the 'Three-fold blessing' over the wine, it also exempts the other drinks from their after-blessing. This is similar to fruit eaten during a meal, where the blessing over bread does not exempt them from an after-blessing, yet the Grace After Meals covers them. So too here with drinks: even if the wine's first blessing didn't cover them because of the interruption of intent, the wine's after-blessing covers them because wine is the 'king' of drinks and establishes the session, just as bread does for a meal. Since wine is considered the primary drink, its final blessing is sufficient for all secondary drinks consumed.</gloss>

**The general rule** according to the *Tur*: if one blessed over wine and drank it, and afterward drank other liquids, one does not need to bless over the other liquids at all—neither before nor after. For the blessing over the wine that was said first, and the blessing said at the end, exempts any drinks consumed. Even if a situation arose where one was required to say a first blessing over the secondary drinks (due to the "interruption of intent" mentioned above), the *after-blessing* of the wine still exempts them.

---

## Rule 13: Containing two specific sections.

**1** One whose son becomes a **Bar Mitzvah**: the father should bless, when the son is called to the Torah: "Blessed is He who has released me from the punishment of this one." <note>original: Baruch she-petarani me-onsho shel zeh</note>. So wrote my teacher of blessed memory in Section 228: to recite this blessing without the Name and Kingdom <note>i.e., omitting "Lord our God, King of the Universe" to avoid a potential blessing in vain</note>.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the laws of blessings from the previous page, shifting from seasonal produce to the specific relationship between ritual hand washing and the blessing over bread. It then transitions into general rules for "doubtful" blessing scenarios and concludes by beginning a new ethical treatise on holiness and personal conduct.</meta>
