<header>The Gate of Letters</header>

<margin>Chayyei Adam, Part 2, 4:50, see there.</margin> **Since they wrote** that their custom was to eat a little bit during the time of drinking so that they would be able to drink, it follows from this explanation that even though the food is not currently before him, it is considered as if it were before him. Since this was their established custom, it is mentioned at the end. If so, the explanation is that one does not need to recite the "Who brings forth" <note>original: Hamotzi</note> blessing over that bread which they eat during the drinking session to enable the drinking; for whenever there is a primary item and a secondary item accompanying it, one recites the blessing over the primary item alone. Even so, they wrote that one requires ritual hand washing <note>original: Netilat Yadayim</note> because of that small amount of food he eats.

<margin>Ibid.</margin> In this regard, they follow the Talmudic view of Rabbi Yochanan that one requires hand washing for bread even when it is secondary and does not require the "Who brings forth" blessing; even so, one must wash his eyes—and this is exactly our case. **And one** should not raise a difficulty from what the Tosafot <note>12th-13th century French Talmudic commentators</note> explained in the chapters "On the Eve of Passover" and "Covering the Blood," or what the Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Yehiel, c. 1250–1327</note> wrote, regarding the case of one who distanced himself <note>interrupted his meal</note>: that the hand washing always depends on the "Who brings forth" blessing. The understanding from their words is that they hold hand washing and the "Who brings forth" blessing are dependent on one another. **But one** can answer that these mentioned commentators did not mean to say that hand washing is *always* tied to the blessing, such that he must recite the "Who brings forth" blessing in every case—whether for eating or for drinking—as mentioned above in the words of Rav Hisda.

**Rather**, it seems to me that this is what they meant: since it is considered "drinking," and he distanced himself such that his mind was diverted regarding hand washing (as the Baraita <note>an early oral tradition</note> explicitly teaches regarding one who distanced himself), this distance is considered a diversion of the mind regarding the "Who brings forth" blessing as well, in a case where that blessing is relevant. For example, if he went out in the middle of a meal, distanced himself, and then returned to eat—then he must wash his hands, as taught in the aforementioned Baraita. This is what Rav Hisda meant by "but for eating." Regarding this, the Tosafot and the Rosh wrote that since we require hand washing, we also require the "Who brings forth" blessing, because it constitutes a diversion of the mind, requiring him to repeat the blessing just as he must repeat the washing for the sake of cleanliness. This follows the view that we do not say "he returns to his original status" (whereas the Tosafot wrote there that if the law followed the other view, even a blessing at the start would not be needed, and this is according to Rav Hisda who said "he returns to his original status"). But regarding the "for drinking" case mentioned by Rav Hisda, the Tosafot and the Rosh did not speak at all.

**And they** did not come now to inform us—by saying that hand washing depends on the blessing—of anything other than to prove in the case of "distancing" that the wine they are drinking there, in that mentioned place, constitutes a diversion of the mind from the meal. Therefore, one must bless before it but not after it; this is the point around which all the words of the Tosafot revolve. And this is why they wrote there, after saying that hand washing implies the "Who brings forth" blessing: "But he does not say the Grace After Meals" <note>original: Birkat Hamazon</note>. See clearly that their main point in that discussion is to inform us that a diversion of the mind requires a new blessing on what one *intends* to eat, but not on what one has *already* eaten. this is to exclude the view of some commentators who believe a diversion of the mind affects the final blessing on what was already consumed (see *Terumat HaDeshen* sign 50, and in sign 10 he brings the commentary of Rashi, Tosafot, and the Rosh who argue on this). And if this were not so, why would the Tosafot and Rosh write that washing depends on the blessing? It refers back to what was discussed by Rav Hisda—that he only said "for drinking"—and they explained that their custom during drinking was
->to eat a little to sweeten the drink, as mentioned above.<-

### Section 2
<margin>The implication of the words of Maggid Mishneh:</margin> Wonder at yourself: how could the Tosafot and the Rosh write that hand washing depends on the "Who brings forth" blessing? For we are dealing here with a case where the drinking is the primary act and the bread is secondary! Let him remember the rule: whenever there is a primary item and a secondary item, one blesses on the primary and exempts the secondary, as noted earlier. **Rather**, one must certainly say that what the Tosafot and Rosh wrote—that hand washing depends on the "Who brings forth" blessing—applies specifically to the "but for eating" case mentioned by Rav Hisda alone. In that case, the washing and the blessing come as one according to the logic of this Baraita, which holds that we do not say "he returns to his original status." Therefore, the Tosafot and Rosh wrote that we require the blessing, but not the Grace After Meals.

Their whole purpose was to prove from here that a diversion of the mind ruins the first blessing for what he wants to eat, but not retroactively for what he already ate, since the Baraita does not mention Grace After Meals. **But** regarding the "for drinking" mentioned by Rav Hisda, where he also washes his hands (as in the Baraita of "distancing"), the Tosafot and Rosh did not say that washing depends on the blessing. For in that case, one is not required to say the "Who brings forth" blessing according to everyone; even if we say there is a diversion of the mind regarding washing, nevertheless, since the drinking is primary and the bread is secondary, the drinking exempts the bread from its own blessing, based on the rule of "primary and secondary,"
<margin>See Rama, end of sign 168.</margin> as explained before us. **Nevertheless**, since we do not find any legal authority explicitly stating that one must wash for "secondary bread," in our case I think it is best for someone who wants to eat bread during drinking (to enable him to drink much) to not eat it [in a way that requires washing], or that he should wash his hands and recite the blessing over the washing, and thus remove himself from all doubt, for blessings
<margin>See Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Ch. 6 of Berakhot.</margin> do not invalidate the act if omitted. **And from this** we see that someone who does not eat during drinking to "sweeten" the drink at all, except when drinking during a meal (meaning after the "Who brings forth" blessing and before Grace After Meals), perhaps this might lead to "misuse of sacred property" <note>original: Me'ilah; here used colloquially for a blessing error</note> because we are not experts. Now it is better to eat for the sake of sweetening the drink or for other things
->unless he knows with absolute certainty that he is eating it only to sweeten the drink, or he should eat without the bread blessing, and may a blessing come upon him.<-

<margin>See sign 167</margin>
### The Eighth Rule
This is what the *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, 14th century</note> wrote in sign 167: If he forgot and put food into his mouth without a prior blessing—if they are liquids, he should swallow them and finish them, and then bless over them while swallowing. This is considered "prior to the enjoyment." This is according to the view of the Rosh. However, the later authorities argue with him, holding that he should swallow them but *not* recite the first blessing, as the opportunity has already passed and the meal cannot be "repaired." This is a case of "doubt in blessings," where we are lenient; see the *Shulchan Aruch* and the *Rama* <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles</note> on this. **And if** they are fruits that would become
->disgusting if removed from his mouth, he should move them to one side, bless, and then swallow them. If they do not become disgusting, such as beans, he should spit them out until he blesses.<-

### The Ninth Rule
If he is in doubt as to whether it is "fruit of the tree" or "fruit of the earth," he should recite the general "by whose word" <note>original: Shehakol</note> blessing. If he said "by whose word" over anything, he has fulfilled his obligation, even over bread and wine. So wrote the *Tur* in signs 202 and 206, and the *Beit Yosef*. See also Rule 8, sign 10, and Rule 3, sign 3.

### The Tenth Rule
This is what is written in the *Shulchan Aruch* in sign 204 and sign 167: For all blessings, if one is in doubt whether he blessed or not, he does not bless, neither at the beginning nor at the end, except for Grace After Meals, because it is a Torah-mandated obligation <note>most other blessings are rabbinic, but Grace After Meals is derived directly from Deuteronomy 8:10</note>.

### Now
It is time to speak of the laws of covering and its purity, and of the holiness of the "source" <note>a euphemism for the reproductive organs/sexual conduct</note> in general and in particular, regarding "turning away from evil and doing good."

### Regarding "Turning Away from Evil"
I have not come to mention the severity of forbidden relations <note>original: Arayot</note>, wasted seed, or the impurity of the menstruant <note>original: Niddah</note>, for we are not dealing with the wicked who deserve the death of the body and the death of the soul, and whose lives are cut off into perdition—may we be saved. The People of Israel are holy, and the Torah commanded: "You shall be holy" <note>Leviticus 19:2</note>. Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, 11th century</note> explained: "Wherever you find a 'fence' <note>a restrictive boundary</note> against forbidden relations, you find holiness." According to our words, the concept of holiness is extra abstinence, as in the principle: "Sanctify yourself through that which is permitted to you" <note>Talmud, Yevamot 20a</note> by making for yourself fences and safeguards. This is Rashi's precision: "where you find a *fence* for forbidden relations," and he did not simply say "forbidden relations," for that is obvious. Rather, he said the *fence* and the safeguard, like vows which are a fence for abstinence. I will mention a few of them, as we learn in Tractate Bava Batra, the chapter "Possession of Houses," page 50: "And he who shuts his eyes from seeing evil"—Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba said: This refers to one who does not look at women when they are standing over the laundry. What are the circumstances? If there is no other way, he is "compelled" <note>not at fault</note>. If there is another way and he goes there anyway, he is a wicked man. It must be that there is no other way, yet even so, he should "hide his soul" <note>look away</note>. And we learn in Tractate Eruvin, chapter "They Make Partitions," page 18, and in the last chapter of Berakhot, page 61, and in the first chapter of Tractate Kallah: One who counts out coins into a woman's hand from his own hand, or from her hand to his, in order to gaze at her—even if he was as great in Torah as Moses <note>original: as the one who received the Torah from Mount Sinai</note>, the verse says: "Hand to hand, the evil one shall not go unpunished" <note>Proverbs 11:21</note>; he shall not be cleansed from the judgment of Hell. And we also learn in Tractate Kallah, first chapter: Yehuda bar Achai bar Yoshiya says: Anyone who gazes at women will eventually come to transgression. Anyone who turns himself away from transgression and does not do it, even if he is an ordinary Israelite, is worthy of offering an offering like a High Priest <note>original: Kohen Gadol</note> upon the Altar, as it says: "And he sent the young men of the children of Israel..." <note>Exodus 24:5</note>. Anyone who guards himself and shuts his eyes from transgression in this world... and the Divine Presence is among the ministering angels, as it says: "And they envisioned God, and they ate and drank" <note>Exodus 24:11</note>. And we also learn in Tractate Berakhot, chapter "One Who Sees," page 61: Rabbi Yochanan said: Better to walk behind a lion than behind a woman; behind a woman than behind an idol; behind an idol than behind a synagogue while the congregation is praying. But they only said this when there is no other path, and he is not leading a donkey, and he is not riding a camel, and he is not wearing phylacteries <note>original: Tefillin</note>. But if one of these is the case, 
we have no concern. And we learn in Tractate Shabbat, chapter "With what may a woman go out?", page 60: It was taught in the school of Rabbi Ishmael:
"Sinsinim" <note>clusters</note>—just as thorns and briars are to Israel, so were the people of that generation, because their eyes went astray after forbidden relations. And Rav said:
"Sinsini"—what are the thorns? The verse refers to the tribes with the ornaments on their faces for whoever wants, for whoever is able to look...

It concludes by introducing the concept of holiness through self-restraint, citing Talmudic warnings against immodest gazing.</summary>

<meta>The previous page discussed the laws of blessings, specifically the criteria for ritual handwashing when eating bread that might be secondary to another food or drink. This page continues that legal analysis, citing various medieval authorities to establish when the blessing on a "primary" food exempts a "secondary" one and whether ritual requirements like handwashing still apply in those cases.</meta>

# The Gate of Letters

He eats it primarily, and he only eats the olive-sized portion of bread in order to sweeten the bitterness of the outer thing <note>referring to a primary food that is sharp or bitter</note>, as is explained there in the Talmud. Even so, the Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Yehiel, c. 1250–1327, a prominent legal authority</note> compared this to the law of the "Hear O Israel" <note>original: Shema</note> prayer. We can clearly conclude from this that he holds that in any case of a <term>primary and secondary item</term> <note>original: Ikar ve-Tafel; a legal principle where the blessing on the main food covers the side dish</note> in the world, the primary item exempts the secondary, even if he only eats the secondary item to prevent harm from the first food.

**And furthermore**, there is clear proof from what the Tosafot <note>12th-13th century French and German commentators</note> wrote regarding the Mishnah in the Talmud in the chapter "All Manners of [Seeds]": Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna were sitting together... they brought dates and pomegranates before them. Rav Hamnuna took and recited the blessing over the dates first, etc. The Tosafot wrote there, and these are their words: "And you did not eat them as an accompaniment to bread, for if so, the bread would be the primary and they would be secondary, and we have learned that one blesses over the primary and exempts the secondary," end of quote. Here you see explicitly that if he had used them to accompany the bread, then the bread would exempt the dates and pomegranates because the primary exempts the secondary. This is true even though this secondary item is not coming to remove a prior harm—for certainly if he ate the bread alone without dates and pomegranates, the bread would not harm his throat—and even so, the Tosafot wrote that if he accompanied the bread with them, it would follow the law of primary and secondary, and one would bless over the primary, etc. 

As for why the Tur <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, author of the Arba'ah Turim legal code</note> mentions regarding the law of primary and secondary above that [the secondary is eaten] "so it will not harm his throat," etc., it is because the Tur wanted to find a case where even bread could be secondary to something else. He could only find such a case where one eats something very salty and eats bread with it so it won't harm his throat. The Tur’s main intention here is to inform us that anything in the world can be secondary to something else. Even bread, which is the most important of all foods, can be secondary—for example, if one ate salty fish and ate bread with it to prevent it from harming his throat, he recites the blessing over the fish and exempts the bread since it is secondary. Do not say that bread is never secondary because of its importance; he comes to teach us that sometimes it is indeed secondary. This is easy to understand.

<margin>This is from the author.</margin> And my teacher <note>likely referring to the Shulchan Aruch HaRav or a similar authority</note> wrote in his Shulchan Aruch, and these are his words: "And some say if the secondary item is more beloved to him, he blesses over it and afterward over the primary. The rule that one blesses over the primary and exempts the secondary applies only when he eats them together or eats the primary first. But if he ate the secondary first—for example, if he wants to drink and wants to eat first so that he does not drink on an empty stomach <note>original: aliba de-kanya; literally 'on the heart of the pipe/throat'</note>, or if he ate berries to sweeten the drink—he blesses over the food first, even though it is secondary to the drinking. For how could the primary exempt it later with its blessing retroactively when he has already enjoyed the food without a blessing? In such a case, he only recites the general 'By whose word' <note>original: Shehakol</note> blessing, since it is secondary to something else," etc. 

It seems to me that from the general principle that where there is a primary item and an accompanying secondary item, one blesses over the primary, etc., as mentioned above, we can derive this law: regarding those people who sometimes eat bread during a drinking session so they are able to drink—if the bread was before him at the time of the blessing over the drink (for the secondary is only exempted by the blessing on the primary when the secondary is before him at the time of the blessing on the primary, as the Mishnah states: "and with it a secondary item," and as explicitly written that the blessing on the primary does not exempt the secondary unless the secondary is placed before him at the time he blessed over the primary; so it is also clearly implied in the Tosafot there in the passage beginning "Like those who eat fruit," etc., see there), let him bless over the drink according to its proper blessing and exempt the bread, since it is secondary to the drinking. One should not distinguish in this matter between a case of "food and food" versus "drink and food," as the Maharayi <note>Israel Isserlein, 1390–1460</note> wrote in the Terumat HaDeshen in the book of responsas, section 18, see there. And even if the bread was not initially before him when he blessed over the drink, but his mind was set upon it and he expected they would bring it to him, it is considered as if it were before him, and the blessing over the drink exempts the bread.

->This is the conclusion<-

**And do not** be surprised that we compare the law of blessings over commandments to the law of blessings over pleasures. For the Rosh, in the tenth chapter of Pesachim (which the Tur brought in section 432 regarding the blessing of searching [for leaven]), which is a blessing over a commandment, compared it to the "Who brings forth" <note>original: Hamotzi</note> blessing for a meal, which is a blessing over pleasure. He argued that just as one who finished eating and intends to eat again can later engage in idle chatter and does not need to repeat the blessing over the bread, so too here: if one started searching, there is no concern for the blessing if he later engaged in idle chatter. So too, we shall do the same in our comparison, as we compare the law of blessings over commandments—such as ritual slaughter and circumcision—to the law of blessings over pleasures. 

(Or if his mind was clearly set on it, even if the bread was not initially before him, but it was the standard practice to always bring a little food during the drinking session so they could drink, it is considered as if it were before him.) Since it is their habit, when he blesses at the beginning, he blesses with this in mind. And so it must be said regarding the Talmud in the chapter "All Manners of [Seeds]" regarding what they said there: "Why do I need to say that wine [drunk] before the meal exempts wine after the meal? Only on Sabbaths and Festivals, since a person establishes his meal over wine," etc., see there. Thus, he exempts it with the blessing over the drink, just as with all types of food that we are accustomed to: even though they are not on the table at the time we recite the "Who brings forth" blessing, they do not require a blessing at all. Since it is common to bring various foods during a meal, the blessing over the bread and the meal exempts them. 

But if the bread was not before him at the time of the blessing over the drink, and he also did not have it in mind at the time of the blessing over the drink that they would bring it to him, and then in the middle of drinking he decided to eat bread—and it is also not their habit to bring bread every time they drink, but only sometimes—then he certainly must recite the "Who brings forth" blessing when they bring it to him afterward. Since he changed his mind, it no longer falls under the law of secondary and primary at all. 

However, regarding the matter of <term>ritual hand washing</term> <note>original: Netilah</note>, there is no difference at all whether the bread was before him at the time of the blessing over the drink or not. In any case, he must wash his hands just as he would for a primary meal of bread. Since the Sages required hand washing for bread in general, they did not distinguish between primary and secondary. For this is how we should establish the law, according to their logic: rather, we must say the Rabbis did not make a distinction (since it is bread in its own right), and especially in a common matter like this. (This reasoning has support even in Rabbinic decrees, as seen in the Tosafot in the chapter "The Man Who Betroths," in the passage beginning "And it turns out to be a 'strange woman' retroactively," etc., see there.) 

Furthermore, follow the reason for the rule: the reason for hand washing is because of "a trace of impurity" <note>original: Serach Tumah</note>, meaning perhaps he will touch <term>Terumah</term> <note>the portion of produce given to the Priests, which must be eaten in ritual purity</note> and make it impure. Even though Terumah does not apply in this day and age, we decree as a safeguard lest the Temple be rebuilt soon, because Terumah is a serious matter. And let us say that wherever there is a decree because of a trace of Terumah for when the Temple is rebuilt, then what does it matter if it is a touching of bread that requires the "Who brings forth" blessing or a touching of bread that does not require it? Is it not the same bread? In either case, it becomes impure by the touch of unwashed hands. Just because it is secondary to drinking and exempt from the "Who brings forth" blessing, is it not bread? Is it not capable of becoming impure? 

According to this reasoning, the Sages required washing for something dipped in liquid (see General Rule 8, Section 6), even though the liquid is secondary to the item being dipped. This is easy to understand. And so it is implied by Rashi in Tractate Shabbat, who explained the Talmudic passage (in the chapter "The Appointed Official Said to Them") regarding a Baraita <note>an early oral tradition</note> which the Tur brought in Section 176: "The law of a meal: a man who goes out to urinate washes one hand and enters. Rabbi Chanin and his colleague differ: he washes both hands and enters. And when he washes, he should not wash outside because of suspicion, etc., until Rav Chisda said: We only said this regarding drinking, but for eating, he washes outside," etc. Rashi explained: "The law of a meal," meaning this law was stated among the laws of the meal. A man who leaves the middle of a meal to urinate washes one hand—the one with which he handled the urine—but if he delayed for a while, he washes two hands. Since he delayed for an hour or two, he diverted his attention from his meal and was not careful to guard his hands, and hands are "busy" <note>constantly touching things</note>. He should not wash outside so they don't say about him that he didn't wash at all. "We only said he should not wash outside" except when he does not need to eat anymore and is only entering to drink, for they were accustomed to lingering over drinks after the meal. (The explanation of "distanced" is after they removed their hands from the bread but before they recited the Grace After Meals). "However, he must wash lest he put a piece of bread into his mouth," end of quote. 

Here you have it explicitly according to Rashi: even though he does not need to eat anymore, and the primary reason he is returning is to drink, as Rashi explicitly explained, he still requires hand washing lest he eat bread, which is secondary to the drinking. It is obvious that the washing is not because of the "Who brings forth" blessing, for Rashi used the phrasing "lest he put a piece into his mouth" and did not use the simpler phrasing "lest he recite the blessing over bread without washing." From this, we see that Rashi holds, according to this Baraita, that one does not need to recite the blessing over this bread because it is secondary to the drinking—since he does not need to eat anymore and only enters to drink, as Rashi explained. And the small amount of bread he eats now, he eats to flavor his drink, as mentioned above. Therefore, even though he might need to recite the blessing over the drink (since it is after the meal, and the established law is that wine during the meal does not exempt wine after the meal), the blessing over the drink exempts the bread since it is secondary. Following the rule that whenever there is a primary item and an accompanying secondary item, one blesses on the primary, etc. Even so, he holds that he requires hand washing just as if it were a primary meal of bread, because the concern for the impurity of Terumah remains in place, as mentioned above.

**And so** the students of Rabbeinu Yonah <note>13th-century Spanish scholar</note> also explained explicitly there in the chapter "These are the things," regarding the case where he "delayed" mentioned above, which was brought by the Rif <note>Rabbi Isaac Alfasi</note> and the Tosafot. And here one might ask: how can he say "we only said this for drinking," given that one does not need to wash for drinking? The answer is that their custom during a drinking session was to eat a little bit so that they would be able to drink. Therefore, they said he needs to wash because of that small amount he eats. And he must do it in front of them so his companions see that he abandoned his hands and then washed them, and they won't suspect him of being someone who is not careful to wash his hands as if he were eating. But when the primary activity is eating, they would not suspect him of failing to wash his hands. From my teacher.

<summary>This page analyzes the laws of "Primary and Secondary" foods, establishing that blessings on a main item (like wine) can exempt secondary items (like bread eaten for health or flavor), though ritual handwashing remains a strict requirement for bread regardless of its status.</summary>

# The Gate of Letters
### Page 95
->**The 25th Letter**<-
<meta>catchword: for them</meta>

Is it just because of habit? As we say in the Haggadah <note>the narrative/homiletic sections of the Talmud</note> in the chapter "The Presumptive Ownership of Houses" <note>original: Chezkas HaBatim; Bava Batra 58a</note> regarding our forefather Abraham, that he would lay his head in Sarah's lap while she looked for lice in his hair. And they said: "Let Rabbi Banna’ah enter, for he is well aware that the 'Evil Inclination' <note>original: Yetzer HaRa; the personification of the impulse to sin</note> does not exist in this world" <note>meaning, at that high level of holiness, there is no physical temptation</note>. However, I am not saying that it is permitted to be secluded with forbidden women <note>original: Arayot; women with whom a man is biblically forbidden to have relations</note> just because one is not familiar with them, or to say that we do not fear that seclusion will lead to a forbidden act. For we have learned that we do not escort the dead and their burden, etc. One may not be secluded with any of the forbidden women mentioned in the Torah, except for certain exceptions. Rather, I am saying it is possible to suggest that when the Sages forbade handing a vessel or doing other things that are not very familiar, they only forbade it with one's wife while she is a *Niddah* <note>a woman during her menstrual period, during which physical contact is restricted</note>, because he is familiar with her. But regarding other women with whom he is not familiar, there is a difference between someone he is used to and someone he is not. This is the end of the quote. However, he did not explicitly mention the permission for other forbidden women to eat with him from the same bowl; he only mentioned handing a vessel and such. But the matter of eating with her, he did not mention. And it is already known what our Sages, of blessed memory, said: "Great is a morsel of food, for it brings people close." Despite all this, it seems to me that since the world is accustomed to being lenient with other forbidden women <note>meaning social interactions that are not secluded</note>, one should not change the custom except regarding a married woman <note>original: Eshet Ish</note>. And the reason for being lenient with other forbidden relatives is that the "Evil Inclination" is blinded so as not to be tempted by them in public; since they are relatives, there is no loss in being lenient. But with a married woman, it is proper to be strict. Even though regarding handing a cup and such, one need not be strict even with a married woman—based on the reason written by the Rashba <note>Rabbi Shlomo ben Aderet, c. 1235–1310</note> that he is not "familiar" with her—nevertheless, regarding eating with her from a single bowl, it is proper to be strict. Indeed, it is written explicitly in *Binyamin Ze'ev* <note>a 16th-century legal work</note>, sign 147, not to eat with a married woman from the same bowl. And even with a married woman, one is not obligated to be so strict except when eating with her alone from one bowl; but when the entire household eats together with her, one should not change the custom. However, if it is just him alone with her, I forbid doing so, even when it is not technically a forbidden seclusion—such as when the door of the house is open or many people are in the house—nevertheless, this shared eating leads to affection.

It is written in the *Knesset HaGedolah* <note>a 17th-century legal commentary</note> on the *Tur*, *Even HaEzer* section 21: The *Mordechai* <note>Rabbi Mordechai ben Hillel, d. 1298</note> wrote in the chapter "Even Though," that Rabbi Baruch says that even though one may not be served by a woman in the manner of a maidservant, it is permitted in the way that Abigail said to David: "To wash the feet of the servants of my lord" <note>1 Samuel 25:41</note>. And that which is implied in the Jerusalem Talmud—that it is forbidden—refers to matters of seclusion in a place of seclusion. But in a bathhouse, since many people are present there, it is permitted. From here [we see] that daughters and maidservants may wash us in the bathhouse. This is the end of his quote. But I say: Let this matter be forgotten and never spoken of! It is forbidden to let such a thing cross one's lips. I suspect that some mistaken student wrote this on his own and attributed it to his teacher. These are the words of the *Knesset HaGedolah*. And the *Darchei Moshe* <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles, c. 1520–1572</note> in his glosses added to reject this opinion of Rabbi Baruch. And leave aside his piety in this matter, for he should have been at least as strict as the Priests. Especially according to what I found in the *Ralbag* <note>Rabbi Levi ben Gershon, 1288–1344</note> in his name, who says it is not proper to rely on Rabbi Baruch in the face of the rejection by our Sages of blessed memory. And regarding Abigail’s words, "to wash the feet of the servants of my lord," she said this out of humility, to indicate that it would be fitting for her to be a wife to one of the servants of her master and to wash his feet, as is the custom of a woman for her husband. These are the words of the *Ralbag*. Therefore, it seems right to be strict, and who can say otherwise? There are other matters of abstinence to mention; however, the People of Israel are already warned and are holy. Even regarding forbidden relations, I will not speak at length.

**But** I have come to speak at length and with great intensity regarding the "Fury of the Transgression" <note>referring to a specific sexual sin</note>, the great and severe sin of wasting seed in vain—may the Merciful One save us. It is said in Tractate *Niddah*, at the beginning of the chapter "Every Hand" <note>Niddah 13a</note>: It was taught that Rabbi Eliezer says: "Anyone who holds his member and urinates is as if he brings a flood upon the world." Rabbi Eleazar said to him: "But won't the sparks of urine splash on his feet and make him appear to have a damaged organ <note>original: beruach shefichah; referring to an anatomical defect</note>, thereby casting a slur on his children that they are illegitimate <note>original: mamzerim</note>?" He replied: "Better that he cast a slur on his children as being illegitimate than that he make himself wicked for one moment before the Omnipresent." And we ask there: Why is it so severe? Because he spills seed in vain. For Rabbi Yohanan said: "Anyone who spills seed in vain is liable for death, as it is said: 'And what he did was evil in the eyes of the Lord, and He killed him also'" <note>Genesis 38:10, referring to Onan</note>. Rabbi Isaac and Rabbi Ammi said: "It is as if he spills blood, as it is said: 'You who inflame yourselves among the terebinths, under every leafy tree, who slaughter the children in the valleys' <note>Isaiah 57:5</note>—do not read it as 'slaughtering' (*shochtei*) but as 'squeezing' (*sochtei*)." Rav Ashi says: "It is as if he worships idols; it is written here 'under every leafy tree' and it is written there regarding idols, 'upon the high mountains and upon the hills and under every leafy tree.'"

**See there**, Rabbi Judah said: "One who brings himself to an erection intentionally should be under a ban of excommunication." And let the master say it is simply forbidden? Because he incites the Evil Inclination against himself. Rabbi Ammi said: "He is called a transgressor, for such is the way of the Evil Inclination: today it tells him 'do this,' and tomorrow it tells him 'go and worship idols,' and he goes and worships." If you wish, I can say that Rabbi Ammi said: "Anyone who brings himself to forbidden thoughts is not permitted into the presence of the Holy One, blessed be He; it is written here, 'And it was evil in the eyes of the Lord,' and it is written there, 'For You are not a God who desires wickedness; evil shall not dwell with You'" <note>Psalm 5:5</note>. This is the end of the quote. And the *Zohar* was even stricter regarding this ugly sin, in the portion *Vayechi*, on the verse: "Woe to the wicked, for it shall be ill with him, for the reward of his hands shall be done to him" <note>Isaiah 3:11</note>. They asked: Why "the reward of his hands"? Rabbi Isaac said: This includes one who commits adultery with his hands to produce and destroy his seed in vain. They have established that such a person does not see the face of the Divine Presence <note>original: Shekhinah</note>, as it is written: "For You are not a God who desires wickedness; evil shall not dwell with You." And it is written: "And Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord" <note>Genesis 38:7</note>. So too here, "Woe to the wicked, for it shall be ill with him"—woe to that sinner who makes himself "evil." "For the reward of his hands shall be done to him" includes one who commits adultery with his hands to produce and destroy his seed in vain. And for this sin, the world suffers more than for all others. And if you ask: Why is he called "evil"? It is as we said, he makes himself evil, and it is written: "evil shall not dwell with You." While all other sinners may ascend [from their punishment], this one does not ascend. And if you say: What about other sinners who kill people? They too have a way to ascend. But this one does not ascend. Why? Because those others kill the children of other people, but this one kills his own actual children and spills vast amounts of blood. And regarding other sinners of the world, it is not written "and it was evil in the eyes of the Lord," but here it is written, "And what he did was evil in the eyes of the Lord." Why? Because it is written: "and he spilled it on the ground" <note>Genesis 38:9</note>. Rabbi Judah said: "There is no sin in the world that does not have a path of repentance except for this one; and there is no sinner who does not eventually see the face of the Divine Presence except for this one," as it is written: "evil shall not dwell with You." Rabbi Isaac said: "Fortunate are the righteous in this world and the world to come, of whom it is written: 'And your people shall all be righteous, they shall inherit the land forever...'" <note>Isaiah 60:21</note>. End of quote.

**See** how strictly the *Zohar* treats this sin, more than all the sins in the Torah! For regarding no other sin were Er and Onan so severely punished. And because it is pushed away from the upper dwelling, it is like a broken clay vessel that has no repair and no purification; woe to him that he was created! **However**, in order to save the soul that has sinned in this and regrets it and wants to enter this "Gate" in which the righteous enter—to say: "Behold, listen to this, woe, woe to him!"—[I say] he must consider the actions he must do all the days of his life in this world. See and sanctify yourself like this, and then the stain will be wiped away.

**First**, I will come to save from eternal death the reader of this passage who might think that there is no repentance for one who has committed this sin, and thus the sinner might despair and say, "As I am lost, I am lost," and follow the desires of his heart in hopelessness. Rather, I have come to awaken the sinner to rise with alacrity to arouse repentance and not to delay a single moment. For indeed, the words of this passage are not to be taken literally—that repentance does not help—for there is nothing in the world that cannot be fixed through repentance. Even one who denied the fundamental principles of faith, as our Sages learned from the verse "Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God" <note>Hosea 14:2</note>. And King Manasseh, who denied God and filled Jerusalem [with blood] from end to end and committed all the abominations, the Holy One, blessed be He, accepted him in repentance. And behold, I will copy what my godly father, my teacher, of blessed memory, wrote on this matter in the book *Emek Beracha*, and also what I wrote there in the glosses; and this is our language: One must know that nothing stands in the way of repentance. Even if one committed every transgression in the world, there is repentance for them. For even Manasseh, who placed an idol in the Temple and committed every transgression in the world, when he repented, the Holy One, blessed be He, accepted him. And Jeroboam ben Nebat, who sinned and caused the masses to sin—if he had wanted to return, the Holy One, blessed be He, would have accepted him, as seen in the chapter "Helek" <note>Sanhedrin 102a</note>, where the Holy One, blessed be He, grabbed him by his garment and said to him: "Return, and I, you, and the son of Jesse <note>King David</note> will stroll together in the Garden of Eden," etc. And our Sages said explicitly: "Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God"—even if one was a denier of the fundamental principles. And it was taught in the chapter "Rosh Hashanah": The School of Shammai says there are three groups on the Day of Judgment... down to: the "sinners of Israel with their bodies" go down to Gehenna <note>Purgatory/Hell</note> and are judged there for twelve months; after twelve months, their bodies are consumed and their souls are burned, etc. But the heretics and the informers... go down to Gehenna and are judged for generations upon generations, and their worm shall not die and they are not consumed. This is the end of the quote. And the proof is that the *Tosafot* of blessed memory wrote that all these cases in the discussion refer to when they did not perform repentance. And so the *Tosafot* explained in *Bava Metzia* in the chapter "The Gold," on the statement regarding those who go down and do not come up: "And all of them are cases where they did not perform repentance, for repentance is effective for everything." And there is an opinion that says that penitents <note>original: Ba'alei Teshuva</note> are greater than those who were righteous all their lives. This is the end of the *Tosafot* in the place mentioned. And the Rambam <note>Maimonides, 1135–1204</note> wrote in the "Book of Knowledge," in the Laws of Repentance, chapter 3, and the *Tanya* <note>a 13th-century Italian halakhic work, not the Chabad text</note> cited it in sign 72: "And these are the ones who have no portion in the World to Come, but are cut off and lost and judged for the greatness of their wickedness forever and ever: the heretics, the atheists, those who deny the resurrection of the dead, and those who deny the Torah..." and he listed many more who have no portion in the World to Come. And he wrote at the end: "All this applies if each of these dies without repentance. But if he returns from his wickedness and dies as a penitent, he is among the members of the World to Come, for nothing stands in the way of repentance. Even if he denied the fundamental principles all his days and at the end he repented, he has a portion in the World to Come," etc. And he elaborated further on this, but I must be brief. And it is already known and mentioned...

Regarding the small finger of a woman, it is as if one looks at the "place of nakedness" <note>original: "makom hatoraf," referring to the private parts</note>. We also learn in the chapter "He whose [dead] relative lies before him" <note>original: "Mi Shemeto," Berachot 24a</note> that Rabbi Isaac said: A handbreadth of a woman [exposed] is considered nakedness <note>original: "ervah"; a legal term for sexual impropriety</note>. Regarding what? If you say to look at her, Rav Sheshet already said: Why did the Torah list jewelry? <note>to show that looking even at a small finger for pleasure is forbidden</note>. Rather, it refers to one's own wife during the recitation of the Shema prayer. Rav Hisda said: A woman’s leg is considered nakedness, as it is said, "Uncover the leg, pass through the rivers" (Isaiah 47:2) and then "Your nakedness shall be uncovered." Samuel said: A woman’s voice is nakedness, as it is said, "For your voice is sweet" (Song of Songs 2:14). Rav Sheshet said: A woman’s hair is nakedness, as it is said, "Your hair is like a flock of goats" (Song of Songs 4:1). We also learn in the chapter "Helek" <note>Sanhedrin 92a</note> that Rabbi Eliezer said: Anyone who gazes at nakedness, his "bow is emptied" <note>original: "kashto nineret"; a euphemism for the loss of spiritual/physical vitality</note>, as it is said, "Your bow was made quite bare" (Habakkuk 3:9). And we learn at the end of the chapter "Holy Things" <note>Avodah Zarah 20b</note> in a teaching: "Keep yourself from every evil thing" (Deuteronomy 23:10)—this means a man should not gaze at a beautiful woman, even if she is single, nor at a married woman even if she is unattractive, nor at a woman's colored garments, nor at a male donkey with a female donkey, nor at a male pig with a female pig, nor at birds when they are mating.
</margin>

Bad checks for the master Rav Nachman bar Isaac: looking at the "separated" <note>original: "nivdal"</note> is enough.

# The Gate of Letters

In Tractate Avot, we learned: "Do not converse much with a woman." They said this regarding one’s own wife; how much more so <note>original: "kal vachomer"</note> regarding the wife of another? From here the Sages said: Anyone who converses excessively with a woman causes evil to himself, neglects the study of Torah, and eventually inherits Gehenna <note>the place of spiritual purgation</note>. Even the light conversation between a man and his wife is brought up against him in judgment. For we learn in the first chapter of Hagigah (5b): Rabbi Ila was going up the stairs and heard a child reciting the verse, "For behold, He who forms mountains and creates the wind, and declares to man what his conversation was" (Amos 4:13). Our Sages of blessed memory remarked on this: even if one is as strong as an army, when he is told that his Master testifies against his conversation, does he have a remedy? What is this "conversation"? Even light conversation between a man and his wife is told to a person at the time of their death. We also learn in Tractate Derech Eretz: Do not converse much with a woman, for the entire conversation of a woman is nothing but lechery. The beginning of adultery is laughter with women; through laughter, they come to transgression. They are the ones who draw a man toward sin and lead to adultery. In Tractate Avodah Zarah and the first chapter of Avot, it is said: Laughter and lightheadedness accustom a person to forbidden relations <note>original: "ervah"</note>. We also learn in Tractate Eruvin, in the chapter "How do we bless": Rabbi Yose the Galilean was walking on the road and met Beruriah <note>a famous female scholar and wife of Rabbi Meir</note>. He asked her: "By which way shall we go to Lod?" She said to him: "Galilean fool! Did the Sages not say 'Do not converse much with a woman'? You should have said: 'Which way to Lod?'" Therefore, anyone who possesses the fear of sin should save himself from this net that is spread for all men, which makes one forget and leads to adultery, which is more difficult than all other transgressions. For all other sins, a person can commit alone, but adultery cannot be done except by two—a man with a woman or a woman with a man. Thus, their sin and the one who causes them to sin are intertwined.

**And it is fitting** for those who go to dances with women, for they violate all the warnings of our Sages. It is even fitting for one who counts money from his hand into her hand <note>a metaphor for close physical proximity or flirtation during business</note>, for he is considered like an idolater. This is the conclusion: "He shall not go unpunished" (Proverbs 6:29). How much more so when a boy and a girl actually play together for the sake of lechery, for the Satan dances in the middle of the dance. They think they are only looking at her colored clothes, but he is looking at her garments, her face, and the faces of women laughing. He also engages in lightheaded conversation with her, even if she is a single maiden. Regarding this, the "Enemy" <note>the impulse to sin</note> flees when one sets a covenant for his eyes: "How then could I gaze at a maiden?" (Job 31:1). Especially since most of them are in a state of menstrual impurity <note>original: "Niddot"</note>. For such women, there is the prohibition of "nakedness" in any event; he defiles himself and is called "unclean," and "his dwelling shall be outside the camp" <note>Leviticus 13:46, used here metaphorically to describe spiritual distance from God</note>. Therefore, whoever has done one of these things has followed a bad culture and must repent. Afterward, he should remain in his dignity and honor all his days, adding vow upon vow to distance himself from the entrance of her house, so that it shall "neither be seen nor found" <note>terms usually applied to leaven on Passover, here applied to the temptation of sin</note>. It is proper for every man to forbid his wife to him while she is a *niddah*, as we learned: "A man who has a discharge <note>original: "zav"</note> shall not eat with a woman who has a discharge" <note>original: "zavah"</note>, and it is forbidden to touch, speak [flirtatiously], or the like. These are forbidden all the more so <note>original: "kal vachomer"</note> with a married woman who is a *niddah*, toward whom her husband is strict. For regarding all these, a married woman is forbidden in seclusion <note>original: "yichud"</note>, and certainly forbidden in all these other matters. Regarding something similar to this, it was written in the *Hagahot Ashri* <note>glosses on the code of the Rosh</note> in the chapter "One who [washes his] head" in Tractate Shabbat, regarding a student who studied much but died in the middle of his days. The Tanna <note>Sage</note> taught: Even though he kept the laws of forbidden acts, for it is said "the leaven of forbidden relations" <note>original: "se’or arayot"</note>, even seclusion is forbidden—specifically that she should not sleep in her garment and he in his garment [in the same bed]. Even general closeness is forbidden because "we say to the Nazirite: go around, go around, but do not come near the vineyard." This is my opinion to correct the language of the gloss: it is forbidden for her to sleep in her garment and him—meaning by himself—referring to his wife while she is a *niddah*. The explanation of the gloss is that even though it is permitted to be secluded with one's wife while she is a *niddah*, we still apply an "all the more so" logic to forbid these matters with other forbidden women. Then it says there is a "new law" regarding the *niddah*: that she is forbidden in his garment and he in her garment. This is proven in the first chapter of Shabbat (13a), which compares a *niddah* to a married woman: just as with a "neighbor's wife" he is forbidden in his garment and she in hers, so too with a wife who is a *niddah*. Thus, everything forbidden with a *niddah* is certainly forbidden with a married woman.

**Therefore**, one must correct the text to forbid it where it is forbidden. We do not read "it is forbidden for the leaven of forbidden relations," but rather "it is forbidden for forbidden relations [to sleep] in her garment," etc., based on an "all the more so" argument from *niddah*. For it would be difficult otherwise: where would we know the prohibition of the contact of garments elsewhere? It was only said regarding a married woman. For example, young men, even those who are meticulous, eat with a married woman from the same bowl, yet with one's own wife who is a *niddah*, this is forbidden! Our Sages said this even though he is with her. Similarly, giving or extending an object to a married woman [is often done lightly], but it entered my mind to find merit for the world <note>to justify the common lenient practice</note> because they think the prohibition is only when there is physical substance to the contact. While with other forbidden women it is forbidden because seclusion is like being with her, and it is a "novelty of closeness," with these forbidden women, a man is prone to treat them as permanent strangers. Therefore, when he is secluded with her, that is the primary closeness and love. But regarding seclusion with his wife [who is a *niddah*], where there is a permanent dwelling, there is no arousal of love in mere seclusion. By this, we can resolve the difficulty raised by the Tosafot <note>medieval commentators</note> in the first chapter of Shabbat. They were amazed that seclusion is forbidden by the Torah, yet we do not learn the laws of "him in his garment and her in hers" from the laws of a married woman. According to my reasoning, it is settled: Seclusion is biblically forbidden, but sleeping in garments is only rabbinically forbidden <note>original: "miderabbanan"</note>. Therefore, we should have forbidden seclusion by the comparison, but permitted sleeping in garments without seclusion—for example, if a servant was present to prevent privacy. This is their conclusion. And according to the logic I wrote, the words of the Tosafot are well-explained, though they left the matter unresolved. Thus, the law remains in its place as implied by the *Hagahot Ashri*. However, in a Responsum of the Rashba <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Aderet</note>, he gave a reason to permit certain matters that do not lead to habitual closeness, saying they are only forbidden with a *niddah* because a man is familiar with her. As it says in the first chapter of Shabbat: Ulla would kiss his sisters, and his opinion differs from that of Rav, who said: Ulla [prohibits] any closeness in the world. And the law follows Rav.

**The Answer:** According to what they said, "Do not draw near" means no closeness in the world. There is no difference between his forbidden relatives, like his daughter or sister, and other relatives, or a married woman; there is no difference between the time of their impurity and the time of their purity. They are always forbidden from any closeness, for regarding all of them it is written: "None of you shall approach any anyone who is near of kin to him" (Leviticus 18:6). If we cannot control our hands with them during their time of impurity, we could never control them, even in their time of purity. However, in all these cases, it is possible that there is no biblical destruction in closeness that does not involve uncovering nakedness; rather, it is a Rabbinic prohibition to prevent transgression. As Rav said: Ulla [says] any closeness at all is forbidden because "we say to the Nazirite: go around the vineyard." They only spoke of closeness that leads to habitual sin, like sleeping with her even in her garment, or kissing. This applies even to his wife who is a *niddah*—sleeping in their garments—as all these things accustom one to forbidden relations. Similarly, even extending a vessel from the hand of his wife who is a *niddah* to his hand is forbidden because he is familiar with her, and a small amount of closeness brings a fear of habit. But with other women with whom he is not familiar, these types of closeness, such as extending a vessel and the like, do not constitute a habit of transgression. Regarding the matter of a man who divorces his wife and then stays with her in an inn in the chapter "The Evening Prayer": Shamai says she does not need a second divorce from him, but Hillel says she does. We also say that a woman divorced after the betrothal <note>original: "erusin"</note> needs a second divorce because he is not familiar with her. In the Gemara, we established this like Abaye... witnesses of seclusion and a heart for a heart... [the text becomes highly technical regarding legal witnesses and physical intimacy]... for we say they are witnesses of seclusion and witnesses of intimacy. Here too, one could say it is a stringency... and we say there in the first chapter of Shabbat: Rav Nachman said to his daughters... [referring to sleeping arrangements and modesty]. And it remains that even though there is this regarding his wife...

<meta>The previous page concluded the discussion on visual modesty and the prohibitions regarding looking at or hearing women other than one’s wife. This page shifts focus to the mechanics of repentance (Teshuvah) for sexual sins, specifically addressing whether such sins can be fully atoned for and the rigorous penance required by medieval authorities like the Rokeach and Maimonides.</meta>

<page-num>99</page-num>
<header>Gate of the Letters</header>

Thus, he has not performed a "complete repentance" <note>original: "teshuvah sheleimah"</note> which acts like a brother to him to cover over all his deeds. This clearly shows you that repentance is effective; if so, what is the meaning of what was said earlier, that repentance does not help [for this sin]? The holy master, Rabbi Isaac Hayut, wrote as follows: "Every repentance requires the act of turning back to happen in the very limb with which one sinned. However, a sin regarding the Covenant <note>original: "brit," referring here to the sign of circumcision and by extension, sexual purity</note> does not depend solely on a repentance of the 'Covenant' limb; rather, it requires a powerful repentance as if he had damaged all his limbs." This is also implied by the language of the *Zohar*, which says that repentance is like a brother to him to cover all his deeds. The reason for this seems to be that for all other transgressions, the most excellent repentance is when the sinner rectifies the specific sin he committed and the matter in which he acted wickedly. For example, if he sinned *with his cheeks* <note>original: "belahi"</note> or with a lying tongue, his mouth should speak truth; if he was foolish, let him occupy himself with wisdom and the Torah which was missing from his tongue. If he sinned with evil thoughts, let him shatter them and return the words of Torah to his heart. If he sinned with haughty eyes, let him be humble and downcast of eyes. If he sinned through the desire for [fine] clothing, let him wear sackcloth and ashes. Likewise, with all the limbs through which he sinned, he should strive to fulfill the corresponding commandments. This is sufficient for him because the transgression did not spread throughout the "full stature of the man" <note>original: "shi'ur kumat adam"; a mystical concept of the human form reflecting the divine</note> but only in a specific limb, and by rectifying that limb, all is fixed. However, the seed <note>original: "zera"</note> is the root and source of the entire human stature, and from the seed, the human is formed. Even though it is revealed through a specific limb, its root is in the brain, and afterwards, in its descent through the spinal cord, it exits through the organ. Though it is revealed there, it contains the power of all his 248 limbs and 365 sinews <note>The traditional Jewish count of body parts and veins/commandments</note> and his entire stature. Therefore, even if he performs repentance with that specific limb—by performing ascetic penance <note>original: "siggufim"</note> and guarding that place so it is not damaged further, keeping it holy and pure—nevertheless, his entire stature was defiled. He must find a rectification for his entire stature, both through penance as if he had sinned in every single limb, and through extra holiness to sanctify every single limb. Then "he shall return and be healed." Now, regarding this matter, if he follows the path of repenting for other sins—meaning only in the place and limb where he sinned—"there is no repentance." His intention is that the beginning of repentance should be to rectify this sin and perform penance, and afterwards to use "ink and signets" <note>meaning to ensure a permanent mark of change</note> so he never stumbles again. Nevertheless, he must add to this and perform repentance for all his limbs as if he had sinned in all of them, for in truth, this [sin] includes them all. This is the explanation of the matter according to the path and resolution of the Rabbi <note>referring to Rabbi Hayut</note>.

# However
It seems to me that it can be resolved in another way according to the intent of the Torah mentioned above, which said there is no repentance for this sin. It begins with the case of a perfectly righteous man, God forbid, who destroyed the "human stature" upon his heart. If he sinned and committed a certain transgression several times, and afterwards regrets it and desires repentance, he must know how many times he committed the transgression. This is so he can perform repentance for the sin the same number of times as he committed it. As the Ari of blessed memory wrote, and as found in the *Emek Bracha*: "One who sinned twenty-eight times, if he performed the repentance as written by the *Rokeach* <note>Rabbi Eleazar of Worms (c. 1176–1238), an influential mystic and author of the law code Sefer Ha-Rokeach</note>—namely the four types of repentance: the Repentance of Return, the Repentance of the Fence, the Repentance of the Weight, and the Repentance of the Writ <note>These are specific ascetic programs involving fasting and self-denial</note>—one time for the prescribed period, he is forgiven. **But** one who sinned many times must perform the written repentance many times, year after year, according to the count of the times he sinned." Repentance as found in our books will not depart [from this rule]. It is not enough that he will not do it again; he must fulfill "The Repentance of the Weight" <note>original: "Teshuvat Ha-mishkal"; the idea that the pain of penance must equal the pleasure of the sin</note> in its perfection. And this is not only regarding many women; before his repentance, he is obligated to repent for each and every one. For this is a complete law: even if he did them unintentionally <note>original: "shogeg"</note> and in a single state of unawareness, he is liable for a sin offering for each one. Even though they are all of the same category of sin, since they are distinct bodies, he is liable for each one, as Maimonides wrote in the ninth chapter of the Book of Sacrifices, in the Laws of Unintentional Sins:

# And these are
his words there: "One who has relations with many forbidden women <note>original: "arayot"</note> in one state of unawareness, even though they are all of one category, since they are distinct bodies, he is liable for each one. How so? If he had relations with five menstruating women, or five of his sisters, or five of his daughters, he is liable for each body," etc. See there. And in the chapter "The Woman," regarding one who had relations with many animals in one state of unawareness, she is liable for a sin offering for each and every animal because their bodies are distinct. This is like being possessed by many men in one state of unawareness, where she is liable for a sin offering for every single man. See there: "A woman whose husband went to a country across the sea and she heard her husband died, or witnesses came saying he died, and she remarried—whether by her own decision or by the court—and it became known that her husband is alive... if she married many men or committed adultery with many men, she is liable for a sin offering for every single man because they are distinct bodies, even though it was all in one state of unawareness." Thus far his words. The *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* <note>SMaG, by Rabbi Moses of Coucy</note> wrote the same in the Laws of Sacrifices to Atone for Unintentional Sins, sign 213. <insert>(And if)</insert> this is said regarding an unintentional sinner—who is certain and [yet] brings a sin offering for each one—how much more so if a man intentionally <note>original: "mezid"</note> commits many abominations with many women. He must perform the repentance written in the *Rokeach* for each and every one, even a hundred times, according to the number of people he sinned with. Even if he dies in the midst of that repentance—as we found with Rabbi Eleazar ben Dordia previously in Step 4. **However**, even if he sinned with one woman many times, even though it is one type of transgression and the "bodies" are not distinct—such that in an unintentional case he would only be liable for one sin offering, as Maimonides wrote in the place mentioned: "One who has relations with one forbidden woman many times in one state of unawareness, even if many days passed between acts, as long as he did not find out in between, he is considered one unintentional sinner and is only liable for one offering," etc.—**even so**, regarding an intentional sinner, if he comes to perform repentance, he is obligated to perform repentance for each and every act. This is by the power of "The Repentance of the Weight" written by the *Rokeach*, that one must weigh his suffering against his pleasure. That is, according to the value of the pleasure he enjoyed with the woman—in hugging, kissing, and relations, whether a little or a lot—so shall he cause pain to his body. From this, we automatically understand that if he had relations many times, he must weigh for the repentance the number of pleasures of the acts he enjoyed. This is based on logic. Furthermore, an intentional sin is not like the unintentional sin mentioned above. Maimonides wrote that for one woman and many acts, one is only liable for one offering because an unintentional sin depends on "unawareness," as it is written [in the Torah]. The proof is that even if it were unintentional, if he had knowledge in between, he would be liable for each one. And this person [the intentional sinner] knew and was warned before the sin, after the sin, and during the sin... he knew his Master and intended to enjoy the forbidden act... it is possible that it is a complete law that he is obligated to perform repentance for every single act of lying down and sleeping with her, since he repeated the sin and transgressed it. I understood this as well from what is written in the *Repentance of Rabbeinu Yonah* <note>Rabbi Yonah Gerondi, 13th-century author of "The Gates of Repentance"</note>, Gate 1: "Know that one who repeats one transgression ten times, even if he is careful with all other transgressions, he is considered as if he transgressed distinct sins. And so our Sages said: 'If they say to a Nazirite: do not drink, and he drinks; do not drink, and he drinks—he is lashed for each one.'" After we wrote all this in a true script, I found support from what Maimonides wrote in the *Book of Holiness*, Laws of Forbidden Intercourse, Chapter 3, explicitly like my words: "One who has relations with one of the forbidden women many times is liable for 'spiritual excision' <note>original: "karet"</note> or court-ordered death for every single act. Even though the court cannot kill him more than once, the acts are counted for him as many transgressions." Thus far his words.

# Come and See
what a great man testifies for me: Maimonides, of blessed memory, who wrote explicitly that one who repeats a sin—even though it is the same type of transgression and the bodies are not distinct—nevertheless, if it were possible to kill him with two deaths, we would kill him at the end for every single act he sinned in. But since he surely dies from the first death, why should we give him a second death? Since he is already a "dead man" <note>original: "gavra katila"; a legal term for someone already sentenced to death</note>. Nevertheless, if there is no completion of the judgment below, he has a judgment above, and it is counted for him as many transgressions regarding the punishment of the World to Come.

# And Consequently
it is precisely "excision" <note>original: "karet"</note> for every single act. As mentioned above, if he wishes to fulfill his duty toward Heaven and be saved from the punishment of the World to Come, it is obvious that he must perform repentance for every single "excision" individually. For the soul is not rectified by a single penance; it remains impure until he afflicts himself with the repentance written in the *Rokeach*, penance after penance, according to the number of "excisions" he committed. Then he is forgiven. This is remembered even without witnesses and warning, as the *SMaG* wrote explicitly in the Laws of Marriage. Furthermore, it seems to me there is proof for this from a Responsum of Rabbi Joel <note>possibly Rabbi Joel Sirkes (the Bach), though the text refers to an earlier Rabbi Joel</note> in sign 18 or sign 12, regarding a question about an adulterous woman. He replied that her repentance is very difficult, and "her breach is as great as the sea; who can heal her?" Since she was rooted in sin for 18 weeks, if we come to examine her, a [single] fire would not be enough for her to perform a complete repentance for every transgression. Even if she only committed adultery once, God forbid, her law is to accept suffering. But perhaps she would not have the strength to accept harsh suffering and return in complete repentance since she is young and tender in years. He elaborated on this a bit and wrote at the end: "I returned to the words of the early authorities, that we cannot burden her with the suffering of her law on our own initiative. It is known that her sin is too great to bear; she committed two evils: she was unfaithful to her husband by her adultery and she desecrated the mountain..." And then he added: "even one time... and her heart should be in cold and snow every single day, and in the heat of the sun before flies..." as Rabbi Eleazar the author of the *Rokeach* wrote, and Rabbi...

<meta>The previous page discussed the specific requirements for repenting for sins of the "Covenant," or sexual purity, noting that while difficult, repentance is never impossible. This page broadens the scope to discuss the most extreme cases of rebellion and apostasy in Jewish history—King Manasseh and the sage Elisha ben Abuyah—to prove that the door to repentance is always open, even when it seems divinely barred.</meta>

<page-num>155</page-num>
<header>Gate of the Letters</header>

# Gate of the Letters

They have a portion in the World to Come <note>original: "Olam HaBa"</note>. Our Sages of blessed memory expounded (in Tractate Yevamot and the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah, on the verse: *If the iniquity of the house of Eli shall be atoned for with sacrifice and offering, etc.*): "With sacrifice and offering it is not atoned, but it is atoned through words of Torah and acts of loving-kindness." We see from here that repentance is effective for every type of transgression, for every sin, and for every wickedness.

As for what we say in Tractate Hagigah, in the chapter "One may not expound," regarding the Heavenly Voice <note>original: "Bat Kol"</note> that went forth and said: *Return, O backsliding children, except for Acher* <note>Elisha ben Abuyah, a 2nd-century sage who became a heretic and was thereafter called "Acher," meaning "The Other."</note>—this was because his repentance was difficult <note>literally "with difficulty," or perhaps "bitter"</note>, for he knew the Glory of his Master and yet intended to rebel against Him.

But what of Manasseh? He was an apostate who sought to provoke [God] to anger! And even so, when he repented, the Holy One, Blessed be He, accepted him. As we say in the chapter of Rabbi Eliezer ben Joshua: "Come and see the power of repentance. Come and see from Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, who committed all the evil abominations in the world and did much evil in the eyes of the Lord to provoke Him... until the captains of the King of Assyria came and put him in a bronze pot <note>according to legend, he was tortured in a copper cauldron</note>... and there he called out to all the other gods to whom he had sacrificed, but not one of them called back to him or answered him or saved him. Finally, he said: 'I shall call to the God of my ancestors with all my heart; perhaps the Lord will answer me as He did with all His wonders.' And when he called to the God of his ancestors, God was entreated by him and heard his prayer, as it is said: *And he prayed to Him, and He was entreated of him...*" At that moment, the ministering angels stood and sealed all the windows of Heaven, saying before Him: "Master of the Universe! A man who placed an idol in the Sanctuary—will You accept him in repentance?" God said to them: "If I do not accept him in repentance, I am locking the door in the face of all penitents!" What did the Holy One, Blessed be He, do? He tunneled a special opening <note>original: "chatira"</note> for him beneath His Throne of Glory from a place where no angel has authority. This is what is meant by the verse *And He was entreated of him*—the word *vaye'ater* <note>entreated</note> is related to *vaye'ater* <note>his prayer</note> and his supplication. Rabbi Levi said: "In Arabia, they call a tunnel *atira*." Thus far the quote.

## And it appears to me
That the "apostate to provoke" regarding Acher and the "apostate to provoke" regarding Manasseh do not fall under the same category, but rather two different levels. As stated in the *Kuzari* <note>A 12th-century philosophical work by Judah Halevi</note>, Acher recognized the Truth within himself and realized clearly that [his path] was false, yet his King [God] was his Glory and there was no help but Him, yet he intended to rebel against Him, saying: "Heaven forbid, perhaps there are two authorities in Heaven!" Thus, he stirred up a lie within himself, and for this reason, he was banished from the worlds. This was not the case with Manasseh; though he was an apostate to provoke, it is not said of him that "he knew the Glory of his Master [and rebelled]" in that same way. The wise will understand.

## And furthermore
Even for Elisha ben Abuyah (Acher), had he persisted and increased his prayer and devoted himself to great and difficult self-mortifications as Manasseh did—and since his Torah was received through great mercy <note>see earlier in Sign 52</note>—even though he heard from behind the Curtain <note>original: "pargod," the heavenly veil</note> the words "except for Acher," he should not have restrained himself from seeking mercy, even though his honor was severe. We find such a teaching regarding Rabbi Eleazar ben Dordia in the chapter *R.E.Z.*: They said of him that he did not leave a prostitute in the world whom he did not visit. Once, he heard there was a prostitute in the coastal cities who took a chest of gold dinars as her fee. He took a chest of dinars and crossed seven rivers to get to her. At the moment of the act, she passed wind and said: "Just as this wind will never return to its place, so Eleazar ben Dordia will never be accepted in repentance." He went and sat between mountains and hills and said: "Mountains and hills, seek mercy for me!" They said to him: "Before we seek mercy for you, we must seek it for ourselves..." He said: "Sun and moon, seek mercy for me!"... He said: "Stars and constellations, seek mercy for me!"... Finally, he said: "The matter depends on no one but me." He placed his head between his knees and wailed in weeping until his soul departed. A Heavenly Voice went forth and said: "Rabbi Eleazar ben Dordia is invited to the life of the World to Come."

The Gemara concludes there that since he was so deeply involved in heresy <note>original: "minut"</note>, Acher should not have despaired of repentance. Even though the Heavenly Voice went forth and his companions said "except for Acher," he should have done his part, even if he were to die in the midst of repenting.

So too wrote the author of *Reshit Chokhmah* <note>The Beginning of Wisdom, a 16th-century kabbalistic ethical work</note> in the "Gate of Holiness," chapter 17, as follows: "The general rule is that there is nothing that cannot be rectified through repentance. That which was explained as being 'beyond the reach of repentance' means only that the repentance is very difficult. Indeed, part of the difficulty of repentance is that they show the person that it does not depend on repentance [for him]. Yet, there is nothing that stands before repentance. Even if you heard: 'Return, O backsliding children, except for so-and-so,' like the case of Elisha ben Abuyah, do not worry. For in the end, Elisha ben Abuyah was accepted, for if he had not even repented [he was still partially saved], how much more so if he had repented, it would have helped him more and more. It was only that they closed the doors of repentance before him, and he needed to persist until the door opened. This is like the saying: 'Everything the Master of the House tells you to do, do—except for "Leave."' That is, the Holy One, Blessed be He: everything He tells you to do regarding repentance, do. But if He says to you 'Leave'—meaning stay behind and do not enter, as in the case of Acher—do not listen to Him! Rather, enter within, for this is the true desire of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and He is merely testing you." Thus far the quote.

<gloss>Acher entered into the Pardes and ruined it, yet was still accepted eventually because he was greater than those who were just proven wrong. Therefore, it was appropriate to accept his repentance. This is unlike a regular sinner who holds onto a bit of weakness in his hand.</gloss>

## For further
clarification of this matter, I will build for you from what I have written in the book *Likutey Chokhmah* <note>Gatherings of Wisdom</note> at the end of the "Gate of Awe" on the verse *Shomer yatzmiach* in the Prophets... regarding the nature of the end and the goodness for the soul... for one who serves through the path of wisdom from below... if he has no fear... he may find the good in the knowledge of his heart...

## And behold
it is true and correct... everything I mentioned above proves this matter... the reason is that Truth follows its path... to hold onto the Truth... even if it is against the way of this world... for this is the evil of the heart... therefore his sin was greater than Manasseh's. And this self-knowledge is the knowledge of "L.P.Y."... as I explained, Acher recognized the Truth within himself and knew clearly that He is the King of Glory, etc., only he harbored some doubt and relied on his own wisdom... and not every person is wise enough to understand this... therefore I have come to simplify and I found his words... ready for every intention...

## Furthermore
I learn regarding Manasseh... that the Holy One, Blessed be He, accepted him because He desired that he should be a living example of repentance... and the matter of "except for Acher" is that the Holy One, Blessed be He, is a lover of kindness and devises means so that his banished ones are not cast off from him. Therefore, he is a consumer of souls and devises means that they should perform repentance. But if a man does not wake himself up to do repentance, the Holy One, Blessed be He... and this is "Return, O backsliding children"—He opens for them a doorway to repentance, except for Acher. And this is sufficient.

## Behold
that there is nothing in the world that stands before repentance. And even though they said "except for Acher," that refers to sinning and then repenting [on a loop], and furthermore, this sin is the sin of the Generation of the Flood who corrupted their way... and for all this, the Holy One, Blessed be He, wanted them to repent and would have forgiven them. As Rashi writes at the beginning of the portion of *Noach*, that He troubled them for 120 years with the building of the Ark specifically to announce to them that they should return and perform repentance. In the portion of *Vayakhel*, the text elaborates there on the severity of the blemish of the Sign of the Covenant...
