# The Gate of the Letters

...that he should not, etc., establish his dwelling in the Holy Land; or, if he is a man who seeks an elevated remedy, let his "holy place" be the "four cubits of Law" <note>original: "ד' אמות של הלכה" — a Talmudic expression meaning that even in exile, God’s presence is found where the law is studied</note> and holy gatherings to connect with his God. They gave a sign for this: "Son of Holiness" <note>original: "בר קודש"</note>, when he is alone or holy. And in the explanation of the verse, "Neither shall he go out of the sanctuary" <note>Leviticus 21:12</note>, it means he should not cease his study. And so it is written in *The Gate of Holiness*, Chapter 7: "Furthermore, one must acquire holiness of place, as we find mentioned in the Torah in the portion *Acharei Mot*: 'a holy place.'"

There are two aspects to this: either a place becomes holy through the labor of Torah and prayer—such as a study hall or a synagogue—or it is a holy place because it is set apart and separated from other people. Creating a fence between oneself and others is a great preparation for "cleaving" to the Divine <term>Dveikut: An ecstatic state of attachment to God</term>. This was the way of the sages who withdrew from inhabited areas, known as the "Desert Sect" <note>original: "כת המדברים" — medieval ascetics who sought isolation in the wilderness to avoid the distractions of society</note>, as cited by the author of *Duties of the Heart* <note>Rabbi Bahya ibn Paquda</note>. It is a condition of spiritual withdrawal to desire solitude, for in this, a person demonstrates in his soul that he has no connection to the people of this world at all—just as it will be true after his passing. Therefore, from now on, he shows the "exile of his soul" in this world, desiring to cleave only to his God, may He be blessed, with whom he is destined to be joined in an essential and complete union.

Similarly, it was written in the book *Hovot HaLevavot* <note>original: "ח"ח" referring to Duties of the Heart</note> regarding a certain man who entered a city to return its inhabitants to the service of God. He found them all wearing the same color of clothing, with their graves situated at the entrances of their houses, and he saw no women among them. He was amazed and questioned them, and they answered him regarding every detail. Regarding the fact that he saw no women among them, they replied: "What did we see that caused us to separate from women and children? Know that our unique community has a town nearby. When one of us needs something from his companion, he goes there, fulfills his need, and returns to us. This is because we saw that their presence brings upon us temptations of the heart and much upheaval, toil, and trouble. We found rest from all of this by distancing ourselves to choose the matters of the World to Come and to loathe this world."

We also find this with Elisha the Prophet: he required "holiness of place" to increase his sanctity. This is what the Shunamite woman did for him, saying: "Behold now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God who passes by us continually. Let us make a small upper room on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick" <note>2 Kings 4:9–10</note>. We see that because of his holiness, he required a prepared place—namely, a small upper room. This was a place of relative withdrawal from people, setting aside the usual physical habits of humanity, symbolized by the bed, table, chair, and lamp.

And so, there are two aspects to the holiness of place. If it is possible for both to exist as one in a man's home—in his study hall or the synagogue—how good is his portion! For he will certainly acquire spiritual merit there. Regarding the one who occupies himself with Torah and acts of kindness and is frequently found in the synagogue, the Sages said that such a person is recognizable in those places where he is accustomed to sitting; there people seek him out. This man is present day by day in the synagogue until, when one asks his neighbor, "Where is so-and-so found?" they answer that he is found in the House of Study. Just as the High Priest was commanded "Neither shall he go out of the sanctuary," so too one who wishes to be sanctified should sanctify himself in a holy place—the synagogue or the study hall.

It is also good to seek solitude through the closeness of a companion, for as our Sages of blessed memory said: "Increase friends for yourself." Rabbi Hayyim Vital <note>original: "רח"ו"</note> wrote elsewhere about the virtues of seclusion (*hitbodedut*), for then one can be spared from all sin and merit the traits of cleaving to Him, may He be blessed. This is not the place to elaborate on that teaching, but the intention is that by being in the "holy land" of the soul through seclusion in a holy place, one becomes truly holy.

We also find holiness and purity in the garments of the body. There is a hint to this in the verse "And they shall make holy garments" <note>Exodus 28:4</note>. Rabbi de Vidas wrote in *The Gate of Love*: "Even though these matters appear as the words of Rabbi Hayyim Vital regarding the diligence of ritual immersion... nevertheless, since the law is established, it is truly a matter of purity. It is fitting for one who wishes to purify himself that his clothes be clean of oil, filth, and stains."

**And if** one is obligated to be careful of this, how much more—a million times over—must he be careful of the "impurity of criminal iniquity" in his garments! He must ensure there is no forbidden **Sha'atnez** <note>original: "שעטנז" — the biblically prohibited mixture of wool and linen in a single garment</note>, for it is a great prohibition. The impurity of this sin is severe, for one who wears *sha'atnez* clothes himself in the "Satan" <note>The Hebrew word "Sha'atnez" is treated here as an acronym and a linguistic play on the word "Satan"</note>. As we have seen with our own eyes in our generations, the head of the rabbinical court in the city of Speyer—a mother city in Israel—after much investigation, found many garments that were a stumbling block for the people. Many new fabrics—such as "Strakes" or those with "new lips" <note>referring to borders or trims</note>—have arrived that are woven with mixtures of wool and linen. Therefore, one must investigate and inquire after this. Women's clothing especially must be clean and inspected, as it is common to find *sha'atnez* in the sewing. We have seen many new types of fabrics coming from distant lands which the world assumes are purely of wool or hair, but are actually mixed with linen threads. Therefore, regulations were made to correct this.

In places where "secluded ones" are known, one must be careful near the heel, where a linen thread is often used during the craftsmanship, and it must be removed. Furthermore, there are things one must be reminded of, such as what was written regarding the stockings called *hosen* <note>Germanic term for leggings/tights</note>. If they are made of cloth and have linen ribbons to tie them, it is forbidden if one makes knots at the ends of the ribbons so they cannot be removed. If the ribbon is not permanently attached and can be pulled out, it is permitted.

I also saw there that it is forbidden to wear two pairs of stockings—one of linen and one of wool—one over the other, if it is impossible to remove the inner one without the outer one, for this is considered a "connection." It is not like wearing two shirts one over the other. It is proper to be careful in this.

I say that this is correct and balanced, as brought in the *Beit Yosef* <note>The legal code by Rabbi Joseph Karo</note>: "How can a man's heart embolden him to act against a matter explicitly stated in the Talmud?" I also found a moral rebuke and true trembling from my great master, the pious Rabbi Zalman <note>original: "מהר"י סג"ל" referring to the author of *Yesh Nochalin*</note>, who wrote: "I am among those who rebuke the matter of *sha'atnez* regarding the custom of sewing wool cloth with hemp threads for beauty. Even though they use hemp, there is a great stumbling block, for we see that most hemp is not as good or easy for sewing as linen threads. Certainly, the tailor will switch them, and he will embitter the man's soul." Even though the Rama <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles</note> wrote that if a Jew gives the tailor hemp threads, we do not fear he will switch them, in our times the way of the tailor is problematic. The non-Jews know the truth: that the vast majority of Jews do not check the threads. Even if the tailor does not intentionally intend to make the Jew sin, while he is busy with his work, he does not focus on always reaching for the hemp thread; he simply takes whatever comes to his hand first. He is not trembling with fear of causing a Jew to stumble. Thus, it is inevitable that a linen thread will be mixed into the garment.

Our words are not for those who wish to excuse things with "wind and vanity" or by citing leniencies while they see with their own eyes that the reality is different. One who is truly God-fearing will admit the truth and not place his trust in a non-Jew's casual conversation. He should distance himself from the stumbling block that occurs every hour he wears a garment of forbidden mixtures. Even if there is only a doubt, we have already mentioned above in the name of the Arizal <note>original: "הר"י ז"ל" — Rabbi Isaac Luria</note> that the spiritual damage of a "doubtful transgression" is sometimes more fearsome than a certain one.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on spiritual purification and the "Gate of the Letters," moving from the ritual bath to the holiness of physical space and the sanctity of garments, specifically the laws of mixed fabrics.</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters 106

One who has not been privileged to establish his residence in the Holy Land, or is prevented from doing so by force, yet has hope modeled after the Holy Place to have a "place of four cubits of Law" <note>A Talmudic expression referring to a private space dedicated to Torah study and divine service</note> for solitude, to be alone with his God. They have already given a sign regarding the word "Holiness" <note>original: "קודש" (Kodesh)</note>: when a person is alone <note>original: "ב' ד' ר' ל' לבדו" (an acronym/pun on being alone)</note>, then he is "holy." And he shall clothe himself and see that "from the Sanctuary he shall not go out" <note>A reference to Leviticus 21:12, applied here to mean staying within one's spiritual boundary</note>, meaning from the place of his holiness. These are the words of the *Reshit Chochmah* <term>Reshit Chochmah: "The Beginning of Wisdom," a 16th-century kabbalistic ethical manual by Rabbi Elijah de Vidas</term> in the Gate of Holiness, Chapter 6: A person needs to acquire a "place" for holiness, just as we find at the end of the section *Acharei Mot* regarding the "holy place."

There are different levels to this: either a place becomes sanctified through the study of Torah and prayer, such as a Study Hall or a Synagogue, or a holy place that is secluded and set apart from other people. A place distant from other people is a great preparation for "attachment" <term>Deveikut: A state of meditative cleaving or attachment to the Divine</term>. Therefore, the early sages would set themselves apart from inhabited areas and were called the "Sect of the Meditators," as mentioned by the pious author of *Chovot HaLevavot* <term>Chovot HaLevavot: "The Duties of the Heart," an 11th-century work of Jewish philosophy by Bahya ibn Paquda</term>. This is one of the conditions of asceticism: to desire solitude, for in this, one demonstrates in his soul that he has no connection to the people of this world at all—which is the truth after his passing. Therefore, from now on, he illuminates his soul in this world and does not wish to cling to anything but his God, may He be blessed, to whom he is destined to cling in his very essence, if he merits it.

So too, it is written in *Chovot HaLevavot* regarding a certain person who entered a province to teach the residents the service of God. He found them all wearing the same color of clothing, saw graves by the doors of their houses, and saw no women among them. He asked them about these things, and they answered him concerning every matter, as explained there in *Chovot HaLevavot*. Regarding the third point—that he saw no women among them—they answered him: "As for what you see, that we have separated from women and children, know that they have a city nearby. When one of us needs something from them, he goes to them, fulfills his need, and returns to us. This is because we saw the distraction that enters our hearts from trade and the great loss, and we recognized the exhaustion and trouble in its pursuit and desire. Because of all this, we chose to focus our hearts on matters of the World to Come and to despise this world."

Similarly, we find with our God that He established the "holiness of place" to make His sanctity beloved. Consider what the Great Shunammite woman did for the prophet Elisha: "Behold now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God who passes by us continually. Let us make a small upper chamber on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick" (2 Kings 4:9-10). Behold, because of his holiness, he required a specific preparation: a "small chamber," which is a sign of withdrawal from other people, and the most necessary natural preparations that humans enjoy—namely, a bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick. These represent asceticism in a balanced way, as the pious author of *Chovot HaLevavot* wrote regarding the three types of asceticism.

By this preparation and by dwelling in the Synagogue and the Study Hall, one returns to the two aspects of the holiness of place. If it is possible for both to be in one—such as a person meditating in his own study hall or synagogue—how good is my portion! For he will certainly acquire additional holiness in his soul. As our Sages of blessed memory said: "The Holy One, Blessed be He, says: Anyone who occupies himself with Torah and acts of kindness and is frequent in the Synagogue, I consider it as if he redeemed Me and My children from among the nations of the world." Their saying "frequent in the Synagogue" implies constant presence in the Synagogue, just as other people are found in the places where they usually sit. This person is found most of the day in the Synagogue, so that when a man asks his fellow, "Where is so-and-so to be found?" they answer him that he is "found in the Synagogue." This is the meaning of "from the Sanctuary he shall not go out." In this sense, one who wishes to be sanctified should sanctify himself in a holy place, like a Study Hall or a Synagogue.

A second good way is meditation through the acquisition of a companion, for our Sages said: "Either a companion or death" <note>A famous Aramaic proverb from the Talmud, Ta'anit 23a, emphasizing the importance of social/intellectual connection</note>. And it is explained in the *Sifrei* on the verse "Two are better than one": from here they said a person should acquire a companion for himself to read with him, study with him, eat with him, and to whom he can reveal his secrets. All these are the words of Rabbi Chaim Vital <note>original: "רח"ו" (Rabbi Chaim Vital, the primary disciple of the Arizal)</note>. It is clarified elsewhere regarding the virtues of solitude that one will then be saved from all sin and merit reaching the level of "attachment" <note>Deveikut</note>. This is not the place to expand on this inquiry, but the intention is to be in the Holy Land and also to have a holy place for meditation—perhaps even a "Holy of Holies."

Furthermore, concerning the matter of holiness and purity in the clothing of the body: a hint to this is "And they shall make holy garments." Jacob said to his sons, "And change your garments." These are the words of the *Reshit Chochmah* in the "Gate of Love," Chapter 11: Although these seem to be two separate things—first, purification by immersion, and second, "change your garments"—nevertheless, since the law places them together, it belongs to the category of purity. It is proper for one who wishes to purify himself that his clothes be pure from filth and impurity, and that they should not be stained with oil or honey.

If one is obligated to be careful in this, how much more so—a thousand times a thousand—must he be careful regarding the "stain of the eye" in his garments, namely the prohibition of *Sha'atnez* <term>Sha'atnez: The biblical prohibition against wearing a garment made of both wool and linen</term>. This is a great prohibition, and this "stain of the eye" is a more severe impurity than a garment stained with oil. For *Sha'atnez* is an acronym for *Shua* (combed), *Tavi* (spun), and *Noz* (woven) <note>A traditional rabbinic etymology for the word</note>. This ignorance is common among many, for there are sinners who do not know better. We have seen with our own eyes, while serving as the Head of the Rabbinical Court in the Holy Community of Nikolsburg <note>original: "קק"אג" - likely Nikolsburg (Mikulov) or a similar major community</note>, and also in the surrounding settlements, that after investigation and inquiry, we found several matters that are an "unintentional sin for the whole community."

There are types of threads called "Chenille" <note>original: "שניליי'"</note>, or in the vernacular "Velvet" <note>original: "טליד" - likely *veludo*</note>, and "Bursa" <note>original: "בשורות"</note>, and "Satin" <note>original: "ס"א מטראקס"</note>, in which they mix wool thread with silk thread and linen. Some of them mix wool and linen threads, and this requires investigation and repeated inquiry. Similarly, in the decorative borders of women's garments called "Shayvolo" <note>original: "שייו"לו"</note>, the tailors were not careful about using *Sha'atnez* threads in the sewing. We have also seen many new types that have arrived recently from distant lands; people always assume they are made of wool or hair, but wool and linen threads are mixed within them. Regarding all this, we established regulations and corrected all the ways.

Also in the high stockings called "Vakin" <note>original: "ואקי"ן" - likely *Wams* or long hose</note>, there is linen thread near the heel, placed there during the manufacturing, and it must be removed. Furthermore, there are things that require a reminder to warn about them, such as the laws of "double garments" mentioned in the Tosefta. As Rabbi Yochanan taught regarding the "double hose" called "Wizen" <note>original: "ווייזין" - *Hosen*</note>, where one is made of wool and silk and the other of linen, or a strap in the loop of the Tefillin to tie them: it is forbidden if he made knots. One should not take them out from there... <note>The text here becomes very technical regarding knots and sewing</note> only after he makes a knot, and on the other side he should not make a knot so that the cord can be pulled back and removed; then it is permitted.

**Furthermore**, it is forbidden to wear two stockings, one of linen and one of wool, one over the other, since it is impossible to strip off the bottom one without the top one; they are considered "joined." This is not like wearing two shirts one over the other. It is correct to be careful in this. And I say it is very correct, for it is mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud and cited in the *Beit Yosef*.

**Furthermore**, I found ethical rebuke and true Torah from my great brother, the pious Rabbi Y. Segal <note>The author's brother</note>, who wrote in the glosses: "The glossator says: This too is among the rebukes for the sin of *Sha'atnez*. It is the custom with wool hats to sew loops for the ears; even though they commonly use hemp threads, many of them are 'mixed' <note>original: "דבושל" - perhaps a corrupted term for mixed or deceptive</note>. For we see with our own eyes that the vast majority of hemp is not good for sewing like linen threads are. Certainly, the tailor will substitute and exchange it."

Now, I know in my humble opinion that the *Remah* <term>Remah: Rabbi Moses Isserles, the primary Ashkenazi halakhic authority</term> wrote that if a Jew gives the tailor hemp threads, it is permitted, as we do not fear he will switch them since the matter can be tested—linen threads turn white when burnt, while hemp threads just burn. This is the common practice, though some are stringent. However, from the words of the *Remah*, the weakness of this custom is apparent, which is why he mentioned the opinion of the stringent. How much more so in our times! The main reason for the leniency—that the non-Jew is afraid to switch them—does not apply, for they know that many Jews do not check after them. It is a certainty that we should fear substitution. Even if occasionally it happens that hemp threads are good for sewing, the tailor, while occupied with his work, will not trouble himself to always look for the hemp thread; he will simply take whatever comes to his hand first. He is not anxious about causing the Jew to stumble. One cannot escape the fact that a linen thread will be mixed into the garment.

Anyone who is "God-fearing" will be strict with himself. Our words are not for those who wish to brush aside these ways with "wind and the breath of their mouths," speaking publicly to permit what the legal authorities discussed. Even though we see with the eye of our intellect and heart that the conditions of earlier times do not apply to us, when people examine my words, their hearts and minds will tell them that this is the correct version, and they will see the truth. One should not place trust in the "famous lady" <note>A metaphor for public opinion or a specific local leniency</note> nor in a non-Jew "speaking innocently" <term>Mesiach le-fi tumo: A legal concept where a person's statement is trusted if they didn't know it had legal consequences</term>. One should distance himself from this great stumbling block, which occurs every time and every hour he wears the garment. This is not just a doubt, but a matter that cannot escape suspicion based on what we have mentioned. As we mentioned above in the name of the *Chassid* <note>Rabbi Judah HeHasid</note>: "The matter of a 'doubtful transgression' is more serious than a 'certain transgression.'"

<margin>Truth</margin>

This is the love and longing written of: "And Abraham went as the Lord had spoken to him." Before he came to the Land, he did not yearn, but after he came the first time and saw in a prophetic vision the splendor of the Land's holiness, he then truly longed for it. This is the reason for the proximity of the passage about Amalek to the entry into the Land... God gave Israel three gifts only through suffering: Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come. Therefore they said in the *Chapters of Rabbi Nathan*: "Be joyful and trembling over the commandments." The word "And it shall be" regarding the dwelling in Israel hints at the joy, and the proximity to Amalek hints at the "trembling" over the commandment... the sufferings of the Land of Israel come from the nations or from illnesses... as it is said: "And no inhabitant shall say, 'I am sick'; the people who dwell there shall be forgiven their iniquity" <note>Isaiah 33:24</note>. This is hinted at in the final letters of the verse: "And it shall be when you come to the land..." <note>The author uses a complex Hebrew cipher (Gematria/Acronym) here to link the verse to the idea of being "smitten" (נכה) yet forgiven.</note> Through the troubles in the Land, sins are cleansed and diminished... specifically light sins that are renewed... and at the time of death, he goes straight to Eden. But those who come to the Land and do not take to heart that they are in the King's Palace, and instead rebel and sin... the verse says: "But when you entered, you defiled My land and made My heritage an abomination" <note>Jeremiah 2:7</note>. It is written: "When you come to appear before Me, who has required this at your hand, to trample My courts?" <note>Isaiah 1:12</note> It should not enter their minds that after their death they will remain in the Land of Israel; rather, in their death, the "Outer One" <note>a demonic force</note> will inherit them... Therefore, every man should be sharpen his focus when coming to the Land of Israel, to have double the fear of Heaven that he had outside the Land, and know that he dwells in the King's house. Thus far his words.

# The Gate of the Letters

One cannot be, etc. <note>original: "אין יכול ליהו' וכו'" — likely a shorthand reference to a previous legal discussion about being exempt from a vow or obligation to travel</note> and who is the one who prevents this? Therefore, one should not pay attention to these words of his. Certainly, the "preventer" is the danger of the road; when travelers are in a state of presumed danger, they are not held guilty <note>original: "אין להם אשם וזופה" — "Zofah" likely refers to a penalty or divine rebuke</note>. So wrote the Rashbatz <note>Rabbi Shimon ben Tzemach Duran (1361–1444), a major legal authority</note> in a responsa, and the *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo’s commentary on Jewish law</note> cited him in Section 110 regarding the aforementioned laws. For if one is compelled to go up to the Land of Israel, it is only when it is possible without danger; but if there is danger, it is forbidden to endanger oneself. However, one who merits and arrives there without danger—blessed is he, and how good is his portion to dwell in the "Shadow of the Almighty," <term>Zel Shaddai: A poetic term for Divine protection</term> for it is the gate of heaven. And through this, he merits legal decisions <note>meaning he gains clarity in Torah study</note>. Our teacher Rabbi Israel <note>Rabbi Israel Isserlein (1390–1460), a German authority</note> wrote in Section 88 as follows: "As for what you wrote to me regarding your ascent to the Land of Splendor <note>a biblical name for Israel</note> and to the Holy City—may it be rebuilt speedily in our days—asking if it is a commandment now even for a scholar, given that due to our sins we have no gathering of youths and Torah study there; know that there is certainly great praise and merit for a person dwelling in the Land of Israel, and especially in the Holy City, for the benefit of the World to Come and also for this world. However, we have heard many times that there are worthless men there, Westerners <note>likely referring to North African or Maghrebi immigrants of that era</note> who are considered entirely wicked, informers and oppressors. They harass and confuse the Ashkenazim <note>Jews of German/Eastern European descent</note> who are observers of the Torah and practitioners of kindness. Their livelihood is distant and meager. Who is the fool who would turn aside there? The hardships are great, and could one withstand all this? Besides the great wickedness of the Ishmaelites <note>Muslims</note> who are there. Therefore, every man must look into himself, calculating the needs of his body and his money, to see in what way he can stand in the fear of God and in the keeping of His commandments, for this is the whole of man." Thus far his words. Our Sages of blessed memory went to great lengths on this subject at the end of the tractate *Ketubot*: "The Sages taught: A person should always dwell in the Land of Israel, even in a city where the majority are idolaters, and let him not dwell outside the Land, even in a city where the majority are Israelites. For everyone who dwells in the Land of Israel is like one who has a God, and everyone who dwells outside the Land is like one who has no God, as it is said: 'To give you the land of Canaan, to be your God' <note>Leviticus 25:38</note>. Does this mean that one who does not dwell in the Land has no God? Rather, it is to tell you that anyone who dwells outside the Land is as if he worships idols, etc." And this teaching refers even to the time of the Land's destruction, as mentioned at the beginning: "even in a city where the majority are heathens." This would not be the case if it were only during the time the Temple stood. And many Amoraim <term>Amoraim: Rabbis from the 3rd to 5th centuries whose discussions form the Gemara</term> expanded there on the virtues of dwelling in the Land of Israel. Rabbi Elazar said: "Anyone who dwells in the Land of Israel lives without sin." Rabbi Elazar also said: "The dead outside the Land will not live <note>referring to the resurrection</note> except through the 'rolling through tunnels.'" <note>original: "גלגול מחילות" — a mystical tradition that those buried in the diaspora must travel through underground tunnels to Israel to be resurrected</note> Rabbi Jeremiah bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: "Anyone who walks four cubits in the Land of Israel is assured that he is a child of the World to Come."

<margin>There is cause to doubt the order... similar to section 36... what is this "sprinkling"... similar to the wings of horses... since the branch was distanced... the merit of our ancestors... Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob... it is like one who has a God, and understand this.</margin>
**When** Rabbi Elazar went up to the Land of Israel, he said: "I have escaped one [sin]," etc. When Rabbi Zera went up to the Land of Israel, he could not find a ferry to cross, so he grabbed onto a rope bridge and crossed. A certain heretic said to him: "Hasty nation! You put your mouths before your ears <note>referring to Israel saying 'We will do' before 'We will hear' at Sinai</note>, and you still remain in your hastiness!" Rabbi Zera replied: "A place that Moses and Aaron did not merit to enter, who is to say that I will merit it? <note>I must hurry before the opportunity is lost</note>" Rabbi Abba would kiss the cliffs of Acre, etc.

<margin>And so in the chapter *Arakhin*... Rabbi Yochanan... Tanchuma... the secret of the Land of Israel... and those who bring their children to Torah study... bringing them closer to Abraham.</margin>
**And it is** stated there that Rav Yehuda said: "Anyone who ascends from Babylon to the Land of Israel violates a positive commandment, as it is said: 'They shall be carried to Babylon, and there shall they be until the day that I visit them' <note>Jeremiah 27:22</note>." But this refers specifically to ascending from Babylon; as for ascending from other lands outside the Land of Israel, there is no one who disputes its merit.
The *Sefer Charedim* <note>The Book of the Devout, by Rabbi Elazar Azikri (1533–1600)</note> writes: "It is a positive commandment from the Torah to dwell in the Land of Israel, as it is said: 'And you shall possess it and dwell in it' <note>Deuteronomy 11:31</note>. Our Sages said in the *Sifrei* that this commandment is equal to all the commandments of the Torah. Furthermore, anyone who leaves the Land of Israel to dwell outside the Land should be in your eyes like an idolater, as it is said: 'For they have driven me out this day from abiding in the inheritance of the Lord, saying: Go, serve other gods' <note>1 Samuel 26:19</note>." And it is found in the tractate *Berakhot* <note>likely intended as *Baba Batra* or a Midrash</note> that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai said: "Elimelech, Machlon, and Chilion were punished only because they left the Land for outside the Land... Rabbi Isaac said: Heaven forbid! Even if they had found only bran to eat, they should not have left. Why were they punished? Because they should have begged for mercy for the people of their generation, and they did not." This is from the storehouse of our Sages, of blessed memory. He further wrote on page 88: "Every Jewish man must cherish the Land of Israel and come to it from the ends of the earth with great passion, like a son to his mother's bosom. For the beginning of our suffering—the 'weeping for generations' <note>referring to the Spies' report in the desert</note>—was because we despised it, as it is said: 'They despised the pleasant land.' And in the merit of the 'hammers of the Torah' it is written: 'For Your servants cherished her stones and favored her dust,' and the verse concludes, 'You will arise and have mercy on Zion.' Therefore, the Amoraim would kiss its dust and its stones upon arriving. And how good and pleasant it is to sing the 'Song of Friendship' composed by Rabbi Yehuda Halevi, of blessed memory, with great love; the beginning of the song being: 'O Sacred Land, precious and chosen,' etc. So do we sing over Zion, as did Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai, every New Moon eve with great joy, praying that God will not drive us from her. Even those near and far who are outside her should yearn for her and love her. Just as He chose them, so He chose the Land of Israel and designated it for them. They are not called 'One Nation' except when the Land is with them, as it is written: 'And who is like Your people Israel, one nation in the land?' We find in the Midrash that the Holy One, blessed be He, told Abraham our father the first time to go through the Land and see it, then return. After he returned, He gave him permission to go back to the Land for five years. During those five years, he yearned to return and go, and he said this verse: 'Oh that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and be at rest... I would wander far off, I would lodge in the wilderness, Selah' <note>Psalms 55:7-8</note>. It is better to lodge in the deserts of the Land of Israel than to lodge in the palaces of lands outside the Land. He was longing and bowing as he went, 'And Abraham went as the Lord had spoken to him.' Before he arrived, he did not yearn for the Land, but after he came there the first time and saw in a prophetic vision the precious glory and holiness of the Land, he longed for it intensely. From him we learn for all generations, we his offspring, to be as longing as he was. Even if one dwells there in distress—on this condition we enjoy it, for it is through suffering. This is certainly the reason for the juxtaposition of the portion of Amalek <note>the archetypal enemy of Israel</note> and the entry into the Land in the portion of *Ki Tavo*. As the Sages said: 'Three good gifts did the Holy One, blessed be He, give to Israel, and He gave them only through suffering: Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come.' Remember that at the first entry, Amalek came. Heaven forbid, in the 'paving of the exiles,' when they want to come to the Land of Israel, Amalek is ready for them on the way. As our eyes see today, let the Lord see and judge. The verse begins with the word *Vehayah* ('And it shall be'), which is one of the twelve permutations of the Holy Name, hinting that one who dwells in the Land of Israel cleaves to God—the opposite of one who dwells outside the Land. The word *Vehayah* hints at what our Sages said: 'Wherever it says *Vehayah*, it is a language of joy.' Rabbi Moses Zacuto <note>The Remaz (1625–1697)</note> wrote: 'The 613th commandment is dwelling in the Land of Israel; every moment a person is in the Land, he fulfills this commandment.' It is known that the primary reward for a commandment is for the great joy in performing it, 'because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy.' Therefore, the inhabitant of the Land of Israel must be constantly happy in his constant commandment. He must also be in fear and trembling, as Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai wrote: 'Any commandment not done in love and fear is not a commandment.' Thus they said in the *Chapters of Rabbi Nathan*: 'Be joyful and trembling over the commandments.' The word *Vehayah* by the commandment of dwelling in the Land hints at the joy, while the proximity to the portion of Amalek hints at the bitterness in the commandment—the 'strap' that hangs over it. The sufferings of the Land of Israel, whether from the nations or from illnesses, are a form of atonement, as it is said: 'And the inhabitant shall not say: I am sick; the people that dwell therein shall be forgiven their iniquity.' This is also hinted at in the final letters of the verse: *Vehayah Ki Tavo El Ha'aretz Asher Hashem Elokecha Noten Lecha Nachalah* — the final letters [of *Nachalah Necha*] hint at being 'stricken' <note>original: "נכה" — from the word for stricken or broken</note> and yet living. This means he is cleansed of his sins, as explained in the verse 'Perhaps I shall be able to strike them' <note>Numbers 22:6</note>. The meaning is that through the troubles in the Land, sins are worn away and forgiven. But those who come to the Land of Israel and do not take the King's Palace to heart, but are rebellious, sinful, and increase in feasting and revelry, of them the verse says: 'But when you entered, you defiled My land and made My heritage an abomination' <note>Jeremiah 2:7</note>. And it is written: 'When you come to appear before Me, who has required this at your hand, to trample My courts?' Let it not enter their hearts that after their deaths they will remain in the Land of Israel; rather, in their death they will be driven out like dogs, heaven forbid. All the wicked who die in the Land of Israel, their souls are cast outside the Land, as it is said: 'And the souls of your enemies, He shall sling them out as from the hollow of a sling.' In the future, the Holy One, blessed be He, will take hold of the corners of the earth and shake it of all impurity, casting it outside the Land, as it is said: 'That it might take hold of the ends of the earth, and the wicked be shaken out of it.' The Remaz wrote in the portion *Acharei Mot* regarding the verse on forbidden relations, 'and the land was defiled, therefore I did visit the iniquity thereof': although these relations are personal obligations and not dependent on the Land, nevertheless the essence of all commandments is to perform them in the Land of God. So it was taught in the *Sifra*: 'And the land shall not vomit you out.' The Land of Israel is not like other lands; it does not sustain transgressors. Behold, the Kutim <note>Samaritans</note> were not punished in their own lands, but when they came to the Land of God and acted according to their former ways, He sent lions against them to kill them. Therefore, every man should tremble upon coming to the Land of Israel, to be more God-fearing than he was outside the Land, and he should know that he is in the King's Palace." Thus far his words.

<summary>This page discusses the immense spiritual superiority of living in the Land of Israel, framing it as a supreme commandment that requires joy, yet warns that the Land's holiness does not tolerate sinners.</summary>
<keywords>Land of Israel, Aliyah, suffering, joy, Sefer Charedim, holiness of place, divine presence, exile, atonement, afterlife</keywords>

<header>The Gate of the Letters</header>

# The Gate of the Letters

<margin>Regarding this, whoever allows anything of anger to rest in his hands, all these [forces] take him to the side of anger, which is the evil "Other Side" <note>original: *Sitra Achra*, the kabbalistic term for the realm of evil</note>, the side of impurity... and they raise him up and he is brought close to that side, and they proclaim in all those firmaments and say: "Woe to so-and-so who strayed after an alien god and worshipped another god!" And at that time, a second voice calls out: "Woe to them, for they have strayed from Me..." <note>Hosea 7:13</note>. How worthy is the man who guards his ways and does not stray to the right or the left, so that he does not fall into a deep pit from which he cannot rise. End of quote.</margin>

<margin>The secret of Anger and the secret of Will <note>original: *Ratzon*</note> are now explained. The Will from Above is entirely good; no evil dwells in His presence. It is the strength and emanation of the Attribute of Justice, holy and pure, and its purpose is the essence of good. With this, we can understand the statement from the Zohar mentioned above regarding the "Anger of the Sages" <note>A Talmudic concept that a scholar's anger is actually a fire for the sake of the Torah's honor</note>: it is good for the honor and preservation of the Torah. However, one who swears out of anger—that is an "alien god." Now, I have already explained that the world was created through Will, and it is known that the world was created through the Torah, as the Sages said: "The Holy One, blessed be He, looked into the Torah and created the world." If one begins with anger <note>original: *Aph*, which means both "anger" and "nose," the first organ of breath</note>, he denies the creation of "something from nothing." Therefore, the angry person has no portion in the Torah, as it says in tractate *Pesachim*: "Anyone who becomes angry—if he is a sage, his wisdom departs from him; if he is a prophet, his prophecy departs from him." And in tractate *Kiddushin*: "The Divine Name is only handed over to one who is in the middle of his years and does not become angry." He brings a story from the *Sefer Charedim* <note>A 16th-century ethical work by Rabbi Elazar Azikri</note> about the pious Rabbi Jacob Ashkenazi of blessed memory, who was a wondrous sage in wisdom and wanted to teach his wisdom to Rabbi Judah the Pious <note>Leader of the German Pietists in the 12th-13th century</note>. But first, he tested him in the matter of anger, for they had a tradition not to hand over the wisdom except to one they had tested with anger and found he did not lose his temper. They tested him three times, etc.</margin>

**"And the Lord** God took the man and placed him..." <note>Genesis 2:15</note> to work it and to guard it. Against our will, the soul is clothed in anger <note>or "the nose"</note>, or it is driven out from the Garden of Eden. Its place is prepared in the "shame of the Garden of Eden," which is Gehenna <note>Hell</note>, if he does not return in complete repentance. As it says in tractate *Nedarim*: "Rabbi Yannai said: Anyone who becomes angry, all types of Gehenna rule over him, as it is said: 'Remove anger from your heart and put away evil from your flesh' <note>Ecclesiastes 11:10</note>, and 'evil' refers only to Gehenna." Similarly, they said in the *Tikkunim* <note>Tikkunei Zohar, a foundational kabbalistic text</note>, Tikkun 48: "How worthy is he who allows the Divine Presence <note>original: *Shekhinah*</note> to dwell [within him], which is not approached by the sadness of the spleen or the anger of the gall, for that is the fire of Gehenna." About this it was said: "You shall kindle no fire in all your habitations on the Sabbath day" <note>Exodus 35:3</note>. And it is certainly so: anyone who is angry is as if he kindled the fire of Gehenna. End of quote. If I were to write of the evils that come from anger, and conversely, the lofty levels that arise from Will, it would take much seed and many parchment rolls!

Therefore, a person must force himself and conquer his inclination, ensuring that all the days of his life he does not fall into anger. Is it not better for him to suppress his inclination than to lose all the holiness that was within him and all the commandments he performed? His prayers are then confined within "four cubits" <note>meaning they do not ascend to heaven</note>. He should think that the Holy One, blessed be He, brought this matter to his hand to test him. 

The Rabbi <note>likely referring to Rabbi Moses Cordovero</note> wrote in the "Gate of Humility," Chapter 3: There is another way to make one's anger subside—he should think that through this, his sins are being atoned for. Sins are atoned for either through accepting suffering, through fasts, sackcloth, and ashes—as King David did—or through the death of children, which provides atonement and purification. Indeed, death itself atones for everything, even the desecration of God's Name, if repentance preceded it. Now, all these are difficult for a person to suffer, and they are very bitter—especially the death of children or one's own death. Since a person subjects himself to self-afflictions to atone for his sins—and sometimes these cause a neglect of Torah study and prayer—it should be pleasant for him to receive light suffering that does not involve the neglect of Torah. He should receive with love the insults and shaming he hears, knowing that the Holy One, blessed be He, loves him by sending him such light suffering to cleanse his sins. The one who insults him is merely a "wicked strap" <note>term: *retzu'ah bisha* — a tool of divine discipline</note> used to lash him, as it says: "O Assyria, the rod of My anger" <note>Isaiah 10:5</note>. 

It is proper for him to pray to the Holy One, blessed be He, in all his prayers—especially in the Evening Prayer <note>Ma'ariv</note>—that the Holy One, blessed be He, grant him the merit of the attribute of humility and submissiveness, and that he should hear his own insult [without reacting] and conquer his inclination. Through this, he will find favor before the Holy One, blessed be He, and what he has sinned until now through anger and pleasure will be forgiven. Since this is his request, he will not become angry or answer his reviler. These two things for acquiring humility I heard from the mouth of my teacher, of blessed memory. End of quote.

Further, in the "Gate of Humility," Chapter 5, he wrote several things to remind a person to nullify anger: "Further things to be saved from anger were written by Rabbi Isaac of Acre <note>A 13th-14th century kabbalist</note>, of blessed memory, in his book: 'One night, on a Sabbath eve, I was contemplating what a person should do so as not to become angry. I felt as if someone was saying to me: Is it not true that an angry person is a fool? Be an intellectual. An intellectual follows the essence of the matter and does not set his heart or mind after the appearance of his eyes or the hearing of his ears regarding physical things or insults meant to anger him. He should not pay them any attention at all, but strive after the essence—meaning, the status of the one speaking or doing them. If he sees that the speaker or doer is a fool and an ignoramus, his mind and his anger should immediately distance themselves. If he is a wise man and an intellectual, his anger should likewise distance itself. For if he is a fool, he should think: "He is a disturbed madman acting without knowledge; his words are no more than the chirping of birds, the barking of a dog, or the braying of a donkey." Regarding the wise man, he should recognize that he speaks for his own good and benefit, and he should receive his words and rejoice in them.'"

"Furthermore, I will let you hear good advice to ease anger: when you have dealings with a person who is not good, make a firm resolution in your heart to suffer from him all kinds of insults in speech and deed. For when a person prepares himself to be insulted by another, it will not come upon him suddenly and he will not become angry. He should do this until he is saved from him, and afterward flee from him, like the parable of the merchant, etc. And through this, he shall live." End of quote.

I have summarized here the words of the Pious One <note>Rabbi Bahya ibn Paquda</note>, author of the *Duties of the Heart* <note>original: *Chovot HaLevavot*, an 11th-century ethical classic</note>. One method he mentions is for a person to think of his end—that death will come to him suddenly, his desires and hopes will cease, and he will be placed in the grave. This should happen when a person considers his obligation to serve God for His many kindnesses and great goodness, and how he has neglected the commandments and how his arguments and excuses will fail on the Day of Reckoning. His spirit shall pass away in a moment, as it is written: "For behold, the day comes, burning like a furnace..." <note>Malachi 3:19</note>. And "who can endure the day of his coming?" 

This matter is explained in the Zohar, on the verse "And the men were afraid because they were brought into Joseph's house" <note>Genesis 43:18</note>: Rabbi Yose says: "Woe to the children of men who do not know and do not look at the paths of the Torah! Woe to them at the hour when the Holy One, blessed be He, comes to demand judgment for their deeds, and the body and soul stand to give an account... that is a day of anger, a day when the mourners open [their mouths] and the masters of judgment stand... at that time the serpent stands ready to bite him, all his limbs tremble, and his soul separates from his body and goes wandering, not knowing which path it will take or to which place they will raise it. Woe to that day of anger and wrath!" Therefore, a person should provoke <note>or "incite"</note> his inclination every day and remember that day before him... for we have learned: "A person should always incite the Good Inclination against the Evil Inclination." If it leaves him, good; if not, let him engage in Torah, for there is nothing that breaks the Evil Inclination like Torah. If it leaves him, good; if not, let him remind himself of the day of death to break it. End of quote.

And when a person takes to heart that he is being judged for his pride and anger, and that all his deeds are written in a book and no sin is quickly erased—as it is written: "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron and a point of diamond" <note>Jeremiah 17:1</note>—then through a change of mind and repentance, it is scoured and cleaned. Furthermore, there is nothing that cancels the "clinging to God" <note>original: *devekut*</note> more than anger. Therefore, a certain Rabbi said that on a day he was angry, he would not pray. Since man is made in the "Image of God" <note>original: *Tzelem Elohim*</note>, as explained in the Gate of Holiness, he must cling to the Holy Name. King David said: "What is man that You are mindful of him... You have made him ruler over the works of Your hands; You have put all things under his feet" <note>Psalm 8:5-7</note>. But through anger, the soul departs from him, and instead of being "above all," he becomes "under all," like a husk <note>original: *kelippah*</note>, as explained above.

Another thing to nullify anger, written in the *Chovot HaLevavot*: when someone reveals his shame to him, he should pity his own soul for its shortcomings and not seek excuses to take revenge or justify himself. Rather, he should say as Judah said: "She is more righteous than I" <note>Genesis 38:26</note>. He should not strive to embarrass the one who told of it, nor blame him for revealing it...

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual and metaphysical dangers of anger, equating it to idolatry and the fire of Hell. It offers practical kabbalistic and ethical advice for cultivating humility, such as viewing insults as divine atonement and remembering the day of death.</summary>
<keywords>Anger, Humility, Repentance, Gehenna, Soul, Evil Inclination, Torah, Chovot HaLevavot, Zohar, Divine Will, Tzelem Elohim</keywords>

<meta>Continuity with previous page: This page continues the alphabetical or thematic "Gate of the Letters," moving into the discussion of the letter Resh (or the concept of Ratzon/Will). The catchword from the previous page, "Sitra," refers to the "Sitra Achra" (the Other Side), which is the main subject of the warnings on this page regarding anger.</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

**The Letter** [regarding] **Will**: Know, my sons, that the virtue of Will <note>original: *Ratzon*—referring to a state of being favored, or having a settled, peaceful will</note>—meaning that one should be eternally content, not becoming frustrated or incensed—is the opposite of the levels of arrogance. Conversely, the trait of anger is an evil and wretched thing; there is no evil in the world like this evil. As our Sages of blessed memory said in Tractate Shabbat, in the chapter "The Weaver": "One who becomes angry is like one who worships idols." Of him, it is said: "There shall be no alien god within you" <note>Psalm 81:10</note>. In the Zohar, portion *Tetzaveh*, this is discussed at length. It comments there on the verse: "Cease from the man in whose nostrils is breath, for of what value is he?" <note>Isaiah 2:22</note>. For the Holy One, blessed be He, created man in the Supernal Image <note>original: *dyukna ila'ah*</note> and breathed into him a holy spirit comprised of three parts, as we have established: *Nefesh, Ruach,* and *Neshamah* <note>the three kabbalistic levels of the soul: the vital/animal soul, the spirit/breath, and the higher intellectual soul</note>. Above them all is the *Neshamah*, which is a supernal power used to know and guard the commandments of the Lord. Because of this, this holy soul enters into [divine] service. But if a man pollutes it, he departs from the service of his Master. Since these three powers—*Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah*—are all one and function as one, they are patterned after the Supernal [arrangement]. Therefore it is said: "He who walks with the wise shall become wise." 

And if we see this man, in whom all these levels resided before they were firmly established, how do we know who he is? How is he recognized? By testing him. If he is endangered by his own anger, we know and recognize who he is. If that holy soul remains firm during the time of his anger and is not uprooted from its place to be replaced by that "alien god," then he is a man as he should be; he is a servant of his Master, a complete man. But if that man does not guard the soul, and uproots that supernal holiness from its place to allow the "Other Side" <note>original: *Sitra Achra*, the realm of evil/impurity</note> to dwell in its stead, then surely this is a man who rebels against his Master. It is forbidden to draw near to him or to associate with him. This is the meaning of "He tears his soul in his anger" <note>Job 18:4</note>. He literally tears and uproots his soul because of his rage, and in its place, he settles [the impurity]. If he had settled holiness within his anger, he would not uproot it from its place. But instead, he tears the holy soul and defiles it because of his nostrils <note>a pun on the Hebrew word for "anger" (*aph*), which also means "nose/nostrils"</note>. Even the breath <note>original: *neshamah*</note> is profaned in his nostrils; "for of what value is he?" Such a man is considered an idolater. One who speaks with him is as if he speaks with literal idolatry, because literal idol worship dwells within his rage. Not only that, but he uproots supernal holiness from its place and settles an "alien god" in its stead. What is written of an "alien god"? "You shall not bow down to an alien god." In this same way, it is forbidden to even look at his face. 

And if you say, "What of the anger of the Sages?"—the anger of the Sages is good in all its aspects. For we have learned that the Torah is fire, and the Torah blazes within the scholar, as it is written: "Is not My word like fire? says the Lord." The anger of the Sages in matters of Torah is for the sake of the Torah's honor; it is all for the service of the Holy One, blessed be He. But if it is regarding other matters, it is not the service of the Holy One. For every sin a man commits is like literal idolatry, and it is forbidden to bring it near him. And if you say, "But it is only a passing moment of anger, and then he returns to his place [of holiness]," the truth is that he has already uprooted the holiness of his soul from himself and his place, and that "alien god" has strengthened within him and will not leave him... [The anger] uroots him from the worlds. To bring holiness back upon himself afterward is not easily done. Rabbi Yose said: "Is he truly defiled?" He replied: "Come and see. At the moment he uproots the holiness of his soul and allows that 'alien god' to dwell in his place, the man becomes defiled and is called 'unclean.' It is forbidden to approach him, for the [divine] Image has been uprooted from him. And once it is uprooted, we must wait until he repents to his place." He said: "Woe, how many are the defilements that are driven out!" He replied: "Other defilements are different; they cannot do more than they do. But this [anger] is the worst of all. Impurity issues from his body and his flesh; the entire body is defiled. While other impurities of the world only affect the outer body, here, 'Cease from the man in whose nostrils is breath,' for he has exchanged the holiness of his Master because of his nostrils. This is the impurity of impurities... he is surely considered like an idol." 

See, this is anger, which is the "Other Side" of idolatry, as we have said. A man must guard himself from it and separate himself from it. Therefore it is written: "Do not make for yourself molten gods" <note>Exodus 34:17</note>, so as not to damage your soul. And immediately after it is written: "The Festival of Matzot you shall guard." This is the side of holiness that a man must guard and not exchange for the "Other Side." If he exchanges it, he is defiled and defiles all who come near him. "The Festival of Matzot you shall guard"—this is the place called "Guarded" <note>original: *Shamor*</note>, and it is certainly written that you must guard it. Thus far the quote [from the Zohar].

<margin>Zohar, portion *Vayechi*</margin>

And these are the words of the *Reshit Chokhmah* <note>a famous 16th-century kabbalistic ethical manual by Eliyahu de Vidas</note> in "The Gate of Humility," Chapter 2: When a man contemplates what Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explained in this passage—that the one who is angry uproots all the holiness within him, which is the *Nefesh, Ruach,* and *Neshamah*—it is because the three are tied together as one. This is why it is written "He tears his soul." Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai informs us in this passage of the great severity of the punishment. Let it not be said that the damage is only to the *Nefesh* <note>the lowest soul level</note> alone; that is not the case. Rather, all the holiness within him departs, for once he has drawn upon himself the "Shell" <note>original: *Kelipah*, the husk of evil</note> called the "Black Covenant," he brings a handmaid to rule in the place of the Matriarch. As it is written: "Princes tremble" <note>referring to the displacement of holy authority</note>—this is literal idolatry, similar to the sin of placing an image in the Temple, which causes the Divine Presence (*Shekhinah*) to flee from there. Therefore, once he has drawn an "alien god" (which is idolatry) into himself, his body and soul remain empty... The *Shekhinah* is the opposite of the *Kelipah*. Just as it was said, "The chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him" <note>Genesis 40:23</note>, so too the *Shekhinah* does not return to him until he repents. 

He adds regarding the "Festival of Matzot" that this is the side of holiness. The concept is that "God has made one thing opposite the other" <note>Ecclesiastes 7:14</note>. Just as the *Shekhinah* includes all the supernal attributes, and through care and guarding one ascends, as explained in "The Gate of Awe," Chapter 1—so too the "alien god" which stands against it includes all the forces of impurity. He is the one who denies Providence, as we explained in "The Gate of Awe," Chapter 8. Therefore it is said that all who are arrogant are drawn from this *Kelipah*, and the punishments are explained here. Behold, the *Shekhinah* only dwells upon a broken and contrite heart. Once a man becomes angry, his heart grows haughty against [God], and the rebellious "alien god" dwells upon him, which is the sum of all impurity. Therefore, it is forbidden to associate with him. Because the worship of idols is called "sacrifices to the dead," and an offering to an idol defiles either by carrying it or by being under the same roof, according to Rabbi Yehuda ben Batyra (as they said in Tractate Chullin, in the chapter on the slaughtering of gentiles). Regarding defilement by carrying, it was taught: Rabbi Yehuda ben Batyra says: "From where do we know that an offering to an idol defiles by carrying? As it says: 'They attached themselves to Baal Peor and ate the sacrifices of the dead.' Just as a corpse defiles by being in the same tent, so too an offering to an idol defiles by being in the same tent." Thus far his words.

I heard from the mouth of my teacher, Rabbi Isaac Ashkenazi <note>original: *Ha-Ari*, the father of Lurianic Kabbalah</note>, of blessed memory, that "He tears his soul" means he makes it *treifa* <note>unfit/torn, like an animal that cannot be eaten</note>. We can be precise about this based on the language of the Zohar, which says: "he tears his holy soul and defiles it because of his anger." It says "defiles it" because it is a *treifa*, and a *treifa* is considered dead, for a torn thing cannot live. It is appropriate that he be defiled... for his holy soul was dwelling within him, and once he brought in the *Kelipah*, it is like a lung-adhesion <note>original: *sircha*, a defect making meat non-kosher</note> that takes hold and defiles the soul. So he said below: "The soul and everything is defiled." This is not like a wise beast that is a *treifa*, which does not defile if slaughtered with a kosher knife; rather, he makes it a *nevelah* <note>a carcass of an animal that died without proper slaughter</note>, for he slaughtered the soul with the knife of his rage. And when the Zohar says "uproots," this "uprooting" refers to the urooting of the "signs" <note>the trachea and esophagus, the "signs" of ritual slaughter</note>. This is also the language of the Zohar: "He tears his soul in his anger... he tears and uproots his soul." Uprooting the "signs" is an act that ruins the slaughter, making it a carcass (*nevelah*) that defiles by carrying. Just as uprooting the "signs" is a disruption of the natural order of things, so too the angry man uproots the holiness whose nature it is to dwell within every creature. By his own hand, he uproots it from its place. Thus, the word "tears" <note>original: *toref*</note> has two meanings, and both are true. Accordingly, an angry man who is a Priest <note>a *Kohen*</note> defiles himself with impurity, for all souls are from the side of Abraham, who is called a Priest. Since through anger he kills his soul, and a corpse defiles, the Priest becomes defiled by the dead. Thus far the words of the *Reshit Chokhmah*.

<margin>*Sefer HaMusar*, portion *Bereshit*</margin>

**A hint** as to how one should respond to his fellow, and why the trait of anger is as it is. Its hint is the Will. When the matter is explained, it will surely bring a **great awakening**. The **secret** of the Will is great and awesome, as explained at length in *Orchot Tzaddikim* <note>an anonymous 15th-century ethical work</note>. The secret is that it "arose in His Will," blessed be He, to create the world through His good Will, generously and without compulsion, only to fulfill His trait of goodness to do good for others. He desires existence and the good of His creations. "Opposite this, God made the other" <note>Ecclesiastes 7:14</note>: He created good and He created evil. This evil exists for the sake of the good, for if there were no evil (which is Judgment), the good would not be sustained. In this regard, [the word] *Mah* <note>Hebrew for "What," numerical value 45</note> is transformed into *Mah*... and this is explained at length in the aforementioned introduction. 

Everything is included in the Good Will. The attribute of His goodness flows from the purity of Unity. Nothing descends from Above except to one who awakens it and draws it upon himself. One who separates himself from Unity [brings] Judgment upon Judgment. This is true Judgment, for her entire life is herself... because her vitality was awakened. Anger is the opposite of Will, for it comes from the root of the "Other Side," Sammael <note>the primary archangel of evil in Kabbalah</note>, which is composed of [the letters] Yod, Vav, and Zayin. That which is drawn from him is "Nostril" and "Wrath" <note>original: *Aph* and *Chemah*</note>... the powers of anger. As we find with the Serpent, the power of Sammael and the corruption began with the "Nostril" <note>referring to a midrashic interpretation of the serpent's speech</note>, as the Sages said: "They began with the nostril." The sign of this is that the serpent opens... and all of it is the chariot of Sammael, who rebels against his Master... his name is "Earth of Eternity." These things are explained in the words of our Sages in the Gemara. 

The reason for this is that the Will indicates His blessed Unity, while anger is drawn from an "alien god" who rebels against Him, becoming a throne and a tent for the "Other Side." Whatever a man does in anger is an empty act; it is all an offering to that "alien god." In the Zohar, regarding one of the Halls of Impurity <note>original: *Heikhalot*</note>, they said that there is a supervisor named *Pistatrita* and many officers of law, and they take up evil words. When anger rests upon a man, this supervisor *Pistatrita* seizes the word that the man threw out in his rage, ascends, and says: "This is the sacrifice that so-and-so offered to our side!" For every side of tranquility is from the side of faith, but from the side of [anger]...

It draws on the Zohar, the Reshit Chokhmah, and the teachings of Rabbi Isaac Luria to warn that anger is a form of spiritual suicide and defilement.</summary>

<meta>Continuity with previous page: This page transitions from the discussion of the letter Resh and the dangers of anger into a broader exploration of the power of speech and the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet. It focuses on the sanctity of the mouth and the severe spiritual consequences of misusing the gift of language.</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

The meaning of the twenty-two letters in our holy tongue was revealed to him through His secret. The term *Kesher Kuzeh* <note>original: "קשר כוזה"—likely a reference to a kabbalistic cipher or protective name</note> also alludes to what is required by the word *Keva* <note>meaning "fixed" or "established"</note>. Through this, we can understand the high level of the early sages, may they rest in peace, whose prayers were answered immediately. This was because they were careful not to blemish the twenty-two letters, which are the five phonetic origins <note>The five locations in the mouth where sounds are produced: the throat, palate, tongue, teeth, and lips</note> fixed in the mouth, as explained in the *Shelah* <note>Rabbi Isaiah Horowitz's work, *Shnei Luchot HaBerit*</note> and regarding other things that blemish the tongue. Therefore, their prayer would pierce the heavens and ascend to the highest heights to awaken Divine Mercy. Similarly, it says in the *Zohar* that when Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, may he rest in peace, was engaged in Torah study, many thousands and tens of thousands of ministering angels would listen to his voice. The reason for this was that the five phonetic origins of their mouths were pure, refined, and unified across all worlds. The sound and speech that emerged from their mouths became a source of "pleasant spirit" <note>original: *nachat ruach*—a state of divine satisfaction</note> above. However, when there is a blemish in the five origins, the breath of prayer and Torah emerging from the mouth comes out through a defect or "adhesion" <note>original: *sirkha*—a term from laws of kosher slaughter referring to a lung lesion; here used metaphorically for a spiritual blockage in speech</note>. It is impossible for such speech to achieve unification above, for "anything that has a blemish shall not be offered" <note>Leviticus 22:21</note>. So it is said in the *Faithful Shepherd* <note>original: *Ra’aya Mehemna*—a section of the Zohar</note>: just as the five lobes of the lung must all be open without any adhesion to receive the sound, so too the five "rectifications" of the mouth <note>the phonetic groups</note> must all be open without any adhesion. These five are: *Aleph-Chet-He-Ayin* in the throat; *Bet-Vav-Mem-Pe* in the lips; *Gimel-Yod-Kaf-Qof* in the palate; and *Dalet-Tet-Lamed-Nun-Tav* <note>the lingual letters</note> require speech, and the speech of the lung must be in them without any adhesion or delay at all. And the mystery of the name *Y-H-V-H* is "before he finished speaking," <note>Genesis 24:15</note> and it shall be attached and emerge—this is the prayer of speech. Concerning this, it is said: "If my prayer is fluent in my mouth, I know it is accepted" <note>Mishnah Berakhot 5:5</note>. But if there is an adhesion and it emerges with delay, "I know it is rejected" <note>original: *me-turaf*—torn or invalid</note>, just as a lung with an adhesion is non-kosher.

Regarding the source of the twenty-two letters, it is said: "Let He see no unseemly thing in you" <note>Deuteronomy 23:15</note>. The Hebrew word for "thing," *davar*, also means "speech." Thus, one should not see speech used in vain. For the "Covenant of the Tongue" and the "Covenant of the Organ" <note>circumcision</note> are aligned one against the other. Just as one must not waste seed in vain, so too with speech. Furthermore, [speech] in vain is also considered "unseemliness." This is the meaning of "Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin" <note>Ecclesiastes 5:5</note>, for speech leads to the sin of the flesh, which is the wasting of seed, as explained in the *Zohar* and cited in the *Derech Chaim* <note>A work on ethics/Musar, likely by the Maharal of Prague</note> in the Gate of Holiness, Chapter 1, and also in Chapter 10. The reason is that speech is fashioned in thought. Anyone who knows that the brain—which is the place of thought—must be spiritual, specifically through the words of the Sages and the Torah, for the secret of the Sages is the secret of Thought. Speech emerges through the two rows of teeth fixed in the mouth, which correspond to the thirty-two paths of Wisdom, as I have elaborated in other chapters. Thus, the source of speech is in the intellect on the side of the Soul. But from the perspective of the Body, "silence is better than speech." This is what the Tanna <note>Mishnaic sage</note> meant: "All my days I grew up among the Sages, and I found nothing better for the body than silence" <note>Pirkei Avot 1:17</note>. He did not say "nothing better for the Soul," but "nothing better for the Body," because from the body's side, speech is physical. Therefore, he used the negative phrasing: "I found nothing better for the body than silence." All this was his point: "From the moment I grew up among the Sages, from the perspective of Wisdom, speech is good; but from the perspective of the body, it is not so—silence is better."

**Behold**, for sinful speech, there is no measure or limit to its punishment, as our Sages have elaborated regarding the four classes that do not receive the Divine Presence: the class of **S**corners, the class of **F**latterers, the class of **L**iars, and the class of **S**landerers. The mnemonic for these classes is **H-M-S-L** <note>original: חמש"ל — Chet (Chanufim/Flatterers), Mem (Mesaprei Lashon Hara/Slanderers), Shin (Shekarim/Liars), Lamed (Leitzim/Scorners)</note>.

<margin>...and the fire shall not be extinguished.</margin>

**And if** I were to go on at length to mention the greatness of their sin and their punishment as mentioned in the Talmud, Midrash, and Zohar, the book would grow too long. I have come only to inform you that these are the "Four Primary Categories of Impurity," and their derivatives are like them. Their sin is as great as one who denies the Essence [God] or worships idols. These are the ones who descend to Gehenna. Excluding the *Chashmal* <note>likely a reference to a type of angelic energy or a specific sin-cleansing process</note>, flattery is mentioned in *Derech Chaim*, Gate of Holiness, Chapter 2: Flattery is severe, as it is weighed against idolatry, sexual immorality, and murder. How do we know idolatry? As it is written: "Their faces are like flames and their hearts are not right." <note>This section provides proof-texts linking flattery to the cardinal sins</note>. Why is the rope of the bed inclined? How do we know sexual immorality? As it is said: "If a man sends away his wife... shall not that land be greatly polluted?" <note>Jeremiah 3:1; the Hebrew word for "polluted," *chanof*, is the same as "flattered"</note>. How do we know murder? As it is written: "And they polluted the land with blood." Flattery against the one being flattered involves four things: First, one who worships idols in this time is not a convert through a prophet who shows him the idol’s importance and miracles; but the one who flatters regarding the Torah has many arguments [against him]. Second, an idolater acts from the wickedness of his heart; if the truth were clear to him, he would not worship it. Third, the idolater worships a thing of God <note>a created thing</note>, but the flatterer has no end to his "worship" [of people]. Fourth, the idolater does not leave [the faith] because of a crown given by men, and his denial of God is public; but the flatterer's denial is not visible, and people trust him, allowing him to harm them in ways the wicked of the world cannot. All their tongues are called flattery...

<margin>And the seal of the Holy One, Blessed be He, is Truth: Mem</margin>

**And the seal** of the Holy One, Blessed be He, is Truth. "One who guards truth" is the numerical value of the names *Y-H-V-H* and *Adonai* <note>The combined gematria of these names is 91</note>. It is also [the value of] "Amen" <note>91</note>. Thus, one who lies denies this Name, which is the seal of the Holy One, Blessed be He. **M** for Slanderers (*Mesaprei Lashon Hara*): It is taught in Tractate Arachin in the school of Rabbi Ishmael: Anyone who speaks slander increases sins corresponding to the three [cardinal] transgressions: idolatry, sexual immorality, and murder. "This shall be the law of the leper" (*Metzora*)—meaning one who brings out an evil name (*Motzi Shem Ra*). Regarding idolatry, it says: "This people has sinned a great sin." Regarding sexual immorality: "How can I do this great evil?" Regarding murder: "My sin is too great to bear." **L** for Scorners (*Leitzim*): concerning them it is cried out that they shall be for a derision. It is brought in the *Kavanot of the Mishnah* that one who scorns is like one who denies the whole Torah and denies the Holy One, Blessed be He, as the Kabbalists have written. If so, why should I go on at length and bring the words of our Sages and the authors regarding the great punishment of these four classes, the four "Fathers of Damages" and "Fathers of Impurity," since it has been clarified that all those who worship idols have no [portion] in the world to come. And it is written in *Faithful Shepherd*, Gate of Holiness, at the beginning of Chapter 2, in the name of the Kabbalists, that the definition of the four classes mentioned corresponds to four impure animals: the **Satan** <note>possibly a scribal error for the *Sair* or a specific desert creature</note>, the **Hare**, the **Camel**, and the **Pig**. A mnemonic: the aforementioned classes are reincarnated into these four impure animals. (The explanation of these four classes is found at length in Chapters 10 and 13 of the Gate of Holiness; look there). However, one must know that one needs to be very strict and distance oneself by thousands of leagues from these traits and anything resembling them—such as various types of flattery, even in a small matter. There is flattery between a man and himself before the Omnipresent, and flattery between a man and his fellow. Flattery of oneself is when one does a good deed and desires that people see him doing so, especially for honor and the like; this person is not serving the Omnipresent with a pure heart, but for the sake of people to show himself off. Flattery between a man and others is well known.

**Similarly**, the class of Liars does not only mean one who lies in weights and measures or in business and the like, but even in optional, everyday speech, one who lies is included in the class of Liars. **Similarly**, Slanderers does not only mean one who invents a bad reputation for his fellow, but even if the bad reputation has already emerged and he mentions it—and not even a "bad name" specifically, but even a small, light thing that causes damage is considered slander...

<margin>From the "Seat of Scorners," as we learned: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradion says, "Two who sit together and no words of Torah pass between them, this is a 'Seat of Scorners.'" It seems he is scoffing at the Torah as if it is not important in his eyes; otherwise, he would not be idle from it. **And how much more so** when one is engaged in Torah and stops in the middle of study for idle chatter. In Tractate Avot, it was taught: "Anyone who stops studying the words of Torah and engages in idle conversation is fed glowing coals of broom wood." **And from the scoffers** of the words of the Sages, it is brought in Tractate Eruvin that they are judged in "boiling excrement." And it seems to me that this includes anyone who says [dismissively] of any logic brought in the Gemara...</margin>

**Furthermore**, one who whitens the face of his fellow <note>shames him in public</note> and one who calls his fellow by a nickname has no portion in the World to Come. The Gemara asks: Is "calling by a nickname" not the same as "whitening the face"? It answers: Even if he is used to it—meaning even if others already call him that, and even not in his presence, it is forbidden. There is great wonder at the blindness and wickedness of the people of the world who sin in this and destroy themselves. God forbid we should be among those of whom it is said: "All descend to Gehenna and ascend, except for these who descend and do not ascend: the one who calls by a nickname... and the one who whitens the face..." Therefore, one who guards his soul will distance himself. If he has stumbled, he should regret the past and ask his fellow: "Please, forgive me," and he should do repentance for this and be careful all his days, and then it will be good for him. **The magnitude** of slander includes gossip (*rekhilut*). It is forbidden to believe it... these are the ones who are lashed. In the chapter "Arachin" and "Pesachim," Rav Sheshet said... if so, anyone who speaks slander, accepts slander, or testifies falsely is worthy of being thrown to the dogs, as it is said: "You shall cast it to the dog" <note>Exodus 22:30</note>, which is adjacent to the verse "Thou shalt not carry a false report." And even if he does not believe the gossip, he must still be concerned for it and is permitted to guard himself, as is explained in the words of our Sages. Similarly, regarding scoffing, even a small word is like vanity... one is a scorner. Not only that, even if he does not speak scoffing, but he sees that he is able to engage in Torah and does not do so, sitting idly, he is called [a scorner].

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual mechanics of speech, warning that the purity of one's mouth is essential for prayer to be accepted. It categorizes the four classes of people excluded from God's presence—Scorners, Flatterers, Liars, and Slanderers—linking their sins to cardinal transgressions and impure animals.</summary>
