# The Gate of the Letters

<note>The author provides instructions on how to respond to an accuser.</note> One should say to him: "My brother, what you have observed of my bad deeds is true, but there is so much more you do not know about me, which the Holy One, Blessed be He, in His hiddenness, has long endured. If the full extent of my evil deeds and iniquities were revealed to you, you would flee from me." One should humble himself before the Creator and acknowledge that God has revealed only a small portion of his faults so that he might repent. If the things spoken against him are false, the one who speaks them loses his own merits. It was said of a certain pious man <note>original: "chassid"</note> that when he heard someone had spoken ill of him, he sent that person a bowl full of the finest fruits of the land. He wrote to him: "It has reached me that you have sent me a gift of your merits and rewards; this is my way of repaying you." 

One of the pious said: "Many people will arrive at the Day of Judgment, and when their deeds are shown to them, they will find in the book of their merits good deeds they never performed. They will say, 'We did not do these,' and it will be said to them, 'The person who spoke against you and recounted your disgrace performed them.' Likewise, when people find merits missing from their books, they will seek them at that time, and it will be told to them, 'You lost them when you spoke against so-and-so.'" Some will also find sins in their record they did not commit; they will be told, "These were added to you because of so-and-so, whom you slandered," as it is written: *And render unto our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom* <note>Psalm 79:12</note>. We have skipped some of his language here to avoid length. 

Regarding the concept of added merit, it is said of the generation of King David, when Shimei ben Gera cursed him: *Let him alone, and let him curse; for the Lord hath bidden him. It may be that the Lord will look on mine affliction, and that the Lord will requite me good for his cursing this day* <note>II Samuel 16:11–12</note>. The "good" mentioned refers to the merits of Shimei, which would return to David in exchange for the curse he accepted. 

The way to nullify anger is to contemplate the many ruins that follow from it. One who angers easily and is not long-suffering may come to commit murder. As it is told in the *Sefer Hasidim* <note>A 12th-century book of Jewish ethics and stories from Medieval Germany</note>: There was a son who honored his father greatly. The father said, "As you honored me in life, honor me in death. I command you to spend one night in a valley and restrain your spirit so that you do not speak." After the father's death, the son went to study. He left his wife pregnant without knowing it and was delayed on the road for many years. When he returned to the city, he arrived at night and went up to the room where his wife was sleeping. He heard the voice of a young man kissing her. He drew his sword to kill them both, but remembered his father's command and returned it to its scabbard. He then heard the mother say to the young man, "It has been many years since your father left me. By the life of this child, he would be old enough now for me to find him a wife." When he heard this, he said: "Open to me, my sister, my love! Blessed be the Lord who restrained my anger, and blessed be my father who commanded me to restrain my anger for one night, otherwise I would have killed you and my son." They rejoiced with great joy.

To ensure anger does not return to the heart, one should recall the words of the sage: "No man ever insulted me more than once, for the first time I endure the insult, and I do not give him the chance to insult me a second time." The sage also said: "He who cannot endure one thing will endure many things." And: "If you take revenge, you will be pained; if you forgive, you will be elevated." Forgive the one who does you evil, and give to the one who withholds from you.

<margin>May he be acceptable to his brothers and be desired by his brothers.</margin>

Just as one is warned not to be angry, one is warned not to provoke a companion to anger, for both are essentially the same. One should clothe oneself in "will" <note>original: *ratzon*—favor or divine will</note>.

**The words** of the wise are heard in quietness. One whose nature is such will never come to anger. "Heard in quietness" means with a tranquil spirit and not with pride. One who holds onto the trait of humility will naturally never be angry, for he endures and overlooks offenses. "Quietness" also implies moderation rather than haste or great noise, as I expanded upon regarding the letter *Mem*. One should lead people with the quality of quietness—meaning patience—and not be hasty in conflict or in action. Then, one will never come to anger and will not cause the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah: The dwelling of the Divine Presence in the world</term> to depart from him. His character will become a throne for the Divine Presence. Your sign for this is that the Divine Presence is not found in the wind, nor in the noise, nor in the fire <note>Reference to Elijah the Prophet in I Kings 19</note>. The "wind" is the spirit of pride; the "noise" is the opposite of patience; the "fire" is the heat of anger. Only in the "still small voice" does the Divine Presence dwell.

<margin>Then he clings to the Holy One, Blessed be He, who sits in the highest heights, the Cause of all causes. For if the will is to do the will of the Creator, and if they make him wait for his command, and if God forbid he transgresses, he shall not rest or be quiet until they are reconciled through his repentance, prayer, and charity, nullifying his will before the Will of the Place <note>original: *HaMakom*—a name for God</note>.</margin>

**One** who possesses this trait and the elevation of the spirit reaches the level of "Will" <note>original: *Ratzon*</note>. He becomes a master of will between himself and his companion, and how much more so toward the Divine Presence.

<margin>Our Sages, of blessed memory, told a story of a certain pious man who, whenever he went to his bed, would say: "Let it be permitted and forgiven to all who distress me." How much more so if he had distressed his companion—he would seek forgiveness from him. There is a secret in the blessing: today the secret of Mercy and Judgment is known, and the night is the opposite—the secret of Judgment and Accusation. In it, all the beasts of the forest creep, including anger and wrath. Especially at the time of sleep, which is a portion of death, it is appropriate to awaken the "Will."</margin>

**They brought** this forth to clarify that one must awaken the Higher Will and repair any distortion before lying down to sleep. He wrote there at length about this. This is hinted at in the verse: *In his day thou shalt give him his hire* <note>Deuteronomy 24:15</note>, so that he does not awaken the secret of anger in the following night. Specifically during sleep, when the soul ascends above, it should not arrive with a blemish. Thus, every man is obligated to repair the matters of each day on that day, so that no day is lacking, and the days are complete and attached to the secret of "Will." I have already written that the proclamation was made with "Will," and the conclusion of each day—*And there was evening and there was morning*—suggests that even though the quality of evening is the opposite of morning, one should see to it that the evening becomes morning, unifying them into one day. This is the essence of repentance. This is why it warns every day: *And God saw that it was good*. The Lord is good and upright, therefore He directs sinners in the way <note>Psalm 25:8</note>, which is the path of repentance. As it says in the Midrash: They asked Wisdom, "What should a sinner do?" They asked Prophecy... They asked the Torah... They asked the Holy One, Blessed be He, and He said, "Let him perform repentance." This is why "The Lord is good and upright."

---
### The Letter Resh is completed.
---

**The Letter Shin: Silence <note>original: *Shetikah*</note>**
We have learned: Simeon, his son, says, "All my days I grew up among the Sages, and I have found nothing better for the body than silence" <note>Pirkei Avot 1:17</note>. Why does it say "I found nothing better," rather than simply "I found silence to be good"? It is known that the excellence of man is that he is a "speaker." The order of the levels of existence is: Inanimate, Vegetative, Animal, and Speaking <note>A standard medieval classification of the soul's powers</note>. Through speech, man is equal to the angels, for external speech is drawn from internal speech. The levels of man in his spiritual intellect are: Vital Soul, Spirit, and Super-soul <note>original: *Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah*</note>, which correspond to Action, Speech, and Thought. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explained that speech comes from the "Holy Living Creatures" <note>original: *Chayot HaKodesh*—high-ranking angels</note>, which is the level of Spirit <note>original: *Ruach*</note>, as it is written: *He makes his angels spirits*. Through speech, man has the power to cling to holiness. Regarding this, it is said: *Who knows the spirit of man that goes upward, and the spirit of the beast that goes downward?* In the Torah, it says: *And man became a living soul*, which the Targum <note>The Aramaic translation of the Bible</note> renders as "a speaking spirit." If the speech that leaves a man's mouth is not holy, but is merely "breath of the mouth," it is a breath containing sin. Even if it contains no sin but is merely empty words, it is then "vanity of vanities" and "striving after wind," and it does not possess the human vitality that ascends upward; rather, he and the beast are equal.

**It is found** in the *Tikkunim* <note>Tikkunei Zohar</note> that there are five rectifications for the mouth, as stated in the *Sefer Yetzirah* <note>The Book of Formation, an ancient mystical text</note>: the gutturals (A-H-Ch-E), the labials (B-V-M-P), the palatals (G-I-K-K), the linguals (D-T-L-N-T), and the dentals (Z-S-Sh-R-Ts). These are the "perfect stones," the 22 letters that are the pattern of the Holy One, Blessed be He. Regarding them, Jacob said: *And he lay down in that place*. The 22 letters are for "bequeathing to those who love me" <note>A play on the Hebrew word *Yesh* (310), but here linked to the 22 letters</note>. 

In the *Sefer Yetzirah*, it says that the Holy One, Blessed be He, fixed in our mouths 22 letters through five origins: engraved in the voice, hewn in the spirit, and fixed in the mouth in five places. Rabbi Hayyim Vital <note>The primary disciple of the Ari, the great 16th-century Kabbalist</note> wrote that my teacher [the Ari] explained that the word "fixed" <note>original: *kevuot*</note> teaches us a great matter: there are five phonetic origins in the spiritual worlds that are the root for all speech. They descend and are revealed from world to world until the Holy One, Blessed be He, in His love for man, fixed these letters in the mouth so that man could cling to his Creator. When he speaks these letters below in his Torah study or prayer, he moves and awakens the Higher Roots above. This is the meaning of "fixed"—it is like a chain; when a man moves one end of the chain in his hand, he moves the entire chain, no matter how long it may be. Similarly, it says at the end of *Sefer Yetzirah*...

<summary>This page concludes the ethical discussion of the letter Resh, focusing on the dangers of anger and the virtues of forgiveness, before transitioning to the letter Shin, which explores the mystical and linguistic power of silence and speech.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the discussion on the spiritual and ethical implications of the letter Resh (symbolizing anger and evil) and transitions into the letter Shin (symbolizing silence and the refinement of speech). It specifically addresses the dangers of cursing and the proper way to speak during times of mourning.</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

->28 I 28a<-

...as it came out of his mouth, so they established it, end of quote. How many common people have brought upon themselves curses and blasphemies in this manner! Furthermore, one should be careful not to curse himself in a moment of anger, for through anger, the "husks" <note>the *kelipot*, or spiritual layers of impurity</note> are purified and gain strength. There are certain forces called "cursers of the day" who take that self-inflicted curse and fulfill it, God forbid. Such a person is like those who prepare evil for themselves, as explained in the Zohar regarding King David: because he said "the man [who did this] is a son of death," <note>2 Samuel 12:5</note> his own spirit caught him <note>David unknowingly pronounced a death sentence upon himself for his own actions</note>. This is the meaning of: "The Holy One, Blessed be He, causes the living soul to fall into the hand of Dumah <note>the angel of silence/death</note>," as King David said: "Unless the Lord had been my help, my soul had almost dwelt in silence <note>original: *Dumah*</note>." 

Concerning such matters, our Sages of blessed memory said: "A person should never open his mouth to the Satan," as we learn in the chapter 'He Whose Dead [Lies Before Him]': Rabbi Simeon ben Lakish said, and it was also taught in the name of Rabbi Yosei: "A person should never open his mouth to the Satan." Rav Yosef asked: "What is the scriptural source for this?" As it is said: "We should have been almost like Sodom" <note>Isaiah 1:9</note>, and what did the prophet respond in the very next verse? "Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom." It is said earlier in that passage that a mourner, when accepting the divine justice <note>the *Tzidduk HaDin* prayer</note>, should not say: "Master of the Worlds, I have sinned much before You, and You have not punished me even one-thousandth of what I deserve." Likewise, it is proper that a man should not curse his wife, for she is "half of his body," and the two together are a "complete man." If he curses her, he is found to be cursing himself.

It seems to me that the warning for all these matters is derived from the verse: "And the names of other gods you shall not mention" <note>Exodus 23:13</note>. All blemishes of the tongue stem from the "External Side," which is the realm of "other gods." Thus King David said: "Guard your tongue from evil" <note>Psalm 34:14</note>; the intention is to avoid all words that give a "grasp" to the Evil One <note>Samael</note>. When one guards his tongue, he merits life and goodness, as it says: "Who is the man who desires life, who loves days..." end of quote. 

King Solomon, peace be upon him, warned: "Be not rash with your mouth, and let not your heart be hasty to utter a word before God; for God is in heaven, and you upon earth; therefore let your words be few" <note>Ecclesiastes 5:1</note>. Great care is needed to guard one's mouth and tongue so as not to stumble into any [disrespectful] hint toward the Heavens—such as those who say in a tone of wonder: "May the Creator forgive me, but why is this so? Why is that so? How could God have created this?" This is a severe transgression, for everything was created with wisdom, uprightness, truth, and justice.

One might say in the name of the Rashal <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria, a 16th-century legal authority</note> regarding the Talmudic tractate *Bava Kamma*, in the chapter 'An Ox that Gored': that nothing bad happened to the dog of Rav Samuel bar Yehuda. <note>The author is discussing a specific story about comforting a mourner</note>. When Samuel bar Yehuda's daughter died, the Sages went to comfort him. Ulla said to him: "What can we do? It is impossible to change it." Samuel replied: "What have I to do with the comforts of the Babylonians? It is a slight against Heaven!" <note>meaning: the phrase implies that if we *could* change God's decree, we would</note>. This "Babylonian comfort" is a slight toward the One Above, for by saying "What is there to do?" they imply: "If it were possible to do something, we would do it." This sounds as if they are complaining against the attributes of the Holy One, Blessed be He, as if He killed the person unjustly. While a human king might be cruel and kill another's son unjustly, and people find it hard to bear but cannot defeat the king—God's greatness is such that all His words are justice. Presumably, He killed the child justly, for there is no injustice before Him. Therefore, we are obligated to receive the decrees of the Omnipresent with love and to bless Him for both the good and the bad. 

Ulla then began to comfort him differently, noting that the Holy One said to Moses: "Do not distress Moab," <note>Deuteronomy 2:9</note> even though they had begun to act corruptly and hired Balaam. Even so, the Merciful One spared them because of Ruth the Moabitess, who was destined to descend from them. If from a commoner a good thing was destined to emerge, how much more so from the daughter of a great Sage! <note>Ulla's second argument: If a child dies, perhaps they were not destined to bring forth good descendants, or their soul's journey was already complete</note>. 

However, it does not seem to me that the Rashal's words are entirely correct when he says the law does not follow Ulla. In every place where the Talmud mentions "The Rabbis" <note>original: *Rabbanan*</note> without qualification, it refers to the students. It is likely that the students of Ulla were the ones who initially offered the comfort, and when they heard Ulla's critique, they changed their practice. Or perhaps they were simply used to that phrasing and knew no other. 

The Rashal also brings proof from the Ramban <note>Nachmanides</note> and the Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note>. However, this is not a strict prohibition of law, but rather a "measure of piety" <note>term: *midat chassidut* - an act of spiritual excellence beyond the letter of the law</note> because of the verse "Be not rash with your mouth." It is a matter of ethical conduct. In Tractate *Avot* <note>Ethics of the Fathers</note>, there are thousands of excellent things to do or avoid which the Rambam <note>Maimonides</note> or the Rosh might omit in their legal codes, even though they are traditions from Sinai. These are "matters of excellence" and traditions of the Sages. Perhaps the Rif and the Rosh omitted them for the sake of brevity. 

Regarding Ulla’s comfort: "If she were worthy, she would not have died." I believe Ulla's point was that if a person—even a righteous one—is not destined to bring forth a specific "holy seed" or fulfill a certain purpose, they may be taken from the world. God alone knows the secrets of causes and the mystery of the "cycle of souls" <note>term: *sod ha-gilgul* - reincarnation</note>. It is possible the righteous person had already completed their soul's correction. This was Ulla's comfort: "The daughter of a Rabbi, though she was certainly righteous, the Knower of Secrets knew she was not prepared for a further purpose; otherwise, she would not have died." Therefore, one should not be overly distressed. While one must grieve for the loss, one should not be "awakened" to such great bitterness as if an injustice occurred. 

As for those who die due to the "sins of their fathers," this too is true, but they also were not destined to produce a great righteous descendant; otherwise, they would not have died. David also said: "Can I bring him back again?" <note>2 Samuel 12:23</note>. This is different, for David fasted and repented *before* the child died. After the death, he acknowledged that repentance cannot bring back the dead until the future resurrection. 

Finally, the Rashal writes: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Johanan: "The Holy One, Blessed be He, does not withhold the reward of any creature, even the reward for pleasant speech." Because the elder daughter of Lot called her son "Moab" <note>meaning 'from father'</note>, God told Moses: "Do not distress Moab... in war," meaning only war was forbidden, but they could be subjected to forced labor <note>original: *angaria*</note>. But because the younger daughter called her son "Ben-Ammi" <note>meaning 'son of my people,' a more modest term</note>, God said: "Do not harass them... at all," not even with forced labor. 

One must be careful in his speech and deeds. God is exacting with those who do not use refined language, "sifted like fine flour." We see this in the Torah: God used eight extra letters to say "that which is not clean" rather than simply writing "the unclean" <note>Genesis 7:2</note>. Even though there is no actual sin in saying "unclean," the Holy One showed His honor and Holy Spirit to teach us "the way of the land" <note>original: *derech eretz* - proper etiquette</note>. I have received from the "Early Ones" that they were careful not to use the common word for "eggs" <note>note: *beitzim*, which also means testicles</note> but used a euphemism. The reason is that whatever comes out of a person's mouth cleaves the firmaments and remains there until the night, when the soul ascends and encounters that word...

It also explores the theological nuances of comforting mourners, debating whether certain traditional phrases show a lack of faith in divine justice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the ethical and linguistic exploration of the "Gate of Letters," focusing on the sanctity of speech. # The Gate of the Letters

If one finds a difficult passage in the Gemara <note>The Talmudic commentary</note>, or in Rashi, or in the Tosafot <note>Medieval commentaries on the Talmud</note>, or any other resolution, and says the explanation is "far-fetched" or "vile," or says "if I had said this, they would laugh at me"—he commits a great transgression. Since I have heard such talk many times, I am warning you about the weight of these letters. Consider Rabbi Joshua, who spoke with the First and Second <note>referring to generations of scholars</note> regarding the blessings and the House of Shammai, yet his view was set aside. I feared he might abandon his path because of the fasts <note>spiritual disciplines</note>. This is the general rule: "For it is not an empty thing" <note>original: *ki lo davar rek*, Deuteronomy 32:47</note>, and our Sages of blessed memory interpreted this: "if it seems empty, it is from you" <note>meaning the lack of understanding lies with the reader, not the text</note>. All their words are truth and justice, full of taste, knowledge, and command, while our intellect is limited.

I saw from my teacher and master, the pious Sage Maharash <note>Rabbi Shmuel, of blessed memory</note>, that when he heard his students say, "But this questioner is crazy!" or "How could he suggest such a thing?" or similar phrases, he would administer "lashes of rebellion" <note>disciplinary measures</note> so that the student would repent for how the matter was phrased. He trained his students to always speak with honor, such as: "The words of the questioner are not understood by me because of their great depth," or similar respectful language.

The Rabbi <note>likely Rabbeinu Yonah</note> wrote that the category of "mockery" <note>original: *leitzanut*</note> includes those who play with dice and all kinds of games. It is not just about two people sitting together without Torah discussion between them; even involving oneself in games is a form of mockery similar to the types of games mentioned in the tractate *Avodah Zarah* <note>the Talmudic tractate on Foreign Worship</note>. They said of such things: "Nor sat in the seat of the scoffers" <note>Psalm 1:1</note>. This refers to stadiums and circuses, where one watches snakes, sorcerers, and clowns. This is the "seat of the scoffers." In addition to the prohibition of theft <note>associated with gambling</note>, it is written there that those who play dice and other games during the New Moons or Festivals—woe to their souls, for they have dealt themselves an evil blow. The festival days are actually days of judgment, as we learned in *Rosh Hashanah*: at four times of the year the world is judged—at Passover for the grain, at Shavuot for the fruit of the trees, at Rosh Hashanah all who enter the world pass before Him like a flock of sheep, and on Sukkot they are judged for the water. Since all festivals are days of judgment, the Sages said that Sabbaths and Festivals were given to Israel only for the study of Torah. They further said that a person should always see himself and the world as half-meritorious and half-guilty; if he performs one merit, he tips himself and the entire world toward the scale of merit. If not, Heaven forbid, he tips the scale toward guilt. Thus, the sinner who engages in games and lightheadedness during these times is more severely judged than during the rest of the year. I say, Heaven forbid, that the New Moons were created to be a time of atonement! Furthermore, on Rosh Hashanah and the Festivals, there is an "extra holiness" in the soul, as the Kabbalists <note>Jewish mystics</note> say: the five levels of the soul—*Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, Chayah, Yechidah*—enter according to the order of the occasions: New Moons, Festivals, Yom Kippur, Sabbath, and the World to Come. The one who plays games comes and desecrates them. Therefore, you and I must ensure that no games are ever found among you, for the days of your life were given to you to be spent in supreme holiness.

### The "Father of Fathers" of Impure Speech
This is obscene language <note>original: *nivul peh*</note>, which is the side of dark destruction; may it be an eternal disgrace. In addition to the evil a person does to himself, he causes evil to the world. Even one who hears it and remains silent is considered like the speaker, as stated in the chapter "With what [may we light]" <note>original: *Kama Madlikin*, Shabbat 33a</note>: "Because of the sin of obscene language, many troubles and harsh decrees are renewed, the youth of Israel die, and orphans and widows cry out but are not answered." It says: "Therefore the Lord shall have no joy in their young men, neither shall have mercy on their fatherless and widows; for every one is a hypocrite and an evildoer, and every mouth speaks folly. For all this His anger is not turned away, but His hand is stretched out still" <note>Isaiah 9:16</note>. It is also stated there by Hanan bar Rava: "All know why a bride enters the bridal canopy; yet, anyone who speaks obscenely about it, even if a decree of seventy years of good was sealed for him, it is turned to evil." Rav Hisda said in the name of Rav: "For anyone who speaks obscenely, Gehenna <note>Hell</note> is made deep for him, as it says: 'The mouth of strange women is a deep pit'" <note>Proverbs 22:14</note>. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak says: "Even one who hears and remains silent [is punished], as it is said: 'He that is abhorred of the Lord shall fall therein.'"

### Woe
to the one who does such things! How will he become a curse and a widow? <note>idiomatic for misfortune</note> He brings his soul down to the underworld for nothing, for what profit is there in filth? Thus says the *Menorat HaMaor* <note>"The Candelabra of Light," a 14th-century ethical work</note>: We have seen people who are tortured with fire and death and all kinds of coercion, enduring all the pressure and yet they do not admit anything with their mouths that would incriminate them. Even though they might be killed today or tomorrow, they endure suffering to gain a moment of life and will not utter a word to incriminate themselves. How much more so should one refrain when no one is forcing him to speak obscenely! This is a great disgrace; he should know it is a great prohibition and a criminal iniquity. One should also know that by defiling his mouth and tongue with impure speech, all his words of Torah and prayer become stained and rejected from their holy dwelling place. He receives punishment for them, for he is like one who brings an honorable gift to a king, but inside the gift box, he has placed excrement. Rabbi Elazar said: "A person may be beautiful and praised, but if his mouth produces obscenities, he is like a beautiful palace <note>original: *triclinium*</note> that has a tannery <note>notoriously foul-smelling</note> built inside it. Every passerby says: 'How beautiful this palace would be, if only there weren't a tannery pipe running through it!'" Even speech that is not prohibited but is simply idle talk <note>original: *devarim betelim*</note> is a flaw, for the mouth was created only to be a vessel of service for the holiness of Torah and prayer. 

### And Speech
of social interaction, such as honest business dealings, is called a "matter of commandment" <note>a *mitzvah*</note>. For "Torah combined with a worldly occupation is excellent." His intention should be for the sake of Heaven—engaging in business so that God may grant him favor and he will not have to rely on charity, Heaven forbid. His reward will be great.

### The Severity
of oaths, vows, and excommunications: It is known to all that one who utters an oath, even a true oath, brings punishment upon himself. It would have been better for him had he not been created. Although the Torah and the Sages have spoken at length about this in the Talmud, Midrash, and Zohar, the essence is: a person should guard his soul from letting any oath cross his lips all the days of his life. This includes even the lightest of oaths that do not mention God’s name, such as swearing "by my head," "by my father’s life," "by my mother’s life," or by his wife, his home, or his children. People often do this in anger or to verify their words. One should habituate himself to a specific phrase to use instead, and avoid all swearing. My teacher, the Sage, Pious, and Holy one, used to say "Without a vow" <note>original: *bli neder*</note> and "Without an oath." This should be your phrasing for doing or not doing something, even when speaking loudly or in anger. Teach this to your children as well, so they may walk in the path of my teacher, the Sage. Happy is he in the Upper World!

### It is Written
in the *Tur* <note>the code of Jewish law</note>, Yoreh Deah section 203, that if one is pledging charity in public and must pledge with them, he should say "without a vow." There is a doubt regarding the meaning: does it mean he should simply say the amount and the phrase "without a vow" is understood, or must he explicitly speak the words "I want to give this, but I say it without a vow"? It seems to me the second interpretation is correct, for normally a pledge is legally a vow even if the word "vow" is not used. 

### The Severe Prohibition
of uttering a curse: The *Tur* (Choshen Mishpat section 27) writes that even one who curses himself violates a prohibition. One is not liable for lashes unless he curses using the Name of God or one of His descriptive titles. However, even if he curses in the languages of the nations, it is included in the titles. If he says "Cursed be so-and-so," it is a curse. There are lashes for this if there was a warning before witnesses. But even without a formal warning, or if the Name is not used, or if it is phrased as "May so-and-so not be blessed by God," it is still a prohibition even if there are no lashes. People are often not careful about this, Heaven forbid.

### It is Written
by Rabbeinu Yonah in *The Gate of Holiness*, chapter 7: "One should not curse someone even if they do not hear it." The Zohar also says: "One who curses his friend... even if the word has no audible sound to the person, that sound rises above, and many destructive forces join it... until it reaches the great abyss... and many judgments are scattered upon that person..." Sometimes an evil word comes out of the mouth...

# The Gate of the Letters

From his mouth—as they have established—and the pious author of the *Duties of the Heart* <note>original: *H"H*, referring to *Hovot HaLevavot* by Bahya ibn Paquda</note> wrote how much the common folk stumble in this by uttering curses and blasphemies. Furthermore, one must be careful not to curse himself in anger, for in the chambers of the "shells" <note>term: *Kelippot*—the kabbalistic concept of impure spiritual husks that conceal divine light</note> there are forces called "cursers of the day." These forces take that curse which he leveled against himself and fulfill it, Heaven forbid. Such a person is among those who do evil to themselves, as explained in the Zohar <note>The primary work of Jewish mysticism</note>. Because David said, "The man is a son of death" <note>referring to 2 Samuel 12:5</note>, the angel Duma <note>term: *Duma*—the angel in charge of the souls of the dead</note> seized upon him. Had the Holy One, Blessed be He, not helped him, he would have fallen into the hand of Duma, as it is written: "Unless the Lord had been my help, my soul had almost dwelt in silence" <note>Psalm 94:17; "silence" is a pun on the name Duma</note>. Regarding such matters, our Sages of blessed memory said: "A person should never open his mouth to Satan" <note>A warning not to invite misfortune through speech</note>, as we study in the chapter "One whose dead [relative lies before him]": Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, and it was also taught in the name of Rabbi Yose, "A person should never open his mouth to Satan." Rav Yosef said: "What is the biblical verse for this? It is written: 'We should have been like Sodom' <note>Isaiah 1:9</note>. What did the prophet answer them? 'Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom.'" It was said there previously that one should not say, while accepting Divine justice: "Master of the Worlds, I have sinned much before You, and You have not exacted from me even one one-thousandth." Similarly, it is proper that he should not curse his wife, for the couple is "half a body," and the two of them together are a "complete human." If he curses her, it results in him cursing himself. The warning for all these categories is: "Make no mention of the name of other gods" <note>Exodus 23:13</note>. All blemishes of the tongue stem from the "External Side" <note>term: *Sitra Achra*—the side of impurity</note>, which is "other gods." Similarly, the King <note>referring to King David in the Psalms</note> said: "O Lord, guard my tongue from evil." The intention is that all things which give a "hold" to the Evil One—who is Sama <note>term: *Sama*—referring to Samael, the Accuser</note>—must be avoided. When one guards his tongue, he merits the "Tongue of Life" <note>original: *Leshon HaChayim*</note> and not the opposite, as it is said: "Who is the man who desires life, who loves days..." <note>Psalm 34:13</note>. Thus far are his words. King Solomon, may peace be upon him, warned and said: "Be not rash with your mouth, and let not your heart be hasty to utter anything before God; for God is in heaven, and you upon earth; therefore let your words be few" <note>Ecclesiastes 5:1</note>. Great care is needed to guard one's mouth and tongue so there is no hint of [disrespect] toward the Heights <note>meaning Heaven/God</note>, such as those who say in a tone of wonder: "May the Creator forgive me, why is it like this?" or "How did He create this so?" This is a severe transgression; everything is done with wisdom, integrity, truth, and justice.

## And there is
the Rashal <note>original: *Rashal*, Rabbi Solomon Luria, a 16th-century legal authority</note>... regarding [the Talmudic tractate] Bava Kamma, Chapter 4, "An ox that gored four or five": Ulla arrived in Babylon, and a daughter of Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda died. The Sages said: "Rise, and let us go to console him." Ulla said to them: "What do I have to do with the consolation of the Babylonians? For it is blasphemy <note>term: *gidufa*</note> against the Heights! For they say: 'What can be done?' implying: 'If it were possible to do [something against God's will], we would do it!'" <note>This is a critique of the phrase "What can we do?" as it implies one would resist God if they had the power</note>. The explanation is: when they say "What can be done?", it implies that the misfortune is hard upon them, but we lack the power to fight with the Holy One, Blessed be He. But if it were in their hands, they would have acted. If so, they are complaining against the attributes of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and it appears in their eyes as if He killed without justice. This is acceptable for a mortal king; if he killed someone's son and it seemed to them that he killed without justice, it would be hard for them and they would want to protest, but they lack the power to act and win against the king. But even the exile in tractate Bava Metzia [is based on] words of justice, and presumably He killed with justice, for no iniquity exists before Him, may He be exalted. Therefore, we are obligated to receive the decrees of the Omnipresent with love and to bless for the good. He [Ulla] went alone and began to console, saying: "What is written? 'The Lord said... do not distress Moab' <note>Deuteronomy 2:9</note>. Even though they began with corruption and hired Balaam, nonetheless the Merciful One had pity on them because of Ruth the Moabitess." [He reasoned:] if a daughter of his master <note>referring to the deceased girl</note> was worthy to have something good come from her, all the more so [she would have lived]. But the Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note> did not cite all this, as it bears no practical legal consequence <note>original: *nefka mina l'dina*</note>, because the law does not follow Ulla over the Sages. Rather, it applies to whoever comes to this matter. It appears that [Ulla's logic] was actually a source of pain for the mourner to be told: "If she were worthy, [she would have lived]"—on the contrary, the honor of the mourner should imply her praise, not her disgrace. As for saying "What can you do?"—Heaven forbid, the pain and the crying are real, but you cannot bring the person back. One knows this themselves... Why do we not examine this also? But if he could return her, [would he have] sinned? Rather, it is permitted to console in this way so there is no side of pain... on the contrary, it is hard for him. And why was there crying and prayer before the child died? Obviously, if he is worthy and good comes from him, the Omnipresent will pity him. However, many times children die for the sins of their fathers, even if they are great and worthy... the son of Rabbi Hanania ben Teradion proves this.

## And it does not
appear to me that his [Rashal's] words are correct when he said the law does not follow Ulla. Wherever the Talmud mentions "the Sages" <note>original: *Rabbanan*</note> without qualification, it refers to the students of the academy... and all of them were considered like students to Ulla. As soon as they heard this from Ulla's mouth, their spirits surely weakened. If Ulla had not gone to console, why would they have gone? Perhaps they were already used to consoling with that phrase... I saw another version in the writings of the Riva <note>Rabbi Isaac ben Asher</note> of blessed memory... [The discussion continues on the nuances of Ulla’s consolation and the etiquette of mourning]. Regarding what the Gaon [Rashal] questioned... Ulla was disagreeing with the Babylonian style of consolation, "What is there to do?", but not with the act of consoling itself. Regarding the difficulty of "If she were worthy..."—with all due respect, the Rashal corrected this by writing: "If she was worthy for good to come from her, all the more so [she would have lived]." The intention is that she was upright and prepared for life... sometimes a completely righteous man or woman is not "prepared" for certain descendants. The generation that knows He is blessed knows the causes; it is possible the righteous person was already perfected through the secret of reincarnation <note>term: *gilgul*</note>. This was Ulla’s consolation: even though she was certainly righteous, He who knows secrets knows she was not meant for this [further life], otherwise she would not have died... therefore, why distress yourself so much? Even though one must grieve for the loss, the void is not so great as you make it... Regarding David saying "I shall go to him, but he will not return to me"—before the child's death, David fasted and repented, but after, he said repentance cannot bring the dead back until the future [resurrection]. This is not "blasphemy." But the "What can I do?" of the common people implies that if they could, they would fight the decree. This is blasphemy. So it appears to me. I found in the Maharaz <note>Rabbi Ze'ev Wolf</note> who cited this story and concluded: one should accept the decree of the Omnipresent with love, as it is said, "Shall we receive good [and not evil?]"... thus far his words.

## Furthermore,
the Gaon Rashal wrote in the aforementioned chapter: "Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yohanan: The Holy One, Blessed be He, does not withhold the reward of any creature, even the reward for pleasant speech." Because the elder [daughter of Lot] called her son "Moab" <note>meaning "From Father," an immodest name</note>, God told Moses: "Do not distress Moab, and do not contend with them in war"—meaning no war, but they could be forced into labor. But the younger [daughter] who called her son "Ben-Ammi" <note>meaning "Son of my people," a more modest name</note>, God said: "When you come near the children of Ammon, do not distress them and do not contend with them at all"—not even forced labor. A great principle is found here: a person must be careful with his speech... even more so, the Holy One, Blessed be He, even regarding the letters... [discussion of the modesty of language in the Torah]. I received from the early authorities that they were careful not to let any [improper word] come [into their mouths]. I will hint to you a simpler reason: "Every spirit/breath <note>original: *ruach*</note> that leaves the mouth of a human, if it is a holy word, it ascends and cleaves the heavens and stands in the place of the Image until it enters its place..."

It highlights that every word uttered has a cosmic impact, ascending to the heavens to create spiritual effects.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Gate of the Letters," moving from the general sanctity of speech to specific prohibitions regarding the mockery of Sages, the dangers of foul language, and the severity of oaths and curses. It maintains a focus on how the physical act of speaking shapes the spiritual state of the soul.</meta>

<header>The Gate of the Letters</header>

# The Gate of the Letters

When a person has free time to study Rashi or Tosafot <note>Two foundational medieval commentaries on the Talmud</note> or some other explanation, and they say, "This is a far-fetched answer," or "If I had said that, people would laugh at me"—such a person commits a great sin. Since I have heard this many times from those who speak with arrogance, I warn against it with a thousand warnings. Consider Rabbi Joshua, who once spoke [sharply] to the House of Shammai <note>One of the two major schools of thought in the early Rabbinic period</note> saying, "I am ashamed by your words, O House of Shammai!" He later regretted it, and his teeth became blackened from the many fasts he took on as penance. This is the general rule: "It is not an empty thing" <note>Deuteronomy 32:47</note>, and our Sages of blessed memory interpreted this to mean: "If it seems empty to you, it is because of you." Everything they said is truth and justice, written with taste and knowledge, and it is only that our own intellect is too limited to grasp it. I saw my master and teacher, the pious Sage Maharshal <note>term: Maharshal—Rabbi Solomon Luria (1510–1573), a major authority in Jewish Law</note> of blessed memory, that when he would hear a student ask, "Was the questioner crazy?" or "How could this be an answer?" and the like, he would strike him with "lashes of rebellion" <note>term: Markot Mardut—a form of disciplinary punishment</note> until the student performed the repentance he prescribed. He accustomed his students to always speak in a respectful tongue, saying for example: "The words of the questioner are not understood by me in their full depth," or similar phrasing.

The author of *Reshit Chokmah* <note>original: "The R"H"—refers to the kabbalistic work *Beginning of Wisdom* by Elijah de Vidas</note> wrote that the category of "mockery" includes those who play with dice and all kinds of games. It is not only about two people who sit together and speak no words of Torah; the act of gaming itself is a form of mockery similar to the types of entertainment mentioned in Tractate Avodah Zarah. The Sages said these are "the seat of scoffers," for the rabbis taught: One who goes to stadiums or camps and sees there the sorcerers, the charlatans, clowns, mimes, jugglers, or acrobats—this is a "seat of scoffers." This is in addition to the prohibition of robbery involved [in gambling]. It is also written there: Those who play dice and other games during the Festivals and Holidays—woe to their souls, for they have dealt themselves evil. The days of the Festivals are actually days of judgment, as we learn in the Mishnah of Rosh Hashanah: "At four times the world is judged: On Passover for the grain, on Shavuot for the fruit of the trees, on Rosh Hashanah all creatures pass before Him like a flock of sheep, and on Sukkot they are judged for water." Since all Festivals are days of judgment, the Sages said that the Sabbaths and Festivals were given to Israel only so they could occupy themselves with Torah. Our Sages also said: A person should always see himself and the world as if it were half-merit and half-guilt; if he performs one good deed, he tips himself and the entire world toward the side of merit. If not, Heaven forbid, he tips the scale toward guilt. Thus, one who sins through gaming or lightheadedness is more severe than one who brings bad tidings for the year. I say this also regarding the New Moon <note>Rosh Chodesh</note>; look into the "Time of Atonement" <note>A prayer recited on the New Moon</note>.

There is another reason: on Festivals and Holidays, there is an additional holiness in the soul. As the Kabbalists say, there are five levels of the soul: *Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, Chayah, Yechidah* <note>These represent levels of the soul from the most physical/vital to the most divine/singular</note>. These levels arrive in order of the holidays—Festivals, Yom Kippur, Sabbath, and the World to Come. The one who plays games comes and desecrates them. Therefore, my children, I have come to warn you and your descendants and the descendants of your descendants: let no game ever be found among you all the days of your lives. Through this, you will merit to cling to the Supernal Holiness.

## The "Father of Fathers" of Impurity
Speech that is foul language <note>term: Nevilut Peh—obscene or dirty talk</note> is a path to the abyss. It may be considered impure and lead to eternal distancing [from God]. In addition to the evil a person does to himself, he causes evil to the world. Even the one who hears it and remains silent is like the one who spoke it. As stated in the chapter "With what may we light" <note>Shabbat 33a</note>: Because of the sin of foul language, many troubles and harsh decrees are renewed, the "youths of the enemies of Israel" <note>note: a euphemism for the Jewish people themselves</note> die, and orphans and widows cry out but are not answered. For it is said: "Therefore the Lord shall have no joy in their young men, neither shall have mercy on their fatherless and widows; for every one is a hypocrite and an evildoer, and every mouth speaketh folly. For all this His anger is not turned away, but His hand is stretched out still" <note>Isaiah 9:16</note>. Why is His hand still stretched out? Rabbi Hanan bar Rava said: Everyone knows why a bride enters the bridal canopy <note>i.e., for intimacy</note>, but anyone who speaks foully about it, even if a favorable decree of seventy years had been sealed for him, it is turned to evil. Rabba bar Shila said in the name of Rav Hisda: For anyone who speaks foully, Gehenna <note>Purgatory/Hell</note> is made deeper for him. Rav Nachman bar Isaac says: Even one who hears it and remains silent [is punished], as it is written: "He that is abhorred of the Lord shall fall therein" <note>Proverbs 22:14</note>.

## Woe to One Who Does Such Things
How can a person invite a curse and a ban upon himself? For no gain, he leads his soul to the grave. What profit is there for a fool in his folly? The *Menorat HaMaor* <note>term: *The Lamp of Light*—a 14th-century ethical work by Isaac Aboab</note> says: We find that when people are forced with whips, fire, and water, and all kinds of afflictions to confess things they have done wrong, they endure all the pain and do not admit anything with their mouths that would lead to a death sentence. Even though they know they may be strangled or their lives shortened, they endure the pressure to gain even a temporary life. How much more so should a person, who is not being forced to speak foully and gains no pleasure from such speech, restrain himself? By speaking it, his sin becomes too great to bear, and it brings eternal death.

Know this: one who defiles his mouth and tongue with the impurity of speech—whether by one of the things mentioned or by any other—all his words of Torah and his prayers become defiled. They are placed "outside the camp" <note>Refers to the biblical quarantine for the ritually impure</note>. He receives a double punishment for them. He is like a commoner who pushes his way into the King’s presence and gives him a gift in a vessel used for excrement; the King is doubly offended. Our Sages said: Rabbi Eliezer said, a man may be handsome and praiseworthy, but if he utters a disgusting thing from his mouth, what is he like? He is like a beautiful, well-built palace that has a sewer pipe from a tannery fixed inside it. Everyone who passes by says, "How beautiful this palace would be, were it not for the sewer pipe inside it."

Even speech that is not prohibited but is merely "idle talk" <note>term: Bitul Torah—time spent on vanity instead of study</note> causes damage. The vessels of the Temple were sanctified for the Torah and prayer, and so is the speech of man. Rabbi Levi said: "If only we had two mouths!" Because with the mouth that one speaks words of Torah, it is not fitting to speak mundane words. This is the secret of the "Confession" <note>referring to the Viduy prayer</note>... if only we had two mouths, the mouth of Torah and prayer would remain guarded and pure.

## Necessary Speech
Speech regarding business and honest trade is called a "matter of a commandment" <note>mitzvah</note>, for "Torah is good when combined with a worldly occupation." His intention should be for the sake of Heaven—that he engages in business so that poverty does not cause him to transgress the Torah, Heaven forbid. Then his reward is great.

## The Severity of Oaths and Vows
It is known to all that one who utters an oath—even a true oath—his sin is too great to bear. Even if he possesses Torah and good deeds, it will not help him. Our Sages discussed this at length in the Talmud, Midrash, and Zohar. Therefore, one who guards his soul should distance himself from letting an oath cross his lips all the days of his life. Even "light" oaths that do not mention the Name of God—such as swearing "by the life of my head" or "by this table"—should be avoided. The word "Chas" <note>A common expression of "God forbid" or an oath-like interjection</note> is also a form of an oath. He should be very careful and warn his wife, his household, and his descendants forever. Since it is human nature to mention God's name or His attributes when angry or when trying to verify a statement, one should accustom oneself to a specific phrase to use instead. My master and teacher, the pious Maharshal, was accustomed to always say, "Without a vow and without an oath." This was his version of a commitment: "I will do this" or "I will not do this," or even when speaking loudly in anger to someone, he used this language. He accustomed his students to do the same. You too, my children, adopt this language, you and your descendants forever, and follow the path of my teacher, the Sage, the Pious, and the Holy—happy is he in the Upper World.

## It is Written in the Tur (Yoreh Deah)
In section 203, it states that if a person is pledging charity in public and must pledge with them, he should say, "Without a vow" <note>original: *Bli Neder*</note>. There is some doubt as to what this means: does it mean he should just say the amount and not use the word "vow," or does it mean he must explicitly state the words "without a vow"? It seems to me the second explanation is correct, because normally a pledge is legally considered a vow even if the word "vow" is not mentioned. This is like the law of one who says, "I will be a Nazirite," and his friend hears and says, "And I too"—he also becomes a Nazirite.

## A Strict Prohibition on Uttering Curses
The *Tur* <note>The *Arba'ah Turim*, a foundational code of Jewish law</note> (Choshen Mishpat, section 27) writes: Even one who curses himself is liable, as it is written, "Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently" <note>Deuteronomy 4:9</note>. One is not legally liable [to a court] unless they curse using the Name of God or one of His attributes. But since cursing with an attribute is liable, it follows that cursing in any language is liable, because the names the Gentiles use for the Holy One, Blessed be He, are considered "attributes." If one says "Cursed be so-and-so," it is a curse. A curse can contain within it a ban, an oath, or a malediction. While one might not receive physical lashes unless there were witnesses and a prior warning, there is nonetheless a severe prohibition. Since people are often not careful about this, I have come with a great warning.

## It is Written in Reshit Chokmah (Gate of Holiness)
In Chapter 7, it says: One should not curse even someone who does not hear it. The Aramaic translator <note>Targum Onkelos</note> explains "Do not curse the deaf" as meaning anyone who does not hear. So too, it says in the Zohar: One who curses his friend, if the friend is present and is shamed, it is as if he spilled his blood. But even if the friend is not there and he curses him, that word does not simply vanish. Every word that comes out of a mouth has a "voice," and that voice ascends on high. Many "prosecutors" <note>spiritual accusers</note> join with it until it reaches the place of the "Great Deep," and many judgments are stirred up against that person. Sometimes a bad word comes out of the mouth...

<meta>This page continues "The Gate of the Letters." While the previous page focused on the gravity of speech and respect for Sages, this page transitions into the spiritual economy of time—how each day must be accounted for—and introduces a triad of spiritual disciplines: Silence, Self-Examination, and Passionate Desire for the Divine.</meta>

<header>The Gate of the Letters</header>
<sig>Chapter 28</sig>

The day consists of twenty-four hours, and when the cycle of the day is complete, a different spiritual influence begins for the following day, following the mystery of the "permutations of the letters of the Name" <note>original: *gilgulay tzirufay otiyot ha-Shem*; this refers to the Kabbalistic idea that God recreates the world every moment using different combinations of the Hebrew alphabet</note>. Therefore, one must correct any wrongdoing on that very day, just as a "fast for a dream" <note>A traditional practice of fasting to avert a bad omen from a dream</note> must be done on the same day. These matters are discussed at length elsewhere. In this regard, all of a person’s days are completed, and every single day remains recorded through the actions one performed and the rectification of one's flaws.

Regarding this, I have interpreted the verse: "The fear of the Lord adds days, but the years of the wicked shall be shortened" <note>Proverbs 10:27</note>. This is puzzling—do we not often see the wicked man prolonging his life in his wickedness, while the righteous man perishes? Furthermore, why does the verse mention "days" for the righteous and "years" for the wicked? The matter is this: the righteous are called "living," but the wicked, even in their lifetime, are called "dead." If one performs a good deed during the day, they have acquired that day’s vitality and a connection to eternal life, for they chose the good. But when one performs an evil act—woe!—they are distanced from the root of the act. Even if they sit idle, doing neither good nor evil, they have not acquired vitality.

Now, the days of the lives of the wicked are vanity; sometimes many years pass without them doing good. It follows that all those years merely add "vanity of vanities," and they are all dead. The righteous person, by contrast, is meticulous about every single day, seeking to acquire vitality within it. Thus, as long as the righteous person is alive, they are a "living fire," abundant in action, adding vitality every single day. This is the meaning of "The fear of the Lord adds days." The wicked person, even if they appear to live many years, is merely a "wicked elder" <note>term: *Zaken Ashmai*—a term for an unrefined or sinful old man</note>; it is possible many of their years were "shortened" because they were dead spiritually. You might think he is seventy years old, but perhaps he is not even eight years old in terms of meaningful life.

**Regarding** the adding of "day upon day," it is explained in the Zohar <note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism</note> that this is why it is written: "And Abraham was old, coming into days" <note>Genesis 24:1</note>, and similarly, "And the days of Jacob drew near" and "the days of David drew near." This is because every single day entered the account of their vitality. This is also why Torah scholars are called "elders" <note>term: *Zaken*—meaning both "old man" and "sage"</note>, because every day they are alive, they become more of an "elder" than they were yesterday.

Through this, we can understand the words of our father Jacob, who said to Pharaoh: "The days of the years of my life are one hundred and thirty years; few and evil..." <note>Genesis 47:9</note>. The word "few" is difficult; how could he say this when he might yet live many more years? Rather, Jacob spoke out of humility. He said: "The days of my life that I have truly *lived* are 130 years, but I am afraid they are 'few' because of the 'evil' way I conducted myself, sometimes walking in an evil path, God forbid." This is how Jacob spoke in the way of humility.

**The general principle** that emerges: every single day, a person must examine their actions at the end of the day, return to God, and sanctify themselves. Just as the Sabbath is "holy to the Lord" and points toward the World to Come—a world that is entirely Sabbath—so too the "Psalm, a song for the Sabbath day" <note>Psalm 92:1</note> is better than the whole week. The entire week is called "Sabbath" <note>A play on the Hebrew word *Shavua* (week), which shares a root with *Sheva* (seven)</note>, because every day must contain some of the sanctity of the Sabbath. The six days of labor are the branches, and their root is the Sabbath. This teaching will be explained at length later in the tractates of *Hullin* and *Shabbat*.

Therefore, just as the Sabbath hints at the world that is entirely Sabbath and entirely good, the whole week is called "Sabbath." Regarding the six days of creation, it is written: "And God saw that it was good." Thus, one must grasp onto the "Good" and perform the "Tree of Life" daily. If one has caused a flaw, they should fix it through Repentance <note>term: *Teshuvah*</note>, as hinted in the verse: "Good and upright is the Lord; therefore He instructs sinners in the way" <note>Psalm 25:8</note>.

**Regarding** this, it is said: "Who is the man who desires life?" <note>Psalm 34:13</note>—meaning eternal life—and wants to know the action he should perform to "live by them"? He must look at three things. The first is: "He loves days, to see good"—meaning he checks himself every day. If he has flawed something, he fixes it through repentance and acquires a higher level every day to add holiness. He should be a "lover of days," becoming an "elder coming into days," adding days as mentioned above. This "adds peace and honor," like "And God saw that it was good." As I explained, this means grasping onto the Good of the World to Come, which is entirely good.

The three steps are: **Examination** (*Bedikah*), **Silence** (*Shetikah*), and **Longing** (*Chashikah*). I have already written my hints above regarding the Patriarchs... the word "Watch" (*Netzor*) contains the letters of "Will" (*Ratzon*). Although the verse says "Watch your tongue from evil," it can also be interpreted as a hint to our instruction.

**S** is for *Shetikah* (Silence), from the word *Shabbat* (Sabbath). It includes all virtues. For the matter of silence applies to both the mouth and the heart. The mouth, in its literal sense, saves one from the many sins of the "imaginative faculty," such as oaths, vows, gossip, evil speech, hypocrisy, strife, insults, curses, lies, mockery, and the like. Then, one draws upon themselves the trait of humility and rises from level to level.

Silence also applies to the heart: one's heart should not hasten to bring a thought into action. Just as speech is forbidden, so too is a [sinful] thought forbidden. One must silence the "alien thoughts" in their heart, for they are all thoughts of flaw. One must nullify envy, hatred, lust, [seeking] honor, and sinful thoughts, which are "harder than the sin itself." As the Sages said: "The tongue is the pen of the heart." It is also written, "I said in my heart," for a thought in the heart is indeed a thought, and afterward, it comes into actual speech through the movement of the lips, and its voice is heard via the tongue.

**E** <note>The author uses the letter Ayin from "Netzor" to emphasize the heart/eye/source</note>. He said: "Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking guile." The matter is repeated with double intent. "Keep your tongue" refers to the heart, which is the root of the tongue, for the tongue is its pen. It says "from evil" rather than "from speaking evil" because in the heart there is no actual speech, only thought. Afterward, regarding the speech heard through the "outlet of the lips," it says, "and your lips from speaking guile." He mentioned "evil" in relation to the heart, as Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai taught: a "bad heart" includes all evils, and a "good heart" includes all goods. Regarding the lips, he says "guile," for it is the way [of the hypocrite] to have one thing in the mouth and another in the heart, and that is all guile.

For this we pray: "My God, guard my tongue from evil and my lips from speaking guile," for this matter is all-encompassing. Thus, we have explained **S** from *Shabbat*, which is *Shetikah* (Silence). **H** <note>Hebrew letter Chet</note> is for *Chashikah* (Longing). Silence is a great principle, as hinted in the word **Teshuvah** (Repentance), which includes silence, cleaving, and desiring, as I have written at length in the *Ten Utterances*, in chapters 3 and 4. I wrote there that the virtue of silence relates to "turning from evil" (negative commandments) and "doing good" (positive commandments). I wrote there at length that one should serve God with "all your heart"—with both your inclinations, the Good Inclination and the Evil Inclination. That is, when one wants to follow the Good Inclination, they should take the "heat" of the Evil Inclination—namely, the craving, longing, and flame—and apply that passion to the commandment. After directing that passion, they should overcome their impulse and place their desire toward the glory of the Creator. Thus, the power of the Evil Inclination is joined to the service of God, both in "shalt-nots" and in "thou-shalts."

**This** is what is meant by: "Turn from evil and do good"—both negative and positive commandments. "Seek peace"—meaning with all your heart, joining your two inclinations together. And he adds: "and pursue it"—to be a pursuer of his "pursuer," which is the Evil Inclination, and conquer it with strength. This is a very exalted matter which I mentioned above in the explanation of "Who is a hero? He who subdues his inclination" <note>Ethics of the Fathers 4:1</note>—meaning one who transforms the evil into good. Look above at length. This is the essence of longing and desire—using the trait of the Evil Inclination to do good. Then, the good is done with a powerful passion. This is the **H** for *Chashikah* (Longing), for "seeking and pursuing" is longing.

Behold, these are **S-B-CH** <note>original: *Shevach*—meaning Praise or Excellence</note>: **S**ilence (*Shetikah*), **E**xamination (*Bedikah*), and **L**onging (*Chashikah*). These three include the commandments, the character traits, and the entire Torah; then it is "well with him forever."

**Therefore**, every single day before going to sleep, a person should be accustomed all the days of their life to gather their children and household. They should arouse themselves and examine the day's deeds. If there was any sin, they should repent and rectify it. Or, if there was any neglect of Torah study or any commandment, they should take it upon themselves to fulfill them, strengthening themselves to uphold the laws and be courageous. They should always add in holiness.

**One should** clothe themselves in the virtue of Silence—this is the quality of "warming up"—and afterward, they should cleave to the virtue of Passion, Longing, and Desire. Then the verse will be fulfilled: "And you who cleave to the Lord your God are all alive today" <note>Deuteronomy 4:4</note>.
