<meta>This page continues the "Gate of the Letters," transitioning from the conclusion of the letter *Shin*—which deals with the sanctity of speech and silence—to the letter *He*, which focuses on *Teshukah* (passionate desire) for the Divine. The text emphasizes that refined speech is a reflection of a person’s inner spiritual roots and introduces a daily practice of self-examination.</meta>

# The Gate of the Letters

...and I will enter before the King, as it is written: "Guarding the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your bosom" <note>Micah 7:5; here interpreted as guarding one's speech to protect the soul</note>, and then that word is awakened and a person merits it. This is sufficient for those who understand.

**We learn** in the first chapter of Tractate Pesachim: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, "A person should never allow a degrading word to leave his mouth, for the Scripture bypassed eight extra letters just to avoid an unrefined expression." As it is said: "From the animals that are *not clean*" <note>Genesis 7:8; the Torah uses the longer phrase "not clean" instead of the shorter, more blunt word "unclean" (*tamei*)</note>. Rav Ashi said: "It bypassed nine letters," as it says: "If there be among you any man that is *not clean* by reason of a nocturnal accident" <note>Deuteronomy 23:11</note>. And let us say ten? There is also the "and" of "and clean." Rav said: "It bypassed ten letters," as it says: "For he thought, something has befallen him, he is *not clean*; surely he is *not clean*" <note>1 Samuel 20:26</note>. It was taught in the school of Rabbi Ishmael: "A person should always speak in a refined tongue," for regarding a man with a discharge, the Torah calls his seat a "riding-place," but regarding a woman, it calls it a "sitting-place" <note>A subtle distinction in Biblical Hebrew terminology to preserve modesty</note>. And it says: "You shall choose the tongue of the crafty" <note>Job 15:5</note>, and it says: "And my lips shall speak knowledge clearly" <note>Job 33:3</note>. Why these additional verses? You might say this only applies to the Torah, but in the words of the Sages, it does not; therefore, come and hear: "You shall choose..." And you might say this only applies to the words of Sages, but in mundane matters, it does not; therefore, come and hear: "And my lips shall speak knowledge clearly." We also say regarding this: There were two students sitting before Rav. One said, "This tradition has made us as tired as a *fatigued swine*," and the other said, "This tradition has made us as tired as a *fatigued kid*." Rav would not speak with the first student again <note>Because the first student used a "degrading" animal as a metaphor</note>. There were two students who stood before Hillel—and some say before Rabbi Judah the Prince—one was Rabbi Yochanan. One asked, "Why do we harvest grapes in ritual purity but not olives?" The Sage said, "I am certain that this student will one day issue legal rulings in Israel," and it was so. There were three priests; one said, "My portion of the showbread was the size of a bean," one said, "Mine was the size of an olive," and the third said, "Mine was the size of a lizard's tail." They investigated his lineage and found a blemish of disqualification in him. Thus, it is found that a person’s speech testifies to his character and his spiritual root.

**Furthermore**, even in mundane matters like business and the like, one should be precise in their language, as found in Tractate Eruvin, in the chapter "How do we extend the borders." The people of Judea were precise in their language. A Judean once said, "I have a cloak to sell." They asked him, "What is the color of your cloak?" He replied, "Like beets of the earth." The people of the Galilee were not precise in their language. A certain Galilean once went around asking, "Who has *amra*?" They said to him, "You foolish Galilean! Do you mean a donkey (*chamor*) to ride, wine (*chamar*) to drink, wool (*amar*) for clothing, or a lamb (*imar*) for slaughter?" <note>This is a famous Talmudic joke about the Galilean accent, where the guttural letters were slurred, leading to total confusion</note>. There was another who came before the judges... see there, for they discuss this at length.

## The Letter Shin is Completed

**The Letter He:** *Teshukah* (Passionate Desire). This is the longing and love for the Blessed Creator, His holy Torah, and His commandments; to observe, perform, and fulfill everything with great joy. One should rejoice in the merit of serving God and clinging to Him. This is the secret of the "Trembling Ones" <note>The *Charedim*, a term for those who tremble at God's word</note>: a condition for the fulfillment of a commandment is the great joy in the commandment itself, for every single commandment is like a signet ring sent to him by the Holy One, Blessed be He. According to the greatness of the joy, so shall the reward increase. Thus did the pious master and Kabbalist, Rabbi Isaac Luria <note>The Ari, 1534–1572</note> of blessed memory, reveal to his confidant <note>Rabbi Chaim Vital</note> as the secret of how he attained the gates of wisdom and the Holy Spirit: it was as a reward for rejoicing in the performance of every commandment with an infinite, boundless joy. He said: This is what is written, "Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joyfulness and with gladness of heart, by reason of the abundance of all things" <note>Deuteronomy 28:47</note>. The "abundance of all things" means more than all the pleasures of the world, more than gold, fine gems, and pearls. And from the strength of this joy in fulfilling the Torah and commandments, he will do everything with great alacrity and intense desire. All the books of the pious describe the way of the lover... and a wonderful sign of the soul's love for Him who loves it with a whole and upright heart is found in the songs of Moses, the Children of Israel, Miriam, Deborah, Joshua, the sons of Korah, David, and Solomon. Through the Holy Spirit, they said, "A maskil, a song of loves" <note>Psalm 45:1</note>, and it is written, "The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's"—to the King to whom peace belongs. Out of the abundance of his love, he sang songs to Him. It is also written, "Be ravished always with her love" <note>Proverbs 5:19</note>; Rabbi Abraham ben David explained this as a term for song. The early and later Sages likewise sang before Him, such as Rabbi Judah Halevi, Rabbi Judah the Pious, Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra, and their colleagues. Just as in worldly matters a lover's passion for his beloved will banish sleep from his eyes, so too one who loves and believes in his Creator will awaken from his sleep with the sweetness of His memory, as it is written: "Happy is the pious one who does not sleep except upon the beds of his love," and he does not tire of the sweetness of His memory. He rises to praise and be tested before Him, to be in solitude and to delight in the greatness of His Torah, as David said: "At midnight I will rise to give thanks to You" <note>Psalm 119:62</note>. David was a faithful lover to Him, as it is written: "I love You, O Lord, my strength" <note>Psalm 18:2</note>, and Rashi explains "I love You" based on the Aramaic translation of "and you shall love" as "and you shall cherish." It is also written, "So He gives to His beloved sleep" <note>Psalm 127:2</note>, which the Sages interpreted as referring to Torah scholars who banish sleep from their eyes to toil in Torah. The word "beloved" should not be taken from its simple meaning: the lover, out of great passion and love for the Blessed One, banishes sleep to delight in His Torah. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai wrote in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot, page 181): "My soul desires You in the night" <note>Isaiah 26:9</note>; at night a person must rise out of love for the Holy One, Blessed be He, to labor in His service until the morning breaks and a thread of loving-kindness is extended over him. It is taught: Fortunate is the portion of that man who loves the Holy One, Blessed be He, with this love, for the word "mercy" (*racham*) is linked to "passion" (*chashuka*). All the thoughts of his heart are bent on doing His will and walking in love and connection. So too, the soul calls our Creator its "faithful lover," as it is said, "God is the rock of my heart and my portion forever" <note>Psalm 73:26</note>, and "I sleep, but my heart is awake" <note>Song of Songs 5:2</note>, which the Sages explained as referring to God. It is the way of a lover to call his beloved "soul of my soul," meaning it is as difficult to part from her as it is for the soul to depart the body, which is as bitter as death. So the faithful lover of the Creator calls to Him from his soul. Thus the Zohar says (Parashat Acharei Mot, page 180): "My soul desires You in the night, even with my spirit within me will I seek You..." It says "my soul desires You" because the soul actually comes from Him; it says "I will seek You" <note>Hebrew: *ashachre-cha*</note> when it should say "one seeks You" <note>*yishachre-cha*</note>. Rather, it is taught: The Holy One, Blessed be He, is the Spirit and Soul of everything, and Israel says: "You are my soul and my spirit, therefore I desire to cling to You and seek Your favor." For "love is as strong as death," and its strength comes from the soul. I have already expanded on this in the "Four Essays," specifically the third and fifth essays, explaining the terms "clinging," "passion," and "desire" in various contexts. There, the matters of passion, love, and clinging—both in positive and negative commandments—are explained at length. This is the "stream" of what I have written in these last three letters: *Shin*, which represents the level of clinging of the will and constant attachment, the virtue of Silence, and the virtue of Passion. These are general principles for the service of God, the preservation of the Torah, and the fulfillment of commandments. They are a great foundation for the elevation of character traits. If these three are performed, this "triple-threaded cord" will not easily be broken; they connect and bind a person to the highest levels until he is "clinging to his wife" <note>A metaphor for the soul's union with God</note>. For the love and clinging of the Holy One, Blessed be He, with the Assembly of Israel is compared to the union of a bridegroom and bride, as it says, "As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you" <note>Isaiah 62:5</note>, and like the love of a man for his wife, as mentioned countless times in the Prophets and the words of the Sages. 

I hereby give a mnemonic for these three praised virtues, which are the "Praise of the Words of Torah" <note>The Hebrew word for "praise" is *Shevach*, spelled *Shin-Bet-Chet*</note>:
\* **S**ilence (*Shetika*)
\* **E**xamination (*Bedika*)
\* **P**assion (*Chashika*)

For **Examination** is the factor that enables the will to investigate every day before going to sleep and see if one is in favor with the Blessed Creator. These three are found in the context of a man’s marriage to a woman: one who **passions** for a woman and wishes to take her must **examine** and investigate her lineage and family (as detailed in the laws of lineage in *Tur Even HaEzer*, section 2). What is the sign of high lineage? One who hears his own insult and remains **silent**. Just as in a lower marriage there is Passion, Examination, and Silence, so too in the "marriage" to the Blessed Creator, these three are present, for which I gave the mnemonic "Praise of the Words of Torah": **S**ilence, **E**xamination, and **P**assion. There is a hint to this in the praise of the Seventh Day (Sabbath), for it is known that the Sabbath alludes to the "World that is entirely Sabbath," and the praise for the time of union alludes to the Supernal Union. Therefore, I will explain these three matters further, as they are hinted at in the verses: "Who is the man who **desires** life... **guard** your tongue... turn from evil and **do good**; seek peace and pursue it" <note>Psalm 34:13-15</note>.

**Examination:** Every day before going to sleep at night, one should see if they are in the favor of the Blessed Creator or in a state of anger. One must fear being caught in the "attribute of night," which is Judgment and Anger, as I explained at length under the letter *Dalet*. "Favor" (*Ratzon*) is a great virtue—that a person should rectify his distortions on that very day, as the Zohar hints regarding the verse: "In his day you shall give him his hire" <note>Deuteronomy 24:15</note>. We learned that Rabbi Eliezer says: "Repent one day before your death." His students asked him, "Does a person know on which day he will die?" He replied, "All the more so, he should repent today, lest he die tomorrow; thus, all his days are spent in repentance." This repentance should occur before one goes to sleep, for sleep is one-sixtieth of death; thus, every day a person rectifies his soul before his "death," even in its literal sense.

**Our Sages** of blessed memory said: "If you see a Torah scholar who committed a transgression by day, do not think ill of him by night, for he has certainly repented." It is possible that based on the secrets of the *Tikunim*, it was said regarding this: "His body shall not remain all night upon the tree" <note>Deuteronomy 21:23</note>—meaning, let not the "carcass" of the sin he committed remain upon the "Tree of Life" <note>The scholar himself</note>, for he certainly repented. It is also possible that "thinking ill of the *bed* of a Torah scholar" refers not just to his death, but to the actual bed he sleeps in, for he certainly repented before going to sleep. I have expanded on this elsewhere in the explanation of the four times of repentance: 1. "In his day you shall give his hire" (daily); 2. Every Sabbath eve; 3. Every New Moon eve; 4. The Great Day of Atonement. Each time period includes those before it, and the day includes...

Always from the perspective of their lack, in order to give them His Torah and to receive their service, so that one who guards the Torah and labors in true service may conduct themselves according to the Law. However, the Holy One, Blessed be He, saw that the world could not endure through the system of Strict Justice alone, so He partnered it with the Attribute of Mercy. The meaning of this "partnership" is that if a person performs Repentance <note>Hebrew: *Teshuvah*</note>, then the Attribute of Strict Justice is transformed into the Attribute of Mercy. But if not—alas and woe!—"let the law pierce the mountain" <note>A Talmudic idiom meaning that strict justice must be applied without compromise if no repentance is found</note>. Therefore, the "Pillar of Repentance" follows, which is linked to the Day of Atonement <note>Yom Kippur</note> and the Festivals along with the New Year <note>Rosh Hashanah</note>, representing the partnership of the Attribute of Mercy with the Attribute of Justice. From this partnership, the "Pillar of the World" is drawn forth, following the secret of **"the accuser becomes the defender"** and there is peace in all things. From the standing of peace <note>original: *shalom*</note> is drawn a "time of favor" for prayer; for when there are accusers, prayer is pushed back by those battle lines, as will be explained later in its proper place. Therefore, the "Pillar of Prayer" follows the "Pillar of Peace," and to prayer belongs the "Pillar of Justice/Charity," as it is written: "I, in justice, shall behold Your face" <note>Psalm 17:15; often interpreted as giving charity before prayer</note>, as will be explained later in its proper place. This is the chain of the "Pillars" according to the order of the seasons: "they shall be for signs, and for festivals, and for days and years." And behold, I shall arrange this with the help of Him who dwells in the Heavens, blessed be He who gives strength to the weary and power to the weak. I have come to it with mercy and supplications, that true and correct words should emerge from me and through me, according to our laws.

->Words given in eighty-one <note>literally "9x9"</note> aspects:<-

->Tractate Chullin: The Pillar of Truth. It contains three chapters: The Chapter of "The Mitzvah is a Lamp," the Chapter of "The Torah is Light," and the Chapter of "The Reproof of Instruction."<-

## Chapter: The Mitzvah is a Lamp
It is written in the Ten Commandments: "Six days you shall labor and do all your work, and the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God," etc. Yet in the portion of *Vayakhel* <note>Exodus 35:2</note>, it is written: "Six days work shall be done, but on the seventh day there shall be to you a holy day, a Sabbath of Sabbaths to the Lord." The change in language is difficult: in the Ten Commandments, it says "You shall labor" <note>Hebrew: *ta'avod*</note> and "you shall do" <note>Hebrew: *ve-asita*</note>, whereas in *Vayakhel*, only "doing" <note>Hebrew: *asiyah*</note> is mentioned. Furthermore, regarding "doing," there is a change in the vowel points, for the Torah speaks in the language of command <note>active</note>, but in *Vayakhel* it says "shall be done" <note>Hebrew: *te'aseh*, which can be read as a passive or reflexive form</note>. There is also a change in that the Commandments say "a Sabbath to the Lord your God," but *Vayakhel* says "there shall be **to you** a holy day... to the Lord"—it says "to you" and also "to the Lord." One must also examine that in *Vayakhel* it says "And on the seventh day," etc., and the "day" refers to the concept of service.

The "Holy Service" is that we are servants to the Blessed Name, and the purpose of creation is "to serve it and to guard it" <note>Genesis 2:15</note>—to guard, to do, and to fulfill all the words of the Torah. Thus, "Service" <note>Hebrew: *avodah*</note> is the work of Heaven. "Doing" <note>Hebrew: *asiyah*</note> is physical work, which is also a commandment—to conduct business in good faith. These two which were mentioned—Heavenly work and physical work (business in good faith)—are the questions asked of a person at their initial judgment: "Did you conduct your business in good faith? Did you set aside fixed times for Torah study?" Therefore, it comes as a command: "Six days you shall labor and do all your work." Regarding the "Holy Service," it says "Six days you shall labor," for they correspond to the six thousand years of the world's existence, and the Sabbath corresponds to the "world that is entirely Sabbath," for then it will be "a Sabbath to the Lord your God," because "today is for doing them, and tomorrow <note>the afterlife</note> is for receiving their reward." Regarding physical work, which is business in good faith, it says "and you shall do" as a command, for it too is a commandment.

The faith required in physical work is divided into two parts: Part one is the business between a man and his fellow, such as buying and selling. Part two is the work a person does by themselves, such as a craft. Part two is hinted at in *Vayakhel*, which says "work shall be done" <note>passive</note> rather than "you shall do" <note>active</note>. For the Sabbath rest from labor is like what we find regarding the "pious ones of old," whose Torah study was their primary occupation and their work was "done by others" <note>or "done on its own"</note>. But when one engages in trade, the commandment is greater when he does it himself, for then he acts in good faith with his fellow—this one deals with that one, and he himself deals with him. Regarding this, the Commandments say: "and you shall do all your work"—you yourself shall buy and sell, and then you shall see that your "yes" is righteous and your "no" is righteous <note>an idiom for total honesty</note>. But *Vayakhel* speaks of physical labor, which is better if performed by others, appearing as if it were done "on its own." Therefore, it says "shall be done" <note>passive</note>. This is why it concludes, "And on the seventh day it shall be to you a holy day," etc.—He did not say "on your days," which one might have thought, but "on the seventh day." In addition to the idea that work should be "done on its own," it says "on the seventh day it shall be **to you**"—meaning for all your needs, it should be considered in your eyes on the seventh day as if "all your work is finished," as the *Tur* <note>a 14th-century legal code</note> writes in *Orach Chaim* section 306: Although thinking about one's business is permitted on the Sabbath, nevertheless, for the sake of "Sabbath Delight" <note>Oneg Shabbat</note>, it is a religious duty not to think of them at all, and it should be in his eyes as if all his work is completed.

Therefore, regarding labor: the Holy Service and the work of business are both "holy," except that one is "holy" and the other is "holy of holies." The Holy One, Blessed be He, commanded us to labor and to act in both. Thus, I will explain several matters of innovation regarding both for the purpose of practice, and for this reason, the chapter is called "The Mitzvah is a Lamp."

Regarding "Heavenly Work," the *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* <note>The "SMaG," a 13th-century legal work</note> wrote in Positive Commandment 4: "Of the 613 commandments given to Israel, there is no commandment that serves as a **sign and a testimony** except for three: Circumcision, Sabbath, and Tefillin <note>Phylacteries</note>, as the word 'sign' <note>ot</note> is written regarding all three. These three are a sign and a testimony for Israel that they are servants to the Holy One, Blessed be He. And 'by the mouth of two witnesses shall a matter be established.' Every Jew is not a 'complete' Jew unless he has two witnesses that he is a Jew. Therefore, on Sabbath and Festivals—which are called 'Sabbath'—the Sabbath itself is called a 'sign,' and one is exempt from Tefillin because it is sufficient that he has two witnesses: the Sabbath and Circumcision. But on a weekday, every person is obligated to don Tefillin so that he has two witnesses: the sign of Tefillin and the sign of Circumcision. Anyone who does not don Tefillin has only one witness that he is a Jew. Therefore, they considered such a person 'excommunicated by Heaven.'"

If you ask: Since Tefillin is a sign and testimony like Circumcision and Sabbath, why was it [neglected]? Rabbi Yochanan said: Every commandment for which the Jews did not sacrifice themselves <note>during times of persecution</note> is still "weak" in their hands, such as Tefillin. And because all three are "signs and testimonies," each one is weighed against the entire Torah. The secret <note>Hebrew: *Sod*</note> of Circumcision is that thirteen covenants were made over it. Torah, Tefillin, and Sabbath are mentioned together in several places. He gave them the Torah and Commandments and "made known to them Your holy Sabbath." And regarding Tefillin: "so that the Torah of the Lord shall be in your mouth."

In the *Tikunei Zohar*: "Those who guard the sign of the covenant <note>circumcision</note>... are like the letter *Yod*. Those who guard the sign of the Sabbath are like the letter *Yod*... for the masters of the Mishnah established that a man should not be found with fewer than two [signs]." It is written: "You shall not take the mother with the young" <note>Deuteronomy 22:6</note>—these are the sign of the Covenant, the sign of Sabbath, and the sign of Tefillin. On weekdays, these are Tefillin and Circumcision; on Sabbath, they are the sign of the Covenant and the sign of Sabbath. It is written of them: "You shall surely send away the mother" <note>interpreted mystically</note>. If Tefillin are [missing], one must show their presence every day, so that the Divine Presence <note>Shekhinah</note>—which is the letter *Yod*—is not found alone without the Holy One, Blessed be He. A person must not be found on any day with fewer than two [signs], otherwise, it is said of him: "a whisperer separates close friends" <note>Proverbs 16:28</note>—separating the Lord of the world from the Divine Presence.

In Tractate Chullin, which deals with "profane" <note>non-holy/weekday</note> matters, it is appropriate to speak of the matter of Tefillin, and also the matter of Circumcision, the second sign and testimony. Even though Circumcision also applies on the Sabbath, nevertheless, "that which is frequent takes precedence over that which is infrequent." We will also lean toward the laws of Circumcision that apply on weekdays but not on Sabbath, such as a circumcision not in its proper time <note>e.g., a delayed circumcision for a sick baby</note> which does not override the Sabbath. Also, if a mohel <note>circumciser</note> removed his hands from the circumcision, he may not return on the Sabbath for the "shreds" of skin that do not invalidate the circumcision. Thus it was ruled: a baby born in the 7th or 8th month is not circumcised on the Sabbath. There are many more laws where the commandment of Circumcision is more established on weekdays than on Sabbath; therefore, it is fitting to mention the matters of Circumcision here.

Likewise, whenever there is a place for Tefillin, it is the true place to mention them. Here in Tractate Chullin, it is also fitting to mention the matters of Mezuzah and Tzitzit <note>ritual fringes</note>, which are related to one another. As it says in the chapter *HaTechelet*: Rabbi Eliezer ben Jacob says, "Anyone who has Tefillin on his head and arm, Mezuzah on his door, and Tzitzit on his garment is assured that he will not sin, for it is said: 'A three-fold cord is not quickly broken' <note>Ecclesiastes 4:12</note>. And it says: 'The angel of the Lord encamps round about them that fear Him, and delivers them.'" If you ask why it brings the second verse "and it says," the intention is that if he only brought the first verse regarding the "three-fold cord," one might say: how do we know the "three-fold cord" refers to these three (Tefillin, Mezuzah, and Tzitzit)? Perhaps it refers to the Passover sacrifice, Mezuzah, or other commandments? To answer this, he brings the verse "The angel of the Lord encamps **round about**"—for then the commandments surround him. Tefillin surround the arm and the head, the Mezuzah at the entrance of the house surrounds all that is within it, for the entrance makes the house surrounded on all four sides, and all within is guarded. So too the Tzitzit...

The catchword "The World" from the previous page transitions into the discussion of the pillars upon which the world stands and endures.</meta>

# Chapter of the Ten Commandments

**And I shall speak** of the ten virtues <note>Hebrew: *maalot*</note> that are mentioned here and there. Six of these are the words of the Sages of the Mishnah in the first chapter of the *Ethics of the Fathers*: "On three things the world stands: on the Torah, on the Divine Service <note>Hebrew: *Avodah*; originally referring to temple sacrifices, later to prayer</note>, and on Acts of Lovingkindness." Furthermore, "On three things the world endures: on Justice, on Truth, and on Peace." Three additional things are common in the words of our Sages of blessed memory, and they are: Repentance, Prayer, and Charity. This makes nine holy things, and "the tenth shall be holy" <note>A reference to Leviticus 27:32 regarding the tithe</note>, a recorded category that includes them all: the foundation of **Faith** <note>Hebrew: *Emunah*</note> in Him, may He be blessed. This is hinted at the end of Tractate Makkot: "Habakkuk came and established them upon one: 'But the righteous shall live by his faith'" <note>Habakkuk 2:4</note>. This serves as a parallel to the Ten Commandments, where the first utterance—the oneness of faith—includes all the commandments, which is: "I am the Lord your God." This follows the Midrash cited by Nachmanides <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nachman, a 13th-century scholar</note>, which says that the Holy One, Blessed be He, said: "Accept My kingship, and afterward I shall decree commandments upon you." This is also a parallel to the Ten Sayings <note>Hebrew: *Ma'amarot*; the utterances by which God created the world</note>, as the word "In the beginning" <note>Hebrew: *Bereishit*</note> is also considered a Saying. It is the Saying that includes all others, hinting that the Blessed Name is the First, there is no beginning to His precedence, and He brought forth and renewed the worlds.

**And behold,** ten times <note>seasons or periods</note> cycle through each and every year, in which these ten virtues are remembered and enacted. Each time is called by the name of a "Tractate" <note>Hebrew: *Masechet*; a volume of the Talmud</note> that comes forth for that specific time. In each tractate, one "Utterance" will be explained—that is, one pillar out of the ten aforementioned pillars. Each tractate will have three chapters, and these chapters will deal with matters according to the verse "For the commandment is a lamp and the Torah is light, and the way of life is the rebuke of discipline" <note>Proverbs 6:23</note>. This is how this composition begins, and the entire work follows this sequence. That is: the section of Contemplation <note>intellectual study</note>, the section of Deeds, Commandments, and Secrets, and the section of Ethics—which involves asceticism, vigilance, and the "extra" holiness that a moral person adds to increase sanctity. Through this, one will be aroused to a great awakening and reach a state of benefit, as many benefits emerge from the fulfillment of the commandments, both in the fear of God within and without.

**And the ten times** are: 1. The six days of Creation; 2. The Sabbath; 3. Passover; 4. Shavuot; 5. The fast of the Ninth of Av <note>Tisha B'Av</note>, including all fast days; 6. Rosh Hashanah; 7. Yom Kippur; 8. Sukkot; 9. Hanukkah; 10. Purim. These ten times are called by names: The "six days of Creation," which are the weekdays, are called by the name "Tractate Chullin" <note>Chullin refers to "profane" or non-holy items, suitable for the workweek</note>. For the Sabbath, "Tractate Shabbat." For Passover, "Tractate Pesachim." For Shavuot, "Tractate Shevuot" <note>meaning "Oaths"</note>, named for the Festival of Weeks <note>Hebrew: *Shavuot*</note> but also because of an actual oath <note>Hebrew: *shevuah*</note>, as we are eternally sworn from Mount Sinai. For the Ninth of Av, the time of the fasts, it is called "Tractate Taanit" <note>Fasts</note>. For Rosh Hashanah, "Tractate Rosh Hashanah." For Yom Kippur, "Tractate Yoma" <note>The Day</note>, for on this day He shall atone; it also includes the general concept of Repentance, which is a daily requirement, as the Tanna <note>Mishnaic sage</note> said: "Repent one day before your death," as will be explained at length. For Sukkot, "Tractate Sukkah." For Hanukkah, which is for praise and thanksgiving, it points to the Pillar of Prayer, as our Sages said: "Prayers were established corresponding to the daily offerings" <note>Hebrew: *Tamid*</note>. Thus it is called "Tractate Tamid," also because of the Hanukkah lights, as it is written: "To kindle a lamp continually" <note>Hebrew: *ner tamid*</note>. See Nachmanides at the beginning of the portion *Behaalotecha* regarding the lamps, where he hints they refer to the Hanukkah lights. For Purim, its name is "Tractate Megillah." To these ten times, the ten aforementioned virtues belong:
*   **The Foundation of Faith:** The existence of the Blessed Name is recognized through the renewal of the world, for which you have thought of a proof, as will be explained shortly; therefore it is linked to Tractate Shabbat.
*   **The Pillar of Truth:** Behold, the creation of the six days of action—the "head" <note>first letters</note> of the words "The-will-sing [of]-me Truth" <note>original: *R-N-Y Emet*</note>, as the author of the *Turim* wrote: "In-the-beginning Created God" <note>original: *Bereishit Bara Elohim*</note>, the final letters spell "Truth" <note>original: *Emet*</note>. Likewise, the seal of the six days of action is Truth: "...which God created to do" <note>original: *bara Elohim la'asot*</note>, the final letters spell "Truth" <note>Hebrew: *Aleph-Mem-Tav*</note>. This informs us that the seal of the days of action—days of business and trade—is that a person's general conduct must be in Truth, as will be explained at length; therefore it is linked to Tractate Chullin.
*   **The Pillar of Kindness:** This is Passover, for they were redeemed through the side of Kindness <note>associated with</note> Abraham, as explained in the Zohar and many places, and will be explained at length in its place. Israel was also awakened through His kindness, as it is said: "I remember for you the kindness of your youth... your following Me into the wilderness" <note>Jeremiah 2:2</note>.
*   **The Pillar of Torah:** The purpose of the Exodus from Egypt was for the Torah, which was given on Shavuot. Therefore, it is linked to this time, as it says: "When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain." Thus, this pillar is linked to Tractate Shevuot.
*   **The Pillar of Service:** This is in place of the sacrifice, as will be explained at length. On the fast day when the Temple was burned, from whence the Service came—nonetheless, it is called "Discipline" <note>Mussar</note>, for in the future it will be overturned to become an eternal building, an eternal House, and an eternal Service. It will turn to joy and gladness, bringing light out of the darkness, for darkness causes the light to be even greater, as will be explained later in its place. Therefore, this pillar is linked to Tractate Taanit.
*   **The Pillar of Justice:** Rosh Hashanah. It is the Day of Judgment Above and Below; this is the judgment below, therefore it is linked to Tractate Rosh Hashanah.
*   **Repentance:** This is specifically associated with Yom Kippur. Therefore, the matters of Repentance are linked to Tractate Yoma.
*   **The Pillar of Peace:** This has a connection to the festival of Sukkot, which follows Yom Kippur. We then merit the attribute of the "Shield of Peace" <note>original: *machatzi hatzinor* - potentially a reference to the 'Sukkah of Peace'</note>, where the Accuser is turned to good, or Peace and Joy. Through the matter of the "Water-Drawing Celebration" <note>Hebrew: *Simchat Beit Hashoavah*</note>, these matters will be explained at length in their place. This is the Festival of Ingathering, and the sign of the Blessed Name is "Peace... the fat of the wheat will satisfy you." Therefore, this pillar is linked to Tractate Sukkah.
*   **Prayer:** This was established in place of the daily offerings <note>Tamid</note>, therefore it is linked to Tractate Tamid and belongs to the time of Hanukkah, which was established for praise and thanksgiving.
*   **Charity:** We are more commanded and obligated in this during the days of Purim, as "gifts to the poor," etc. Therefore, it is linked to Tractate Megillah.

**And now** I have come to mention them according to the order of the year's cycle: that is, Weekdays <note>Chullin</note>, Sabbath, Passover, Shavuot, the Ninth of Av, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Sukkot, Hanukkah, and Purim. Even though this is not the order of the Pillars as they were first mentioned, according to the order of times, this is a "set and living" order "for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years" <note>Genesis 1:14</note>, according to the order of their cycle.

**Also,** the unfolding of the Pillars follows the order of the times: "In the beginning He created" the six days of the week, the Pillar of Truth, Tractate Chullin. Afterward, the Sabbath on the seventh day, Tractate Shabbat, and then His existence, may He be blessed, was revealed. The world was created with Kindness, as it is said: "The world shall be built with kindness" <note>Psalm 89:3</note>, and this is the festival of Passover. The purpose of creation was for the sake of the Torah, as our Sages of blessed memory said: "'In the beginning'—for the sake of the Torah and for the sake of Israel who would receive it." The "sixth day" <note>Hebrew: *yom hashashi*</note> has an extra letter *He* <note>numerical value 5</note>, indicating that all of creation was suspended until the sixth of Sivan <note>the day the Torah was given</note>. This is the festival of Shavuot, and it is the Pillar of Torah. The world was also created for the sake of the Service <note>sacrifices/worship</note>, as we learned in Tractate Taanit in the chapter "In three periods," where they would read every day from the account of Creation. They said in the Gemara: "From where do we know these things?" Rabbi Jacob bar Aha said in the name of Rabbi Assi: "If not for the *Maamadot* <note>groups of laypeople who stood by during sacrifices</note>, the heavens and the earth would not endure." As it is said: "And he [Abraham] said: Lord God, whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it?" Abraham said before the Master of the Universe: "Perhaps Israel will sin before You, and You will do to them as You did to the generation of the Flood and the generation of the Dispersion?" God said to him: "No." Abraham said: "Master of the Universe, let me know whereby I shall inherit it?" God said: "Take for Me a three-year-old heifer, and a three-year-old goat, etc." Abraham said: "Master of the Universe, this is well when the Holy Temple exists, but when the Holy Temple does not exist, what will become of them?" God said to him: "I have already established for them the order of sacrifices. Whenever they read them, I credit it to them as if they had offered them before Me, and I forgive them for all their iniquities." Thus, the world was created for the sake of the Service as well. This is why I have established the Pillar of Torah... <note>sentence continues into the theological justification of substituting study for sacrifice</note> even though the world was created with Kindness, as I wrote, it was nevertheless with the intent and thought to conduct it with Justice—meaning with Awe... but it arose in God's thought that the world should be conducted according to the line of Justice, to merit the innocent and convict the guilty without waiver. Therefore, the Pillar of Justice now belongs and is linked to Rosh Hashanah, on which the world was created. Thus, the order is proper: He created the world...

<meta>The previous page established the "Ten Pillars" upon which the world stands, concluding with Faith as the tenth and central foundation. This page transitions from the philosophical categorization of these pillars to their practical application within the Jewish calendar and the specific study of Tractate Chullin, which the author associates with "The Pillar of Truth."</meta>

The world, due to its deficiency, lacked a vessel to receive His Torah and to honor His service, and it was meant to be conducted according to the strict line of Law—punishing those who did not guard the Torah or serve with true devotion. However, the Holy One, Blessed be He, saw that the world could not endure on the Attribute of Law <note>Hebrew: *Middat HaDin*; strict justice</note> alone, so He partnered it with the Attribute of Mercy <note>Hebrew: *Middat HaRachamim*</note>. The meaning of this "partnership" is that if one performs Repentance <note>Hebrew: *Teshuvah*</note>, then the status is transformed from the Attribute of Law to the Attribute of Mercy. If not, woe and alas, "let the law pierce the mountain" <note>A Talmudic idiom (Sanhedrin 6b) meaning justice must be carried out regardless of the consequences</note>. Therefore, the "Pillar of Repentance" is naturally connected to Yom Kippur <note>The Day of Atonement</note>, and the combination of Yom Kippur with Rosh Hashanah <note>The Jewish New Year</note> represents the partnership of the Attribute of Mercy with the Attribute of Law. From this partnership flows the "Pillar of the World," following the secret that "the prosecutor becomes the advocate" <note>original: *kategor na'aseh sanegor*; a mystical concept where the forces of judgment are transformed into forces of merit</note> and there is peace in all things. From the Pillar of Peace flows the "Time of Favor" for Prayer, for when there are prosecutors, the cycles of prayer are like the arrays of battle, as will be explained later in its proper place. Therefore, the "Pillar of Prayer" follows the "Pillar of Peace." To Prayer belongs the "Pillar of Charity/Justice," as it is written: "As for me, in righteousness (*tzedek*) I shall behold Your face" <note>Psalm 17:15</note>, and as will be explained later. Behold the unfolding of the Pillars according to the order of time: "and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years" <note>Genesis 1:14</note>. And now, I shall arrange them with the help of the One who dwells in the heights; blessed is He who gives strength to the weary and power to the powerless. I have come to it with mercy and supplications, that true and correct words should emerge from me and through me, according to our custom.

# Tractate Chullin: The Pillar of Truth, etc. Chapters: The Lamp of Mitzvah, Torah is Light, The Chapter of Moral Rebuke

<margin>
In Leviticus it is written: "Six days shall work be done, and on the seventh day it shall be holy for you, a Sabbath of Sabbaths to the Lord." It is difficult to understand the change in language from the Ten Commandments, where it says "Six days you shall labor and do (*ve'asita*)" <note>Active voice</note>, whereas in the portion of *Vayakhel*, only "doing" is mentioned. Furthermore, regarding "doing," there is a change in vocalization: in the Commandments, it is in the imperative, but in *Vayakhel* it says "work shall be done" (*te'aseh*) with a *tzere* <note>indicating a passive voice: "it shall be done"</note> rather than a *patah* <note>which would indicate the active "you shall do"</note>. There is another change: in the Commandments it says "a Sabbath... to the Lord your God," but in *Vayakhel* it says "it shall be holy for you, a Sabbath... to the Lord"—it says both "for you" and "to Me." We must also scrutinize why *Vayakhel* says "and on the seventh day" and "the seventh day." Regarding the language of "Service" (*Avodah*): this refers to the Holy Service, for we are servants to the Blessed Name, and the purpose of creation is to serve Him and guard Him—to guard, to do, and to fulfill all the words of the Torah. Thus, "Service" is Heavenly Work, while "Doing" is the work of physical action, which is also a commandment: to conduct business in good faith. These two that I mentioned—Heavenly Work and the work of action (faithful business)—are the questions asked of a person at their initial judgment: "Did you conduct business in good faith? Did you set fixed times for Torah?" Therefore, it comes as a command: "Six days you shall labor and do all your work." Regarding the Holy Service, it says "Six days you shall labor," corresponding to the six thousand years [of the world's existence], while the seventh day is the Sabbath, corresponding to the World that is Entirely Sabbath. Then it is "a Sabbath to the Lord your God," to act and hasten to receive their reward. Regarding the work of action, which is faithful business, it likewise says "and you shall do" as a command, for it too is a mitzvah. However, the work of action is divided into two parts: Part 1 is the business between a person and their fellow, such as buying and selling. Part 2 is the work a person does for themselves, such as manual labor. Part 2 is hinted at in *Vayakhel*, which says "work shall be done" (*te'aseh*) with a *tzere* [passive] rather than a *patah* [active]. This suggests a state of "doing" similar to what we find regarding the "pious ones of old," whose Torah was their permanent occupation and their work was done for them by others <note>i.e., it seemed to happen "on its own"</note>. However, when one engages in business, it is actually a greater mitzvah for him to engage in it himself than for others to do it for him. Likewise, for one who deals faithfully with his fellow, this is "doing" in which he himself is engaged. Regarding this, it says "Torah matters and doing all your work"—you yourself shall conduct business, and then you will see that "your 'yes' is righteous and your 'no' is righteous." But *Vayakhel* speaks of manual labor, which would be better if performed by others, thus it is "done on its own" <note>passive</note>; therefore it says "shall be done" (*te'aseh*). And on the seventh day it shall be "holy for you"...
</margin>

**Chapter: The Lamp of Mitzvah.** It is written in the two versions of the blessings: "Six days you shall labor and do all your work, and the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God," etc. and in the portion of *Vayakhel* it is written, "Six days work shall be done, and on the seventh day it shall be holy for you, a Sabbath of Sabbaths to the Lord." It is difficult to understand the change in language from the Ten Commandments, where it says "labor and do," whereas in *Vayakhel* it only mentions "shall be done." Even within "doing," there is a change: in the Commandments, it is in the imperative, but in *Vayakhel* it says "shall be done" (*te'aseh*) with a *tzere* [passive] rather than "you shall do" with a *patah* [active]. There is another change: in the Commandments, it is "a Sabbath to the Lord your God," while in *Vayakhel* it is "holy for you, a Sabbath of Sabbaths to the Lord." It says both "for you" and "to Me." We must also scrutinize why *Vayakhel* says "and on the seventh day." Regarding the language of "Service" (*Avodah*): this was the Holy Service; we are servants to the Blessed Name, and the purpose of creation is to serve Him and guard Him—to guard, to do, and to fulfill all the words of the Torah. Thus, "Service" is Heavenly Work, while "Doing" is the work of physical action, which is also a commandment: to conduct business in good faith. These two that I mentioned—Heavenly Work and the work of action (faithful business)—are the questions asked of a person at their initial judgment: "Did you conduct business in good faith? Did you set fixed times for Torah?" Therefore, it comes as a command: "Six days you shall labor and do all your work." Regarding the Holy Service, it says "Six days you shall labor," corresponding to the six thousand years, while the seventh day is the Sabbath, corresponding to the World that is Entirely Sabbath. Then it is "a Sabbath to the Lord your God," to act and hasten to receive their reward. Regarding the work of action, which is faithful business, it likewise says "and you shall do" as a command, for it too is a mitzvah. However, the work of action is divided into two parts: Part 1 is the business between a person and their fellow, such as buying and selling. Part 2 is the work a person does for themselves, such as manual labor. Part 2 is hinted at in *Vayakhel*, which says "work shall be done" (*te'aseh*) with a *tzere* [passive] rather than a *patah* [active]. This suggests a state of "doing" similar to what we find regarding the pious ones of old, whose Torah was their permanent occupation and their work was done for them by others. However, when one engages in business, it is a greater mitzvah for him to engage in it himself than for others to do it for him. Likewise, for one who deals faithfully with his fellow, this is "doing" in which he himself is engaged. Regarding this, it says "Torah matters and doing all your work"—you yourself shall conduct business, and then you will see that "your 'yes' is righteous and your 'no' is righteous." But *Vayakhel* speaks of manual labor, which would be better if performed by others, thus it is "done on its own"; therefore it says "shall be done" (*te'aseh*). And on the seventh day it shall be "holy for you." It does not say "to the Lord," for then it would be mandatory, but it says "and on the seventh day," meaning that when it says "work shall be done," it means "on the seventh day it shall be for you" etc. It must be considered in your eyes on this day as if all your work is done. As the *Tur* <note>A 14th-century legal code</note> writes in *Orach Chaim* section 306: even though thinking about one's business is permitted on the Sabbath, it is nonetheless a mitzvah to conduct oneself as if one does not think of them at all, and it should be in his eyes as if all his work is completed. Therefore, both the service of Holy Work and the work of business are also "holy," except that one is holy and the other is the "Holy of Holies." The Holy One, Blessed be He, commanded us to do both. This is explained in some novel matters regarding action, which is why this chapter is called **The Lamp of Mitzvah: Heavenly Work.** The *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* <note>A 13th-century legal code</note> wrote in Positive Commandment 4: "Of the 613 commandments given to Israel, there is no commandment that serves as a sign and a witness except for three: Circumcision, Sabbath, and Tefillin. Regarding all three, it is written 'Sign' (*Ot*). They are three signs and witnesses for Israel that they are servants to the Holy One, Blessed be He. 'By the mouth of two witnesses shall a matter be established.' Every Jew is not 'complete' unless they have two witnesses that they are Jewish. Therefore, on Sabbath and Festivals—which are called 'Sabbath,' and Sabbath is called a 'sign'—one is exempt from Tefillin, for he already has two witnesses that he is Jewish: the Sabbath and the sign of the Covenant of Circumcision. But on weekdays, every man is obligated to don Tefillin so that he has two witnesses: the sign of Tefillin and the sign of Circumcision. Anyone who does not don Tefillin has only one witness that he is Jewish. Therefore, they are considered as being 'ostracized by Heaven.' And if you ask: since Tefillin are a sign and witness like Circumcision and Sabbath, why was it 'pushed away' <note>neglected</note> by the mouth of all Israel? According to all the explanations of our Rabbis, any commandment for which they did not sacrifice their lives during times of persecution is still 'loose' in their hands, such as Tefillin. Because the language of 'sign and witness' is used, each one is weighed against the entire Torah. Circumcision is weighed against the Torah, and thirteen covenants were made over it, corresponding to the 'Covenants of the Torah.' Tefillin and Sabbath are also mentioned together in several places. After He gave them Torah and Mitzvot, He said 'And You made known to them Your holy Sabbath' and regarding Tefillin: 'So that the Torah of the Lord shall be in your mouth.' In the *Tikkunei Zohar*: those who guard the sign of the Covenant within its boundaries are seen by the Lord; and those who guard the sign of the Sabbath within its boundaries... the masters of the Mishnah established that a person should not be found with fewer than two [witnesses]. It is written 'You shall not take the mother with the children' <note>Deuteronomy 22:6</note>... and in the Zohar it says these are the sign of Tefillin and the sign of the Covenant of Circumcision, and on Sabbath the sign of the Covenant and the sign of the Sabbath. It is written of them 'You shall surely send away the mother and take the children'—the 'Mother' [the Divine Presence] needs to show that they are Jews like every man every day, so that the *Shekhinah* <note>Divine Presence</note>... is not left alone without the Holy One, Blessed be He. A person must not be found on any day with fewer than two, otherwise it is said of him 'he separates an intimate friend,' meaning he separates the Master of the World from the *Shekhinah*. Of the Covenant of Circumcision, it is said 'it is an eternal salt covenant.' The sign of Tefillin is the feminine aspect (*Nukva*) and the sign of the Covenant is the masculine aspect (*Dechura*). The secret of the word is: 'Who shall go up for us to heaven?' (*Mi ya'aleh lanu hashamaymah*). The first letters of these words [in Hebrew] spell 'Circumcision' (*Milah*), and the final letters spell the Name of God (Y-H-W-H). In Tefillin, the feminine aspect is hinted at: 'And it shall be for a sign on your hand' (*yadcha*), which can be read as 'a weak hand' (*yad kehah*)." Thus far the quote. Therefore, here in Tractate Chullin <note>meaning "Profane" or "Weekday" matters</note>, which deals with the days of the week, it is appropriate to speak of Tefillin and Circumcision, the second sign and witness. Even though it applies on Sabbath as well, the rule is: "That which is frequent and that which is infrequent, the frequent takes precedence." Furthermore, the laws of Circumcision that apply on weekdays do not all apply on Sabbath, such as a circumcision not in its proper time, which does not override the Sabbath. Also, regarding a child born in the seventh or eighth month, one does not circumcise on Sabbath. Since the laws of Circumcision are more established and common on weekdays than on Sabbath, it is appropriate to mention the matters of Circumcision here.

---

->And since the conclusion of the discussion on Tefillin is to mention them, the true place is here in Tractate Chullin; it is also appropriate to mention here the matter of Mezuzah and Tzitzit, which follow and are connected to one another.<-

As it says in the chapter *HaTechelet* <note>Menachot 43b</note>: "Whoever has Tefillin on his head and arm, a Mezuzah on his doorway, and Tzitzit on his garment is assured that he will not sin, as it is said: 'A threefold cord is not quickly broken' <note>Ecclesiastes 4:12</note>. And it says: 'The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear Him and delivers them.'" If one only brought the first verse regarding the threefold cord, one might ask: how do we know the cord refers to these three—Tefillin, Mezuzah, and Tzitzit? Perhaps it refers to the Passover sacrifice or other commandments? Therefore, he brings the verse "The angel of the Lord encamps *around*," showing that these commandments surround him. He has four surrounding things: the Tefillin on his head surround the head; the Mezuzah at the entrance of the house; and the third surrounds all that is within.

<columns>2</columns>
By wrapping himself, the entrance of the house is surrounded on all four sides, and all that is within is guarded. So too the Tzitzit
on the four corners of the garment; the garment surrounds the wearer. It was necessary to bring also the
first verse, "The threefold cord," for otherwise I would say the cord [metaphorically] delays if all three are not 
together. Therefore he brings the threefold cord. And on the Sabbath, when there are no Tefillin, the Sabbath takes the place of Tefillin. And for the 
Recitation of the Shema, we remember these three in the first and second paragraphs: Tefillin and Mezuzah, and then
the paragraph of Tzitzit. In the first two paragraphs, it says "when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way,
and when you lie down."

<meta>The previous page discussed how the Attribute of Mercy was partnered with the Attribute of Law to allow the world to endure, specifically through the mechanism of Repentance. # Chapter of the Ten Utterances

<image-desc>A large rectangular woodcut headpiece with elaborate floral scrolls and acanthus leaves. In the center, a decorative oval frame contains a seated figure, flanked by cherubs or human figures entwined in the surrounding foliage.</image-desc>

**He shall speak** of ten virtues mentioned here and there. Six were observed by the Sages of the Mishnah <note>The earliest layer of the Talmud, compiled around 200 CE</note> in the *Ethics of the Fathers* (Chapter 1): "On three things the world stands: on the Torah, on the Temple Service, and on Acts of Loving-kindness." And: "On three things the world is sustained: on Justice, on Truth, and on Peace." Three additional things were commonly cited in the words of our Sages of blessed memory: Repentance, Prayer, and Charity. These comprise nine holy things, and the tenth is the "Holy of Holies" <note>The most sacred part of the ancient Temple</note> which includes them all: the Foundation of Faith in the Blessed Creator. This is hinted at the end of Tractate *Makkot*: "Habakkuk came and established them [the commandments] upon one: 'But the righteous shall live by his faith'" <note>Habakkuk 2:4</note>. This mirrors the Ten Commandments, where the first utterance—the oneness of faith—includes all the commandments: "I am the Lord your God." This follows the Midrash cited by Nachmanides <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nahman, a 13th-century scholar</note>, which says the Holy One, Blessed be He, said: "Accept My sovereignty first, and afterward I shall decree commandments upon you." It also mirrors the "Ten Utterances" of Creation; as our Sages said, "In the beginning" is also considered an utterance, and it is the utterance that includes all others, hinting at the Blessed Name, who is first and has no beginning to His priority, and who brings forth and renews the worlds.

**And behold**, ten times <note>Significant dates or seasons</note> are mentioned throughout every year, in which these ten virtues are remembered and enacted. Each time is called by the name of a *Masekhet* <note>A "Tractate" or volume of the Talmud</note> that is appropriate for that season. In each tractate, one "Utterance" will be explained—that is, one pillar out of the ten pillars mentioned above. Each tractate will contain three chapters, and these chapters will cover topics according to the verse: "For the commandment is a lamp, and the Torah is light, and the way of life is the reproof of instruction" <note>Proverbs 6:23</note>. This book begins with and revolves around this center: namely, the section of Intellectual Inquiry, the section of Deeds and Ethics, and the section of Secrets and Allusions—which include abstinence, caution, and zeal. These are the "Moral Instructions of Mordechai" <note>A reference to the author, Mordechai</note> to increase holiness. Through this, one will be stirred to a great awakening and reach a state of benefit, as many benefits emerge from fulfilling the commandments, including health, pleasantness, and strength.

**The ten times** are: 1. The Six Days of Creation; 2. The Sabbath; 3. Passover; 4. Shavuot; 5. The fast of the Ninth of Av (including all fasts); 6. Rosh Hashanah; 7. Yom Kippur; 8. Sukkot; 9. Hanukkah; 10. Purim. These ten times are called by names:
*   The **Six Days of Creation**, which are the mundane days, are called by the name *Tractate Chullin* <note>original: "Masekhet Chullin"; literally "Profane/Ordinary Matters"</note>.
*   The **Sabbath** is *Tractate Shabbat*.
*   **Passover** is *Tractate Pesachim*.
*   **Shavuot** is *Tractate Shevuot* <note>A play on words: Shavuot means "Weeks," while Shevuot means "Oaths"</note>, because we are "oath-bound and standing" from Mount Sinai.
*   The **Ninth of Av** is *Tractate Taanit* <note>Fasts</note>.
*   **Rosh Hashanah** is *Tractate Rosh Hashanah*.
*   **Yom Kippur** is *Tractate Yoma* <note>Aramaic for "The Day"</note>, because on this day He atones, and it includes the concept of Repentance, which is "a matter for each day," as the Teacher said: "Repent one day before your death," as will be explained at length.
*   **Sukkot** is *Tractate Sukkah*.
*   **Hanukkah**, which is for Praise and Thanksgiving, points to the pillar of Prayer (as our Sages said, "Prayers were established corresponding to the daily offerings"). It is called *Tractate Tamid* <note>Daily/Perpetual Offering</note>, also because of the Hanukkah lights, of which it is written, "to raise a perpetual lamp." See Nachmanides at the beginning of the portion *Behaalotecha* regarding the lights, which hints at the Hanukkah lights.
*   **Purim** is called *Tractate Megillah* <note>The Scroll of Esther</note>.

To these ten times, the ten virtues belong:
*   **The Foundation of Faith**: The existence of the Blessed Creator is known from the renewal of the world, for which you have considered the proof as will be explained soon; therefore, it is attached to *Tractate Shabbat*.
*   **The Pillar of Truth**: Behold, the creation of the workdays is headed by Truth, as the author of the *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher</note> wrote: "In the beginning God created" (*Bereshit Bara Elohim*) ends with the letters that spell *Emet* <note>Truth</note>. Similarly, the seal of the six workdays is "which God created to do" (*Asher Bara Elohim La'asot*), the final letters of which spell *Emet* <note>Truth</note>. This informs us that the seal of the workdays—days of business—must generally be conducted with Truth, as will be explained at length; therefore, it is attached to *Tractate Chullin*.
*   **The Pillar of Loving-kindness**: This is Passover, for they were redeemed through the kindness of Abraham, as explained in the *Zohar* and many places. Israel also awakened His kindness, as it is said: "I remember for you the kindness of your youth... your following Me in the wilderness." The purpose of the Exodus from Egypt was for the "Torah of kindness on our tongue," as it says: "When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain"; therefore, this pillar is attached to *Tractate Pesachim*.
*   **The Pillar of Torah**: The Torah was given on Shavuot; therefore, this pillar is attached to the holiday of Shavuot.
*   **The Pillar of Service**: This has a connection to *Tractate Taanit*, for the fat and blood that are diminished [during a fast] take the place of a sacrifice, as will be explained. Although the Temple was burned on the fast day [the 9th of Av], ending the Service, it is nonetheless called "Instruction," for in the future it will be overturned to become a sublime building and eternal Service, turning to joy and gladness—light out of darkness for the Jews. Darkness causes the light to be even greater, as explained later; therefore, this pillar is attached to *Tractate Taanit*.
*   **The Pillar of Justice**: Rosh Hashanah is the Day of Judgment, when the judgment below is hidden above; therefore, it is attached to *Tractate Rosh Hashanah*.
*   **Repentance**: This is specifically related to Yom Kippur; therefore, matters of Repentance are attached to *Tractate Yoma*.
*   **The Pillar of Peace**: This relates to the holiday of Sukkot, which comes after Yom Kippur when we have merited peace from the adversary Sama[el] <note>The personification of evil/the prosecutor in Jewish thought</note> who is turned to good, or simply peace and joy. The matter of the "Joy of the Water-Drawing House" hints at this. This is also the Festival of Ingathering, and the sign of the Name is "Your border is peace, He satisfies you with the fat of wheat"; therefore, this pillar is attached to *Tractate Sukkah*.
*   **Prayer**: Established in place of the daily offerings (*Tamid*); therefore, it is attached to *Tractate Tamid* and belongs to the time of Hanukkah, which was established for Praise and Thanksgiving.
*   **Charity**: We find its obligation most prominent during the days of Purim, as "gifts to the poor," etc.; therefore, it is attached to *Tractate Megillah*.

**And now, I have also** come to mention them according to the order of the year's cycle: that is, the mundane workdays, Sabbath, Passover, Shavuot, the Ninth of Av, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Sukkot, Hanukkah, and Purim. Even though this is not the order of the virtues as they were first mentioned, this chronological order is superior and shall be "for signs and for seasons, and for days and years" according to their cycle.

The unfolding of the pillars follows the chronological order: "In the beginning," the six workdays were created—the Pillar of Truth, *Tractate Chullin*. Afterward, the Sabbath on the seventh day—*Tractate Shabbat*—and then His Blessed existence was revealed. The world was created with kindness, as it says, "The world shall be built with kindness"—this is the holiday of Passover. The purpose of creation was for the sake of the Torah, as our Sages said: "*Bereshit* (In the beginning) means 'for the sake of the Torah' and for the sake of Israel who would receive it." The "sixth day" <note>Genesis 1:31</note> has an extra letter *He* to show that all of creation was suspended until the sixth of Sivan <note>The date of the giving of the Torah</note>; thus, the holiday of Shavuot is the Pillar of Torah. Also, the world was created for the sake of the Service, as taught in *Tractate Taanit* (Chapter 4): they would read the account of creation every day. The Gemara asks: "From where do we know these things?" Rabbi Jacob bar Aha said in the name of Rabbi Assi: "Were it not for the *Ma'amadot* <note>Groups of laypeople who stood by during Temple sacrifices</note>, heaven and earth would not endure, as it says: 'And he said, Lord God, whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it?' Abraham said: 'Master of the Universe, perhaps Israel will sin before You and You will do to them as You did to the generation of the Flood?' The Lord replied: 'No.' He said: 'Master of the Universe, let me know how I shall inherit it.' He said to him: 'Take for Me a three-year-old heifer...' <note>Genesis 15</note>. Abraham said: 'That is fine while the Temple stands, but when the Temple no longer stands, what will become of them?' God said: 'I have already enacted for them the order of sacrifices; whenever they read them, I credit it to them as if they had offered them before Me, and I forgive all their iniquities.'" Thus, the world was also created for the sake of the Service. The reason the Pillar of Torah precedes it is because of its splendor; that which is not frequent is not as worthy as the Pillar of Torah, which is constant splendor. This is especially true of the Service when the Temple is not standing, for then the rectification of the Pillar of Service is the reading of the sacrificial portions, as mentioned in this passage. And even though the world was created with Kindness, as explained, it was nevertheless with the intention to conduct it with Law—that is, He created it out of generosity, not necessity, but only from His kindness and goodness to do good if one follows the good path. But it arose in His thought that the world should be conducted according to the line of Law, to merit the innocent and convict the guilty without wavering. Therefore, the Pillar of Justice now applies, and it is attached to Rosh Hashanah, on which the world was created. Behold, the order is proper: He created the world...

# Gate of the Letters

<margin>
S"N"S <note>Possibly a manuscript reference code</note>
And so it is written in all the writings of my teacher, Rav Nachman <note>Rabbi Nachman of Regensburg, a noted medieval authority</note>, who explained to me that we hold the commandment of "overnight stay" <note>Hebrew: *linah*; referring to specific laws of duration</note>... [the text here contains fragmented citations regarding Rabbi Yose and the sequence of stairs/levels].
</margin>

It should be upon his garment and return to the "Small Tallit" <note>The *Tallit Katan*, a fringed garment worn under the shirt</note> which he wears at all times, and not just during the time of prayer alone. This fulfills the verse "at all times let your garments be white" <note>Ecclesiastes 9:8</note>. The reason, according to the *Zohar* <note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism</note>, is to constantly fulfill the commandment: "And you shall see it [the fringe] and remember." Because of those who might mock <note>referring to historical periods where wearing religious garments openly could lead to ridicule or danger</note>, we also wear the Small Tallit under our clothing. As for me, I take the two fringes that are in front and pull them out through the clasps of the garment so that I see them always, and this is the proper way to conduct oneself.

The placement of the fringes on the corner should be a distance from the corner—both in the length and the width of the garment—equal to the "joint of the thumb" <note>roughly 1 to 1.5 inches</note>. It should not be more than three thumb-breadths, for if it is more, it is no longer considered the "corner." If it is less than the thumb's joint, it is "under the corner," whereas the Torah says, "upon the corner." Some of the common folk are not careful about this; therefore, I have come to remind and warn them.

The author of the *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo, 1492–1575</note> at the end of Section 11, page 16, wrote in the name of the *Malbush* that one must hang the fringes along the length of the shawl and not its width. So too wrote the *Rokeach* <note>Rabbi Eleazar of Worms, c. 1176–1238</note>. In the *Hagahot Maimoniot*, it is written: "The Ra'am <note>Rabbi Eliezer ben Samuel</note> wrote that one must place the fringes along the length and not the width... so that it hangs over the edge." This was the practice of the Maharam <note>Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg</note> to be precise that the fringe hangs over the corner while the person is wrapped in it. Though there were different views on whether length or width matters most, the consensus is that it should not hang diagonally from the very point of the corner. Rashi <note>the preeminent medieval commentator</note> explained that it should be slightly higher than the actual edge so that the attachment touches the corner.

However, Maharil <note>Rabbi Jacob Moelin, c. 1365–1427</note> wrote it is proper to hang the fringes downward toward the earth, yet specifically on the side of the corner as it says "on the corners of their garments." One should not change the custom of the blessings. The *Beit Yosef* wrote that he saw the custom of winding the thread: 7 times in the first section, 9 in the second, 11 in the third, and 13 in the fourth. All these windings total 40, which is the numerical value <note>gematria</note> of "The Lord is One" <note>YHVH (26) + Echad (13) equals 39; the author notes that adding 1 for the "Name" itself brings it to 40</note>. However, there is a preferred custom: 7, 8, 11, and 13 windings. These together total 39, which is the exact numerical value of "The Lord is One" <note>YHVH (26) + Echad (13) = 39</note>. Why would one need to add one more for the Name? The Name itself is already hinted at, as the "filling" of the Name <term>Milui</term><note>A mystical calculation where each letter's name is spelled out</note> also carries profound meanings.

The Maharshal <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria, 1510–1573</note> of blessed memory gave a sign for this: "39 lights are needed for the Tallit." The word for Tallit <note>טלית</note> has a numerical value that, with the 8 strings and 5 knots, hints at the 613 <note>Taryag</note> commandments. The windings should number 39, which is the "Dew [Tal, numerical value 39] of Lights." Furthermore, the first two sets of windings (7 and 8) equal 15, corresponding to the first two letters of the Divine Name <note>Yod and Heh</note>. The next 11 windings correspond to the latter letters <note>Vav and Heh</note>, and the final 13 correspond to the word "One" <note>Echad</note>. Likewise, the strings and knots total 26, the value of the Name *Yod-Heh-Vav-Heh*.

The verse says, "And you shall see them and remember all the commandments of the Lord." The *Zohar* notes that seeing them is like seeing the Divine Presence. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai said: "Anyone who is careful with the commandment of fringes merits welcoming the Divine Presence." The *Beit Yosef* (Section 24) cited a responsum from the Rivash that one should look at the fringes while wrapping oneself and reciting the blessing.

The *Tur* <note>The code of law by Rabbi Jacob ben Asher</note> wrote (end of Section 8) that one must be careful to cut the ends of the strings to make them eight *before* winding them. If he winds them and only then cuts the ends, they are invalid. Also, common people must be careful not to cut the ends of the strings with a metal knife, for it is said "you shall not lift up iron upon them" <note>Exodus 20:22; iron, used for tools of war, should not touch objects of peace and life</note>. Instead, one should sever them with their teeth—for there are 32 teeth, corresponding to the 32 strands of the fringes <note>8 strings on 4 corners</note>. This is cited in the name of Rabbi David, the son of our teacher Joel.

My father and teacher, of blessed memory, wrote in *Emek HaBerakhah* (Section 52) that one must check the fringes. This doesn't just mean the part that hangs loose, but also the wound part <note>the *Gedil*</note> and the "head" of the strings where they are inserted into the corner. One must check especially where the strings separate at the bottom, for if even one string is severed at its base or within the wound part, it may render the entire garment invalid.

**I have written** this to caution common people who do not know to be careful **regarding** the placement of the Tallit. It is proper that those fringes that were originally positioned near the head should always remain at the head. Since they have attained a higher level of holiness, they should not be demoted. Therefore, the custom is to make a "Crown of Glory" <note>the *Atarah*, a silver or silk border</note> as a marker for the top so they do not swap them or put the upper ones at the bottom. **Proof** for this matter I found in the stories of our Rabbis in Tractate *Shabbat* (Chapter *HaBoneh*), where the Sages wrote on the beams of the Tabernacle so they would know which one was the mate of the other. Rabbi Ami said: "'And you shall set up the Tabernacle according to its fashion'—does wood have a 'fashion' or 'justice'? Rather, it means a beam that merited to be placed in the North shall always be in the North, and the South in the South."

On this matter, I found in the Maharil <note>Rabbi Jacob Moelin</note> regarding the laws of the Sukkah <note>the ritual hut for the festival of Tabernacles</note> that his teacher, Maharash, would mark the wooden boards 1, 2, 3 to ensure their order was never changed from year to year. The Rama <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles, 1520–1572</note> wrote in his glosses that some have a custom not to sleep in a Tallit that has fringes, nor to give it to a non-Jewish launderer to wash, so that the commandment is not treated with contempt. However, many are lenient regarding sleeping in them. In my opinion, even those who are lenient do so during the "nights of commandment" <note>Sabbath nights</note> specifically while at prayer, but not with the Small Tallit worn under daily clothes.

**Regarding the matter of Tefillin:** One is obligated in the positive commandment of Tefillin <note>phylacteries</note> to place them on his head and arm all day long. This was the practice of the Sages of the Talmud. When they reclined for a formal meal, they would remove them and place them on the table until the time for the grace after meals. This practice of wearing them all day has largely ceased because Tefillin require a "clean body" <note>physical cleanliness and focused mind</note>. However, I have seen "men of ascent" <note>spiritually elite individuals</note> even in these times who wear Tefillin all day. Rabbi Chaim Vital wrote in *Gate of Holiness*: "If a person cannot wear them all day for fear of bodily cleanliness, he should at least wear them during the time of prayer." In the *Tikunim* <note>Tikunei Zohar</note>, it is explained that a prayer is only complete when one is wrapped in a Tallit and Tefillin. It says: "And all the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of the Lord is called upon you, and they shall be afraid of you." This refers to the Tefillin of the head. When a person wears the Name on his head during prayer, his enemies fall before him.

Therefore, it is proper that every prayer should be conducted while wrapped in fringes and Tefillin, except for the evening prayer. The custom has already spread in the Land of Israel to wear Tefillin even during the *Mincha* <note>afternoon</note> prayer, and this is how one should act. This is also the custom of the Jewish Diaspora throughout the Islamic lands. One must be careful and "bold as a leopard" <note>Ethics of the Fathers 5:20</note> to stand firm against mockers and not be prevented from performing the commandment.

**My father and teacher wrote** in *Emek HaBerakhah* (Section 15) that it is good to take water and wash the place where the Tefillin are placed before putting them on. Since they are a matter of holiness, you must sanctify yourself. You already know the saying of the Sages: "Tefillin require a clean body." One must recite the blessing on the hand-Tefillin after placing it on the bicep but *before* tightening the strap. Similarly for the head-Tefillin, after placing it on the head but *before* fastening it. This is because all commandments require the blessing to be said "passing before their performance" <term>over la-asiyatan</term>. The *Beit Yosef* explains that the tightening is the actual "act" of the commandment. If one were to bless before even touching the Tefillin to the arm, it would be "too far before" the act. Thus, we bless in the moment between placement and fastening.
