<meta>This page continues the discussion of practical holiness and the "signs" of the covenant, specifically focusing on the interpretation of the verses from the Shema and the laws governing the ritual fringes (Tzitzit). It transitions from the philosophical meaning of "sitting in the home" to the technical requirements for the prayer shawl.</meta>

"And when you lie down and when you rise," for sitting is beautiful in the home, as it is written: "Happy are those who dwell in Your house." This means it is proper for a person to be **sitting within the four cubits of the Law** <note>original: "daled amot shel halakha"; a term referring to the immediate personal space dedicated to religious study and practice</note>. He should not go outside, but rather remain settled and listen to all the "laws of the house"—that is, the Torah and the commandments that apply in the home day by day: all the laws of forbidden and permitted foods, ritual purity and impurity, and every matter of holiness. Afterward, the verse says: "And when you walk on the way." While on a journey, "walking" is appropriate rather than "sitting," for on the contrary, one must walk according to his path so that he may return quickly to his home and to the service of the Name <note>God</note>. Nevertheless, regarding walking on the way, the verse says: "Happy are those whose way is upright, who walk in the Torah of the Lord." This means a person is happy when he is "upright" with the Lord even while on a journey—a time when one’s focus on the Name often diminishes—yet he still walks in the Torah of the Lord, never separating from the Torah and the commandments, and does not treat any prohibition lightly, as travelers often do. Furthermore, his Torah study and prayer will endure; one who merits this is fortunate. Afterward, the verse mentions the time of lying down and the time of rising, which are night and day, including the entire cycle: "And there was evening and there was morning." This cycle repeats. Regarding this, the letters *Vav* and *Zayin* are used to remind us of the day: the *Vav* and *Zayin* of the **ritual fringes** <note>Tzitzit</note>, the *Zayin* of **phylacteries** <note>Tefillin</note>, the *Zayin* of the **doorpost scroll** <note>Mezuzah</note>, the *Zayin* of **circumcision**, the *Zayin* of business dealings, and the *Zayin* of the Torah's path on the journey. This cycle encompasses the order of night and day from the six days of creation, detailing the order and custom a person should follow. However, the order of Sabbaths and Festivals will be explained in their proper place.

The conclusion of our tractate is like the connection mentioned at the opening of the Tabernacle: all the blessing is the blessing of the face, and take all the remainder within it. Regarding these three perfections, it is said: "And you shall walk after the Lord," and "to love Him with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might"—these correspond to the three life-forces of the body. Furthermore, these are the levels of acquisition: first in the body, and then in money. In all of them is the perfection of the commandments, representing three aspects: the three names of the King by which a person is surrounded. Man is at the center, a symbol of this. The recognition of this begins with the opening "in your house, and when you walk on the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise." It is proper that through your hand, they shall be "as frontlets between your eyes, and you shall write them on the doorposts of your house." Like a crown, the ritual fringes, phylacteries, and doorpost scrolls are tied above everything else. Regarding the verse "when you sit, and when you walk, and when you lie down, and when you rise," for the Sabbath return is holy; the rule is that without these, there is no peace for him—whether he stands, sleeps, sits, or rises. Regarding all the commandments, the words "all when you sit" and "all when you rise" refer to the time of sleep and the time of rising, which represent the change of place and sleep in his house. "And when you walk on the way" refers to the outside, where the paths are opened for you. Between those who stand and those who walk, there is no void; a person must always have a counting of the heavenly hosts before him. Those who are stationary are called "standing," while those who move are "walking." The order of the three paths in the worlds of the living requires one to be "sitting" to remember and speak from a settled mind. Thus, "when you walk on the way" refers to the order of the world. But regarding the "ten who walk," when should one be stringent in walking? This refers to the "walking" that exists in atonement. Through this, his sign remains in perfection, standing in the final covenant. These are "when you lie down and when you rise," as mentioned at the beginning: this refers to the grave, and then the rising among those who stand.

<column-break/>

## The Matter
The ritual fringes, as discussed in the chapter *HaTekhelet* <note>The Blue Dye</note>: Great is the commandment of **ritual fringes** <note>Tzitzit</note>, for it is considered equal to all the commandments combined, as it is said: "And you shall see it and remember all the commandments of the Lord." This is according to the *Tur* (Orach Chaim) and the *Rambam* <note>Maimonides</note>. Even though a person is not strictly obligated to buy a four-cornered cloak just to become obligated in fringes—rather, the obligation only applies if he *chooses* to cover himself with a four-cornered cloak—nevertheless, it is good and proper for every person to be careful and diligent in the commandment of fringes. One should have a **small garment** <note>Tallit Katan</note> with fringes to wear all day, because the primary purpose of the commandment is to remember the other commandments, and one needs this reminder every hour and every moment. An analogy for this is a person who warns his friend about a certain matter and ties a knot in his belt so that he will remember. Therefore, there are **five knots** corresponding to the five books of the Torah, and **four corners** on every side he turns to remind him. Nowadays, the fringes are made of two strands, different from the time when the **cerulean blue dye** <note>original: "Tekhelet"</note> was available. In those days, the commandments were not as numerous <note>referring to later Rabbinic fences</note> and not everyone could review them constantly, which is not the case now. This is the end of his words.

### And in the Chapter
*HaTekhelet*, an angel found Rav Katina and saw him wearing a linen garment in the summer and a heavy cloak in the winter <note>garments that were not four-cornered and thus exempt from fringes</note>. The angel said to him: "Katina, Katina! A linen sheet in summer and a cloak in winter—what will become of the commandment of fringes?" Rav Katina replied: "Do you punish a person for failing to perform an optional commandment?" The angel said: "In a time of

---

**Divine Wrath** <note>original: "Ritcha"; a time of heavenly judgment</note>, we indeed punish for it." The *Mordechai* <note>a 13th-century legal authority</note> writes in the name of the *Tosafot* of Sens: a person who has a four-cornered cloak but tries to find ways to evade the obligation is punished. This specifically applied in their days when they were accustomed to wearing four-cornered garments. However, since it is not our custom to wear four-cornered garments, we are not punished even in a time of Divine Wrath. Still, pursuing the commandment is considered "performing a commandment in the best possible way" <note>original: "Mitzvah min hamuvchar"</note>. As we say: Moses did not long to enter the Land of Israel for its fruit, but rather to fulfill the commandments that depend on the Land. The reward for this is great, as it is considered equal to all the commandments combined. So it is written in the *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* (SMaG). However, in the *Tosafot* (Chapter 1 of *Arachin*), it is derived that Moses desired to enter the Land to fulfill its commandments, and it would be proper to punish in a time of Divine Wrath one who evades them. There it is stated: "Woe to those who do not have phylacteries on their head and phylacteries on their arm and fringes on their garment." The *Tosafot* there explain that this refers to someone who *has* them but does not wear them; alternatively, even if he does not have them, he should try to obtain them, just as we find with Moses. According to this, although our custom does not lead to a punishment for evasion, one should still follow Moses' example. It is written in the name of **Rabbeinu Yonah** <note>13th-century scholar</note> that a person will be punished in times of trouble for not having the kindness in his heart to bring himself within the scope of the commandment. Therefore, one should follow the path of the pious and be sure to wear a four-cornered garment with fringes, as this commandment is exceedingly beloved. By bringing himself into a state of obligation, he fulfills the commandment in the best way according to the Torah. **Rambam** ruled that the Torah obligation only applies to garments of wool or linen; other materials are only obligated by Rabbinic decree. Even though other authorities like *Tosafot* and the *Mordechai* hold that all materials are obligated by the Torah, a "God-fearing person" should satisfy all opinions. The later authorities write in the name of **Maharil** <note>Rabbi Jacob Moelin</note> that one should not use a silk prayer shawl, but rather one of wool. Regarding those made of silk, the *Agudah* writes that the custom is not to recite the blessing over them unless they have wool corners. Scrupulous individuals recite the blessing first over a small wool shawl and then put on the silk one. Regarding the size: one must ensure the shawl is large enough to cover the head and most of the body of a "small child" who can walk in the market alone without needing someone to watch him. Some define this as a child of nine years, while the *Sefer HaChinuch* says a child of six or seven. The *Beit Yosef* cites the *Terumat HaDeshen* saying that the custom for the "small shawl" <note>Tallit Katan</note> is to have a neck-opening and be large enough to cover the head and most of the back. At the time of the blessing, one should wrap it over the head and let it fall back. It appears the custom is to wear the small shawl under the shirt. The primary purpose of the commandment is constant remembrance. The **Zohar** <note>the Book of Splendor</note> in the portion *Shelach Lecha* states: Any person who does not merit in this world the "garment of the commandment" will be embarrassed in the afterlife when he stands before the King. It says: "At all times let your garments be white." You have been shown that one must be diligent in the commandment of fringes, both small and large, for this is the secret of being wrapped in the "shroud of the commandment."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of practical religious duties, moving from the general concept of Torah study in the home to the specific physical "signs" of the covenant: the Tefillin (phylacteries) worn on the head and arm, and the Mezuzah (doorpost scroll).</meta>

**Tractate Chullin** <note>original: "Masachet Chullin"; though the header says Chullin, the text begins by discussing the laws of Tefillin found in Tractate Menachot, Chapter "Ha-Komets."</note>
Page 29a 1 Z

Of blessed memory. The chapter "The Handful" <note>original: "Ha-Komets"; refers to the third chapter of Tractate Menachot</note> discusses the phrase "between your eyes." This refers to the height of the head. Does it mean the height of the head, or does it mean literally "between your eyes"? It is stated here "between your eyes" and stated elsewhere regarding mourning "you shall not make a bald spot." Just as there it refers to the height of the head, the place where one makes a bald spot, so too here it refers to the height of the head, the place where one makes a bald spot <note>original: "karcha"</note>. The *Nimukei Yosef* <note>A 14th-century Talmudic commentator</note> explains that the "place that makes a bald spot" refers to where there is a lot of hair. See there <note>original: "ayen sham"</note>. We learn from here that the primary requirement for placing the <term>Tefillin</term> <note>Phylacteries; small leather boxes containing Torah verses</note> is that the entire box must be placed on the hair-covered part of the head. One who is not careful about this not only fails to fulfill the religious obligation <note>original: "chovat mitsvah"</note> of Tefillin, but it is also considered "the way of the heretics" <note>original: "derekh minut"; referring to those who reject the Oral Tradition and place the Tefillin literally between the eyes on the forehead</note>. This is as the Sages of the Mishnah taught in the third chapter of Tractate Megillah, and Maimonides <note>original: "Ha-Rambam"</note>, of blessed memory, brought it in the *Book of Love*, the Laws of Tefillin, Chapter 4: "One who places the Tefillin on his forehead... this is the way of the heretics." Rashi explains that such a person does not believe in the tradition <note>The Oral Law</note> but says "between your eyes" means literally between the eyes, and "upon your hand" means literally on the palm. But the Sages learned through a verbal analogy <note>original: "gezerah shavah"</note>: it says "between your eyes" here, and it says elsewhere "you shall not make a bald spot between your eyes." Just as there it refers to the top of the head—the place where hair grows—so too here it refers to the place where a baby’s brain is soft <note>The fontanelle</note>.

See there. A person should be careful that the strap between the box and the knot is slightly shorter than the circumference of the head, so that the straps surrounding the head are tightened firmly. Then he will not come to commit a transgression as mentioned, and it will be good for him. Thus far his words. I received a tradition from my teacher and father-in-law, the righteous teacher Solomon Luria <note>original: "ShLL" (Shlomo Luria), the famous 16th-century scholar known as the Maharshal</note> of Lublin, regarding what the Sages said—and it was brought by the *Tur* in Section 8 and the *Beit Yosef* in Section 25, and likewise in the *Shulchan Aruch*—that regarding Tefillin, every time one touches them, he should recite a blessing. This means if they slip and he touches them to return them to their place. But he said that in this current era, when we only wear Tefillin during the time of prayer, one does not need to bless if he touches them to return them to their place. Certainly, as long as one is engaged in holy matters, this is not called "distraction" from the Tefillin, for they too are a holy matter. These laws were only stated for one who wears Tefillin all day long and conducts all his business in Tefillin; then he might easily become distracted. Furthermore, it is only considered a "distraction" when one is involved in laughter or frivolity, as the *Tur* wrote in Section 44. Since during prayer there is no laughter or frivolity, his intention is correct.

I also heard from my teacher Solomon Luria that when he removed his Head-Tefillin early in the morning, he would remove it with his left hand and not his right. No one knew his reason, and his wisdom died with him. However, although his specific reason was hidden, it seems his reasoning was that the right hand is considered the "strong hand," and if he used his right hand to remove them quickly, it would look as if the Tefillin were a burden to him. Therefore, he removed them with the left hand, which takes more time, so it does not appear as a burden. Furthermore, we find that the early pious ones would wait an hour before prayer and an hour after prayer so that the service would not seem like a burden. Likewise, the Sages said in the first chapter of Berakhot: "One who leaves the synagogue should not take large strides," and Rashi explains this is so he does not appear to be fleeing a burden. Moreover, the original commandment was to wear them all day, but because we require a "clean body"—that one should not pass gas in them— and one must not be distracted from them while wearing them, and not every person can be so careful, the custom became not to wear them all day, as the *Tur* wrote in Section 37. Since according to the strict law we are obligated to wear them all day, and it is only because of our lowliness that we cannot keep them in purity that we remove them, one must remove them with humility and weakness, using the left hand—the "weak hand" that does not rule as much. Through this, his service will be recognized. This was his reason for removing the Tefillin—because he could not maintain them in purity. He should humble his soul, similar to what the *Maharil* wrote in the Laws of Sukkot regarding those physical boards: when they leave the Sukkah <note>The ritual hut for the holiday of Tabernacles</note>, they should leave with humility and a heavy head <note>seriousness</note>, like a slave departing from his master. This is the reason for this matter, and it is a worthy reason; it is proper to do so when removing Tefillin.

---

### The four portions of the Head-Tefillin must be placed in four compartments. Therefore, it seems to me that one should protest against those who make the parchment portions very large, in such a way that the portions are not entirely contained within the "houses" <note>The upper boxes</note>, but rather some of the scrolls are within the "base" <note>original: "titura"; the lower flange of the Tefillin</note>. The base is made very high just so the scrolls will fit, but the law requires the scrolls to be entirely within the "house" as the *Tur* (Orach Chaim 50) states. Rava said: "It is forbidden to remove Tefillin in front of one's teacher," as it is written "and he raised his hand against the king." Rabbi Yochanan said: "One who removes Tefillin before him [his teacher]... what is the remedy? He should wrap his head first, and then the students wrap theirs." Rashi explains that one should turn his face to the side out of fear of the teacher's majesty and remove them away from his presence. He also wrote that the reason is that he uncovers his head, and uncovering the head is a disgrace before a "king" <note>The teacher</note>. Our great teacher, the Maharal <note>Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague</note>, of blessed memory, wrote: From this reason, it seems that even in the service of a student who is assisting his teacher, he should remove them with his left hand. Perhaps they feared another reason: that he is removing the "yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven" <note>The Tefillin</note> and it is not proper to do so before his teacher until he sees his teacher doing the same. Furthermore, there is a matter of ruling on a law in front of his teacher; by removing them, he signals that he is no longer obligated in them at that time, and one should not do this without the teacher's instruction. Thus far his words. According to the second reason, it is only forbidden if he removes them before sunset... but for practical purposes, one should fear the words of Rashi. So it was ruled in the *Shulchan Aruch*: "One should not remove Tefillin before his teacher, but should turn to another side out of awe and remove them away from his face." I found that for this reason—that the student commits an act of flattery when he uncovers his head—the *Maharshel*, of blessed memory, said not to remove Tefillin in front of a Torah scroll, for it is a disgrace to the scroll to uncover one's head toward it. Rather, he should turn himself to the side. Certainly, if one is overcome by a cough, a sneeze, or saliva, he should turn his face from the holy place. In the name of the great Rabbi and Gaon, our teacher Rabbi Shachna <note>Shalom Shachna of Lublin</note>, of blessed memory, I heard an explanation of the prohibition against removing Tefillin before a teacher: by removing them, he prevents himself from serving his teacher. This is because every task a slave does for his master, a student does for his teacher. If he is in a place where people do not recognize him, and he does not have Tefillin on his head... he might be mistaken for a slave. If he has Tefillin on his head, he can perform menial tasks like removing shoes for his teacher even in a place where he is unknown, because Tefillin prove he is a free Jew (as slaves are exempt from Tefillin). If he removes them, he might avoid such service to escape being called a slave. One who prevents his student from serving him is as if he prevents kindness from him and removes the fear of heaven. As for the "remedy" of wrapping his head first, this follows the same logic. In a place where people don't know them, the student must still serve the teacher; the concern is only when there is a "detriment," such as when the teacher is wearing Tefillin and the student is not. Then there is proof he is a slave, because why else would he not be wearing them? But when the teacher also removes his, the "detriment" is gone, and there is no fear he will be called a slave; then he is obligated to remove and carry the teacher's shoes. Meditate on this.

---

### The matter of the Mezuzah is a positive commandment to write the portions of "Hear" <note>Shema</note> and "And it shall come to pass if you obey" and to fix them upon the doorpost of the house, as it is written: "And you shall write them upon the doorposts of your house and upon your gates." One must be very careful with this. As the Sages said: "Anyone who has Tefillin on his head and arm, Tzitzit on his garment, and a Mezuzah on his door is presumed not to sin," because the Mezuzah contains the seal of the Holy One, Blessed be He. Always, upon his coming in and going out, he will remember the Unity of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and place His fear upon his face so that he does not sin. Anyone who is careful with it will have his days and the days of his children lengthened, as it is written: "So that your days and the days of your children may be multiplied." If one is not careful, they will be shortened, for from a "yes" you can hear a "no." Likewise, the Sages interpreted that for the sin of the Mezuzah, one's sons and daughters die young, as it is written: "The blood of the souls of the poor innocents... you did not find them in a breach." This is found in the chapter "With what may we light" <note>Tractate Shabbat, Chapter 2</note>. Rashi explains: "In a breach" <note>original: "bamachteret"</note> refers to a doorway that has no side-posts. The verse says "not in a breach did I find them"—meaning their doorposts were found complete according to my commandments—"yet for all these things you struck them." This verse follows "In vain I have struck your children." From this, we understand that a person is obligated to bring himself into a situation where he is liable for the duty of a Mezuzah. If he makes his doorway in a way to exempt it, he is punished. We see this in the chapter "The Blue Thread" <note>Tractate Menachot, Chapter 4</note> regarding Tzitzit <note>ritual fringes</note>: one is punished in a time of Divine wrath if he does not bring himself into the obligation of Tzitzit. It is possible to say that one who has a house with many rooms fit for a Mezuzah should be careful and quick to install beautiful Mezuzahs to fulfill this. We have a rule: "Do not be disgraceful before the commandments," especially a holy commandment like this which contains the Unity of the Name and the acceptance of the commandments. One should see that his hand is within four cubits of the Mezuzah. How good and how pleasant it is to put the reed containing the Mezuzah inside a vessel of clear glass <note>original: "kli zkhukhit"</note>, for then the letters of the name *Shaddai* <note>Almighty</note> shine through the glass vessel. I have seen pious men and men of deeds acting thus. A holy man should be told: when he comes to fix it, he should place it in its spot—that is, in the cavity he has made—and before fixing it, he should bless: "Blessed are You... who has commanded us to fix a Mezuzah." The place for fixing it is within the space of the doorway, within the handbreadth closest to the outside, at the start of the upper third—that is, from two-thirds of the height of the doorway and above. Below this measurement, he should not place it; but from this measurement and above... <meta>catchword: and upward</meta>

<summary>This page details the precise physical placement of Tefillin on the head and the respect required when wearing or removing them in the presence of a teacher. It also introduces the laws and spiritual significance of the Mezuzah, emphasizing that it protects the home and leads to long life.</summary>
<keywords>Tefillin, Mezuzah, head placement, Maharshal, Shulchan Aruch, Rashi, respect for teachers, doorpost, long life, holiness</keywords>

# Tractate Chullin 
<note>original: "Masachet Chullin"; while the header names this tractate, the content continues the laws of Tefillin, likely part of a broader legal compendium.</note>

<margin>
23, etc. 
And the combing there, where they depart and rely on the heads, etc., see Chapter 2. 
And the prohibitions in Chapter 1 according to the Rosh, it is appropriate to bless over both of them, and this is the opening blessing. 
From the teaching of the Rosh: high up on the nape and not low on the throat where the nape actually meets the center of the head, and not leaning toward the face, either here or there as mentioned below in Chapter 18, regarding the seventy. And if he is a claimant, he should bless before their removal... in Chapter 80, 106 there... and these are the words: and he blesses over them because their removal is for both of them until the actual hour that he tightens them on his head, etc.

**Chullin** itself, to leave it, and he brought it earlier <note>original: "ibala"; a common abbreviation for "see there"</note>: Behold, we see that one must bless before performing the act of the commandment and close to it. If one were to bless over the <term>Tefillin</term> <note>Phylacteries</note> of the hand and the head before placing them, it would not be "close to their performance," for two actions are still missing before the completion of their performance: namely, the placement and the tying on the arm, and the placement and the tightening on the head. Therefore, one must bless over the Tefillin of the arm after placing it on the <term>Kiboret</term> <note>The bicep muscle</note> but before tying them to the arm; and for the head, after placing them on the head but before they are tightened.

**And** that which **Maimonides** <note>original: "Ha-Rambam"</note> mentioned regarding this law only concerning the Tefillin of the arm, and did not also include the Tefillin of the head—that one blesses over them before tightening them and after placing them on the head for the same reason of "before the performance" mentioned above: **Maimonides** follows his own reasoning, for he holds that we do not bless over both of them except for one blessing, which is "to lay" <note>original: "le-haniach"</note> (unless one makes an interruption between them, in which case he would bless "on the commandment of Tefillin" over the one for the head). Many other authors wrote this as well, such as the *Tur* and the *Beit Yosef* in the mentioned chapter. However, the *Tur* was precise in following the method of his father, the **Rosh** <note>Rabbi Asher ben Yehiel, 13th-century legal authority</note> of blessed memory, that we bless two blessings even without an interruption. Therefore, the second blessing was mentioned, namely at the time when he tightens them on his head and his arm as mentioned above, for just as the tying on the arm is the completion of their performance, so is the tightening. And it would be "and he blesses to lay on its proper place" as mentioned above, which is the completion of the performance on the head. This is also implied by the precise language of our master in his *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo’s commentary on the Tur</note> and his *Shulchan Aruch*, where he wrote clearly that one must bless over the Tefillin of the arm after placing it on the bicep before tying it, for this tying is their "making." See there in the text. And he wrote on this: "And therefore, for the head-tefillin, before he tightens them on his head." Thus, he is precise: "before he tightens them on his head," and not "before he places them on his head," which implies he holds that one blesses

**over them** specifically before tightening and not before placing them for the reason stated above. This is a true precision and worthy of attention. And so wrote **Rabbeinu Yonah** in the *Book of Fear* <note>original: "Sefer Ha-Yir'ah"; a 13th-century ethical work</note>, and these are his words: "He shall place the Tefillin of the arm on the left arm above the joint called the *Kuber* <note>likely a phonetic rendering of the bicep area</note> in the vernacular, slightly toward the heart, and shall wrap to lay Tefillin. Afterward, he shall place it on the head toward the brain and bless on the commandment of Tefillin," end of quote. My father and teacher <note>original: "A"M"; abbreviation for Avi Mori</note> of blessed memory wrote further: He should place the strap of the hand on the arm but should not remove it immediately after tying so that it does not move from its place, since he will bless over it "to lay Tefillin." It is good to do this so that if it moves, he will be secure and it will not be tight, whether it was before the placement of the head-tefillin or after the placement, or if he comes into doubt whether he needs to go back and bless over it or not. In Tractate Shabbat 72b, at the end, the author of *Chullin* wrote: if the hand-tefillin moved before the placement of the head-tefillin, he tightens them and does not need to go back and bless over it; but if the hand-tefillin moved and then the head-tefillin moved, he blesses and tightens, end of quote. **And it shall** remain placed there until the completion of the placement of the head-tefillin, and then he shall remove it and wrap the strap around the arm. Its very placement shall be distinct from then on without a strap on its back. And the **Maharil** <note>Rabbi Jacob Moelin, 14th-century authority on Ashkenazic custom</note> wrote, and it is written in the book *Chesed L'Avraham* <note>original: "Ch"Y"; likely referring to Chayei Adam or similar, but the context points to mystical/halakhic synthesis</note> in the name of the **Zohar**, and the *Beit Yosef* brought it in Chapter 27, that one must bring the hand-tefillin close to the head-tefillin <note>referencing the mystical union of the two</note>... and immediately after tying the Tefillin of the arm on his arm, he should place the Tefillin of the head before finishing the wrapping of the strap on his arm, and afterward he completes the wrappings around his arm. My father and teacher of blessed memory wrote the reason for this. And we, the inhabitants of the Land of Israel, and similarly those who dwell in all the kingdoms of Ishmael <note>Muslim lands</note>, whose actions follow the acceptance of the **Zohar**, are accustomed to laying the Tefillin of the arm while sitting, as explained in the Zohar and by other Kabbalists. For the Tefillin of the arm corresponds to the attribute of *Malchut* <note>Sovereignty; the feminine aspect of the Divine</note>, about which it is said, "And I saw the Lord sitting on a high and exalted throne," following the secret of the woman who sits beneath her husband. But the Tefillin of the head is done while standing, out of honor for the King, who is in the aspect of the Male world. Furthermore, we wrap the straps around the arm seven times, corresponding to the seven maidens who are fit to be given to her from the King. Based on this, the custom spread in these lands to do the wrappings of the

<margin>
23, etc. 
The signs of Sukkah were established as a sign, Chapter 14, by heart. The sign of Tefillin is "He shall be sitting on a throne."
</margin>

**straps** immediately after placing the hand-tefillin on the bicep, before placing the head-tefillin. Therefore, he should not place the strap of the hand on the back of the hand at all, since he is already circling the strap seven times on the arm. **And these are the words** of the *Tikkunim* <note>original: "Ha-Tikkunim"; referring to Tikkunei Zohar</note>: "And God created man in His image, in the image of God He created him." This is the commandment of Tefillin. Come and see: everyone who places Tefillin on his head and on his arm ascends every day toward all the living creatures of the Chariot, and the wheels, and the seraphim, and the whole host appointed over their prayers. And he is a precious son in the likeness of the King. He who wears Tefillin—about him it is said, "And God created man in His image, in the image of God He created him." "In His image" refers to the Tefillin of the head, in the mystery of the Tefillin of the Master of the World. They are the Supernal Shekhinah <note>Divine Presence</note>. Tefillin on his head is the Central Pillar, and in it is the hollow of the three first chambers. And the Central Pillar includes two spheres. And the Supernal Mother is the Tefillin on his head; it is the Tefillin that is prepared every day. And the opening of the Tefillin of the head is the Lower Shekhinah, and she is bound to him, and about her it is said, "And his soul is bound to his soul." And the living creatures were in Judah... in the binding which is the strap wrapped on the left finger—this is his wedding sanctification <note>original: "kiddushin"</note>, and it is a ring wrapped on the third finger, and through this, she is bound with him and is beautiful, and he is with her. End of the Zohar's words. **The greatness** of one who lays Tefillin is that he resembles his Creator... as stated by some regarding the intention of Tefillin... and from what was explained, the strap that we wrap on the finger is the wedding ring that the groom gives to her. From here, my master, of blessed memory, used to say that it is not proper to wrap the strap on the finger until the Tefillin of the head is placed, which is the secret of the Male; for if the Male has not yet arrived, from where does the wedding sanctification come? And this is the custom of most of Israel, and it is not proper to change the custom. And so my master of blessed memory used to say, that the wrapping on the finger must be done while standing, for the male who sanctifies does so while standing. Afterward, he said the reason for standing is for the word, and the preceding, and the soft, and the tastes, and the decision, as I wrote at the beginning of the methods in the printed edition of Maimonides. And the student Jacob, and the language is distinct, as our Rabbis wrote in the Beginning of Rabbi Ishmael... in the chapter "The Handful is Great" <note>Menachot 36a</note>, if one **blesses one** or **blesses two**. Rashi explained: if he did not speak [between them], he blesses one for the arm and for the head. If he spoke, he blesses two: "to lay," which he already blessed on the arm, and he returns and blesses "on the commandment of" for the head—making two. Thus wrote the Rif, Maimonides, and other authorities. Some say if he did not speak, he blesses one, "on the commandment," for the head. If he spoke, he blesses two for the head, for he must return and bless "to lay." Thus wrote Rav Amram and the *Halakhot Gedolot* <note>8th-century legal code</note> and the tradition of the Rashbag <note>Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel</note>. The tradition of the Rashbag, peace be upon him, is this: the Tefillin of the arm and the head correspond to "Remember" and "Observe" <note>The two versions of the Sabbath commandment</note>. Just as "Remember" and "Observe" were said in a single utterance, so too one blessing is for both of them. End of quote. Although the *Beit Yosef* wrote that there is a slight interruption in the explanation of the Zohar, nevertheless, the truth is the spirit of his path, and so he ruled... but see in the book... that this version is in their books. Therefore, every God-fearing person should not enter himself into a doubt of a "blessing said in vain" <note>original: "berakhah levatalah"</note>. For what will it help what he says afterward, "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever," if he is blessing a rebellious blessing if it is in vain? My father and teacher of blessed memory wrote further: **Every man should be careful** that the straps surrounding his head should not be loose, but rather tightened with a complete tightening on his head. For if they are loose, the knot will not be exactly behind him, truly opposite the nape. All the legal decisors wrote that the knot must be at the back of the head, truly high on the nape, aligned with the middle of the head, and not leaning toward the face this way or that way. And we learn in the chapter "The Handful": Rav Judah said, the knot of the Tefillin must be high up, so that Israel shall be "on high," and it must face inward, so that Israel shall be "inside." End of quote. Rashi explained that the knot should be high on the nape opposite the face and not low down opposite the throat. And if the straps surrounding the head are not placed properly, tightened and strong, then the knot will not be in its proper place as mentioned, and it will sometimes be pulled onto his head and sometimes down on his neck. Furthermore, if the strap surrounding the head is loose, it will turn over in an instant, and this is a "great sin," as it is found in the chapter "These may Shave" <note>Moed Katan 25a</note>: Rav Huna had his Tefillin strap turn over, and he fasted... and the **Rosh** wrote in the Laws of Tefillin: "The response of the Gaon: one whose strap turns over is required to sit in fast," for the meaning is he needs a fast, etc. See in Yoreh De'ah... in the *Zohar*, changing the service to help is guarded from another sin. For when the straps surrounding the head are loose, then the "box" <note>original: "ketzitzah"</note> of the Tefillin descends from the high part of the head to a low place on his forehead between his eyes. This is not correct, for the essence of the commandment is that the box should be placed on the place of the hair. Your sign is: "his locks are wavy" <note>Song of Songs 5:11</note>—it should be surrounded by the hair—and not on his forehead. In this way, it will be on the height of the head. And our Sages said...

<meta>Continuity Note: The previous page concluded a technical discussion on the laws and blessings of Tefillin (phylacteries). This page shifts abruptly to the ethical and legal requirements of business conduct, specifically the concept of "faithfulness in negotiation" and the moral weight of keeping one's word.</meta>

# Tractate Chullin
<note>original: "Masachet Chullin"; while titled Chullin, the text here focuses on civil law and business ethics, quoting Tractate Shevi'it and Tractate Bava Metzia.</note>

**"The spirit of the Sages finds pleasure in him"** <note>original: "Ruach Chachamim Nocha Heimenu"; a rabbinic expression of approval for someone who acts beyond the strict letter of the law.</note>—this is not so, for we must explain that this refers to anyone who fulfills his word, even when no money has changed hands. For if money had been given, it would not be enough to merely say the Sages are displeased; rather, he would be required to accept the **"He Who Punished"** curse, <term>Mi She-Para: A formal curse recited in court against one who backs out of a deal after money has been paid but before the goods are moved.</term> as we learned in the chapter "The Gold." Rather, we must say the end of the Mishnah deals with a case where he did not yet pull the object to acquire it nor give money. And although at a glance the simple reading of the Mishnah does not seem to imply this, nevertheless, the Mishnah can be interpreted well when we analyze the addition of the word "all" <note>original: "kol"</note>. When it says "all movables," it refers to both complete movables and incomplete movables—meaning coins, which relative to other coins are called "movables"—they are acquired through "pulling," as we learned: "Gold acquires silver..." 

Afterward, the end of the passage says: "And anyone who fulfills his word"—meaning even without pulling the object—and fulfills his word in every circumstance, whether there was money or there was no money, then the "spirit of the Sages finds pleasure in him." And if not, the spirit of the Sages does not find pleasure in him. The text does not descend now into the distinction between money and no money regarding the "He Who Punished" curse, because this is not its primary place. Nevertheless, it indicates by the language of "all" at the end that even without pulling and without money, this anonymous Mishnah supports the view of Rabbi Yochanan in the chapter "The Gold" (page 49), where Rav and Rabbi Yochanan disagree regarding "mere words." <note>A legal debate over whether a verbal agreement alone creates a moral obligation.</note> Rav believes there is no **lack of faithfulness** <term>Mechusar Amanah: A person who breaks their word is considered untrustworthy or "lacking in faith."</term> in them, while Rabbi Yochanan believes there is a "lack of faithfulness" in them. 

One should not interpret the Mishnah according to Rav and say that the end only deals with a case where he did not pull the object but *did* give money—and specifically in that case, if he retracts, the Sages are displeased. If you ask: "But isn't he then obligated to accept the 'He Who Punished' curse?" we would have to say that "He Who Punished" is itself the definition of "the Sages are displeased," meaning he must receive the Sages' curse. This is as the Tosafot wrote in "The Gold" (page 48) regarding the <term>Baraita</term> <note>External teaching from the time of the Mishnah</note> of Rabbi Shimon the Prince: "He who retracts on words, the spirit of the Sages is not pleased with him." Rava said: "We only have the expression 'the spirit of the Sages is not pleased with him.'" And the Tosafot wrote: "If you say, what is Rava teaching us? The Baraita says the same thing!" They answer that he teaches us that "the spirit of the Sages is not pleased" is *not* the same as the "He Who Punished" curse. If so, we should also say according to Rabbi Yochanan—who holds that retracting is a lack of faithfulness—that the interpretation of the Mishnah regarding "the spirit of the Sages" refers to "He Who Punished." However, this is not so, for that initial thought is void and not logical in any way. For on page 49, when the Gemara challenges Rav from the teaching of Rabbi Shimon, Rav does not interpret "the spirit of the Sages" as "He Who Punished." It is not logical at all to interpret it that way.

Thus, the anonymous Mishnah in Tractate Shevi'it leans toward the words of Rabbi Yochanan. Indeed, all the legal decisors have ruled like Rabbi Yochanan. I only brought this Mishnah to derive from it that even in a case of **"two markets,"** <term>Trei Tar'ei: A situation where the market price changes between the verbal agreement and the actual transaction.</term> one who fulfills his word is someone the Sages are pleased with. The general language "one who fulfills his word" implies that in whatever situation, he stands and fulfills it. This is unlike the *Ba'al HaMaor* and his faction who think that in a "two markets" situation, one who retracts is not considered "lacking in faith." Rather, it is like the majority of decisors who hold that even in "two markets," if he retracts, he is "lacking in faith," as cited in the *Knesset HaGedolah* and agreed upon by Maharacha. 

The words of Rav Chisda even derive from the Torah, as found in "The Gold" (page 49): It was taught that Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda says: "What is the meaning of the verse 'A just *hin* (measure) shall you have'? Surely a *hin* is included in the *ephah* measure? Rather, it teaches that your 'yes' (*hen*) should be just." This means that when you say "yes" or "no," fulfill your words and make them just. From this teaching, the Gemara challenges Rav (who says words carry no obligation). Abaye explained Rav's view as meaning one should not speak one thing with the mouth and another in the heart; meaning he should say it sincerely and not intend to change it. But if the market price changed later and he retracts because of the price change, there is no "lack of faith" there. Note that Abaye's explanation is according to Rav, but according to Rabbi Yochanan—whose view is the law—even in the case of "two markets," one who retracts is "lacking in faith." 

And so, one who promises his friend merely by word to do him some good or service, or to give him free gifts, is obligated to be faithful to his word. Regarding a gift, they only said this applies to a small gift, for the recipient relied on it when he was promised. But for a large gift, there is no "lack of faith," for the recipient did not truly believe he would give it until he acquired it through formal means. If a person is obligated to pay at a certain time, he should set a long enough time from the start so that he does not turn out to be a liar. I heard that regarding this it is said: "The lip of truth shall be established forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment" (Proverbs 12:19). This means one who has a "lip of truth" is established forever because he extends the time long enough so that within that time he can fulfill his word faithfully. But one who speaks for "a moment" and retracts tomorrow has a "lying tongue." The intention is that shortening the time leads to lying.

***

**And if** the matter of conducting business with faithfulness is so significant even regarding a mere promise, how much more so—a thousand times over—must a person be careful not to come to **robbery** or even the suspicion of robbery, even for less than a penny’s value. For there is no sin mentioned like robbery; the decree of the generation of the Flood was only sealed because of robbery, for it says "the earth was filled with violence," as Rashi explains there. Know that it is impossible for a man to have a penny less or a penny more than what the Holy One, Blessed be He, decreed for him year by year. A person should not say, "If so, I will sit idle," for the Torah already said: "And the Lord your God will bless you in all that you *do*." Our Sages of blessed memory said: "I might think even if he sits idle? Therefore, the text says: 'In all that you do.'" A small amount of action is required for the blessing to rest upon. But if he takes and robs and extorts what God did not command, he commits a sin for nothing. 

The weight of the sin of robbery is very great; even when he dies, he has no rest until he returns the stolen object to the victim or his heirs. This is the secret hinted at in the phrase "and they shall follow after him"—meaning he must fix it in his lifetime, even if he must go a great distance, so that after death he is not forced to wander far to reincarnate and return it.

From the enactments of the **Men of the Great Assembly** <note>An ancient body of 120 scholars who established many Jewish prayers and laws.</note> in the order of the prayers, we see the greatness of the matter of robbery. The climax of the year is the Days of Repentance and Prayer, and the climax of the Days of Repentance is **Yom Kippur**, and the climax of Yom Kippur is the **Ne'ilah** <note>The "Closing" prayer at the very end of the Day of Atonement.</note> prayer. It is then that the Men of the Great Assembly established that we say:

> In the text of the prayer: "And You have given us, Lord our God, in love, this Day of the Fast of Atonement, an end, pardon, and forgiveness for all our iniquities, **so that we may cease from the oppression of our hands.**"

Let a person not think that when he conducts business faithfully he loses out; on the contrary, the Holy One, Blessed be He, blesses the work of his hands, as we learn in *Vayikra Rabbah*: Rabbi Levi said, "Blessings bless their owners, and curses curse their owners." How so? "If you do thus, 'it shall be yours'—what to carry and give, what to buy and sell." For it says, "it shall be yours"—blessings bless their owners. How do curses curse? "There shall not be in your bag... there shall not be in your house..." (Deuteronomy 25:13-14). The Holy One, Blessed be He, says: "I said a full and just stone 'shall be yours'; if you do so, you will have what to carry and give. But if not, you will not have what to carry and give."

In Tractate Tamid (page 28) it is taught: Rabbi says, "Which is the straight path a person should choose? He should love rebuke..." and some say, "He should hold fast to excessive faithfulness," as it is said, "My eyes are upon the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me" (Psalms 101:6). Included in business faithfulness is also that when a man sells his merchandise, he should not overpraise it, and when he buys, he should not excessively disparage it. Anyone who speaks truth in his heart and does not want to speak a lie—even things he merely thinks—his words are fulfilled, as it says, "You shall decree a matter, and it shall be established for you" (Job 22:28). A man of truth in all his dealings, whether in buying or selling or in lending, should always say his final intent at the first word. Those who deal with him will become accustomed to knowing that he does not change his word, nor will he add or subtract. 

There are many prohibitions and warnings regarding the lender, the borrower, and even the guarantor and the witnesses. In the book *Minchat Zekenim*, it says that one who lends with interest will not rise at the Resurrection of the Dead. How many lose their property because of this money? Specifically, some students of the Sages perform a "Business Agreement" <note>original: "Iska"; a legal framework allowing for investment that bypasses the prohibition on interest by treating the lender as a partner in profit and loss.</note> but do not follow the law correctly. The only permission is through the formal *Iska* document. How could they think to deceive the Eye Above? Therefore, I command you: as you have seen from me, so shall you do. Remind the borrower if he is an unlearned person. Here is the version of the document:

> "Before us came Person A and Person B and said to us: 'Be faithful witnesses for us... how we received 100 [coins] immediately... to deal with them and to profit 20... and the lender shall have this amount of the profit, and for this we have received the wage for our labor equally. And after the profit of this amount... it shall be at whatever time... and this is upon our responsibility.' And he lent them, and this aforementioned document shall be for a certain time, and we are the borrowers."

<summary>This page discusses the legal and ethical obligations of keeping one's word in business, emphasizing that verbal agreements carry moral weight ("the spirit of the Sages"). It warns severely against robbery and usury, citing the Ne'ilah prayer and providing a template for a legal business partnership (Heter Iska) to avoid charging interest.</summary>

# Tractate Chullin
<note>original: "Masachet Chullin"; while the header names this tractate, the content is a collection of various laws and ethical teachings (Likutim) including Mezuzah, Circumcision, and Business Ethics.</note>

<margin>Above all, the placement of the Mezuzah is anywhere up to a handbreadth <note>original: "tefach"; approx. 3-4 inches</note> away from the lintel. Nevertheless, my master and father of blessed memory <note>original: "A.D.R." / "A.D.Z.L."</note> taught that it is a commandment to place it in the upper third of the doorpost. Since I have seen homes that are not careful in this matter, I have come to remind and warn. One should intend for the "head" of the Mezuzah—that is, the side starting with "Hear O Israel" <note>original: "Shema"</note>—to face inward, and the final line to face outward. This follows the Ashkenazi custom <note>German/Eastern European Jewish tradition</note> of those who are meticulous to let the parchment protrude and fix the Mezuzah at a slant. However, in those lands that follow the custom of Rashi and Maimonides <note>Two of the most influential medieval Torah scholars</note>, where the Mezuzah must be standing upright, the length of it should be the length of the doorpost's frame, and one should intend for the "Shema"—meaning the end of the scroll—to face outward.</margin>
Above all, the placement of the Mezuzah is anywhere up to a handbreadth away from the lintel. Nevertheless, my master and father of blessed memory taught that it is a commandment to place it in the upper third of the doorpost. Since I have seen homes that are not careful in this matter, I have come to remind and warn. One should intend for the "head" of the Mezuzah—that is, the side starting with "Hear O Israel"—to face inward, and the final line to face outward. This follows the Ashkenazi custom of those who are meticulous to let the parchment protrude and fix the Mezuzah at a slant. However, in those lands that follow the custom of Rashi and Maimonides, where the Mezuzah must be standing upright, the length of it should be the length of the doorpost's frame, and one should intend for the "Shema"—meaning the end of the scroll—to face outward.

## The Matter of Circumcision
In Tractate Shabbat, in the chapter "Rabbi Eliezer," it was taught that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: "Every commandment that the People of Israel accepted upon themselves with joy, such as circumcision <note>original: "milah"</note>—as it is written, 'I rejoice at Your word'—they still perform it with joy." The explanation of "with joy" is that they perform it with a feast. We also find in the Midrash Tehillim: "But I will hope continually, and will yet praise You more and more." It is brought in the Midrash Rabbah: "Come and see that a person has no one dearer to him than his children, yet to do the will of his Creator, he sees his son's blood spilled for circumcision and accepts it upon himself with joy." Not only this, but he spends money and makes that day a day of celebration, even though he was not explicitly commanded to have a feast. This is the meaning of "I will hope continually." In the Book of the Zohar <note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism</note>, it says: "Fortunate is the portion of one who brings this offering with joy before the Holy One, Blessed be He, and he should rejoice in this portion all that day," as it is written, "Let all who take refuge in You rejoice; let them ever shout for joy."

If there is a commandment to rejoice with physical joy, how much more so with spiritual joy, which is a state of "clinging to God" <note>original: "deveikut"</note>. Amidst this joy, a great happiness should awaken in his heart, and he should glorify and praise the Name, may He be blessed, for having granted him a son and allowing him to enter him into the Covenant of Abraham our Father <note>original: "Brit Shel Avraham Avinu"</note>, to be sealed with the sign of the holy covenant which the Name gave us. We, His servants, carry the holy seal. This should generate a great joy in the soul. Within this joy, he should open his mouth at the moment the circumciser <note>original: "Mohel"</note> is ready to perform the act and say: "Behold, I am prepared and ready to fulfill the positive commandment which the Creator commanded me, to circumcise my son, for the sake of the unification of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and His Divine Presence <note>original: "Shekhinah"</note>..." 

Immediately after the circumcision, he should pray to the Name that He return a holy and pure soul to the child, that he may learn and teach, keep and perform, and uphold the Torah. He should bless the child, following the custom of the later authorities to bless him. Thus it is brought in the Targum Yonatan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note> on the portion "Vayechi" regarding the verse "By you shall Israel bless, saying...": "The House of Israel shall bless the infant on the day of his circumcision, saying..." And if others are standing there, they say: "Just as he has entered the covenant, so may he enter..." as it is brought in the chapter "Rabbi Eliezer of Circumcision." We say, "to enter him into the covenant of Abraham our Father," and those standing there respond, "Just as he has entered the covenant, so may he enter into Torah, the wedding canopy <note>original: "Chuppah"</note>, and good deeds." These are the commandments of the son that are incumbent upon the father. This is the proper order: a person should always learn Torah, then marry a wife, and then perform good deeds. Even though one is obligated in the commandments at age thirteen, he is not subject to heavenly punishment until twenty, and eighteen is the age for the wedding canopy.

It is customary to prepare a "Chair for Elijah" <note>original: "Kiseh Shel Eliyahu"</note> as explained by the legal decisors and in the Zohar. The Zohar states: "Rabbi Abba said: Whenever a man takes his son to enter this covenant, the Holy One, Blessed be He, calls to His heavenly entourage and says: 'See what a covenant My children have made in the world.' At that moment, Elijah, of blessed memory, arrives and flies across the world in four wings to be present there. Therefore, we have learned that a person must prepare a special, honorable chair for him." It is written regarding Elijah, "What are you doing here, Elijah?" and "I have been very zealous for the Lord... for the children of Israel have forsaken Your covenant." God said to him: "By your life, wherever my children fix this holy sign in their flesh, you shall be present." Rabbi Meir ben Gabbai wrote in the book *Tola'at Yaakov* that one must explicitly say: "This is the chair of Elijah, remembered for good." If they do not say this, he does not come. So I saw in the Midrash of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

## Commandments
The Redemption of the Firstborn <note>original: "Pidyon HaBen"; the ritual of redeeming a firstborn son from a Priest (Kohen)</note> is a very great commandment. According to the Midrash Shocher Tov, King David said to the Holy One, Blessed be He: "With what shall I serve You? I am Your pledge through all the limbs within me. On my head I place Tefillin; I do not round the corners of my hair; I act as a patron <note>original: "syndicos" / "Sandak"</note> for circumcised children." 

Regarding the Protection Night <note>original: "Shmira"</note>: After we perform the redemption, the father should not sit on the covered chair next to the *Sandak* <note>The person who holds the baby during circumcision</note>. One must also seek out a righteous man to perform the circumcision, as it says in the Midrash: "Let the pure come and deal with the pure." One should not take a circumciser who is known to be an укреп <note>unclear/corrupt: likely meaning a person of poor character</note>. The pious Rabbi I. Segall, when he served as a *Sandak*, would wash and immerse himself in a ritual bath <note>original: "Mikvah"</note> to hold the infant in purity. He said the commandment of the *Sandak* is greater than that of the *Mohel* because the *Sandak's* legs are like an altar, as if he is offering incense to Heaven. For this reason, Rabbi Pinchas wrote that one should not serve as *Sandak* for the same father's children multiple times, but rather a different *Sandak* for each son. This is based on the Talmud in Yoma: a Priest who offered incense once never did so again, because the incense brought wealth. Therefore, they would give the opportunity to a different Priest each time to enrich him. Similarly here, since the *Sandak* is greater than the *Mohel*, Rabbi I. Segall said he is called to the Torah before the *Mohel*. 

It seems the *Mohel* should also immerse in a ritual bath, as he is like the Priest performing the service. The blood of circumcision is like the blood of a sacrifice. Circumcision is on the eighth day, just as a sacrifice is acceptable from the eighth day onward. Thus, the *Mohel* is the officiating Priest and the *Sandak* is the Altar. Regarding the fact that those standing there must stand, Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg brought proof from the verse "And the people stood in the covenant." This is also cited by the Tashbetz, the Mordechai, the Kol Bo, and the Abudraham. Therefore, one must be careful to stand.

The Torah says, "Watch yourself and watch your soul diligently." This implies a child needs protection. One should be vigilant for the newborn child against Lilith <note>In folklore, a demoness believed to endanger infants</note>, who is prepared to harm children. The primary protection is to stay awake at night until the circumcision, learning Torah and engaging in good deeds. This is also a charm to make the house full of light. I also found in one book a wonderful charm: to take a small piece of stone <note>unclear: possibly "Mila" (word/circumcision) or "Melah" (salt)</note>... this is "holy flesh" and is beneficial. It is a commandment to be very meticulous with all I have written to provide extra protection, as a sign of: "And you shall keep My covenant."

## The Matter of Conducting Business Faithfully
In the chapter "With What May We Light," Rabbi said: When a person is brought in for heavenly judgment, they ask him: "Did you conduct your business faithfully? <note>original: "Nashata ve-Natata be-Emunah"</note> Did you set fixed times for Torah study?" This implies that first they ask about business. However, in the first chapter of Sanhedrin, it says a person’s judgment begins only with words of Torah. The Tosafot <note>Medieval commentators</note> resolved this: "With What May We Light" refers specifically to the order of the questions asked, but punishment begins first for not setting times for Torah. 

The *Tur* <note>The code of law by R. Jacob ben Asher</note> brings this in a different version: they ask him, "Did you set fixed times for Torah? Did you conduct business faithfully?" It is possible the *Tur* had a different manuscript, or as the *Beit Yosef* wrote: Our teacher [the Tur] believes the judgment indeed begins with Torah, and the Talmudic passage just lists things without being strict about the order. Nevertheless, the takeaway is that one should first set times for Torah and then go to engage in business. The mnemonic for this is "Truth and Faithfulness" <note>original: "Emet ve-Emunah"</note>—"Truth" refers to Torah, and "Faithfulness" refers to business.

### We Learned in a Mishnah
At the end of Tractate Shevi'it: "All movables are acquired through 'pulling' <note>original: "meshikha"; the physical act of moving an item to finalize a sale</note>... wherever the Sages spoke...". Therefore, regarding one who does not fulfill his word, the spirit of the Sages finds no pleasure in him. One should not interpret the end of the Mishnah as applying only to the beginning—that movables are acquired by pulling and not by money. Rather, even if money was given without pulling, if he reneges, the spirit of the Sages finds no pleasure in him. For then we could say that when there was neither pulling nor money, but only words, it does not fall under the category of...

# Tractate Chullin
<note>original: "Masachet Chullin"; though titled after the tractate concerning dietary laws, this section continues a collection of various ethical and ritual teachings.</note>

Regarding the firstborns, for the mothers of the firstborn etc., "and sanctify..." He said to him: "Happy are you and happy is your nation that you dwell within it." Until here [is the quote]. And is it not the blessings of the Torah portion *Ekev* <note>Deuteronomy 7:12-11:25</note> from where we derive this?
The explanation: "Your land" requires a tithe <term>Ma’aser; the practice of setting aside a tenth of one's produce</term>, and likewise "the fruit of your womb" requires a tithe. And regarding this circumcision of a son, it seems to me that it is compared to a human requiring a tithe. This means one should eat for nine days and fast on the tenth. 
The support for this matter is the verse: "On the tenth of the month... you shall afflict your souls" <note>Leviticus 16:29, referring to Yom Kippur</note>. Behold, the "tithing of the person" <note>original: "erom asuri"</note> is more beloved before the Holy One, Blessed be He, to fast on it. One should also eat [on the ninth], which is the reason for the verse "and you shall call for yourselves on the first day." The four days between Yom Kippur and the festival of Sukkot are permitted to them and do not enter the "account" [of sins], because the year consists of 354 days; if you remove the tenth [Yom Kippur], there remain four days. Therefore, He was lenient regarding those four days because they did not reach the threshold of a tithe—they did not even reach half of one. The count begins on the 15th of Tishrei <note>The first day of Sukkot</note>, which is called "the first" to begin the commandment of tithing. This is the meaning of "the first for the account of sins" <note>A Midrashic concept that the four days between Yom Kippur and Sukkot are sin-free because everyone is busy with religious duties</note>—meaning, the four days that preceded it are not subject to the tithe and have no sins in them. But the 16th day is for the account of sins, for one is obligated to tithe from it and to fast on its tenth day. And according to the Midrash of Rabbi Tanchum: even if one already fasted on the tenth of that month [Yom Kippur], which was for the atonement of the Holy Day that God chose as the tenth for His love, now on the 16th of Tishrei one begins the days subject to tithing. This commandment of the tenth is a great commandment. For this reason, one must count all the days of his life—the days that the Blessed Name sustains and provides for him—to fast on the tenth day. The providence of the Blessed Name should not move from before his eyes, and therefore he should observe it with love.

Since we have learned that one is obligated to tithe his days, we must know how we count the days and in what manner their "tithe" is performed. There are several ways before you. **The first way** is to count every ten days of the entire year, and the tenth is holy for the commandment of the tithe—"he shall not substitute it nor exchange it" <note>Leviticus 27:10</note>. If it falls on Shabbat or other days on which we do not fast, since it is deferred, it is deferred, and we do not fast on them. One should not postpone it to the following day. If the tenth day arrives on a day when one would fast anyway—whether an obligatory fast or a voluntary one—we do not say "he paid his debt with the tithe" or "the tithe with the debt," but rather the tenth should be moved to the following day, or the commandment of that tithe is fulfilled by it and the day counts for both. **The second way** is that if the tenth day falls on the Sabbath or a day on which one would fast anyway, it is deferred, and one need not worry about the following day; he is not obligated to fast on it, and they fast for the obligation of the tithe [only on a weekday]. **The third way** is according to Rashbam the Duke <note>original: "Rashbam HaDuchos"; likely a specific local authority or a family title</note>, and he added to the ancient ways regarding a "returning fire" <note>likely a reference to a specific lunar or calendar calculation</note> whether it is deferred or not. 

But regarding the count of days until the tenth, everything is counted. The *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo, 1488–1575</note> raised another doubt, and it is a great one: should we count Sabbaths and Festivals within the days, even though we do not fast on them? Or perhaps days on which one already fasts? Behold, they are not subject to tithing, for "holiness does not emerge from holiness," as is found in the *Rabbot* <note>Midrashic collections</note>. For the Prophets are above, and the Levites [are below]... <note>The text here becomes highly elliptical/symbolic regarding the hierarchy of holiness</note>. Therefore, **the first way is the primary one**, and so one should do: count every ten days for the whole year starting from the 15th of Tishrei. The tenth day—even if it is Sabbath, or the eve of Sabbath, or a Festival—the fast of the tenth is holy; he shall not substitute it nor exchange it. Support for this is found in "the tenth of the month," even though within those ten days there are Sabbath, Festivals, Rosh Hashanah, and the Fast of Gedaliah. 

I have a slight proof from the words above where it was written that according to the explanation "upon which [the staff] passes," it means the tenth when you count from bottom to top. It is like a pit that you need to take him out of and put Simeon in his place, even if he was counted within the ten. Later this will be explained more. And should you say: since we conclude that the tenth is holy, and if you say "it is deferred, it is deferred," then there is a loss of those days on which we do not fast. If those tenths fall on Sabbath or Festivals, it turns out that one does not fast for those weekdays in which he ate. It seems to me the answer is like the "response of the birds" <note>original: "teshuvat barburim"; likely an idiom for a swift or sharp answer</note>: when we set the boundaries of the year, those Sabbaths and Festivals on which we do not fast amount to more than ninety days. These ninety days have nine days that are not subject to the tithe. The second answer: you remove nine days that you do not fast, and you put in their place nine days on which you *do* fast, such as the Four Fasts <note>Tzom Gedaliah, 10th of Tevet, 17th of Tammuz, 9th of Av</note>, the Fast of Esther, and the Monday-Thursday-Monday fasts <note>original: "Behab"</note>... Although we don't worry about this, let us return to our proof from the tribe of Levi, which is a "tithe" from Simeon... for one out of ten is a tithe. It is not specifically the tenth that is forbidden... the tenth is holy, as I have explained. Until here are his words.

In my eyes, it seems that this law does not need such [complexities], and certainly it is so: the tenth shall be holy, whether on a weekday or on Sabbath. On Sabbath and Festivals, since the essence of the holiness is that the tenth be an "offering," there is a practical difference for one’s conduct. For example, if it falls on Sabbath or a Festival, he should nonetheless have a "Day of Repentance" to examine his deeds, to reflect on repentance, and to make resolutions for holiness. He should contemplate how to improve his actions. As it is written in the *Tur* <note>The code of law by Jacob ben Asher</note>, Orach Chaim section 595, that it is appropriate to make "Days of Repentance"—they are called Days of Repentance, not "Days of Fasting." Therefore, "Shabbat Shuva" <note>The Sabbath of Return</note> is also a day of repentance even though fasting is forbidden on it. So too with every tenth day: certainly if it falls on a weekday, he should fast; but if it falls on a day when one cannot fast, it should nonetheless be a day of repentance. And if it falls on a public fast day, he should increase his repentance. As for what was said about "delaying the count from the 15th of Tishrei" and that the four days between Yom Kippur and Sukkot do not count—this does not seem correct to me, for certainly every single day is present in a person’s account. As for the phrase "the first for the account of sins," there are many explanations for it. 
The proper order should be as follows: all the days of his life he should count from Rosh Hashanah. Yom Kippur is the tenth of the month. From the day after Yom Kippur, he should begin to count ten days, and the fourth of the month <note>Cheshvan</note> will be holy to him. Thus it shall ascend every year. At the end of the year, if the count does not align perfectly, he should either make the days after the last tenth all holy, or start the count fresh from Rosh Hashanah, as is the universal custom.

# Let us return to the matter of business, and the traveler who speaks of the way.

In Tractate *Berakhot*, in the chapter "The Prayer of the Dawn," Elijah said to Rav Yehuda: "Go <term>consult; or "ask permission of"</term> your Creator when you go out on a journey; go consult your Creator and then go." Rabbi Yaakov said in the name of Rav Chisda: "This refers to the Traveler's Prayer." One must contemplate this language: "Go consult the King." Will the Holy One, Blessed be He, answer him and give him advice? 
I heard an explanation that it follows the rule: "One does not stand [to pray except with a heavy head]." They said of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa that when he would pray for the sick, he would say "this one shall live" and "this one shall die." They asked him: "How do you know?" He replied: "If my prayer is fluent in my mouth, I know it is accepted; if not, I know it is rejected." Until here [is the quote]. This is the law: one should pray the Traveler's Prayer, and if it is fluent in his mouth, then he may go securely on his way, for then he knows the Holy One, Blessed be He, is answering his call. If not, he must guard himself against danger, God forbid. Every person of understanding should take this to heart.

The *Tur* wrote in section 110 that the Maharam of Rothenburg <note>Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg, c. 1215–1293, leader of German Jewry</term>, when he went out on a journey, would say [the Traveler's Prayer] after the "May it be Your Will" blessing <note>The morning blessing for Torah or for bestowing kindness</note> in order to join it to the blessing of "He who bestows kindness" so that one blessing is adjacent to another. One should not interpret this to mean that Maharam always did this specifically [before leaving the house], for he did this when he went out on his way before the time for those blessings had arrived. But if the time for the morning blessings arrived before he went out, he certainly would not delay their blessing. And how could he say the Traveler's Prayer before going out? Is not the law that one does not say the Traveler's Prayer until he has "taken hold of the way"? As it says in the chapter "The Prayer of the Dawn": "When does he pray? Rav Chisda says: At the moment he takes hold of the way." One cannot say he is "on the way" just because the horse is ready and he has prepared himself to go, for even if he is moving, a cause might suddenly arise that delays him and he does not go; thus the prayer and the blessing would be in vain. Rather, the explanation must be that he has *literally* taken hold of the way—that he is on the road. 
If so, the proof returns to its place. It seems to me that Maharam did not do this on the first day he traveled, unless he traveled before the light of dawn, before the time of the order of blessings. But when he was already on the way and had been traveling for several days—and the law is that one must say it every single day as long as he is on the journey—then every day he would conduct himself thus. Even though he has not yet left his lodging, since he has reached the time of the order of blessings, he would join it [the Traveler's Prayer] etc., because while he is on the road, even if he is at an inn, it is called "taking hold of the way." What I wrote—that it requires that specific similarity of being on the road—applies to the first day of his departure from the city. But afterwards, it is always called "taking hold of the way," even when he is in an inn. So should every person conduct himself if the inn is in the middle of the journey. If he wakes up before saying the order of blessings, he should join them like Maharam. If he goes during the day, he should bring himself to an obligation of a blessing, such as by urinating or the like, and then join them. And afterwards, all the days he is on the way, every single morning he should join it to "May it be Your Will" as is the order.
My master and father of blessed memory wrote regarding the business of the blessing: when one goes out on a journey, it is good to give charity, as it is said: "Righteousness <note>In Hebrew, *Tzedek* (Righteousness) is the root of *Tzedakah* (Charity)</note> shall go before him and shall set him on the way of his steps" <note>Psalm 85:14</note>.

<summary>This page discusses a spiritual practice of "tithing one's days" by fasting or reflecting every tenth day, and details the laws and mystical signs surrounding the Traveler's Prayer (Tefilat HaDerekh).</summary>
