# Going Forth
<margin>The assembly <note>original: "Knesset"</note> rustles with thrift; in any case, he was not precise like the baskets of redemption, and a cup of 462 parts is prepared.</margin>
From the seventh of the six days of work (for the seventh is holy), the seventh of the six days, along with the addition of holiness at its beginning and its conclusion, rises to twenty-four hours. It provides four hours to each and every day. Even though the addition at the conclusion of one day is the addition at the beginning of the following day, it nevertheless counts for both. How so? The day is twenty-four hours. The seventh part of twenty-one hours is three hours. Three hours remain, which are three times 720 parts <note>A 'part' or 'chelek' is a traditional unit of time, 1/1080th of an hour</note>. Take a ninth of this; these are 462 parts of the 560-part addition. 650 [parts] of twilight until the eve of the New Year; 140 with 462 is 1002 parts, which is 78 parts less than a full hour. Calculate six times 78, which equals 468. One must add from the profane to the holy on the Eve of the Sabbath. As the Maharal <note>Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague</note> wrote, six times four hours equals twenty-four. Thus, the page is filled with 460 parts, and the seventh part of this is the total holiness of the Holy Sabbath day, the entire day itself. 

And you will see that a hint to this comes from the six mentions of "Light" followed by a full day. That is: "And God said, let there be **light**," "and there was **light**," "and God saw the **light** that it was good," "and God divided between the **light** and the darkness," "and God called the **light** Day." Here are five times, and with the word "Day," which is itself a light, that makes six. Thus: "it was evening and it was morning, one day."

<margin>The assembly of the 7th at the end, to be added to the holiness of the two spirits <note>original: "nefashin"</note> that were already sanctified.</margin>
This alludes to the Sabbath, which includes everything and is entirely light, both evening and morning. From its light, it is "one day," unique. It is the central point, and the six [weekdays] are the surrounding circle. Therefore, it is written "one day" <note>Genesis 1:5</note>. According to the order of the section, which refers to the first day, it should have written "the first day." However, "no scripture leaves its literal meaning," yet through the hidden path, the verse comes to hint at this. 

From all this judgment, one can essentially understand what Rabbi Eliezer said: "Repent one day before your death." His students asked him, "Does a person know on which day he will die?" He replied to them, "All the more so, let him perform repentance <term>Teshuvah</term> <note>Literally 'Return' to God</note> every day, for in every day there is a Sabbath, which is the World to Come." And "better is one hour of repentance in this world..." etc. Regarding this, they wrote a hint in the Zohar: "**On his day** you shall **give** his **reward**" <note>Deuteronomy 24:15</note>—to perform repentance "the matter of the day on its day," and not to let the worker's wage remain overnight. This means to oversee one's actions so they are completed. Therefore, the first letters of "**B**eyomo **T**itten **S**ekharo" <note>On his day give his reward</note> spell **Shabbat**, to hint at all the aforementioned. I have further come to reveal a secret in this matter regarding performing repentance for the day's matter on its day.

<margin>The assembly and the secret of its holiness above in the manifestation of Will, rustling at night.</margin>
One should also add repentance every Friday. Its secret will be explained according to what we wrote above: that the days are branches from the five. Incidentally, I will explain all four levels of atonement and the four times of repentance: 1) Every day toward evening. 2) On the Eve of the Sabbath. 3) On the Eve of the New Moon. 4) The great day of repentance, Yom Kippur. Behold, the one famous in the "Gate of Intentions" <note>A work by Rabbi Isaac Luria, the Ari</note> revealed his secrets, and I am here expanding his words so they may enter the heart of the wise to understand and contemplate, to hear, to learn and to teach, to observe and to do. 

It is necessary to preface this with two introductions. First Introduction: All spiritual branches emerging from their source emerge and then return. The branches spread from the Source, and return and return to the Source, and emerge again and return, cycling back until the time of every "desire and will" that brought them into existence—Blessed be He—until they return to their Source and rest there. This is like the sphere of **Binah** <term>Understanding</term>, for as the Kabbalists say, *Binah* is called *Teshuvah* <note>Repentance/Return</note>, because there the "living creatures" <note>Chayot/angels</note> return. From *Binah* the [six] extremities emerged, and everything that cascades from them. It is proper for those who bring them [the actions] back to ensure their deeds are good and do not damage the branches, so they may return to the Source as they emerged. This is as the Sages said: "The soul was given to him... just as it was given to you in the morning... Blessed are you in your coming and blessed are you in your going"—that your departure from the world should be like your arrival. Therefore, a person must perform repentance and clean the damage from the branches before they return to the Source. If, God forbid, the branches return to the Source damaged, the damage approaches the Source, and then his repentance is difficult. 

Second Introduction: The departure of the branches from their Source and their return follows the principle of "by the word of the Lord they shall journey, and by the word of the Lord they shall camp." *Binah* is the root and source of the six extremities <note>the six emotional attributes</note> which are the cause of all the Work of Creation. These six attributes are comprised of Judgment and Mercy. Thus, there are two sets of the letter *Vav*, and two Names of *YHVH*, from which the twelve months of the year cascade within *Binah*. For this reason, they are twelve like *Binah*, and even though they are sometimes six in *Tiferet* <term>Beauty/Harmony</term>, they are still from the side of *Binah*, which is the root of *Tiferet* that includes the seven extremities. For from *Binah*, light went out to the "World" <note>Olam</note>, and "World" implies a perimeter. It is known that "Year" <note>Shana</note> relates only to the light of the Sun, not the light of the Moon, for the Moon is related to "Month" <note>Chodesh</note>. To the Sun, months do not relate, only the year. The solar year and the lunar year are not equal. The solar year is ten days longer. Even so, the year is established as complete when those days are 355 days, like the numerical value of "Year" <note>Shana = 355</note>. 

Nevertheless, the solar year, which is 364 days, is longer. But know that this is corrected through the secret of the leap year; the years "lend and sustain and subtract" from one another. One month is added every three years, and sometimes every two years, so that in every cycle they come into alignment. The lunar months are returned to the lunar years. If you divide the leap month among the years, it adds fifteen days to every year for the Tishrei of the year, even if it is only 353, 354, or 355. Whether the calendar is "short," "ordered," or "full," in conjunction with the leap year it reaches 315. Out of these 315, 355 days are the count of the "Year" <note>Shana</note>, and they are the branches. The ten extra days are the sources of the 355 days; they are the **Ten Days of Repentance**, corresponding to the ten spheres <term>Sefirot</term> within *Binah*. Thus, everything is in the perfection of twelve months, corresponding to the twelve permutations of the Name **YHVH**, which are the extremities within *Binah*, included in Judgment and Mercy. So too are the permutations of the Name **EHYH** <note>I Shall Be</note> within *Binah*, totaling 62. 

This is the aspect of the root of the cascading of the Building Above, which is why it is called *Binah*—for she is the "**Mother of the Children**" <note>original: "Im HaBanim"</note>. She is the aspect of *Binah* with fifty gates, forty-nine of which are from her essence, hidden like the [five] spheres. They are the root for twenty-one, which are the days of repentance that are the "Head" of the year and its source, and the days which are 355 like the count of "Year" <note>Shana</note>, and three "handfuls" from it. When these ten days of the Tree of Knowledge <note>possible scribal error for Ten Days of Repentance</note> enter their Source—meaning the tenth day of repentance, the ten hidden ones in *Binah*—these are the days of repentance where the upper three [spheres] are. Therefore, *Binah* is Repentance, in the secret of returning things to their Source. It is found that a man who has distanced himself through his actions must repair his deeds and untie every blemish to draw near and return to his Source, as it is written: "Seek the Lord while He may be found, call upon Him while He is near." Every single day, he rises further and draws closer to his Source. That is: the first day of the days of repentance is *Malchut* within *Binah*, the second day is *Yesod* within *Binah*, the third is *Hod* within *Binah*, and so on, until the tenth day, which is *Keter* <term>Crown</term> within *Binah*. This is the Great Day of Repentance, **Yom Kippur**. When a man performs repentance below, he draws near, and those gates of repentance are opened for him. Then he is called "Holy," and he enters the innermost sanctum on the tenth day, which is the supreme holiness of those ten sources—the Crown within *Binah*. When he is cleansed below of every blemish and merits to enter there, then Yom Kippur means that every blemish is wiped away. For such is the meaning of "Atonement" (*Kapparah*): an expression of wiping/cleansing, as Rashi wrote on the portion of *Vayishlach*. After Yom Kippur, the branches, which are the days of the year, begin to be drawn down. In this respect, Yom Kippur is also called "New Year" <note>Rosh Hashanah</note>. Thus is explained the secret of the Great Yom Kippur, which is the secret of bringing the branches of the year into their Source. The secret of the twelve permutations of the Name **YHVH** is their unification with the twelve permutations of the Name **EHYH**.

<margin>The assembly at the end of the seasonal times, every day and three, and they cease by the hand of ten, see there.</margin>

# Now
The times of repentance will be explained. Every Eve of the New Moon <term>Rosh Chodesh</term> is called a "Minor Yom Kippur" <note>Yom Kippur Katan</note>, for it too is a return of the branches to their Source, "by the word of the Lord they journey, and by the word of the Lord they camp." The same applies to the Eve of the Sabbath, and so too every day: "Repent one day [before death]." These are twelve branches, which are the twelve months gathered in each and every year. The year gathers twelve months, which are the twelve Names of *Havayah*, the twelve diagonal boundaries. These are the twelve permutations that are formed from the four-letter Name, like this:

Y-H-V-H, Y-H-H-V, Y-V-H-H... <note>The text lists various letter combinations of the Name</note>

Behold, in every month, one *Havayah* (permutation) from these twelve acts. This is the division into the four seasons of the year: three months, three permutations starting with the letter *Yod*, they act upon one season. They are three "living creatures" <note>Chayot</note> for one season which contains three months. Similarly, three permutations starting with the letter *He* act upon the second season. Three permutations starting with *Vav* act upon the third season. And three permutations starting with the second *He* act upon the fourth season. In this manner, the four letters of the Name **YHVH** are the heads of the seasons of the year. From each and every letter of these four letters, three permutations branch out. They are three branches from a single letter of the four letters of the Name **YHVH**, the Source. Thus, from each letter of the Source *YHVH*, there are three branches, totaling twelve branches—twelve permutations—one permutation for each month. And so the months, each and every month of these twelve months, has twelve permutations acting within them. It returns to be a gathering and a source for the four Sabbaths in every month... as there are four seasons in the year...

# Tractate Chullin

<margin>
Note: The author only explained 1/18th parts, and the sixth part of the part that is calculated precisely; however, there is no end to the calculations, and the end result is exactly 462 parts.
</margin>

Subtract from the seventh of the six workdays (for the seventh of the six days, with the addition of holiness at its beginning and its end, amounts to twenty-four hours, providing four hours for each and every day. And even though the additional departure time of one day is the additional entry time of the following day, it counts for both). 

How so? A day is twenty-four hours. The seventh part of twenty-one hours is three hours. This leaves three hours, which—if multiplied three times by 1080 <term>Halakim (parts); 1080 parts make one hour in the Jewish calendar</term>—yields 462 parts. The additional holiness is 540 parts; thus we arrive at 1,002 parts, which is 78 parts less than a full hour. If you calculate six times 78, it equals 468. One must add from the "profane" <note>ordinary weekday time</note> to the "holy" on the Eve of the Sabbath. As mentioned, this adds four hours per day; six times four is twenty-four, and from this, the entire principle of holiness is formed, which is the holy Sabbath day in its entirety. 

It appears that this is hinted at in the six mentions of "Light" followed by a full "Day" in the account of Creation: *And God said, Let there be light; and there was light. And God saw the light, that it was good; and God divided the light from the darkness. And God called the light Day.* <note>original: Genesis 1:3-5</note> Here are six mentions including the word "Day," which is a single light, just as it says: *And there was evening and there was morning, one day.*

<margin>
Note: There is no need for this distinction; it is added to the holiness of the secular, which has already been established.
</margin>

This alludes to the Sabbath, which is entirely "day" and entirely "light," where evening and morning unite, and then it becomes the "One Unique Day." This "addition" of time is the center point, while the six days are the surrounding circle or branches. Therefore, it is written "One Day" <note>Yom Echad</note>; although the order of the passage refers to the first day and should have said "the First Day," the scripture never loses its literal meaning, yet in a hidden way, the verse comes to hint at this: 

From all this, one can understand the reason behind the teaching of Rabbi Eliezer: "Repent one day before your death." His students asked him: "Does a person know on which day he will die?" He replied to them: "All the more so, he should repent every day, for every day contains a Sabbath, which is the World to Come." For "better is one hour of repentance in this world..." <note>than all the life of the world to come (Ethics of the Fathers 4:17)</note>. Regarding this, they wrote a hint in the Zohar based on the verse: *On his day you shall give his reward* <note>original: "Byomo Titen Secharo," Deuteronomy 24:15</note>, referring to performing repentance. One should perform it "day by day" and not let the "worker's wage" <note>the soul's restoration</note> remain overnight—meaning one should oversee the actions one has performed. Therefore, the acronym for **"B'yomo" "Titen" "Secharo"** <note>the first letters Bet, Tav, and Shin</note> spells **Shabbat** (Sabbath), hinting at all the above. I have further come—

<margin>
Note: I have already investigated above the intention to establish merit for the Place (God), blessed be He; the end of what is above is better every day, and for all those who are early with verses, see there.
</margin>

—to reveal a secret regarding this matter of performing repentance "day by day." Also, one should add repentance every Eve of the Sabbath. This will be explained according to what I wrote above: that the days are branches of the Sabbath. 

By the way, I will explain the four divisions of atonement, which correspond to four times for repentance: 
1. Every day at evening time. 
2. On the Eve of the Sabbath. 
3. On the Eve of the New Moon <term>Rosh Chodesh</term>. 
4. The "Great Day of Repentance" <note>Yom Kippur</note>. 

Behold, the author of *The Gate of Gates* revealed this secret, and I am expanding his words so they may enter the heart of the wise, to understand, to listen, to learn, and to teach, to keep, and to perform. 

First, one must provide two introductions. 
**The first introduction:** All spiritual branches that emerge from their source go out and return. That is, the branches spread from the Source, return to their Source, and go out and return again. Such is their existence until the time of every desire of the One who brought them into being, blessed be He, when they return to their Source and rest there. This is associated with the divine attribute of **Binah** (Understanding), which the Kabbalists call "Teshuvah" (Repentance/Return), for that is where the "living beings" <note>Chayot/Spiritual energies</note> of the universe return in song and joy. 

One must distinguish if their deeds were good and did not damage the "branches," so that they may return to the Source just as they emerged. As our Sages said: "Give the soul back to Him as He gave it to you," and "Blessed are you in your coming and blessed are you in your going"—that your departure from the world should be like your arrival. Therefore, a person must perform repentance and repair any damage to the branches before they return to the Source. For if, God forbid, the branches return to the Source damaged, then the damage is brought close to the Source itself, and then repentance is much more difficult.

**The second introduction:** The emergence of the branches from their Source and their return follows the rule of "By ten they journey and by ten they encamp" <note>referring to the ten Sefirot, or Divine Attributes</note>. **Binah** (Understanding) is the root and source of the **Six Extremities** <term>Chessed through Yesod; the six emotional attributes</term>, which are the cause of all the Works of Creation. 

These six attributes are comprised of both Judgment and Mercy, totaling twelve. These correspond to the twelve permutations of the Name **YHVH**, from which the twelve months of the year branch out. Although the year is sometimes associated with the attribute of Beauty <term>Tiferet</term>, it is ultimately from the perspective of **Binah**, which is the root of the "Six Extremities." For from **Binah**, light goes out to the "World," and the "World" is the circumference. 

It is known that the "Year" <term>Shanah</term> refers only to the light of the Sun, not the Moon. To the Moon, we attribute "Months," and to the Sun, we attribute "Years." When the year is a solar year, and the twelve lunar months are short of the solar year, we intercalate <note>add a leap month</note> so that the lunar months eventually align with the solar years. 

If the intercalated part were applied to every single year from Tishrei to Tishrei, it would be 355 days, even though it is only 354 or 356 days depending on whether the year is "deficient," "ordered," or "full." Nevertheless, with the intercalation, the count is 355. Out of these 355 days (the numerical value of the word **Shanah**/Year), ten days are the sources of the year. These are the **Ten Days of Repentance**, corresponding to the secret of the ten **Sefirot** within **Binah**. 

Thus, everything is in perfection: the twelve months correspond to the twelve permutations of the Name **YHVH**, which are the Extremities within **Binah** comprised of Judgment and Mercy. Likewise, the permutations of the Name **EHYH** <note>I Will Be</note> in **Binah** are twelve. This is the root of the "branching out" from above. This entire Name is called **Binah**, for she is the "Mother of the Children." 

In her hidden essence, ten Sefirot are concealed within her. These are the root for those ten days of repentance which are the "Head" and Source of the year. The days that number 355 are branches from her. When these ten days of the year enter their Source—that is, into the Ten Days of Repentance (meaning the ten hidden Sefirot of Binah)—one must repair his deeds and remove all damage to return to his Source. As it is said: *Seek the Lord while He may be found, call upon Him while He is near.* 

Every day, the soul rises higher and approaches its Source. The first day of the Ten Days of Repentance is the **Malchut** (Kingship) of Binah; the second day is **Yesod** (Foundation) of Binah; the third is **Hod** (Splendor) of Binah; and so on until the tenth day, which is **Keter** (the Crown) of Binah. This is the "Great Day of Repentance," **Yom Kippur**. 

When a person performs repentance below, he draws near and the "Gates of Repentance" are opened for him. Then he is called "Holy," and he enters into the "Innermost Sanctum" on the tenth day, which is the highest holiness of those ten sources—the **Keter** of Binah. If he has ascended from below free of all damage, he merits to enter there. Then Yom Kippur "wipes away" all damage, for that is the meaning of *Kapparah* (atonement)—a language of "wiping away" or "cleaning," as Rashi explains in the portion of *Vayishlach*. After Yom Kippur, the branches (the days of the year) begin to spread out again. In this sense, Yom Kippur is called "The Head of the Year" (Rosh Hashanah) along with the first of Tishrei.

Thus, the secret of the Great Yom Kippur is explained: it is the secret of bringing the branches of the year back into their Source. This is the secret of the twelve permutations of the Name **YHVH** paired with the twelve permutations of the Name **EHYH**.

**Now**, the times of repentance will be explained: 
- Every Eve of the New Moon <term>Erev Rosh Chodesh</term> is called a "Minor Yom Kippur" <term>Yom Kippur Katan</term>, for it is also a return of the branches to their source. 
- The same applies to the Eve of the Sabbath. 
- And so too every single day: "Repent one day [before your death]."

These are the twelve branches, which are the twelve months gathered in every year. The "Year" gathers the twelve months, which are the twelve *Havayot* (Beings/Names), the twelve "Diagonal Borders" <note>Kabbalistic term for the boundaries of spiritual space</note>, which are the twelve permutations formed from the four-letter Name, like this:
Y-H-V-H, Y-H-H-V, Y-V-H-H, H-V-Y-H, H-V-H-Y, H-Y-V-H, V-Y-H-H, V-H-Y-H, V-H-H-Y, H-H-Y-V, H-H-V-Y, H-Y-H-V. 

In every month, one of these twelve permutations is active. These are divided into the four seasons of the year: 
- Three permutations starting with **Yod** (Y) act in one season (three months).
- Three permutations starting with **Heh** (H) act in the second season.
- Three permutations starting with **Vav** (V) act in the third season.
- Three permutations starting with the second **Heh** (H) act in the fourth season.

In this way, the four letters of the Name **YHVH** are the "Heads" of the seasons of the year. From each and every letter of these four letters, three permutations branch out. These are three branches from each letter of the Source. In total, there are twelve branches—twelve Names—one for each month. Thus, each month of these twelve months has a Name acting within it, and it returns to be a collection and Source for the four weeks within it. That is to say, just as there are four seasons in the year, so too the Name is divided...

And it was, and it was the deed which he shall perform, and he who hears will merit and increase his learning, for there is no measure to the attributes of God. Why is it written: **"Which a man shall do and live by them"**? <note>Leviticus 18:5</note> I shall begin with the order of the night and afterwards the order of the day. This is how the Teacher <note>original: "Tanna"</note> began the Mishnah: "From what time may we recite the *Shema* in the evening?" and so on. The Talmud explains that the Teacher does this for two reasons. First, the order of the verse is: "when you lie down and when you rise." Second, the Teacher learns from the creation of the world: **"And it was evening and it was morning."** <note>Genesis 1:5</note>

Regarding the order of the night: at the outset, one must link the entrance of the night with the departure of the passing day through the service of the Blessed Name, either by performing a commandment or by engaging in Torah study. Likewise, one must link the departure of the night with the entrance of the day. This matter is explained in the *Zohar*, and it is hinted at in the aforementioned verse: **"And it was evening and it was morning, one day."** This implies that one should link the evening and the morning, both at their departure and their arrival, so that they become a single unity in the Oneness of the Creator.

Our Sages of blessed memory already hinted at this when they established the blessings of the *Shema*. Before the recitation of "Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One," they established that we should mention the attribute of day at night, and the attribute of night during the day. That is: "Who forms light and creates darkness" <note>said during the day</note> and "Who brings on the evenings... who opens the gates" <note>said at night</note>. This is meant to remove from the hearts of the heretics <note>original: "Minim"</note>—may their names be blotted out—the idea that the one who created the day did not create the night. The verse "And it was evening and it was morning" also alludes to this: both night and day belong to the Lord.

The Blessed Creator made a sign in their creation to demonstrate this. Specifically, at sunset, the sun becomes red and radiant so that the darkness is inclusive of light. Similarly, before the day illuminates at dawn, the darkness is great. Onkelos <note>The famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic</note> translates the verse "and the darkness was felt" as: "after it is stirred, it shall receive the night." All this is to show the inclusion and unity of all things. Therefore, a person must observe a decree that shall not pass: to join and link the entrance of the day with its departure through the study of Torah and the service of the Blessed Name.

<column-break/>

<margin>This is hinted at in the division of the alphabet according to the "BiT-YaP" cipher <note>An ancient cryptographic system where letters are swapped</note> explained in the *Kuzari*.</margin>

They said in the Talmud, in the name of Rabbi Joshua ben Levi: Children <note>original: "dardeki"</note> in the study hall said things the likes of which were not said even in the days of Joshua son of Nun.
**A-B** [Aleph-Bet]: *Aleph Binah*—learn understanding.
**G-D** [Gimel-Dalet]: *Gomel Dalim*—be kind to the poor. Why is the foot of the *Gimel* stretched toward the *Dalet*? Because it is the way of a benefactor <note>Gomel</note> to run after the poor <note>Dal</note>.
And what is the reason the foot of the *Dalet* is stretched back toward the *Gimel*? So that the poor person should make himself available to the benefactor.
And why does the *Dalet* turn its face away from the *Gimel*? To show that he should give to him in private, so that the poor person should not be ashamed.
**H-V** [He-Vav]: These are the names of the Holy One, Blessed be He.
**Z-Ch, T-Y, K-L** [Zayin-Chet, Tet-Yod, Kaf-Lamed]: If you do this, the Holy One, Blessed be He, sustains you, shows you favor, is good to you, gives you an inheritance, and binds a crown <note>Keter</note> for you in the World to Come.
The **bent Nun** and the **straight Nun** [נ ן]: A faithful person who is bent will eventually be a faithful person who is straight <note>humility leads to uprightness</note>.
**S-E** [Samekh-Ayin]: *Semokh Aniyim*—support the poor.
The **bent Pe** and the **straight Pe** [פ ף]: An open mouth and a closed mouth <note>there is a time to speak and a time to be silent</note>.
The **bent Tzadi** and the **straight Tzadi** [צ ץ]: A righteous person who is bent will eventually be a righteous person who is straight.
**K** [Kof]: *Kadosh*—Holy.
**R** [Resh]: *Rasha*—Wicked. Why does the *Kof* turn its face away from the *Resh*? The Holy One, Blessed be He, says: "I cannot look upon the wicked."
And why is the crown of the *Kof* turned toward the *Resh*? To say that if the wicked person repents, I will bind a crown for him like My own.
And why is the foot of the *Kof* suspended? So that if he repents, he can enter through the opening.
**S-T** [Shin-Tav]: *Sheker* [Falsehood] and *Emet* [Truth]. Why are the letters of "Falsehood" close to each other in the alphabet, while the letters of "Truth" are far apart? Because falsehood is common, but truth is hard to find.
<note>This section is a mystical meditation on the shapes and positions of the Hebrew letters as moral lessons.</note>

The alphabet contains the whole Torah. One who is wise will reflect on these signs. Sometimes a person is like the letters, rising or falling. One must understand all this. A person who can accept the heavens upon himself is like a branch ready to be taken and merit the stars of heaven.

The secret of the Holy One, Blessed be He: Why is it that Israel is not answered even when they labor in prayer? It is because they do not pray in the plural. One should always pray in the language of the community, saying "Save us," "Heal us," "Pity us." The Maharal of Prague <note>Rabbi Judah Loew</note> wrote that our intention should be for the collective of Israel. When we say "Pity us," we mean the entirety of the people. All that we pray for is for the sake of the Divine Presence <note>original: "Shekhinah"</note> which dwells among us.

---

**And behold,** it was already mentioned in the *Zohar* above regarding the matter of Repentance <note>original: "Teshuvah"</note>: "In his day you shall give him his wage." A person must perform this every day and examine the deeds of that day so that they are rectified, and "the sun shall set and he shall be pure" before the next day enters. Now, perhaps the time will be short, for one must examine and also repair what was spoiled and find the right paths. The time is short because the time for prayer arrives, as does the time for linking the night to the day through Torah study and the Recitation of the *Shema*.

In this matter, I will enlighten you and teach you the way you should go: At sunset, one should reflect on repentance and make a firm resolve in his heart to examine and repair all his transgressions when he has leisure later before going to sleep. Even if the repentance was not fully completed by sunset, he is called a "Penitents" <note>Ba'al Teshuvah</note>. This is similar to the law regarding one who refuses to obey a legal judgment: they write a "note of shunning" <note>original: "shamma"</note> against him, but as soon as he says "I am coming to court," even if the judgment has not yet been carried out, they tear up that note. So too in this case: as soon as he contemplates repentance and resolves to perform a complete repentance, he is called a Penitent, on the condition that he later completes the repentance and its rectification before going to sleep. On this, the Sages hinted: "If you see a Torah scholar commit a sin at night, do not think ill of him by day, for he has surely repented" before he went to his bed.

**The first thing** is the acceptance of the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven through the Recitation of the *Shema*. We learned at the beginning of Tractate *Berakhot*: "From what time may we recite the *Shema* in the evening? From the time the priests enter to eat their heave-offering," which is from the time the stars emerge. Our master Rabbeinu Yonah wrote: When we say that from the emergence of the stars onward is night, it means specifically three medium-sized stars. If there are fewer, it is not yet night. We say in Tractate *Shabbat*: one star is day, two is twilight, and three is night. We do not mean large stars that are visible during the day, nor small stars visible only in deep night, but medium ones. Since not everyone is an expert in distinguishing medium from small stars, one must be careful to wait until the small ones are visible.

However, in all the lands of Ashkenaz <note>Germany and Central Europe</note>, the custom is to recite the *Shema* earlier during the Evening Prayer. The legal authorities <note>original: "Poskim"</note> sought to find a reason for this custom, as explained at length by our rabbis. The *Tur* of blessed memory wrote that out of necessity they acted thus, because the community gathers for the Afternoon Prayer <note>Mincha</note>, and if they did not recite the *Shema* and pray the Evening Prayer <note>Maariv</note> until the stars emerged, everyone would have gone home, and it would be a great burden to gather them again later. Thus, they would end up not praying at all. Therefore, this custom was adopted.

Observe that he did not permit praying the Evening Prayer before the stars emerge except for the reason that one is praying with the community. It follows that an individual living in a village, or if he is on the road where there is no community, must wait until the stars emerge. The *Kol Bo* wrote in Section 9: "The time for reciting the *Shema* is from the emergence of the stars, and one who does so before then has not fulfilled the obligation, unless it is with the Leader of the Congregation in a place where there is a local council <note>original: "Chever Ir"</note>." The reason is based on the verse: "It is a time to act for the Lord; they have made void Your Torah." If they were to pause between the Afternoon and Evening prayers and each man went to his tent, they might become lazy or forget to return to pray at the proper time (the emergence of the stars), and the recitation would be cancelled entirely. But in a place where there is no community, it is better for the individual to wait and recite it at its proper time.

## Chapter: The Way of Life – Ethical Rebuke

The commandments mentioned above—Fringes <note>original: "Tzitzit"</note>, Phylacteries <note>original: "Tefillin"</note>, the Doorpost Marker <note>original: "Mezuzah"</note>, Circumcision <note>original: "Milah"</note>, and Business and Commerce—one should take ethical instruction from them regarding the three "perfections" we mentioned above (which will be discussed further at length in their proper place). These are: the perfection of the Soul (which is the Intellect), the perfection of the Body, and the perfection of Wealth. Within this "triple-threaded cord," everything is included. 

For the **Phylacteries** on the arm are placed opposite the heart, and the Phylacteries on the head are placed upon the brain; this is a reminder for the perfection of the Intellect—to take shelter in the source of wisdom and for the heart, which is the dwelling place of understanding. "The heart understands" <note>A common Talmudic idiom</note> so that a person may sanctify their wisdom and understanding. 

The **Fringes** <note>Tzitzit</note> which surround the body serve as a reminder for the perfection of the Body. It is written that the Fringes have eight strings and twelve <insert>five</insert> knots <note>The author likely refers to the custom of windings/knots</note>. 
- In the first string: to merit regarding commandments and transgressions dependent on the **Eye**. 
- In the second string: commandments and transgressions dependent on the **Mouth**. 
- In the third: **Swallowing**. 
- In the fourth: commandments and transgressions dependent on the **Ears**. 
- In the fifth: the **Nose** and its sense of smell. 
- In the sixth: <unclear>the torso/skin</unclear>. 
- In the seventh: commandments and transgressions dependent on the **Hands**. 
- In the eighth: commandments and transgressions dependent on the **Feet** and the **Genitalia** <note>original: "Ervah"</note>. Thus far.

The **Mezuzah**, which is at the entrance of the house, concerns one's coming and going—that which a person gathers into their house. The custom is to bring things in and take things out, and all should be done in "Truth and Faithfulness" <note>original: "Emet ve-Emunah"</note>. This is the secret of "Conducting business in good faith." That is, what a person brings into their house—meaning what they earn—should be earned faithfully. Also, afterward, what they take out (spend) should be in faithfulness, so that they do not spend on vanity or excessive lusts, but rather all spending should be for the sake of Heaven. He himself should transform the "necessary" into the "sacred" and spend on Torah study, the poor, and acts of kindness, according to the blessing with which the Lord has blessed him. 

Furthermore, a person should take ethical instruction when he is wrapped in Fringes, clothed in Phylacteries, and sealed with the "Sign of the Holy Covenant" <note>original: "Oth Berit Kodesh," referring to circumcision</note>. I mean to say, if he remains in his holiness and has not sinned, then he is sealed with the seal of the Holy One, Blessed be He. And this—the Holy One, Blessed be He—is "Truth" <note>original: "Emet"</note>. This is the secret of the Name **Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh** <note>I Am That I Am</note>. The Kabbalists explain that "Ehyeh" (numerical value 21) times "Ehyeh" (21) equals 441, which is the value of the word **Truth** <note>original: "Emet," Aleph=1, Mem=40, Tav=400</note>. And the letters of "Ehyeh" contain the essence of the Name that is not pronounced by its letters, namely Y-H-W, which also equals 21 <note>Yud=10, Heh=5, Vav=6</note>, for the final "Heh" is a double.

It is stated in the *Book of Creation* <note>original: "Sefer Yetzirah"</note> that the six permutations of Y-H-W are the six seals of the six directions: He sealed the Height (Up), the Depth (Down), the East, the West, the North, and the South, as seen there at length. This is cited in the books of the Kabbalists: So too the person clothed in Phylacteries—**"And all the peoples of the earth shall see that the Name of the Lord is called upon you"** <note>Deuteronomy 28:10</note>—this is the seal of the "Height," for the Divine Presence is above his head. The seal of Circumcision, which is the "conclusion of the body," is the seal of the "Depth" (Down). (It is also forbidden for a person to bring himself to arousal without a commandment, for that would bring "heat" toward the earth—thus completing the six directions). And the four Fringes correspond to the four directions (East, West, North, South). 

So shall a man remember throughout the six days of work, which are sealed by the six directions and the aforementioned "constriction" <note>original: "Tzimtzum"</note>. Let him be awakened each and every day according to the nature of its blessing. It is written: **"In the heavens above and on the earth below"** <note>Deuteronomy 4:39</note>—these are His seals, which correspond one to another. "In the heavens above," so to speak, refers to the Holy One, Blessed be He; "and on the earth below" refers to Man, who was made in the Image and Likeness. To this, the First Day and the Sixth Day hint: [on the first day] the heavens and earth were "sealed" because of the Unification of the World, and on the Sixth Day, Man was created and placed on the "sealed earth," corresponding to the Upper Realm.

Behold, it was already mentioned above in the introduction to *The Generations of Man* that the four "walls" of the world are: Hanukkah, Prayer, Charity, and Torah Study (which is equal to them all). Look there. 
- **The Second Day:** "Let there be a firmament..." and He called the firmament "Heaven." This firmament refers in its secret to the "Firmament above the heads of the Living Creatures" <note>original: "Chayot," referring to Ezekiel's vision</note>. So they said in the *Midrash of Rabbi Nehunia ben ha-Kanah* and in *Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer* (Chapter 4): On the second day, the Holy One created the firmament and the angels, etc. But were not the heavens and earth created on the first day? Rabbi Eliezer said: This refers to the firmament above the heads of the Living Creatures. This is the secret of the Throne, as it is written: "The heavens are My throne." At the end of Tractate *Yoma*, it says: "Great is repentance, for it reaches up to the Throne of Glory." And He said, "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water"—this is Repentance, which is turned toward all "waters" (tears). "Streams of water run down my eyes" <note>Psalms 119:136</note>; the gates of tears are never locked. The essence of Repentance is "drawing water" [of tears], and of this it is said: "Many waters cannot quench love." 
- **The Third Day:** The creation of plants and their growth through "interpenetration." "The herb of the field before it grew, for the Lord God had not sent rain... and there was no man..." <note>Genesis 2:5</note> to pray for rain. [Thus, Day 3 relates to Prayer].
- **The Fourth Day:** The creation of the Luminaries, which point to the Written Torah and the Oral Torah, as our Sages of blessed memory mentioned in the Midrashim and as the commentators have elaborated. In Tractate *Shabbat* (Chapter "He who let the darkness fall"): "One who is born on the fourth day of the week will be a wise man" (a scribal error: <note>The text corrects itself or notes a variant</note>) because the luminaries were hung on that day. 
- **The Fifth Day:** The creation of the fish, which hints at matters regarding the virtue of **Charity**. There is one who scatters and yet increases, and the Holy One sends a blessing. Likewise, the fish and human beings [on Day 5]—he who lacks from them, they are "shining faces" and many. And on Day 7 [the Sages] expounded: "Cast your bread upon the waters..." In the chapter "He who let the darkness fall": "One born on the fifth day will be a performer of acts of kindness." Why? Because the fish and birds were created on it. Rashi explains: "One does not toil for their food; rather, they are sustained by the kindness of the Holy One, Blessed be He." Thus far his words. The essence of Charity is to give prepared food, for the benefit to the poor man is immediate.

Behold, it is explained through all I have written: the order of times, the order of days, the order of salvations, and their use is explained clearly. They are all equal for the good, providing an awakening in a pure heart to understand and be wise each and every day according to its blessings—to be awakened to the matter of that day and the letter of the Name that serves within it, to be a "Chariot" <note>original: "Merkavah"</note> for it. The general rule is to perform His words on their day, both in the literal sense—e.g., Day 1 points to His Oneness, to fix His Oneness in one's heart and have His awe upon one's face always; Day 2: Repentance; Day 3: Prayer; Day 4: Torah; Day 5: Charity; and Day 6: let a man remember he was created below in the Image and Likeness, so to speak, to be "god-like." He should also meditate on the secrets of each day, which correspond to the six Supernal Attributes. How a person can become a Chariot for each attribute is explained above at length. Afterward, he should think: "Which letter of the Name [is active]?" and contemplate what the Chariot to it is. Then he will be sanctified with supernal holiness. "The Holy One gives wisdom to the wise," and "He who comes to be purified is assisted." And now I shall record the beauty of each and every day...

He wrote: The body has twenty "pearls," the secret of the letters *K-M-N-P-S* <note>Final forms of Hebrew letters</note>. In the writing of the letters, they are straight and elongated... in this world they are "closed/bent" and in the future they will return to their straight form... This relates to the perfection of deeds and specifically to the faculties dependent on the body. There are "surroundings" that encompass the body, pointing to the body as it is with the three foundations... and this is the secret of the "Crown." <meta>This page continues the discussion on the timing and requirements for religious duties, specifically transitioning from the general laws of atonement and cycles to the specific laws of the Evening Shema and the spiritual conduct required before sleep.</meta>

# Tractate Chullin
### Page 123

He holds that people must go and lie down until midnight, and from that point onwards the time for the Recitation of the Shema <note>original: "Kriyat Shema"</note> has passed. It follows that they would be exempt from the Shema, for although Rabbi Simeon holds that the time lasts all night, the rule is that when an individual disagrees with the majority, the law follows the majority, as seen in the Talmud. Or, perhaps the Sages agree with Rabban Gamliel’s interpretation that the phrase "when you lie down" means the entire time people are asleep, which is the whole night. Consequently, the time for the Shema lasts all night, and when the Sages said "until midnight," they meant this only as a preferred requirement <term>L'chatachila: the ideal way to perform a commandment initially</term> to keep a person far from transgression. However, after the fact <term>B'di'avad: a legal status where an action is accepted even if not done ideally</term>, one is obligated to recite it until the pillar of dawn <note>original: "Amud HaShachar"</note> rises. Rabban Gamliel replied to them: "You are obligated to recite it if the dawn has not yet risen," for the words of the Sages were intended only as a preference and a safeguard.

Regarding the question of what exactly they disagree upon: since both agree that the ideal time begins when the stars come out, and both agree that the essential time lasts until the dawn, it seems to me that their dispute concerns the ideal timing <note>original: "L'chatachila"</note>. If a person does not wish to eat or sleep that night, the Sages hold that even so, it is forbidden to delay the recitation past midnight as a safeguard. But Rabban Gamliel is not concerned by this, just as with the Prayer <note>referring to the Amidah</note>, where a person is permitted to wait to pray at any point during its designated time. What we wrote above—that Rabban Gamliel agrees with the earlier teaching—refers to the teaching that one should not say, "I will eat a little and sleep a little," lest sleep overcome him. However, if he has no intention of eating, drinking, or sleeping, Rabban Gamliel holds that the ideal time lasts the whole night. The Sages, however, hold only until midnight as a decree, lest he fall asleep since the night is prone to it.

One could also say their dispute concerns someone who began a permissible activity while it was still broad daylight, such as a great feast that extended into the night. The Sages hold he is obligated to stop when midnight arrives as a safeguard, while Rabban Gamliel holds he need not stop. Thus, everything is settled. Whatever the case may be, the law follows the Sages: a person must distance himself from transgression and be mindful of all such concerns.

# The Matter of the Nightly Shema and the Order and Praise to be Recited in the House of Prayer

The order of the night is taken from *Emek HaBeracha* <note>The Valley of Blessing, a work by the author's father, Abraham Horowitz</note> by my father and teacher, of blessed memory, with my own annotations. It is good to study throughout the night close to the time of sleep, and even on the shortest summer nights, one should study at least a small amount so that he falls asleep from words of Torah. Our Sages said in the first chapter of *Avodah Zarah* and in *Chagigah* (chapter "One may not expound"): "Anyone who engages in Torah study at night, the Holy One, Blessed be He, draws over him a thread of kindness <note>original: "chut shel chesed"</note> during the day," as it is said: "By day the Lord commands His kindness [and at night His song is with me]" <note>Psalms 42:9</note>. Furthermore, this fulfills the verse "you shall meditate on it day and night."

Even if it is difficult, as mentioned above in the name of the author of *Birkat Abraham* who testified in the name of his teacher, the Mahari Colon <note>Rabbi Joseph Colon, a major 15th-century Italian halakhist</note>, that when he was heavily burdened with communal affairs and lacked time to study, he would open a book seven times a day and read a line or two, and do the same at night. Thus he fulfilled "you shall meditate on it day and night," for "whether one does much or little, provided his heart is directed toward Heaven" in times of duress. So wrote the *Tur* <note>The standard code of Jewish law</note> in section 238.

Regarding nightly study, it is even more significant than daytime study, especially for scholars. As our Sages said: "The song of Torah is only at night," as it is said: "Arise, cry out in the night" <note>Lamentations 2:19</note>. We learn in *Eruvin* that Rafram bar Chama said: "Night was created only for review." We also learn in the chapter "One may make partitions": "Rav Judah said in the name of Rav: Any house where words of Torah are heard at night will never be destroyed." Therefore, since the night hours are quiet and conducive to study, which cancels many sins, how much more so if a person failed to complete his daily quota of study—he should complete it immediately that night and not delay it at all. As seen in the chapter "He who dwells," Rav Aha bar Jacob would "borrow" from the day and "repay" at night—meaning he had a fixed daily quota, and if he was busy during the day, he would complete it immediately at night. So far are the words of the *Ammud HaTamid* <note>The Eternal Pillar</note> in the aforementioned place.

The *Tur* also wrote in the Laws of Torah Study: "Although a person is obligated to study by day and night, most of one's wisdom is acquired at night. Therefore, one who wishes to merit the crown of Torah should be careful with all his nights, not losing even one to sleep, eating, drinking, or idle chatter, but dedicating them to words of wisdom and Torah." Maimonides <note>Rambam</note> wrote similarly in the *Book of Knowledge*: "A person only learns the majority of his wisdom at night." I have already written on this partially in my small composition titled *Beit Abraham* <note>The House of Abraham</note> regarding the Sages' statement that "the nights were created for the rest of scholars."

Every person should practice the conduct of the night by engaging in Torah study at sunset. The *Zohar* says regarding the morning watch that one should "link the departing night and the incoming day with Torah." The reason for both is the same: it is proper to bind and unify the attribute of Day with the attribute of Night, and Night with Day. This is the secret of "And there was evening and there was morning, one day" <note>Genesis 1:5</note>; understand this.

Torah study serves as a great protection so that a person does not forget and experience a nocturnal emission <term>Keri: accidental seminal discharge, considered a state of ritual impurity</term>. The sin of wasting seed is considered very grave, as seen in the chapter "Every Hand" and mentioned by all legal authorities, and in *Kappur Sachi* section 240. The author of *Reshit Chochma* <note>Beginning of Wisdom, a 16th-century kabbalistic ethical work</note> spoke at length about the severity of this sin in the "Gate of Holiness," citing the *Zohar* that while all sins in the world have a path to repentance, this one does not. He questioned this, noting that nothing stands in the way of repentance, for even King Manasseh was accepted by God. The conclusion of his long discussion is that it is not a "simple" repentance; because the sin strengthens the Evil Inclination for the future and creates many spiritual obstacles, the person is often not granted the opportunity to repent easily. He requires many self-afflictions <note>original: "sigufim"</note>, and the penitent may become weary and fail to do what is necessary; this is what "no repentance" means.

However it may be, listen to me: one who has accidentally wasted seed and has not yet committed more serious transgressions, the path of repentance is before him. He must increase his charity greatly and perform double, difficult fasts until the gate opens, for a locked door is not opened quickly. If a person studies Torah before sleeping, the Torah protects him from this, as the Sages said: "Anyone who goes to sleep from words of Torah, he will not be visited by bad tidings," for it is said: "He shall abide satisfied; he shall not be visited by evil" <note>Proverbs 19:23</note>. Without this, it is known that one who wastes seed is called "evil," as the Sages expounded on the verse "Keep yourself from every evil thing"—that one should not have impure thoughts by day so as not to come to a discharge by night. When one is "satisfied" with words of Torah, the Torah heals this ailment.

Therefore, every man of Torah should not lie down until he has read much Torah, so that he is "satisfied" with it. Just as a person satiates himself with food until he is weary and cannot eat more, so should he satiate himself with his Torah. One who does not do so and goes to sleep without words of Torah, and then sees a discharge at night—even if by accident—is considered liable for his own soul's impurity, for "a mistake in study amounts to a deliberate sin." This is especially true for an unmarried man, who should never lie down to sleep until he has read much Torah.

However, if he occupied himself with Torah during the day and is satisfied with it, he is not strictly obligated to extend his study at the beginning of the night if it will prevent him from rising for the midnight watch <note>original: "Ashmura"</note>. "The wise man has his eyes in his head" <note>Ecclesiastes 2:14</note>; he should manage his affairs with judgment. If he completes enough Torah during the day that he cannot do more at the start of the night, he should still engage in a little Torah to link the night to the day, as is known to those who know the hidden wisdom <note>original: "yodei chen," i.e., Kabbalists</note>. The author of *Reshit Chochma* spoke at length on this, and I will not copy his words here to avoid being wordy.

After studying enough to be satisfied before lying down, he should examine his deeds. *Reshit Chochma* says the order of the night is as follows: before he sleeps, he should examine what he did that day and write his deeds on a card so as not to forget them, to fulfill "my sin is ever before me" <note>Psalms 51:5</note>. This is also in *Sefer Hasidim* and the *Zohar*: every single night before one sleeps or dozes, a person must perform an accounting <note>original: "cheshbon"</note> of the work he did that whole day and ask for mercy for his failings. Why at this hour? Because at this hour, the "Tree of Death" begins to hold sway in the world, and people "taste the taste of death" <note>referring to sleep</note>. Therefore, at this time, one must account for his deeds and confess them, for it is the hour of death; such people are called "Masters of the Accounting."

The mnemonic for this is: "Repent one day before your death," for sleep is a taste of death, as the Sages said: "Sleep is one-sixtieth of death." Regarding confession <note>original: "Vidui"</note>, *Reshit Chochma* wrote further in the "Gate of Holiness" in the name of the *Zohar* that it is very good to weep while confessing one's sins. When the soul ascends by means of a tear, it rises through the splendors of the world to the Holy World, for "all gates are locked except for the gates of tears."

Then he should recite the Shema. One must be as precise in the "Shema on the Bed" as in the Shema recited in the synagogue. It should be read with awe, fear, and intense intention <note>original: "kavanah"</note>, for some say the primary Shema by which a person fulfills his obligation is the one read before his bed; that which we read in the synagogue is only so that we may "stand in prayer from within words of Torah." The *Tur* brings various opinions on this in section 238; therefore, one should intend in both to fulfill the will of the Almighty. After the recitation, he should go to sleep. Regarding the statement of Rabbi Joshua ben Levi that "even though one recited the Shema in the synagogue, it is a commandment to recite it on his bed," the commentators explained that "on his bed" means adjacent to his bed at the moment he wishes to go to sleep.

The *Kol Bo* <note>A 14th-century ritual compendium</note> wrote in section 29, and the *Beit Yosef* cited it in section 239, that all Israel have the custom not to eat, drink, or speak after the Shema recited on the bed. They rely on the verse: "Commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. Selah" <note>Psalms 4:5</note>. Similarly, our teacher Yerucham <note>Rabbi Yerucham ben Meshullam, 14th-century provencal scholar</note> wrote...

<summary>This page discusses the legal and mystical requirements for the evening, focusing on the timing of the Shema and the immense importance of studying Torah before sleep to protect against spiritual impurity. It details the practice of "soul accounting" (cheshbon hanefesh) and confession before bed, viewing sleep as a minor form of death.</summary>

# Tractate Chullin

<note>Although the heading reads "Tractate Chullin," the text content is a commentary on Tractate Berakhot, specifically the beginning of the first chapter regarding the laws of the Recitation of the Shema and the evening prayer.</note>

One should pray with the congregation and recite the Shema with its blessings and pray, and not separate from them. Afterward, at the **emergence of the stars**, one should recite the Shema from its beginning to its end, in its proper sections, but without a blessing. This path is the preferred one among the three paths mentioned in the words of our Rabbis. Let this be like the beginning of *Berakhot* <note>The first tractate of the Talmud</note>, and since his intention is for the sake of Heaven, he should say in his soul: **"For the sake of the unity of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and His Presence, through the Hidden and Concealed One."** <note>original: "L'shem yichud kudsha brikh hu u-shkhinteih..." - a mystical formula intended to unify the spiritual realms through the performance of a commandment.</note> Let it not be light in your eyes that he recites the Shema and prays with the congregation <note>earlier than the stars emerge</note>, for there is support for their custom as they permitted it in a time of pressing need, even though they do so quite early. 

One can bring proof from **Jacob our father**, as it says, "And he encountered the place," <note>Genesis 28:11</note> establishing the evening prayer. He prayed while the day was still at its height, because the sun set suddenly. The Holy One, Blessed be He, said: "This righteous man has come to my lodging place; shall he depart without staying the night?" One cannot say that Jacob our father, peace be upon him, prayed but did not recite the Shema until nightfall, for that is not so. The legal decisors have already ruled, etc., and it is possible to "link redemption to prayer" <note>the practice of reciting the prayer immediately after the blessing of redemption</note> even for the evening service, unlike the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda who said the prayers were established in the middle.

And these are the words of the **Tosafot** <note>Medieval commentators on the Talmud</note> in the chapter "The Morning Prayer": regarding the establishment of the evening prayer, it is a wonder that it says in the chapter "The Sinew that Displaced" that when Jacob reached Haran, he wanted to return, saying, "Is it possible I passed the place where my ancestors prayed?" etc. From this it is proven that he prayed the evening prayer during the day, since he had already prayed and intended to return. This poses a difficulty for our custom <note>to pray early</note> and the first chapter <note>of Berakhot</note> which says the time for prayer is not until the stars emerge. But according to what we explained, that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda who said the time for the Afternoon Prayer lasts until **mid-afternoon** <term>Plag HaMincha: a halakhic time of day, roughly 1.25 proportional hours before sunset</term>, it is settled. Our custom is appropriate, for on the contrary, it is good to pray slightly while it is still day. These are the words of the Tosafot.

According to the decisors who rule like our Mishnah—that the time is specifically at the emergence of the stars—and who justify the custom based on "pressing need," etc., one must say that Jacob did so because of a pressing need. For if he had stayed, he would have been distressed over having passed his ancestors' place without praying. Since he wished to return and walked swiftly to reach the place of his fathers to pray, the Holy One, Blessed be He, prepared a lodging for him and performed the miracle of **"the leaping of the way"** <term>Kfitzat HaDerekh: a miraculous shortening of a journey</term>. Therefore, he was forced to pray while it was still day to fulfill this commandment. Certainly, there is support for the custom during pressing times, and afterward, when the stars emerge, he should recite the Shema. The entire night is the time mandated by the Torah <note>original: "D'Oraita"</note>, and "both are equally good," and I apply to them the verse "they shall stand together."

In the first chapter of *Berakhot*, it was taught: The Sages made a **safeguard** <note>original: "Siyag"</note> for their words so that a man would not come from the field in the evening and say, "I will go to my house and eat a little, and drink a little, and sleep a little, and afterward I will recite the Shema and pray," and sleep would snatch him away, resulting in him sleeping all night. Rather, a man comes from the field in the evening, enters the synagogue—if he is accustomed to reading the Bible, let him read; and if he is accustomed to studying Mishnah, let him study—and he recites the Shema and prays, then eats his bread and recites the Grace after Meals. 

The **Tosafot** wrote there, and **Rabbeinu Yonah**, may his memory be a blessing, wrote: from here it is implied that from the moment the time for the evening Shema arrives, he may not eat a meal until he recites the Shema and prays the evening service. From the Tosafot, it is implied that specifically from the actual time of the evening Shema is he forbidden to eat. However, if the time for Shema has not yet arrived—for example, an hour or half an hour before night—the proof is that before the emergence of the stars, he may begin to eat. 

So wrote the **Tur** in section 231 regarding that Baraita <note>External oral tradition</note>: "so that a man should not come from the field in the evening and say, I will eat a little, etc." He writes: "it follows that when the time for Shema arrives, it is forbidden to set a meal until he prays." From the fact that he wrote "when the time arrives," it implies that before the time, it is permitted to start eating. **Rabbi Ovadia** <note>Bartenura</note> wrote the same in his commentary on the Mishnah: "and the Sages made a safeguard... however, initially, once the time for the evening Shema arrives, which is from the time the stars emerge, it is forbidden to dine and certainly to sleep until he recites Shema and prays," etc. Here you have it explicitly that he wrote "initially"—meaning from the emergence of the stars—it is forbidden to dine, implying that before the time of the stars' emergence, it is permitted to eat.

However, the **Rif** <note>Rabbi Isaac Alfasi</note> wrote at the beginning of the Mishnah of *Berakhot* against this: "There are Sages who say... until midnight," for we say later in the law that "a man should not come from the field in the evening, etc." He writes: "even when he comes from the field before the time of Shema, he might say 'since the time for Shema has not yet arrived, I will eat and drink first'; rather, he should go and recite Bible first and study until the stars emerge, then recite Shema and pray, and afterward eat," etc. From his words, he is more stringent with us, that even **before its time**, it is forbidden to eat. 

The **Beit Yosef** <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo</note> wrote on this in section 232 that this refers specifically to half an hour before, as is the law regarding the Afternoon Prayer. So also wrote the **Shulchan Aruch**. But in the words of our teacher **Rabbeinu Yonah**, it is clearly proven from this Baraita that it refers to one coming from the field before the time of Shema arrives. For if the time had already arrived, he would not say "if he is accustomed to reading, let him read; to study, let him study, and then recite Shema," because surely once the time arrives, he must recite Shema first and only then read or study. This is a decisive refutation of the Tosafot, the Mordechai, the Tur, and Rabbi Ovadia. 

It must be that it refers to when the time has not yet arrived. This is also implied by the language "comes from the field in the evening" and not "at night," meaning at the time of sunset. From that moment, it is forbidden to start eating, etc. And the Baraita intended this; even according to the opinion that they only argue regarding the end of the time—which is until the dawn—there is no dispute regarding the safeguard at the beginning. **Rabbeinu Yonah** also wrote that there are two interpretations.

According to this, one must ask: In the first Mishnah of *Berakhot*, what do the Sages and **Rabban Gamliel** argue about? Since even Rabban Gamliel holds that ideally one must recite the Shema immediately when the time arrives at the emergence of the stars, and after the fact, if he did not recite it, the Sages would surely admit that even after midnight they should recite it. For if we say they do not recite it at all, it is difficult: since Shema is a Torah commandment, how can the Sages exempt him from it? 

Teacher **Rabbeinu Yonah**, at the beginning of *Berakhot*, was sensitive to this question and answered it with forced adjustments. First, he answered that the Sages hold that after midnight, one recites it without blessings, and he debated this. Afterward, he answered that the Sages hold he should not recite it at all, for **the Sages have the power to uproot words of the Torah.** <note>original: "Yesh koach b'yad chakhamim la'akor davar min ha-Torah."</note> 

He wrote: "It seems to me that the explanation is this: the Sages hold that even the Shema, which is from the Torah the entire night, one does not recite after midnight. For the Sages can exempt him from a positive commandment whenever they do so as a safeguard or for the fulfillment of the commandment itself. We see this with the **Lulav** <note>The four species used on Sukkot</note>, whose commandment is from the Torah on the first day, yet when the first day of Sukkot falls on Shabbat, the Sages exempted people from taking it due to a decree lest one carry it four cubits in the public domain. And regarding a linen sheet in **Tzitzit** <note>Ritual fringes</note>, even though the Torah obligated it—for the Torah permitted **Shaatnez** <note>The forbidden mixture of wool and linen</note> in the matter of Tzitzit, as it is written 'Do not wear wool and linen together' followed immediately by 'Make for yourself twisted threads,' implying that a thread of linen with the blue wool is permitted by the Torah—even so, the House of Shammai exempted him because of a decree concerning night garments. That is to say, even though if he wore it by day he would be obligated by the Torah to place Tzitzit on it, they exempted him from wearing it without Tzitzit since the night is not the time for Tzitzit. For the commandment of Tzitzit only applies by day, as it is written 'And you shall see it and remember,' implying that whenever there is sight, there is remembrance, and when there is no sight, there is no remembrance. They decreed the day because of the night. Thus, he is obligated by the Torah not to wear a linen garment by day without the blue wool fringe, and yet the House of Shammai exempted him from the blue wool because of a decree lest he wear it at night and violate the prohibition 'Do not wear wool and linen together.' And since the law follows the House of Shammai, here too, even though the commandment of Shema lasts all night from the Torah, the Sages exempted him because of a safeguard, as we have written." These are his words.

However, his words are far-fetched in my eyes. For certainly the Sages have the power to uproot a Torah law through "sitting and doing nothing" <note>original: "Shev v'al ta'aseh" - passive non-performance</note> except when the concern comes from another side, such as the Lulav on Shabbat, where the concern is that he might carry it, which is a separate prohibition. In that case, the commandment would be fulfilled through a transgression. Similarly, regarding Tzitzit on a linen sheet, they decreed so that he would not commit a separate transgression. But to cancel the commandment of Shema after midnight just so he will be diligent to recite it another time before midnight? How is one greater than the other? Now he is certainly canceling the Shema, while the "other time" is only a doubt if he will cancel it! This is forced.

Furthermore, another difficulty for all his explanations: what did Rabban Gamliel answer his sons? That the Sages only spoke of "distancing" <note>original: "Har-chak-a"</note> but in reality, they are obligated. According to the Rif's explanation, the Sages hold he should not recite it, and the rule is that the law follows the majority. If so, how could Rabban Gamliel obligate his sons to recite it since the Sages hold he should not? Rabban Gamliel himself taught his sons that the law follows the majority, as found in the Gemara's explanation of this Mishnah. This is a great wonder regarding Rabbeinu Yonah.

I can only justify his words by saying that he did not have the version of the Mishnah that says "If the dawn has not risen, you are **obligated** to recite." Rather, he must have had the version "you are **permitted** to recite." This version exists in some manuscripts. But Rashi in the Gemara wrote: "We do not read 'permitted' but 'obligated'." Yet even the version "permitted" does not work well according to Rabbeinu Yonah's method, for the question returns to its place: how can the Sages uproot a Torah-mandated Shema? 

What will you say? That they did so for a safeguard? If so, why did they give a person permission <note>to recite it after midnight</note>? They should have prohibited it like all other decrees! Therefore, all these things do not seem correct to me. And although we are not worthy to disagree even with a student of the students up to ten generations, nevertheless, my heart has emboldened me to examine this Mishnah, which is the very first Mishnah of the Six Orders of the Mishnah. 

I say that the teacher has left me room to distinguish myself. Accept the truth from whoever says it. I shall explain the Mishnah according to how it is explained in the Gemara: that there are three disputes in the matter. Rabbi Eliezer holds the time is until the end of the first watch; the Sages say until midnight; and Rabban Gamliel says until the dawn rises. They disagree on the verse "when you lie down." Rabbi Eliezer says "when you lie down" refers to the time people **go** to lie down, which is until the first third of the night. This covers the entire time of the evening Shema. But the Sages and Rabban Gamliel hold that "when you lie down" means the entire time people **are lying** in bed, which is the whole night. Only the Sages were more stringent because of the safeguard, limiting it to midnight. When Rabban Gamliel's sons came from the wedding hall and said "we have not recited Shema," they were in doubt regarding the Sages' view: did they interpret "when you lie down" like Rabbi Eliezer, with the Sages only...

<summary>This page analyzes the timing of the evening Shema and prayer, debating whether the Sages' "midnight" limit is a strict legal cutoff or a cautionary safeguard. The author critiques Rabbeinu Yonah's view that the Sages could completely cancel a Torah obligation for the sake of a safeguard.</summary>
