<meta>This page continues the discussion of the laws of prayer and ritual purity, moving from the timing of the Shema to the mystical significance of the midnight hour and the laws of washing hands upon waking.</meta>

### Tractate Chullin

...in his heart and wrote their order upon him. I have explained from the words of our teacher Joseph <note>likely referring to Rabbi Joseph Caro, author of the Shulchan Aruch</note> in his arrangement, and everything is explained above; see there. In a manuscript on the *Tur* <note>The Arba'ah Turim, a seminal code of Jewish law</note> at the end of section 7, our great teacher Rabbi Isaac Aboab wrote in the name of a *Gaon* <note>an eminent rabbinic authority from the early medieval period</note> that a person who urinated and then delayed his intention to urinate again, it is proper to bless the "Who Formed Man" blessing <note>original: "Asher Yatzar," the blessing for bodily functions</note> for both times together. And if he delayed significantly, it is as if the first instance was nullified, and he should not pray the Morning Prayer <note>Shacharit</note> but should pray the Afternoon Prayer <note>Mincha</note> twice. This law is strange in my eyes. Is the matter so holy? If he delayed his intent to urinate and then wished to recite a blessing over food, everything depends on the opinion that if there is intent, one must recite the blessing of "Who hears prayer" <note>Shma Koleinu</note>. If he has already fulfilled it, he returns to bless twice the blessing over food <note>Birkat HaNehenin</note> for the joy. It seems to me that specifically regarding this blessing, since the blessing of "Who gives life" is hidden within it—which is the restoration of the soul to the body of man—it is similar to the prayer of the afflicted. For in prayer, one improves the words, and the custom is to rely on a support for every blessing that is not recited over a person's bed, such as the blessing over fruit and blessings of enjoyment and the like. Having missed it once, he cannot bless twice, for "a twisted thing cannot be made straight." <note>A quote from Ecclesiastes 1:15, meaning a missed opportunity for a specific mitzvah cannot be regained.</note> My opinion is that he only needs to bless once, as one who arranges a blessing over an action he performed, even if he did it twice. I wrote this in my commentary on the Alfasi <note>Rabbi Isaac Alfasi, known as the Rif</note>. Regarding the Succa canopy, one must pray with eyes toward that world, to pray a supplication and find understanding, to pay every blessing of thanks and praise. These are memories of eternal kindness for all, in every land.

<column-break/>

At night, the whole world tastes the taste of death, and their souls ascend on high. If they are not worthy, the spirits push them away, and they go wandering through the world. But the souls of the righteous who are worthy ascend on high, and many gates are opened for them, and they are brought up to the place called "His Holy Place," where all souls appear before the Holy One, Blessed be He. This is the model of the place where Israel appears before the Holy One, which is called "The Assembly of Israel." This involves the eighteen letters of the Name <note>Y-H-V-H</note>. We recite songs for two hours until midnight. These are called the "Mourners of Zion," those who wept over the destruction of the Holy House. At the middle hour of the night, they say, "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and also wept" <note>Psalm 137:1</note>. These are those who wept by the rivers of Babylon with Israel. From where do we know they wept there? As it is said: "Behold, their brave ones cry without" <note>Isaiah 33:7</note>. We conclude with: "Remember, O Lord, against the children of Edom," and this is the Jerusalem version. At that hour, the Holy One, Blessed be He, awakens and kicks through many firmaments, shaking twelve thousand worlds. He lows and weeps, as it is written: "The Lord roars from on high, from His holy habitation He utters His voice" <note>Jeremiah 25:30</note>. He remembers Israel and the destruction of the Temple and says: "Woe, that I have destroyed My house, burned My palace, and exiled My children among the nations." He drops two tears into the Great Sea. At that hour, a flame is stirred from the north side, and a wind strikes that flame, which then strikes the wings of the rooster and it crows. Then it is midnight. The Holy One has no rest until He descends into the Garden of Eden to play with the souls of the righteous of Israel. A sign for this: "I remembered, I, the poor one..." He asks: "Who is this who rises at midnight to sing and praise?" For when God enters Eden, all the trees and all the souls of the righteous say: "Lift up your heads, O gates" <note>Psalm 24:7</note>. Happy is he who joins them and rises to labor in Torah to participate with those singers. They say: "Behold, bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord who stand in the house of the Lord" <note>Psalm 134:1</note>. For his reward is in Jerusalem. For one whose awakening of praise comes from the north, then a psalm is sung... as it is written: "O God, do not be silent" <note>Psalm 83:2</note>, and "So that my glory may sing to You and not be silent" <note>Psalm 30:13</note>. When a voice is heard in heaven, the Living Creatures <term>Chayot</term> <note>a high order of angels</note> ascend from below. The Holy One silences all the heavenly host to listen to that voice. The Assembly of Israel and all the host of angels listen to that voice, as it is written: "O you who dwell in the gardens, companions listen for your voice; let me hear it" <note>Song of Songs 8:13</note>. When the Holy One draws a thread of kindness over the Assembly of Israel, He casts upon them all who join with her at night. Because his mind is proud, this matter was said at midnight.

---

->**The matter of the holiness of the [marital] union was explained at length above under the letter 'Kof' for Holiness; see there.**<-

---

**It is written** in the Zohar, portion Vayeshev, page 150: "A traveler opened with weeping..." Come and see the secret of the matter: no human being in the world does not taste the taste of death at night, and an unclean spirit <term>Ruach Tum'ah</term> rests upon that body. When the soul returns to the body, that spirit is removed. This has been stated as a secret... a filth of impurity remains. Therefore, a person should not put his hands to his eyes because of that unclean spirit until he washes them. When he washes them, he becomes sanctified and is called holy. How should he be sanctified? He requires kindness <note>Chesed</note> from above... to be sanctified from the joy of the wedding feast. This vessel is meant to receive the impurity, and to be sanctified from it.

The Kabbalists wrote: When a person sleeps at night, the soul leaves his body and immediately an impure spirit rests upon his hands. The reason is that night and dust are called the powers of impurity. Therefore, when it rules over his hands, one who walks four cubits <note>approx. 6 feet</note> with impure hands is liable for death by the Heavens, for he brings a "strange god" <note>meaning idolatrous or impure energy</note> upon his hands. Regarding this, the verse says: "And he sent tents to the singers" <note>a mystical interpretation of a verse</note>. Therefore, one should distance himself from ugliness and anything similar to it, and distance himself from the side of impurity so that the side of holiness and purity may rest upon him. These waters require two vessels: an upper vessel to be sanctified from—symbolizing the world of holiness—and a lower vessel to receive those impure waters, which symbolizes the "shell" <term>Kelipa</term> <note>the outer layer of impurity in Kabbalistic thought</note>. Because a man is impure until he washes his hands, he should only receive water from one who has already washed, as it is said: "And the pure one shall sprinkle upon the impure" <note>Numbers 19:19</note>. It is forbidden to pass one's hands over the eyes because the spirit of impurity rests upon them—and these are three spirits—therefore one must wash them three times to remove them. It is forbidden to use those waters for any purpose, and forbidden to pour them out except in a sloped place so that people do not step on them and be harmed.

**This is** the order of the day: If he receives water from another person, whether a child or an adult, the one pouring should wash first and then pour for the other, as it is hinted: "the pure upon the impure." For how can he remove the spirit of impurity from his friend while it still clings to him? Rather, he should purify himself first and then purify others, as in the matter of "Gather yourselves and then gather" <note>Zephaniah 2:1, interpreted as 'correct yourself before others'</note>. This strictness applies specifically to the morning washing for the reason we mentioned, but during the rest of the day for other washings, one need not be so strict. One who is overly strict in this is considered strange. If one asks: "How can he receive water from the impure when he himself is impure?" one can say that the spirit does not wish to remove the impurity from him... but his power and form come upon him to remove it. But a man who has not yet been purified and desires his impurity has no power to remove another's impurity until he himself is purified. A person of soul must be very careful not to walk four cubits with "filthy hands"—those upon which the spirit rested at night—which gives power to the "Sammael" <note>a name for the primary force of evil/impurity</note> to rule over him. It is said: "There shall be no strange god within you," and this is as we wrote, for it is not proper to give it power and dominion even for a single moment, lest the "Sammael" cling to him. The matter is that for every washing of the hands, such as when exiting the bathroom, he needs his hands washed immediately. Even though he does not need to pour three times, for even if the spirit of impurity touched it, the Zohar says that when a person leaves the bathroom, he should not engage in marital relations during that hour because there clings to him...

### Tractate Chullin

->**Gloss**<-
However, in the <term>Gemara</term><note>The core text of the Talmud</note> in the chapter titled "One Who Sees" <note>Berakhot chapter 9</note>, it implies that within the general category of the verses of blessings, there are various times. According to his words and their force, it is not far-fetched for one who skips, etc. For by the power of tradition, one should add from the order of the Book of Curses, etc. The arrangement of the "Who causes sleep to fall" <note>original: "HaMapil," the blessing recited before sleep</note> blessing is as mentioned, and the verse... etc. This is explained in the *Book of Ethics* <note>Sefer HaMusar</note>, chapter 4, that after the <term>Shema</term><note>The central Jewish prayer "Hear O Israel"</note>, one should say the "Who causes sleep to fall" blessing. The reason for this is looked into, for one should immediately follow with the blessing of "Who causes sleep to fall," which is the blessing of sleep. It is already known that it is forbidden to interrupt between the blessing and the sleep for which one is blessing. And even though he might have things in hand and sometimes interrupts a great deal against his will between the blessing and sleep, this is not like those exemptions mentioned elsewhere, and he is not required to fix every matter as is appropriate for it. And so it is in the *Book of the Reed* <note>Sefer HaKaneh</note>, and it is written there: "Our Sages, of blessed memory, said: When a person enters to sleep on his bed, he should say the order of the Bedtime Shema... 'Who causes sleep to fall' from the bond of sleep... until 'The Enlightener of the whole world in His glory,'" end of quote.

<column-break/>

...his, in section 239. One should read the Shema close to his bed, and they do not eat, drink, or speak after the Bedtime Shema, but rather one sleeps immediately, as it is said: "Commune with your own heart [upon your bed, and be still]" <note>Psalm 4:4</note>. And if he reads the Shema and cannot sleep immediately, then he should return and read it several times, one after the other, until he sinks into sleep, so that his reading is close to his sleep, end of quote.

From here it is implied that the reading of the Shema should be the final thing he reads close to sleep; thus proved our Master, <term>Nissim Gaon</term>, end of quote.

The *Tashbetz* <note>Rabbi Shimon ben Tzemach Duran</note> wrote in section 250: And he says "For Your salvation I hope, O Lord" <note>Genesis 49:18</note> three times: "For Your salvation I hope, O Lord; I hope, O Lord, for Your salvation; O Lord, for Your salvation I hope; I hope for Your salvation, O Lord; O Lord, I hope for Your salvation; O Lord, for Your salvation I hope," etc. until he says, "I was glad when they said to me" <note>Psalm 122:1</note> in order to mention Jerusalem. And he repeats every night before sleep and reads the Ten Commandments in the portion of *Va'etchanan*. And so wrote the <term>Maharshal</term><note>Rabbi Solomon Luria</note> in his responsa; see there. 

One who urinates at night must distance himself four cubits from the waste and wash his hands, and turn himself so his heart does not see his nakedness <note>a requirement for modesty during prayer</note> to bless "Who formed [man]" <note>Asher Yatzar</note>, etc. And one should not lie down when he is excessively sated until the food in his bowels is digested, as Maimonides wrote in the *Book of Knowledge* in the Laws of Character, chapter 4: "A person should not sleep on his face or on his back, but only on his side; at the beginning of the night on his left side, and at the end of the night on his right side. And he should not sleep close to eating, but should wait after it about three or four hours. And he should not sleep during the day," end of quote. And so it was in the *Candle of Illumination* <note>Menorat HaMaor</note> in the fourth lamp, and it was brought in the *Paths of Faith* <note>Shivilei Emunah</note> in the seventh path, and it concludes there as follows: "And the reason for this is because the liver is situated on the right side, and when one sleeps on the left side, the liver rests upon the stomach and warms it with its heat, and by this, the food is digested quickly. And after the food is digested, it is proper for him to turn onto his right side so that the stomach may rest and the waste of the food may descend," end of quote. 

One should meditate on Torah and commandments until he sleeps. A person should not eat excessively at night, for it increases sleep, and likewise, he should be careful not to become intoxicated with wine, for that also increases sleep according to nature. A man must rise at midnight, as we say in the first chapter of Berakhot: Rav Acha said: Thus said David, "Never did midnight pass me by in sleep," etc. And after he wakes from his sleep, he should praise and thank the Holy One, Blessed be He, that He awakened him from his sleep to life. And the author of the *Beginning of Wisdom* <note>Reshit Chochmah</note> in the "Gate of Holiness" elaborated on the obligation incumbent upon us to rise at midnight according to the <term>Zohar</term><note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism</note>. He wrote there that one should not eat at night except for types of preserves that draw away the <unclear>vapors</unclear>, so he can stand with a settled heart to engage in Torah without sleep, etc. (For if he eats much, it increases the smoke <note>referring to metabolic "vapors" believed to cause drowsiness</note> that rises to the brain, and therefore most of those who produce vapors and smokers increase sleep in a person). Until... and so the Holy One, Blessed be He, returns the souls to Israel at midnight so they may engage in His Torah... and all the living creatures... the souls at midnight so that a person will take it to heart and say: "Not for nothing did the Holy One, Blessed be He, return my soul to me, but for this deed or so that I may engage in Torah," etc. 

And after we have explained the obligation incumbent upon us to rise, and how great the reward is, it is our desire to explain further intellectual awakenings to urge a person. Our Master Jonah <note>Rabbi Jonah Gerondi</note> wrote at the beginning of the *Book of Fear* <note>Sefer HaYirah</note> that in the morning when a person wakes from his sleep, it is proper that he place the love of the Creator in his heart for His kindness in returning his soul to him, for how many went to sleep on their beds and did not rise? And regarding this we say, "Who restores souls to dead bodies." And then he should not sit on his bed in a lazy manner, but should think: "Behold, the King calls me to His service!" How diligent would he be to rise if a fire fell in his courtyard? Although these words of his were regarding the matter of prayer, it is proper to learn from them regarding the matter of rising at midnight, for we have already said that at midnight the Holy One, Blessed be He, returns the souls to the bodies so they may engage in Torah, etc. Until he wrote in the chapter "Berakhot": A lyre was hung above David's bed, and when midnight arrived... immediately he would rise and engage in Torah until the pillar of dawn ascended, etc. It is also proper to understand the rooster... at midnight... for he used to go on the way and take a rooster with him... behold, the early Sages did not rely on their wisdom and piety to wake at midnight and needed assistance, how much more so us. Therefore I say, one who does not have a rooster should seek a friend who does not sleep until midnight so he may wake him exactly at midnight, and his friend has a reward, etc. And if he is in a place where there is no other... it is proper not to lie in a spread-out bed and not to stretch out his whole body. And I heard that the Sage, the Honorable Rabbi M. Ish-Nah, would not sleep in a spread-out bed, but rather a seat-bed, and said it was his way to sleep on top of a single box with his feet hanging, and he would rise at midnight... and no man knew of this until after his death when his wife told it, etc. And he elaborated there on such matters very much... and a God-fearing person will read from there and then pass [the service of] the Lord with all his heart, all his soul, and all his might. (And they have already elaborated on the praise of rising at midnight in the Zohar, portions: Noach, Lech Lecha, Toldot, Vayechi, Beshalach, Terumah, Pekudei, Tazria, Acharei Mot, Kedoshim, and more in other places in this Zohar and in the *Tikkunim* countless times. See how great the lot of this commandment is; happy is he who fulfills it). And there is no need to say to bless "Who formed [man]," etc.

### Valley of Blessing

<margin>At the end of *Orach Chayim* <note>The section of the Code of Jewish Law dealing with daily life.</note></margin>
At the end of any matter, everything possible should be done so that we do not interrupt needlessly. This is clearly implied by what the *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Yosef Karo’s commentary on the Tur.</note> brought regarding the words of the *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, author of an influential legal code.</note>: "And if he goes immediately to the synagogue, he may wish to wait to recite the blessing **'Regarding the Washing of Hands'** <note>original: *Al Netilat Yadayim*</note> until his arrival at the synagogue," etc., as we wrote above nearby. And the *Beit Yosef* said there: "I have already written in Chapter 4 in the name of the *Maharam* <note>Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg.</note> that one does not recite the blessing **'Regarding the Washing of Hands'** when he washes his hands until his arrival at the synagogue." And to reconcile this, he wrote here that the matter depends on his will: if he wishes, he blesses immediately, and if he wishes, he waits until his arrival at the synagogue. Our great teacher, Rabbi Isaac Aboab, of blessed memory, wrote that the *Semaq* <note>The "Small Book of Commandments" by Isaac of Corbeil.</note> wrote similarly. He further wrote that there is reason to doubt this, for since all commandments require a blessing to be recited "immediately before their performance" <note>original: *over le-asiyatan*</note>, and they only permitted the blessing for washing to be delayed because it was not fit to bless beforehand due to the hands being unclean, therefore, for that same reason, since one blesses before drying the hands, it is considered as being before the washing. If so, it is legally required that he blesses as closely as possible. 

Perhaps his opinion in this matter is that since these morning blessings are recited in the synagogue, therefore the blessing for washing may also be joined with the final ones if one wishes, even though it is not in its proper place. This is possible even though one could distinguish here that the blessing for washing hands is a "blessing of the commandment" <note>A blessing recited over a specific ritual action.</note> which must be prioritized, while the others are "blessings of praise" which can be said after their performance, as the legal decisors wrote on this, including the *Rosh* <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel.</note> at the end of the tractate *Berakhot*. Furthermore, this fits the reason the Rabbi wrote later (meaning the *Tur* in *Orach Chayim* Chapter 46) that our arrangement of these blessings in the synagogue is for the sake of the unlearned <note>original: *Am HaAretz*</note> who do not know them, so they may answer "Amen." 

But according to the reason he wrote—that we do this because the hands are not clean—it would not be proper to do this. However, one might reply that since we do not recite the later blessings immediately after washing, but rather leave them for the synagogue, this blessing is also included with them and no distinction should be made, end of quote. 

The *Ne'or* <note>Likely referring to a specific commentary or the "Light" of a scholar.</note> wrote that he asked Rabbi Jacob Moelin <note>The *Maharil*, a leading authority on Ashkenazic custom.</note> how it is possible for a person to wash his hands in the morning and wait to recite the blessing **'Regarding the Washing of Hands'** until the synagogue. Is this not an **interruption**? <note>original: *hefsek*; meaning a change of place and a lapse of attention, even if no time passed in between.</note> He replied that there is no famous reason for this, but it seems to me that this was enacted to wait for the order in the synagogue so the unlearned may hear, answer "Amen," and fulfill their obligation through these blessings. Even though we sometimes bless in the synagogue even when there is no unlearned person present, nonetheless, they did not distinguish between cases (just as we found regarding the eighteen-fold prayer <note>The *Amidah*.</note> which was enacted for the early generations whose synagogues were in the fields; even though that reason no longer applies, the blessing did not move from its place). According to the explanation, it seems that one who recites the morning blessing **'Regarding the Washing of Hands'** and afterwards does not bless in the synagogue acts correctly, end of quote from the *Ne'or* and the *Beit Yosef*.

Your eyes see how the great later authorities wondered even about the simple act of walking to the synagogue between the washing done at home and the blessing **'Regarding the Washing of Hands'** recited in the synagogue, even if he did not interrupt with any idle speech in between, and they forced themselves to search for reasons for this. 

And now we do this—waiting for the blessing until our arrival at the synagogue—and they could find no reason for this except so the unlearned might hear and answer "Amen" and fulfill their obligation, as stated above. (For we may intentionally interrupt between the washing and its blessing if the interruption is for some benefit, as mentioned nearby in the gloss, and this walking is for the benefit of the unlearned as mentioned here inside.) If not for this, one could not interrupt between the washing and its blessing. If so, how can people interrupt by **reciting Psalms** <note>original: *Tehillim*</note> between the washing of hands and the blessing? Is this not an **interruption**? (And it is simple that in any place where it is forbidden to converse, it is forbidden to speak even in the **Holy Tongue** <note>Hebrew.</note>, as written by the *Tosafot*, the *Mordechai*, the *Ria*, and the *Kol Bo* in Chapter 30, and the *Tashbetz* in the Laws of Prayer, Chapter 204.) It is without reason, for they could delay the recitation of Psalms until after finishing the morning blessings or after finishing the entire prayer. Why did they see fit to say it between the washing and the blessing, to "separate those who are joined"? Why this and for what? We do not strike even a humble submission by a hair’s breadth. For the *Tur* only said in Chapter 6 that one may interrupt between the morning washing and its blessing specifically for the interruption of walking, as he wrote: "And if he goes immediately to the synagogue," etc., but regarding an interruption of words in between, who said this was allowed?

<margin>*Orach Chayim*</margin>
And if you say, where would one get the idea to distinguish between these two types of interruption—meaning between the interruption of walking and the interruption of speech—since both are considered an interruption? (Meaning that a change of place alone is called an interruption even if one does not speak in between, as stated above in the name of the *Ne'or*.)

One may say that they can be distinguished in two ways. **The first way** is that the *Tur* only permitted the interruption of walking between the washing and the blessing from his house to the synagogue, as explained in his words brought above, where he wrote in the cited chapter: "And if he goes immediately to the synagogue and wants to wait to bless... until his arrival at the synagogue," etc. There is a great reason in this: to fulfill the obligation for the unlearned, as mentioned in his words in Chapter 46. 

(Gloss: And even though the *Tur* did not explicitly write this reason here, nonetheless it is heavily hinted at by his language in the aforementioned Chapter 6, saying: "And if he goes immediately to the synagogue and wants to wait to bless **'Regarding the Washing of Hands'** until his arrival at the synagogue so that he may arrange them with the rest of the morning blessings, it is in his hand," end of quote. Why did he need to say "to arrange it with the rest of the blessings"? Surely saying "he wants to wait... until his arrival at the synagogue, he has permission" would be enough if it weren't to enlighten us on the benefit resulting from waiting for the blessing until the synagogue. This benefit is that we merit many of the later ones who do not know how to bless, and they will answer "Amen" after him and fulfill their obligation. We find this regarding the other morning blessings, which they enacted to be arranged in the synagogue for this reason, as the *Tur* wrote in Chapter 46: "According to the order of the *Gemara*, it was proper to bless each one at its time, but because the hands are not clean, they enacted to arrange them in the synagogue; and also because many of the unlearned do not know them, they enacted to arrange them in the synagogue so they may answer 'Amen' after them and fulfill their obligation," end of quote. 

Behold, the *Tur* wrote here that they enacted to say the morning blessings in the synagogue to benefit the unlearned, even if he did not explicitly mention the blessing for washing hands, for the morning blessings include this. The *Tur* did not need to write this explicitly in Chapter 6 because he relied on what he wrote in Chapter 46, as mentioned nearby. End of gloss.) 

Since they have an obligation and their blessing is needed, we must find a remedy for them to fulfill their obligation, for "All Israel are sureties for one another." This is not the case for an interruption of other walking, or even the interruption of reciting Psalms, which there is no obligation to say now, but rather one can say them at a later time, as stated above. If so, the interruption for Psalms is a "needless interruption." 

**The second way** is that the *Tur* only permitted the interruption of walking between the washing and the blessing in a case where there is no **lapse of attention** <note>original: *hesach hada'at*</note> from the washing, which is included in going from his house to the synagogue without any delay at all. This is evident from his explicit language: "And if he goes immediately to the synagogue and wants to wait," etc. The word "immediately" simply means without interruption. Then, from the time of washing until his arrival at the synagogue, his mind is on the washing and there is no lapse of attention. When a person's mind is on the matter, it is not considered an interruption (as explained above in Part 1, Ten General Principles). But for one who does not go immediately to the synagogue after washing, but interrupts in between with some matter, or goes but does not engage in the blessing of his mouth but rather says supplications and requests or Psalms after arriving at the synagogue before the blessing **'Regarding the Washing of Hands'**, I would say the *Tur* agrees that he should not do so because of the interruption and lapse of attention. For we cannot say his mind is on the washing since he interrupted so much in between; he did not remember the matter and will forget it.

<margin>Chapter 185</margin>
And in this, the *Tur* agrees in *Orach Chayim* Chapter 185, writing: "One who left the privy and wanted to wash his hands for a meal, they asked *Rashi* if he needs to wash twice. He replied: 'They asked my teacher, Rabbi Jacob of Bricaire, and he said he must wash twice—reciting on the first washing **"Who formed man"** <note>original: *Asher Yatzar*</note> and on the second **"Regarding the washing of hands"**... and the *Maharam* of Rothenburg used to follow the practice of Rabbi Jacob of Bricaire, for if he did it in one washing, reciting **"Who formed"** and then **"Regarding the washing,"** it would be an interruption'" (meaning that he interrupts with the "Who formed" blessing between the washing and the blessing for washing hands). "So too did my father, the *Rosh*, of blessed memory, practice," end of quote. 

Now, this is an argument from the minor to the major <note>original: *kal v'chomer*</note>: If the blessing **"Who formed man,"** which is only one blessing and it too comes from the current life-necessity (meaning he hastens his hands because he also left the privy, which is similar to the purity of hands for a meal without a privy) as the *Beit Yosef* wrote in Chapter 158 in the name of the *Tur*—even so, it is considered an interruption between the washing and the blessing **'Regarding the Washing of Hands'**. How much more so are supplications, requests, or Psalms—whose interruption is long and which do not have the same immediate necessity as the "Who formed" blessing—how much more so are they an interruption!

(Gloss: And if you say that one should reverse the logic and say, on the contrary, that the recitation of Psalms, which are "optional matters" <note>original: *divrei reshut*</note> in that if he wants he says them now and if he wants he doesn't, are not counted as an interruption; but the blessing **"Who formed man"** after leaving the privy, since it is an obligation for him to bless now, is more of an interruption because it is a matter of obligation? This would be according to the principle: "Anything that is fit for mixing, the lack of mixing does not hinder it," etc. <margin>until here</margin> And so he judged according to what the *Tur* wrote in *Orach Chayim* Chapter 65 regarding the interruption of the *Shema* in filthy alleyways, and these are his words there...)

### Tractate Chullin <note>Though the header says 'Chullin'—a volume of the Talmud dealing with dietary laws—the content of this page focuses on 'Orah Chayim,' the laws of daily conduct.</note>

In it, the "ox of the bathroom" <note>original: *shur de-veit ha-kise*—a Talmudic reference to a spiritual danger or demon associated with latrines</note> which damages it; this appears to be because of the **spirit of impurity** <note>original: *ruach ha-tumah*—a harmful spiritual residue believed to rest on the hands after sleep</note>, thus concludes his words. And it seems to me that as soon as one wakes up and no longer wishes to sleep, even if he has not yet risen from his bed and remains lying down, he should wash his hands so that the spirit of impurity departs from him. Since the holy soul has returned to him, he should not give any place to impurity. I found this suggested somewhat in the *Zohar* <note>The primary work of Jewish mysticism</note> on Genesis: that one must wash immediately upon waking, even if he does not yet intend to get up. (However, it is forbidden to be uncovered on his bed, unless he is meditating on words of Torah—and I have already written that one who meditates on Torah does not need to recite a blessing). One should not stand up from his bed naked, nor should he put on his shirt while sitting; rather, he should take his shirt and insert his head and arms while still lying down, so that he is covered even while in his place. This is how Rabbi Yosei boasted: "The beams of my house have never seen the hem of my shirt." Let a person not say: "I am in my innermost chambers in a dark house; who sees me and who can testify against me?" for "the whole earth is full of His glory," and before Him, "darkness is as light." Amen. The reason for this is that the limbs of a man hint at higher spiritual things, as Job said: "From my flesh I shall see God," even regarding the holy union. Therefore, it is not proper to reveal them, for "it is the glory of God to conceal a matter." One should be meticulous to put on his shirt the right way and not turn it inside out, as Rabbi Yochanan said: "Who is a scholar? One who is meticulous with his shirt." The reason for this is that it is the covering of the holy body, and as was mentioned, the inner side is pure and clean while the outer side receives impurity; therefore, it is not proper to make the inner part outer or the outer part inner.

<margin>
Page 63, End of Section...
One should not doubt the fact that this is not found in the chapter *Kira* on page 49, to say that... Rabbi Papa said: his hands against his face... like the loaves of the *Avrekh* of the house... and he concludes it is not difficult... as explained in *Chullin* and by Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, the preeminent medieval commentator</note>... facing the wall and there is no issue of modesty... to cover it as a garment... since the Holy One, Blessed be He, fills the earth with His glory... and as said regarding the choice of modesty and covering himself... only when done with modesty... but here it is decided according to those who bring the first reasoning... and the main point is that he adds all his words... so that the purpose of this walk is to ascend higher... and this reason is pressing... and it is better for him.
</margin>

<column-break/>

**And when he puts on** his shoes, he should put on the right one first but not tie it; then he should put on the left one and tie it, and afterward tie the right one. For we learn in the chapter *Bameh Isha*: Rabbi Yochanan said, "As with **Tefillin** <note>Phylacteries; ritual leather boxes containing Torah verses</note>, so it is with shoes." We raise an objection: one puts on the right first... Rav Nachman bar Isaac said: "A God-fearing person fulfills both opinions." Mar the son of Ravina would do this: he put on the right and did not tie it, put on the left and tied it, and then returned and tied the right. It is explained in the book *Kaneh* that the reason for the right and left is that just as the Tefillin are placed on the left first... for the **Tefillin of the Head** is on the head, representing the Community of Israel... therefore one must illuminate the hand which corresponds to the Attribute of Sovereignty (*Malchut*). Similarly, when one goes to place the Tefillin on the head, then the "Woman" <note>A Kabbalistic reference to the Divine Presence</note> is in her house and blesses, saying, "Blessed are you to the Lord, my daughter." So too with the shoe: one puts it on the left first like Tefillin... and the reason the *Baraita* <note>An ancient oral tradition not included in the Mishnah</note> said the right first is because the **Tefillin of the Hand** contains the letter *Yod*, which indicates Mercy. When a person wants to go up to the King, he takes permission from the "Wealthy One," and therefore puts the Tefillin of the hand on first. But regarding the shoe, which is on the left foot, prepare your way with the left shoe, but put on the right first and then the left... Rabbi Isaac fulfilled both: he puts on the right and does not tie, then puts on the left and ties; thus he intends to ascend and create a holy connection, all in one day.

**And one who knows** the secret of the shoe—"How beautiful are your steps in sandals"—the matter will be clarified for him even more, and it will be expanded upon, God willing, in the secret of the prohibition of wearing leather shoes on **Yom Kippur** <note>The Day of Atonement</note>. There it will also be explained why the blessing "Who has provided me with all my needs" is linked to putting on shoes. If a person restrains himself, it is because it is written: "Prepare to meet your God, O Israel," for it is not the honor of the King to come before Him with a belly full of filth. On the level of Truth <note>Kabbalistic interpretation</note>, this waste in man is like the dross and the judgment, the soot that comes from silver. One must clear himself of it so as not to awaken its likeness or give it a portion in prayer... this is the meaning of "Prepare to meet your God" and not toward something else. Our Sages said: "One who holds back his openings transgresses the prohibition of 'Do not make yourselves detestable.'" Do not make your souls detestable—specifically your souls. And in Tractate *Berachot*: "For this let every pious man pray at a time of finding"—this refers to the bathroom. This means when a man prays, he should first relieve himself. This is the meaning of the verse "Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all my innards, His holy name." Even the innards of a man... must bless the Lord. Therefore, one must check himself well when he comes to pray; one should not bring a belly full of waste before the Holy One, Blessed be He, to bless Him. (It seems this is why Rabbi Yochanan said: "One who wishes to accept upon himself the **Yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven** completely should relieve himself, etc." so that his whole body is whole... for if his belly is full of waste, he does not accept it with his whole soul, and his acceptance of the Yoke is flawed). One should be modest in the bathroom, as explained above in the laws of modesty.

**And when he relieves** himself, they said in *Berachot* in the chapter *Ha-Ro'eh* that he should wipe with the left hand and not the right, because with the [right] hand one points to the notes of the Torah <note>the musical accents or cantillation marks</note> and eats with it... and with the left he should not wipe with all fingers. With the middle finger he should not wipe, because the strap of the **Hand Tefillin** is wrapped around it, and it binds the higher sanctities... how could he wipe himself with something that is bound to holiness? We learn this through an *a fortiori* argument: if one does not wipe with the right because it shows the Torah's notes, how much more so this middle finger, which is itself involved in the performance of the commandments and the Torah.

**Afterward**, when he has washed his hands, he should immediately arrange the blessings one after another. By right, they should have been recited immediately upon waking—each blessing for its specific action—and this is how the Sages of the Talmud acted. So too is it written in the *Zohar*. Although we wait until our hands are clean, nevertheless, as soon as they are clean, one must arrange them.

**Since** there are many fine points and various laws regarding interruptions between blessings, I will copy all that is written in the book **Valley of Blessing** <note>original: *Emek Bracha*</note> by my master and father, of blessed memory, along with my own glosses from Section 7 to the end of Section 10. We can learn many excellent things from them. These are his words there on page 28:

## Valley of Blessing

**The Tur wrote** in Section 6 as follows: "And if he goes immediately to the bathroom and wishes to wait to recite the blessing **'Regarding the Washing of Hands'** <note>original: *Al Netilat Yadayim*</note> until his arrival at the synagogue, so that he may arrange it with the other morning blessings, he may do so," etc. However, he should act as if he is occupied until he arrives there, and he should not interrupt at the outset between the washing and the blessing with any matter or speech. (But after the fact, if he did interrupt with words between the washing and the blessing, it is not considered an interruption requiring him to wash a second time. Even at the outset, he may interrupt if necessary for a blessing, such as to say to his fellow "A good morning to you" <note>original: *Tzafra de-marei tav*</note> or to ask after someone's peace out of respect... especially since such an interruption is minor and does not distract his mind from the washing). This is not like what I have seen many do, rising early for the synagogue and saying supplications, requests, and Psalms, and afterward, when the Cantor recites the blessing **'Regarding the Washing of Hands'** out loud, they bless with him, even though it is not explicitly permitted (as the *Tur* wrote in Section 46... brought in the name of the *Agur*). They also answer after him with the blessing for washing hands in a loud voice. It is revealed to all that these people recite this blessing in a way that is not in accordance with the law, for they did not bless immediately after washing, and now after they have said supplications and Psalms, they bless after the Cantor's blessing. This blessing will not be accepted, in my opinion, since they interrupted so much between the washing and the blessing. For the great rule is like the law of every blessing: to bless "immediately before their performance," and they only permitted the blessing for washing hands to be recited afterward because his hands were not clean from the night's sleep... as the *Rosh* <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note> wrote. The *Tur* brought this in Section 4 and Section 158. But certainly, the law dictates that we should bless immediately.

# The Valley of Blessing, Page 126

And afterward, he should begin with the second [act]. So too in our case: since he has begun to engage in the commandment of ritual washing, it is proper for him to complete it—that is, to recite the blessing "**concerning the washing of hands**" <note>Hebrew: *Al Netilat Yadayim*</note> immediately after washing at home, or in the synagogue upon his arrival there, before he begins other matters. Even though these other matters are also the recounting of the Creator's praise, [it is an interruption]. (For the blessing he recites over the washing is the completion of the washing he began.) Specifically, the interruption of reciting **Psalms** <note>Hebrew: *Tehillim*</note> at that time is a significant interruption. <note>Glosses of the Maharal: They are currently without a commandment, because reciting Psalms is not a commandment tied specifically to this hour; he could postpone the Psalms until after the blessing over washing, as mentioned above and explained in the introduction.</note>

**But** for the sake of a commandment that is a "passing hour" <note>meaning a time-sensitive obligation that will be missed if not done immediately</note>, it is certainly permitted to interrupt. It is not even a question whether it is permitted to interrupt for something necessary for the washing itself—such as walking from his home to the synagogue to arrange the blessing over washing together with the other morning blessings as mentioned above—for that is clearly permitted. Rather, even if he interrupts between the washing and the blessing for the sake of a general commandment, he may do so if it is a "passing hour." For regarding the interruption between the prayers of *Yishtabach* and *Yotzer Or*, [the Sages] said that it is a "transgression in his hand," yet even so, for communal needs or to designate charity for one who comes to be supported by the poor-fund, it is permitted to interrupt, as the **Tur** <note>The *Arba’ah Turim*, a 14th-century code of Jewish law</note> wrote in Section 54. My teacher of blessed memory wrote there: "From this spread the custom in many places to bless the sick or to allow a person to demand justice in the synagogue between *Yishtabach* and *Yotzer Or*, for all this is considered 'for the sake of a commandment.'" These are his words. Our Sages of blessed memory further said: (as brought in the code of the **Tur**, Section 218) regarding one who was reading [the Shema], in between the sections he may greet an honorable person out of respect and return greetings to any person. In the middle [of a section], he may greet someone out of fear and return greetings out of respect. We learn from all this that even in a place where they said it is forbidden to interrupt, it is permitted for the sake of a commandment, specifically if it is a "passing hour" for that commandment. And it is known that "one who is engaged in a commandment is exempt from [another] commandment." <note>This is a fundamental legal principle: performing one religious duty excuses a person from having to perform another at that same moment.</note> Since that hour is passing, he can complete the beginning of the commandment of washing by blessing over it immediately upon his arrival at the synagogue, without the interruption of reciting Psalms, and afterward he can say Psalms as he wishes.

(So too, regarding what people are accustomed to: they interrupt for things like a hater or an enemy, a thief, a donkey, or a leopard, and similar things. Regarding these interruptions we are accustomed to when arriving at the synagogue—it is not difficult at all. For it is certainly proper and right for anyone called by the name "Israel," upon entering the synagogue (which is a **"Minor Sanctuary"**), to accept upon himself the yoke of the awe of the Sanctuary, to glorify it, and so on, and not be like a group of commoners. For it was said that it is forbidden for a person to go to his friend's door to greet him before he has prayed, yet even so, they said if he happens upon him, he may greet him. (Tur Section 89). How much more so regarding the Divine Presence and the glory of the Temple: when he happens upon this holy place and enters it, he should bow, prostrate, glorify, and exalt the Name of God, and then recite the blessing over washing. Therefore, these interruptions are not considered significant. Furthermore, they are brief matters, and being incidental, they are not considered an interruption. This is unlike the recitation of Psalms, which is a significant interruption and a distraction, since they say so many chapters that they lose sight of the washing and it is forgotten.)

**And further**, there is another reason why reciting Psalms is not like those brief interruptions. For those interruptions are common among the House of Israel and have been forbidden or permitted from world's end to world's end upon entering the synagogue. It is like what was said regarding the verse "O Lord, open my lips"—since the Rabbis established it, it is considered like a "long redemption" <note>part of the prayer itself</note> and is not an interruption. Although it is not exactly the same—as "O Lord, open my lips" was an enactment of the Sages of the Talmud, whereas these interruptions are merely a general custom—nevertheless, since it is the custom to say them, they are not an interruption because they are all for the sake of prayer. This is not the case with the recitation of Psalms, which is not an ancient custom. For I have heard it said that this custom only spread recently in these lands to recite it communally. And even if now the whole congregation does not say it, but only the leaders of the community, [it remains an interruption]. This is not the case with verses like "**How goodly are your tents**" <note>Hebrew: *Mah Tovu*—the traditional opening verse said upon entering a synagogue</note>, which all of Israel says equally upon entering the synagogue. Therefore, they are not considered an interruption. Thus, it seems it is not proper to interrupt between the washing and the blessing with any supplication, request, or Psalm, except for the verses of "How goodly" and "But I, in the abundance of Your kindness," according to the custom. For "you have only that which has been made custom," and "do not add to their words."

Thus, those people who do not bless immediately after washing upon entering the synagogue, but instead say supplications and requests or Psalms first, and only afterward—when the **Prayer Leader** <note>Hebrew: *Shaliach Tzibbur* or *Shatz*</note> recites the blessing aloud—they recite the blessing along with him, they have fulfilled their obligation. <note>Glosses of the Maharal: See there, for they have inherited their reward, etc.</note> But if those people did not interrupt between the washing and the blessing, and blessed immediately after washing in their homes or immediately upon arrival at the synagogue, and then they repeat and bless again after the Prayer Leader's blessing—this is even worse, for it is a **blessing said in vain** <note>Hebrew: *Beracha LeVatala*—a serious prohibition against using God's name unnecessarily</note>, being a blessing over an act already completed. This must not be done, as mentioned above in the name of the **Agur** <note>A 15th-century Halakhic work</note>. How good and right it would be if they would begin with the blessing over washing immediately upon arrival at the synagogue, and afterward say Psalms before the prayer of *Baruch She'amar* or after the service, so they do not interrupt between the washing and the blessing. But what can we do, since most communities, nearly all of them, have already accustomed themselves to start with Psalms first?

Alas, I have found those pious and distinguished men who conduct themselves in the House of the Lord with honor, rising early to study Torah... before the Prayer Leader begins the blessing aloud... they should prepare to rise a bit before the beadle calls to the synagogue, enough time so they can say the blessing over washing in their homes from a **Prayer Book** <note>Hebrew: *Siddur*</note> immediately after washing. (For ideally, one should not interrupt after the blessing over washing until he completes at least the entire order of morning blessings). They should do this at home or in the synagogue always upon arrival, before they begin saying Psalms, and they should not interrupt between the washing and the blessing. Even if they hear the Prayer Leader's blessing afterward, they should only answer "Amen."...

As the **Agur** says, this should be done before *Baruch She'amar*... but if so, it is enough that the people saying Psalms do not repeat the blessing after the Prayer Leader in the early morning, only Amen. And according to what was said above, why does the Prayer Leader repeat it to answer Amen aloud? Since not the entire congregation is blessing after him... furthermore, one does not say Amen after his own blessings, as the Sages said: "Anyone who answers Amen after his own blessings is disgraceful." The **Tur** brings this (in Section 188 and 215). One must answer that there are always people found every morning in the synagogue, especially in the large and well-known communities, who do not say Psalms in a group but come to the synagogue after the Psalms are finished, just as the Prayer Leader begins to recite the blessing aloud. They fulfill their obligation through him. Even if they all said it together in a group, there are always youths... to say the blessing aloud after the completion of Psalms. Therefore, it is good, so that even the "Psalm-sayers" themselves—those who set a time to start early in the morning with friends—it is inevitable that one or two or more of them might be delayed in coming to the synagogue until the Prayer Leader starts. We do not know which one will be "fitting" to arrive exactly at that time... Therefore, for the masses who are not part of the Psalm group, or the youths, or the Psalm-sayers themselves who arrive late... they have the custom to give something to charity for their group because they missed the set time for Psalms. It is possible those people arrive exactly when the Prayer Leader says the blessing... and they answer after him. For them, the order of washing followed by the blessing is correct. For those who interrupted with Psalms or other requests between washing and the blessing... they do not repeat it again... the Prayer Leader's Amen is not in vain. Just as we find in Grace after Meals... the Prayer Leader always blesses and [they answer] Amen... even if there is no one who is not an "expert" <note>Hebrew: *Baki*—referring to someone who doesn't know the prayers and needs to listen to the leader to fulfill their obligation</note>... as brought above in the name of the **Agur**.

<note>Glosses of the Maharal: Even in a congregation where everyone has prayed and everyone is an expert in prayer, and there is no one who is not—</note>

It highlights the tension between the legal requirement for immediacy and the communal tradition of early morning study and song.</summary>

--- Page 285 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical legal discussion regarding whether certain actions or recitations constitute a "forbidden interruption" (hefsek) between the ritual washing of hands in the morning and the recitation of the corresponding blessing. The author is debating whether reciting Psalms or the "Asher Yatzar" blessing creates a legal break that would require re-washing or invalidate the sequence.</meta>

# The Valley of Blessing

...and prayer and sickness <note>original: "u-tefilah u-machalah"</note>, so ends his words. Here too, one might say that since the blessing of **Who formed man** <note>The *Asher Yatzar* blessing, recited after using the bathroom, thanking God for the proper functioning of the body.</note> is an obligatory matter to say now after leaving the bathroom, it constitutes a significant interruption. Therefore, the Halakhic authorities <note>The *Poskim*</note> wrote that one who leaves the bathroom and wishes to wash his hands for a meal must wash twice, because the *Asher Yatzar* blessing interrupts between the washing and the blessing **"concerning the washing of hands"** as mentioned above in Chapter 4. The same rule applies to the morning washing: the *Asher Yatzar* blessing is also an interruption between the washing and the blessing over the washing because it is an obligatory matter. However, if one interrupted with "discretionary matters" <note>Non-obligatory speech or actions</note> between the washing and the meal and its blessing—and similarly if one interrupted the morning washing with discretionary matters, or even by reciting **Psalms** <note>Hebrew: *Tehillim*</note>, which is also called a discretionary matter since he is not strictly obligated to say them at this exact moment—one might think this does not count as an interruption. 

But this is not so. Regarding the laws of interruption, the *Asher Yatzar* blessing is also considered like a discretionary matter, because it is not tied to a specific time; rather, whenever one performs his needs, he blesses. If he had not performed his needs now before the meal, he would not be reciting it. If so, it falls under the category of discretionary matters. This is stated explicitly in the **Code of Jewish Law** <note>The *Shulchan Aruch*, the foundational legal code written by Joseph Karo in the 16th century.</note> in Section 178, which says: "A person who naps during his meal—this is not an interruption. Similarly, if he interrupted with other discretionary matters, such as needing to use the bathroom and the like," so ends his words. 

If so, since we find according to the **Rosh** <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, a prominent 13th-century German-Spanish scholar.</note> and his colleagues that they hold that *Asher Yatzar* interrupts between the washing and its blessing for one who leaves the bathroom and wants to wash for a meal... it follows that even if reciting Psalms is considered a discretionary matter, it still constitutes an interruption between the morning washing and its blessing. This is just as we find that the *Asher Yatzar* blessing interrupts between washing and the meal, even though it is considered a discretionary matter. Certainly, the act of washing is one and the same, and what constitutes an interruption in one case constitutes an interruption in the other. This is simple to understand. <margin>Inside the gloss</margin> • People who recite Psalms might say they have something to rely upon when they interrupt with Psalms between the washing and the blessing, based on what the Rosh wrote (in the chapter "Covering the Blood" and brought by the *Beit Yosef* in Section 609) regarding the incident of Rav’s students. He wrote: "We do not find a concern for an interruption between an action and the final blessing, etc." It seems to my humble opinion that the Rosh's words here and his words there are all one.

**And I say** regarding those people who say this: you should not desire their view nor listen to them. For what the Rosh wrote in that place—that we do not find a concern for an interruption between an action and the blessing—refers specifically to the act of Rav's students mentioned in Section 609. (It is not a general rule for other places like our current case). The text there states: Rav’s students were sitting at a meal, and Rav Yeba the Elder was standing over them. They said, "Give us [the cup] and we shall say the blessing [Grace after Meals]." Afterward, they wanted to drink. He said to them: "This is what Rav said: once you have said 'Give us and we shall bless,' it is forbidden for you to drink." Why? Because you have "removed your mind" <note>Hebrew: *Hesach HaDaat*; a legal state where one ceases to focus on a particular activity, ending the legal continuity of that act.</note> from drinking. Since you removed your mind from drinking, it is forbidden to drink until after the Grace after Meals. 

However, the **Tosafot** <note>Medieval commentators on the Talmud</note> and the Rosh wrote there that "removing one's mind" does not disqualify the final blessing for what one already ate. They explained that "it is forbidden for you to drink" means you cannot drink *unless* you recite a new blessing over the wine, but by reciting that blessing, it is permitted to drink before Grace after Meals. They brought proofs for this interpretation (see above in Principle 7, Chapter 6). It is on this that the Rosh comments, writing that we do not find a concern for an interruption between an action and the final blessing. Meaning: even though they removed their minds from eating and drinking by saying "Give us and we shall bless," there is no concern that this interruption makes it forbidden for them to eat and drink further in this meal until they say Grace after Meals (which is the "final blessing" the Rosh mentioned). One can interrupt between the act of eating and the final blessing (the Grace after Meals). 

To establish the truth for you, I present the words of the Rosh and what he added there: "Some explain that it is forbidden to drink until you have said Grace after Meals, but this is not correct... for removing one's mind is a factor for the *first* blessing [before eating]... but it is not a factor for the blessing over what one already ate. For if he eats again and recites Grace after Meals for both sittings, we find no concern for an interruption between the act and the final blessing. We only worry about an interruption between the *first* blessing and the act, such as between washing hands and the blessing over bread." These are clear words: all the Rosh's words in this matter refer only to matters of a meal. 

Consequently, that clause stating "we do not find a concern for an interruption between an action and the final blessing" refers to the gap between the act of eating and the Grace after Meals recited at the end. This is learned from the context; all the clauses before and after speak of meal interruptions. Specifically, an interruption between eating and Grace after Meals, or between washing hands and the blessing over bread. But the matter of an interruption between the morning washing and its blessing—our current subject—is not mentioned there at all. Furthermore, if the Rosh's opinion were as suggested here—that there is no concern for interruption—he should have said "we do not find *anywhere* a concern for interruption," which would include the morning washing. Since he did not write that, but referred specifically to the incident of Rav's students, it implies it does not apply to our case. Moreover, how can you say the morning blessing is a "final blessing"? It is a single blessing belonging to the act of washing itself!

**And further**, when you examine it well, these cases are not alike at all; they are as far apart as the East is from the West. It is understandable why the Rosh is not concerned about an interruption between the act of eating and the final blessing (Grace after Meals), for there is a great reason: as long as one is not hungry again from that food, he can still bless. Since the time for the blessing has not passed, what does it matter if there was an "removal of mind" in between? But in our case, the blessing for morning washing (which is a **Blessing of the Commandments** <note>Hebrew: *Birkat HaMitzvot*; a category of blessings recited before performing a religious duty.</note>), the proper time for it is *before* the washing, just like all other such blessings which must be recited "prior to their performance." It is only because we cannot mention God's name [while our hands are unwashed] that we recite it after washing, as mentioned above in the name of **Mahari Abohab** <note>Rabbi Isaac Aboab, a 15th-century Spanish talmudist.</note>. Therefore, as soon as our hands are clean after washing, the obligation of the blessing falls upon us. Why should we interrupt for no reason? Since the time for the commandment has arrived and it is possible to fulfill it, we should fulfill it! 

Even though reciting Psalms or petitions is also a commandment, and whoever increases their requests for mercy gains merit, it is nonetheless proper to bless over the washing first. This is because it is the first commandment he began, and our Sages said: "To one who begins a commandment, we say: 'Finish it!'" This is the same reason we "do not pass over commandments" <note>Hebrew: *Ein ma'avirin al ha-mitzvot*</note>; as the commentators explained, one should not set aside a commandment that comes to hand first in order to perform another. This is also the reason for the order of removing Tefillin, as mentioned in the *Tur* Section 28 and in the *Kol Bo* (page 9): one places the hand-tefillin into a case so that he will encounter the arm-tefillin first when he goes to wear them again, for if he encounters the head-tefillin first, he would have to set it aside [to do the arm first], and a person should not set aside a commandment that comes to hand to engage in another. We also say in the Mishnah in the chapter "Covering the Blood" <note>From Tractate Chullin in the Talmud</note>: if one slaughtered a hundred wild animals in one place, one covering suffices for all. Rabbi Judah says: if he slaughtered an animal, he should cover the blood and *then* slaughter the bird. The **Ran** <note>Rabbi Nissim of Gerona, 14th-century scholar.</note> wrote on this: it is proper to cover the blood of the first and finish its commandment completely (for covering is the completion of the slaughter) before starting the second. We see that where commandments are distinct, one must finish the first commandment...

<summary>This page argues that the blessing for morning hand-washing should be recited immediately after washing, without interrupting for Psalms or other prayers. The author refutes the idea that legal precedents regarding meal-time interruptions apply to this morning ritual, emphasizing the principle of completing a commandment once it has begun.</summary>

# The Valley of Blessing
### Page 127

One hour before the start of the *Selichot* <note>Penitential prayers recited in the early morning during the month of Elul and between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.</note> and after completing the *Selichot*, the Prayer Leader <note>Hebrew: *Shliach Tzibbur*, abbreviated here as Sh-Tz.</note> returns and recites the blessing **"Concerning the washing of the hands"** <note>Hebrew: *Al Netilat Yadayim*, abbreviated in the text as *A.N.Y.*</note> aloud at the pulpit in order to fulfill the obligation for the unlearned. This follows the principle that for all commandments, even if one has already fulfilled their own obligation, they may still help others fulfill theirs, as discussed previously. —I have written what appears correct to me based on my intentions and for the sake of Heaven; though I am small and humble, "he who listens shall listen, and he who refrains shall refrain" <note>A paraphrase of Ezekiel 3:27, meaning the author presents his view regardless of whether it is accepted.</note>.

<margin>8. And if it is not his intention to go immediately after washing to the Synagogue, and he wishes to recite the blessing **"Concerning the washing of hands"** immediately after washing etc., this is according to the book *Birkat Avraham*.</margin>
In his home, he must then immediately recite the blessing **"Who formed man"** <note>The *Asher Yatzar* blessing recited after using the bathroom.</note> and all other morning blessings, one after another. This is because one must not create an interruption between the blessing over washing and the sequence of blessings, just as one must not interrupt between the blessing over bread and eating, or between washing for a meal and the meal itself, according to the *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, author of an influential code of Jewish law.</note> and those who follow him (as written in *Orach Chaim*, Section 166). The reason is that they only established the blessing for washing in the morning for the sake of the **Recitation of the Shema** and the **Standing Prayer** <note>The *Amidah*.</note>, or at the very least for the sake of the sequence of morning blessings which are matters of holiness. Therefore, every person should be careful at the outset to recite the blessing for washing over a "complete" morning washing, wherein he will recite all the blessings of praise without interruption, at least until the Section of the Daily Offering <note>The *Parashat HaTamid*, a section of the morning service.</note>. Otherwise, it would be a "blessing in vain" over the washing of hands, for one must not interrupt between the blessing and the matter for which we are blessing. One must not interrupt by waiting, nor by idle activity, nor by changing locations. (For changing location is considered like a "diversion of the mind," as the *Tur* wrote in Section 178, even if one does not interrupt with speech.) Upon this idea the spirit and intention of most of that mentioned book revolves, especially the fourth part, and you will find what we have innovated there.

It appears that we read "Washing of the Hands" in the *Matteh Moshe* and the *Rosh* <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, a 13th-century German-Spanish scholar.</note>, and these are his words regarding the verses (in the chapter "One who sees"): "And when he wakes up, let him say 'My God, the soul...' etc. until he washes his hands and says **'Blessed art Thou... concerning the washing of hands.'** Because a person's hands are 'active' <note>Meaning they likely touched covered parts of the body while sleeping.</note> and it is impossible not to have touched 'unclean flesh' during the night, they established a blessing before he recites the *Shema* and prays, etc." See there. And it appears that if he has no water, he should wipe his hands with a pebble or dust and recite the blessing "Concerning the cleanliness of hands," for a person is obligated to clean his hands at the time of prayer, as said above, for it is written: "I will wash my hands in purity" <note>Psalm 26:6</note>. From this we may learn that the same applies to the Afternoon Prayer <note>*Mincha*</note> and the Evening Prayer <note>*Ma'ariv*</note>: if he relieved himself and washed his hands, he recites the blessing for washing. However, throughout the rest of the day, when he relieves himself, he only needs to recite **"Who formed man"**, for the blessing over washing was only established for a meal or for prayer. Just as when he washes he says "Blessed be He who removes sleep from my eyes..." and "May it be Your will that You accustom us to Your Torah..." until "Blessed art Thou... who bestows kind favors to His people Israel." Nowadays, the custom is to recite these blessings after washing his hands, and as long as his hands are not clean, he should not recite the sequence. As for the rule that "for all commandments, one blesses prior to their performance," and these are blessings of commandment where we say "and commanded us," one must recite the blessing first. However, blessings of vision or praise, such as these, can be recited afterward. Nevertheless, from the language of the Talmud, it implies he can recite all these blessings before washing his hands, and this supports my words that they only established the washing of hands for the *Shema* and the Prayer.

<margin>The blessing of the *Rosh* at the beginning of his words above.</margin>
These are his words; and I have brought all this from the words of the *Rosh* because we will need them later.

<margin>It implies explicitly that he holds there should be no interruption.</margin>
Because a person's hands are active, they established a blessing (meaning the blessing for washing) before he recites the *Shema* and prays.
Between the blessing of washing and the *Shema* and Prayer, since the blessing was established for their sake; for one must never interrupt between a blessing and the matter for which we recited the blessing.
And so wrote the *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo.</note> in the *Tur*, Section 52: "Even the children of the sages of Israel said with love," and these are his words: "But Rabbenu Yonah wrote in the name of Rabbi Meir that one should not interrupt between the blessing and the thing over which one blesses, and such is the consensus of the *Ramah* and the *Ramban* <note>Nahmanides.</note>," thus far the *Beit Yosef*. Furthermore, it is proven from the words of the *Rosh* above that he holds one must not interrupt between the blessing for washing and the *Shema* and Prayer, in the name of the Sages of the Mishnah: "Because a person's hands are active... they established a blessing before he recites *Shema* and prays... from this we learn that the same applies to the Afternoon and Evening Prayers if he relieved himself and washed his hands, he recites the blessing for washing." From this it is proven that the *Rosh* treats the night and even if he did not relieve himself—or if he did relieve himself, whether major or minor needs—the same regarding the Afternoon and Evening prayers: both require washing and a blessing.

<margin>It implies from this that he equates them in all matters, just as we learned regarding the washing for the Afternoon and Evening prayers.</margin>
That they were not careful about reciting the blessing for washing even if he relieved himself and wiped, or minor needs and rubbed, except when he wishes to pray immediately without any interruption at all, as the *Tur* wrote in Section 7. The *Rosh* would not recite the blessing for washing all day unless he had relieved himself and wiped or rubbed his hands and was going to pray (meaning Afternoon or Evening prayers) immediately afterward.

<margin>From the use of the word "immediately," it clearly implies that if he were not going to pray immediately, he would not recite the blessing for washing at the time of relieving himself, even if he wanted to pray a short while later.</margin>
For the word "immediately" indicates this, as the *Tur* wrote in Sections 166 and 192 regarding washing for a meal: "And he should dry his hands well and recite the *HaMotzi* blessing **immediately**." And he wrote there that the *Rosh* was accustomed not to interrupt and not to speak, and when he was reclining at a meal with others, he would wash last so as not to interrupt and not to speak. Thus far.

<margin>Thus, the word "immediately" means "at once," without interruption between the matters discussed. So too regarding the blessing over hands for the Afternoon or Evening prayer...</margin>
...where the word "immediately" is written, it also means "at once," without an interruption between the washing and the Afternoon or Evening prayer. This is similar to the morning washing mentioned above. This is what I said previously, that the source of his words (meaning, what the author of *Birkat Avraham* wrote about not interrupting between the morning washing and the *Shema* and Prayer) stems from what the *Rosh* wrote in his rulings, etc. Therefore, it is proper for every person to conduct themselves in this manner, as I brought above in the name of the book *Birkat Avraham*: that he should not interrupt in the morning between the blessing for washing and the *Shema* and Prayer, or at least between the sequence of blessings until the Section of the Daily Offering, since the *Rosh* agrees with him on this.

<margin>And one should not challenge what I brought above in the name of the author of *Birkat Avraham*, who holds that the blessing for washing in the morning was established for the *Shema* and Prayer—for if so, why the entire sequence of blessings alone? What connection do the morning blessings have with the Prayer to equate them? Furthermore, the *Rosh* did not mention in his words the...</margin>
...consensus we reached (it seems to me they established the blessing for the morning washing) except for the *Shema* and Prayer alone, and not the sequence of blessings. One could say that the author of *Birkat Avraham* reasoned in the aforementioned fourth part that the request we say in the morning among the other morning blessings—which begins "May it be Your will that You accustom us to Your Torah and make us cling to Your commandments..." until the conclusion "Who bestows kind favors to His people Israel"—is like a form of the Eighteen Benedictions <note>The *Amidah*.</note>, and like a form of the "Abundant Love" blessing <note>*Ahava Rabbah*, the blessing before the Shema.</note>, and like the *Shema* itself, and like the "True and Firm" prayer. He elaborated there a bit on this, see there. (And do not distance yourself from what the author of *Birkat Avraham* wrote... because the request "May it be Your will" is like the *Shema* and Prayer, it is considered like *Shema* and Prayer regarding the morning blessing for washing. For we find that the *Tur* wrote in Section 238 similarly: "As for the custom of interrupting with the verses of 'May our eyes behold' and the *Kaddish*—this was because in the early days their synagogues were in the fields, and they were afraid to stay there until the time of the Evening Prayer, so they established to say these verses which contain eighteen mentions of God's name corresponding to the eighteen blessings of the Evening Prayer." Now, one might ask: what is the connection between these eighteen mentions of the Name and the eighteen blessings? Rather, you must say that in a time of necessity, a mere hint is sufficient. The same applies here. Furthermore, it is written in the *Kol Bo* that we are accustomed to say "There is none like our God" on Shabbat and Festivals to complete the count of one hundred blessings... they said the one hundred 'structures' found in "There is none like our God" each count as a blessing, etc. See there.) If so, since they are similar in nature, the author of *Birkat Avraham* holds it is proper for this reason to recite the blessing for washing for them, just as for the actual *Shema* and Prayer. And the *Rosh* also holds this view regarding the morning washing, even for the sequence of blessings alone, as mentioned nearby in the name of *Birkat Avraham*. And when the *Rosh* wrote that the blessing for washing was only established before *Shema* and Prayer, he did not mean specifically the literal *Shema* and the eighteen-blessing Prayer, but also these morning blessings; when gathered together, they are called "*Shema* and Prayer" regarding the blessing for washing for the reason mentioned above. Indeed, it is not surprising that the *Rosh* holds that morning blessings stand in the place of Prayer regarding the morning washing. But if you were to say that the *Shema* and Prayer the *Rosh* mentioned regarding the morning washing refer to the literal *Shema* and Prayer, but for the morning blessings alone, even if said all together, he would not bless over washing—it would be a contradiction within his own words. For in his rulings, as brought above, he said the blessing was only for *Shema* and Prayer, and he wrote the same in a Responsum (Rule 4). But afterward, in that very same Responsum—which the *Tur* brought in *Orach Chaim* at the end of Section 46—he wrote: "One who rises before the light of morning to study should recite the blessing for washing, 'Who formed man,' 'My God, the soul,' and the entire sequence of blessings until the Blessing of the Torah, including the Blessing of the Torah, and then study." Thus, you see he wrote here that one recites the blessing for washing for the sequence of blessings alone, for certainly when he rises before the light of morning, the time for *Shema* and Prayer has not yet arrived. If so...

<summary>This page analyzes the legal requirement to ritualistically wash hands and recite the accompanying blessing specifically before the Morning, Afternoon, and Evening prayers, emphasizing that there should be no "interruption" (speech or significant delay) between the washing and the prayer. The author harmonizes different opinions to argue that even the morning blessings (Birkot HaShachar) are significant enough to warrant the washing blessing, as they function as a preliminary form of prayer.</summary>
