<meta>This page continues the technical legal discussion regarding the timing of the blessing "Concerning the washing of hands" (Al Netilat Yadayim). The author is specifically addressing the practices of "The People of Psalms"—groups who gather early to recite the entire Book of Psalms—and the communal role of the Prayer Leader (Shliach Tzibbur) in helping others fulfill their ritual obligations.</meta>

# The Valley of Blessing
### Page 128

Nevertheless, the Prayer Leader should descend before the Ark and repeat the prayer in order to uphold the ordinance of the Sages. This is the rule for any matter established by our Sages for a specific reason: even if that specific reason is occasionally absent, the Rabbinic ordinance remains in force as a safeguard, lest the original circumstance return. Otherwise, the Sages would be making their words subject to varying measurements and inconsistent rules. 

If the "People of Psalms" <note>Groups of pious individuals who gather to recite the Book of Psalms in its entirety, often before the morning service.</note> would do this—namely, reciting the blessing **"Concerning the washing of hands"** <note>Hebrew: *Al Netilat Yadayim*, often abbreviated in the text as *A.N.Y.*</note> privately along with the other morning blessings before they begin the Psalms—they would rectify three things that are otherwise disordered:

1.  **Immediate Blessing:** Reciting the blessing immediately after washing. It is not proper to interrupt between the washing and the blessing based on everything I have written above.
2.  **Timing of Morning Blessings:** It brings the morning blessings closer to the time of their relevance. According to the order of the Talmud, one should ideally recite each blessing at the moment the benefit occurs <note>For example, saying the blessing for "opening the eyes" when one first wakes up.</note>. However, because one’s hands are not yet clean, the Sages ordained saying them after washing. Since one cannot say them at the exact moment, it is best to at least say them as soon as possible after washing.
3.  **The Torah Blessing:** When one recites all the morning blessings one after another immediately after washing and before the Psalms—as they are written in our Prayer Books up to the "Section of the Daily Offering"—they include the **"Blessings over the Torah."** This is very good, as it also covers the recitation of the verses of the Psalms, which are the core of the Torah. Even those who believe that one does not need a blessing for verses said as a plea for mercy rather than formal study would agree that it is improper to say many chapters of Psalms without the Torah blessing. This was also written by Rabbi Chaim Abulafia <note>A prominent 18th-century Rabbi and Kabbalist.</note> in his work on the Code of Jewish Law.

Even if they were concerned about the length of the interruption between the washing and the blessing, why should they not be "returning" to the better practice? "One who is ahead in performing a commandment" should not be discouraged. As the Talmud says in the tractate *Berakhot* (in the chapter "The Morning Prayer") regarding the **"Traveler’s Prayer"**: "Since I can do it better, do not call it worse." <note>original: "Mahiyot tov al tikra ra." A legal principle meaning that if a better or more meticulous way to perform a commandment is available, one should take it.</note> The Talmud relates that Rav Chasda and Rav Sheshet were traveling together. Rav Chasda stood still to pray. Rav Sheshet (who was blind) asked his attendant what Rav Chasda was doing. When told he was standing to pray, Rav Sheshet said, "Help me stand too, so I may pray; since I can do it better, I should not do it worse." Rashi explains: "Since I am able to pray while standing because my companions have stopped, I will not call it 'bad' by praying while walking, even though walking is technically permitted."

<margin>13</margin>
## But
Even though it might be technically permitted to interrupt with Psalms between the washing and the blessing, it is still a case of "do not call the better way bad." It would be proper to be strict and wait a brief moment before starting the Psalms. One can recite the hand-washing blessing immediately after washing along with the sequence of morning blessings, as it is not such a great burden. 

Even a regular Prayer Leader who recites Psalms with the congregation at the pulpit can do this: he should recite the hand-washing blessing and the other blessings to himself at home or in the synagogue before starting the Psalms. This ensures he does not interrupt between washing and the blessing. Even though he will repeat them later with the congregation in a traditional melody, these repeated blessings are not "blessings said in vain." It is the established custom to repeat the morning blessings in the community to fulfill the obligation for the unlearned. This has been the practice since ancient times, as noted earlier in the name of the *Knesset HaGedolah*. The *Tur* <note>The *Arba'ah Turim*, a foundational code of Jewish law by Rabbi Jacob ben Asher.</note> writes: "They ordained the arrangement of these blessings in the synagogue so that the unlearned might hear them, answer 'Amen,' and thereby fulfill their obligation." 

Therefore, even if one has already blessed privately, he may repeat them with the congregation to help others. This follows the rule that <insert>in their order</insert> "Even if one has fulfilled his own obligation, he may still help others fulfill theirs" <note>original: "Af al pi she-yatzah, motzi."</note>. This is specifically true if they are said aloud so others can answer "Amen." (Note: If they are said silently and his voice is not heard by the congregation, then the principle of "one who hears is like one who speaks" does not apply, and the blessings would indeed be in vain if he already said them privately.) 

This does not contradict what was cited earlier in the name of the *Agur* <note>A 15th-century legal code.</note> regarding not repeating the blessing at the synagogue. The *Agur* was likely not referring to a case of helping others fulfill their duty. Regarding helping others, Rashi explains that "All of Israel are responsible for one another" <note>original: "Kol Yisrael arevim zeh bazeh." This is a fundamental concept of Jewish communal responsibility.</note>; since one's fellow has not yet fulfilled the commandment, it is as if the person himself has not fully fulfilled it. 

This is also why the Prayer Leader repeats the main Prayer aloud for those who are not proficient. My teacher also wrote this in the Code of Jewish Law regarding the Shofar: even if the one blowing the Shofar has already fulfilled his duty, he may recite the blessings again for the sake of the community. We see the same at the Passover Seder; one might lead the Seder at home several times for different people, repeating the blessings over the Matzah and Bitter Herbs even though he has already eaten and is no longer personally commanded to eat more at that moment. He can bless because he is acting on behalf of others. 

However, at the very least, the Prayer Leader should not say the hand-washing blessing *alone* (without the other morning blessings) immediately after washing before starting the communal Psalms. Doing so would make that blessing seem isolated and "in vain," as it would be separated from the rest of the morning blessings which were ordained to be said together. Therefore, I say it is proper that when the cantors say the morning blessings early in the synagogue, they should say them within the hearing of the congregation, at least up until the blessing "Who bestows bountiful kindness." By singing them, everyone can answer "Amen," and they will be saved from the concern of "blessings said in vain."

## And Without
Even without this specific reason, it is a worthy custom for the Prayer Leader to say all the morning blessings aloud to benefit the public with the opportunity to answer "Amen," for the reward for answering "Amen" is great. 

(A further note: what I wrote above—that a Prayer Leader should not say the hand-washing blessing by himself if it will be separated from the other blessings by the recitation of Psalms—this is specifically when there is a long interruption. However, during the days of *Selichot* <note>Penitential prayers</note> and the High Holy Days, it seems to me the Prayer Leader *can* bless privately immediately after washing before starting the *Selichot*. Even if the other morning blessings don't follow immediately, the verses of the *Selichot* themselves are sufficient to maintain the "connection." They are verses of mercy and contain many mentions of God's names, from "To You, O Lord, is the righteousness" until the end. These verses are essentially the Names of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and are saturated with the "Thirteen Attributes of Mercy" which never return empty. They are holy. 

The *Shibbolei HaLeket* <note>A 13th-century Italian halakhic work.</note> notes that the Thirteen Attributes should only be said with a congregation. Rabbi Avigdor Katz also ruled that they require a quorum of ten because they are <insert>matters</insert> of sanctity (*Devarim she-bi-kdusha*). We also mention the Patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob), Moses, Aaron, David, Solomon, the Tribes, and the Matriarchs. We say the *Ateinu* prayer, the liturgical poems (*Piyyutim*), and the Sanctification (*Kaddish*). Since we mention such holy matters in the *Selichot*, they should be considered equivalent to the *Shema* or the Prayer itself in terms of allowing the blessing over washing to be validly connected to them.)

## And Even
Furthermore, the *Shema* and the Prayer itself are alluded to within the *Selichot*. This is seen in the section "Guardian of Israel," where we say "those who say Hear O Israel," and "those who sanctify Your name," and "those who declare the threefold sanctification" (referring to the *Kedushah*). Just as in the main Prayer we fall on our faces for supplication (*Tachnun*), so too after *Selichot* we say the *Tachnun* ending with "We know not what to do." Therefore, it is entirely appropriate for the Prayer Leader to recite the blessing for the washing he performed...

<meta>This page continues the technical legal discussion regarding the proper sequence and timing of the morning blessings, specifically the relationship between the blessing over washing hands and the subsequent prayers. The author continues to argue against separating these rituals by time or location.</meta>

# The Valley of Blessing
### Page 128

...one who brings [bread] for eating, for the reason that these actions are requirements for the blessing of "Who brings forth" <note>Hebrew: *Hamotzi*, the blessing over bread.</note>, as the *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher (c. 1269–1343), author of the *Arba'ah Turim*, a foundational code of Jewish law.</note> wrote in Section 167. If so, since this walking is for the purpose of the washing and its blessing, we should also say here that it does not constitute an interruption. This is what the Sages meant when they said that an interruption between a blessing and the act (eating) is only permissible if it concerns the needs of the meal—this applies specifically *post-facto* <note>Hebrew: *Bedieved*—referring to an action that is technically acceptable after the fact, even if not ideal.</note>. For if one spoke between the blessing and the eating about matters necessary for the meal, such as "bring salt" or "bring the appetizer," it is not considered an interruption to the extent that he must repeat the blessing. This is unlike speaking about matters unrelated to the meal, which would require repeating the blessing, as the *Tur* wrote in the aforementioned section.

However, *ideally* <note>Hebrew: *L'chatchila*—referring to the most proper or preferred way to perform a commandment from the start.</note>, one certainly should not interrupt between the blessing and the eating even with these matters. This was explicitly written by the *Beis Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo (1488–1575), author of the *Shulchan Aruch*.</note> in the name of the *Kol Bo* <note>An anonymous 13th-14th century legal work.</note>. Likewise, the *Maharam* <note>Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg (c. 1215–1293).</note> ruled in his *Shulchan Aruch* that one should not interrupt at all, even to say "bring salt." If so, in our case—the interruption between the blessing of "Concerning the washing of hands" <note>Hebrew: *Al Netilat Yadayim*, often abbreviated in this text as *A.N.Y.*</note> and the rest of the blessings—we should say the same: even if the interruption is for the sake of the washing blessing (such as the aforementioned walking from one's home to the synagogue to complete the other blessings, the *Shema*, and the prayer for which the washing was ordained), one still does not have permission to do so *ideally*.

Just as one should not *ideally* interrupt between the blessing of bread and eating even for things necessary for the blessing—for example, slicing the bread after the blessing is considered an interruption according to the *Tur* in Section 167, even though it is necessary for the meal. Why? Because he could have partially sliced the bread before the blessing. Therefore, slicing it fully between the blessing and eating is considered an interruption such that it is not proper to do so *ideally*. So too in our case: if he blesses "Concerning the washing of hands" in his home and then walks to the synagogue to arrange the blessings there, this "change of location" in the middle is an interruption. Even though the blessings in the synagogue are the purpose of the washing, it is not proper to do so *ideally* because there is an interruption of "change of place" in between. Rather, he should wait to recite the blessing for washing hands in the synagogue so he can immediately join the other blessings to it without an interruption. (Unless his intention is to recite all the other blessings at home immediately after the washing blessing.)

It is only *post-facto* that it is not an interruption. For instance, if he blessed "Concerning the washing of hands" at home alone and then went to the synagogue to arrange the blessings there, it is not an interruption that would require him to repeat the washing blessing, since the walking is for the sake of the ritual. But *ideally*, one should not interrupt, even for things necessary for the blessing, similar to the "bring salt" example above. 

I am not saying these two interruptions (washing vs. bread) are identical in every way, but only regarding when the interruption is for the sake of the matter itself. In both cases, *ideally* one should not interrupt, but *post-facto* one need not repeat the blessing. However, if the interruption is for something *unnecessary*, they are not equal. While an unnecessary interruption between bread and eating requires a new blessing, we do not find it explicitly stated in any book that one who speaks between the washing blessing and the morning blessings must repeat the blessing. We should not enter into the doubt of whether a blessing is required, as blessings are not [always] strictly preventative <note>Meaning, the lack of a perfect sequence doesn't necessarily invalidate the act entirely.</note>. However, one should be careful not to interrupt at all from the moment of the washing blessing until completing at least all the morning blessings. If he was not careful, it is a transgression, as if he said the washing blessing in vain, as I mentioned above in the name of the author of *Berachat Avraham*.

**The general rule of everything written here regarding the morning washing is this:** Immediately upon reciting the blessing "Concerning the washing of hands" at home or in the synagogue, the blessing must be "sustained" there—meaning he should immediately arrange at least the entire order of morning blessings. He should not interrupt with a delay in time, idle chatter, or a change of place. For it was for all of these (or for the *Shema* and the Amidah prayer) that the washing blessing was ordained, and not for the blessing of "Who formed man" <note>Hebrew: *Asher Yatzar*.</note> alone. Even if he wants to recite the blessing "My God, the soul" <note>Hebrew: *Elohai Neshamah*.</note> and the blessings of the Torah to study, he has not fulfilled his obligation properly until he completes the entire order of blessings one after the other, in their entirety, as stated two or three times.

Therefore, those people who rise before dawn to study or engage in other business, wash their hands, and recite "Concerning the washing," "Who formed," and "My God, the soul," but then stop and wait until daylight to recite "Who gives the rooster understanding" and the rest—they are not acting correctly. According to what I wrote in the name of the *Berachat Avraham* and the opinion of the *Rosh* <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel (c. 1250–1327).</note> (as the *Hagahot* and *Beis Yosef* also seem to agree with the *Rosh*), they should not interrupt between the washing and the completion of the morning blessings. Otherwise, why would the *Rosh* require one to touch their covered places or use the restroom [to justify a new washing] before the morning prayers? He could just wash once and save the blessings for later. Clearly, the *Rosh* holds that one should not interrupt between the washing and the blessings. I have written what appears correct to me for the sake of Heaven, to separate people from the possible prohibition of "a blessing in vain." May my teaching drop as the rain <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 32:2.</note>.

->The order of the blessings, one after the other: [1] Concerning washing hands, [2] Who formed...<-

It appears to me that one should not say in the blessing of "Who formed man" <note>Hebrew: *Asher Yatzar*.</note> "Healer of the sick," but rather "Healer of all flesh." For it is said in the Gemara: "One who enters the privy says... when he leaves he says: 'Who formed man with wisdom... it is impossible to stand before You.' How does he conclude? Rav says: 'Healer of the sick.' Shmuel said: 'Abba <note>A nickname for Rav.</note> has made everyone into sick people! Rather, say: Healer of all flesh.' Rav Sheshet said: 'Who does wonders.' Rav Pappa said: 'Therefore, let us say both: Healer of all flesh and Who does wonders.'" This is the language of the Gemara. Since Shmuel challenged Rav, and the Gemara did not refute him, we see the law follows Shmuel—we do not say "Healer of the sick." Furthermore, the law usually follows the *Rosh*, and the *Rosh* wrote: "The conclusion of the Gemara is Rav Pappa's statement to say both... but Rav Pappa only included 'Healer of all flesh' in his version." This is also the version of the *Alfasi* <note>Rabbi Isaac Alfasi (1013–1103), also known as the *Rif*.</note> and Maimonides <note>Hebrew: *Rambam* (1138–1204).</note>. Rashi explains that "Healer of all flesh" corresponds to the act of excretion, which is a healing for the entire body. I also saw this in the Spanish prayer books, and in the book *Matteh Moshe* (Section 35), and the *Tur* likewise did not say "Healer of the sick."

## My God
**The soul... Who gives the rooster understanding...** Regarding what is written in the *Shulchan Aruch* that in a place where [the blessing] "Who has not made me a gentile" [is problematic], one should say "Who has made me a Jew"—one should not actually say this. For if he said that, he would not need to say "Who has not made me a slave." It is understandable if one says "Who has not made me a gentile," then "slave," then "woman"—these three blessings follow a hierarchy of commandments, as the *Beis Yosef* wrote in Section 47. We first bless "Who has not made me a gentile" because they are not commanded in the law at all; then "Who has not made me a slave," because although they have some commandments, they are restricted; and then "Who has not made me a woman," because although she is more significant than a slave, she is not obligated in all commandments. But if he says "Who made me a Jew" at the start, everything is included! Why would he go back and bless "Who has not made me a slave"? It is possible that the printers changed the language here out of fear of the nations in exile <note>Original: "Galuyot"—referring to the censorship of Jewish prayer books by Christian authorities who found the "Who has not made me a gentile" blessing offensive.</note>, which is understandable. The version in the Gemara and in the *Alfasi* is simply "Who has not made me a gentile."

It also analyzes the specific wording of the Asher Yatzar blessing and addresses potential censorship in the text of the "Who has not made me a gentile" blessing.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the morning rituals, specifically focusing on whether the blessing over washing the hands should be performed immediately upon waking or delayed until one reaches the synagogue. # The Valley of Blessing

And upon what should he recite the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" <note>Hebrew: *Al Netilat Yadayim*, often abbreviated as *ANI* in the text</note> if not upon the sequence of Morning Blessings that he requires before the light of morning? If so, the difficulty returns. Furthermore, there is a difficulty within that same response mentioned above; for his Excellence <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, known as the *Rosh* (c. 1250–1327)</note> wrote: "The rule of the matter is that one should not recite the blessing 'On the Washing of the Hands' except in a place where the Sages established it, such as when one washes his hands to eat, or as they established it in the morning when he rises from his bed and his hands are soiled from touching hidden parts of the body, and he must pray, he must wash, etc." Here you see that he wrote at the beginning of this response—just as he wrote in his legal rulings in the chapter *HaRo'eh*—that the Sages only established the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" for eating and for prayer <note>Specifically the *Amidah* prayer</note>. 

This implies that for the sequence of Morning Blessings alone, one does not recite "On the Washing of the Hands." If so, how did he write at the end of that very same response that one who rises early to study should wash his hands and recite the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" for the sequence of the blessings alone, as mentioned? If so, it seems there is a contradiction from the beginning of the response to its end! Rather, we must say that according to the *Rosh*, the sequence of Morning Blessings is considered like the Recitation of the *Shema* and the Prayer itself regarding the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands," for the reason mentioned nearby in the name of the *Blessing of Abraham*.

Alternatively, we can say that what the *Rosh* wrote in his rulings and his response—that the washing of hands and its blessing were only established for the *Shema* and the Prayer—refers to the actual *Shema* and Prayer, not just the sequence of blessings. And what the *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, author of the Four Rows of Jewish Law</note> wrote in Section 47—that one who rises before the light of dawn to study should recite "On the Washing of the Hands," "Who formed man," "My God, the soul," and the entire sequence of blessings—implies clearly that he holds one recites "On the Washing of the Hands" even for the sequence of blessings alone. This is also how it appears at the end of the mentioned response. These words are correct exactly as written; they are right and proper, but they refer to two different circumstances. Everything depends on the occasion and the time, and according to the change of time, the law changes. "A word in its season, how good it is!" <note>Proverbs 15:23</note>. 

Sometimes there is a time when it is better to attach the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" to the sequence of Morning Blessings—even if they are said alone—rather than waiting to recite the blessing until the *Shema* and Prayer. Other times, it is better to wait with the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" in order to attach it to the *Shema* and the Prayer as well. This is the straight path a person should choose for himself: If he rises before the light of dawn, when the time for *Shema* and Prayer has not yet arrived, he should recite the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" immediately, combined with the rest of the Morning Blessings up until the Section of the Continual Offering <note>The *Tamid* section of the liturgy</note> (except for the blessing "Who gave the rooster understanding," as the *Tur* wrote in Section 46). It has already been mentioned above that all the Morning Blessings stand in the place of the *Shema* and Prayer regarding the ability to recite "On the Washing of the Hands" for them, just like the *Shema* and Prayer themselves.

And it is better to recite the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" in conjunction with the other blessings after he has risen from his bed, rather than waiting until the light of dawn, so as not to distance these blessings so far from the time of their subject matter. For it would have been proper to recite each one at its specific time, but because the hands are not clean from the night's sleep, the Sages established that we recite them after washing, as mentioned above in the name of the *Rosh* (and so it is in the *Tur*, Section 46). However, reason dictates that we should recite them at least as close as possible, as mentioned above in Section 6 and below in Section 9.

However, for one who wakes from his sleep and rises after the dawn has broken and goes immediately to the synagogue, this reasoning becomes stronger. Then it is better to wait with the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" until he comes to the synagogue, so that he may recite it with the other blessings, the *Shema*, and the Prayer without any interruption in between. The reason is that the primary establishment of the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" was for the sake of the *Shema* and the Prayer, as the *Rosh* wrote. Therefore, when the time for the *Shema* and Morning Prayer arrives as he rises in the morning, it is not proper to interrupt between them with the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" [said earlier], since the actual *Shema* and Prayer are imminent. It was specifically for one who rose before dawn that the *Rosh* wrote to recite the sequence of blessings until the Section of the Continual Offering. Even though he does not attach the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" to the actual *Shema* and Prayer, we do not mind, because it is impossible to attach them since their time has not yet arrived. (And to wait so long to recite "On the Washing of the Hands" and the other Morning Blessings is not proper to do, for one should not separate the blessings from the time of their subject matter so much; it is proper to attach them to the time of their subject matter as much as possible). Regarding this and similar cases, our Sages were accustomed to say: "Where it is possible, it is possible; where it is not possible, it is not possible."

Thus, since it is not possible to attach the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" to the actual *Shema* and Prayer because their time has not yet arrived, it is proper to rely on the Morning Blessings in this time of need and recite the blessing for the washing because of them, just as one would for the actual *Shema* and Prayer. But when he rises from his bed after the morning has lightened and wants to go immediately to the synagogue, surely it is better to wait with the blessing until he arrives at the synagogue, so that he may arrange it with the other blessings and attach the actual *Shema* and Prayer to one another, since the primary establishment of the blessing was for their sake.

As for what the *Tur* wrote: "And if he goes immediately to the synagogue and wants to wait to recite the blessing etc.," this refers to his own will, as mentioned in Section 6. From the fact that he wrote "and goes immediately to the synagogue," it is obvious that he is speaking of the daytime. Even so, he wrote that the matter depends on a person's will—if he wants, he blesses immediately; if he wants, he waits until he comes to the synagogue. However, he means to say that the "permission" is in his hands, according to the judgment of choice: if he wants to bless, he blesses immediately, and if he wants, he waits. One might think these two choices are equal and both are good, but this is not so. For I have already explained in the second answer that for one who goes to the synagogue upon rising—such as in the summer when the time for *Shema* and Prayer has already arrived—it is better to wait with the blessing until he arrives there. For the true time of the blessing is close to the sequence of blessings, *Shema*, and Prayer, for which the blessing of washing was primarily established.

Rather, his intention in writing "permission is in his hand" means that he has the legal right to do so. He comes to teach us that he is *permitted* to do this, so that you should not say there is a prohibition in the matter due to the "interruption" between the washing he performed in his house and the blessing he will recite in the synagogue. For one should not interrupt between the washing and the blessing, as mentioned in Sections 7 and 5. Based on that logic, it would be forbidden to wash his hands in his house unless he also recited the blessing there, or he would have to wait to wash his hands until the synagogue so that wherever he washes, the blessing would be without the interruption of a "change of place." For a change of place is considered like a distraction of the mind, even if he does not interrupt with conversation, as in the case of a table in a house. Therefore, the *Tur* informs us: "If he goes immediately to the synagogue and wants to wait to recite the blessing until he arrives, to arrange it with the other blessings, the permission is in his hand." It is permitted to do so, and the walking is not considered an interruption, because through this walking he fulfills the commandment of the blessing more perfectly than if he had blessed at home in conjunction with the other blessings at the place of washing and then walked to the synagogue. In that case, he would be interrupting with his walking between the blessing and the actual *Shema* and Prayer.

But this is much better: to bring the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" close to the *Shema* and the Prayer, since the time for them has arrived and he wishes to go immediately to the synagogue. This is how it appears to me to interpret the *Tur's* words here, even though it is a bit of a forced explanation.

And if you say it is still difficult: what the *Tur* wrote in the aforementioned Section 7, after writing "And if he goes immediately to the synagogue and wants to wait etc. the permission is in his hand," he then wrote immediately after: "However, if he blesses 'On the Washing of the Hands' and 'Who formed man' <note>Hebrew: *Asher Yatzar*</note> immediately, some say he must say 'My God, the soul' <note>Hebrew: *Elohai Neshamah*</note> immediately after... and some say he does not need to say it immediately after." This implies that ideally, he could also recite the washing blessing in his house without the entire sequence of blessings, only with "My God, the soul" alone. (And he would attach "My God, the soul" to it because it is a blessing adjacent to its fellow, according to the opinion of the *Rosh*). Does this not contradict everything written above on this matter? (Namely, that it is proper to join the washing blessing to the *Shema* and Prayer, or at least to the full sequence of Morning Blessings). 

One can answer that the *Tur* only wrote this according to the opinion of those who say <note>likely referring to the *Geonim* or specifically Saadia Gaon</note> that one recites the washing blessing every day after tending to his needs for the sake of the "Who formed man" blessing alone, as the *Tur* mentioned in Section 7. But according to the *Rosh* and those who follow him—and according to our custom where we do not recite "On the Washing of the Hands" all day long—even if he blessed in his house early in the morning, even with the "Who formed man" and "My God, the soul" blessings, he would still recite it in the synagogue or in his house with all the other blessings as mentioned above. 

The main thing the *Tur* comes to inform us here is this: if it is his practice throughout the day to recite "On the Washing of the Hands" and "Who formed man" after relieving himself because it is a matter of sanctity, as the *Tur* wrote in the mentioned section, then some say he must say "My God, the soul" immediately after because it is adjacent to the blessing of "Who formed man." Do not wonder that the *Tur* deliberates according to a view he himself does not hold, for we find he did the same regarding this very blessing in Section 473 regarding the Passover Night, where there is a dispute if one recites the washing blessing on the first dipping. He wrote at the end: "And one who wishes to satisfy the doubt should bring himself into an obligation of washing from another side, such as by touching his feet or rubbing his head." The *Beis Yosef* wrote there: "And what he wrote, that one who wishes to satisfy the doubt should bring himself into an obligation of washing... this is according to the reasoning that our Master <note>The *Tur*</note> wrote in Section 7, that after relieving oneself one recites 'On the Washing of the Hands.' But according to the opinion of the *Rosh*, who wrote that one does not bless 'On the Washing of the Hands' after relieving himself unless he wants to pray..." This concludes the point. Thus, what the *Tur* wrote here is the law according to one opinion, even though he himself does not hold by it.

And if you further question what I wrote several times—that one should not interrupt between the washing blessing and the sequence of blessings even with a change of location—and yet this walking is for the sake of the blessing so that he can arrange the other blessings in the synagogue, for the Sages did not establish the washing blessing in its perfection until he sets his heart to bless it with the other blessings for which it was established? If so, it is similar to bringing salt or an appetizer, which does not constitute an interruption between a blessing [and the act]...

<summary>This page analyzes a perceived contradiction in the writings of the Rosh and the Tur regarding whether the blessing for washing hands is tied to the Morning Blessings or the main Prayer service. The author concludes that the timing depends on when one wakes up and that walking to the synagogue is a "necessary" act that does not count as a forbidden interruption.</summary>

<header>The Valley of Blessing</header>

# The Valley of Blessing

They would wash their hands for the Recitation of the *Shema* <note>The central declaration of Jewish faith, recited twice daily</note> and for Prayer <note>The *Amidah* or standing prayer</note> because of the verse "I will wash my hands in purity," as mentioned earlier in Chapter 8 in the name of the *Rosh* <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, a 13th-century legal authority</note>. And when they had completed washing their hands for the *Shema* and Prayer, they would recite the blessing over them before the washing, just as with all other blessings over commandments, which are recited prior to their performance. But as for us, who cannot recite each and every morning blessing at its proper time because our hands are not [ritually] clean as mentioned (and as long as our hands are not clean, one may not mention the Holy Name), it is proper at the very least that we recite the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" <note>Hebrew: *Al Netilat Yadayim*, abbreviated in the text as *ANI*</note> immediately after the washing. We should not interrupt between it and the washing with other blessings, since it is a blessing over a commandment. Therefore, it is our custom to begin with the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" first, in order to keep it close to the act of washing. Afterward, we recite the other blessings, which are blessings of praise for the order of the world and its conduct in the early morning, as mentioned above, following the principle of "the first first, and the last last." Even though the *Rosh* arranged them in the chapter *HaRo'eh* according to the order of the Talmud, the blessing for washing is always functionally first.

But we begin with a different reason as to why we start with the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" even though it is the last of the actions a person performs when rising in the morning. This is based on the response given by the *Rashbi* <note>Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the traditional author of the *Zohar*</note> (brought by the *Beit Yosef* <note>The comprehensive legal code by Rabbi Joseph Karo</note> in his notes on Chapter 4, which is also written in the margins of the *Mordechai* in the chapter *Elu Devarim*). He was asked why they established the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands" in the morning, since this blessing was originally only established for bread during a meal. He elaborated somewhat in his response until he finally wrote:
<margin>Morning of the Dawn</margin> That the Morning Prayer is different from the Afternoon and Evening prayers. That is to say, in the morning we become a "new creation," as it is written: "They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness" <note>Lamentations 3:23</note>. We must thank God for creating us for His glory, to serve Him and bless His Name. For this reason, they established all those blessings in the morning that we recite every single day. Therefore, we must sanctify ourselves and prepare our hands from a vessel, like a Priest <note>Kohen</note> who sanctifies his hands from a vessel before his service. Based on these words, it is proper that we begin with this blessing because of its sanctity, like a Priest standing to serve and bless His Name in the Holy Temple, who would wash his hands from the Basin <note>The *Kiyor*</note> first and then bless. Even though this is a small matter, we perform a symbolic version of this in our synagogues, which are for us a "Minor Sanctuary" during our current exile until the arrival of our Messiah.

And immediately <margin>In Chapter 1</margin> after the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands," one should bless "Who Formed" <note>*Asher Yatzar*, the blessing for the functioning of the body</note>. The *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, author of the four-part legal code</note> also arranged them one after the other in Chapter 6. Also, from what the *Beit Yosef* brought in his notes in this chapter and in Chapter 4—that the people of Spain <note>Sephardic custom</note> practiced reciting "On the Washing of the Hands" and "Who Formed" each in their own home, and then in the synagogue they would begin from "My God, the Soul"—it implies that these blessings are inherently connected to one another.

And even though <margin>Chapter 6</margin> the blessing "Who Formed" should have been delayed until the end, before the blessing "Who removes sleep," according to the order of the world's conduct—for usually the way of the world is that after one puts on his shirt and puts his hand over his eyes, and then puts on his shoes and fastens his belt and wraps his head-covering, he then enters the bathroom to attend to his needs—nevertheless, it seems to the aforementioned authorities that the blessing "Who Formed" should be said immediately after "On the Washing of the Hands." Perhaps the reason is that since the blessing "Who formed man" concerns a permanent matter and was established for the creation of man with wondrous wisdom, as the commentators of blessed memory explained regarding the phrase "Who formed man with wisdom" and "Who acts wondrously." As it says in the Midrash, man is like a skin-bottle full of air, etc., and besides this there are many good qualities, etc., that the Blessed Name bestowed upon man in his creation, which we exalt with this blessing (as the *Beit Yosef* cited from the *Tur*). Therefore, it is worthy to be at the head of all the blessings of praise. Furthermore, it comes from the start of the day, as the *Beit Yosef* wrote. Therefore, it is proper to attach it immediately after the blessing "On the Washing of the Hands."

And the blessing "My God, the Soul" <note>*Elokai Neshamah*</note> is proper to move forward and recite immediately after "Who Formed," before the other morning blessings, because it comes first in time. For first, a person wakes from his sleep, and because of this, it is placed earlier in the Talmud. After saying "My God, the Soul," it is proper to attach the blessing "Who gives the rooster understanding," for a person is woken by the sound of the rooster. This is the order in the Talmud. This is especially true according to the explanation of the author of the *Akeidah* <note>Rabbi Isaac Arama, 15th-century philosopher</note> in Gate 55, who wrote that it is proper to attach it to "My God, the Soul." He wrote there: "If the awareness of the received kindness awakens, and the understanding of the proper reward... upon what does the world stand?" until he said, "Behold, we receive from Him, may He be blessed, specific acts of righteousness and kindness; however, they are all included in two categories necessary for our existence: Vitality and Knowledge, and Sustenance." These are explained in the verses "He gives a soul to the people upon it, and a spirit to those who walk on it," for He, may He be blessed, returns souls to dead corpses when they live on the earth. And it is also said: "For the Lord gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding," which is the bestowal of His knowledge and intellect. And it is also said: "The eyes of all look to You... You open Your hand," for He prepares the sustenance and needs without which it is impossible to stand. For all of this, we are obligated to return the proper reward to our Creator. Therefore, the Sages arranged the order of our praises in our morning blessings: they said "My God, the soul You have given me" and concluded with "Who restores souls to dead corpses." This is the first matter. Regarding the second, they attached "Who gives the rooster understanding." And regarding human needs, they arranged all the other blessings, for they are many: opening the eyes of the blind, straightening the bent, clothing the naked, etc., until the one who "has not withheld any necessity." This is the end of his words for our purposes. And indeed, this is correct: according to his explanation, it is proper to attach the blessing "Who gives the rooster understanding" to "My God, the Soul," and it is also proper to say it before the other blessings established for physical needs, so that the blessings established for these three categories follow one after the other according to their rank and importance. For certainly Vitality and Knowledge—for which these two blessings were established—precede other needs in importance.

As for the three customary blessings: "Who has not made me a Gentile," "a slave," or "a woman," <margin>In the *Tur*, Chapter 40</margin> the *Tur* wrote in Chapter 40 that in the Ashkenazic prayer books, they are written immediately after "Who gives the rooster understanding," but in Sephardic prayer books, they are written at the end, after "Who removes sleep." There is no concern in changing this, but it seems better to arrange them immediately after "Who gives the rooster understanding," as they are written in our prayer books. They are connected to one another. Even though the content of these blessings shows they were not established based on the order of the world's conduct, but rather as praise and thanks to the Omnipresent for choosing us from all nations and bringing us close to His service, and giving us His Torah and its commandments—which are not applicable to Gentiles—and the exemption from time-bound commandments [for women]... we praise the Creator that we are among those commanded and active, for in this our reward is complete, as the Sages said: "Greater is one who is commanded and acts." For this reason, it is proper to attach these three blessings to "Who gives the rooster understanding." For you already know that "Who gives the rooster understanding" was established for the wisdom and understanding given by God, and it is also known that the essence of wisdom and understanding is in the Torah and its commandments. Thus, it is proper to attach these three blessings to "Who gives the rooster understanding" since they deal with these matters.

(Note: The author of *Tola'at Yaakov* <note>A mystical commentary on the prayers</note> wrote: "Regarding 'Who has not made me a Gentile,' you should look into a hidden secret in this blessing. For all the blessings we mentioned above should logically be recited every day. But this blessing—he should have recited it only once from the day he was born! The same applies to 'Who has not made me a slave' and 'a woman.' But the intention here is that when the soul ascends at night to the upper world, if he is righteous, many heavenly ministers take hold of it and lead it to its proper place. But if he is wicked, many angels of destruction come out to meet it... and they place it in the place of a defiled Gentile, or a slave, or a woman. But when a person wakes from his bed, if he knows himself to be righteous, he blesses 'Who has not made me a Gentile,' meaning He did not leave me in the place of a Gentile.") According to this reason too, it is proper to attach these three blessings to "My God, the Soul." Afterward, he should arrange the rest of the blessings, such as "Clothing the naked," "Opening the eyes of the blind," etc., following one another in the manner mentioned above. This is the straight path before a man, following the order of the world and human conduct early in the morning, one after the other, intertwined like sisters.

Furthermore, one should bring himself every day into the obligation of these blessings so as to fulfill the opinion of every man. For the *Rambam* <note>Maimonides, 12th-century philosopher and legalist</note> wrote in Chapter 6 of the *Laws of Prayer* (and the *Beit Yosef* brought this in Chapter 46) that any of these blessings that one is not obligated in, he does not recite. The custom of reciting all of them one after another in the synagogue—whether one was obligated or not—is an error in their hands, and it is not proper to do so. Even the *Rosh* and the *Tur* who wrote that all the blessings regarding the order of the world (such as "My God the Soul," "Who gives the rooster understanding," "Who spreads the earth") should not be omitted even if one did not hear the rooster or walk on the earth—they only said this specifically for those. But those blessings regarding physical benefits, such as "Clothing the naked," "Crowning Israel," "Who provides for all my needs," and "Straightening the bent"—if one does not benefit from them, such as if he stayed in bed and did not dress or belt himself, he does not bless them. They follow the opinion of the *Tosafot* <note>Medieval commentators on the Talmud</note> on the chapter *HaRo'eh*...

# The Valley of Blessing

<margin>And it is according to its writing and its language <note>This likely refers to the standard text of the Code of Jewish Law being discussed.</note></margin>

<gloss>Meaning, in the days of the Sages of the Talmud.</gloss>

<gloss>Because their hands were considered "sanctified" and prepared, they were careful to wash their hands and stand in a manner that allowed them to say the blessings in purity. But for us, who cannot be so careful to remain in such a state of purity, the authorities established that we should say them after the ritual washing, as written by Rabbenu Yonah and the Rosh at the end of the third chapter of Berakhot, and the Tur brought this in Section 46.</gloss>

<term>Explanation: <note>In Hebrew: *Pi*, an abbreviation for *Perush*</note></term> When a person wakes from his sleep and wishes to rise from his bed, first and foremost he puts on his undershirt, as the *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, 14th-century legalist</note> wrote—that he should put it on while still lying down. Therefore, it is appropriate to first recite the blessing: **"Who clothes the naked"** <note>Hebrew: *Malbish Arumim*</note>. After putting on his shirt, he passes his hands over his eyes using a sheet or his shirt <gloss>meaning, it is forbidden to touch the eyes with the hands before washing due to the danger of morning impurities, as written in the Orach Chaim, Section 4</gloss> because his eyes are still bleary from sleep. Therefore, it is appropriate to recite afterward: **"Who opens the eyes of the blind"** <note>Hebrew: *Pokeiach Ivrim*</note>. Afterward, he sits up on his bed and stretches his limbs; therefore, it is appropriate to recite afterward: **"Who releases the bound"** <note>Hebrew: *Matir Asurim*</note>. After sitting on the bed, he stands up from his bed; therefore, it is appropriate to recite: **"Who straightens the bent"** <note>Hebrew: *Zokef Kefufim*</note>. After he has moved his feet from the bed and placed them on the ground, it is appropriate to recite: **"Who spreads the earth over the waters"** <note>Hebrew: *Rokea Ha'aretz Al HaMayim*</note>. After his feet have descended to the ground, he puts on his shoes. Presumably, a person’s shoes are prepared near his bed so they are ready if he needs to go out at night, lest he strike his foot against a stone. Since they are ready before him and he puts them on before his other clothes, it is appropriate to recite: **"Who has provided me with my every need"** <note>Hebrew: *She'asah Li Kol Tzorki*</note>. After putting on his shoes, he goes to put on his outer garments for the day, for presumably a person's fine clothes are not kept right next to the bed where they might get dusty or soiled by the feathers of the pillow and blanket. Since he must walk to them to put them on, he should recite: **"Who establishes the steps of man"** <note>Hebrew: *Asher Hechin Mitz'adei Gaver*</note>. After he has put on his clothes and his belt is upon them, it is appropriate to recite: **"Who girdles Israel with strength"** <note>Hebrew: *Ozer Yisrael BiGevurah*</note>. Once he is dressed and belted, he covers his head with the specific head-covering for the day, for until now his head was presumably covered with a nightcap—as it is a mark of piety for a person's head to be covered at night just as it is during the day. Now, when he has finished his garments and wishes to go out, he covers his head with the specific covering for the day. Therefore, he should recite: **"Who crowns Israel with splendor"** <note>Hebrew: *Oter Yisrael BiTifarah*</note>. Then follows the blessing **"Who removes sleep [from my eyes]"**, which was established for the washing of the face, which is the final act. Therefore, its blessing is at the end. According to this, the blessing of "Who crowns Israel" should properly be at the end, just before the blessing of "Who removes sleep." After all these mentioned acts, he washes his hands and washes his face. Indeed, they are arranged in the Talmud one after the other at the end of the blessings, as it says there: "When he washes his hands, let him say 'On the washing of the hands' <note>Hebrew: *Al Netilat Yadayim*</note>; when he washes his face, let him say 'Who removes sleep...'" and such is the version of the *Rosh*. From this, we see why we begin with the blessings... until what the *Rosh* wrote <gloss>in the chapter "HaRoeh" and brought above in Section 8</gloss>. We shall explain these blessings further. Nowadays, the custom is to recite these blessings after washing the hands, for as long as one's hands are not clean, one should not recite them in order. As for the rule that all blessings must be recited "prior to the performance" of the deed, that applies to the blessings over commandments where we say "and commanded us"—one must first bless the Holy One for what He commanded us to bring us closer to His service. But a blessing of thanks and praise, such as these, can be recited afterward <gloss>and so wrote the Radbaz in the chapter on Passover, see there</gloss>. Based on these words, it works out well that we begin with the blessing over washing the hands, as it must be "prior to the performance" since it is a blessing over a commandment. Even though this specific blessing over washing hands cannot truly be "prior to its performance" for the reason the *Rosh* wrote—that a person’s hands are constantly active and it is impossible not to have touched a "soiled place" during the night <gloss>as the Tur also wrote in Sections 46 and 158</gloss>—nevertheless, logic dictates that we should bless as close to the washing as possible and not interrupt between the washing and the blessing with other blessings. This is also found in the foundations of the *Rosh* in the name of *Maharam of Rothenburg* regarding one who leaves the latrine and wishes to wash his hands to eat, etc. I have elaborated on this in Section 7. But regarding the rest of the mentioned blessings, since they are blessings of thanks and praise, it is not so strictly required if we interrupt slightly between them and the actions they describe. Regarding the fact that they arranged it <gloss>meaning the blessing "On the washing of the hands"</gloss> in the Talmud at the end, that was specifically for them, as they would say each blessing at its specific time before the washing. Thus, they would wash their hands only after they had said all the blessings; they only instituted the washing of the hands for the *Shema* and for Prayer. Even though their hands were clean, they would still recite all these blessings before the washing. Nevertheless...

<column-break/>

And let no one mistake the Gloss written in the *Shulchan Aruch* Section 46 regarding what is written inside: "One must bless every day **'Who made me a Jew'**" <note>This was a variant of the blessing "Who did not make me a gentile."</note>. It is written there in the glosses: "Even a convert can recite this, but he should not say 'Who made me a Jew' if he was originally a gentile, for he was a gentile at first." This is the language of the Gloss there. From the words as they are written here in the Gloss, one would understand that the *Maharam* <note>Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg</note> believes that in this version—where it is written that one must bless every day "Who made me a Jew"—it is the version of our ancestors, intended to be said in place of "Who did not make me a gentile," and the aforementioned Gloss refers to that, saying "even a convert may bless this way." Heaven forbid that a holy mouth should say such a thing! For it is already known that one who blesses "Who made me a Jew" and afterward blesses "Who did not make me a slave" and "Who did not make me a woman" is reciting a "blessing in vain" <note>Hebrew: *Bracha Levatala*—a serious liturgical error</note>, as mentioned earlier. This is similar to what the *Tur* wrote in Section 46: "If he went ahead and blessed 'Who straightens the bent' before he blessed 'Who releases the bound,' he should not recite the latter." Rather, this Gloss is a spiritual error and was printed by mistake. It seems to me that it should be as written by Rabbi Moshe <note>The Rema</note>... whose name is the source of all the glosses in his *Shulchan Aruch*. It seems he can bless **"Who made me a convert,"** and "soul-making" is also called "doing/making," as it is written: "And the souls that they made in Haran." Blessed be the God of salvations who saved us from this error. [The list of blessings includes:] **"Who did not make me a slave," "Who did not make me a woman," "Who clothes the naked," "Who opens the eyes of the blind," "Who releases the bound," "Who straightens the bent," "Who spreads the earth over the waters," "Who has provided me with my every need," "Who establishes the steps of man," "Who girdles Israel with strength," "Who crowns Israel with splendor," "Who removes sleep," and "Who grants knowledge."** These are the core blessings. As for **"Who gives strength to the weary"** <note>Hebrew: *HaNoten LaYa'ef Koach*</note>, even though there is a good basis for saying it, as the *Tur* wrote in Section 46, nevertheless, since it is not mentioned in the Talmud, one should not say it, as the *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo</note> wrote. Many other legal authorities did not mention it either. Similarly, the blessing **"Who uplifts the humble"** <note>Hebrew: *Magbiha Shefalim*</note> should not be said for this same reason. These are the words of the *Maharshal* <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria</note>: "Afterward, when he saw me reach the Morning Blessings... I skipped 'Who uplifts the humble' because this blessing appears neither in the Gemara nor in the words of the Geonim <note>Early medieval sages</note>. Even Maimonides and the *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* did not mention it. I also found in the *Leket* <note>A collection of customs</note> that one should not say it... and regarding 'Who gives strength to the weary,' I also do not practice saying it since it is found in neither the Babylonian nor Jerusalem Talmud. No author brought it, except that the *Tur* once wrote regarding the Ashkenazic prayer books that it was established based on a Midrash... And it is surprising, for in the Responsa of the *Tashbetz*, it concludes that regarding the practices of the Talmud, no person has the authority to institute or add a new blessing, even the Geonim do not have that authority. Therefore, it seems right not to say it." This is what I wrote in my great work on the first chapter of *Ketubot*. The general rule is: any blessing not mentioned in the Gemara or by the legal authorities should not be said by an individual. One should be even more careful not to change the version mentioned in our Talmud. Regarding the petition arranged after the seventy-two verses beginning with the name "The Lord, God of Israel," which concludes with the blessing "Who hears prayer"—and similarly the conclusion of some other printed petitions—it is an error for whoever concludes them with a formal blessing, for this blessing is not mentioned in the Talmud or legal authorities and has no basis anywhere. Therefore, whoever says it, recites a blessing in vain. Instead, he should say, **"Blessed are You, Who hears prayer"** (without mentioning the Divine Name). I have written the order of these blessings one after the other because I have seen some prayer books where they are written out of order; for example, "Who straightens the bent" is written before "Who releases the bound," or "Who establishes the steps of man" is written before "Who has provided me with my every need," or "Who opens the eyes of the blind" before "Who clothes the naked." None of this is correct. The primary order is one after the other as I have shown here, derived from the Gemara (in the chapter "HaRoeh") which mentions them in this specific order, according to the version of the *Rosh*. The exception is the blessing "On the washing of the hands," which is mentioned in the Gemara last, before the blessing "Who removes sleep," but we are accustomed to saying it at the very beginning of the blessings for reasons I will mention soon, with God's help. When you look at the sequence of these blessings one after another, you will see they are truly arranged according to the order of the world and the conduct of a person rising from his bed (early in the morning), as I will explain further on, with God's help.

And even though in their days they would say each one at its specific time, as implies the language of the Gemara and as the *Tur* brought in Section 46—saying "When he wakes from his sleep, let him say 'My God, the soul...'; when he hears the sound of the rooster, let him say 'Who gave the rooster understanding...'; when he dresses, let him say 'Who clothes the naked'; when he puts his hands to his eyes, let him say 'Who opens the eyes of the blind,'" and so on for all of them—implying they blessed each one at its moment even before washing...

<summary>This page discusses the proper order and source of the Morning Blessings, arguing that they should follow the logical physical actions of waking up and that only blessings found in the Talmud should be formally recited with God's name.</summary>
<keywords>Morning Blessings, Birkhot HaShachar, Talmud, Halakha, Maharshal, Rosh, Rema, prayer order, ritual washing, Netilat Yadayim, blessings in vain</keywords>

# Tractate Chullin
<note>While the header identifies this as the Talmudic tractate "Chullin" (concerning dietary laws), the content of this page consists of liturgical poetry, Kabbalistic instructions, and ethical guidance.</note>

Remember the footsteps of Your Messiah <note>original: "ikvot mashiḥecha"</note>; remember Your congregation which You acquired of old, the tribe of Your inheritance which You redeemed, this Mount Zion where You have dwelt. Remember, O Lord, the affection of Jerusalem; the love of Zion do not forget forever. Remember for us the Covenant of the Patriarchs, as You said: "And I will remember My covenant with Jacob, and also My covenant with Isaac, and also My covenant with Abraham will I remember, and the land I will remember" <note>Leviticus 26:42</note>. Where are Your former loving-kindnesses, O Lord, which You swore to David in Your faithfulness? Rise up to help us and redeem us for the sake of Your kindness. Value our ancient mercies as in the days of our troubles; and if not for our sake, act for Your sake. Rise, O Lord, and plead Your cause; remember our reproach from the hand of the base man all day long. Why has the wicked man spurned God <note>original: "AHEI," a common substitution for the Divine Name</note>, saying in his heart, "You will not require it"? Search out the wickedness of the wicked and the evil man until You find no more. You, O Lord, are enthroned forever; Your throne is from generation to generation. Why do You forget us forever, and forsake us for so long? Turn us back to You, O Lord, and we shall return; renew our days as of old. For You have utterly rejected us; You are exceedingly angry with us. Have You utterly rejected the cities of Judah? Does Your soul loathe Zion? Why have You struck us so that there is no healing for us? We hoped for peace, but there is no good; for a time of healing, and behold—terror! We know, O Lord, our wickedness and the iniquity of our fathers, for we have sinned against You. Do not spurn us, for Your Name's sake; do not dishonor the throne of Your glory. Remember, and do not break Your covenant with us. For You have utterly rejected us; You are exceedingly angry with us. 

Turn us back, Master of the Universe, to Your Sanctuary forever. O Lord, God of Israel, stand up from the Throne of Judgment and sit upon the Throne of Mercy, and have compassion on us for Your sake, and for the sake of our ancestors, and for the sake of the pious and the upright in their hearts, and for the sake of all those killed for Your Unity <note>original: "yichudecha," referring to the declaration of God's oneness</note>, and for the sake of all those burned for the sanctification of Your Name, and for the sake of all whose blood was shed for Your Unity—the blood of the souls of the poor and the innocent who poured out their lives unto death, and beneath the <unclear>yoke</unclear> lowered their heads. They followed after You and were killed for You all day long. They would offer before You burnt offerings and sacrifices, prepared as a pleasing aroma—the head and the pieces. And they, in their deaths, were happy and joyful, saying to me: "I am ready for song and for its leaders, and I will offer myself, my fat, and my blood. I will give my rest and my head, my flesh, the fruit of my womb, and the sin-offering of my soul." And a soul fainting, wallowing in blood, a heritage passed from fathers to sons, a judgment to rise for them as a voluntary peace-offering, a favor for them before the Lord. 

Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but to Your Name give glory, for the sake of Your kindness and Your truth. Why should the nations say, "Where is their God?" And You shall grant us our inheritance and remove us <note>from exile</note>, for You are our hope, Gracious and Merciful One. May our troubles be before Your eyes; see our affliction and plead our cause, and let our grievance rise before You at all times—the grievance of Your Great Name which is profaned among the wicked; profaned by those who reproached You and gave their glory to another. And may the bloodshed of those called by Your Name be <unclear>avenged</unclear>. O our God, look upon those who reproach You, and do not cover their iniquity, and let their sin not be blotted out from before You. And let all the nations know that You are the Lord, the Holy One of Israel; and they shall sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and stand in awe of the God of Israel. 

Please remember Your children, the poor and the needy who look forward to Your salvation. Our Father in Heaven, You are righteous and You are pious, and all Your deeds are in faithfulness. May Your mercies be rolled upon Your children who are in the land of their captors, and bring out from the prison-house those who sit in darkness and the bound—the prisoners of hope. Open <note>their eyes</note> and strengthen <note>them</note>. Remember for us, O Lord God of Israel, that You sanctified Your people Israel from among seventy nations; and it was good that You separated the tribe of Levi to stand and serve and to give thanks to Your Name, and Israel to achieve atonement through them. And now, through our many iniquities, our resources are cut off, and our glory is cast down, and we have been emptied of all good, and we have nothing but our prayers and the outpourings of the sources of our hearts. For we are thirsty for Your mercies like a weary land for water, crying out before You with a broken heart, pouring out our speech before You so that the Lord may hear and answer. Remember for us what You commanded us in Your Torah: "If your brother becomes impoverished and his hand falters, you shall uphold him" <note>Leviticus 25:35</note>. And we are Your children and Your toddlers, Your delights. Have mercy on us in Your great compassion, and fulfill for us what was said by Your prophet: "For My own sake I will do it, for I will not give My glory to another" <note>Isaiah 48:11</note>. You have made us a <unclear>reproach</unclear>, You have afflicted us, we have seen years of evil. Send the Redeemer to redeem us and save those who remain upon Your land. Return us, our children, and may Your blessings be upon us. Let those who dwell in the dust awake and sing, and may eternal joy be upon their heads, as it is said: "And the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with singing, with everlasting joy upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away" <note>Isaiah 35:10</note>. Awake now! For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but My kindness shall not depart from you, and My covenant of peace shall not be removed, says the Lord who has compassion on you. Awake now! "And I will restore the captivity and have mercy on the House of Israel, and I will be jealous for My Holy Name" <note>Ezekiel 39:25</note>. And the prophet said further: "As a man whom his mother comforts, so will I comfort you; and you shall be comforted in Jerusalem" <note>Isaiah 66:13</note>. May it be His will.

-> Psalm 9, 87, 107 <-

**Father** of Mercy, who does good in His favor to Zion; may You build the walls of Jerusalem. Have mercy on Zion as You said, and establish it as You spoke—a constant redemption. Hasten the salvation and return to Jerusalem with great mercies through Your prophet: "My house shall be built, says the Lord of Hosts, and a measuring line shall be stretched out over Jerusalem" <note>Zechariah 1:16</note>. And it says further: "Proclaim, saying: Thus says the Lord of Hosts: My cities shall again overflow with prosperity, and the Lord will again comfort Zion and again choose Jerusalem" <note>Zechariah 1:17</note>. And it says: "For the Lord has comforted Zion; He has comforted all her waste places, and has made her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of the Lord; joy and gladness shall be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of song" <note>Isaiah 51:3</note>. And the first of the prophets, Moses our Teacher <note>original: "MRAH"</note>, said: "If your outcasts are at the ends of the heavens, from there the Lord your God will gather you, and from there He will take you" <note>Deuteronomy 30:4</note>. Our soul waited for the Lord; He is our help and our shield. For in Him our heart shall rejoice—<note>The letters of "rejoice," *Yismach*, are an anagram for *Mashiach* (Messiah)</note>—for in His Holy Name we have trusted. Let Your kindness, O Lord, be upon us, even as we have hoped in You. The Lord will not forsake His people for the sake of His great Name. And may it be the will of the God of my mouth... <note>abbreviated prayer</note>.

**And this** was the order written by the students of the Ari, of blessed memory <note>Rabbi Isaac Luria, 16th-century Kabbalist</note>, and it is found in the *Book of Intentions* <note>Sefer HaKavanot</note>. When he rises before midnight <note>original: "chatzot laila"</note>, which is the hour when, so to speak, "In secret places my soul shall weep" <note>referring to God's mourning for the Temple</note>, he should rise and wake from his sleep, wash his hands, and tend to his needs. He should sit before the *Mezuzah* on the ground—not even on a pillow—in the darkness. He should cover his head like a mourner, wrapped in grief, and begin by saying, "By the rivers of Babylon..." <note>Psalm 137</note>. He should bring to mind the Destruction of the House <note>the Temple</note>. In "A Psalm of Asaph" <note>Psalm 79</note>, he should meditate on the killing of the righteous. "Remember O Lord..."—this should be brought up in place of the circumcision <note>a complex Kabbalistic meditation</note>. He should intend that "the Lord's strength was for us." He should say, "The crown of our head has fallen," and meditate on the word "fallen" <note>Hebrew: "nafela"</note>, which relates to the falling of the Divine Presence. He should meditate on the word "Youth" <note>Hebrew: "na'ar"</note>, which is a title for the angel Metatron. "For this our heart was faint"—the letters of "faint" <note>H-D-V-H</note> are inverted to become "suffering" <note>D-V-H</note> all day long. For these things... the eighteen edges. He should say the lament "Upon my palaces..." and afterward the verses from Isaiah: "Look down from heaven and see..." "For You are our Father..." until "our congregation." Afterward, the verses "You had mercy on your walls..." until "they passed through its gates." "O God, do not be silent." "You will arise and have mercy on Zion, for Your servants desire..." "Who builds Jerusalem, the Lord." "As the deer pants..." "Judge me, O God." "May the Lord answer you in the day of trouble." "God be gracious to us." And one should crown the Lord with all his heart, and meditate on the four expansions of the Name <note>Kabbalistic permutations</note> *MATZPAD*, *YEDID*, *EHEYEH* <note>Technical names for Divine attributes in Lurianic Kabbalah</note>.

And immediately when the day shines, he should run to the synagogue to be among the first ten, as our Sages of blessed memory said. The matter of the order of prayer will be described at the end, God willing, in the section on the House of Prayer. And immediately when he leaves the synagogue, he should go to the Study Hall to study Torah, to fulfill: "They go from strength to strength" <note>Psalm 84:8</note>.

**And if** afterward he engages in business, he should do so in good faith. He should intend to remove his hands from what is not his boundary. His work should be temporary and his Torah study permanent. If he returns to his studies whenever he is free, his Torah is called his "profession." When he pauses to eat, it should be in holiness and purity, as it is written: "For the sake of..." and "Holy." Afterward, he should wash every day and designate a measure of "acts of loving-kindness" <note>gemilut chasadim</note> to fulfill that which is said: "The kindness of God is all day long." When the time for the Afternoon Prayer <note>Mincha</note> arrives, he should run to the synagogue to be among the first ten. Afterward, he should say, "Evening, morning, and noon I will speak..." <note>Psalm 55:18</note>. For the patterns of repentance are engraved, and he should complete the repentance and the confessions, and repair what was damaged through the power of the Zohar. At night, he should return to the order of the night as mentioned above, and then he shall ascend on high.

"As my law": meaning my foundation, my hope, my shell, all the nations I have passed. "As my law, the shell of all the nations": many nations, like the "overturning of many nations."

Explanation: "In the footsteps of Your Messiah": in the initial tribulations, hidden beneath the <unclear>foundation</unclear>, so that he cannot come to the world, God forbid.

Explanation: This is a cry and a plea: "Where is that which You swore to David in Your faithfulness?" and why is it that You forsake us now?

Explanation: Do not be mistaken; for our deeds, act for Your sake, for our quarrel is Your quarrel. For the <unclear>base man</unclear> will mock us, for he has seen in You the power to <unclear>do evil</unclear>.

Explanation: For every <unclear>reproach</unclear> of Your spirit is toward us, because "You will not require." And do not cover up what he says and does.

Explanation: Remember his youth and his strength. You shall require the <unclear>shame</unclear> to say that "You will not require," as mentioned above. For it is as if He is in His <unclear>glory</unclear> and You are not doing so. Explanation: We know that You are enthroned forever, and likewise "Why do You forget us?"—that You should not forget us at all. For You are the one who said "I am the Lord," so Your promise exists.

And he should bind his strength with rising and <unclear>clapping</unclear>, and all should go according to the Names in the revelation of the Ari, of blessed memory. And the *Zohar* wrote <unclear>concerning this</unclear> that his whole body should not walk upright, but should be bowed and low. And when he does this because he is accepting the consequences of his sins, it is permitted. And so did King David, peace be upon him, as it is said: "I went about gloomy and bowed down..." and he goes and <unclear>weeps</unclear> and completes <note>the prayer</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Morning Blessings (Birkhot HaShachar) and transitions into the proper order of study and the mourning for the destroyed Temple in Jerusalem.
