<page-num>121</page-num>
<header>The Valley of Blessing</header>
<meta>catchword: footsteps</meta>

<margin>And even though the *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo, 16th-century author of the Shulchan Aruch</note> wrote in *Orach Chayim* Section 46 <note>original: "סימן מ'" - the text says 40, but likely refers to 46</note> as follows: "And regarding the *Kol Bo* <note>A 13th-century legal compendium</note>, he wrote that the custom spread in those lands to recite them [the blessings] in order. Similarly, Rav Natronai, Rav Amram, and the other Geonim <note>Leaders of Babylonian academies, c. 600–1000 CE</note> established the practice to recite them all in order. Even if one did not perform the specific action, he does not bless for himself alone, but rather he blesses the Name [God] on behalf of the whole world for performing all these goodnesses and kindnesses for everyone at all times." End of quote.</margin>

And there is proof for this, see there. And even though the *Beit Yosef* wrote in *Orach Chayim* Section 46 as follows: "And regarding the *Kol Bo*, he wrote that the custom spread in those lands to recite them in order. Similarly, Rav Natronai, Rav Amram, and the other Geonim established the practice to recite them all in order. Even if one did not perform the specific action, he does not bless for himself alone, but rather he blesses the Name on behalf of the whole world for performing all these goodnesses and kindnesses for everyone at all times." End of quote. This implies from his words that even blessings meant for one's specific enjoyment may be recited even if one was not obligated in them, etc. Nevertheless, since we find that the *Tosafot* and the *Rosh* <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, 13th-century German-Spanish scholar</note>—whose waters we drink and whose words we generally do not deviate from—and all their words are like streams of fire to us, it is better for us to be cautious. Therefore, one should not recite these blessings unless he has become obligated in them. This is also the opinion of the Rambam <note>Maimonides</note>, as was brought above. It is proper to be concerned with their words and not enter into a doubt regarding a "wasted blessing" <term>Bracha Levatala</term><note>A blessing said in vain, which is a violation of taking God's name in greed</note>. We should prepare ourselves to fulfill the requirement properly. 

I found a similar case in the *Tur* <note>The code of law by Rabbi Jacob ben Asher</note> *Orach Chayim* in Section 600 regarding the law of the *Kiddush* <note>Sanctification prayer over wine</note> on the second night of *Rosh Hashanah* <note>The Jewish New Year</note>. It says: "And regarding the blessing of Time (*Shehecheyanu*) on the second night during *Kiddush*, and on the second day for the *Shofar* [ram's horn], Rashi wrote in a response: 'My teachers say we only say the blessing of Time on the first day, for the two days are considered a single long day. But I say one must say the blessing of Time, and such is the custom in my place and all places I have passed...'" It concludes that even if there is a doubt, one says the blessing. However, the Geonim wrote that one should *not* say the blessing of Time on the second day. On this, the *Rosh* wrote: "It is good that a person takes a **new fruit** and places it before him, and recites *Shehecheyanu* having the fruit in mind as well, thus exiting the doubt." This was the custom of Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg. 

Since this is the case there, certainly in our matter we should be concerned with the words of the *Tosafot*, the Rambam, and the *Rosh*. We should bring ourselves every morning to a state of obligation for the blessings to satisfy all opinions. This is how one should do it: He should bless in order, the first first and the last last. From the moment he wakes up, while still lying in his bed, he should put on his shirt <note>original: "כותנו" - tunic or shirt</note>. After dressing, he should intend to pass his hands over his eyes using a sheet or his cloak to open his eyes. Afterward, he should sit a little on his bed and intend to "rejoice his bones" which were bound all night. Then he should intend to straighten himself, then descend from his bed and intend for his feet to touch the actual ground to stand for a moment before putting on his shoes. Then he should walk a bit in his room to put on his daytime clothes, which are not placed so close to his bed. He should gird his belt and cover his head. When he washes his hands and face, he should also intend to wash the residue from his eyes caused by sleep, and this will be the "one who removes sleep from my eyes." This means through this washing, he removes all slumber from his eyes. After performing all these actions with intention to make himself obligated in the blessings written above, then his actions will be proper before the Blessed One to recite the blessings in order according to everyone.

---

# The Blessing of the Torah would be more proper after "My God, the soul..." to also exempt the verses said before the Section of the Daily Offering

As I wrote in Section 46, see there. And according to what I wrote above—that it is good to connect the blessing "Who gives the rooster understanding" to the blessing of "My God, the soul..." <note>Elohai Neshamah</note> according to the explanation of the *Ba'al Akeidah* <note>Rabbi Isaac Arama, 15th-century philosopher</note>—I said it is good to delay the **Blessing of the Torah** until after the first "Blessed art Thou" which is the end of the morning blessings and the Daily Offering. It is possible that the *Tur* was not strict that the Torah blessing be specifically immediately after "My God, the soul," but only that it be before the verses of study. Since no verse has been mentioned until now, I said it is good to mix the Torah blessings with everything attached to them—namely the Priestly Blessing and "These are the things..."—immediately after the blessing "Who bestows good kindnesses," which follows the first "Blessed art Thou." This is connected to the blessing of "good kindnesses," for there is no greater kindness than Him giving us His holy Torah, which is the life of our lives and the length of our days, His precious vessel that He delighted in every day. The Torah itself is called "kindness," as it says: "And the Torah of kindness is on her tongue" <note>Proverbs 31:26</note>. Connecting kindness to kindness is preferable.

---

# And after saying the Torah blessings with all that is attached to them, he shall begin and say "May it be Your will that You save me today from the brazen..." and "A person should always be God-fearing"

And he should say from here on in the order written in the prayer books (*Siddurim*). And if he rises to study before the light of morning, it is good to say the entire order of blessings and praises one after another in the manner mentioned, including the Torah blessing and its attachments until the Section of the Daily Offering. This is better than waiting until the light of morning, so as not to distance these blessings so far from the time of their subject matter. Even though he is not performing the actions at that moment because his hands were unrefined from the night <note>And because of this, after he washes his hands and they are clean, he should bless immediately and hasten to arrange the blessings so as not to distance them from their subject. This was mentioned several times above in Section 7 and 8, and so it is in the Responsa of the Rosh, Rule 4, Section 1, brought by the Tur at the end of Section 46 and the Beit Yosef in Section 4</note>. And thus wrote my father and teacher, the *Rosh*: "Those who rise early to study before the dawn should bless 'Who fashioned [man],' 'My God, the soul,' and the entire order of blessings and the Torah blessings. But the Section of the Daily Offering he should not read until the day breaks, for it stands in place of the offering of the sacrifice, whose time is only by day. Likewise, the blessing 'Who gives the rooster understanding' should not be recited until the day." End of quote. It is also good to first recite the Section of the Binding of Isaac (*Akeidah*), the Section of the Manna, the Ten Commandments, and other verses of mercy, supplication, and requests. And the *Beit Yosef* wrote in *Tur Orach Chayim* Section 1: "It is good to say them (meaning the Ten Commandments, so that he remembers the standing at Mount Sinai every day and his faith is strengthened; and the Section of the Binding to remember the merit of the Patriarchs before the Holy One, and also to subdue his inclination to the service of God just as Isaac bound his soul; and the Section of the Manna so he believes that all his sustenance comes through Divine Providence)." It is good to have intention in all this at the time of reading each section. It is also good to pray before the morning light over the Destruction [of the Temple] and the Exile, as the *Rosh* wrote (in the first chapter of *Berakhot*), and the *Tur* brought it in Section 1: "It is proper for every God-fearing person to be pained and worried at that hour, and to pour out supplications over the destruction of the House [Temple]..." etc., from *Emek HaBerakhah*.

---

# And behold, regarding 
I have seen many versions of the supplications and the awakening of the Destruction. I have mentioned these two passages to be said before the body of the prayer for the Destruction, so that a person may be moved to pain himself when remembering the destruction, as if the Divine Presence itself <term>Shekhinah</term> is in pain:

### For this our heart is faint, for these things our eyes are dim; for Mount Zion which is desolate, foxes walk upon it <note>Lamentations 5:17-18</note>. Zion has become a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation. Our holy and beautiful house where our fathers praised You has been burned with fire, and all our pleasant things have become a ruin. O Lord God of Hosts, how long will You not have mercy on Your city? And this Jerusalem which You have been angry with these many years, how long, O God, shall the adversary reproach? Shall the enemy blaspheme Your name forever? How long shall Your glory be in captivity in the hand of the adversary? Until when shall there be weeping in Zion and mourning in Jerusalem? Give Yourself no rest, do not keep silent, and do not be still. For behold, Your enemies make a tumult, and those who hate You have lifted up their head. How long, O Lord, will You look on and be silent? When will You arise and be a refuge? O Jealous and Vengeful One, be jealous for Your name which is praised among all nations but is being desecrated. O Lord, God of vengeance, God of vengeance, shine forth <note>against the four destructions</note>. Lift up Yourself, Judge of the earth; render a recompense to the proud. O Hope of Israel, its Savior in time of trouble, why should You be as a man astonished, as a mighty man that cannot save? Yet You, O Lord, are in our midst, and Your name is called upon us; do not leave us. Why do You forget us forever, and the smoke of Your anger burn against the sheep of Your pasture? Why, O Lord, do You stand afar off? Why do You hide Yourself in times of trouble? Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction and oppression? Remember, O Lord, against the children of Edom the day of Jerusalem, who said, "Raze it, raze it, even to the foundation thereof!"

<header>Tractate Chullin</header>

The honor of the day <note>Friday</note> comes before the honor of the night. There are those who interpret this to mean precisely on the afternoon of the Eve of the Sabbath, and similarly every day due to great wealth; however, there is at least a prohibition against entering the Sabbath while one is so full that they have no appetite. End of quote. The Rema <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles, the 16th-century Polish authority on Jewish law</note> wrote in his glosses to Section 249 that a meal whose set time falls on the Eve of the Sabbath—such as a circumcision <term>Brit Milah; the covenant of circumcision</term> or the redemption of the firstborn <term>Pidyon HaBen; a ceremony where a firstborn son is redeemed from a Kohen</term>—is permitted, as mentioned above, and this is the simple custom. End of quote. 

When I spoke words of Torah in the Holy Community of Krakow with our teacher and master, the pious Gaon <note>A title for a supreme Torah scholar</note>, our teacher Rabbi Solomon <note>likely Rabbi Solomon Luria, known as the Maharshal</note>, of blessed memory, it happened that there was a redemption of the firstborn on the Eve of the Sabbath. He did not want to go to the formal setting of the circumcision meal <note>The text mentions a circumcision meal here, but the event was a redemption of the firstborn; he likely means the celebratory meal in general</note>. He stated that the Rema concludes there that the simple custom to eat meat on those days is merely a general custom; regardless, the practice is that we do not eat more than the minimum ten men <term>Minyan; a quorum of ten</term> required for the formal setting of the circumcision meal, etc. 

Rabbenu Yonah <note>A 13th-century Spanish rabbi and moralist</note> wrote in his work—end of quote—and from here we see that they only eat meat for the quorum and no more. Behold, the prohibition of eating meat on those days is merely a general custom. Regardless, the practice is that they do not eat more than the quorum for the formal setting of a circumcision meal, etc. And regarding what we see in the Gemara <note>The Talmud</note> concerning "poisoning" <note>likely a reference to eating too much before the Sabbath</note>, all the more so if there is a quorum, they should not eat more. And I said to him: This is proof! It is well and good there, where one can find a solution by setting the meal with dairy foods, and the many guests can recline for whatever food they desire; but on the Eve of the Sabbath, no solution can be found, for setting a formal meal is prohibited whether it is meat or dairy. Perhaps it is permitted? He rejected my words on the grounds that "there is no true joy without meat," and this is simple to understand.

## Matter
The sixth day <note>Friday</note> compared to the Sabbath is like the relationship between This World and the World to Come. For a person prepares all their needs from the Eve of the Sabbath for the Sabbath, since on the Sabbath it is forbidden to prepare or act. If not for one's preparation on the Eve of the Sabbath, what would they eat on the Sabbath? Similarly, our Sages of blessed memory said: "He who toils on the Eve of the Sabbath will eat on the Sabbath." So too, one who prepares Torah and good deeds in This World will eat from them there <note>in the afterlife</note>. But one who did not toil there, what will they eat? And one who did not toil on the Eve of the Sabbath, what will they eat on the Sabbath? In this regard, they said "What will he eat?" and did not say "He shall not eat." For if they had said the latter, it would imply it was possible to eat but he was being punished by not eating. By saying "What will he eat?", they meant it is impossible to eat after the time of the commandment has passed, for the commandment itself is the food, and he did not prepare it. If so, what can he eat? Therefore, one should examine their deeds, awaken in repentance, and repair every ruin. I have already expanded on this in my work *Matnat Chiloni*. 

Afterward, one should trim their nails and go to immerse in the ritual bath <term>Mikveh</term>, like a woman purifying herself from her menstruation, for there is no impurity like the impurity of sins. This is the reason for this "awakening" mentioned in the legal codes, that one is obligated to trim their nails every Eve of the Sabbath. As the Renu <note>possibly a reference to a specific authority or work like 'Rabbenu'</note> wrote in Part 3: One removes three things on the Eve of the Sabbath: nails, thorns... a righteous person burns them, a pious person buries them, and a wicked person throws them away. It is bad, and there is a concern that a pregnant woman might pass over them and miscarry. This is from the words of our Sages in the chapter "Three Who Ate" <note>original: "שלשה שאכלו" — Berakhot, Chapter 7</note>. *Sefer Chasidim* <note>The Book of the Pious, a 12th-century German work</note> wrote not to shave or cut on Thursday, because the nails begin to grow on the third day, etc. He should trim his nails on the Eve of the Sabbath, starting from the left hand with the ring finger and ending with the thumb. On the right hand, he starts with the index finger and ends with the ring finger. One should not change this order. If he does not take them one after the other, it is because it is hard for the memory <note>meaning it causes forgetfulness</note>. End of quote. Abraham gave a sign for this order: Right hand: 2, 4, 1, 3, 5 <note>original: "א"חב"ד" — a mnemonic for the sequence of fingers</note>; Left hand: 4, 2, 5, 3, 1. This is also found in the writings of the Ari, of blessed memory <note>Isaac Luria, the 16th-century mystic</note>. 

(Regarding the order of trimming nails, it is written in *Sefer HaMusar*, Chapter 4: How does one trim them? Start with the ring finger, then the pinky, then the middle, then the index, then the left thumb... and let your Sabbath be on the Eve of the Sabbath... Afterward, one should eat in an elevated place... The name of God will be fulfilled upon him... But on the right hand, start with the thumb and end with the ring finger. End of quote. Here you have what was written in the *Sechel Tov* and *Abudarham*). Seven things require washing, and one of them is one who trims his nails, as taught in Tractate Berakhot. End of quote. 

A person should be careful in trimming their nails every Eve of the Sabbath. Through this, he fulfills the principle that "one commandment leads to another," for when the nails grow, he will be careful of the excess or the dirt that is between the nails. One should be concerned, perhaps, with every trimming, for this is the high level: anything external that intervenes <term>Chatzitzah; an obstruction that invalidates ritual immersion</term> during immersion also intervenes during washing. Regarding immersion every Eve of the Sabbath, it is a great holiness and contains holy secrets, as has been explained. The secret of the Mikveh and the matter of immersion on the Eve of the Sabbath was explained above at length under the letter *Kuf* for *Kedushah* <note>Holiness</note>; see there. 

Before the Mikveh, it is good to warm the body with hot water, as stated in the chapter "With what may we light" <note>Shabbat, Chapter 2</note>: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: This was the custom of Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai on the Eve of the Sabbath: They would bring him a tub full of hot water, and he would wash his face, hands, and feet. The *Mordechai* wrote: The *Ra'avyah* wrote that we learn from here it is a commandment <term>Mitzvah</term> to wash one's face, hands, and feet in hot water on the Eve of the Sabbath. It is also a commandment to wash the head on the Eve of the Sabbath, as we say in the chapter "The Trial is Finished" <note>Sanhedrin, Chapter 6</note>... this was on the Eve of the Sabbath, and he was scrubbing his head. It is also written in the chapter "Why also..." <note>likely referring to a Talmudic passage</note>... it was the afternoon of the Eve of the Sabbath, and the herald called out... Rava was washing his head. End of quote. The Maharash wrote in a gloss in the language of the *Aruch* that one should not wash for the Sabbath until close to evening, so that he may dress himself immediately, for this is the honor of the Sabbath.

## And Before
the immersion, one should read the weekly Torah portion "twice the scripture and once the translation" <term>Shnayim Mikra ve-Echad Targum; the practice of reviewing the weekly portion twice in Hebrew and once in the Aramaic Targum Onkelos</term>. One should not read the portion and the fulfillment of the sixth day until after midday. Although regarding the "Awe-inspiring One," they wrote <margin>The students of the school of Segre <note>original: "קלכסי סקר'" - likely a reference to a specific school of scholars</note> wrote: One should only read the Translation with the cantillation marks <term>Trop; the musical system for chanting scripture</term> if the Scripture itself is read with the marks... for these letters, vowels, and marks only exist in the Written Torah.</margin> there, and it would seem that if one completes it with the congregation, it is fine. Nevertheless, for the most choice way to perform the commandment, one should only read it on Friday after midday. It is written in the holy writings of the Ari, of blessed memory, that this is because at that time the "husk" <term>Kelippah; a spiritual shell of impurity</term> separates from the holiness, and afterward, with intention, the flow of influence is drawn down, followed by the holiness of the Sabbath. This matter will be explained later. According to the foundational secret in the first chapter of Berakhot: Rav Huna bar Yehuda said in the name of Rabbi Ami: A person should always complete his portions with the congregation—twice the scripture and once the translation—even verses like "Atarot and Dibon" <note>Names of places in Numbers 32:3 that lack a typical Aramaic translation</note>. For anyone who completes his portions with the congregation, his days and years are lengthened. 

There are reasons and nuances for reading the verse, the scripture, and then the translation over it, and then returning to read the verse in scripture. They do this until the entire portion is finished. Some believe it is better to say the verse and read the translation upon it—that is, the translation—and after reading the explanation, to return to the verse. But this is not so, for the language of the Gemara implies twice the scripture and afterward the translation. This is also proven in the Zohar and the words of the Kabbalists, as will be explained later in my secret. Even according to the revealed reason written by some commentators, it is good to read the translation at the end. They wrote: The reason is that the Torah was given three times: first at Sinai, second in the Tent of Meeting, and third "explained well" <note>Deuteronomy 27:8</note>. Because of this, we read every verse twice, and the completion of the translation corresponds to "explained well." 

The *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, 14th-century author of the Arba'ah Turim</note> wrote in Section 285 that "Atarot and Dibon" is part of the portion even though it has no translation <note>in Aramaic</note>. According to this, even names like "Reuben and Simeon" and the like must be read three times. Some explain that the Sages specified "Atarot" because there are books in which the Jerusalem Translation is written for them. They mentioned "Atarot and Dibon" even though there isn't much translation for you there. According to this, "Reuben and Simeon" would not need to be read three times. Nevertheless, the custom is to be strict, following Rashi. 

It seems to me regarding the matter of reading the verses "May God bless you..." etc., "May God shine His face..." "May God lift His face..." <note>The Priestly Blessing</note> that one should read them each twice and then the translation. For those who are accustomed to returning and reading "Reuben and Simeon" three times, they should do the same for all verses. It appears from Rabbenu Yonah, who wrote: "And even Atarot and Dibon"—he specified this verse because it has no translation, saying that even verses without translation must be read three times. This does not seem right, for we find many other verses without translation, such as the verses of the Priestly Blessing and many others; why did he not mention them? From this I conclude: according to those who are strict to read "Reuben and Simeon" three times, they should also read the Priestly Blessing three times. And even though it has a translation, as found in our Bibles for these chapters, it is possible that this translation was not received from Sinai. Therefore, one should read the scripture three times. Perhaps the translation is a received translation but was not available in the time of Rabbenu Yonah. 

After these intentions, I found in the book of our teacher Rabbi D. Luria <note>David Luria</note>, of blessed memory, who wrote extensively on the blessing of one who "completes" [the portion]: our mind is completed through the Torah. This is because it has no translation and one must complete the scripture with another reading—twice scripture and once translation. It is logical that the text was written by Moses and not by the translator. End of quote. 

The *Tur* further wrote there: the most choice way to perform the commandment is to complete it before one eats on the Sabbath. If one did not complete it before eating, he should complete it after eating, before the Afternoon Service <term>Mincha</term>. From then onward, since the next portion begins, the time has passed. Our Sages said: the most choice way is to complete it before one eats, etc. So too wrote the *Tosafot*, the *Rosh*, and the *Mordechai* in the Midrash: that Rabbi [Judah the Prince] commanded his children: "Do not eat bread on the Sabbath until you finish the entire portion." It implies from their words that he only commanded that they should not delay reading it until after the meal. But if they did it earlier and read it before the Sabbath, it is also included in the most choice way to perform the commandment. This also appears from the words of Maimonides <term>Rambam</term> in his explanation of the Laws of Prayer and from the glosses there.

# Tractate Chullin

And these are the words of the holy beloved <note>a respectful reference to a classic text, likely the Zohar</note> in the Torah portion of *Vayechi*, which Rabbi Shimon explained in the portion of *Bereshit*: It is a great and grand counsel from the Torah regarding how a person should bind themselves to the upper holiness, conduct themselves within it, and never separate from the upper desires. Such a person needs to conduct themselves according to the time—meaning, to know which *Sefirah* <term>Sefirah; one of the ten divine attributes or emanations in Kabbalah</term> is ruling at that moment, to bind themselves to it, and to perform the spiritual rectification appropriate to that ruling attribute. 

It begins with the night, the time a person lies on their bed. This dominion is "Night," the attribute of *Malchut* <term>Malchut; "Kingdom," the lowest of the ten Sefirot, associated with the physical world and the Divine Presence</term>. As one goes to sleep, sleep is a semblance of death, and the "Tree of Death" <note>original: אילנא דמותא (Ilan de-muta)</note> rules. What should one do? One should rectify and prepare to bind themselves to the secret of holiness—namely, the secret of the attribute of *Malchut* in its holy aspect. For this, one should go to their bed and accept the "Yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven" <note>The recitation of the Shema prayer</note> with heartfelt intention. 

If one rises at midnight, they are able to distance themselves from the "Husk" <term>Klipah; literally "shell" or "peel," representing spiritual impurity or forces that conceal godliness</term> ruling over them, remove evil from their flesh, and clarify and rectify the *Shekhinah* <term>Shekhinah; the Divine Presence in the world, often depicted in Kabbalah as being in "exile" and needing "rectification" through human deeds</term> through the study of Torah. Concerning this it is said: "When you lie down, it <note>the Torah</note> shall watch over you" from the external forces, "and when you wake, it shall converse with you"—it shall bind itself with him and he with it. The form of his soul shall then ascend to the Garden of Eden with the *Shekhinah*, who enters there with the righteous. Thus we have learned that he too delights with the righteous and with Abraham, for they all listen to his voice. Behold, he has truly escaped from death and reached the secret of the upper life, binding himself to the secret of the Garden of Eden. 

The light of *Tiferet* <term>Tiferet; the attribute of "Beauty" or "Harmony," often associated with the sun and the written Torah</term> then begins to sparkle upon him—the light that shines in the Garden of Eden of the righteous. Similarly, it is explained in the portion of *Terumah*: When dawn breaks and the "pillar of the morning" rises, he also begins to enter the synagogue. He binds himself to the Three Patriarchs at the entrance of the synagogue by saying: "And I, through Your great kindness, shall enter Your house..." (Psalm 5:8). He includes himself in the secret of *Tiferet* and the Divine Name <note>original: אהוי"ה (A-H-W-Y-H)</note>, which includes Kindness (*Chesed*), Strength (*Gevurah*), and Beauty (*Tiferet*). 

He enters the "Assembly of the Kingdom" <note>the Synagogue</note> and focuses his intention on the verse's reference to the Three Patriarchs: "Your kindness" refers to Abraham; "I will prostrate myself toward Your holy Temple" refers to Isaac, from whose side comes the act of prostration—to bow one's stature before the attribute of Judgment to keep the "Living One" <note>the soul/vitality</note> from being pushed away from it; then the Torah of your lips shall be heard, and the flow of Mercy shall be drawn upon it from above to sweeten it. "In awe of You" refers to Jacob, of whom it is written: "How awesome is this place" (Genesis 28:17). 

This is how one integrates their power of thought, speech, and action: for the "thought" we mentioned is the intention (*kavanah*), the "speech" is the verse, and the "action" is the coming to the synagogue and the prostration before His Temple. Before prayer, he stands in the synagogue, his mouth a flowing spring, saying "My soul longs, even faints..." (Psalm 84:3). The intention is to be in the House—the Synagogue—rectifying the *Shekhinah* with all the power of his intention during prayer. When he leaves there, he ascends in the secret of Torah and binds himself to it in the secret of the "Attribute of Day," conducting himself all day until the time of the Afternoon Prayer (*Mincha*). 

Then he binds himself to Strength (*Gevurah*), for he has already bound himself to Kindness (*Chesed*) during the morning prayer and to the secret of Beauty (*Tiferet*) through the study of Torah. In the evening, he binds himself to Strength again. All this is within the "Attribute of Day" when he comes to the synagogue to unify in the secret of Strength, just as he did on the side of Kindness. Through this, he binds the *Shekhinah* with him at his meal, to "bestow kindness upon the soul" <note>Proverbs 11:17</note>—the animalistic part of himself that receives the food. 

After he has reached the time of the Afternoon Prayer and bound himself to Strength, he waits for evening. Then *Tiferet* descends to *Malchut*, and he is with her. In the night prayer, he binds himself by coming to the synagogue with the aforementioned intention. He binds himself to the "Bed of Tiferet" <note>a mystical term for the union of divine attributes</note> to enter into union. He leaves the synagogue and unifies himself truly with *Malchut* alone, through the secret of accepting the Yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven. This is his cycle throughout the day, aligned with the cycle of the *Sefirot*, always clinging to the light that rules at that moment. This is the essence as found in the portion of *Bereshit*, and the rest is collected from many places in the Zohar. It is comprehensive advice for a person to always remain bound to holiness, so that the "Crown of the Shekhinah" never departs from his head. End of quote.

---

# Chapter of the Mitzvah's Lamp

Rav Chisda said: A person should always wake up early to provide for the expenditures of the Sabbath, as it is said: "And it shall be on the sixth day, they shall prepare that which they bring in" (Exodus 16:5)—they should prepare it immediately. 

In the work *Kanfei Yonah* <note>by the Kabbalist Rabbi Menahem Azariah of Fano</note>, Part 4, Sign 15, it is written: It is good for a person to buy all their Sabbath needs on Friday and not on Thursday, provided he is certain they will not be lacking. Everything he buys, he should say, "For the honor of the Sabbath." End of quote. It appears that this applies specifically to matters of food, which are more tasty and flavorful if bought on the Eve of the Sabbath <note>Friday</note>, similar to the translation of "food for the soul" on a Festival day. However, for items that are good, prepared, and beautiful when bought before Friday, it is proper to do so, or even to buy them earlier and say, "I am buying this for the honor of the Sabbath."

In the *Midrash Tanchuma*, Rabbi Judah said: Even if a person is busy on Friday morning, it is a commandment to rush because of the twilight, as it is said: "And it shall be double" (Exodus 16:5). The Rema wrote in the *Shulchan Aruch* (Section 251): A person should diminish their study a little on Friday to prepare the Sabbath needs. Even if he has many servants to serve him, he should prepare something himself for the Sabbath needs, for it is his personal religious duty (*mitzvah*). This is more significant than doing it through a messenger. Rashi explained that when a person physically occupies their body with a commandment, they receive a greater reward. 

See what is written in *Netiv* and *Bnei Bnei Yisrael* on the verse "And remember to observe the Sabbath"—meaning to prepare for the honor of the Sabbath, just as "the cattle which he had made" (Genesis 18:7) implies preparation. The Torah guides us that everything a person needs to prepare and do should be done by the person himself. Even though his servants might do his work, he must do something himself to finish the preparation. This is why Rav Pappa used to singe the head of the animal, and Rabba would salt the *shibuta* <note>a type of fish, possibly a variety of mullet or carp</note> fish. So too it is written in the *Tur* (Section 254): Even if he has many slaves to serve him, he should prepare something himself for the Sabbath needs, regardless of his dignity. As stated in Chapter 22, Rav Chisda would slice the beets—meaning the vegetables for the Sabbath meal—and Rabba and Rav Joseph would chop wood.

The author of *Tola'at Yaakov* <note>Rabbi Meir ibn Gabbai</note> wrote regarding the secret of the Sabbath: One must prepare their home from before evening for the honor of the Sabbath. There should be a lit lamp, a set table, and a made bed, for all these are "the honor of the Sabbath." Even if a person is distinguished and it is not his usual way to buy things from the market or occupy himself with household chores, he is obligated to do things for the Sabbath needs with his own body. This was the honor of the early Sages: one would chop wood for cooking, one would cook or scald meat, one would roll wicks, and some would go out and buy food for the Sabbath. Anyone who increases these actions is praiseworthy.

Your eyes see the "great ones of the world," the "men of renown" from of old, who acted this way: making the Sabbath for the Lord, for the sake of the Name of the Lord. Whoever sees these actions as heavenly work and their own honor—they were assured the honor of the Sabbath. Who would not do so? The *Tur* concludes on this in the mentioned section: From them, a person should learn, and not say "I will not diminish my dignity," for this *is* his dignity—that he honors the Sabbath. End of quote.

It is famously said of her: "As a lily among the thorns" (Song of Songs 2:2), for the wicked surround and clothe her. This is the secret of "removing idols from the land"—referring to the Upper Land—especially on the Holy Sabbath day, which is the secret of the attribute of *Malchut*, hence she is called "Sabbath the Queen" and also "Bride." This corresponds to the final attribute which includes all the upper lights that shine toward its face. 

This is alluded to by the Sabbath candles: one for "Remember" and one for "Observe," as seen in the *Bahir*—"Remember" for the male and "Observe" for the female. This is the secret of the unification of the upper lights in the "Sukkah," in the secret of "And there shall be peace in your borders," as the Kabbalists wrote that this alludes to the attributes of *Yesod* <term>Yesod; "Foundation," the ninth Sefirah</term> and *Malchut*. See the works called "The Lamps of Peace," and his words will be well understood by whoever has merited to benefit from the radiance. This is the wisdom of Kabbalah. 

From this, we learn that it is very "sweet to the palate" <note>spiritually beneficial</note> to make the bed and remove the "idols" <note>the spiritual husks/spiderwebs</note> from the house and to set it with lamps and a made bed—which is the "Bed of King Solomon," as explained at length in the *Tikunim* on the portion of *Vayechi*.

Every Friday near the Sabbath, one should equate it with the *Shekhinah*, as the Sages said: "And they shall prepare that which they bring in." This refers to the grinding of the knife. I found an innovation in the name of the book *Chayei Olam* which proves this from the phrase "And they shall prepare *et*," comparing it to other verses.

# Regarding
<margin>The time for lighting</margin>
The time for lighting is mentioned in the chapter "With what may we light" <note>the second chapter of Tractate Shabbat</note>, where the household of Rav Joseph would delay the lighting. Rav Joseph said: We have learned, "The pillar of cloud shall not depart by day, nor the pillar of fire by night," which tells us that the pillar of cloud completes the time for the pillar of fire, and the pillar of fire completes the pillar of cloud. This was the opinion of the earlier scholars. An old man said to him: We have learned, "provided that one does not light too early and does not light too late." Regarding this, the *Beit Yosef* <note>the commentary by Rabbi Joseph Karo</note> wrote in Section 263 that the *Tosafot*, the *Rosh*, and the *Ran* wrote in the beginning of the chapter "The Prayer of the Dawn" regarding Rav, who would pray the Sabbath prayer on Friday afternoon from the "midpoint of the afternoon" <term>Plag HaMincha; approximately 1.25 seasonal hours before sunset</term> onwards. He would light the candle and accept the Sabbath upon himself from that early hour. This is what we mean in the chapter "With what may we light" regarding the lighting of the candle: "provided that one does not light too early." What is considered "too early"? Once he accepts the Sabbath upon himself at that moment, he can accept the Sabbath while it is still day, provided it is from the midpoint of the afternoon onwards. The *Tur* wrote similarly in Section 263, saying: "The *Tosafot* explained that from the midpoint of the afternoon onwards, one may light the candle and accept the Sabbath through the Evening Prayer, provided one waits to recite the *Shema* until its proper time, which is the emergence of the stars." This does not violate the rule "provided he does not light too early," for it is not considered early since he accepts the Sabbath at that very moment. In any case, one should not light the candles earlier than the midpoint of the afternoon, which is an hour and a quarter before nightfall. The custom in these communities was not to light two hours before nightfall, especially in the summer days, when this is called *Sabel* <note>likely an acronym or local term referring to a burden of waiting or a specific liturgical issue</note> because the day is still very much at its height. Therefore, it is proper for every pious person to be stringent and rectify this as much as possible, commanding his wife to light between the Afternoon and Evening prayers after the community has prayed the Afternoon prayer. Then everything is ready to receive the Sabbath, and it appears as a gesture in honor of the Sabbath. For the reason one should not light too early is that it is not recognizable that he is lighting for the sake of the Sabbath; however, in this manner, it is clearly recognizable. It seems right to me to light the candles with olive oil or pure oil, and not with the oils used in some places where they light with candles of wax or tallow... it is written by the author of the *Tur* regarding women: "and take oil." There is a great dispute among the giants of the world about this, as mentioned at length by the *Tosafot* and the *Rosh*, and brought in the *Tur* Section 264. The *Beit Yosef* wrote there: if one placed it inside wax around the wick and made a candle from it, etc. At the beginning of our chapter, we learned regarding wicks: "from here on, they are invalid; regarding oils, they are plain/simple." This means there was no need for them, however, regarding a "pouch" <term>termia; a protective layer or holder</term> for the wick, it was needed. Rashi explained that this was necessary because people were accustomed to making a kind of long wick with another wick inside it, as we do. But the *Tosafot*, the *Rosh*, and the *Razah* questioned the words of Rabbi Yochanan, suggesting that all wax candles should be forbidden. They explain that if one places a wax candle in oil, the oil should be forbidden. We learn that "from here on they are plain," meaning that since it contains valid oil, it is permitted. However, a wax candle without oil would be forbidden. The *Rosh* further wrote that the *Rif* <note>Rabbi Isaac Alfasi</note> had the version: "lest we decree wicks on account of oils," which follows Rashi’s view. Thus, it is the custom in Germany and France to light wax candles. The *Ran* wrote that this is also the opinion of the *Ri*, *Ramban*, *Rashba*, and the *Smag*. The *Mordechai* and the *Nimukei Yosef* wrote that tallow or fat is permitted according to Rashi. This also appears to be the opinion of the *Rosh* and the *Nimukei Yosef* since they cited Rashi’s words without qualification. Similarly, it is found in the responsa of Rav Sherira Gaon and the Elder *Ri* that wax is permitted even though it is not oil. This is also the opinion of Maimonides. In another place, the *Rosh* mentioned a responsum by Andrea which he does not rely upon. The *Maggid Mishneh* <note>commentary on Maimonides</note> wrote that it seems to him this was Maimonides' opinion as well. In my own eyes, I see no proof in Maimonides’ words, for it clearly seems he did not write this law as a permission; since it is not explicitly mentioned in the Talmud, he does not tend to rule on it. He does not clarify the opinion of the Gaonim or the Sages of Narbonne. Rather, it seems that if wax alone is made into a wick and placed in a lamp full of oil, like a **pennant** or wool, they might have some tradition to make a wick from wax in this way. He agreed with the words of the Gaonim, but since the *Rosh* and several great later authorities permitted it, and it is a Rabbinic decree, one may rely on them. Also, because the opinion of the *Rif* in his own community was to permit it, as explained by the *Rosh*, one should rely on him more than on a responsum written in the name of the *Rif*. And so is the common practice. Thus, the *Beit Yosef* followed his method of deciding according to the two out of three major authorities: the *Rif*, Maimonides, and the *Rosh*. The *Beit Yosef* held that the *Rif* also agreed with the *Rosh* that it is permitted. But when you look closely at this matter, it is not so. Even though the *Rosh* wrote this, it was because he had not seen the responsum of the *Rif* which forbids it. Had he seen the *Rif*'s responsum, he certainly would not have explained the *Rif*’s words according to Rashi. According to the words of Rashi, *Tosafot*, and the *Rosh*, it is permitted to light with wax using those candles made of three parts called **candles** <note>original: קנדל"יש (candellas)</note>, where the wax is on the wick, and it goes without saying that it is permitted to put those **candles** inside an oil lamp to light. But the Sages of Narbonne and the Gaonim forbid lighting those **candles** because of the wax, but they allow putting them inside a lamp and pouring oil over them to light. It seems to me from the words of our Master and the responsa of other Gaonim that it is forbidden to light with wax or tallow in any manner, whether placing a piece of wax in the lamp in place of oil, or wrapping the wax like a wick such as a **candle**, and even placing the **candle** in a lamp and pouring oil over it is also forbidden, for it is like wrapping something one may light with around something one may not light with. And when the Talmud says "wax was necessary," implying there is a permission for a wax candle, the meaning is that it is permitted to make a wick from the wax itself to place in a valid oil lamp, because wax itself, although forbidden to light as fuel, is only forbidden when it stands on its own (such as when wrapped around a linen wick). But when it does not stand in place of the oil but rather in place of the wick, it is fine. This explanation is where the difference lies between the *Rosh* and the *Tur* and the other decisors regarding our Master's words. For the *Rosh* and the *Tur* wrote that our Master's opinion was to permit **candles** of wax according to Rashi’s words, and because they did not see our Master’s responsum, they explained "wax was necessary" according to Rashi. But since our Master explicitly forbids it in a responsum, it cannot be explained that way. Rather, it means: "Lest we decree that making a wick like a thread out of wax is forbidden even though it is only a wick." And according to this explanation, everything is settled well, and this is the opinion of Maimonides and our Master. This is also implied by the *Ramban* in the *Book of Wars*, where he wrote: "I was compelled to answer this because I saw that our Great Master <note>the Rif</note> wrote in a responsum that it is forbidden and there is no doubt about the matter." It seems simple that because the *Rif*’s words could be interpreted in two ways, he relied on the responsum. This also appears to be the view of the author of the *Ma'or*. The truth is that his words should be interpreted as forbidding, since he explicitly revealed his mind in a responsum. The *Rosh*, who did not see the responsum, wrote what he wrote. Thus, according to the *Rif* and Maimonides, it is forbidden, and so it should be examined.

# The Second [Case]
<margin>Ashkenazi custom</margin>
Section 263: He wrote as follows: "I found in an Ashkenazi responsum: when two or three householders eat in one place, each one recites a blessing over his own lamp, even though there is already plenty of light." Although some have hesitated about this, nevertheless some have the custom to do so. In this matter, there are three ways to justify it: every bit of additional light brings more peace to the home and extra joy in enjoying the light in every corner. In the *Shulchan Aruch*, he concluded in sub-section 2 and wrote: "It is correct to be careful regarding a doubt about blessings, and only one person should recite the blessing." But the *Rema* <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles</note> wrote in his gloss: "But we do not practice this way." It seems to me that in any case, regarding a single lamp that has many mouths <note>branches</note>, no one should recite a blessing except for one woman alone. Even the *Rema* only wrote this when each one has a lamp in a different corner, and even then, the words of the *Ri* are more logical, to remove oneself from the doubt of a blessing said in vain. All the women should stand together and one...

# Tractate Shabbat

It seems somewhat that specifically on the Sabbath before eating is when it is considered the "choice fulfillment" of the commandment, and not before then. This is the end of his words. However, it has already been proven in the books of the Kabbalists <note>Jewish mystics</note> that one should read the "Two parts Scripture and one part Translation" <note>original: *Shnayim Mikra ve-Echad Targum*; a traditional Friday practice of reading the weekly Torah portion twice in Hebrew and once in the Aramaic translation of Onkelos</note> on the eve of the Sabbath. This is the most choice way to fulfill the commandment: to complete the reading on Friday. During the public Torah reading in the synagogue, one should not read along, but rather look at the Torah scroll and listen to the Cantor <note>Reader</note> as he reads from the Torah; he should remain silent, only hearing and focusing his intention.

When the Sages said one should "complete it with the congregation," they did not mean he should read *simultaneously* with the congregation (i.e., with the Cantor), but rather that he must complete the reading while that specific weekly portion is still being read by the congregation. This window exists from Sunday onwards until the Afternoon Service (*Mincha*) of the coming Sabbath, at which point a new portion begins. For the weekly portion always governs the time from Sabbath afternoon to the next Sabbath afternoon; after that, its time has passed. All of this is according to the strict law. However, for the "choice fulfillment" of the commandment, one should wait to read the "Two parts Scripture and one part Translation" until Friday after midday, and then complete it.

I found this explained in the words of Rabbeinu Yonah <note>Rabbi Jonah of Gerona, a 13th-century ethicist</note>, who wrote: "A person should always complete his sections with the congregation," meaning that before the congregation reads the portion in the synagogue, he should read it at home. This is the end of his words. His phrase "with the congregation" means *prior* to the congregation, similar to the phrase "The pious ones would pray *with* the sunrise," where Rabbeinu Yonah explains that "with" means just before the sun rises. Just as we say "on the eve of the Sabbath *with* the darkness," we do not mean actual darkness, but just before darkness.

There are also differing customs. Some read every single verse twice and then the translation for that verse. Others complete the entire weekly portion twice in Hebrew and then read the translation a third time. However, I have received the "choice path" to follow the plain meaning of the Talmud’s language: to read every *parasha* twice and then the translation. Here, *parasha* refers to a small paragraph—either "open" or "closed" <note>referring to the physical spacing in the Torah scroll</note>—rather than the entire weekly portion. This is according to what Rashi wrote on the book of Leviticus: "to give space between one section (*parasha*) and another." Similarly, the language of the Talmud in Berakhot (page 9) refers to "one hundred sections (*parashiot*) in the book of Psalms." 

This explains the precise language of the Sages: "A man should always complete *his* sections (*parashiot*)..." Why use the plural "sections" instead of "the portion"? Because "section" does not refer to the whole weekly reading, but to the paragraphs within it. This is helpful because people do not all begin reading at the same time. As I wrote regarding the law, one may start from Sunday onward; one person starts today, another tomorrow, until one has only a few sections left and another has more. Therefore, the Sages said "complete his sections with the congregation." I have also received the tradition that even when a section ends in the middle of a verse—as in the verse "And it was after the plague" in the portion of *Phinehas*—one should stop there to complete the reading of that section. 

When one reads, he should set his heart and mind to contemplate what he is reading—whether it be the commandments of the Torah, character traits, or ethical paths—to extract benefit from every matter. He should read in order to learn, to teach, to keep, and to do. At the very least, it is desirable for a man to always contemplate these three things, which form a "triple cord that is not easily broken" <note>a reference to Ecclesiastes 4:12</note>: 
1. **The Lamp of Commandment:** The 613 commandments. 
2. **The Torah of Light:** Being wise and understanding the secrets of the Torah. 
3. **The Path of Life:** Ethical rebukes and the discipline of character traits.

Every man will find these according to his own intellect and the breadth of his knowledge. And you, my sons (may their Rock and Redeemer protect them), I shall open for you a gate in every weekly portion for these three categories. From what I show you, you shall see and do likewise, adding more and more, for the Torah has no fixed measure or time that would ever be "enough."

The work here is great regarding our current topic. Therefore, I shall make a separate pamphlet of this, with God's help, and it shall be titled "The Written Torah." This pamphlet will be established as a supplement to the "Ten Utterances" <note>referring to the author's larger work, *Shenei Luchot HaBerit*</note>. It is a great and mighty commandment to prepare for the Sabbath by checking the Torah scroll to ensure not even a single letter is missing or extra, and that no letter is resting against another. Even regarding the "defective" and "full" spellings <note>original: *chaserot v'yeterot*; words spelled with or without vowels like *vav* or *yod*</note>... one must see that everything is in order. Our Sages said: "If one corrects even a single letter, it is as if he wrote the entire scroll." One commandment leads to another, for he then enables the public to fulfill their obligation with a kosher scroll. If even one letter is missing, it is invalid.

Since this topic has come to my hand, let me say something complete and great regarding a ruling that has spread among the people. In the *Levush* <note>Rabbi Mordecai Yaffe's code</note>, sign 143, the Maharshal <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria, a 16th-century authority</note> ruled that another Torah scroll should be taken out only when an actual error is found that changes the meaning. But for a spelling variation that doesn't change the meaning, he felt it wasn't necessary. However, even one missing letter makes a scroll invalid! The Rema <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles</note> wrote that for spelling variations (full/defective), we don't take out another scroll because our scrolls are not perfectly accurate anyway. But for a change in the *reading* of the word or an obvious error—even if the meaning doesn't change—for example, if one wrote *Keshev* instead of *Keves* <note>original: כבש / כשב; both mean "lamb," just with letters swapped</note>, it is clear to me that one must take out another scroll.

<margin>
In sign 143, it is explained that if a mistake is found in a Torah scroll in the synagogue, if the meaning of the word remains recognizable, they may finish the reading in that scroll. This is based on the Jerusalem Talmud. End of his words.
</margin>

Regarding the reading of the Megillah <note>the Scroll of Esther</note>, the Jerusalem Talmud says we are not overly pedantic about minor errors. Rav Isaac bar Abba and Rav Hananel were reading "the Jews" (*Yehudim*), one read it with one *yod* and one with two, and neither corrected the other. Some say this only applies to errors where the language and meaning remain identical. But if any meaning is changed—like *zakhur* (remembered) vs. *zakhar* (male)—one must correct it. The *Kol Bo* says if the Cantor made even a single error in a letter, we make him go back until he reads it precisely. Though some are lenient if it doesn't change the meaning, I believe even for such errors one should return and read it correctly. Because of these concerns, I say it is a great commandment to check the Torah scroll every Friday and every Eve of a Holiday.

Mahar"i Israel wrote in sign 100 that it is specifically on the Eve of the Sabbath that it is an obligation to "complete the portions," but one does not need to do so for the holiday portions. However, it is my custom to complete the portions for holidays, the additional portions, and the four special Sabbaths as well. For even if you might say one is not strictly obligated, he nonetheless receives a reward as one who studies Torah.

## Courtyard Mergers (Eruvei Chatzerot)

It is a great commandment. Our Sages said that when King Solomon enacted the "Courtyard Merger" <note>term: *Eruv*; a ritual meal that allows residents of different houses to carry items in a shared courtyard on the Sabbath</note>, a Heavenly Voice emerged and said: "My son, if your heart is wise, [My heart will also rejoice]." How is it done? We take a piece of bread from each house and place it in one of the houses of the courtyard, so that we now view it as if they all live in that one house. 

The *Agur* <note>a 15th-century halakhic work</note> records that the great leader of the generation, Rabbi Jacob Moelin (Maharil), was asked about the custom in some German communities to make the *Eruv* with bread and leave it in the synagogue all year. He replied with great concern. The Maharil himself would not rely on the communal *Eruv* made on the Eve of Passover for the whole year, fearing it might become spoiled or lost, leading to a transgression. He was accustomed to placing an *Eruv* every Friday. This was also the custom of Maharshal. 

When one performs this, the bread should belong to someone else <note>to create a partnership</note>. One cannot use his small son (if he is supported by him), nor his wife, to acquire it for the group. When granting ownership, the bread must be lifted one handbreadth from the ground. I was asked when one should eat the "Eruv-bread," and I replied: our custom is to set the *Eruv* every Friday. On the Sabbath night, I use that bread as my "double-loaf" (*Lechem Mishneh*) for the blessing, as was the custom of my teacher, the Maharshal. Regarding the blessing "Who has sanctified us... concerning the commandment of the Eruv," it seems to me one should not recite it unless he intends to not be covered by the communal *Eruv* performed by the town.

# Tractate Shabbat

<margin>
**Measures of Conduct**
Take candles, and your mnemonic is: "You shall do no work" <note>Exodus 20:10</note>.
Rabbi Shimon said: Until the profane time <note>the weekday</note>, there are 18 hours, and your mnemonic is: "All the kings are peace and one" <note>A mnemonic for the 18 hours of the Sabbath's onset</note> for the whole day.
On the Sabbath, even the wicked in Gehenna <note>the afterlife realm of purification</note> rest; therefore, he who displays anger on the Sabbath commits a double sin. They have already given a sign for this: "You shall kindle no fire in all your habitations on the day of the Sabbath" <note>Exodus 35:3</note>—this refers to the fire of dispute and the heat of anger.
The letter *Aleph* <note>representing the number 1</note> signifies that you have heard this: "You shall kindle no fire..." it should be like a "Great Love."
Furthermore, one angel is good and another is evil. If one is found far off, weakened, or sent away, a "staff of strength" and a "standing rod" <note>metaphors for divine support</note> are provided. The good angel says, "May it be Your will that it be so for another Sabbath," and the evil angel <note>forced to respond</note> says "Amen." We find this matter explained well in the Midrash of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai <note>the Zohar</note>: When a person comes from the synagogue on Sabbath eve, the *Shekhinah* <note>the Divine Presence</note> spreads over everything like a mother over children. At that hour, "Thy dread shall fall..." and "Only with your eyes shall you behold..." for "You, O Lord, are my refuge... no evil shall befall you" <note>referencing Psalm 91</note>.
This occurs when a person comes to his home and receives his guests <note>original: *ushpizin*</note> with joy. When the *Shekhinah* sees a lamp burning, a table set, and the bed made, and a man and his wife in joy and peace, she says: "This is mine, this is Israel in whom I take glory." But if, Heaven forbid, the *Shekhinah* departs, the angels depart with her. Looking into this, we see that if his forces <note>impure spirits</note> are with him, the spirit of impurity hovers over him and he is removed. This refers not just to the man, but to the woman; she is called "Fire" (*Esh*), and he is called "Fire" (*Esh*). <note>The Hebrew words for Man (*Ish*) and Woman (*Ishah*) both contain the letters for Fire (*Esh*), plus the letters of God's name (*Yud* and *He*). Without God, only fire remains.</note>
Regarding this, it is said: "Do not desire the delicacies of one with an evil eye," whose "table is full of filthy vomit." Therefore, one must be careful to receive the Sabbath with joy, setting the lamp, the table, and the bed for the honor of the Presence of the *Shekhinah*.
And so says the *Sefer Hasidim* <note>Book of the Pious</note>: Better a meal of herbs on the Sabbath where there is love between a man, his wife, and his household, than a fatted ox and hatred with it. A person should not say, "I will buy Sabbath delicacies," while knowing he will quarrel with his wife, father, or mother. Avoid strife, for "Better a dry morsel and quietness with it than a house full of feasting with strife." This applies to both the Sabbath and Festivals. This is the meaning of "And you shall honor it, by not following your own ways" <note>Isaiah 58:13</note>—that your speech on the Sabbath should not be like your speech on weekdays.
</note>
</margin>

<margin>
In the secrets of the letters:
The end of the letter *Khaf* transforms into the letter *He*, representing that the entire day is *Chesed* <note>Kindness</note>.
"The Lord will command His loving-kindness in the daytime" <note>Psalm 42:9</note>, for even the night is like day in His kindness.
</margin>

**Character Traits** of piety and extra holiness: one should be ready for the needs of the Sabbath, completing heavy labors by midday. From midday onwards, all involvement should be in the sanctity of the Sabbath, which is entirely Sabbath—namely, in awakening toward repentance, rectifying one’s deeds, and the study of Torah. All members of the household should do this until the time the day enters. The Sabbath day must be entirely characterized by grace, kindness, peace, and "Great Love."

**My Father and Teacher,** of blessed memory, wrote in *Emek HaBeracha* <note>The Valley of Blessing</note> that within that sanctity, one should allow a small pause between the physical pouring <note>of preparations</note> and the ultimate purpose, so that there is no "turning back," Heaven forbid. Likewise, in the prayer *Vaykhulu* <note>"And [the heavens] were finished"</note>, when one reaches "God blessed," he should be careful not to distance the word "God" (*Elohim*) from the word "at" (*et*), but should emphasize the letter *Aleph* of "at" very much, lest he "widen" <note>mispronounce</note> it. Regarding this, it is written: "Be not rash with your mouth." This is explained in chapter 7. Rabbi Mordechai bar Joseph used to say after the reading of *Bameh Madlikin* <note>"With what may we light," the Mishnaic chapter on Sabbath lamps</note>: It was taught that Rabbi Hanina said a person should check his pockets on Sabbath eve as it gets dark, lest he find something <note>and carry it accidentally</note>. Rav Joseph said: This is a great law for the Sabbath. Afterward, one says "Lord, Open..." <note>the start of the Amidah prayer</note>. Through this, if one accidentally prays the weekday prayer, he finishes that blessing, as stated in the chapter *Mi She-meto* and explained in the *Tur*, section 288. I found one who weighed this carefully: he should be anxious all week, for it is a sign of the matter mentioned in the chapter *Kadosh*, that one should examine his deeds and awaken in repentance.

### Matters of Sabbath prayers and their mysteries will be explained later in the section on the House of Prayer.

<margin>
It was written in the glosses on the chapter *Bameh Madlikin*: A "gross stride" <note>a very long step or running</note> takes away one five-hundredth of a person's eyesight. What is the remedy? To restore it through the *Kiddush* <note>sanctification prayer over wine</note> of Friday evening.
This means that since a gross stride takes one part in five hundred of the light of a person's eyes, the remaining parts are quickly restored to us.
In the Tractate Shabbat, it says that even applying [medicine] on the eye is forbidden if it is done in a way that is clearly for healing.
I found among the novellae of the *Mordechai* <note>Rabbi Mordechai ben Hillel</note>: I asked the *Maharam* <note>Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg</note>, since it is an obligation to eat near the lamp, how is it that people customarily leave the lamp in the house and eat in the courtyard? He replied that the lamps were commanded for delight (*Oneg*) and not for distress. If he enjoys the light of the courtyard more, it is clearly permitted. However, it seems to me that this is only permitted for the meal in the courtyard, but the *Kiddush* should be in the place of the lamp, since it is specifically tied to the honor of the Sabbath. This is especially true according to what I found written in the name of *Sekhel Tov*: the reason for two lamps corresponds to what they said about a gross stride taking away one five-hundredth of eyesight.
The number five hundred is significant; even by looking at the lamps during the *Kiddush*, he will have healing. Also, a man has 248 limbs and a woman has 252; together they equal the numerical value of twice "Light" (*Or*), representing the union of man and wife. Therefore, when he looks at the lamps during *Kiddush*, he receives healing. According to this, the custom of blessing two lamps on the Sabbath is also settled—they symbolize the union of man and wife, in the manner of the "appointed time for scholars." It follows clearly that one should only perform *Kiddush* in the place of the lamp. Because of this, it seems that if one has several rooms and moves from room to room, he must have a lamp in every place where there is a fear he might stumble.
I received from those who are meticulous in the commandments that perhaps this is what they meant when they said: "He who is regular with the lamp [will have wise children]," meaning in many places.
</margin>
<margin>
And there is an allusion.
</margin>

**The Holy Foundation** will be explained soon in the second chapter. The *Kol Bo* <note>a 13th-century ritual work</note> states: When one begins to say "The sixth day, and the heavens and the earth were finished," these words in their initials stand for the crown of the Name. When they begin, he should cast his eyes upon the lamps, and during the *Kiddush*, he should look at the cup, just as one does with the Cup of Blessing. This is the end of his words.

**You shall call the Sabbath a delight** <note>Isaiah 58:13</note>. Our Sages, of blessed memory, spoke at great length about delighting in the Sabbath. Maimonides <note>Rambam</note> writes in the Laws of Sabbath, chapter 30: What is this "delight"? It is what the Sages said: one must prepare a very rich dish and a spiced drink for the Sabbath, all according to a person's wealth. Anyone who increases spending for the Sabbath and the preparation of many good foods is praiseworthy. At the very least, one delights it with good bread, fish, and meat, and wine. There is a hint in this: "Delight" (*Oneg*) and the Name of God have the initials for Wine (*Yayin*), Fish (*Dagim*), and Meat (*Basar*). Our Sages said: mustard and fish. The matter of their words is that "Delight" (*Oneg*) also equals the small numerical value of 6. It is known that the "Seventh Gate" is the chosen one, and the Sabbath is the foundation and head of them all. The number [of meals] alludes to the fifty meals <note>of the year</note>. Therefore, it seems right to celebrate the Third Meal also with two loaves of bread (*Lechem Mishneh*), according to some authorities. Our Sages said, "Anyone who delights *the* Sabbath," and they did not say "Anyone who delights *on* the Sabbath," because a person's intention should not be to delight himself, but rather to perform the delight for the sake of the honor of this Sabbath. "And you shall call the Sabbath a delight" is like one who invites an important and great person and makes a feast in his honor—the expense and the pleasure are for the guest. So too is the explanation of the Zohar: "And you shall call the Sabbath"—that you should invite it as a guest, preparing it properly with fine clothing and acquisitions. Therefore, those who are stingy with their clothing and covering do not truly wish to follow the sweetness and the pleasure of beautiful garments. Furthermore, from their excessive eating, "a deep sleep falls upon them." Nevertheless, who are those called "delighters of the Sabbath"? Not those who delight themselves on the Sabbath. Therefore, one should manage his affairs with judgment. The wise man has "eyes in his head"; when he sits to eat in the morning, even though he eats appropriate foods, the intention is not to fill his belly, for that is not called "rest" or "delight," but rather the destruction of the food and the body, and a loss to the soul, as he will be unable to stand on a "good pillar" when he comes to engage in Torah and commandments, as we have explained. Rather, the matter is that he should eat and drink with joy and a good heart, food that is good and beautiful.
