<meta>This page continues the discussion of the laws and spiritual preparations for the Sabbath, moving from the mystical dangers of anger to the practical and symbolic rituals of candle lighting, food preparation, and the "Spice of the Sabbath."</meta>

# Tractate Shabbat

...and one person recites the blessing, and the rest respond "Amen," for when ten people perform a single commandment, one blessing suffices for all of them. During the summer, one must make long candles that will stay lit until nightfall; otherwise, it would be a **wasted blessing** <note>original: "Beracha Levatala"; a blessing said in vain because the primary purpose of the lamp is to provide light when it is actually dark</note>. In the *Mordechai* <note>a major 13th-century German legal code</note>, in the chapter "With what may we light," it says it is mandatory to dine in the place where the candle is lit for the sake of **Sabbath delight** <note>original: "Oneg Shabbat"</note>. This is also cited in the name of the *Agudah* and appears in the *Agur* (Section 368). It is also written that those who light candles in the corners of the house but eat in the courtyard—if the candles are not long enough to stay lit until night, it is a wasted blessing. The *Tosafot* <note>medieval commentators on the Talmud</note> also wrote that one must dine where the candle is lit for the sake of Sabbath delight.

**When a woman** gives birth, on her first Sabbath after the birth, the husband lights the candles and recites the blessing. Among the new insights I found, Rabbenu Bahya <note>a 13th-century Spanish scholar</note> wrote on the Torah portion *Yitro*: it is fitting for a woman to pray to the Blessed Name at the time of lighting the Sabbath candles—which is a commandment specifically placed upon her—that the Lord grant her children who "shine in the Torah." This is because prayer is more readily heard at the moment a commandment is performed. In the merit of the Sabbath candle, which is light, she will merit children who are masters of the Torah, which is also called light, as it says: "For a commandment is a lamp, and Torah is light" <note>Proverbs 6:23</note>. Our Sages likewise taught: "He who is accustomed to lighting the lamp will have sons who are Torah scholars." I have also received a tradition that at this time, the woman should read the *Haftarah* <note>the weekly reading from the Prophets</note> of Rosh Hashanah—the prayer of Hannah—up until the verse "And He shall exalt the horn of His anointed."

Regarding the matter of **insulating food** <note>original: "Hatmanah"; the practice of wrapping pots to keep them warm for the Sabbath day</note>, my father and teacher (of blessed memory) wrote in his ethical will, *Yesh Nochalim*: "Admonish your wives regarding the preparation of the oven where they place the hot food for the next day. This must be done before the sexton calls out in the synagogue. They should not open it until the next morning to take out the food." This is unlike what some women do, opening the oven on Friday night after leaving the synagogue by means of a non-Jew to take out food for the night meal, and then resealing it via the non-Jew for the sake of the next day’s lunch. In my opinion, this is strictly forbidden. Even if one argues it is permitted in the summer—since we often leave the synagogue an hour or two before dark and the prohibition of work after "accepting the Sabbath" is only rabbinic at that stage—nonetheless, in the winter, we leave synagogue very close to nightfall. If one opens and reseals the oven then, it constitutes a new act of insulation on the Sabbath itself, which causes further cooking and is forbidden by all opinions. Furthermore, if you permit it in the summer, people will mistakenly do it in the winter as well.

All labors performed for the Sabbath must be done with **alacrity and joy**. Just as one receives a reward for the "seeking"—that is, preparing for the Sabbath from the conclusion of the previous Sabbath—one also receives a reward for the "withdrawal"—that is, hurrying to cease all work when the time of the "Sabbath addition" arrives. This is hinted at in the Divine Name *Shaddai* <note>traditionally interpreted here as "She-dai," meaning "He who said 'Enough!'"</note>. The Torah mentions "A Sabbath of solemn rest" <note>Shabbat Shabbaton</note> and "A solemn rest of Sabbath." This implies there should be a "solemn rest" before the Sabbath (preparation) and a "solemn rest" after the Sabbath (extending the holiness as it departs). 

This matter is explained in the Talmud (Tractate Bava Kamma, page 32): Issi ben Yehuda admits that if a person is running in the public domain on Friday afternoon and causes damage, he is exempt because he is running with "permission" <note>performing a religious duty</note>. What is this "permission"? It refers to the tradition of Rabbi Hanina, who said: "Come, let us go out to meet the **Sabbath Bride, the Queen**." Others say: "To meet the Bride, the Sabbath Queen." Rabbi Yannai would wrap himself in his cloak and stand, saying: "Come, O Bride! Come, O Bride!"

I believe there are three distinct levels here: The first mentions the "Bride Queen," the second the "Sabbath Bride Queen," and the third simply the "Bride." The first refers to the rush to prepare. The Sabbath is called both a Bride and a Queen; she is a "Bride" when she is being sanctified, and a "Queen" when she is united with the Supernal King. This is why our Sages established three different prayers for the Sabbath <note>referring to the Evening, Morning, and Afternoon Amidah prayers, which unlike weekday prayers, have different middle sections</note>. They correspond to the stages of a wedding:
1.  **Evening Prayer:** Corresponds to the *Kiddushin* <note>betrothal</note>.
2.  **Morning Prayer:** "Moses shall rejoice," corresponding to the joy of the groom with the bride.
3.  **Musaf (Additional) Prayer:** Corresponds to the *Additions* <note>Tosefet</note> the groom adds to the marriage contract <note>Ketubah</note>.
4.  **Afternoon Prayer:** "You are One," corresponding to the private union of the groom and bride.

One must prepare feasts for the night and the day, as if they were the "betrothal feast" and the "wedding feast," all to honor the Queen. This is why we say "Let us go out to meet the Bride Queen"—it means we run to prepare these feasts. Then, when the time comes, one changes clothes and wraps oneself in fine garments to receive her. This is why Rabbi Yannai would wrap himself and say, "Come, O Bride," signaling that the Bride has arrived for the feast.

<column-break/>

<margin>
**A Gloss**
From here we learn that it is not just wrapping the challah, but all preparations to cook and finish the food for the Sabbath are considered "with permission." If one causes damage unintentionally while rushing for these needs, he is exempt from payment.
</margin>

...Rabbi Issi ben Yehuda says a person is liable [for damages while running] because he is acting unusually, but he admits on Sabbath Eve at twilight that the person is exempt, for he runs with permission to arrange and prepare for the honor of the Sabbath. If two people were both running and injured one another unintentionally, they are both exempt, and such is the law.

Whatever a person buys, prepares, or cooks for the Sabbath, he should say: **"I am buying (or cooking) this for the honor of the Sabbath."** By doing so, holiness spreads into that food, and it acquires a spiritual fragrance. This depends on the person’s own level and the sincerity of his thoughts. This relates to the story in the Talmud: The Roman Emperor said to Rabbi Joshua ben Hananiah, "Why does the Sabbath food have such a fragrant aroma?" He replied, "We have a certain spice called 'Sabbath' that we put into it." The Emperor said, "Give me some of it!" Rabbi Joshua replied, "It only works for those who keep the Sabbath; for those who do not keep the Sabbath, it does nothing." In truth, this "spice" is the act of the person saying, "This is for the honor of the Sabbath." This speech has an effect. It is also a good custom to **taste the food** on Friday to ensure it is properly seasoned and will be eaten with appetite. As I found written: "One who tastes the Sabbath dishes merits life." After all these actions, one enters into the repairs/rectifications of the Sabbath...

<summary>This page discusses the practical and mystical preparations for the Sabbath, including the laws of candle lighting, insulating food, and the symbolic comparison of the Sabbath to a royal bride. It emphasizes the "Spice of the Sabbath," a spiritual fragrance achieved through intentionality and the verbal dedication of preparations to the holy day.</summary>

<keywords>Sabbath candles, Oneg Shabbat, Hatmanah, Rabbenu Bahya, Issi ben Yehuda, Bride Queen, Sabbath Spice, intentionality, Yesh Nochalim, wedding symbolism</keywords>

--- Page 300 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Sabbath laws, focusing on the spiritual sanctity of the day, the proper conduct during Torah readings (especially for a groom), and the requirement to complete one hundred blessings.</meta>

<margin>Even with his wife, a man must act with sanctity, and one who sanctifies himself merits worthy children.</margin>

**"On the Sabbath day it shall be opened, and on the day of the New Moon it shall be opened"** <note>Ezekiel 46:1</note>, for at that time there is an "Extra Soul" <note>original: "Neshamah Yeteirah"; a spiritual enrichment believed to descend upon Jews during the Sabbath</note> and marital union is beautiful. I found this written in the name of the holy Arizal <note>Rabbi Isaac Luria, the foundational 16th-century Kabbalist</note>. It is also stated in the Midrash regarding the verse, "Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs" <note>Isaiah 56:4</note>—these are those who restrain <note>original: "hameresim," a play on words between "eunuchs" (sarisim) and "restraining/crushing" (meresim)</note> themselves all the days of the week until the Sabbath, "who shall keep My Sabbaths" <note>Isaiah 56:4</note>, for these are the Sabbaths dedicated to the Name, which is the primary time for marital intimacy <note>original: "Onah"</note>. The word "shall keep" <note>original: "ve-yishmoru"</note> is used in the same sense as "and his father kept the matter" <note>Genesis 37:11, implying waiting with anticipation</note>, and as the Sages said: "waiting for him at the entrance." Their reward, which He shall give them in the World to Come, is "a monument and a name better than sons and daughters" <note>Isaiah 56:5</note> that people have in this world. I also found that the phrase "those who taste it merit life" <note>from the Sabbath hymn "Me'en Olam Ha-ba"</note> alludes to the "taste" of intimacy. The Sages hinted at this by the proximity of the verses: "You shall be holy" followed by "Every man, his mother and father you shall fear, and My Sabbaths you shall keep" <note>Leviticus 19:2–3</note>. Behold, a man is obligated to sanctify himself at the time of union, and wherever you find a boundary set against immorality, you find holiness. Even with his wife, one must act with sanctity, and he who sanctifies himself merits worthy children. Indeed, there are three partners in [the creation of] a human: the Holy One, blessed be He, the father, and the mother. This is the meaning of "You shall be holy, for I am holy," and the text juxtaposes the father and mother with the Sabbath because the time for union is on the Sabbath. There is a revelation of this in the Zohar; see there.

---

**And on the Sabbath day,** one should not stand at the grave <note>meaning, should not wake up early for work or sorrow</note> early as on other weekdays. The *Mordechai* <note>Rabbi Mordechai ben Hillel, a 13th-century legal authority</note> wrote in the chapter "All Sacred Writings" regarding the common custom where people wake up early all week to go to the synagogue to pray or study, but on the Sabbath, they sleep longer in the morning. This is the reason: for every weekday, it is said regarding the Daily Offering <note>original: "Tamid"</note>, "in the morning, in the morning," but regarding the Daily Offering of the Sabbath, it does not say "in the morning," but rather "And on the Sabbath day" <note>Numbers 28:9</note>. This phrasing implies a later time, as is understood in Tractate Yoma. Rabbi Yehuda bar Yehuda heard this reason in the city of Rome from the mouth of Rav Hai Gaon <note>the last of the great Babylonian leaders, 10th century</note>.

**When the groom** begins to read from the Torah, the eyes of all the people should be upon the Torah scroll. The most excellent way to perform this commandment is for every individual to have a *Chumash* <note>a printed Pentateuch</note> in hand and follow along word for word with everything the groom reads. In this way, one will not turn his thoughts to any other matter in the world, for it is a time of great favor. It is criminal to speak while the groom reads from the Torah; even to speak of [other] Torah matters is inappropriate. Rather, one should only listen to the words coming from the mouth of the reader and focus on them. He who speaks or causes a disruption <note>original: "ha-meshaneh"</note> "has despised the word of the Lord" <note>Numbers 15:31</note> and is liable to judgment—may the Lord save us. Also, they must not distract themselves from the reading so that they may answer "Amen" after those who bless over the reading. After the "Barchu" <note>the call to prayer</note>, one should focus on "Blessed is the Lord who is blessed," and it is considered as if they had recited the blessing themselves. 

This also serves to complete the count of one hundred blessings <note>Jewish tradition encourages saying 100 blessings daily; on the Sabbath, the standard prayer is shorter, leaving a "deficit"</note> on the Sabbath, which a person cannot complete through the Grace After Meals or the standard prayers—since the Sabbath prayer is missing twelve blessings in each of the three services, totaling thirty-six. One completes the count by focusing on the blessings of those called up to the Torah and answering "Amen," and likewise for the blessings of the *Maftir* <note>the concluding Torah portion and Prophetic reading</note>. We see that this adds thirty blessings to the count. One should not be lenient in this matter at all; even one who is tired or has studied much should not neglect this. Even a Torah scholar <note>original: "Talmid Chacham"</note> involved in other holy studies should stop while the groom reads, for the Torah is the root of all teachings, and the entire Torah consists of the Names of the Holy One, blessed be He. We have nothing greater in this world than this; its words are eternal and the entire universe is sustained by them. It is the summation of all wisdoms, and there is nothing in the world not found within it. If it seems "empty" to us, it is only because of our limited understanding. Every person of spirit should honor the Torah and not desecrate it in the eyes of the unlearned <note>original: "Ammei ha-aretz"</note>. If they see scholars ignoring the reading to discuss their own affairs, it leads to a great desecration. Therefore, one must listen as if hearing the Torah given anew at Mount Sinai. As the Sages said, the words should be "as if they were given today." Remember the commandment of *Haqhel* <note>the biblical assembly every seven years</note>, where even infants were brought to hear, even though they lacked understanding, simply to receive a reward for the sanctity of the act. So too, one should warn those standing near him to remain silent and listen. He who does so is praiseworthy, for he brings merit to the many, and it is said of him: "Anyone who honors the Torah, his body will be honored by others."

**It is forbidden** to fast on the Sabbath until the sixth hour <note>approximately midday</note>. The *Mordechai* wrote that one should even delay the prayer... My grandfather wrote in *Emek Beracha*: it is good to study some Torah on the Sabbath before eating, as it says in the *Yalkut*: "From here they said, a man should rise early on the Sabbath and go to the synagogue and Study Hall, read the Torah and the Prophets, and then go home and eat and drink to fulfill the verse 'Go, eat your bread in joy'" <note>Ecclesiastes 9:7</note>. The *Kolbo* <note>a 14th-century ritual work</note> wrote that some hurry to Kiddush. The authorities wrote that a man is obligated to recite one hundred blessings every day, and on Sabbaths and Festivals when the prayer lacks blessings, he completes them with various fruits. This is explained in Tractate Menachot. We have seen that the "Amen" answered to the Torah reader and the *Maftir* helps complete this count. Therefore, I say it is good that when fruits are served during the Sabbath meal, one should wait to eat them until after the Grace After Meals <note>original: "Birkat Hamazon"</note> to gain the "after-blessing," though on weekdays one should not do this to avoid an unnecessary blessing. In every Sabbath meal, one should recite the Grace After Meals over a cup of wine, even if he is alone, unlike his weekday custom, to honor the beloved Sabbath meal.

<column-break/>

This is surprising, for the verse "And on the Sabbath day" was not written regarding his own standing or the Musaf offering, as the *Mordechai* explained. Regarding the Daily Offering of the Sabbath, it does not say "in the morning" but "And on the Sabbath day," whereas the weekday offering explicitly says "one in the morning." This implies that the Sabbath morning service is slightly delayed to allow for the Additional Offering <note>original: "Musaf"</note> or to distinguish the day. The term "On the Sabbath day" refers to the entire duration of the day. This is consistent with what Rashi <note>the premier 11th-century commentator</note> wrote regarding the timing of the meal: on weekdays, people would eat at the fourth or fifth hour, but on the Sabbath, they would stay longer in the synagogue and return home later, at the sixth hour. They would wake up early to go to the synagogue but stay later in prayer and study than they would on weekdays. This delay is part of the "Sabbath delight" <note>original: "Oneg Shabbat"</note>, as the soul is sustained by the spiritual light of the day before the body is sustained by food. This is the secret of the "Extra Soul."

The same is implied in the chapter "All Sacred Writings" <note>Tractate Shabbat, page 119</note>: they would study and preach before the meal. It is told there that Rav Sheshet would sit in the sun during the summer and in the shade during the winter to make himself uncomfortable so that he would finish his study and be eager to eat <note>this is a common Talmudic story about ensuring one eats the Sabbath meal with an appetite</note>. This ensures that the time of eating is a time of pleasure and not a burden.

<meta>This page continues the instructions for the Sabbath, transitioning from the holiness of the person to the practical and spiritual conduct of the Sabbath day, specifically focusing on the three required meals, the rituals of breaking bread, and the laws regarding lighting candles.</meta>

...is small and well-prepared, etc. Digestion is improved when food is small in quantity but high in quality, provided one does not fill his belly. One should drink three cups of wine to gladden his heart—though this depends on the individual—and he should rise from the joy of his eating to establish his study. Or, he may sleep a little to rest his head and limbs, and afterward sit to study, engaging in the depths of the Law <note>original: "Halakha"</note> according to his intellectual capacity, until the time for the Afternoon Prayer <note>original: "Mincha"</note> arrives. He should pray his prayer properly and depart in peace. From then on, he shall set his table to eat the Third Meal <note>original: "Seudah Shlishit"</note>. He should eat it with joy and a good heart to fulfill the verse, "And you shall call the Sabbath a delight" <note>Isaiah 58:13</note>, drawing it out for the appropriate amount of time. He should mention words of Torah at the table as we have written, and bless after his food over a cup of wine. Then he shall depart in peace to study or to the synagogue to arrange the songs and praises for the "Awe-inspiring in Praises" <note>God</note>, blessed and exalted be He, all according to the place and time. So too wrote the Abudraham <note>a 14th-century commentator on the liturgy</note> in the name of a certain scholar: that this is one reason according to the plain meaning <note>original: "peshat"</note> for why the Holy One commanded us to eat three meals. For if a person does not fill his stomach when he knows there is another meal to eat, his mind remains clear. However, if he knows there is no other meal, he will fill his belly with his food and fall into a deep sleep, neglecting the Torah and his attachment to God. For the Sabbath is holy, and one must remain attached to holiness.

# And to eat
Three meals on the Sabbath, as Rashi <note>the preeminent medieval French commentator</note> of blessed memory taught in the 17th chapter of the Laws of Sabbath. This is derived from the fact that the word "Today" <note>Hebrew: "Ha-Yom"</note> is written three times regarding the Sabbath food: "And Moses said: 'Eat it **today**, for **today** is a Sabbath to the Lord; **today** you will not find it in the field'" <note>Exodus 16:25</note>. This teaches that one must prepare three meals. From our language, it sounds as if this is a Torah commandment. The "Delight" <note>Oneg</note> consists of even a single meal from a great table. The Zohar <note>the foundational work of Jewish mysticism</note> states that all the tables of Israel are arranged by the angels in that heavenly palace when the Sabbath enters. Thousands upon thousands and myriads upon myriads of angels are appointed over the tables, watching how the "Delight of Sabbath" <note>Oneg Shabbat</note> is arranged. If an angel sees the table set with all kinds of delights, he blesses the table: "Then you shall delight in the Lord... and the Lord shall answer you" <note>Isaiah 58:14</note>. Then he asks for a long life in the morning, "For thus shall the man be blessed," and all the angels answer "Amen." But when one does not provide Sabbath delight, the angel pushes the table away, and that table is cast out to a place called *Gage* <note>a mystical reference</note>, where the letters of "Delight" (*Oneg* - עג"נ) are reversed to "Plague" (*Nega* - נג"ע). They curse it, saying, "May a curse come upon it... he did not desire blessing, so may it be far from him" <note>Psalm 109:17</note>. May the Merciful One save us. This is the language of the Zohar; look at its words and rejoice.

Regarding the two loaves <note>original: "Lechem Mishneh"</note>, it is written in the *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo's commentary</note>, section 274: It was ruled like Rabbi [Judah the Prince], that one should break <note>the bread</note> from the whole loaf. Ravina said to Rav Ashi: "Does this not look like gluttony?" He answered: "Since he does not do this every day but only now, it does not look like gluttony." Rashi explained "over the whole meal" as meaning a large slice that would suffice for the entire meal. However, the Rashba <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Adret</note> wrote in the chapter "How do we bless" that he does not return to this explanation, but rather it means breaking bread from the loaves placed before him to eat. Similarly, Rav Hai Gaon explained that if a person blesses on the Sabbath over two loaves and breaks one, like Rav Kahana, it is well. And if he breaks for himself enough for the whole meal, like Rabbi Zera, it is also well. Our master <note>Maimonides</note> and the *Magen Avraham* also wrote like Rashi. The *Taz* <note>Rabbi David Ha-Levi Segal</note> wrote two explanations and did not decide between them. In the book *Even Ha-Ezer*, the words of the Rashba are clarified: Rabbi Zera broke enough for the entire meal. Rashi explained this as a large slice, but the Rashba argues this isn't gluttony; on the contrary, it is "a generous eye." Furthermore, one must break bread over two loaves. This is my custom, even though I found it in the name of the Gaon Rabbi Solomon Luria. 

Nonetheless, for the Third Meal, one only breaks bread over one loaf. In the *Kaf Ha-Chayim* <note>or "Kinfey Yona"</note>, it says that for every Sabbath meal, one should declare: "This is the meal of the complete faith." On the table, one should arrange twelve loaves. For the Evening Meal, he should say: "This is the meal of the Holy Field and the Small Face <note>original: "Zeir Anpin"</note> and the Holy Ancient One." By this merit, a man is saved from the birth pangs of the Messiah. For the Morning Meal, he arranges eight loaves and says: "This is the meal of the Holy Ancient One..." By this merit, he is saved from the judgment of Gehenna <note>Hell</note>. For the Afternoon Meal <note>Mincha</note>, he arranges four loaves and says: "This is the meal of the Small Face..." By this merit, he is saved from the war of Gog and Magog. In every meal, he should not cut his bread, but use two loaves, intending for the upper and lower loaves to correspond to mystical emanations. He always breaks from the right-hand loaf. On the night following Sabbath <note>original: "Motza'ei Shabbat"</note>, he arranges three loaves, and by this merit, he is saved from the "beating of the grave" <note>original: "Chibut Ha-Kever"</note>. He recites twenty-six blessings, corresponding to the numerical value of the Name of God, blessed be He.

# It is fitting
For every meal to have a man prepare himself from the start, as is found in the chapter "With what may we light" regarding Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. He saw an old man holding two bundles of myrtle <note>original: "Asa"</note> running at twilight. They asked him, "What are these for?" He said, "For the honor of the Sabbath." They asked, "Would not one suffice?" He replied, "One corresponds to 'Remember' <note>Zakhor</note> and one corresponds to 'Observe' <note>Shamor</note>." He said to his son, "See how beloved the commandments are to Israel!" Even though we light two candles—one for "Remember" and one for "Observe"—nevertheless, a God-fearing person fulfills both. There are other reasons for lighting two candles. I have seen meticulous people use two bundles of myrtle since it is mentioned in the Talmud. The *Kol Bo* <note>a book of laws and customs</note> wrote that one should not eat while it is still day, so as not to be too early or too late. The *Tashbetz* wrote that the Maharam <note>Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg</note> used to eat on Friday night exactly at sunset, not waiting for actual night, nor eating while the day was still very long, as people do at weddings.

<margin>
I also found in the "New Responsa" near the end: one should not eat during the summer until near sunset. He cited many proofs not to be too early or too late. See also the book *Sefer Chasidim*, section 266: One who ate while it was still day on Sabbath, such as for the Third Meal, and three stars had not yet appeared... he is exempt from reciting the Grace after Meals over a cup... regarding the three meals, what he ate before sunset... see there in the supplement.
</margin>

# If
The candle goes out, it is forbidden to tell a Gentile to light it for him. Similarly, on Saturday night near dark before one has prayed. The Rama <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles</note> wrote: "Some say it is permitted to tell a Gentile to light a candle for the Sabbath meal because they believe telling a Gentile is permitted even for a primary labor in the context of a commandment <note>original: "mitzvah"</note>." Based on this, many are lenient to command a Gentile to light candles for a meal, especially a wedding feast or a circumcision, and no one protests. However, one should be stringent where there is no great need. And I say, where there is no great need, it is certainly forbidden according to most authorities. I have seen in distinguished communities that they sit in the dark on Saturday night, even at a wedding feast, until the congregation has said "Bless the Lord," and only then does one who has prayed light the candles. You, my children, be very careful, since many break boundaries and are lenient.

The conjugal rights <note>original: "Onah"</note> of Torah scholars are specifically designated for Friday night, as the Sages interpreted the verse: "Who yields its fruit in its season" <note>Psalm 1:3</note>—this refers to the intimacy of scholars from Friday night to Friday night. (Rabbi Solomon Luria wrote that the acronym of "And the children of Israel shall keep the Sabbath" <note>Exodus 31:16</note> spells "Coming" <note>Hebrew: "Biah," referring to intimacy</note>). In the Zohar, it is written that "keeping" the Sabbath refers to a person guarding himself all the weekdays and saving his strength for the Sabbath. The secret is "to the eunuchs who keep My Sabbaths"—referring to those who restrain themselves in the Garden. The righteous person who holds onto the Covenant, the child born from that union is a "tzadik" <note>righteous person</note>. Know that during the six work days, the gate of the inner courtyard shall be closed, but on the day...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Sabbath rituals, specifically focusing on the transition from the holy Sabbath to the workweek through the ceremony of Havdalah (Separation) and the Melaveh Malkah (Escorting the Queen) meal.</meta>

[A parable is told] of a king whom the people escort with joy and with songs. Therefore, we are accustomed to perform the **Havdalah** <note>The ceremony marking the end of the Sabbath</note> while standing, even though it would technically be appropriate to sit—especially when one person fulfills the obligation for their fellow through the blessing, which usually requires sitting as mentioned in the legal codes. This is because the way one "escorts" a guest is by standing.

The book *Tola'at Yaakov* <note>A 16th-century Kabbalistic commentary on the liturgy by Meir ibn Gabbai</note> writes in Section 77: The reason we add from the "weekday to the holy" at the conclusion of the Sabbath is to demonstrate and show that we do not wish for the "Holy Personhood" <note>The extra Sabbath soul</note> to depart from among us. Their departure is very difficult for us, and therefore we delay it. Out of great affection, we escort the Sabbath with songs and praises, similar to the verse, "We would have sent you away with mirth and with songs" <note>Genesis 31:27</note>. So it is said in the Midrash: A parable of a bride and a queen whom they escort with songs and praises. It was already hinted at above that the secret of the Sabbath is that she is called a "Bride," and "New Faces" <note>original: "panim chadashot"—a term used for wedding guests</note> have come here—meaning in the Sabbath prayers. Since the Bride has come anew, she must be brought in with songs and praises, and similarly, she should be escorted out with songs and praises when she departs.

Therefore, it is a good and proper custom to sing hymns at the entrance of the Sabbath and at its departure. The *Tur* <note>The Arba'ah Turim, a foundational code of Jewish law</note> wrote regarding this in Section 295: It is common to mention **Elijah the Prophet**. The author of the *Ittur* explains the reason is that he is destined to announce the Redemption. It is stated in the Talmud <note>Tractate Eruvin</note> that Israel is assured that Elijah will not arrive on a Friday or a Holiday <note>so as not to disrupt preparations</note>. Therefore, we pray that since the Sabbath has passed and he is now able to come, may he come and bring us good tidings.

The *Maharil* <note>Rabbi Yaakov Moelin, a primary source for Ashkenazic custom</note> says: The reason we are accustomed to say verses about Elijah and hymns based on his name is because it is stated in the *Tosefta* that on Saturday nights, Elijah—of blessed memory—sits under the Tree of Life and records the merits of those who keep the Sabbath.

My teacher and Rabbi <note>referring to Rabbi Moses Isserles, known as the Rama</note> wrote in his *Shulchan Aruch*, Section 296: During Havdalah, one should fix their eyes on the cup and the candle. We pour out some of the cup of wine before finishing the blessing "Who creates the fruit of the vine" so that the cup is not "lacking" <note>completely full</note>. The reason for the spilling is that we say in the language of the Sages: "A house in which wine is not spilled like water will not see a sign of blessing." We also pour from the cup after Havdalah, extinguish the candle in it, and wash the eyes with it out of love for the commandment.

However, I heard in the name of the *Maharshal* <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria</note> that their custom was not good, for it looks like a disgrace to the commandment. Rather, only at the time of mixing the cup for Havdalah, one should fill it to its very brim, more than is necessary, so that it overflows. On the ground, he should "pour out like water" <note>original: "yishpoch kemayim"</note> before he begins. After drinking the Havdalah cup, he should pour from it. There are those who are precise and begin to pour into the cup when they start saying "Behold, God is my salvation," and continue until they reach "And from the wells of salvation," at which point they pour so that the wine flows over the lip of the cup.

It is worthy for a person to strive and seek wine for Havdalah, as Rabbi Yochanan said: Three are among the inheritors of the World to Come, and they are: one who dwells in the Land of Israel, one who raises his children for Torah study, and one who recites Havdalah over wine at the conclusion of the Sabbath. What does this mean? That he leaves over wine from the Sanctification <note>Kiddush</note> for the Havdalah. Rashi explains: This refers to one who has only a little wine and prevents himself from drinking it on Friday night [to save it for Havdalah]. The *Tur* brought this in Section 296, and the *Tzedah LaDerech* by the Radbaz concludes: Anyone who recites Havdalah over wine is beloved... and it acts as a spiritual remedy <note>original: "segulah"</note>. The Arizal <note>Rabbi Isaac Luria, the great Kabbalist</note> said: One who recites Havdalah over wine will have children worthy of rendering legal rulings. This is also found in the *Tur* in the aforementioned section.

The *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo</note> wrote in Section 297 in the name of the *Mordechai*, and it is also in the *Shulchan Aruch*: One takes the wine in the right hand and the myrtle in the left, blesses the wine, then takes the myrtle in the right and the wine in the left and blesses the myrtle... and then returns the wine to the right.

<column-break/>

# It was written
by the *Tur* in Section 297: It is the custom in all places to bless over the **myrtle** <note>original: "hadas"</note>, and the custom of our ancestors is Law. In Section 300, the *Beit Yosef* wrote in the *Shulchan Aruch* to bless over the myrtle wherever possible. My teacher wrote in his *Shulchan Aruch*: It is not appropriate to bless over dry myrtle because it has no scent; rather, one should use other spices. This is the custom in these lands. However, in many places, they place myrtle together with the other spices to satisfy all opinions. One should heed his words, for it is not an empty matter; the *Knesset HaGedolah* wrote that the masters of Kabbalah say there is a "secret" in the myrtle when blessing it on Saturday night. (The *Zohar*, Portion Vayakhel, mentions the myrtle having "three leaves" as a wonderful mystery regarding the secret of the Name of 72. One who fears Heaven should fulfill these words).

One must look at their fingernails before blessing "Who creates the lights of the fire," because it is written: "And God saw the light, that it was good; and God divided..." <note>Genesis 1:4</note>. I found that those who are precise say this commandment is performed best by blessing over a **torch**. (A gloss in the *Sefer Chasidim* says: On Saturday night, one should not take wood called *Kyat* to perform Havdalah or bless over it because its smell is bad, and one needs something good, as written in the *Book of Traditions*).

The reason for the torch is that since the blessing is "Who creates the lights <note>plural</note> of the fire," there must be a torch where many flames are seen. We are accustomed to look at the fingernails (and it is further written in the tradition: they stand looking at the palms of the hands so they may benefit from the light). My teacher wrote in his *Shulchan Aruch*: One should look at the fingernails of the right hand and see the skin of the left hand. One should fold the fingers into the hand so that they see the nails together with the palm, and they should not see the "face" <note>inner side</note> of the fingers.

*Tola'at Yaakov* says: Fourteen camps are arranged from that light and are called "Lights of the Fire." We fold four fingers of the right hand against the light, which is a hint to those camps, the secret of the "Lower Chariots" that shine from the light—the secret of the Bride, the Assembly of Israel, who rules over them like a <unclear>Arsikion</unclear>. One should not look at the back of the fingers, which are a hint to the lower lights, of which it is said, "And you shall see my back" <note>Exodus 33:23</note>. The inner parts are a hint to the upper lights, of which it is said, "But my face shall not be seen." One should not fold the inner fingers before the light because they are internal and do not shine like the light below; they shine from the Upper Light above. But the backs shine from the lower light, therefore we fold the backs of the fingers toward the light to hint that from the "face" <note>inside</note> they shine, etc. His words follow the *Zohar*. Our Sages taught in the laws of Havdalah: This is the custom—first one brings the fingers into the hands and bows the lower part, then stretches them out, and behold, there is light in the place of darkness. So wrote the *Knesset HaGedolah* in the name of *Shibbolei HaLeket*... one blesses because it is proper to benefit from the light.

One should not drink the Havdalah wine until they sit. In the Responsa of *Maharil*, Section 38, Rabbi Zalman did not drink the Havdalah cup until he sat, likely because "a scholar should not eat while standing and should not drink while standing."

Regarding the washing of the face [with wine] to show affection for the commandment: We arrange the table to eat on Saturday night even if one only needs an olive's bulk of food, in order to **"Escort the Queen."** In Section 300: For there is a bone in man called the *Luz* <note>a legendary indestructible bone</note> and it is only sustained by eating on Saturday night. The author of *Tzedah LaDerech* wrote: Just as we bless over spices to restore the soul, so too is the order of the table. To go from one thing to its opposite is strange; as we go from rest to labor, we should hold a beautiful candle, more than other weekday nights, and honor the table and say verses of joy.

A person must be very careful with this meal of Escorting the Queen and spend money on it, as taught in Tractate Shabbat, page 119: For Rabbi Abbahu, they would prepare a third-born calf on Saturday night, and he would eat only its kidney. When his son Abimi grew up, he said, "Why waste so much? Let us leave the kidney from the Friday meal." They left it, and a lion came and ate [the calf].

One who fasts on Saturday night because they are making a break from the honor of the day should strive to prepare this meal afterward. He should study the passages and words composed for this meal and its secret, and may the words of his mouth be acceptable as if he had performed it. So did Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai on the eve of Passover that fell on the Sabbath; he engaged in the secrets of the Torah in place of the Third Meal.

# It was written
in *Reshit Chokhmah* <note>A 16th-century moral-mystical work by Eliyahu de Vidas</note>, Chapter 3 of the Gate of Holiness: The holiness of the Sabbath is in **Thought, Speech, and Action**. In Chapter 4, he wrote that speech, thought, and action are hindered [without holiness] according to the *Zohar*, for they represent the Soul, Spirit, and Breath <note>Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah</note>. It is known that they grow stronger on the Sabbath... I have not come except to awaken people to certain things that many have neglected, to serve as a reminder.

Regarding "Doing Good," one must sanctify through **Speech**, which is the sanctity of the day in prayers and over the cup, and to increase songs and hymns. As I brought above, one must bring in the Sabbath with songs and praises and escort it out with songs and praises. One should also speak the words of the Sages from Tractate Shabbat, page 118, before each of the three meals: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi said in the name of Bar Kappara: Anyone who fulfills the Three Meals on the Sabbath is saved from three tribulations—the birth pangs of the Messiah, the judgment of Gehenna <note>Hell</note>, and the war of Gog and Magog.

"The birth pangs of the Messiah"—for "Day" is written here, and there it is written, "Behold, I send you Elijah the Prophet before the coming of the **day**..." "The judgment of Gehenna"—for "Day" is written here, and there it is written, "That **day** is a day of wrath." "The war of Gog and Magog"—for "Day" is written here, and there it is written, "On the **day** that Gog shall come."

Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Yose: Anyone who delights in the Sabbath is given a boundless heritage, as it is said, "Then you shall delight in the Lord... and I will feed you the heritage of Jacob your father" <note>Isaiah 58:14</note>. Not like Abraham, of whom it is written "Arise, walk through the land in the length of it and in the breadth of it," nor like Isaac, of whom it is written "For to you and to your seed I will give all these lands," but like Jacob, of whom it is written "And you shall spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south." Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: He is saved from the subjugation of the kingdoms... Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the laws and spiritual atmosphere of the Sabbath, moving from the conclusion of the day (Havdalah) back to the internal experience of the Sabbath itself, specifically regarding emotional expression, fasting, and the balance between rest and study.</meta>

**Tractate Shabbat**

So it seems to me, and so I have found: if one is obligated to fulfill the command to "call the Sabbath a delight" [Isaiah 58:13], it follows through an "a fortiori" argument <term>kal va-chomer</term> <note>A logical inference: if a lesser case is true, the more important case must certainly be true.</note> that one should not grieve with any sorrow; and it follows as an even stronger argument that one should not weep. Even weeping by way of repentance for one’s sins is forbidden on the Sabbath, for so it may be learned from the Book of Nehemiah, Chapter 8 <note>Where the leaders told the people not to mourn or weep because the day was holy.</note>. However, one who fasts on the Sabbath due to a disturbing dream <term>ta’anit chalom</term> is permitted to regret, weep, and supplicate. This is also written in the book *Seder HaYom* <note>A 16th-century book of daily Jewish practice by Moshe ben Machir.</note>, as follows: "If one saw a dream and his soul is grieving such that it is appropriate to fast for it, he is permitted to live in sadness and with a heavy heart... for the little bit of joy lost through the soul's affliction is outweighed by the flesh's delight in being relieved of its worry." Since they permitted him to fast for the benefit of his soul and the preservation of his body—for through this he will find righteousness, life, and honor—even when he "sits alone and is silent" [Lamentations 3:28]. Regarding his sins or iniquities: let him not recount them, and they will tear up a seventy-year decree against him through God's mercy on his affliction and his sighing on a day when all the world is at ease while he is in pain. It turns out that the sighing is a rest for him.

And it seems to me that even though he regrets before his King and confesses in his heart with a full mouth, saying "I have sinned, I have been iniquitous, I have transgressed, remove my sin and let me not die," this is permitted to him on the Sabbath because it is a matter of saving a life <term>pikuach nefesh</term>. Just as they permitted fasting due to the fear of a life-threatening situation—lest some decree was issued against him and he needs to annul it even on the Sabbath—for this same reason it is permitted to confess and say "I have sinned..." and it shall be considered a righteous act for him to return to his God from whatever sin he has committed. He should not let the opportunity pass, for "man does not know his time." For this reason, it seems to me right to "turn the dream to good" <note>A ritual of reciting positive verses to neutralize a bad dream.</note> on the Sabbath. And even though one does not ask for their personal needs on the Sabbath, and the Sages said that one who asks for his needs seven times will have it decreed against him from heaven, there is no need to fear this here, for regarding the saving of a life—or even a doubt thereof—one violates the Sabbath. All the more so here, where he does not actually violate the Sabbath laws, and it is a commandment to be with a group to "make the dream good" because he restores the soul of the one fasting or dreaming.

One who fasts on the Sabbath must not waste the day in vanity; rather, he should sequester himself in the Synagogue or the House of Study, or in a modest place, and read or study, each according to his level. He should request of our God that He accept his fast and annul every evil decree from him. He should not sit among those eating nor among those playing, and should distance himself from delight the entire day. Thereby, he will be filled with mercy from Heaven and find shelter under God's wings, and his request will ascend.

And the Rema <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles, a major legal authority.</note> wrote in his glosses [to Shulchan Aruch, section 288]: "One for whom it is a delight to weep so that the pain leaves his heart is permitted to weep on the Sabbath." Even though there is no proof from there for one who weeps out of repentance—for on the contrary, that person weeps in order to feel pain—nonetheless, since he feels pain in order that the punishment for his sins will depart from him, this pain becomes a delight to him. And even if in general times of repentance one should not do so, nonetheless, when the day itself causes it, such as in a dream fast, it is permitted to him specifically on that day.

And thus wrote the *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo's commentary on the Tur.</note> in section 288: It is written in the *Agur* in the name of the *Shibbolei HaLeket* that it is found in the Aggadah <note>Homiletic or narrative traditions.</note> that they found a student of Rabbi Akiva weeping on the Sabbath, and he said: "This is a delight for me." Some prove from here that a person in mourning finds it a delight not to eat; since it is almost forbidden for him to eat, it would cause him pain to do so. Therefore, the *Kol Bo* writes in section 25: It is possible to say that specifically fasting for business matters or out of despair is what is forbidden; but one who fasts out of repentance and piety, his fast is a delight to him and is permitted. Nevertheless, it is not appropriate for a person to make a habit of this, and you will not find anyone who excels in piety who fasts on Sabbaths, Festivals, or New Moons, except for Yom Kippur. As Maimonides wrote in the first chapter of the Laws of Fasting: a person who fasts every day finds eating on the Sabbath to be a pain due to the change in his habit. We have seen many pious men and men of deed who were sad on the Sabbath for this reason, and I heard the same regarding Judah the Pious <note>A 12th-century leader of the Chassidei Ashkenaz.</note>, that he would do so. Similarly, we say in the Talmud [Tractate Pesachim]: "Mar the son of Ravina used to sit in a fast the whole year, except for Shavuot, Purim, and the Eve of Yom Kippur." But without such a circumstance, it is forbidden. However, the Rashba <note>Rabbi Shlomo ben Aderet, a 13th-century authority.</note> wrote in a response that the case of Mar the son of Ravina was specifically regarding a dream fast, for otherwise it would be forbidden. This must be the interpretation so that he does not disagree with all the other Tannaim and Amoraim <note>The Sages of the Mishnah and Talmud.</note>. Even if you say he refers to a general fast, we do not abandon the majority of the Sages to follow a single opinion, especially in a matter of strictness that leads to...

---

-> ...bringing proof to the matter. <-

### And Fasting
<margin>
See also *Sefer Chasidim* [Book of the Pious], section 161: One who finds delight in weeping so that suffering does not come upon him (God forbid) is not considered to be violating the Sabbath. It appears this applies when he fears a trouble coming upon him, whether through a dream or an occurrence. But if it is due to repentance for his sins, it is forbidden on the Sabbath.
</margin>
A dream: since it has come to my hand, let me say a word about it, for I have seen many people who are lenient and fast on the Sabbath when they feel low. It has already been explained that in this time, one should not fast a dream fast on the Sabbath, for we are not experts in the interpretation of dreams to know which are good and which are bad. The world is accustomed to fast only for three specific types of dreams, as explained in section 288. However, it seems to me that even for these, one should not fast unless his soul is grieving and his heart is in pain, for only then is the fast a delight for him; otherwise, it is not. When people have asked me about their dreams on the Sabbath, I was accustomed to rule for them in most cases that they should not fast on the Sabbath, so that they may fulfill the commandment of Sabbath delight. Instead, they should take upon themselves a voluntary fast during the weekdays. Since one who fasts on the Sabbath would have needed to "fast for his fast" <note>A penance fast for having fasted on a holy day.</note>, let him now take upon himself two days. Even though the Sages said it must be "on that very day," nonetheless, accepting it on that day is sufficient, since his intention is for the sake of Heaven—not to desecrate the Sabbath. The acceptance is considered like the deed itself, for a time of distress is different. As we see in Tractate Ta'anit, page 8: In the days of Rabbi Judah, a fast was decreed by Heaven... but they could not fast [on that day]. Rabbi Judah said to them, "Let us accept it upon ourselves..." and the decree was annulled. He was asked, "From where do you know this?" He replied, "As it is written: 'Then he said to me, fear not, Daniel, for from the first day that you did set your heart to understand and to fast before your God, your words were heard' [Daniel 10:12]."

---

### And the one who fasts
on the Sabbath must "fast for his fast" <note>Perform a penance fast on a weekday to atone for the lack of joy on the Sabbath.</note>. They wrote that one is not specifically obligated to fast on Sunday. The book *Tola'at Yaakov* writes: "Know that one who fasts on the Sabbath cancels the Supernal Delight and the boundary of the Congregation of Israel which is completed on this holy day. If afterward on Sunday—a time when the weekdays rule—he fasts, he atones for the end of it before the Holy One, Blessed be He... This is why it is written 'Do not say I will repay evil' [Proverbs 20:22]. This sin is punished in this world and the next. Therefore, he must fast immediately on Sunday, the time of the dominion of that spirit of the weekday... and in this, he finds healing and returns the 'theft' he stole [from the Sabbath]." Happy is the one who cleaves to the holy faith and strives always in the service of the Omnipresent to do what is right in His eyes, to cleave to Him, as it is said: "And you who cleave to the Lord your God are all alive today" [Deuteronomy 4:4].

---

### Sleep on the Sabbath
is a delight, provided one does not overindulge in it too much, so that it does not lead him to the neglect of Torah study. For Sabbaths were only given for rest <note>original: "eersa"—a bed/couch</note> and joy. It says in the Midrash: The Torah said before the Holy One, Blessed be He, "Master of the Universe! when Israel enters the Land, this one runs to his vineyard and that one runs to his field—what will become of me?" He said to her, "I have a partner that I am pairing with you, and her name is Sabbath; for on it they are idle from their work and can occupy themselves with you." And it says in *Midrash Tanchuma* on the portion *Vayakhel*: The masters of Aggadah would say: from the beginning of the Torah until its end, there is no portion that begins with the word "Assembly" <term>Kehillah</term> except for this portion alone. And why so? The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moses: "Go down and make for Me large assemblies regarding the matter of the Sabbath, so that all the generations coming after you will learn to assemble communities every Sabbath and enter synagogues and study halls to learn Torah in public." Rabbi Alexander said: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Israel, "If you assemble every single Sabbath... and read the Torah and the Prophets, I consider it as if you have made Me King over My world." For so the Prophet Isaiah explains: "You are My witnesses, says the Lord, and I am God" [Isaiah 43:12]—you testify about Me that I am God in the world. And even though it says in the Jerusalem Talmud: "Rabbi Chaggai said: Sabbaths and Festivals were only given for eating and drinking," while Rabbi Berechiah said: "Sabbaths and Festivals were only given for occupying oneself with words of Torah," the *Tanchuma* explains that they do not disagree. What Rabbi Berechiah said refers to workers who are busy with work all week, and on the Sabbath, they gather to study Torah. What Rabbi Chaggai said refers to Torah scholars who are weary from Torah study all week, and on the Sabbath, they find delight [in rest]. God forbid that one should spend the whole day only in delight, but rather one should enjoy delight more than other days; but it is forbidden to separate from the Torah. Everyone agrees the Torah was given on the Sabbath. On the contrary, a person is obligated to innovate new insights in the Torah every Sabbath, as it is written in the Zohar: When the "Extra Soul" <term>Neshama Yeteira</term> <note>The additional spiritual capacity granted to a Jew on the Sabbath.</note> returns to its place, the Holy One, Blessed be He, asks it, "What new insight did you innovate in the Torah?" One should also honor the Sabbath at its departure with the order of parting, with songs and by setting a meal. My father and teacher, of blessed memory, used to be in "The Valley of Blessing" <note>Reference to the book *Emek HaBeracha*.</note> and would say the blessing with a melody, well and beautifully, in order to escort the Queen <note>The Sabbath Queen</note> with joy and with songs.

<summary>This page discusses the emotional and physical requirements of the Sabbath, weighing the obligation of joy against the distress of bad dreams and the necessity of repentance. It emphasizes that while sleep and food are essential delights, the primary purpose of the Sabbath remains public Torah study and spiritual growth.</summary>

# Tractate Shabbat

...which is like a serpent before its Creator. Therefore, our Sages of blessed memory said that the authority of a man after seventy years becomes like a serpent. This applies to one who did not bow during the *Modim* prayer <note>The "We give thanks" section of the Amidah prayer.</note> to the right, and ten prostrations corresponding to the man who was created on the right. To the left, ten corresponding to the woman who was created on the left. And in the belly, nine corresponding to the earth which was cursed with nine curses, for it is like the belly. Until here are his words <note>original: "עכ"ל", an abbreviation for "until here are his words," used when finishing a quote.</note>. That is to say, the belly caused these nine, and He decreed nine types of labor; one who damages them enters into the thirty-nine curses. But one who is careful is blessed, for the Sabbath is blessed to the Lord, as it is said, "And He blessed it" [Genesis 2:3]. And according to this hint from the *Rokeach* <note>Rabbi Eleazar of Worms, a 12-twelfth-century scholar and mystic.</note>, the Tanna <note>A sage from the era of the Mishnah.</note> taught in the chapter *Klal Gadol*: "The primary categories of labor are forty minus one." One might ask: why not just say thirty-nine? Rather, the Tanna used the language of the verse regarding lashes, "Forty he shall strike him" [Deuteronomy 25:3], meaning to say the sum of forty <note>original: "מנין סכום ארבעים", implying the number that leads up to forty but does not reach it.</note>. (And there is a hidden secret as to why the verse spoke of "forty"). These thirty-nine labors correspond to the thirty-nine curses, and the secret of the thirty-nine lashes is why the Tanna used that specific phrasing. It is difficult to conclude that "The Lord blessed the Sabbath day" for a blessing and not for a curse; may a person always be a light...

->Knesset<- <note>Likely an abbreviation for a specific communal or legal heading.</note>

...is called in Heaven "Sabbath," which is weighed against the entire Torah and hints at the world that is entirely Sabbath <note>A reference to the World to Come.</note>. One is obligated to study all the laws of the Sabbath in the works of the earlier and later legal authorities <term>Rishonim and Achronim</term> in order to observe, perform, and fulfill them. There are many matters in which the world is not careful, and through their transgressions, they stumble—such as <term>Amirah L'Goy</term> <note>Asking a non-Jew to perform labor on the Sabbath.</note>, which is a rabbinic prohibition <term>Shvut</term>, and many types of <term>Muktzeh</term> <note>Objects that are "set aside" and forbidden to be handled on the Sabbath.</note>. For example, I have seen many people holding chickens in their hands when they flee outside; they stumble through the prohibition of instructing a non-Jew or by handling it themselves. In the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Shabbat, it says: it is forbidden to move cattle, beasts, or birds. Nevertheless, it is permitted to overturn a basket before chicks so they may climb up and down on it, but while they are on it, it is forbidden to move the basket. One may "lead" cattle, beasts, or birds in a courtyard—that is, holding them by the neck and the sides and walking them if the animals need it—provided one does not lift them in a way that their feet are uprooted from the ground. They are *Muktzeh* and it is forbidden to move them, except for a chicken, which should not be "led" because it lifts itself off the ground, resulting in the person carrying it. But one may push a goose from behind with the hands so that it enters the coop.

<margin>
This is found in Chapter 9 of the Laws of Sabbath and in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 3. Regarding broken vessels: it is written in the "Old" Jerusalem Talmud that if a stone or metal vessel was broken even before the Sabbath, it is forbidden to move it on the Sabbath. But in the "New" version, Chapter 308, it says even if it broke on the Sabbath, if it is still somewhat fit for use, it is permitted to move it. In the *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* (Semag), it says this is specifically for a private domain. The *Kol Bo*, the *Shulchan Aruch* (Chapter 308, Section 10), the *Tur*, and the *Shiltei HaGibborim* all seem to agree that this is specifically on the Sabbath day, and only if it has no use at all for any other work except its original purpose, and not for making other things, but only for holding fruit or other items. All this is to fulfill the duty of the Sabbath in a place where there is enough to perform work.
</margin>

<margin>
The *Mordechai* <note>13th-century legal authority.</note> wrote in the name of the *Avi HaEzri* that the requirement to place a "loaf of bread or a child" on a corpse <note>A legal workaround to allow moving a corpse on the Sabbath to prevent it from being disgraced or burned.</note> only applies to a naked corpse. But if the corpse is covered, one may move it. However, his clothing... it seems to me that this is not the opinion of Rashi or other legalists...
</margin>

<margin>
One must ask the Rabbis if there is a concern regarding the prohibition of "dyeing" <term>Tzovei'a</term>. According to the author who says "there is no prohibited way of dyeing with food," it is permitted. However, it is proper for every Jew who eats berries or other staining fruits to be careful not to touch his clothes or the tablecloth with stained hands, for that would be a "sub-category" of dyeing. If blood comes out of a wound, it is forbidden to place a cloth over it <note>Because the blood will dye the cloth.</note>. But if one colors his bread with fruit juice, we do not mind, for there is no "dyeing" in food. Regarding women's jewelry on the Sabbath, it is explained in the Tractate and in Chapter 301 that a woman should not go out wearing a signet ring into a courtyard that does not have an *Eruv* <note>A legal boundary that allows carrying on the Sabbath.</note>. One must warn women about this in places where there is no *Eruv*.
</margin>

<margin>
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Hanina... regarding contracting <term>Kablanut</term> <note>Hiring a non-Jew to do work at their own pace.</note>: inside the Sabbath boundary <term>Tehum</term> it is forbidden; outside the boundary, it is permitted. An important person <term>Adam Chashuv</term> is different. Some say Mar Zutra... they were taking bricks from Mar Zutra's place and building with them on a Festival without his knowledge...
</margin>

<column-break/>

According to the plain meaning <term>Peshat</term>, we can answer and say that the primary labors are indeed forty, and they are taught as "minus one." <note>The text here enters a complex linguistic and legal debate about the counting of the 39 Melakhot, referencing the *Tosafot* (medieval commentators) on Tractate Shabbat, page 70, and the views of Rav Ashi regarding whether "plowing" and "sowing" or other sub-categories are counted separately.</note> The *Tosafot* explain that even though they are sub-categories <term>Toldot</term>, they are still considered primary categories <term>Avot</term> because they were performed in the Tabernacle <term>Mishkan</term>... A sub-category is exactly like its primary category in terms of the penalty. The labors that were performed in the Tabernacle are the "fathers" (primary), and even though they are thirty-nine for the purpose of the sacrifice, there is still the sub-category of "dyeing"...

# Warnings on Trapping and Moving Objects

Sometimes people stumble in several matters, such as the snare of "trapping" in a group. The *Rema* <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles, 16th-century author of the Ashkenazi glosses to the Shulchan Aruch.</note> ruled at the end of Chapter 306 that it is forbidden to trap a beast or a bird that is in one's possession. He further wrote: if a beast is frightened, it is forbidden to catch it on the Sabbath. I have seen many times people taking a bird that has escaped and putting it back...

The "Old" Jerusalem Talmud says it is forbidden even if it broke before the Sabbath, and certainly if it broke on the Sabbath. The *Rema* brought this in Chapter 308, and the laws of *Muktzeh* are very long. However, I am not dealing with simple matters or Rashi's commentary alone. People take wood and stones on the Sabbath and throw them, but those who fear the Lord and are knowledgeable must keep their eyes on the details of these matters. When you delve into the laws of *Muktzeh*, you will find that even a vessel whose primary work is permitted <term>Keli she-melachto l'heter</term> is only permitted to be moved for a specific need—either for the use of the object itself or for the use of the place it occupies. But to move it for no need at all is forbidden. Regarding sacred scrolls and food, it is permitted to move them even for no need at all, as written by the *Beit Yosef* in Chapter 308.

Regarding the "loaf or child" workaround for a corpse mentioned by the *Mordechai*: he claims if a corpse is clothed, it can be moved. But this does not seem to be the view of Rashi. I have a definitive refutation of his words from the chapter *Bameh Madlikin* (page 30), where Solomon asked the House of Study: "My father [David] is dead and lying in the sun; what shall I do?" They answered him: "Place a loaf of bread or a child upon him and move him." Now, King David was certainly clothed! One cannot suggest that he was naked, God forbid. This is a great difficulty against the *Mordechai*. We cannot say that he was stripped to be anointed with oil for healing and then died naked, for it would be a disgrace to leave a king in the sun. Rather, he must have died instantly, and the place was sunny. Therefore, the law remains: one specifically needs a loaf or a child.

Regarding "sorting" <term>Borer</term>: the *Rema* wrote in Chapter 319 that two types of fish are considered two types of food, and it is forbidden to sort one from the other except by hand for immediate consumption, even if the pieces are large and recognizable. But if it is all one type, even if one picks large pieces from the small ones, it is not called "sorting." In large feasts where types of fish are mixed together, the servers are not careful about this; therefore, one must warn them.

# Further Warnings

It is forbidden to calculate sums of money, or measures, or counts, as explained in Chapter 324. I have come as one who reminds and warns about this, for the world is not careful. These are things mentioned in the Mishnah and Talmud. The *Rosh* <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, 13th-century scholar.</note> was careful not to urinate in the snow <note>Because it creates a "path" or "hole," which could be seen as a form of building or digging.</note>, and so it is proper to be careful. The *Beit Yosef* wrote at the end of Chapter 320, citing the *Shibbolei HaLeket*, that one should ask the Rabbis about the concern of "dyeing" when eating berries... <note>Repeats the warning about staining clothes with fruit juice or blood, and the prohibition of women wearing signet rings where there is no Eruv.</note>
