<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the sanctity of the Sabbath, specifically focusing on the mystical significance of the three Sabbath meals, the Havdalah ceremony marking the end of the Sabbath, and the spiritual implications of Sabbath delight.</meta>

<page-num>141</page-num>
<header>Tractate Shabbat</header>

The Higher Light is revealed, the secret of the "Ancient of Days" <note>original: "Atik Yomin" — a Kabbalistic term for the highest, most ancient level of the Divine crown (Keter)</note>, and from here there is proof that the third meal must be performed at the time of the afternoon prayer <note>original: "Mincha"</note>. This is not like those who perform the third meal in the morning, immediately after the [second] meal where they recite the Grace after Meals, and then remove the tablecloth and return to perform the third. There is no mention here of the Sabbath meal being performed in halves, nor of the third meal, whose proper time is at the afternoon prayer, because it corresponds to the Ancient of Days, who is revealed at that hour. There is further proof from the Bible in the chapter "All Sacred Writings" <note>A chapter in the Talmud, Tractate Shabbat 117b.</note>: if a fire breaks out on the night of the Sabbath, one may rescue food for three meals; in the morning, one may rescue food for two meals; and at the afternoon prayer, one may rescue food for one meal. There is even further proof from what we learned in the first chapter of Tractate Pesachim: when the 14th of Nisan <note>The eve of Passover.</note> falls on a Sabbath, everything [leavened] is removed before the Sabbath, and one leaves over food for exactly two meals. One must leave over exactly two meals because leaven becomes forbidden from the sixth hour <note>Mid-day</note> and onwards; this implies that the time for the third meal is only at the afternoon prayer. 

Our teacher Tam <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Meir (1100–1171), a leading French Tosafist.</note> was accustomed, when the 14th of Nisan fell on a Sabbath, to eat "enriched matzah" <note>term: <term>Matzah Ashirah</term> — Matzah made with fruit juice, oil, or honey instead of water, which is not considered "bread of affliction."</note> for the third meal, kneaded with oil and honey. For our Sages, of blessed memory, did not say "anyone who eats matzah on the eve of Passover is like one who cohabits with his betrothed in the house of his father-in-law" except regarding "bread of affliction" <note>plain matzah used for the Seder</note>. However, enriched matzah is permitted, for the obligation of "bread of affliction" does not take effect until the evening. 

It is written in the Midrash of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai <note>The Zohar</note>, may peace be upon him, that he was accustomed to set the table on the 14th of Nisan that fell on a Sabbath and engage in the "Work of the Chariot" <note>term: <term>Ma'aseh Merkavah</term> — Early Jewish esoteric mysticism based on the vision of the prophet Ezekiel.</note> in place of the third meal, saying: "This is the meal of the King." It is a hidden secret, and there is a mnemonic for these meals: "And you shall call the Sabbath a delight (*oneg*)" and "A river goes out of Eden to water the garden." The Hebrew words Eden, River (*Nahar*), and Garden (*Gan*) correspond to the order of the meals. The **Garden** (G) corresponds to the night meal, representing the Bride <note>The Shekhinah</note> who is called a "locked garden." The **River** (N) corresponds to the morning meal, the secret of the "Beauty of Israel" (*Tiferet Yisrael*), which is the Sabbath day. The **Eden** (E) corresponds to the afternoon meal, representing the Higher Eden. Thus far are his words. 

However, according to the tradition of the godly Ari <note>Rabbi Isaac Luria (1534–1572), the father of contemporary Kabbalah.</note>, of blessed memory, it follows the first opinion: the night meal is for the "Feminine of the Lesser Countenance" <note>original: "Nukba de-Zeir Anpin"</note>, the morning meal is for the "Holy Ancient One" <note>original: "Atika Kadisha"</note>, and the afternoon meal is for the "Lesser Countenance" <note>original: "Zeir Anpin" — the emotional attributes of the Divine</note>.

## The Secret of Havdalah
Regarding the "Worm of Jacob" <note>A poetic term for the Jewish people</note> and the enlightened ones, one should smell spices at the conclusion of the Sabbath as the choicest way to fulfill the commandment. One should use myrtle (*Hadas*) to hint at the place of the souls from which they go out to dwell with Israel on the Sabbath, and to which they return, and from which they derive their existence. That tree from which the souls fly forth is called "Myrtle," as it is said, "And he stood among the myrtle trees." Queen Esther was named "Hadassah" <note>Myrtle</note> after it. 

The blessing over the fire hints that the fire of the "North" <note>A reference to the attribute of Judgment</note> was hidden and stowed away on the eve of the Sabbath. Because it is forbidden to awaken it at all on the Sabbath, as it is written: "You shall not kindle fire [in all your dwellings on the Sabbath day]," when Israel blesses it at the conclusion of the Sabbath, it goes out to serve its post as in the beginning. Four camps of light radiate from that river and are called "Camps of Fire." We bend the four fingers of the right hand toward the candle; they are a hint to those camps, the secret of the "Lower Chariots" that radiate from the "Splendor" <note>original: *Hod*</note>, the secret of the Bride as a soul. "And you shall see my back, but my face shall not be seen" <note>Exodus 33:23</note>. The existence and validation of the light is found by looking at the back of the fingers, which are a hint to the "Lower Lights" of which it is said, "And you shall see my back." But the inner palms are a hint to the "Higher Lights" of which it is said, "And my face shall not be seen," and one must not gaze at it. Therefore, we do not bend the inner part of the fingers before the candle, because they are internal and do not radiate from a lower candle, but rather they radiate from the Higher Light above. But the back [of the fingers] radiates from the lower candle; therefore, we bend the back of the fingers toward it to hint that they radiate from it. 

There is another reason for looking at the fingernails: the nails hint at the secret of another cause, as we wrote above in the laws of cutting nails in the section on Sabbath. Furthermore, since the "Accuser" <note>original: *Sitra Achra* / The Other Side</note> spreads through the world at the conclusion of the Sabbath, we look at the nails to consider the power in this so that one is not harmed. They are the "saved lights" of which it is said "And He made for them..." <note>Referencing the garments of skin/light made for Adam</note>. One blesses the One who created him to save him from every trouble. 

In the Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer <note>Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer, chapter 20/21.</note>, it says that at twilight [on the first Saturday night], Adam sat and pondered in his heart, saying: "Woe is me, perhaps the serpent who tripped me up will come in the evening and bruise my heel." A pillar of fire was sent to him to illuminate the darkness from all evil. Adam stood up and rejoiced in his heart and said: "Blessed are You... Creator of the lights of the fire." From here you already know that at the conclusion of the Sabbath we bless the light that comes out of the wood and the stones, which is not the case on Yom Kippur, as we ruled in Tractate Pesachim in the chapter "The Place Where They Are Accustomed." The reason is that the Sabbath is like the general structure called "Trees," as it is said, "The trees of the Lord are satisfied," and the standing is called "The Stone of Israel." Even the higher beings are called "Stones" because they are a structure. Therefore, we bless at the conclusion of the Sabbath over the light that comes out of the wood or the stones. But Yom Kippur is above the structure, and we only bless upon it over light that "rested" <note>Fire that was lit before the holiday and kept burning.</note>. "House of Jacob, come and let us walk in the light of the Lord."

## And He Blesses
"He who distinguishes between the holy and the profane," etc. Let us explain: there are four "distinctions" <note>original: *havdalot*</note> corresponding to the four "Husks" <note>term: <term>Kelipot</term> — Mystical shells or husks of impurity that conceal the Divine light.</note> that surround the world of Emanation (*Atzilut*). These are the "stormy wind," "great cloud," "flashing fire," and "a radiance around it." These are the secret of the ten lower crowns called the "Outer Husks." These husks act as a partition between Israel and their Father in Heaven when sins cause it. Regarding this it is written, "But your iniquities have made a separation..." The Divine Presence (*Shekhinah*) clothes itself in them during the weekdays to fulfill "and His kingdom rules over all" and to fulfill "God reigns over the nations." This is the secret of "In all their affliction, He was afflicted" and it is written "I am with him in distress." The secret is that when they were exiled to Egypt, the Shekhinah was with them, in order to guard His son. They are like the shell in the hand of the one who peels it; they are the "evil" within the Tree of Knowledge, and these matters are ancient. Remember that on the Sabbath, the Holy One, blessed be He, clothes Himself in the "good" part of the Tree of Knowledge—these are the secret of "Holy, Holy." But at the conclusion of the Sabbath, He departs from them and clothes Himself in the aforementioned Husks to lead the world. Because the garments of the Sabbath are of the level of "Creation" and these Husks can mingle with them, they [the Sages] instituted for us to make a distinction at the conclusion of the Sabbath. This is the secret of "diverse kinds" (*Kilayim*) and "forbidden mixtures" (*Shaatnez*). Of one who blesses over them, the verse says, "For he has defiled the sanctuary of the Lord." 

But the Higher Lights, which are of the level of "Emanation" (*Atzilut*), no impurity touches there, nor does it mingle with them. This is the secret of the Havdalah: "He who distinguishes between the holy and the profane"—the Higher Lights are holy, and the lower ones are profane. "Between light and darkness"—the secret of the Higher Lights, which are the Hidden Light, and the outer ones, which are the Husks. "Between Israel and the nations"—Israel is from Emanation, from the trunk of the Tree, a holy place; but the nations are impure, attached to the impure place, which are the aforementioned Husks, and one must distinguish between them. "And between the seventh day and the six days of labor"—which are profane. He who distinguishes between them is one who does what is good in the eyes of the Lord. Thus far are his words. 

He further wrote: You already know what our Sages, of blessed memory, said regarding the secret of the tree with which Adam sinned—lest he [sin] again. They forbade the joy of the grapes... and gave it to him... the "cup of staggering," the "cup of His wrath." Corresponding to this, the woman received the blood of menstruation, the secret of the "filth" that the serpent cast into Eve. And because it was written that this separation from Adam was caused by wine, women do not taste the Havdalah wine. In the future, the Holy One, blessed be He, will strip away the Husk and appear to Israel face to face without any partition, as it is written, "Your Teacher shall not be hidden anymore, but your eyes shall see your Teacher." This will be at the time when the verse is fulfilled: "He will swallow up death forever," and it is written, "and the sun shall be ashamed"—the secret of the well-known Minister [of impurity] and the filth within it. Then the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, like the light of the seven days, on the day that the Lord binds up the breach of His people and heals the stroke of their wound. Thus far are his words.

## The Secret of Delight
The delight of Torah scholars from one Sabbath eve to the next—I have already written above that the first letters of "The **B**en-children of **I**srael shall **K**eep the **S**abbath" <note>original: **V**e-shamru **B**enei **Y**israel **E**t **H**a-shabbat. The translator notes the initials spell *Bi'ah* (intercourse).</note> form the word "Bi'ah" (intimacy). This is the secret of the "eternal covenant." It says "it is a sign" (*Ot hi*); it is written *hi* (she) but read as *hu* (he). This is the secret of the union and the unification of "Remember" and "Keep." The "Holy Covenant" is the Unified One. 

As it is written in *The Tree of Life* in the seventh gate: this is the time for Torah scholars, the "seed of peace." The Sabbath represents the secret of "Foundation" (*Yesod*), and "Victory" (*Netzach*) and "Splendor" (*Hod*) are the two testicles. Therefore, when there is peace in the home, which is the secret of the "Illuminator," then the Torah scholar is included, for Netzach and Hod are called "disciples of the Lord." Torah scholars would intend in this matter to use their beds on Friday night in order to draw down a "New Spirit" into the child. For then, certainly, there is a New Spirit from the side of the returning cycle. And if you find difficult the prophet's statement, "and a new spirit I will give within you," which implies the future and seems to say there is no New Spirit now—one may answer that the prophet's statement was in a general sense. However, for those individuals whom God calls, there is a New Soul even in this time. Thus far are his words.

<meta>This page transitions from the general laws of the Sabbath to the specific intersection of the Sabbath and Passover laws, particularly when the Eve of Passover falls on a Saturday. It moves from mystical Sabbath reflections into the practical Halakhic (legal) complexities of selling and removing leaven.</meta>

<page-num>141</page-num>
<header>Tractate Passover</header>

In my inquiries in the "Higher Light" <note>original: "BeHeL" – possibly referring to the author's own work or a specific region</note> in the land of Russia, I questioned those Jewish *Arendars* <term>Arendar: A Jewish leaseholder who managed estates, taverns, or mills in Eastern Europe</term> who possess storehouses of leaven <note>original: "Chametz"</note> and glassware. What investigations did they conduct when they sold these items to non-Jews before Passover, and how do they conduct themselves? They used to say that it has been the custom from time immemorial to sell the entire room to the non-Jew and to leave the key with him. In this, they were very lenient. Consequently, that leaven remained over Passover, making it "leaven owned by a Jew during Passover," which is forbidden for any benefit. This is certainly true if the room is closed and locked within the house and the non-Jew has no permission to enter there; that is obvious. But even when the non-Jew has permission to go there and take what he wishes, nevertheless, how did the non-Jew acquire these barrels <note>original: "Chavot," likely "Chaviyot" (barrels/vats)</note> that remain in the Jew's domain, if not through an act of acquisition? When the non-Jew acquires all the barrels for the purpose of a legal purchase of movable goods within the domain of the renter, such a thing is impossible in the case of large shops.

<column-break/>

<note>This column contains highly abbreviated and fragmented notes, likely referring to tax codes or specific commerce customs.</note>
Tax collectors... thick tax... specifically on the Great Sabbath... regarding the matter of the table and the value mentioned regarding the secret... according to its meaning, hidden places and garments, and it passed with permission... like the shopkeepers... 19th [day] related to the table and seven amounts... 19th for the times of the table and flowing into the secular... on the mouth of "take and live"... already there was and seven cleanings... and separates the exchange... existence for Passover... from the matter of "the bush was not consumed."

<column-break/>

And if he sold him the room and, along with it <note>original: "Agav" – a legal mechanism where movable goods are acquired by virtue of acquiring the land they sit upon</note>, everything placed within it, then he would need to legally acquire the land. Maimonides <note>original: "Rambam"</note> wrote in Chapter 4 of the *Laws of Sale* and Chapter 1 of the *Laws of Acquisition* that a non-Jew does not acquire land from a Jew except through a deed <note>original: "Shtar"</note>, and a Jew does not acquire land from a non-Jew except through money. This is also explained in the *Shulchan Aruch* and the *Tur* (Choshen Mishpat, Section 194). Therefore, I have made it a custom that the *Arendars* should sell the room with everything inside it through a legal contract and provide him with a deed of sale. Furthermore, even when the deed of sale is written in our own language <note>Yiddish or Russian-influenced Hebrew</note>, stating to the non-Jew: "This specific room is sold to you with everything inside it," that is sufficient. If we do not do this—woe! I was careful not to derive benefit from their leaven after Passover. Because of this, I must make it known to be careful about this. Even though one might find a way that does not require a deed—namely, according to what the *Beit Yosef* wrote in Section 194 regarding a Jew buying from a non-Jew—if the non-Jew tells the Jewish buyer, "I am acquiring this through money alone," he acquires it. If so, let us say the same regarding the law of a non-Jew buying from a Jew: let the non-Jew say, "I am hereby acquiring this, for the money alone has acquired it for me." Even if he then acquires the five measures of wisdom without a deed, one must still make it known and prepare the matter well so that his mind is resolved to truly buy it. However, if he is in a place where the custom among merchants is to transfer movable goods by the "handing over of the key" <note>original: "Masirat Mafteach"</note> to the buyer, that is sufficient, and one does not need to be stringently careful. One must know clearly that such is the custom, and then the arrangement of the leaven for the non-Jew is effective, as explained in the glosses of Rabbi Moses Isserles <note>original: "HaGahat ReMA"</note> in Choshen Mishpat Section 201. But it is forbidden to use any trickery or deception against the non-Jew so that he lacks the ability to go to the room and take [the leaven] whenever he wishes. Regarding this, it is said: "And you shall fear your God... I am the Lord" <note>Leviticus 25:17</note>—matters entrusted to the heart.

The *Hagahot HaNiglah* <note>Rabbinic commentary</note> at the beginning of Tractate Passover wrote that Abraham ben David of Posquières <note>original: "Ra'avad"</note> said: the reason the Mishnah uses the word "Or" <note>which can mean light or night</note> is to say that at the start of the night, while there is still some light, it is fitting to check [for leaven] so that one does not become lazy or forget. Since the first hour has light, the Tanna <note>Mishnaic sage</note> used the word "Or" for the sake of "refined language" <note>original: "Lishna Ma'alya"</note>. He did not say "at the beginning of the night of the 14th we search for leaven," for even if that reason of refined language were not there, the Tanna would not have lacked for words. He meant to say that the removal [of leaven] must be performed with the light of day so that one does not become lazy. These are his words, of blessed memory. Rabbeinu Yerucham also wrote this in the name of the *Ra'avad*. Therefore, one must be careful in this. One should be extremely careful to move from the mundane to the mundane, and from commandment to commandment; let them wait until after they have drawn the "rested water" <term>Mayim Shelanu: Water drawn at dusk and left to cool overnight, used for baking Passover Matzah</term> for the commandment, and then immediately check for leaven. For the time for drawing the water is close to twilight, as the *ReMA* wrote in his gloss at the beginning of Section 455. Then, immediately after bringing the water, he should check.

**Regarding** the eating of leaven and its removal on the Eve of Passover: I have seen among the masses that they are not careful; they eat after the fourth hour of the day. One transgression drags another along; they are drawn after the methods of the masses <note>unclear: "Chasun"</note>. Here, when there is the end of the hour when it must be burned, then there are two opinions, and they do not fulfill the commandment of burning the leaven—see the books. Also, the nullification <note>original: "Bitul"</note> that they recite is not a valid nullification, for it is after the time of the prohibition, and at that point, the leaven is no longer in his possession. For they have the custom not to nullify until after it is burned. This practice is bad in my eyes; we should apply a "fortiori" reasoning <note>original: "Kal Vachomer"</note> in our hearts, especially regarding a commandment that comes to a person only once a year. Therefore, my sons, I command you: be very careful to wake up early in the morning, and be precise and exacting for the commandment. In this way, their hidden rewards will multiply, and they will merit and bring merit to the public.

# **C**ustom
When Passover falls on the Sabbath, it is the custom of the "Holy Association" <note>original: "HaCh" – likely "Hevra Kadisha" or a specific Hasidic group</note> to make a "rich meal" with "enriched Matzah" <term>Matzah Ashirah: Matzah made with fruit juice, eggs, or oil instead of water; its use is debated in Jewish law</term>. However, in those countries where it is not the custom to eat enriched Matzah, one should set the Third Meal <note>original: "Seudah Shlishit"</note> with meat and fish. If he sets the meal with fruit, let him take fruit from the Seven Species <note>Wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, and dates</note>. As the *Beit Yosef* wrote in the *Tur* (Orach Chaim Section 291), one fulfills the obligation on this Sabbath with the third meal in this manner, for some say one fulfills it with any food. Though we do not generally rule this way on other Sabbaths, now, in a time of pressing need, it is different. It is stated in the *Tur* that one should complete the third meal with words of Torah.

As it says in the Zohar <note>original: "v'z.l. b'P. Amar" – likely quoting Parashat Emor</note>: "The Sabbath meal of the Jews is of several types: one for the sake of the Matzah and Bitter Herbs, and one for the sake of the [Passover] sacrifice... and since bread is not found from the seventh hour onwards, a small piece of breadless food is not the proper order. And if you say it should be with wine—wine is permitted because it gladdens the heart. But truly, one should toil in the delights of the Sabbath... on this day, the 'Holy Apple Orchard' is blessed, and the upper and lower worlds are blessed. This day is the existence of the Torah." Rabbi Abbahu said: This is what Rabbi Shimon [bar Yochai] used to do—at the time when the Sabbath meal was removed from the table, he would engage in the "Work of the Chariot" <note>original: "Ma'aseh Merkavah" – deep mystical/Kabbalistic study</note> and would say, "This is the meal of the King who invites the kings, his sons."

We can say by way of a hint <note>original: "Remez"</note> that one should complete this meal with a <term>Tarnima</term> <note>original: "Tarnima" – a Talmudic term for a snack or dessert, here interpreted homiletically</note>, meaning through the study of Torah, based on the expression "Abaye found Rava..." where they would speak words of Torah. This is the salvation from the matters of the day—one who finds desire on Passover.

The *Tur* wrote in Section 447: Regarding the commandment of leaven in one's house, if it is during the Intermediate Days <note>original: "Chol HaMoed"</note>, he must remove it immediately. If it is a Festival day, some say he should overturn a vessel over it until the night when he can remove it. But on a Festival day, one cannot move it to remove it. It goes without saying that if he nullified it, so that there is no biblical prohibition remaining, it is obvious he cannot move it. But even if he did not nullify it, such that there is a biblical prohibition, even so, he should not remove it since he cannot destroy it according to the law—which according to Rabbi Judah must be by burning. Such is the law for leaven that remains when Passover falls on a Sabbath after the fifth hour. It seems to me that this refers to a case where no non-Jew is present; but if a non-Jew is present, he should tell the non-Jew to remove the leaven. This is not only if he did not nullify it—where he would be transgressing a biblical law—where it is permitted via a non-Jew, but even if he did nullify it, which is only a rabbinic prohibition. Nevertheless, the positive rabbinic commandment of "you shall remove leaven" <note>Exodus 12:15</note> comes and applies even if he nullified it. This is like the proof of Rav Nachman... and do not say that a biblical "do not" <note>negative commandment</note> is pushed aside by a positive commandment like circumcision... or forbidden mixtures in ritual fringes <note>original: "Kilayim in Tzitzit"</note>. And as for the Shofar on Rosh Hashanah when it falls on the Sabbath, the Shofar does not push aside the Sabbath... there it is different... for at the moment he transgresses the Sabbath rest, he is not yet fulfilling the positive commandment of the Shofar, for the blowing comes afterward. But if the transgression and the fulfillment happen at the same moment, the positive commandment pushes aside the negative... this is the rule: a positive commandment pushes aside a negative one.

The *Tur* wrote at the end of Section 428: "I saw in Barcelona that the meticulous ones would bake everything they needed for the Festival before the start of the Festival, so that if even a tiny amount of leaven were to fall in, it would be nullified before the time of the prohibition." This is a beautiful custom, and I follow it. "And you shall guard the Matzot" <note>Exodus 12:17</note>—one needs extra guarding. First, one must see that the dough does not sit for even a single moment without being worked. If they left it without working it for the time it takes to walk a "mil" <note>approx. 18-24 minutes</note>, it becomes leaven. This is a quarter of an hour and a 20th part of an hour. The *Hagahot Maimoniot* wrote in the name of the *Re'ah*: this measure is in a house without fire, but if there is fire or extra heat, it hastens the fermentation. One must pay attention to the circumstances. If one works it by hand, it is protected; but if it is left without work, it ferments immediately. See the Responsa of the *Rosh* (Rule 14). What people are accustomed to—rubbing the dough with their hands after they have prepared it for baking, saying "it shouldn't sit still"—has no substance. This is not "working" the dough; on the contrary, because of the rubbing, the dough will heat up and ferment [faster]. Those who place a mark or a roller on the Matzah—there is no benefit or wisdom in this... it is more correct...

# Tractate Shabbat

Regarding the incident of the Golden Calf, [the jewelry] was taken from the men and given to their wives as a memorial that the women did not participate in that sin; end of quote. <note>original: "Ekh"l" – a common abbreviation for "end of his words." This refers to the Midrashic tradition that women refused to contribute gold to the Golden Calf, and as a reward, they were given the New Month as a personal holiday on which they refrain from certain labors.</note> And Rabbi Isaac says that heavy labor is forbidden even for men [on the New Month], as the *Nimukei Yosef* <term>Nimukei Yosef: A 14th-century commentary on the Talmud by Rabbi Yosef Habib</term> also cited there.
In the "Great Gloss" <note>original: "B'GH"</note> it is written in the name of Rabbeinu Yerucham, of blessed memory: regarding the primary custom of not performing labor [on the New Month], they should not do any labor at all. For I have seen many women who err and say, "We must not spin wool, but we may do other work." It is proper for them to either forbid all labor according to their custom or permit all labor; end of quote. And I have seen women who err by thinking they should only avoid labor performed for wages, but they continue to sew household garments and the like. This should not be done; since they have the custom not to do labor on these nights, they should abstain from it entirely. Yet, it is possible that originally they only took it upon themselves to distinguish the day from a weekday and did not intend to forbid labors not done for profit; end of quote. It is proper to be mindful of the words of Rabbeinu Yerucham.

## Concerning
the blessing of *Hallel* <term>Hallel: A prayer service of praise consisting of Psalms 113–118, recited on festivals and the New Month</term> on the New Month: there is a dispute among the great authorities. Some say the congregation recites a blessing at the beginning "to read the Hallel" and at the end "May all Your works praise You," while an individual reciting it alone does not bless. Others say that even the congregation does not bless, neither at the beginning nor the end; this is the opinion of Maimonides <note>Rambam</note>, and such is the custom in the entire Kingdom of the Land of Israel and all its surroundings. However, Rabbi Moses Isserles <note>Rema</note> wrote in his glosses that even an individual should bless, following the opinion of the Rosh and Rabbeinu Tam. He wrote that, nevertheless, a person should be careful to pray with a congregation so that he can bless with them. In my opinion, an individual should not bless at all, neither at the beginning nor the end. Even in a congregation, it is difficult for me to bless, for the evidence of those who do not bless is very strong, as is clear from their words. Even though the congregation does bless, one should not add a blessing for an individual, for in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we take the lenient path <note>original: "Safek berakhot l'hakel" – a legal principle stating that if one is unsure if a blessing is required, it is better to omit it to avoid taking God's name in vain</note>. And so is the custom of the Sephardim, not to bless.

### ->I have written some laws of the Sanctification of the Moon above<- <margin>And look there</margin>

## We learned
<margin>The author, line 6</margin>
in *Tractate Soferim* <term>Tractate Soferim: One of the minor tractates of the Talmud, focusing on the scribal laws and public readings</term>: one does not bless over the moon except at the conclusion of the Sabbath, when one is fragrant and his clothes are fine. It is written in the "Hagahot Mordechai" that if one blesses on a weekday, he should put on Sabbath clothes. So it is also written in the "Rectifications of the Festivals" by the Mahar-i <note>likely Rabbi Isaac of Vienna</note>: when he would hasten to bless on a weekday, fearing the time might pass or to avoid missing the opportunity, he would change his clothes.
There is a beautiful custom in the Kingdom of the Land of Israel and its surroundings to recite verses and passages after the Sanctification of the Moon, followed by the "Rabbi’s Kaddish" <note>Kaddish D'Rabbanan</note>. It is proper to say on a weekday evening, "Praise God in His sanctuary..." etc. The school of Rabbi Ishmael taught: Had Israel only merited to greet the presence of the Divine <term>Shekhinah: The Divine Presence</term> once a month, it would have been enough for them. Abaye said: Therefore, we must bless while standing. There is a tradition from the pious Mahar-i Riva of Regensburg to say: "The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills. My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag. Behold, he stands behind our wall, gazing through the windows, peering through the lattice"; end of quote. The matter of this Sanctification is so that [God’s name] shall be magnified and sanctified, and the Great Name shall be whole, and then the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun. <gloss>This month shall be unto you the beginning of months; it shall be the first month of the year to you</gloss> <note>Exodus 12:2</note>. There appears to be a double phrasing in this verse: it says it is the "beginning of months" and then says a second time "it is the first for you." Perhaps the verse speaks of two types of intercalations <term>Intercalation: The adjustment of the calendar, such as adding a leap month</term>: the intercalation of the month and the intercalation of the year. "This month shall be unto you" refers to the sanctification of the month as Rashi explained; "it is the first for you" refers to the intercalation of the year. As Samuel said, "We do not intercalate Nisan in Nisan," and the renewed month of Nisan is the first.
But by way of a mystical hint <note>Remez</note>, we can say the verse suggests "This month is for you the head of months," encompassing all of them. It is the "Head of Months" because every single day is like a New Month, as the *Tur* wrote in Section 429 in the name of *Tractate Soferim*: we do not fast in Nisan because on the first of Nisan the Tabernacle was established, and the twelve Princes <note>Nesi'im: The leaders of the twelve tribes of Israel</note> brought their offerings, etc. It seems to me a good custom to observe every month the thirteen days of the fast of the Community of Israel. This relates to seven great secrets which drew down spiritual abundance, each to his own tribe for all time. It was not for nothing that the Torah wrote out each tribe and detailed their offering, even though they were all identical. It would have been appropriate to say briefly, "And so did this Prince offer, and so did that Prince offer." Rather, each one had unique secrets. In this way, the *Midrash Rabbah* explains different reasons for each Prince. In the words of our Rabbis, these are wondrous secrets attained by those to whom God has granted a portion of this true wisdom called [Kabbalah]. This section awakens the holiness of the day, just as the Sephardim are accustomed to say at every season the Psalms relevant to that day. I found written in the holy writings of the Arizal <term>Arizal: Rabbi Isaac Luria, the foundational 16th-century Kabbalist of Safed</term> and in their commandments in chapter 32... regarding the end of vows for each tribe individually.

## Furthermore
<margin>It seems to me regarding the holiness of the Torah portion of the "Oaths" <note>likely the portion regarding the tribal offerings</note> until "Thus he made the festival," it corresponds to the tribe of Levi. As seen in the Midrash, Aaron was distressed that he had no part in the Princes' offerings. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: "You are prepared for a greater greatness"—referring to the lighting of the Menorah. These twelve days were all holy, and their essence later relates to the twelve tribes and a holiness in memory of all sanctities. Afterward, the 14th of Nisan is the day they brought the Passover offering, followed by Passover itself. Since most of the month passes in holiness, it is customary to treat the whole month with holiness and not to fast. It seems to me that those who have a custom to fast on every Eve of the New Month should fast on the Eve of the New Month of Iyyar. Even though we observe holiness all month and a voluntary fast is avoided, this fast—which one has taken upon himself for every month of the year—should be observed as an obligation. Greater than this, the *Beit Yosef* wrote that one should fast a fast he took upon himself as an obligation even before Passover during the days of the Princes' offerings. His language is: "It implies to me that students who have a constant practice to fast on Mondays and Thursdays all year because of the desecration of God's name among the nations while Israel is in exile, and because of the glory of the Temple that was burned... also in the month of Nisan they should fast." One should not cancel those fasts because of the Princes' offerings. Certainly, one should fast after Passover the fast of the Eve of the New Month which he obligated himself to all year. With this, it seems to me we can resolve the verse in Section 429: at the beginning it is written that from the New Month of Nisan until the "Binding of the Festival" <note>Isru Chag: The day after a pilgrimage festival</note> we do not fast or eulogize. Then he brings proof from *Tractate Soferim* that says one does not fast until Nisan passes. Even though it seems possible to resolve this another way—that the period until *Isru Chag* refers only to eulogizing, but fasting is forbidden the whole month—the *Beit Yosef* says there is no proof from *Tractate Soferim* regarding eulogies. We can say the *Tur* finds it logical that since we do not fast until *Isru Chag*, it is proper not to eulogize on those days. But concerning what I wrote above about the difference between voluntary and obligatory fasts, we can also resolve the words of the *Tur*: until *Isru Chag*, one does not fast even an obligatory fast like a Nazirite or the anniversary of a parent's death; but from the middle of the month onward, one would fast for a parent's anniversary or the Eve of the New Month. This is what seems correct to me.</margin>
It will be explained later regarding the secret of the twelve tribes and the secret of the renewal of the world... and not for nothing does the matter of Passover begin, which demonstrates the renewal of the world from the 18th of Nisan... God commanded the Passover offering... the Princes began their offerings from the New Month of Nisan and finished on the 12th of Nisan.

## Laws
### Of the Custom
of Passover: [The laws] are very numerous, more than other prohibitions. Therefore, a person must be very meticulous and not rely on the members of his household alone, but must supervise both the ritual scalding <note>Hag'alah</note> and all the removals of leaven. Especially regarding the making of the Matzot, to see that they are made with alacrity without a moment's delay.
It is a custom to be stringent and scald all vessels, even drinking vessels used for cold liquids. Nevertheless, one must be precise when boiling them in the vat: first scald vessels used for cold things, then vessels used with boiling liquids as primary vessels <term>Kli Rishon: A vessel that was on the fire, which has a higher heat-transfer status in Jewish law</term>, then vessels used with hot things as secondary vessels <term>Kli Sheni: A vessel into which hot liquid was poured from a primary vessel</term>, such as bowls and spoons, and finally the pots, vats, and kettles.
I found written by Rabbi A. Shor, of blessed memory, in the Laws of Passover: All Israel is accustomed to making bread on the Eve of the Great Sabbath <term>Shabbat HaGadol: The Sabbath before Passover</term>, the great according to his greatness and the small according to his smallness, and they call it "Challah."
The meaning in the vernacular is "Bread of the Synagogue," and they distribute them to the poor. In days when they were careless with the dough-offering <note>original: "Sh'Nakhla" – likely referring to the *Challah* tithe</note>... very much with the grain; end of quote. And I heard in the name of the Gaon Maharal that he meant: every person should bake one *Challah* or one cooked dish out of trust for Passover, for perhaps there was a concern of leaven there... and perhaps that "Challah" is the "Challah of God" that the Sages obligated for Passover.
It is proper for a person to sanctify himself with this holiness: to give from his flour to the poor so they may eat before Passover, and then the flour for Passover will be even more holy.

**The custom** is to make it roasted <note>referring to the *Zroa*, the shankbone</note>; we sear it and do not roast it on a [metal] spit, but only over coals. The reason is that it serves as a memorial to the Passover lamb, and the Passover lamb was only roasted on a spit of pomegranate wood. **The Wisdom** of Passover in *Lev Yosef* <note>A rabbinic work</note> says one needs two types of meat; nevertheless, it was not heard from Rav Yosef that the meat must be roasted. Since Rav Huna simply states one does not need roasted meat, who is it that disagrees? Therefore, it is better for the two cooked items to be boiled, which is preferable. After this, I found in the *Tosafot* <term>Tosafot: Medieval commentaries on the Talmud</term> there, in the words of Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah: "two types of meat." It is better that they be cooked and not roasted, so they do not resemble [the sacrifices] at all, but are merely a memorial." So far his words; and this is how I have led the public. He shall place all these things in a bowl <note>The Seder Plate</note> and arrange the bowl before him so that he does not have to "pass over" the commandments. He should wrap the Matzahs in a cloth to cover the "shame of the bread" <note>A concept where the bread is covered while the wine is blessed</note>, as we prioritize the wine for Kiddush. When he begins "We were slaves" <note>The *Avadim Hayinu* section of the Haggadah</note>, he shall reveal them from above a little to fulfill "the bread of affliction" <note>original: *Lechem Oni*</note> upon which many words are answered. He also said that it is proper in his eyes to place the vegetable for dipping in the bowl closest to him, more so than the Matzahs, for it is proper that the Matzahs be close [but] one must not pass over the commandments <note>Meaning, one should reach for the item used first without reaching over items used later</note>. **And on the night** when our lips [offer prayers], the Men of the Great Assembly established the prayer to correspond to the daily offerings. The Mincha prayer corresponds to the afternoon offering. It was the custom in the time of the Holy Temple that the Passover lamb was slaughtered after the afternoon offering. In order to "render the bulls of our lips" <note>A biblical phrase meaning that prayer replaces animal sacrifice</note>, it is proper to engage in the order of the Passover sacrifice after the Mincha prayer, according to what I have copied briefly from the *Seder HaYom*: "The Passover offering is brought from the lambs or the goats, a male in its first year. It is slaughtered in the Courtyard <note>original: *Azarah*</note> anywhere after midday on the fourteenth [of Nisan], after the slaughter of the afternoon offering and the cleaning of the lamps. One does not toss the blood of the Passover lamb until the afternoon offering is slaughtered and its blood tossed. They would stir the blood of the Passover lamb so it would not congeal until the blood of the daily offering was tossed. Afterward, they slaughtered the Passover lamb... and the tossing of the blood was a single tossing against the Base [of the altar]. How was the slaughter performed? The first person in the line would receive the blood and give it to his fellow, and his fellow to his fellow, and the priest closest to the Altar would toss it... then return the empty vessel to his fellow, and his fellow to his fellow. There were rows of priests with silver bowls and rows with gold bowls. These bowls did not have [flat] bases, lest they set them down and the blood congeal. Afterward, they would hang the Passover lamb and flay it entirely, tear it open, and remove its entrails until the waste was removed. They would take out the sacrificial fats... and the priest would burn them on the Altar... the slaughtering and the tossing of the blood and the burning of the fats override the Sabbath, but other matters do not override the Sabbath. Similarly, they do not carry it [home] when it falls on the Sabbath... they would wait with their Passover lambs on the Temple Mount... when the Sabbath ended, they would go out and roast their Passover lambs. They were divided into three groups... the Courtyard was filled, the doors were locked... while they were slaughtering and offering the fats, they would recite the Hallel. If they finished, they would repeat it a second and third time. With every reading, they would blow three blasts on the shofar. When finished, the first group left and the second entered... After all had left, they would wash the Courtyard even on the Sabbath because of the blood. How was the washing done? A stream of water passed through the Courtyard, and they would block its exit so it would overflow and wash away all the blood and dirt, then they would open the exit and the floor would be left clean and beautiful. This was the honor of the House. If the lamb was found to be unkosher <term>treif: torn or physically defective</term>, it did not count for him until he brought another. This is the matter in brief." **The zeal** of a person is to be diligent regarding the word of God, to read this in its time, so that the reading replaces the offering. He should feel sorrow over the destruction of the House and plead before the Creator of the world to build it quickly in our days; end of quote. If he wishes to elaborate more on its laws and statutes, how good and pleasant that is, and whoever expands on it is praiseworthy. **And afterward**, he shall wear his clean and honorable clothes to receive the joy of the festival with gladness and joy, elegant and refined. It is fitting for him to do so and to give thanks and praise to Him who performed all these miracles and wonders for our ancestors and for us, as our Rabbis said: "He brought us out from slavery to freedom." Therefore, we must show this within ourselves: to rejoice in the salvation of our God, to remember and know the great kindness the God of our ancestors did for us, taking us from the iron furnace <note>Egypt</note> and taking us from the fifteen levels of filth in which we were submerged among the idolaters. We had almost forgotten the covenant of our ancestors, but He unified us as a treasured people and crowned us with His Torah and commandments. Happy is the people for whom this is so! Who is it that understands this and will not tremble with awe? Everything will end, but he should enjoy according to his ability... doing the commandment with full knowledge and proper intention, and not in a casual way as a "commandment of men learned by rote." **Afterward**, when he receives the holiday and prays the evening service, he should pray with full intention and joy to give thanks: "This is the day the Lord has made, let us rejoice and be glad in it." Specifically in the sections regarding the Exodus from Egypt, he should be aroused with full intention to thank and praise the Name of God. **And he shall return** to his house and conduct himself, and his wife as a queen, and the members of his household as children of kings. They should honor the table with silver and gold vessels and every precious and honorable thing they have, according to what God has granted them. All this is to show the strength of His glory in every place. And the holiness of this night and all the miracles that were seen... He who enjoys his food or his drink... from all nations and sanctified us with His commandments. Therefore, it is proper for a person to be extra careful not to speak any mundane conversation on this night... and they should not be separated from clinging to God for a single moment, but all should engage in the commandments of this night and in telling the miracles of our Rock and publicizing the miracle to his household. And if he is merited a portion of honor and knows the secrets of these matters, he should engage in them. There is another reason not to speak any conversation until after eating the *Afikoman*: because the blessing over the "fruit of the earth" made over the *Karpas* also applies to the eating of the *Maror*, as the Rashbam wrote and the Rosh agreed. # Tractate Pesachim

Fearful that it might come to leavening, he should hire her <note>a worker</note> and then return to pick it and roll it once more. This is also found in the writings of the Maharil <term>Rabbi Jacob Moelin (c. 1365–1427): A leading authority on Ashkenazic custom</term> in the name of the *Rokeach* and the *Agudah*. In order for the impression to be fixed in the heart—to be careful and diligent in the pursuit of the commandments—the Maharil established the practice of saying at every action of the commandment: "For the sake of the commandment of Matzah." This applies whether one is making the matzot, drawing the water, measuring the flour, or mixing the water into the flour. This is because the sifting and the flour are considered as one stage. The proof for this is from a case of doubt where one person provides water and another provides flour to knead dough for an *Eruv* <note>a ritual boundary</note>, questioning if the *Eruv* counts for both. It is proper to precede the mixing and the drawing of water by nullifying the crumbs of dough that fall from one's hand before they have the chance to become leavened. After they have leavened, they are no longer in his jurisdiction to nullify, as the time of the prohibition has passed. Therefore, he should nullify them before they can reach the state of leavening, for sometimes there are crumbs that are significant <note>original: "chashivi," meaning they have enough volume to not be automatically ignored</note>, like the "gleanings of the stalks." As for what was said regarding crumbs usually being considered ownerless <term>Hefker: Property that is ownerless and may be taken by anyone</term>—this refers to crumbs that fell away on their own without being moistened. Regarding this, he wrote that sometimes there are crumbs that are significant. Rabbi Zalman Runkel <note>A 14th-century Rabbi of Mainz and teacher of the Maharil</note> distinguished this: when we say generally that "crumbs are ownerless," it refers to bread crumbs. However, dough crumbs, since they are still fit for further kneading, are more significant and are not automatically nullified. And the Maharil wrote that these are different because they are significant; perhaps after baking, they will sweep the house and gather them together, making them worthy of consideration. Many err in this, saying simply "crumbs are ownerless," implying that all crumbs are naturally ownerless. This is a complete error, as I have written. Rather, one should say before kneading: "All the crumbs that fall from this dough shall be nullified and ownerless." This is stated in the *Rokeach*, section 273, as well as by the Maharil and in the *Orach Chayim* <note>The code of Jewish Law</note>. It is the custom of women when they take *Challah* <term>Challah: The portion of dough set aside and given to the Priests (Kohanim) in Temple times; today it is burned</term> from the matzah dough to either fold the dough in two or take from the two ends. The evidence that this is not done well is because it heats the dough through this friction—literally the rubbing of their hands in joining the dough from end to end around the rolling pin.

And similar to this, the Maharil wrote regarding the preparation of the matzot: "As for what people are accustomed to, rubbing their hands over the matzot after they have been shaped but before they are baked, saying 'they shouldn't be left idle'—there is no substance to this. This is not 'engaging' with the dough; on the contrary, because of the rubbing, they will heat up more and become leavened." In my humble opinion, this custom spread among women by mistake, as two terms were confused. It is like what the *Tur* wrote in section 456: "Because one must be precise with the measurement of the dough so as not to increase it due to the fear of leavening, it is better to reduce it; therefore, it is good to bring the doughs together at the time of separating the *Challah* in case there was not enough for the required measure." What people are accustomed to doing—bringing the ends of the dough together—is a confusion of these laws. It is proper to protest this and instead ensure that during the separation of the *Challah*, one person stands over the dough at its edges while a second person rolls it with the rolling pin so that it does not sit idle.

# Some laws of Challah are explained above under the letter K for *Kedushah* (Holiness).

<margin>165</margin>
**It is proper** to supervise the vessel in which one kneads. If one kneads several doughs one after another in it, and when measuring flour into the vessel, crumbs of dough from the first batch stick to the vessel and remain there without being worked, they must be removed so that the vessel is clean. When it is clean <gloss>meaning for the illness</gloss> <note>This likely refers to a specific hygienic or ritual concern</note>, it is proper to have prepared "preparations," which are sets of two kneading vessels. Immediately after the first dough, one is ready; empty the second vessel and clean it, while the second dough is rushed into the second vessel, and so on in a cycle. This is good and beautiful, and so it is proper to do.

**The Beit Yosef** <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo's commentary on the Tur</note> wrote in section 451 that for the "flat griddle" <note>original: "platt"</note>, the custom is to perform *Hag'alah* <term>Hag'alah: Ritual koshering of a vessel by immersion in boiling water</term>. However, it is possible to say that if one throws it into the fire and heats it in the oven extensively, it is permitted, as "the way it absorbs [forbidden substance] is the way it expels it." This is from the *Tosefot Yeshanim* on Maimonides. It was written in the fifth chapter: an object used to wash bread has no remedy through *Hag'alah* because its use is via fire <note>and therefore requires *Libun*, or heating to a glow</note>. It is written in the *Terumat HaDeshen* and the *Mordechai* and the *Smak* that one should be stringent and not kosher a warming vessel for matzah through *Hag'alah* because it is considered used via fire. I found that it is proper for every person, when baking on Passover, to have two shovels, for fear that perhaps one matzah will become leavened, and it would not be proper to remove another matzah with that same shovel. Therefore, when a woman removes a matzah from the oven and is in doubt if it has leavened, she should wait until the shovel is washed, or she should remove the other matzot with a different shovel.

**Those** women who brush the matzot with salt water and the like and return the matzot to the oven to bake well must be careful not to remove the matzot from the oven to the table until the doubt is removed from their hearts that they are certainly baked. While they are still hot, leavening can continue from them.
**I was asked** about a grain of wheat found in hot goose fat on Passover. At first, it occurred to me to permit it, because "fruit juice does not cause leavening" <note>A halakhic principle that pure fruit juice, without water, does not ferment grain into prohibited chametz</note>. Afterward, I reconsidered, and perforce fat does not have the law of fruit juice, as the *Rokeach* forbade it—and the *Tur* cited it in section 467—regarding a roasted chicken on which a grain of wheat was found, stating it is forbidden. From this, we see that fat is not considered like fruit juice. One cannot say this refers to a case where the chicken was salted, for he stated his words generally and should have specified. Furthermore, the *Tur* says at the end of section 462 that "salt with oil does not cause leavening," so we must conclude that in all cases involving a roasted chicken, the wheat forbids it. The reason, in my opinion, is that since the wheat has been soaked in water for several days, it already contains the power of water (especially in "the city of Awen" <note>likely a coded reference to a specific locality like Frankfurt</note> where wheat fell into the water). And even though the *Gahot Maimoni* wrote in chapter 5 in the name of the *Smak*, and the *Beit Yosef* cited it in section 462: "It is permitted to knead with wine even though it is impossible for wine not to have a drop of water that falls into it during the harvest," nevertheless, one need not fear the water as it is nullified. The *Smak* wrote: "Even though it is impossible for wine not to have a drop of water, and even initially they are accustomed to adding water during the harvest... nevertheless, one need not fear the water since the water was already nullified in the wine before they kneaded the dough." One must say that this is not comparable; there, the water is a tiny amount, but here, the soaking water is a large amount and covers it entirely—so it appears to me. I have heard some meticulous people who warn their wives not to walk on Passover with a tallow candle <note>made of animal fat</note> to look into the pot to see how the food is cooking, since they were not careful about leavened vessels at the time of its making, and some of the fat might fall in. Rather, they should take a wax or oil candle in their hand; this is a meticulousness of "fear of sin." On the eve of Passover, a person should ensure he is always devoted throughout the entire day to the service of the Name, blessed be He, in fear and in love. "In fear" means the fear of sin, so that he fulfills "On the first day you shall remove leaven from your houses," for the Torah said leaven is prohibited on the eve of Passover from the sixth hour and onwards, and the Sages forbade it two hours earlier. He should be careful and diligent to destroy the leaven and nullify it with speed and diligence as I wrote above. He should reflect on repentance and search his deeds, thinking how to destroy the "Evil Inclination" so that it shall no longer be seen or found with him. Afterward, he should barber himself in honor of the holiday, specifically before midday. From midday onwards, it is a holiday because of the sanctity of the Passover Sacrifice, and he should occupy himself only with matters of the festival. He should go to the bathhouse and immerse himself in honor of the festival, for "He has chosen us from all the nations." The secret of immersion was explained above. He should engage with great love and the joy of the Place, blessed be He, and involve himself in performing the commandments in holiness, purity, and extra care. He should not rely on the members of his household, but see with his own eyes the heating of the oven, checking if the embers spread through the whole oven, for the flame alone is not enough. He should reflect on the engagement of the commandments so that there is not a moment without engagement. Afterward, he should engage in matters needed for the night, like arranging the plate and preparing the needs of the day. His table should be set while it is still day in order to eat immediately when it gets dark. Even if he is in the House of Study, he should rise, for it is a commandment to hurry and eat for the sake of the children so they do not sleep. Also, everything must be prepared; he should not delay, for any delay caused by the children might hinder the order of the Seder, as one must hurry so that the *Hallel* <note>psalms of praise</note> is also read before midnight. He should prepare the *Karpas* <note>vegetable</note> and vinegar or salt for dipping, the *Maror* <note>bitter herbs</note>, the *Charoset* <note>sweet paste</note>, and two cooked items. The *Tur* wrote in section 473: "And two cooked items: one in memory of the Passover lamb and one in memory of the Festival Offering (*Chagigah*), of whatever type he wants." The custom is meat and an egg. And the custom is to take a shankbone <note>original: "Zroa"</note> as a hint to "with an outstretched arm." Some say when Passover falls on the conclusion of the Sabbath, one does not take these items... because the *Chagigah* does not override the Sabbath. But Rabbi Peretz wrote that one should not worry, since they are only for memorial, and on the contrary, one who is meticulous in this appears as if he is making actual sacrifices. And so wrote the author of the *Ittur*. A person should change three things, and there is no need to bring all of these before every single person, but only before the master of the house, and he will distribute to all. In the *Beit Yosef*, he brought the words of the *Kol Bo* who wrote: "We say in the Jerusalem Talmud that the custom is to take a shankbone and an egg, meaning 'The Merciful One desired to redeem us with an arm and with mercy' <note>a pun on *Zroa* (arm) and *Beia* (request/mercy)</note>." He also wrote: "Suitably..."

<meta>This page continues the technical and liturgical discussion surrounding the Passover Seder, specifically transitioning from the laws of preparing Matzah to the nuances of the Haggadah text, the selection of bitter herbs, and the requirements for the Afikoman and the Counting of the Omer.</meta>

# Tractate Pesachim

...to You for our redemption and the redemption of our souls, and we shall thank You with a **new song** <note>original: "shir chadash"</note> for our redemption. This means that here and later on we should include two additional words. However, the intention of the *Tosafot* <term>Medieval French and German commentators on the Talmud</term> was not that the wording must be exactly identical, letter for letter, but rather their intention was the addition of two words in general, both here and later. That is to say, here we say "a new song" <note>original: "shira chadasha" - feminine form</note> and later "a new song" <note>original: "shir chadash" - masculine form</note>. Therefore, it is taught in our tractate that this does not refer only to the beginning of their words, as the *Pnei Yehoshua* <note>Rabbi Jacob Joshua Falk, 1680–1756</note> wrote, "and let us say before Him a new song." Just as the *Maharshal* <term>Rabbi Solomon Luria (1510–1573), a major Polish posek and communal leader</term> emended, it does not refer to everything mentioned in their words up to this point regarding the blessings. One must distinguish regarding redemption in the matter of the "song": sometimes it is in the masculine and sometimes in the feminine. On this, they concluded and said that it is taught: all "songs" <note>referring to past redemptions</note> are in the feminine form, and so on.

There is a necessity for this when adding these two words to "and let us say before Him," according to the version of the *Tosafot* and the glosses of the *Mordechai* <note>Rabbi Mordechai ben Hillel, 13th-century German scholar</term> mentioned above. In any case, one must say them in the feminine form, "a new song" (*shira chadasha*). The reason they include this here is that the version of "and let us say before Him Hallelujah" written in the Mishnah and the prayer books is not connected to what precedes it. For it began with the past, saying, "Therefore we are obligated to thank... who performed miracles for our ancestors and brought us out from slavery to freedom... and from subjugation to redemption." This all speaks of the past, yet it concludes "and let us say before Him Hallelujah," which speaks of the future. Therefore, the liturgists established "and let us say before Him a new song" so that everything refers to the past. The flow of the words is thus: "Who performed miracles for our ancestors... and brought us out... and a new song was said before Him." This refers to the Song of the Sea <note>The song sung by Moses and the Israelites after crossing the Red Sea</note>. This song is said in the feminine, as it says there, "this song" <note>original: "et ha-shira ha-zot"</note>. According to this, one must read it as *ve-ne'emar* <note>meaning "and it was said" - past tense</note> and not *ve-nomar* <note>meaning "and we shall say" - future tense</note>. Indeed, I found it punctuated this way in the book of the *Mordechai* of Rabbi Isaac Bezalel, of blessed memory: with a *segol* under the *nun* and not a *cholam*. If it is with a *cholam*, then it is future tense; however, when it is with a *segol*, it is past tense, meaning that a "new song" was already said before Him—referring to the Song of the Sea.

One must also be precise according to the *Tosafot* and the *Mordechai*: if I found it punctuated "and a new song was said before Him," why did they write that one should say this Haggadah followed by what is written in the Mishnah? One cannot say that the *Tosafot* and the *Mordechai* delete the word "Hallelujah" from the Mishnah, for they wrote their words and did not write "except for the word Hallelujah," which is the "new song." They did not write that we do not include the word "Hallelujah." Furthermore, it is impossible to say we don't say "Hallelujah," for if so, the Tanna <term>a sage from the period of the Mishnah</term> would be referring to the adjacent Mishnah which asks "Until where does he recite?" The School of Shammai says "Until a joyous mother of children," and the School of Hillel says "Until a flint into a fountain of waters." Who would have mentioned "Hallelujah" if we didn't recite it?

It seems to me that the *Tosafot* and the *Mordechai* believe the word "Hallelujah" mentioned in the Mishnah is not part of the continuous song that one must say, but is merely a sign—a simple marker—to indicate that the word "Hallelujah" should be near the start of the *Hallel* <note>the psalms of praise</note>. This teaches that after finishing "and a new song was said before Him," he should start and say *Hallel*. This is what "Until Hallelujah" means. The fact that the word "Hallelujah" is not part of the recited text but only a marker is proven by the words of the *Tosafot* and the *Mordechai* who wrote: "And let us say before Him a new song," and no more. They did not write "and let us say before Him a new song, Hallelujah."

Rather, we learn from this that they disagree, and the word "Hallelujah" is not part of the recited text. However, both the *Maharshal* and those who wrote in the glosses of the *Rokeach* stated that after the Haggadah, before starting *Hallel*, one should say "and let us say before Him a new song, Hallelujah," as per the ruling of the *Mordechai* and the *Tosafot*. Therefore, it is difficult to reconcile his words, and we must explain that a new song has already been said before Him—namely the Song of the Sea—and also "Hallelujah" was already said before Him, in the manner our sages said: "Praise, O servants of the Lord—and not servants of Pharaoh."

But this does not sit well with the subsequent Mishnah regarding "Until where does he recite?" for according to this, nothing was mentioned regarding the saying of *Hallel*. We must say that the word "Hallelujah" mentioned in the words of Rashi is only a transcription of the language of the Mishnah and not his own thought, meaning one should say the word "Hallelujah." Look closely into this. I have pressed myself to resolve everything correctly according to the version of the *Tosafot*, the *Mordechai*, and the *Maharshal*, even though the explanation is a bit far-fetched.

### **Bitter Herbs** <note>original: "Maror"</note>
Your sign is four. We learned in the chapter *Kol Sha'ah*: "These are the vegetables with which a person fulfills his obligation on Passover..." until "...they may fulfill it with them whether they are moist or dry." In the Gemara, Rav Hisda said: "They only taught this regarding the stalk, but regarding leaves, moist ones are valid, dry ones are not." The *Kessef Mishneh* <note>commentary by Joseph Karo</note> wrote in Section 473: "The *Hagahot Maimoniyot* wrote that for any vegetable, the stalk is valid, and this is not the root." The *Pnei Yehoshua* wrote similarly. In the Jerusalem Talmud, it defines what is called a "stalk" and what is called a "root." I will bring you what is noted for our eyes:

Rabbi Isaac said: It was taught in the first chapter of *Sukkah*: "Three stalks and in them three stems." Rashi explained: "Stalks are roots." For this reason, it seems, Maimonides wrote "and not roots," meaning the small roots that turn to the side when it is connected to the earth. But the large root within it is called the "stalk." So it is written there. And in the *Radaph*, he wrote: "If he takes a root, he should take what is above the ground, such as the top and what is adjacent to it." But he should not take what is below the ground, for that is the root. And it is written: specifically the stalk and not roots. In the *Agudah*, Section 80 in Tractate *Eruvin*, in the name of Rabbi Isaac: "And so it is proper to act." For I heard them saying in the name of the Gaon Rabbi Shaphna that everything beneath the ground is called a root, and it is only called a stalk if it emerges above the ground near the leaves. Therefore, when preparing the *Maror*, one should take the upper part with the head of the cutting.

### **Commandment** <note>original: "Mitzvah"</note>
All the Matzah that one eats during the meal should be eaten with intention, and one recites the blessing over it... from what Rabbi Joshua ben Levi said: "Anyone who eats an olive-sized amount of Matzah while reclining has fulfilled his obligation." This implies that a householder who is not being fed from his own table does not fulfill the obligation by just eating an olive-sized piece in a single gulp, but rather must eat it all while reclining. So it is in the *Maharil*.

### **Afikoman**
The *Mahari Padwa* <note>Rabbi Meir Katzenellenbogen, 1482–1565</note> said: One must eat the equivalent of two olive-bulks, which is like a chicken's egg. For the egg-size is from the rest of the Matzot, and one fulfills the obligation with an olive-bulk that was half-dry and eaten when one is satisfied and for the purpose of satisfaction. If one cannot eat it all, he should at least not eat less than an olive-bulk, and it must be done while reclining. It should be eaten before midnight. The *Rokeach* <note>Rabbi Eleazar of Worms, c. 1176–1238</note> wrote: The eating of the Afikoman should not be a burden or a toil for him... for one who eats it as "gross eating" <note>eating while already overfull</note>, about him it is said, "and transgressors shall stumble in them." Regarding the matter of the invitation for the Grace After Meals (*Zimmun*), the *Maharil* wrote at the end of *Emek HaBerakha*.

### **Obligated** <note>original: "Chayav"</note>
A person is obligated to occupy himself with the laws of Passover and the Exodus from Egypt, and to explain the miracles and wonders that the Holy One, Blessed be He, performed for our ancestors, until sleep overcomes him. However, the "Hamapil" blessing <note>the blessing before sleep</note> must be recited, for this blessing is not for protection but is a blessing over sleep itself; this is simple.

### **He Wrote** <note>original: "Katav"</note>
The *Kolbo* <term>Anonymous 13th/14th-century collection of Jewish laws</term> wrote: "Rabbi Asher <note>The Rosh, c. 1250–1327</note> wrote: There are people who have the custom to minimize their eating on the first day of Passover so that they will eat Matzah with appetite on the second night." And so it is written in the sermons of Ibn Shu'aib <note>Rabbi Joshua ibn Shu'aib, 14th-century Spain</note> that the *Ramban* <term>Nachmanides (1194–1270)</term> used to act this way. From here, men of action have the custom not to eat *charoset* on the first day of Passover, just as they practiced on the Eve of Passover.

**The matter** of the Counting of the Omer is a great matter and a supreme holiness that people draw upon themselves, as explained later. Therefore, one must arouse repentance in his heart and be holy and pure. There is a great error in the version that the common people are accustomed to say: "That today IS the first day" <note>adding the Hebrew prefix 'she-' (that)</note> or "is two days," etc. For the chanter should not use the prefix *she-*, but should say "Today is the first day" or "the second," etc., without the *she-*. From the word "Today" onwards is the commandment of counting, which fulfills the positive commandment "and you shall count for yourselves." The blessing "Blessed are You... Who has sanctified us... regarding the Counting of the Omer" is the blessing over the commandment. Therefore, whoever hears the blessing from his fellow should say "Amen" before the fellow begins to count "Today is such-and-such."

### **And he counted**
The book *Ma'arekhet Ha-Elohut* <term>A 14th-century Kabbalistic work</term> wrote in the seventh gate: "Since the counting is for the Omer, it seems that the counter must say 'Today is such-and-such,' and the prefix *she-* should refer back to the word 'Omer' in the blessing. Or, he must say 'Today is such-and-such of the Omer.'" This latter way is the primary one.

### **Counters**
Up to seven weeks. When he counts seven days, he should say "Seven days which ARE one week," for "week" (*shavuah*) is masculine. Thus Rashi explained explicitly regarding "complete this week" in the portion of *Vayetze*. And for eight days, he should say "which are one week and one day," and so on always, for one must count both days and weeks.

### **He Wrote**
The *Rashba* <term>Rabbi Solomon ben Adret (1235–1310), a leading Sephardic authority</term> wrote in a response: A congregation that erred on a cloudy day and recited the blessing on the counting of the Omer, and then returned... the law is that he should say "Today is seven days" even if it is actually nine, because that day is the ninth day and they did not act according to clear testimony. For the essentials are not counted until the stars come out. Thus it is proper to do... and the Gaon *Maharshal* would not eat until the stars came out, for he said perhaps he would forget the counting in the preoccupation of the meal, and before the stars came out he was not permitted to count. We say the "May it be Your Will" prayer after the counting because nowadays the counting is only a Rabbinic obligation since the Holy Temple no longer stands. Therefore, we say "May it be Your Will that the Temple be rebuilt," and then it will be from the time of the Torah and we will fulfill its commandments. And there are those who are perfect and say... what is the connection between the Temple service and mentioning it with the Counting of the Omer? Is not the Counting of the Omer...
