<margin>SMaK <note>Sefer Mitzvot Katan, a 13th-century legal code</note>, section 157</margin>
<margin>The Great Sage Rabbi Isaac <note>likely referring to Rabbi Isaac Luria, the Arizal</note> wrote in his Seder arrangement that one should take the "pious" bread <note>Matzah made with extra care</note> to remove himself from doubt, for Rabbi Isaac holds that one is required to recite the Grace After Meals over the *Karpas* <term>the vegetable dipped in salt water</term>, whereas according to the words of the Sages, it is not necessary.</margin>

# Tractate Pesachim

...cups so that he fulfills his obligation with the blessing over the fruit of the vine. If so, how can he interrupt or pause between them with matters that are not relevant to the Seder? When one blesses the Matzah and the Bitter Herbs, he should also intend for the blessing to cover the "sandwich" <note>the *Korech*, where Matzah and Maror are eaten together</note>. It is also proper that when blessing the eating of Matzah, his thoughts should include the eating of the *Afikoman* <term>the final piece of Matzah eaten as dessert</term> that will be eaten at the end. Since this is the case, how could he interrupt? Aside from this, a person should consider that this commandment comes to him only once a year, and afterward all these precious desires—these commandments—will pass from him. Therefore, at their proper time, he should bless them, love them, and cling to them, never separating his thoughts from them. I have seen "men of ascent" <note>spiritually elevated individuals</note> who cherished the commandments; they would kiss the Matzah, the Bitter Herbs, and the ritual objects during the performance of the commandment. So too, those who merit entering and exiting <note>the synagogue or the performance of a deed</note>, and likewise the Four Species of the Lulav—it is all to show love for the commandment. This can be learned from what Maimonides <note>Rambam</note> wrote at the end of the Laws of Ritual Fringes, that it is customary to kiss the *Tzitzit* <term>ritual fringes</term> when one looks at them, all for the sake of cherishing the commandment. Happy is the one who serves the Lord with joy, a good heart, clinging, desire, and delight.

### The Law of the Four Cups

<margin>So it is written in the first chapter.</margin>
The size of the cup should be such that it holds a *revi'it* <term>approx. 3.3 to 5 fluid ounces</term> after it is diluted with water. The *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, 14th-century halakhist</note> wrote in section 472 that one does not need to drink the entire cup, but only the majority of it. The *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo's commentary on the Tur</note> adds: regarding what was written that one needs the majority, this is indeed implied by the Talmud. However, the *Tosafot* <note>Medieval French and German commentators</note> wrote that ideally, one should drink a full *revi'it*, and this is also implied by the words of the *Rosh* <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note>. The *Kol Bo* <note>13th-14th century legal work</note> wrote that if the cup was large and contained two *revi'it* measures, if he drinks it in two parts, one after the other, he fulfills the obligation. My master and father added: if it was a large cup containing two or more *revi'it* measures, he may drink it in two or more parts according to its size and fulfill the obligation. After he has drunk a "cheekful" <note>the amount of liquid that fills one side of the mouth</note>, even from a small cup that does not hold a full *revi'it*, he should give his children and the small members of his household to drink. Maimonides, however, wrote that one must drink the majority of every cup, even if it holds many *revi'it* measures, and so wrote our teacher Rabbi Solomon Luria <note>the Maharshal</note>.

<margin>Additionally, we claim that the Cup of Blessing alludes to the Divine Presence, which is called "Face," and it is known and explained regarding the tractate that they receive sixty and sixty <note>mystical numbers</note> and the angel Sandalfon follows them wherever they go, and he will expand his "Galsaktanim" <note>an esoteric/Kabbalistic term for divine garments or shields</note> with you.</margin>
When one blesses the wine, the cup should be full so that the bread does not "see its shame" <note>a poetic way of saying the bread should be covered while the wine is being blessed</note>. When reciting the Haggadah, the bread should be uncovered, for it is called "the bread of affliction" <note>original: *lechem oni*</note> because we "answer" <note>a pun on *oni* (affliction) and *onin* (answering/reciting)</note> many words over it. When one reaches the section beginning "Therefore it is our duty" <note>original: *Lefichach*</note>, he should take the cup in his hand, and when he mentions the bread, he should [cover it]. When reciting the paragraph "And it is this that has stood for our ancestors," he should hold the cup in his hand until he finishes the passage "The Holy One, Blessed be He, saves us from their hand." This is according to the Kabbalah and the Ancient Wisdom. At that point, the bread should be covered; afterward, he should set the cup on the table and reveal the bread until the "Therefore" section.

**We remove** the Seder plate from the table when saying "Why is this night different?" <note>original: *Mah Nishtanah*</note> until "We were slaves," and this takes the place of moving the table <note>as was done in ancient times</note>. As explained in Tractate Pesachim, page 115: "Why do we remove the table? The school of Rabbi Yannai said: So that the children will notice and ask." Abaye was sitting before Rabbah and saw them removing the table from before him. He said to them: "We haven't eaten yet! Why are they taking the table away from me?" Rabbah said to him: "You have exempted us from saying 'Why is this night different?'" Rashbam <term>Rabbi Samuel ben Meir, 12th-century French commentator</term> explains: You exempted us from saying "Why is this night different" because it is taught later: "The son asks his father, and if not, he asks himself: Why is this night different?" Since he asked out of his own heart, we do not need to recite the formal "Why is this night different." It is impossible to answer my son's words except by saying "because we were enslaved in Egypt, we do all these things." However, others do not understand why this is considered an interruption. The *Tosafot* write: the removal of the table is so the child recognizes and asks—meaning, through this, he will come to ask about other things. But regarding the specific question of why we remove the table, he is not exempted from the formal "Why is this night different." The Talmud only mentioned the beginning of Abaye's question. This interpretation is a bit strained. Therefore, it appears according to what I have received: when the child asks why we remove the plate, we answer him: "Because we will not eat now, nor will we eat until we have spoken words of praise and thanks." Then the child says: "How is this day different from other days?" and then we answer "We were slaves," and automatically we are exempt from saying the formal "Why is this night different." (Afterward, I found this also in the rulings of Rabbi Simcha). This applies to everything the child might ask, such as at the first dipping of the vegetable: "What is the meaning of this?" and so on. We pour the second cup before the meal so he will ask "Why is this night different?" We answer him that slaves of kings and ministers [did thus] so that the ancestors would live for the eating, and this matter is continuous. Then the child says: "What is this day? How is this day different from other days?" and then we respond and tell of the miracles of Egypt, how we went out to freedom with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. One should break the middle Matzah into two. The early Rabbis said that the blessing of "Hamotzi" <note>the blessing over bread</note> should be over the second piece, but it is forbidden because "one does not pass over commandments" <term>a principle that you must perform a ritual as soon as it is available</term>. But now, the "Hamotzi" is over the first piece, and there is no commandment in breaking the Matzah into two, and the third piece remains whole. One recites the "Hamotzi" over the first piece and the blessing for "eating Matzah" over the second. One must bless the eating of Matzah over the broken piece, as is the way of a poor person. If he had broken the third, he would bless the eating of Matzah over the third, but one does not pass over commandments. Note that there is a different version in the Jerusalem Talmud. Half is placed under the bed for the *Afikoman*, in memory of "their bundles wrapped in their cloaks upon their shoulders" <note>Exodus 12:34</note>. The Sage Maharashat wrote that it is proper to wrap it in a cloth and place it between the knees, not just to hide it. The Maharal wrote to take a large portion for the *Afikoman*, and so wrote the Maharshal. This is to fulfill what is in the Book of Tanya. I found in the name of Rabbi Z. Meir that the commandment of Hallel <term>Psalms of Praise</term> is to recite it while standing. I found the reason in the name of the scholar Rabbi Benjamin bar Abraham the Physician: based on the verse "Praise, O servants of the Lord, who stand," meaning, praise the Name while standing, as it is said, "And the people stood." In the Temple court, they would recite it during the slaughter of the Passover offering while standing, for there is no sitting in the Temple court. As for why we recite it on Passover nights while sitting, it is because it is divided and not recited all at once, rather it is divided for its sections. Furthermore, one is sitting at the table with a cup in hand; if he stood, his mind might be distracted by the meal and the cup might fall from his hand. Like Rabbi D. Meir, I found that because the way of the Passover Hallel is the way of reclining and freedom, we do not burden them to stand. Therefore, even though one sits, he sits in awe and fear, and does not recite the Hallel in a lightheaded manner, but with gravity and reverence.

**Concerning** the blessing of "Hamotzi" and the eating of Matzah: I, the author, will write the custom of my master and father. He would take the three Matzahs—that is, with the broken piece in the middle—and bless "Hamotzi" over the whole ones to fulfill the "double bread" <term>Lechem Mishneh</term> with two whole loaves, and also to fulfill the "bread of affliction" <note>Lechem Oni</note> with the broken piece. Afterward, he would set down the third and hold in his hand the first and the second (the broken piece) and bless over both together for "the eating of Matzah." He would break off a *kezayit* <term>the size of an olive</term> from each together. Thus, he fulfills all opinions and doubts. This is because there are opinions that one should bless "Hamotzi" over the whole ones and "eating Matzah" over the broken one, and there are opinions that say the opposite. Therefore, to satisfy both, one holds both in his hand and recites "Hamotzi" and "eating Matzah" one after the other. So wrote the *Tur* at the beginning of section 475. One must break off an olive-sized piece from each. This is from the "Laws of Customs," where a question was raised: why is it necessary to eat an olive-sized piece from the Matzah used for "Hamotzi"? For a blessing over food, even a tiny amount suffices. It makes sense for the Matzah used for the commandment of "eating Matzah," for it is written "bread of affliction," and the way of a poor person is a broken piece, and by law, that is an olive-sized piece. But according to what we said—that one uses both because of doubt over which Matzah is for which blessing—one is forced to eat an olive-sized piece from each. This is the language of the "Deep Gleanings" <note>original: *Likutei Amok*</note>, section 3. In the Haggadah, in the text of "Therefore we are obligated," our versions conclude "and let us say before Him: Hallelujah." This is the explicit version in the Mishnah, Tractate Pesachim, page 116. However, in the Glosses of the *Mordechai*, it is written: "and let us say before Him: a new song" <note>original: *shira chadasha* - feminine</note>. So too wrote the *Tosafot* on page 116, that this is the version, as I have transcribed below. So also wrote the *Maharshal* in his responsa and in his prayer book for the Passover Seder. We have thus learned that the versions in our prayer books that say "Hallelujah"—though found in many legal authorities—are incomplete versions. The true version is "and let us say before Him: a new song." Do not pay attention to what the *Tosafot* said: "it seems to me that it should be 'a new song' [masculine: *shir chadash*] regarding our future redemption," for that is taught in our Mechilta <note>an ancient midrashic work</note>, and regarding all "songs" <note>of the past</note> the feminine language [*shira*] is used, except for the song of the future which is in the masculine. (This is because there is no exile after that redemption). This is a third opinion—that they agree to say "a new song" [masculine], but not according to the text written by my masters, the *Hadarni*, the *Hagrani*, and our Rabbi, who wrote to say "a new song" in the feminine. The *Tosafot* wrote the version in the masculine, "a new song" [*shir chadash*], but this is nothing but a scribal error in the words of the *Tosafot*. It should say: "The version is: and let us say before Him: a new song [feminine]." So too is the emendation of the *Maharshal* in his work *Chochmat Shlomo*. With this, the explanation of the words of the *Tosafot*, the *Beit Yosef*, and the version "and let us say before Him: a new song" is complete. And so we will bring later.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the performance of religious duties, transitioning from the laws of the Passover Seder to a broader ethical discussion on the nature of kindness and social obligations, specifically the joy of a wedding, visiting the sick, and burial.</meta>

[To speak with him <note>likely referring to a groom or a poor person</note> with good words, to appease him, and to say to him, "Do not set your eyes upon money, for God shall be with you," and similar words that enter the heart.]

**And that** which we said above—that the primary commandment of bringing joy to a bride and groom <note>Hebrew: *Simchat Chatan v'Kallah*</note> is greater than other acts of kindness—is specifically when it is "True Kindness" <term>True Kindness (*Chesed shel Emet*): An act done purely for the sake of heaven without expecting repayment, typically used for burying the dead, but here applied to selfless acts for the living</term>, performed for the sake of Heaven and not for the sake of receiving a reward. One should follow the ways of his Creator, may He be blessed, who performed True Kindness with Adam and Eve and blessed them. At the end of the eighth portion <note>in Midrash Rabbah</note>, Rabbi Simlai said: We find that the Holy One, Blessed be He, blesses grooms—from where do we know this? From the verse, "And God blessed them." From where do we know He adorns brides? From the verse, "And the Lord God built the side" <note>Genesis 2:22; the Rabbis interpret "built" as "braided her hair" or "adorned her"</note>. From where do we know He visits the sick? From the verse, "And the Lord appeared to him [Abraham] in the plains of Mamre" <note>Genesis 18:1, while Abraham was recovering from circumcision</note>. From where do we know He buries the dead? From the verse, "And He buried him [Moses] in the valley." Rabbi Samuel bar Nachman said in the name of Rabbi Jonathan: He also shows a welcoming face to the mourner, as it is written, "And God appeared to Jacob again... and blessed him." And what blessing did He bless him with? Rabbi Jonathan said: The blessing of mourners. 

It is difficult to understand why Rabbi Simlai did not count the comforting of mourners, which is mentioned twice: "And it was after the death of Abraham, that God blessed Isaac," which is the blessing of mourners, and likewise He blessed Jacob with the blessing of mourners. It seems that Rabbi Simlai only counted the order of the levels of acts of kindness, which are three, one above the other, in terms of how a person performs them. The first level is the joy of grooms and brides; one might fear perhaps he does it for repayment, so that they might also make him happy, or his son, or that they might sit together in a court of law. Visiting the sick is a higher level, for every sick person is in a state of doubt whether they will live or die; if they die, they will not repay the favor, and despite this, the person performs kindness with them despite the uncertainty. The third level is the highest level, and that is True Kindness: the burial of the dead, for one does not expect any repayment at all. 

This Rabbi Simlai mentioned here is the same one in the Tractate Sotah, page 14, where Rabbi Simlai taught: The Torah begins with acts of kindness and ends with acts of kindness. It begins with kindness, as it is written: "And the Lord God made for Adam and his wife coats of skins and clothed them." And it ends with kindness, as it is written: "And He buried him in the valley." This concludes his words. 

One might ask: What is gained by noting it is at the beginning and the end? The entire Torah is holy! Rabbi Simlai's intent is as we explained here; his intention was to use a shorthand. That is, the joy of grooms and the care for the dead. When there is a beginning and an end, there is necessarily a middle between them. His intent is that regarding the Holy One, Blessed be He—whose end is in His beginning and His beginning is in His end—all are equal. He means to say: Just as the end, the burial of the dead, is True Kindness even among human beings, so too with the Holy One, Blessed be He, even the first case, the joy of brides and grooms, is performed as True Kindness.

<insert>
->Concerning the Rabbis<-
The Rabbis, Nissim, Razi, and Jonathan discussed the verse regarding Jacob and why it does not say "and He comforted him," to show a higher level... to show him a welcoming face... one should learn from this to speak good words to him and show a pleasant face.
</insert>

->To this they hinted:<-
They repeated his words: What is the joy of the groom? It is like clothing the naked; just as He, blessed be He, performs kindness and it is True Kindness, so should you. To this hints the word "Truth" <note>Hebrew: *Emet* (אמת)</note>: the *Aleph* (א) is at the beginning, the *Mem* (מ) is in the middle, and the *Tav* (ת) is at the end. These correspond to the three levels mentioned above, that they should all be True Kindness. Through this, we can explain a statement in the Midrash Rabbah, portion 8: "Kindness and Truth have met, Righteousness and Peace have kissed." Kindness said: Let Man be created, for he performs acts of kindness. Truth said: Let him not be created, for he is entirely full of lies. Righteousness said: Let him be created, for he performs charity. Peace said: Let him not be created, for he is entirely full of strife. What did the Holy One, Blessed be He, do? He took Truth and threw it to the ground, as it is written, "And He cast Truth to the ground." 

It is difficult to understand why the Blessed One needed to cast Truth to the ground. Are not the attributes of the Holy One, Blessed be He, such that He leans toward kindness when merits and sins are equal? Furthermore, here Kindness and Righteousness are balanced against Truth and Peace. The reason Man should not have been created was a concern that he would have no peace. The intent is: Kindness said "let him be created" for the merit of kindness, but Truth said "let him not be created" because the kindness of human beings is not "True Kindness" but is done for repayment; if so, what merit is there in his kindness? Righteousness said "let him be created" for the merit of charity. Peace said "let him not be created" because the essence of charity is intended to bring peace... but in our many sins, it often leads to anger and strife, and thus the "face of the house" is bad and full of quarrels. What did the Holy One, Blessed be He, do? He cast Truth to the ground, meaning Peace will merit through Kindness. And what was Truth's claim? That human kindness is not True Kindness. But since there exists also the power of True Kindness in our society—that which we do with the dead to bury them in the "land of the living"—this is "Truth shall spring from the earth." The general rule is: anyone who performs a commandment should see to it that his thought is not for any repayment or peace from the world, but only to perform kindness essentially and to walk in the ways of the Blessed One.

# Visiting the Sick

<margin>
Visiting the sick <note>Hebrew: *Bikur Cholim*</note> is a Torah-mandated obligation, as we derive in Tractate Nedarim, chapter "Ein Bein HaMudar," page 40. Rabbi Simeon ben Lakish said: From where in the Torah do we know the obligation to visit the sick? As it is written: "If these men die the common death of all men, and be visited after the visitation of all men..." What does this imply? Rava said: If all men are sick and cast upon their beds, and people visit them and say... It was taught: Visiting the sick has no fixed measure. What does "no fixed measure" mean? Rav Yosef thought to say there is no measure to the reward. Abaye said to him: Is there a measure to the reward of any commandment? For we have learned: "Be as careful with a light commandment as with a weighty one, for you do not know the reward of the commandments." Rather, Abaye said: Even a great person must visit a small person. He also said: Even a hundred times a day. And in Tractate Bava Metzia, page 30, Rav Yosef taught: "And you shall show them"—this is the house of their lives; "the way"—this refers to acts of kindness. And at the end, "visiting the sick" and "burial," "the work"—this is the law; "that they shall do"—this refers to acting beyond the letter of the law. The Master said: "And at the end, visiting the sick"—is this not already included in acts of kindness? It is necessary to specify it, for even one born under the same astrological sign <note>Hebrew: *Ben Gilo*</note> must go, even though a *Ben Gilo* takes away one-sixtieth of the illness <note>and might thus become weakened himself</note>, even so, he is required to go. This concludes the quote.
</margin>

This obligation involves the body, the soul, and money. How so with the body? One should run and busy himself with all the patient's needs, provide him with all his medicines, and exert his body greatly for these needs. There is a story of a student of Rabbi Akiva who fell ill, and the Sages did not enter to visit him. Rabbi Akiva entered to visit him, and because he swept and cleaned the floor before him, the student lived and said to the Rabbi, "My teacher, you have revived me!" How so with the soul? One should pour out his soul in supplication to pray to the Blessed One to send the patient a complete recovery. How so with money? To see if the sick person lacks the funds for his needs and to strive to provide for him, etc. And it is worthy even of the greatest acts of kindness.

## In the First Chapter
of Tractate Shabbat, page 12: It was taught that one who enters to visit the sick on Shabbat should say: "It is Shabbat, which forbids crying out, and healing is soon to come." Rabbi Meir said: "She [the Sabbath] can have mercy." Rabbi Judah says: "May the Place <note>a name for God, *HaMakom*</note> have mercy on you and on the sick of Israel." Rabbi Yose says: "May the Place have mercy on you among the sick of Israel."... Upon entering, he says "Peace," and upon leaving, he says: "It is Shabbat, which forbids crying out, and healing is soon to come, and His mercies are many; rest in peace." 

Whom does the ruling follow? That which Rabbi Hanina said: One who has a sick person in his house must include him among the sick of Israel. Like whom? Like Rabbi Yose. And Rabbi Hanina said: It was with difficulty that they permitted comforting mourners and visiting the sick on Shabbat. Rabbah bar Hana said: When we would follow Rabbi Eleazar to ask after his health... sometimes he would say, "May He visit you in peace," and sometimes he said, "May He lead you to peace." How could he do this? Did not Rabbi Judah say: A person should never ask for his needs in the Aramaic language? And Rabbi Yochanan said: Anyone who asks for his needs in Aramaic, the ministering angels do not attend to him, for the angels do not recognize the Aramaic language! A sick person is different, for the Divine Presence <note>Hebrew: *Shekhinah*</note> is with him, as Rav Anan said in the name of Rav: From where do we know that the Divine Presence supports the sick person? As it is written: "The Lord will support him upon the bed of suffering." 

It was also taught likewise: One who enters to visit the sick should not sit upon the bed, nor upon a chair, but should wrap himself and sit before him, because the Divine Presence is above the head of the sick person, as it is written: "The Lord will support him upon the bed of suffering." And Rava said in the name of Rabin: From where do we know that the Holy One, Blessed be He, provides for the sick person? As it is written: "The Lord will support him upon the bed of suffering." This concludes the intent. And he noted "not on the bed and not on a stool." It appears that specifically when the sick person lies low, one should not sit higher than the head of the sick person. It also appears that even if the visitor sits lower than the sick person, he should not sit right at his head... it is clear that one must sit lower than the patient... as the Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, 13th-century scholar</note> explained. Our Rabbis taught: One who enters to visit the sick should not sit on the bed, nor on a stool, nor on a chair, nor on any high place, but rather <note>not</note> above the head of the sick person, but rather wrap himself, etc. It seems clear that the beginning considers the types of seating and the manner, and afterward says "and not at his head," meaning even if he is sitting low. Do not be mistaken by the language "above the head of the sick person"—it implies that if he is lower it is permitted even at the head; for "above" does not mean height, but rather the direction of the feet...

<header>Tractate Pesachim</header>

# Tractate Pesachim

The Counting of the Omer <note>The 49-day period between Passover and Shavuot</note> is not dependent on the building of the Temple; it is a personal obligation <term>Personal obligation (*Chovat HaGuf*): A commandment that falls on the individual regardless of whether they are in the Land of Israel or if the Temple stands</term> and is practiced in all places of residence. I found in the name of the scholar Rabbi Benjamin, son of Abraham the Physician <note>original: "R. Benjamin bar Abraham HaRofé"; likely R. Benjamin Anav, a 13th-century Italian scholar</note>, of blessed memory, that even though the counting itself does not depend on the Temple, the actual reaping and bringing of the grain offering *does* depend on the building of the Temple. In the Diaspora—in the regions of Poland, Bohemia <note>original: "Piham"</note>, and all those kingdoms, as well as in Germany <note>original: "Ashkenaz"</note>—where it is the custom to pray the Evening Service <note>Arvit</note> while it is still broad daylight <note>During the long summer days in Northern Europe, communities often prayed early before stars appeared</note>, there are nevertheless modern holy groups that gather to pray the Evening Service at its proper time <note>at nightfall</note>, as I have seen in that great city of Israel, Prague <note>original: "PR"A," an abbreviation for Prague</note>. Happy is the one who joins them, for a commandment is most beloved when performed at its proper time. Even if it is not possible to do this all year round, it is proper for anyone who has the fear of God in his heart to join them during the days of the Omer, for then "one commandment leads to another" <note>a Talmudic proverb</note>: reciting the Shema at its proper time and counting the Omer with the congregation.

## Regarding "And You Shall Rejoice in Your Festival"
The specific ways one should experience the joy of the holiday will be discussed at length later, in the section on the Festival of Sukkot. Regarding birds that are stuffed with meat and eggs: it is permitted to sew them shut on a festival day, provided that the thread was already placed in the needle before the start of the holiday. One must be careful not to cut the thread on the holiday itself. It is also the custom to burn the remaining thread left on the bird after sewing. This is recorded in the Shulchan Aruch, section 509. It is necessary to inform the women who are not experts in the law and to teach them these details. One may not prepare on Shabbat for a weekday, nor for a holiday; however, one may prepare on a holiday for Shabbat. Similarly, one may not prepare from the first day of a holiday for the second day, and it is forbidden to do even a small or easy preparation. I was asked if women are permitted to light the candles on the first day of the Diaspora holidays <note>the second day added outside of Israel</note> at twilight for the sake of the second night of the holiday. I permitted it, comparing it to the candle of the synagogue, which is a "perpetual lamp" that one is allowed to light on the first day at twilight for the sake of the night. This is not called a "useless candle" because the act of lighting itself is a commandment at that moment. The same applies here. Even though they recite the blessing for the sake of the night, it is of no concern; is it not true that every Friday we add time and light candles while it is still day and recite the blessing? On the contrary, in my view, it is a greater commandment than the common practice where women do not light the second night's candles at all until they return from the synagogue after the evening prayer, for then, by the time they arrive home, it is already quite dark, and that is not ideal. This is how I have seen it.

In some communities in the Diaspora, every homeowner takes the candle he prayed by and places it in the sand in the designated place where all the candles are kept. This involves a strict prohibition, as explained in the Shulchan Aruch, section 514: a wax candle that is tilted to be lit on a holiday, and one is concerned that it will burn down entirely, and wants to place something around it before lighting to prevent it from burning further so it will extinguish when it reaches that point—this is forbidden because it is considered "extinguishing." The correct path is for every homeowner to take his candle and bring it to his house. In this way, he is saved from a transgression and performs a commandment, for he lights it during the dark of night. Our Sages, of blessed memory, said: "Why did Saul merit kingship? Because he lit lamps in dark alleys." This will be a light for the world and an answer for him; he was observant for the sake of kindness, as will be explained. It is proper to explain a bit about the attributes of kindness.

Whoever wishes to cleave to the Divine Presence <note>Shekhinah</note> should learn from the attributes of his Creator. If he habituates himself to these attributes, he will find himself cleaving to the Divine Presence. This is as we learn in the first chapter of Tractate Sotah, page 14: Rabbi Hama, son of Rabbi Hanina, said: "What is the meaning of the verse, 'After the Lord your God you shall walk'? Is it possible for a human to walk after the Divine Presence? Is it not written, 'For the Lord your God is a consuming fire'? Rather, it means to follow the attributes of the Holy One, Blessed be He. Just as the Holy One, Blessed be He, clothes the naked—as it is written, 'And the Lord God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them'—so too, you should clothe the naked. The Holy One, Blessed be He, visits the sick—as it is said, 'And the Lord appeared to him [Abraham] in the plains of Mamre'—so too, you should visit the sick. The Holy One, Blessed be He, comforts mourners—as it is said, 'And it came to pass after the death of Abraham, that God blessed Isaac his son'—so too, you should comfort mourners. The Holy One, Blessed be He, buries the dead—as it is written, 'And He buried him [Moses] in the valley'—so too, you should bury the dead."

Blessed be our God, in whose abode there is joy! The measure of reward is much greater than the measure of punishment. We find that the Holy One, Blessed be He, rejoiced with great joy at the wedding canopy of Adam. As we learn in Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer, chapter 12: The Holy One, Blessed be He, made ten wedding canopies for Adam in the Garden of Eden, all of them of precious stones and pearls. Now, for every groom, we make only one canopy, but for the King Messiah, they will make seven canopies, as it is said: "You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone was your covering: the ruby, the topaz, and the diamond; the beryl, the onyx, and the jasper; the sapphire, the emerald, and the carbuncle, and gold; the workmanship of your settings and your sockets was in you on the day you were created." These are the ten canopies. The angels would play drums and dance like women <note>meaning in circles or with specific instruments</note>, as it says, "the workmanship of your settings..." on the day Adam was created. The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to the ministering angels: "Come, let us perform acts of kindness for Adam," for the world stands upon the attribute of performing kindness. And the Holy One, Blessed be He, said: "Kindness is more beloved to Me than the sacrifices and burnt offerings that Israel will one day offer before Me on the altar," as it is said: "For I desire kindness and not sacrifice." And the ministering angels walked before him like friends who bring joy to the wedding canopies, as it is said: "For He shall give His angels charge over you," and this "way" refers only to the way of grooms. The Holy One, Blessed be He, is like a groom—just as a groom stands and blesses the groom and bride within their canopy, so the Holy One, Blessed be He, stood and blessed Adam and Eve, as it is said: "And God blessed them, and God said to them..." We also learn in Tractate Bava Batra, in the chapter "One who Sells a Ship," page 75a: Rabbi Hama bar Hanina said: The Holy One, Blessed be He, made ten wedding canopies for Adam in the Garden of Eden, as it is said: "You were in Eden, the garden of God..." Mar Zutra said: These are the precious stones mentioned in the verse. We also learn in Tractate Eruvin, in the chapter "One who Makes Partitions," page 18: "'And He brought her to the man'—this teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He, acted as a groomsman <note>original: "shoshbinut"</note> for Adam." Thus far the quote. Adam did not speak after his groomsman... and their songs were, as it were, like the joy of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and from Him, the supernal angels learned. And just as the angels played drums and danced, so it is proper to honor and cherish a groom and bride, since it is the will of Heaven. Similarly, David danced before the Ark.

In Tractate Ketubot, in the chapter "The Woman," page 17a: Our Rabbis taught: How does one dance before the bride? The House of Shammai says: "The bride as she is" <note>describing her exactly as she appears</note>. But the House of Hillel says: "A beautiful and graceful bride." The House of Shammai said to them: "According to your words, if one married a woman who was lame or blind, would they say to her, 'A beautiful and graceful bride'? But the Torah said, 'Keep far from a false matter'!" The House of Hillel said to the House of Shammai: "According to your words, if someone makes a bad purchase in the market, should his friend praise it to his face or disparage it to his face? Surely, he should praise it to his face!" From here the Sages said: "A person’s mind should always be pleasant with people." When Rav Dimi came, he said: This is what they sing before the bride in the West <note>the Land of Israel</note>: "No eye-paint, no rouge, no braiding—and yet a graceful doe!" It was said about Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai that he would take a branch of myrtle and dance before the bride, saying: "A beautiful and graceful bride." Rabbi Samuel bar Rav Isaac would dance with three branches <note>tossing them and catching them</note>, throwing one and catching one. Rabbi Zeira said: "The old man is embarrassing us!" But when Rabbi Samuel passed away, a pillar of fire separated between him and the rest of the people. And there is a tradition that a pillar of fire only separates for one or two people in a generation. Rabbi Aha said: "The old man’s 'folly' <note>his branch-dancing</note> benefited him." Rav Ada bar Ahava would carry the bride on his shoulders and dance. The Rabbis said to him: "May we also do this?" He said to them: "If she is like a wooden beam <note>original: "k'shura"</note> to you—yes; and if not—no." From all this, we see the obligation to be pious and to hold onto the ways of the early Sages, and to perform kindness for grooms for the sake of Heaven, to honor them and praise them, and from God, may He be blessed, his reward will be complete. Our Sages particularly mentioned the joy of a groom, saying: "Anyone who enjoys a groom's banquet and does not bring him joy..." because the bride can be viewed in different ways; if she is like a beam to him, he should act like the elder, and if not, not. Furthermore, one should increase his efforts and use clever ways to make the groom happy and praise the bride before him, for if the groom is happy and good-hearted, he will love the bride and pursue her, and that is her true joy.

## And Regarding
the matter of bringing a bride to the canopy, the Sages mentioned the bride and did not say "the groom." They explained that in ancient Israel, the custom was to take the bride from her father's house and bring her to the groom's house, and the groom would bring her in to him. However, the essence of the commandment is "Bringing in the Bride" <term>Hachnasat Kallah: Providing a dowry and wedding necessities for a poor bride</term>—assisting with her dowry and clothing so that she is able to enter the canopy. I found this written: it is proper for a person to toil in this with his body, his money, and his might, and to be one who acts and causes others to act. However, those who are accustomed to deceiving the groom in any way they can regarding the matter of his dowry, and also to force him to go to the canopy even though they have not given him the full dowry they promised him—this is not a proper custom, and the law protects the groom. On the contrary, we see in the final chapter of Ketubot: "One who pledges money to his son-in-law and then defaults—she should sit until her hair turns white." Admon says: "She can say, 'If I had pledged for myself, I would sit until my hair turned white. Now that my father has pledged, what can I do? Either marry me or release me!'" Rabban Gamliel said: "I see the words of Admon." Thus far the quote. And even according to Admon's words, we cannot force the groom to bring her in <note>to marry her</note> if the promised money is not paid, even though he has already betrothed her. And understand this. Behold, those who deceive the groom think they are performing a commandment so as not to embarrass a Jewish daughter, but in my view, it is not proper for a groom except in a very small matter. Regarding what the Levites mentioned... that when they finish the acquisition... the groom resolves in his heart... but this is a great commandment to go and pursue and strive for him all that is possible... and certainly it is possible to speak with him...

# Tractate Pesachim

And let it be said: "I have no pleasure in the death of the one who dies, says the Lord God; return and live forever." [Ezekiel 18:32] "Forever, O Lord, Your word is settled in heaven." [Psalm 119:89] Your word is true and stands forever; may Your words be verified and come before You as a pleasing offering, that You may atone for my sins, forgive my iniquities, and pardon my transgressions. Blot out and remove those committed willfully, unintentionally, under duress, or by choice—in speech, thought, and deed; those revealed to me and those hidden from me; what I did in my childhood, my youth, my middle age, and my old age, whether in this incarnation <term>Incarnation (*Gilgul*): The kabbalistic concept of the soul returning in different bodies to achieve perfection</term> or in another. Remove and forgive everything. And in the hour <note>original: "בשוגע" (likely a typo for בשעה)</note> of my end, as I depart from this world to return to You, I hereby accept death with love for You. "To You, O Lord, I lift up my soul." [Psalm 25:1] May it be Your will, O Lord my God and God of my fathers, that my death be an atonement for all my sins in the world, from the greatest to the least. Receive my soul with joy as You take it from me. On the day of my going before You, please favor my journey; send angels of mercy to come out toward me, and may they say with one voice as I enter, "May your coming be in peace." May they bring me to the Garden of Eden, and there may my dwelling be, where I shall delight in the radiance of Your light for all days. There shall be the place of my glorious rest and the "Hidden Light" <gloss>meaning: eternal pleasantness</gloss> before You. May You be my hiding place and my shelter, and under the shadow of Your wings give me my portion. Hear my supplication, hasten my salvation, O Eternal God; You are my light for generations and my salvation, for in You I have trusted. "May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be pleasing before You, O Lord, my Rock and my Redeemer." [Psalm 19:15]

This is an ancient prayer founded upon the Name of 42 <term>Name of 42 (*Shem Mem-Bet*): A mystical name of God derived from the 42 letters of the prayer *Ana B'Koach*</term>. This is the language of the *Pardes* <note>Referring to *Pardes Rimmonim* by Rabbi Moshe Cordovero</note> in the Gate of Specific Names, at the end of Chapter 13: The Rashbi <note>Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the traditional author of the Zohar</note>, peace be upon him, wrote that every name containing six letters corresponds to the six wings of the Seraphim, as it is said: "Each one had six wings" (in Isaiah). He said this name is good to recite at night before sleeping, and likewise for a person near their passing. For by these wings, as written in Isaiah, "with two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew," the soul flies upward and hopes to be saved from the angels of destruction and all harmful spirits, and will merit the life of the World to Come. Thus far his words. And I have received a tradition that those who guard the dead <term>Guards (*Shomrim*): People who sit with a body from death until burial to honor the deceased and protect the soul</term> and sit around them from the moment of death until they are hidden in the dust of the grave, should sit in a tight circle around the body like a breastplate so that no "external force" <note>impure spiritual entities</note> can enter between them. They should recite this prayer constantly without a moment’s pause, not diminishing it even a thousand times.

Afterward, tell him that he should arrange his affairs for the members of his household—if he has money in the hands of others, or others have money in his hand, or if he wishes to command that something be done according to his will. Specifically, he should remember to leave something for the poor, for the sanctuary, for the "Gemilut Chasadim" <note>acts of loving-kindness</note> societies, or for the burial society. For it is a duty for every man, from all his toil, at this hour to leave something to the holy funds, for that is his "portion in life." The Recanati <note>Rabbi Menahem Recanati, 13th-14th century Kabbalist</note> wrote in the portion of *Vayechi*: Some Kabbalists said a person must be careful at the time of death that none of his limbs remain outside the bed. For whatever remains outside this "five" <note>likely referring to the bed's protective boundaries</note> will not be gathered and will not be buried—meaning in the "Upper Burial"—but is given to the beasts of the field to consume. This hint is very great, because surrounding the bed are those called "destroyers and punishers" <note>impure spirits</note>... Therefore, he must be gathered unto his people and not live for the "Beasts of Impurity." This is the meaning of the "gathering" mentioned regarding the righteous. Thus far his words. His words are clear to "those who know grace" <term>Those who know grace (*Yodei Chen*): An idiom for students of Kabbalah</term>, for the bed symbolizes the attribute of *Malchut* (Kingship) of the Shekhinah, from where the souls are quarried. Therefore, any limb that is outside the bed is disqualified as "extraneous" and shall be called "unclean, unclean." Correspondingly, the soul remains flawed in its holiness. He who guards his soul will keep distance and be careful, and merit a good old age. Thus far his words.

<margin>Repentance</margin>
Repentance one day before your death is good; therefore, a person should perform kindness for himself and run toward his forgiveness while still healthy, preparing himself for the [final] place. Let these shrouds be prepared before him, for several reasons... <unclear>strengthen</unclear>... these can be made in holiness, purity, and cleanliness by <unclear>righteous women</unclear> such as these, etc. In the *Sefer Hasidim* <note>The Book of the Pious, a 12th-century ethical text</note>, it says perhaps he will die and be buried on a Festival by Gentiles, and they will not <unclear>hesitate</unclear> to deal with his shrouds. Furthermore, the making of shrouds <unclear>with spices</unclear> in his grave and preparation for death serves as an altar for the one buried... and the shrouds themselves can cause an awakening in his heart to always remember the day of death. The shrouds should be heavy... and not like those who wrap themselves in their own souls... his soul which is most exalted... and in the chapter "These are the Knots"... and he should have a boundary within them and sweetness.

[Numbers 6:24-26]. And if the patient is able, he should also say the psalm of David: "The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not...

# Tractate Pesachim

The beginning and the end are before Him, and his head is the most elevated part, and this is easy to understand. We can further learn from the language of the Baraita <note>An ancient Jewish oral tradition not incorporated into the Mishnah</note> which states that one should "wrap oneself"—this means one must wrap themselves in a cloak as they do when going to the synagogue, out of respect for the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah: The indwelling presence of God, believed to rest at the head of a sick person's bed</term> that dwells at the head of the sick person.

**If** the act of kindness in visiting the sick is considered great when one attends to their physical needs and their life, then it is an "all the more so" argument <term>Kal Va-Chomer: A logical inference from a minor premise to a major one</term> regarding attending to the needs of their soul. This means seeing to it that the sick person confesses and feels better through a broken heart, complete regret, and a request for forgiveness and pardon from the Blessed Name. One should also have them settle their affairs while they are still alive, and not do as the common people do, who wait to speak of such things with the sick person until the soul is being crushed <note>original: "דבודכה של נפש," likely referring to the final moments of life</note>, at which point the sick person lacks awareness and cannot reflect on complete repentance. For the essence of repentance is regret, the abandonment of sin, and the specific confession of every single one of one's iniquities, asking for forgiveness with a broken heart and weeping. One must be of sound mind for this. Therefore, those who are wise act early; when they notice the person is in danger, they should say to them: "It is good to give thanks to the Lord and to pray to Him, for He is the true Physician. This confession is nothing other than a prayer before the Blessed One, just as we do every day in the synagogue." As our Sages of Blessed Memory said: "Many have confessed and did not die, and many did not confess and died." Through this, may God grant them a complete recovery.

Before anything else, one should tell the sick person to ask for forgiveness from anyone they have sinned against, whether in speech or in action. If they hold another's money in any way, they should arrange to return it, for the Blessed Name is very exacting regarding matters between a person and their fellow. Likewise, they should forgive anyone who has sinned against them, whether in word or deed, whether through theft or a slight to their honor. For if they do not, the Blessed Name will not forgive their own sins when they ask for forgiveness now. As our Sages of Blessed Memory said: "He who bears iniquity and passes over transgression"—to whom does He bear iniquity? To one who passes over the transgression of others.

The person should be told that the standard confession will now be read before them word for word, and even though it is general, they should reflect in their heart on their specific sins, perhaps categorizing them under these general types. If it is a woman <note>original: "אשת עמיתו," literally "his fellow's wife," here used generally for a married woman</note>, she should specifically reflect if she neglected the three commandments: ritual purity, the dough-offering, and the lighting of the Sabbath candles. There should be an intention of total regret, and a resolve that if God grants them recovery, they will not sin in these ways again. Anyone who expands upon their confession is praiseworthy.

## In the Zohar
In the portion of *Pekudei*, it says: whoever watches over the sick and strives to bring them to repentance, such a person acts as a "defending angel" <note>original: "מלאך המליץ טוב"</note> and causes them to be saved from the harsh decree, redeems them from death, and grants them life. Regarding such a person it is said: "Blessed is he who considers the poor." [Psalm 41:2] Thus far the quote. Blessed is the sick person who awakens this in themselves before others have to awaken it in them.

## In the Chapter "Bameh Madlikin"
Our Rabbis taught: one who falls ill and is near death, they say to him, "Confess," for all who are executed confess. Just as a groom is affected by wine, so too everyone who confesses has a portion in the World to Come. For so we find with Achan, etc. The *Beit Yosef* <note>A 16th-century legal commentary by Joseph Karo</note> wrote in the name of the *Shitah Chakhamah* that the verse "that soul shall bear its guilt and shall confess" [Leviticus 5:5] is a foundational principle for all who are dying, that they require confession. Thus far his words. The order of the confession is copied here from the *Tur*, Yoreh Deah, chapter 338, with various versions, and I shall gather them together one by one to present them:

He should answer and ask for forgiveness from everyone he has sinned against and ask for the good favor of those around him to help him with prayer. He should perform complete repentance, wash his hands, wrap himself in *tzitzit* <term>Tzitzit: Ritual fringes worn by Jewish men</term>, and say: "The Lord God is truth, His Torah is truth, Moses His prophet is truth, and blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever." He should recite "Ashrei" [Psalm 145] until the end of the psalm, and "A prayer of David: Incline Your ear, O Lord, and answer me" [Psalm 86], and "For the Leader, with stringed instruments, a song" [Psalm 67], and "I lift my eyes to the Lord" [Psalm 121]. Afterward, he should say with great intention:

# I Acknowledge
I acknowledge before You, O Lord my God and God of my fathers, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, God of gods and Lord of lords, in heaven above and on the earth below; there is none else. Creator of heaven and earth, Who performs kindness and justice on the earth, Who was, is, and will be. My healing is in Your hand, and in Your hand is the will that You heal me with a complete recovery, for You are the merciful Physician King. And if I die, may my death be an atonement for all my sins, iniquities, and transgressions that I have committed before You from the day of my birth until this day. My youth and my old age are known to You, whether committed under duress or by will, whether intentionally or unintentionally, whether openly or in secret, whether without intent or by my hand, whether in thought, action, speech, hearing, sight, touch, taste, or smell. May everything be bypassed and may the prayer for which I was redeemed <note>The text here is slightly garbled in the original manuscript</note> and the sins I committed from the day I was on the earth until this day—whether in this incarnation or in other incarnations <term>Gilgul: The kabbalistic concept of reincarnation</term>—be forgiven. For to You, O Lord, belongs salvation; in You is my hope. My God, please forgive a good person and pardon, for You are a gracious and merciful King.

<margin>
My transgressions number in the thousands, tens of thousands, and myriads. Even if I am full of iniquity and lacking in merit, You are the One who bears iniquity, transgression, and sin, and cleanses.
</margin>

# Please
O Lord, Creator, You created me, raised me, protected me, provided for me, and sustained me until this day. But I, in my evil folly, have acted and angered You with my bad deeds day by day, and my hand has not ceased from sinning. May it be Your will to grant me mercy. O Lord, I acknowledge before You my transgressions, sins, and iniquities. You are full of mercy; I rely on the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in kindness and truth, keeping kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin, and cleansing.

Have mercy on me for the sake of Your great mercies and Your vast kindnesses. Do not remove Your Divine Presence from me and do not hide Your face from me. Bring me out from darkness to light and from bitterness to sweetness. For the sake of Your great kindness, You created repentance before You created Your world, for You knew that the inclination of man's heart is evil from his youth. Therefore, there is none besides You to pardon and forgive, and to spare the struck. Therefore, I, the sinner, who am but flesh, blood, and worms, filth and pollution, offer my supplication and request before You: please forgive my sins, bypass my guilt, and cleanse me of my iniquity. Is this not Your attribute from the day You created Your world—to pardon and forgive those who return to You? Here I am, O Lord, be gracious to me, and not according to the works of my hands shall I return; do not repay me according to my deeds. In Your attribute of goodness and kindness, deal with me. Erase my intentional sins and bypass my transgressions. Cast into the depths of the sea all my sins, like clouds that will never be remembered or visited again. With what shall I come before You, and with what shall I be found pleasing so that I may be atoned for all my sins, iniquities, and transgressions that have passed and gone?
->If through repentance and confession I may be found pleasing<-
Here I am returning and confessing before You, O Lord my God and God of my fathers: I have sinned, I have transgressed, I have acted perversely, and it was not worth it for me.

<margin>
Instruction: While still in health, one should write a will regarding their property... I have done this and that... suddenly on a horse... my heart and my spirit... with all my heart and all my soul... blessed is the one who leaves... and if I have sinned since the day of my birth, I have taken it to my heart to make for myself a heart of flesh and a pure heart... like a convert or a child newly born...
</margin>

# And Now
O Lord my God, after I have returned, I have regretted; and after I was made aware, I struck my thigh; I was ashamed and also humiliated. And if through prayer and supplication we are forgiven, here I am offering my supplication before You—as the eyes of a servant to his master and the eyes of a maid to her mistress, so my eyes are lifted to You, O Lord God. And if through weeping and crying out You forgive, behold, in secret my soul shall weep because of my sins, and in my chambers my spirit shall groan over the multitude of my transgressions. And if through a broken spirit You atone, behold, my heart is broken within me. And now, O Lord my God, Who stretches out a hand in repentance to those who return and assists those who come to be purified, open Your hand to receive me in complete repentance before You. Hear the prayer of Your servant and do not ignore me. May there be before Your Throne of Glory righteous advocates to speak on my behalf and to bring my prayer to Your ears. And if through my many iniquities there is no advocate for me and none to find merit for me, please show me kindness from Your Throne of Glory, just as You tunneled a path for Menasseh <note>A reference to the Midrash that God made a special "tunnel" under the Throne of Glory to accept the repentance of the wicked King Menasseh when the angels tried to block it</note> when he cried out to You from the midst of distress. For we rely on Your promise written in Your Torah: "And from there you shall seek the Lord your God and you shall find Him, if you search for Him with all your heart and all your soul." And the words of Your prophets are written, saying: "Seek the Lord while He may be found, call upon Him while He is near. Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts... for He will abundantly pardon." And it is said: "Who is a God like You, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression for the remnant of His inheritance? He does not retain His anger forever, because He delights in kindness." And it is said: "Say to them: As I live, says the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live; turn, turn from your evil ways; for why will you die, O house of Israel?"

<header>Tractate Pesachim</header>

<margin>Even before his eyes fail and his strength is exhausted, we are all considered as dead; such is the nature of all living things. Nevertheless, when a sin brings about a cause for death, it is as if he were already dead, and his thoughts become heavy. However, in the labor of Torah and good deeds, there is life. This is the hint in the saying: "The righteous, even in their death, are called living" <note>A famous Talmudic aphorism from Tractate Berakhot 18a</note>. Through this, he cleaves to the Living God, for he will have an "eternal foundation" when he is at peace with everything, just as at the moment his soul departs—since he has subdued himself and lives forever with the Lord, which is what is sought.</margin>
"And you shall obey my voice; for the Lord your God is a merciful God; He will not fail you, nor destroy you, nor forget the covenant of your fathers which He swore to them." "The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord; He is their strength in time of trouble." "He shall not be afraid of evil tidings; his heart is firm, trusting in the Lord." "The sun shall no longer be your light by day, nor for brightness shall the moon give light to you; but the Lord will be to you an everlasting light, and your God your glory."
"You shall winnow them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the tempest shall scatter them; and you shall rejoice in the Lord, and shall glory in the Holy One of Israel."
"Then you shall delight yourself in the Lord, and I will cause you to ride on the high places of the earth, and feed you with the heritage of Jacob your father; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken." "Delight yourself also in the Lord, and He shall give you the desires of your heart."

# Prayer

**Master** of the Universe, in Your hand is power and might to make great and to strengthen, and to humble man even unto the crushing of the soul <note>original: "דביכוחה של נפש"</note>, and nothing is hidden from You. In Your hand is the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh; therefore, may it be Your will to grant strength and fortitude before this illness, to heal it, to strengthen it, to restore it, and to revive it according to Your will and my will. May his merits come before You, and cast all his sins and transgressions into the depths of the sea. May Your mercy suppress Your anger, even if perhaps a decree was made to remove him from the world at this time; for You are righteous and Your judgments are upright, and one must not question Your mercy. However, let him not be gathered by "evil judgments" and the multitude of human transgressions. May no cruel messenger <note>original: "חמאל אכזרי," likely a reference to a destroying angel</note> be sent against him with chariots of pain. May illnesses depart from him, and all the evil spirits that emerge from the "branches of his soul" <note>original: "מסנסי נפשו"</note>. Let his death be like that of all men among Your righteous servants, like "drawing a hair out of milk" <note>An idiom for a painless, peaceful death</note>. May his soul be gathered unto You, and may angels of peace come out to meet him and lead him to rest in the shadow of Your wings, Selah, Amen. Thus far I have found <note>indicating the scribe is copying from another source</note>.

<margin>And there in the matter of the end... [illegible]... it is better to inherit.</margin>
**I found** in the book *Ta'amei Mitzvot* <note>Reasons for the Commandments</note> by the Rabbi, Rabbi Menachem of Babylonia <note>A 16th-century Italian kabbalist</note>, section 4, where he spoke at length regarding the punishment for one who emits seed in vain. He wrote that the fool who wastes it in his hair <note>unclear metaphor</note>... there the forces of impurity are found, and from there evil spirits are created. After his death, they do not depart from him but accompany him, for they are his "children" (and there is no greater pain than this), may the Merciful One save us. Therefore, the ten "intelligences" <note>likely referring to the Ten Psalms of the Tikun HaKlali or a similar spiritual remedy</note> should be rectified day by day to emerge from the pit. Thus far are his words.

And happy is every one who fears sin, who is wise and prepares for his end. He should review his deeds and actions, for all His ways are justice; a God of faithfulness and without iniquity, righteous and upright is He. Righteous and upright is He to His creatures, pure and unique in His action. Who can say to Him, "What are You doing?" He fashions his face and the work of his hands... everything He has made for His sake. For He brings down to the grave and brings up; the Rock is righteous, and the Creator of every deed, and acts with kindness in all He does. Therefore, in all His desire, who can say to Him "What are You doing?" The Rock is righteous and upright, there is no iniquity in His ways, for He is called "Kind" and "Pious." His work is pure and His paths are righteous, even when hidden from His face... mercy yearns for him, for we are all the work of His hands. The Rock, the soul of every living thing is in Your hand; our days are full. Have mercy on the remnant of the sheep of Your hands, and say to the Angel: "Stay your hand!" <note>A plea to stop the Angel of Death</note>. O Rock, have pity from the heavens; act in Your kindness... Look now at the fewness of the nations, for You are full of mercy, and give comfort to the mourners. O Rock, this is the way of all the world; gather and perform kindness, all of you. For nothing is hidden, and my soul is for eternal life. The Rock.

**In the chapter** "The Weaver" <note>Tractate Shabbat, chapter 13</note>, it is taught: Rabbi Shimon ben Eleazar says, "He who stands over the deceased at the moment the soul departs is obligated to rend his garment. To what is this comparable? To a Torah scroll that has been burned." <note>This highlights the infinite value of a human life</note>. Behold, man is like the Tablets of the Covenant: five fingers against five, just so. The human body is like the Tablets, and the letters are the souls. When they fly away, the Tablets are broken. And just as the Tablets were placed in the Ark, so too is man placed in a casket <note>The Hebrew word "Aron" means both the Ark of the Covenant and a coffin</note>.

## The Commandment of Escorting the Dead, Weeping over a Worthy Person, and the Great Obligation of Eulogizing a Torah Scholar

All these things are well known and famous. So too is the comforting of mourners.
**Acts of Loving-kindness** such as welcoming guests will protect you. "Let your house be open wide," etc. In Tractate Shabbat, the chapter "One may clear away" <note>Chapter 18</note>, Rabbi Yochanan said: "Great is hospitality, even more than rising early for the House of Study." Rav Dimi of Nehardea said: "Even more than rising early for the House of Study." Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: "Hospitality is greater than receiving the Divine Presence," as it is written: "And [Abraham] said, My Lord, if I have found favor in Your sight..." <note>Genesis 18:3; Abraham asked God to wait while he tended to travelers</note>. When guests come to one's house, he should receive them with a pleasant countenance and immediately set bread before them to eat, for perhaps the poor person is hungry and is ashamed to ask. Therefore, one must give him bread and warm food and show him a shining face. Even if he only has a small thing, let him eat bread in front of them and warm their hearts in public. In this way, he will be a "restorer of the soul." He should not tell them his troubles, for he will break their spirit if they think that by their coming, he is saying "we barely have peace in the city" during the meal. He should show himself as pained that he cannot provide more, as it is said: "And if you draw out your soul to the hungry"—meaning, "it grieves my soul that I have no more to give you." One should know how much the guest wants to eat, for perhaps he was accustomed to delicacies; if he is of "good breeding" <note>original: "בן טובים"</note>, one should provide a worthy lodging. How great is the beauty of kindness! And if the guests stay overnight, he should have them sleep in the best of his beds as is fitting for them, for rest is a great thing... it gives him more satisfaction than the one who feeds and waters him. He should provide them with a "loaf of bread for the journey," for "because of a piece of bread a man will transgress" <note>Proverbs 28:21</note>—this refers to the one who did not provide it. We see the gravity of this from the fact that because of a loaf of bread [not given], the matter unfolded until the priests of Nob were killed <note>A reference to 1 Samuel 21-22, where a lack of hospitality led to a massacre</note>. One who does not escort a guest and does not give him provisions for the way is as if he spills...

May it be Your will, O Lord my God and God of my fathers, that You receive my soul with joy when You take it from me. On the day of my passing before You, please find my journey acceptable. Send the angels of mercy to come out toward me, and may they say with one voice: "Enter in peace," as I enter the Garden of Eden. There may my dwelling place be, and let me delight in the radiance of Your light. There shall be the glory of my rest, and let the hidden light <note>Original: "Or Ganuz"; the primordial light of creation reserved for the righteous</note> before You be my shelter and my canopy. Place my station under the shadow of Your wings. Hear my supplication, hasten my salvation; do not turn Your ear from my relief and my cry, for You are the God of my salvation in whom I have trusted. May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before You, O Lord <note>original: "YEHUD"; a mystical variant of the Tetragrammaton</note>, my Rock and my Redeemer.

**Pi-Yehudiv** <note>A mystical term or title</note>: How good it is for a man to enter the world that is entirely good <note>the Afterlife</note> when he accepts the suffering of death with joy and love for the sake of His Name, as mentioned in the Zohar. Therefore, he should justify the Divine Decree upon himself, saying: "The Lord is righteous and upright," etc. Then his heart will burn with the joy of accepting death with a good heart, saying: "To You, O Lord, I lift up my soul." He should meditate on the word "Asha" (I lift), which consists of the letters <gloss>God</gloss> with <gloss>the People</gloss> <note>a mystical letter-substitution</note>, which hints at the 42-Letter Name. Through this name, his soul is extracted from the "shells" <term>Kelipot: spiritual husks or forces of impurity</term> that cling to it. He should consider the soul as the part of God which He gave, as I will explain later.

<margin>For my support and my stay.</margin>
According to a hidden treasure of a great Kabbalist, it is written: <gloss>And from the wise man</gloss>, the strong and exalted Rabbi Joshua, known as Shalish, I heard what he received from his teacher: that when a man’s soul is being taken out, the Accuser <note>The Satan</note> leans on his right and his left and says to him, "Deny the God of Israel!" But the soul finds grace. If he should come to a point of admission, what is the remedy to turn the Accuser away? He should meditate on the letters Y, K, G.

<margin>The essence of the day: if he is not in his right mind at that time, they should say and inform him through others, or have his son or his friend read it before him; they should read his studies, and this will be good for him.</margin>
<margin>The signature of these names is found, for example, at the end of the verse: "For the Lord God is a sun and shield" (Psalm 84:12), the letters L, H, A, V, V. These are the 65 Great Names mentioned in the *Makhtesh*. See the "Gate of Prayer" by the Arizal <note>Rabbi Isaac Luria, the foremost kabbalist of the 16th century</note>.</margin>
<insert>Tzamerkhad</insert> <note>A mystical name derived from the final letters of the first verses of Genesis</note>. This name emerges from the end of the verses of the first portion of Genesis until "One Day." Its numerical value equals "Rashaon." And the name "The Lord God," etc., is L, H, A, V, V, which are the 65 Great Names mentioned in the *Makhtesh*. See the "Gate of Prayer" by the Arizal.
<margin>And you shall visualize in your soul the name of his soul and lead it without any trembling or fear. Behold the name "My Name is Blessed." With heart-felt intention, when saying "The Lord is God," he should intend that the Attribute of Justice and the Attribute of Mercy are unified. The name "Yedid" <note>Friend/Beloved</note> equals 26 <note>the value of the Tetragrammaton</note>, and the soul is L, P, H, etc. Then the first letters equal 26, the value of the name of the Lord, and the second letters equal 86, the value of *Elohim* (God/Justice). Thus, the unification is found: "Blessed be He." The name of the Lord in its full spelling <note>Gematria/Miluy</note> equals 45, and what is written in Your Name is 86, like *Elohim*. "The Lord, the Lord is God." He should meditate on the writing of the Name for six years <note>meaning: throughout his life's stages</note>, letters corresponding to the six wings of the Seraphim... and the word "He" (Hu) includes everything. Especially the unification of "I am that I am" (Exodus 3:14). The general rule of these are the 42-Letter Names explained in the book *Pardes* at the end of the third chapter of the "Gate of Names." The 42-Letter Name has six branches that subdue the power of the Satan so as not to burn the two wings... and one should remember this at night before sleeping, and so too a person near his passing. For these wings—with two he covers, etc., and with two he flies. The soul flies upward and can be saved from the angels of destruction and all damaging forces and the Accuser, so they do not agitate the scholars of the Talmud. And the Kabbalist of Metatron <note>the highest angel</note> hides the glory of Rabbi Moshe above. For these names are included with him at the time of his passing. When the soul leaves the body, they should say "Ana BeKoach," etc., until "Receive the song of Your people, strengthen us, purify us, O Awesome One." Intend this at the time the soul leaves <gloss>*</gloss>. As long as the soul has not yet departed, they should repeat these names and the unifications. I found a hint in the verse <gloss>*</gloss> "And you <gloss>*</gloss> who cling <gloss>*</gloss> to the Lord your God <gloss>*</gloss> are all alive <gloss>*</gloss> today." The initials of "You who cling to the Lord" equal 42. And when saying "Into Your hand I commit my spirit," intend the acronym "Be'er" (Well), which is the secret of the "Well of Living Waters" above. For these combined names equal "Be'er," namely: *Ehyeh*, *Yehovah*, *Adonai*. Finally, <gloss>*</gloss> "You have redeemed <gloss>*</gloss> me, <gloss>*</gloss> O Lord," the initials are P, A, Y, which is one of the names of the 72-Letter Name and equals "Yehudiah."</margin>

# **Chapter**
Torah is Light. The holiday of Passover is the pillar of Kindness <term>Chesed: the divine attribute of benevolence</term>. "The worm of Jacob" <note>a reference to the Jewish people</note> according to the tradition of the Sages. Passover corresponds to the days of ascent, which are entirely kindness and mercy, returning from the "Upper Sin," the source of mercy. Therefore, no Accuser <note>Satan</note> can strike then, as is explicitly stated. Matzah hints at the "First Light," of which it was said, "Let there be light." Therefore, eating Matzah on the first night is an obligation, and from then on it is optional, provided one does not eat leaven (*Chametz*). It is written, "The world is built on kindness," for the Blessed Name created the world with His kindness, as it is written, "The kindness of the Lord fills the earth." The Blessed Name did not need the world; He only created it so that there would be creatures to receive His goodness, or so they could prepare themselves for good, or that it might be good for them forever. In the Tractate of Rosh Hashanah, Rabbi Eliezer says: In Tishrei the world was created; and Rabbi Yehoshua says: In Nisan the world was created. The words of both are true. In Tishrei the world was created and renewed out of nothing (*ex nihilo*), but this was not known or publicized to the masses, and the [nations] deny it, saying the world follows its natural course from eternity. However, in Nisan, the signs and wonders that Moses performed in Egypt revealed to our Teacher [Moses] the shattering of the natural order and the renewal of creation. This happened when the zodiac was at its most choice point: Aries <note>the Ram</note>, which is the first of all the signs and represents honor. And the whole world saw that He is the God of gods and Lord of lords who created "something from nothing." Therefore, it is in His power to destroy them, uproot them, or build everything according to His will, blessed be He. Thus, the renewal of the world that occurred in Tishrei became known and publicized to the servants of the Lord, to the whole House of Israel, etc. "Observe" and "Remember" are the duties mentioned: for by "Remembering" <note>Zakhor</note> the Sabbath day, the Creation is remembered—"for in six days the Lord made," etc. And by "Observing" <note>Shamur</note> the Sabbath day, the Exodus from Egypt is remembered—"and remember that you were a slave in Egypt," etc. These two concepts unify together. They found a hint that "Remember" and "Observe" were spoken in a single utterance. Likewise, it is written "Observe the month of Spring" <note>Passover</note>. This is the matter of the Names of the Torah... for we see the end in the beginning and the beginning in the end. Behold, all the signs and wonders that Moses did, etc., and "In the beginning God created," etc. The signs and wonders are the renewal of the creation of "In the beginning." For this reason, it is called "Pesach" (Passover), because [God] "skipped over" and hovered. Incidentally, I will explain the counting of the Omer: "And you shall count for yourselves from the day after the Sabbath, from the day you brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven complete Sabbaths shall there be. Until the day after the seventh Sabbath, you shall count fifty days" (Leviticus 23). Behold, the interpretation of "the day after the Sabbath" refers to the day after the first festival day [of Passover], as is known from the translation and from Rashi. "Seven Sabbaths" means weeks. Why does the Torah call the festival "Sabbath"? To equate it to the week of seven. Also, regarding "count fifty days"—is it not actually 49 days? The fiftieth day is the aspect of the "Face of the Sabbath," which chooses and publicizes the renewal of the world, for "the Lord made the six days of work and on the seventh day He rested." Thus, the days of Passover and the [Omer] days are like the seven days of Creation. This is the meaning of the counting. Rabba said: It is a commandment to count the days and a commandment to count the weeks. Maimonides <note>Rambam</note> already wrote in the section on Genesis that the days of Creation hint at the days of the world's existence: for a thousand years [is as a day], and thus the world exists for six thousand years and one is destroyed—meaning it rests, just like the Sabbath.

<margin>In the tractate Bava Metzia, the chapter "One who hires workers"</margin>
**A**nd there is a great reward for one who serves guests by himself, just as we find with Abraham regarding what he did for the angels, even though they appeared to him as desert-dwellers. As the translation says, Rav Judah said in the name of Rav: Everything that Abraham did for the ministering angels himself, the Holy One, Blessed be He, did for Abraham's children Himself; and everything he did for them through a messenger, the Holy One, Blessed be He, did for his children through a messenger. "And Abraham ran to the herd" <note>Genesis 18:7</note>—and "a wind went forth from the Lord" <note>Numbers 11:31</note>. "And he took butter and milk" <note>Genesis 18:8</note>—and "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you" <note>Exodus 16:4</note>.
