### Rich Matzah
<margin>As we say in Tractate Chagigah, and so too the Generation of the Flood etc. Freedom etc.</margin>
...concerning the week, as it is said: "As for me, I will behold Your face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with Your likeness" <note>Psalm 17:15</note>. "I shall be satisfied when I awake" is a higher level than "beholding Your face," and this is simple to understand. 

The "Wicked" <note>The Wicked Son from the Haggadah.</note> represents the ten generations that were not refined and were argumentative even in the days of [darkness]. He says "What" <note>original: *Mah*</note>, as in "What is this service to you?" because he is arrogant. The "Wicked One" is the questioner who thinks only of his own pleasure and not the service of the Name [of God]. He says, "What is it to us that we should serve Him?" Similarly, the Generation of the Flood said to God, "Depart from us" <note>Job 21:14</note>; their success was purely material. As it says, "They send forth their little ones like a flock" <note>Job 21:11</note>. So too the Generation of the Division <note>The builders of the Tower of Babel</note>; for all of them, their pleasure was everything. The matter of "to them and not to him" <note>The Haggadah's response to the Wicked Son</note> follows the simple meaning: "If I am not for myself, who will be for me?" <note>Pirkei Avot 1:14</note>. Everything a person does only for the moment, he does not do for his true self, but "leaves his wealth to others" and his body perishes. But when I act for my [eternal] self, how very important I am!

Now, the questioner is liable for the "accidental damages," which are the Plagues of Pharaoh. For "The Lord hardened his spirit." Therefore, these wicked ones remained in Egypt and died during the "Days of Darkness" <note>The three days of the plague of darkness</note> and were attached to Pharaoh. This is why it concludes: [If he had been there] he would not have been redeemed, but would have remained with Pharaoh in his domain, which is the domain of darkness.

The "Explanation" in the portion of *Toldot*: One who does not know how to deceive is called "Simple" <note>original: *Tam* — also translated as "pure" or "innocent."</note>. Jacob was called *Tam*, reflecting the beauty of Adam. So too was the first Adam on a weekday before he ate from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, which is the mechanism of knowing how to deceive. They deceived him through the secret of "A wandering Aramean was my father" <note>Deuteronomy 26:5</note>, which refers to the "Cunning Serpent." This continued until he crushed the "Simple" (*Tam*) into "Dead" (*Met*) <note>A Hebrew wordplay where the letters of *Tam* (תם) are rearranged or altered to *Met* (מת)</note>, and added the letter *He* of the "Life of the Worlds." 

Behold, the "Simple Son" is a "paid guardian" who walks in simplicity. Just as I [God] am with you, so you should be with Me in exchange for my service; he is a paid guardian. So too, Jacob was a "Simple Man" (*Ish Tam*) while he was with Laban. The status of Adam as a "paid guardian" was because he was meant "to work it and to guard it" <note>Genesis 2:15</note>. Regarding the verse "I will greatly multiply..." <note>Genesis 3:16</note>, the letter *He* is missing, proof that it was added when the Serpent said, "Your eyes will be opened and you will be like gods." The Simple Son asks, "What is this?" and the answer is given: the One who acts remains as He is. For his whole aim is to be "in exchange for his toil." Even if he is fearful afterwards, the "strengthening of the Exodus" from the plagues and the joy is mandatory. Afterwards, it becomes his duty to serve Him even if He does not provide abundance at this moment. As I explained the verse: "I am the Lord... on the condition that you accept My yoke." In the book *Duties of the Heart*, it says that at the end, a person may lack the good things he attains through God so that he can truly fulfill his service.

"The one who does not know how to ask" refers to one who, although he was needed in his generation, was like those in the generation of Abraham our Father, etc. For there was no need to prohibit him... the "outcry of Sodom" etc. He began to ask questions and requests. But regarding "And God said to Noah, the end of all flesh has come," Noah did not ask for anything! This [failure to ask] exempted his generation on the condition that he would remain "Noah" <note>The name Noah shares a root with "rest" or "comfort."</note>, meaning there would be a remnant for the preservation of the world so the world would not be entirely lost, and they would later be fruitful and multiply. This is why Noah is called a "Man of the Earth," meaning for the sake of the Earth. See what I have written in the Torah regarding the "Wickedness of Noah" at length. Behold, Noah was a "Righteous Man" yet also a "Man of the Earth." Nevertheless, he needed to be "Simple" (*Tam*). 

And it says: "You open [the conversation] for him"—give him the beginning. This is like the explanation of the verse "You have begun [to show Your servant]" <note>Deuteronomy 3:24</note>. This is achieved through the sacrifices. "Who gave Me something beforehand that I should repay him?" <note>Job 41:3</note>. Who made a <term>Mezuzah<note>A scroll placed on doorposts.</note></term> before I gave him a house? Who made <term>Tzitzit<note>Fringes on a four-cornered garment.</note></term> before I gave him a cloak? Through this, Moses merited the giving of the Torah. As it says, "On that day you shall tell him," interpreting the verse "And he said on that day, is it not because my God is not in my midst?" <note>Deuteronomy 31:17</note>. I explained in another discourse that this refers to an awakening specifically on the Sabbath day when troubles depart, and not before. 

Thus, there are "Four Sons" <note>original: *Kanim* — literally "stalks" or "types."</note> in the statutes of the Passover. And "The Lord" <note>represented by the letter *He*</note> is against these, as in "All the commandment which I command you," that He should have mercy on the commandments. Rather, the commandments and Abraham our Father—who is the Wise One, the Mighty One, and the True Guardian, as it says, "Who will keep my charge (*mishmarti*)"—specifically "my charge," which is the "Guarded Matzah" (*Matzah Shmurah*) in the secret of "And they baked the dough... for it was a night of guarding." The night was "divided" for him, as explained on the verse "And he divided the night against them." 

On the day the Lord made a covenant with him, he was given the good news of the Egyptian exile. It was "good news," as our Sages said. And it is written in Egypt using the suffix of the name of God (*Yah*)—"In the land of Egypt" (*Mitzrayim*). I have already explained that "servants of Pharaoh" refers to the "Hebrew Husk" (*Klipah*) that seeks to be arrogant and rebellious. Therefore, Abraham is the <term>Chariot<note>original: *Merkavah* — In Kabbalah, the Patriarchs are the "wheels" or "vessels" for Divine manifestation.</note></term>, as our Sages of blessed memory said: "The Patriarchs are the Chariot." This is represented by the letter *Chet* (ח), which is the opposite of Gehenna. I have elaborated elsewhere on the verse "Is it not true that if you do well, there is uplifting?" meaning: the living Chariot and the bearing of the Throne. "But if you do not do well, sin crouches at the door"—this is the "cutting off," the opposite of the Garden of Eden. 

This is the explanation of the Midrash Rabbah on the portion of *Lech Lecha*: "Behold, a smoking furnace and a flaming torch." Shimon bar Abba in the name of Rabbi [Yochanan] said: Four things were shown to him—Gehenna, the Kingdoms, [the Torah, and the Sacrifices]. He said to him: "As long as your children are busy with two of these, they are saved from the other two." Some explain: through two they are judged. God said: "What do you prefer? That your children descend into Gehenna or into the Kingdoms?" 
<margin>Rabbi Chanina bar Papa said: Abraham chose the Kingdoms for them.</margin>
And Rabbi Chama bar Chanina said: Abraham chose the Kingdoms, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, chose the Kingdoms for him. For it would have been [impossible] "unless their Rock had sold them and the Lord had delivered them" <note>Deuteronomy 32:30</note>. And they were sold to you so that the Lord might turn the "wise" into fools. 

<margin>See the book *Yafé To'ar* at length; it seems that even the "Kingdoms" will be in the strongest possible sense.</margin>
This is the "Four" mentioned. Rabbi Chanina said... and see the book *Yafé To'ar* at length. It seems that Rabbi Yuda also agrees with Rabbi Chanina, for the matter of Gehenna has two faces. One is for evil—to cover their dust and make them into dust. Concerning this, "two youths" came to choose the subjugation of the Kingdoms. The "Service of God" is a Gehenna that is for good, meaning it refines the "Husk" and the "Filth." As it is written: "In a script, their writing is as their heat." 

The Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note> said: the intention is that freedom comes, as in the portion of *Shemot*: "And it came to pass in those many days, that the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel sighed from the labor." Nachmanides already asked: why does it say "In those *many* days"? I found in the *Sefer HaGerushin* composed by the divine Rabbi Moshe Cordovero, of blessed memory, that Egypt's "Ministering Angel" was diminished from his greatness and became the Prince of Gehenna. In my eyes, the reason is that when the Holy One, Blessed be He, brought down the Prince of Egypt...

## The Rich Forehead
<note>Hebrew: *Mitzach Ashirah*.</note>

The Accuser stands constantly before the Holy One, blessed be He, in order to mislead and [bring] guilt upon humanity, and to invoke judgment upon them. But once a person steps forward and specifies his sins, one by one, that Accuser finds no opening for his mouth, and he cannot claim judgment against him. For the person has already sought judgment first, and then spoke. The Accuser might say, "So-and-so did such and such," but the person has already preceded him by detailing his sins. Since the Accuser sees that he has no opening for his mouth above, he then departs from him entirely. This is if he repents properly; if not, the Accuser becomes a creditor because the person is found to be a habitual sinner before the Holy One, blessed be He. Until here are the words [of the holy Zohar].

It is clear from this statement that the words of the story <note>The telling of the Exodus on Passover.</note> make an impression above and awaken the power of redemption, just as there. The Holy One, blessed be He, rejoices in that story, and it causes the awakening of redemption, similar to the secret of "brokenness in supplication for the sake of the High One" which was explained at length in its place. Then silence and peace are achieved above, strengthening the stronghold of peace. And thus, peace on all sides. The verse says: "Let them give thanks to the Lord for His kindness, and for His wonders to the children of men" <note>Psalm 107:8</note>. And the verse will be: "Salvation belongs to the Lord; Your blessing be upon Your people. Selah" <note>Psalm 3:9</note>.

The intention is that our salvation belongs to the Lord, so to speak—to Him is the salvation in the secret of the <term>Shekhinah<note>The Divine Presence, often described as being in "exile" with the Jewish people.</note></term> in exile. Thus, the elevation of salvation reaches Him above all. And "Your blessing be upon Your people, Selah"—we, His people, need to bless Him as if it were only for our sake, even though in truth, His need is our need.

And the Sages said: "Let them give thanks to the Lord for His kindness"—even though it is the kindness of the Holy One, blessed be He, meaning the kindness reaches Him, nevertheless, "His wonders are for the children of men," to live and to praise. Furthermore, it can be explained according to the Zohar mentioned above: when we praise the Name for the kindness He performed, it triggers an awakening for more abundance to flow. Therefore, it begins in the singular, "His kindness" (*hasdo*), and ends in the plural, "and His wonders" (*nifla'otav*). For when one sings over the kindness already done, it causes a further awakening of influence to add to the first; this is "and His wonders."

> <gloss>Until here... [A brief scribe's or printer's note regarding the placement of the text and references to other sections].</gloss>

The summary of the matter is that through the telling of His wonders, a cleaving is created between Him, may He be blessed, and us. The darkness and the cloud that intervene and separate Him from us are removed. In the true elevation, He will be elevated for us as God, and we will be for Him a people. And as on that day, He will be our God...

# Tractate Pesachim

## Guarded Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Shmurah*. This refers to the special matzah guarded from moisture from the time of harvest.</note>

It is missing the height <note>The author uses a mystical shorthand here, likely referring to the numerical value or the physical "height" of the letters</note> on the letters D-D <note>Dalet-Dalet</note> just as our Sages of blessed memory said, "whether it is *mahiya* or *tamehiya*," for David is his name, therefore it is written "missing" <note>A reference to "defective" spelling in the Torah where letters are omitted</note>. However, the reading is in its "fullness," its height alluding to the secret of the Fullness <note>The *Miluy*, a Kabbalistic method of expanding letters into names</note>. And that which is called "Peace Offerings" <note>Hebrew: *Shelamim*</note>, its height alludes to it being clarified within the secret of the name Y-H-V-H. This is the secret of the "broken Yod" of the word "Peace" <note>Numbers 25:12, where the letter *Vav* in *Shalom* is traditionally written with a crack</note>, and it is alluded to in the case of Phinehas, who is Elijah. These offerings are called "Peace Offerings," for "He shall be" <note>Hebrew: *Yihyeh*</note> in the end of days; therefore, "This is the law of the peace offerings" is written last. And in the middle, the letters Y-H Y-H for God interrupt the "Sacrifice of Aaron." For at the time when the Holy Temple stood, there was peace in the world through the sacrifice of Aaron; the covenant of life and peace was with him. This connects the Y-H to the Y-H so that it somewhat resembles the nature of the redemption—and in the future, it will be the essence of it, and not just a portion. However, in the portion of *Vayikra* <note>Leviticus</note>, the "Peace Offerings" are completed in their whiteness, as you have seen above in the words of the Zohar regarding the matter of *Vayikra*: "from within the darkness comes light," meaning the advantage of light over darkness. This is the matter of the "Sin Offering" and the "Guilt Offering" which exist in the secret of the exile of the letters Y-H; it is written "Holy," for the darkness will turn into a great light. This is not the case with the letters Y-H in their sanctity, which remain constant, but the letters V-H <note>The latter half of the Divine Name</note> will turn into the "Holy of Holies," for out of darkness comes light, and out of the bitterness of the lettuce <note>the *Maror*</note> [comes sweetness]. Therefore, the "Peace Offering" is the center, in the middle, to remember that out of distress comes relief. Regarding the destruction of the Temple, it is written "all hearts are faint" <note>Hebrew: *Davay*</note>, the secret of *Davay* is that it is not "Peaceful" <note>Shalamim</note>. Its fullness is at the thresholds, and one who examines it will find that the first *He* is within the bending, and the last Y-H is within the Dalet, in the secret of the generation, until the changing of the first letters—the *Vav* and the last *Vav*. This is the "Fullness," meaning male and male, like the *Sekkusi* and *Tziriti* <note>unclear grammatical or mystical terms</note>, everything is full. And this is its form, and it is overturned, meaning "your doors shall be changed," so that the last *Aleph* will turn into a *Lamed* in the secret of "His spirit," concerning which it is written...

## Rich Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Ashirah*. Matzah made with juice or oil instead of water, often discussed regarding its suitability for the Seder.</note>

"And anyone who tells [the story of the Exodus] all that night is praiseworthy." This refers to the Zohar in Parashat Bo: "This commandment follows that one: to tell the praise of the Exodus from Egypt, which is an obligation upon a person to speak of this praise forever." We have established that every person who tells of the Exodus from Egypt and rejoices in that story with joy is destined to rejoice with the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah: the indwelling presence of God</term> in the World to Come, which is the greatest joy of all. This is a person who rejoices in his Master, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, rejoices in that story. At that hour, the Holy One, Blessed be He, gathers all His heavenly entourage and says to them: "Go and hear the story of My praise which My children are telling, rejoicing in My redemption!" They all gather and come and give thanks to the Holy One, Blessed be He, for all those laws and mighty deeds, and they acknowledge the holy nation He has on earth, who rejoice in the joy of their Master's redemption. Then, strength and might are increased above. Through that story, Israel gives strength to their Master, like a king whose strength and might are increased when his subjects praise his power and give him thanks; then all fear him and his glory is exalted above all. Therefore, one must praise and tell this story in this manner. It is an obligation for a person to speak constantly before the Holy One, Blessed be He, regarding all those miracles He performed.

And if you should ask: "Why is it an obligation? Does not the Holy One, Blessed be He, know everything—all that was and all that will be? Why publicize this before Him when He already knows?" Indeed, it is certainly necessary for a person to publicize it and speak before Him of all that He has done. This is because those words ascend, and all the heavenly entourage gathers and sees them, and they all give thanks to the Holy One, Blessed be He, and His glory is exalted over them above and below. In the time when they speak and specify their sins for all that they have passed through—if you should ask why this is necessary:

->Incense<-
<note>Hebrew: *Miktara*. Likely referring to the burning of sacrifices or a transition in the homily.</note>

Their iniquities [are specified now], but in the future, they will give thanks and praise. The order of the service is based on resolution and repentance, so that all sin—which comes from the "thought of sin"—should cease. The thought leads to the deed; this is why the "Olah" <term>Burnt Offering</term> comes before the "Chatat" <term>Sin Offering</term>, for the Burnt Offering comes to atone for the thoughts of the heart, as our Sages explained. In this way, the secret of "turning from evil" is fulfilled, and afterward "shining" away the evil. "Peace" is "doing good" through the cleaving that will occur in the future. "When a soul brings a 'Minchah' <term>Meal Offering</term>," it will be like the matter of the meal offering during the time of Elijah, for Elijah the Prophet will come and herald the redemption. Then there will be "Peace Offerings" <note>Shalamim</note>—the peace that will burst forth from the upper realm, and "Halleluyah" will be fulfilled. As it is said: "Let every soul praise God, Halleluyah, Amen!"

### Rich Matzah: Second Homily

| Matzah | Shall be eaten in a holy place | "It shall be eaten" is redundant, for it is written at the beginning of the verse: "And that which is left of the meal offering... they shall eat." And in Tractate Yebamot page 80, it brings: |

We have learned: Rabban Gamliel used to say: Anyone who has not said these three things on Passover has not fulfilled his obligation, and these are: The Passover Offering, Matzah, and Maror... One must ask: How are these commandments different from all other commandments in the Torah, that he felt the need to state the reason for these specific three? And why is there an "uttering" over them? The pattern is that there are "Three Crowns": the Crown of Torah, the Crown of Priesthood, and the Crown of Kingship—and the "Crown of a Good Name" rises above them all. As we shall explain, these three symbols correspond to these three crowns, and their essence is in the Crown of a Good Name, meaning the Name that teaches Goodness. It is written "grace and clay" <note>unclear wordplay on *chen* and *chomer*</note> as we explain regarding the "Eternal Offering" slaughtered by the groups, one after another. The "Good Name" appears to me to refer to that which teaches of goodness and kindness, rising above etc. "Pasach" <note>Passed over</note> means He pitied and had compassion. "Matzah" refers to the three matzot of the Seder order, corresponding to the breads of the Thanksgiving offering, as stated in the *Tur* <note>The code of Jewish law</note> at the end of section 475, regarding the "Good Name." This refers to the "Guarded Matzah" <note>Matzah Shmurah</note> which teaches of true freedom from the "circle"—meaning the shells <note>impure spiritual forces</note> and their portions in judgment and love. And the third is "Maror," the bitterness of the commandment from the best... a "Good Name," for it is called *Chassa* <note>Aramaic for lettuce and "mercy"</note>, for the Merciful One had mercy on us and redeemed us. Thus there are three upon three, and the Good Name is above them. An example for this statement is that two crowns are drawn from the three... as it is said regarding the "pious ones," that the Crown of a Good Name is above them. "Three good gifts I gave to this nation through the hands of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam." Moses is called "Sun," for it is written "And she saw him, that he was good," and our Sages said his name was "Tov" (Good). Concerning their weeping, as it is found in Tractate Ta'anit chapter 1: It is taught that Rabbi Yosei the son of Rabbi Yehuda says: "Three good sustainers stood up for Israel, and they are: Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. And three good gifts were given through them: the Well, the Cloud, and the Manna." The Well...

# Tractate Pesachim

### Rich Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Ashirah*. This refers to matzah made with liquids other than water, such as fruit juice or eggs, which is generally richer but not valid for the primary obligation at the Seder according to many authorities.</note>

<margin>Matzah</margin>
And corresponding to these: based on three, they are these three commandments: Passover, Matzah, and Bitter Herbs (*Maror*). Matzah corresponds to the Exodus from Egypt, and to the three gifts: the Manna, the Well, and the Clouds. The one that includes them all is the Manna, which came in the merit of Moses. That which rises above them all at our will is found to be purely spiritual, corresponding to the spirituality of the Cloud and the Well. As for the Bitter Herbs, it was in his <note>Aaron's</note> merit, of blessed memory. Rashi brought their words: the "cakes of matzot" <note>Exodus 12:39</note> that Israel brought out of Egypt were with them, and the three matzot symbolize the three aforementioned gifts. Through this, the difficulties I raised at the beginning of the chapter "The Workers" (which I transcribed above) are answered. Our Sages of blessed memory said: "Cakes of Matzot," for it was Passover, and these three are included in Matzah. The taste of the Manna was like this, but while Rabbi Jose said they were in the merit of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, the matter is that in the merit of these three, they were sustained in the wilderness for forty years. These were only a likeness of those three at the time of the Exodus from Egypt, before those three actually began. While Israel were still like guests, the example of these three was in the merit of Abraham as a reward for how he honored his guests. This is the model before the Manna descended; the taste of the Manna was like the "cakes of matzot" they brought out of Egypt. And before the Cloud was revealed—as it is said, "The Lord went before them... in a pillar of cloud"—it was already revealed in Egypt, in the likeness of the Cloud. This is what is written, "I carried you on eagles' wings," which Rashi explains as the day Israel came to Raamses. This is in the manner of what is written in the Book of Daniel: "And behold, with the clouds of heaven," which is the likeness of the Cloud before the pillar of cloud was revealed. The likeness of the Well existed before the revelation of Miriam’s Well, as it is written in the portion of *Beshalach*: "And the waters became sweet." This is similar to the Well that was inherited from the streams, an allusion to my heart <note>The author uses "my heart" likely as a personal insight or a common mystical trope</note>, "and the waters became sweet there." And as it is written there regarding the thirsty, "and the community had no water," we learn from this verse that the Well was in the merit of Miriam. Importance has already been given there to a "verbal analogy" <term>Gezera Shava: A method of Talmudic interpretation linking two laws based on identical words</term> using the word "there" (*Sham*), similar to the law of the "Beheaded Heifer." Just as our Sages interpreted it, I also say this verbal analogy of "there" alludes to this. Thus, we have the likeness of the three gifts given through the three Shepherds in the wilderness; their likeness was with Israel at the time of their departure from Egypt. This likeness was in the merit of Abraham who honored guests, for Israel in that city were like guests to the Holy One, blessed be He. Then Abraham was revealed, as Rabbi Cordovero wrote in the *Book of Expulsions*:

"It is written: 'As in the days of your coming out of the land of Egypt, I will show him [wonders].' My teacher asked: it should have said 'I will show you,' just as it says 'your coming out.' He answered: This is the meaning of 'And He brought you out in His presence,' which means 'Like His presence'—this refers to Abraham our ancestor. Since he exited the exile in the 'Vision Between the Pieces,' it was necessary to show him the final redemption. This is the meaning of 'in his presence'—in the presence of Abraham. Similarly, since the revealed redemption should be described as such, the verse says 'I will show him'—meaning I will show Abraham, just as he saw at the Exodus from Egypt." End of quote.

This is the allusion of the Matzah with its three branches. The Bitter Herbs also have three laws: the stalk, the leaves, and the lettuce—the choice way to perform the commandment. The one that includes everything corresponds to the second bitterness during the building of the Holy Temple. Or, the three are like the crowns: the Crown of Torah, the Crown of Priesthood, and the Crown of Kingship, and the Crown of Torah includes them all, as is known. To this they alluded: "Lettuce is the choice way to perform the commandment" regarding Bitter Herbs, referring to the Crown of Torah. The size of the Bitter Herbs is like an olive, based on the idea that "one should be satisfied with food as bitter as an olive." And it is written: "And they shall take to you pure olive oil, beaten," which is explained in the Zohar regarding the Torah: it says that masters of the Torah must be like a piece of the Torah, which is called *Tushiyah* <note>Wisdom/Resourcefulness</note>, and it is bitter like an olive. This is the source of sustenance, for the olive, too, the Holy One, blessed be He, chose it to be sweetened. This is the "fast opening" of the Torah with the verses. And it is found in the chapter "At All Times" (page 32) that at its beginning it was soft and at the end it became hard; so we find regarding words of Torah in the Tractate Ketubot, in the chapter "A Young Woman who was Enticed." Rabbi Isaac said: "In that hour, a person should roll with his son in the study of Torah until twelve years of age, and from then on, he should be strict with him for his livelihood." I have established its foundation regarding the Passover of the future, for then the essence was seen at the end, and the end at the beginning, and the middle includes them both—namely, these three: Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come. These are the three groups of the Passover women. And behold, remember that the Passover is named because "He passed over" in Egypt, as it says, "And He passed over Egypt." This indicates the nullification of idolatry and the nullification of the heavenly ministers who strengthen the firstborn. This is why it says, "He passed over and the thresholds shook." The Passover of Egypt alludes to the Passover of the future, when it will be fulfilled that "On that day the Lord shall be one and His name one." The Passover lamb in Egypt was taken on the Sabbath, which is called "The Great Sabbath" <note>Shabbat HaGadol</note>, pointing toward the future which is "entirely Sabbath." It is found in the *Tur* that the Sabbath before Passover is called the Great Sabbath, etc. See the two questions asked and their answers at length; I also wrote other answers elsewhere. However, I say further: the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded to slaughter sheep for the Passover, which superficially seems prohibited <note>Because the Egyptians worshipped sheep</note>. Therefore Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, called them... and even though the sheep of Israel were not worshipped, nonetheless it is written "Draw out and take for yourselves"—draw from what you have and take from the market. Even if you have, take from the market, or one Israelite from another (so that it is not something worshipped by an Israelite... see *Beit Yosef* at the end of section 148). Nevertheless, it says "take" plainly, implying even from a Gentile. You cannot say it means "withdraw from idolatry" by buying specifically from an Israelite, for if that were the meaning, why say "draw from your own"? The point is that a "worshipped animal" is forbidden as a sacrifice for *other* purposes, but to sacrifice it for this purpose itself—to show that this idol is null and void—is permitted. This is like the calf we used for the... and we ask, "Does a prosecutor not become a defender?" <note>A legal principle: an object used for a sin cannot be used for a mitzvah</note>. But it is different here, for it is to atone for the act of the Calf itself. Regarding that sin, the rule "a prosecutor does not become a defender" does not apply; it only applies when entering in golden garments to the inner sanctum, for then one is occupied with a different service. Therefore, the Blessed One commanded to take specifically on the tenth of the month, because the tenth of the month was the Sabbath. Our Sages of blessed memory said: regarding one who keeps the Sabbath, even if he worshipped idols like the generation of Enosh, he is forgiven. Thus, the Sabbath is the nullification of idolatry. And if it had fallen on other days of the month, it would have been a commandment...

<column-break/>

### Guarded Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Shmurah*. This heading marks the transition to discussing the special matzah and the mystical nature of the Seder night.</note>

...to say "it is the night." There are wondrous secrets in this, some of which were explained in the Zohar (Portion *Bo*), and at length in the explanation of the *Pardes* <note>Referring to *Pardes Rimonim* by Moses Cordovero</note> in the "Gate of Emanations," chapter two, see there. These are the perfect Sages who occupy themselves with the secrets of that night; that is to say, the ultimate purpose of time is that night. They revealed wondrous secrets until the spark reached those who are the students, who debated in wisdom and told according to their perception, for the Torah has many faces. Our Sages said: "The time has arrived for the morning Shema." This was not just an announcement, but an answer to their debate and their intention. "The time has arrived for the morning Shema"—meaning, the night is called the time of the "Evening Shema," and when the time for the "Morning Shema" approaches, it is still called night, but in the masculine form. As is known, the attribute of Night is feminine, and the attribute of Day is masculine. This is the likeness of the act, and their intention was as explained in the Zohar, as follows:

"It is written: 'If there be a young girl (*Na'arah*), a virgin betrothed...' Because as long as she has not received the male, she is called 'Youth' (*Na'ar* - masculine form). Once she receives the male, she is called 'Young Girl' (*Na'arah* - feminine form). So too, the Night is a 'Youth' (*Na'ar*) when it has not received the male. And even though it is written 'A night of guardings for the Lord,' the male was destined to be united with her. At the hour she is united with the male, it is written 'This is that night for the Lord'—a night of guardings, male and female. And everywhere it is written 'It is that night,' after male and female are found as one, praise is given only to the male." End of quote.

The *Pardes* there expanded on the explanation, see there.

# Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah said: "Behold, I am like...":
This is a Mishnah in Tractate Berakhot. Before this, we learned there: "We mention the Exodus from Egypt at night," which refers to the portion of *Tzitzit* <note>Numbers 15, which mentions the Exodus</note>. Some explain "I did not merit/I was not victorious" <note>A play on the word *Zachiti*</note>; it is implied from their words that they bring this as evidence that the Sages disagree with Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah regarding the Future to Come. It is difficult: why did they not disagree earlier when he said "We mention..."? Furthermore, since Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah did not know the interpretation of Ben Zoma, why did the Sages disagree? Rather, it seems they do not disagree on the core law, but rather Ben Zoma and the Sages differ on the derivation of the verses. Both believe that "the days of your life" refers to the fixed lifespan. Ben Zoma believes "the days" means the days, and the nights are not included in "life," as I saw in the chapter "Rabbi Akiva," that in the future they will deduct from our father... from the seventy years of a man's life, half is nights. But the Sages say "all the days of your life" includes this world—meaning the judgment, the day, and the nights. This world is called "the days of your life" because this world has a limit. And the word "all" is to include [the nights]. With this, the expression "Behold I am like seventy years old" is clarified; for seventy years is the fixed year of our life, as it is said, "The days of our years among them are seventy years." If Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah were actually seventy years old, it would be for a memory, and it was logical for him to interpret like Ben Zoma to establish "the days of your life" upon this fixed limit.

# Tractate Pesachim

### Guarded Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Shemurah*. This is matzah made from grain that has been "guarded" or supervised against moisture from the moment of harvest to ensure no fermentation occurs.</note>

"We have waited for Him, this is the Lord; we have waited for Him, let us exult and rejoice in His salvation" <note>Isaiah 25:9</note>. The word "This" (*zeh*) acts as if one is pointing with a finger: "This is He." "And we shall rejoice in His salvation"—meaning the salvation that comes from Him to save us. Furthermore, "in His salvation" can be interpreted as His own salvation, as it were <note>A mystical concept where God's presence, the *Shekhinah*, is redeemed alongside the Jewish people</note>, as it is written: "For I have desired that His Great Name be magnified and sanctified," etc. This is the essence of the passage: "Anyone who tells at length [of the Exodus]... behold, such a person is praiseworthy." This means that the Lord, blessed be He, is Himself praised, glorified, and sanctified through our telling, and we have merited through our waiting for Him to declare, "This is my God" and "This is the Lord for whom we have waited."

This is the secret of "And God led the people around" <note>Exodus 13:18</note>; He surrounded us so that there was no separation between us. In the Midrash, regarding "And God led the people around," it is said that even a poor person in Israel must not eat until he reclines (*hesibah*), for thus did the Holy One, blessed be He, make them recline <note>The act of reclining at the Seder table symbolizes freedom, mimicking the dining habits of ancient nobility</note>. Thus, the secret of reclining is explained. With this, the four answers are completed.

### The Narrative
<note>Hebrew: *Ma'aseh*. This refers to the famous story in the Haggadah about the five Sages who spent the entire Seder night in Bnei Brak discussing the Exodus.</note>

"It happened that Rabbi Eliezer..." and so on, until the end. Regarding the morning recitation of the *Shema*, one must connect the Exodus from Egypt to both day and night. For the Exodus from Egypt publicizes the "renewal of the world," which demonstrates God's truth and His blessed unity. Now, our Rabbis said that one must include the "attribute of day" in the night and the "attribute of night" in the day within the framework of the *Shema*. Specifically, in the morning blessing, we say "Who forms light and creates darkness," and in the evening blessing, "Who brings on the evening twilight with wisdom" and "opens the gates." This is to show that one God created them both, unlike the heretics <note>The *Minim*, likely referring to dualists or Gnostics</note> who say that He who created the day did not create the night.

These blessings were established before the *Shema*—"The Lord is our God, the Lord is One"—and after the *Shema* in the blessings of "True and Firm" (morning) and "True and Faithful" (evening). There, we mention the Exodus from Egypt, which is the proof of this unity. It should be a bond between day and night. We see in the wisdom of the Creator, blessed be He, that He encamped the people near the night. And the day, as its name implies, was destined to come, or it was darkened beforehand, as the Targum <note>Ancient Aramaic translation/commentary</note> says regarding the verse "And the darkness was felt." Therefore, the Zohar writes that one must bind the night to the day and the day to the night through blessings and sanctifications.

This was the primary intention of these holy Tannaim <note>Sages of the Mishnaic period</note>. They certainly began in the evening to bind the night to the day, and they did not stop all night until they had also bound the day to the night. This obligation is most intense on that night: to engage in the story of the Exodus and the wonders that prove this unity, as I have explained. A great hint may also be found here: I have seen in most accurate versions the phrase "all *that* [masculine] night" (*kol oto ha-laylah*). This is difficult, as it should say "all *that* [feminine] night" (*otah ha-laylah*), since "night" (*laylah*) is typically a feminine noun.

->S.G.S.<-
<note>Likely an abbreviation for a concluding phrase like "Siyum Gemara Selah" or a specific scribal mark.</note>

According to the plain meaning, we can say that they "acquire" the night by day, as it will be in the future: "And the night shall shine as the day" <note>Psalm 139:12</note>. In that context, "night" is treated as masculine. Since the night is sweetened by the day and becomes a "great night" <note>A night of great significance or light</note>, the Exodus that happened by day makes the night take on a masculine form; therefore, it says "that [masculine] night."

Another difficulty: how could the students speak in the presence of their teachers to say "the time for the morning Shema has arrived"? Did their teachers not see this for themselves? Furthermore, what does it matter if the time for the *Shema* arrived? Since they began the Seder while it was permitted, and according to our way of thinking, "Torah study takes precedence and the hour does not pass," why should they stop? To answer this, I will provide a brief introduction regarding the verse: "It is a night of vigils for the Lord... this is that night of vigils for the Lord" <note>Exodus 12:42</note>. The repetition in this verse is difficult, as is the phrasing "this is that night." It should have said...

<column-break/>

### Guarded Matzah
The purpose of the Egyptian exile and the redemption was to receive the Torah, as it is written: "When you take the people out... you shall serve God on this mountain" <note>Exodus 3:12</note>. This refers to the receiving of the Torah. The Torah is the "service" that the Holy One gave to us—a great yoke that weakens human strength. Preceding this was the yoke of the "husk" <term>Klipah: literally "shell" or "husk," referring to the forces of spiritual impurity that conceal the divine light</term>, which was the yoke of Egypt.

Afterward, regarding the gift of the Land of Israel: they only merited it through the preceding "husk," which was the forty years they spent in the wilderness where they died. Therefore, it is always mentioned in their lifetime in the desert: "When you come to the land," "In your coming to the land." For the "husk" of the Land of Israel is the suffering in the wilderness.

Furthermore, regarding the gift of the World to Come (*Olam Ha-Ba*): the preceding "husk" consists of the four exiles which refine, cleanse, and purify the people, leading them to repentance. Those who calculate the exiles find four, corresponding to Babylon, Media/Persia, Greece, and Edom <note>Rome/the West</note>. They do not count the Egyptian exile (which lasted 210 years, though the actual servitude was only 86 or 117 years) because these four are the "husk of darkness" that precedes the light of the World to Come. This is the "Hidden Light" from the six days of Creation, which the Holy One, blessed be He, set aside for the righteous in the future.

There are four stages before the World to Come arrives: the victory of the day, the Sabbath-like rest (where "nothing compares to it in this world"), the process of repentance through the power of exile, and then the World to Come which follows a person's death. This is followed by the Messianic era and finally the Resurrection of the Dead.

This explains the Midrash Rabbah on the verse "And the earth was without form and void (*tohu va-vohu*), and darkness was upon the face of the deep" <note>Genesis 1:2</note>. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish interpreted the verse as referring to the four kingdoms: "Without form" is the Babylonian kingdom; "and void" is the Median/Persian kingdom; "and darkness" is the Greek kingdom, which darkened the eyes of Israel with its decrees, telling them, "Write on the horn of an ox that you have no part in the God of Israel." "Upon the face of the deep" refers to the Wicked Kingdom <note>Rome</note>, which is as fathomless as the deep. "And the spirit of God hovered"—this is the spirit of the Messiah. By what merit does it come? It hovers over the "water"—the merit of repentance, which is compared to water, as it is written, "Pour out your heart like water."

One might ask why the author of *Keritot* changed the terminology? The purpose of "In the beginning... and God said, let there be light" is as Rashi explained: this light was hidden for the righteous in the future. It is impossible to merit this light without the preceding "husk," namely the four exiles mentioned above, which refine and cleanse us. Only then will the Messiah come and God will say, "Let there be light." The "renewal of the world" was something from nothing (*Yesh me-Ayin*), and the final redemption from Egypt will be similarly miraculous, as I have elaborated elsewhere in my writings.

There are fifty "something from nothing" gifts. The Torah: the whole world was considered as "nothing" (*Ayin*) until the receiving of the Torah. Rashi notes on the verse "The sixth day" that all of creation was suspended until that moment. The Land of Israel is also "something from nothing," as all other nations are as "nothing" compared to it; it is a land that the Lord seeks out, and from its essence, all other lands are sustained. It was conquered from thirty-one kings. The Land of Israel possesses ten levels of holiness. The World to Come is also called "nothing" (*Ayin*), for it is the source of everything. In the future, every righteous person will inherit 310 worlds <note>Based on the numerical value of the word *Yesh* (310)</note>. This "Something" (*Yesh*) comes from the power of the "Nothing" (*Ayin*)—that is, from the Torah and Mitzvot performed in this world.

Let us return to the matter of the three places: Torah upon leaving Egypt, then the World to Come, and finally the perfection of all. The first level, the Exodus from Egypt, began the joy of the light, as it is written: "And for all the children of Israel, there was light in their dwellings." This "light" refers to the Torah. Rabbi Simon said: the word "Light" appears five times in the creation story, corresponding to the Five Books of the Torah. Afterward, the Torah is described as the moon in its fullness, as seen in the Midrash. In the future, the "Hidden Light" will be fully revealed—the light of Zion, which will be for the Lord as an everlasting light.

The Egyptian redemption was from the "feminine" world, but the Torah itself is spoken in the "masculine" language. In the future, "The Lord will go before them"—He and His court. When they merited the Holy Temple, it was because "From Zion shall go forth the Torah." Afterward, in the future, a "New Song" will be sung in the masculine form (*Shir Hadash*). "He has made a memorial (*Zecher*) for His wonders"—the word *Zecher* <note>Masculine</note> has the numerical value of 228, related to "The Lord commanded the blessing, even life forever."

Therefore, at the Exodus from Egypt, these three <note>Torah, Priesthood, Kingship</note> were not yet called "Crowns," but only "gifts" from the Cloud, the Well, and the Manna. Even though the Torah was given, it was not yet in its perfection. The sign of this is that the people said, "You speak with us..." and retreated from the desire to "see our King." Only with the building of the Holy Temple did the light increase and the "moon" become full. Or, these three are the "Crown of Torah, Crown of Priesthood, and Crown of Kingship" in the aspect of the gift of the Land of Israel. In the future, with the revelation of the Hidden Light, the essence of the Torah will be "Perfect," as I explained elsewhere. This is the "Upper Land of Israel." As our Sages said: "I will not enter the Jerusalem of Above until I have built the Jerusalem of Below." They shall go from strength to strength, from the World to Come to the Resurrection of the Dead.

The explanation of these matters is as follows: at the revelation of the Torah, these three came from the Cloud, the Well, and the Manna. At the revelation of the Land of Israel, they became the three Crowns. And in the end, at the final revelation, it will be as "God said: Let there be light." The end is rooted in the beginning.

# Tractate Pesachim

## Rich Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Ashirah*. This refers to matzah made with fruit juice or eggs rather than just water. In a mystical sense, it represents a "richer" or more complex level of divine illumination.</note>

Redemption initially comes only from the side of the "Female World" <note>In Kabbalah, this refers to the *Shekhinah* or *Malchut*, the receptive aspect of divinity</note>. Later, in the Land of Israel with the building of the Temple, the light of the moon in its fullness adds a higher level. This is represented by the numerical pattern 3-4-3. In the future, when the "Hidden Light" is revealed, the pattern will be 3-3-6. You will find a wondrous hint of this: in the reverse alphabet (*Tashrak*), you find the 3-4-3 pattern. This relates to the phrase "And the gold of that [land] is good" <note>Genesis 2:12</note>; the gematria <note>Jewish system of assigning numerical value to letters</note> of these phrases reflects the 4-3-3 structure. The *Tur* <note>A foundational code of Jewish law</note> already wrote in section 286 that the reverse alphabet indicates the process of redemption.

The beginning of Israel’s holiness occurred when they left Egypt, corresponding to the start of the standard alphabet (*Aleph-Bet*), at which time the pattern was 3-4-3. In the future, according to the reverse alphabet, it will be 3-3-6. In the middle period—which refers to the strength of the Land of Israel—it was also 3-4-3. This is hinted at by the tribe of Gad, who went at the head of the army to conquer the land. It is written of Gad, "He tore the arm and even the crown" <note>Deuteronomy 33:20</note>. We find the 3-4-3 hint in the verse "Gad, a troop shall troop upon him" <note>Genesis 49:19</note>.

The first three levels include the middle three and the final three, for the middle ones are branches of the first, and the final ones are branches of branches. All connect back to their root. Then, the Divine Name *Adonai* <note>original: אדנ"י</note> is joined with the first three levels. This is the secret of the Temple Treasury chamber, where the half-shekel was collected, gathering the essence of every Jewish individual into the "Well of the Covenant" in the Assembly of Israel. This is the secret of the three baskets of three *seah* each <note>A measurement used in the Temple</note>—the secret of three sets of three. Then everything is generalized into the number 4, which is the "Aleph, Bet, Gimmel" they used to write on the baskets. This is also the secret of the Altar in the time to come.

"Toward the face of the Menorah" <note>Numbers 8:2</note> refers to the light of the moon in its fullness, where the middle is most praised, following the 3-4-3 pattern. Regarding the principle "We ascend in holiness and do not descend": this refers to the progression of light. At first, one cannot reach the "Great Light" directly, so we move from strength to strength, year by year. In the end, the light is most praised, representing the "Great Light" and the 3-3-6 pattern.

From this, we can understand why Rabbi Yehuda gave the mnemonic *Detzach, Adash, Beach* <note>A mnemonic for the Ten Plagues: Blood, Frogs, Lice; Wild Beasts, Pestilence, Boils; Hail, Locusts, Darkness, Firstborns</note>. These correspond to the ten Divine Names. As the Kabbalists explain, the root is the number 10. *Detzach, Adash, Beach* follows a 3-3-4 pattern. As mentioned, when Israel left Egypt, they reached the lower level of "4."

The core of the matter is Pesach, Matzah, and Maror, which are three sets of three. These correspond to the "Crown of Torah," the "Crown of Priesthood," and the "Crown of Kingship." We must still explain the "Crown of a Good Name" which rises above them, and the staff that rises above them in the World to Come. I have found that after the Resurrection of the Dead, they are all called a "Good Name." This explains the difficulties I raised in my commentary on the Mishnah.

Regarding the Unique Name of God <note>The Tetragrammaton, Y-H-V-H</note>: the first two letters, *Yud* and *Heh*, are holy on their own. However, the last two, *Vav* and *Heh*, are not found to have independent holiness in the same way. Yet, you should know that "Greatness" is hinted at within them. These refer to the three levels of the Name *Adonai*. There are levels of the soul (*Neshamah*), and then a "Soul for the Soul" as explained in the Zohar. There is a difference between the soul's attachment to us and its attachment to the Blessed Creator. This is the meaning of "No eye has seen, O God, besides You" <note>Isaiah 64:3</note>, which refers to the secret of the "Additional Soul" (*Neshamah Yeterah*).

This is explained in the *Gate of Vowel Points*: the points *Cholem* (above), *Shuruk* (middle), and *Chiriq* (below) draw light into the letter *Vav*, which represents "Beauty" (*Tiferet*). The *Cholem* (the dot above) represents the "Sovereignty" (*Malchut*) in her high seat with her husband.
1. Her first position: with the first three levels, the secret of *Cholem*.
2. Her second position: the light of the moon equaling the light of the sun, the secret of *Melafom* <note>A vowel point where the dot is in the middle</note>.
3. Her third position: below, under the "feet" of the *Vav*, the secret of *Chiriq* <note>A vowel point where the dot is below</note>.

I wrote earlier that the first level was when Israel left Egypt. When they ascended and reached the "Fifty" <note>The fifty days to Sinai</note>, the attachment changed. The letter *Vav* indicates the Holy One, Blessed be He, who is the "Place of the World" <note>The six directions/edges of the world</note>. In the hidden realm, the *Vav* includes the six upper "edges." This is the name Y-H-V-H vocalized with a *Cholem*. *Chiriq* hints at the Name *Adonai* at the feet of the final three levels. *Melafom* indicates the Name *Adonai* when it is equal.

This explains a puzzling Midrash in *Shir HaShirim Rabbah*: "A crown with which his mother crowned him" <note>Song of Songs 3:11</note>. Rabbi Simeon bar Yochai asked Rabbi Eliezer: "Have you heard from your father what this crown is?" He replied with a parable: A king had an only daughter whom he loved dearly. He called her "My Daughter." His love grew until he called her "My Sister." It grew further until he called her "My Mother." So too, the Holy One, Blessed be He, loved Israel and called them "Daughter." His love increased and He called them "Sister." Finally, He called them "Mother." Rabbi Simeon stood and kissed him on the head, saying: "If I only came to hear this, it would be enough."
The secret is this: "Daughter" is the first level (the lower three). "Sister" is the second level...
<meta>catchword: ...the equality [of the moon and sun]</meta>

## Guarded Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Shemurah*. This section moves from mystical structures to the text of the Haggadah itself.</note>

To his teachers, he made known the excellence of the Torah, which is of ultimate perfection. As our Sages taught: "It is not an empty thing for you" <note>Deuteronomy 32:47</note>—and if it seems empty, it is *from you*, because it is hidden from you. But the Giver of the Torah is Blessed, and He knows that it is not an empty thing. The Torah is a reflection of the Blessed One who gave it. Thus it says:
->**"Blessed be the Place, Blessed be He"**<-
The Blessed One is both "Revealed" and "Hidden."
**Revealed:** From the perspective of His actions in His world, He is called "**Place**" (*Makom*), for He is the "Place of the World" <note>A classic Rabbinic term: God is not contained by the world; the world is contained within God</note>.
**Hidden:** From the perspective of His essence, which even the ministering angels must ask, "Where is the place of His glory?" His essence is known only to Himself, and this is "**Blessed be He**."

Correspondingly, He gave the Torah in both a revealed and hidden state. Regarding what is revealed to us and our children, the Haggadah says, "Blessed be He who gave the Torah to His people Israel." Regarding the subtle, hidden things known only to Him, it says, "Blessed be He."

The author of the Haggadah provides this introduction because he wants to reveal the mysteries of the **Four Sons**. He begins by saying, "**The Torah speaks corresponding to four sons**," meaning that the Torah assumes all the sons are together at one table. When Israel was in their land, numerous as the sand on the seashore, there were many groups for a single Passover offering. Without doubt, in every gathering, there was a mix of all these types of sons.

This introduction also answers a question: "Even if we are all wise... it is a commandment upon us to tell of the Exodus."
**The Wise Son—what does he say?** His words are framed as a question. He takes the verses written regarding the general Torah and applies them specifically to the Passover, since the Exodus is mentioned there as well. When the Wise Son asks this, his intention is surely not just the literal meaning. If it were, why would he ask it specifically now on Passover? Rather, his words are borrowed from the language of wisdom, and his intention concerns something specific to Passover.

He finds a difficulty in the "**Testimonies**" (*Edot*), "**Statutes**" (*Chukim*), and "**Laws**" (*Mishpatim*) mentioned regarding Passover.
**Testimonies:** These are commandments we do as a "memorial" to an event, such as Maror (bitter herbs) to remember "and they embittered their lives." These are testimonies of what happened in the past.
**The Difficulty:** If these are "Testimonies" (where the reason is known), why are they also called "**Statutes**" (*Chukim*)? A "Statute" usually refers to a royal decree where the reason is *not* known.
And if you suggest that "Statute" here doesn't mean a hidden decree, but rather a "universal statute" for the whole world and not just Israel—that contradicts the fact that Passover is called a "**Law**" (*Mishpat*). A "Law" in this context is something specific to Israel, as it says, "He has not dealt so with any nation; and as for His laws, they have not known them" <note>Psalm 147:20</note>.

So the Wise Son asks: If "Statute" means a royal decree, it contradicts "Testimony." If "Statute" means a universal law, it contradicts "Law" (which is specific to Israel).
The answer given to him is: "**One does not eat dessert [Afikoman] after the Passover lamb.**" In the chapter "Arvei Pesachim," one authority interprets the word *Afikoman* as "Bring out the vessels..."
<meta>catchword: ...which is to say</meta>

# Rich Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Ashirah*. Historically, this refers to matzah made with "richer" ingredients like wine or oil, but here it serves as a heading for a "richer" mystical interpretation of the Passover story.</note>

The Holy One, Blessed be He, took us for Himself. Therefore, the "Passover of Egypt" <note>The original Passover event in the Book of Exodus</note> was characterized by taking the lamb on the tenth of the month and tying it to the bedposts. This was done to merit the attribute of "alacrity" from our God. This lamb was forbidden as a sacrifice elsewhere, and for this reason, specifically, the Sabbath before Passover is called "The Great Sabbath" <note>Shabbat HaGadol</note>. The Passover of Egypt points toward the Passover of the future, which will be different and under a different name. Thus, these three levels are yours: they are three times three, hinting at three degrees of ascent. They correspond to the three things the Israelites lived by: the Cloud, the Well, and the Manna <note>The three miraculous gifts that sustained the Israelites in the desert</note> upon their departure from Egypt, similar to the receiving of the Torah. Afterward, there are three "houses" or crowns: the Crown of Torah, the Crown of Priesthood, and the Crown of Kingship, corresponding to the time of the giving of the Land of Israel and the building of the Holy Temple. And in the future, in the World to Come, we will see the "end within the beginning," and there will be three: Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come. These are the nine levels of Israel, and the tenth is "Holy"—meaning the collective of the Assembly of Israel <note>Knesset Yisrael</note>, for they are a single unity. This is as we say in prayer: "You are One, and Your Name is One, and who is like Your people Israel, one nation." The essence of their unity is that their soul is "a part of God above." Because of this power, His Name, may He be blessed, is partnered with our names.

I will reveal a bit: even Israel is partnered with His hidden Name. Just as we counted nine levels for Israel plus the tenth which is "Holy," so too with His Names, may He be blessed, which may not be erased. There are three levels, one on top of the other, which are three times three. How so? The first level consists of three Names: *Ehyeh*, *Yah*, and the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter Name of God, Y-H-W-H</note> with the vowel points of *Elohim* <note>God as Judge</note>. The second level is *Elohim* and the Tetragrammaton with the vowel points of *Cholem*, *Sheva*, and *Kamatz* <note>These are specific Hebrew vowel signs</note>, the sign for which is the word *Chashak* <note>original: "חש"ק", a mnemonic for the vowels mentioned</note>. The third level is "The Lord of Hosts" <note>Adonai Tzevaot</note>, "The Lord," and *Yahiu*. These are three sets of three. Furthermore, there is a tenth level, which is the Name *Adonai* <note>pronounced "My Lord"</note>. This Name corresponds to the Assembly of Israel, for it is from this Name that the souls descend, being "a part of God above," as explained in the books of the Kabbalists. Thus it is written: "Let my Lord (*Adonai*) go among us" <note>Exodus 34:9</note>, and "In the assemblies, bless God, the Lord (*Adonai*), from the source of Israel" <note>Psalm 68:27</note>, for that Name is the source of their souls.

You will also find that there are sixty-five families in Israel, as Rashi <note>A famous 11th-century French commentator</note> explained on the verse "The Lord set His love upon you... though you were the fewest of all peoples" <note>Deuteronomy 7:7</note>. The numerical value of the Name *Adonai* is also sixty-five. This is the meaning of "This is my Name forever, and this is my memorial [to all generations]" <note>Exodus 3:15</note>. The phrase "This is my Name" points specifically to the hidden Tetragrammaton mentioned above. However, the phrase "and this is my memorial" is difficult terminology; what is it pointing to? "Memorial" usually implies something else entirely, like the saying: "Not as I am written [the Tetragrammaton] am I read [Adonai]." Furthermore, why do we change the pronunciation specifically for this Name? One cannot say it is because the vowel points of *Adonai* and the vowels of the Tetragrammaton are the same (*Chashak*), for it is still difficult to explain why the Name "Lord of Hosts" is read with those same vowels. We must distinguish that in "Hosts" (*Tzevaot*), the *Kamatz* vowel comes before the *Cholem*.

<insert>
Sign 60.
A certain tractate writes at the end, according to the simple meaning of the matters from Tractate Adonai: The end of laughter is the end, for the completion of the book... in the melodies of the Sages, the verse of the Kingdom of the Shekhinah <note>the Divine Presence</note>... which is the prayer of remembrance.
</insert>

Nevertheless, the core of the matter regarding "This is my Name and this is my memorial" is that what we mention aloud—*Adonai*—is "My Name." That is to say, it is hinted at within the Tetragrammaton through a "substitution" <note>term: *Temurah* — a Kabbalistic method of swapping letters for their neighbors in the alphabet</note>. The substitution for the letters of the Tetragrammaton (Y-H-W-H) are the neighboring letters: B-W-Z-W. This is the hint: "And its substitution shall be holy" <note>Leviticus 27:33</note>, meaning the Name of God with the substitution B-W-Z-W adds up to sixty, the numerical value associated with *Adonai*. The Name *Adonai* is the source of the souls of Israel, and they too exist in the mystery of substitution. This follows what our Rabbis said, and what Rashi brought in the section *Ki Tetze*: "A curse of God is hung" <note>Deuteronomy 21:23</note>, which is compared to two twin brothers... <note>A Midrashic parable where a king and a commoner are twins; when the commoner is hanged for a crime, people think the king is being hanged. It explains why God is "pained" by the death of the wicked.</note> Thus, the phrase "This is my Name and this is [my memorial]" is resolved as "this is myself."

The root of the matter is that the Tetragrammaton indicates God's essence, which is hidden and beyond our comprehension. Our connection to Him is through His actions and through the Assembly of Israel, upon whom His specific providence rests. Since the Name *Adonai* is the source of Israel, we find ourselves—in terms of our souls—positioned within the three levels of Names I mentioned. In the first three, we always find the Name *Adonai* paired, as in: "My Lord (*Adonai*) God, what will You give me?" <note>Genesis 15:2</note>, or "My Lord God, how shall I know that I shall inherit it?" <note>Genesis 15:8</note>. This shows the mention of *Adonai* in the first three levels. Similarly, in the middle three, there is "God, God, the Lord" with the *Chashak* vowels, and it is mostly read as *Adonai*. Furthermore, the Torah mentions the Name *Adonai* alone several times without the Tetragrammaton. This confirms that the Name *Adonai*, the source of Israel, exists in three ascending levels. As Israel ascends, the divine flow is elevated from higher and higher places. This is explained in the Midrash (*Vayikra Rabbah*) regarding "giving signs." Many interpretations exist, but I will explain it according to what I have written.

I must first introduce a teaching of our Rabbis from Tractate Megillah, in the chapter "He who reads [the Megillah] standing." Regarding the rule that one does not read fewer than ten verses in the Torah, Rava said: "The first person to read four verses is praiseworthy, the second is praiseworthy, and the third is praiseworthy." The first is praiseworthy because of the "three baskets of three *seahs* each" used to take up the contribution for the Temple chamber, marked '1, 2, 3' to know which was filled first. The middle reader is praiseworthy because it is written "toward the face of the Menorah shall [the lamps] cast light," showing they face the western lamp, which faces the Divine Presence. Rabbi Yochanan said: "From here we see the middle is praiseworthy." The last is praiseworthy because "we ascend in holiness and do not descend." These three levels are the 3-by-3 I explained. When the flow comes from *Adonai* in the first three, the order is 4-3-7. When it comes from the middle three, it is 4-3-7. When it comes from the last three, it is 4-3-7. The highest level for Israel is 3-3-3. The middle level is 3-4-6. The lowest level is 3-3-6. I wrote above that the 3-3 level of Israel began with the dawning of light when they left Egypt, when "all the children of Israel had light." This continued until the receiving of the Torah. However, when they said [to Moses], "You speak with us," they "turned backward." This is the sign 3-4-20... <note>The text becomes more technical and numerical here</note>.

<column-break/>

# Guarded Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Shmura*. This refers to matzah made from grain that has been "guarded" against moisture from the moment of harvest.</note>
## Section

The command of *Tsitsit* <note>Ritual fringes</note> hints in its plain meaning to the Exodus from Egypt; see Rashi on the portion *Shelach Lecha*. "Blessed is the Place [God], Blessed is He! Blessed is He who gave the Torah to His people Israel, Blessed is He! Corresponding to the four sons [the Torah speaks]: one wise, one wicked, one simple, and one who does not know how to ask." 

Several difficulties arise here. First, what is the connection between the Name *Shachaf* <note>original: "שחף", possibly a scribal error or a specific mystical reference to the context of Israel</note> and the matter of Israel? Why does it say "Blessed is He" in relation to the four sons—the Wise, the Wicked, etc.? And then again, "Blessed is He who gave the Torah, Blessed is He"? Furthermore, the phrasing "The Torah spoke *against* [corresponding to] four sons" is difficult.

Another major question raised by commentators: the answers given to the four sons here in the Haggadah are not the same as the answers provided for them in the Torah itself. In the book *Zevach Pesach*, the author discusses this at length. Furthermore, what is the relevance of the law "one does not conclude the Passover meal with *afikomen*" <note>the final piece of matzah</note> to the "Table of Wisdom"? 

Regarding the Wise son's question: "When your son asks you tomorrow, 'What are these testimonies, statutes, and laws?'" as stated in the portion *Va’etchanan* <note>Deuteronomy 6:20</note>—this refers to the whole Torah, not just the laws of Passover. The Sages explained that if your son asks "tomorrow"—meaning in the future—you should answer "We were slaves... and the Holy One took us out." It follows that once they are answered that they are His servants, it becomes our obligation to fulfill everything He commanded us, and the core is the "sweetness" <note>original: "חרוה", likely *cherut* (freedom) or *chayut* (vitality)</note> of our existence. 

Yet another difficulty: according to the Haggadah, the answer to the Wise son is "Tell him according to the laws of Passover: one does not conclude after the Paschal lamb with *afikomen*." This implies the Wise son didn't know the laws of Passover, which contradicts his description as "Wise." 

Regarding the Wicked son: the Haggadah says, "had he been there, he would not have been redeemed." It should have said "he *was* not redeemed" in the past tense, since it is speaking directly to him. 

Regarding the son who doesn't know how to ask: "You must open [the conversation] for him." Why use the language of "opening"? It should have said "You shall tell him." 

Further, in the Wicked son's answer, the Haggadah quotes the middle of a verse: "It is because of *this* [what the Lord did for me]" <note>Exodus 13:8</note>, but it does not quote the beginning of the verse. 

There are also questions about the order of the sons. Why does the Haggadah not list them in the order they appear in the Torah? The Haggadah starts with the Wise son, then the Wicked (who is also a type of "wise" man, but one who is wise for evil), then the Simple son who asks a partial question, and finally the one who doesn't know how to ask. But in the Torah, it starts with the Wicked son <note>Exodus 12:26</note>, then the one who doesn't know how to ask <note>Exodus 13:8</note>, then the Simple son <note>Exodus 13:14</note>, and finally the Wise son in the book of Deuteronomy. 

Furthermore, the Wicked son speaks in the plural: "What is this service to *you*?" <note>Exodus 12:26</note>, while the other sons are addressed in the singular. In the answer to the Wicked son, it says "And you shall say" (plural), rather than "And you shall say *to him*" (singular) as it does with the others. 

Finally, in the verse for the son who doesn't know how to ask: "And you shall tell your son on that day, saying..." <note>Exodus 13:8</note>. The word "saying" seems redundant since it already said "you shall tell." 

Therefore, I say that the author of the Haggadah (*Baal HaMaggid*) felt these difficulties and through them understood the inner meaning: that the Torah indeed spoke to four different types of children, even if only three are explicitly mentioned in the context of Passover. As mentioned before, the Wise son's question in *Va’etchanan* refers to the whole Torah, yet it is also hinted at regarding Passover. This serves as an introduction to his words...

## Rich Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Ashirah*. This term usually refers to matzah made with juice or oil, but here it serves as a title for a "richer" mystical interpretation.</note>

It is stated in the "Investigation of Judgment," Part 3, Chapter 6, and Part 4... regarding the secret of the sacrifice: "When a man brings an offering to the Lord, from you and of you" <note>A mystical reading of Leviticus 1:2, suggesting the person is the offering</note>. This is the meaning of "And Moses brought Aaron and his sons near," as well as Nadab and Abihu in the **burning of their souls** as the parts of the burnt offering. As it is said, the sin-offering strengthens the verses written after it: "and a fire went out from before the Lord." Who truly knows the matter of the sacrifice offered by Aaron and his sons? It is likely, as seen in great petitions, that they were softened above, or their souls flew away and they became like Isaac, of whom it was said, "I have offered him up."

So it is written at the end: "And he came down from performing the sin-offering." This closeness cannot return to its original state unless Aaron, through his own choice, offered himself. Thus, he was both the sacrifice and the one offering it. All this took place during the dedication of the Tabernacle; then the principle was fulfilled that **"the priests eat and the owners are atoned,"** for through their closeness they were offered. In terms of their "closeness," they are the priests, but in relation to Moses our Teacher, they are the "owners" <note>the ones bringing the sacrifice</note>. Thus Aaron and his sons were both the priests and the owners. This spiritual eating is very refined, like the spiritual **Banquet of the Righteous** in the future. It is even more refined than the eating of holy sacrifices. The "Meal Offering" (*Mincha*) was similar to this, for it is a "remembrance of God," representing a broken spirit. All sacrifices are about submission, but the Meal Offering most of all. As Rashi says: "Who usually brings a meal offering? A poor man." Therefore, the eating of the *Mincha* was more delicate than other holy offerings. This is why the commandment to eat it is mentioned and warned about more strictly in the *Mincha*.

For this reason, it was commanded "it shall not be leavened," referring to the "kneaded leaven" <note>symbolizing the ego or the "evil inclination"</note>. Therefore, the priest's meal offering was "entirely consumed for the Lord, a fire-offering of pleasing aroma." Furthermore, Isaac our patriarch, who is the essence of "Service" <note>Avodah</note>, is a burnt offering to the Lord. The Afternoon Prayer (*Tefillat Mincha*) was established in place of the meal offering, for there is no burnt offering without a meal offering. This is why this prayer is called *Mincha*. And regarding the coming of the Messiah, it is written: "A poor man riding on a donkey." This represents the three forms of Matzah: 1) the commandment to eat, 2) it shall not be baked as leaven, 3) do not bake it as leaven. These correspond to **Pesach, Matzah, and Maror**. One does not fulfill the obligation except by reciting the words over them. This hints at the **"Crown of a Good Name"** which rises above them and is more spiritual. This is the law regarding the laws of Passover.

(And the measures of the commandments... the laws of leaven and matzah and all the laws... and afterward to preach:) "This is the law of the Meal Offering"—may it be that we are answered in the Mincha prayer, which is the sacrifice of the poor, and may it herald our righteous Messiah, "A poor man riding on a donkey," fulfilling the verse: "For You will save the poor people." May the salvation be near, Amen.

---

### Third Homily for the Great Sabbath occurring on the Portion of Metzora
<note>The "Great Sabbath" is the one immediately preceding Passover. "Metzora" is the Torah portion dealing with the laws of the leper.</note>

**For the one being purified:** "Two live, pure birds," and so on. Just as perfection consists of three matters—perfection of the **soul**, perfection of the **body**, and perfection of **wealth**—as it is said of Jacob our patriarch: "Jacob arrived whole" (whole in body, whole in wealth, whole in his Torah). So too we find the commandments of impurity: "Ritual impurity of the dead" occurs upon the departure of the soul; then there is impurity that issues from the body (the leper, the *zav*, etc.); and then there is the impurity of houses and vessels, which are a person's wealth (land and movable goods). This is certainly not a trivial matter.

There is surely a secret regarding the "impurity of houses." Regarding the language "And I will put [a plague]" <note>Leviticus 14:34</note>, Rashi writes that this was "good news" that was given to them. But if He did not "give" it, what would we say? Nachmanides writes: "This leprosy is not natural at all, and does not exist in the world [normally], nor do plagues on houses. But when Israel is perfect before God, the Spirit of God is upon them always to keep their bodies, clothes, and houses in good appearance. When one of them commits a sin, a deformity appears in his flesh, garment, or house to show that God has departed from him." Therefore the verse says, "I will put a plague of leprosy in a house in the land of your possession," for it is a stroke from God in that house. It only applies in the Land of Israel, which is the inheritance of God... because that matter only occurs in the **Chosen Land** where the Honorable Name dwells. It further states that a house only becomes impure after the conquest and division of the land, when every person recognizes his own portion... for then their minds were settled to know the Lord.

However, a difficulty arises: in the case of clothing, it should also have said "And I will put." Furthermore, if it only applies in the Chosen Land where the Name dwells, then Jerusalem—which is even more chosen for holiness—should certainly be subject to it. Yet, in reality, Jerusalem and outside the Land do not become impure through plagues. This is because it is written "in the house of the land of your **possession**," and Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes. According to the one who says Jerusalem *was* divided among the tribes, then Jerusalem *does* become impure, except for the holy places like the Temple and Synagogues. Another difficulty: "This shall be the law of the leper." Wherever "This is the law" (*Torat*) is written, it comes to include something—what does it include here? "And he shall be brought to the priest," and afterward it says, "And the priest shall go out." At first glance, the language is contradictory.
