<column-break/>

## Guarded Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Shmura*. Matzah that has been guarded from moisture from the time of harvest.</note>

Regarding the dispute between Rav and Shmuel: one says the "disgrace" [we start the Haggadah with] is "We were slaves," and the other says the disgrace is "In the beginning our ancestors were idolators." We fulfill the words of both. It is understandable why we mention the disgrace of slavery, for from the "iron furnace" of servitude we were refined. But why mention the disgrace of idolatry? This is based on the verses from Joshua that the *Maggid* <note>the narrator of the Haggadah</note> brings. Why did he not mention Ishmael explicitly, but only hinted at him by saying "and I multiplied his seed"? Whereas Esau he mentions explicitly. I will explain this entire section in Joshua, Chapter 24, from "And Joshua said to all the people" until they "descended to Egypt," and afterward "Now therefore fear the Lord" until "and His voice we will obey."

This section is difficult and deep, for it is very puzzling. He said, "Now therefore fear the Lord and serve Him in sincerity... and if it seems evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose for yourselves..." Is choice really given in the matter of His service? What difference does it make what they choose? Furthermore, they answered graciously, "Far be it from us to forsake the Lord," yet Joshua said, "You cannot serve the Lord." His words seem to contradict themselves.

Before I can explain, I must preface a few principles. 1) "For the Lord's portion is His people, Jacob is the lot of His inheritance." We are tied in our souls to the Ultimate as with a **rope** (*Hevel*); one end is above and one end is below. This hints that the Blessed Name and the People of Israel are "face to face" by means of this rope, the level through which souls are tied to their source. This is the matter of the "division of the nations," for their vitality only reaches a certain limit and no further. Thus Israel is the "Inner Face" and the nations are the **Shell** (*Kelippah*). 2) I have already elaborated elsewhere that even the Shell, though it is a shell, has a root above in holiness. This is the secret of the names of Isaac and Samael <note>the archetypal angel of evil</note>; though he is the Angel of Death, his root is in the name *El*. In the future, the Shell will be purified from its source; the evil and impurity will perish, but the good and holiness will remain. This is the refinement of the Shell by the Holy, like Terah from whom came Abraham, the head of believers. Through this, the Shell was blessed and its impression remained in the Holy, like a convert who enters the Covenant of Abraham. This is a great merit for the Patriarchs and for Israel, that through them comes the refinement to give life.

In the final stage, there are two levels: the Shell itself and the Root of the Shell above. There are levels from below to above: 1) The essence of the Shell. 2) The "clothing" of holiness, which is the higher head and root that clothes itself within the Shell. This is why I have written at length elsewhere about the three levels: the Head and the Root in their own holiness without "clothing." This is the secret of **"And I will pass through the land of Egypt"**—by way of "passing through" and not by "clothing," for He was revealed in His Glory and His Essence. He "divided" the portion of the Lord for all nations and the princes above, to whom the nations are attached. This is their own level, the lower level, and He divided them so that they do not grasp onto the Holiness, even in the level of "clothing." They reach only as far as the essence of the lower level.

 מסכת פסחים

## Guarded Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Shamurah*. While this usually refers to matzah guarded from moisture, here it introduces a teaching on the spiritual "guarding" of the Passover sacrifice.</note>

That is to say, they should not eat the Passover offering in two different places. This matter serves as a response to the Vilna Gaon <note>original: "גר"א" (Gra), Rabbi Elijah of Vilna, a 18th-century scholar</note>. Another interpretation: "My statute" <note>Hebrew: *Chuki*</note> refers to a matter that has no apparent logical reason. One might have reasoned the opposite: that the Holy One, Blessed be He, would go from house to house to eat, similar to how the redemption of the Holy One, Blessed be He, moved from house to house. Note that the very essence of the question regarding the Passover offering is aimed at the wicked person. The language used by the wise man is a burden from this, and he is gracious. Therefore, the Torah does not mention the "Wise Son" here regarding the Passover offering. This is why it says: "And you, say to him according to the laws of Passover," meaning, regarding the topic of the "Afikoman" <note>the final piece of matzah eaten</note>, answer him that "we do not conclude the Passover meal with a dessert." But regarding the question itself about the general Torah, the answer is as written in the book of Deuteronomy <note>original: "ואתחנן" (Va'etchanan)</note>. Note that at first, the Wise Son spoke because the language of "My Teacher" <note>Rabbi</note> hinted that the Torah mentions here the Wicked Son, or that the speakers are "your children" in the plural, like the gathering of the "Kol Bo" <note>a medieval halakhic work</note>. It is written: "And you shall say, it is a Passover sacrifice to the Lord, who passed over the houses of the Children of Israel when He struck the Egyptians and saved our houses." He did not say "to him," because regarding the cloud, one might think he only thought it. He speaks against all those reclining. This is how the Wise Son's question should be. And "set the teeth of the wicked on edge" <note>a phrase from the Haggadah's response to the Wicked Son</note>. The response to the Wise Son is this: "He saved our houses," passing from house to house. If so, it is a statute <note>a law beyond human logic</note>, and this is why "we do not conclude," as I wrote above. The matter of "teeth" refers to the simplicity of "He saved our houses" and not those of the Egyptians. Likewise, regarding the Wicked Son, if he had been there, he would not have been redeemed.

**"And you shall tell"** <note>Hebrew: *Ve-Higgadta*</note>: My teacher and guide taught, regarding "your son on that day, saying," this refers to the one who does not know how to ask. One might doubt him; perhaps he is not even a member of Israel because you did not tell him about the commandment, and he is a denier. Therefore, he does not take care to engage in discussion. Or, it is due to his own lack of capacity. Therefore, the commandment comes: "You must open the conversation for him." Perhaps he will open his mouth in denial and then return, adding to the first wicked one. Therefore, "tomorrow you shall entice him" and "tell your son." Also, "face him to say" <note>Hebrew: *le-emor*</note> is a language that suggests he should not say this to the wicked one in this way: "Because of this, He did for *me* and not for *him*." This is why it is explained in various places that this is a response to the wicked person. Therefore, the language "he would not have been redeemed" is used in the third person, because he is speaking with the one who does not know how to ask, telling him to say so to the wicked one, rather than speaking with the wicked one directly. He only speaks within the assembly of those reclining. This Passover offering is for the Lord, and it is mentioned in study. Therefore, it says "Even you, set his teeth on edge" regarding what he will say to him afterward. They bring him out of the category of "one who does not know" into the category of "Israel." Therefore, he brings the verse "Because of this..." The phrase "Because of this" is the formula that the one who does not know how to ask should say. One might think it should be told from the first of the month; therefore, the Torah says "On that day." If on that day, one might think while it is still day <note>before the holiday begins</note>; therefore, it says "Because of this"—I only say it at the time when matzah and bitter herbs are placed before you. People ask a question here, even though I wrote above regarding the "Four Sons" how it is answered. Nevertheless, it is repeated to prove it. Everyone asks: the phrase "while it is still day" refers to the eve of Passover, when there was great business with the Passover offering, a large gathering in Israel... the son would ask in wonder, "What is there to eat, and what is all this?" Because of the preoccupation with the tasks, the father has no time to answer his son properly. Therefore, the Torah said, "And you shall tell your son on that day," meaning, when he asks while it is still day, wait until the evening when they are placed before him. Now remember, then you will be free from your occupations, and then I will tell you all the matters, even regarding the matters of the Passover offering.
"What does the Torah teach..." see the letters... in the chapter "On the Eve of Passover."
The son begins with the disgrace and concludes with the praise.
And so-and-so...

## Rich Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Ashirah*. This term usually refers to "egg matzah," but here it is a heading for a "richer," more complex mystical commentary.</note>

The Equality. He said it is the first level. We find a similar example in the statement regarding the obligation of Israel, using the masculine language in the Midrash "Kohelet Rabbah" <note>an ancient commentary on Ecclesiastes</note>: "There is one, and there is no second." "There is one"—this is the Holy One, Blessed be He, as it is said, "The Lord our God, the Lord is One." "And there is no second"—He has no partner in His world. Also, "he has neither son nor brother." "He has no brother" from where? But He *does* have a brother, for the Holy One, Blessed be He, is to Israel. He called them "sons," as it is said, "You are sons to the Lord your God," and He called them "brothers," as it is said, "For the sake of my brothers and friends." "And there is no end to all his labor"—to all that He did in the seven days of Creation. "For whom do I labor and deprive my soul of good?" If the righteous do not stand and gather commandments and good deeds before Him, then all that the Holy One, Blessed be He, created in His world is nothing. Therefore, this statement is astonishing. It is also not understood: "He has no brother, no son"—is it not possible to have a son and not a brother? There is another astonishing Midrash in the blessing of the Torah portion "Yitro" <note>Jethro</note>, which is close to this Midrash. It says: "God is One; 'I am the Lord your God.'" Rabbi Abbahu said: This is a parable of a mortal king who rules and has a father, a brother, or a son. The Holy One, Blessed be He, said: "I am not so. I am the first, for I have no father; and I am the last, for I have no brother; and besides Me, there is no God, for I have no son." Thus far the Midrash. Now, I have explained above the order of the three levels from the name *Adonai* <note>the Divine name meaning "My Lord"</note>: the Source, the Root, and the Radiance. These three levels are hinted at in the three points of the letter *Yod*. The more internal meaning is what is hinted at in the vowels, which hint at the "Extra Soul" <note>Hebrew: *Neshama Yeterah*</note> mentioned above. The connections of "Large," "Sister," and "Mother" mentioned in the Midrash "Chazit" correspond to the three first levels hinted at in the words. The more internal ones are the three mentioned in the points of the letter *Yod*, and they are stated in the masculine: Son, Brother, and Father. The essence of these statements, which are all languages of affection, indicates three levels of attachment of the internal souls of Israel to fulfill what is written: "And you who cleave..." But this does not mean there is an actual partnership, Heaven forbid. It is like what is said in the Torah portion "Bechukotai": "And I will walk among you and I will be your God." Rashi explains: "I will stroll with you in the Garden of Eden and you will not be terrified of Me." One might think you will not fear Me; therefore, the verse says, "And I will be your God." This is what is meant by "I am the first, for I have no father," even when you rise to the highest level. And regarding the middle level, it is said "I have no brother," even though you are called so by way of affection. And regarding the lower level, it says "I have no son." Specifically from here, "two to do them," and "he has no brother" hints that even though He loves Israel, as it is written "For the sake of my brothers and friends" and "You are sons to the Lord your God," nevertheless it is not literally so, for "I am the Lord your God." Therefore, he rightly questioned: "He has no brother," for even when they rise to the level of equality, you say it is not literally so. How much more so when they are at the lower levels! The meaning is that the plain sense of the verse does not show us that there is no partnership with Him; on the contrary, the plain sense is the opposite—that the Holy One, Blessed be He, loves Israel, as we find in the Torah that He called them "Sons," and afterward they reached an even greater level and He called them "Brothers." The explanation of the verse here is thus: The Blessed Name is One; He created His world alone, not for His own sake, but only to benefit the creatures. He chose the nation of Israel and called them "Son." And even though in truth "Son" and "Brother" do not apply to Him as partners, the verse proclaims the levels: He called them "Sons," then they rose to a higher level and He called them "Brothers." All this is when one engages with the commandments. This is the connection of the matter. Then it is not difficult why He mentioned "Son" and "Brother," for he recognized the order of levels one after another. Everything follows from the "letters of the mother"; they are communal, hinted at in the three attachments of the name *Adonai* in three places. These are from the side of the "Female World." And in these three points of the letter *Yod*, which are mentioned as Son, Brother, Father, and are even more internal, they are the secret of the "Good Name" <note>Hebrew: *Shem Tov*</note> that rises above the three first crowns. Behold, the letter *Vav* indicates the masculine... and the *Heh* indicates the feminine... Therefore, these three which are feminine are hinted at in the "filling" of the letter *Heh*... And in the verse, the word "He" <note>Hebrew: *Hu*</note> is written with a *Vav* but read as "She" <note>Hebrew: *Hi*</note> with a *Yod*; thus it is unified with the masculine. The matter of the "fillings": when the name of four letters is filled with *Heh*... it equals the numerical value of "Son" <note>Hebrew: *Ben* = 52</note>, corresponding to the level of "Daughter," both being the first level. When filled with *Aleph* or *Yod*... it equals the value of "Man" <note>Hebrew: *Adam* = 45</note>, made in the image and likeness, which is the second, middle level: "Brother" and "Sister" are equal. When filled with *Yod*... it is the highest level: "Father" and "Mother," for the *Yod* includes all holiness and hints at the three upper levels. Thus, the letters *Vav* and *Heh* of the Name, even though they are not inherently as holy as the letters *Yod* and *Heh* which form a Name on their own, nevertheless hint at a great matter. For now, the Name is not complete in these letters *Vav* and *Heh*; they are hidden until the future... "His Name is Great." Then the Name will be complete in its letters and the Throne will be complete... then all will be equal in holiness "inside and within" <note>in the Holy of Holies</note>. But now, so to speak, the pious are not "inside and within" the Palace and the Tent of Meeting, but rather, metaphorically, in the Courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. This is hinted at in "the Courtyard of the Tent of Meeting" in the Torah portion *Vayakhel*... it mentions "its pillars" in the masculine and "its pillars" in the feminine. This hints at the letters *Vav* and *Heh*. Through this, the language "from its oil and from its fat" is also answered... hinting at the secret of the Name. It says "in a holy place, in the Courtyard of the Tent of Meeting." I asked earlier: why only "in the Courtyard"? Rather, it hints at this: that which is now in the Courtyard will in the future be "inside and within." Even though at that time the Name was complete, nevertheless, everything that is destined to be hidden is like... until the future. This is hinted at in the Courtyard of the Tent of Meeting...

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the Passover sacrifice and the responses to the "Four Sons." ## Rich Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Ashirah*. While this term usually refers to matzah made with wine, oil, or honey, the author uses it here as a heading for "rich" or deep intellectual commentary.</note>

<margin>The Rabbi <note>original: "מהר''י" (Mahari), likely referring to a specific teacher or the author's own gloss</note></margin> regarding all these matters: the essence of this teaching is to be understood plainly—that the Holy One, Blessed be He, is both revealed and hidden. He is revealed through His actions but hidden in His true essence. Similarly, the Torah is revealed, yet contains a hidden dimension. One might ask: what is this teaching coming to tell us? Is this not something known and explicit to every beginning student? <note>original: "בר רב דחד יומא" (bar rav de-chad yoma), an Aramaic expression for a student of only one day, meaning a novice.</note> We also need to clarify what is "revealed" about Israel and what is "hidden" within them. The meaning of this statement is that God is the "Revealed," and the "Hidden" refers to the Primordial or Sealed aspect. These two are bound together, and all this will be explained with God’s help. Regarding the word "In the beginning" <note>original: "בראשית" (Bereishit)</note>, the Sages taught that the Holy One, Blessed be He, created all worlds for the sake of the Torah and for the sake of Israel, in order to bestow goodness upon others. The entire creation exists so that Israel might receive the Torah, know His Name, and bow before His divinity for their own good, thereby meriting eternal existence. They further said that the Holy One, Blessed be He, created the world using the "Holy Tongue" <note>Hebrew: *Lashon HaKodesh*, referring to Hebrew</note>. This is what the commentator Rashi notes when he says a woman should be called *Ishah* because she was taken from *Ish* (man); from here we learn the world was created with the Holy Tongue. We must look closely: it should have said that when God created the world, He spoke in the Holy Tongue. Similarly, when Israel was redeemed from Egypt to receive the Torah, they were redeemed only in the merit of the Holy Tongue. These three things—God, the Torah, and Israel—are bound together. When He makes His divinity known through the creation of the world, so too the Torah and Israel are linked. This is the version of the blessing we chose: "Who chose us from all nations and exalted us above all tongues," meaning our Torah is above every other language because the Holy Tongue is the source. The matter is thus: among all the seventy languages of the nations, there is no language that does not have some words from the Holy Tongue mixed into it, such as the word "two" found in various dialects <note>original: "ש''ט בכתפי... פת באפריקי", the author refers to a Talmudic teaching that certain foreign-sounding words in the Torah are actually 'two' in other languages like Coptic or African dialects</note>. Do not think that our Holy Torah is mixed with the languages of the nations; rather, think of it the other way around: every nation has some "holy" words mixed into theirs. However, Israel and the Holy Tongue are entirely holy and spiritual, distinct from all other languages. The reason is that although the other nations stem from the "side of impurity," they still have some root or hold in the upper holiness. However, Israel is like the "inner face," and Israel is entirely holy; therefore, the Holy Tongue is entirely theirs.

**But** we must explain what the "Holy Tongue" is and why it is called such. Earlier scholars have already addressed this. Maimonides in *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "מורה נבוכי'" (Moreh Nevuchim)</note> wrote his view, which Rabbi Moshe Zakuto <note>original: "רמ''ז" (Remez)</note> quoted and compared in the section on the Golden Calf, though he disagreed. Nachmanides <note>original: "רמ''בן" (Ramban)</note> explained there that it is called "Holy" because it is the language in which God speaks to His prophets and angels, and the names of the Patriarchs are called by this language. But we still need to know why God chose this specific language. The earlier scholars left me room to distinguish myself here. Alongside this explanation, I will clarify a great and powerful inquiry: Why does the Torah mention physical rewards and punishments, but does not explicitly mention spiritual and eternal rewards? Now listen to me, and let your souls be sanctified. In *The Guide for the Perplexed*, he discusses "divine attributes" based on the human form mentioned in the Bible, such as "the eyes of God," "the hand of God," "the feet of God," and the entire stature of man. This is mentioned in the verse: "Upon the throne was a likeness like the appearance of a man." However, one must know in their heart that the Creator is not a physical body and cannot be perceived as one. *The Guide for the Perplexed* explained these attributes his way, and the author of *The Holy Service* <note>original: "עבודת הקודש" (Avodat HaKodesh) by Meir ibn Gabbai</note> explained them at length according to the path of Loving-kindness. To understand this well, we must first establish two premises. Premise 1: As explained in the book *The Orchard* <note>original: "פרדס" (Pardes Rimonim) by Moshe Cordovero</note>, our holy letters are not arbitrary symbols like those of other nations. Rather, they are spiritual essences carved from Above. Premise 2: Also explained in *The Orchard*, a physical "eye" is not called an "eye" because of its physical substance, but because of the power of "sight" which is called an "eye." Similarly, a "hand" is not essentially the limb, but the power of "action" or "taking." In the Talmudic tractate Gittin, they discuss "hands" that are not "proven" <note>term: *Yadayim she-einan mochichot* (unproven hands) — a legal concept regarding whether an ambiguous statement has legal force</note>, meaning the power of acquisition. When the Sages say a minor girl "has no hand," they do not mean she is missing a limb, but that she lacks the legal power to receive marriage or divorce. Likewise, the common phrase "there are feet to the matter" means the matter has a basis or support. This is the explanation for all the limbs. Now we come to the explanation: the "Eye" itself refers to Divine Providence, which cascades down from above through thousands upon thousands of levels, one above the other, until its physical reflection in man—the power of physical sight—is called an "eye." Just as the four physical elements are an extension of the spiritual...

<column-break/>

## Guarded Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Shamurah*. This section comments on the standard text of the Passover Haggadah.</note>

<margin>Shield of Abraham <note>original: "מגן אברהם" (Magen Avraham), a famous 17th-century commentary on the Code of Jewish Law</note></margin> Israel is compared to the booths (*Sukkot*)... for our King has been our refuge from of old. From of old, He has been our refuge, literally. Just as a garden is fenced, He protected us when we were few. As I wrote, he will save his house alone, to educate us that there is none above Him. We were in exile and were not redeemed in booths, yet we remained attached to Him, blessed be He. Even in a time of distress, the Passover offering reminds Israel that even when we are crushed with suffering, we have not been forgotten by Him. It is written: "They shall call, and He shall answer." Even if we have sinned, His love and attachment to us—or to Israel—will not be harmed.

It did not occur to me that you could not pass before the "Jealous God" <note>original: "אל קנא" (El Kanna)</note>. That is to say, I do not want you to be attached to other gods at all. I do not want you to be in exile except through the attachment to His Oneness and His Providence. Or as they accepted and said, "We will serve the Lord," meaning Him alone. This focus began with Abraham the Hebrew, who received it from his ancestors and it was refined through him: "And I took your father Abraham." After that, they were not just called "Ancestors," but specifically Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and we are the branches among them. "Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt." This phrasing is difficult; it should have said "and they went." But "Descended" implies a spiritual descent from above, a great decline, as the ten tribes were destined to go down there. The matter of the years in Egypt was set in motion for Israel.

**Blessed** is He who keeps His promise to Israel... This is difficult: why does the Haggadah bring the beginning of the verse "and they shall serve them and they shall afflict them," which is not a "good" promise? We can answer that out of the darkness comes light. When the good comes, the preceding evil is remembered to increase the joy. Or we remember it to explain the reason for eating bitter herbs (*Maror*), because "they embittered their lives." Our father Abraham saw in his vision that a servant would inherit him, as he said to God: "What will You give me... and the steward of my house is Eliezer of Damascus." God replied: "This one shall not inherit you, but one who comes from your own body." That is, this servant will not inherit you. However, to understand the "contraction" or limitation: "He who comes from your body" eventually became "we were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt." Thus, "and they shall serve them" was actually part of the good promise, as God "calculated the end" <note>original: "חישב את הקץ" (Chishev et ha-Ketz)</note> to fulfill what He said to Abraham. In the Talmud, Rabbi Hama bar Guria said in the name of Rav: A person should never favor one son over the others, for because of the weight of two shekels of silk that Jacob gave to Joseph more than his other sons, his brothers became jealous of him, and the matter evolved until our ancestors went down to Egypt. The Tosafot <note>medieval commentators</note> ask: Even without this, wasn't it already decreed "and they shall serve them and afflict them"? Perhaps they would not have been decreed such heavy affliction if not for this. For the 400 years began thirty years before Isaac was born. This is the view of the Great Rabbi, Rashi. However, the "Wisdom of Solomon" <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria, the Maharshal</note> erased this in the Tosafot and corrected the text to say that the 400 years began from the birth of Isaac. This is still not perfectly understood. It must be explained thus: we see that God was lenient in every way, so such a harsh affliction would not have been decreed. The Gaon <note>the Vilna Gaon</note> found room to distinguish himself in explaining the Tosafot. They have a difficulty with the verses: If the decree was 430 years from the "Covenant between the Pieces," why does the verse say 400 years? And if the prophecy doesn't count until Isaac was born (when they became "strangers"), then the 400 years fits, but later the verse says "the residence of the children of Israel... was 430 years." Therefore, the Tosafot believe the decree was indeed 400 years from the Covenant, but because of the sin with Joseph, the exile was extended by another 30 years—as Joseph was 30 years old when he stood before Pharaoh. Thus the decree was "calculated" <note>term: *Chishev* — God calculated the timing to favor Israel</note>. The Haggadah says "Blessed is He who calculated the end," for the servitude and the awakening were all foreseen, but free will was given. If not for the Joseph incident, the 400 years would have started from the "Seed" being strangers. God "calculated" to make it as He said.

**And it is this [promise]** that has stood... This is difficult: previously it was talking only about Egypt, but now it talks about "every generation" that stands against us to destroy us. Also, the section "Go and learn [what Laban sought to do]" refers to a time before Egypt. Furthermore, why say "in every generation they stand against us... and the Holy One, Blessed be He, saves us"? What is the greatness in that? It would be better if they never stood against us at all so we wouldn't need saving! In Tractate Sotah, Rabbi Ezra explains: In the merit of the righteous women, Israel was redeemed. When they went to draw water, the Holy One, Blessed be He, would prepare...
<note>The text ends mid-sentence with the catchword "prepare."</note>

<summary>This page explores the mystical nature of the Hebrew language as a divine tool of creation and analyzes the Haggadah's "Blessed is He who keeps His promise," specifically calculating how the 400-year Egyptian exile was fulfilled and influenced by the sale of Joseph.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the Passover themes, specifically transitioning from the nature of the "Hidden" and "Revealed" into a detailed comparison between the Exodus from Egypt and the purification laws of the leper (Metzora). ### Tractate Pesachim: Shmurah Matzah

### Rich Matzah
<note>Hebrew: *Matzah Ashirah*. In a legal sense, this refers to matzah made with juice or oil, but here it serves as a title for "enriched" or deep homiletical commentary.</note>

<margin>This was written concerning the "leprosy of our distress." Our Sages of blessed memory said that the "Abomination of the Egyptians" refers to Pharaoh, who said, "The Nile is mine." Our Sages said he was afflicted with leprosy so that he could not flee. It is written: "And you shall take a bundle of hyssop and dip it in the blood that is in the basin, and strike the lintel and the two doorposts." Why a bundle of hyssop? To burn away the spirit of impurity and to show his "buttons" <note>likely a metaphor for spiritual points of connection</note> like those places of complete faith. For it says, "And He will pass over the door and not allow the Destroyer to enter your houses to strike you," because He sees the Holy Name inscribed upon the entrance. Close to this, the Ibn Ezra wrote on this portion: "The cedar wood and the hyssop... behold the leper, the afflicted house, and the impurity of the dead are similar to the Passover of Egypt."</margin>

Truthfully, regarding the verse "And he shall be brought to the priest," the Sages asked: what is the practical difference of this portion? The theme of the day—the Exodus from Egypt—has a resemblance to the leper, and vice versa. Concerning the great Redeemer and Prophet <note>Moses</note>, like whom none have arisen, it was also through leprosy that he was "brought" when his hand became leprous. It is written: "This shall be the law of the leper" <term>Metzora: A person afflicted with a spiritual skin disease caused by gossip</term>. The King of Egypt was like a "shut-in" leper who had no passage, just as Israel in Egypt were like a shut-in leper. The "bundle of hyssop" mentioned in the Exodus is exactly like that brought for the purification of a leper. The leper, the afflicted house, and the impurity of the dead are all in the likeness of the Passover in Egypt.

This matter of removing the "evil spirit" requires explanation. Our Sages said on the verse "This is the law (*Torah*) of the leper": This is the law of the "Motzi-Ra" <note>original: "מוציא רע" (one who brings forth evil), a Hebrew wordplay on "Metzora"</note>, for leprosy comes because of Evil Speech <term>Lashon Hara: Derogatory speech or gossip</term>. In Tractate Erachin, Rashi explains: Why did the Torah say a leper should bring two birds for his purification? Because he committed an act of "chirping" (gossip), the Torah said let him bring a "chirping" sacrifice. So too, from a murky mind comes evil speech. This is why Moses' hand was stricken with leprosy—due to his murky words <note>referring to Moses saying "They will not believe me"</note>. In the Midrash, Rabbi Yannai said: Even Solomon proclaimed, "He who guards his mouth and his tongue, guards his soul from distress (*mi-tzarot*)." Do not read it as "from distress" (*mi-tzarot*), but "from leprosy" (*mi-metzora*). The Zohar also expounds that his "soul" is his "breath of life." One might ask: we see many people who speak gossip and yet are not stricken with leprosy? The answer is that their *souls* are stricken with leprosy. Leprosy is a stroke from God. We find this in Egypt: Israel was not redeemed except for the merit that there was no gossip among them. On the contrary, they consumed "holy gossip" <note>an ironic phrase suggesting they shared only good or necessary things</note>. I saw in the Midrash Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Kapra: By the merit of four things Israel was redeemed from Egypt: 1) They did not change their names; Reuben and Simeon went down, Reuben and Simeon came up. 2) They did not change their language; for the "mouth that speaks to you" spoke in the Holy Tongue. 3) They did not speak gossip; for they were told to ask their neighbors for gold and silver, and the matter remained private among them. Not one of them informed on his fellow. 4) They were not promiscuous.

This is known in the laws of the "Ohel" <note>Tent</note> and the scriptural interruption. It is written "The name of his mother was Shelomith daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan." This contradicts what Moses said: "And Moses was afraid and said, 'Surely the matter is known!'" Rashi explains that Moses was worried because there were informers among Israel. He said, "Perhaps they are not worthy of redemption." The "matter was known" why Israel was persecuted more than all seventy nations. But I see that they *were* worthy. We cannot say there were informers but they repented and were thus redeemed, for we see Dathan and Abiram <note>famous biblical antagonists of Moses</note> stayed in their impurity. Rather, we say there were no informers *except* those mentioned by the text, namely Dathan and Abiram, just as it publicized Shelomith. If they were the only ones, why was Moses afraid? The answer is that once he saw them, he feared there were many more like them. But in truth, there were only those few, and the text publicized them because they did not repent. Or, perhaps there were more who did repent. Thus, they were redeemed in the merit of not being like Dathan and Abiram.

Consider this: regarding the merit of not being promiscuous, it is clear—wherever you find licentiousness, "confusion" <note>original: *andralmusia*, a Greek-derived term for chaos or divine plague</note> follows. How could they be redeemed? So too with gossip, for the sin of gossip is greater than the three cardinal sins. As the Sages said: Saul's generation were righteous but lost battles because there were informers among them; Ahab's generation were idolaters but won battles because there were no informers among them.

Regarding the high status of the Holy Tongue and not changing names: why is this so great? The Zohar (Parshat Acharei Mot) teaches that there are three levels bound together: The Holy One, Blessed be He, the Torah, and Israel. Each level has a "Hidden" and a "Revealed" aspect. "He tells His words to Jacob, His statutes and laws to Israel." There are two levels: Jacob and Israel—one revealed and one hidden.

The elders did not understand anything but the second level, and they thought that Joshua was only warning the "middle" ones. They thought they would return to the second level in their redemption. To this they replied, "Far be it from us to forsake the Lord."

<column-break/>

They have no attachment to the Divine Name even in the "middle." A level higher than this is the "Righteous among the Nations" who have an attachment to the Divine through the medium of the Prophet. The third level is Israel in the Diaspora; even if they serve idols, they do so in "purity" <note>meaning, without the intent of actual betrayal, but out of circumstance</note>. Every "oppressor" of Israel becomes a "head." This is the secret of the "Head" I mentioned—the third level. Israel lived among the nations in the midst of their impurity. Even though the celestial prince of that nation caused loss, their attachment is only at the "heads." It is like the light of the sun shining through glass; it is not delayed by the glass but shines through it. Even if we sin by serving idols, it is still "in purity."

Behold, "Esau is a brother to Jacob," and they were in one womb. Esau drew the filth (*zohama*), even in exile. For Jacob became subject to Esau, yet Jacob was refined for his children, who are in the aspect of the "Head" of Esau. Wherever Israel is exiled, they become the "head"—meaning for Israel's sake. This resulted from the "merging" of Jacob and his sons, who were twins. The filth entered Esau and did not remain in Jacob. Therefore, Esau was separated so he would not harm Israel. They were not truly brothers, for "the child of a maidservant is like her" <note>a legal principle regarding status</note>. Therefore, there was no "merging" in Isaac. This is why it says, "And He knew Abraham regarding his son," for he was in the aspect of a Canaanite. Sarah said, "Drive out this handmaid and her son," and the Sages agreed with her. He shall not inherit with my son. From him came the hand of impurity.

Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt, into the "Pit," to be completely refined for the sake of the Glory of Heaven. This explains the portion of Joshua: he mentioned they were in the land of Egypt to be refined. God led Abraham to the land of Canaan to subdue the "Husks" (*Klipot*) <term>Klipot: Mystical 'shells' or 'husks' that conceal the divine light and represent evil</term> and to awaken holiness. These places are the "hard husks," as it says "the practice of the land of Egypt" and "the practice of the land of Canaan." They were refined. Joshua’s concern was that they should not be cut off by their sins from the supernal holiness, for "the Lord's portion is His people." Even if they sin and "forsake," they can still serve the Lord within the husk, like Abraham our forefather. Even in Canaan, they would be at the third level I mentioned—where it is merely a "passage" and not "garbing" oneself in the husk. The "Head" remains holy. Thus, a person returns to the "Other Side of the River" <note>the Jordan</note>. There, at the "Other Side of the River," was the worship of idols and the Canaanites. Joshua said "Choose for yourselves," for there the "Husks of the Seventy Princes" begin. It started in Babylon in the days of the Generation of the Dispersion, and from there the light of Abraham dawned to nullify it. Afterward came the practices of Canaan and Egypt, which were even more corrupt. Abraham went to Canaan to shine light there, but the filth was still uncertain among Israel—whether they were in darkness there. Regarding the Egyptian husks, they had already "passed over" and were refined and redeemed. Therefore Joshua said: "Choose for yourselves," whether to be truly among the nations who are not attached even through a medium, and to serve other gods literally among the nations.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and mystical exploration of the Torah's structure, transitioning from the symbolic meaning of the Exodus rituals to a deeper analysis of the relationship between the "Hidden" (mystical) and "Revealed" (legal) aspects of the Torah. It specifically addresses how the physical commandments performed in this world reflect eternal spiritual realities.</meta>

### Tractate Pesachim: Shmurah Matzah

**Even though** it is explained in the *Book of Formation* <note>original: *Sefer Yetzirah*, an ancient Jewish mystical text</note> that the chain of emanation is without number until it reaches this lowest boundary, nonetheless, the root of the lower is in the upper, and the upper in the one above it, rising higher and higher until the Essential Supernal Root. It is further said that the Torah has a "hidden" and a "revealed" dimension. The meaning here is that the revealed is the hidden, and the hidden is the revealed. For just as the Holy Language <note>Hebrew</note> emerges from holiness and emanates downward—as I have explained elsewhere—so too are the practical commandments which a person performs and through which they live the "life of souls." These correspond to the 600,000 letters in the Torah <note>A traditional idea that there are 600,000 letters in the Torah, matching the 600,000 souls of Israel</note>, for the law for the Torah and for its engravings is one and the same. Although the Torah has become "physicalized" through descending levels, its words shine most brightly. If Man had not sinned, he would not be purely material but purely intellectual, and "the earth would be filled with knowledge" <note>Isaiah 11:9</note> even within his earthly nature. But now, no intellectual part remains in him except the heart, as is the secret I have written elsewhere regarding the verse: "Man looks at the eyes, but the Lord looks at the heart" <note>1 Samuel 16:7</note>. For when the first Man followed his eyes—as it is written, "pleasant to the eyes" <note>Genesis 3:6</note>—the heart was no longer seen in him. Before man sinned, he remained in the Garden of Eden "to work it and to keep it" <note>Genesis 2:15</note>. Our Sages interpreted "to work it" as the positive commandments and "to keep it" as the negative commandments, which he fulfilled in a different, more spiritual manner, as explained in the *Pardes* <note>Likely *Pardes Rimonim* by Moshe Cordovero</note> in the "Gate of the Soul." Thus, Man and the Torah are one and the same, and your sign for this is: **"This is the Torah of the man"** <note>Numbers 19:14; here interpreted mystically to mean the Torah and Man share the same structure</note>.

This hints at the 248 limbs and 365 sinews <note>The traditional count of components in the human body</note> corresponding to the 613 commandments. The 600,000 letters of the Torah correspond to the 600,000 souls of Israel. The matter of "working it and keeping it" refers to the souls. Nevertheless, they emerge from the source of holiness, one corresponding to the other, for the reward of a commandment is the soul and the spiritual body of the commandment itself. This is the meaning of the Sages' statement: "If a person sanctifies himself a little below, they sanctify him much from above." For example, regarding the ritual fringes <note>*Tzitzit*</note>: now that we are in our physical state, they are merely physical strings. However, in the higher realms, reaching the very peak of the levels where they sparkle, they are exalted things. See the verse: "No eye has seen, O God, besides You" <note>Isaiah 64:3</note>. So it is with all commandments. This is why "the reward for a commandment is the commandment itself" <note>Ethics of the Fathers 4:2</note>—meaning its root. See the work of Recanati <note>Menachem Recanati, a 13th-century Kabbalist</note> on the essence of punishment and reward from God.

We view the "preparation" in the way of reward and punishment like that of a human king, but the one who develops his intellect to see things differently understands what is written: "it is his reward," meaning a necessity. For the reward of the commandment is the commandment itself, as one attaches oneself to its spirituality. This is why "one commandment drags another commandment along," and similarly with sin: the punishment for a sin is the sin itself—its root in the "shells" <note>*Kelipot*, the kabbalistic term for forces of impurity</note>. For the revealed and the hidden in the Talmud and in practice are all one, unified in the secret of the Holy Language. Even the mundane physical aspects are refined through the purity of the holy. Through this, the matter of the revealed and hidden parts of the entire Torah is clarified. Behold, the world thinks the hidden is something entirely different from the revealed.

**However**, this is not so. Rather, the hidden has simply become thickened and physicalized, and that is its "revelation." This is the interpretation of the verse: everything exists in the intellect according to its proper context. Just as copper can be made to resemble gold, yet remains a lower level of composition, so is the "revealed" in relation to the "hidden." A similar idea was explained by the Rabbi <note>Maimonides</note> in the *Guide for the Perplexed* at the beginning of his book. Through this, we can understand the statement of our Sages in Tractate Sukkah regarding Rabbi Zakkai: "He did not leave out Scripture, Mishnah... [down to] a Great Matter and a Small Matter." The "Great Matter" refers to the *Work of the Chariot* <note>*Ma'aseh Merkavah*, or Divine Mysticism</note>, while the "Small Matter" refers to the legal debates of Abaye and Rava <note>Famous Sages of the Talmud</note>.

The earlier commentators wondered: are not the debates of Abaye and Rava the very life and light of our existence, the "peg" upon which everything hangs? How could he call them a "small matter"? In the *Ein Yaakov* <note>A collection of Talmudic legends</note>, the opinions of the Rashba and others are cited. The explanation is this: the legal debates and analysis establish the laws of the Talmud, which are the fulfillment of the Written Torah in their clarity, so that man may understand the performance of the commandments "which a person shall do and live by them" <note>Leviticus 18:5</note>. The true meaning of this verse is that the vitality within these debates is exactly what I have said: that the physical commandments of our Torah are both physical and eternal. One must "do them today" in order "to receive their reward tomorrow." The reward is not external; it is the commandment itself. Just as a small piece of writing below appears tiny, but its source above is great, so too is the performance of a deed today: it is a "small matter," yet its root above in the Divine Chariot is a "great" and eternal matter. The small matter is literally the great matter, just as a grain of wheat grows into a full stalk. Thus it is clear that the Oral Torah—which is the "revealed" part that man performs—is itself the "hidden" secret of the Written Torah, which is entirely comprised of God's names and the *Work of the Chariot*. This is the meaning of the "two great lights": the "greater light" and the "lesser light." The masters of truth <note>Kabbalists</note> have already written that the secret of the Sun and the Moon is the secret of the Written Torah and the Oral Torah. Now, in the time of souls, they are a "greater light" and a "lesser light," as mentioned: a "great matter" and a "small matter." In our exile, these two great lights are rooted in a single "Crown of Torah." This is hinted at by the fact that the entire Oral Torah is contained within the Written Torah. From this, we understand "The Torah is light," for it shines from the attribute of Strength (*Gevurah*). In the Midrash on Genesis, Rabbi Simon says the word "light" appears five times, corresponding to the Five Books of the Torah. In Tractate Sanhedrin, regarding the verse "He has placed me in darkness like the eternally dead," Rabbi Jeremiah says this refers to the Babylonian Talmud. At first glance, this seems contradictory—is it not light that enlightens our eyes? Is it not our brilliance and light? Why call it "the eternally dead"? Furthermore, the Midrash explains that the light mentioned at the beginning of the Torah refers to the Five Books, and it says there that "He separated the light" and God hid it. This makes sense if it refers to the light visible to humans, which can be hidden. However, the matter is one and the same: the person who merits it gains the "hidden light," which is the "Garments of Light" <note>spelled with an *Aleph*</note>, a topic I have elaborated on elsewhere—this is the hiding of the Torah's light. The simple meaning and the homiletic interpretation of Rabbi Simon are one. It is clear from our words that the Torah itself, in the Holy Language, is entirely the secret of His names. The practice of the Torah, "to work it and to keep it," is entirely the *Work of the Chariot*. Then the Torah is entirely a clear light. Only when Man became physicalized was the light removed—meaning the "Garments of Light" [spelled with an *Aleph*] were replaced by "Garments of Skin" [spelled with an *Ayin*] because of sin. Since it is skin <note>materiality</note>, the life-force was removed from this.

<column-break/>

They are like you; just as you strive for liberation, so do they. <margin>This refers to the "possessions" that are mine essentially—meaning their guiding star (*mazal*) that they used to worship. They will humble it with a few people, as it is written: "with seventy souls."</margin> A question arises: what does this come to teach us, that they were few? Is it not explicitly written in the portion of *Vayigash* that they were only seventy souls? Rather, he states the reason they merited such increase was because they were few. This is like the verse: "It was not because you were more numerous... for you are the fewest" <note>Deuteronomy 7:7</note>, meaning because you diminish yourselves, as the Sages interpreted. This caused the few to become many. The "fewness" hints at the "multitude," for there were seventy souls, and each one of them was equal to an entire nation, as there are seventy nations. Behold, God allotted the nations to the heavenly hosts, and they are placed under them. But "He placed His name, the Lord your God, upon you," and you are considered "as the stars of the heavens" over whom the nations have no dominion, for you are like stars forever and ever.

**"And he became there a great nation"** etc. He interprets the word "great" both in what precedes it and follows it. "A great nation"—distinguished, as the Sages said: "The academy never ceased from our ancestors." A teacher taught: "Amram was the leader of the generation." He was great and powerful, encompassing both quantity (numbers) and quality (strength/heroes). "And numerous, as it is said..." meaning not only did the academy never cease, but he chose to go from perfection to perfection. Unlike what Jacob said regarding Laban's house—"I will return in peace"—which would have meant merely returning to his original state of perfection. Rather, it says "and you shall be for peace," which refers to "ornaments upon ornaments," except that we were "naked and bare" <note>Ezekiel 16:7</note> due to the primordial Serpent who was "cunning" <note>same Hebrew root as 'naked'</note>, as I have elaborated elsewhere.

**"And they dealt ill with us"**—it is easy to humble them. "And they dealt ill with us" <note>Hebrew: *vaya-re-u otanu*</note>—our Sages explained this means they made us into "evil ones" (*re'im*) and sinners like themselves, for every sinner is a fool. "And let us deal wisely with them" <note>Exodus 1:10</note>. Wisdom is sometimes sent to the physical masses, as it is written: "for with clever stratagems you shall wage war." And that which is written, "and it shall go up from the land," refers to what was said above regarding the homeland. "And numerous like the sprout of the field..." and "it shall go up from the land like the sprout of the field." "And they afflicted us with their burdens"—this affliction refers to marital relations, so that offspring would not emerge. This was against the "quality" mentioned above regarding strength. "With hard labor"—this was to prevent the "quantity" or increase in numbers. "And we cried out..." It is difficult to see what new point is being made by citing verse after verse. Rather, it is to reconcile the three different ways God is mentioned. Regarding "And we cried out," it says "to the Lord, the God of our fathers." Regarding "And He heard," it mentions only "the Lord." Regarding "And He saw," it mentions no name at all. To this, he answers: Israel prayed by the merit of the Patriarchs, but the Holy One answered them for His own sake, as He promised: "I am the Lord, I am faithful." What is the proof that Israel prayed through the merit of their fathers? It says: "And the king of Egypt died, and they groaned... and they cried out." This verse is difficult; on the contrary, they should have been happy [that the king died]! Rashi wrote what he wrote, but there is another difficulty: "And God knew"—it's obvious He knows, so what does this teach us? I heard an explanation: when a king dies, all his people weep, cry out, and eulogize him. Anyone who does not do so offends the king's honor. Thus, all of Egypt were crying and weeping, and Israel also cried out. But Israel's cry was from the hardship of the labor. "And the children of Israel groaned from the labor." The whole world thought they were crying like the king's other servants over his passing, but "And God knew"—He, may He be blessed, knew the hidden thoughts: that they were actually crying out to God and praying about the troubles of the labor. Certainly, a cry without speech is not a "prayer." Rather, the case was that they spoke during their crying: "O God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob!" Their intent was to awaken the merit of the fathers, while the listeners understood...

# Tractate Pesachim

Spreading from one cause to another through the world of the celestial spheres and upward into the world of angels is the secret of the **Chariot** <note>The *Merkavah* or Divine Chariot, a central theme in Jewish mysticism regarding the vision of God’s throne</note>: Michael, Gabriel, Uriel, and Raphael. Michael corresponds to **Water**, Gabriel to **Fire**, Uriel to **Air**, and Raphael to **Earth**. However, their foundations are rooted in spirits and waters of a light within a light, a skin of light, rising higher and higher. These are the four camps of the Divine Presence: the **Man**, the **Lion**, the **Ox**, and the **Eagle** <note>These are the four faces of the "Living Creatures" seen in the Prophet Ezekiel’s vision of the Divine Chariot</note>, which become increasingly refined and spiritual as they ascend. The four letters of the Divine Name <note>The Tetragrammaton (Y-H-W-H)</note> are called Fire, Water, Spirit, and Earth; their purity and spirituality are beyond measure, beyond searching, and beyond understanding—there, these names exist in their true essence. 

Afterward, through the **Chain of Emanation** <note>term: *Hishtalshelut* — the process by which divine energy steps down through various levels to create the physical world</note>, these elements rule over the four Living Creatures, then through the emanation into the four camps of the Divine Presence, then into the world of the spheres, and finally into this world, where they are called water, fire, air, and earth. However, above, in the four letters of the Name, they are "Water, Fire, Air, and Earth" in essence. This is because the letters are not merely agreed-upon symbols like the alphabets of other nations; rather, they are the functional power of hidden spiritual forms. The shapes of the letters, their sharp points, and their "crowns" <note>Small calligraphic flourishes on certain Hebrew letters</note> all indicate how God understood and clarified existence. 

Thus, we say that the matter of Divine Providence is "Eye" in its essence; for the root of the letter combination for "Eye" (*Ayin*)—comprised of the letters *Yod*, *Vav*, *Dalet*, *Nun*—follows the secret that the descending letters are themselves the essence of the thing. This applies to His Providence, and likewise the combination of the letters *Yod*, *Resh*, *Dalet* <note>Spelling out the word "descend"</note>. The letter *Yod* at its root is a Divine power of His kindness, which then descends. The same applies to the "Gevurot" <note>The Divine attribute of Judgment or Strength</note> on the left side. The secret is that everything in the world is an emanation from the essence of these Names. These Names are "borrowed" terms—just as we speak of the "handles" of vessels or the "legs" of a chair as borrowed metaphors for the power of gripping or the power of standing. 

The same is true for all names of the parts of the human stature; they exist in spirit, and through emanation, they are the model of what is above. The "Southern Foundations" are called by these terms as a metaphor. This is the meaning of "Man in our image"—a "Man" seen upon the Throne. It means that there is a "measure of the stature" in essence: a true Hand and a true Foot. Just as with every word we speak in our tongue, the **Holy Language** <note>Hebrew</note> implies that these things exist essentially in the Holy One, blessed be He. We only use this language because it was hidden within our souls as it descended from the holy place. This is the nature of the Holy Language: it emanates from the eternal Holy Tree, and we use it for physical matters by way of metaphor and through the power of emanation. This is the explanation of all laws: they rise from level to level, one higher than the other, "Hand for a Hand" and "Eye for an Eye"—from level to level. 

This was the wisdom of the first Man (*Adam*) in the naming of the creatures. Through the strength of his perception of the Holy Language, he attained knowledge of every created thing and its root above. It will be explained that the "vitality of the soul" is not mentioned directly as a spiritual essence in the Torah. On the contrary, spiritual realities are mentioned in their essence, while physical things are mentioned by way of "borrowing" or metaphor. For example, "I will give you your rains" (*geshem*) <note>Leviticus 26:4</note>—these physical objects are not actually called "Geshem" in truth. The word *Geshem* is a holy term for the spiritual flow and nourishment above. It emanates and descends until, in the physical world, it manifests as those drops that make things grow, which are then called "rain" (*geshem*) by metaphor. The word *Geshem* "pierces" and descends from the essence of the "Holy Substance" through all worlds. In all those worlds, the term is a metaphor; the true spiritual essence is only found in the holiness of the Holy One, blessed be He. There, it is spiritual and awake. In our worlds, it is a borrowed term according to the level of each world. As for the end of these promises: "Blessed is the One who grants Man knowledge."

<margin>All these matters are mentioned in the compilation *Chesed L'Avraham* Part 2, from the "Siftei Nofek," regarding the "Appointed Times," their width and depth. See also my own "Writing of Truth" (*Ktav Emet*) on the portions *Vayechi* and *Toldot*, pages 68, 69, and 60.</margin>

And what was partially explained is that Man is not a living god, for "Eye for an Eye, Hand for a Hand, Foot for a Foot" means they are called such in the Holy Language because everything spreads from the Supernal Root. That which emanates through the chain of emanation thousands and tens of thousands of times through all the worlds—without limit—until the power of human sight is formed, which is his providence; therefore, the name "Eye" is borrowed for him.

And so it was with the creation of the worlds, both spiritual and physical. At first glance, the physical are not spiritual, but in truth, they are all grasped together and linked as one matter. They simply proceed and emanate from one state to another: from Emanation (*Atzilut*) to Creation (*Beriyah*), from Creation to Formation (*Yetzirah*), and from Formation to Action (*Asiyah*) <note>The Four Worlds of Kabbalistic cosmology</note>. They change through millions of levels without number. Every time they emanate, they become more "thickened" or material. This one has this quality, and that one has that; this is extremely refined spirit, and that is not as refined, until it becomes increasingly thick as it moves toward this physical world. Everything that exists in the upper worlds exists in the lower worlds. From this, we can understand the saying that the Holy One, blessed be He, is "Hidden and Revealed"—meaning the revelation of His Godliness is made known through the creation of this world. His creation was a descent from spiritual to spiritual until it reached the physical. The revelation is the "hidden," and the "hidden" is the revelation. Thus the world was created through the Holy Language, for He created it with the letters of the 
<meta>catchword: Alphabet</meta>
Alphabet.

"And he stayed there" <note>Deuteronomy 26:5, from the Passover Haggadah</note>—this teaches that Jacob did not descend to Egypt to become permanently settled. When Jacob perceived the "Spheres" (*Ofanim*) there in Egypt, he saw that every "face" was impure and surrounded by an external veil. Therefore, "He descended there," but he did not intend in his mind to stay and be swallowed up. For if he had, he would have been immersed like the "dead," as I wrote in my deep writings regarding the "Food of Egypt." If he had stayed one moment longer, he would have been—God forbid—swallowed up. Therefore, Jacob did not intend to settle. And thus, his ears heard... I found written in the pamphlet of the **Arizal** <note>Rabbi Isaac Luria, the foremost 16th-century Kabbalist</note> regarding the soul's "rain" (*geshem*)... just as the Ministering Angel of Esau admitted to the blessings, so too Pharaoh said, "Your brothers have come to you," meaning your brothers

are similar.

...similar to them, like small fish in their bellies. What is the meaning of this great matter? Our Sages have already revealed the concept of the "New Song" <note>original: *Shirah Chadashah*</note>. When the term is feminine, it refers to redemptions of the past; but for the future, it says "A New Song" <note>original: *Shir Chadash*</note> in the masculine. This is the secret of the "Direct Light" and the "Returning Light." Direct Light is the secret of the Male world, and Returning Light is the secret of the Feminine. 

This is also the secret of the feminine's adornment with a mirror. For a mirror reflects when the light of desire or the Returning Light strikes it. This is visible to the eye as the foundation of the Supernal Feminine—the "Womb" of the 600,000 souls of Israel who fruitfully multiply. For holy souls, in the secret of their reincarnation, are many in the place of "Building Purity." This is the secret of "The mother of all living." Joseph is the secret of "Gathering" (*Asifah*), as said of the righteous. All of this is hinted at in these names: the souls of Israel that rose to 600,000, for there it is possible to receive the Torah.

Accordingly, in the "Return," there are 600,000 letters which are the root for the 600,000 souls. This is their kingdom. They see in the mirror because this redemption was a "New Song" (feminine). Through the "Mirrors of the Legions" <note>A reference to the mirrors used by Jewish women in Egypt to encourage their husbands, mentioned in Midrash</note>, they established legions of 600,000 to draw down the root of the 600,000 souls from the womb of the Supernal Feminine. But in the future, there will be a "New Song" (masculine) from the Male world. For the souls of Israel were separated and did not have the strength to rise—that is, the part belonging to the wife's house. But "her husband shall establish it and build it," and he will go... as it is written: "Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you" <note>Isaiah 60:1</note>. This is the Direct Light.

From this, the words of the Haggadah are clarified: "Blessed is He who keeps His promise to Israel." One might ask: what does "keeps" mean, since we see we were enslaved and are in exile among the nations through Divine wrath? "And it is *this* that has stood" <note>referring to the "Ve-hi She-amdah" prayer</note>—meaning the Feminine aspect above helped, and the redemption came from the side of Returning Light. Therefore, it was not an eternal redemption. This is the reason that in every generation they rise against us, but the Holy One, blessed be He, saves us from their hand. However, in the future redemption, "she shall no longer rise" alone; rather, the Lord Himself will arise, as it is written: "Now I will arise, says the Lord" <note>Psalms 12:6</note>. 

Pharaoh hinted at this: he did not decree death except upon the males. For it is known that the "Direct Light" is the Male world. "Go and learn what Laban the Aramean sought to do" <note>A quote from the Haggadah</note>. Jacob did not go down to stay, but only to sojourn. But Laban sought to "uproot everything." Laban is **Balaam** <note>A common mystical association identifying the two biblical figures</note>, and Balaam had a hold in all the worlds. Concerning him, it is said "An Aramean destroyed (*oved*) my father." He descended to Egypt, for the man Laban descended to Egypt because he is Balaam, and he established his grip in Egypt to uproot everything, so that Israel would have no holding—neither in the Male world nor the Feminine world. As the Sages said: "The daughters are my daughters, and all that you see is mine" <note>Genesis 31:43</note>. The word "He" (*Hu*) refers to the "Seer," for the prophet was formerly called a Seer. Therefore, Balaam’s spirit dwelt among the nations...

"And he went down to Egypt, compelled by the Divine Word." This is difficult, as the language of "descending" usually implies a voluntary action. It seems the author of the Haggadah is not merely explaining "And he descended," but the opposite. He is answering the difficulty regarding the secret revealed above: that Laban is Balaam. Now, most Kabbalists agree that the secret of reincarnation only applies to Israel and not to the nations. To this, he says: "An Aramean destroyed my father and went down to Egypt"—this was "compelled." For in truth, this measure does not usually apply to the nations, but here it was by Divine decree... for a reason known only to Him, may He be blessed.

# Rich Matzah
<note>original: "Matzah Ashirah" — typically refers to matzah made with fruit juice or eggs, but here used as a title for a deeper discourse on the bread of affliction/faith</note>

And it is written: *This is the Torah which Moses set* <note>Deuteronomy 4:44</note>, for the **Torah of Moses** is the **Talmud** <note>The body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law and legend</note> that he achieved and directed. The law is the "Torah" that a person hints to themselves through intensive analytical study and the "eddies" of the legal discussions. He understood that everything is contained within the written word, for there was no darkness before him, as his face radiated light; he was like a **shining mirror**. Our Sages, of blessed memory, said that he is equal to 600,000 <note>The number of adult Israelites in the Exodus</note>, for 600,000 souls correspond to the 600,000 letters of the Torah.

Returning to the matter: the **Written Torah** is a "secret" and a "hint." A **secret** <note>term: *Sod* — the mystical or hidden meaning of the text</note> is a great matter, like the *Work of Creation*. A **hint** <note>term: *Remez* — the allegorical or suggestive meaning</note> is what the Sages call "the Proclamation." The **Oral Torah** is the Talmud—the debates of Abaye and Rava. The Written Torah is in the **Holy Language** <note>Hebrew</note>, and the "hint" of the Oral Torah is in **Aramaic** <note>original: "Targum"</note>, which is the language that approaches the Holy Language. This is the secret of reading "twice the scripture and once the translation." The scripture, which is the Written Torah, includes two parts, and the translation is one. 

As I have written, this change—the **Babylonian Talmud**—is represented by the translation (Aramaic). However, the **Land of Israel**, in its high degree, is the secret of the Holy Language. The matter revealed in the Holy Language is the "Center"—the **Foundation Stone** from which the world was established, located in the Temple and in Jerusalem. In the first chapter of Tractate Shabbat, it is taught in the name of Rabbi Meir: "Anyone who is permanently settled in the Land of Israel, eats his daily food in ritual purity, speaks the Holy Language, and recites the *Shema* morning and evening, is assured a place in the World to Come." Thus, the high status of the Holy Language is linked to the Land of Israel, for from there the light goes forth, and "the Torah is light."

This is the meaning of the passage in the chapter "The Seller of a Ship": Abaye said, "One of them is better than two of us," but when one of us goes up there (to Israel), he is better than two of them. For Rabbi Jeremiah, when he was here (in Babylon), did not understand what the Sages were saying, but when he went up there, he called us "foolish Babylonians." 

Regarding this, there is a statement in Tractate Chullin: "And three souls... change." Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rav: "These are the wicked of the nations who emerge from Israel in every generation; sometimes two are here and one is there, sometimes two are there and one is here." The point is that after the "change" in the Babylonian style here, they reverse it there, becoming equal to two of the former. The matter is as I explained: "twice scripture and once translation." The Land of Israel is the Holy Language—there is the **Secret** and the **Hint**. The "Hint" refers to the matters of the Oral Torah, but there it is found in great depth because it is closer to the Source, being in the Holy Language, much like the biblical verses themselves. 

This is not the case in the **Babylonian Exile**, where commonness entered, characterized by the secret of "translation" and a sense of "darkness." Because of this, "a man dies" from the many wanderings, and sometimes errors occur, requiring one to "extract light from the darkness." From this power, disputes multiply. In the chapter "The One Who Performs Levirate Marriage," Rabbi Oshaya said: "What is the meaning of 'And I took for myself two staffs, one I called Pleasantness and one I called Injurers' <note>Zechariah 11:7</note>? 'Pleasantness' refers to the scholars of the Land of Israel who treat one another pleasantly in the law. 'Injurers' refers to the scholars of Babylon who injure one another in the law." 

Isaac said: "These are the scholars in the Land of Israel who are gentle with one another in the law, like oil." Conversely, those in Babylon are "bitter" toward one another in the law. Thus, the scholars of the Land of Israel emerge as "shining oil," for "Torah is light." Light and joy are found in the "hint" of the Oral Torah there, and they do not get as "heated" in analytical debate as they do in Babylon. Therefore, they occupy themselves much more with the **Secrets of the Chariot** <note>term: *Maaseh Merkavah* — the highest form of Jewish mysticism</note>, which is a "great matter." The Babylonian scholars, conversely, occupy themselves with "commotion" and almost entirely with "small matters"—the debates of Abaye and Rava. 

Therefore, in the Land of Israel, it is "twice scripture" with the "translation" in each. But when "one of us" (a Babylonian) who has already learned the ways of analytical debate goes up to Israel to learn the Secrets of the Chariot, he is better than two of them. For in the Secrets of the Chariot, one must also employ deep and sweet analysis. Regarding the chapter of the Chariot, a person is asked: "Did you glimpse the Chariot?" which means: "Did you analyze the wisdom?" In the **Zohar**, there is a place for questioning and a place where one cannot ask. When one reaches the level of "the black and the dove," he is at a higher degree to fulfill "you analyzed with wisdom." 

It has been explained that the advantage of the Land of Israel is greater than Babylon, though the wisdom of "small matters"—the debates of Abaye and Rava—is greater in Babylon. From this, we can explain a puzzling statement in the **Jerusalem Talmud** (Tractate Pesachim): Rabbi Hiyya taught: "The Torah speaks of four sons. The **Wise Son** says: 'What are the testimonies, statutes, and laws which the Lord our God commanded you?' You should say to him: 'With a mighty hand the Lord brought us out of Egypt.' The **Wicked Son** says: 'What is this service to you?'—meaning 'What is this burden you tire yourselves with every year?' Since he excludes himself from the community, you should set his teeth on edge and say: 'Because of this the Lord did for *me* when I left Egypt'—for *me* and not for *him*; had that man been in Egypt, he would never have been redeemed. The **Simple Son** <note>original: "Tippesh" — literally 'foolish' or 'dull', often replaced by 'Tam' (simple/innocent) in the standard Haggadah</note> says: 'What is this?' You should teach him the laws of Passover: 'One does not conclude the Passover meal with an **Afikoman**.' What is Afikoman? That one should not get up from one group and enter another. And the **One Who Does Not Know How to Ask**..." 

Behold, your eyes see that the matter is reversed from the order of "Wise to Simple" in our standard Haggadah. I have already explained: the "Wise Man" in the Land of Israel deals with the secrets of the Torah and uses little analytical debate. The opposite is true in Babylon. Thus, the "Wise Man" of the Land of Israel is considered "Simple" in Babylon in terms of analytical debate, and the "Wise Man" of the Diaspora is "Simple" in Israel in terms of...

"My dove, my perfect one" <note>Song of Songs 6:9</note> refers to the heights of the supreme level. The number 2 hints at her second place, and 3 hints at her third place. He praises and flows from the dwelling; then she is "facing the Menorah," giving light. This is not as high as the first supreme level. Sometimes, it is thus in the "West" (the Land of Israel), and it returns: 3, 4, and another 3, which is called "three who ascend in holiness," for it starts below at a small holiness and then ascends. The sign is 3, 4, 3, and it returns. When Israel left Egypt, they were not yet at the peak of holiness. The **Zohar** says they were like one who is impure and comes to wear white and be purified. It is known that during the "Chain of Emanation," ten spheres were created, and in them, you find the sign 3, 4, 3. And he came to reveal a new thing to us that was not explained above regarding the "bringing out" in the Torah. This is that there were two signs in the staff even within the blood, as it is written: "And Aaron's staff swallowed their staffs." The matter follows a path of effort here. In these wonders, this is meant to suggest a "comparison" <note>term: *Gezera Shava* — a legal interpretive tool</note> from afar. The novelty in the **Plague of Blood** was that the blood did not occur by chance, but the water essentially became blood, like blood that comes from heat. This is why it says "Blood and Fire." Furthermore, there was a novelty even within the miracle: there was a "pillar of smoke," which is not in the nature of water. ## Another explanation: these 10 words indicate all 10 plagues.

And this is not difficult at all. Afterward, a new section begins: "These are the ten plagues, etc." Rabbi Yehuda gives them signs <note>Dtzach Adash Beachab</note>. Many commentators ask: what is the benefit of providing these signs? It seems we can say that the miracles of Israel were steeped in Judgment, and the "system" of the plagues should have rightfully fallen upon Israel as well, Heaven forbid. Only the Holy One, in His mercy and kindness, gave "redemption and deliverance" and transformed the matter into something else. Just as the "Blood" that Pharaoh saw—where he said, "See, evil is before your faces"—was transformed into the **blood of circumcision**. Thus the signs were given. The first sign, **Dtzach** (Blood, Frogs, Lice): the first plague of this set is Blood, and it was transformed into the blood of circumcision. The second sign, **Adash** (Wild Beasts, Pestilence, Boils): the first plague of this set is Wild Beasts, through which we are cleansed of our sins in another way... The third sign, **Beachab** (Hail, Locusts, Darkness, Firstborn): the first plague of this set is Hail, which was fulfilled in the days of Samuel... The Rabbi comes to teach us that just as we find with the first signs that were fulfilled for Israel through the Attribute of Judgment and then turned into life and redemption through the Attribute of Mercy, so too with all of them. I will add further: a "precious soul/stone" is like this matter.

Regarding the "Signs" (plural), if we consider the **Atzilut** <note>term: *Atzilut* — the World of Emanation, the highest of the four worlds in Kabbalah</note>, it is three sets of three, and **Kingship** <note>original: *Malchut* — the tenth Sephirah</note> is the tenth. As with the measure of the appearance... as explained in the Zohar and the *Tikunim*, and brought in the *Pardes* in the Gate of Vowel Points: the vowels **Holam**, **Shurek**, and **Hireq** hint at the Sephirah of **Tiferet** <note>Beauty/Harmony</note>. The vowel points indicate that **Malchut** has three "places" regarding its union with Tiferet. **Holam** <note>The dot above the letter</note> is when she sits on high, the secret of "a crown of glory for her husband." Her first place is the secret of "on the day the Lord God made Earth and Heaven," where the Earth (Malchut) is raised to the Heavens. Her second place is the secret of "the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun," where both are equal; then her ascent is in the middle three, the secret of **Shurek** <note>The dot in the middle of the letter</note>. Her third place is when she is below, under the letter Vav; about this it is said: "And his feet shall stand..." and then she is measured in the secret of... the secret of **Hireq** <note>The dot below the letter</note>. This is hinted at in Tractate Megillah: Rava said, "The first person who reads four verses is praiseworthy... for this praises the generations." The middle person who reads four is praiseworthy because of the "Western Lamp." The last person who reads four is praiseworthy for "ascending in holiness." The "Contribution of the Chamber" is the elevation of the degree upon which all sacrifices and incense rely. This shows the three "places" of Malchut from top to bottom...
