<meta>This page continues the mystical and legal discourse regarding the importance of the Shavuot vigil and the study of Torah, specifically focusing on the "Oral Torah" (the Mishnah) and the unique merit of studying at night. It transitions from the supernatural voice (the Maggid) to a collection of traditional sources (Talmud, Midrash, and Zohar) that reinforce these themes.</meta>

# Tractate Shavuot

## The Mishnah
The letter *Shin* <note>The second letter of the word "Mishnah"</note> of the Mishnah is refined and resonates with the *Tzadi* of Isaac, which represents the attribute of Strict Judgment. This judgment is transformed into the *Shin* of *Yishak* <note>original: ישחק - a variant spelling of Isaac (Yitzhak) meaning "he shall laugh"</note>, signifying the joy and gladness that will exist in the future. This is hinted at in the tradition of Rabbi Isaac regarding the letter *Shin* and "laughter," as is explained to those who know the "Graceful Wisdom" <note>A traditional euphemism for Kabbalah</note>. Behold, the redemption draws near, and the "Gate of Freedom"—the Fiftieth Gate, the Gate of Redemption—is resonating. This alludes to the *Shekhinah* <note>The Divine Presence, viewed in Kabbalah as feminine</note> who is in exile; with these movements of study, one brings her out of the bitter and hasty exile. Thus far [the words of the Maggid]. **And these are the words** of the introduction to the section *Vayechi* (page 156, side 3): "Know that a person must engage in the Written Torah by day and the Oral Torah <note>The Mishnah and its commentaries</note> by night, each matter in its proper time. Similarly, our Sages of blessed memory said in *Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer*: 'During all those forty days that Moses stood on the mountain, he would read the Written Law by day and repeat the Mishnah by night.'"

In the same way, the Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and expansion of the Bible</note> interprets the verse "My beloved is dazzling and ruddy" <note>Song of Songs 5:10</note> with this language: "The Assembly of Israel, who is like the praise of the Master of the World, says to that God: 'It is my will to worship Him, for He is draped in a garment as white as snow by day, occupying Himself with the twenty-four books of the Torah, the words of Prophecy, and the Writings. And by night, He occupies Himself with the Mishnah, the Six Orders. And His appearance is as bright as fire because of the greatness of wisdom and reasoning, as He reviews the traditions of the Law every single day, and He is destined to publicize them to His people on the Great Day.'" The word "dazzling" (white) refers to the Written Torah, which is why it mentions a white snow-like garment. The "ruddiness" (redness) alluded to in the word "ruddy" refers to the Oral Torah, which emerges from the "Bride" <note>The Shekhinah/Oral Law</note>, whose "appearance is as bright as fire." This refers to the scholars of every generation, which is why it says "His appearance is as bright as fire," hinting at the "consuming fire" <note>Deuteronomy 4:24</note>.

This is the same "preciousness" that they should guard at the conclusion of the fast <note>Tractate Ta'anit</note> regarding the nights. It is said: "One who does not add [to his study time] shall be gathered [pass away]." What does "add" mean? Rabbi Joseph taught: "His mother shall bury him." <note>A harsh Talmudic idiom for a shortened life</note>. The intention is that study at night is the Oral Torah, which serves as a "Chariot" <note>A mystical vehicle</note> for the "Mother," which is the attribute of *Malkhut* <note>Kingship/Sovereignty, the lowest of the ten Divine emanations</note>.

We find that the night is a time more prepared for Torah than the day, because during the day a person is more occupied with business. Therefore, they said in the third chapter of *Ethics of the Fathers*: "Rabbi Hanina ben Hakhinai says: One who stays awake at night, or travels alone on the road and turns his heart to idleness, is liable for his life." This means that since these are times free from business and work, they are appropriate for self-rebuke and study; one who does not do so wastes his time and endangers his soul. The Psalmist alluded to this: "And it was throughout the night," even unto the "watch of the morning." Therefore, David would rise at midnight to read the Torah.

We also expound in Tractate *Menachot*, in the chapter "Behold I take upon myself a tenth," on page 110: "'Behold, bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord by night' <note>Psalm 134:1</note>—these are the disciples of the wise who engage in Torah at night; the Scripture considers them as if they were engaged in the Temple service." We also learn in the first chapter of *Avodah Zarah* (page 12) and in Tractate *Hagigah* (page 3): "Rabbi Levi said: Anyone who engages in Torah by night, the Holy One, blessed be He, draws over him a thread of grace by day, as it is said: 'By day the Lord will command His grace, and in the night His song is with me' <note>Psalm 42:9</note>. Why will He command His grace? Because in the night His song [the Torah] was with me." Some say that Rabbi Simeon ben Lakish said: "Anyone who engages in Torah in this world, which is compared to night, the Holy One, blessed be He, draws over him a thread of grace in the World to Come, which is compared to day." We also learn in Tractate *Eruvin* (page 65): "Rabbi Judah said: The moon was only created for study."

We also learn there, in the chapter "One who makes partitions" (page 18): "Rabbi Joshua ben Eleazar said: Any house in which the words of Torah are heard at night will never be destroyed, as it is said: 'But none says, Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night?'" <note>Job 35:10</note>. Another says it refers to their souls and merit, as we learn in the chapter "Yom Kippur" (page 77): "'He gives to His beloved sleep' <note>Psalm 127:2</note>—Rabbi Isaac said: These are the wives of the scholars, who drive sleep from their eyes in this world [to support their husbands' study] and merit the World to Come." If a scholar does not engage in study at night with his wife <note>meaning, while she sleeps or supports him</note>, as we learn in the chapter *Helek* (page 92): "Rabbi Eleazar said: Any house in which words of Torah are not heard at night, fire consumes it, as it is said: 'All darkness is hidden for his treasures; a fire not fanned shall consume him; it shall go ill with him that is left in his tent' <note>Job 20:26</note>. There is no 'remnant' <note>original: שריד - *sarid*</note> except for a scholar, as it is said: 'And among the remnants whom the Lord shall call.'" All this is because Torah learned at night is preserved and settled best, as one is free from distractions. Therefore, how good and pleasant it is that the study of the Oral Torah, which requires great concentration, was designated for the night.

**The SMaG** <note>Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, a 13th-century legal code</note> wrote in the section on Negative Commandments (Part 3): "One who treats the Torah lightly, even for a long time, violates a negative commandment, as it is said: 'Lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life.' And in the chapter 'Two Loaves,' it says he violates two negative commandments. In *Ethics of the Fathers* we learned: 'One who forgets a single matter from his study, Scripture considers him as if he were liable for his life.'" We also learn in the third chapter of *Yoma*: "Rabbi Hamnuna said: Forgetting even one thing from one's study causes exile for one's children, as it is said: 'And you have forgotten the Torah of your God, I will also forget your children.' Rabbi Abbahu said: He is even removed from his greatness, as it is said: 'Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you from being a priest to Me.'" It seems to us that when they said one who turns away from Torah violates a commandment, he violates it every single day.

It is taught in *Yoma* (page 35): "The poor man, the rich man, and the wicked man come to judgment before the Holy One, blessed be He. They say to the poor man: 'Why did you not engage in Torah?' If he says, 'I was poor and preoccupied with finding sustenance,' they say to him: 'Were you any poorer than Hillel the Elder?' He used to work and earn half a *denarius*; half he gave to the guard of the House of Study, and half for the sustenance of his household. One time he found nothing to earn, and the guard would not let him enter. He climbed up and sat by the skylight to hear the words of the Living God. That day was the eve of the Sabbath, and three cubits of snow fell upon him. In the morning, Shemaya said to Abtalion: 'Every day the house is bright, but today it is dark!' They looked up and saw the form of a man in the skylight. They went up, cleared the snow, bathed him, and sat him before the fire, saying: 'This man is worthy for us to desecrate the Sabbath for him.'

They say to the rich man: 'Why did you not engage in Torah?' If he says, 'I was rich and preoccupied with my properties,' they say to him: 'Were you any richer than Rabbi Eleazar ben Harsom? His father left him a thousand villages on land and a thousand ships at sea, yet he never once went to see them. Instead, he sat and engaged in Torah all day and all night, placing a sack of flour on his shoulder and going from city to city to study Torah.' They ask the wicked man: 'Why did you not engage in Torah?' If he says, 'I was handsome and preoccupied by my impulses,' they say to him: 'Were you any more handsome than Joseph the Righteous? Every day the wife of Potiphar tried to seduce him with words, changing her clothes evening and morning, offering him a thousand pieces of silver to lie with her, but he would not listen to her.' Thus, the poor, the rich, and the wicked are all held liable for not engaging in Torah."

This passage requires explanation. It is difficult: what was the "evil" of the rich man that he replied, "I was rich and preoccupied"? He should have used his wealth to sustain the Torah rather than being so preoccupied with business. Also, what would be the answer for the poor man who was preoccupied with food? After all, he and his work were few. This is even more difficult regarding the wicked man. It would seem, "What have I to do with his Torah?" for it is written: "And to the wicked, God said: 'What right have you to recite My statutes?'" Furthermore, if he has an excuse for not studying, he is still liable in judgment for being wicked! Moreover, why does he say "I was preoccupied with my impulses"? All the more so he should have studied, as our Sages said: "If this repulsive one [the evil impulse] meets you, drag him to the House of Study!"

The matter is that each one wants to be exempt under the rule that "one who is engaged in a commandment is exempt from other commandments." The rich man's claim is based on what the Sages emphasized regarding the reward of those who support Torah scholars with their money. As it says in the last chapter of Tractate *Ketubot* (page 102): "Anyone who makes use of the light of Torah, the dew of life revives him; and anyone who does not make use of the light of Torah, the dew of Torah does not revive him." When he saw him suffering, he said, "My Master, I have found a resting place for them from another source: 'Those who cling to the Lord your God [are all alive today].'" We also learn in *Genesis Rabbah*: "All of them [the tribes] shall dwell toward the sea... and all of them belong to Issachar." Now, Issachar was greater than Zebulun, as he is listed first in the genealogy. However, because Issachar engaged in Torah and Zebulun engaged in commerce and came and fed him, the Scripture mentions Zebulun first <note>In the blessing of Moses: "Rejoice, Zebulun, in your going out, and Issachar in your tents"</note>. It says: "It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it" <note>Proverbs 3:18</note>—not "to those who toil in it."

We learn in *Leviticus Rabbah*: "To those who hold fast to it"—this refers to those who support the hands of Torah scholars and assist them with their money, like Shimon the brother of Azariah. Because Azariah would go out in commerce and come and put food into Shimon's mouth, the Torah is called by Shimon's name. We also learn in *Midrash Tanchuma*: "'It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it'—had it said 'to those who toil in it,' there would be no hope for others. But it says 'to those who hold fast,' meaning those who support the hands of its students." Similarly: "'Cursed is he who does not uphold the words of this Torah'—had it said 'who does not learn,' there would be no hope for others. But it says 'who does not uphold,' meaning who does not support the hands of the students." And in the Torah portion of *Bereishit*, it says: "'A good understanding have all those who do them'—these are the students of Torah. Those who toil in Torah are not called 'doers,' because through their toiling they are simply studying. But those who support them are called 'doers' [of the commandment], and of them it is written: 'His praise stands forever.'"

Behold, the status of one who supports the hands of Torah scholars is very great. Therefore, the rich man claims that he supports many students who engage in Torah. He thinks this is sufficient for his generation and that he is not obligated to study himself, since he hires others with his money and helps the Torah. Therefore, he occupies himself with the authority of his gathered wealth and ignores the words of Torah. Ben Harsom makes him liable, for he certainly supported the Torah with his great wealth—as he was a man of kindness and holiness—yet despite all that, he engaged in Torah day and night.

The poor man claims: "Even though I did not engage in Torah, it is as if I engaged in the Torah..."

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the spiritual and legal merits of Torah study, specifically addressing the proper balance between dialectical reasoning (Pilpul), the study of the Mishnah, and the study of the Talmud. It transitions from general principles of truthful study to mystical interpretations involving the Divine Presence (Malchut) and the rectification (Tikkun) of the soul.</meta>

# Truth
The matter is like "a good, sharp pepper" <note>original: פלפלא חריפתא (pilpela charifta) - a Talmudic idiom for a sharp, penetrating argument</note>. In the chapter "The Middle Gate" <note>Bava Metzia, page 31a</note>, Rava said: At the time when a person is brought in for judgment in the afterlife, they are asked: "Did you conduct your business faithfully? Did you set aside fixed times for Torah study? Did you engage in deep analysis <term>Pilpul: a method of Talmudic study involving intense dialectical reasoning and hair-splitting analysis</term> with wisdom?" etc. However, all this was said regarding a "Pilpul of Truth." A person can achieve great depth in every single law through the power of questions and answers, analyzing them to extract the paths of the true, simple meaning <note>the "Peshat"</note>, whether in the commentary of Rashi or the Tosafot <note>medieval French and German commentators</note>. Just as we pray, "Grant us our portion in Your Torah," we can add to our analysis by examining and understanding the difficulties raised by the Tosafot and other challenges found within the flow of the Talmudic discussion. The Torah was given to all of Israel, for the "Crown of Torah" is laid out for everyone. Let no one think, "Who am I, and what am I, to look into and walk among great and wondrous matters?" For one who studies for the sake of Heaven and exerts himself in the study—"If you have labored and found, believe it." All these analyses, where the "Torah burns within him," serve as a "chariot" for the attribute of Sovereignty <term>Malchut: the lowest of the ten Divine emanations in Kabbalah, associated with the Oral Torah and the physical world</term>, which is called the Oral Torah and represents the attribute of Justice. This applies specifically to a "Pilpul of Truth." However, regarding a "Pilpul of Falsehood," it is written: "He who speaks lies shall not be established." In the first chapter of Eruvin, it was taught: There was a veteran student in Yavne who could prove a lizard was ritually pure using 150 reasons <note>this is a classic example of sophisticated but ultimately false logic, as the Torah explicitly states a lizard is impure</note>. The Tosafot ask: What greatness is there in such sharpness to purify what the Torah explicitly forbids? Rabbenu Tam answers there... see the source. Thus, it is difficult to see what merit there is in an analysis that is not based on truth. This note is sufficient.

### And on the Matter
of studying Mishnah and Talmud, and which of them one should spend the majority of his time reviewing: It is found in the "Middle Gate" <note>Bava Metzia, page 33a</note> that our Sages taught: Those who engage in the study of Scripture perform a deed that is both a virtue and not a virtue; those who engage in Mishnah perform a virtue for which they receive a reward; but in Talmud, you have no greater virtue than this. Yet, one should always run to the Mishnah more than the Talmud. This itself is difficult! You said that in Talmud there is no greater virtue, and then you said one should always run to the Mishnah? Rabbi Yochanan said: In the days of Rabbi <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, the redactor of the Mishnah</note>, this teaching was taught because everyone had abandoned the Mishnah and gone after the Talmud. He then returned and taught them: Always run to the Mishnah more than the Talmud.

---

->Secret Matters<-

I found in the commentary on the portion of *Yitro* regarding the search for your path: He wrote that the Written Torah is like a prayer, while the Oral Torah is drawn from the attribute of Sovereignty. He wrote that the laws that are decided with the inclusion of the Name of Heaven... <margin>The time for the incense of prayer and these two times are for Torah study</margin> the time for the incense of the morning prayer and the time for the incense of the afternoon prayer. This is written in the Book of Proverbs: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord." However, the Rabbi, the author of *Tosafot Yom Tov*, wrote in his book on the tractates *Keritot* and *Ketubot* (page 8) that the foundation and the laws of wisdom, Mishnah, and Talmud are more and more significant because one who has received the tradition... and he should return to wisdom and the rectification of the soul. For the Oral Torah, every time a person engages in it, he creates a "birth," and for every answer, they receive great reward, strength, and hidden light. This light is placed in the "Sovereignty" <note>Malchut</note> to provide it with the strength of the "Hidden Mem" <note>A reference to Isaiah 9:6, where the letter Mem appears in its "closed" final form in the middle of a word, representing a divine mystery</note>. For the Mishnah is like the "Crown of the Oral Torah," and through it, four things hidden from the eyes of all living beings are rectified. All those who are emanated for Israel are awakened from above to shine and bring down their power below. This is the secret of the "Iron sharpens iron" <note>Proverbs 27:17</note>; just as iron sharpens its fellow, so do scholars sharpen one another in Jewish Law.

<column-break/>

->Secret Matters<-

The great teacher Rabbi [Joseph] Karo wrote... and he said: Also, a person's habit of studying Torah before leaving the synagogue for his business indicates the secret of "connecting prayer to Torah," which is to link the attribute of Sovereignty to the Beauty of God. Therefore, it is good to set aside times for Torah, for Sovereignty is "Time," and you have times of Judgment and times of Mercy, times of Day and times of Night. Therefore, one fixes a time for Torah by day and by night. This is the secret of the Mishnah—it has the same letters as *Neshamah* <note>Soul</note>. When a person studies Mishnah, he provides "food" for the soul to ascend to the highest level. I found it written that the Mishnah is the "Crown of the Oral Torah," and through it, there is a great rectification for the four things hidden from the eye of every living thing. All those emanated to Israel are awakened from above to illuminate and bring their power below. First, the letter *Mem* of the word *Mishnah* rectifies and sweetens the *Mem* of the phrase "To the increase of [le-marbe] the government" <note>Isaiah 9:6</note>, which is closed and sealed until the "End of Days," but is opened through the study of the Mishnah.

---

And how much more so in our time, when we have merited the commentaries of the Rambam <note>Maimonides</note> and Rabbi Bartenura <note>the standard commentator on the Mishnah</note>, who explain the Mishnah according to the consensus of the Talmud and also record the final legal ruling. Thus, the merit of the Mishnah is great. For when they originally said "Talmud has no greater virtue than this," it was because studying the Mishnah without the Talmud meant one would not know the actual laws, for they would not know the reasoning. Sometimes a person might compare one case to another that is not actually similar and thus give a mistaken ruling. Regarding this, it was said in Tractate Sotah (Chapter 3): "Those who repeat Mishnah laws are the destroyers of the world." <note>Because they rule based on the Mishnah without understanding the underlying Talmudic debate</note>. They are "destroyers of the world," yet they are also "settlers of the world." But now, in our time, the majority of one's occupation should be in the Mishnah, to study it with a clear heart and mouth according to the plain meaning, and to review it until it is fluent, according to the Rambam and Bartenura. Then everything is rectified. The Law follows the Talmud in its general principles and in truthful analysis. Happy is the one who merits the Mishnah, such that the Six Orders of the Mishnah are fluent in his mouth, for it shall be "sustenance for the soul" to ascend on high to the first level. Your sign for this is: **Mishnah** (משנה) has the same letters as **Neshamah** (נשמה - Soul).

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the spiritual dangers of secular philosophy compared to the sanctity of Torah study. It draws on a lineage of medieval and early modern authorities to argue that "external wisdoms" (philosophy) are fundamentally incompatible with the "internal wisdom" of the Torah. It then transitions into practical advice—fifteen specific methods—for successful and holy Torah study.</meta>

# The Distancing from Philosophy

The **distancing** from the study of philosophy and its prohibition is clarified in the words of both the early and later sages. To bring all their words here would be a burden upon me, yet I will present a few of them. The Geonim <term>Geonim: the leaders of the Babylonian academies, roughly 6th–11th centuries</term> showed this in the *Ein Yaakov* regarding the tractate *Chagigah*, in the discourse on "Four who entered the Orchard" <note>original: Pardes — a famous Talmudic allegory for mystical/philosophical inquiry</note>; see there.

**Rabbeinu Asher** <note>original: The Rosh (1250–1327), a leading legal authority</note> wrote in his Responsa (Principle 28): "Even though I do not know your 'external wisdoms,' blessed be the Merciful One who saved me from them. For they use signs and wonders to lead a person away from the fear of God and His Torah... let our Torah not be like your idle chatter, your 'wisdom of logic' which all the sages of the generation have distanced." He continues: "For the wisdom of the Torah and the wisdom of philosophy do not travel the same path. The Sage [Solomon] said, 'None that go to her return' <note>Proverbs 2:19</note>, meaning that one who first enters this [secular] wisdom cannot leave it to let the wisdom of the Torah enter his heart. He will not be able to repent from natural philosophy and will not succeed in standing upon the wisdom of the Torah, which is the path of life. His heart will always be toward natural science, and it will occur to his spirit to equate the two wisdoms and bring proof from one to the other, thereby perverting judgment. For they are two opposites, rivals to one another, and they cannot lie together in one place."

Furthermore, see the "Pillars of Faith" written by the **Rashba** <note>Rabbi Shlomo ben Aderet (1235–1310), a preeminent scholar in Barcelona</note> in his responsa, where he expanded on this: "There are those who wanted to make the Greek books the foundation, making them the primary thing and the Torah of God secondary... they treat the bitter as sweet and the sweet as bitter. I have seen the pressure they exert against the Torah and its sages, almost uprooting the roots and abandoning the Torah. While there may be a few useful pages in those books, they contain many damages... If the Sages of blessed memory said not to meditate on the *Book of Sirach*, how much more so these books which cause one to turn away from God and the Torah." He expressed great anger toward the residents of the city of Florence for their engagement with external wisdom and for silencing the Torah scholars of their generation.

The great prince and sage **Rabbi Isaac ibn Albalia** <note>referred to here in a complex citation alongside the Radak</note> wrote: "When did the Holy Scriptures become so disgraced that they are treated wickedly through the measures of wisdom... and when did a person repent for his sins through Greek wisdom?" 

The pious **Rabbi Joseph Yaavetz** <note>15th-century thinker who witnessed the Spanish Expulsion</note>, in the introduction to his *Book of Beliefs*, complained about the philosophers among our people: "When I investigated their many words, a flame burned within me, for the 'fringes' <note>meaning the outer edges or identity</note> of Israel had flown away. I saw that in all these generations, those who went too deep into philosophical inquiry denied [the faith]."

It is further explained in *Sefer HaYashar* <note>The Book of the Upright, an ethical work often attributed to Rabbenu Tam</note> that among the things that nullify the service of God are "evil wisdoms." This refers to wisdoms that damage faith, like external wisdoms and philosophy. A servant of God has no need to diligently study them; rather, he should distance himself with all his strength. For whatever benefit they might offer, he will lose his faith. Many who were "wise in their own eyes" thought they were ascending, but they did not know they were distancing themselves from faith. Those who enter philosophy do not believe unless they are shown a number or a physical foundation; thus, their faith wavers. But when one studies with a sage who is not pious, he will fall into the pit of doubt and destroy his faith. This rule should be kept in your heart: "Fear the Lord."

In the work *Asiah Kushir*, it is written: "If one occupies himself with external wisdom... he should cast this occupation away, for the damage that comes from it is greater than the benefit. Those who base their faith on their own human understanding... are those who cling to external wisdoms. Even if he thinks he is pious and that these wisdoms cannot sway his faith, he is actually distancing himself little by little without feeling it. He thinks he is holding onto his Torah, but he does not know he is very far from it."

The Kabbalist Rabbi [Meir ibn Gabbai] wrote at great length in his book *Avodat HaKodesh* <note>The Holy Service, a 16th-century Kabbalistic classic</note> (Part 'The Purpose,' chapters 6–9 and Part 'Secrets of the Torah'). In these chapters, he revealed their shame in public and warned very strongly against them.

# The Two Women

He said that King Solomon, peace be upon him, founded the Book of Proverbs as an allegory based on two women: one beloved and one hated. The hated one represents the philosophers—the "adulterous woman," the "strange woman" who speaks with smooth words. She seduces a person, and he does not know it will cost him his soul. On the other hand, the "wise woman," the "woman who fears the Lord," she shall be praised—this is the Torah of our lives, the heritage <note>original: Morashah</note> given to us by Moses. Do not read it as *morashah* (heritage), but as *me’orasah* (betrothed). 

He concluded: "How good is our portion and how pleasant is our lot, to fill our bellies with Scripture, Mishnah, Talmud, and verses, and afterward to engage in the wisdom of Kabbalah. Then one is sanctified with great holiness, and his soul will walk on a paved path to the House of the King, to the place from which it came, and it will be uplifted and magnified... and included in all the supernal lights."

# Fifteen Paths to Torah Study

I found that there are fifteen paths required for engaging in Torah:

1. **The First Path:** The study should be with a great sage and in the company of distinguished colleagues. As our Sages said: "A sword against the solitary" <note>Ta'anit 7a</note>—this refers to scholars who study Torah alone, whereas it should be done in partnership.
2. **The Second Path:** One should look into books written by the great sages of Israel, which increase general principles through conciseness. One should not pay attention to works with many words but little fruit.
3. **The Third Path:** A person should focus on what he reads and reviews to know the explanations and the intent of the statements.
4. **The Fourth Path:** One should be diligent in creating "signs" <note>mnemonics</note> for what he reads, reviews, or learns.
5. **The Fifth Path:** One should always study in the same group, and not one group today and another tomorrow for the same subject.
6. **The Sixth Path:** One should always look at the physical books, the handwriting, and the "binding" <note>contextual connections</note>; this should be the place of his analysis and building.
7. **The Seventh Path:** Engagement in Torah should be with a voice and tangible speech, so that he hears what comes out of his mouth. It should not be in silence or a low voice like a mourner, but with the exertion of all the organs of speech and the powers of the body. Maimonides wrote: "Anyone who makes his voice heard during his study, his study will endure; but one who reads silently quickly forgets."
8. **The Eighth Path:** One's study should be with a melody, whether in Scripture or Mishnah. For this reason, you find ancient books of the Mishnah written with vowels and musical notes.
9. **The Ninth Path:** The books should be in *Ashurit* <note>the standard Hebrew square script</note>.
10. **The Tenth Path:** The books should be in beautiful handwriting, not poorly written.
11. **The Eleventh Path:** That he should have [a mentor/companion] to accompany him.
12. **The Twelfth Path:** The studies and the learning should be with joy, pleasure, composure, and patience. A person should not be [distressed] while engaged in Torah.
13. **The Thirteenth Path:** Engagement in the Torah should be "for its own sake" <term>Lishma: studying for the purpose of connecting to God and fulfilling His will, rather than for ulterior motives like status</term>, to achieve what is proper.
14. **The Fourteenth Path:** One should designate and fix a set time for Torah study, and during that time, clear his mind of every other occupation or thought.
15. **The Fifteenth Path:** To pray to God that He give him wisdom, understanding, and a good memory. These are the "Straight Paths of the Lord," and the righteous walk in them.

->Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to engage in the study of Torah for its own sake.<-

Rabbi Meir says: "Anyone who engages in Torah for its own sake merits many things..." and we also learn in the chapter *Helek*...

# Tractate Shevuot

->Within the Torah, the entire matter of Torah study is the "Torah of Kindness." As our Sages of blessed memory <note>original: ARZ"L — *Adoneinu Rabbenu Zikhronam Livrakha*</note> asked: "What is the Torah of Kindness? It is one who learns Torah and teaches it to others." Regarding this, they said: "And those who justify the many [shall shine] like the stars forever and ever" <note>Daniel 12:3</note>—these are the teachers of children. I say that regarding the fast I have chosen <note>Isaiah 58:6</note>, which is to provide for my children and the members of my household, I am also included among those who "justify the many." For our Sages taught: "One who performs charity at all times" <note>Psalms 106:3</note>—this refers to one who supports his sons and daughters while they are young. Behold, my Creator, it is said of a poor man who exerts his whole body to feed them: regarding this, the "careful one" is called to account for the "wickedness" mentioned in the passage. This does not mean he is actually wicked, but rather it refers to one born under a bad astrological sign <note>original: *mazal tekhunah ra'ah*</note> with a disposition toward wickedness, yet he conversely conquers his desire. He asks: "What is the ultimate purpose of Torah study? That it should bring us to action, and that one should overcome the degraded Evil Inclination." The "wicked man" says: "Since I do this, it is as if I have labored in the Torah." A man who strives, Joseph <note>referring to the biblical Joseph's resistance to Potiphar's wife</note>, through the love [of God] he overcame his desire... for they acquire [merit] above all the Torah he learned and followed from Shem and Eber <note>The legendary academy of the ancestors of the Jewish people</note>.<-

<margin>
<note>This note appears to be a kabbalistic calculation or mnemonic</note>
KNS"S (From before a great hint at the end of the verse between "one who serves God"... why "serves for the light"... to say the secret of the 130 years... they did not pass the 100... it is still called "they did not pass"... and so all the judgments... from the nature of the world... the letters of the Name... from their deeds... to hint... 15). And so it is mentioned: the teacher from below who was remembered by them... in the translation of Jonathan <note>Targum Yonatan: an early Aramaic translation/commentary on the Prophets</note> on page 72.
</margin>

**One who desires** to learn so that the material remains in his hand and he can express it clearly with his mouth: as we learn in Tractate *Eruvin*, chapter "How do we provide a boundary" <note>original: *Keitzad Me'abrin*, page 54a</note>. It is told that Bruriah <note>a famous female scholar of the Talmudic era</note> came across a student who was whispering his studies quietly. She said to him: "Is it not written, 'Ordered in all things and secure' <note>2 Samuel 23:5</note>? If the Torah is 'ordered' in all your 248 limbs, it will be 'secure' [remembered]; if not, it will be forgotten." And we say there that Shmuel said to Rabbi Yehuda: "Sharp one! <note>original: *shinena* — a term of endearment for a brilliant student</note> Open your mouth when you study so that it will remain with you and grant you long life, as it is said, 'For they are life to those who find them' <note>Proverbs 4:22</note>—do not read it as 'to those who find them' (*lemotza’eihem*), but as 'to those who express them' (*lemotzi’eihem*) with their mouth." And we also say there that Abaye asked: "What is the meaning of the verse, 'For it is pleasant if you keep them within your belly' <note>Proverbs 22:18</note>? When are the words of Torah pleasant? At the time you keep them in your belly. And when can you keep them in your belly? At the time they are established together upon your lips." Rabbi Zera said [it is derived] from here: "A man has joy by the answer of his mouth" <note>Proverbs 15:23</note>—when is there joy for a man? When he answers with his mouth. Rabbi Yitzhak said from here: "For the matter is very close to you..." <note>Deuteronomy 30:14</note>—when is the matter very close to you? At the time it is in your mouth and in your heart to do it. Another said from here: "You have given him his heart's desire, and the request of his lips..." <note>Psalms 21:3</note>—when have You given him his heart's desire? At the time of the request of his lips. One who wishes to learn must constantly review his studies and prepare and remember them, as we learn in the fifth chapter of *Ta'anit* (page 7). Rav Hisda said to a student whose study was as difficult for him as iron: "This is because your Mishnah <note>the foundational code of Jewish law</note> is not organized," as it is said, "If the iron is blunt and one does not whet the edge" <note>Ecclesiastes 10:10</note>. What is the remedy? Increase your sessions [of study]. If one's study was organized from the beginning, he should review the text 40 times, corresponding to the 40 days in which the Torah was given, before coming before his teacher. Rabbi Abahu, when he would return to review the text, would do so 24 times, corresponding to the Torah, Prophets, and Writings <note>the 24 books of the Hebrew Bible</note>, before coming before Rava. If one does not review his learning, he will forget it, as we learn: Rabbi Joshua ben Levi said, "Anyone who learns Torah and does not review it is like a man who sows but does not reap." Others say it is like a woman who gives birth and then buries her child. If one can review his study even 100 times—one who reviews 100 times is called "one who serves God," as we learn in the fourth chapter of *Chagigah* (page 9b): "Then you shall return and discern between the righteous and the wicked, between him who serves God and him who does not serve Him" <note>Malachi 3:18</note>. Is "righteous" not the same as "one who serves God"? Is "wicked" not the same as "one who does not serve Him"? Rather, "one who serves Him" refers to one who reviews his lesson 101 times, whereas "one who does not serve Him" refers to one who reviews his lesson only 100 times. The student asked: "And because of one extra time, he is called 'one who does not serve God'?" He replied: "Yes. Go and learn from the donkey-drivers' market: ten miles for one *zuz* <note>a silver coin</note>, but eleven miles for two *zuz*." And one who has the capacity for study but causes Torah to be forgotten from Israel through his neglect by not reviewing his study, is destined to give an account in judgment, as we learn in *Kiddushin*... Rabbi Ishmael said... if a matter is clear to you, do not hesitate, but say it immediately, as it is said: "Say to wisdom, 'You are my sister'" <note>Proverbs 7:4</note>.

**It is stated** in Tractate *Berakhot* (page 38): Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba used to review all his studies and every type of lesson before his teacher, Rabbi Yochanan. Tosafot <note>medieval commentaries on the Talmud</note> write: "This does not literally mean 'all' his studies, but rather whatever he learned over a 30-day period, he would review everything before him on the 30th day."

**At the end** of Tractate *Berakhot*: "Silence <note>original: *Has*</note> and then analyze." This follows the view of Rava, who said: "A person should always learn Torah [the basic text] first, and afterward he should contemplate/analyze it." Rashi explains: "Silence" means to be quiet and listen until the text is fluent in your mouth, even if it is not yet fully settled or understood by you. Afterward comes "priesthood" <note>a metaphor for higher analysis</note>—ask what you have to ask and find resolutions until it is settled for you and you can contemplate it. See also the Ya'avetz <note>Rabbi Jacob Emden (1697–1776)</note>. And in the fourth chapter of *Avodah Zarah*: "A person only learns Torah in a place that his heart desires" <note>Avodah Zarah 19a</note>. This is also found in Tractate *Shabbat*, chapter "With what [garments] may a woman [go out]": Rav Kahana said: "By the time I was 18 years old, I had finished the entire Talmud, but I did not know that a verse never loses its plain meaning <note>term: *Peshat* — the literal or direct historical sense of a scripture</note> until now." What does this come to teach us? That a person should learn the text and review it even if he does not know what it is saying, as it says, "My soul is crushed with longing" <note>Psalms 119:20</note>—even if he does not know all the reasons. Afterward, he should return for all the reasons, and it will be difficult for his understanding, and he should not run... this is specifically... at 18 years old. From this it is proven that a person should first finish the subject, and afterward it will unfold. I have seen many of our scholars behave this way: they learn one tractate throughout the entire Talmud, and from two tractates they learn one quickly without great depth, and afterward they learn another tractate slowly with depth, analysis, and review.

**After** one has "filled his belly" with the Bible, Mishnah, and Talmud, he should engage with awe, fear, holiness, and purity in the **Wisdom of Kabbalah** <note>the Jewish mystical tradition</note>—in the *Zohar*, the *Tikunim*, their commentaries, and other holy books that draw from the source of the well of the *Zohar*. Many rulings have already been written concerning the study of the Wisdom of Kabbalah. The general rule is that a person is obligated to know the Name of the Blessed One. One who has not seen this wisdom has never seen light in his days; he is like one who walks in darkness. I have mentioned these matters at length above in the chapter "Ten Utterances." I remember the honor of Elijah the Prophet, remembered for good... I found it written: Just as among priests, there is one who earns only one-eighth of a coin for his livelihood by digging treasures for days, and another who earns twenty a day by digging pits... and an old worker who bores pearls earns much more profit in a day without difficulty. Not everyone earns the same in a week; all are craftsmen, but the one whose labor is more refined earns more in one day. So too, one who knows the "secret" (*Sod*) of the commandments—for example, if Reuben, Simeon, and Levi ate together... and Levi knew the mystical intentions <note>term: *Kavanah* — the focused spiritual aim or meditative intent during a prayer or act</note> of the Grace After Meals while holding the cup of blessing, while another performed the same commandment but did not know the secrets of the blessing. Behold, both performed one commandment, but there is an advantage to Levi's reward over the other's reward like the advantage of light over darkness. This applies to all other commandments, and this is simple to those who know the "True Wisdom" <note>original: *Hen* — a common shorthand for Kabbalah</note>. It is true that just as the reward of one who knows the secrets of the commandments is very great, so too is his punishment if he transgresses or neglects a commandment. Nevertheless, a person should not use this as an excuse to neglect the commandments, saying, "Neither the act nor its reward," for the Lord our God will settle accounts with every person. In our simple understanding, God does not punish based on the depth of Kabbalah, as the nations of Seir and Paran did when they refused the Torah. However, knowledge is necessary, and there are four conditions: first, a proper heart full of fear and love of God; second, that he be a master of the Book of the *Zohar*...

**In Tractate *Berakhot*** (page 20): One who is engaged in the "Work of the Chariot" <note>term: *Ma'aseh Merkavah* — the highest form of early Jewish mysticism</note> does not interrupt even for "Amen, May His Great Name be Blessed." The reason in the Wisdom of Kabbalah is that one must not distract his mind from the matter he is engaged in until he completes it. It goes without saying that he must not engage in any [mundane] talk... even regarding general Torah matters. One who interrupts with idle talk is fed coals of broom-wood <note>a metaphor for spiritual punishment</note>. Fortunate is he who guards his mouth and tongue; he shall live in the company of God.

Nevertheless, the obligation is upon the recipient to learn with even greater strength and greater power; his mouth shall not cease from study day and night, literally, to learn and to teach, to keep, to do, and to fulfill.

# Honor
<margin>
We say in the Gemara <note>The Talmud</note> that action is superior when learning for oneself, but study is greater when teaching others. This is because whoever teaches his friend's son Torah is considered as if he gave birth to him. Therefore, study is called "greater" because it possesses two benefits: both the deed and the study. This is the essence of the words of the Tosafot <note>Medieval French/German commentators</note> and the Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, 13th-century legalist</note>. Therefore, our Master wrote in Sign 246: "A commandment that can be performed by others — let him not cease from his Torah study; but if not, he should perform it and then return to his learning." This is agreed upon by all the legal authorities <note>original: *Poskim*</note>, and there is no need to elaborate further here.
</margin>
Included in the category of "Torah study for its own sake" <note>original: *Torah Lishmah*</note> is that one's study should direct him to rectify his actions. Clearly, a dispute regarding this arose among the Sages of Israel. It is found at the end of the first chapter of Tractate Kiddushin: "Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders were once reclining in the upper story of Nitza's house in Lydda. This question was asked before them: Is study greater or is action greater? Rabbi Tarfon answered and said: Action is greater. Rabbi Akiva answered and said: Study is greater. They all answered and said: Study is greater, for study leads to action." This concludes the citation.

Several commentators have raised a difficulty: since action is the ultimate goal, and it is known that the goal is greater than the thing which leads to the goal, then according to this logic, action should be greater! They wrote what they wrote, but I only wish to present the words of our masters, the commentators of the Talmud, by whose words we live—namely, Rashi and the Tosafot. It is found in Tractate Bava Kamma, the first chapter: "The Sages taught: They already did for him as he did for others—this refers to Hezekiah, King of Judah, before whom thirty-six thousand armed soldiers went out to show that he fulfilled the Torah. Rabbi Yohanan, when he would enter the bathhouse, they would do the same for him, except they would place a Torah scroll on his bed and say, 'This one fulfilled what is written in this.'" Today we also do this: we bring the scroll out for a funeral, but we do not leave it there. Furthermore, we might leave it there, but we do not say "He fulfilled." 

Rabba bar Hanna said: "I was walking with Rabbi Yohanan to listen to his teachings. When he went to the bathhouse, I asked him a matter of law, but he did not explain it to us until he washed his hands, put on tefillin <note>phylacteries</note>, and said a blessing. Only then did he speak to us. He said: Even 'He fulfilled' may be said; but 'He taught' may not be said." And the Master said: "Study is great because it leads to action." This is not a contradiction: one refers to learning for oneself, the other to teaching others. Rashi explains: "Leads to action" implies action is actually superior; when learning for oneself, action is better. But when teaching others, teaching is superior to the deed; therefore, we do not say "He taught" <note>meaning teaching is so great a merit it is beyond what we can testify about a person at their funeral</note>. 

Furthermore, the Master said: "Torah study is great because it leads to action." Rashi explains there that even so, action is superior. But Rabbeinu Tam <note>a leading 12th-century Tosafist</note> finds this difficult, for on the contrary, from the passage in the first chapter of Kiddushin, it is proven that study is literally greater! There, the Elders in the attic in Lydda concluded that study is greater because it leads to action. Rabbeinu Tam explains that the meaning is as follows: since we say "He fulfilled," we are implying that he studied, for if he had not studied, how could he have fulfilled? For study leads to action. He does not initially consider the distinction between learning for oneself and teaching others. However, regarding Rabbi Yohanan, he did not say "He taught," because teaching others is certainly superior, as it brings the many to action when he teaches them. 

In the *She'iltot* of Rav Achai Gaon <note>8th-century legal work</note>, he says regarding Rabbi Yohanan putting on tefillin before speaking: the Talmud asks, how could he put on tefillin before saying the teaching? Is not study greater than the deed? It answers: there is a difference between learning for oneself and teaching others. Learning for oneself is great because it leads to action, but teaching others is not "greater" than a personal obligation like tefillin. Therefore, he put on tefillin first. 

I will first explain the words of the Tosafot, for one might ask on Rabbeinu Tam's explanation: why does the Talmud need to say that for personal learning, the deed is superior? Since both the passage here and the one in Kiddushin deal with the same principle, it should have simply answered that "He fulfilled" refers to teaching. There is another nuance in Tosafot where they say "it did not occur to him at that moment to distinguish." What does this mean? It's obvious the questioner didn't think of the answer! These two points can be resolved as one: certainly, the questioner knew that it is impossible to fulfill the law without studying it first. One can certainly perform an action without teaching others, but one's own fulfillment depends on one's own study. If so, why did he find it difficult? He surely knew that "He taught" is not said. It must be that even the questioner knew this, but it didn't occur to him to distinguish between the act of learning and the act of teaching within the statement "Study is greater." He thought "Study is greater" included both. Therefore, he asked well: since he fulfilled the law, he must have learned it. Even if he didn't teach others, the two types of study are equal in status, and since both are greater than action, why do we say "He fulfilled" but not "He taught"? Thus, he was forced to answer that "Study is greater" refers to teaching others; but for personal study, action is greater. They are distinct in their levels: action is better than personal study, but teaching others is better than action. 

Now, one shouldn't challenge Rabbeinu Tam by saying: if teaching is greater than action because it leads to action, then personal study should also be greater than action for the same reason. This is not a challenge, because action is the ultimate goal, and therefore superior to the study that leads to it. The commentators only questioned the case of teaching, which is superior to the deed because it contains two matters: the study itself and the good deed of teaching one's fellow. This is certainly the ethical explanation: study that leads to action has the deed within it. But in personal study, one must choose: is study or action superior? Rashi explains that "leading to action" proves action is the essence. This is the plain meaning: study leads to the goal, and the goal is superior. 

Now I will settle the challenges against Rashi. Some say that for a person who has not yet learned, they should be told to study first, as they are "empty." But for one who has already learned, action is better than study. This is Rashi's view. He holds that "Study is greater" means it has the "right of priority" <note>original: *din kadima*</note>. It is better that he learns first so he doesn't lose out on commandments, for he won't know what to do. If he doesn't learn, woe to him! Laws will be hidden from him, and he will commit prohibitions and miss many active commandments. The true goal is the deed. But for one who already knows the laws, nothing is better for his soul than performing a commandment. For the commandments are the end goal. Therefore, at the end of the first chapter of Bava Kamma, the Talmud correctly questions why "fulfilled" is superior to study: because action is the goal. The answer is that personal study is superior only because it contains the potential for the deed within it. Regarding teaching others, the deed is superior. We must conclude that if one does not yet know the laws of the actions, study must come first, and study is "great" in terms of priority. 

The conclusion from both views is: "It is not the study that is the essential thing, but the action." <note>Pirkei Avot 1:17</note>. Therefore, one should strive after good deeds. This applies to one's own study; but to teach others is even superior, as it includes both study and the good deed of teaching. And for one who does not know the laws, study is "greater" and must be done first. This is how Rashi's words must be understood, and it is likely Rabbeinu Tam agrees, even if he interprets the Talmudic passage differently. All this only applies if a commandment comes his way that can be performed by others. But if it cannot be done by others, he must perform the commandment and then return to his study, as Maimonides <note>Rambam</note> ruled, cited in the Tur, Sign 246. Regarding a commandment that is currently incumbent upon him, he must stop his study and do it. This is clear from the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Pesachim, which the Rosh cites: if one is going to study with his teacher and remembers he has leaven <note>chametz</note> in his house, he must return and destroy it; nullification is not enough. The Jerusalem Talmud says: "Here the Rabbi taught that action is greater than study." This is also cited in the Beit Yosef, Sign 444. Even when teaching others, if a commandment falls upon him to perform, he must prioritize the deed and then return to teaching. This is seen in the story of Rabbi Yohanan putting on tefillin before teaching others. At first glance, this is difficult: if teaching is greater, why did Rabbi Yohanan prioritize tefillin? According to the version in the *She'iltot*...

<summary>This page explores the foundational Jewish debate on whether Torah study or practical action (mitzvot) is superior. It concludes that while action is the ultimate goal, study is "greater" because it is a prerequisite for correct action and because teaching others is itself a supreme act of kindness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the purpose of Torah study, transitioning from the obligation of action to the spiritual and ethical requirements of studying "for its own sake." It explores the cosmic consequences of one's intentions and the practicalities of how a scholar should be supported by the community.</meta>

# Helek 
<note>original: "Helek" — the name of the eleventh chapter of Tractate Sanhedrin, which discusses the afterlife and the merits required to earn a portion in it.</note>

<margin>Helek, page 90, side B</margin>
On page 90, side A, Rabbi Alexandri said: Anyone who occupies themselves with the Torah for its own sake <note>original: "Lishmah" — meaning study motivated by love of God rather than for status or reward</note> is as if they make peace in the Heavenly Assembly and the Earthly Assembly, as it is said: "Or let him take hold of My strength, let him make peace with Me; peace he shall make with Me" (Isaiah 27:5). And Rav said: It is as if they built a Heavenly Palace and an Earthly Palace, as it is said: "And I have put My words in your mouth... to plant the heavens and lay the foundations of the earth" (Isaiah 51:16). And Rabbi Yohanan said: It is as if they protect the entire world, as it is said: "And in the shadow of My hand I have covered you." And Rabbi Levi says: It is as if they bring redemption closer to Israel, as it is said: "And to say to Zion: You are My people."
And when one occupies themselves with it for its own sake, it becomes an elixir of life for them. As we learn in the final chapter of the tractate on Foreign Worship <note>original: "Avodah Zarah"</note>: So it is taught, Rabbi Banna'ah says: Anyone who occupies themselves with the Torah for its own sake, their Torah becomes an elixir of life for them, as it is said: "It is a tree of life..." (Proverbs 3:18), and it says: "It shall be health to your navel..." (Proverbs 3:8), and it says: "For whoever finds me finds life..." (Proverbs 8:35). But if one does not occupy themselves with it for its own sake, it becomes an elixir of death for them. As our Sages of blessed memory said: Anyone who occupies themselves with the Torah not for its own sake, it becomes an elixir of death for them, as it is said: "My doctrine shall drop [ya'arof] as the rain" (Deuteronomy 32:2), and the word "arifa" refers only to killing, as it is said: "And they shall break the heifer’s neck [ve-arfu] there..." (Deuteronomy 21:4).
The meaning of "for its own sake" is the intention that one should occupy themselves with the Torah to fulfill what the Blessed Name commanded us: "And you shall teach them." One should consider the Torah to be like a royal decree that a king writes to his servants, telling them what to do and what to avoid doing. So the Holy One, Blessed be He, gave the Torah to His people Israel, His faithful servants, on the condition that when they read the Torah, Prophets, and Writings, or study the Mishnah, Talmud, and Legal Codes <note>original: "Poskim"</note>, they should do so with the resolution: "Whatever I find there regarding what to do and what not to do, I will fulfill as a faithful servant." And whatever is not within my power to fulfill due to some obstacle, if I can cause others to fulfill it, I will do so with alacrity. This is what we say in the blessing "Accept [our prayer]": "...and put in our hearts to discern and to understand, to hear, to learn and to teach, to observe and to do and to fulfill."
And these things that I have spoken of include the laws, namely from the positive and negative commandments—matters of the forbidden and the permitted, the impure and the pure, the innocent and the guilty—unless one learns paths of ethical instruction and the cultivation of upright character traits and learns them in order to fulfill them. And the "secrets" <note>original: "Ra'zei" — likely referring to Kabbalah or deep philosophical inquiries</note> which involve investigations, knowledge, and perceptions—one should learn them so that they may know His Blessed Name and His greatness and the hidden mysteries of His commandments. Then their heart will be inflamed to fear Him and to love Him. This is the conclusion of the blessing "Great Love": "...and enlighten our eyes in Your Torah, and make our hearts cling to Your commandments, and unite our hearts to love and fear Your name." How good it is when one opens the book to say: "Behold, I wish to learn so that my study will lead me to action, to upright character traits, and to the knowledge of the kindness and guidance of the Creator," doing so for the sake of the unity of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and His Presence <note>original: "Shekhinah"</note>.

<margin>Chapter five of Tractate Avot <note>Ethics of the Fathers</note></margin>
This is what is called "Torah for its own sake." And we learn in Tractate Berakhot, in the chapter "One who Recites," on page 17: Rav was habitually saying: "The goal of wisdom is repentance and good deeds, so that a person should not read and study and then kick <note>meaning to rebel or show disrespect</note> his father, his mother, his teacher, or someone greater than him in wisdom," as it is said: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord... to all who perform them" (Psalm 111:10). It does not say "to those who study them," but "to those who perform them." For those who perform them not for their own sake, it would have been better for them had they not been created. Therefore, a person must occupy themselves with Torah for its own sake; he should not use it to make himself great, nor to derive physical benefit from it. As we learned in the fourth chapter of Avot: Rabbi Tzadok says: Do not make them a crown to magnify yourself with, nor a spade to dig with. Hillel used to say: One who makes use of the Crown [of Torah] shall pass away. This teaches that anyone who benefits from the words of Torah removes their life from the world.
And we learn in Tractate Nedarim, in the chapter "Konam," on page 62: It is taught, "To love the Lord your God"—so that a person should not say, "I will read so that they will call me a Wise Man; I will study so that they will call me Rabbi; I will study so that I may be an Elder and sit in the Academy." Rather, learn out of love, and honor will eventually come, as it is said: "Bind them upon your neck..." (Proverbs 3:3), and it says: "Her ways are ways of pleasantness..." (Proverbs 3:17), and it says: "It is a tree of life..." (Proverbs 3:18). Rabbi Eleazar says: Do things for the sake of their Doer, and speak of them for their own sake. Do not make them a crown to magnify yourself with, nor a spade to dig with. And this is an argument from the lesser to the greater: if in the case of flesh and blood, when a person does work for the sake of his employer, he fulfills his employer's will, how much more so for one who makes use of the crown of the Torah! Woe to the person who is haughty regarding the words of Torah, as our Sages of blessed memory have elaborated greatly on this, and the parchment is too short to contain their words. Only, let him be humble and lowly in spirit. "One commandment leads to another," as we learned in chapter four: Ben Azzai says: "Run to a minor commandment as to a major one..." and do not be quick to falsehood. Return and labor in the Torah and receive wisdom from it, for they said: "Great is the one who acts for the sake of Heaven," and it is greater than the renunciation of money. For "he is taking a life as a pledge"—meaning the one who is guarded, for the souls of Israel and the Torah are one, as will be explained later at length.
And how very great is this sin in the eyes of one who says a simple meaning of a verse in a book, or something he heard, and does not mention the name of the one who said it or wrote it! Regarding the matter of meditating on words of Torah, our Rabbis of blessed memory have already warned about this, and it was agreed in Tractate Avot in the Mishnah of Rabbi Yohanan the Shoemaker in chapter five: "Any assembly that is for the sake of Heaven will endure."
Regarding the criticism of those who benefit from the power of their Torah: nevertheless, there are distinctions in this. Certainly, one who learns Torah so that they will have a great name and be honored, and people will benefit them, or one who maintains an academy so that they will have an income—their punishment is great. But one who takes benefit so that they can study and not be interrupted by having to seek their sustenance—this is certainly permitted. There is an explicit verse: "...to give the portion of the priests... so that they might hold fast to the Torah of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 31:4). And in the fifth chapter of Berakhot, Abaye said (and some say Rabbi Isaac): "He who wishes to benefit, let him benefit like Elisha <note>The prophet Elisha accepted the hospitality of the Shunammite woman</note>, and he who does not wish to benefit, let him not benefit like Samuel of Ramah <note>The prophet Samuel traveled at his own expense</note>, as it is said: 'And his return was to Ramah, for there was his house' (1 Samuel 7:17)." And Rabbi Yohanan said: Everywhere he went, his house was with him. The matter is that Samuel did not need those things, but Elisha did.
Furthermore, it is said there: One who constantly passes by—Rabbi Yossi bar Hanina said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Jacob: "Whoever hosts a Torah scholar <note>original: "Talmid Hakham"</note> in their house and lets them benefit from their possessions, the Scripture considers it as if they were sacrificing the daily offerings." And in the chapter "One who Hires Laborers," it is said: "Their teeth... the life of the world and life from them" <note>unclear citation, likely referring to the merit of supporting scholars</note>. And this was the claim of Ben Azzai, and he explained that "their teeth" refers to the troubles of not letting them benefit from one's possessions. And in the chapter Helek, page 100: "Anyone who does not let a Torah scholar benefit from their possessions will never see a sign of blessing, Heaven forbid." Even a small amount that is worthy of giving to benefit and help a Torah scholar—whoever does not do so bears their sin.
And we learn in the Jerusalem Talmud <note>original: "Yerushalmi"</note>, in the final chapter of Second Tithe: Rabbi Jonah would give the tithe to Rabbi Aha, not because he was a priest, but because he labored in the Torah. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Shekalim chapter five: Rabbi Hama bar Hanina and Rabbi Hoshaiah were walking in those synagogues of Lydda. Rabbi Hama said: "How much wealth did my ancestors sink here!" Rabbi Hoshaiah said to him: "How many souls did your ancestors sink here! Were there no people who could labor in the Torah?" Rabbi Abin made these gates of the Great Study Hall. Rabbi Mani came to him and said: "See what I have made!" He replied to him: "And Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces (Hosea 8:14). Were there no people who could labor in the Torah?" Thus, you see with your own eyes that these Sages criticized those who spent their money on the building of a synagogue—even though it is a great commandment—and called them "forgetters of their Maker" because they did not choose the better path, which is to give to those who occupy themselves with the Torah.
And in the Book of Splendor <note>original: "Sefer Ha-Zohar"</note>, in the section Vayichi, they said:

<margin>In the Book of the Zohar, section Vayichi</margin>
And I will bring blessings upon the one who takes the bread from his mouth and gives it to the mouth of Issachar <note>The tribe of Issachar traditionally represented the scholars, supported by the tribe of Zebulun</note>. From here we learn: anyone who supports a Master of Torah receives blessings from above and below. Not only that, but he merits two tables <note>success in both this world and the next</note> which another person does not merit; he merits wealth that is blessed in this world, and he merits having a portion in the World to Come.
Similarly, in Midrash Rabba at the end of the section Behar: Rabbi Tarfon gave Rabbi Akiva six centaria of silver and said to him, "Buy us a property so that we may occupy ourselves with Torah and find rest." Rabbi Akiva took them and divided them among the scribes and teachers and those who labor in the Torah. After some days, Rabbi Tarfon stood with him and said, "Show me the property you bought." He took him to the scribes and teachers and those who labor in Torah... and said, "This is the property I bought for you."
In Tractate Yoma: "He who wishes to pour wine upon the Altar should fill the throat of a Torah scholar." And similarly in Tractate Ketubot: "One who brings a gift to a Torah scholar is as if they were sacrificing the First Fruits." Behold, it is a great commandment, and see the reward for one who lets a Torah scholar benefit! And the Torah scholar is permitted to receive it so that they may be strong in the Torah of the Lord. If the Torah scholar were not permitted to receive it, then the giver would be transgressing the law: "Do not put a stumbling block before the blind." Why would it be considered a great commandment to benefit him? On the contrary, it would be considered a sin! Rather, it is as I explained.
Certainly, there were "men of ascent" <note>highly pious individuals</note> in Israel who ate dust and did not want to benefit, like the story of Yohanan ben Amram in the last chapter of Bava Batra, and like Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa, and like Rabbi Eleazar ben Pedat, who were very poor. Certainly, people would have given them much money, but they did not want to benefit. These are the "men of ascent," and they are few. However, one who benefits and receives in order to be able to hold fast to the Torah of the Lord without interruption is permitted. This general rule I hand over to you, my children: if you and those like you and your descendants merit to maintain an academy and to conduct yourselves by taking a rabbinic salary, you may take a rabbinic salary in order to maintain the academy and establish students. But do not maintain the academy for the sake of taking a rabbinic salary, for then it would be a "spade," Heaven forbid.
The ultimate goal of the matter is that one should study Torah for the sake of Heaven, and not for any honor or any money. If honor comes at the end because people honor him, he can receive enough to provide for the needs of his household. And even if it is more than what he needs, it is permitted, on the condition that it is doubly and triply clear that in his Torah study, his only intention was for the sake of Heaven and nothing else. And afterward, when the honor came to him on its own, he did not use any trickery or even a thought toward this; it simply came on its own because generous people arrived whose intention was for the sake of Heaven and not for any other reason. Then he is permitted to receive.
And with this matter, what Rashi wrote in the chapter "The Order of Fasts" (Taanit 21a) is settled. These are his words: "Rabbi Yohanan reigned—they appointed him Head of the Academy. It is the custom that whoever is the Head of the Academy, they would magnify him from their own and enrich him, as we say regarding the High Priest in the Sifra and in Yoma: 'The High Priest among his brothers'—magnify him from the resources of his brothers." End of quote. According to my introduction, if the recipient's study is for the sake of Heaven, both the taking and the giving are for the sake of the Name.

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual necessity of studying Torah with pure intentions ("for its own sake") and clarifies the ethics of communal support for scholars, distinguishing between forbidden self-aggrandizement and the virtuous act of supporting study for the sake of Heaven.</summary>
