# Tractate Shevuot

...And the teacher explained: "If to desecrate" <note>Hebrew: *le-chalel*. This likely refers to a teaching on the sanctity of life and lineage</note> meaning that they should serve the Blessed Name. For the primary purpose of the offspring that the righteous desire is to have children who are masters of good deeds. Therefore: "Honor your father and your mother." 

Behold, the first five commandments are between Man and the Omnipresent <note>Hebrew: *HaMakom*, a name for God implying He is the "place" of the world</note>, and their root is "I am the Lord your God." Corresponding to them are the five commandments between Man and his fellow:

**Thou shalt not murder** — Man is made in the [Divine] Image, and murder is therefore an act against "I am the Lord your God."
**Thou shalt not commit adultery** — This corresponds to "You shall have no other gods." One must cling only to his wife, just as the Lord is the [only] God, within the secret of "I am the Lord your God," which is the Supernal Union.
**Thou shalt not steal** — This refers to the "chariot" <note>Hebrew: *merkavah*, a mystical structure</note> of kidnapping souls, which separates a Jewish soul from its source. This corresponds to "Thou shalt not take [the Name in vain]." I have written regarding the dignity of Man in the upper realms, and I previously cited Recanati <note>Rabbi Menahem Recanati, a 13th-14th century Italian Kabbalist</note> regarding "Thou shalt not take," that one who does so separates, as it were, soul from soul—that is, the Name *YHVH* from *Elohim*.
**Thou shalt not bear false witness** — This corresponds to "Remember the Sabbath day," which is the testimony of Creation and the sustenance of the world, as I have written. Since the essence of Creation is Man, one must not bear false witness against him.
**Thou shalt not covet** — This corresponds to "Honor your father and your mother." 

First, I will introduce a passage from the Zohar <note>The foundational text of Jewish mysticism, written in Aramaic</note>: "The commands 'Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, do not covet' — no musical accent <note>Hebrew/Aramaic: *ta'am*, meaning both 'musical note' and 'reason'</note> was placed to stop between them. For if there were no stopping accent, there would be no restoration for the worlds, and it would be forbidden for us to ever take a life, even one who [legally] violated the Torah. But since there are stopping accents, it is [only] forbidden for an Israelite [to murder]."

**Thou shalt not commit adultery** — If there were no stopping accent, it would be forbidden even to procreate or to be with one's wife for the joy of the commandment. But since there is a stopping accent, it is [only] forbidden for an Israelite [to commit adultery].
**Thou shalt not steal** — If there were no stopping accent, it would be forbidden even to "steal the mind" <note>A Hebrew idiom for deception</note> of one's teacher in Torah, or the mind of a sage to learn from him, or for a judge to use legal deception to uncover a fraud. But since there is a stopping accent, it is [only] forbidden for an Israelite [to steal property].
**Thou shalt not bear false witness** — Against your neighbor. Here, there is no stopping accent because the testimony of the Torah is a general principle. In all matters of Torah, the judge and witness are meant to teach humanity the path of self-improvement, as it says: "I am the Lord who teaches you for your benefit, who leads you in the way you should go." 
**Thou shalt not covet** — There is no stopping accent here at all. One might say even the "donkey of the Torah" <note>Metaphor for a student who carries much knowledge but lacks deep understanding</note> is forbidden [to covet]. However, come and see: in all other commands, the Torah speaks generally, but here it specifies: "your neighbor’s house, his field, his servant," etc., regarding worldly things. But the Torah itself is always "coveted" and a "delight" for the spirit, length of days in this world and the next. 

One may ask: why does the text change for "Do not covet," lengthening it and specifying details? It should simply say "Do not covet" and have a stopping accent like the others. It seems this command is unlike the others; the others have a "permitted" side <note>e.g., legal execution or marital relations</note>, though that permission is not constant. Therefore, "Do not murder," "Do not commit adultery," and "Do not steal" are grouped to warn whoever violates the law, yet "He shall live by them" is also written. Regarding "Do not covet," however, the Torah itself *should* be coveted. Just as the prohibition has no fixed time and is eternal, the "coveting" of the Torah must be eternal. This corresponds to "Honor your father and your mother," who represent the Written and Oral Torah. Thus, it is clear that all Ten Commandments were spoken in a single utterance, revolving around the word "I [am]," five against five: the Torah of God and the Torah of Man.

These two concepts—the Torah in Seven Voices and the Torah in Five Voices—represent either the essential union of Beauty <note>*Tiferet*</note> and Sovereignty <note>*Malkhut*</note> as "Two Great Luminaries" of equal stature, or the aspect of the Seven Voices, the Great Luminary...

<column-break/>

...And this means that Sovereignty was unified with the [higher levels] through the Foundation <note>*Yesod*</note> and [Understanding].
And all the places are opened with complete mercy and flow simply in the secret of blessing. From the depths of the [Divine] Names, everything becomes submissive to Him so that they may flow. All the flow that is breathed into a person comes through this. And then the soul [reaches] the Gates of the Divine Presence <note>*Shekhinah*</note>... 

In the first stage, the attributes are acquired as general principles. Then, the "Ten" are included in each general principle, so that each one is comprised of ten. Observe how the *Sefirot* <note>Divine emanations</note> are comprised of seven, and from the Divine Presence <note>*Shekhinah*</note> downward they are comprised of ten, which is the secret of Wisdom <note>*Chokhmah*</note> and above. When the secret of the Union is completed in the Crown <note>*Keter*</note>, mercy rests upon them to flow in a totality of ten. These are the "Seven" multiplied by ten: Beauty, Sovereignty, and Foundation are unified. 

This is the meaning of the [spiritual] elevation in the daytime. In the world of Unity, He flows to the seven, which is the "Seven of Building." When they are included together, they become seventy... These are the "Seven Voices" that were heard... The Divine Presence <note>*Shekhinah*</note> reveals the Names of the Lord... for the *Sefirot* in their essence are the mystery of the King... 

There are "Faces within Faces." Each *Sefirah* is comprised of ten... See the book *Pardes* <note>*Pardes Rimonim* by Moshe Cordovero</note> in the first gate. So too in other places... If these inclusions [of the *Sefirot*] did not exist, the world could not exist...

The "Five Voices" represent the inclusion of Foundation and Sovereignty within Beauty... but when they are mixed, even though the *Sefirah* itself is not changed, Foundation and Sovereignty are "captured" by Beauty. This creates the "Seven *Sefirot*." 

The secret of the "Ten" is the Pillar of Cloud... and the "Seven" correspond to the portion of the Chariot... which raises Israel. For "Righteousness" <note>*Tzedek*</note> purifies from the side of the "End." These influences are particularly found in the [sacred] books... and in the future, Israel will merit the primordial light through the restoration [of these attributes]. 

Regarding the "Seven Nations" <note>The nations inhabiting Canaan before the Israelites</note>, they were like a "shell" <note>*Kelipah*</note> that is "evil," even more evil than the soul itself. This is what is meant by "He will not let you go," etc. In the Zohar, portion *Beha'alotkha*, it is explained that there is a "Bone" and "Flesh" and "Soul." The Soul is the delight, but the others are the husks...

It is written "Good" regarding the Torah... This refers to the Foundation <note>*Yesod*</note>, the source of the "Sign" <note>The Covenant</note>. For the word "Good" <note>Hebrew: *Tov*</note> appears in the Torah... and when the light and the Torah and the Beauty [are unified]... mercy comes... as I have explained...

<margin>Salt—remember; Salt—add; Salt etc. until the end of the sign: Sword. Voice, salt etc. Kohani, Kasni, Poni, Sini, Korah, Kabal. In the transmission of trade, these words require investigation or a simple explanation. Furthermore, because the "Radiance of the Pious One" <note>original: "Keren HaChasid." This likely refers to a specific sage or a mystical light associated with a holy person</note> was greatly distressed, he said one must hide these words and guard them in truth, in heaven, and in fear, for these matters are hidden before the Holy One, Blessed be He.</margin>
In a place where there is a doubt regarding a Name <note>Refers to the Names of God, which have specific laws of sanctity in scribal practice</note>, whether it is secular or holy: how should the scribe act? Should he sanctify it or not? I have received a practical legal tradition to follow the Translation <note>original: "Targum." Usually refers to the Aramaic translation of the Bible (Targum Onkelos), which distinguishes between when a word like "Elohim" refers to God or to judges/idols</note>. According to the consensus of the Translation, so shall he do, and we do not deviate. It is also possible to say, "I am writing for the sake of sanctity," and the scribe should think in his heart: "If this name is holy, I am writing it for the sake of its sanctity entirely; and even if it is secular, I am writing it for the sake of the sanctity at its head and its root." This is easily understood. This is included in the concept of "making wise the simple," <note>Psalm 19:8</note> for even in "simplicity" <note>original: "petyut," also implying folly or openness</note> there is wisdom at its beginning. Also, regarding "making wise the simple," you must know that the Hebrew language is only a covering <note>original: "mekhasay." The author suggests the outer language hides deeper truths</note>, and behold—

<margin>miracle <note>original: "nes," also meaning "banner" or "sign"</note></margin>
In every place where there is a need to explain the end of a verse as being "truncated" <note>original: "katzar"</note> or the like, it is all according to the measure of our understanding. But in truth, for one who understands the wisdom and the hints of the language in its fine grammatical points, he would understand the matter without needing a "conclusion" <note>original: "siyum"</note>. It is only because the matter is "empty" <note>a play on the verse "it is not an empty thing from you"</note> to us that we must transpose words or force the meaning. However, there is great hidden wisdom where the matter is exactly as its literal meaning without any external conclusion. I believe this even regarding the Mishnah, where the Talmud says "the text is missing a part" <note>term: <term>Chasuri Mechasra</term> — a Talmudic principle where the Sages assume a line of text is missing from a Mishnah to make it align with the law</note>. This is only according to the measure of our understanding. But our Holy Teacher <note>Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the redactor of the Mishnah</note> composed the Mishnah with Divine Inspiration and with choice and deeply profound poetic language hidden within it. If it were understood, we would not need to claim something is "missing." Therefore, the language of the Mishnah is no less than the Scripture itself. This is the meaning of "no verse departs from its literal meaning" <note>term: <term>Ein Mikra yotze mi-pashuto</term> — the principle that even with allegorical interpretations, the plain meaning remains valid</note>. All things are literally as they are to those who understand, and it is "not an empty thing," except from us, and so we must transpose. After I wrote this, I found similar words in the book *Adnei Levanon* <note>a work by Rabbi Meir ben Isaac Eisenstadt</note>, page 110: Our Sages said, "no verse departs from its literal meaning." When they said "no verse departs," they did not say "the verse is only interpreted literally." This means that according to the "seventy faces of the Torah," <note>The idea that the Torah has 70 levels of meaning</note> not one of them contradicts the literal meaning. Perhaps the literal meaning is one of the seventy. If so, no scholar has the right to offer an explanation that contradicts the literal meaning by saying "this verse is missing four or two words" or "half of it is reversed" without necessity. Rather, the verse is as it is. In the measure of providence, there are many verses where we feel we must add a word or two because of the "literal" sense; this is not because of the verse itself, but because of our own lack, for we do not understand the Holy Tongue—not even in the way it resembles the languages we are immersed in during our exile.

<margin>Remember and His covenant in writing etc.</margin>
How beautiful is the layout for the homiletic study of the Talmudic discussions of Rashi and Tosafot, which are all founded in wisdom! However, it is a mistake in my eyes not to stop between one pamphlet and another according to the year. May God be with you. And "behold the Oral Law," <note>original: "ve-chaze she-be'al peh"</note> and there I will place it next to the pamphlet called "The Written Torah."
And the "He" [of the Name] "makes wise the simple": even though one understands and contemplates the verse, he is still "simple" if he transposes and flips the excellence of the letters. But the letters themselves "make wise." Also, "the testimony of the Lord is faithful" refers to the Oral Law. Furthermore, "The testimony of the Lord" <note>original: "Edut Hashem"</note> in Gematria <note>Jewish numerology</note> equals "Talmud" <note>Both equal 480</note>. This is the testimony between the Blessed Name and His dwelling place. The Holy One, Blessed be He, commanded: "The Oral Torah—you are not permitted to write it down." The reason is that the Holy One, Blessed be He, gave "signs" to Israel to distinguish them, just as Jacob gave signs to Rachel so that Laban would not deceive him. So too it is written regarding the Torah, "to give craftiness to the simple." This was for the sake of the nations of the world, so they would not copy it. For it was revealed and known before Him that they would copy the Written Torah and claim, "It is ours." But in the future, the Holy One, Blessed be He, will ask: "In whose hand are the signs that I delivered mouth-to-mouth? That one is My own." Then Israel will come with their signs. This is explained in the Midrash brought by the Tosafot in Tractate Gittin, chapter *HaNizakin*, page 60: "Were I to write for him the many things of My Torah, they would be accounted as a stranger's" <note>Hosea 8:12</note>. This means the nations of the world wrote down the Torah. If everything had been written for Israel, the nations would have copied it all. Therefore, He said, "I wrote the majority of My Torah" as a metaphor, and the compassion is in what I *did* write for you, lest they be considered "strangers" who copy it. This is hinted at in the Sages' statement in Tractate Avodah Zarah: In the future, the Holy One, Blessed be He, will take a Torah scroll in His lap and say to the nations, "Is there anyone among you who fulfilled *this*?" And "this" refers only to the Torah, as it is said, "And *this* is the Torah which Moses set." It is difficult to understand why the Sages used such a long phrasing; they should have simply said, "And *this* is the Torah."

<margin>Acquire. And even now that the speaking voice has been written down, it belongs to him to hear from the mouth of a scholar. "It is time to act for the Lord, they have made void Your Torah" <note>Psalm 119:126, used to justify writing the Oral Law</note>. The Holy One, Blessed be He, was the one who placed it in the heart of the early ones to write it down from their mouths at the time of the copying of the Oral Law, and they gave the signs as is known. Blessed be He and blessed be His name.</margin>
The letter Aleph [of the Name] represents: The Torah is called by the name of the Holy One, Blessed be He—"The Torah of the Lord"—and it is called by the name of Moses—"The Torah of Moses." The matter is that the Written Torah is entirely His Name, and the Oral Torah is entirely the "mouth of Moses" <note>original: "pishat Moshe"</note> as we will explain later, and it is called by his name. It is already known that "This" (masculine) and "This" (feminine) <note>original: "Zeh" and "Zot"</note> refer to the Written and Oral Torah. The Written Torah is called *Zeh* ("This"—the "Luminous Mirror") and the Oral Torah is *Zot* ("This"—the "Non-Luminous Mirror"). In the future, the Holy One, Blessed be He, will ask for the signs, which is the Oral Torah. This is why it says *Zot* in the language of a mission to ask—for the intention is not the Written Torah, but the Torah of which it is said "And *this* (*Zot*) is the Torah which Moses set," which is the Oral Torah. This is easily understood. This is "making wise the simple," to give the simple "craftiness" to save them from deception. "Signs" are a Torah requirement. This is the matter of the "covenant" mentioned in Tractate Gittin, chapter *HaNizakin*: Rabbi Yochanan said, "The Holy One, Blessed be He, did not make a covenant with Israel except for the sake of the oral matters, as it says: 'For according to the mouth of these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel.'"

### The Excellence of Those Who Study It

"The mandates of the Lord are upright, rejoicing the heart." Above, in the introduction to *Toldot Adam*, I spoke at length regarding the phrasing "He gave the Torah" versus "He gives the Torah." For the Holy One, Blessed be He, still gives the Torah every day in a revealed way. This is not to say there isn't another explanation for this. One explanation is that He "did not add" <note>Deuteronomy 5:19</note>, and another is the opposite: He "did not cease." Both are true. He "did not add" at that specific time to reveal more than He did, but He "did not cease" because all the prophecies of the prophets and all the innovations of the scribes in every generation and its scholars are contained within it. Everything that a student innovates was already in the power of that Voice, and now its time has arrived according to the generation to come to light. Thus, all the words of our Rabbis, the enactments, the fences, and the customs—everything is from Sinai. See above at length. All of this belongs here as well. There it was also explained well that "these and these are the words of the Living God" <note>A famous Talmudic phrase indicating that multiple valid opinions can exist</note>. To this the verse hints: "The mandates of the Lord are upright." The word "mandates" <note>original: "Pikudei"</note> is a language of appointment, like the "officers of the congregation." It hints at every generation and its scholars and seekers. It is also a language of "deposit" <note>original: "Pikadon"</note>, hinting at what was deposited and hidden in that Voice which had not yet come to light, but comes to light in every era through the scholars of each generation. These are the "mandates of the Lord." Even if it seems the Blessed One did not command them except through the Rabbis, in truth, the Lord commanded them, and now they are revealed to the light. Regarding them it is said: "I will never forget Your mandates." Your mandates are where the spirit of the Lord speaks through them, for souls are the spirituality of the Torah and the commandments. They are the threads of the flames spreading out from that "Great Voice." This is the Torah that the Holy One says in the name of the scholars: "My son Meir says thus..." etc. This is why we pray: "Give us our portion in Your Torah," that we too may merit that the Holy One, Blessed be He, says things in our name. It also means: "Give us our portion in Your Torah"—that the words of Torah we innovate should be saturated with words of truth which are *Your* Torah. That is, that which was in the power of this Great Voice, so that we do not, heaven forbid, innovate things that are not true. In the innovation of a true thing, that is our portion, but in truth, it is His Torah. We are merely the ones who bring the words of the Sages to light through our souls, which are from the source of this matter. This is the explanation of our Sages: "A scholar is superior to a prophet." That is, the aspect of Wisdom is more refined than the aspect of Prophecy. As our Sages said in Tractate Megillah regarding the insight that "no prophet is destined to innovate anything from now on"—meaning from the aspect of Prophecy, the Holy One does not give a "new" Torah beyond what was given through Moses, our teacher, peace be upon him (except for temporary rulings). However, from the aspect of Wisdom, the scholars understand one thing from another and bring the hidden to light according to the soul's aspect of what they already grasped and understood at the Standing at Mount Sinai in the aforementioned Great Voice. Now, with the revelation of these souls, it is revealed to the light in this time. Through this, we can explain the statement in Tractate Shabbat, chapter *HaBoneh*, where Rabbi Yochanan says: "ANOKHI" <note>The first word of the Ten Commandments, "I"</note> is an acronym for "I Myself wrote and gave" (*Ana Nafshi Ketavit Yehavit*). The Rabbis say it stands for "A pleasant saying, a writing, a giving." Others say "ANOKHI" refers to the books... give heart to this. This is a hint to seek the acronym backwards or why he changed the language... Before I explain this statement, I must preface that "writing" refers to the Written Torah and "saying" refers to the Oral Torah. Likewise, "writing and giving"—that is the Oral Torah, as it is written: "He put wisdom in his mouth." And this is "writing," and this is—

One must examine the word **except a voice** [Deuteronomy 4:12]. Is "seeing" not inapplicable to a "voice"? Furthermore, it is not within the realm of faith to say "except a voice." From the strength of this difficulty, we are forced to say that they even saw a **form** within the voice. That form which all of Israel perceived at the standing at Mount Sinai was not a human form, but rather the form of the **letters** from which the voice and the speech are made. I have already informed you that they are divine, living powers. And since we have a true root-principle that nothing which emerges from the thought of the Blessed and Exalted One returns empty—whether in His thought or in His speech—for everything produces fruit, whether for good or for bad, to the extent that [the Sages] said that His thought to punish the wicked creates forces of judgment, and the reverse is also true. If so, His "good word" which He spoke to Moses His servant when He said, "I am the Lord your God," and all the Ten Utterances—those very words they heard and **saw with their eyes**: the letters of that speech. For they were engraved and hewn in flames of fire, as it is said: "The voice of the Lord hews out flames of fire" [Psalm 29:7]. They saw them with their eyes, and for this reason the scripture says, **"And all the people saw the voices and the torches and the mountain, etc."** [Exodus 20:15]. Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "They saw that which is normally heard, which the mouth cannot speak, etc." <note>Rashi explains the miracle of "synesthesia" at Sinai, where the people saw the sounds</note>. Perhaps he intended this [mystical explanation]. This is the end of his quote.

And it is written in the portion *Va'etchanan*: "**And it was, when you heard the voice... behold, the Lord our God has shown us His glory and we have heard His voice**" [Deuteronomy 5:20-21]. Thus, the "seeing of the letters" is the testimony that "God is in our midst" and "He showed us all these." And it says **"making wise the simple"** [Psalm 19:8] to let us hear the great level of the letters of the Torah, for they bring wisdom to the one of whom they said "the letters make wise."

The author of the *Pardes* <note>Rabbi Moshe Cordovero in his "Pardes Rimmonim"</note> elaborated greatly on this in the "Gate of Letters," chapters one and two, and I copied from them into *Toldot Adam* <note>A work by the author of this manuscript</note> in the investigation of the Holy Tongue. Look at what is written above, for it is needed here. There it is clarified that one who reads the Torah "for the sake of Heaven" to contemplate the words—even if he does not understand, and the precision of the letters did not come easily to him, and he remains "simple" as he was—nevertheless, he has a "cleaving" <note><term>Dveikus</term>: mystical attachment to the Divine</note> to the Wisdom, and it will benefit him in the future. This is the meaning of "making wise the simple." Therefore, it was taught that it was written "Assyrian" <note>The standard block script used in Torah scrolls</note> to be said by heart <note>The text here is likely discussing the visual requirement of reading from a scroll</note>, so that one may be "mounted" upon the sight of its letters.

Similarly, it is written in the book *Kad HaKemah* <note>A 14th-century work of ethics by Rabbenu Bahya</note> under the entry "Torah," and these are his words: "Reading the Torah is a great commandment even if he does not understand what he reads, provided that he knows he is reading. For sometimes a person reads a portion of the Torah but does not realize he is reading because he is thinking of other things; he does not fulfill his obligation. But when he knows he is reading, it is a great commandment and he has a great reward. This is what they taught in the first chapter of *Avodah Zarah*: 'A person should always learn, even if he does not know what he is saying, as it says: *My soul is crushed with longing* [Psalm 119:20]...'" <note>The Sages interpret "crushed" (ga-re-sah) as "learning" (girsa), suggesting one should "grind" through the text even without full comprehension</note>. And the blessing followed him.

I also found it written—and it is a wonder—that the scripture says, "**And you shall meditate upon it day and night**" [Joshua 1:8], etc. This teaches that "meditation" <note>Hebrew: *Hegina*</note> alone—that is, the reading—has a specific "remedy" <note><term>Segulah</term>: a spiritual or supernatural property</note>. And how much more so if it is accompanied by good understanding and the attainment of its secrets! This remedy also clings to the Prophets and the Writings <note>The other two sections of the Hebrew Bible</note>, and their reward changes into another language, provided they are in the Holy Tongue.

The ancients called the twenty-four [books of the Bible] "The Sanctuary." They said: "I will return and dwell," just as the Sanctuary was the cause for the continuation of the Divine Presence among the Children of Israel, as it is written: "And they shall make for Me a Sanctuary and I will dwell among them" [Exodus 25:8]. So too this Holy Book: because of it, there was Divine Providence within the letters by increasing the reading of it, and it is the cause of its [Israel's] existence during this long exile. And just as the Sanctuary, through the service of the inner matters, is the cause for God to atone for our sins, so too the one who engages in this book—the Sanctuary—with desired intent, diligence, and guarding it in the heart, is the cause for God to forgive our sins, as it is said: "I will put My Torah within them... for I will forgive their iniquity" [Jeremiah 31:32-33].

Because this book, the Sanctuary, changes in its "remedy" into a Sanctuary, the ancients mapped it out:
*   **The Torah** corresponds to the **Holy of Holies**, for it corresponds to the world of the Intellect, to the God of Israel and the Angels.
*   **The Prophets** correspond to the **Sanctuary** [the *Heikhal*], which is the source of the Table, the Menorah, and the Altar of Incense; it corresponds to the world of the Spheres [the stars/planets].
*   **The Writings** correspond to the **Hall** [the *Ulam*] and the **Courtyards**, which correspond to the lower, physical world.

They called it the "Sanctuary of God" because it sanctifies [us] in this exile. The engagement, the meditation, and the reading in them alone is part of the "Service" [the *Avodah*]. For as it were, the Name is not complete...
...the true [service] appropriate for a man, and that which draws down the Influence, the Divinity, and the Providence through a remedy attached to them. This we have seen through experience and the senses, for when the scholar engages in this book, the Sanctuary, everything is revealed, as it is written: "And they read in the book of the Torah of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading" [Nehemiah 8:8]. There were deep meanings and a cleaving of Divine Providence upon them when they ascended from the time of the Exile. Until here [ends the quote].

Twenty-eight... and my fathers to him... stories and inks... twenty letters.

Happy is the man who makes an effort every week to go to the synagogue to read the Torah portion from within the Torah scroll. I have a tradition regarding what is stated in Tractate *Berakhot* and Tractate *Shabbat* regarding Rav Ami and Rav Assi: even though they had thirteen synagogues, they would only pray "between the pillars." This means **between the pillars of the Torah scroll** that was open before them. They would study from it and be precise with its letters, and when the time for prayer arrived, they would pray with their faces toward the Torah scroll.

I must also provide another moral instruction to those who say the words of Torah in a rush, because of the "heat" in their mouths, and also the portions of the thirty-two Princes <note>Numbers ch. 7, which lists identical offerings by the tribal leaders</note>. Since the words are repetitive and they double them in their hands so quickly, it is a great "exhausting labor" on such a day. This is a "sore evil" [Ecclesiastes 5:12]... our teacher and many spiritual worlds [rely on this]. It was not for nothing that the words were repeated! Happy is the one who is precise with the breath of his mouth and the sight of his eyes upon the letters of the Torah.

<meta>This page continues the mystical and philosophical exploration of the Revelation at Sinai, specifically focusing on the nature of the Divine Voice and the relationship between the Written Torah and the Oral Law. It references the debate regarding whether the Israelites heard the actual words of God or merely a sound, engaging directly with the views of Maimonides (the Rambam).</meta>

<header>Tractate Shevuot</header>

the essence itself, and this is the "Voice" which is from the heavens, as it is written: "From the heavens He made you hear His voice." And it is written: "A likeness [you saw not; only a voice]," which refers to the "Likeness of the Letters." As I mentioned above, this is the secret of the Torah, which is written "black [fire] upon [white fire]," <note>A traditional metaphor for the Torah's origins; the "black fire" represents the ink/letters and the "white fire" represents the parchment/spaces.</note> without end and without limit. How so? According to how it is written and arranged in its letters. Our intention here regarding the creators of the Oral Torah <term>Torah she-be-al-peh; the tradition of legal and spiritual interpretation passed down by the Sages</term> is that it stems from the Written Torah. However, the letters of the Torah have many "faces" arising from many combinations; words can be formed from letters in different ways and through various perspectives, a thousand thousand, ten thousand myriads, without limit and without end. Furthermore, through the substitution of its letters <note>Referring to systems like Atbash, where letters are swapped according to specific ciphers.</note> in all types of alphabets and permutations, it becomes infinite. As stated earlier regarding the excellence of the Torah, these wonders were revealed only to the "children of the upper chamber" <note>An idiom for elite scholars or mystics.</note> with all their strength. All of this is contained within the "Great Voice which did not cease" (Deut. 5:19). Every prophet received from it, and even everything a diligent student will innovate in the future was already received then. That is to say, they stood there, and from there it is now being revealed. In this regard, the Oral Torah is like a small portion of the Written Torah. Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Elazar do not disagree on this; rather, the difference between them lies in the meaning of "permission." One speaks of the aspect of "not ceasing" and calls this "writing," for even though the specific reading is hidden from us, the primary "faces" of its letters are written before us. Regarding this, He said: "I have written for him the many things of my Law." Rabbi Yohanan, however, holds that this cannot be called "writing" since we do not know the [hidden] reading; therefore, he speaks of the aspect that "He did not continue" to reveal it. The verse "I wrote for you the greatness of my Torah" is phrased as a wonder... and regarding this, the conclusion is with the portion of Reuben. Some say they do not disagree at all, but merely speak from two different perspectives. We say that the writing and the speech became a "pleasant original utterance"—the Oral Torah, which is even more precious in terms of how it grows. And He replied: "Writing," which is the Written Torah as it is written before us. This is the support... I saw the "children of the upper chamber," and they are few, like the Babylonian craftsmen. It was through the righteousness of the letters with which heaven and earth were created—meaning the hidden letters—for the Holy One, Blessed be He, looked into the Torah and created the world. Some say the Torah is "writing"... the spiritual abundance prepared for the wise. All the innovations and prophecies of the prophets, and the innovations of the sages and students, all come from the "faces" of the Torah that were hidden and which they brought to light. Everything is within the letters of the Torah; thus the Torah is "writing," and the Written Torah "did not cease" and will never cease. And "faithfully" refers to that Oral Torah, as I expounded above. It is also possible to interpret "faithfully" in the sense of "In all my house he is faithful" (Num. 12:7), which was the Holy One's response to Moses regarding the Oral Torah.

## Returning
to the matter of the verse: "The precepts of the Lord are right" (Psalm 19:9). What are "the precepts of the Lord"? The "precepts of the Lord" refer to "every generation and its sages." Those who bring the hidden into the light are "right," for "the ways of the Lord are right; the just walk in them, but the sinners stumble therein" (Hosea 14:10). Regarding these [sages], it says they "rejoice the heart," while regarding those [sinners], they are an "abomination to their hearts." The heart is full of wisdom, a flowing spring that never ceases, and in it is the "Heart of Israel." The Holy One, Blessed be He... as the Sages expounded on the verse "And I will give you a submissive heart," even unto your own heart, for He is the Heart of Israel and the Holy One, as it is said: "my heart and my portion." This is from the perspective of the souls clinging to Him, which is why the hidden was revealed through them.

<margin>The Rabbi <note>referring to Maimonides/Rambam</note> explained in the *Guide for the Perplexed* that the "Voice," the essence which was heard, was not... the Torah was given... and it is forbidden to hear the words, but rather the Voice is a created voice from heaven, and He made His voice heard. The "Heavens" refers to the "Beauty of Israel" <term>Tiferet Yisrael; a mystical attribute associated with the Written Torah</term>. Regarding the hearing of the voice at that holy assembly, whether all the speech heard by Moses reached Israel or not—the Rambam did not speak clearly on this, for his opinion is that the "speech" was for Moses alone, and only the "recognition of the sound" reached Israel.</margin>

## Toward the Perfection
of the matter mentioned above, it is necessary to elaborate and make known the excellence of those who received the Torah, and the excellence of every single generation that was there and received their portion. The Great Teacher <note>Maimonides</note> held that they did not perceive "speech" at all, but rather that massive Voice created without breath or letters. Moses would then tell Israel what he heard. He claimed this is what the scripture intends by saying "I stood between the Lord and you," and "Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice." He wrote that this indicates the speech was his, and they only heard the massive Voice. It says, "When you heard the voice," and "You heard the sound of words [but saw no image]." Wherever "hearing words" appears, he interprets it as hearing the Voice, while Moses made the words known and publicized them. He said this was his view, and that it is what appears from the Torah and the majority of the words of the Sages. However, when he [Maimonides] encountered the statement of the Sages that "I [am the Lord]" and "You shall have no [other gods]" were heard directly "from the mouth of the Might" <note>From God Himself</note>, which implies these two commandments reached Israel just as they reached Moses, he turned away from the "straight path" (the literal meaning of the words) and sought "many calculations." He argued that "from the mouth of the Might" refers to logical proof. He claimed these two—the existence of God and His unity—can be achieved through human contemplation. Anything known through proof is equal for the Prophet and for anyone else who knows it. He claimed there is no advantage... only from the side of prophecy did the Torah say, "You have been shown to know." These are his words, and this is the summary of his opinion on the "Day of the Assembly": that what reached Israel was a sound alone, not a collection of letters, but for Moses, the speech descended in a connection of letters, and he made it heard to Israel. He said the power of the Ten Commandments was... but the primary Sages of Truth <note>The Kabbalists</note> also disagreed with him in their "Holy Service," and they spoke at great length in explaining the words of faith which you shall understand forever. This [faith] is that all Ten Commandments reached Israel exactly as they reached Moses, for the Divine Will was to establish faith so that all Israel would be prophets in the entire Torah generally, and would not need any intermediary. This is because the Ten Commandments are the root of everything.

We shall not desecrate the dispute... as it is spoken in the scripture... But for any matter that has no hint in the Scripture and is not stated within it... and they received it through the methods of logic, regarding those specifically they said "Law given to Moses at Sinai."

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the Revelation at Sinai, specifically exploring the relationship between the Written Torah and the Oral Law. It addresses the philosophical question of how much of the specific details of the law were originated by Moses versus being directly dictated by God, using the first word of the Ten Commandments as a focal point for this inquiry.</meta>

# Tractate Shevuot

Rabbi Yochanan said: "I" <note>original Hebrew: *Anokhi*, the first word of the Ten Commandments</note> is an acrostic for **"I Myself have written and given"** <note>original: *Ana Nafshi Ketavit Yehavit*</note>. Resh Lakish said: It refers to the "Writing and the Teaching"—the Written Torah was given, and that which is Oral is also entirely from the mouth of the Almighty. He came to teach us in this noble statement that perhaps we might form an understanding from certain statements which hint at how Moses our Teacher (peace be upon him) testified to the Oral Torah from his own mind. Yet, he aimed for the truth. This is found in the Midrash <note>A genre of rabbinic literature that interprets biblical texts</note> regarding the verse "And it was when He finished [speaking] to Moses" <note>Exodus 31:18</note>: the word "finished" <note>Hebrew: *kelloto*</note> is written in a way that suggests a "bride" <note>Hebrew: *kallato*</note>, implying something was missing. From this, it appears that the Holy One, blessed be He, handed over only general principles, and it is said that Moses our Teacher, peace be upon him, understood the details on his own. Similarly, in the *Midrash Rabbah* at the end of the portion *Ki Tisa*, it says regarding the verse "Write for yourself": The ministering angels began saying before the Holy One, blessed be He, "Are You giving permission to Moses to write whatever he wishes to say to Israel? 'I' have given you the Torah; 'I' am the one who wrote it and gave it to you!" The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them, "Heaven forbid that Moses would do such a thing! And even if he did, he is trustworthy, as it is said: 'Not so My servant Moses; in all My house he is trustworthy' <note>Numbers 12:7</note>."

From this, it is implied that Moses understood from his own intellect. To save us from such claims, God said: **"I Myself have written and given,"** meaning that the Holy One, blessed be He, Himself gave the Written Torah and He Himself explained it—that is, the Oral Torah, with its generalities, its details, and its fine points. Thus our Sages of blessed memory said in a *Baraita* <note>A tradition from the era of the Mishnah not included in the main text</note>: "And He descended to Moses on Mount Sinai." What does this teach us? Was not the entire Torah said from Sinai? Rather, it tells you that just as the Sabbatical year was stated with its generalities, details, and fine points from Sinai, so too all the commandments, their generalities, details, and fine points are from Sinai. 

Behold, here is an example: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, "In booths <term>Sukkot</term> you shall dwell seven days." Afterward, He informed him that this booth is an obligation for males and not for females; that it applies to those who are settled and not travelers; and that a booth must be made only from that which grows from the ground; and that one may not roof it with wool, nor with silk, nor with vessels—even those made from things that grow from the earth, such as cushions or garments. He also informed him that eating, drinking, and sleeping in it for all seven days is an obligation; and that its interior space must be no less than seven handbreadths long by seven handbreadths wide; and that the height of the booth must be no less than ten handbreadths. When the Prophet [Moses], peace be upon him, came, this commandment was given to him along with its explanation. So it is with all six hundred and thirteen commandments: the commandment is in writing, and the explanation is oral.

This is the language of the work *Avodat HaKodesh* <note>A 16th-century Kabbalistic work by Meir ibn Gabbai</note> in Chapter 22 of the "Section on Divine Service": Since one has already ascended in the understanding of the generalities of the book, for the entire Torah is emanated from the Supreme Wisdom, which is the Wisdom of God—the Supreme Thought which cannot be grasped at all. Regarding this it is said: "For My thoughts are not your thoughts" <note>Isaiah 55:8</note>; the word "your thoughts" is written without the letter *Vav*. Thus they said in the Midrash of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai <note>The Zohar</note>, peace be upon him: "Come and see: The Thought of the Holy One, blessed be He, is supreme; it is the head of all. From that Thought, paths and trails spread out to find a place for the Holy One to dwell, and to be established in the Palaces of the Holy One, blessed be He. From that Thought, the watering of the Garden of Eden flows and goes forth to water everything. From that Thought, the Written Torah and the Oral Torah are found, for in that Thought, the upper and lower worlds exist." 

The order of the matter is that the Written Torah and the Oral Torah—which are the letters *Vav* and *Heh* of the Great Name <note>The Tetragrammaton, Y-H-V-H</note>—were emanated from the Supreme Thought. The two Torahs that we received from the mouth of the Almighty, which are the Written Torah and its explanation, the Oral Torah, were emanated from them, fixed, and engraved from them. The source of everything is that Thought which is hidden from the eyes of all living things; grasping it is impossible. Just as that Source is impossible to grasp except by the will of the True Willer—who in His wondrous Thought desired to hew from it the two great channels, the Written Torah and the Oral Torah—so too, it would be impossible for us to know His will if He Himself did not inform us and explain His will to us. For this reason, just as we required the tradition from His mouth for the Written Torah which was hewn from that Source, so we required the tradition from His mouth for the Oral Torah, which is the explanation of that "hewing." This is the Torah that Moses set before the children of Israel; he brought in his hands the signs of that Source from which it was hewn to indicate its place, and it came inscribed and sealed with that Great Ring that encompasses all.

## However

The matter in these statements is that once the Holy One, blessed be He, gave the two Torahs—the Written and the Oral—to Moses our Teacher, peace be upon him, Moses' intellect was strengthened. He understood "one thing from another" through great analysis <term>pilpul</term> without end or limit, as if it were the "beauty of the tradition" <note>A phrase referring to the aesthetic and intellectual depth of legal debate</note>. In what is found in the Tractate Nedarim <note>OCR says "Ein bein ha-modar," referring to the chapter in Nedarim</note>, page 37, they said: Rabbi Yochanan asked, "What is the meaning of the verse: 'And I will give you the stone tablets, and the Torah, and the commandment, which I have written to teach them'?" <note>Exodus 24:12</note> "Which I have written"—these are the Ten Commandments. "The Torah"—this is the Scripture. "The commandment"—this is the Mishnah <note>The core text of the Oral Law</note>. "Which I have written to teach them"—these are the Prophets and the Writings. "To teach them"—this is the Gemara <note>The rabbinic analysis of the Mishnah</note>. This teaches that all of them were given to Moses from Sinai. On page 38, it says: "Take your waste [chips of stone] for yourself" <note>Exodus 34:1</note>; just as the waste was yours, so too the "sharpening" <note>The depth of the legal analysis</note> was given to you. 

It is written concerning the matter of giving it to Israel: "He who has a bountiful eye shall be blessed" <note>Proverbs 22:9</note>. Rav Chisda concluded: "And the Lord commanded me at that time to teach you." Another explanation: "I have taught you statutes and ordinances, as the Lord my God commanded me." See also: "And now write for yourselves this song"—the "Song" refers to the Torah, "so that this song may be a witness for Me among the children of Israel." It was merely the "waste" <note>The leftovers from carving the tablets, symbolizing the extra wisdom Moses gained</note>. In the matter of the Midrash for the portion *Ki Tisa*, the Holy One, blessed be He, answered the angels: "Heaven forbid that Moses writes from his own mind; he writes only as I call out." According to this explanation, even if he adds through the strength of analysis, "in all My house he is trustworthy." Heaven forbid that he should be considered inferior to a king's palace; the kingship of the Oral Torah belongs entirely to Moses, as will be explained later.

<column-break/>

## Speech

Is pleasant... some say that this can be explained according to what is found in Tractate Gittin, the chapter "Ha-Nizakin," page 60: Rabbi Eleazar said: The Torah

## Speech

is mostly written and a minority is oral, as it says: "Though I write for him the majority of My Torah, they are accounted as a stranger's" <note>Hosea 8:12</note>. But Rabbi Yochanan said: The majority is oral and a minority is in writing, as it says: "For according to the mouth of <note>meaning: by means of</note> these words" <note>Exodus 34:27</note>. But is it not also written, "I write for him the majority of My Torah"? He said: This refers to the Oral Torah, which is like the Written Torah. "Though I write for him the majority of My Torah, they are accounted as a stranger's"—this is because they are too difficult to learn by heart, as Rashi explains. "Majority in writing" means most of the Torah depends on the interpretation written through "general and particular" <term>klal u-prat</term>, "verbal analogy" <term>gezerah shavah</term>, and the other rules by which the Torah is interpreted. Its minority is oral—that which has no hint of learning in the Torah but was told to Moses orally. "For according to" etc. refers to the chosenness of the eternal covenant. This "majority," however, is a wonder: Should He have written the majority of His Torah for them? Behold, in that which I did write for them, they were accounted like a stranger! Therefore the Rabbis said it was a "Pleasant Speech."

There are thirteen rules by which the Torah is interpreted, and they are called the "Covenant." The Rabbis agree with Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that the majority is the "Speech"—that is, the Oral tradition. Therefore, he preceded "Speech" to "Writing." And he called it "Pleasant Speech" according to the verse "Pleasantness is at Your right hand forever" <note>Psalms 16:11</note>. The Torah was given from the right hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, so to speak—the majority of the Torah is in the "Right," like a task performed with two hands where the right hand is dominant. Regarding "sweeter than honey," they said: "Pray for pleasantness... to behold the pleasantness of the Lord." Afterward, "I have written and given." "Writing" refers to the thirteen rules by which the Torah is interpreted. This writing is also called by the Name [Y-H-V-H], which is the Oral Law, as mentioned above. Even though the writing is interpreted thus, nevertheless it is the Name. The Rabbis follow Rabbi Yochanan there; therefore, he interprets the acrostic **"I"** <note>Anokhi</note> as: **"Pleasant Speech I have Written and Given"** <note>original: *Amirah Ne'imah Ketavit Yehavit*</note>. Rabbi Yochanan himself does not interpret it this way here because it is more convenient for him to interpret his acrostic as: **"I have Given, Written, are Trustworthy, Speech"** <note>original: *Yehavti Ketivah Ne'emanin Amirah*</note>. They follow Rabbi Eliezer there, who holds that the Written Torah is the majority. Therefore, he preceded "Giving" and "Writing" to "Speech," and said "Given and Written"—meaning they are "Trustworthy Speech" as well. He did not say "Pleasant," which implies the most important. "Equal" implies it is the majority, because "Pleasantness is at His right hand" as mentioned above. Therefore he said "Trustworthy." It seems to me this should be explained according to Rashi’s commentary in "Ha-Nizakin."

## Indeed

It seems to me to explain there, with God's help, that this "Written Torah" is meant literally, as it is written before us. And some say, and our Rabbis—one says this and one says that—and the language is precise, meaning there is a difference in how they interpret. The matter is as I wrote above: "A great voice that did not cease" <note>Deuteronomy 5:19</note>—meaning it never stopped.

# Tractate Shevuot

### 49b 49 On the Matters

They fell from their holy place and the high level they had attained, returning to being those who learn and forget—for hearing from the mouth of the Master is not like hearing from the mouth of the student. When they were driven out due to their sins and lost what they had lost, they returned to their initial request, saying: "We wish to hear from the mouth of the King." The response was that this is impossible until the Time of Perfection. Furthermore, it can be proven that all the Commandments reached Israel just as they reached Moses. This was explained earlier in the portion: that the Voice that made the Commandments heard was not a created voice, but a unique, emanated voice. It was further explained that in the World of Unity, there is no Voice without Speech, for there, Voice and Speech are one. It is impossible to have Voice without Speech because they exist in a single unity; for the Voice is the "Great Name," symbolized by the phrase "a great voice that did not cease," and the Speech is the Fire. From this—from between the Voice and the Fire—the Torah was given. One who separates the Voice from the Speech is "cutting the shoots" <note>original: *mekatzetz binetiot*—a Talmudic idiom for heresy, specifically separating divine attributes that should be unified</note> of the Name. And concerning this, it says "And God spoke," which is the "Final Voice" that Israel perceived, which is the Speech. One who lacks the Voice is without Speech because they are hearing [together], as it is written: "The voice of the living God speaking." The Voice and Speech are together; one does not exist without the other. Those who say that what reached Israel in the other Commandments was only a Voice without the inclusion of letters were following the Great Teacher <note>referring to Maimonides</note> of blessed memory, who proposed a "created voice" for the Commandments. However, it has already been explained that a Voice without Speech is only possible according to their view—that the Voice could be without Speech because they maintained it was a created thing. But according to the accepted Truth <note>Kabbalistic tradition</note> which we have explained, that Voice is impossible without Speech. Once this is established and accepted, it is clear beyond any doubt that all the Commandments reached Israel just as they reached Moses.

The high level that Israel possessed at the receiving of the Torah was shared by us, our children, and our children’s children until the end of all generations; they were all there. As the sages of blessed memory said in the chapter "Helek" <note>The tenth chapter of Tractate Sanhedrin</note> regarding the secrets of the Torah: The Torah shall not cease from their descendants. To establish this firmly, since it was impossible for every generation to physically be there on that day, it was through Divine Wisdom and the Supreme Will that all souls destined to be created were actually present there. As the Tradition explains to the holy scholars of Israel, and in the Midrash of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (peace be upon him), they said: "All of them stood at Mount Sinai... and each one saw what was appropriate for them to see." Thus, all the generations of the world entered into the tradition of the Covenant and were bound by the surety, the Torah, and the Divine Unity. It is impossible for this bond to be loosened for any generation at any time, for so it was established Above and accepted below. One should not question or reflect further upon this. We believe what was said in the *Midrash Shocher Tov*: "Give Me guarantors who owe Me nothing." And so it says, "The Lord did not make this covenant with our fathers [alone]." They said to Him: "Grace, grace! For they owe You nothing." He said to them: "The infants." Immediately, they brought the infants from their mothers' breasts and the fetuses from their wombs. Their mothers' bellies became like a vision of glass, and they saw the Holy One, blessed be He, from within the womb and spoke with Him like infants who have not yet seen the light. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: "Are you guarantors for your fathers, that if they do not fulfill the Torah, you will be held accountable for them?" They said to Him: "Yes." He said to them: "I am the Lord your God." They said: "Yes." He said: "You shall have no other gods before Me." They said: "No." And so it was for every single commandment; they answered "yes" to the positive and "no" to the negative. He said to them: "From your mouths I give the Torah to them," as it is said: "Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings You have established strength"—and "strength" means nothing other than the Torah, as it is said: "The Lord will give strength to His people." Therefore, when Israel neglected the Torah, the children were held accountable, as it is said: "And you forgot the Torah of your God, I also will forget your children." Our sages said: "In the future, a woman will give birth every day." Rabbi Hiyya said: "As it were, I too will be forgotten, but the children will return and clarify Me," as it is said "I also will forget." Rav said: Their mothers' bellies became like <unclear>a luminous mirror</unclear>. Immediately the infants separated from their mothers and the fetuses separated from their navels. Rabbi Levi said: The last miracle was like the first—the bellies of their mothers returned to how they were, the infants returned to their dwellings, and the fetuses returned to their navels. Both groups opened their mouths and sang song, as it says: "Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings You have established strength." The Sages of Truth <note>Kabbalists</note> asked: How is it possible for fetuses in their mother's womb to speak with the Holy One? But there is a secret in this matter: they certainly spoke with the Holy One <term>face to face</term> <note>original: *p.b.p.*—*panim bepanim*</note>, because the "Crown of Israel" is called the "Mother of all creatures" and is called "Womb." For in the Kingdom (*Malchut*) of the Lord, all the souls of the entire world are formed before they come into this world. Just as there are souls below, there are other souls of a similar form Above. All those souls stood at Mount Sinai when the Torah was given, as it says: "With him who is standing here... and with him who is not here," meaning all the souls already created and those not yet created stood at Sinai. This is the secret of the Midrashic statement that "their mothers' bellies became like a vision of glass," which is a parable for the "Mother of all living" in which all images and countenances are formed. She is the "Assembly of Israel" in which all souls are gathered and included until the time comes for them to dwell in bodies. This is why the Midrash says their bellies became <term>as a luminous mirror</term> <note>original: *aspaklaria ha-meira*—a clear lens of prophecy</note> when she is in union with her Beloved. The "surety" involves the obligation to the merit of the ancestors and to warn them not to sin, lest the punishment for their evil fall upon their offspring; let them keep the Torah and its commandments and not transgress, lest their children be seized for their iniquity and die young. As it says in the *Alphabet of Rabbi Akiva*: If his children die in his lifetime, they say to him, "Why did your children die in your lifetime?" And as it is said: Rabbi Eleazar said a person must oversee his children until thirteen years of age, and from then on he must say: "Blessed be He who has released me from the punishment of this one." They accepted the surety of the "Subjugation of Souls" and took upon themselves the Yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven, entering the tradition of the Covenant of the Torah while still in the "Womb," which is the Supernal Mount Sinai, just as those below accepted it while standing at the terrestrial Mount Sinai. Thus, the Covenant is established and accepted Above and below. All were included; none were exempt. For the Supernal Torah—the secret of the Written Torah—was at Sinai, the secret of the "Final Hey" <note>The last letter of the Tetragrammaton, associated with the Shekhinah</note>. There, all future souls received it, for the Written Torah and the Oral Torah are in one Unity. There, Israel heard them and accepted them at Mount Sinai below. This perception is impossible except through prophecy, and for this reason, all of Israel ascended to it, and 600,000 stood before Him at Horeb; all of them were prophets regarding these two Torahs in our hands. This is why they asked to see His glory and greatness and hear His voice. They aimed well when they said: "All that the Lord has spoken, we will do and we will hear." They wanted to remove any doubt or protest that might arise at any time—that some person boasting of prophecy might come to deny what they believed and heard with their own ears. Therefore, they wanted to stand upon the Truth which leaves no doubt, so they would remain steadfast in their faith and faithful to their covenant. This elevation and excellence that Israel had at the receiving of the Torah was even higher than the level of the angels. Because of this, the angels were moved to a kind of "jealousy of scribes," as it says in Tractate *Shabbat*, chapter *Rabbi Akiva*: Rabbi Joshua ben Levi said, when Moses ascended to the Heights, the ministering angels said before the Holy One: "Master of the Universe, what is one born of a woman doing among us?" This statement is well known. According to this, it is explained in the book *Midrash Shmuel* on the verses: "Forever, O Lord, Your word stands firm in heaven; Your faithfulness is to all generations... they stand this day for Your judgments... unless Your Torah had been my delight." Regarding this complaint: when Moses ascended to the Heights, the ministering angels said: "Your word stands firm"—referring to the debate between Moses and the angels when he went to receive the Torah. For the angels were saying it should be given to them: "What is man that You are mindful of him?" They meant: "Lord, Your word (the Torah) should remain 'forever' with the 'standing ones' <note>the angels</note>; give it to us and not to humans." One might wonder what would happen to those below and how they would survive without the Torah. To this they replied: "Your faithfulness is to all generations"—meaning, for the generations of men, the faith they have in You is sufficient for them. Just as the world existed through faith from creation until the giving of the Torah, let it stand on faith alone now. "They stand this day for Your judgments"—the angels stood with the humans to see who would merit the Covenant. It seemed more logical to give it to the angels, who are holy ministers of the Supreme, rather than to "cloudy" human beings in the lower world. But Moses argued: "Unless Your Torah had been my delight"—the Torah is entirely concerned with human matters, such as "You went down to Egypt," "You were enslaved to Pharaoh," "Do not murder," "Do not commit adultery." Is there an Evil Inclination among you angels? Through these arguments, the lower beings [merited] the Torah.

<meta>This page serves as the philosophical and mystical foundation for the passage provided in the previous translation. While the previous snippet described the consequences of the Israelites' fear—their "fall" from a state of perfect memory—this page explains the initial state of the Revelation at Sinai. It details how the 613 commandments are encoded within the Ten Commandments and argues against Maimonides' view that the Israelites heard only a sound rather than distinct words.</meta>

# Tractate Shevuot

### The 613 Commandments

The **613 Commandments** <note>original: *Taryag Mitzvot*</note> are general principles from which all else emerges; they are the roots and foundations for all the laws, which act as branches and specific judgments. To demonstrate this, the Ten Commandments contain exactly **613 letters** from the beginning until the word "your neighbor" <note>the end of the tenth commandment</note>, not including that final word. Similarly, the Sage <note>likely referring to the author of the *Sefer ha-Chinuch* or *Charedim*</note> elaborated in the introduction to the "Positive Commandments" that the Holy One, Blessed be He, made all of Israel hear them. Every individual reached the levels of **prophecy** and heard the Word themselves without an intermediary. 

The Holy One, Blessed be He, foresaw that false prophets would arise in the future to mislead the world with forged religions. Therefore, He spoke with His own "mouth," as it were, while all the souls of future generations were present. This ensures that if anyone ever attempts to change the religion, we can say to him: "You speak a lie. If the Blessed Name desired this change, He would have told us publicly, just as the public revelation occurred at the Giving of the Torah." At that time, He gave us the Ten Commandments—which encompass all 613—in a public forum, proving that Moses was His faithful prophet. Thus, the people would believe everything Moses told them later regarding the specific details of the commandments. This is the meaning of the verse: *“Behold, I come to you in a thick cloud, that the people may hear when I speak with you, and believe you forever”* (Exodus 19:9).

I have transcribed this at length above. However, if the view of **Maimonides** <note>the Rambam</note> were correct—that they did not hear distinct letters but only a general, miraculous sound—then the aforementioned purpose would, Heaven forbid, be nullified. Furthermore, the plain meaning of the verses contradicts Maimonides, for the text says: *“Has any people heard the voice of God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard, and lived?”* (Deuteronomy 4:33). This clearly explains that they heard both the Voice and the Speech.

The work **The Holy Service** <note>original: *Avodat HaKodesh* by Meir ibn Gabbai</note> states: To further indicate this, the text says after the Ten Commandments, *“These words the Lord spoke to all your assembly...”* (Deuteronomy 5:19). Initially, everyone heard all Ten Commandments uttered in a single, miraculous divine speech. Afterward, He repeated them, detailing each commandment individually. At that point, the people could no longer endure the intensity and said to our teacher Moses: *“You speak with us”* (Exodus 20:16). Upon the second repetition, we only heard "I am" and "You shall not have" directly from the mouth of the **Almighty** <note>original: *mepi ha-gevurah*</note>. This is why our Sages taught: *"I am" and "You shall not have" were heard directly from the mouth of the Almighty.*

However, as I mentioned, everyone initially heard all Ten Commandments when they were spoken as one. I have already written the reasons for this "single utterance" above. The book **Secrets of the Torah** <note>likely *Sefer Ha-Peliyah* or a similar Kabbalistic text</note> explains: A proper reason can be clarified—these ten were chosen because they include the entire Torah and all the commandments, being their roots. Because they are the foundation of everything, it was necessary to hear them from the mouth of the Almighty. Through them, heaven and earth and all things in the upper and lower worlds were sealed; from them, all things emerge and extend.

Thus, the Ten Commandments were, in their essence, the roots of all commandments. The **Supernal Light**, the source of life, is the root of all existence. From it, lights were emanated and unified according to the number **620** <note>the numerical value of *Keter*, meaning "Crown"</note>, corresponding to the **620 letters** in the Ten Commandments. From there, the "Supernal Torah" is emanated, which includes the 613 commandments. Branching out from the Ten Commandments is the **Divine Presence** <note>original: *Shekhinah*</note>, called the "Crown of the Seven Days of Creation." This is understood through the name *Ehyeh* <note>meaning "I Will Be"</note>, where the beginning is the letter *Aleph* and the end is *Kaph* <note>forming "Ak," or 21, but here likely referencing a Gematria structure where Aleph is 1 and Kaph is 20</note>, signifying "Goodness for Israel."

The first utterance, **"I am"** (*Anochi*), includes all other commandments; it is their essence and root. It is the secret of "Accepting the Kingdom of Heaven" and the sum of all principles from which all parts of the Torah are derived. *Anochi* indicates God's existence, and from that existence, the laws—which are the King's decrees—become obligatory. The Name of the Lord indicates His vitality, which gives life to all things; He is the one who renews and brings them forth, the only True Ancient Being. From this root, the "True Beliefs" are derived, which the Torah calls the "Testimonies of your God," indicating His guidance and providence. From this also comes the part called **Commandments** <note>original: *Mitzvot*</note>. *“Who brought you out of the land of Egypt”* is the cornerstone of infinite merit.

This noble Utterance is the root and essence of all the commandments, which are the entirety of the Torah. Even though the patriarchs already possessed the tradition of these principles, and some were grasped through what they witnessed in Egypt, the Holy One, Blessed be He, wanted them to achieve this through **prophecy**, seeing it with their own eyes so it would be verified with absolute strength. These are the great pillars upon which all faith stands.

The second utterance, **"You shall not have other gods before Me,"** teaches **Unity**. By saying "before Me" <note>literally "on My face"</note>, He indicated all these principles: existence, eternity, providence, and power—that He is One in all of them. "My face" refers to His "Inwardness." By saying "beside Him," He warned them not to seek these things from anyone else, for they will not be found in any other power or created being. All others are "other" to Him.

These two "roots" reached Israel in their perfection directly from the mouth of the Almighty because they are the core of faith. They did not need Moses to explain anything to them. While all the commandments reached them from the mouth of the Almighty, they subsequently required the explanation of Moses for the other eight. In these first two, however, they attained the same perfection as Moses himself. 

Our Sages said, *"I am" and "You shall not have" we heard from the mouth of the Almighty.* This phrasing does not mean they *only* heard those two, for all scriptures testify they heard all words from the Almighty. Rather, it means that for the other **611 commandments** <note>The word "Torah" equals 611 in Gematria</note> included in the other eight utterances, they required Moses to explain the plain meaning and details. These are the laws "which Moses commanded us." Israel grasped the generalities of all commandments, but the specific details were heard from Moses—except for the first two, which required no further explanation.

Our Sages also received a tradition that at Sinai they grasped all the nuances and details of the Torah, the arrangements of the sections, and the shapes of the letters. They saw the interpretations that future prophets and scribes would one day derive. Not only this, but they grasped the secrets and the underlying reasons. As it says in the **Midrash of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai** <note>the Zohar</note>: *"Every single word was filled with many meanings... these were the commands, the prohibitions, the secrets..."* 

They saw the voices. It does not say they "heard" the voices, but that they *saw* them, just as it is written *“And they saw the God of Israel”* (Exodus 24:10). They looked into the voices and perceived great wisdom. All future generations and souls yet to be born were there. They reached the highest level of prophecy, achieving a perfect grasp of the Torah, its traditions, its wisdom, its secrets, and its reasons. From that one Voice they perceived, everything else multiplied and emerged.

To highlight the perfection of this perception, the Midrash says: At the moment Israel heard *"I am the Lord your God,"* the study of the Torah was **fixed in their hearts**. They would learn and never forget. They said to Moses: *"Moses, our teacher, become our mediator <note>original: perezvin</note>, for there is a 'death' between us <note>the overwhelming nature of the voice</note>; you speak with us and we will hear."* 

But once they made this request, the **Evil Inclination** returned to its place, and they returned to being people who learn and forget. They said: *"Moses is flesh and blood, and his teaching passes away."* They went back to Moses and said: *"Would that God would reveal Himself to us a second time! Would that He would 'kiss me with the kisses of His mouth'! Would that the Torah be fixed in our hearts as it was before!"* 

Moses replied: *"This is not for now, but for the Future to Come,"* as it is said: *“I will put My law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts”* (Jeremiah 31:32). The intention was to perfect them in a way more wondrous than their natural capacity. They were raised from their lowly state to a miraculous level of prophecy. God did not withhold His goodness; He spoke from heaven so they would always be upright, like the **ministering angels** who stand before Him with no distraction or forgetfulness. 

The purpose of giving the Torah was to return the "Crown of Perfection" to Israel which existed before the **Original Sin** <note>of Adam</note>. This perfection is only possible if one acts without distraction. By fixing the Torah in their hearts, their learning would be permanent. When they heard the word *Anochi*, they achieved that supernal perfection and secret wisdom. But when they became overwhelmed by this perfection, they distracted their minds and said, *"You speak with us."* At that moment, they **fell**...

### Revealing the Excellence of the Converts

They are under the wings of the *Shekhinah*, while Israel is compared to the wings themselves. <note>A common Kabbalistic distinction: converts are sheltered *by* the wings, while Israel *is* the wings of the Divine Presence.</note>
As for the elders and the souls that were created... <note>The following text is in a dense Rabbinic Hebrew script, discussing the lineage of Jethro and Ruth.</note>
From a great Sage, our Master Rabbi [name unclear], I received that the secret of the convert is found in the book *Yalkut Reuveni* regarding the resolution of late difficulties. Our teacher also taught us to add here... and to erase the words...
Regarding the matter of Boaz and Ruth: Boaz saw with "holy eyes" that she was worthy of being taken as a wife, for she was a holy soul. She would not see sleep at the time she was to be joined to the *Shekhinah*. He was afraid that a blemish might fall upon him through this act, but just as Jethro and the others overcame their past, so too did she. 

Therefore, he exerted himself to speak words of holiness to her, contrary to the intentions of the scoffers. This is based on what our Sages said in the Midrash regarding the verse "and she sat at his feet." He placed a crown upon her so that the Destroyer would not touch her. It is like the parable of a king... as brought in the chapter "These are the ones who are exiled." 

Concerning Ruth, she was forty years old <note>A traditional Midrashic view of Ruth's age</note> when she came to be gathered under the wings [of God]. She was beautiful in her deeds. It is known what the Sages said on the verse "and you went to a people you did not know yesterday or the day before." This means she accepted the Torah even before it was fully revealed to her. Her reward was complete. 

It was fitting that from her should come the kingship of the House of David. The name **Ruth** (ר-ו-ת) <note>Numerically 606</note> plus the seven laws of Noah equals **613**, the number of the commandments. Alternatively, the name hints at her being "saturated" <note>a pun on the Hebrew root R-V-H</note> with words of Torah. This is the secret of Tamar and Ruth, who both acted for the sake of Heaven to establish the Davidic line. 

In the Scroll of Ruth, there are many hints. When Boaz says, "Stay this night," it refers to the "night" of the exile, until the "morning" of the redemption comes. He gave her six measures of barley, hinting at the six righteous men who would descend from her, including the Messiah. 

The matter of Jethro is also significant. Even though he was a priest of Midian, he recognized that "the Lord is greater than all gods." He contributed a portion to the Torah. This teaches us that the "sparks of holiness" are found even among the nations, and they must be gathered back to their source.

### The Excellence of the Poor

The *Tosafot* <note>Medieval commentators on the Talmud</note> wrote in Tractate Shabbat... even though they were outsiders... Jethro was a "righteous convert" (*Ger Tzedek*). The name **Ruth** also indicates the "addition" of commandments that she accepted upon herself.
Our Sages noted that Israel is the holy nation, and even their "refuse" is more precious than the finest of the nations. 

This is mentioned in the secret of the name **Ruth**, who was the ancestress of the Kingdom of the House of David. The lineage of David is connected to the "shakings" and "refining" of souls. The secret of the "fallen booth of David" is that it will be raised through these sparks. 

Regarding the debate of "an Ammonite [man] but not an Ammonite [woman]," <note>The legal ruling that allowed Ruth, a Moabite woman, to marry into Israel despite the biblical prohibition against Moabite men</note> there is great discussion. The name **Tamar** and the name **Ruth** share a mystical connection in the letters. Our teacher explained that all of this is part of the secret of the "levirate marriage" (*Yibbum*) and the restoration of lost souls. 

There are hints in the Scroll of Ruth regarding the "receiving of the ears" <note>likely referring to hearing the Torah</note>. When she fell on her face before Boaz, it symbolized the submission of the soul to the Divine. Boaz spoke to her "at the time of the meal," which hints at the "Future Feast" for the righteous. 

When Boaz said, "I have found favor in your eyes," he was hinting at her essential holiness. Even the King of Moab recognized that Israel was "too mighty for him." This "might" comes from the soul of David, which was already hidden within Ruth. 

Everything points to the acceptance of the Torah. Just as Israel said "We will do and we will hear," Ruth said "Your people shall be my people, and your God my God." This is the ultimate "Peace to the one who is far," bringing the distant ones under the canopy of truth.

This page expands on the concept of the "Spark of Moses" present in every generation and explains why the Torah, though composed of Divine Names, had to be given to "one born of woman" rather than celestial beings.</meta>
