<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of Moses' personal stringencies to the laws of communal mourning, specifically regarding the fast of Tisha B'Av (the Ninth of Av) and the general prohibition of music and luxury as a remembrance of the Temple's destruction.</meta>

# Tractate Ta'anit

A minor point: it is written in *Terumat HaDeshen* <note>A 15th-century collection of legal responsa by Rabbi Israel Isserlein</note>, section 100, that it seems even washing in cold water is forbidden [during the week of Tisha B'Av], even though the language of Maimonides <note>The 12th-century philosopher and legalist, also known as Rambam</note> implies the custom of prohibition applies specifically to hot water. It appears that the *Or Zarua* and the *Mordechai* <note>Medieval legal authorities</note> disagree with him on this custom. Regarding the custom of the *Maharil* <note>Rabbi Jacob Moelin, a primary source for Ashkenazi custom</note>, he wrote only regarding this specific week. In my youth, I saw people washing in rivers even during this time, and the authorities did not protest, though one who is stringent shall be blessed. These are his words. And the *Maharshal* <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria, a 16th-century authority</note> wrote that the custom is not to wash even in cold water. In the words of the *Maharal* <note>Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague</note>, he wrote that it is permitted to wash one's head on the Friday before the "Sabbath of Vision" <note>original: "Erev Shabbat Hazon," the Saturday before Tisha B'Av</note>, but specifically with cold water and not hot, and even this is barely permitted. It seems to me that one who is accustomed to immerse in a ritual bath every Friday in honor of the Sabbath—according to the secrets of the later great Kabbalists as explained earlier in Tractate Shabbat—should not cancel this immersion even on the Friday before Tisha B'Av. However, he should not wash excessively, but only the amount required for the immersion he performs every Friday. And see the book of Isaiah regarding this: "And all your deeds shall be for the sake of Heaven."

# Law
<margin>At the end of section 500, the *Mordechai* wrote at the beginning of Tractate Moed Katan that Rabbi Shmuel of Bamberg would say the blessing "Who creates the lights of the fire" out loud without a cup of wine.</margin>
He would not say the blessing over spices <note>Normally part of the Havdalah ceremony marking the end of the Sabbath</note> because that is a pleasure, and so wrote the *Hagahot Maimoniyot*. Also, the *Sefer Mitzvot Katan* wrote that one blesses "Who creates the lights of the fire," and Rabbi Abraham wrote that we do not bless over the cup until after the fast of Tisha B'Av concludes. We do not smell fragrant woods because on the night of Tisha B'Av one should not create "pleasure for the spirit," but we do bless over the light before reading Lamentations <note>original: "Eichah"</note>. From what he wrote—that he would not say the blessing over spices because it is a pleasure—it would seem that since a fast is meant to "afflict the soul," one should avoid smelling spices on any fast day. Certainly, according to the *Ra'avyah* <note>Rabbi Eliezer ben Joel HaLevi of Bonn</note>, whom the *Tosafot* cite in Tractate Chagigah (page 13), it is permitted to wash in hot water on the other three fasts, and the *Bet Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo</note> wrote in section 550 that this is the common custom. It is obvious then that there is no place for these stringencies [on minor fasts]. However, one who is stringent upon himself like the father of the *Ra'avyah*—not to wash in hot water for three days—should be stringent in this as well, even though they are not entirely alike; for washing is a pleasure of the body, while scent is a pleasure of the soul, yet it still provides "pleasure for the spirit." One should not raise an objection from the fact that marital relations are permitted [on minor fasts], for that is specifically at night when the fast has not yet begun until dawn for those who do not begin the fast from the evening before. But on the day of the fast itself, one who is stringent in washing should be stringent in this too. And on Yom Kippur, it seems simple to me to be stringent not to smell spices. I will write more on this later in Tractate Yoma with God's help.

# When it Occurs
<margin>Regarding one who stops eating while it is still day, following the Sephardic custom, it is always prohibited. Regarding the custom of women to sleep on the ground, some say it is a mistake... regarding spices... it seems the stringent should not separate... and regarding this I saw in my travels a memory of the head on the night of Tisha B'Av... as I wrote to be in another place.</margin>
When Tisha B'Av falls on a Sunday, or on a Friday and is pushed to Sunday <note>meaning the 9th falls on the Sabbath and the fast is observed on the 10th</note>, some women do not know how to pray the Evening Service and thus have not said the Havdalah prayer. Since we do not perform Havdalah over a cup of wine until after the fast, every man must warn the women of his household that on fast days they should not light a fire to cook for the night, or when cooking for their children, until they have said: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, Who distinguishes between the holy and the profane."

# It Appears
It appears to me that those who fast on the night of the tenth [of Av] and maintain the fast through the tenth day, it is a good custom for them to say the prayer *Nachem* ("Comfort") in the supplications of the Afternoon Prayer of Tisha B'Av. One could even say *Nachem* in the Evening, Morning, and Afternoon prayers if they are still fasting. This is implied by Maimonides. For what prohibition is there if one were to mention "Comfort" every day of the year? One can add personal requests in any of the middle blessings of the *Amidah* <note>The standing prayer</note> that match the theme of the blessing. Now, while one sits in fast and because of the Destruction, it is a good thing to do this and to say *Nachem* during the Tisha B'Av Afternoon Prayer—the time when the fire was set to the Temple—and to say it until the end of the fast.

# Custom
It is the custom everywhere to go to the cemetery on Tisha B'Av, for Tisha B'Av is a communal fast. This is based on what was done during fasts for rain, as mentioned by the *Tosafot* in Tractate Ta'anit (page 16). Furthermore, it says in *Eichah Rabbah* <note>A Midrashic collection on Lamentations</note> that the righteous even in the grave pray for Jerusalem. This was cited by Rabbi Hayyim in the name of Rabbi Isaac Luria <note>the Arizal</note>. It seems to me that one should not go in a large group, for this is not a social gathering, and it leads to "idle chatter" <note>original: "shichat chulin"</note> and distracts the mind from mourning. Rather, one should go alone or with one other so as not to stop speaking of the matters of the Destruction and to be awakened to mourning. **Always** one must remember the Destruction and make a remembrance of it in all his actions. As the Sages said: A man plasters his house but leaves a square cubit <note>term: "amah al amah"</note> without plaster as a memory of the Destruction. Regarding those in the Diaspora who build additions and houses and make square black shapes on their walls and write upon them "A Memory of the Destruction"—this is a mockery and a joke in my eyes, for on the contrary, this is a decoration! One who fears the word of God should not deviate from the words of our Sages and should leave a square cubit unplastered.

# And So
<margin>The space is empty here.</margin>
Many are not careful about what our Sages said: When a man makes a feast and sets a table for friends, he should diminish it slightly and leave an empty place without the engraved plates that are fit to be placed there. I saw in the homes of the great, when they prepared their homes for their daughter's wedding with beautiful tapestries <note>original: "coverlets"</note> on the four walls, they left an empty space a cubit wide in the middle. Likewise, they said when a woman makes silver or gold jewelry, she should leave out one type of ornament so that it is not a "complete ornament." Concerning this, my heart faints within me when I see the bad custom among women who are filled with ornaments and jewelry, and what are called in the local language "stockings," garments, and jewelry that they deck themselves with... if only there were two necklaces. They follow the many customs of the nations who are envious [of wealth], while the noble and modest women withdraw their hands from this. It is proper to act this way in every single thing to fulfill: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill; let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth if I do not remember thee, if I do not set Jerusalem above my chiefest joy."

At the end of Tractate Sotah, it was taught: Since the Sanhedrin was abolished, song was abolished from the wedding-feast houses, as it is said: "With song they shall not drink wine." It is forbidden to use instruments, or even singing by mouth, unless the singing consists of words of praise and thanksgiving [to God]. It is only a "joke" <note>meaning permitted</note> to gladden a groom and bride on their wedding day; then even musical instruments are permitted. They were very strict about this at the end of Sotah. There it says: Rav Huna said, "The ear that hears music shall be torn out." Rava said, "Music in a house leads to destruction at the threshold." Rav Huna said, "The singing of boat-pullers and cattle-drivers is permitted, but that of weavers is forbidden." The explanation is: the song of boat-pullers who pull ropes is only to encourage them in their work. And cattle-drivers sing while they plow only to lead the oxen into the furrows, for the oxen move to the sound of the song which is pleasant to them. But the song of weavers is only for "joking" <note>frivolity</note>. One should distance himself from this... And even though the *Shulchan Aruch* wrote in the name of the *Tosafot* that even without a feast it is forbidden only for one who makes a regular habit of it—like the Exilarch <note>the leader of the Jewish community in Babylon</note> who would stand and lie down to music—nevertheless, all the legal decisors stated their words plainly, implying that for all people it is forbidden. This is logical, for it is no less than the "song of weavers" which is forbidden. **Furthermore**, there is a fear that the joy of song will lead to "frivolous laughter." The Sages said at the beginning of the chapter "One does not stand": It is forbidden for a man to fill his mouth with laughter in this world. The *Knesset HaGedolah* wrote that Maimonides explains this refers specifically to the time of Exile, and so wrote Nachmanides. But Rabbeinu Yonah explained that even not in times of Exile this is said, for excessive joy causes a person to forget the commandments. It seems to me that Rabbeinu Yonah is correct, for the text says "in this world" and not "during the time of the Destruction." This teaches us that filling one's mouth with laughter is always forbidden until the actual time of the Redemption. From this, one must refrain from laughter, and especially at this time... even with instruments, there is a prohibition because of the Exile... and one who is careful will see the consolation of Zion.

# Regarding
The matter of fasting: In the first chapter of Tractate Ta'anit (page 11), Shmuel said: "Anyone who sits in a fast is called a sinner." He holds like the Tanna <note>Sage</note> Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, who said: "What is the meaning of the verse 'And [the priest] shall make atonement for him, for that he sinned by the soul' (Numbers 6:11)? Against which 'soul' did this [Nazirite] sin? Rather, it is because he pained himself by abstaining from wine. And does this not suggest a fortiori <note>original: "kal v'chomer"</note> reasoning? If this one who only pained himself by abstaining from wine is called a sinner, how much more so one who pains himself by abstaining from everything!" But Rabbi Elazar says: "He is called holy," as it is said: "He shall be holy, he shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow long." If this one who only pained himself regarding one thing is called holy, how much more so one who pains himself regarding everything! And for Shmuel, how does he explain the word "holy"? That refers to the [physical] hair...

It also addresses the general prohibition of music and excessive laughter during the Exile, emphasizing a lifestyle of restrained joy.</summary>

It maintains the previous page's focus on personal stringency and the proper spirit of observance.</meta>

# Tractate Shevuot

The festival of **Shavuot** <note>original: "Atzeret," a Talmudic name for Shavuot</note> contains within it the deepest secret of the *Sefirot* <note>Divine emanations in Kabbalah</note>, hinting at the end of the Sabbatical and Jubilee cycles, as it says: *“And you shall sanctify the fiftieth year.”* I have already elaborated on this above. At this time, a person's inner cries are heard by Him, for it is *“a solemn assembly for the Lord your God.”* These three elements—the festival, the Sabbath, and the Jubilee—draw forth the three types of perfection: **Action**, **Speech**, and **Thought**. 

**Action** corresponds to the beginning of the world, called the “days of action,” for in them the Lord acted—and even on the Sabbath, He created “rest.” **Speech** corresponds to the Giving of the Torah, as it says: *“And God spoke all these words.”* **Thought** corresponds to the ultimate World to Come, where everything is intellectual; that is the realm of Thought. This “threefold cord” of Action, Speech, and Thought must be present in every good deed. I have written at length about this in the appropriate legal sections. It is also clarified in the verse: *“Observe the words of this covenant and do them, so that you may act wisely in all that you do.”* The word *“Observe”* refers to the Mishnah—that is, the study—as Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, the preeminent medieval commentator</note> explained elsewhere; this is the aspect of **Speech**. *“And do them”* refers to **Action**. *“So that you may act wisely”* refers to **Thought**. Therefore, it is fitting to be spiritually awakened on this day and resolve to sanctify oneself in these three areas, following the principle of *“Turn from evil and do good.”* Regarding the Giving of the Torah, it is written: *“On this day”*—meaning that every single day the Torah should be in your eyes as if it were given today, as Rashi explains. Therefore, every day we pray for this in the blessing of “Abundant Love” (*Ahavah Rabbah*): to learn, to teach, to observe, to do, and to fulfill. *“And enlighten our eyes”* refers to the wisdom found in pure **Thought**.

## Clarification
Previously, there was a great debate: is study greater or is action greater? Does a person stop their studies to perform a commandment? There are many legal distinctions in this matter. From this, a person should be stirred: if it is sometimes forbidden to stop studying even for a commandment, how could it ever enter one's mind to stop studying for idle chatter or to sit in idliness? Happy is the one who hears these words and is filled with the resolve to return to the Torah of the Lord day and night. May He return to him forever.

->The Tractate of Shevuot is completed with the help of the Living God, the source of salvation.<-

# Tractate Ta’anit: The Pillar of Service

->I have already hinted above that a fast takes the place of a sacrifice; therefore, the two concepts are closely linked.<-

## Chapter: The Lamp of the Commandment
->Laws of the Ninth of Av, Laws of Fasting, and the Matter of Service:<-

<margin>Mitzvah</margin> It is a great religious duty to mourn on the Ninth of Av <note>Tisha B'Av, the fast day mourning the destruction of the Temple</note> and to recite lamentations starting from the evening. The core of the lamentation is the Scroll of Lamentations (*Eichah*), which was said with Divine Inspiration through the prophecy of Jeremiah. Therefore, it seems to me to be a good custom for every individual to go back and read the Scroll of Lamentations to themselves the following day. For always, the obligation of the day is superior, just as we find regarding the Sabbath that the "honor of the day" is superior to the "honor of the night." We find a similar rule regarding the reading of the Megillah <note>The Scroll of Esther on Purim</note>: a person is obligated to read it at night and repeat it during the day. The *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher's 14th-century legal code</note>, section 559, brings the words of *Tractate Soferim* which states: some read the Book of Lamentations in the evening and some delay it until the morning. Therefore, I say we should fulfill both. One cannot say it must be specifically at night or specifically during the day; a person sees that the day is a better time to awaken oneself to weeping and mourning. It is written: *“She weeps bitterly in the night,”* and some say the mourning is at night because anyone who mourns Jerusalem at night is answered. Rashi explains on Lamentations: *“She weeps bitterly in the night”* because it was then that the majority of the Sanctuary was burned, as it lasted through the evening of the next day. Even though the community does not do this—reading it only at night—it is still proper for the individual to do so. A person should do what is best for themselves. One who examines the simple meaning of the Mishnah would conclude that it should be read at night to fulfill *“She weeps bitterly in the night.”* And if one fasts through the ninth day and reads it also on the tenth day, he fulfills the burden of all who mourn for her. Furthermore, I found in Rashi’s commentary on Tractate Ta’anit that the mourning of the day is greater than that of the night. Proof comes from the Talmud (Ta'anit 12b): when they said work is forbidden, they meant only during the day, but at night it is permitted. Although this is not absolute proof that mourning during the day is greater than the night—since work was forbidden during the day so that people wouldn't think one has completely distracted oneself from mourning—nevertheless, there is a basis for the argument.

<margin>The Beit Yosef</margin> In section 554, the *Beit Yosef* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo, author of the Shulchan Aruch</note> agreed that one who reads the Torah on the Ninth of Av should say the blessing *“Blessed is the True Judge”* before the blessing over the Torah. The *Bach* <note>Rabbi Joel Sirkis</note> wrote that this is the common custom, and so it appears in the *Tur*. When reading at night, I have not seen people practicing this, perhaps because there is a doubt whether the blessing applies to reading Torah, Mishnah, or just hearing the news of the destruction. Since there is a doubt, we do not make the blessing. However, it seems to me that the reader should say *“True Judge”* both when reading the Torah and before the Scroll of Lamentations. One should not ask what the connection is between the blessing and the Torah, for the reading on the Ninth of Av is specifically a reminder of the Destruction and the Exile.

<margin>Many</margin> of the unlearned people, and even some students by force of habit, stumble and are not careful about removing their shoes. They put their shoes back on after midday. This custom is a cause for grief. O children of God, do not walk in that path with them! For everything the Sages forbade remains forbidden until the night, just like eating and drinking. It is only regarding customs not mentioned in the Talmud—such as sitting on the ground—that the later authorities were lenient after midday. But Heaven forbid one should be lenient with what was forbidden in the Talmud. This error surely spread from merchants who walk outside in the streets of the gentiles and feel they must wear shoes; however, it is explicitly taught: one who goes out on a journey may wear shoes, but when he enters the city, he must remove them.

<margin>When there is</margin> mud or filth, and one must go to the bathroom or for some other necessity where it is permitted to wear shoes: it seems to me that he should swap them, putting the right shoe on the left foot and the left on the right. This creates a "change" <term>shinui: a deviation from the normal way of doing an act to signify it is not being done for pleasure</term> and serves as a reminder of the removal of shoes. Since this protects him from the mud, it is good to do. I have support for this from the Talmud, Tractate Ta'anit page 12: Rabban said to Rav Sheshet, “We see the Rabbis wiping their shoes [as if they are wearing them] and they are not concerned with the fast.” He replied, “Perhaps they are also eating!” Abaye and Rava would enter [the study hall] and put on their shoes at the entrance. Mar bar Rav Ashi and Mar Zutra would swap the right for the left and the left for the right. The Rabbis of the house of Rav Ashi would go out normally, following Samuel who said: “There is no public fast in Babylonia except for the Ninth of Av.” Rashi explains that the Rabbis came to the fast and followed Samuel’s view. 

<margin>From</margin> what is appropriate, one should be stringent on the other three fasts—the Fast of Gedaliah, the Tenth of Tevet, and the Seventeenth of Tammuz—just as on the Ninth of Av, since they all relate to the Destruction. However, we are not as careful with the communal practice unless the community can withstand it. Therefore, they were only stringent on the Ninth of Av itself. It is clarified in the *Sefer HaPardes* <note>A work attributed to the school of Rashi</note> that for any individual who feels they can withstand it, it is better than two hundred other fasts to be stringent upon themselves and stop eating while it is still day <note>starting the fast at sunset the night before, even for the minor fasts</note>. It seems to me that this stringency applies specifically to eating and drinking—so that the fast lasts a full day and night—but for other matters, one need not be stringent. However, if one is stringent in those things as well, let it be between himself and God, so that it does not appear as pride (*Yohara*), and a blessing shall come upon him.

<margin>Wrote Avi HaEzri</margin> <note>Rabbi Eliezer ben Joel HaLevi, known as the Ra'avyah</note>: Our ancestors practiced not washing from the first day of the month of Av, and we must uphold this because of the verse: *“Do not forsake the teaching of your mother.”* This is also found in the *Mordechai* at the beginning of Tractate Moed Katan.

<sig>The Humble One</sig>

# Tractate Ta’anit
### 51a
**Page 201**

...with faith and tranquility, and he should hasten to return to his Master.

<margin>
The language of the **Tur** <note>The Arba'ah Turim, a foundational 14th-century legal code</note> in Section 549 regarding these days on which one fasts: He wrote that according to the Torah, one who fasts on these days should not eat or drink until evening. On the **first of Nisan**, from the 6th [hour] until the end of the [day], see there. However, our version of the **Bahag** <note>Ba'al Ha-Halakhot Gedolot, an early medieval legal authority</note> contains slightly different versions. It is written in the **Tur** that on the **26th of Nisan**, Joshua bin Nun died; but in the **Kol Bo** <note>A 13th-14th century legal work</note> (Section 63), it says he died on the **28th**. However, in our version of the **Bahag**, it is written like the **Tur**, that Joshua died on the 26th, and it is the custom to follow the majority of versions. 

The **Tur** wrote that on the **18th of Av**, the "Western Lamp" <note>The central lamp of the Temple Menorah</note> was extinguished in the days of King Ahaz; however, in our version of the **Bahag**, it says the 17th of Av. The **Kol Bo** agrees with the **Tur** on the 18th. 

The **Tur** wrote that on the **17th of Elul**, the scouts who brought an evil report of the land died; but in our **Bahag** and **Kol Bo**, it says the **7th of Elul**. 

The **Tur** wrote that on the **5th of Tishrei**, Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Akiva ben Joseph were killed; in our **Bahag**, it says the **10th**, but the **Kol Bo** follows the **Tur**. 

The **Tur** wrote that on the **2nd of Tishrei**, a decree was issued that our ancestors would die by the sword, famine, and plague because of the incident of the Golden Calf; in the **Bahag**, there is a different version which seems to be a scribal error. The **Kol Bo** says: "On the **6th**, it was decreed that they would die by sword and famine; on the **7th**, those who made the calf died." On that day, the son of the sage Rabbi Yehonatan (of blessed memory) was killed; see the *Novellae of Hotshef* <note>Likely a local or specific commentary title</note> regarding two days of fasting. 

The **Tur** wrote that on the **2nd of Marheshvan**, Zedekiah's eyes were blinded and his sons slaughtered before him; in the **Bahag** and **Kol Bo**, it says the **6th**. 

The **Tur** wrote that on the **28th of Kislev**, King Jehoiakim burned the scroll written by Baruch ben Neriah; in our **Bahag**, it says the **8th**, and in the **Kol Bo**, the **5th**. 

The final ruling is that even one who wants to be stringent and fast according to all versions should not fast on the 28th of Kislev, because that is **Hanukkah**, and since the version is not universally agreed upon, we do not fast.
</margin>

## They Said
->The ancients said that the letters of the word **Fast** <note>Hebrew: T-A-N-I-T (תענית)</note> relate to the saying of our Sages: "The merit of a fast is the charity [given]." The explanation is that when a person fasts, he lacks bread and food and feels pain; he then senses the suffering of the poor person who constantly lacks bread—how he suffers and hurts—and thus he has mercy on him. And so it is written:<-

My father and teacher, the Rabbi of blessed memory, wrote in the book *Emek Beracha* <note>"Valley of Blessing," a work on the reasons for the commandments</note> that one should give his money to charity on the day of a fast to fulfill the verse: *"And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might"* <note>Deuteronomy 6:5</note>. This means that the money for the food he did *not* eat today should be given to the poor to bring them close. If he does not do this, it looks as though he did not fast for the sake of Heaven, but only to save money on his meal! 

One can find a hint of this in the words of the Prophet <note>Isaiah 58:7</note> who said: *"Is it not to share your bread with the hungry?"* The verse specifies "**your** bread"—the bread that was meant for your portion—excluding the bread of his wife and children for whom he is obligated to provide. If he only has enough to sustain them narrowly, he should at least give his own portion. I found this in a manuscript. 

This also alludes to what King David said to Solomon his son <note>1 Chronicles 22:14</note>: *"Behold, in my poverty (ba-on'yi), I have prepared for the house of the Lord a hundred thousand talents of gold..."* This is difficult: why would he say "in my poverty"? We wish all the people of God were as "poor" as he! On the contrary, he should have said "In my wealth I have prepared." But the explanation is known: after the incident with Bathsheba, David was a great penitent. The essence of repentance is fasting. He surely gave the value of his meals [to the Temple]. This value amounted to the talents of gold; for every single fast he undertook, he dedicated the cost of that meal to the Most High. Thus, by adding them up one by one, the total reached one hundred thousand talents of gold and a million talents of silver. This is what is meant by *"In my poverty"*—meaning, "through my fasting (innui) and self-affliction, I prepared these," to say that they came from what I saved through the power of my fasts and dedicated to Heaven. I found this also in the **Jerusalem Talmud** (Tractate Pe'ah), which cites this verse and asks: "What is the meaning of 'in my poverty'? If he had this amount in hand before dedicating it, he was wealthy!" They answered: "In my poverty (be-on'yi)" means "in my fasting"—for he would fast and dedicate the cost of his meal to Heaven. This is clearly as explained above.

## The Custom
->It was the custom to fast on the anniversary of the death of one’s father and mother every year. In my opinion, it is also a beautiful custom to fast on the day one’s primary teacher <term>Rabbi Muvhak<gloss>A teacher from whom one has gained the majority of their Torah knowledge</gloss></term> died, for a person is obligated in the honor and awe of his teacher even more than that of his father. **Maharik** <note>Rabbi Joseph Colon, 15th-century Italy</note> wrote in Root 31 that if the anniversary of a father's death falls on the Sabbath or Rosh Hashanah, it should be delayed until the next day. It is proper to act thus even though the **Rema** <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles, 16th-century Poland</note> wrote that this is not our custom; however, if the next day is also a day on which one does not fast, then since it has been delayed, it is set aside entirely.<-

## The Rema wrote
The **Rema**, in his gloss on the **Tur** (Yoreh Deah, Section 400), regarding the fast for the anniversary of a parent's death, said: "If this fast falls on the Eve of Sabbath (Friday), he may finish the fast as with other fasts." See also Orach Chaim, Section 249. However, his words are somewhat obscure. I am here to clarify what the **Gaon Maharshal** <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria, 16th-century Poland</note> wrote in a responsum on this matter. His conclusion is that it depends on the *first* time: if the first time the anniversary falls on a Friday, he has the choice whether to complete the fast until nightfall or not. If he does not complete it then, he never needs to complete it when it falls on a Friday. But if the first time it fell on a weekday and he completed it, then he is forever obligated to complete it, even when it falls on a Friday.

## In Tractate
**Berakhot**, Chapter 1: **Rava** would not decree a fast on a cloudy day, because it is said: *"You have covered Yourself with a cloud so that no prayer can pass through"* <note>Lamentations 3:44</note>. Therefore, the beginning of a fast must be on a day when a person can take to heart the words of Rabbi Yannai... Rava would not decree a fast on a cloudy day, even if it were possible that the next day would be clear, for he could not know if the next day would be cloudy as well.

# The Wellspring of Service
## And let them make
->Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them. The verse should have said "dwell in **it**" <note>referring to the physical building</note>; rather, it says "among **them**" <note>referring to the people</note> because every person is obligated to make himself a sanctuary. This is a constant requirement. It is written that the **Tefillin** <note>Phylacteries</note>, which contain the secret of the Divine Chariot, are the sanctuary a person places upon himself. A person must also purify himself and all<-

his limbs, and then he takes the form of the Tabernacle and the Sanctuary. 

The *Bechinat Olam* <note>likely "Bechinat Ha-Olam" or a similar philosophical/exegetical work</note> (Portion Terumah) says: It is known that the Tabernacle and its vessels are all physical representations intended to help us contemplate the higher spiritual forms which they mirror. Among the wonders included in it is that the Tabernacle consists of three parts: 
1. **Inside the Veil** (The Ark-cover); 
2. **Outside the Veil** (The Tent of Meeting); 
3. **The Courtyard of the Tabernacle**. 

These correspond to the three parts of existence: 
1. **The World of Angels** (Separate Intelligences); 
2. **The World of Spheres** (The Stars and Planets); 
3. **The Lower World** (Our physical world). 

So too, we find that **Man**, who is the essence of everything, is a "Microcosm" mirroring existence in its three parts. Man is divided into three realms: the Realm of Speech (Intellect), the Realm of Vitality, and the Realm of Nature. 

The **first part** of the Tabernacle—inside the veil where the Ark, Tablets, and Cherubim were—represents the most inner and hidden things. They are the "Chariot" for the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah<gloss>The manifest presence of God in the world</gloss></term>. This corresponds to the **World of Angels**, which are hidden, separate forms and intellectual beings that serve as the Throne for the Holy One. Corresponding to these in Man is the **Realm of Speech**, which is the **Head**—the dwelling place of Wisdom where the Intellect flows into the brain. The perfect righteous person is a "Chariot" for God; like the Patriarchs of the world, the Divine Presence rested upon them. This is the significance of the Tefillin placed on the head, corresponding to the brain and the heart, which mirror the two Cherubim. From here you can understand the power of one who wears Tefillin.

The **second part** is outside the veil—the Tent of Meeting. There stood the Table, the Menorah, and the Incense Altar. These were distinguished, inner vessels, but not as high as the first ones. These correspond to the **World of Spheres**, which are distinguished beings that "declare the glory of God," and the world is sustained by their movement. Corresponding to these in Man is the **Realm of Vitality**, which is the **Heart**, for all life depends on it and the whole body is sustained by its movement.

The **third part** is the Courtyard of the Tabernacle. In it was the Bronze Altar, the Altar of Burnt Offering, upon which sacrifices were offered. This corresponds to **this Lower World**, which is the realm of "generation and corruption" <note>A philosophical term for the physical cycle of birth and decay</note>. Corresponding to this in Man is the **Realm of Nature**, from the navel downward, for from there comes generation (reproduction) and the beginning of the body's eventual decay. Corruption is the cause of generation, for if there were no decay in the world, there would be no need for new generation. Thus you have learned that the Tabernacle in its three parts corresponds to the three parts of existence, regarding which King David said: *"Bless the Lord, you His angels... Bless the Lord, all His hosts... Bless the Lord, all His works"* <note>Psalm 103:20-22</note>. 

And so says the **Zohar** (Portion Shelach Lecha): When the Holy One created man, He created him to correspond to the celestial firmaments...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on Tractate Ta’anit, moving from the calendar of fast days into the ethical and ritual laws of fasting. It specifically addresses the debate over whether fasting is a virtuous act of holiness or a sinful neglect of the body, the laws of fasting after a disturbing dream, and the communal obligation to cry out to God during times of distress.</meta>

## Tractate Ta’anit

And even though they called such a person a "sinner," he is only called a sinner because he afflicts his own soul. But did Rabbi Ami really say this? For Rabbi [Elazar] said: A person should always assess himself as if a holy being dwells within his innards, as it is said, <note>Hosea 11:9</note> "The Holy One is in your midst; I will not come in fury." There is no contradiction: one case refers to someone who is physically able to afflict himself, while the other refers to someone who is not able to afflict himself without harm.
<margin>Resh Lakish said: He is called "pious" (*chasid*).</margin>
As it is said, <note>Proverbs 11:17</note> "A man of kindness brings good to his own soul." This concludes that point. And these are the words of the **Tosafot** <note>Medieval commentators on the Talmud</note>: Samuel said that anyone who sits in a fast is called a sinner. This is difficult, as we say in the chapter "He Who Causes Injury" <note>Tractate Bava Kamma</note> that while one is permitted to injure oneself, others who injure him are liable. There, the Gemara explains that Samuel's view—that one may injure oneself—refers specifically to one who "sits in a fast." This implies that according to Samuel, a person who fasts is *not* called a sinner! However, the Tosafot explain: certainly he is a sinner, as we say here, and that is the established order. Nevertheless, the commandment (*mitzvah*) he performs by fasting is greater than the transgression of afflicting himself. This is similar to the commandment of the Nazirite <note>One who takes a vow of abstinence</note>; for we say that one who sees a *Sotah* <note>a woman suspected of adultery</note> in her disgrace should abstain from wine. Nonetheless, there is still a small degree of "sin" involved. This is comparable to one who fasts a **"Fast for a Dream"** (*Ta’anit Halom*) on the Sabbath; because he nullified the joy of the Sabbath, his divine sentence is torn up, but he is punished for the fast of the Sabbath. What is his remedy? He should "fast for his fast" <note>fast again on a weekday to atone for fasting on the Sabbath</note>. This concludes their words. And it seems to me that even Samuel would agree that one who has afflicted himself because of a severe or minor transgression certainly must rebuke himself; he is permitted to be stringent with himself and fast until he knows clearly that no "stain" or trace of the sin remains. Samuel’s words [about being a sinner] were only said regarding one who is pious, holy, and pure, who has never tasted the taste of sin—such a person should not fast. The matter of the verse <note>Numbers 6:11</note> "for that he sinned against the soul" is explained as follows: This person who accepted Nazirite status surely estimated for himself how much time he needed to be a Nazirite to refine himself. Thus, he performed a commandment by abstaining from carcasses. But if he became ritually impure during that time, the law is that his previous days fall away; thus, he caused himself more affliction than he originally designated. In this "excess" affliction, he has "sinned against the soul."
<margin>And Rabbi Elazar holds that he is always called "holy" in the first chapter.</margin>
See there. And we say that even if there is an "iniquity of the filling" <note>an obscure reference to incomplete repentance</note>, even for one who did not sin in permitted matters, everything is still caught up in the sin of "Evil Speech" (*Lashon Hara*) or in the failure to afflict oneself [when necessary]. These are the words of the **Sefer Nekudat HaChasid**: "nullification [of the fast] is a nullification of Torah study..." and regarding the measure of character traits and the transgressions in which a person is immersed, therefore he should fast and fast again, even according to Samuel. If only it would suffice! Perhaps God will have mercy. According to this, we find that for Rabbi Elazar and Resh Lakish, even if one did not sin and fasts, he is called "holy" and "pious." This applies specifically when he is physically able to afflict himself, like the case of Ravina who would sit in a fast the entire year, as mentioned in Tractate Pesachim. But if he cannot endure the affliction, Samuel said (and Resh Lakish himself agreed) that a Torah scholar is not permitted to sit in a fast because he diminishes his "Heavenly work" <note>his Torah study</note>. This applies when he has not sinned. But if he has sinned, he must measure his state, feel pain, and even cancel his study [to fast]. I have expanded on this in the ruling on "He Who Causes Injury" in my explanation of the Sugya <note>Talmudic discussion</note> in the Written Torah, on Parashat Naso. And these are the words of the **Keneset HaGedolah** <note>17th-century halakhic work by Rabbi Chaim Benveniste</note>: In the first chapter of Shabbat, Rav Chama bar Guria said in the name of Rav: "A fast is as good for a dream as fire is to flax." And Rav Chisda said: "Provided it is on the same day." And Rav Yosef said: "Even on the Sabbath." One must remember this great secret: one must see to nullify it and fast immediately, specifically on that very day. And it is a simple matter that immediately after the dream, one should not taste anything, even if it is the middle of the night, and he should not wait to start the fast until daybreak as one does with other fasts. Indeed, I found written in the name of the **Rashba** <note>Rabbi Shlomo ben Aderet, 13th-century Spanish scholar</note> that if a person sleeps in the afternoon and has a bad dream that requires a fast, he must fast for a full twenty-four hour period (*me’et le’et*). I found this in the collection... and so ruled the **Mahari** in the name of **Maharash**, who fasted on the Sabbath when he slept a midday nap and had a dream for which one fasts; he would fast from that half-day of the Sabbath onwards until midnight, and then he would perform Havdalah and eat. He said this was equivalent to a full day, like the first day, and this is the meaning of "a fast for his fast."
<margin>Thus far I have found.</margin>
Behold, he begins the fast immediately. Furthermore, it seems to me he should separate from his wife and not engage in marital relations; for when a bad dream happens to him, he needs to be in a state of repentance (*teshuvah*), anxiety, and pain. It is logically certain that he should not behave with levity, even on the Sabbath. This "half-day" timeframe is also practiced. And since the law of Resh Lakish is to fast and nullify the pleasure of the Sabbath and the three meals, how much more so this matter! And so it will be explained later regarding the "Time of Favor," that it is forbidden to engage in marital relations; so too now, it is a "time of trouble" for the dreamer.

***

**Regarding** this matter, that it must be on the same day and start immediately, the measure of engaging in repentance, prayer, and upright awakening: I have seen a custom where people are diligent to "improve the dream" (*Hatavat Halom*) <note>a ritual of reciting positive verses to change a dream's omen</note> immediately in the morning. This is unlike what most of the world does—improving the dream after the fast—because "the zealous perform commandments early."
<margin>This is nothing; God [gave] Daniel water which...</margin>
And one cannot say that the merit of the fast helps to incline the interpretation of the "improvers" <note>the three people who perform the ritual</note> so that they are heard. For as soon as one has set his heart to fast, it is considered as such here; since he accepted the fast and began it. The proof is that by law, the one fasting should say the *Anenu* ("Answer us") prayer <gloss>also</gloss> in the Evening Prayer preceding the fast. Even if he eats after praying the Evening Prayer, he is obligated to pray *Anenu* in the Evening, Morning, and Afternoon prayers <gloss>again</gloss>. It is only because of the concern that he might be overcome by a "ravenous hunger" (*bulumos*) <note>a medical state of extreme weakness/hunger</note> that the Sages feared a "blessing in vain" and enacted that one should only say *Anenu* in the Afternoon Prayer (*Mincha*) of the fast day itself. But regarding the "improvement," its time is immediately. I found that the sage **Rabbi Solomon Almoli** <note>A 15-century physician and dream interpreter</note> wrote in the "Book of Dream Interpretation" (*Sefer Pitron Halomot*) which he composed: "The matter of the enactment to say after the improvement: 'Do not trust to cut [the dream] for good, and let your heart be good, for God has already accepted your deeds.'" The intention of this verse <note>Ecclesiastes 9:7</note> is that since for all dreams for which they perform this improvement, they are accustomed to fast during the day, and at night after the fast they perform the improvement, they say to him at the end: "Now, after all you have done, go and eat without a fast anymore, for God has already accepted your deeds through what you did in your fast and your repentance." According to this, if someone performs the "improvement" but did not fast, or if they perform it in the morning when it is not yet the <gloss>time</gloss> for eating, one should not say this verse. However, everyone is accustomed to saying it regardless. The **Rambam** <note>Maimonides, 12th-century philosopher and codifier</note> wrote that one should not say it because its initial letters form the word *Abel* ("Mourner"). If one wishes to say it, they should say: "Go in your desire with joy and eat your bread," or "Go, eat your bread with joy." This concludes his words. I agree with the Rambam not to say it, and let his dream be improved through the "anointing of his taste" which I wrote.
The **Rambam** wrote at the beginning of the "Laws of Fasts": It is a positive commandment from the Torah to cry out and sound the trumpets for every trouble that comes upon the community, as it is said, <note>Numbers 10:9</note> "against the adversary that oppresses you, then you shall sound an alarm with the trumpets"—meaning, for anything that distresses you, such as drought, plague, locusts, and the like.
<margin>Cry out over them and sound the alarm and merit.</margin>
This is one of the paths of repentance: that when a trouble comes and they cry out over it and sound the alarm, everyone will know that it is because of their evil deeds that evil has come upon them, as it is written, <note>Jeremiah 5:25</note> "Your iniquities have turned away these things." This realization will cause the trouble to be removed from them. But if they do not cry out and do not sound the alarm, but rather say "this thing happened to us according to the way of the world, and this trouble is a mere happenstance (*mikreh*)," this is a cruel way! It causes them to stick to their evil deeds and adds other troubles, as it is written in the Torah, <note>Leviticus 26:27-28</note> "And if you walk with Me in happenstance (*keri*), then I will walk with you in the fury of happenstance"—meaning, when I bring trouble upon you so that you will repent, if you say it is "happenstance," I will add to you the fury of that happenstance.
<margin>And from the words of the Scribes...</margin>
...to fast for every trouble that comes upon the community until they receive mercy from Heaven. This concludes his words. Behold, when they decree a fast because of some trouble, it is a twofold matter: the repentance they perform and, see, the fulfillment of the Rabbinic positive commandment to fast in a time of trouble. And this Rabbinic commandment is great, for it stems from a Torah commandment: "If the adversary who oppresses you comes...
->...then you shall sound an alarm, etc." and fasting is included in the sounding of the alarm.<-

***

**And this** positive commandment is also incumbent upon an individual to whom some trouble has happened: he should decree a fast upon himself and examine his deeds. So too should all those connected and joined to this trouble do. Then he will find acceptance through repentance, and this repentance stands as a fulfilled commandment. He should say during the "Acceptance of the Fast": "Behold, I accept upon myself a private fast to fast tomorrow as my Lord God commanded me, for the sake of the Unification of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and His Presence (*Shekhinah*), through the Hidden and Concealed One." The wording "as my Lord God commanded me" is appropriate according to what is found in the chapter "With what may we light" <note>Tractate Shabbat</note> regarding the formula of the blessing for a Rabbinic commandment, where we say "and He commanded us." Where did He command us? Rav Acha said: "From 'you shall not deviate'" <note>Deuteronomy 17:11</note>; Rav
->Nehemiah said: "Ask your father and he will tell you, your elders and they will say to you" <note>Deuteronomy 32:7</note>. This concludes the point.<-

***

**The Rambam** wrote in the first chapter: It is proper that anyone fasting, whether an individual fasting for his trouble or his dream, or one fasting with the community for their trouble, should not conduct himself with luxuries. He should not act with levity, nor should he be happy and good-hearted; rather, he should be anxious and mourning, as it is said, <note>Lamentations 3:39</note> "Wherefore does a living man complain, a man for his sins?" This concludes his words. One who does not do so has achieved nothing but the physical affliction of depriving himself. For the purpose of the fast is to subjugate the physical matter (*chomer*) and strengthen the intellectual power (*koach ha-sikhli*), and to be uplifted toward the World to Come, where there is neither eating nor drinking, but only enjoying the radiance of the Divine Presence. Thus, he should also intend to be attached to God all day long in repentance, prayer, charity, and "Torah study is equal to them all." How much more so should he "turn from evil" to distance from himself every trace of sin and every base character trait. Specifically, he must guard
->from anger<-
which is the greatest blemish in the world. For anger is a "strange god," and [an angry person] is like an idolater. Since he is empty of food and drink, he must overcome his anger. We find this also in the *Sefer HaYashar* <note>The "Book of the Upright," a 13th-century ethical work</note>. He should also not rejoice in any futile joy; rather, his whole aim should be his attachment to the Blessed Creator. And even if some business transaction happens to him during the day, he should conduct it
->with faith.<-

<summary>This page explores the spiritual and legal requirements of fasting, debating whether it is an act of holiness or sin, and provides specific instructions for fasting after bad dreams and during communal distress. It emphasizes that the physical act of fasting is meaningless without internal repentance, the subjugation of the physical self, and the avoidance of anger.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Tractate Ta’anit, specifically focusing on the ritual of reciting the "Order of Sacrifices" (Korbanot) as a substitute for actual Temple offerings. It transitions from the general laws of fasting to the daily liturgy that facilitates atonement through study and speech.</meta>

## Tractate Ta’anit

Consider Sign 1 <note>original: "Siman Aleph" - referring to the first section of the Shulchan Aruch, the Code of Jewish Law</note>, but there is no time to say it in the congregation. And even that which I mentioned above, there is no time to say it in the congregation; rather, "the zealous rise early for the commandment" <note>A Talmudic idiom meaning those who are eager to perform God's will do so at the earliest opportunity</note> to stand at daybreak and read the Portion of the Daily Offering <note>The *Tamid*, the sheep offered every morning and afternoon</note> individually, along with everything attached to it, at dawn. Afterward, one should say the Portion of the Burnt Offering and the Meal Offering, etc., before the "Blessed is He who Spoke" prayer <note>Baruch She'amar, the opening of the morning psalms</note> if he has time.

At the beginning, he should say: "Master of the Universe, when the Holy Temple stood, a person who sinned would bring a sacrifice..." as it appears in the aforementioned Sign 1 of the "Way of Life" <note>Orach Chaim, the first volume of the Code of Jewish Law</note>. Afterward, he should say: "Abraham said before the Holy One, Blessed be He: 'Master of the Universe, perhaps Israel will sin and You will treat them like the generation of the Flood?' He replied to him: 'Take for Me a three-year-old heifer...'" as it appears in the second chapter of Tractate Ta’anit and in the chapter "The People of the City" <note>In Tractate Megillah</note> until the words: "And I will forgive all their iniquities."

He should further say what is stated at the end of Tractate Menachot: "Rabbi Isaac said: What is meant by the verse, 'This is the law of the sin offering' and 'This is the law of the guilt offering'? It means that whoever occupies himself with the law of the sin offering, it is as if he had offered a sin offering; and whoever occupies himself with the law of the guilt offering, it is as if he had offered a guilt offering." He should also say what is written at the end of Menachot: "It is written: 'In every place, incense is offered and presented to My name' <note>Malachi 1:11</note>... in every place, and so on."

Afterward, he should say the portions as they are ordered one after another in the Book of Leviticus: **Burnt Offering**, **Meal Offering**, **Peace Offering**, **Sin Offering**, **Suspensive Guilt Offering**, and **Certain Guilt Offering**.

The **Portion of the Burnt Offering** begins at the start of Leviticus until "And when a soul brings an offering" <note>Leviticus 1:1–2:1</note>, and also in the portion of *Tzav*: "This is the law of the burnt offering" until "it shall not be extinguished" <note>Leviticus 6:1–6</note>, as explained in the name of the "Way of Life." The **Portion of the Meal Offering** is in Leviticus from "And when a soul brings an offering" until "you shall offer salt" <note>Leviticus 2:1–13</note>, and also in *Tzav*: "This is the law of the meal offering" until "all who touch them shall be holy" <note>Leviticus 6:7–11</note>. The **Portion of the Peace Offerings** is in Leviticus: "And if his sacrifice is a peace offering" until "you shall not eat" <note>Leviticus 3:1–17</note>, and also in *Tzav*: "And the Lord spoke... He who offers his peace offering" until "the children of Israel" <note>Leviticus 7:28–38</note>. The **Portion of the Sin Offering** is in Leviticus: "And if one soul shall sin" until "a guilt offering to the Lord" <note>Leviticus 4:1–5:13</note>. The **Portion of the Certain Guilt Offering** is in Leviticus: "And the Lord spoke... a soul that shall sin" until "his guilt before the Lord" <note>Leviticus 5:14–26</note>, and also in *Tzav*: "And this is the law of the guilt offering" until "it shall be his" <note>Leviticus 7:1–7</note>.

For all these portions were repeated because of the new laws introduced in them, as the commentators explained. By reviewing all the repeated portions regarding the matter of the sacrifices one by one to find the tally of innovations, you will find that it was proper for each person to recite them, especially for the Peace Offerings. Even though they are not adjacent to each other in the Torah, "there is no 'earlier' or 'later' in the Torah reading" <note>A principle that the sequence of the Torah is not necessarily chronological or restrictive for liturgy</note>.

In the text of the Burnt Offering portion, he should say after it: "May it be the will of the Master of all worlds..." as the *Tur* wrote in Sign 1. He should do the same for the Meal Offering, Peace Offering, and the Suspensive Guilt Offering. However, for the Sin Offering and the Certain Guilt Offering, he should not say this, because they are not brought as voluntary gifts <note>These are mandatory for specific sins, unlike the others which can be donated voluntarily</note>. Rather, he should say after the Sin Offering the language written by the **Maharshal** <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria, a 16th-century Polish legal authority</note> in his responsa, as follows: "After the portion of the Sin Offering he should say: 'Master of the Universe, if I am liable for a sin offering, may it be Your will that this be considered and accepted before You as if I had offered a sin offering in its proper time.'" He should say the same after the portion of the Certain Guilt Offering.

On Shabbat and Festivals, he should only say the Portion of the Daily Offering and its associated texts. But the portions of the Burnt, Meal, and Peace offerings—which are individual sacrifices brought by vow or donation—it seems to me he should not say them, because vows and voluntary offerings are not sacrificed on Festivals <note>A legal technicality in the Talmudic Tractates Shabbat and Beitzah</note>. Certainly, he should not say the portions of the Sin and Guilt offerings, as we do not bring those on those days. We also follow the custom of not saying the "Psalm of Thanksgiving" <note>Mizmor L'Todah, Psalm 100</note> on Shabbat and Festivals, because the Thanksgiving offering is an individual sacrifice, and individual sacrifices are not offered on Shabbat and Festivals, as taught in the name of *Shivilei HaLeket* <note>A 13th-century Italian halakhic work</note> in Sign 9. This was also written by the **Rosh** <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, 13th-14th century</note> in the chapter "He Whose Dead [Relative Lies Before Him]," as follows: "We do not pray a voluntary prayer on Shabbat because there is no voluntary sacrifice on Shabbat."

The reason for all of this is that the reading is considered as if they actually sacrificed, as our Sages of blessed memory said: "Whenever they read them, I credit it to them as if they offered them before Me." For this same reason, some commentators wrote to be careful to recite the verses of the Incense (*Ketoret*) from a written text and not by heart, because the recitation stands in place of the offering; if one omits one of the ingredients, the Sages say he is liable for death.

From the words of the **Tur**, it seems one should only say the sacrificial portions at the time appropriate for offering them, as he wrote: "However, the portion of the sacrifices is better said during the day, for that is the place and time of the offering, and its time is by day." Furthermore, how could one say on Shabbat and Festivals after the Burnt or Peace offerings, "May it be Your will that this be considered... as if I offered it," when if the individual sacrifice itself were offered on this day, one would be liable 

->to a sin offering!<-
<note>Closing a quote from the work *Emek Beracha* (Valley of Blessing)</note>

***

**A**nd these are the words of my great brother, our teacher **Rabbi S.G.L.** <note>Likely Rabbi Shmuel Segal or a similar relative of the author</note> in his glosses: Be careful and be cautioned according to these words. I say, whoever has committed a sin for which the Torah requires a sacrifice, even if he has performed complete repentance, he should be eager to occupy himself with the portion of the sacrifice that comes for that specific sin, so that his atonement may be complete. For since the Sages received the tradition that there is a remedy for this—as they said, "Whoever occupies himself with the portion of the Sin Offering..." and as the Midrashim warned about this—we are not permitted to be lazy in completing our atonement. "And whoever increases the study, this is his."

The sacrificial portions are: Burnt Offering, Meal Offering, Peace Offering, Sin Offering, the "Sliding Scale" Offering, and the Guilt Offering. It is proper to arrange them in the order mentioned, for I have not seen them arranged as such in any other place. Also, because of the new laws introduced in them: the Burnt Offering begins from the start of *Vayikra* until "And when a soul brings an offering," and from the start of *Tzav* until "it shall not be extinguished."

Note that the verse, "And the priest shall put on his linen garment..." <note>Leviticus 6:3</note> in this portion, which refers to the commandment of removing the ashes, is not an active service at the time of the Burnt Offering; rather, its commandment is before the offering of the Daily Sacrifice. Therefore, one should say this verse with the portion but not say it with the intent of performing the service, but rather as one reading the Torah. The same applies to the verse "And he shall strip..." which follows it.

The **Meal Offering portion** is in *Vayikra*: "And when a soul brings a meal offering..." until "you shall offer salt," and in *Tzav*: "This is the law of the meal offering." The **Peace Offering portion** is in *Vayikra*: "And if his sacrifice is a peace offering..." until "an eternal statute for your generations," and in *Tzav*: "This is the law of the sacrifice of the peace offering which he shall offer to the Lord, if for a thanksgiving... or a vow or voluntary offering" until "and the meat that touches [anything unclean]," and afterward "And the Lord spoke... speak to the children of Israel, he who offers the sacrifice of his peace offerings" until "from the children of Israel."

The **Sin Offering portion** is in *Vayikra*: "And if one soul shall sin in error..." until "and it shall be forgiven him," and the adjacent portion: "And if he brings a lamb as his offering" until "and it shall be forgiven him," and in *Tzav*: "And the Lord spoke... this is the law of the sin offering" until "and every sin offering that is brought [into the Sanctuary]." If he wishes to read the two sin offering portions together, he should not intend for both to be for his obligation, but only one of them; for the other, he should intend to be merely "reading the Torah," so it does not look like he is bringing two sin offerings for one sin. Similarly, if he reads the Burnt Offering portion for a sin he committed that requires a Burnt Offering, he should read one for the atonement of the sin and the others as "reading the Torah" or as a voluntary Burnt Offering, so it does not look like he is bringing two Burnt Offerings for one sin. This is as the *Tur* and the **Maharam** <note>Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg, 13th century</note> wrote: that one should not say the Daily Offering portion twice for the sake of the obligation, so it does not look like he is offering two Daily Offerings—similar to what we mentioned above in the name of the decisors regarding the Incense formula.

The **Sliding Scale Offering portion** <note>A sacrifice whose value changes based on the wealth of the sinner</note> is in *Vayikra*: "And if a soul shall sin and hear [a voice of adjuration]..." until "to the priest like a meal offering." He should read one of the portions for his obligation. The **Suspensive Guilt Offering** is in *Vayikra*: "And if a soul shall sin and do [one of the things forbidden]..." until "a guilt offering to the Lord," and in *Tzav*: "And this is the law of the guilt offering" until "it shall be his." The **Certain Guilt Offering** is in *Vayikra*: "And the Lord spoke... a soul that shall sin and commit a trespass..." until the end of the section, and in *Tzav*: "And this is the law of the guilt offering." And the portion of the law in *Tzav*: "And this is the law of the sacrifice of the peace offerings... if for a thanksgiving..." until "he shall not leave any of it until morning."

Regarding the Burnt Offering brought in the heat <note>likely referring to the specific timings or voluntary nature</note> and the Peace Offerings... <note>The text here becomes slightly elliptical, discussing the specific libations (wine/meal) that must accompany the meat</note>. Therefore, after reading their portions, he should read the portion of their meal offerings and libations in their proper order from the verse "And you shall make them a fire-offering to the Lord" until the end of the verse. If he does not say the portion of the meal offering and libations, how can he afterward say "May it be Your will... as if I offered a Burnt Offering in its time"? For if one offered a Burnt Offering without its meal offering or libations, it would not be "good in the eyes of the Lord." Furthermore, since anyone who occupies himself with the portion of the sacrifices for the sake of the offering is in the place of the one offering the sacrifice, it must be performed according to all its statutes and laws.

Now, let us remember the matter of the sacrifices and what they come to atone for:
The **Burnt Offering** (*Olah*) comes for one who transgressed and neglected a positive commandment, or for a sin committed through the thoughts of the heart. He should return in repentance with regret and by abandoning the sin, and the Torah [says it shall be] "for that which he sinned," just as one confesses at the time of the sacrifice. Thus he should say: "Please, O Lord, I have sinned, I have transgressed, I have rebelled, and I have neglected such-and-such a positive commandment. Behold, I return in complete repentance before You, and I have abandoned the way of the wicked. May I have salvation, and please atone for my sins, iniquities, and transgressions..." as it is written: "Let the wicked forsake his way, and the man of iniquity his thoughts; let him return to the Lord and He will have mercy on him, and to our God, for He will abundantly pardon."

Afterward, he should read the Portion of the Burnt Offering and intend in his heart that the act of saying the portion stands in place of the act of offering to atone for that sin he committed, just as one must intend at the time of the sacrifice, as it says: "And they shall lean their hands..." and "May it be Your will... as if I offered a Burnt Offering in its time." He should intend it for the sake of the atonement of the sin.

The **Sin Offering** (*Chatat*) is brought by one who stumbled accidentally (*b'shogeg*) in a matter that, if done intentionally, would incur "spiritual excision" (*karet*). For example, if he accidentally ate forbidden fat (*chelev*), or desecrated the Sabbath with one of the prohibited labors, or stumbled by eating leavened bread on Passover. He should return in repentance as mentioned above, and the confession is for "that which he sinned." He should say: "Please, O Lord, I have sinned, I have transgressed, I have rebelled, and I have stumbled accidentally and committed such-and-such a sin. Behold, I return..." as above. And afterward,

<meta>catchword: He shall read</meta>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Tractate Ta’anit regarding how prayer and personal conduct serve as a replacement for the Temple sacrifices. It expands on the mystical connection between the human body, the Land of Israel, and the structure of the Holy Temple, emphasizing that the individual's "table" and "thought" now function as the altar of atonement.</meta>

<page-num>18</page-num>
<header>Tractate Ta’anit</header>

And he called out and gave him strength and power in the middle of the body, for there the heart dwells, which is the strength and nourishment of the entire body. All the limbs of the body are invited there to be nourished. The heart is seen as held and strengthened by the highest place above, which is the brain of the head that dwells on high, and it leaves its mark within it. These are tied to one another in this established way. The Holy One, Blessed be He, brought him forth and made him into one body, and He fixed the limbs of the body around the heart. To this side and that side, it dwells in the center, and the entire body and all those limbs are nourished by that heart, which is the strength of everything, and everything depends on it. That heart is tied to and unified with the upper brain that dwells above. 

Similarly, when the Holy One, Blessed be He, created the world, He arranged the Great Ocean <note>original: "Yama de-Okyanos"</note> to surround the entire inhabited world. The settlements of all seventy nations all surround Jerusalem, and Jerusalem is in the center of all habitation. Its beginning surrounds the Temple Mount, and the Temple Mount surrounds the Women's Court, and the Women's Court surrounds the Chamber of Hewn Stone <note>The seat of the Sanhedrin, the supreme religious and judicial body</note> where the Great Sanhedrin sat. We have learned that no one was permitted to sit in the Temple Courtyard except for the kings of the House of David alone. The Chamber of Hewn Stone surrounds the Hall <note>The *Ulam*, the entrance hall to the Temple</note>, and the Hall surrounds the Altar, and the Altar surrounds the Sanctuary <note>The *Heikhal*</note>, and the Sanctuary surrounds the Holy of Holies <note>the *Kodesh Ha-Kodashim*</note>. There the Divine Presence <note>The *Shekhinah*</note> dwells, along with the Ark-cover, the Cherubim, and the Ark. This is the "heart" of all the land and the world, and from here, they are all nourished, just as the places of settlement are like the limbs of the body. And the heart is nourished by the brain of the head, and they are seen as bound one to the other. This is as it is written: "The place, O Lord, which Thou hast made for Thee to dwell in" <note>Exodus 15:17</note>—this corresponds to the realm high above. This is the end of his words.

After a person awakens to the realization that he is the image of the Tabernacle and the Temple, he should offer a sacrifice within it, which is prayer. These are the words of the *Tur* <note>The foundational code of Jewish law by Rabbi Jacob ben Asher</note> in the section *Orach Chaim*, Sign 90: Prayer stands in the place of sacrifice, as it is written: "So will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips" <note>Hosea 14:3</note>. It is also written: "To serve Him with all your heart" <note>Deuteronomy 11:13</note>. Now, is there "service" in the heart? Rather, what is the service of the heart? You must say: this is prayer. Therefore, one must be careful that it be like a sacrifice in its intention <note>*kavanah*</note>. One should not mix in any other thought, just as a foreign thought invalidates a holy sacrifice. It must be done while standing, similar to the Temple service, as it is written: "To stand and to serve." He should serve and place his feet together like the priests during the service. He should fix a specific place for prayer, just as each sacrifice had a fixed place for its slaughter and the sprinkling of its blood. Nothing should intervene between him and the wall, just as in the Temple, an intervention <note>a *chatzitzah*</note> invalidated the space between the priest and the vessel or between him and the floor. It is proper for him to have fine garments designated for prayer, like the priestly garments, although not everyone can afford to spend lavishly on this. Nevertheless, it is good to have special trousers for prayer for the sake of cleanliness. After he has modeled his prayer after the sacrifice, it rises as a "pleasing aroma" before Him to offer his burnt offering, and an angel turns it into a crown for his Creator. This is the end of his words.

---

## Further
The fulfillment of the sacrifice now consists of these three perfections: perfection of the body, perfection of wealth, and perfection of the Torah. Their sign is *GMN* [Wealth <note>Mamon</note>, Body <note>Guf</note>, Soul <note>Nefesh</note>]. The sacrifice from the perspective of the perfection of the soul is in the place of Torah study. Our Sages of blessed memory said: The Torah atones as if one had offered all the sacrifices, for it says: "This is the law <note>Torah</note> of the burnt-offering, of the meal-offering, and of the sin-offering, and of the guilt-offering, and of the consecration-offering, and of the sacrifice of peace-offerings" <note>Leviticus 7:37</note>. Anyone who occupies himself with Torah is as if he offered them all. The sacrifice from the perspective of the perfection of the body is fasting, as will be explained later. The sacrifice from the perspective of the perfection of wealth is a person's table, set and prepared also for the poor. As we learn in the chapter "Who are those who say": Rav Judah said in the name of Rav: Three things prolong a person's days and years: one who lingers at his table. "Lingering at the table" is explained as waiting to see if a poor person might come to eat from his bread. Proof is brought for each point, giving the reason for the meal at his table: "Perhaps a poor man will come and he will give to him," as it is written: "The altar of wood, three cubits high..." and it is written: "And he said unto me: 'This is the table that is before the Lord'" <note>Ezekiel 41:22</note>. The verse begins with an "altar" and ends with a "table." Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Eleazar both said: As long as the Temple stood, the Altar atoned for Israel; now, a person's table atones for them. This is the end.

---

## Further
The fulfillment of the sacrifice now in this time of exile is through three things: action, speech, and thought. For the sacrifice on the Altar required these three: Action is the act of the sacrifice itself. Speech is the confession, for without it, "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination." The essence of the sacrifice must be repentance, as explained in Tractate Berakhot, chapter "One whose dead [relative lies before him]," page 23. Thought—for it must be "for its own name"; any sacrifice slaughtered for a different purpose did not count for the owners toward their obligation. Also, thought can invalidate a sacrifice. Just as thought invalidates a sacrifice, so must a person offer himself to the Holy One, Blessed be He, in action, speech, and thought. So wrote the *Tze'enah U-Re'enah* <note>A popular interpretive work on the Torah</note> on the portion of *Vayikra*: Because human actions are completed through thought, speech, and action, the Blessed Name commanded that when a person sins, he should bring a sacrifice. He should lean his hands upon it, corresponding to action. He should confess with his mouth, corresponding to the place of speech. He should burn in the fire the fat and the membrane covering the innards, the kidneys, and the lobe of the liver—for these are all the "vessels" of thought and those that entice one to sin and bring it from potential to action. When their internal parts are removed and offered and burned in the fire of the One who does His work, he should sprinkle its blood on the Altar, corresponding to his own blood and soul. This is so that a person will think while doing all these things that he sinned against his God with his body and soul, and it would be fitting for him to spill his own blood and burn his own body, were it not for the mercies of the Blessed Name, who took from him a substitute in the form of an animal sacrifice—its blood instead of his blood, its life instead of his life, and the main parts of the sacrifice's limbs instead of his own limbs. This is the end of his words.

---

# The Person
How does one offer oneself in action? This refers to the sign of mourning for Jerusalem, which he shows in all his actions and in all his intentions regarding Jerusalem, in the spirit of "Rejoice with her, all you who mourn for her" <note>Isaiah 66:10</note>. For mourning mentions and "destroys" the destruction, and this destruction is for the sake of building; through mourning, the memory of Jerusalem is awakened for good. A hint to this: immediately upon the destruction of Jerusalem, the Messiah was born, as mentioned in *Midrash Rabbah* on Lamentations. Therefore, one should not mourn on the Sabbath, for the building of the Temple does not override the Sabbath.

## How in speech?
"So will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips," and our Sages of blessed memory said: Anyone who occupies himself with the portion of the sacrifices is as if he offered the sacrifices.

## How in thought?
<margin>How? He says in his heart that he is ready to surrender his life for the sanctification of the Blessed Name <note>*Kiddush Hashem*</note>, and then the verse is fulfilled in him: "When any man of you bringeth an offering" <note>Leviticus 1:2</note>—that he offers himself to the Blessed Name.</margin>
He says in his heart that he is ready to surrender his life for the sanctification of the Blessed Name, and then the verse is fulfilled in him: "When any man of you bringeth an offering"—that he offers himself to the Blessed Name.

---

# Also
The matter of thought is this: when one occupies himself with the portion of the sacrifices, it is not enough to merely speak with his lips. Rather, he must understand everything he says and apply his thought to it, because thought is effective in the sacrifice. Therefore, our Sages of blessed memory said: "Anyone who *occupies* himself <note>original: "osek"</note> with the portion of the sacrifices," and they did not say "Anyone who *recites*," because "occupying" implies understanding the matter, for that is what constitutes "occupation." And regarding the matter of occupying oneself with the portion of the sacrifices, one must clarify which portions and their order.

These are the words of my father and teacher, may his memory be for a blessing in the life of the world to come, in the book *Emek Beracha*: When one reaches the portion of the Daily Offering <note>The *Tamid*</note>, he should read from the portion of Genesis <note>*Ma'aseh Bereshit*</note>, every portion of that day and the day following it. For example, on Sunday, he should first read "In the beginning..." etc., and also the portion "And God said, Let there be a firmament..." until "And there was evening and there was morning, a second day." In this manner, he should read all six days of creation, each portion belonging to its day and the portion belonging to the next day, until on Friday, he reads "And God said, Let the earth bring forth..." and also "And the heavens were finished..." until "which God created to make." This is exactly what they used to do in the Temple: they would read the Work of Creation every day at the time of the service, as seen in Tractate Ta’anit (in the chapter "Three Periods"): The men of the "Standing Guard" <note>The *Ma'amadot*, lay representatives who assisted at the Temple</note> would read from the Work of Creation. On the first day of the week: "In the beginning" and "Let there be a firmament." On the second day: "Let there be a firmament" and "Let the waters be gathered." After he has read the portion of the day, he should begin to say the Portion of the Laver <note>The *Kiyor*</note>, for it was the first service. Afterward, he should say the Portion of the Removal of the Ashes, as written in the *Shulchan Aruch*, Sign 1. Afterward, he should say the portion "And this is what you shall do upon the altar..." in the portion of *Tetzaveh* until "to speak unto thee there," for it is like the portion of the Daily Offering and is a command for all generations, as it says there: "a continual burnt-offering throughout your generations." Afterward, he should say the portion of the Daily Offering: "And the Lord spoke..." in the portion of *Pinhas* until its order. It was repeated because of many new matters introduced in it, as Rabbi Moses ben Nachman <note>Nachmanides</note> explained on the portion of *Pinhas* regarding the two lambs. After it, he should say the verse: "Then shall the offering of Judah and Jerusalem be pleasant unto the Lord..." as the *Tur* wrote in Sign 48. Afterward, he should say: "Abaye was arranging the order of the Altar system..." and from here it should be written in an infinite way <note>perhaps meaning without interruption</note> the "Preparation for the Incense" until "throughout your generations." Then the portion of the Ingredients of the Incense and its preparation, because after the offering of the Daily Sacrifice, they would burn the incense. Afterward, the Priestly Blessing, because after that, he blesses the people, as it is written: "And Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people, and blessed them; and he came down from offering the sin-offering, and the burnt-offering." Thus, after the service comes the blessing, as decided in the Gemara, chapter 4 of Megillah, and so it is in Sign 1. And it would be proper to attach to this the portions of the Burnt Offering, the Meal Offering, the Peace Offering, the Sin Offering, and the Guilt Offering, as it is written—
