# Chapter: Torah is Light
**The Matter of the Ninth of Av** • It is written: "Rejoice with her in joy, all you who mourn for her" <note>Isaiah 66:10</note>. And it is written: "Thus says the Lord: The fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall become joy and gladness for the House of Judah" <note>Zechariah 8:19</note>. From the words of the Prophets and the Writings, and the words of our Sages of blessed memory in the Talmud, the Midrashim, and the Zohar, the great obligation to mourn for the destruction of the Holy Temple and for the Exile <note>original: "Galut"</note> has been clarified. 

The reason for this matter is for the sake of the honor of the Divine Presence <note>original: "Shekhinah"</note>, for because of our sins we were exiled from our land, and, as it were, the Divine Presence is in exile and joy is destroyed. The enemy stems from the side of the "husk" <note>original: "Qlippah"; in Kabbalah, this refers to the forces of evil or impurity that conceal holiness</note>, the "Other Side" <note>original: "Sitra Achra"</note>. The glory of the House of the Lord was burned; there is no burnt offering and no sacrifice. Prophecy and the Holy Spirit have ceased, while the spirit of impurity has spread. The people of the Lord, the nation of Israel, were given over to the plague, the sword, famine, captivity, and plunder. Even today they are among the nations like a lamb among wolves. Her crown has fallen and her head is sick—this is the desecration of the Name of God. Woe to us, for we have sinned; our ancestors and we ourselves have not been purified. They surely weep <note>original: "qa bakhayu"</note> because we caused all of these things. When we take this to heart through fasting, weeping, lamenting, and an awakening of the heart to cry out, "Turn us back, O Lord, to You, and we shall return," then the cloud and the mist—which is the "husk"—are consumed and diminished. They are broken by the power of the sorrow and regret, and the suffering also scours away the sins.

## In the Conclusion
As discussed later, at the time of the Redemption, we will not only return to the high level of greatness we once had, but there will also be a great advantage to the future light across many levels. 

Thus, the end is better than the beginning. What was, as I mentioned at length in the introduction to *Toledot Adam*, was explained in the Spanish book <note>The OCR here contains garbled text, likely referring to a medieval philosophical or kabbalistic work</note> regarding the chapters of Titus <note>Referencing the Roman general who destroyed the Second Temple</note> and the "husks." The advantage and our uplifting come from the power of the darkness of the troubles. The great amount of mourning <unclear>is from...</unclear> It is a natural thing that it adds to itself a great new light for the future. For through the growth of mourning at the beginning, it is as if the Temple were destroyed just now. They will be strengthened by the power of the great intention regarding the destruction <unclear>...</unclear> Those who mourn in their own sight as if the destruction happened now, and as if blood was spilled, and who always mourn in mourning—they are blessed. They mourn with all the blessings in many matters in the place where the "husks" were submitted. Then the great light will be there without any interruption of a screen or mixture. Thus all the exiles and troubles find their place. And now, when the holiness of the veil is found, and its repair is found, they will come at the end of days for the good, and they are for the purpose of the essence of good itself. 

With this, the Midrash on Lamentations is explained <unclear>...</unclear> It is difficult: what is the questioner asking? There was a desecration of God's name in the eyes of the nations, and as if one would think <unclear>...</unclear> it is impossible that the Holy One, Blessed be He, would send punishment in vain. On the contrary, we find that in one instance He was gracious <unclear>...</unclear> but to strike blows for no reason, God forbid! This is also called a "futile action" from which no eternal purpose emerges. Furthermore, "the Lord has afflicted her" <note>Lamentations 1:5</note> means that this should not be an action without eternal good; rather, the blows and the suffering are to take vengeance from them for what they transgressed... because of the "multitude of her transgressions." That is to say, the blows and sufferings subdue the "husks" which are called the "multitude of her transgressions." For due to our many sins, the "husks" spread, and they are many while the holy ones are few. Regarding them it was commanded: "Do not follow a multitude to do evil" <note>Exodus 23:2</note>. The blows, the troubles, and the sorrow of the Temple’s destruction subdue and nullify the "husks" which are now a ruin. In the future, not only will there be a multitude of praises, but "the knowledge of the Lord" will spread from the small to the great. For this good, the Ninth of Av is called a "Festival" <note>original: "Moed"</note>, because out of the distress comes relief. This is the meaning of "Rejoice with her in joy," and as it is written that the fasts will become "joy and gladness." A hint of this appears in our Holy Torah, as our Sages said, "tomorrow" <note>original: "machar"</note>. I found in the notes of the Ari of blessed memory <note>Rabbi Isaac Luria, the preeminent kabbalist of Safed</note> that the words are literal, for there is a "tomorrow" that is after a long time. There will be "a feast to the Lord tomorrow" <note>Exodus 32:5</note>, which refers to the 17th of Tammuz, for it will become joy and gladness.

## Furthermore
You shall contemplate and see a wondrous matter. "A word in its season, how good it is!" <note>Proverbs 15:23</note>. We see that the Torah portions always read on the Sabbaths of the "Three Weeks" <note>original: "Bein HaMetzarim," the mourning period between the 17th of Tammuz and the 9th of Av</note>—namely *Matot*, *Masei*, and *Devarim*—mention the victory over the nations and the division of the Land. This is the opposite of the "evil time" of those days. Sometimes the portion of *Pinhas* is also at the start of the Three Weeks, containing all the "Festivals of the Lord." Rather, the matter is as I said: the troubles will turn into festivals, and the Exile causes the establishment of the Land in the future. In the place of darkness and its deeds, it is said that "food was turned into a holiday." There is a great hint at the conclusion of the section on the Festivals, namely at the end of the portion of *Pinhas*, where it says: "And Moses spoke to the children of Israel according to all that the Lord commanded Moses" <note>Numbers 30:1</note>. The adjacent portions then say: "And Moses spoke to the heads of the tribes" <note>original: "Rashei HaMatot"</note>. It would have been appropriate to say, "And the Lord spoke to Moses saying, 'If a man makes a vow...'" as is written elsewhere. Why does it say "And Moses spoke" to interrupt the matter? 

But it is not answered simply. Rather, the matter of the "Heads of the Tribes" has a connection to the Festivals. For the Festivals ceased with the destruction of the Temple; the months, the Sabbaths, and the holidays rested, for "the joy of our heart has ceased." These "Heads of the Tribes" are "the crown of our head has fallen"—the Great Sanhedrin <note>The high court of 71 sages</note> that Nebuchadnezzar exiled. This came to them by the power of "If a man makes a vow," for they permitted the vow and the oath to the righteous, as will be explained later. But in the future, the crown shall return after the Exile, and the "tribes" <note>The word *Matot* means both tribes and staffs/branches</note> will have their "departures for their journeys" <note>A reference to the portion *Masei*</note>. "These are their journeys according to their departures," as will be explained later. Therefore, after the journeys, the division of the Land is mentioned. Afterward, that which is written in the portion of *Devarim* will be fulfilled: "May the Lord... increase you a thousand times more and bless you as He spoke to you" <note>Deuteronomy 1:11</note>, without limit to our blessing. Then the Ninth of Av will be a great Festival.

## A Matter
This is hinted at in our Holy Torah in the story of our father Jacob wrestling with the angel, who is the guardian angel of Esau <note>identified in tradition as Samael</note>. Esau is Edom <note>The Roman Empire and the subsequent Western world in rabbinic thought</note>, who destroyed our Holy and Beautiful House twice—the First Temple and the Second Temple. Regarding the Second Temple, it is explicitly stated: "Remember, O Lord, against the children of Edom the day of Jerusalem, who said: 'Raze it, raze it, to its very foundation!'" <note>Psalm 137:7</note>. And Jeremiah the prophet prophesied against the "daughter of Edom." Even the First Temple was destroyed by the power of the guardian of Edom, who is Samael, who is the Accuser <note>original: "Satan"</note>, who is the Evil Inclination. For it is known that the First Temple was destroyed for the sin of idolatry, and it was all drawn from the filth of the sin of the Golden Calf, which was the first to sin. Because of this, they later committed many transgressions; the generation of Jeroboam also made calves. Moses' servant <unclear>...</unclear> came from the Accuser who mixed up the world and showed them the guardian of Edom, Samael the Serpent, to mislead them. Even in the Second Temple, where there were no "strange sins" <note>idolatry</note>—for the Men of the Great Assembly had succeeded in nullifying the "Accuser" of the Inclination for Idolatry, as explained in the Aggadah—nevertheless, he came and mixed up the world with jealousy and hatred. For the Second Temple was destroyed for the sin of "baseless hatred" <note>original: "Sinat Chinam"</note>, and we have still not been purified of this sin, due to our many iniquities. Therefore, the "Son of Jesse" <note>The Messiah</note> has not yet come. The general rule: the sin of the First Temple was due to transgressions between man and God, namely idolatry, which is the opposite of "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul." The sin of the Second Temple was due to transgressions between man and his fellow, namely baseless hatred, which is the opposite of "And you shall love your neighbor as yourself."

## And All
this is hinted at in the matter of Jacob's wrestling with the angel, the guardian of Esau. For there, in a hint, is the matter of the Ninth of Av. The Zohar on the portion of *Vayishlach* says: "In a human being there are 248 limbs corresponding to the [positive] holy commands... and they were given to be performed. Correspondingly, there are 248 angels in whom the Divine Presence is clothed... and corresponding to them are the [365 negative] commands, which were given to prevent [sin], corresponding to the 365 days of the year... and corresponding to the angel Samael..." <unclear>...</unclear> "Therefore the Children of Israel do not eat the sinew of the thigh <note>original: "Gid HaNasheh"</note>." # Tractate Ta’anit

One should read the section regarding the **Sin Offering** <note>original: "Chatat"; an offering for unintentional sins</note> and focus his heart as mentioned previously. The **Sliding-scale Offering** <note>original: "Oleh v'Yored"; a sacrifice where the cost varied according to the person's financial means</note> is brought by one who was adjured by an oath to testify for his fellow, but suppressed his testimony, whether unintentionally or willfully. It is also for one who swore "with his lips" regarding something he would do—such as eating, traveling to a certain place, sleeping, or any other action—concerning matters within his power to do or not do. This applies even if the matter is nonsensical or physically impossible, such as swearing to move the **Leviathan** <note>A legendary sea creature, here used as a metaphor for an impossible task</note> from place to place. If he swears to do one of these things and forgets, thus violating his oath, or swears not to do it and then forgets and does it, [he is liable]. This also applies to an oath regarding the past, such as falsely swearing he did something when he did not, or vice versa. What should he do to achieve complete atonement? He should perform full repentance and confess, as mentioned before. The merit of reading the section of the **Sliding-scale Offering** will suffice to count as the sacrifice the Torah required of him. He should focus his intent as we wrote above.

The **Suspensive Guilt Offering** <note>original: "Asham Talui"</note> is brought by one who is in doubt as to whether he committed a sin punishable by **spiritual excision** <note>original: "Karet"; a severe spiritual penalty</note>. For example, if two pieces of fat were before him—one being **forbidden fat** <note>original: "Chelev"</note> and the other being **permitted fat**—and he ate one but does not know which, he should return in repentance and regret, and read the section of the Suspensive Guilt Offering.

The **Certain Guilt Offering** <note>original: "Asham Vadai"</note> is brought by one who held his fellow’s money (valued at a **Perutah** <note>the smallest copper coin</note> or more) and denied it—whether it was a deposit, a business partnership, theft, robbery, withholding wages, or a lost object he found and denied. If he swore falsely about it, he must first return the property to its owner, repent, and feel regret for the sin. In place of the sacrifice the Torah required, he should study the section of the Certain Guilt Offering and focus his heart as described above.

The **Meal Offering** <note>original: "Minchah"</note>, **Peace Offering** <note>original: "Shelamim"</note>, and **Burnt Offering** <note>original: "Olah"</note> may also be brought as voluntary gifts. The **Thanksgiving Offering** <note>original: "Todah"</note> is brought by one who experienced a miracle and is obligated to give thanks to God for the kindness and wonders performed for him. He should read the corresponding Torah portion and stand, focusing his heart on the idea that the recitation of these sections stands in place of the physical sacrifice.

The *Tur* wrote that after the section of the Burnt Offering, one should say: "Master of all Worlds, may it be Your will that this be considered and accepted before You as if I had offered a Burnt Offering in its proper time." After the Meal Offering, one says the same, and likewise after the Peace and Thanksgiving offerings. If one reads the Burnt Offering section because he is liable for a sin that requires it, he should focus his intent during the reading and the "Master of all Worlds" prayer on atonement for that specific sin. If he reads it voluntarily, he should focus on the pleasure it brings to God, as our Sages said: "It brings satisfaction to Him who spoke and the world came into being."

For other sections whose sacrifices atone for specific sins, we already wrote that one should focus on the specific sin being atoned for. After the Suspensive or Certain Guilt Offering, if he is indeed liable, he says the "Master of all Worlds" prayer accordingly. Regarding the **Sin Offering**: although it is only brought for a known sin, one should nevertheless read the section every day. Even if he is not certain he sinned, he should read it out of doubt. He should intend that if he did sin, the reading should count as a sacrifice to atone for him; if he did not sin, it should be considered like regular Torah study. The *Ram"b* <note>Likely referring to Rabbi Moses Isserles or Maimonides, depending on the specific code cited</note> noted that he would still receive a reward for Torah study.

Regarding the **Sliding-scale Offering**, even though it is not always applicable, one should say it every day with the same intent. After the Sin Offering, one says: "Master of all Worlds, if I have become liable for a Sin Offering, may it be Your will... as if I offered it in its proper time; and if not, let this be as if I am merely reading the Torah." Regarding the Guilt Offering, he says: "If I am liable for a Guilt Offering..." This was written by the *Maharil* <note>Rabbi Jacob Moelin, a major authority on Ashkenazic custom</note> in his responsa.

The section of the **Suspensive Guilt Offering** should be said every day even if one is not definitely liable, because it was also brought voluntarily. Our Sages noted that the "Pious Men of Old" <note>original: "Chasidim HaRishonim"</note> would volunteer a Suspensive Guilt Offering every day (except the day after Yom Kippur). 

<margin>Restricted</margin> Some would also take a vow of **Naziritehood** <note>A vow of abstinence from wine, hair-cutting, and contact with the dead</note> specifically <margin>Daily</margin> so that they would become liable for the Guilt Offering of a Nazirite, which could then be offered. The Gaon *Maharam"z* <note>Rabbi Moshe Zacuto</note> wrote that before the section of the **Daily Offering** <note>original: "Tamid"</note>, one should say the section of the **Laver** <note>original: "Kiyor"</note> from the portion of *Ki Tissa* ("And you shall make a copper laver..."), as it was the first task of the Temple service. Then the section of the **Removal of the Ashes** (*Trumat HaDeshen*), followed by the Daily Offering and the sections on the **Incense** (*Ketoret*). This includes the recipe for the incense and the verses "Aaron shall burn incense upon it..."

I also found in the Sephardic prayer books that after the Daily Offering, they would offer the Incense and then the **Priestly Blessing**, for the priest would bless the people at that point. Then one says the "Order of the Arrangement" <note>original: "Seder HaMa'arakhah"; the procedure for arranging wood on the Altar</note> according to the Sage Abaye. The *Tur* records the formula: "Master of all Worlds, You commanded us to offer the Daily Offering in its time and the Incense in its season... but now, because of our sins, the Temple is destroyed and the offerings have ceased... You said, 'We will pay the bulls with our lips' <note>Hosea 14:3; meaning prayer replaces animal sacrifice</note>. Therefore, may it be Your will that this be accepted as if I offered the Daily Offering in its time and stood at my station."

It is also written that one should say the verse: "And he shall slaughter it on the side of the altar northward before the Lord." The Midrash states that God said: "Whenever they read this verse before Me, I remember for them the **Binding of Isaac** <note>original: "Akeidat Yitzchak"</note>." One should say this before the sacrificial portions. 

Regarding Shabbat and Festivals: since no individual sin or guilt offerings were sacrificed on those days—only the Daily and Additional (*Musaf*) offerings—one should not focus on the "atonement" aspect of those individual sacrifices when reading them on Shabbat. Instead, he should read them simply as Torah study. The book *Emek Berakhah* suggests that some do not read these portions at all on Shabbat, but the author here argues that since we recite the Mishnah of *Eizehu Mekoman* <note>A chapter of the Mishnah detailing where various sacrifices were slaughtered</note>, there is no reason to avoid the biblical verses, provided one does not intend for them to count as an actual sacrifice brought on that day. However, it is better to engage in Torah study related to the themes of the specific Shabbat.

# Tractate Ta’anit
<note>Tractate Ta'anit focuses on fast days, repentance, and historical tragedies, particularly the destruction of the Temple.</note>

They led her <note>referring to the Divine Presence or the soul of Israel</note> out from Jerusalem. Furthermore, Rabbi Judah said regarding the land: the first was the exile of Israel. Therefore, the famous question arises: what entered the minds of such exalted individuals <note>referring to the spiritual leaders or the Sanhedrin</note> to permit a "bolt for the outside"? <note>This refers to a technical legal discussion about a door-bolt (Nagar), but here it serves as a metaphor for whether an oath can be dissolved.</note> For if one makes a vow based on the knowledge of his fellow, it cannot be dissolved except in his presence. And regarding the dwelling of Moses, "let his prayer not be united," etc. The Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, 13th-century legal authority</note> wrote that the **Sanhedrin** <note>the supreme legislative and judicial council in ancient Israel</note> were forced to act due to fear of the King. They and the King were obligated to honor the King of Kings, the Holy One Blessed Be He. It is possible that the Sanhedrin actually sinned because they saw what would happen. 

The beginning of the discourse starts with: "Do not let the section of vows be light in your eyes." One might ask: why would it be light? Rather, this is the explanation: if one makes a vow, it is as if he built a forbidden altar. If he fulfills it, it is as if he offered a sacrifice upon it. Let him go to a wise man who will dissolve it for him. Nevertheless, let the dissolution not be light in your eyes, for see what happened to the Sanhedrin. Even Zedekiah <note>the last king of Judah before the Babylonian exile</note> was completely righteous, yet it entered his mind that he could despise an oath. Tosafot and the Ran <note>medieval Talmudic commentators</note> wrote, and the Beit Yosef <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo</note> cited them, that it was for the sake of a commandment, because Zedekiah was greatly distressed that he could not reveal the matter and was being hindered from the service of Heaven. 

One should also consider the matter of the "chariot" and how a king like him would be humbled by this. Furthermore, the merit of Abraham, the merit of Jacob, and the merit of Isaac were not mentioned here. Yet we find the opposite in the chapter of "Rabbi Akiva" regarding the verse: "For Abraham did not know us, and Israel <note>Jacob</note> did not recognize us" (Isaiah 63:16). Also, the tying of their hair to the tails of horses certainly hints at the verse: "For the Lord God does nothing [without revealing His secret to His servants the prophets]" (Amos 3:7). 

Jacob corresponds to the Three [Kingdoms], and Moses to the Two. The kingdom of Babylon is compared to a lion, and this tribe is compared to a lion—"A lion’s whelp is Judah" (Genesis 49:9). Thus, the kingdom of Babylon falls at the hand of Daniel, who comes from the tribe of Judah. Benjamin corresponds to the kingdom of Media; this one is compared to a wolf and that one is compared to a wolf. Benjamin is a "ravenous wolf" (Genesis 49:27), and the kingdom of Media is compared to a bear <note>original: "Dov"</note> which is like a wolf in the language of the Targum <note>Aramaic translation</note>. At whose hand does the kingdom of Media fall? At the hand of Mordecai, who comes from the tribe of Benjamin. 

Levi corresponds to the kingdom of Greece. This is the third tribe and that is the third kingdom. Both have "tripled" letters <note>referring to mystical groupings of Hebrew letters</note>. One blows horns and the other blows horns; one wears special garments and the other wears special garments. They were many in number but fell by the hand of the few. By what merit? By the belt of Moses, as it is said: "Smite the loins of those who rise against him" (Deuteronomy 33:11). At whose hand does the kingdom of Greece fall? At the hand of the Hasmoneans, who are from the tribe of Levi. 

Joseph corresponds to the kingdom of Edom <note>Rome</note>. Both possess "horns." Joseph is described as "his horns are the horns of a wild ox" (Deuteronomy 33:17), and regarding Edom it says "ten horns" (Daniel 7:7). One resisted sexual immorality <note>Joseph and Potiphar’s wife</note> and the other is attached to it. One honored his father and said, "I fear God" (Genesis 42:18), while of the other it is written, "he did not fear God" (Deuteronomy 25:18). At whose hand does the kingdom of Edom fall? At the hand of the **Anointed for War** <note>original: "Meshuah Milchamah"; a priest or leader designated for battle</note> who comes from the descendants of Joseph.

One might ask: why did the Holy One Blessed Be He not reveal His secret to the prophets until now? Perhaps the exiles are different. The Holy One Blessed Be He said to Moses: "I will be what I will be" (Exodus 3:14), meaning I will be with them in this exile and in other exiles. It is known why the Lord revealed this to our father Abraham, as it says in Midrash Genesis Rabbah on the portion of "Lech Lecha": "Dread" refers to Babylon, "Darkness" refers to Media, "Greatness" refers to Greece, and "Falling" refers to Edom. 

Another question: why was the merit of Jacob not mentioned? It says "Three against Two," but there were four kingdoms. If he did not know all four, how could it be said that God revealed His secret? Or how did he not receive the knowledge from his father Isaac, who received it from Abraham? Furthermore, in Tractate Berakhot, it says the kingdom is "like a bear," referring to the Persians who eat and drink like a bear, are hairy like a bear, and have no rest like a bear—implying it is literally like a bear. Up until now, we have found comparisons between them.

---

# Genesis
<note>In Hebrew, *Bereshit*. This section uses the story of Creation as an allegory for Jewish history.</note>

In the word *Bereshit* (In the beginning), there is a hint to the Four Kingdoms, as found in the Midrash. "And the earth was **unformed**" (*tohu*)—this is the kingdom of Babylon. "**And void**" (*vohu*)—this is the kingdom of Media. "**And darkness**"—this is the kingdom of Greece, which darkened the eyes of Israel with its decrees, saying to them: "Write on the horn of an ox that you have no portion in the God of Israel." "**Over the face of the deep**"—this is the wicked kingdom <note>Rome/Edom</note> which is as unfathomable as the deep. Just as the deep has no limit, so too the wicked. 

"**And the spirit of God hovered**"—this is the spirit of the **Messiah** <note>original: "Mashiach"</note>, as it is said: "And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him" (Isaiah 11:2). By what merit does this spirit come? "Hovering over the face of the **water**"—by the merit of **Repentance** <note>original: "Teshuvah"</note>, which is compared to water, as it is said: "Pour out your heart like water" (Lamentations 2:19). 

Rabbi Hiyya the Great said: At the beginning of the creation of the world, the Holy One Blessed Be He foresaw the Holy Temple built, destroyed, built, and destroyed. "In the beginning God created"—behold, it is built. "And the earth was unformed and void"—behold, it is destroyed. "And God said: Let there be light"—behold, it is built and perfected in the future to come, as it is said: "Arise, shine, for your light has come" (Isaiah 60:1). 

We find something similar: that the Holy One Blessed Be He informed the three pillars of the world of the exiles, for the world was created in their merit: Abraham, Moses, and Jacob. Regarding Abraham, it was through his merit that the world was blessed. Regarding Moses, it is said: "He saw the beginning for himself" (Deuteronomy 33:21). Regarding Jacob: "Thus says the Lord who created you, O Jacob, and formed you, O Israel" (Isaiah 43:1). The Holy One Blessed Be He said to the world: "Who created you? Jacob created you. Who formed you? Jacob formed you."

To each of them, God revealed the kingdoms. To Abraham: "Take for Me a tripled heifer"—this is Babylon; "a tripled goat"—this is Media; "a tripled ram"—this is Greece. To Moses, the Lord also showed that they would undergo kingdoms. Jacob, the "head of the exiles," actually went into exile. One should take all this to heart; the ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous walk in them. That which appears to be the destruction of a building is actually "tearing down in order to rebuild" <note>a principle where destruction is a necessary step for a greater construction</note>. Then the eternal, pure building will emerge. 

The fire that burned the Temple is the cause of its future rebuilding with holy fire. In the verse "From on high He sent fire into my bones" (Lamentations 1:13), the final letters of the words spell "Messiah" <note>original: "Mashiach"</note>. In a manuscript of the Rokeach <note>Rabbi Eleazar of Worms</note>, it says that the Messiah was born on the day of the destruction. Evil is the cause of ultimate good for three reasons: 
1. The husk (*kelipah*) precedes the fruit, just as night precedes day. Light emerges from darkness. If the husk were not created first, it would be mixed within the fruit; thus, the husk allows the fruit to be pure. The "cup of staggering" for the nations preserves the "stored wine" for Israel. God wants to bring us to the wine cellar that is refined from all dregs caused by the first sin. Then the cloud will vanish, and there will be light. This is the secret of "the advantage of light over darkness." The vitality of light comes from the preceding darkness. 
2. The exiles we suffer save our souls from **Gehinnom** <note>the purgatorial afterlife</note>. The exiles are the furnace and the refinery. 
3. The exiles arouse us to return in repentance.

This is the explanation of the Midrash.</margin>

# Tractate Ta’anit
<note>This tractate of the Talmud deals primarily with the laws of fast days and the commemoration of national tragedies.</note>

They ate from it but did not drink, and because of this, the Holy One, Blessed be He, knew everything. A hint was given to them regarding Jacob: **"And a man wrestled with him"** <note>Genesis 32:25</note> during all the days of the year and throughout all of Jacob’s limbs, but he could not find a way to harm him except through that **sciatic nerve** <term>Gid HaNasheh: the forbidden nerve in the hindquarters of an animal</term>. Immediately, Jacob’s strength weakened. Among the days of the year, the angel found the day of the **Ninth of Av** <note>Tisha B’Av, the date both Temples were destroyed</note>, for on that day, judgment was strengthened and decreed against us, and the Sanctuary was destroyed. Anyone who eats on the Ninth of Av is as if he ate the forbidden sciatic nerve. Thus far are his words. And those 345 angels are the angels of harsh judgments. **Sammael** <note>Often identified as the guardian angel of Esau/Rome and a figure of spiritual opposition</note>, the harshest of them all, is the spiritual essence of the sciatic nerve. And the word *Et* <note>a Hebrew grammatical marker</note> is used to include the Ninth of Av, for the numerical value of the letters of *Et* hints at the Ninth of Av.

**These are the words** of the Recanati <note>Rabbi Menahem Recanati, a 14th-century Italian Kabbalist</note>: The sciatic nerve has five branches on the right and five branches on the left, totaling ten, corresponding to the ten classes of impurity that surround the Divine Chariot, as it is said: "The wicked walk on every side" <note>Psalms 12:9</note>. This nerve is close to the area where these impure classes dwell. Therefore, one who eats it draws upon himself a spirit of impurity, for one limb strengthens another limb. The term *Nasheh* <note>meaning "removed" or "displaced"</note> suggests a drawing out, for through it, one is removed from the service of the Blessed Name. Therefore, the Children of Israel do not eat the sciatic nerve, as they are careful to avoid the forces of impurity. Behold, the enemies of our father Jacob (peace be upon him) were all powerful, and the guardian angel of Esau—who comes from the spirit of impurity—could not prevail against him except at the sciatic nerve, where he found a place to take hold. Thus far are his words. And you already know that the primordial Serpent originally had legs which were cut off; therefore, the "shells" <term>Kelipot: kabbalistic term for forces of evil or concealment</term> desire to take hold of the thigh, as the Sages said: "The weariness in the legs of the scholars comes from them" <note>referring to spiritual friction from these forces</note>.

**And I found** in the book *Akedat Yitzchak* <note>a 15th-century philosophical commentary by Rabbi Isaac Arama</note> on the portion of *Vayishlach*, that he added to the words of the Zohar and wrote: In this verse is a hint to the four fasts of the year which were drawn upon us from the displacement of the hip socket. The word *HaNasheh* <note>the nerve</note> is like the word for "the year" (*HaShanah*), meaning the Children of Israel shall not eat because of the events of the year: the 3rd of Tishrei, the 10th of Tevet, the 17th of Tammuz, and the 9th of Tammuz <note>This likely refers to the fasts of Gedaliah, the Siege of Jerusalem, and the breaking of the walls</note>. The word *Et* includes the Ninth of Av, totaling the four fasts. Thus far are his words.

<margin>
As mentioned above.
The Ninth of Av. And the reason it precedes... to hint to you... his kingdom... and understand.
</margin>

**And now** I will explain the matter well. I have already written that Esau is **Edom** <note>traditionally identified with the Roman Empire</note>, and his heavenly guardian was the one who destroyed the two Temples. This is the secret of "And he wrestled" (*vaye’avek*). Rashi explains this in two ways:
1. From a language meaning "to be attached or entwined."
2. From the word for "dust" (*avak*).
Our Sages of blessed memory said: "He touched the socket of his thigh"—this means Sammael could not prevail against Jacob himself, but he touched the "socket of his thigh," referring to the generations of descendants who would be pulled toward idolatry. From here we derive the concept of "dust." So it is taught in the Tractate *Avodah Zarah* <note>"Foreign Worship/Idolatry"</note>, Chapter 1: If an Israelite goes to a pagan festival, the "dust" or residue of the idolatry is forbidden because he was "attached" to it. Regarding this, the hint of "dust" appears.
This "dust" corresponds to the Golden Calf, the sin of which extended to the time of the destruction and "pushed away the legs" <note>damaged the foundation</note>. This "dust" hints at the destruction of the Second Temple, which was caused by **unfounded hatred** <term>Sinat Chinam: baseless hatred between people</term>. The Sages said: "Most people stumble in theft, a minority in sexual immorality, but all in the 'dust' of the evil tongue <note>Lashon Hara: gossip/slander</note>." This was the sin of the Second Temple. They also hinted at this in the word "dust" (*Avak*), which points to the story of **Kamtza and Bar Kamtza**, whose petty social feud caused the destruction of the Temple, as told in the Talmud, Tractate *Gittin*.

<margin>
As mentioned above.
Regarding the generations of the Kingdom of Israel, which is like the sign of the Moon... he strove with God and with men... to the end... of the thought, the end of the action.
</margin>

**He said** to Jacob: "Let me go, for the dawn has risen." See Rashi’s commentary on the portion of *Vayishlach*. The "morning" hints at the kingdom of Saul, which was the beginning of the rising of the Kingdom of Israel. See Rashi at the end of *Vayishlach*, for Edom established eight kings before Israel had a king. Once eight kings reigned in Israel from Saul onward, the kingdom of Edom was nullified. This is the hint of the angel of Edom saying to Jacob: "Let me go—is this news not enough for you?" But Jacob was not satisfied and said, "I will not let you go unless you bless me." Then the angel told him that in the future, his name would be called "Israel." He brought him news that after the exiles, in the final redemption, the verse will be fulfilled: "For you have striven with God and with men." This means the destruction of the First Temple was a decree from God (due to idolatry), and the Second Temple was against "men" (due to social hatred). But in the future, you will have striven and prevailed with both—there will be perfection in everything. Jacob was still not satisfied, for he understood that there are times of mourning and times of joy. In the future, there will be joy and greatness for Israel, but during their exile, it is "bitter in the light." Therefore, he asked to know the angel’s name so he could adjure him in times of trouble. I found this written in the *Tziyuni* as well. The angel replied: "Why is it that you ask my name? You have no need for this." For even the evils of the destruction and the exiles—though they appear evil and ruinous—are actually the cause of the blessing. There will be a greater light that emerges from the power of the darkness. This is the secret of "And he blessed him there"—meaning even in the "place" of the curse, it will be turned into a blessing and become a time of gladness and joy.

# Sermon for Portion Matot

"And Moses spoke... If a man makes a vow..." <note>Numbers 30:2</note>. In *Eichah Rabbah* <note>a collection of Midrash on the book of Lamentations</note>, Rabbi Eleazar said: "Do not let the section of vows be light in your eyes, for because of the section of vows, the Great Sanhedrin <note>the high court</note> of King **Zedekiah** were killed." When Jeconiah was exiled, King Nebuchadnezzar appointed Zedekiah over five kings, as it is written: "And send them to the king of Edom, and to the king of Moab..." <note>Jeremiah 27:3</note>. Zedekiah used to enter and leave the king’s presence without permission. One day, he entered and found Nebuchadnezzar tearing the flesh of a **live rabbit** and eating it. Nebuchadnezzar said to him, "Swear to me that you will not publicize this." Zedekiah swore to him. How did he swear? Rabbi Yose bar Hanina said: He swore by the Inner Altar. Later, the five kings were sitting and mocking Nebuchadnezzar in front of Zedekiah. They said to him, "The kingship does not fit Nebuchadnezzar; it fits you, for you are of the seed of David!" Zedekiah also mocked him, saying, "I saw him tearing and eating the flesh of a live rabbit!" The kings’ messengers went and told the King, "That Judean who enters and leaves your presence without permission said to us, 'I saw Nebuchadnezzar tearing and eating the flesh of a live rabbit.'" Immediately, Zedekiah rebelled against the king. Nebuchadnezzar came and sat in Daphneh of Antioch. The Great Sanhedrin went out to meet him. When he saw that they were all people of distinguished form, he ordered chairs to be brought and sat them down. He said to them, "Interpret the Torah for me." They would read portion after portion and translate it for him. When they reached the portion of vows—"If a man makes a vow"—he asked them, "If one wishes to retract it, can he or not?" They said to him, "He may go to a wise man, and the wise man releases him from his vow." He said to them, "It seems to me that you released Zedekiah from the oath he swore to me!" Immediately, he ordered them to be brought down to the ground. This is what is written: "The elders of the daughter of Zion sit on the ground and keep silence; they have cast dust..." <note>Lamentations 2:10</note>. They began mentioning the merit of Abraham, of whom it is written, "I am but dust and ashes." They put on sackcloth, mentioning the merit of Jacob, of whom it is written, "He put sackcloth on his loins." What did the enemy do to them? <meta>This page continues the discussion of the spiritual dimensions of the Jewish exile, moving from the symbolism of Jacob’s struggle with the angel to the historical "Four Kingdoms" that dominated Israel. It focuses on how human actions affect Divine strength and the specific character of each period of suffering.</meta>

# Tractate Ta’anit
<note>This tractate of the Talmud deals with communal fasts and the history of national calamities.</note>

<margin>
They sat on the ground, as is the custom of the Sanhedrin, following the statement we are currently discussing: **"To whom You have done this"** <note>Lamentations 2:20</note>. **"Thus shall you say to them"** <note>Jeremiah 10:11</note>. **"What can I compare to you?"** <note>Lamentations 2:13</note>. Even the nations admit that this is a **"wise and understanding people"** <note>Deuteronomy 4:6</note>. And from the *Aleph-Bet* <note>The alphabetical acrostic in Lamentations</note>, we see the reversal where the letter *Pe* <note>meaning "mouth"</note> precedes the letter *Ayin* <note>meaning "eye"</note>. In the giving of the Torah, the "mouth" said **"We will do"** before the "eye" said **"We will hear,"** seeking to see with the eye of the spirit. But now, in the incident of **Bar Kamtza** <note>The famous story of a social slight that led to the destruction of the Second Temple</note>, he spoke with the speech of his lips, yet his eyes were distorted. This reversal of *Pe* and *Ayin* represents the spreading of a false report—may God have mercy. And it is said that even if they had not reversed the order and had spoken the truth, they would still have been punished for the sin of **Lashon Hara** <term>evil speech/slander</term>. The scripture records the truth of the matter as it happened. **"How [Eicha] has the gold become dim!"** <note>Lamentations 4:1</note> corresponds to the great humiliation and the "wondrous descent" from the loss of the **Kingdom**, as we fell under our enemies. For this "Eicha" is a lament for the kingdom of Josiah and his people, the children of Zion, about whom it is certainly said: "The children of Israel are the children of kings." **"I am the man"** <note>Lamentations 3:1</note> represents the trouble born out of former relief. For Jeremiah kept this bitterness within him; he had been at the height of greatness and worldly desire, for he was a reincarnation of Solomon, as the Kabbalists have written.
</margin>

He hovers from the heavens and makes me hear, saying: **"Today His feet..."** and **"Under His feet..."** <note>Exodus 24:10</note>. The **"Pride of Jacob"** <note>Psalms 47:5</note> refers to the study halls, which are the fortresses of the "guardians of the city." Concerning the living creatures <note>divine beings in Ezekiel's vision</note>, it is said: **"I am the man who has seen affliction"** <note>Lamentations 3:1</note>. The prayer **"Remember, O Lord"** <note>Lamentations 5:1</note> is also established against the four "Until when?" questions mentioned previously, but from a different perspective—namely, "Remember that we are poor and needy." 

There are four levels of compassion for the poor. The highest level is: **"Praiseworthy is he who is wise toward the poor"** <note>Psalms 41:2</note>—meaning even before the poor person arrives, he is wise and contemplates, "Perhaps this person is in need." Another interpretation: **"Until when will You forget me forever?"** <note>Psalms 13:2</note> and not place me in Your memory; regarding this, we lament, **"Remember, O Lord."** 

The level below that is when one sees the poor person ready to ask, and he begins to help him and does not **"hide his face,"** which corresponds to **"Until when will You hide Your face from me?"** And his eyes rise upward to see a bit of the "Divine Countenance" <note>Hebrew: *Ma'at*</note>, and regarding this, we lament, **"Look [and see our disgrace]."** 

The lower level is when the poor person feels shame and asks, and the giver grants his request; this is **"Until when shall I take counsel in my soul"** <note>Psalms 13:3</note>, coming like a poor man at the door. **"A prayer of the afflicted when he is faint"** <note>Psalms 102:1</note>; the prayer is the soul, as the prayer is built in the body and soul. Regarding this, we lament, **"See our disgrace,"** for we come as those who are poor and empty before the Lord of Righteousness, and **"to us belongs shame of face"** <note>Daniel 9:7</note>, for the one who asks in prayer is like a beggar seeking help. 

The level below that is to look upon every face during the **redemption of captives** held by an enemy who has overcome them. This is **"Until when shall my enemy be exalted over me?"** <note>Psalms 13:3</note> and regarding this, **"Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers"** <note>Lamentations 5:2</note>. Thus, these are the laments of the section "Remember."

The four alphabetical acrostics correspond to the **Four Kingdoms** <note>Babylon, Persia/Media, Greece, and Rome/Edom</note>. How so? In every "trouble born of relief," since we were exiled from our land, we have had no true relief. Throughout the time of the Second Temple, there were wars and troubles—the trouble of bitter dread. We were troubled even in the kingdom that was "slumbering" for Mordecai, over a morsel of bread <note>original: "sumsa de'lachma"</note>, and the evil man [Haman] sought to rule over us when **"man rose up against us"** <note>Psalms 124:2</note>—meaning a common man and not a king. 

The Greek exile brought the nullification of Torah and good deeds, as they said: "Write on the horn of the ox [that you have no part in the God of Israel]." This trouble was prolonged into the exile of **Edom** <note>Rome/the West</note>, may God have mercy on us. Let us explain the words of Abarbanel <note>Don Isaac Abarbanel, 15th-century statesman and philosopher</note>: Rabbi Azariah said in the name of Rabbi Judah bar Simon: "Whenever Israel performs the will of the Omnipresent, they add strength to the Power on High, as it is said: **'Through God we shall do valiantly'** <note>Psalms 60:14</note>. But when Israel does not perform the will of the Omnipresent, as it were, they weaken the great Power on High, as it is said: **'You neglected the Rock [Tzur] who begot you'**" <note>Deuteronomy 32:18</note>. 

Rabbi Judah bar Simon said in the name of Rabbi Levi bar Paitat: "When Israel performs the will of the Holy One, Blessed be He, they add strength to the Power on High, as it is said: **'And now, I pray, let the power of the Lord be great'** <note>Numbers 14:17</note>. And when they do not perform His will, they weaken the great Power on High, and they themselves **'walked without strength before the pursuer'**" <note>Lamentations 1:6</note>. 

Rabbi Huna, Rabbi Aha, and Rabbi Simon spoke in the name of Resh Lakish, and the Rabbis in the name of Rabbi Hanina: It was forbidden to mention His name in Jerusalem... the word *Eicha* <note>original: "איכה"</note> has the numerical value of "loss of strength." We learned in the first chapter: "I have no strength." The Holy One, Blessed be He, said: "A time will come when I will do this to you: **'And they shall go without strength before the pursuer.'**" Rabbi Aha said: "Just as Israel was only exiled through a 'full' pursuer <note>meaning a powerful, complete enemy</note>, so they shall only be redeemed by a 'full' redeemer, as it is written: **'And a redeemer shall come to Zion'** <note>Isaiah 59:20</note>." 

One might ask: what is the difference between these opinions? Why are these four answers necessary? And why the "pursuer" when they were already "without strength"? These correspond to the Four Kingdoms. 
1. **The Exile of Babylon**: Trouble out of relief. The source and life of Israel is in the heights; they are called **"children of God"** <note>Psalms 82:6</note>. Then, **"Through God we shall do valiantly."** By "God" [Elohim], I mean that from the greatness of the past, we know the power. When we are called "Elohim," it is as if we were on the land belonging to one of the two nations and the Divine Presence was above our heads—then **"Through God we shall do valiantly."** Understand this well. But when we fell, then **"the Rock who begot you was weakened"**—the "Image of God" was weakened. This is the doubling of the phrase **"and they walked without strength,"** meaning the life-force was gone. **"Now, before the pursuer."**

The mention of "Place" <note>Hebrew: *Makom*, a name for God</note> is significant. When we, as it were, resemble the one called *Elohim* like His name, then He is the "Place of the world" <note>the sustainer of all existence</note>.

The teaching in the name of Resh Lakish speaks of the **Exile of Media**. Therefore, it mentions the title of the Holy One, Blessed be He, for "He is Holy" in exile, and "Blessed is He" is hidden. Understand this. It speaks from the perspective of **"a slave when he reigns"** <note>Proverbs 30:22</note>. For the verse **"And now let the power be great"** was said by Moses regarding the wickedness of Israel compared to the nations, so that they should not say, "He lacked the ability..." But now, in the era of fallen ones and ruling slaves, this is **"they walked without strength before the pursuer,"** meaning the one who rules over them now is a "pursuer" without human strength—a commoner and not a king ruling over us.

Rabbi Huna, Rabbi Aha, and Rabbi Simon in the name of Resh Lakish speak of the **Exile of Greece**—the troubles of nullifying the Torah. Therefore, they went "without the strength of the Lord" to engage in the Torah, of which it is said: **"The voice of the Lord is in strength"** <note>Psalms 29:4</note>.

Rabbi Aha speaks of the **Exile of Edom**—a prolonged trouble. In this state, as it were, the Name is not complete. Now, the promise **"And I will fill the Sanctuary"** is not fulfilled until the future, when I shall fill it thereafter. Now the "pursuer is full." Therefore, **"they walked without strength."** Why? Because our strength has been exhausted by the length of the exiles. And now, he who is not worthy of Zion, a redeemer will come to him. The word for "Redeemer" <note>Go'el</note> is written lacking a letter, for the deficiency is on the side of evil. But He will act for His great Name's sake, for the Divine Presence is in exile. And in the future, **"A redeemer shall come to Zion"** written fully. Understand this; your matter is one of Kingdom.

And behold, they are "two that are four." All of Greece... for this causes "trouble out of relief," which leads to the nullification of Torah and Divine Service. This is why the commentators were brief regarding the exile in Egypt—to consult how God saved the Service, so that they would accept the yoke of Torah and Service through goodness. But how can one experience delight when all good is forbidden? When a person is honored through goodness, he cannot pull the yoke. Similarly, we find Babylon and Greece resemble each other, just as Greece is hinted at in the "Firstborn." So too we find a parallel: as it is brought in the chapter *Helek* <note>Sanhedrin 94b</note>: "The descendants of Sisera taught Torah in Jerusalem; the descendants of Sennacherib taught Torah in public—and who were they? Shemaya and Avtalyon. The descendants of Haman taught Torah in Bnei Brak—and who was it? Rav Shmuel bar Shilat. Even of the descendants of that wicked one [Nebuchadnezzar], the Holy One, Blessed be He, sought to bring them under the wings of the Divine Presence." The angels said before the Holy One: "Master of the Universe! One who destroyed Your House and burned Your Temple—will You bring him under the wings of the Divine Presence?" This is what is written: **"We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed"** <note>Jeremiah 51:9</note>. 

Media and Edom also resemble each other—**"a slave when he reigns"**—it is a trouble that continues without pause. Not only is one not enslaved by him, but the situation is reversed and he enslaves him. So too we find Media and Edom are similar in themselves, for they are from the seed of Esau. For the essence of the Median exile [Haman] was the wicked one, the grandson of Amalek, the grandson of Esau.

### **And Just As**
The blessings of Moses our Teacher were similar to the blessings of Jacob our father in a single pattern, so too are these "rectifications"—namely the Four Kingdoms—which are meant to rectify us and return us in our end. They follow a specific pattern. For Greece and Edom are the patterns of Babylon and Media. It is already known that the place of Jacob and Moses is holy; one came to reveal the rectifications—Jacob was there, one from within and one from without. So it is in all their matters. Now I will explain the statement. It begins by saying: **"For He has revealed His secret to His servants"** <note>Amos 3:7</note>, meaning He gave them a hint and made a sign through them. For the Fathers are a sign for their children. 

Behold, the exiles of Babylon and Media, which are "trouble out of relief" and "a slave when he reigns"—the Holy One, Blessed be He, placed these signs in Jacob. How so? There is no relief or joy in the world... I mention this regarding the "living creatures" [Chayot]. This is why **"Jacob’s bed was complete,"** meaning all his children were holy, for the "bed" was complete in every way. Yet all their troubles were this: the trouble of Rachel, the trouble of Joseph, the trouble of Simeon, the trouble of Benjamin. And it is written: **"The elder shall serve the younger,"** but it was reversed, so that Jacob our father accepted him as a master.

### In the Level

Not from you, for you were constrained by it." This was an atonement for the trouble of the nullification of Torah in the days of Greece, for its fulfillment came through great trouble. And corresponding to the exile of Edom—the "prolonged trouble"—is the Rebuke found in the Mishneh Torah <note>Deuteronomy</note>, as is known that the Rebuke in the Priestly Code <note>Leviticus</note> is against...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Jewish suffering and exile, transitioning from the symbolic fall of the "Kingdom" to a detailed sermon on the Torah portions of Mattot and Masei. It examines the "Ten Horns" of Israel's power, the relationship between the joy of Passover and the mourning of the Ninth of Av, and the spiritual purpose behind the long years of displacement.</meta>

# Sermon for the Portions of Mattot and Masei

Based on the book of Lamentations, where it is written: **"He has cut off in fierce anger all the horn of Israel"** <note>Lamentations 2:3. In biblical imagery, a "horn" symbolizes strength, dignity, and power.</note>. Our sages teach that there are ten "horns" belonging to Israel: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, the Torah, the Priesthood, the Levites, Prophecy, the Holy Temple, and the People of Israel themselves. When the people sinned, these honors were taken from them—as it says, "He has cut off in fierce anger"—and they were given to the nations of the world. This is what is meant by the verse: "And concerning the ten horns that were on its head" <note>Daniel 7:20, referring to a vision of a beast representing world empires</note>. Yet, when Israel returns to God in repentance, the Holy One, Blessed be He, restores them to their place, as it says: "All the horns of the wicked I will cut off... but the horns of the righteous shall be lifted up" <note>Psalm 75:11</note> and "He will exalt the horn of His Messiah" <note>1 Samuel 2:10</note>.

But wait—how can we say that the Holy One gave the nations Prophecy, Priesthood, and the Levites? <note>Since these roles are unique to the covenant with Israel.</note> Rather, it means that these "horns" are established through the nations in the sense that the nations' actions drive Israel to repent, and through that pressure, the people are refined until they stand firm and improve themselves. Then, the "horn of His Messiah" is revealed. We see that the Four Kingdoms <note>The traditional four empires that exiled Israel: Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome</note> were mentioned even at the beginning of Creation, but at the end of the process, "the spirit of God" <note>Genesis 1:2</note> is the spirit of the Messiah. This spirit hovers "over the face of the waters," and "water" symbolizes Repentance. This process transforms intentional sins into merits. 

This is the meaning of the Midrash at the opening of Lamentations regarding Rabbi Abin’s teaching. He links the first night of Passover to the night of Tisha B'Av <note>The Ninth of Av, the major day of mourning for the Temple</note>. He says: "Because He satiated me on the first night of the festival of Passover, He has turned me back on the night of Tisha B'Av with wormwood" <note>Original Hebrew: *Hadrini le'anah*. This is a play on words noting that the day of the week Passover begins is always the same day of the week Tisha B'Av falls on.</note>. This means that just as we bless God for the good, we must realize that the "evil" or suffering is also for our ultimate good. The fast will eventually turn into a day of joy and gladness. When a person gives their life to this truth, the fast of the fourth and fifth months will truly be transformed into celebration.

In light of this, we can explain a difficult Midrash in *Lamentations Rabbah* regarding the verse: "For the Lord has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions" <note>Lamentations 1:5</note>. The Midrash asks: "Is it possible it was for no reason?" and answers, "Scripture says: 'for the multitude of her transgressions.'" This is puzzling. Would anyone think the Holy One, Blessed be He, gives punishments for no reason? We find "free gifts" given for the sake of good, but never for evil, for God "delights in kindness" <note>Micah 7:18</note>. 

This statement can be explained in three ways. We will also address the command to mourn for Jerusalem and to remember the destruction daily, as mentioned in the *Zohar* and other holy books. Whoever increases their weeping for Jerusalem is worthy to see its consolation. However, one might wonder: Don't all the prophets, the masters of Truth, and even the wise men of the nations say we should accept suffering with love? To cry over the past is a "vain action" <term>poyel hevel; a futile effort</term>. Furthermore, it is known that sadness is a great barrier to wisdom and spiritual perception. Indeed, Prophecy only rests upon a person in a state of joy. 

However, based on what we said earlier, three benefits emerge from this mourning:
1.  **Awareness:** By contemplating the loss of our spiritual normalcy and the greatness of the destruction, we feel the weight of our sins. We realize our iniquities caused this. We then feel shame, our sins are "ever before us," and we search our deeds.
2.  **Atonement:** The exiles serve as a substitute and atonement in place of the punishment of *Gehinnom* <term>Purgatory/Hell</term>. Perhaps because of our deeds, we have built up a heavy debt. Therefore, we mention the trouble of the destruction so that the Holy One might "join our thought to deed." I mean that He considers the brokenness of our hearts as if we were actually undergoing the physical cleansing, until the debt is paid through our "shattering of heart."
3.  **Refinement:** The suffering acts as a "smelting pot" so that the *Kelipah* <term>husk or shell of evil</term> is removed entirely. Then, in the future, the inner light will shine. 

Regarding these three things, the scripture says: "Why should a living man complain?" <note>Lamentations 3:39</note>. That is, why complain about the trouble if the purpose is that he should truly be "alive"? The verse then explains how to reach the goal of this sadness:
*   Against the **first** reason, it says: "Let us search and examine our ways, and return to the Lord" <note>Lamentations 3:40</note>. This refers to the sins of our fathers and our own sins.
*   Against the **second** reason, it says: "Let us lift up our heart with our hands" <note>Lamentations 3:41</note>. This means the desire of our heart is counted as if it were a physical action.
*   Against the **third** reason, it says: "We have transgressed and rebelled; You have not forgiven" <note>Lamentations 3:42</note>. This "not forgiving" is actually for the good. For if You had forgiven and made it easy for us, the defect would have remained at its root. The light would not shine clearly because the dregs would still be mixed with the wine, and our sins would not be "turned into merits." Therefore, You—to whom we cling, for our souls are a "portion of God from above"—did not forgive, so that the defect could be fully transformed into merit. 

This explains the Midrash: Even though the affliction is from the Lord, one might think it is "for no reason"—meaning there is no purpose other than useless pain. But the scripture says "for the multitude of her transgressions," meaning a purposeful end comes from this: one remembers the sins to repair what is hidden. Alternatively, "for no reason" could mean that the sadness achieves nothing; but "for the multitude of her transgressions" implies it serves as the atonement necessary for those sins. We have not yet been purified of our errors and our attachments, and this "multitude of transgressions" is why we are not yet clean.

A third way to read it: One might say, "Is it possible [we are punished] for no reason?" meaning "Is it only because we were cast away from the High Table <note>A metaphor for the Temple and Divine presence</note>?" We might think our sin is only a burden to us because of the punishment and the exile from our Father's table. To this, the verse says: "for the multitude of her transgressions" and not "for the multitude of the transgressors." As the Talmud says in the first chapter of *Berakhot*: "Let sins cease" <note>Original Hebrew: *Yitamu chata'im*</note>, not "let sinners cease." Similarly, "Cursed be their anger" <note>Genesis 49:7</note>—it is the anger that is cursed, not the people. This means the *Kelipah* (the husk of evil) will depart. 

Now, even in the decrees of exile, there is the name of Mercy. All exiles exist for the ultimate purpose of Redemption. This secret was revealed to Abraham, Moses, and Jacob—the three pillars of the world for whom the world was created. Abraham is the head of the believers; Jacob's "bed was perfect" <note>meaning all his children remained righteous</note>, representing the whole assembly of Israel; and Moses is the essence of the Torah. The exiles refine these qualities.

The *Zohar* mentions: "Fortunate are the righteous who subdue the Nefesh <note>the lower soul</note> into the Ruach <note>the spirit</note>, and the Ruach into the Neshamah <note>the higher soul</note>, and the Neshamah into the Holy One, Blessed be He," to be saved from the punishment of *Gehinnom*. This is the secret of the soul's purity:
*   The **Nefesh** (lower soul) relates to the sacrifice: "When a soul sins."
*   The **Ruach** (spirit) relates to Repentance: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit." This is the spirit of prophecy.
*   The **Neshamah** (higher soul) is the "pure and holy soul" without dross or defect.

Abraham represents the descent into exiles to save the *Nefesh* from *Gehinnom*. Jacob represents the perfection of the "bed" to remove the filth of the "husk." Moses represents the light of the Torah, the secret of the *Neshamah*, which includes all 600,000 souls of Israel.

This is why Psalm 79 begins: "A Psalm of Asaph: O God, the nations have come into Your inheritance." The Talmud asks: Should it not be called a "Lament of Asaph" instead of a "Psalm"? <note>The word *Mizmor* usually implies a joyful song.</note> Rather, it is indeed a "Psalm" because they "looked and saw if there was any pain like my pain" <note>Lamentations 1:12</note> and understood its ultimate purpose. The Four Kingdoms correspond to four general forms of all the evil troubles mentioned later in the sermon. This is hinted at in Psalm 13, where "How long?" <note>Original Hebrew: *Ad Ana*</note> is repeated four times:
1.  **External trouble:** "How long will You forget me?"
2.  **Internal trouble:** "How long will You hide Your face from me?" (When the "light of the King's countenance" which gives life is hidden).
3.  **Loss of Torah:** In the exile, there is no Torah and no good deeds. "How long shall I take counsel in my soul?" (Having to invent strategies/prayers to replace the Temple service).
4.  **The Rule of the Enemy:** "How long shall my enemy be exalted over me?"

These correspond to the three things mentioned by our Sages: **Children, Life, and Sustenance** <note>Hebrew: *Benei, Chayei, u'Mezonei*</note>. They are hinted at in the verse: "And He will bless your bread" (Sustenance), "There shall not be a woman who miscarries" (Children), and "the number of your days I will fulfill" (Life) <note>Exodus 23:25-26</note>. 

In Lamentations, the "widow" <note>Lamentations 1:1</note> hints at the loss of these:
*   Regarding **Sustenance**: "They seek bread" <note>Lamentations 1:11</note>.
*   Regarding **Children**: "For these things I weep... my children are desolate" <note>Lamentations 1:16</note>. 
At the giving of the Torah, the children were the "guarantors." But through the Golden Calf, that was canceled. Now the verse is reversed: "For these things I weep." 

Our Sages said that **Children, Life, and Sustenance** do not depend on merit, but on *Mazal* <term>spiritual flow/fortune</term>. This is difficult—is it not said that "Israel has no *Mazal*" <note>Meaning they are above the influence of the zodiac</note>? Rather, it means that like Repentance, these things are "suspended" <note>Hebrew: *tola*</note>. When there is merit, they are certain. But when they depend on *Mazal*, they are "suspended" because Israel is above that system. This is why the prophet says to the nations: "It is not for you, all you who pass by the way" <note>Lamentations 1:12</note>. For while the nations are under the stars and constellations, Israel's fate is cast down from heaven...

It links the calendar of mourning (Tisha B'Av) to the calendar of joy (Passover) to show that both serve a divine purpose in the development of the Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the destruction of the Temple and the mourning for Zion, transitioning into a mystical and ethical discourse (Drush) on the Torah portions of Mattot and Masei. It explores the themes of vows, the journey of the soul, and the ten 'horns' of Israel's power.</meta>
