<meta>The previous page likely discussed the fundamental duties of a judge and the general prohibition of bribery during a trial. This page continues with specific categories of bribery and judicial ethics, concluding with the requirement for equal treatment of litigants.</meta>

->Tractate Rosh Hashanah: The Pillar of Judgment Below<-

<margin>2. Prohibition of receiving a bribe even after the judgment</margin>
Even if the bribe was given and he <note>the judge</note> was acquired through this bribe—even if it was intended to favor the truth of the Torah—it is written: "and it blinds the eyes of the wise." **2. The prohibition of receiving a bribe even after the judgment** is found in the *P'nei Moshe* <note>a commentary on the Jerusalem Talmud</note> on this chapter, citing the Rav <note>Rabbi</note>, as follows: Rav Chama had killed a man <note>original Aramaic: *קטול גברא* - likely referring to accidental manslaughter</note>. Rav <note>Rabbi Pappa</note> said to him: "Rav Chama, go and look into his judgment, and if you see a way to save him from being destroyed or exiled, do so." Two witnesses came and testified that he had definitely killed. Then two other witnesses came and testified against one of the first two, saying in the presence of the residents that he had stolen a *kav* <note>a measure of volume</note> of barley, and the other said he stole a *kav* of barley, but this happened before the robbery <note>original: *הורשא*</note>. Rabbi Mordechai Yosef said: "The law follows Rabbi Yosei." Rav Pappa said to him: "This applies only where the Author of the Mishnah did not specifically follow Rabbi Meir." Rav Chama came and kissed Rav Pappa’s feet and wished to serve him <note>literally "received his feet"</note> for all his years <note>original: *וקבליה לכרעיה דכולהו שני'*</note> to speak on his behalf to the king to exempt him from the tax. However, the Sages are already exempt from the head-tax, so this was not considered "delayed bribery" <note>term: *שוחד מאוחר* - a gift given after the trial as a 'thank you,' which is still legally problematic</note>. Thus ends his words. From this, we see that it is forbidden even after the fact. See also where it is hinted: "The judgments of the Lord are true, they are righteous altogether" <note>Psalm 19:10</note>—meaning both before and after the judgment. Regarding this, he <note>Samuel the Prophet</note> hinted: "Whose ox have I taken?" <note>1 Samuel 12:3</note>. This is known: a person who sells an ox to its owners, meaning it is not "owned" by its owners <note>the judge</note>, but on the contrary, he knows the "eating" he is eating <note>benefiting from the gift</note>. Thus, one who accepts a bribe after the judgment was not "owned" by the litigants <note>during the trial</note> since in the field of judgment he had no prior knowledge, only afterward did he eat what was given to him.

<margin>3. Bribery through asking for favors</margin>
**3. Bribery through asking for favors** <note>term: *שוחד שאלה* - benefit derived from borrowing items or requesting personal favors</note>, as explained in the *Tur* <note>an authoritative code of Jewish law</note>, *Choshen Mishpat* section 9: a judge who is accustomed to asking for favors is forbidden from judging unless he also provides benefits and asks for favors from the other party in return. This is also hinted at in "they are righteous altogether." Regarding this, it is hinted: "Whom have I oppressed?" For one who borrows a vessel and does not lend one in return is effectively indebted for the rental fee of that vessel, and when he does not pay it, he is "oppressing" <note>original: *עושק* - oshek</note>. As it is written: "What is oppression? It is the withholding of a worker's wages," and similar matters.

<margin>4. Prohibition of taking payment for a verdict</margin>
**4. Prohibition of taking payment for a verdict**, as we learned in the Mishnah: "One who takes a fee to judge, his judgments are void." The Ran <note>Rabbi Nissim of Gerona</note> wrote in the chapter "The one who consecrates" that by Rabbinic decree, his judgments are void. Note that it does not say "that judgment" is void, which implies that it is not only the specific case where he took a fee that is void, but *all* judgments he makes are void, unless it is known he did not take a fee for them. Thus ends his words. The *Tur* (*Choshen Mishpat* 9) wrote: If he only takes "compensation for lost time" <note>term: *שכר בטלה* - sechar battalah; payment to cover what the judge would have earned at his regular job during the trial hours</note>, it is permitted, as per Rabbi Eliezer. This applies if he has a known trade he would have been doing at the time he had to judge, and he says to the litigants: "Give me what I am losing from my work." If they give him the wage of that labor from which he was idled, it is permitted, provided he receives it from both parties equally. This is also hinted at in "they are righteous altogether"—that both parties should benefit equally from the "compensation for lost time." Regarding this, he said: "Whom have I crushed?" <note>1 Samuel 12:3</note>. Radak <note>Rabbi David Kimhi</note> wrote that "crushed" (*ratzoti*) is a language of oppression and crushing. Jonathan <note>the Aramaic translation</note> translated "Whom have I oppressed? Whom have I coerced?" One might say: "oppressed" refers to coercion, and "crushed" refers to willingness <note>voluntary gifts</note>. Even if a payment is taken for a verdict where both parties are willing—meaning they give it voluntarily—it is still considered "coercion" because they feel compelled by the judges. Therefore, there is no permission for this unless they specifically take what was previously decreed as the "city wage," and the townspeople established and accepted that the litigants would pay a fee if they required a verdict from the judges. The fixed amount should be paid equally, whether the case is for a hundred *maneh* or a small verdict. Let them be "righteous altogether."

<margin>5. Arbitration</margin>
**5. Arbitration** <note>original: *בוררות* - borrerut</note>: "This one chooses for himself [an arbitrator] and that one chooses for himself [an arbitrator]." See in *Choshen Mishpat* section 13 how it elaborates on the humility of the arbitrator who tries to find merit for his side, and how it is better if they choose more, etc. The conclusion of his words is that each litigant should present his merits before his chosen arbitrator so that the rights of both are clarified equally. See there. And Jonathan hinted at "righteous altogether." Then the truth will emerge. Regarding this, he said: "From whose hand have I taken a bribe <note>original: *כופר* - kofer; literally 'ransom'</note> that I should hide my eyes from him?" Meaning: I have heard both sides equally, and I have contemplated them, just as I looked into the merits of the one who chose me.

<margin>6.</margin>
**6.** The *Beit Yosef* wrote in *Choshen Mishpat* at the beginning of section 4: A judge of "absolute truth" <note>term: *דיין אמת לאמיתו* - din emet l'amito; a judge who perceives the underlying reality of a case, not just the surface arguments</note> is one who repeats it in his heart. Whether this one or that one wins, it is a "matter of the heart." Only the Holy One, Blessed be He, who knows thoughts, can truly stand over this. Therefore, the Scripture required a "voice" to testify, saying "Witness!" And this is "The judgments of the Lord are truth," and "God stands in the congregation of the Divine." When it is an absolute judgment of truth—the "truth of the truth"—all the judgment becomes a partnership with the Holy One, Blessed be He. This is "they are righteous altogether"—as if to say, the Divine Presence and the judge are together.

<margin>9. He told him the judgment: either he comes out innocent or guilty, he comes out well.</margin>
### In the Chapter
In the chapter "With what [animal] may it go out" <note>Tractate Shabbat 56a</note>, Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Jonathan: Anyone who says the sons of Samuel sinned is only mistaken, as it is said: "And it was when Samuel was old... and his sons did not walk in his way." It was his *ways* they did not follow, but they did not actually sin. How then do I fulfill "they turned aside after lucre"? It means they did not act like their father. Samuel the Tzaddik <note>the Righteous</note> used to travel to all the places of Israel and judge them in their own cities, as it says: "And he went from year to year in a circuit to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, and judged Israel." But they did not do so; rather, they sat in their own cities in order to increase the fees for their court attendants <note>term: *חזניהם* - chazzanim; here meaning court clerks or bailiffs</note> and their scribes. Thus it ends. In the chapter "One may hang" <note>Tractate Shabbat 139a</note>, Rabbi Malai said in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Simeon: What is the meaning of "The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of the rulers"? "The staff of the wicked"—these are the judges who became a staff <note>a burden/tool of punishment</note> for their court attendants. "The scepter of the rulers"—these are the Torah scholars who teach the laws. Mar Zutra said: These are the Torah scholars who teach public laws to the judges. Rabbi Elazar ben Malai said in the name of Resh Lakish: "For your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken lies, your tongue mutters wickedness" <note>Isaiah 59:3</note>. "Your hands are defiled with blood"—these are the judges. "And your fingers with iniquity"—these are the scribes of the judges. "Your lips have spoken lies"—these are the "lawyers" <note>term: *עורכי הדיינין* - orchei hadayanim; literally "arrangers of the judges," advocates who coached litigants</note> of the judges. "And your tongue mutters wickedness"—these are the litigants themselves. Thus ends his words. Therefore, judges must take extra care upon themselves, their attendants, and their scribes, that they do not take more than what was fixed for them by the town elders. They should also warn with all their strength the litigants' advocates and the litigants themselves not to speak lies.

<margin>10. Love compromise</margin>
### Whoever
Whoever is being sued for money that is in his possession is forbidden to seek pretexts and excuses to evade payment so that the other party will agree to a compromise <note>term: *פשרה* - pesharah</note> and forgive him for the rest. This is from *Terumat HaDeshen* <note>a 15th-century collection of responsa</note> section 306, where he elaborated on the commentary of the Tosafot in the chapter "An ox that gored four or five," for at first glance it does not seem so. The Maharshal, in his *Yam Shel Shelomo* section 18, brought the words of the *Terumat HaDeshen* and explained the words of the Tosafot in one context, concluding as the *Terumat HaDeshen* did, that it is not good. The Ya'avetz <note>Rabbi Jacob Emden</note>, in a clear response, said there is no side of permission to seek excuses in order to reach a compromise.

<margin>11. Prohibition of accepting a judgment if his mind leans toward one of them</margin>
### In the Chapter
In the last chapter of *Ketubot* <note>Tractate Ketubot 105b</note>: A person should not judge someone he loves or someone he hates. For one who is loved, he will not see his guilt, and for one who is hated, he will not see his merit. Therefore, every judge should examine what is in his heart and fulfill "You shall fear your God"—referring to matters given over to the heart. He should refrain from judging unless the two litigants are equal in his heart. How much more so if his mind is close to one of them for another reason, such as a fee from the side of the law <note>original: *פ"מ ש"ה למסכת לנפשיה*</note>. Such an obligation falls upon the town elders: if it is clear in their hearts that this judge is close to this person, they should disqualify him from sitting in judgment. For the disqualifications of a person that the Sages stated due to proximity <note>family relations</note>—"you shall give a boundary"—this applies to ordinary people. But if one recognizes the mind of men, that a "close love" still exists in the heart of this judge, they should prevent him from sitting in judgment and not pay attention to the formal boundary of proximity given by the Sages. Even without family relation, if it is known that he loves him very much, they should not seat him in judgment, and they should not rely on what is permitted by the letter of Torah law. For Torah law was stated only for the average case. Regarding such a thing, it was said: "Jerusalem shall not increase," except that they based their words on Torah law. Because I have seen this stumbling block many times, therefore I am crying out about this, standing and repeating it.

<margin>12. Prevention of the judge's pride</margin>
### And Even
And even if the judge knows within himself that the two litigants are equal in his eyes, but he understands that one litigant suspects him of favoring the other's friendship more—as Moses our Teacher understood from the words of the daughters of Zelophehad, who suspected him of having a total grievance in his heart against Zelophehad—therefore "he brought their cause before the Lord." See there.

### In the Chapter
In the chapter "The Oath of Testimony" <note>Tractate Shevuot 31a</note>, the Sages taught: From where do we know that if two come [to court], one dressed in rags and the other dressed in a cloak worth a hundred *maneh*, that we say to him <note>the rich man</note>: "Dress like him," or "Dress him <note>the poor man</note> like you"? The verse says: "Keep far from a false matter." The *Tur* explained that this commandment was repeated even for a judge who knows that the heart of this rich man is against you because of his importance, and he might say: "How can I embarrass such an important person in court?" "Keep far from a false matter." Since there is a psychological injury in this claim, the truth of his holiness is to shame his face in court, and he is sick in this. It is possible that this is included in what Maimonides wrote in several places: concerning the "good news" of the judges of Israel—that were it not for the Talmud's rule of seating the litigants and witnesses to remove conflict, we would not have the strength to establish the laws of the religion on their foundation. Thus ends his words. In Section 3, in the name of the Maharshal of blessed memory: even though we do not have the power today to say "dress like him," nevertheless, the judges should say to the rich man: "Do not fear, and do not be comforted by the honor practiced toward you in all the courts of Israel; speak your words." And if his heart is strengthened and he is not humbled...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the mystical significance of the holidays, moving into the secrets of the Shofar and the Ten Days of Repentance. It draws heavily from the Zohar and the teachings of the Ramak and the Ari.</meta>

# **Behold**

It is known that the emanation of the "Building" <note>The lower seven Sefirot, which form the structure of the emotional world</note> consists of three lines: the line of Kindness (*Chesed*), the line of Judgment (*Din*), and the line of Mercy (*Rachamim*). These are the secret of the letters **Aleph-Mem-Shin** mentioned in the *Book of Formation* (*Sefer Yetzirah*), which represent Air, Water, and Fire. 

The line of Kindness is the secret of the Higher Waters; Strength (*Gevurah*) is the secret of Fire; Beauty (*Tiferet*) is the secret of Air; and Kingship (*Malchut*) is the Higher Earth. It has already been explained in many places that the "husks" <note>The *Kelipot*, or forces of impurity</note> take hold around the edges of this Building. However, in Understanding (*Binah*), which is the root of the Building, everything is guarded and there is no touch of the external forces <note>Original: "No touch of a Gentile," a metaphor for impure spiritual influences</note>. This is the secret of the World to Come.

Understanding is called "Repentance" (*Teshuvah*) because it is there that the emanations of the Building return. When a person has caused damage through their sins, but then stops, abandons them, repairs the damage, and returns with all their heart, they awaken that root of the Building. Everything then becomes purified, and the Accuser <note>The prosecuting angel</note> departs because he has no grasp there. One awakens this power through the Shofar, as the breath that leaves the mouth is composed of water, fire, and air. The water is the moisture in the mouth, and the fire is the heat of the breath, representing the **Aleph-Mem-Shin**. By the lower **Aleph-Mem-Shin**, the root of the Supernal **Aleph-Mem-Shin** is awakened—the secret of Understanding and Repentance. These three are present in the world of Action (*Asiyah*), and Repentance awakens itself through the awakening of "a right and new spirit within me" <note>A reference to Psalm 51:10</note>. This is the **Aleph-Mem-Shin**.

Thus says the *Zohar* in the portion of *Emor*: Rabbi Abba was sitting before Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and said, "Surely, many times I have asked about this Shofar: what is it referring to? Until now, my mind has not been settled on it." He replied to him, "Surely, this is the secret of Israel, the shield of Israel on the Day of Judgment. It is called a *Shofar* and not a *Keren* (horn). This is because a *Keren* is known to be attached to Judgment, which we do not want. But we have learned in words and in practice that this matter is meant to show and awaken hidden things. Come and see: when that Supernal Shofar, in which all lights are found, ascends and does not shine upon the Building, then Judgments are awakened and thrones are set for the house of judgment. And if this is the 'Ram of Isaac,' it is called strength, might, and the praise of the Patriarchs." This concludes the quote.

He is saying that the secret of the Shofar is to awaken the Supernal Shofar, which is Understanding. From Understanding emerges the Voice, which is Beauty (*Tiferet*), composed of fire, water, and air. The intention is to transform Judgment into Mercy. Therefore, we do not blow a simple animal horn (*Keren*), for the horn hints at the attribute of Judgment—the attribute of Kingship—and we do not seek to awaken Judgment, but rather to awaken Mercy. He says that when the Supernal Shofar—from which all lights flow—ascends and does not shine upon the Sefirot of the Building (who are its children, nursed by it), and the flow of Mercy is withdrawn upward, then in the hiding of the face of Mercy, Judgment is awakened. He says the "Ram of Isaac"—the Supernal Shofar—is the strength and power of *Gevurah* <note>Strength/Judgment</note>, from the language of "the mighty (*eilei*) of the land he took." To use this secret, we must take a ram's horn to hint at the ram of Isaac. This is the strength and praise of the Supernal Patriarchs, with which the Patriarchs are crowned, so that the portion of Strength is included within them. Then the rule of Judgment is transformed into Mercy through the *Teruah* <note>The broken, sobbing sound of the Shofar</note>. Therefore, the scripture says, "It shall be a day of *Teruah* for you," meaning to nullify the Judgment. This is the awakening from above that you must trigger; without your awakening, there would be no awakening from Above.

->Here is the secret of the blasts in detail and the secret of the Shofar blessings as I found them<-
->In the words of the Divine Rabbi Moses Cordovero, of blessed memory, in his work on the Ten Days of Repentance<-

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>In the Gemara</margin>
The ten Sefirot within Understanding, which is Repentance. With the Shofar below, one awakens the Shofar Above, which is Understanding. This is the meaning of the verse "to hear the sound of the Shofar": "To hear" refers to Kingship; "the sound" (*Kol*) refers to Beauty (*Tiferet*). For the Voice is composed of water, fire, and air, and this is Beauty composed of Kindness and Mercy. This inclusion within Understanding is called the "Sound of the Shofar." Regarding the Voice and its movement: a simple, straight blast (*Tekiah*) corresponds to Kindness, which is the "outstretched right hand" to receive those who return. The broken sounds (*Shevarim*) correspond to Strength. The sobbing sound (*Teruah*) corresponds to Beauty. The word *Teruah* relates to "friendship" (*Re'ut*), but also contains Judgment, as in "You shall break them (*Teruo'em*) with a rod of iron." Thus, there are three sounds representing Peace, Strength, and Beauty. The cantor's voice exiting the Shofar is explained this way in the *Tikkunim*.

### **However**
In the *Zohar*, portion of *Phinehas*, it says the *Teruah* is in Kindness, *Shevarim* in Strength, and [the final blast] in Kingship. "Happy is the people who know the *Teruah*"—using the language of "And Adam knew (*yada*) Eve his wife" <note>Implying intimate connection</note>. The second straight blast is Beauty. Both these and those are the "words of the living God." This is the resolution: Truly, the *Teruah* is in Beauty, but from the perspective of its attachment to Strength and Judgment. This clarifies that one aspect is Kingship, and of this it is said, "a voice from one of his sides," meaning the side of Kingship, which is the side of Strength within it. The second side is its leaning toward Kindness, which is the essence of Beauty—the second straight blast from the side of simple Kindness.

### **This is**
The sequence of blasts known as *Tashrat*, *Tashat*, and *Tarat* <note>Acronyms for Tekiah-Shevarim-Teruah-Tekiah, etc.</note>. The intention is to sweeten the forces of Judgment on this day. Therefore, we first awaken Kindness from its source, which is the first straight blast exiting the Shofar. This hidden essence contains all the sounds of the Shofar, including the Kindness within the Beauty of Understanding. The primary intention is to place the forces of Judgment—the *Shevarim* and *Teruah*—in the middle. The second straight blast, the power of Kindness from the sides, then tips them toward the side of Mercy and sweetens them. This is the second resolution—namely Wisdom. This is the first time. The second time, we draw down to the forces of Judgment the sweetness within them, from the Kindness mentioned above. Because the power of the day is so strong, one must soften the voice in a whisper during the silent prayer blasts. The third time is to raise them to their actual place as at first, which is Beauty... afterwards, each of the attributes of Judgment is dealt with individually to sweeten it specifically. This is the secret of the 100 blasts. The darkness of the "Higher Earth" <note>Kingship</note> is covered so it does not see the power of the Accuser who demands Judgment. Through the Shofar, the power of Mercy is awakened; the cloud vanishes, and the son enters to be with his Father.

### **Afterward**
I spent time with important individuals and found delightful pamphlets—"No eye has seen a God besides You"—this was the hidden *Zohar* until the arrival of the Man of God, the Ashkenazi Rabbi, Isaac Luria (the Ari), of blessed memory. He raised the secret of knowledge, and they established the custom of blowing one hundred sounds: 30 sounds while sitting <note>Before the main prayer</note>, 30 sounds during the silent prayer, and 30 sounds in order during the repetition of the prayer, totaling 90, and after the completion of the prayer, the final sounds are accepted. Even though there are differing customs—"every river has its own course"—nonetheless, God has granted us beautiful insights that support the foundation of every place according to its custom.

# **Tractate Rosh Hashanah: Torah Or**

One says a person should spend a year in repentance <note>The Hebrew "Y"E" likely stands for "Yehi Ratzon" (May it be Your will) or a similar liturgical shorthand, here referring to the practice of dedicated penitence</note> and brings this verse: "Good and upright is the Lord; therefore He instructs sinners in the way." This is what the scripture means by "The ways of the Lord are upright" <note>Hosea 14:10</note>—using the plural "upright." This implies a double "uprightness": He made the person upright initially, and when they sin and return, He restores them to being upright once more. All these thoughts and the "Return of Elul" <note>The month preceding Rosh Hashanah</note> occur during the month of Elul at the time of the Shofar blasts, which should be done with joy, awe, and fear. This is the essence of the Shofar blasts: that there shall be a "Return to the Lord our God." It is also appropriate to reflect on this before entering into the <term>Unification of the Deep Sefirot</term> <note>The process of harmonizing different aspects of the Divine through prayer and intention</note> regarding the Shofar of Rosh Hashanah, some of which will be explained later with the help of God, blessed and exalted be He.

**Regarding the matter**
of the fast on the Eve of Rosh Hashanah, the <term>Tur</term> <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher's seminal code of Jewish law</note> brings the <term>Midrash Tanchuma</term> <note>A collection of homiletic teachings</note> on the verse "And you shall take for yourselves..." It concludes that on the Eve of Rosh Hashanah, the Holy One, blessed be He, waives one third of a person's sins. During the Ten Days of Repentance, He waives the second third, and on Yom Kippur, He waives everything. One might ask: this does not seem equal for every soul. Sometimes one person's third of sins is twice as heavy or numerous as another's. Thus, God would be waiving more for one than the other. For example, if one person has ten sins and another has thirty, God waives ten for the one with thirty, but only three-and-a-third for the one with ten. This is certainly a difficult point. Why would He, whose "work is perfect and all His ways are justice," act this way?

It occurred to me to say that the "waiving" mentioned here does not refer to the sins a person commits themselves—for "anyone who says the Holy One is a 'waiver' [of justice] shall have his life waived" <note>A Talmudic warning that God does not simply ignore sin without repentance</note>. Rather, it refers to the sins for which "all Israel are <term>sureties</term> <note>Hebrew: *Arvut*; the concept of communal responsibility where Jews are spiritually responsible for one another</note> for one another." On the Eve of Rosh Hashanah, the Blessed Name waives one third of this communal responsibility. Then, during the Ten Days of Repentance, the second third, and so on.

In this same vein, the Priestly Garments used to atone, as our Sages of blessed memory said: "The Breastplate atones for [errors in] judgment; the Ephod atones for idolatry; the Robe atones for evil speech (*Lashon Hara*)." One must ask: was not the destruction of the Temple caused by these very sins? How could the people be punished if the Priests were atoning for them? We must conclude that the Priestly Garments only atoned for the *communal responsibility*, but not for the actual sinners themselves. Likewise, all the atonements mentioned by our Sages—such as the goats of Yom Kippur, both the one offered inside and the one sent outside, which atoned for accidental and intentional sins—all refer to the communal responsibility.

This is hinted at in the words of the Tanna <note>Mishnaic Sage</note>: "If I am not for myself, who will be for me?" This means: If I do not repair myself—meaning the sins that are mine, which I committed personally—who will repair them for me? Certainly, those sins that are not "mine" except through communal responsibility can be repaired by another means, namely the Priestly Garments. But those sins that are my own, no one can repair them but me. I found this also in the book *Avodat Yom HaKippurim*, stating that Priestly Garments atone for communal responsibility.

It also occurred to me to explain the fast of the Eve of Rosh Hashanah this way: Even a truly righteous person who has not sinned personally may still have many sins through communal responsibility—perhaps even more than a wicked person. For a wicked person who is a surety for a righteous person is responsible for only a few sins, whereas a righteous person who is a surety for the wicked is responsible for many. According to the first logic, it was difficult why the righteous person's few sins wouldn't be fully forgiven on the Eve of Rosh Hashanah. According to this second logic, it would seem unfair to the wicked person who is responsible for so little.

The true path is this: one should not wonder how a sin can be forgiven in this world without the specific repentance belonging to that sin. Every sin has a unique repentance: "Repentance of the Coming," "Repentance of the Weight," "Repentance of the Rav," or "Repentance of the Scripture" <note>These refer to specific ascetic and spiritual regimens designed to "balance" specific sins</note>. Even when one performs complete repentance, it is still an act of Divine Kindness that God accepts it. Could a person who sins against a flesh-and-blood king save himself just by repenting? Therefore, when the sin is great and the person is lowly, even with specific repentance, it still requires a measure of mercy for the Blessed Name to accept it. Regarding this, it is said that the first fast—the Eve of Rosh Hashanah—causes the Holy One to waive one third of the previous year's "complete repentance." This fast makes the repentance acceptable. Then, during the Ten Days of Repentance, the process continues. Now, the difficulty is resolved; it doesn't matter if one has many sins or few. Whoever has many sins must perform many acts of repentance, and for the one with few, one repentance suffices.

->**Rosh Hashanah**<-

This is the Day of Judgment, and all who enter the world pass before Him <term>like sheep</term> <note>Hebrew: *B'nei Maron*; can also be translated as "like soldiers" or "as through a narrow pass"</note>. This day was established as the Day of Judgment from the beginning of Creation, for Adam was created on Rosh Hashanah; on that same day he sinned, and on that same day he was judged and emerged with a pardon <note>Hebrew: *dimos*, from the Greek *demosios* or *dimissio*</note>, as stated in the Midrash. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Adam: "You are a sign for your children; just as you were judged on this day and pardoned, so shall they be judged on this day and pardoned."

The matter is this: since this is the time of Creation, when the Blessed Name renews His world, every year at this time He visits His world and decrees what shall be from the beginning of the year to its end. He creates the world anew. When a person repairs their deeds and is pardoned, they become like a new creation. Since the King sits on the Throne of Judgment, the "sons of God" <note>Angels/prosecutors</note> come to stand before the Lord.

This is the meaning of the Zohar (Parshat Pinchas), where Rabbi Shimon begins by saying: "'And it was the day' <note>Job 1:6</note>—wherever it says 'And it was the day,' it implies distress. 'And it was in the days of' also implies distress. 'And it was the day' refers to a day of pain, which is the day of Rosh Hashanah, a day of harsh judgment upon the world. 'And it was the day that Elisha passed over to Shunem'—that was Rosh Hashanah. In every place 'And it was the day' refers to Rosh Hashanah, which is Judgment."

On this day, the "sons of God" come—these are the High Court, the literal "sons of God" who are close to Him. They are seventy nations <note>spiritual representatives</note> who always surround the King and are wiser than the world regarding the guilty and the upright. When they stand for judgment—the primary judgment of all—who is there who does not fear the Name of the Holy One and honor the Torah and His commandments? Who does not care for the glory of the Holy Name, that it not be profaned on earth? Who does not care for their own honor? Who does not honor this Name?

On the day of Rosh Hashanah, seventy thrones stand for judgment over the world. There are many "masters of shields" <note>defenders</note> and accusers standing above. These are on the right to merit and those are on the left to find guilt, to remember the sins of the world and the sins of every individual, etc. (Until here [the Zohar quote]).

**These are the words**
of *Tola'at Ya'akov* <note>A 16th-century Kabbalistic work by Meir ibn Gabbai</note> in the section on Tractate Beitzah: "'Blow the Shofar at the new moon, at the hidden time (*bakiseh*) for our festival day' <note>Psalm 81:4</note>. Which festival has the moon 'hidden'? It is Rosh Hashanah." Rosh Hashanah is the time when the world is judged in the Supernal Court (meaning <term>Malchut</term> <note>the Sefirah of Kingship</note>). If it were judged solely by the Supernal Court of the secret of "the Fear of Isaac" <note>pure Judgment/Gevurah</note>, the world could not endure the intensity of the judgment. So it was at the time of Creation: had He not joined the Attribute of Mercy with the Attribute of Judgment, the world would not have stood. Furthermore, this month is the seventh month, and the number seven awakens judgment. On this day, the "uncircumcised one" <note>the husk of impurity/the Accuser</note> hovers over the creation and "covers the moon" <note>the spiritual source of the Jewish people</note>. Darkness covers the earth and his power is great. When judgment is awakened above, then "Isaac’s eyes were dimmed from seeing" <note>Genesis 27:1</note> and he called Esau his great son. This is because God made it so that they would fear Him. The advised counsel is to blow the Shofar to remove the accuser so he does not cover the moon or separate it from the Sun <note>The Sun represents the Sefirah of Tiferet/Mercy</note>. This is the secret of "the moon is covered," the secret of the final letter *He* of the Divine Name being covered by the power of darkness and the "foreskin" <note>impurity</note>, and her soul is bitter for her children.

**And in the Midrash**
of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, I saw another reason for the awakening of judgment on this day: when the Higher Luminary (meaning <term>Binah</term> <note>the Sefirah of Understanding</note>), which is the "Seventh Assembly," desires to send flow and blessing and renew goodness in the world, it observes the deeds of the world. (For from *Binah*, judgments are awakened). It looks to see if the world is acting properly and if they are worthy of that good. If it sees the world is not worthy, it withholds the good until the wicked are finished. This causes a delay in the union Above, and the Attribute of Judgment is awakened. It is written "his eyes were dimmed from seeing"—instead of looking with a "good eye" from the side of the Right without judgment, the eyes are dimmed from seeing the aspect of Mercy. Because of this, the Satan who emerges from that side is awakened and seeks permission to destroy. He covers the Covenant so as not to give light to the moon. This is the meaning of "at the hidden time (*bakiseh*) for our festival day." However, because the Holy One does not wish to destroy His handiwork, He gave us the counsel to "Blow the Shofar at the new moon, at the hidden time" to break the "Kisseh" (the cover) that hides the moon from shining. (End of his words).

**And furthermore**, God has granted me the merit of a second pamphlet that explains the first pamphlet; both are equally good, therefore I have copied them both together with the help of Heaven:

# First Pamphlet

**The reason** our Sages of Blessed Memory said that the blowing of the Shofar confuses the Accuser <note>original: "Satan"</note> is because the Shofar is intended to sweeten the Divine Judgment and to draw out the voices in their entirety—breath, water, and fire—within that "Great Shofar." For when the Judgments are awakened, the power of Samael <note>The angelic name of the Accuser/Satan in mystical literature</note> grows strong, but when they are diminished, he has no power or spiritual sustenance at all. For this reason, during the first set of blasts <note>The "sitting" blasts performed before the main prayer</note>, there is a sweetening of the Judgments, but not to a great extent. However, after the blasts performed while standing <note>The "standing" blasts during the Musaf prayer</note>, there is an essential sweetening of the Judgments, and because of this, he becomes confused. 

And now, it is necessary to make known the secret of the Shofar blowing and its intention, so that we may merit to confuse the Accuser and subdue him. For it is a great thing that you are able to subdue him on the Day of Judgment, so that he will have no power to prosecute against Israel, and the merit of the many will depend on you. Know that the one who blows the Shofar, before he blows, while the congregation is saying the liturgical poem, should say these verses to himself and focus on these two names and what lies between them:

<margin>(These are two instances of the name YHVH, and interleaved between them are the letters of the word **K**-**R**-**A** **S**-**T**-**N** <note>Meaning "Tear the Satan"</note>, which is called "The Satan.")</margin>

->**K-Y-R-H-A-V-E-S-H-T-V-N-H**<-
<note>This is a mystical cipher interleaving the letters of "Tear the Satan" (Kra Satan) with the Four-Letter Name of God (YHVH) repeated.</note>
->The place of the two Names and what is between them:<-

# And these are the verses:

<columns>2</columns>
* **K** (Koph): You have heard my voice; hide not Your ear from my sighing, from my cry.
* **R** (Resh): The beginning of Your word is truth; and every one of Your righteous ordinances endures forever.
* **E** (Ayin): Be surety for Your servant for good; let not the arrogant oppress me.
* **S** (Shin): I rejoice at Your word, as one that finds great spoil.
* **T** (Teth): Teach me good discernment and knowledge; for I have believed in Your commandments.
* **N** (Nun): Accept, I beseech You, the freewill offerings of my mouth, O Lord, and teach me Your ordinances.

<column-break/>

**After** these verses, he should say this prayer and focus within the words on the idea that the breath rises and sings to burn away the "veils" that separate. He should say: "May it be Your will, O Lord my God, God of Judgment, that this shall now be a time of favor before You. And in Your many mercies and great kindness, may You tear all the veils that separate between You and Your people Israel this day. And remove from before You all the accusers and prosecutors against us.

Upon Your people Israel, seal the mouth of the Accuser <note>Satan</note>, and let him not prosecute against us, for our eyes are turned toward You. I will exalt You, my God the King, God of Judgment, who hears every prayer and the Shofar-shout <note>Teruah</note> of Your people Israel today with mercy."

# And the Essential Point

**And the essential point** of the intention lies in the two Names mentioned above, each of which is placed within the four letters of the Divine Name <term>YHVH<explanation>The Tetragrammaton, the most sacred four-letter name of God</explanation></term> in order to sweeten it. Afterward, he should say: "God has ascended with a shout," and so on, as it is written in the Sephardic prayer book. He should take the Shofar in his right hand and intend that the lip of the Shofar corresponds to the "Hand" <note>Yad</note> which is in <term>Chokhmah<explanation>Wisdom; the second of the ten Sefirot or divine emanations</explanation></term>. The Shofar itself corresponds to the "Constellation of Judgment," which is <term>Binah<explanation>Understanding; the third Sefirah, often associated with the "Divine Mother" and the source of the Shofar's sound</explanation></term. And regarding that which is brought in the Talmud, "so that it may be seen here and there," the upper visible part corresponds to the <term>Keter<explanation>Crown; the highest and most hidden Sefirah</explanation></term>, whose loftiness has no end. The lower visible part corresponds to <term>Da’at<explanation>Knowledge; the Sefirah that mediates between the upper and lower realms</explanation></term>, which influences all the worlds.

And when he blows, he should intend the Name YHVH which is formed by the voice and the Shofar together in this manner. This is the short explanation: The first **H** (He) is the breath that enters. The **V** (Vav) is the sound drawn through the Vav from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the secret of **A-G-S** <note>An acronym for Air, Water, Fire</note>—which are Air, Water, and Fire. Jacob is Air, Abraham is Water, Isaac is Fire. The final **H** (He) is the breath that exits. Afterward, he shall say the blessing.

And when he says the words "the sound of the Shofar," he should intend two "sounds": to hear the lower sound that awakens the upper sound, and also to draw the breath that comes from the Crown <note>Keter</note> down to the lower world in the secret of Understanding <note>Binah</note> and the secret of the musical notes. Regarding the word **Shofar**, he should intend the name **Elohim**. The letter **Shin** <note>Numerical value 300</note> is the "full" name Elohim which sums to 300—spelled out like this: *Aleph-Lamed-Pe, Lamed-Mem-Dalet, He-Yod, Yod-Vav-Dalet, Mem-Mem*. The letter **Pe** <note>80</note> equals the simple name Elohim <note>86</note> when using the "Vav" of the spelling. And the letters **Dalet-Shin** sum to Elohim in a specific calculation. Behold, one must intend to sweeten these three "Elohims" through the word **Kol** <note>Voice/Sound</note>, which is the combination of the names **Ehyeh, YHVH, and Adonai**. And the name **Yah** <note>Yod-He</note> plus **Chesed** <note>Kindness</note> equals the numerical value of **Kol** (136).

One must intend to sweeten the five letters of "Elohim" and the three numerical counts of "Elohim" mentioned (the Shin, Pe, and Dalet) and the one that includes them all, making nine. This is the secret intention of "To hear the sound of the Shofar"—to sweeten the word "Shofar" (which consists of three Elohims and its letters) through the word "Kol" (which is the names YHVH, Ehyeh, Adonai, and Yahu). And the meaning of "To hear" <note>Lishmoa</note> is related to "And Saul gathered" <note>Vayishma</note>, an expression of gathering. Its meaning is to gather the light of the "Sound" (Kol)—which is YHVH, Ehyeh, Adonai, Yah—to sweeten the five letters of Elohim and the three calculations that sum to Shofar, and the "inclusive" one as stated. Then he shall bless the "Shehecheyanu" blessing.

# The Intention of the Blasts while Sitting

**The first Tashrat** <note>Tekiah-Shevarim-Teruah-Tekiah</note> is to awaken the Patriarchs from their place: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; weak judgment and harsh judgment. The **second** is to draw the Patriarchs down to the lower attributes (Netzach, Hod, Yesod); weak judgment and harsh judgment. The **third** is to return them to their place; weak judgment.
**The first Tashat** <note>Tekiah-Shevarim-Tekiah</note> is to awaken the Patriarchs in their place; weak judgment. The **second** is to draw the Patriarchs to the lower attributes; weak judgment. The **third** is to return them to their place; weak judgment.
**The first Tarat** <note>Tekiah-Teruah-Tekiah</note> is to awaken the Patriarchs from their place; weak judgment. The **second** is to draw them to the lower attributes; harsh judgment. The **third** is to return them to their place; harsh judgment.

**Also**, one must intend in the "sitting" blasts a hint to awaken the World of Action <note>Asiyah</note> in its three aspects: the receiver, the thing itself, and the influencer. These are hinted at in the final letter of the Four-Letter Name, and in the Name YHVH with two different vowel points, and the name Adonai, and the attribute of Kingship <note>Malkhut</note>. One must intend that he is awakening the Patriarchs from their place and remember this name as stated.

# These are the Shofar Blasts of the Repetition of Musaf

Since they belong to the World of *Briah* <note>The World of Creation, the second of the four spiritual realms in Kabbalah</note> in its three aspects and four expansions, they are hinted at in the first letter *Heh* [ה] of the Four-Letter Name <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHVH</note>, and in the Name YHVH when it is vocalized with the vowels of *Elohim* <note>original: יְהֹוָה; the vowels for the name Elohim are used here as a meditative tool</note> and in the Name YHVH vocalized with the *Tzeirei* vowel like this: יֵהֵוֵה. One must focus their intention during these blasts to return the Patriarchs to their source, corresponding to the letter *Heh*.

<note>Gloss in Rashi script</note>
(Annotation): The general intention is to wipe out the Accuser <note>original: "S-K-L-S," a common cipher for the Satan/Accuser</note> and to sanctify the "Pelat-Yelo" <note>A mystical name or concept</note> through the three sets of blasts mentioned. Each set consists of three sequences (T-Sh-R-T, T-Sh-T, T-R-T). The first set (Sections 19-21) corresponds to the attribute of *Malchuyot* (Kingship) in the World of *Briah*. Section 19 is for the first T-Sh-R-T; Section 20 for the T-Sh-T; and Section 21 for the T-R-T. The second set (Sections 22-24) corresponds to *Zichronot* (Remembrances) in *Briah*. Section 22 is for T-Sh-R-T; Section 23 for T-Sh-T; and Section 24 for T-R-T. The third set (Sections 25-27) corresponds to *Shofrot* (Shofars) in *Briah*. Section 25 is for T-Sh-R-T; Section 26 for T-Sh-T; and Section 27 for T-R-T. Here, too, the simple blasts (*Tekiot*) are for Abraham and Jacob, but the broken blasts (*Teruah*) are shared by Isaac and Jacob. This is the order of this pamphlet for every set of three sequences, arranged according to the Foundation of Existence. End of annotation.

# WONDERING AWE

The intention refers to the World of Formation <note>original: *Yetzirah*; the third of the four spiritual realms, associated with the emotions and the breath</note> in its three aspects. They are hinted at in the letter *Yod* [י] of the Four-Letter Name <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHVH</note>.
The Name should be visualized with the *vowel point* <note>original: *nekudah*</note> for this world, which is the Name YHVH with the *Holam* vowel <note>A dot above the letter representing the 'O' sound</note> on the letter *Shin* <note>Likely referring to a specific permutation or the letter's placement in the meditative structure</note> and in the attribute of Beauty <note>original: *Tiferet*</note>.
This occurs during the Shofar blasts in order to draw down the light of the Patriarchs <note>original: "ABG," an abbreviation for Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob</note> into the lower emotional attributes <note>original: "NHY," referring to the sephirot of Netzach (Victory), Hod (Splendor), and Yesod (Foundation)</note>.
Each one is according to its specific quality, and one should focus the intention on this Name:

-> <note>Permutations of Divine names used for meditation</note> Y-K-R-V-A-H Y-S-H-T-Z-N-H <-
-> Y-H-V-H [with various vowels] Y-H-V-H [with Holam vowels] <-

And so it is found in the pamphlet at the end, until here.

<meta>This page continues the technical and mystical instructions for the Shofar blasts, specifically focusing on the symbolic relationship between the sounds and the Patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob) as well as the transition from the "sitting" blasts to the "standing" blasts during the Rosh Hashanah service.</meta>

### TORAH LIGHT

And behold, the "wail" <note>original: *yelul*; the rapid, sobbing sound of the Shofar, also known as Teruah</note> belongs to the secret of the "stands" that we find. Have we not learned that the *Shevarim* <note>the three medium, "broken" blasts</note> are soft and the "wails" are harsh? In the Torah portion of *Emor*, Rabbi Shimon <note>Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the traditional author of the Zohar</note> explained three sets, each including three parts—the order of the three-by-three blasts. The **First Set** belongs to **Abraham** and includes his companions with him, for he is represented by the first *Tekiah* <note>the long, straight blast</note>, which is certainly "simple." It first awakens the mercy of "Father and Mother" <note>original: *Abba v'Imma*; the higher Divine attributes of Wisdom and Understanding</note>. With the second sound, the voice rises, changing and breaking the power of Judgment <note>original: *Din*</note>, and **Isaac** is weakened before his father. In the third sound, which is "simple" for the others, **Jacob** is awakened along with Abraham, and they support Isaac, causing the Judgments to be nullified. The **Second Set** appears to be primarily in the place of Judgments, to appease the mind of Isaac. In the first *Tekiah*, he awakens Abraham to the "groaning" <note>original: *nehiya*</note>, for that is the dwelling place of the Judgments, and they receive him between them. The second sound carries the divided voice of the attribute of Isaac along with the lower severities of pure Judgment. This causes the voice not to need strengthening, nor do the Judgments prevail, because they are humbled before the "pious elder" <note>original: *saba chasida*; a reference to the attribute of Mercy or the Ancient of Days</note>. In the third "simple" blast following it, the sound rises to Jacob to bring him down there as well; they support Isaac and the Judgments with him, silencing them. The **Third Set** is entirely within the secret of "Jacob’s inheritance without borders" <note>a mystical concept of infinite expansion</note>. He rises with Abraham, and they support Isaac between them, and all the Judgments are subdued. This is the general rule of the commandment and the secret according to the Torah law. In the discourse "The Hosts of the Lord," we explained that which Rabbi Abbahu established <note>Rabbi Abbahu is the Talmudic sage who standardized the modern Shofar sequence</note>, and all the traditions are beautifully agreed upon in all their parts with what is explained in the Torah law regarding why the Sages established thirty sounds—one should look there.

**And behold**, the author of the Pamphlet first took this general teaching in three aspects, any of which could potentially be the Torah law: whether the blower in the three sets "groans and wails" <note>performing both Shevarim and Teruah</note> consecutively, or "groans" alone, or "wails" alone. He explained the general intention of each of these modes briefly, and then descended into the secret of the appropriate and superior intention of their words. Thus, we have thirty sounds performed while "sitting" <note>original: *miyushav*; the blasts sounded before the Musaf prayer</note>, in which all Israel are equal. Their order is *Tashrat*, *Tashat*, *Tarat* <note>Acronyms for the combinations of Tekiah (T), Shevarim (S), and Teruah (R)</note>. He explained that all three of these are in the place of the first *Tekiah* of the first set, for they are all included in the ten attributes of the *Keter* <note>The "Crown," the highest Sephirot</note> which he hid within the first *Tekiah*, which is pure Kindness <note>original: *Chesed*</note>. There are sections of the pamphlet that provide a basis for the establishment of thirty sounds during the "Standing" prayer <note>the *Amidah* recited silently</note>, which serves as a model for the totality of the second set, which contains ten links, and for the Cantor’s Repetition <note>original: *Chazarat HaShatz*</note>, which serves as the model for the totality of the third set.

**It is known** that all the commandments are "repairs for the Divine Presence" <note>original: *tikkunei Shekhinah*</note>, which occurs through the "building" on this day—the day on which Adam and Eve were created. Their full stature was repaired from the lower attributes <note>original: *NHY*; Netzach, Hod, and Yesod</note> of the Small Face <note>original: *Zeir Anpin*; the emotive Divine attributes</note>. Likewise, the three-by-three blasts he performed for her established the structure of Understanding, Knowledge, Kindness, Might, Beauty, Victory, Splendor, and Foundation. The tenth sound in each part of this commandment may correspond to the Kingdom <note>original: *Malkhut*</note> within it. This is very fitting, so that the ten sounds of the "May it be accepted" prayer shall complete it as a "perfect Crown" <note>original: *Keter*</note>, she too being composed of ten attributes. And for us, who have only sixty sounds—thirty while sitting and thirty while standing during the Cantor’s Repetition of the *Musaf* prayer—we can direct our intention during the first thirty to all three sets of the Torah. For even though the Judgment within the first set begins soft and ends harsh (by preceding the *Shevarim* to the *Yelalah*), since they are all under one sign, there is no concern for them above. One should intend to receive help from "Father and Mother." The **Second Set** should be entirely "soft" <note>merciful</note>, since its foundation is in the place of Judgments, to appease them so they do not prevail at all. The **Third Set**, even though it is entirely "harsh" <note>judgmental</note>, there is no objection, since it is silenced at its root and is mitigated quietly. Anyone who intends in all three—*Tashrat*, *Tashat*, and *Tarat*—to fulfill the Torah obligation in every possible way without interruption is praised. One should intend in the first set for the general commandment of the Torah, according to the first path for building the "middle nest" within it, which has extra attributes. Similarly with the multiple and directed sounds... in the second, according to the secret of the sounds of the Cantor’s Repetition, where each blessing has ten sounds, intended to establish the "Crown of the Torah" <note>original: *Keter Torah*</note>, which is balanced. In all that is seen, it is the "Awe" <note>original: *Nora*</note> that causes the Accuser <note>original: *Satan*</note> to be afraid in his strength, as you know from the Rabbi, that they appear in the "Pillar of the Profane" in the attribute of Victory <note>*Netzach*</note> to establish the Crown of the Torah. It is certainly right to intend this according to the custom of the Yeshivas, where they only blow *Tashrat* for the Sovereignty verses, *Tashat* for the Remembrance verses, and *Tarat* for the Shofar verses.

**However**, regarding the division of the Patriarchs for each of the hundred sounds, it is better not to awaken "harsh Judgment" <note>original: *dina kashya*</note> near **Isaac**, who is himself harsh. Rather, it should always be one harsh and one soft. Therefore, harsh Judgment is appropriate near **David**, who is soft, so that Judgment does not prevail over him in the company of **Jacob**. In the sign of *Tarat*, it is settled—for it is not good otherwise that harsh Judgment should be near Isaac; it should awaken the "Goodly Choice" of Jacob <note>original: *bechir yafay ma’or*; a poetic title for Jacob</note>. According to this, it is possible that the *Shevarim* near Isaac alone would be harsher than the "wails" <note>Teruah</note>, because Jacob joins with David to sweeten them. Yet the Accuser is still in his strength, though not in full force. But in the "Standing" sounds, there are two advantages in the sign of *Tarat*: even though its void is harsh Judgment by its own nature, nothing is mentioned near it except David, whose judgment is "soft," with Jacob helping him as he always does in the sign of *Tashrat*. Therefore, it is certainly in strength, for "in his shadow he dwells," and "no evil occurrence" shall strike. The initials of "Shofar" <note>Hebrew: שופר</note> and the numerical value of the four words together with "Tishrei" return David to his place among the tribes... and Isaac near the harsh wails, for "they shall not hurt nor destroy in all My holy mountain." Nevertheless, "a groom who is separated at the beginning of the year" is not the proper way. Jacob enters near his father, since he is his "close redeemer," in the "simple" blast afterwards. Everything follows the conclusion, which is in Mercy. With this, all the passages from the Zohar that seem to contradict each other regarding the division of these sounds will be reconciled; study it and you will find it so.

**According to our way**, the secret of the Pamphlet is stable and correct regarding the marking of the Patriarchs near the thirty "sitting" sounds. However, in the "standing" blasts, since in every way our intention in them is for the "Crown of the Torah"—which is itself the World of Emanation <note>original: *Atziluth*; the highest of the four worlds</note>—its order is arranged near the Patriarchs according to the exchange of "May it be accepted" without any change. Whether there are sixty standing sounds or thirty, there is no difference in this at all. Always, the general intention for the appropriate Names is according to the order of the Pamphlet in four divisions. It was possible to attribute the first array to the totality of the "sitting" blasts, the second to the Sovereignty verses, the third to the Remembrance verses, and the fourth to the Shofar verses. Or, what is more logical according to what we explained: that her Crown, which is certainly entirely of Emanation, is balanced with all that is seen. The sounds of Sovereignty, Remembrances, and Shofars would then all be "repairs for the Crown," even if we intend for the first array of Names in the three *Tashrat* sounds of the sitting blasts, and for the second in the three *Tarat* sounds of Creation—like a beautiful bride to be adorned in Might with harsh Judgment alone, for the husks <note>original: *klipot*; spiritual forces of evil</note> therein are impure and pushed away from the Holy. The fourth is entirely within the totality of the "standing" blasts, and this is sufficient.

**And this for you** is the proper division for the intention of the blowing for us blowers of the sixty sounds, which is equal to the thirty "sitting" sounds, along with those who are accustomed to blowing only forty sounds. All is according to the way we are destined to explain in our assumptions—the additions in the middle of the Pamphlet in their proper places.

**And behold**, the author of the Pamphlet responded here in detail how one should intend during each sound of the sixty. But I have not copied it, since they were already hinted at above in the first pamphlet in the brief glosses, and the wise student will understand from there. However, regarding the division of the four arrays of the Names, one should intend according to this as follows: before the first three *Tashrat* sounds of the "sitting" blasts, he should intend for these:

-> Y-K-H-R-V-A-H Y-S-H-T-V-N-H <-
-> Y-D-V-D HASHEM ADONAI <-

<margin>And before the three *Tashat* sounds of the sitting blasts, he should intend for these:</margin> -> Y-K-H-R-V-A-H Y-S-H-T-V-N-H <-
-> Y-V-D-V-D-V-D-Y-A-D-V-D <-

<margin>And before the three *Tarat* sounds of the sitting blasts, he should intend for these:</margin> -> Y-K-H-R-V-A-H Y-S-H-T-V-N-H <-

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the laws of the Shofar and how they symbolically relate to the process of repentance. It specifically addresses the varying levels of reward in the afterlife and the different degrees of repentance.</meta>

<header>Torah Light</header>

<margin>An explanation from the book *Ten Principles of the Ways of Repentance* which a penitent <note>Hebrew: *baal teshuvah*, literally "master of return"</note> should cling to. Each of the mentioned laws hints at a general path of repentance, as will be explained with Divine help. This is the author's intent regarding the specific words and the various "pillars" upon which all other details of repentance rest, for their specific details are certainly numerous and a book could not contain them, as they are beyond counting. Before I explain how the general paths of repentance emerge from these mentioned laws, we will first present some introductory concepts from which the truth and faith may be observed.</margin>

# These are
The laws—meaning the laws of the Shofar—which I have seen fit to mention here one by one to reach a count of eleven. My intention is to learn from them eleven general principles for the paths of repentance that a penitent should follow.

## First
One must know that there are differing levels and ranks among the wise and the righteous in the World to Come <note>Hebrew: *Olam HaBa*</note>. The proof comes from what our Sages of blessed memory said <note>note: original quote from the Talmud, Tractate Megillah 28b</note> regarding the verse "Before His elders shall be glory": this teaches that for every single person, a dwelling place is given according to their specific honor. This is also precise in the Mishnah which states, "All Israel has a portion in the World to Come," implying a specific portion for each individual according to their honor. Our Sages also said in the chapter *HaShoel* <note>Tractate Shabbat 152a</note> regarding the verse "Because man goes to his eternal home": this teaches that for every righteous person, a dwelling is made according to their honor. It is like a king of flesh and blood who enters a city; though they all enter through one gate, when they stay overnight, each one is given a dwelling according to their rank. Similarly, our Sages said that the holiness of the Levites was such that no creature could stand within their partition. And from the teaching that "in the place where penitents stand, even the perfectly righteous cannot stand" <note>note: this suggests the penitent's rank is greater than the righteous person's</note>, we also learn that everyone has a specific rank before the Creator, one above the other, in the World to Come. This extends to the unique measures of the Patriarchs, the level of Moses himself, the level of Aaron himself, and all other people—each is given a dwelling place according to their honor.

## Second
One must know that just as the rank of a pious person in the World to Come is greater and higher than the rank of a righteous person, so too are there levels within the rank of the penitent. We learn this from what our Sages said in the Talmud <note>Tractate Yoma 86</note>: There is a contradiction between the verse "Return, wayward children" <note>original: *shuvu banim shovavim*</note> and the phrase "you who were wayward." Rashi explains: when you repent out of love, I consider you as if your initial sin was due to foolishness and youth. Yet it is also written, "I will heal your waywardness," implying that from here on you are like a person who was sick and has been healed, but the name of the sickness still clings to him. This distinction is between repentance from **love** (where the sin is uprooted from the start) and repentance from **fear** (where the sin is merely "healed"). Rabbi Judah says there is a contradiction between the word "children" (implying penitents are called children) and the verse "for I have mastered you" (implying they are called servants). There is no contradiction: one refers to repentance from love and fear (where they are called wayward children), while the other refers to repentance through suffering (where they did not return until they were afflicted with pain; these are called servants). Resh Lakish said: Great is repentance, for intentional sins are treated like accidental errors <note>Hebrew: *shegagot*</note>. But did he not also say that intentional sins are treated like merits <note>Hebrew: *zechuyot*</note>? There is no contradiction: one is from fear, the other is from love. Thus you see clearly that there are different levels among penitents themselves. A person who repents from love has a higher rank in the World to Come than one who repents from fear. The same applies if both repent from fear or both from love—one may still be greater than the other, such as if one repented immediately after the sin while the other delayed, or if one repented while still in the "heat" of his youth while the second waited until old age, as will be explained in the third introduction.

## Third
One must know what the author of *Menorat HaMaor* <note>The Candelabra of Light, a famous 14th-century ethical work</note> wrote: "As long as a person regrets his sin and performs complete repentance, his repentance is accepted and he is chosen and honored before the Holy One, blessed be He. However, there are seven levels, each greater than the next."
1.  The best level is repentance done **immediately**, which is accepted at once. Regarding this, Rabbi Abbahu said that in the place where penitents stand, even the perfectly righteous cannot stand.
2.  The second level is one who was immersed in sin for many days or years but repented during the **days of his youth**, while still in his full strength and vigor. Of him it is said, "Remember your Creator in the days of your youth." Saadia Gaon explained this as repenting while still having the strength to commit the sin as before, but refraining out of regret. Our Sages asked: Who is a true penitent? One who has the opportunity to sin again—same woman, same place, same time—and restrains himself.
3.  The third level is one who is still in his youth but the **opportunity** to sin is not as available as before, or he is embarrassed before other people to pursue his desires as he once did. Even so, his repentance is accepted because he is still in the stage of youthful vitality.
4.  The fourth level is one who repents out of **fear of death** or fear of a divine decree, as we find with the people of Nineveh.
5.  The fifth level is one who regrets his sin after **great troubles** and evils have befallen him. The Holy One, blessed be He, in His great kindness, accepts him, as it is written: "When you are in distress and all these things have come upon you... you shall return to the Lord your God."
6.  The sixth level is repentance in **old age**, when his physical strength has weakened. Even though he did not repent in his youth, if he returns with all his heart, his repentance is accepted. Of this it is said, "You turn man back to dust <note>Hebrew: *daka*, also meaning 'crushed'</note>," meaning until the time a person is crushed and weakened, God still says, "Return, children of men."
7.  The seventh level is for one who was a sinner all his days and stood in his transgression until the day he **died**, seeing that his time was near. Our Sages said in *Ethics of the Fathers*: "Repent one day before your death." Even this repentance is accepted, though each level receives a reward according to its quality. 

However, one who persists in his wickedness even on the day of death and passes away without repenting is a complete heretic. He does not believe in the Day of Judgment and destroys his body and soul. Therefore, Solomon in his wisdom warned: "Whatever your hand finds to do with your strength, do it," meaning repent while you still have your strength, for there is no repentance or remedy in the grave. As it is written: "In the underworld, who shall thank You?" Our Sages hinted at this: "Prepare yourself in the lobby <note>this world</note> so that you may enter the banquet hall <note>the world to come</note>."

**This** is also explained in the *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* <note>The Great Book of Commandments</note> regarding the Laws of Repentance: Although the one who repents in old age or illness—where it is impossible for him to do what he did in his youth—is not the "excellent" form of repentance, it is nonetheless accepted and he is called a penitent. Even if he transgressed all his life and repented on his deathbed, his sins are forgiven.

**Similarly**, it is written in the *Repentance of Rabbeinu Yonah*: "There are many levels to repentance, and according to these levels, a person draws closer to God. While forgiveness is found for all repentance, the soul is not completely purified—as if the sins never existed—until the person purifies his heart. It is like a garment that requires washing; the degree of whiteness depends on the intensity of the washing." As it is written: "Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity."

<meta>The transcription at the very bottom "nu b 2 6 5" seems to be a structural or filing note from the original scribe.</meta>

# The Way of Life: Rebuke of Moral Instruction

And even if he pays every sum and all the money in the world, he is not forgiven until he seeks forgiveness from him. Rabbi Isaac said: One who aggravates his fellow, even with mere words, must appease him and should bring many friends with him <note>to act as mediators or witnesses to his sincerity</note>.

<margin>**And we say**</margin> (in the second chapter of Tractate Yoma): This is the teaching of Rabbi Isaac: [The verse says] "From all your sins before the Lord [you shall be cleansed]"—this implies that for transgressions between man and God, Yom Kippur <term>Yom Kippur: The Day of Atonement</term> provides atonement. But for transgressions between a man and his fellow, it does not atone until he appeases his fellow. And these are the words of Maimonides <note>original: "Ha-Maimoni"</note> in the Laws of Repentance, Chapter 2: Repentance and Yom Kippur only atone for transgressions between man and God, such as one who ate forbidden food or had a forbidden sexual union and the like. But transgressions between man and his fellow—such as one who injures his fellow, or curses his fellow, or robs him, and the like—are never forgiven until he gives his fellow what he owes him and reconciles with him. Even if he returned the money he owed, he must still reconcile with him and ask him to forgive him. And even if he only aggravated his fellow with words, he must appease him and approach him repeatedly until he is reconciled. And we learn in the Jerusalem Talmud (in Tractate Yoma) that the one who was insulted should himself go to appease the one who insulted him <note>This refers to a pious practice of a victim making themselves available so the offender can easily apologize</note>, and not through a mediator. And thus says the *Menorat HaMa'or* <term>Menorat HaMa'or: "The Candelabra of Light," a popular 14th-century work of Jewish ethics</term>: If the sin involves words of the lips, even if he pays all his debts, he must seek forgiveness. As we learn in the first tractate <note>Bava Kamma</note>, in the chapter "The Injurer": even if he gives him all the "rams of Nebaioth" <note>a biblical reference to a massive sacrifice</note>, he is not forgiven until he seeks forgiveness from him, as it is said: "And now, return the man's wife..."

<margin>**We have learned**</margin> from all this that for a sin between a person and their fellow, one must reconcile with their fellow. It is not like the practice I have seen in some places—due to our many sins—where just before the Cantor begins *Kol Nidre* <term>Kol Nidre: The opening prayer of Yom Kippur</term>, friends go to one another in the synagogue to ask for forgiveness. But such a person does not actually hate his friend, nor does his friend seek his harm. His friend will simply say to him that he never knew anything bad of him, only good. Thus, their "asking for peace" and their meeting to forgive one another happens in a place where forgiveness was not even needed, for they were at peace all their days. But those who actually hate one another remain in their places and do not go to one another! A person should not wait for his fellow, but should go to him with a humble spirit <note>original: "Be-rosh rami," literally "with a high head," here used ironically or to mean "promptly"</term> and seek a compromise between two enemies who are "wise in their own eyes," where each thinks he is the righteous one. Let the righteous one learn from the story of the Great Sage who, despite his greatness, showed humility by going to a certain butcher <note>A reference to a story in the Talmud where Rav went to appease a butcher who had offended him</note> to the outskirts of town, despite the words he had against him in his heart. Even though the butcher was the one who sinned against him—as Rashi explains in that passage—how much more so should every person behave toward their equal. And certainly, one should go to one greater than himself to appease him, and the ear shall hear, and the words of his mouth shall answer him, until he says: "I have known [your sincerity]" and says "I have forgiven." According to this, go and act.

<margin>**Fourteen**</margin> One must know that in every place where I mention the word *Shofar* <term>Shofar: The ram's horn blown on the New Year</term> regarding these laws I brought above, my intention is that the Penitent <note>original: "Ba'al Teshuvah"</note> is called by this name. The Sages hinted at the Penitent using the name *Shofar* because the Penitent must "beautify" <note>original: "le-shapper," a wordplay on Shofar</note> and improve his deeds. So it is said in the Midrash: "Blow the horn (*shofar*) at the new moon"—meaning, renew (*hadesh*) your deeds; "Shofar"—meaning, beautify (*shappru*) your deeds. Furthermore, *Shofar* is an acronym for *Shfel Ruach* (Lowly of Spirit), for so must a Penitent be: lowly of spirit and walking bowed down, as mentioned above in Introduction 4.

<margin>**Fifteen**</margin> One must know that in every place where I mention in the laws "if it was punctured," or "cracked," or "broken," it refers to sin. For the man who sins separates the divine spark, breaks the fence, and shatters a break. As it is said in the Psalms: "I have broken the paths of the profligate" (Psalm 119) <note>This is a non-standard citation/interpretation</note>. Rabbi David Kimhi <note>Radak</note> explained: "I prevented man from walking in the paths of the wicked." The author of the *Akedah* <note>Rabbi Isaac Arama</note> also compared sin to breaking, as he wrote in the section *Shoftim* regarding the symbolic hints of the alphabet: Sins caused the Tablets to be broken. He says there: When Moses went up to repair the breaking of the first Tablets, it represented what they lost of the purity of their souls. For the philosophers describe the soul as a tablet prepared for writing. The Torah is written upon it in purity, and within it is the power of the "Godly soul that You gave me which is pure." The truth is that the souls themselves are the Tablets, "the work of God," and "the writing is the writing of God engraved upon them." If iniquities defile them, erase their writing, and break them, one must strive to "hew second Tablets" and write upon them the things that were on the first. This is a duty all year round, and especially during the days of awakening. Thus, you see clearly that he compared iniquities to breaking. Consequently, it is understood that "sealing" <note>repairing a hole in the shofar</note> refers to the return to repentance. For the sealing of the break is its repair. As the Sages said on the verse "And they sewed fig leaves": the word "sewed" implies they set their hearts to mend what they had torn. As the folk saying goes: "One who sins much must patch much" <note>original: Judeo-German/Yiddish phrase regarding many sins requiring many "patches" or acts of repentance</note>. This means that one who has sinned greatly must perform great and many acts of repentance.

<margin>**Sixteen**</margin> One must know that the Penitent, after completing his own repentance, must also bring others back to the service of the Creator, as the verse says: "Gather yourselves and gather" <note>Zephaniah 2:1, interpreted as 'correct yourself and then correct others'</note>. And King David says in the Psalm of Repentance <note>Psalm 51</note>: "I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners shall return to You." Now, I shall review the introductions briefly with a slight elaboration:

---

<margin>1</margin> This informs us that there are different levels and ranks among the wise and the righteous in the World to Come.

<margin>2</margin> This informs us that one Penitent may be at a higher and loftier level in the World to Come than another Penitent.

<margin>3</margin> This informs us that Repentance has seven levels. The highest of all is that which is done immediately after the lapse... up to one who sins for many days... and repents while he is still in his full strength and vigor and subdues his impulse... in the same situation and with the same woman... meaning that the choice and the woman are available and nothing prevents him except the fear of sin. Regarding such repentance, our Sages said: "In the place where Penitents stand, even the perfectly righteous cannot stand." The lowest level is one who does not repent until close to his death.

<margin>4</margin> This informs us that humility is the essence of repentance; he should be lowly of spirit before every person and his soul should be like dust to all.

<margin>5</margin> This informs us that nothing stands in the way of repentance; even if one did all the evils in the world and repented, he is healed.

<margin>6</margin> This informs us that the sinner must repair the sin itself; with the very thing he sinned, he should make amends.

<margin>7</margin> This informs us to perform repentance in order, so as not to perform the later steps first or delay the earlier ones.

<margin>8</margin> This informs us of the "Weighted Repentance": if one sinned with one woman many times, he must perform the repentance written in the *Rokeach* <term>Rokeach: A 12th-century legal and ethical work by Rabbi Eleazar of Worms</term> as many times as he sinned with her. Certainly, if he sinned with many women, he must increase his repentance according to the number of women and the number of acts.

<margin>9</margin> This informs us that if he sinned with a woman only once, he only needs to perform the penance once, and should not afflict his body more than the time prescribed in the *Rokeach*. What King David meant by "My sin is before me always" will be explained there.

<margin>10</margin> This informs us that if a person committed many sins, both light and severe, he should perform repentance for each one individually and not bundle them together to repent only for the most severe.

<margin>11</margin> This informs us that one should repent even for a "doubtful transgression"... and the punishment for a doubt is more stringent than for a certainty.

<margin>12</margin> This informs us that a person should not publicize his sins that are between him and God.

<margin>13</margin> This informs us that if a person pained his fellow, even with words, he has no forgiveness forever until he reconciles with his fellow.

<margin>14</margin> This informs us that wherever "Shofar" is mentioned in these laws, it refers to the Penitent.

<margin>15</margin> This informs us that wherever "punctured," "cracked," or "broken" is mentioned in these laws, it indicates sin—"your break is great like the sea." And "sealing" indicates repentance.

<margin>16</margin> This informs us that the Penitent, after repenting, must bring others back to the service of God.

<summary>This page concludes a list of sixteen principles of repentance, emphasizing the necessity of interpersonal reconciliation and using the Shofar as a primary metaphor for the penitent's soul. It stresses that true atonement requires both the restoration of social harmony and a proportional, humble return to God.</summary>
