<meta>This page continues the discussion on the spiritual significance of the Jewish festivals, specifically focusing on how they correspond to the three Patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It bridges the physical enjoyment of the holidays with spiritual service and the ethical requirement to provide for the poor.</meta>

# Pillar of Peace

It is explained according to the interpretation of *Penehu* <note>Likely a reference to a specific commentator or a work titled "Face of..."</note> that when the physical powers are strengthened, the powers of the soul are awakened. For example, the "tasty foods" of Isaac <note>Refers to Genesis 27:4, where Isaac asks for a meal to prepare his spirit for blessing his son</note> and so on; look and see what was written above. This is the inner meaning of it, and no further explanation is needed, though others have elaborated on it more. However, look at this which I found, desired, and saw as a "light for my path" <note>A poetic reference to Psalm 119:105</note>. In the book *Orach Chayim*, Section 406, it is written: The Festivals were established corresponding to the Patriarchs. **Passover** corresponds to Abraham, as it is written: "Knead it and make cakes" <note>Genesis 18:6</note>, and it was then Passover. **The Festival of Weeks** <term>Shavuot|The holiday celebrating the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai</term> corresponds to Isaac, for the sounding of the Shofar <term>Shofar|A trumpet made from a ram's horn</term> at the giving of the Torah was from the horn of the ram <note>The ram sacrificed in place of Isaac at the Binding of Isaac</note>. **The Festival of Booths** <term>Sukkot|The autumn harvest festival where Jews dwell in temporary huts</term> corresponds to Jacob, as it is written: "and for his livestock he made booths" <note>Genesis 33:17</note>. Thus far are the words of Chapter 42 of the *Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer*.

This matter demands an explanation <note>Hebrew: "Darsheni," a term indicating a text requires deeper midrashic analysis</note>. According to the plain meaning, this is difficult: are not all the reasons for the festivals already written in the Torah? Passover is because the Lord "passed over" <note>A wordplay on the Hebrew 'Pesach'</note> the houses; the commandment of Matzah is because the dough of our ancestors did not have time to rise, etc. The Festival of Weeks is the time of the giving of our Torah and the offering of the "Two Loaves" corresponding to the two Torahs <note>The Written and Oral Torahs</note>. The Festival of Booths is because "I made the Israelites dwell in booths," etc.

I answer that their overall intention in this matches what I mentioned recently. It is to teach the people knowledge, so that every person remembers the Patriarchs of the world during their festival. The "deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children" <note>A classical rabbinic principle</note> to act as they did. Aside from the reasons explicitly written in the Torah, they should perform the Passover in its appointed time just as our father Abraham (peace be upon him) did at the time of Passover. This is hinted at in our shorthand <note>Notarikon</note>:

<margin>*Service *Acts of Kindness *Torah</margin> They also performed these three things: **Service**, which is the service of the Blessed Name. One should remember the theme of the day, for the memory of the kindness of the Holy One, Blessed be He, which He performed for our ancestors and for us, is a "complete service." We remember His kindness and offer praise before Him with voice and melody, singing songs and psalms because He performed all these miracles for our ancestors and for us, bringing us from slavery to freedom and from the physical body to joy. We must not be ungrateful. By remembering His kindness and wonders, we perform the commandment set for us with zeal and precision. In this way, we fulfill the idea that "perfect service" is the service of the soul combined with the service of the body.

The service of the body consists of taking pleasure in food and drink, as written in the Torah regarding the commandments of the festivals: "You shall sacrifice peace offerings and eat there and rejoice." The service of the soul is to thank, praise, and remember His miracles. Then the service will be complete. One must also perform **Acts of Kindness** on a holiday even more than on other days—namely, sending portions of food to others. As Ezra said: "Send portions to those who have nothing prepared" <note>Nehemiah 8:10</note>. As mentioned below: "If you gladden Mine [the poor], I will gladden yours." Finally, **Torah**: because one must study Torah on a festival, as it is uniquely suited for this. As it is taught at the end of Tractate Megillah: "And Moses declared the festivals of the Lord to the children of Israel"—Moses ordained for Israel that they should inquire and lecture on the matters of the day: the laws of Passover on Passover, etc.

Now, regarding the "cakes" Abraham made on Passover and "Acts of Kindness" on all festivals: **The Festival of Weeks** corresponds to Isaac, etc. The intention is that when we remember the sounding of the Shofar of the Torah, which was from the ram of Isaac, we should turn our hearts and inclinations to the service of the Blessed Name, just as Isaac surrendered his soul. Also, the memory of the ram's horn of Isaac should awaken us to repentance, just as we blast the ram's horn on the New Year <term>Rosh Hashanah|The Jewish New Year and Day of Judgment</term>. These days are remembered and observed for repentance because they are days of judgment.

**The Festival of Booths** corresponds to Jacob, etc. Since Sukkot is the time of the harvest, and his house is full of all good things—grain, wine, and oil—more than any other time of the year, there is a danger. As mentioned previously, food and drink can lead a person to pursue their physical nature, and the heart may go astray, leading one to forget the Blessed Name. As Moses our teacher (peace be upon him) said: "Lest you eat and be satisfied... and your heart grows haughty and you forget the Lord." Therefore, it says Sukkot corresponds to Jacob, of whom it is written: "and for his livestock (*miknehu*) he made booths." This follows what the author of *Shevil Emuna* wrote: "A righteous man knows the soul of his animal" <note>Proverbs 12:10</note>. This refers to the "animal soul" within him. Just as a booth <note>Sukkah</note> is a temporary dwelling of limited size—just enough to hold one's head, most of one's body, and a table—so too was the eating of our father Jacob. His physical needs, hinted at by the word *miknehu* <note>meaning 'his livestock' but interpreted here as 'his acquisitions' or 'his physical needs'</note>, were always temporary and limited. He only sought "bread to eat and clothing to wear." Thus, on Sukkot, a person should remember Jacob and not focus solely on filling the belly and physical pleasure. Rather, one should intend to awaken the physical powers only to better awaken the spiritual power.

Jacob is mentioned here more than the other Patriarchs because we do not find among the holy fathers anyone who suffered and gave himself over to physical acquisitions as much as Jacob. He went after his wealth with a "whole heart" <note>referring to his integrity in working for Laban</note> for the needs of his children and wives. It might have seemed that this hindered his meditation compared to the other Patriarchs. Therefore, the text mentions that even while working, Jacob was meditating. As the Midrash says: "He lay down in that place"—implying that for the twenty years he was in Laban's house, he did not sleep. He was occupied with his "animal soul" (the sheep) by day, but his heart was with the Torah.

The Festival of Booths is the "Festival of Ingathering." When a person finds rest and quiet after toil and labor, their joy is very great. They might turn their heart to idleness from the words of Torah. This is the opposite of what our Sages said: "Sabbaths and Festivals were only given for the study of Torah." Therefore, they emphasized this on Sukkot more than other holidays.

All these intentions are proper for a person to bring up during the festivals of the Lord. It is certainly not a "vain thing" <note>Deuteronomy 32:47</note> that our Sages said the festivals correspond to the Patriarchs. Besides the simple meaning—to remember the merit of the fathers—by this merit, may the Lord bring forth our judgment like light during these three pilgrimage festivals. Amen, so may the Lord our God do.

Before I finish speaking of the laws of the holidays, I will bring one more verse: Solomon the King said in the book of Ecclesiastes: "On a good day, be in good" <note>Ecclesiastes 7:14</note>. It does not say "be good," but "be **in** good." The extra letter hints that a person should be "good" in two ways on a holiday.
1. **Good for himself:** in food, drink, and clothing for him and his household.
2. **Good for others:** meaning he should send portions to those who have nothing prepared.

As the *Tur Orach Chayim* states in the laws of the festivals (Section 529): The commandment of the holiday is to divide it—half for the House of Study and half for eating and drinking. One should not be stingy with holiday expenses. One must honor and delight in it just like the Sabbath. Maimonides wrote: A person is obligated to be happy and "good-hearted" on the festival—he, his wife, his children, and all who join him. How does he make them happy? For the small children, he gives nuts and treats. For the women, he buys clothes and jewelry according to his means. And he is obligated to feed the stranger, the orphan, and the widow along with other poor people. But one who locks the doors of his house and eats and drinks with his children and wife, and does not feed and give drink to the poor and the embittered of soul—this is not the "joy of a commandment," but the "joy of his stomach." Regarding such people, it is said: "Their sacrifices are like the bread of mourners." A person must do everything on the festival that brings joy to the heart—eating, drinking, walking, and gladdening his household. Just as he must gladden his own, he must gladden "the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow who are within your gates." The Holy One, Blessed be He, said: "You have four members of your household (son, daughter, servant, maidservant); if you gladden Mine [the poor], I will gladden yours."

# Torah Or

And this is the "fallen booth of David" <note>Amos 9:11</note> and the "booth of peace" and the "virgin of Israel." Thus far. And that which was now a temporary dwelling will return to being a permanent dwelling, for if [text unclear] the secret of the World to Come. The dispute between Rabbi Judah and the Sages <note>Tractate Sukkah 2a</note> regarding whether the Sukkah must be a temporary or permanent dwelling—both are true, for "both these and those are the words of the Living God," and this suffices for the person of understanding. 

And in this way, the days of Sukkot, although they hint at the ten intermediate days <note>Between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur</note>, nevertheless, by their entry into Understanding <term>Binah|The third of the ten kabbalistic Sefirot, associated with the divine womb or mother</term> and the three highest emanations being counted as one, there are ten Sefirot <term>Sefirot|The ten attributes or emanations through which the Divine is revealed</term>. Therefore, a Sukkah that is not ten handbreadths high is invalid, and one higher than twenty cubits is invalid. For the "half-shekel" and the "full shekel" represent the number four, which is the letter *Yod* in its spelled-out form <note>Y-W-D equals 20</note>. This is the secret of the ten Sefirot from top to bottom in the "Direct Light" and the ten from bottom to top in the "Returning Light," following the secret that "their beginning is wedded to their end, and their end to their beginning." I have written more great and wonderful secrets on this matter regarding the verse "In Salem also is His tabernacle" <note>Psalm 76:3; "Salem" (Shalem) is linked to "Shalom" (Peace)</note>; you will find them above in the introduction titled *Toledot Adam* in the discourses on the blessing "Who forms the luminaries." It is worthy of careful study in 그 place, as well as what I wrote at the end of that introduction regarding the discourses on "Feminine Waters" and "Masculine Waters." May your eyes see and your heart rejoice.

And in the chapter "The Stolen Lulav" <note>Tractate Sukkah 37b</note>, Rabbi Jeremiah asked Rabbi Zera: "What is the reason we recite the blessing over the Palm Branch?" He answered: "Because it is taller than all of them." He then asked: "Then let us lift the Citron and bless over it?" But rather, because its species is the tallest of all. We have already made it known that the Palm Branch <term>Lulav|The closed frond of a date palm</term> corresponds to the spine, and is thus found to be taller than the other species. It is supreme over "all the nations of the earth," and its inheritance is "without borders," the secret of the "broad places of the river," the source of blessings. Therefore, we bless over it and not over the other species, and through the "Crown of the Kingdom," the branches are blessed. 

Thus far you will find in the book *Tola'at Yaakov* <note>The Worm of Jacob, a 16th-century kabbalistic commentary on the liturgy by Meir ibn Gabbai</note> page 73. See there the secret of the "wavings" in the six directions. Each time one waves three times, totaling eighteen wavings. *Tola'at Yaakov* (page 73) says: "As we learned in the *Book of Formation* <term>Sefer Yetzirah|An ancient Jewish mystical text</term> of our father Abraham, peace be upon him, in the first chapter, thirteen paths, and He fixed them in His great Name Y-H-W and sealed with it the six directions. He turned upward and sealed it with Y-H-W, etc." He says that from this Name, which is Y-H-W, six permutations were made, and they are the six names mentioned there, each name consisting of three letters, totaling eighteen letters. He sealed all six directions with them... And know that every day of the festival hints at one "Eighteen," as is known regarding the hint of the eighteen wavings... and the secret of the seven circuits <term>Hakafot|Ritual processions around the synagogue altar</term> corresponds to the Sabbatical cycles. Therefore, we circle once each day for each Sabbatical cycle, and on the seventh day, seven circuits to combine the cycle of them all, for they all have one Father and one God created them. And on the eighth day is the secret of the Jubilee, as mentioned above.

The *Recanati* <note>Rabbi Menahem Recanati, a 13th-14th century Italian kabbalist</note> wrote (on the portion *Emor*) that one must join the Citron <term>Etrog|The citrus fruit used on Sukkot</term> with the other species so as not to separate them from the "Building" <note>The structure of the Sefirot</note>. 

And this secret was revealed to me in a dream on the first night of the festival of Sukkot, when a certain pious Ashkenazi man named Rabbi Isaac was staying with me. I saw in the dream that he was writing the Name [of God] with *Yod* and *Heh*, but he was distancing the final *Heh* from the first three letters. I said to him, "What is this you have done?" and he replied, "This is the custom in our place." In my dream, I rebuked him and [text unclear], but he did not understand. The next morning, at the time of taking the Palm Branch, I saw that he was only waving the Palm Branch and its species without the Citron. I then understood the interpretation of my dream, and he changed his practice. Thus ends the account. 

This general principle of this holy renewal is the name Y-H-W-D <note>The four letters of the Tetragrammaton with a Dalet added</note> which has the numerical value of 30. The 15th of the month, ten days and five days after Yom Kippur, is Sukkot. Six days after the first day of Sukkot is Hoshana Rabbah, the "Closing," the secret of the final *Heh*, the "Small Feast" as is known, which returns to its understanding... that is Y-H-W-D. 

The secret of the "Pillar of Peace" is the secret of the "Exile," and the masters of Israel are called "Israel," for even though they are separated below, nevertheless, above in the secret of their souls, they are a single unity... for they are "the Lord's portion." And the "branches" who wish to return to their root must be an example to their root—meaning they must be united below as well. When there is separation below among the branches, it causes, as it were, separation and "cutting of the plantings" above. Look at how far the matter reaches! Therefore, the entire House of Israel must pursue peace and be one in peace and perfection without blemish, to resemble their Creator, for His Name is "The Lord is Peace." On this, the hint is given: "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 18:13</note>. The meaning is: since you are "with the Lord your God" as part of the Lord's portion, you must be wholehearted. And when you are wholehearted, then you shall be "with the Lord your God" in His very presence, and your eyes shall behold Him.

## Finished the Chapter "Torah Or"

<margin>In the book *Menorat HaMa'or* <note>The Candelabra of Light, by Isaac Aboab</note>, Candle 3, Part 4, Chapter 1, he wrote words of moral instruction regarding the hint of the Sukkah, saying: "Leave your permanent dwelling and sit in a temporary dwelling" <note>Tractate Sukkah 20b</note>.</margin>

### Chapter 4: Moral Rebuke

Their intention was that this commandment of the Sukkah comes to teach us that a person should not place his trust in the height of his house, its strength, or its fine repair, even if it is filled with all good things. Let him not trust in the help of any man, even if he be a "giant of the earth" and a ruler... but let him place his trust in the One who spoke and the world came into being, for He alone has the power and the faithfulness, and He does not retract what He promises, as it is written: "God is not a man, that He should lie" <note>Numbers 23:19</note>. He alone is the refuge and the hiding place... and to awaken man to this, the commandment of the Sukkah comes at this time, after the "gathering of the granary and the winepress" in the Land of Israel... because this is a time of joy for all, when the storehouses are full of all good things, and the man has already gathered into the city, plastering his roof and strengthening the repairs of his house to be protected from the storm and rain. Perhaps he might say [words of pride], therefore He commanded him to go out of his strong house and sit in a booth, so that he will be stirred and place his trust in the Name, may He be blessed, and take to heart that all the good that came to him from the field came solely by the will of God. And on this they hinted by making it from the "waste of the granary and the winepress," to say that this one who gathers fruit to eat and uses the waste to cover the booth is like a person paying a fee—that all the protection of his body and all that he has is from the Blessed Name, and he should not trust in what he possesses. Thus far his words.

The author of the *Akedah* <note>Isaac Arama, 15th-century philosopher</note> also wrote in the portion *Emor* words of moral instruction hinted at in the Sukkah; see there. Also, although in Chapter 2 I wrote the true secrets of the Sukkah, nevertheless, do not let your hand rest from thinking on this and taking moral instruction. And since these words have come to my hand, I will make known what is in my heart. I have seen the Children of Israel building houses like the fortresses of princes, making permanent dwellings in this world and in an impure land. And even though [the Sages said] the houses of the righteous are destined to be moved to the Land of Israel, nevertheless, their intention and their crawling <note>Meaning their obsession with physical property</note> is to have a heritage to leave to their children, as if this inheritance was given to him and his seed forever. This appears, Heaven forbid, as a distraction from the Redemption. 

Therefore, my sons (may God preserve them), even if God gives you great wealth, build houses only according to the necessity of your needs and no more. Do not build towers and increase in grandeur and greatness. Only have a dwelling for your generations according to your honor and its beauty, to be secluded in them for Torah and Repentance. Go and see what Jonadab son of Rechab commanded his sons: "You shall not build houses... but you shall dwell in tents" <note>Jeremiah 35:7</note>. This does not apply nowadays, to live in tents; but I say this to leave aside magnificent buildings beyond the necessity of a dwelling, and to use the rooms for the honor of seclusion for His Blessed Name.

# The Pillar of Peace

Therefore, our Sages of blessed memory warned about anger for this reason. And it is written there at the end of the chapter that the most praiseworthy trait for every wise person—through which he will have peace in this world and the world to come—is that he should not become angry, but rather forgive his insults, overcome his natural inclinations <term>Middot|Literally "measures," referring to one's character traits or emotional reactions</term>, and forgive anyone who has sinned against him. By doing this, his own sins will be forgiven by Heaven, as we learn in the first chapter of Tractate Rosh Hashanah (page 17): Rava said, "Whoever passes over his measures <note>original: "HaMa'avir al midotav" - meaning one who ignores personal slights and does not insist on his "due" retribution</note>, [Heaven] passes over all his transgressions, as it is said: 'He bears sin and passes over transgression' <note>Micah 7:18</note>. To whom does He bear sin? To the one who passes over transgression [committed against him]." Thus far are his words.

**Included** in the category of Peace is the duty to honor all people <note>original: "Beriyot" - literally "creatures," implying all of God's creations</note>. "Who is honored? He who honors others" <note>Ethics of the Fathers 4:1</note>, whether with his money or his physical person. And in Tractate Berakhot (at the end of page 60), the Sages taught: "We do not show honor [by yielding the way] on roads, nor on bridges, nor with dirty hands." And the Tosafot <note>A group of medieval commentators on the Talmud</note> explain: "We do not show honor, etc. And if you ask: But didn't we say in the Tractate Shabbat, in the chapter 'With what may a beast [go out],' that Levi and Rav Huna bar Hiyya were traveling on the road, and Rav Huna's donkey preceded the donkey of Levi, and Rav Huna wanted to clear his mind regarding Levi <note>meaning, he wanted to show him respect by letting him go first</note>? This implies we *do* show honor on the roads! The answer is: when they set out on the road together, they show honor; but if each is going his own way and they happen to meet on the road to one place, they do not show honor." Thus far his words. This is the perfection of peace in his body. In his intellect, how so? He should teach Torah to his fellow and to his fellow's son, for the Torah is Peace, as it is said: "The Lord will give strength to His people; the Lord will bless His people with peace" <note>Psalm 29:11</note>. Also, in worldly matters, he should give proper advice to his fellow to save him from mishap and damage, showing compassion and mercy regarding his interests and such.

# Chapter: Torah is Light

Regarding the matter of the four days between Yom Kippur and Sukkot: I wrote in the first chapter that through the effort one puts into the commandments of the Sukkah and the Lulav <note>The "Four Species" waved during the holiday</note>, it serves as a reminder to be sanctified through them and to turn away from evil. This is the "contemplation of repentance." Afterward, the days of the festival themselves are essentially holy, for in them we fulfill the commandments of the Sukkah and the Lulav, as if these four days were titled by the commandments themselves. Know that everything is hinted at in the secret of the letter *Yod* (י), the secret of the Ten Days of Repentance. When the *Yod* is spelled out fully <note>In Hebrew, the letter Yod (י) is spelled Yod-Vav-Dalet (יוד)</note>, the "filling" letters <note>The Vav (ו) and Dalet (ד)</note> also equal ten. I already wrote above in the first discourse that while we say there are ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, the language is seemingly imprecise, as there are only seven days between them. I wrote there what I wrote, and I wrote that it also hints at the ten days between Yom Kippur and Hoshana Rabbah <note>The seventh day of Sukkot, seen as the final day of judgment</note>. For we find that Yom Kippur is called "Rosh Hashanah," as it says "on the tenth of the month... the Day of Atonement shall be completed" <note>Ezekiel 40:1 mentions the "beginning of the year" on the tenth of the month</note>. And Hoshana Rabbah is when the sealing of judgment is finished, and Yom Kippur is completed in its fullness and its end. Since the name "Rosh Hashanah" applies to Yom Kippur, and the name "Yom Kippur" applies to Hoshana Rabbah, understand that both are ten-day periods, like the eight days between Yom Kippur and Hoshana Rabbah. However, the first Ten Days of Repentance are the primary ones; they are the essence of the Ten Days, while those that follow are branches of repentance. This is the "filling" of the letter *Yod*: the filling is the letters *Dalet* (ד = 4) and *Vav* (ו = 6). The *Dalet* represents the four days between Yom Kippur and Sukkot, and the *Vav* represents the six days of Sukkot. After the *Yod* is completed in its spelling, the day following it is the day of the final sealing.

**The Secret of the Sukkah:** Thus are the words of *Tola'at Ya'akov* (page 70): For this reason, our Sages of blessed memory said that the Name of Heaven rests upon the Sukkah, as it is taught in Tractate Sukkah, first chapter: Rabbi Judah says, "From where do we know that just as the Name of Heaven rests upon the festival sacrifice <term>Chagigah|The peace-offering brought to the Temple during the pilgrimage festivals</term>, so the Name of Heaven rests upon the Sukkah? The verse says: 'The Festival of Sukkot, seven days for the Lord' <note>Leviticus 23:34</note>—just as the festival sacrifice is 'for the Lord,' so the Sukkah is 'for the Lord.'" The secret of this is that the Sukkah is "Great," meaning the place of Jacob's birth. The secret of the Sukkah is "In booths shall you dwell seven days" <note>Leviticus 23:42</note>, the secret of the arrangement of matters of the Higher Wisdom <term>Chokhmah|The second Sefirah, associated with the flash of intuition</term> hidden within the sparkle of the beginning of thought, from the place where there is no knowledge or boundary, until the Infinite <term>Ein Sof|The Infinite, God as He exists prior to any self-manifestation</term>. The soul of that thought, as it turns to illuminate the World to Come, reveals Wisdom upon its face, and from it emanates the Six Ends <note>The six directions/emotions of the divine structure</note> along with the "Seventh Daughter," the Mother of Solomon. These are the seven days of the Sukkah. Therefore, the word "In booths" (*ba-sukkot*) is written defectively <note>Missing the letter Vav</note>, hinting at the secret of the "Tenth" which is seen through it—the secret of the luminaries. The seven days of the Sukkah are the Higher Sukkah, which stands as a light to strengthen the "Good Oil" upon the booth of the generation. This matter is explained in the Zohar, section *Emor*: for sometimes "Sukkot" is written full (with a Vav) and sometimes "Sukkot" is written missing a Vav. Thus far is the secret of the Sukkah; look into it. **SKH** (סכ"ה) <note>Numerically 85, or a reference to the Sukkah covering</note> refers to the "Upper Mother" <term>Ima Ila'ah|The divine persona of Binah/Understanding, viewed as a protective mother</term> who covers them like a mother over her children. For the Sukkah, which is the "Building," is included in both Beauty <term>Tiferet|The central Sefirah, representing harmony</term> and Sovereignty <term>Malchut|The final Sefirah, representing the physical world and the Divine Presence</term>. Both are like the Upper Mother, which is the "Year," and into her we enter, and in this shadow we sit for seven days. We are the "shadow of the Sukkah." For Israel, its shadow must be greater than its sunlight, to hint to us that the Attribute of Mercy should prevail over the Attribute of Judgment. Who could endure the heat? For who could stand before the Great Sun? But we come into the shadow of the Sukkah of the sun of absolute Mercy. The shadow of the walls alone is invalid; but the walls are the place where the "Quiet Field" is hidden—from there, an eye was given. This commandment was given from the "Left," and therefore if one covers the roof with something susceptible to ritual impurity, it is invalid. But the walls are of the matter of the "Body." Therefore, after the forgiveness of sin, this commandment was given in the secret of "And Jacob traveled to Sukkot" <note>Genesis 33:17</note>. For the roof-covering <term>S'chach|The organic material used to cover a Sukkah</term>, which is the "Merciful One," the secret of the Right Hand is protected, and there is no contact with the "Body" <note>External forces</note>. Therefore, after the forgiveness of sin, this commandment was given in the secret of "And Jacob traveled to Sukkot," after he sent a gift to Esau—which is the secret of the Scapegoat on Yom Kippur to the power of Esau. We are in the shadow of this Sukkah.

**Afterward,** there is a hint in the matter of Jacob traveling to Sukkot: "And for his cattle he made booths." Thus are the words of *Sefer HaMusar* (page 146): In those days, Israel offers sacrifices for the nations of the world, so that they do not mingle in the joy of Israel with their King. Those nations are like the small branches that have no utility, which are beneath the tree around the roots; they are all blessed by the tree. This is the secret of that "stuttering one" <note>Possibly referring to the spiritual prince of the nations</note>—even though they "destroy the vineyards," they must be blessed by Him. For the nations of the world take hold of the external roots. Sacrifices are offered for them so they do not enjoy the radiance and take a portion of the Higher Life, the secret of the Higher Ascent which is for you alone. Because of this, they [the sacrifices] continually decrease. They live from the Holy, but do not ascend. All those bulls [offered on Sukkot] decrease and go down every day until they reach seven. This is their blessing, the blessing of the small branches. And this hints at the time until after the final sealing, for the sealing is not finished until Hoshana Rabbah. Afterward, Shemini Atzeret is a festival unto itself, and then their [the nations'] hold is abolished. It is written: "On the eighth day, there shall be a restricted assembly <term>Atzeret|A day of festive assembly or "holding back"</term> for you." And thus says *Tola'at Ya'akov* (page 74): The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: "I have held you back before Me, like a king who invited his sons to a feast for set days. When the time arrived [ to leave], he said: 'I beg of you, stay with me one more day, for your departure is difficult for me,'" as seen in Leviticus Rabbah. And in the chapter "The Flute," Rabbi Levi said: "To what do these seventy bulls correspond? To the seventy nations. Why a lone bull [on the eighth day]? To correspond to the lone nation [Israel]." It is like a mortal king whose servants made him a feast; on the last day, he said to his beloved friend: "Make me a small feast so that I may enjoy you." Thus far. The secret of the matter is that the seven days hint at the seven Sabbatical cycles <note>Shmitot</note>. This is the secret of the circuits <term>Hakafot|The ritual of walking around the altar or the synagogue platform</term> they would make around the Altar. After these are completed, it is the secret of the Great Jubilee, and the attachment of the "small branches"—the powers of the 70 nations—is completely abolished. "And there shall be an assembly *for you*," for the sealing is finished in its fullness, and it is good for the good lovers, and it shall be a victory. This is the matter of the Willow <term>Aravah|One of the four species, which is also the subject of a special ceremony on the last day</term> taken on Hoshana Rabbah, as written in the Zohar and explained in the book *Tola'at Ya'akov* (end of page 72). Thus it says there: It corresponds to the "Fear of Isaac" <term>Pachad Yitzchak|A name for the Sefirah of Gevurah/Judgment</term>. It is called "Willows of the Brook" because it grows by the Higher Brook, which is the river that flows out of Eden. And because on this day the judgment is completed, the commandment of the day is the Willow; we strike it on the ground, meaning to destroy the Judgment so it cannot be found, lowering it to the dust. The Willow is shaped like lips, to hint to you that this day is the conclusion of judgment and the end of "evil speech." For on that day, the decrees go out from the King and are given to the "Master of Judgment" to fulfill the judgment. He shall "kiss their lips" and have no more mouth to answer. It is the day the blessings of the nations are finished—for Israel offers seventy bulls for the seventy nations so they may be blessed by our blessings and thereby be with us, for the seventy nations surround the Nest. When the root is blessed, the branches are blessed. This is the completion of their blessing and the beginning of their judgment; it is the beginning of Israel's blessings and the completion of their judgment. And on the next day, they are prepared to delight with their Father in Heaven. Thus far. These matters hint at Yom Kippur and the completion of the judgment that began on Rosh Hashanah, when Satan also comes to prosecute, but now everything is completed for the good. It also hints at a more internal level regarding the completion of judgment and the beginning of the future Redemption, as I have hinted. And I previously hinted at the secret of the "Two Booths"—the Booth of David and the Upper Mother. The "Fallen Booth of David" <note>Amos 9:11</note>—He will establish it. Of her it is said: "She has fallen and shall no more rise, the virgin of Israel" <note>Amos 5:2</note>, which is explained in the Zohar (and found in *Sefer HaMusar*, page 65): There it gives a parable of a matron <note>The Queen/Shekhinah</note> who had a quarrel with the King and left his house until the King's anger subsided. Once his anger was cleared, the redemption occurred and she returned to her place and her house. A second and third time, she left in the King's anger, but the King comforted her and swore she would no longer be exiled time after time, but He himself would go and return her to his merit in the "Station of David," which was not like this in glory. Every time [before] was in the sense of "She has fallen and shall no more rise" <note>meaning she could not rise on her own, but God will now lift her up</note>.

# The Matter of Prayer and the Reading of the Torah Scroll

Every person who succeeds in their prayer through the desire of the heart must ensure that their voice is not heard by others <note>This refers to the "Amidah" or Silent Prayer, where the words are whispered so only the speaker can hear them</note>. For if their voice is heard by another, there is no one who listens to them Above, except for the one who heard it first below. To such an extent must one take care—that they <note>the heavenly beings</note> should not hear that prayer. Likewise, the word of prayer belongs to the Higher World, and a word from the Higher World need not be heard by the physical ear.

**Preparation:** One should make a preparation for their heart to focus. And how should one focus? It says: one should focus before rising to pray. They should sit for a while in quiet and silence, removing all [extraneous] thoughts from their heart. They should begin to think about the greatness of Him who spoke and the world came into being, and about His wonders, His awesomeness, His might, and the kindnesses He has performed for His people. They should think of the goodness and the acts of grace He bestowed upon those who are lacking and flawed—returning good to the guilty, saving them from many troubles, healing their illnesses, and satisfying them from His goodness. Though the person did not act in a way to earn such a reward, God bestowed goodness and merit upon them. One should also think of their own lowliness and insignificance in relation to the Creator; for what is a human but a "driven leaf and stubble"? They should think: "Now I desire to stand before the King to supplicate Him and request my needs and petitions." Truly, they are not worthy or fitting to stand before Him.

**The Theft:** <note>Referring to the "theft" of God’s kindness</note> It is the kindness and perfection of the Creator that He permitted and commanded this, despite the person’s shortcomings in His service. After all this, one should rise and pray. 

**Gravity:** <note>original: ח"ש - חסידים ראשונים</note> One does not stand to pray except from a state of "gravity" <term>Koved Rosh: literally 'heaviness of the head,' meaning a state of serious spiritual submission</term>. The Early Pious ones used to wait one hour and then pray, so that they might direct their hearts toward their Father in Heaven.

**Entering:** When a person stands to pray and another person enters, that entrant causes a disruption to the worshiper's focus. In this, "evil friends" err, for they rush to enter the synagogue at the time the community is reciting the "Verses of Praise" <term>Pesukei D'Zimra: the introductory psalms of the morning service</term> or during the prayer itself, thereby causing a lapse in the focus of the congregation who are unifying the Name of our Creator. Therefore, it is proper to be careful not to enter the synagogue during the time of "Unification" <note>likely referring to the Shema</note> or during the prayer. Similarly, when praying alone, one should pray in a place where they are certain no one will enter, so they may focus.

**The Neighbor:** When one's neighbor—meaning those sitting near them—prays with focus, it becomes easier for them to focus as well. But when those sitting near them are scoffers or pray without focus, it will be difficult for them to focus. Regarding this, it is said: "Woe to the wicked and woe to his neighbor," and "Keep far from a bad neighbor and do not associate with the wicked." 

As written in *The Book of the Pious* <note>Sefer Hasidim</note>, section 772: A God-fearing person must not stand or sit during prayer near a wicked person. For when a wicked person stands in prayer, they are occupied with evil thoughts. When the Divine Presence <note>original: "Shekhinah"</note> dwells, it distances itself from them and hides its eyes, as it is written: *When you spread forth your hands, I will hide my eyes from you...* <note>Isaiah 1:15</note>. This was also the view of Joshua the Pious. And I say: when a righteous person prays with focus, it is not because of the wicked person next to them that their prayer is loathed; rather, as the verse says: *The Lord is far from the wicked, but He hears the prayer of the righteous* <note>Proverbs 15:29</note>. Even though the Lord is far from the wicked, He still hears the prayer of the righteous, even if they are side-by-side.

**Time:** When a person has a period of time drawn from their heart's vision, they can say each request slowly and focus. But when they do not have such time, there is no time free for thought in the mind, except like "the shot of a bow." I saw a certain pious man who measured his focus and the segments of his prayer; he said the Psalm does not provide enough time for a man to focus. If only it sufficed to say the words of the prayer and the reading perfectly! For I see in myself that I hasten to speak, and I do not finish the words of the prayer until the congregation has finished theirs.

**The Conclusion of the Matter:** Regarding focus in "Unification," prayer, and Torah: people are divided into two parts. The first part are those who truly unify the Name, may He be blessed, and pray to Him and bless Him. The second part are those who say the words of Unification but do not unify; they say the words of prayer but do not pray; they say the words of blessing but do not bless. Behold, the first part—those who focus—are very, very few, "a city and its wise men." But the people of the second part have multiplied...

The law has already been decided that "Commandments require intention" <note>Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim, section 60</note>. Prayer specifically requires focus, even according to the opinion that other commandments do not. This is because prayer is a "service of the heart." Rabbeinu Yonah wrote explicitly in the chapter "Ha-Koreh" <note>of Tractate Berakhot</note>: Even one who holds that commandments do not require focus in a matter involving a physical action must agree that a commandment depending solely on speech requires focus. For the speech itself is the entire action; if one has no intent in the speech and does no other action, it is as if they have done nothing at all. 

This reasoning is found in the Mishnah where Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa said: "If my prayer is fluent in my mouth, I know it is accepted." Rashi explained: "If it is fluent and ordered in my mouth, and my supplication flows from my heart to the mouth—for the heart is the root."

And there, in the commentary on "One does not stand" <note>Berakhot 32b</note>, regarding one who says "Hear, Hear" <note>repeating the first line of the Shema</note>, they silence him. It asks: perhaps at first he did not focus his mind, and finally he did? The answer: Is it "companionship" <note>original: חברותא - meaning an inappropriate familiarity or audacity</note> toward Heaven? If he did not focus his mind the first time, they silence him... Rashi explains: This teaches him that he must focus and understand what he is doing.

<margin>
Sefer Hasidim. See the Tur, Choshen Mishpat, Section 109: Prayer is in place of sacrifice. And in the Zohar, Parashat Pekudei: It is written, "To serve Him with all your heart"—this is the service of the heart, the secret of the service of the soul. Therefore, one must be careful of "foreign thoughts" <term>Machshavot Zarot: distracting or secular thoughts during prayer</term>. There should be no doubt in the mind; do not mix in thoughts of doubt. One should pray before the Holy One, Blessed be He, while standing, as in the service [in the Temple], as it is written: "To stand before the Lord." One must bow the feet. Those who enter during the time of service must sanctify their hands and feet, needing to find grace in the Holy Place. Therefore, one must clean their hands of all filth and grime. There should be nothing separating them from the wall. One must remove all things that distract the heart from the essence of prayer. Wear white garments and honorable clothing instead of weekday clothes.
</margin>

Since prayer is the perfection of speech through thought and action, it is specifically in the place of a sacrifice. If it is not so, it is an "invalid prayer," like an invalid sacrifice. In the *Tikkunei Zohar*, they said that an invalid prayer is handed over to "the dog," fulfilling the verse: *You shall cast it to the dog* <note>Exodus 22:30</note>. In *Reshit Chochma* <note>a 16th-century Kabbalistic ethical work</note>, in the "Gate of Fear," chapter 8, it is written that this [the dog] refers to the power of Lilith. It seems a hint to this is found in the verse: *But against any of the children of Israel, a dog shall not whet its tongue* <note>Exodus 11:7</note>, for their prayer is worthy and God hears it, as it says in Exodus: *And God heard their groaning...*

<column-break/>

**The 50th Level** which I mentioned—to pray with the community—is a great and proper thing. It is illuminated in the first chapter of Berakhot (page 8): Rabbi Yitzchak said to Rav Nachman: "Why does the Master not come to the synagogue to pray?" He said to him: "I am unable." He said to him: "Let the Master gather ten people and pray [at home]." He said to him: "It is too much trouble for me." He said: "Let the Master tell the messenger of the community <note>the Cantor/Prayer leader</note> to come and inform the Master when the community is praying." He said: "Why all this [effort]?" He replied: "As Rabbi Yohanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: What is meant by the verse, *But as for me, let my prayer be unto Thee, O Lord, in a time of favor*? When is a 'time of favor'? At the time when the community is praying." Rabbi Yossi bar Hanina said it is learned from here: *Thus says the Lord: In a time of favor I have answered thee...*

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual and practical requirements for prayer, emphasizing internal focus (Kavvanah) over external sound, the necessity of preparing the heart, and the importance of praying with a community during a "time of favor." It also explores the Kabbalistic view of speech as a substitute for Temple sacrifice and warns against distractions or "bad neighbors" during worship.</summary>
<keywords>prayer, Kavvanah, intention, synagogue, community, sacrifice, Sefirot, speech, Rashi, Rabbeinu Yonah, Zohar, Sefer Hasidim, Berakhot, time of favor</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the laws and inner intentions (Kavvanah) of prayer, focusing on maintaining physical and spiritual purity while standing before the Divine, and the precise recitation of the Shema.</meta>

# Matters of Prayer and the Reading of the Torah Scroll

The Great Name [must be approached] in holiness and purity, etc. **The Kol Bo** <note>original: "הכלבו"; a 14th-century halakhic compendium</note> wrote: the Kabbalist Rabbi Heyden, of blessed memory, wrote in the chapter regarding the Order of Prayer that a Cantor should be careful to spit [beforehand] so that saliva does not gather in his mouth when he blesses and sanctifies the Holy King, Blessed be He.

If one was standing in prayer and "sneezed"—meaning a wind escaped from below—he should wait until the scent dissipates and then return to his prayer. If he feels the urge to "sneeze," he should move backward four cubits <note>About 6–8 feet</note>, "sneeze," wait for the scent to dissipate, and then return to his place and say: "Master of the Worlds, You have formed us with many openings and many hollows. It is revealed and known before You our shame and our disgrace—shame and disgrace in our lives, and maggots and worms in our death." Then he returns to the place where he stopped.

**The Shekan"i** <note>An acronym for a commentator</note> wrote that in the work **Terumat HaDeshen** <note>"The Offering of the Ash," a 15th-century book of legal responsa</note>, the author was asked why we do not see even the most meticulous people in our time following this law of moving back four cubits. He replied that it is implied by one of the Great Sages that he would force himself to hold back the wind until the end of the prayer, and this is also evident from the words of the **Rokeach** <note>Rabbi Eleazar of Worms</note>. It is possible the reason [we aren't as strict] is because we only worry about the prohibition of "do not make yourselves detestable" when it involves a major or minor evacuation, but for a mere "wind" during prayer, they did not strictly forbid it.

Nevertheless, one who cannot restrain himself—I do not see a clear side for permission not to distance oneself four cubits, except perhaps for the reason that he would be excessively embarrassed before the congregation if they noticed. This is especially true if he is the Cantor, who would be greatly shamed and disgraced if the many people realized his body was not clean while standing before the Holy One, Blessed be He—and **human dignity** <term>Kevod HaBriyot: the principle that preserving a person's dignity can sometimes override secondary rabbinic decrees</term> is of great importance.

It also seems that the formula "Master of the Worlds..." is not required [in public], as perhaps it was only instituted for one who moves away from his bed, where his shame and disgrace are felt and visible, as the wording implies. For this reason, the Sages only designated the distancing of four cubits and the recitation of "Master of the Worlds" for one praying in private, where there is no public shaming or degradation. One can also prove from the Talmud (Tractate Shabbat) that we do not worry about a Rabbinic prohibition in cases of public degradation. Rava's students once forced him to delay his bodily needs because they had a fixed time for study, and in Tractate Yevamot, it mentions Sages who suffered physical harm because they delayed themselves out of embarrassment in public. They did not fear the prohibition of "do not make yourself detestable" in the face of public shame.

Nonetheless, it is very difficult to create distinctions of the mind that are not even hinted at in the Talmud or the rulings of the Geonim <note>The leaders of Babylonian Jewry, approx. 600–1000 CE</note>. Thus, it follows that one praying at home is obligated to move away and say "Master of the Worlds," while one praying in a congregation should let the scent pass and remain in place due to the shame. However, the suggestion that one doesn't need the formula at all is far from logic. Since the author of *Terumat HaDeshen* himself wrote this as a doubt, it seems to me that one to whom this happens should meditate on the formula "Master of the Worlds" in his heart—for even thought is like speech.

## Concerning
<margin>Blessings</margin>
The laws of one who has experienced a seminal emission <note>Ba'al Keri</note> regarding the reading of the Torah, the Shema, and the Prayer: there are various opinions on this as explained in the **Tur** and **Beit Yosef** <note>Standard codes of Jewish law</note> in Section 88. However, the common custom is that ritual immersion is not required. **Maimonides** wrote in a letter that although the final law follows the lenient view, he himself practiced ritual purity all his days, and this is considered a **measure of piety** <term>Middat Chasidut: an optional act of spiritual discipline beyond the letter of the law</term>.

Indeed, such a man is certainly pure. And one who cannot do so due to certain hindrances should think in his heart while washing his hands about what is stated in the Talmud (Tractate Berakhot, page 15): Rabbi Yochanan said, "Anyone who cleanses his hands and then recites the Shema and prays, the Scripture considers it as if he built an altar and offered a sacrifice upon it, as it is written: 'I will wash my hands in purity and circle Your altar, O Lord' (Psalm 26:6)." Even though Rava did not agree that it is exactly like immersion, Rashi explains that "washing in purity" implies washing the whole body, but the verse specifies "my hands" to teach that the reward for washing hands is like that of immersing the whole body. Thus, one who is pained because he cannot immerse, and walks with a broken heart while washing, is considered as if he immersed—for a good thought is joined by the Holy One to action.

It is forbidden to do one’s personal business before praying once the time for prayer has arrived. However, before the light of dawn, it is permitted. Nevertheless, it seems one should not engage in any matter until they have recited the **Morning Blessings**. Out of fear of Heaven, when one rises from bed after washing, they should meditate on the greatness of the Creator, Blessed be He, and contemplate His wondrous creatures, as it says: "When I see Your heavens, the work of Your fingers..." (Psalm 8:4). They should think of the Standing at Mount Sinai and the Covenant He made with us. We have already mentioned this awakening in Part 2, earlier in this composition.

> Acceptance of the Yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven through the recitation of the Shema should be done with awe, fear, trembling, and sweat, and with great and powerful intention (Kavvanah), as mentioned at length in the Talmud and the Codes, with all precision and by separating the words that are joined together.

## And my teacher, of blessed memory, did not say this in "Emek Bracha"
The author of **Kose Mayim Chayim** <note>"A Cup of Living Water"</note> in Part 2, called **Mekor Chayim** <note>"Source of Life," by Rabbi Mordechai Jaffe</note>, wrote: our teacher Rabbi Meir told us to accept the Yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven in three verses: "Hear, O Israel," "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever," and "I am the Lord your God," etc.

<margin>Israel, a pause at "You"</margin>
"Israel" is a pause; "The Lord our God" is the second pause; "The Lord is One" is the final pause. The meaning should be: "Hear O Israel, He who is called the Lord our God is called One." Or one might say: "Hear O Israel, the Lord our God—the one who made Him our God—He is the Lord who is One." The word "Hear" (Shema) is an expression of "Listen and Hear," as if saying: "Listen Israel, the Lord our God is One."

One should not elongate the 'Aleph' of *Echad* (One) lest it sound like "is not" <note>Hebrew: "Ee" means 'not'</note>, God forbid. Nor should one rush the letter 'Chet,' but rather elongate it slightly to crown Him over the seven heavens and the earth <note>The numerical value of Chet is 8</note>. One must elongate the 'Dalet' of *Echad* to crown Him over the heavens, the earth, and the four directions of the world. Some are accustomed to emphasizing the 'Dalet' significantly, but the **Beit Yosef** and **Maharshal** wrote that it is only necessary to feel the strength of the letter slightly so it does not sound like a 'Resh' <note>Which would change the word from "One" to "Other"</note>.

<margin>Explanation of my teacher's secret</margin>
An explanation of the secret of my teacher from Lublin regarding those who say [technical grammatical points regarding vowel points and the letter Dalet vs Resh]. This was not a mistake of Ezra the Scribe... one should be careful not to make errors.

It is found in the **SMaK** <note>Sefer Mitzvot Katan, 13th century</note> and brought by the **Beit Yosef** in Section 61: one must intend that the 'Aleph' [of Echad] means He is One; the 'Chet' that He is unique in the seven heavens and the earth; and the 'Dalet' represents the four directions.

<margin>And these are his words</margin>
The **Shiltei HaGibborim** <note>"Shields of the Heroes," 16th-century commentary</note> on the **Mordechai** wrote: the measure of elongation for "Echad" is three [beats] for the 'Chet' and three for the 'Dalet'. How so? Crowning Him above and below with the 'Chet' and in the directions with the 'Dalet'. This is also found in the book **Tanya** and the **Shulchan Aruch**. One should pause slightly between "forever and ever" and "And you shall love" to separate the acceptance of the Kingdom of Heaven from the other commandments. This pause should be long enough to reflect in his heart that "The Lord is your God" and "You shall have no other gods," meditating on the Ten Commandments during the Shema, as they are all hinted at in the first paragraph.

Regarding other pauses in the Shema where one must emphasize or punctuate words: such as the 'Ayin' of *Nishma* and the 'Dalet' of *Echad*. One must be careful with the pronunciation of letters so that one letter is not swallowed by its neighbor, such as not saying "ve-charah af" <note>"And his anger will burn"</note> as one word. One must also be careful with two identical letters that follow each other, where the first ends a word and the second begins the next, such as "be-khol levavkha" <note>"With all your heart"</note>. One must separate between words where the first ends in an 'M' and the next begins with an 'Aleph', such as "u-neshatem et." These are all written in the **Tur, Orach Chayim Section 61**. The author of **Be'er Mayim Chayim** counts sixty such instances of words that need to be separated. And this is not just for the Shema, but for any place in prayer or the **Verses of Praise** <term>Pesukei D'Zimrah: psalms recited before the main morning prayer</term> where a word ends with the same letter that begins the next word, or ends with an 'M'.

# Matters of Prayer and the Reading of the Torah Scroll

The Jerusalem Talmud in the tractate of Berakhot <note>The Jerusalem Talmud is a collection of Rabbinic discussions from the 4th century CE</note> discusses synagogues and houses of study that stand outside the Land of Israel. It was ruled that in the Diaspora, those in the East should pray facing West toward Jerusalem, and likewise, the scribe who finishes a Torah scroll in the North should turn its face to the South. All of Israel here in the lands of exile pray by raising our prayers toward Jerusalem and the Holy Temple, and from there, the prayers ascend before the Blessed Creator. Now, I must inform you of the difference between prayer in the Land of Israel and prayer in the Diaspora. Know that prayer in the Land of Israel is like someone who is close to the road to speak with the King; his house is near the King, and there is no adversary <note>original: "שטן"; often referring to a spiritual accuser or obstacle</note>, no evil occurrence, and no destroyer on the path. But prayer in the Diaspora is like someone who needs to speak with the King but his house is very far from the King; on the road, there is deceit, bandits, many evil mishaps, and many wild beasts. Now see how much a person must be careful to purify his body from theft and oppression, and to hurry with purity and simplicity, focusing on the text of his prayer so it is worthy to be accepted, as we have mentioned. In this way, know that there are many delayers and accusers of the prayers of Israel while they travel toward Jerusalem due to the forces of impurity belonging to the nations of the world. Therefore, every person should have within them the strength and thought to purify themselves and to humble themselves in our prayers when they prepare to pray in the Diaspora, so that the Divine Presence <note>original: "שכינ'"; the indwelling presence of God</note> will be worthy to be accepted before the Blessed Creator. I have tasted all his words because I heard many excellent things from his perspective, and it is visible to our eyes from what is written: "But your iniquities have separated between you and your God" <note>Isaiah 59:2</note>. All this applies in the lands of the Diaspora, where the forces of impurity surround the chosen ones. According to his words, there is a great distinction... <margin>The soul of a pious person</margin> what is it for the Great One to do for me, etc. specifically during the time the Temple stood. So it seems to the student from his own mind, though not everything is forced to be accepted as public prayer, as is found in the *Sifrei* <note>An ancient legal commentary on the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy</note> on the portion of Korach... and you shall remember the commentary of **Ramban** <note>Rabbi Moshe ben Nachman, a 13-century scholar</note>, may his memory be a blessing, who would distance [the idea of] who would dare to announce the name of the Blessed Creator... Indeed, the prayer of the public in the synagogues—the matter is not that the Creator accepts every request, rather, a window of opportunity opens for the request and the requester. For every single day there are great ones among us to seek the face of God, and He will entreat them to fulfill [their requests]. And the day they stand in the synagogue and look into it, they lead the prayer... as for this matter, prayer is the service of the heart... just like any other simple path. Regarding the matter of the hearing of the prayer, the Holy One, Blessed be He, is careful with prayer, and the angel of "Kutra" <note>original: "קטרה"; likely referring to the crown of prayer or the angel Sandalphon who weaves crowns for God from prayers</note> sits within the Sanctuary, etc. It is not necessarily that He will answer what one asks, but rather that the Holy One, Blessed be He, receives it... like one who receives all good deeds. A path is open to enter between you and your Tefillin <note>Ritual phylacteries</note> and Mezuzah <note>The scroll on the doorpost</note>... even if he does not see a blessing because of this, nonetheless, the deed is written above and the reward is preserved. So it is with the Tefillin, which in their physical form are elevated above to be given as a crown and a diadem. But for the lower ones who are fixed in their place in the synagogue, in any case, their request—and sometimes they will have peace and health in all their ways—for a complete prayer is like a sacrifice... and the King will send... and everything will be directed toward God and His uniqueness. The prayer of the public is a treasure above. And in the Talmud, tractate Berakhot, chapter "One should not stand," page 32: Rabbi Elazar said, "From the day the Temple was destroyed, the gates of prayer have been locked, as it is said: 'Also when I cry and shout, He shutteth out my prayer' <note>Lamentations 3:8</note>." And afterward **Rashi** <note>The premier medieval commentator</note> explained that although the gates of prayer were locked, the gates of tears were not locked, for it says: "Hear my prayer, O Lord, and give ear unto my cry; hold not Thy peace at my tears" <note>Psalms 39:13</note>. This is what I have tasted from the sages, do not withhold your illness, for it is written that He hears the prayer of the mouth. This means there is no need for anything other than that it be accepted before Him... I found in the Gemara <note>The Talmudic discussions</note> in the chapter beginning "The one who is more careful," that the "tears" mentioned imply that prayer should be seen at all times... and one should pray that it be accepted. And one must understand what the matter of "seeing" is if it is not accepted. Rather, it is like this: if the prayer is worthy, the Holy One, Blessed be He, desires it, meaning it is considered a fulfillment of a positive commandment, even if the Holy One, Blessed be He, hides His eyes from the specific request of the person praying. Nonetheless, the prayer is preserved for the future... and so it is with the prayer of the public.

<column-break/>

The fear of the Lord... for the fear of the daughters of Israel who took it upon themselves that even if they see a drop of blood as small as a mustard seed, they sit [in impurity] for seven clean days <note>A reference to the laws of family purity (Niddah), where Jewish women adopted a stricter standard than the biblical law</note>. **Rava** says... a person who sins... is forced within... his soul to eat... and he passes through the crossing. And afterward, Rav Huna said, Rabbi Zeira said: "One who comes from the synagogue should not enter a house of study to eat... and so it is with the decided laws <note>original: "הלכות פסוקות"; clear, final legal rulings</note> of the Rabbis... and the Braita <note>Teachings from the time of the Mishnah not included in the main text</note> where there is no dispute. The entire chapter... is decided laws. Or perhaps in their days there were not many students. And it seems in my eyes that in the decided laws... regarding the prayer... there are two matters... From the statement of Rabbi Zeira who said "one should not sleep..." regarding the drop of blood like a mustard seed, this was for the purpose of the law, but it was not superfluous in its purpose... I have written above that the wisdom in our time... like a clear explanation... secret and hidden knowledge... one could say this crown belongs to this knowledge. But for every proof that I bring in my mind to Rabbi Ma'as, may his name be exalted, it will be added... and the matter of intention is this: one should direct his heart according to his knowledge and it will be found that nothing is hidden from him... we bring our hearts before Him in supplication and request today to seek His face... and the Holy One, Blessed be He, will accept our hearts as if they were before the innermost chamber... as the **Ra"sh** <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note> wrote in his testament, chapter 146, to pray with intention, and this shall be His will... as it is written: "Commit thy way unto the Lord; trust also in Him, and He shall bring it to pass" <note>Psalms 37:5</note>. And our Rabbis have already replied to him, that in the chapter on Idolatry it says: "A man shall not fill his mouth with laughter in this world"... I bring the words of the **Ra"sh** against those people who have no heart to understand... written on the paper... and so in every letter of the four letters of the Torah <note>Referring to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter Name of God</note>... it is the Lord who is revealed, blessed be His name... hidden things... so one should think... through the lack of his knowledge... nonetheless, in what he understands or blesses, the Holy One, Blessed be He, considers it as if he knew the inner meanings... which are the ten attributes, which are the ten Sefirot <note>The ten emanations of God in Kabbalistic thought</note>, which are His powers, blessed be He, though His essence cannot be known or contemplated even by Himself as He truly is. Regarding the matter of praying with speech: a person should connect with the Great Goodness and Kindness, doing good for the entire congregation... and this is the "Great Good" for Israel... the sages who were in the Diaspora... and the matters are interpreted... the Holy One, Blessed be He, from His nature... so he will find for himself that he speaks with strength... like a son who removes the burden from his father. May the Lord help... according to what our Rabbi wrote... for they are His servants... and certainly there will be a covenant... everything will return to you in peace to the Sanctuary...

->Awakening to the two aforementioned matters from the Rabbis of the community:<-

# Purity
This is a great principle for the Recitation of the Shema, for Prayer, and for all blessings, praises, and study. All the covered places on a person are considered a soiled place because they have traces of sweat; likewise, if one scratches his head, he is obligated to wash his hands. If he stands in the middle of prayer and forgot and touched [a covered place] and cannot go to wash his hands, it is sufficient to clean them with earth or pebbles or by rubbing his hands against a wall. The **Maharal** <note>Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague</note> wrote in the name of the **Rokeach** that a person should not touch the mucus of the nose or the wax of the ear during the time of prayer, since these secretions are called "filth" in the chapter "HaMekabel" <note>A chapter in the Talmudic tractate Bava Metzia</note>. One should be careful with this, and be careful not to beat your flax... in our places, all the secretions of our nose, and no stranger should touch them to throw them to the ground according to custom, and sometimes I took the corner of my cloak and shook it to the ground... **Mahari Segal** <note>The Maharil, a primary source for Ashkenazi custom</note> said regarding one who rises from his study to pray: he must wash his hands and then pray. In the chapter "Three Who Ate" <note>In Berakhot</note> at the end of page 50: If one was eating and brought food into his mouth without a blessing, he should swallow it [if it is not disgusting to spit out]... it says "swallow them in their place" and it says "spit them out." There is no difficulty: one refers to things that are not disgusting, and the other refers to things that are disgusting. For things that are not disgusting, one should move them to one side and bless. The **Rema** <note>Rabbi Moses Isserles</note> cited Rabbi Isaac... in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, because it is said: "Let my mouth be filled with Thy praise" <note>Psalms 71:8</note>. From this it is proven that it is forbidden to leave loose saliva in the mouth at the time one blesses. It appears that all the places of the five organs of speech should be clean. **Rabbi Abraham** wrote that they used to wash their mouths because of the mucus within it, for one must mention the Name.
