<header>The Written Torah – Their Name is Three Camps</header>

There are three from their own perspective, and they are also divided into three types of service: the **Priests** in their service, the **Levites** in their song, and the **Israelites** in their standing <note>original: *ma'amad*—referring to the lay representatives who stood by during the Temple sacrifices</note>. These hint at two conceptual levels. One level is the **Soul, Spirit, and Vital Soul** <note>original: *Neshamah, Ruach, Nefesh*—the three primary levels of the soul in Jewish mysticism</note> according to my explanation, which correspond to the three letters *He-Vav-He* <note>The final three letters of the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter Name of God</note>, and their general manifestation and appearance is in the letter *Yod*, making the full Name *Y-H-V-H*. The second level is that they exist within the secret of the letters *Yod-He-Vav*, which are the root of the line of **Kindness** <note>original: *Chesed*</note> and the line of **Mercy** <note>original: *Rachamim*</note>. It is known that the Priest, Levite, and Israelite correspond to **Kindness, Strength, and Beauty** <note>original: *Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet*—three of the ten *Sefirot* or Divine attributes</note> as written by all the Kabbalists. 

This explains the matter of the **Nazirite**: the commandment comes and says "no razor shall pass over his head," whereas with the **Levites** it is the opposite—"they shall pass a razor over all their flesh." Behold, regarding the Nazirite, the Torah says "the crown <note>original: *nezer*</note> of his God is upon him," just as it is said of the High Priest that the "crown" is upon him, and he is likewise forbidden from contracting ritual impurity from the dead. Since the Priest is from the side of **Kindness**, it follows that the Nazirite’s intention is also from the side of Kindness. His hair hints at the "supernal channels" and the forces of life emanated from the attribute of Kindness; therefore, it is forbidden to destroy them. But the **Levite** is from the side of **Strength** <note>original: *Gevurah*</note>, the forces of **Judgment** <note>original: *Din*</note> from which the "external forces" <note>original: *chitzonim*—referring to demonic or impure energies</note> are stirred to impurity. Therefore, the commandment for them is the opposite: to destroy with a razor and to eliminate the "thorns from the vineyard," for one must eradicate the forces of impurity so they do not take control. Thus, the Priest, Levite, and Israelite also represent Kindness, Strength, and Beauty.

Behold, the center of these camps is the **Ark** containing the Tablets, which hint at the **Name of 72** <note>A mystical name of God composed of 72 three-letter units derived from Exodus 14:19-21</note>, which consists of 72 triple-word units totaling **216** letters <note>original: *Riyu*—the numerical value of 216</note>, as is known. These are the verses: "And he traveled," "and he came," "and he stretched out" <note>Exodus 14:19-21</note>. Likewise, the Tablets were six handbreadths long, six handbreadths wide, and six handbreadths high; thus they are **216** handbreadths in volume. It is explained in the *Zohar* (Portion *Beshalach*, page 52a) that the essence of the Name of 72 is in **Kindness**, and indeed the word "Kindness" <note>original: *Chesed*</note> has the numerical value of 72. Nevertheless, it includes Kindness, Strength, and Beauty, and I have elaborated on this in the *Gate of Specific Names*, chapter five; see there. 

Furthermore, you will find the Name of 72 hinted at in the **Levites**, as it is written: "And they shall be Mine" <note>original: *Ve-hayu Li*</note>. The letters of *Ve-hayu Li-m* <note>a play on the word *Leviyim*</note> are the first two names from the Name of 72. When "72" <note>the Divine Name</note> is joined with "Israel," it equals **613** <note>72 + 541 (Israel) = 613, the number of commandments</note>, corresponding to the entire Torah. Thus the three camps of Priest, Levite, and Israelite, which are three triangles, surrounded their center—the Tablets. These were 14 in their filling <note>a complex gematria calculation involving the letter *Yod* and the name *EHYEH*</note>, totaling **216**; go and calculate. 

From what I have written regarding the Priest, Levite, and Israelite, they hint at two matters: first, the **Vital Soul, Spirit, and Soul** (the letters *He-Vav-He* of Kindness); and second, they hint at the line of **Kindness, Strength, and Beauty** (which are the letters *Yod-He-Vav*). At first glance, the letters *He-Vav-He* and Kindness correspond to the letter *Yod*, and the letters *Yod-He-Vav* and Kindness to the final *He*. However, this will be clarified...

All of this will be explained when I present the matter of the **Four Flags** mentioned by the Kabbalists—what was written on each and every flag. It will also clarify the matter of the **Name of 72** which was inscribed on the flags, as well as the progression of the three worlds of **Creation, Formation, and Action** <note>original: *Beri'ah, Yetzirah, Asiyah*</note>, which are the four "Living Creatures" <note>original: *Chayot*</note> that carry the Throne, the camps of the Divine Presence, and the four elements. 

**Nachmanides** <note>Rabbi Moshe ben Nachman, 13th-century scholar</note> wrote that on the **Flag of Judah** was the form of a **Lion**, based on "Judah is a lion's whelp." On the **Flag of Reuben** was the form of a **Man**, based on the "mandrakes" <note>which Reuben found, and which look like human figures</note>. On the **Flag of Ephraim** was an **Ox**, based on "his firstling bullock, majesty is his." On the **Flag of Dan** was a **Serpent** <note>as the verse says, "Dan shall be a serpent"</note>, though some drawings show an **Eagle**, based on "as an eagle stirs up its nest." The tribe of Dan was the "gatherer of all the camps," and it was similar and hinted at this, even though we find in the *Targum Yonatan* <note>An Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Torah</note> that says the form on Dan's flag was a serpent. I found in the *Tziyuni* <note>A 14th-century Kabbalistic commentary by Menahem Tziyuni</note> in another place that the Kabbalist wrote: they wrote that there were 80 forms of a serpent, hinting at his place, as it is said, "Dan shall be a serpent." And the wings were the wings of an **Eagle**, which indicate his mercies, as it is said, "an eagle stirs up its nest." 

Thus, the four "Living Creatures" that carry the Throne were depicted on the flags. Also, the four flags hinted at the four camps of the **Divine Presence** <note>original: *Shekhinah*</note> and the four elements in the four directions, as explained at length in the *Zohar*. This was also brought by the **Recanati** <note>Rabbi Menahem Recanati, 14th-century Italian Kabbalist</note>. Here are the words of the Recanati in brief: the four flags correspond to the four elements, the four camps of the Shekhinah, and the four Living Creatures that carry the Chariot. When we ascend even higher, all of these correspond to the four attributes: **Kindness, Strength, Beauty, and Kingship** <note>original: *Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Malchut*</note>. 

The four elements below correspond to the high levels of the Archangels: **Michael, Gabriel, Uriel, and Raphael**. 
*   **Michael** is the element of **Water** and unites with the Supernal Waters, the "Waters of Kindness," for he is the Righteous Priest of the Above who atones, because "by kindness is iniquity atoned"; therefore, he is on the **Right**. 
*   **Gabriel** corresponds to the element of the **Great Fire**, and therefore he is on the **Left**, and he is the "Prince of the Host" Above. 
*   **Uriel** is in front of him, corresponding to the element of **Air** <note>original: *Ruach*—spirit/wind/air</note>, and from there light goes out to the world, for he is in the **East**. 
*   **Raphael** is in the **West**, corresponding to the element of **Earth**, and the Sages said he is appointed over the "Earth that Heals" because of the Throne of Glory which is called "Prime Matter" <note>original: *Chomer Rishon*</note>. End of quote. 

I will further copy the language of the *Tziyuni*, and everything I have written will be clarified: The Four Flags are a tradition passed from man to man back to Moses our Teacher, peace be upon him. 
*   The **Flag of Reuben** had the drawing of a **Man**; engraved on it were three letters from the Patriarchs of the world: *Bet* from Abraham, *Tzadi* from Isaac, and *Ayin* from Jacob <note>these letters form the word *Etz*, Tree</note>. These letters were from the Shekhinah, along with three permutations of the Name: *H-V-Y*, *Y-H-V-H*, and *Y-H-V*. 
*   On the **Flag of Judah** was the form of a **Lion**, with the letters *Aleph, Yod, Gimel* from the Patriarchs, and three permutations of the Names *Y-V-D*, *H-Y*, and *Y-H-V-D*. 
*   The **Flag of Ephraim** had the form of an **Ox**, with three letters from the three Patriarchs *Aleph, He, Kof*, and three permutations of the names *Y-H-V-H*, *Y-H-V*, and *Y-H-V*. 
*   The **Flag of Dan** had the form of an **Eagle**, with three letters from the three Patriarchs *Mem, Kof, Bet*—*Mem* from Abraham, *Kof* from Isaac, and *Bet* from Jacob—and three permutations of the Name *H-V-Y-H*, *H-Y*, and *Y-H-V-D*. 

In the rest of the four from Abraham... God added... and the rest of the ten from His Name, making it the Name through which the world was created. The Holy One, Blessed be He, established pillars above and a matter below from the Ark, and so on. Two clouds were engraved with two letters, and when the time came to move the camps, the pillar in which the Holy Name was fixed would move from above the Ark, and four clouds of glory would move... end of the *Tziyuni's* words.

### And I

say that according to the abundance of these letters *He* and *Vav*, the letters *H-V-H* and *Y-H-V* were doubled, which seemingly lacked the letter *Yod* as I mentioned above. Regarding the letters *Y-H-V* that were additional permutations beyond the three permutations of the Name *Havayah* <note>another way of referring to the Name YHVH</note>—there were three permutations on each and every flag corresponding to the three tribes in each flag. This hints at the verse: "Where the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord <note>original: *Ya-h*</note>..." 

The matter of these permutations of the Name *Havayah* on each flag adds up to the **Name of 72**, as seen in the *Sefer HaBahir* <note>An early Kabbalistic text</note> and cited in the *Pardes* <note>the *Pardes Rimonim* by Rabbi Moshe Cordovero</note>: Rabbi Amyurai sat and expounded, "What is written: 'Behold, the heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain You'? This teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He, has 72 names, and they are all fixed in the 72... as it is written 'six of their names on one stone and the six remaining names on the second stone.' And it is written 'these twelve stones'... but these stones are 'stones of remembrance' for the heavens. Ten stones are 72, corresponding to the 72 Names of the Holy One, Blessed be He." Why did it begin with twelve? To teach you that twelve <note>unclear textual reference to *Chagigah*</note> hold... and God has... 28 and a half names. The explanation of the statement there in the *Pardes* is that the general sum of the 12 stones was "according to the names of the children of Israel," and each stone included six, and six times twelve is 72. 

He brought proof because the verse equated them—it appears that just as on these stones there are six names, so too among the Israelites, each one has six names, for they are the 72 Names of the Holy One, Blessed be He. All of this accounts for the **Ark** containing the Tablets, which was **216** handbreadths in volume <note>72 x 3 = 216</note>, and everything revolves around the Name *Y-V-D-D*. For "the Torah of the Lord <note>Y-V-D-D</note> is perfect," meaning the entire Torah flows from the Name *Y-V-D-D*, and from the Name *Y-V-D-D* comes the Name of 72 in three aspects: 
1.  **Frontal:** Namely, the spelling out of *Y-V-D* in its filling... which equals 72. 
2.  **Rearward:** Namely, *Y, Y-H, Y-H-V, Y-H-V-H*, which also equals 72. 
3.  **Permutation:** Namely, the twelve permutations, each from six forces, which also equals 72. 

Thus, the Name of 72 emerges three times from the Name *Y-V-D-D*. It was inscribed on the four flags in the secret of the permutation. Thus the matters of three and four have been explained at length, and everything goes to one place. These are the two letters *Shin* on the **Tephillin** <note>Phylacteries worn during prayer; the head-tephillin has a 3-headed and a 4-headed letter Shin</note>. Also, the essence of the Tephillin is to be twelve. The Tephillin are a Sanctuary. 

What I have written is the general way. Specifically, the portions of **Numbers (Bamidbar)**, **Naso**, and **Behaalotecha** will be explained according to the three camps and the three parts: Priest, Levite, and Israelite, representing Soul, Spirit, and Vital Soul. 
*   Portion **Bamidbar** hints at the **Camp of the Divine Presence**, where the parts of the **Soul** <note>original: *Neshamah*</note> reside. 
*   Portion **Naso** hints at the **Camp of the Levites**, the part of the **Spirit** <note>original: *Ruach*</note>. 
*   Portion **Behaalotecha** hints at the **Camp of Israel**, the part of the **Vital Soul** <note>original: *Nefesh*</note>. 
Each will be explained in its place with the help of God.

# Bamidbar Sinai (In the Wilderness of Sinai)

This book is called the "Book of the Census" <note>original: *Chumash HaPikudim*</note> because of the counting of Israel. From this, we understand that this counting is significant and should never be counted casually. Our Sages, of blessed memory, said that this counting was in order to cause the **Divine Presence** to dwell among Israel. Therefore, I say that this portion among the portions corresponds to the **Camp of the Divine Presence**. The name of the Camp of the Divine Presence is aligned with that which is Above, as our Sages said: "The Sanctuary below is aligned with the Sanctuary Above." 

Behold, in this portion, the census of Israel and the Levites is mentioned, as well as their placement in their spots. In the Camp of the Levites, only the census of the Kohathites was mentioned, for in the Camp of the Divine Presence, the Priests were there. The census of the sons of Kohath is also the appointment of the Priests in carrying the Ark. Our Sages said that in all places the Priests came—at the Jordan, and in the conquest of Jericho, and when they returned it to its place—see the Radak <note>Rabbi David Kimhi, 12th-13th century commentator</note> and some say...

# Written Torah

...the land, etc. "Woe to a sinful nation." <note>Isaiah 1:4</note> And what is written after it? "Come now, and let us reason together." <note>Isaiah 1:18</note> "Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean," etc. To what can this be compared? To a king’s son whose father told him, "Go to school." He went to the [study hall] <note>original: "ללשון"; likely a transcription error for 'the chamber' or 'to study'</note> and began playing with the youths. When his father realized he had not gone to school, he cursed him and made him hear harsh words. Afterward, he said to him, "Wash your hands and come dine with me." So Isaiah says, "I have nourished and brought up children," etc. <note>Isaiah 1:2</note> And when he finishes the entire matter, what does he say? "Come now, and let us reason together."

Similarly with Jeremiah: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: "What do you see, Jeremiah?" and he said, "A rod of an almond tree," etc. <note>Jeremiah 1:11</note> "A seething pot... out of the north the evil shall break forth." <note>Jeremiah 1:13-14</note> And what follows all this? "Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem," etc. "Israel is holy to the Lord," etc. <note>Jeremiah 2:2-3</note> This is a parable of a king who took a wife. He would say, "None is as beautiful as she, none as praised as she, none as settled as she." Her groomsman entered the house and saw her neglected—the house was not organized, the beds were not made. The groomsman said to her, "If only you could hear how your husband praises you in the marketplace! You do not [deserve] this praise based on these actions." The groomsman then said, "If he praises her like this when she is neglected, how much more so if she were prepared!" So it was with the generation of Jeremiah; they were sinning, yet He says to them, "I remember for you the kindness of your youth," etc. Jeremiah said to them, "If only you would hear what He says to you: 'Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem... I remember for you the kindness of your youth... Israel is holy,'" etc. He said, "If He loves them so much at the hour they are sinning, how much more so when they do His will!" Here it says, "For you are not My people," etc., and what follows it? "And it shall be in the place [where it was said to them 'You are not My people,' there it shall be said to them 'You are the sons of the living God']." <note>Hosea 1:9-10</note> These are the words of the teacher.

In general, suffering is for the purpose of love; therefore, the time of anger is also a time of favor. There are three parables corresponding to the three "perfections" <note>The Talmud mentions three things that expand a person's mind: a beautiful home, beautiful vessels, and a beautiful wife.</note>: a beautiful dwelling, beautiful vessels, and a beautiful wife, which I have written about in another <term>derush<gloss>homiletic teaching</gloss></term> in the name of the *Divrei Chaim*. A beautiful dwelling is the Heart; beautiful vessels are the tools of action [the limbs]; a beautiful wife is the Soul. According to the Arizal, <note>Rabbi Isaac Luria, the great Kabbalist.</note> this is hinted at in the verse "You turn man to contrition" <note>Psalm 90:3</note> for the first letters of the Hebrew words for **Dwelling** (*Dirah*), **Vessels** (*Kelim*), and **Wife** (*Ishah*) form the acronym "Contrition" (*Daka*).

And behold, in the first parable [the school], it refers to the "vessels." In the second parable, "Go to school" refers to the [dwelling]. The third parable refers to the "wife." And the "guarded house" is the human body (as I have written). <unclear>Until the keepers of the house do not tremble</unclear>... in the name of the "beauty of the song" of man's life... "and on the earth you shall sleep," <note>Ethics of the Fathers 6:4</note> a hint that he should remember everything on the earth and live. And then the first Midrash comes together: in the desert, like the Tent of Meeting. It spoke of the Tent of Meeting, of His children, and of their rebuke, according to the secret of "And the Lord called to Moses and spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting," which the Zohar explains as "He spoke a little from the Tent of Meeting." From this shall be his end. It is written "And He called," and it is written there "And the Lord God of Hosts called on that day [to weeping and mourning]," etc. <note>Isaiah 22:12</note> And it became a desolate wilderness. And he hinted that in his lifting up <unclear>at evening</unclear>... for everything goes to one place... the daughter of Zion in the future. And he wrote "all" as a hint to the two aforementioned matters as we explained. 

And he hinted at a great wonder regarding the dispute between Rabbi Yohanan and Resh Lakish: "Whoever's way it is to count years" and "Whoever's way it is to count years." <note>A Talmudic debate regarding chronological reckoning.</note> This hints at the count that they disagreed upon, and "these and those are the words of the living God." For you are <unclear>neck</unclear>... and he preceded "all" to "you." And with this, he answers what I have not written... even though I love My people and you are in a low state, let it not enter your minds that I love you more [than others] only for your own good to finish your sin. "And I have likened you to Me," for I am with you in your distress. And in the future, it is written "On that day," etc. So you, in the future, your name and My name shall grow together. And he brought in this Midrash the verse "Yours, O Lord, is the greatness," <note>1 Chronicles 29:11</note> for in the banners [of the tribes] there was the Name... and the Holy One, blessed be He, in the exile took the extra letters *Vav* and *He* [from the Tetragrammaton], as it is written "Hand on the Throne of God," <note>Exodus 17:16, where 'Throne' and 'God' are spelled defectively, missing letters.</note> and the Holy One, blessed be He, placed them in His "foot" (*Regel*). And this is "The Greatness" (*HaGedulah*), the letters of which can be rearranged to spell *Regel* (Foot) plus *Vav* and *He*. And in the future, He will return them, and also the hidden *Aleph* from the Throne, and fulfill the promise to join them. "Stone" refers to the Head and our Source. And we shall keep [the name], which are the letters *Regel*, *Vav*, *He*, *Aleph*...

Pharaoh's spirit... as we elaborated elsewhere.)

### Take a census of the sons of Gershon, etc.

This portion corresponds to the camp of the Levites. For although He placed the charge of Kohath in the portion of *Bamidbar*, because the Kohathites are the ones who carry the Ark—which is also the burden of the Priests, and therefore they are considered within the honor of the Divine Presence—nonetheless, in the portion of *Naso*, everything belongs to the camp of the Levites. It begins with Gershon, who is the firstborn. And [the text says] "They too," etc., for all Levites are meant to be in place of the firstborns.

In Midrash Rabbah, it says: "She [the Torah] is more precious than pearls" <note>Proverbs 3:15</note>—this refers to Kohath and Gershon. Even though Gershon was the firstborn, and we find everywhere that the Torah accords honor to the firstborn, because [Kohath] carried the Ark where the Torah resides, the Torah placed him before Gershon. In the census, it says, "Take the sum of the sons of Kohath," and afterward, "Take the sum of the sons of Gershon," etc. This is because "She is more precious than pearls," and "pearls" (*peninim*) refers to the "inner" (*pnim*) or "prior" (*lifnim*) things of Israel, etc.

### Further

The language of the Midrash: "If a man should ask: Was not Gershon the firstborn? Why then did the Torah precede Kohath in taking the census, and only afterward count Gershon?" You should answer him: Because Kohath was among those who carry the Ark, which is the Holy of Holies, and from him came Aaron the Priest, who is the Holy of Holies... therefore the Torah sanctified Kohath first. And from where do you learn that Gershon did not lose his greatness? Because he was the firstborn, for you find that just as it said regarding Kohath "Take the sum [Naso]," it also said regarding Gershon "Take the sum [Naso]." And when the verse says "They too," it is so you should not say that the reason He counted the sons of Gershon second was because they are of less status than the sons of Kohath.

It seems that this phrase "And from him came Aaron the Priest" mentioned in the Midrash is an answer intended to resolve an additional difficulty beyond the one about Kohath carrying the Ark. The difficulty itself is: Why was Gershon, the firstborn, not among those who carried the Ark? To this, he answered that because Aaron the Priest came from [Kohath], and he is the Holy of Holies and the Ark is the Holy of Holies [they belong together]. We should not find the Midrash's language too brief when it says Kohath preceded Gershon because Aaron came from him, as it might seem difficult to suggest the lineage of the fathers gives way to the sons. Therefore, he had to answer that Kohath [was chosen] for the sake of the holy service of carrying the Ark, and this matter of carrying the Ark had to belong to Kohath specifically because Aaron, who is a Priest, came from him. And since the carrying of the Ark was shared by the Levites and the Priests, they [the Midrash] ask why it mentions Aaron and not Moses, who also came from Kohath and was greater than Aaron. [The answer is] because Moses' sons are called by the name of the tribe [of Levi], but here there was a need for a partnership in carrying the Ark between Priest and Levite; therefore, it mentions Aaron.

### And Since

this Midrash has come to my hand, I will explain it. Behold, by the power of this Midrash, several difficulties in the verses are resolved:
1. In the census of Kohath, it mentions Moses and Aaron, but in the census of Gershon, only Moses is mentioned, and for Merari, neither is mentioned.
2. Why use the term "Naso" <note>Literally "lift up," used for "take a census."</note>? (And the term "Naso," used for the firstborn, was not used for Merari... [this is explained elsewhere]).
3. Why the change in the phrase "by their fathers' houses, by their families"? For Kohath, it says "by their families, by their fathers' houses."

Based on the aforementioned Midrash, all is resolved. In the census of Kohath, Aaron is also mentioned because he was relevant to it, as it says "and from him came Aaron." For Gershon, Aaron is not mentioned. Moses is mentioned for the greatness of Gershon, as it says "They too," etc., and therefore the term "Naso" (lifting up) is used. It says "by their fathers' houses" [first] because the greatness of the "father's house" belongs to Gershon, as he is the firstborn. But for Kohath, it precedes "by their families" because of the family from which Aaron came. And for the sons of Merari, it is written "by their families, by their fathers' houses"—the family is more important than the father's house because Merari was the youngest and the poorest of them; their "family" [status] comes from [the general Levite connection to] Kohath the Ark-bearer and Gershon the firstborn.

And I have already written that Gershon, as the firstborn, represents all the Levites who were given in place of the firstborns of Israel. Therefore, we find written concerning the Levites the phrasing "by their fathers' houses, by their families," just as it is written by Gershon. For so it is written in the portion of *Bamidbar*: "Number the children of Levi by their fathers' houses, by their families." And regarding the matter of the Torah upholding the birthright, he brought the verse "She is more precious than pearls" and interpreted "pearls" (*peninim*) as "inner faces" (*panim bifnim*)... and on this there is a difficulty... from where do we know Gershon did not lose his greatness? Because he is the firstborn. But the end of the passage contradicts the beginning, which said Kohath was preceded so he could carry the Ark!

However, the matter is an "inner" one, referring to the "double" [nature of the soul]. It is as if "Face" (*Panim*) were written twice. The reason for this is for the sake of Man, so that he may acquire the Torah, as I mentioned above regarding the concept of "Let us make Man." And "Man" (*Adam*) is the firstborn of all humanity because he was the first. And behold, Israel are called "Man." Therefore they are called "Sons," as it is written "Israel is My son, My firstborn." However, this birthright preceded the Levites over the Israelites, because they are in the aspect of the "Spirit of Man that ascends," while Israel is the Soul...

# The Written Torah: Three Camps

Regarding the matter of Jerusalem, of which the Sages said that no man ever spent the night in Jerusalem with a sin in his hand <note>original: "לא לן אדם בירושלים וחטא בידו" — a traditional teaching that the daily sacrifices in the Temple atoned for sins every day</note>. For "Righteousness lodged in her," meaning a judgment of righteousness. The Holy One, blessed be He, collects the debt [of sin] little by little in order to sustain the people, as it is written: "You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will visit upon you all your iniquities" <note>Amos 3:2; the idea is that God punishes Israel in small increments to prevent their total destruction</note>.

**And before** the granting of the World to Come, the Blessed Name precedes it for us with the suffering of the three exiles. Then we shall merit the light, and "He will no longer exile you." As found in the Midrash Rabbah on the portion of *Lech Lecha*, our father Abraham chose exile so that Israel would be saved from Gehenna <note>Hell or purgatory</note> and merit the World to Come. Suffering cleanses, and according to their spiritual ascent, they merit to see their world even while in this life. However, one must question the repetitive language used in the teaching that "three gifts were given to Israel through suffering" <note>Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come</note>. Rather, it should be understood through a secret we have heard: that these three good gifts are "doubled," and the goodness is twofold in each of them. 

First, I will preface that there is a distinction between the word "good" spelled with a *Cholam* <term>Cholam: a Hebrew vowel mark producing an "oh" sound, as in *tov*</term> and "good" spelled with a *Shuruk*, which some call *Melupim* <term>Melupim/Shuruk: a Hebrew vowel mark producing an "oo" sound, as in *tuv*</term>. For "good" with a *Cholam* indicates revealed goodness, but "good" with a *Melupim* indicates its inner essence—the essential goodness within it which is hidden. 

We find this in all three gifts: 
Regarding **Torah**, it is written "The law of Your mouth is **good** (*tov*) to me" with a *Cholam*. Yet it is also written, "Teach me **good** (*tuv*) taste and knowledge" with a *Melupim*. 
Regarding the **Land of Israel**, it is written "A **good** (*tova*) land" with a *Cholam*. Yet it is also written, "If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the **good** (*tuv*) of the land" with a *Melupim*. 
Regarding the **World to Come**, our Sages of blessed memory said it is "A world that is entirely **good** (*tov*)." This implies a difficulty for the Sages: why call it "good" with a *Cholam*? They answered that then there will be no distinction between revealed and hidden; rather, everything will be revealed goodness, just like the hidden essence. In this world, the "good" (*tuv*) with a *Melupim* is hidden; it is the internal essence, the "hidden light," and those who seek to ascend must search for it. But in the World to Come, it will be a revealed reality before all people, for it will be a world that is "entirely good." 

The matter of these three is the power of their revealed "good" (*tov*) and their hidden "goodness" (*tuv*). In **Torah**, the "good" (*tov*) is the revealed part—the fulfillment of physical commandments. The "goodness" (*tuv*) is the knowledge of the secrets. In the future, everything will be spiritual and "entirely good." In the **Land of Israel**, the "good land" is the revealed holiness of the physical Temple. The "goodness of the land" (*tuv ha-aretz*) is the Upper Land of Israel and the Upper Temple, to which the physical corresponds. In the future, it will be "entirely good" and fully spiritual, for the Holy One will bring down a Temple from above to below. Regarding the **World to Come**, there is a Lower Garden of Eden and an Upper Garden of Eden, which is more spiritual; these represent the two types of "good." But for eternity, the World to Come will be an "entirely good" eternity. I have already elaborated on this elsewhere.

**And upon this** the portion is explained: "And Moses said to Hovab the son of Reuel... We are journeying to the place of which the Lord said..." He hinted to him these two kinds of "good." He hinted that they were not traveling to the revealed place alone—the "good land"—but rather "we are journeying" toward the place promised by the Lord. This refers to the place hinted at in the portion of *Mishpatim*: "to bring you to the place which I have prepared," which Rashi explains refers to the Upper Temple that corresponds to the Lower Temple. "Come with us, and we will do you good." Moses said that "the Lord has spoken good concerning Israel" alone, and not the pious of the nations, but through your attachment to us, that goodness will be drawn upon you. The matter is as it is written: "The place, O Lord, which You have made for Your dwelling"—hinting at the Upper Temple. And "The Sanctuary, O Lord, which Your hands have established." 

The matter of "hands" refers to the higher hints of the ten fingers of the hands, which represent the Ten Sefirot <term>Sefirot: the ten creative attributes or emanations through which God interacts with the universe</term> as taught in the *Sefer Yetzirah* regarding the covenant. And behold, there are ten toes on the feet, which is a lower level than the fingers. I have written elsewhere that this is hinted at in the verse: "Yea, He loved (*chovev*) the people; all His holy ones are in Your hand." Even when God has love for the nations—meaning the pious among them—there is still a distinction between them and Israel. For the holy ones of Israel are attached to "Your hand"—the ten fingers of the hand. But the nations are related to the ten toes of the feet. This is why Jethro is called "Hovab" here, hinting at the verse "Yea, He loved (*chovev*)." Moses hinted to him that by attaching himself to us, "we will do you good"—you will be like us. Moses needed to give this promise because "the Lord has spoken good" specifically for the benefit of Israel.

"And he said to him: I will not go..." Jethro did not desire the words of Moses, our teacher, peace be upon him, as he thought Moses was speaking only of the literal, physical Land of Israel. He said to him: "Return to your land," for the Lord spoke good only concerning Israel—meaning, from the perspective of strict law, He does not provide this specific good to others, and converts have no portion in it, but "we [Israel] will do good to you." To this Jethro replied, "I will not go [with you], but to my own land," for I do not need your "goodness," as I have a land like yours. And if it is for the sake of the commandments dependent on the Land, "one who is occupied with a commandment is exempt from [another] commandment," for "I will go to my birthplace" to convert my family, as Rashi explains on the verse "And he went his way to his own land."

Then Moses said, "Please do not [leave us]." Moses was very humble, and he recognized the benefit Jethro brought. He saw that Jethro had not understood his words and said: turn back from this path of thinking, for "it is for this reason" <note>original: "על כן" — a play on the biblical text "forasmuch as" or "because"</note> that I spoke. "Inasmuch as you know our encampment in the wilderness"—that we had three banners hinting at the three camps, which is the seal of those who surround the Throne of Glory. You saw that the Divine Presence <note>Shekhinah</note> corresponds to the upper realm. So too is your hint regarding the Eternal House <note>The Temple</note>, that the Lower Temple corresponds to the Upper one which "His hands established." "And you shall be to us as eyes"—this hints at spiritual attachment, as the Sages said: "To see and be seen"—just as one comes to see, so he comes to be seen. This attachment is the "eyes." You have been among us and you have seen. 

After Moses hinted at the intent of his first words, he added more regarding the eternal goodness which is "entirely good." This is why he said, "If you go with us..." Previously he said "atnu" <note>meaning "near us" or "with us"</note> but here he uses the term "immanu" <note>a deeper form of "with us"</note>. For "immanu" implies a greater attachment and unity than "atnu." "Atnu" comes from the language of "we" (*anachnu*), hinting at a plurality—the attachment of many together. But "immanu" is an essential and literal unification, meaning a spiritual unity where in the future we will be one with that hidden, stored-away goodness which is entirely good, and "we will do good to you."

Now, this first journey was on the condition of entering the Land. But they corrupted their way, similar to the sin of Adam who sinned through eating. So too, "they craved a craving" and said, "Who will feed us [meat]?" Just as the Serpent came to the woman to incite her and separate her from her source, here the "Satan of the nation" gathered them. The letters of "they roamed" (*shotu*) are the same as "Satan" <note>The author is playing with the Hebrew letters of the words</note>. The "table" of eating, which ought to be "the table before the Lord," was turned into a "serpent" (*nachash*) that incites and rebels. I have elaborated on this in the book *Ma'or* regarding the holiness of eating under the letter *Kuf* for *Kedushah* <note>Holiness</note>; see there at length. It says, "The meat was still between their teeth, before it was chewed, and the anger of the Lord..." 

Behold, the world stands upon Torah and upon Service <note>Sacrificial service or prayer</note>. I found in the secrets of the *Rokeach* <note>Eleazar of Worms, a 12th-13th century scholar</note> written on the Song of Songs regarding a verse that appears twice with slight variations: "Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes... all of them bearing twins" and "Your teeth are like a flock of ewes... all of them bearing twins." This verse hints at the Service and the Torah. For our Sages said that the Holy One said to Abraham, when he asked "How shall I know [that I will inherit the land]?": "In the merit of the sacrifices." Abraham asked, "That is fine when the Temple stands, but when the Temple does not stand, what will happen?" God replied, "Let them occupy themselves with the portions of the sacrifices," which is the Service. 

It is a received tradition that a person has 32 teeth—16 above and 16 below. "Your teeth are like a flock of ewes" hints at the 16 sheep [sacrificed] every single week: two daily lambs (one morning, one evening) times seven days, plus two lambs for the Sabbath—totaling 16. "Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes" refers to the reading of the Torah. The "shorn flock" in each week is 17 <note>Perhaps referring to the number of people called to the Torah or specific verses</note>. Therefore, a man must prepare his teeth in holiness, meaning through the "Service," and this is why it says the owners are atoned for [through the sacrifice]. Regarding Torah, eating is also good so that one may be healthy and strong to study Torah. But those who sinned, "the meat was still between their teeth..." and their death was their atonement.

**And Moses began** to sin? <note>This likely refers to a difficult passage or a specific interpretation of Moses' role in the incident of the spies or the complainers</note> ... the matter of the journey to the Land of Israel was meant to be led by Moses, and then it would have been like the Garden of the Lord, but they were driven out just as Adam was driven out... this is the connection to the prophecy of Eldad and Medad that "Moses dies and Joshua brings them in."

<margin>For seemingly it is difficult: what connection did this prophecy have to this event?</margin>

<margin>And the matter is somewhat verified by the appointment of the seventy elders, with Moses and Aaron over them, corresponding to the Name of 72 [letters]... "The world is built on kindness." And so it was always the practice, seventy [elders]... I have written regarding the Sanhedrin...</margin>

# Written Torah: The Three Camps

There were beginnings for the three types of death in the world, regarding which it is said, "her feet go down to death." Therefore, Moses said: "Kill me at once" <note>Numbers 11:15</note>, and immediately it says: "The Lord said to Moses: Gather for Me seventy men," etc. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: "You request death every time? Behold, I will draw from the spirit [that is upon you]..." At that moment, Moses knew he would die and not enter the Land, for Eldad and Medad <note>two elders who prophesied in the camp</note> prophesied about this. From here we learn that a person should never curse themselves, for many angels are appointed and waiting for such a moment when a person curses themselves. 

Even though Moses did not immediately face the end because of this, his words had an effect. In the account of the construction of the Tabernacle, Moses' name is not mentioned as Aaron and the princes are mentioned for the dedication of the Altar. This is because he said, "And if not, erase me, please, from Your book" <note>Exodus 32:32, when Moses pleaded for Israel after the Golden Calf</note>. He was punished by having his name erased from a portion of the Tabernacle's description. King David (peace be upon him) also spoke of this: "I said, I will guard my ways from sinning with my tongue; I will keep a muzzle on my mouth while the wicked is before me" <note>Psalm 39:2</note>. This means: while that appointed angel is waiting to answer "Amen" to my self-curse and stands before me to harm me, I will place a muzzle on my mouth so as not to curse myself. Moses was not careful in this, saying "Kill me at once" and "Erase me from Your book." 

Particularly now, when his curse was for his own sake—because he did not want to carry the entire burden of the people alone—his curse was accepted above and he was punished. However, at the time he said "Erase me," his curse was for the sake of all Israel, praying for them regarding the Golden Calf; therefore, he was not punished with actual death then. Nevertheless, his words did not return empty, as he was erased from the portion describing the Tabernacle. This is why Eldad and Medad remained in the camp and said: "Moses will die and Joshua will bring Israel into the Land." Because of this, Joshua came to Moses and said: "My lord Moses, forbid them!" <note>Numbers 11:28</note>. He meant: prevent these words from their mouths so they do not prophesy this. The word "forbid" (*kela'am*) is like "the rain was restrained" (*vayikaleh*)—a literal prevention. But Moses did not seek to prevent them from speaking, saying: "Are you jealous for my sake?" 

**Until** it comes out of your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you: See how far the punishment of those who crave physical desires reaches! Therefore, a person should distance themselves from luxuries and suffice with the minimum, as Jacob said: "And give me bread to eat and clothes to wear" <note>Genesis 28:20</note>. I have expanded on this under the letters *Kuf* and *Kuf Kadima*.

**And the man** Moses was very humble, more than any human: See how great the attribute of humility is! Behold, Moses our Teacher, the choice of all creations and the master of prophets, was praised by Scripture only for his humility. One must pursue humility to the furthest extreme, as we have learned: "Be exceedingly, exceedingly humble of spirit." The text says "more than any human," for there were three humble men: Moses and Aaron said, "What are we?" <note>Exodus 16:8</note>; our father Abraham said, "I am dust and ashes"; and King David (peace be upon him) said, "I am a worm." 
<margin>According to the secret wisdom: *Abraham*, David, *Moses*. I have already mentioned this elsewhere.</margin>
Moses was the humblest of all, for Abraham compared himself to dust and ashes, and David to a worm, but Moses said: "We are nothing at all." This is the meaning of "more than any human" (*Adam*). <note>The Hebrew word "Adam" can be read as an acronym for Adam, David, and Moses, suggesting a lineage of humility.</note>

**And the anger** of the Lord burned against them, and He departed: It is difficult to understand why there was anger only after the Holy One had already spoken to them. It should have written of the anger beforehand. It can be explained that the anger flared because they hesitated to confess their sin and say, "We have sinned." Contrast this with David: when Nathan the Prophet came to him, he immediately confessed and said, "I have sinned," and the prophet told him, "The Lord has also removed your sin."

**And behold**, Miriam was leprous, white as snow: See how far the punishment for gossip (*Lashon Hara*) reaches! Look at what happened to Miriam the Prophetess for a slight conversation she had regarding Moses her brother. Thus the verse says: "Remember what the Lord your God did to Miriam on the way as you came out of Egypt."

**And the people** did not travel until Miriam was gathered in: They showed her great honor. We can learn from here that one who sees a Torah scholar or a righteous person who is stricken, suffering, or lowly, should treat them with even greater honor. For "whom the Lord loves, He rebukes." It is not like in these current generations, due to our many sins, where a scholar who is poor and lowly is despised by people. Woe to them for the insult to the Torah! One who fears the word of the Lord will treat such a person with honor, beauty, and as a crown.

# Blessed are You, O Lord, who has no equal and none besides You, for helping me complete
## Numbers: Naso and Behaalotecha
### Portion of Shlach Lecha
#### This is His name by which He is called; remember it, for the Lord is He who gives strength for valor.

---

**Lamp of Commandment** <term>Ner Mitzvah: The legal and moral requirements of the commandments.</term>
(385) To separate the *Challah* <note>a portion of dough given to the Priests</note>. (386) That they shall make *Tzitzit* <note>ritual fringes</note> on the corners of their garments. And not to follow the straying of the heart and the sight of the eyes, as it is said: "That you do not go about after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you use to go astray." The meaning of this prohibition is that we should not allow our thoughts to wander into contemplations that are the opposite of the knowledge upon which the Torah is built, for one might come to heresy. If a spirit rises in his heart to think those empty thoughts, he should cut his thinking short and return to the true and good paths of the Torah. Likewise, a person should not chase after what his eyes see, which includes not pursuing the lusts of this world, for after them comes evil, shame, and wrath. This is what our Sages said: "After your heart—this refers to heresy; and after your eyes—this refers to lustful thoughts," as it is said of Samson, "Take her for me, for she is right in my eyes."

**Light of Torah** <term>Torah Or: The inner spiritual and mystical meaning of the commandments.</term>
These commandments are the refinement and purification of the soul and body. Regarding *Challah*, it is written: "For not by bread alone does man live, but by everything that comes from the mouth of the Lord." I have elaborated elsewhere in the name of the Ari <note>Rabbi Isaac Luria, the great Kabbalist</note> on this verse. Philosophers have investigated how physical food can cause the soul to remain attached to the body, since the soul does not eat. The matter is that food contains both physical and spiritual elements. There is nothing below that does not have a spiritual flow from above that brings it into existence and tells it "Grow!" Just as there is a connection in the food between the spiritual and physical, so the soul remains attached to the body through food. The soul benefits from the spirituality and the body from the physicality. This is the meaning of "not by bread alone"—meaning, not just from the physical side of it—"does man live, but from that which comes from the mouth of the Lord," which is the spiritual flow within it. Therefore, the Torah commanded us to awaken the power of holiness within the bread and to separate *Challah*, which is the "high portion" given to the Priest who is holy. When he eats it, the dough refines the body and soul of the eater. Adam, the first human, was also the "Challah of the world," perfect in body and soul. When he corrupted his way, he caused "thorns and thistles" to sprout and "by the sweat of your brow you shall eat bread." By lifting the *Challah* and giving it to the holy Priest, the bread is sanctified to become "bread that sustains the heart of man," and purity rests upon it.

**Likewise**, the four *Tzitzit* surrounding the four directions of the body serve to remind one of the 613 commandments, for the word *Tzitzit* plus the 8 strings and 5 knots equals 613 <note>in Hebrew numerology, Gematria</note>. Thus the body is brought to action, as it says: "And you shall remember and do all the commandments of the Lord." They also serve as a memory for the soul, which is carved from beneath the Throne of Glory, as our Sages said: "The blue thread (*Techelet*) resembles the sea, the sea resembles the sky, and the sky resembles the Throne of Glory." This is the refinement of body and soul. Regarding this are the prohibitions "Do not follow after your heart"—which is heresy, the purification of the soul at the level of thought—and "after your eyes"—which are the external permitted desires, so that the body may be a clean body.

**And behold**, these two commandments are called "first" (*Reshit*). Regarding *Challah* it is written: "The first of your kneading bowls." In the Midrash Genesis Rabbah, it is said: "In the beginning (*Bereshit*)—for the sake of *Challah*..." as it says, "the first (*Reshit*) of your kneading bowls." According to the secret wisdom, the Recanati wrote: "From the first of your kneading bowls you shall give a gift... <gloss>(Also hinted at in 62, and see more in 'The Generations of the Body,' for just as the Challah is a commandment for your generations, I have already compared it to the tenth portion which hints at the Assembly of Israel) to bring down its chariots... the study of Torah... a little for the Lord because...</gloss>

### Written Torah — Three Camps — Page 358

In this world, one should not pursue honor; rather, "the wise shall inherit honor" <note>Proverbs 3:35</note> in the future to come. Before one's elders, there is no place for personal honor. <gloss>(Lack of status... and our death... and Joseph for his covering in all fruit...)</gloss> This refers to the "eye of the service" in its grapes, which is prepared for the World to Come <note>A rabbinic metaphor for the spiritual rewards stored for the righteous</note>, as our Sages of blessed memory said. Regarding the wicked in the future, it is written "Behold, the day comes, burning..." <note>Malachi 3:19</note> and it is written "smoke rose up." And behold, it is written "the days were the days of the first ripe grapes" <note>Numbers 13:20</note>; for the Land of Israel is complete and corresponds exactly to the Celestial Land. The Spies "ate the sourness of the fruit" because they too pursued honor to lord over others, as it is written: "Honor removes a person from the world." Upon them was fulfilled the verse: "As vinegar to the teeth and as smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who send him." But the zealous are early to perform the commandment.

**Let us return** to the first matter regarding the mission of the Spies. The intention of the Spies was to pursue honor, and they went from transgression to transgression until they denied God and were cast out from the land below and the Land Above. The intention of the Israelites was to "bring back a report"—meaning they wanted them to tell the truth, but not to "spread an evil report" of lies. Their intent was to see if they could conquer the land through natural means, but even this was evil in the eyes of God, and also evil in the eyes of Moses. The command of the Blessed Holy One regarding the mission of the Spies was, on the contrary, intended to show them with their own eyes that it is *impossible* to conquer them through natural means, for the people are very strong and the cities are great and fortified up to the heavens—unless the hand of God does this. Then they would see that He is the one who gives strength. 

With this, the great question is answered: What was the sin of the Spies at the beginning, before they spread the evil report of the land, such that Caleb had to quiet the heart of the people? For the sin was that they said, "However (Apes), the people are fierce," as the Ramban <note>Nachmanides, a 13th-century commentator</note> wrote. But it is not exactly as the Ramban wrote—for in my view, there is no difference whether they used the word "however" (Apes) or "only" (Rak) or "but" (Ach)—rather, it is as the author of the *Akedat Yitzchak* <note>Isaac Arama, a 15th-century philosopher</note> said. I follow the path of the *Akedat Yitzchak*: the matter is that their use of "However" (Apes) inverted God's intention. Saying "however, the people are fierce" implies a deficiency that would cause them to withdraw because of it. On the contrary, God's intention was for them to see that the inhabitants were fierce, so they would realize that the war belongs to God. As I wrote, the purpose was to see that "the Lord of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress." He who trusts in God, kindness shall surround him.

# ->The Way of Life: Moral Rebukes<-

## ->Portion of Shelach Lecha<-

This is interpreted beautifully in the Zohar regarding the dominion of the Torah, from which the levels of the World to Come change. Regarding one who wishes to become wise, "let him turn South," etc. "And you shall see the Land"—this refers to the Celestial Land. "Is he strong?"—this refers to a hero who subdues his inclinations. "Are they few or many?"—this refers to those who exert themselves in Divine service. For the Divine Presence (Shekhinah) is like a "soft and delicate" thing... for that world... 18,000 worlds... and they went up against the "sword of the faces," Numbo and Sheshai and Ahiman... many divisions of pure and impure, forbidden and permitted, punishments and rewards. And "Hebron" refers to the Written Torah and the Oral Torah. "Seven" <note>Hebron was built seven years before Zoan</note> refers to the "seventy faces of the Torah." "Before Zoan in Egypt"—this refers to "and the wisdom [of Solomon] excelled..." more than all the wisdom of Egypt. See there at length, for the entire portion is explained well regarding the excellence of the Torah and its details, and the matter of the World to Come, etc.

**From this portion**, one should be aroused to see how far the punishment for spreading an evil report (Lashon HaRa) goes. It causes evil to oneself and to the entire world, just like the Spies who caused great evil to all of Israel—an eternal evil throughout the generations. Our Sages of blessed memory said: If these Spies, who only defamed wood and stones (by saying "it is a land that devours its inhabitants"), were punished so, how much more so one who spreads an evil report about his fellow man!

**"And now, I pray, let the power of my Lord be great."** They said in the *Pesikta* <note>An ancient collection of homiletic midrashim</note>, and it is brought in the *Yalkut* on the verse "You neglected the Rock (Tzur) who begot you" <note>Deuteronomy 32:18</note>: When Israel performs the will of the Omnipresent, they add power and might to the Celestial Realm, as it says, "And now, let the power of my Lord be great." But when they provoke Him, they (as it were) "weaken" (Tashi) the Rock who begot them. Behold the power of free will—how far a person's actions reach!

**"And now, let the power..."** until "And God said: I have forgiven according to your word." These verses should be studied well, for from them emerges a great awakening regarding the mention of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy and the fact that whenever Israel performs them, they are answered.

**"And if you err..."** and do not perform all these commandments. This is found in the *Midrash Tanchuma* and cited in the *Yalkut* on the verse "If a soul shall sin in error against any of the commandments of the Lord." This teaches you that anyone who sins unintentionally (B'shogeg) is as if he violated all the commandments of the sea <note>Likely a scribal error for "commandments of the Torah/God"</note>. For it says, "And if you err and do not perform *all* these commandments." And thus wrote the *Reshit Chochma* <note>A 16th-century Kabbalistic ethical work</note>: When it says "And if you err... all the commandments," it should be understood as stated in the Zohar (Portion of Naso): Anyone who fulfills one commandment properly, it is as if he fulfilled all 248 positive commandments, for there is no commandment that is not included within all 248. From the reward for fulfillment, we may know the punishment for the transgressor: one who violates one commandment is as if he violated them all. This is the meaning of "And if you err and do not perform all these commandments." See how much a person must be careful and forever offer rebuke, whether regarding unintentional or intentional sins. "And those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever."

**"And you shall see** them and remember all the commandments of the Lord." This is a great principle.

### ->Yours, O Lord, is the greatness, etc. Yours is the kingdom. With Your help, I have finished the portion of Shelach Lecha.<-

## ->Portion of Korah<-

### ->His name is fitting for him; do not stand in the place of the great.<-

**Ner Mitzvah (Lamp of Commandment):** Commandments 388 to 396 from the count of 613.
388: The commandment commanded to the Priests and Levites to guard the Sanctuary and to walk around it always, every night, all night. This guarding is for His honor, to exalt and glorify Him, not out of any fear of an enemy, Heaven forbid. As it says, "And they shall keep the charge of the Tent of Meeting." The language of the *Sifrei* <note>An ancient legal midrash</note> is: "You and your sons with you before the Tent of Testimony"—this includes the Priests and Levites even on the outside, meaning to guard it and walk around it. 
389: That the Levites shall not carry out the work of the Priests, nor the Priests the work of the Levites. As it says to the Levites, "But they shall not come near the vessels of the Sanctuary and the Altar." Then the verse returns and speaks to the Priests, saying "that they die not, neither they nor you," for just as the Levites are restricted, so is every man restricted from their work. 
390: That a "stranger" (non-priest) shall not serve in the Sanctuary. As it says, "And a stranger shall not come near unto you." 
391: Not to cease the guarding of the Sanctuary. As it says, "And you shall keep the charge of the Sanctuary, etc." and every place where it says "Beware" (Hishamer), "Lest" (Pen), or "No" (Lo), it is a negative commandment.
392: For the redemption of the firstborn of man. As it says, "But the firstborn of man you shall surely redeem." 
393: Not to redeem the firstborn of a clean animal. As it says, "But the firstborn of an ox, or the firstborn of a sheep, or the firstborn of a goat, you shall not redeem; they are holy." 
394: For the Levites to be workers in the Sanctuary, to be gatekeepers and singers every day over the sacrifice. As it says, "And the Levite, he shall perform the service." This commandment is repeated elsewhere in the Torah: "And he shall minister in the name of the Lord his God." The Sages said in Tractate *Eruvin*: Which service is "in the Name of the Lord"? You must say it is song. 
395: That the children of Israel are obligated to give a portion—one tenth. As it says, "For the tithe of the children of Israel, which they set apart as a gift unto the Lord, I have given to the Levites." 
396: That the Levites were commanded to set aside a tithe from the tithe they receive from the Israelites. As it says, "And you shall set apart from it a gift unto the Lord, a tithe of the tithe."

**Torah Or (Light of Torah):** The Torah is called "light" because it illuminates, and it is also called "fire." Just as fire illuminates and one benefits from its warmth by keeping a distance, but is burned by drawing too close—so is the secret of the Torah. One who enters beyond his place, into the innermost sanctum beyond his level, then "he glimpses and is harmed" or "glimpses and dies." As explained elsewhere regarding the death of Nadab and Abihu "when they drew near before the Lord"—it does not say "when they offered," but "when they drew near," for they entered into things too wondrous for them, and thus they died. This is also the secret of the "Graves of Craving," where the people died who craved to gaze upon the Divine. This was the cause of their death, as explained in the book *Brit Menucha* <note>A 14th-century Kabbalistic text on the vowels and Divine names</note>. Therefore, do not stand in the place of the great <gloss>in a place that is greater [than you].</gloss>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the rebellion of Korah from the previous page, transitioning from the narrative of the punishment to the moral lessons derived from it, and finally beginning the next Torah portion, Chukat, which discusses the Red Heifer.</meta>

# Written Torah: In the presence of the great, do not stand <note>A reference to Proverbs 25:6, suggesting humility before teachers or God.</note>

At this turning point, the Holy One, Blessed be He, judged them extensively and decreed death upon them. The Angel of Death arrived to slaughter them, but Aaron held the Angel's hand and would not let him proceed. To this, the Angel of Death replied: "What are you doing? Am I not, like so-and-so, an emissary of the Omnipresent to carry out what the Holy One, Blessed be He, Himself decreed when He brought death upon them? The incense only avails against me when I add to their suffering." To this, Aaron replied: "Moses is also an emissary of the Omnipresent; wait for me until the Lord repents of the evil He spoke of." This is how the matter is to be explained. However, regarding our specific subject, the incense did not avail to save those who sinned specifically *with* the incense—namely, those who grumbled against Moses our Teacher for giving advice to Aaron to have the men offer incense.

## The General Principle
Korah’s jealousy removed him from the world. He sinned regarding the *Tzitzit* <note>The ritual fringes; according to Midrash, Korah challenged the laws of Tzitzit</note>, which are a spiritual rectification for the Levites. Regarding Dathan and Abiram, they were driven by physical desire and sinned at the "entrance of their tents" where the *Mezuzah* <note>The parchment scroll placed on doorposts</note> is fixed as a spiritual rectification. But their intention was "for the sake of Heaven"—to regain the status of the firstborn <note>original: "Bechor"</note>, through which "the wise shall inherit glory." They remembered to clothe themselves in the garment of the *Tefillin* <note>Phylacteries worn during prayer</note>, of which it is said: "And all the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of the Lord is called upon you." This is the meaning of their claim: "For all the congregation are holy, and the Lord is among them." However, they erred and transgressed the rule: "Do not seek what is too wondrous for you, and do not investigate what is hidden from you." They died "in their drawing near before the Lord," for they approached too closely to a higher level of spiritual attainment and were consumed, much like the fire that consumed the sons of Aaron <note>Nadab and Abihu, who also offered "strange fire"</note>, because they sought to attach themselves to that which was beyond their reach. Even though their actions were like those of the wicked, their intention was for the sake of spiritual union (*Devekut*). As for the dispute in the chapter titled *Chelek* <note>The 11th chapter of Tractate Sanhedrin in the Talmud</note> regarding whether Korah's assembly has a portion in the World to Come, this refers specifically to the assembly of Korah that was swallowed by the earth, but not to the assembly of the 250 men who were burned. This is implied by the language of the Mishnah: "The assembly of Korah has no portion in the World to Come... as it is said, 'And the earth covered them' in this world, 'and they perished from the midst of the assembly' for the World to Come; these are the words of Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Eliezer says of them: 'The Lord deals death and gives life, brings down to the grave and raises up.'"

## The Way of Life: Moral Instruction
From the dispute of the wicked Korah, one takes a moral lesson regarding the severity of the punishment for causing division (*Machloket*). See what happened to Korah himself; he was a prince and a great man in Israel, and but for the sin of dispute, he would have been among those who carried the Holy Ark. Dathan, Abiram, and even the little children were lost. Although the Heavenly Court usually only judges those above the age of twenty, here even the children perished—such is the gravity of dispute, as our Sages of blessed memory said. A person is warned and taught the moral lesson to hold fast to peace. Every person of intellect should learn to be among the "disciples of Aaron," a lover of peace. For Aaron saw that despite the dispute—even when they sought to uproot his own honor—he said nothing. Whatever reasons a man can find to mediate peace and extinguish the fire of dispute, he must do. Learn this from Moses our Teacher: though he was the greatest of prophets and a king, he went himself, in all his dignity, to Dathan and Abiram to try and bring them back to peace. Even when they said "We will not come up," he went to them accompanied by the elders of Israel. All of this was for the sake of peace.

**Not** one of them was delayed. Similarly, Samuel of Ramah said: "Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken?" <note>1 Samuel 12:3</note>. There are many moral lessons regarding true justice that emerge from the telling of these matters; I have written at length on this in my work *Amudei HaDin* on the tractate of *Rosh Hashanah*. Look for it there.
**All** the best of the oil, the wine, and the grain—you shall give to the Lord from the very best. Similarly, those who give money to a charity box or to a poor person should give the finest currency that is in circulation without hesitation, and one must be very meticulous in this.

->### The Portion of Chukat<-
->### This is the name by which it is called: The Portion of the Red Heifer<-

**The Lamp of Commandment:** Commandment 397 of the 613 commandments: The burning of the Red Heifer. 398: The laws of ritual impurity from a corpse, as it is said: "This is the Torah: when a man dies in a tent..." 399: The law of the preparation of the purifying waters, as it is said: "And the pure person shall sprinkle upon the impure."

**The Light of Torah:** Because the secret of the Red Heifer is exceedingly hidden, even the early sages who had some knowledge of the ritual found that even that small portion was "closed and sealed" and not fully explained. However, so as not to leave this section entirely empty, I will present a sermon on the portion of the Red Heifer that I composed in my youth. From it, the "Torah shall go forth to light," bringing the commandment closer to human intellect and the plain meaning of the text. This is the text:

<columns>2</columns>
(Happy is the one who is wise and searches and understands the depth of this matter. For this is a hidden secret that a person cannot fully fathom in its depth. Only a wise man will be considered wise [if he acknowledges his limits]. As the philosophers said regarding the Creator, may He be blessed: "The goal of knowing Him is to know that we cannot know Him." That is, we delve so far into the depth of understanding that we conclude it is unattainable. This is hinted at in the verse: "I said I will be wise, but it is far from me." <note>Ecclesiastes 7:23</note>. For the Assembly of Israel is like a daughter... before the Holy One, Blessed be He, and she says she cannot know. To this the verse hints: "I was like a beast and did not know; I was with You." Why did it say "Beasts" <note>original: "Behemot"</note> in the plural? Rather, King David, peace be upon him, spoke through a metaphor: "I was like a beast," etc. Because whoever has an intellect yet still cannot descend to the depth of the matter, [is humbled]. It is impossible for me to attain this, for this is the wisdom of the Priest who deals with purity while he himself becomes impure. This is why it says: "I said I will be wise, but it is far"—meaning, when I attain it, I see it is even further away. There is no wise man except one who realizes his knowledge cannot reach it. This settles the verse in Parashat Vayakhel: "And every wise-hearted man in whom the Lord put wisdom..." <note>The author explores why "wisdom" is repeated in the construction of the Tabernacle, suggesting the sages knew their limits.</note>
<column-break/>
"This is the statute of the Torah" <note>Numbers 19:2</note> etc. It is difficult: it should have said "This is the statute of the *Heifer*." According to what the Mizrachi <note>Rabbi Eliyahu Mizrachi, a 15th-century commentator</note> wrote, this difficulty is resolved. Even though there are several places where the word "statute" (*Chukah*) is used where the reasoning is not a "decree from before Me" (such as "This is the statute of the Passover," where the reason for Passover is clear), here it is different because both "Torah" and "Statute" are written. It would have been enough to use one, as in "This is the Torah: when a man dies in a tent," or "This is the Torah for the burnt offering, the meal offering, the sin offering, and the guilt offering," or "This is the statute of the Passover." In my humble opinion, the difficulty is resolved regardless, for "An eternal statute" refers to the Passover statute as the statute of the *intermingling* <note>original: "Pilush"</note>, the statute of leaven and unleavened bread. "A statute for you and your children" means a fixed matter. Similarly regarding judgment: "I made known the statutes of God." All matters of the Red Heifer are difficult, and why should we lengthen the list of difficulties? However, permission is given to contemplate as much as possible. Rabbi Moshe the Preacher, whom Rashi quotes, proves that "I said I will be wise, but it is far" refers to this. He did not say "I was not wise," for the matter *does* grant some wisdom through hints. But its "inner essence" remains far away. This is also implied in the Midrash where Rabbi Isaac begins: "All this I tested with wisdom; I said I will be wise..." King Solomon said: "I have mastered all of the Torah's portions, but when I reached the portion of the Red Heifer, I would expound on it, research it, and question it, yet I said 'I will be wise, but it is far from me.'" Thus, he *did* expound and research, but he did not stand upon its ultimate clarity, unlike the rest of the Torah.

It then transitions into the laws of the Red Heifer, noting its status as the ultimate "statute"—a law beyond human comprehension that even King Solomon could not fully grasp.</summary>
