# Judges: Six Steps to the Throne (376)

<margin>Only a true prophet</margin>
For a lie is vanity, a work of delusion. This awakens the matter of the false prophet—that one must not listen to him and must not fear him.
"I will raise up for you..." and "...to him you shall listen." <note>Deuteronomy 18:15</note> The **Pillar of Peace**: even in war, we are commanded toward peace, as it is written regarding an "optional war" <note>term: Optional War (Milchemet HaReshut): A war initiated for national interest or expansion, as opposed to a war commanded by God for defense.</note>, "you shall call out to it for peace."
And even in a "commanded war" <note>term: Commanded War (Milchemet Mitzvah): A war mandated by the Torah, such as defending against an attacker.</note> where "you shall not let any soul live," it is because these are wicked and sinful people; their destruction and erasure brings 
life to the world in peace. We are also commanded concerning the peace of the altar, if there is a benefit to it, as it says, "you shall not destroy its trees" even in a time of war. And the matter here 
concerns the Anointed Priest <note>The Kohen Mashuach Milchama, a priest designated to address the troops.</note> who speaks to the many, as it is written, awakening the love of the Place, may He be blessed. Or "peace be to us and war upon our enemies"; therefore, we shall not be broken before the enemy. The **Pillar of 
Torah**: the entire matter of the tribe of Levi is that they shall have no portion in the land. This is because they were chosen for the Pillar of Torah, as it is written: "They shall teach Your laws to Jacob and Your Torah to Israel." 
If they had a portion in the land, this one would run to his vineyard and that one would run to his olive trees, etc.; if so, what would become of the Torah? And thus it is written, "to give the portion of the Lord to those who hold fast to the Torah." Therefore, 
we were commanded to give to them so that they might be free to engage in the Torah without distraction. The Priests were also blessed with holy gifts and divided into watches; nonetheless, during a festival, they share 
equally. They were also given the gifts of the foreleg, the cheeks, and the stomach, and the first of the fleece. The **Pillar of Divine Service**: "you shall not plant an Asherah tree near the altar" and "you shall not erect a standing stone," and "you 
shall not sacrifice that which has a blemish." The **Pillar of Kindness**: the kindness performed for the dead is "true kindness." And in this matter, the six cities of refuge and the "broken-necked heifer" <note>term: Broken-necked Heifer (Eglah Arufah): A ritual performed by city elders when a murder victim is found in an open field and the killer is unknown, signifying communal responsibility.</note> will be explained later.

# And now I will explain their matters one by one

## **The Pillar of Judgment**
"Judges and officers you shall appoint for yourself," etc. First, I will explain according to the plain meaning, and afterward, the secret will be clarified. 
"Judges and officers you shall appoint for yourself." One might ask: it should have said "appoint *over* you," as it says "you shall surely set a king *over* you." And one cannot say that "over you" only 
applies to a king, for our Sages of blessed memory said: "all appointments that you place *over* you should be from among your brothers." This can be settled by the difficulty found in explaining the portion of the King, which 
the early and later commentators struggled with: how did Israel sin by asking for a king, when it is a positive commandment to "surely set a king over you"? As it is found in Tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 23: 
Rabbi Yosi says, "Everything mentioned in the 'Portion of the King' <note>1 Samuel 8</note>, a king is permitted to do." Rabbi Yehuda says, "That portion was only stated to threaten them, as it says, 'you shall surely 
set a king over you,' so that his fear should be upon you." And so Rabbi Yehuda would say, "Israel was commanded with three commandments upon entering the land: to appoint a king, to wipe out 
the offspring of Amalek, and to build the Chosen House [the Temple]." Rabbi Nehorai says, "This portion was only stated in response to their complaint, as it says, 'and you shall say: I will set a king over me' etc." Rabbi 
Eliezer says, "The elders of that generation asked properly, as it says, 'give us a king to judge us'; but the common people among them ruined it, as it says, 'that we also may be like all the nations, 
and our king shall judge us and go out before us.'" And the Rabbi Abarbanel <note>Don Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a statesman and philosopher.</note>, in his commentary on the Torah, brought all these opinions. Regarding Rabbi Eliezer, Abarbanel questioned that the Torah itself writes 
"like all the nations that are around me." See there in Abarbanel what he himself wrote on this matter at length. For one who looks with this intellect, it is possible to explain the words 
of Rabbi Nehorai according to the view of Abarbanel. In the Sifrei <note>An ancient legal commentary on Numbers and Deuteronomy.</note>, Rabbi Nehorai says they only asked for a king to make them worship idols, as it says, "that we may be like all the nations." Against 
this Sifrei, Abarbanel asked: when the Holy One said to Samuel, "Now, listen to their voice," why didn't the Holy One warn them only not to worship idols? It seems to me that the rebuke was hinted at 
in what was said, "it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me," etc. And the *Mahamat* <note>Likely a reference to a specific commentator or work.</note> wrote on the verse "The scepter shall not depart from Judah," etc., that their sin was that they did 
as Samuel did. But wait—if so, there is no generation without sin, for every judge is like Samuel; "Jephthah in his generation is like Samuel in his generation." The clearest of all is the view of the Rabbi in his sermon, and this was 
Rabbi Eliezer's view: that there are two types of leadership. One is judgment according to the Torah, and for this, the Sanhedrin <note>term: Sanhedrin: The supreme judicial and legislative council of ancient Israel.</note> were appointed. The other is "safeguards" beyond the Torah, and this 
is called an "emergency ruling" <note>term: Emergency Ruling (Hora'at Sha'ah): A temporary legal measure that suspends a Torah law to address a specific crisis or societal need.</note> because the hour requires it. Jerusalem was only destroyed because they based their words strictly on Torah law [without mercy or social context]. And on this comes the hint: "And you shall purge the innocent blood," for sometimes we are required to use the knife and punish not according to the law because of the need of the hour. This was the purpose of setting a king, for a king breaks through fences. Regarding this, 
the scripture says, "For there sat thrones for judgment, thrones for the house of David." <note>Psalm 122:5</note> The thrones for judgment are the Sanhedrin; the thrones for the House of David is the throne of the kingdom 
<margin>House of David •</margin> as Rabbi Hillel, who came up from the rivers, said: they judged a righteous judgment according to the Torah. But when there was a need for an emergency ruling, the king would run and break through a fence against 
Torah law. This is the hint in "Justice, justice shall you pursue." The first "Justice" refers to the Sanhedrin, which is righteous judgment. The second "Justice" is for the emergency ruling. Of this, it says "so that 
you may live and inherit the land," for Jerusalem was only destroyed because they stood their words upon strict Torah law. The Israelites in the days of Samuel sinned because they said, "Give us a king 
to judge us." They wanted the king to be the *judge*. This is against the will of God, for to be a judge to judge Torah law—for that, "judges and officers you shall appoint" 
<margin>that is, the Sanhedrin •</margin> and the appointment of a king should be *against* Torah law to make emergency rulings. For this, the language of "setting *over* you" is appropriate, for he rules over you 
<margin>and breaks the judgment given in the Torah •</margin> and before a king was king over Israel, the Court would judge these two matters: that is, Torah law and also emergency 
<margin>rulings •</margin> Thus, Moses our Teacher was called a king, as it says, "And he was king in Jeshurun" <note>Deuteronomy 33:5</note>; he was the head of the Sanhedrin and also a king. Likewise, after the destruction, when there was 
no king in Israel, the princes of the Land of Israel would say: "I heard that they may clarify and punish even not according to the law," etc. According to this, the verse "you shall not turn 
to the right or the left, even if he tells you of the right that it is left and of the left that it is right," etc., is explained. This applies specifically as long as a king has not been appointed in Israel; then, every person 
<margin>for it is difficult to decide</margin> from the Sanhedrin acts with righteous judgment, and the king acts with emergency rulings. When they asked for a king for the purpose of judgment, they sinned. This was the view of Rabbi Eliezer, 
and he divides the verse "set for us a king to judge us like all the nations" into two statements said by two groups: the elders and the common people. It would be difficult to say "set *over* us," so why "for us"? 
Rather, the elders said: "he should be joined *to* us," meaning we are the officers and appointees, and he will only diminish [his own power], but he should also have an appointment in public needs. But the commoners said, "also to judge us," as is explained at the end with lengthy words: "a king shall be over us and we will also be like the nations."
Let us return to the matter: then what is written, "and they shall judge a righteous judgment," is answered. The Sanhedrin—and not the "Justice" that stands against "Judgment" [emergency law]. If so, the double expression of "righteous judgment" [mishpat tzedek] hints at what is written: 
"true judgment to its truth." The Tosafot <note>A group of medieval commentators on the Talmud.</note> wrote in the chapter "Resha'ah" that this excludes "deceptive judgment." And the Tosafot in the fourth chapter of Bava Batra explained their own words, as 
is clarified in the Tur, Chosen Mishpat, section 15: what is called "deceptive judgment," see there. It must be "true to its truth." And this is "righteous judgment" and "Justice, justice shall you pursue." One might ask about 
the repetition. It has already been explained as indicating an emergency ruling. In the Sanhedrin, they said: "Follow a good court"—one for judgment and one for compromise. And in the Sifrei: "From where do we know 
of one who leaves the court acquitted..." etc. See above "Justice, justice shall you pursue" according to the way of "being deliberate": even if a case has already come before you, be deliberate with it now. On this comes the hint: "When 
they have a matter, they come to me, and I judge between a man and his fellow." He explained: when there was now a case for two litigants, even if it was exactly the same 
as a case that had already occurred, nonetheless, I do not rely on what I ruled before. Rather, I judge "between a man and his fellow" now, for perhaps it is different according to who the person is.

## **Do Not Pervert Judgment**
This can be explained in the same way I explained what they said on the verse "right and left": "even if he tells you of the right that it is left," etc. And one might ask: how is it possible that they would say of the right that it is left, etc.? Above, I explained it as "emergency rulings." But 
this is not according to the plain meaning. Furthermore, I questioned what they said: "to the judge who shall be in those days." Would it enter your mind that one would go to a judge who is *not* in his days? 
Rather, it is to tell you that even if he is not like other judges who were before him, you must listen to him; you have no one but the judge of your days. I find this strange—why 
say anything at all? It is known that one cannot go to someone not in his days! One cannot say that the scripture comes to inform us that we should not say we won't listen to this judge because 
he does not compare to the judges before him. Certainly, one cannot say that, for if so, they would immediately not have followed Joshua because he did not compare to Moses, 
and the Torah was given for all generations. It is understandable regarding "to the priest who shall be in those days"—meaning you have no priest but the one in your days—mentioned at the beginning of the portion "Ki Tavo"; there it is not difficult, for it comes 
to teach us that one should not go to a different priestly watch, but specifically to the priest of that watch. But here it is difficult. Rather, the matter follows what is written in the Tur, Chosen Mishpat, section 28, as follows: 
The Raavad <note>Rabbi Abraham ben David of Posquières (c. 1125–1198).</note> wrote that we do not judge now in monetary matters...

<meta>The previous page concludes with a discussion on the spiritual qualities of the patriarchs; this page continues exploring the themes of peace, the anatomy of the soul, and the laws of leadership and the priesthood as found in the Torah portion of Shoftim (Judges).</meta>

->Do not rebuke etc. The pillar of peace is Peace, which is the perfection of every blemish, and one who is rebuked is compared to peace. "Ox and lamb" <note>Hebrew: *Shor ve-Seh*</note> are a hint to Jacob and Joseph. Jacob is called a "lamb," as it is said:<-
->**Redeemer** of Israel. # The Way of Life: Moral Reproof

**Judges** and officers you shall appoint for yourself in all your gates. In <unclear>Be-K-A-N-I-S-H</unclear> they hinted at a moral lesson regarding what we learned in *The Book of Formation* <note>An ancient Jewish mystical text</note>: "There are seven gates in the soul: two eyes, two ears, the mouth, and two nostrils," end of quote. These are the most important gates, located in the head of a person. However, there is also a gate for the Covenant <note>referring to the reproductive organ</note>... and the lower desire, and a person must guard these gates—namely, his seeing, hearing, speaking, and tasting. One must also guard what comes out of the nose, and guard the gate of holiness so that it does not depart, and know that if it is for sanctity... Also the "lower mouth" <note>the digestive/excretory system</note>, so that he does not fill his belly like an animal with vomit and filth. Over these gates, a person must place... judges and officers. That is to say, he must judge himself constantly. This is the meaning of "you shall appoint for yourself," meaning he should always supervise to ensure there is no sin there, for almost all places are a place of peace and a dwelling in his life and in his instruction.

**You** shall not pervert justice; you shall not take a bribe. Our Sages, of blessed memory, warned very, very much against bribery, even "verbal bribery" or a small favor. As [is written]... in the *Tur: Choshen Mishpat* <note>A classic code of Jewish law</note>, how it is proper for a person to distance himself and be as fiery as the quality of <unclear>Sh-L-I-Ch-U-T</unclear> in the portion of *Devarim*, and happy is the one who does this. Because [after taking a bribe]... a closeness of mind enters him and he perverts justice, meaning he overturns his merits [of the briber] excessively. Those who seek deeper meanings said: bribery <note>original: *Shochad*</note> is a hint to "darkened justice" <note>original: *Chashuch Mishpat*</note>, for when the bribe is... the bribe <note>original: *Shochad* - שחד</note> becomes "Five-Hundred and Five" <note>original: *T-Sh-H* - תשה</note>—that is, the letters that follow *Sh-Ch-D* <note>the letter after Shin is Tav, after Chet is Tet, after Dalet is Heh</note> are *T-Sh-H*—for after taking a bribe, you will pervert justice.

**The commandment** of appointing a King is through <unclear>Ch-Ph-Sh-T</unclear>, so that the fear of the kingdom should be upon them. In the fulfillment of the Torah and the commandments, therefore from the *Zohar* <note>The foundational work of Kabbalah</note> regarding the King... that he himself should guard the Torah and the commandments, for "adorn yourself first, and then adorn others." Therefore, the King was commanded to have a Torah scroll... that belongs to him, because the obligation upon him is double that of the rest of the people. For this reason, he was warned against accumulating silver, gold, and many wives, which represent an abundance of desires. Also, an abundance of horses, so that he remains attached to the Blessed Name and places his trust in Him. For "some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we mention the name of the Lord our God." And behold, the Sages expounded... "you shall surely set [a king]"—all "settings" <note>appointments/authorities</note> that you set over yourself etc. I say this also regarding moral reproof: anyone who has any position of authority over Israel must...
->with extra holiness and purity.<-

**And why** is [the section of the Levites] placed next to the section of the King? "The Priests, the Levites, and all the tribe of Levi shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel; they shall eat the fire-offerings of the Lord and His inheritance." For since [the King]... in this praise for honor and glory, they [the Priests/Levites] must therefore be more attached to the Blessed Name and those who dwell upon His words. And "everyone who is greater than his fellow" must be... more meticulous, and "around Him it is very stormy" <note>A Talmudic concept that God is more demanding of the righteous</note>. With this, we can understand what is written afterward: "And if a Levite comes from one of your gates out of all Israel where he resides etc." And it is explained... regarding a Priest <note>original: *Kohen*</note> and not a Levite, so why does he call the Priest a "Levite"? ...It is written "And this shall be the due of the Priests"... [why] does he call the Priest a "Priest" and now he calls him by the name "Levite"? It is known that the Priest is from the side of Kindness <term>Chesed</term> and the Levite is from the side of Severity <term>Gevurah</term>. And behold, the elevation of the Priest is higher than the Levite, and judgment is more meticulous. Therefore, they hinted that the judgment <note>Hebrew: *Din*</note> should be upon the Priest... even though he is from the side of Kindness, nevertheless he himself is judged with the attribute of Judgment <note>original: *Midat Ha-Din*</note>, which is the attribute of the Levite. "Portion like portion they shall eat"—regarding the festival sacrifices, they all take a portion for themselves and are judged with the attribute of Judgment. And it is known that on all the Festivals, the world is judged with the attribute of Judgment, as we learned in the Mishnah: "At four times the world is judged: On Passover for the grain; on Shavuot for the fruit of the tree; on the Festival [Sukkot] they are judged for water; on Rosh Hashanah etc."

**"Be wholehearted with the Lord your God."** This verse includes all the conduct of the character traits and holiness, and that one should be attached to God always—"be wholehearted." Furthermore, there is a great hint in this verse as explained in the *Zohar* in another place: it says that when a man performs a commandment, it adds strength to the "Supernal Image" <note>The Divine form</note>, and through [sin], he blemishes above and below. For when a man sins, it is recognizable in his face, etc. And this is the matter of "the look on their faces witnesses against them." And so it is written, "A man’s wisdom makes his face shine." And the Rabbi Alshich <note>Rabbi Moshe Alshich, a 16th-century commentator in Safed</note> explained what Jacob said regarding Joseph: "I will go and see him," for he wanted to look at the "impression of his face" <note>Hebrew: *Reshimu de-Anpeh*</note>, what it was. And so he said afterward... "that you are still alive," for I am marking the impression of your face, for you are a "living man," and "his face shines toward you," and "in the light of the King's face is life." And regarding this it is written: "Why are you downcast... the salvation of my face and my God," meaning: even if I am greatly pained, is there not a remedy in Repentance <term>Teshuvah</term> to save the impression of the face and also to remove the blemish from the Divine Image? And these two faces... "Face to face the Lord spoke with you." And regarding this... "as he comes to see, so he comes to be seen." From this, a difficult verse in Isaiah will be explained... the prophecy "To You, my heart said: Seek My face; Your face, O Lord, I will seek." The matter of this verse refers to the verse above it: "To behold the pleasantness of the Lord." And he said: Master of the Universe, to You... my heart. You have no need to see the light of the impression of my face, for "my heart speaks with You," as if to say, before You the secrets of the heart are revealed. "My heart and my flesh both sing together to the [Living God]"... and to human beings, "my flesh" alone. "Seek My face"—he uses the plural "seek," for he is speaking to people, saying: "O people, seek My face," and when do I [God]... in this, that they should seek My face, when "Your face, O Lord, I will seek" to behold the pleasantness of the Lord. "Man sees the eyes, but the Lord sees the heart." The general principle is: when a person sins... he makes an impression and a blemish on his face and, as it were, also Above. Regarding this comes the warning: "Be wholehearted with the Lord your God"—the Supernal Image and the lower image. See how far a person's actions reach!

**Who** is the man who has built a house and has not dedicated it? Let him go and return to his house. And one who has planted a vineyard and not redeemed it? Let him go and return. And so, one who has betrothed a wife and not taken her. This alludes to... for there are three times of the World to Come, as mentioned in the Sabbath morning liturgy: "The life of the World to Come, the Days of the Messiah, and the Resurrection of the Dead." The "Life of the World to Come" is the "faithful house" that... is pleasant for every righteous person, a dwelling according to his honor. The "Days of the Messiah"—this is the "taking of a wife," the Holy One Blessed be He and the Assembly of Israel, as it is written: "For as a young man marries a virgin, so shall your sons marry you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you." And after the "Resurrection of the Dead," there will be the eternal state "which no eye has seen, O God, besides You." And the explanation of our Sages is... the [wine] preserved in its grapes from the six days of Creation, and that is the "Vineyard of Hosts." Therefore, the sinner returns from the battle lines, and the Scripture hangs it on these [house, vineyard, wife] because it hints that he did not... understand the way to these three: he did not dedicate the "House," did not redeem the "Vineyard," and did not take the "Wife." "Let him return to his house"—and the matter of "returning" <note>Hebrew: *Yashuv*</note> is that he should perform Repentance <term>Teshuvah</term> and repair...

# 381
# Holiness of the Soul and the Sanctity of Blood

The secret of the commandment of **procreation** <note>Hebrew: *Pru u-Rvu*</note>—a son and a daughter—corresponds to the secret of the letters *Yod* and *Heh* of the Divine Name. The Father and Mother represent the mystical qualities of Wisdom <term>Chokmah</term> and Understanding <term>Binah</term>, while the Son and Daughter represent the qualities of Beauty <term>Tiferet</term> and Sovereignty <term>Malchut</term> <note>These are the letters *Vav* and *Heh* of the Tetragrammaton</note>. When a man and his wife fulfill this commandment, they mirror the "Higher Union" of the Divine Name. There are two arrangements of the Name *YHVH*: one for the purity of the home and one for the cycles of the year. Know that a "clear union" occurs when souls are united and become "one flesh" below just as their souls were united above; this is his true soulmate. Sometimes, a woman is not a man's true soulmate, and he releases her with a bill of divorce <note>Hebrew: *Get*</note>, and she goes to another man. The law requires a bill of divorce to be written in twelve lines, comparing the "leaving" of a marriage to the "becoming" of a new one. Regarding one who divorces his first wife, it is said that "the Altar sheds tears over him." The "first wife" refers to the first mystical union, and the Altar corresponds to the "Valiant Woman" <note>Hebrew: *Eshet Chayil*</note> above. The Recanati <note>Menachem Recanati, a 13th-century Italian kabbalist</note> wrote: just as their bodies were joined, their souls were joined before birth. Therefore, when they separate, they require a "scroll of severance" <note>original: *Sefer Kritut*</note> that must be written specifically for her name, his name, and the name of the city, for this separation occurs even within their spiritual names. The supreme rule is that a clear union mirrors the Divine Countenance. When united in purity, holiness, and modesty, it brings blessing and abundance from the "Higher Covenant" to the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah</term>, creating peace from above to below.

There shall be no **harlot** among Israel, for one who unites with impurity causes the higher abundance to flow toward the "higher concubine"—the harlot of the other side—bringing forces of impurity into the world. Children born of forbidden unions <note>Hebrew: *Mamzer*</note> or from the nations of Ammon and Moab are considered to be influenced by the "unclean spirit" <note>Aramaic: *Ruach Mesava*</note> of the demonic figures Samael and Lilith. Such children are called "strange children" because they were conceived under the authority of "the other side" <note>Aramaic: *Sitra Achra*</note>. However, from a holy union, the souls of Israel are emanated from the Source of Holiness. As it is written: "I am like a leafy cypress tree; your fruit comes from Me." Maimonides <note>The Rambam</note> also speaks of the emanation of Jewish souls from this holy source. The secret of a man's union with his wife is the secret of the "Giver" and the "Receiver." When a man is physically unable to father children—such as one who is "crushed or maimed"—it causes a spiritual defect above, for the "river" of abundance dries up. This is also the reason for the gravity of wasting seed, for it destroys a soul that was worthy of being created. As the verse says, "it is a life that he takes," meaning he ruins and destroys the potential for life.

**The reason** that Edomites and Egyptians are permitted to enter the congregation in the third generation after their conversion is as follows: Abraham our father was the first "righteous convert" and the head of the nations. Waste was removed from him <note>referring to Ishmael</note> and from his lineage until the third generation, which was Jacob our father, whose "bed was complete" <note>meaning all his children were righteous</note>. Jacob and Esau were brothers, but through Esau's lineage and Jacob's blessings, the third generation is permitted. This is why it says, "Do not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother." Similarly, the Egyptian exile lasted many years from the time of Abraham's "Covenant Between the Parts." In Egypt, the souls of Israel were refined in the "iron furnace" until they became a complete nation. They were called "Israel" after our father Jacob, who was the third generation from Abraham.

**The distancing** of the "hire of a harlot" and the "price of a dog" from the House of the Lord is because the House of the Lord represents the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah</term>, while the harlot belongs to the side of Lilith. There, the "dogs" cry out, representing the Angel of Death in the city. Thus David prayed: "Deliver my soul from the sword, my only one from the hand of the dog."

**Know** that there are two types of harlots. One is Lilith, the harlot mentioned above. The second is Machalat, whose name relates to sickness <note>Hebrew: *Machalah*</note> and curses. She appears in dreams and through the joy of frivolity and foolishness. She is the "woman of beautiful form" <note>Hebrew: *Yefat Toar*</note> taken in war, whom the Torah only permitted as a concession to the Evil Inclination. She must shave her head and weep for her father to humble the power of Machalat. Children born from such a union are often "strange children," which is why the Torah portions of the "Beautiful Woman," the "Rebellious Son," and "Execution" are adjacent. Slander <note>Hebrew: *Motzi Shem Ra*</note> also stems from this side of evil. This relates to the concubines of Abraham, to whom he gave "gifts"—our sages say he gave them names of impurity. The name "impurity" <note>Hebrew: *Tumah*</note> indicates a spreading of the half-name. Therefore, a slanderer is punished and must remain married to the woman he shamed to prevent further separation. The secret of **Levirate Marriage** <term>Yibbum</term> and **Shoe-Removal** <term>Chalitzah</term> is very deep, rooted in the secret of Reincarnation <term>Gilgul</term>. The purpose of union is the joining of like-souls, so that the children born are "children of the Lord." One who has no children is considered "dead" in this world and lacks life in the World to Come, for he has diminished the Divine Image.

**And now** we shall first explain a bit of the secret of Reincarnation.
->The secret of the "First" and "Second" Spiritual Unions<-

<columns>2</columns>
Then the matter of *Yibbum* and *Chalitzah* will be clarified. Regarding the secret of the commandment of burial, the Recanati wrote at length. He noted that God "thinks thoughts so that the banished one is not cast off." No one should say that the sparks of the Holy One, blessed be He, are to be abandoned. As long as a person is not buried, their soul cannot undergo reincarnation. It is like a man who cannot marry another woman until he has buried his first wife. Therefore, it is commanded to bury the dead immediately, so the soul may find its "rest" and its proper place. This is hinted at in the verse following the laws of burial: "You shall not see your brother's ox or sheep wandering and hide yourself from them; you shall surely return them." If God returns lost objects to their owners out of great mercy, we must follow His ways. This refers to the "lost" soul of a brother, but not the "loss" of a Gentile, as I alluded to in the secret of the *Ibur* <note>a form of soul-pregnancy or attachment</note> on the verse "and this was the custom in former times in Israel." Regarding these lost and banished souls, it is said: "On that day, a great Shofar shall be blown, and those lost in the land of Assyria and those banished in the land of Egypt shall come." In the blessing of the "Great Shofar," we pray for the gathering of the exiled souls scattered to the four corners of the earth in their various reincarnations.

<column-break/>

And thus says the Zohar (Portion Balak, 188): Everything depends on the secret of the "Image." For when a person departs this world, the Angel of Death takes the body. It is forbidden to leave the body unburied, for as long as the body is not covered by the earth, the soul cannot enter its holy place. The body is a garment, and when it is finished with its work, it must be returned to the dust from whence it came. The Image of the King must not be shamed by being left out. The body was created in the "supernal image" and its design is purposeful. Therefore, one must not see the higher "form" without its "vessel," and it is forbidden to cover it after death in a way that shames it. This is hinted at in the verse: "Do not hide yourself from your own flesh." The body of a righteous person is like a holy scroll that has been worn out. Our sages taught that the angels would hide themselves because they questioned the creation of man, saying, "What is man that You should be mindful of him?" But when they see the holiness of the body even in death, they recognize the Divine purpose. Furthermore, it is said that the grave provides a "cleansing" for the soul so it can be corrected and prepared for the future resurrection. Burial is an act of kindness for the living and the dead, ensuring that the soul finds its way back to its root.

# When You Go Out: Sanctity of the Body and Sanctity of Value

The "forced ones of the earth" <note>An allusion to the Jewish people in exile</note>—all these matters refer to the gathering of the scattered exiles. There are many matters regarding the "reincarnations" <note>Hebrew: *Gilgulim*, the cycle of souls returning to the world to achieve perfection</note> of the names that were scattered.
And here, I shall add a flourish of my own to what is mentioned in this verse:
**“You shall not see your brother's ox or his sheep** straying and ignore them...”
**I will first introduce** what the Kabbalists have said regarding the matters of reincarnation.
Since the words of the godly Rabbi Solomon Alkabetz <note>16th-century Kabbalist and poet, famous for composing 'Lecha Dodi'</note> (may his memory be a blessing for the life of the world to come) are well-ordered, I will transcribe his language, as follows: I say that on the day God created Man upon the earth, He formed within him
types of "lights" <term>Ma’orot: spiritual illuminations</term> which He placed there for the purpose of Emanation. These are His statutes, His ordinances, and His teachings—the positive commandments which a man shall perform and thereby live in the aforementioned world.
This world shall also be a reflection of the 365 negative commandments <note>Hebrew: *Mitzvot Lo Ta'aseh*</note>, as is known. "He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life"—a soul emanated from Him, blessed be He, which ascends with him in its "ascent,"
clothed in and overseen by these commandments, so that not one of them is missing. For if even one of its "ingredients" is missing, he is liable for death and shall not ascend to the designated place.
The distance from that place corresponds to the number of commandments missing. Moreover, if he violated one of the commandments of the Lord which should not be done, He, in His compassion for the work of His hands,
"devises means so that the banished one be not expelled from Him" <note>Quoting 2 Samuel 14:14</note>. He established for them the principle of Reincarnation—which is the return to this world. This principle is divided into three parts corresponding to the three
attributes of the three Patriarchs <note>Abraham (Kindness), Isaac (Strength), and Jacob (Beauty)</note>. There are those who return to this world not because of a commandment they lacked, but to receive punishment for a transgression they committed—yet it is to do "Kindness" <term>Chessed</term> with the children of [the world].
This is explained in the *Book of Wonder* (*Sefer HaPali’ah*), the *Book of the Figure* (*Sefer HaTemunah*), and the *Book of the Sapphire Pavement* (*Sefer Livnat HaSapir*). The scriptural support for this is: "For your sake I have been sent" <note>original: *di-yeta'arvi bi le-ma'anchem*</note>.
These things vary in degree, as is known to those who delve into wisdom. If so, it says that his return was for their need. The secret of the verse "the law of Kindness is in your midst" was not given to be eaten <note>meaning: it is a deep spiritual secret, not for casual consumption</note>,
except from mouth to ear <note>transmitted via oral tradition</note>. This attribute is the "Courtyard of Kindness," the teaching of Abraham. And there are those who come to this world to receive punishment for a transgression for which it is impossible [to atone]
except through the power of the world, for it is the foundation of the King of Kings. Especially when "Strengths" <term>Gevurot: the attribute of Judgment</term> increase, for every wrath and every evil comes from it, according to the secret of "infants and sucklings" <note>referring to souls that die young as a form of purification</note>.
The dead, in their smallness—all this occurs when they have returned in complete repentance. Every human heart shall be moved, even by the agreement of the "fainting soul"; this does not happen to the wicked who seek reward.
The other has transgressed, and if he now returns in repentance, he will rectify the "Breath of Reincarnation." And these who reincarnate, when they have not returned to the Name <note>God</note> in completeness—sometimes, as mentioned in
the words of Elihu: "Lo, all these things God works, twice, thrice, with a man" <note>Job 33:29</note>. They shall no longer reincarnate [as humans] but rather in animals and beasts, pure or impure, the lighter [punishment] first.
"Twice, thrice with a man"—from then on, in a beast. One who has not plumbed the depths of divine knowledge might consider this a far-fetched idea, but let him reflect on the words:
for he [the Sage] brought this reality close even though it is distant and strange to the intellect. Let us return to the matter and say that these reincarnate in the attribute of "Loss," the attribute of Isaac <term>Gevurah/Judgment</term>. And there are those who return
for the purpose of completing the commandments they lacked until now. These shall be [granted] until the "thousandth generation," until they are completed, to emerge from their reincarnation through the secret of Jacob's attribute <term>Tiferet/Beauty</term>.

Israel, and the attribute of Jacob is Beauty <term>Tiferet</term>. The hint is brought

-># In the Beginning: The Blessing of the Torah<-

Which is the second Torah, the <term>Oral Torah<note>Torah she-be’al peh; the traditions and interpretations traditionally transmitted by speech rather than the primary written text.</note></term>, about which they ask, "Who is she?" She points with her tip toward the letter *Aleph* <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, often symbolizing the unity of God and the Written Torah</note>, for the Oral Torah points entirely toward the <term>Written Torah<note>Torah she-bi-khtav; the five books of Moses.</note></term>. For "from man this was taken," <note>original: "ki me-ish lukkacha zot," a pun on Genesis 2:23</note> meaning the Oral Torah is called "This" (*Zot*), as has been explained. She was taken from the Written Torah, which is called "Man" (*Ish*), for "Man and Woman" are known to represent these two—the Written and the Oral Torah. Everything in the Oral Torah is learned from the Written Torah, as is common in the Talmudic phrases "From where do we derive this?" or "From where are these words?" and similar expressions. In the creation of the Light and its hiding, the Written Torah was hinted at, as it says in the <term>Midrash<note>Ancient rabbinic homiletic interpretations of scripture.</note></term>: "Let there be light"—this is the symbol of the Torah, as it is said, "Light is sown for the righteous," referring to the five books of the Torah.

**A**nd I have already written that the concept of "Blessing" (*Berakhah*) is an expansion, like a great, constant, and eternal flow of bounty. This is essentially the nature of the "Hidden Light," for even though it is hidden for now, from it comes the name combined with the letter *Het*, representing the true Blessing. This is the secret of the expansion of the <term>Emanations<note>Atzilut; the highest of the four worlds in Kabbalah, representing pure divine light.</note></term> which have no end or limit, as it says, "And I will increase of the spirit and place it upon them." Currently, we only have the revealed expansion of the Oral Torah. However, the hidden secrets, which are the "Soul of the Soul," remain hidden. Even though there are luminaries of expansion in the secrets called "Souls," the "Soul of Souls" is hidden for the righteous in the future to come. There, the name <term>YHWH<note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God, often associated with the attribute of Mercy and the Written Torah.</note></term> is written forever because it is hidden, but it is pronounced by the name <term>Adonai<note>The name of God meaning "My Lord," associated with the attribute of Sovereignty and the Oral Torah.</note></term>. It is already known that the name YHWH is the secret of the Written Torah, as it says, "And this is the Torah," which is the secret of <term>Tiferet<note>Beauty/Harmony; the sixth divine attribute or Sefirah.</note></term>. The name Adonai is <term>Malchut<note>Kingship/Sovereignty; the tenth divine attribute, associated with the physical world and the Oral Torah.</note></term>, the Oral Torah, and she is the "Blessing" because she is the expansion, like the ten attributes within the Torah of God that are inherited through them. From this is drawn the blessing for dialectic study <note>Pilpul; a method of Talmudic study using sharp analysis and logic</note>, and the blessing is multiplied because one matter is learned from another. In the Talmudic tractate <italic>Gittin</italic>, in the chapter "Ha-Nizakin," they said: at first, the dialectic method was given only to Moses; afterward, it was given to all of Israel. This "remainder" is called by the name of God, as it says, "The Torah of the Lord is perfect," though it is also called the "Torah of Moses." I have written at length on this matter in my introduction to <italic>Toledot Adam</italic> and also in my commentary on tractate <italic>Shevuot</italic>. There, the Holy One, Blessed be He, handed over general principles to Moses, as it says, "And He gave to Moses... when He finished [k-khaloto]," which the Midrash interprets as "He gave him general rules [k-klalot]." From these, Moses understood the Oral Torah, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to him: "It is true, according to your discernment." Therefore, the Oral Torah is named after Moses: "This is the law of Moses" <note>original: "V'zot Mosheh"</note>. This is compared to the physical woman; the Oral Torah, being the secret of sovereignty (*Malchut*), is his wife. As the <term>Zohar<note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</note></term> says: "The Man of God, the husband of the Matronita" <note>The Matronita is a kabbalistic term for the Shekhinah, the Divine Presence.</note>. This is because he stems from the side of *Tiferet*, in the secret of the Wisdom of God from Wisdom (*Chokhmah*) and Understanding (*Binah*). Thus comes the hint: "But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding?" The pious author of <italic>Me'or Einayim</italic> wrote that the hidden Name is found within the name of Moses... <note>The text here engages in complex wordplay between the name Moses (Mosheh) and the divine names.</note>. Therefore, Moses is the "husband of the Matronita" and is called the "Man of God." It is true that ten individuals were called "Man of God": Moses, Elkanah, Samuel, David, Shemaiah, Iddo, Elisha, Micah, Amoz, and the Messiah. However, there is a difference between Moses and the others. "Man of God" as said of Moses means a man who belongs to God—that is, *Malchut*—like "the husband of Naomi." When "Man of God" is said of Phinehas, it means a man who is <italic>like</italic> God, meaning he is attached to Him. Furthermore, we always find his personal name joined to it, as in "Moses, the Man of God." In the Prophets, they are called by his name to remember his name always... unlike the other prophets. Regarding this matter of being called the husband of the Matronita, there is a hint: "A husband does not die except to his wife." This is hinted at in the verse "And Moses died there." The word for "mourning" (*Evel*) has the same numerical value (Gematria) as <italic>Adonai</italic> (61), for this attribute—this bride—mourned for Moses. Upon this comes the hint: "And this is the blessing with which Moses blessed..." I have already written on the meaning of "Blessing."

The Oral Torah is the "Second" and is represented by the letter *Bet* in the word *Bereshit* ("In the beginning"), which points toward the *Aleph* of *Anokhi* ("I am"), the Written Torah. It is also known that the attribute of *Malchut* is called "Blessing" (*Berakhah*), and she is the "Pool" (*Berekhah*) that receives all the emanations in the secret of the hundred silver sockets (*Adanim*) of the Tabernacle, which correspond to the "Hundred Blessings" as explained in the book <italic>Sha’arei Ora</italic>. The Midrash on Psalms says: in the place where Jacob stopped his blessings, Moses began; and where Moses stopped, David began. Jacob stopped with the word "this" (*Zot*), as in "This is what their father spoke to them." Moses began with "this," as in "And this is the blessing." Moses stopped with "Happy are you, O Israel," and David began with "Happy is the man." The matter is this: "This" refers to the Land—the "Upper Land" given to you—which is divided into twelve territories. Corresponding to them are the twelve tribes who were allotted the land below, for the upper reflects the lower, six against six. *Tiferet* brings back the edges, and corresponding to them are those who receive these six. The Written Torah is the letter *He* (5), representing the five books; the Oral Torah is the letter *Vav* (6). There is a hint in the letter *He* and the letter *Bet* in its full spelling—six against six—making twelve borders. From there, Jacob divided the blessings to the twelve tribes who would inherit the Land of Israel. From the place where Jacob stopped, Moses began, for Moses delved deeper to sometimes enter and draw out the blessings. All of Moses’ blessings were of the same nature as Jacob’s blessings, but of a higher and more internal level; that is, the end of Jacob's blessing was the beginning of Moses'. Both were blessing the twelve tribes in their inheritance of the Land of Israel. However, above them all is King David, who is essentially the attribute of *Malchut*. As our Sages said, "One who disputes the kingdom of the House of David is as if he disputes the Shekhinah." He is the summation of all the tribes of Israel; therefore, he is more and more a "depth of blessing," delving into the innermost parts. Where Moses stopped, David himself began. Let us return to the matter: "This is the Torah of the Lord" and "The Torah of Moses"—it is the "Torah of Man." In every generation, the Sages innovate through their analysis to derive one thing from another. This is the Torah that the Holy One, Blessed be He, learns from the mouths of the Rabbis, saying, "My son so-and-so says this, and my son so-and-so says that." The hidden secrets are the "Torah of the Lord," which He reveals to those who fear Him. In the future, He will reveal the Hidden Light which was the *Aleph* mentioned above, and the Oral Torah is the *Bet*. This is what is hinted at here: "The Lord came from Sinai" after mentioning "And this is the blessing with which Moses blessed," which is the Oral Torah. "The Lord from Sinai" refers to the secrets of the Written Torah, which is the Torah of the name YHWH. He said "Bet" and "He"—it is the *Aleph-Bet*. As I will write later, "He shone forth from Seir to them," meaning the Torah was hidden. The kindness of the Hidden Light was intended for the future, but "He shone from Seir to them and appeared from Mount Paran"—here he hints at an expansion of some of that light in a specific measure. He shone from Seir upon Israel from the light of the angels. As it is written in the Zohar in the portion of *Balak*: Come and see, it is written: "The Lord came from Sinai, shone forth from Seir to them, the earth trembled, etc." When the Holy One, Blessed be He, wanted to give the Torah to Israel, He went and turned to all the nations, but they did not accept it. As it says:

So-and-so came and "shone from Seir unto them," but they did not want to receive it. He went to the children of Ishmael, but they did not want to receive it, as it is written: "He appeared from Mount Paran." Since they did not want it, He returned it to Israel. Thus we have learned. Now one must ask: We have learned that there is no sin for a person who scrutinizes the details of the Torah, so I will ask my question to illuminate the words of this verse which does not seem settled. If the Holy One, Blessed be He, came to Seir, to which of their prophets did He appear? And when He went to Paran, to which of their prophets did He appear? If you say He appeared to all of them, we have never found this to happen except with Israel alone, and specifically through Moses. And it has been said that this is how they established the verse to say: "The Lord came from Sinai," and this is "from Seir unto them" and "appearing from Mount Paran." However, "from Seir unto them" and "from Mount Paran"—all this must be known and looked into. I asked this question, but I did not hear or know the answer. When Rabbi Shimon came, I asked him the matter as before. He said to me: This question has been discussed. "The Lord came from Sinai," as it says, "Behold, I come to you in a thick cloud." And from Sinai He came and was revealed to them. "He shone from Seir unto them"—from what He said to the children of Seir, who did not want to receive it, from that He gave light to Israel and added light to them, and they loved Sinai. So too, He "appeared" and gave light to Israel from Mount Paran, by the power of what the children of Paran said—that they did not want to receive it—from this, Israel added love and light more than was fitting. And regarding your question "Through whom did He appear to them?" Come and see: The Lord is the High God, and He revealed the matter through Himself. The Torah came out from the holy upper secret of the Hidden King. When it reached the Left Arm, the Holy One, Blessed be He, saw in a vision of that arm a "bad blood" <note>This refers to the spiritual essence of Esau/Edom, associated with the planet Mars and bloodshed.</note> that was liable there. He said: I need to purify and whiten this arm. If not, that bad blood will lower and damage everything. But it was necessary to clarify every flaw from here. What did He do? He called to the Left and it came before Him. He said to it: Do you want my Torah? It said: What is written in it? He said to it: "You shall not murder." The Holy One, Blessed be He, skipped to the part that was necessary. It said: Heaven forbid! This Torah is Yours, and let it stay Yours; I do not want this Torah. It was beloved and appeared before Him. It said: Master, if You give me all my dominion, let it be removed, for my dominion is over killing, and wars will not exist, and my dominion is over the planet Mars—everything will be canceled from the world. Master of the world, take Your Torah and let me have no portion or inheritance in it. But if it is pleasing before You, here are the people of the children of Jacob—give it to them.

Life for the holy ones would not be recognized if not for the "Seir" <note>Esau</note> and his deeds being like the husks of the nations. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the thirteen hermeneutic principles of Rabbi Ishmael, specifically focusing on the nuances of 'General and Particular' logic versus 'Inclusion and Exclusion' logic, and how specific examples like the laws of firstborns and covering blood illustrate these rules.</meta>

# Oral Torah

And Ishmael <note>Rabbi Ishmael, a 2nd-century scholar famous for his thirteen rules of biblical interpretation.</note> does not expound the principle of **Particular, General, and Particular** <note>Hebrew: *Prat u-Klal u-Prat*; a rule where a specific term is followed by a general term and then another specific term, limiting the law to things similar to the specifics.</note>; therefore, he did not count it. Those verses regarding the **piercing** <note>original: *denuyer* / *v'reka*; likely referring to the piercing of a servant's ear with an awl in Exodus 21:6</note> that we brought above are interpreted by him for a different derivation, as there are those who expound there—so ends his words. 

And there are some who do not expound the Torah according to the meaning of **General and Particular**, but rather according to the meaning of **Inclusion and Exclusion** <note>Hebrew: *Ribui u-Mi'ut*; a method associated with Rabbi Akiva that results in a broader application of the law than Rabbi Ishmael's method.</note>. That is to say, in place of **General, Particular, and General**, or **General and Particular**, he expounds **Inclusion, Exclusion, and Inclusion**, or **Inclusion and Exclusion**. The difference between the 'General and Particular' method and the 'Inclusion and Exclusion' method is explained in the words of Rashi, of blessed memory, in the chapter "The Verdict is Final" <note>Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 6</note>, at the end of the chapter "These are the Injured" <note>Tractate Chullin, chapter 3</note>, and in the chapter "These are the Skins." 

It is this: those who expound **General and Particular** view the **Particular** as an explanation of the **General**. But those who expound **Inclusion and Exclusion** do not see the **Particular** as an explanation, but rather as an **Exclusion** that removes a portion and leaves a portion. From now on, the difference will be clear to you: in many places, one who expounds **General and Particular** concludes that the law includes *only* what is in the **Particular**, and you may not add even something similar to it. But one who expounds **Inclusion and Exclusion** includes everything and excludes only that which is truly unlike it. 

Furthermore, one who expounds **General, Particular, and General** views the **Particular** as the explanation of the **General**, so the law includes only what is in the **Particular**; when the text returns to a **General** term, it only comes to add things *similar* to the **Particular**. However, one who expounds **Inclusion, Exclusion, and Inclusion** includes everything and excludes what is dissimilar, but when the text returns to include again, it includes even that which is dissimilar. It excludes only one thing—the most distant thing—and the Scripture leaves it to the Sages to know which thing is appropriate to exclude. 

Regarding the matter of **Particular and General** and **Exclusion and Inclusion**, the law is the opposite of **General and Particular** and **Inclusion and Exclusion**. **Exclusion and General** <note>original: *Mi'ut v'Prat v'Klal*</note> is essentially like **General and Particular**, including everything. But **Exclusion and Inclusion** is more complex... <note>The text here enters a technical debate about the sequence of inclusions and exclusions in the biblical text, specifically regarding the 'awl' (Exodus 21:6) and whether the phrasing follows a standard linguistic path or a specific legal derivation.</note> It is the way of the master's speech to use the measure of **Exclusion, Inclusion, and Exclusion**, which is not a standard measure. Even if one expounds **Inclusions and Exclusions**, he may still expound it as **General, Particular, and General** because if he expounded it as **Exclusion, Inclusion, and Exclusion**, we would struggle with why the final exclusion was necessary to change the way of the verse... therefore he expounds it as **General, Particular, and General**.

# From a General that needs a Particular, and from a Particular that needs a General
->This measure teaches that the General needs<-
->the explanation of the Particular, and the Particular the explanation of the General<-

Do not be surprised when this measure is compared to the measure of **General and Particular**, for the difference between them is in this matter: in a standard **General and Particular**, each one is clear in its meaning on its own and does not need the other. For example, "From the animals, from the cattle and from the sheep" <note>Leviticus 1:2</note>. "Animals" does not need the explanation of "cattle and sheep," nor do "cattle and sheep" need "animals." Therefore, they said "the General includes only what is in the Particular," because the Particular did not come to explain the meaning of the General (which was already clear), but only to specify from within its category. 

However, in **A General that needs a Particular**, the meaning of the General is not clear on its own; through logic alone, it could mean something else. Then the Particular comes to explain and redefine its meaning. This is why they said **A General that needs a Particular**, such as "and he shall cover it in the earth" <note>Leviticus 17:13, regarding the blood of slaughtered animals</note>. We do not expound this as a standard **General and Particular**, where "the General includes only the Particular," etc., because this is a **General that needs the Particular's explanation**. "And he shall cover" could mean overturning a vessel over it, or mixing it with earth. Indeed, the primary meaning of the word [cover/conceal] usually implies overturning or hiding, as in "you desired them and saw me" or "a faithful spirit conceals a matter" <note>Proverbs 11:13</note>. Thus, when the verse says "in the earth," it explains that this covering must be through actual mixing and mingling. The General needs the Particular to define its meaning, and therefore it is expounded in its place as a **General that needs a Particular**.

A similar example is found in the laws of Firstborns: "Sanctify to Me every firstborn..." <note>Exodus 13:2</note>. One might think this includes a female, but the text says "**Male**." One might think even if a female was born before him, the text says "**Opening of the womb**" <note>Hebrew: *Patar Rechem*</note>. This means that a "firstborn male" is the first one born, but even if a female preceded him, he might still be called a "firstborn" in a general sense. Therefore, "Opening of the womb" comes and redefines the meaning of "firstborn" to mean specifically the very first thing to emerge from the womb. These matters, written by the author of *Halikhot Olam* <note>A 15th-century work on Talmudic methodology by Rabbi Yeshuah ha-Levi</note>, are explained clearly.

In Tractate Bekhorot, page 19, it says: "From a General that needs a Particular and a Particular that needs a General—how so? 'Sanctify to Me every firstborn'—I might think even a female is included. Therefore, the Torah says 'Male.' If it says 'Male,' I might think even if a female was born before him? Therefore, the Torah says 'Opening of the womb.' If it says 'Opening of the womb,' I might think even if he was born after a Caesarean section <note>original: *Yotzei Dofen*</note>? Therefore, the Torah says 'Firstborn'." This is a General that needs a Particular and a Particular that needs a General. See Rashi there. 

The emerging principle is this: a standard General is understood on its own, as is the Particular. Like "From the animals" (General) and "Cattle and sheep" (Particular)—it is clear that cattle and sheep are types of animals. The Particular only comes to exclude wild beasts from the blessing. However, in "Cover it in the earth," the General "Cover it" *needs* the Particular "Earth." Without "Earth," we would interpret "Cover" as overturning a vessel. Even if we allowed mixing, we wouldn't exclude a vessel. Thus the General needs the Particular to exclude the vessel. Similarly, "Firstborn male" and "Opening of the womb" need each other because the General "Firstborn" isn't clear enough on its own—it could mean the first male even if a female was born first. The Particular "Opening of the womb" explains it must be the first birth. But "Opening of the womb" alone isn't clear either—we might think it includes a Caesarean birth. Thus it needs the General "Firstborn" to show it must be a natural first birth in all respects. The Sages elaborated on this in the Baraita in the Gemara.

# Anything that was included in a General Rule and then singled out—it was not singled out to teach about itself alone, but to teach about the entire General Rule.

<columns>2</columns>
**Gloss**
And the *Korban Aaron* <note>A commentary on the Sifra by Rabbi Aaron ibn Chayyim, 16th-17th century</note>, of blessed memory, in the second chapter, says: "Anything" implies something extra, as if to say any matter that was part of a general category and was then excluded to teach a law... it comes to teach about the whole rule. Even though it was singled out, it still teaches about the whole category. According to this, he investigated the arrangement of the words... if it was already part of the general rule, why was it singled out? If it were just for its own sake, it wouldn't need to be singled out, as the rule already applied to it. For example, the law of "Kindling fire" <note>on Shabbat</note> was already part of the general rule of "Do no work." Therefore, its being singled out must be to teach us something about the entire category of "work"—specifically, that just as one is liable for kindling fire individually, one is liable for each type of work individually.
<column-break/>
This is the language of *Halikhot Olam*: This measure in the Torah is to teach about itself and about its general category. The phrasing implies this: as they said regarding Kindling—"You shall kindle no fire" <note>Exodus 35:3</note>. Kindling was already included in the general prohibition "You shall do no work." Why was it singled out? To divide <note>Hebrew: *l'halek*</note>. That is to say, to make the various labors distinct, so that if one performed five labors including kindling in one state of unawareness, he is liable for kindling individually. From there we learn for the others: just as one is liable for kindling individually, so too for all others. This is also the case with **Necromancy and Divination** <note>original: *Ov v'Yidoni*</note>, which were part of the general prohibition against sorcery but were singled out to teach a specific law about the whole category.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the thirteen rules of hermeneutics (interpretation) used to derive the Oral Torah from the written text, specifically focusing on the rule of context and the rule of resolving contradictions.</meta>

<page-num>85</page-num>
<header>Oral Torah</header>

...regarding the plague of leprosy <note>original: "tzara'at"</note> in a house in the land of your possession: "and He shall put the plague..." it is possible etc. Two types are mentioned: either a house made of planks or curtains, or a house built of stones, wood, and earth.
We might know from the air <note>The author uses "air" (avir) here perhaps to refer to the general atmosphere or context</note> which of these it speaks of, or if it speaks of all of them. For this purpose, it was handed down to us at Sinai that we should learn this from the laws stated regarding a "house" at the end of the passage...
and the structural elements of the house. Therefore, when it says "and he shall break down the house, its stones, and its wood," we learn from this that it only speaks of a house built of stones, wood, and earth. As for saying "from its end" <note>learning a definition from the conclusion of a scriptural passage</note>...
if it is explained from its beginning, it is even better, for the nature of this interpretive measure is that the matter should be learned from itself, whether at its beginning or its end. And since it informs us from the end, we learn...
all the more so from the beginning. The Ra’avad <note>Rabbi Abraham ben David of Posquières, a 12th-century French scholar</note> wrote something similar, stating: "The reason it says 'from its end' is because it already mentioned the rule of 'a matter learned from its context' <note>original: 'davar ha-lamed me-inyano'</note>, which might apply even to a nearby subject..."
Like the case of "and you shall slaughter... and you shall eat," or the case of "you shall not steal" <note>referring to the Ten Commandments, where "stealing" in that context refers specifically to kidnapping</note>, where we learn the matter from its context; how much more so do we learn from the beginning of the same subject. This is why it says "from its end."

## Two verses that contradict each other until a third verse comes and reconciles them

**The Ra'avad** explained this rule in the following way: when there are two verses that contradict one another, you are not permitted to reject them or consider them an error. Instead, you must hold the tension between them and the Torah...
until a third verse arrives and decides between them. Then you must act according to the resolution the Torah provides. He [the Ra'avad] taught...
that we learn from this rule that the resolution provided by the Torah in a third verse between two contradictory passages is authoritative. For example, it is written "from the heavens etc." and another verse...
says, "And the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai." The third verse then comes and reconciles them: "From the heavens He made you hear His voice... and on the earth He showed you [His great fire]." From this resolution, you can learn to resolve other cases...
of verses that contradict each other where a third verse does not explicitly appear to reconcile them by our own logic. For instance, we find what the Torah says in the portion of *Acharei Mot* regarding...
[the author discusses various internal contradictions in the laws of sacrifices and land]. He brought proof for his opinion from how the Sages reconciled, through their own logic, the verse that says "and you shall measure outside the city two thousand cubits" and another verse...
that says "from the wall of the city and outward, one thousand cubits round about." Likewise, as we learned in the tractate *Bechorot* <note>Firstborn animals</note>, one verse says "you shall sanctify" and another verse says "you shall not sanctify," and they reconciled them...
by their own logic and harmonized them according to their understanding. However, the language "until a third verse comes" is difficult and seems to have no meaning if it simply means logic; it should have just said...
"two verses... reconcile them." Then it would say, "how does the third verse come?" using the Torah as proof. This is similar to the rule of *Kal VaChomer* <note>an argument from minor to major</note>...
where we find the Torah itself uses the logic of *Kal VaChomer*, and proof is brought from the *Kal VaChomer* of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai which is explicit in the Torah. If so, it is not the way of a teacher of the Oral Torah to...
and logic alone would not dictate this. For who can come after the King? How can one's own mind reconcile two verses that are in total contradiction and absolute opposition? The Ra'avad felt this and was forced to explain that this is a divine guideline: there are two verses that appear to contradict... until the [third verse arrives].
Therefore, from here you learn to resolve two verses that are difficult against each other, and not that one should be rejected or that we should consider the Torah to contain an error. See how the Rabbi struggled with this...
and he only pushed this interpretation to equate this rule with the rule of *Kal VaChomer*. Look into the *Netiv* and *Chiyud*... [he discusses finding these views in the Talmud].
The book *Korban Aharon* <note>A classic commentary on the Sifra/Halakhic Midrash</note> also wrote pleasant things regarding this rule: "To this end, it is worthwhile to explain to you what we understand from the plain meaning of the teacher's words..."
We say there are two types of opposition. The first is opposition without total contradiction or denial, as has been clarified. The second is opposition with total denial, contradiction, and absolute conflict. The first type is that...
which the Sages strived to reconcile and harmonize, so that they do not exclude one another; rather, it is possible for both to be upheld. Come and see the commandment, as this is the beginning...
of the reconciliation which we find explicitly in the Torah: The Ra'avad saw that Rabbi Akiva said: one verse says, "And you shall measure outside the city on the east side two thousand cubits," and another verse says, "from the wall of the city and outward, one thousand cubits round about." One says one thousand cubits and the other says two thousand cubits? How can this be? One thousand cubits...
is for the open space <note>original: 'migrash'</note> and two thousand cubits is for the Sabbath boundary <note>original: 'tchum shabbat'</note>. Rabbi Abba, the son of Rabbi Yose the Galilean, says: one thousand cubits is for the open space, and two thousand cubits are for fields and vineyards. Look and contemplate...
these matters are necessary to see where the city is surrounded. Because of this, these two verses do not truly contradict each other, for 'one thousand cubits' does not exclude 'two thousand' since they refer to different subjects...
through which both verses can be fulfilled. Thus Rabbi Akiva interpreted it: one thousand for the open space and two thousand for the Sabbath boundary. And Rabbi Abba saw that the boundary does not necessarily have to be given...
since it is not for the improvement of the cities but for the improvement of the settlement, whether they are in his flock or wherever they may be from the fields. Therefore he said that these are like two different subjects...
the improvement of the city, and it is appropriate to say in His kindness "it shall be for you the open spaces of the city." To this, he said that one thousand cubits is for the open space, which is an empty, clear area...
as an ornament for the city to have light. And the two thousand around it were given to the Levites as their inheritance; one thousand cubits around the city for the open space, and the rest for fields and vineyards. In this way, the two thousand...
are given to the Levites around the city: of them, one thousand for the open space and the rest for fields and vineyards. Similarly, what was said in the tractate *Arachin* in the chapter "One who consecrates his field": Rabbi Ishmael says, one verse...
says "you shall sanctify" and another verse says "he shall not sanctify." One says etc. How can this be? One may consecrate it as a 'consecration of value' <note>donating the monetary value to the Temple</note> but you may not consecrate it as an 'altar consecration' <note>as a physical sacrifice</note>...
One verse says "you shall sanctify" regarding the firstborn, as it is written "Every firstborn... you shall sanctify," and another verse says "he shall not sanctify," as it is written "But a firstborn... no man shall sanctify it." [The resolution is]...
a 'consecration of value' to bring it for its price, giving its benefit to the priest, but you do not sanctify it as an altar consecration such that another type of sacrifice would apply to it. See and understand that according to...
the statements "you shall sanctify" and "you shall not sanctify," even though they are a positive and a negative, it is not a strong contradiction since there are many types of sanctification. We can establish the positive for one type of sanctification, namely...
value, and the negative for another type, namely the altar sanctification. Indeed, as Rashi explained, the positive command is to sanctify the firstborn by saying "Behold, you are holy as a firstborn," and the negative is against...
another sanctification. Likewise, the contradiction regarding "consecrated to the Lord" and the verse "it shall be for them round about" is not a contradiction because it lacks the term for totality, the word "all." If it...
had written "all the assembly for God" and "all the assembly for you," they would contradict each other in an absolute denial. But as it stands, it says "assembly," "assembly," and "assembly," and does not specify if it is "all" or "part"...
this is an indefinite premise. It is as if it said "part for the Lord and part for you." And Rabbi Ishmael, who said "it is all for the Lord" etc., believes the verse...
uses a broad term. Therefore, he said it is as if it said "all" in both, but that this is not a command but a permission. Meaning: the choice is in your hand—either give it all to the Lord or...
all to yourselves. The intent of the verse is that one should fulfill the commandment with it. This is the "First Type," where the opposition between verses is not an absolute denial but a partial opposition...
Therefore, they do not call it a "contradiction" or a "denial." In such cases, permission is given to our intellect to harmonize them, since the resolution is apparent once we see they do not exclude...
each other. However, in the "Second Type" of opposition, which is absolute denial where they totally exclude each other, this is the rule [the 13th rule]. Its intent is to say that when we see...
verses that absolutely exclude each other, we should leave them alone until the third verse arrives to be the decider between them. For in such absolute contradictions, the power is not given...
to our intellect. See the example they brought for this: one verse says "From the heavens He made you hear His voice," as it says "For from the heavens I have spoken with you," which shows the voice was in the heavens...
and another verse says "And the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai," which is an absolute contradiction, for if He is in heaven He is not on earth, and if He is on earth He is not in heaven...
We said that in such a case, it is not within the power of the intellect to harmonize them, nor should we think they are an error, but rather wait until the third verse comes etc. And this is...
what it says: "From the heavens He made you hear His voice... and on the earth etc." Pay close attention to the phrasing "until the third verse comes," which implies it is a third entity equal to them in that it...
comes from the mouth of prophecy, and it shall be the decider, not you. In this way, the word "until" is settled.

## All the rules are completed; to God be praise and thanks.

**The Rule of Rabbi:** The intention here concerns the matter of the Mishnah. For "Rabbi" <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince</note> is our Holy Teacher; he wrote the Mishnahs and arranged them. Therefore, this general rule will explain...
the Mishnahs. The explanation of "Mishnah" is as "Second to the King" <note>original: 'mishneh la-melekh'</note>, for the Written Torah is the King, and the Mishnah is second to it and its mistress etc...
They are called "Tanna" because the root of that word also means "to repeat" <note>shoneh</note> or "second." It is just that "Mishnah" is the Holy Tongue [Hebrew] and "Tanna" is the language of the Targum [Aramaic]. For the word "and you shall teach them" <note>veshinantam</note> is translated [into Aramaic] as "and you shall repeat them" <note>vetatninun</note> and...
