<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of Talmudic methodology and the principles of legal interpretation, specifically how the Sages determine if a list in the Mishnah is exhaustive or if the author "taught some and omitted others."</meta>

# The Tablets of the Covenant
<note>original: "Luchot HaBerit," the title of the work by Rabbi Isaiah Horowitz</note>

The Hebrew maidservant <note>term: "ivriyah" — a Jewish girl sold into domestic service by her father, usually due to poverty, who serves until puberty or her father's death</note> acquires her own freedom upon the death of her father, etc. Rav Sheshet raised an objection: There are four who receive a "severance gift" <note>term: "ma'anikin" — the gifts a master must give a Hebrew servant upon their release, as per Deuteronomy 15:13</note>, etc. Now, if it were so that she goes free at her father's death, we should see this mentioned as well. And if you were to say that the author "taught some and omitted others" <note>original: "tana veshayer" — a Talmudic principle suggesting a list isn't exhaustive</note>, the text uses the word "these," which implies an exhaustive list... However, there are places where the Sages say "he taught some and omitted others" even when the word "these" appears at the end. For example, in the chapter "These are Said in Any Language," the author omitted the "oath of testimony" and the "oath of utterance," and similarly in other places. The Tosafot <note>note: Medieval French and German commentators on the Talmud</note> concluded that a distinction must be made: wherever many diverse matters are taught together, we say "he taught and omitted" even if it says "these," such as the case in tractate Sotah. But where the text does not teach many diverse matters and still says "these," we do not say "he taught and omitted," as is the case in tractate Kiddushin and its like. Similarly, regarding a specific count, there are places where the teacher taught and omitted even though a number was specified. In the chapter "The One Who Performs Levirate Marriage," Rabbi Hiyya taught: "There are [matters] from the words of the Torah and four secondary prohibitions from the words of the Scribes," and the Gemara concludes there that he taught and omitted, and likewise in many places. This requires careful legal study <note>original: "iyun halacha"</note>; see the Tosafot in the first chapter of Kiddushin. These are the words of the Tosafot in the first chapter of Kiddushin regarding the "four who receive severance gifts," etc., where we say that wherever "these" is taught, we do not say "he taught and omitted."

And they wrote in the second chapter of Ketubot that even though a number is taught, one might say he omitted, unless he teaches (as he does there): "And you cannot say [this] about any one of them." In the chapter "These Young Women," the Tosafot wrote: "Even though in the first chapter the Talmud deduces 'the teacher taught "these" and yet you say he taught and omitted?', here where it is taught at the end..." And at the beginning of the chapter "These are Those Who are Lashed," Rashi <note>note: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, the preeminent 11th-century commentator</note> of blessed memory wrote that "these" is not precise and he indeed taught and omitted. And there the Gemara says: "The teacher taught and you say he taught and omitted?" And in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah, the Tosafot wrote: "One can say that even though the teacher gave a count, one might still say he taught and omitted." They wrote similarly in the chapter "Damages."

# He wrote
The Ramban <note>note: Rabbi Moses ben Nahman (Nahmanides), 13th-century scholar</note> of blessed memory wrote in the first chapter of Kiddushin: "It is preferable for us to uphold the Mishnah and establish it as the opinion of a single individual rather than saying the teacher taught and omitted." At the beginning of the first chapter of Bava Kamma and the second chapter of Ketubot, they discuss whether "half-damages" is an omission; [they conclude] this follows the view of Rabbi Yose the Galilean. And in the last chapter of Sukkah, regarding the "Eve of Passover," it is not an omission, for that follows the view of Rabbi Yehuda. Similarly, in the tenth chapter, the Rashba <note>note: Rabbi Shlomo ben Aderet, 13th-century Spanish scholar</note> of blessed memory in the first chapter of Bava Kamma, page 5, brought what Maharai Karo <note>note: Rabbi Joseph Karo, 16th-century author of the Shulchan Aruch</note> cited in his "Rules of the Talmud."

**When there is a difficulty** between the inference of the beginning [of a text] and the inference of the end, sometimes the Talmud replies and says "it is made" — meaning the teacher strengthened the inference of the beginning to be exactly like the end itself. And sometimes it says "This was taught, but that was not taught" <note>original: "ha lo shana zu"</note>. The matter is: wherever we find a clear tradition elsewhere, then we say "here it was taught [specifically]," but where there is no such tradition, we do not. He wrote similarly in the fourth chapter of Kiddushin; see also Tosafot in the second chapter of Chullin, page 10.

# He wrote
In *Halichot Olam* <note>note: "Paths of the World," a work on Talmudic methodology by Jeshua ben Joseph ha-Levi</note>: Which teacher chooses to mention at the beginning what comes from a derivation <note>original: "midrash"</note> and only then brings what is written explicitly in the Scripture? The reason is that what comes from derivation is more precious to him and he seeks to establish it. For example, at the start of Yevamot, "Fifteen women, etc., and his daughter's daughter, etc." The Gemara explains that he mentioned "his daughter" first because it comes from a derivation and is therefore more precious, so they prioritized it, as at the start of Nedarim. These are his words. And Maharai Karo wrote: "That which comes from derivation, etc. But I say that in some places we say 'when he begins, he begins with Torah law' <note>original: "de-oraita"</note> because it is preferable to him..." It would seem that when we say "what comes from derivation is more precious," it is when he first includes everything together—both what is written in the Torah and what is not—and then returns to specify them, as in the first chapter of Yevamot where it teaches "Fifteen women exempt their rival wives" and then specifies "And these are: his daughter, and his son's daughter, etc." But where he did not first include both the Scriptural and the non-Scriptural together, we say "he began with Torah law." Likewise, at the beginning of the chapter "There are Those Who Inherit," we say "since it comes from derivation, it is more precious."

# Sometimes
There are three teachers mentioned in a dispute, and if there is no difference for the last one between the final teacher and the earlier ones, then the Gemara asks: "Is this not the same as the first teacher?" <note>original: "hainu tanna kamma"</note>. It then answers: "There is a practical difference between them <note>original: "ika beiniyahu"</note> in such-and-such a case." And sometimes it says "there is a difference" and they conclude—meaning, we recognize the difference, but who hid it? There is a question on this: aren't the later rabbis the ones who forbid? The rule we hold is "the later teacher comes to add" <note>original: "tana batra letafuyi ata"</note>. The Tosafot wrote in tractate Eruvin, page 13, that it is not applicable to say "the later teacher comes to add" when there is another teacher who interrupts between them. And in the chapter "With What May We Light," it says "And the Sages say: he shall not light it." From the context, "the Sages" would be the same as the first teacher. The Talmud answers: "There is a practical difference between them regarding Rav Bruna's law, etc., but they did not specify." Tosafot wrote there that "they did not specify" does not apply here to mean the later one adds, but rather to be more stringent. It is surprising that the Tosafot needed this case where there are three teachers, since the rule is in their hands that the later one adds, as the teacher concludes regarding eggs. Likewise here, Nachum the Mede concludes that one may light with boiled tallow in its pure state, and the Sages come to forbid boiled tallow even when oil is added to it. Regarding Rav Bruna, one can say the same: they did not specify. However, in the first chapter of a Mishnah, even where there are three teachers, we say the later teacher comes to add to the first teacher. It says there according to the explanation of Rabbi Ishmael: "Three tables and three rams are forbidden," and the Sages say: "Sometimes they are forbidden and afterward permitted." The Gemara asks: "The Sages are the same as the first teacher?" and answers: "There is a difference between them regarding Samuel's law," who said that by custom it is only forbidden for a single day. The first teacher agrees with Samuel, but the others do not. The explanation is that there, the later one adds to the first. And in the tenth chapter, where three teachers are mentioned and the "world was proven," he wrote that it seems to him that even with three teachers, the middle teacher is more stringent in that tractate, while the last teacher comes to add to the first teacher and they specify. Since the middle teacher is very stringent, the last teacher's mind is not set on adding to that stringency, but presumably comes to add to the first teacher, which is why they specify.

# And in a case
where the first teacher was not mentioned by name, but the later teacher was mentioned by name, and there is another in the Gemara's conclusion which implies that the teacher whose name is specified is himself the first teacher—except that at the beginning his name was mentioned and then he returns to an anonymous statement <note>term: "stam"</note>, and afterward his name is mentioned—the first matter follows the opinion of so-and-so. We find this in Chullin at the start of "All Flesh," where it teaches: "Poultry may be placed on the table with cheese but not eaten, these are the words of the House of Shammai. The House of Hillel say: It may neither be placed nor eaten." Rabbi Yose said: "This is one of the leniencies of the House of Shammai and the stringencies of the House of Hillel." The Talmud asks: "Isn't Rabbi Yose the same as the first teacher?" and answers: "Who is the first teacher? Rabbi Yose." This means: "Whoever says a matter in the name of the one who said it brings redemption to the world." Rashi explains that the teacher forgot and did not mention his name at first, and then went back and mentioned his name. This clarifies several places in the Mishnah where it teaches "in the name of Rabbi Levi" and asks [the same question]. We explain according to Rashi that the teacher forgot and did not mention the name at first, and therefore left it anonymous; after it was written, he remembered the name but did not erase what he first wrote anonymously, because once it is written, it is written, and afterward he fulfilled the commandment to state a matter in the name of the one who said it.

# In the chapter
"One Who Steals Wood," where it says "he is indeed explaining," the Tosafot wrote: It is surprising that the Talmud does not ask, "If so, why do I need the word 'liable' twice?" And in the first chapter of Sanhedrin, why do I need the word "three" twice? In many places the Talmud is precise about this, and in many places it is not. The Rashba wrote: "There are many cases where it asks this, and many where it does not." In the first discussion of Sanhedrin, "Why 'three' twice?" and at the start of Metzia, "this and that" is taught, and at the start of Nedarim, "Why 'forbidden'?" and in the chapter "A Beth Kor," it asks "Why 'I am selling'?" And there are places where it does not ask: in the first chapter of Chullin in the Baraita <note>note: an external teaching not included in the Mishnah</note> of "one who slaughters with a detached object, his slaughter is valid," where it explains the derivation but does not ask "Why 'valid' twice?" And in the chapter "The Sinew that Displaced," regarding impure eggs boiled with pure eggs, it does not ask "Why 'forbidden' twice?" And in the chapter "Disqualified Consecrated Items," the Tosafot wrote: "In every place where it says 'he is liable,' one cannot say 'he is indeed explaining' in those places where it does not ask."

# The way of the Talmud
is to ask: "Since they argue about this, let them argue about that," and it will establish the dispute in both. The answer to this can be in one of three ways: either to say that it took one of them as the point of dispute, implying the dispute applies to the other as well; or to say that the dispute is obvious there, and here it comes to teach us a greater novelty <note>original: "chiddush"</note> that they even argue in this case; or to say that precisely here they argue, but there they do not. These are the three ways: "it is necessary," "all the more so," and "specifically."

# A Mishnah
from which they bring a precise proof, but we ask an objection from a distant part of it, and the end of the text seems to contradict his words, and it concludes: "Rather, from this nothing can be proven." This is like what we say in Bava Batra in the chapter "One Who Sells a Beth Kor" <note>term: "Beth Kor" — a measure of land area, approximately 6 acres</note>: what is the law in an anonymous case? If one says, "I am selling you a Beth Kor of earth," what is the law? If measured by a rope, any small amount less, he must deduct from the price; any small amount more, he must return it. Thus, an anonymous case is like being measured by a rope. But they objected: look at the end of the text, "If he said 'more or less,' then even a quarter-measure per seah..." or
->they shall return<-

<meta>The previous page appears to have discussed the methods of the early sages (Tannaim) such as Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Oshaya. This page continues the methodological analysis of the Talmud, focusing on the Amoraim (later sages) and the structure of their legal inquiries.</meta>

Page 355
->The Oral Torah<-

The ways of Hiyya and the ways of Oshaya <note>Two major sages who compiled external teachings (Baraitot) after the Mishnah was completed.</note>, and each one only knew the other's dispute. It seems to me that when the Talmud asks "Shall we say..." <note>original: "לימא" (leima)</note> and so forth, it is in order to clarify how the law is decided according to the rules transmitted to us—for example, that in a dispute between person X and person Y, the law follows person X. Furthermore, there is another practical application: if we find one of them saying the opposite elsewhere, we may challenge him from his own words <note>literally: "from his own to his own".</note> Also, in passing, the Talmud sometimes explains the words of the early sages (Tannaim) which are obscure. This is the same approach used when discussing a dispute between later sages (Amoraim) as in the chapter "Merubeh" <note>Baba Kamma 62b</note> and at the beginning of Horayot. These are his words.

## Rule of the Amoraim
The role of an Amora <note>A Talmudic sage (approx. 200–500 CE) who "interpreted" or "said" the teachings of the earlier Tannaim.</note> is like that of the Tosefta—namely, to explain the Mishnah. Because in later generations, the hearts [intellectual capacities] were diminished <note>original: "נתמעטו הלבבות"</note> and the explanation of the Tosefta was not sufficient, the Amoraim came and explained the Mishnah at greater length. They also created an explanation for the explanations they had given for the Tosefta. I have already written regarding the meaning of the word "Amora" above in the section concerning "Rabbi."

## The Way
When the Talmud challenges one Amora with the words of another Amora, it says: "Are you casting [the words of] one man against [those of] another man?" <note>original: "גברא אגברא קא רמית" (gavra agavra ka ramit); meaning, why should the opinion of one sage invalidate the opinion of another equal peer?</note> as is found in Sanhedrin in the chapter "Zeh Borrer," and in many other places. Sometimes it says: "The words of person X are a transmitted teaching <note>original: "מימרא" (memra)</note>, and person Y does not agree with that teaching." This is like what we say in the chapter "Hazkat HaBatim" where we challenged Rav Bibi, because Rav Nachman said to Rav Huna: "If one was hung [under duress] and sold, his sale is a [valid] sale," and he replied that Rav Bibi’s statement is a transmitted teaching, and Rav Huna does not agree with that teaching. 

Rashbam wrote there: "It is a transmitted teaching" means that he is saying it in the name of others. But if Rav Bibi had said it in his own name, he would be a "man" [authority], and then we would ask "Are you casting one man against another?" Until here are his words. Therefore, when we challenge one Amora with another, if the words of the one being challenged are his own, the answer is "Are you casting one man against another?" but if his words were the words of another, then the answer is "The words of person X are a transmitted teaching, and person Y does not agree with it."

## And Sometimes
We challenge one Amora with another because the law follows him. In the chapter "D.T." we challenge a teaching of Rav against Rav Hanin, and the R.A.P. <note>likely a reference to a specific commentator or 'the Rosh' (Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel)</note> explained that since Rav was an Amora, we challenge based on his words because he was the leader of the people in the Diaspora in his generation, except for Shmuel. And sometimes we challenge one Amora with another where we are certain that the law follows him, like when it says: "But did not Rav Yehuda and the Sages say: if one stole and the owners have not yet despaired..." and the law is like him.

## And the Ramban
In his novellae on the tractate Bava Batra, wrote that we also challenge from Shmuel because of Rav’s greatness. Similarly, we challenge from Rav Kahana because he was a great man, as we find in the story of Rabbi Yochanan where he was particularly sharp.

## When [the Talmud] Brings
An Amora’s statement regarding the words of a Baraita <note>An "external" teaching from the era of the Mishnah not included in the main Mishnah.</note> or the Mishnah, it is because one could offer a different explanation for that Baraita; therefore, it brought the words of the Amora to clarify it and to derive a primary point from it. So wrote the Tosafot in the chapter "Zeh Borrer." Sometimes it brings an Amora regarding a Baraita simply for additional clarity. Likewise, it brings an Amora when it is known that the Baraita was not studied in the house of Rabbi Hiyya, as the Tosafot explained at the beginning of Shabbat regarding the phrase "thrown according to the group" where they challenged that this seems redundant like the phrase "and he saw, and furthermore the verse says." The Tosafot wrote that it refers to a group of Tannaim, and according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, it brought "thrown according to the group" regarding the Baraita because it was not studied in the house of Rabbi Hiyya.

## The Amora
His way is to explain and not to be obscure, as Rashbam wrote in the chapter "Arvei Pesachim" and Rashba in the chapter "Elu Terefot," whose words are: "The Amora should have explained explicitly, for it is not the way of the Amora to be obscure but to explain." So too wrote the Gaon in a Responsum, that the style is not for the Amora to make us hear a novel point through an inference, for it is not his way to be obscure, but to explain more than the Mishnah and the Baraita. This is the reason for what is found in the Gaon's Responsum, and similarly in the writings of Mahari Colon, that the rule "we do not learn from generalities even where it says 'except'" applies specifically to the words of the Tannaim because they repeated their teachings in a concise way and could not clarify everything necessary. But regarding the words of the Amoraim, we do not say this, for the way of the Amoraim is to explain.

## Sometimes
An Amora will make us hear something that is already explicitly stated in a Baraita. We see the reason for this in what Rashbam wrote in the chapter "Arvei Pesachim": because sometimes not everyone is expert in the Baraita, and even the Amora himself sometimes does not know it. **When** Amoraim are mentioned without specifics, and the subject allows for an interpretation from which it appears they disagree and an interpretation where they do not disagree, we must choose the interpretation [of agreement], even if it is very forced. So wrote the Ran in Shabbat and Bava Metzia.

## It is Not
For the Amoraim to bring into their dispute anything other than the specific point on which they disagree; they should not mention what is agreed upon. We find this in the chapter "Knot Cutheans" <note>likely referring to Menachot</note> where it is taught: "A house does not invalidate a sukkah," and an inquiry was posed to us regarding whether it counts toward the required size. Abaye said: "It does not invalidate and it does not count," while Rava said: "It does not invalidate and it does count." The Tosafot challenged: Why did Abaye and Rava need to mention "invalidation"? They should have only mentioned "counting," which is what they disagree on.

## Rule of Laws
Just as I wrote regarding the Tosefta and Baraitot—that the "Hofesh" <note>likely a term for the editor or compiler</note> refers to those waiting before them, and the Baraitot teach final legal rulings—so too is it the way of the Amoraim to explain the Mishnah as I wrote above. They also added and innovated legal rulings that were not mentioned in the Mishnah, and these are called "Halachot" (Laws). "Anyone who studies laws every day is assured that they are a child of the World to Come."

## Rule of the Academy
These are the "Sons of the Academy" <note>Bnei Yeshivah</note>. Every reasoning in the Talmud is what the Rabbis of the Academy reasoned. Similarly, all anonymous inquiries in the Talmud ("The inquiry was posed to them") refer to the members of the Academy.

## Rule of the Scales of Inquiry
This refers to the "Simplifier" <note>original: "פשטן" (pashtan) - one who resolves the query</note>, for the inquirer has two "scales" <note>original: "כף" (kaf) - palm of a hand or scale-pan</note>: one scale of merit and one scale of liability—meaning to find innocent or guilty, to forbid or permit, to make impure or pure, or to validate or disqualify. It is for this reason he asks if it is "this way or that way," and the Simplifier decides with one statement. Where inquiries are one after another, the way is that the second inquiry is born from the second side of the first inquiry. This is as if to say: "If you will find [reason] to say <note>original: "אם תמצא לומר" (im timtza lomar - a common Talmudic logical bridge)</note> that the first side of the first inquiry is the case, there is no room for the second inquiry; but if you will find [reason] to say the second side of the first inquiry, a different inquiry is still required." 

Sometimes the second inquiry is built on the first side of the first inquiry, saying: "If you will find [reason] to say the first side, a different inquiry is still required." The student must examine every place where there are two inquiries to see if the second is built on the first or second side. Most of the time it is built on the second side, and a minority of times on the first. Sometimes you will find many inquiries adjacent to each other, some built on the second side and some on the first. 

Sometimes we ask many inquiries and all of them say "What is the law? What is the law?" like the first one, as in Bava Batra in the chapter "Mi Shemet": "A house for an atrium, what is the law? One inside the other, what is the law? It stands [unresolved]." <note>original: "תיקו" (teiku)</note>. And so in many places. The way of wisdom, as I wrote, is that one must state the first inquiry, then "if you will find [reason] to say," upon which the second inquiry is built. And from the second inquiry two "what is the laws" result: "if you will find [reason] to say" how you will act in the first inquiry, whether on the second side or the first side. 

And just as an Amora asks an inquiry based on an "if you will find [reason] to say" from his own inquiry, so we find an "if you will find [reason] to say" based on the inquiry of his fellow. In Shevuot, Rava inquired: "One who swears 'I will not eat dust,' in what amount [is he liable]?" Rav Ashi inquired: "One who swears 'I will not eat a grape-stone,' in what amount?" The commentators explained that Rav Ashi asked this based on the "if you will find [reason] to say" regarding the dust. There are very many such cases. When there are many inquiries, and the first says "And if you will find reason to say it is permitted," then all subsequent inquiries follow that "if you will find reason to say it is permitted," and vice-versa. 

We find in the first chapter of Ketubot an inquiry: "What is the law regarding having intercourse for the first time on the Sabbath?" They change the order and say, "If you will find [reason] to say according to Rabbi Yehuda it is forbidden," they should have also said "If you will find [reason] to say according to Rabbi Shimon it is permitted," since they disagree—Rabbi Yehuda says an unintentional act is forbidden, and Rabbi Shimon says it is permitted. *Halichot Olam* says in the name of Rabbi Nachum bar Papa that this is not difficult, for even though they inquired according to Rabbi Yehuda's view that it is forbidden, within Rabbi Yehuda’s own logic there is a side where it is permitted, such as when it is a "destructive act," and from that inquiry a permit also emerges; see there.

## He Wrote
The *Halichot Olam* <note>The classic work on Talmudic methodology by Jeshua ben Joseph ha-Levi</note> regarding the way of the Amora to ask a single inquiry from which we can hear two [answers] depending on the respondent's reply. In another way, he could have asked in the chapter "Elu Terefot," where Rav Kahana and Rav Ashi asked Rav: "If a needle is found [piercing] a rib from here and a rib from there, what is the law?" We challenged: let him ask about one, meaning one rib, and from both of them we would hear two [answers]! He asked him in a language that implies a desire to resolve what is difficult: if [a needle in] two [ribs] makes it "torn" <note>original: "טריפה" (treifah) - unkosher due to fatal injury</note>, then certainly one rib does; and if he returns that a "torn" status results from one, then certainly two do. He was answering the clarity of the two you asked about, implying that regarding one, it is obvious.

<meta>catchword: to you</meta>
100 Q. B.

<meta>This page continues the systematic analysis of Talmudic terminology and the logical structure of Rabbinic debate, focusing on how challenges and inquiries are phrased.</meta>

->**The Oral Torah**<-

It appears from this context that the term *Atkafta* <note>original: "אתקפתא"; a logical challenge posed by an Amora (a Sage of the Gemara) based on reason rather than a quoted text</note> is not a phrasing used for a contradiction against what was said previously, for here the words of the Mishnah and the Baraita <note>A "Baraita" is a tradition from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the final authorized collection</note> are certainly true; rather, it is a difficulty the Sage has that he does not know how to resolve. This also appears from what the Tosafot <note>Medieval commentators on the Talmud</note> wrote in the chapter "The Widow is Maintained" (Ketubot, page 96a) in the entry beginning "A widow who seized movable property etc.," where the one who poses the challenge there only offers a "mere *Atkafta*" and does not necessarily hold that view himself. These are his words.

---

## Is it not?
The word *Mai* <note>original: "מאי"</note> means "What is it?" in the manner common to legal inquiries, as in "What is the law here?" Its meaning is "what is it," namely, is the law like this or like that? Similarly, in the phrase "What are we dealing with?" throughout the Talmud where it says "Is it not?" <note>original: "מאי לאו"</note> one must pause between the word *Mai* (What) and the word *Lav* (Not). That is to say: "What is the nature of this? Is it not so-and-so?" phrased as a wondering question.

---

## What is the difference between them?
This is a question regarding a dispute between *Amoraim* <note>Sages of the Talmudic era</note> about the reason for a law. It asks: "What is the practical difference in the law between them that led them to disagree over the underlying reason?" This is an inquiry into the "legal consequence" <note>Hebrew: *Nafka Mina*</note>. If they have no disagreement in the practical law, why did they come to a dispute over the reason, arguing whether it should be this reason or that reason? And if they do have a practical disagreement, what is that law over which they differ that led them to this dispute in reasoning?

## In what [point] do they disagree?
The phrase "In what do they disagree?" <note>original: "במאי קא מפלגי"</note> refers to cases where they have a dispute in the practical law. This is similar to asking "What is the legal consequence?"—meaning, if they have no disagreement in logic, why did they come to a disagreement in the law? 

Sometimes we find "What is the difference between them?" used in the same sense as "In what do they disagree?", and this is not forced, for the phrasing of "What is the difference between them?" can refer either to the root <note>the underlying logic</note> or the branch <note>the practical application</note>. If it refers to the root, it is like "In what do they disagree?"—meaning, what is the logic they argue over, where one Master holds one way and the other holds another, until they reached a dispute in this law? 

One might need this to explain the law between them, as stated at the beginning of Gittin (page 2a): "Rava said: What is the legal consequence for us to change it?" And Rava said: "Because witnesses are not commonly found to confirm it." And we say: "What is the difference between them? There is a difference between them in such-and-law..." and many such cases, for the Talmud is full of this. 

Even though the phrasing "What is the difference between them?" and "In what do they disagree?" are not always used distinctly, and one can explain either when they argue over a law or a reason, I say that the question "What is the difference between them?" is more precise for reasoning, as I explained—because the intent is to say "There is no practical difference between them, so why do they argue over the reason?" If "What is the difference between them?" is found regarding a dispute of law, it is strange according to the nature of the language. 

So I have found. However, Rav Hai <note>Rav Hai Gaon, a leading 10th-century Babylonian authority</note> held that "Between them" means "In what do they disagree." In the chapter "Interest" (Bava Metzia 63) regarding what is "excessive profit," he is precise as I explained... Rava said "One side of interest," and we ask "What is the difference between them?" meaning "In what do they disagree?" in the chapter "Gold" (Bava Metzia), asking what reason they give for their words. In the first chapter of Sanhedrin, regarding the dispute of those Sages whether we bring a "hollowed" person, it asks "What..." and Rashi explains it as "In what do they disagree?" In the chapters "The One who Places" and "Blue Thread," the Talmud's style is different there than other places... and he continues to explain using the language of "they disagree." He wrote further in the chapters "Daughters of Cutheans" (page 38), "The Miscarrying Woman" (page 22), "The One who Takes Out," and "Ownership of Houses" (page 40), "What is the difference between them? There is a difference between them..." The Tosafot wrote: "It is difficult for the Rabbi, what does it inquire? For they argue over the law explicitly!" And the Rashba <note>Rabbi Shlomo ben Aderet, 13th-century Spanish scholar</note> wrote: "One could say it is not meant precisely, but rather they seek to explain those who argue in general terms..."

## This
The phrase "This statement of So-and-so" <note>original: "הא דפלוני"</note> was not said as an explicit statement, but was inferred from a general rule. Sometimes the Talmud asks: "And if it was inferred, what of it?" and sometimes it does not ask. This matter is not always subject to that objection, but rather it asks whether the statement was said explicitly or inferred. "Explicitly" means it was stated clearly, or it belongs to the resolution "And if it was inferred, what of it?" because since he went to the trouble to establish it with resolutions, saying "rather it was inferred," it appears there is a general intention. 

Like that which is in the chapter "He who comes upon his sister-in-law," Rabbi Akiva bar Avri said in the name of Rabban Simeon ben Gamliel that the law is like Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai. Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi said to him: "Did you hear this from him explicitly, or did you hear it from a general rule?" What was the general rule? For Rabbi Simeon said "Any city..." He replied: "I heard it from him explicitly." And the Talmud asks: "And if it was inferred, what of it? It is different there..." and so on. 

I say: in every place where it says in truth "This statement of So-and-so was not stated explicitly but was inferred," such as in the third chapter of Shevuot where Rav Papa said "This statement of Rabbi Abbahu was not said explicitly but inferred," and many similar cases, it is not appropriate to ask "And if it was inferred, what of it?" because he is simply stating the truth of the matter. The phrase "What is the rule?" <note>original: "מאי כללא"</note> should be read with the vowel *Tzere* <note>a Hebrew vowel indicating an 'ey' sound</note>, meaning: "From what general rule was this understood?"

## He Objects
"So-and-so objects to support So-and-so." Sometimes the Talmud just says "He objects" on its own, and sometimes it says "So-and-so objects to support So-and-so," like in the chapter "Ownership of Houses" (Bava Batra), "Rava objects to support Rava," etc. The Rashbam <note>Rabbi Shmuel ben Meir, 12th-century commentator</note> explained that this was the phrasing used in the House of Study, and likewise "The teaching is in accordance with Rava, and it is a refutation of Abaye."

## Come and Hear
It is the way of the Talmud that when it comes to posing a challenge against an *Amora* from a Baraita or a Mishnah, it first says "They object" <note>Hebrew: *Mitivei*</note>. But when an *Amora* comes to resolve the Baraita or Mishnah that the questioner used to challenge him—by using another Mishnah or Baraita—he says "Come and hear" <note>Hebrew: *Ta Shema*</note>. This means: "The difficulty you raised has been resolved, now come and hear that there is another source." Do not imagine that there is no resolution. 

However, when the Talmud itself comes to pose an initial challenge against an *Amora*, it does not say "Come and hear" but "They object." Sometimes you will find "Come and hear" at the start because it begins a different challenge from a Baraita against another *Amora* using the phrase "Come and hear," or because it brings another *Amora* and challenges him from that same Baraita, it also says "Come and hear." Sometimes "They object" is used against an *Amora* and then it also starts with "Come and hear." The language can sustain both, for "Come and hear" literally means: "Come and hear what I say to you," using this challenge to solve the inquiry.

---

## In Chapter "He who was Struck"
In the chapter [the first of] Makkot, Rav Giddal said in the name of Rav: "A non-priest who ate from a Sin-offering or a Guilt-offering before the sprinkling of the blood [is liable]." Rava objected... "Rather, if it was stated, it was stated thus: Rav Giddal said in the name of Rav: A non-priest who ate from a Sin-offering or Guilt-offering before the sprinkling of blood is exempt." 

It is difficult: why did he need to change the version because of Rava's objection? Let us say that Rav himself is a *Tanna* <note>a Sage of the earlier Mishnaic era</note> and may disagree [with the Baraita]! Our teacher R.K. wrote in his principles of the Talmud: "A simple resolution is that the reason is because they are objecting from the Sifra <note>An ancient halakhic midrash on Leviticus</note>, which is the 'Book of the School of Rav.'" 

But it seems to me we can resolve it another way: here it is different because Rav Giddal said it in the name of Rav, and it is more plausible to say that Rav Giddal made a mistake than to say Rav is a *Tanna* and disagrees. 

Further, our teacher R.I.K. wrote: "Know that we find a matter phrased as a wonder, that is challenged from a Baraita and concluded as a refutation." In the chapter "The Miscarrying Woman," Rav Yosei asked Rabbi: "If a woman miscarries something like a raven and the placenta is attached to it, what is the law?" He said to him: "One does not ask about something that does not exist; a woman does not miscarry the likeness of domestic animals, beasts, or birds..." This was a refutation. 

The Rashba wrote: "It is logical that Rabbi himself recanted and taught that his own previous words were a refutation. For if not so, and we object from a Baraita—if Rabbi did not teach it, where did Rabbi Hiyya <note>Rabbi's primary student</note> get it?" He wrote that the law follows that Baraita. 

But this is not a correct resolution, for if so, the Talmud would not have remained silent and just said "it is a refutation." Rashi wrote: "The refutation of Rabbi, who said it is a thing that is not asked." It seems he intended to resolve this difficulty: if the divisions were in the law, we would ask "If Rabbi didn't teach it, where did Hiyya get it?" But regarding a matter dependent on physical reality—whether it exists or not—if it appeared to Rabbi that it doesn't, he answered based on what people thought. But the Talmud knew that the words of the Baraita are true, that it is a thing that exists. 

Another resolution: the conclusion "refutation" means that the Baraita itself is challenged and the law is not like it. Rabbi said "They object" to challenge the Baraita... and it refers back to Rabbi Yosei ben Saul who said in the name of Rabbi... that from the power of this Baraita we hear that such things never happened.

---

## Many
In many places we find in the Talmud, during a dispute between two *Amoraim*, that the questioner first challenges one *Amora* from a Mishnah or Baraita, and the answerer resolves it for him; then the questioner returns and challenges the second *Amora* from a different Mishnah or Baraita. 

There is a difficulty here even without the dispute of the *Amoraim*: how did the questioner understand the Mishnahs or Baraitas that contradict each other? It was settled for him within their dispute! Why didn't he point out the contradiction between the texts themselves without these *Amoraim*? 

One can answer this in many ways to resolve it in the best manner, but so as not to deviate from the intent of the question, I say: if we can provide a third logic that acts as a decider between the two logics of the disagreeing *Amoraim*—for example, if this *Amora* forbids entirely in all cases, and this *Amora* permits entirely in all cases—the questioner might have held to forbid in one case and permit in another. In that way, the contradicting Mishnahs or Baraitas would have been settled for him, but not according to those two *Amoraim*...

# **Tablets of the Covenant**

### **Ilmela (If not / If it were)**
Sometimes in the Talmud, the word *ilmela* <note>Aramaic: "if not" or "had it not been"</note> is found ending with the letter *Aleph*, and sometimes it appears as *ilmali* ending with the letter *Yod*. Rabbeinu Tam <note>Jacob ben Meir, a leading 12th-century French Tosafist</note> wrote in the *Tosafot* <note>Medieval commentaries on the Talmud</note> for the tractate *Megillah* that in instances where the word means "if it were not," it is not written as *ilmela* with an *Aleph* at the end. However, in instances where it means "if it were like," it is written with a *Yod* at the end, and the letter *Lamed* is vocalized with a *Chiriq* vowel <note>the "ee" sound</note>.

### **Alma (Therefore / Wherefore)**
The meaning of the word *alma* in the Talmud is usually "conclude from this." However, there is an *alma* that means "why," as in "On what [basis] is it taught..." or "Why did so-and-so say this?" In those cases, one must read the *alma* with a *Qamatz* vowel <note>the "ah" sound</note> under the *Lamed*. Rabbi Isaac Canpanton <note>A 15th-century Spanish scholar known as "the Gaon of Castile"</note> wrote regarding the phrase "On what basis is it taught" (*alma tanya*) that I say it is like *al mah* <note>Hebrew: "on what"</note> with the letter *Ayin* interchanged with an *Aleph*. This is also found in the Jerusalem Talmud as *ve-al mah tanya* ("and on what basis is it taught").

### **Amri Tarvayhu (Both of them said)**
Wherever the text says "So-and-so and So-and-so—both of them said," it is known that they are regular disputants <note>Aramaic: *bar plugta*; sages who frequently disagree on law</note> in other places. Examples include Rav and Shmuel, Rav and Yosef, or Abaye and Rava; they are frequently cited as "both of them said," and there are many such pairs.

### **Af Al Pi (Even though)**
"Even though there is no [absolute] proof for the matter, there is an allusion <note>literally "a memory"</note> to the matter." Rabbeinu Yonah wrote at the beginning of tractate *Berakhot* that this is said because the verse does not provide a complete proof. Rashi <note>the primary 11th-century commentator</note> and the Ran <note>Nissim of Gerona, 14th-century scholar</note> wrote in the first chapter of *Pesachim* that the reason they say "Even though there is no proof" is because we do not derive Torah laws directly from the "Words of Tradition" <note>the Prophets and Writings, as opposed to the Five Books of Moses</note>. 

"These and those are the words of the Living God." <note>A famous Talmudic principle regarding legal disputes</note> When two *Amoraim* <note>Sages of the Talmudic era, approx. 200–500 CE</note> disagree on a law or a matter of "forbidden and permitted," and each says "this reasoning seems more logical," there is no falsehood here. This is because each one is stating his own logical reasoning; one master gives a reason for permission, and the other gives a reason for prohibition. One compares one matter to another, while the other draws a different comparison. It should be said that, nevertheless, "these and those are the words of the Living God," for sometimes this reason applies and sometimes that reason applies, as the reasoning can flip based on a slight change in circumstances. This is from Rashi in the chapter "Even though" (*Af Al Pi*). I have elaborated on this concept of "these and those are the words of the Living God" in my work *Yad HaEmet*, in the introduction to my work *Toldot Adam*, and in my commentary on tractate *Shevuot*.

### **Eshtakad (Last year / Previously)**
Sometimes an *Amora* challenges another *Amora*, and the one challenged was silent <note>The Hebrew *Eshtakad* here seems to be a scribal shorthand or specific terminology for "remained silent from before/previously"</note> and does not answer. We are in doubt whether his silence indicates a retraction—that he changed his mind because of the challenger—or if he simply did not care to answer and still stands by his original statement. The rule in this matter is: if the one challenged is a student of the challenger, we say his silence is a retraction. But if the challenger is a "student-colleague" <note>a peer</note>, we do not say his silence is an admission, but rather that he did not concern himself with the words. See the chapter "The One Who Sells the House" regarding the sale of one long boundary and one short boundary, in the dispute between Rav with Rav Kahana and Rav Assi, where Rav remained silent; see the *Tosafot* there.

Regarding the rule "A positive commandment comes and overrides a negative commandment," we do not apply this in all cases. For example, there is no "building" of circumcision over leprosy, or ritual fringes (*tzitzit*) over forbidden mixtures (*kilayim*) <note>The law usually allows wearing wool and linen together if they are ritual fringes</note>. In the original explanation, one is not fulfilling a positive commandment at the exact moment of the act; rather, when one removes the fringes, at that moment he fulfills the commandment of circumcision and uproots a negative commandment. Similarly, with forbidden mixtures in fringes, at the moment the fringes of forbidden mixtures are placed, one violates the negative commandment and fulfills the positive commandment of fringes. However, we do not say "a positive commandment overrides a negative commandment" if one must uproot a negative commandment just to fulfill a positive commandment that comes *later*. This is true even for Rabbinic prohibitions, such as blowing the Shofar on Rosh Hashanah while it is in a tree <note>climbing a tree is forbidden on the Sabbath/Holidays</note>. They do not override the Sabbath laws of the Sages. Even though doing the act immediately is usually better, here, while he is violating the prohibition [by climbing], the commandment is not yet being done, for the commandment is the blowing to hear the sound of the Shofar, and the climbing is merely a preparation for the commandment. The reason a positive commandment overrides a negative one is that a positive commandment is service out of love, while a negative one is service out of fear, and service out of love is greater. This I have found. 

One may not intentionally nullify a Torah prohibition at the outset, but one may nullify a Rabbinic prohibition at the outset. See *Pesachim*, the chapter "At all times," in the *Tosafot*, where this applies to things that have no root in the Torah, such as *Muktzah* <note>items forbidden to be moved on the Sabbath</note>. See also the *Charmos* <note>likely referring to the *Chavot Yair* or another legal code</note> in the Laws of Forbidden Foods, Chapter 15. In the glosses, it is written that some authorities hold that even for things rooted in the Torah, one may nullify the prohibition at the outset—such as milk that fell into a pot containing chicken, which then gave flavor to the pot; one may add more chicken until the flavor is nullified, according to the view that chicken with milk is not a Torah prohibition. This is also cited in the Jerusalem Talmud on Chapter 2.

### **Ein (No/There is not)**
"A prohibition does not fall upon another prohibition" (*Ein issur chal al issur*). This is a great principle for all Torah prohibitions: a prohibition does not take effect if one is already in place, unless both prohibitions occur simultaneously, or if the second prohibition adds new restrictions. The difference between an "added prohibition" (*issur mosif*) and an "inclusive prohibition" (*issur kolel*) is this: an inclusive prohibition is where the latter prohibition adds nothing to the first object itself but increases the number of prohibited items for the person. For example, a carcass (*neveilah*) that a person swore not to eat—the oath adds nothing to the carcass (which was already forbidden), but it increases the prohibitions on the person regarding all foods in the world. We say that since the oath takes effect on other foods, it "includes" the carcass with them, making him liable for the oath as well. An "added prohibition" is one that adds a restriction to the object itself that was previously permitted. For example, a piece of fat from a consecrated offering: it was forbidden to eat as "fat" (*chelev*) but permitted for benefit <note>non-eating use</note>. If it then becomes "leftover" (*notar*), a further prohibition is added, making it forbidden for benefit and disqualified for the altar. Here we say: since the status of *notar* took effect regarding the Altar, it also took effect regarding the person eating it, making him liable both for the fat and for the *notar*.

### **Ein (No/There is not)**
One does not receive lashes for a negative commandment that serves as a warning for a death penalty by the court. The reason is that the Torah does not punish with death unless it first warns "Do not do this." Therefore, when a warning is given for a case involving death, it is intended for that death penalty and not for lashes. If it were the Torah's way to punish without warning—saying "If you do work, you shall die" without first saying "Do not do work"—then I would say the warning was intended for lashes. But now that the Torah only punishes with death after warning, the warning is as if it said: "Do not do any work, for if you do, you shall die." Thus, the warning is for the death penalty, not for lashes. 

The word "Then" (*Az*) always refers to words of prophecy. It does not mean "not to be forgotten," but rather that someone is saying something without a logical reason; so wrote the *Tosafot* in the chapter "Those who are Burned." However, Rashi and the *Tosafot* in the chapter "How do we extend boundaries" wrote that it is a term of praise. But when it says "they treated their words like words of prophecy," it is not meant as praise. 

Rabbi Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: wherever it says "Rabbi So-and-so said [that] Shmuel said," it means Shmuel was his teacher and he heard it directly from him. But wherever it says "Rabbi So-and-so said *in the name of* Rabbi So-and-so" (such as Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai), he did not hear it from him directly, but heard it from another who received it in his name. So Rashi wrote in tractate *Chullin*.

### **Ketav (He wrote)**
The author of *Halikhot Olam* <note>The "Paths of the World," a manual on Talmudic methodology by Jeshua ben Joseph ha-Levi</note> wrote as follows: Wherever there is a dispute between Sages, the Gemara says regarding the latter Sage "So-and-so says," putting the name before the statement, rather than saying "Said So-and-so." Keep this rule in your hand: wherever you find "So-and-so says" (*omer*), it is known that he disagrees. If it says "Said So-and-so" (*amar*), it is known that he does not disagree, but comes to explain or add. Rashbam <note>Samuel ben Meir, Rashi's grandson</note> wrote similarly in the chapter "There are those who inherit" (page 122): "Rabbi Yehuda said..."—he does not come to disagree, because it does not say "Rabbi Yehuda *says*." We find this in the first chapter of *Bava Kamma* (page 13) regarding the laws of minor sacrifices: the words of Rabbi Yose the Galilean, and then "Ben Azzai says..." to include peace offerings. Rashi explains that Ben Azzai is clarifying Rabbi Yose's words. Thus, even though it says "says," he is not disagreeing but clarifying. We find similarly in the first chapter of *Bava Metzia* (page 11): Resh Lakish said a minor girl has no courtyard... Rabbi Yochanan said she has a courtyard... and the Gemara concludes: "This master said one thing and that master said [another], and they do not disagree." And in *Moed Katan*, "Rav Papa said..." and the *Tosafot* wrote that he does not disagree. It appears that even if it says "So-and-so says," he does not necessarily disagree. The Rosh <note>Asher ben Jehiel, 13th-14th century</note> wrote at the end of the first chapter of *Kiddushin*: Rav Ashi placed the words of Rabbi Eliezer after the school of Yannai to show that he disagrees with him; the reason it does not say "Rabbi Eliezer *says*" is because he was not in Rabbi Yannai's generation.

### **Im (Whether)**
"Whether for the Reading or for the Tradition" <note>Hebrew: *Im la-mikra, im la-masoret*</note>. It is written in *Halikhot Olam*: the "Reading" (*Mikra*) is the primary focus, meaning we interpret based on how the word is vocalized/spoken. The "Tradition" (*Masoret*) means we interpret based on how the word is written in the text. This is a dispute in many places. For example, in the chapter "How do we roast" regarding the verse "It shall be eaten" (*ye'akhel*): Rabbi Yehuda holds we follow the "Tradition," and since it is written [without a certain vowel], it implies the person is warned not to eat it in two places. Rabbi [Judah the Prince] holds we follow the "Reading," and we read it as "it shall be eaten" (*ye'akhel*), meaning the Passover lamb is what is warned to be eaten in one group and not two. But one group in two places is permitted. And in *Yevamot* and the fourth chapter of *Sukkah* regarding the word "Sukkah" (written *sukkat*, *sukkat*, *sukkot*): the Rabbis hold we follow the "Tradition," and since it is written twice missing a letter and once full, they derive the number of required walls. But Rabbi Shimon holds we follow the "Reading," as is explained there. One might ask about Rabbi Yannai who said "We follow the Reading," yet in the first chapter of *Kiddushin* he interprets both the Reading and the Tradition together regarding the verse "In his betraying her" (*be-vigdo bah*), where he derives both the language of "betrayal" (*begidah*) and "garment" (*beged*). Rashi explained there that wherever both can be upheld, we interpret both Reading and Tradition. My teacher, Rabbi Y. <note>likely a reference to a specific mentor of the author</note>, noted that this applies where they harmonize, but where they contradict—where if you have one, you cannot have the other—that is where they disagree on whether the Reading or the Tradition is the primary source. Regarding the case of *Sukkah*, they are contradictory. If the meat is rank, do not seek <note>original: *tidrosh*</note>...

<meta>This page continues the author's encyclopedic exploration of the terminology and hermeneutic rules used in the Oral Torah (the Talmud and related commentaries). It follows a thematic/alphabetical arrangement.</meta>

# Oral Torah

The homily on whether the biblical text [original: *Mikra*] or the traditional reading [original: *Masorah*] is primary, and if you disqualify one you do not necessarily disqualify the other—these are his words. This is as Rashi (of blessed memory) wrote in the tractate *Bava Batra*, and the *Tosafot* (of blessed memory) in the chapter "How Do We Roast" and in the first chapter of *Sanhedrin* wrote regarding the difficulties with this. See also the beginning of the chapter "The Robber" in Rashi and *Ketubot* (of blessed memory).

### Do not read...
<note>original: "Al tikrei"</note>
You will find this expression in the Talmud many times. I have received a tradition that whenever they say "Do not read [X] but rather [Y]," it is because there is some difficulty in the text that indicates it should not be read as written, but rather in this alternative way. For example: "Do not read 'your children' [*banayikh*] but 'your builders' [*bonayikh*]." They derived this from the verse "And great shall be the peace of your children" (Isaiah 54:13). The word "your children" is redundant since the beginning of the verse already says, "And all your children shall be taught of the Lord"; it would have been enough to say "and their peace shall be great." Therefore, it must mean "your builders." Similarly, "Do not read 'observing the Sabbath from desecrating it' [*me-challalo*] but 'forgiven is he' [*machal lo*]." This is because the word "Sabbath" is usually feminine, so it should have said *me-challalah* [in the feminine]. Since we find the desecration of Sabbath mentioned in the feminine—as in "those who desecrate it [*me-challeleyha*] shall surely be put to death"—the use of the masculine form [*me-challalo*] suggests the reading "it is forgiven him." I have expanded on this in its proper place. Furthermore, I say that sometimes the sages say "Do not read..." even when there is no textual difficulty, simply because the idea itself was received as a tradition from man to man. To ensure it would not be forgotten by them or their descendants, they established a mnemonic sign [original: *siman*] and "set up markers" for the matter by way of a scriptural support [original: *asmakhta*], saying "Do not read X but Y."

## The Letter Bet

### Berabbi
Whenever it says "Berabbi," such as "Rabbi Shimon Berabbi" and the like, it is a title of greatness and importance. This is how Rashi (of blessed memory) explained it in the tractate *Kiddushin* regarding the lineage of Yudan Berabbi: his name was great in his generation. Whenever "Levi Berabbi" is mentioned, it is a title of wisdom and sharp-wittedness—these are his words. Rabbeinu Yerucham also wrote this in the name of the sage, adding that it is a descriptive title. However, when the text does not mention a specific name but only says "Berabbi," then it is a proper name. In the first chapter of *Makkot*, where it says "Berabbi says," Rashi explains that "Bar" is his name. But in the first chapter of *Zevachim*, where it says "Berabbi says," Rashi wrote: "I do not know who he is, perhaps it is Barzillai," etc. Look there; so it appears to me.

### Taught in Conflict
<note>original: "Be-machaloket shenuyah"</note>
Sometimes in the Mishnah, the text brings two subjects, and the later teacher [original: *Tanna*] disagrees with the second subject that the first teacher discussed. Because he disagrees with the second subject, it implies a question: "He should have disagreed with the first subject!" The Gemara then asks: "Let him disagree with the first case!" It answers: "It is taught in conflict." This means that through the conflict over the latter case, we see that even the first case is a matter of dispute.

### Braita
<note>term: Braita (an "external" teaching of the sages from the era of the Mishnah that was not included in the main collection)</note>
Or a Mishnah that follows one teacher in one matter and another teacher in another matter. It is said in such a case: "This is the view of Rabbi [Judah the Prince]," for he recorded it according to two different opinions. This teacher holds like so-and-so in one case and like so-and-so in another, so as not to create a contradiction... <unclear>sh-n-a</unclear>... the Mishnah is neither according to Rabbi Ishmael nor Rabbi Akiva, and so it is in many places.

### Showing Good
<note>original: "Machvat"</note>
"Do not read 'evil' [but 'good']..." In the chapter "The Morning Prayer" (page 20), regarding the prayer of one who is traveling: how should one pray? Rav Chisda says standing; Rav Sheshet says even while walking. Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Shalom were traveling on the road. Rabbi Chiya stood and stayed in his place. Rabbi Shalom, who had heard his tradition, said: "What is Rav Chisda doing?" (He saw him standing and praying). He said to him: "Set up a disturbance for me too so I may pray." "Do not read 'evil' but 'good'..." I received from my father and teacher, the Honorable Rabbi A. Segal (may his memory be for a blessing in the world to come), that the word "you shall be called" [*tikarei*] should be read with a *chiriq* vowel under the *Tav* and a *qamatz* under the *Qof*. It should be read as "showing that you have the power to do the ultimate good." And the "good" is sufficient—a commandment performed in the best possible way. Why should you be called a "bad man" when you have the power to do the ultimate good?

## The Letter Gimel

### You are pitting one man against another
<note>original: "Gavra a-gavra ka ramit"</note>
This is the way of the Talmud: when it raises a difficulty from the words of one post-Mishnaic sage [original: *Amora*] against another, it says, "You are pitting one man against another." Sometimes it says that the words of so-and-so are merely a "quoted teaching" [*memra*] and so-and-so does not hold by that teaching. This is like what we say in the chapter "The Presumptive Ownership of Houses" regarding Rav Bibi, where Rav Nachman said to the house of Zevachin: "Between me and him..." and it was said that the words of Rav Bibi are a quoted teaching, and Rav Huna does not agree with that teaching. The explanation there is that a *memra* is something one says in the name of others. If Rav Bibi had said it in his own name, he would be considered "a man" [an independent authority], and the challenge "you are pitting one man against another" would apply. Thus, when one challenges one sage with another, and the words being used for the challenge are "sifted" or original, one says: "You are pitting one man against another." But when the words are those of someone else, one says: "These are the words of so-and-so, and he does not hold by that teaching."

### The Matter Itself
<note>term: Gufa (literally "the body"; a Talmudic term used to return to a previously quoted text for its own sake)</note>
Sometimes when the Talmud brings a certain Braita or teaching incidentally, it later makes it the "body" of the inquiry to expand the explanation. This is "Gufa," meaning "the matter itself is required." It was previously secondary, now see it as the essence. Sometimes it says "The Master said" [original: *Amar Mar*]. If they are merely reasons, it uses neither "Gufa" nor "Amar Mar," but begins with the words mentioned above and builds the student's words upon them. This is as if it had said "The Master said." Similarly, in Rashbam (chapter "The Seller of a House"), the Gemara mentions the city and quotes a verse, and at the end says "and he did not say 'The Master said'." The difference between "Gufa" and "Amar Mar" is this: when the Talmud first brought the matter incidentally—either to raise a difficulty or to support a point—it later uses the term "Gufa" or "Amar Mar." But if the Talmud brought a Braita not incidentally but as the main subject, it cannot say "Gufa" afterward, because "Gufa" indicates that what preceded was incidental and now it is being made the essence. If what preceded was already the essence, "Gufa" is inappropriate; rather, one says "The Master said," meaning "The teacher said this, and one may ask such-and-such." The phrase "The Master said" can be used for what preceded whether it was incidental or essential, while "Gufa" can only be said for what was previously incidental. The ultimate purpose of "Gufa" is to signal that the previous proof was not actually a proof because the statement was misunderstood. In the beginning of the first chapter of *Na'arah*, it brings a proof that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, and afterward raises a difficulty... and therefore it is not appropriate to bring a proof from it. One should investigate: if a statement is brought incidentally to provide proof and then subjected to debate, does that discussion diverge from the current topic or not? If it diverges, one must say "Gufa." If it is part of the topic but "Gufa" is said, one must ask why. There are places where the Talmud debates as mentioned... and in that debate, it diverges slightly from the topic but not entirely; in such a case, it is not necessary to say "Gufa," but if it is said, it is not a great difficulty since it did diverge somewhat. In the beginning of the chapter of *Na'arah*, regarding the exclusion of those teachers and asking what is the difference between them, it's difficult because it should have said "Gufa." One could say that since it asks "what is the difference," it is to understand the words of Rabbi Shimon of Timna, and thus it doesn't diverge much and doesn't need "Gufa." You find that everywhere "Gufa" is said, the intent is to bring a new insight [original: *chiddush*] to what preceded. If it brings no new insight, one should not say "Gufa." This raises a difficulty for us in the chapter "These are Forbidden," regarding the section "The Lung that was Pierced," where it brings a teaching of Rava as support... and then brings that same teaching again using the word "Gufa" without adding any new insight at all. It can be answered that since it wanted to bring many other rulings in Rava's name, the Talmud restarted from the first ruling mentioned regarding the lung and then listed many others, all in the name of Rava. From this, you learn that wherever you find "Gufa" without a new insight, the intention is to gather together all the rulings stated by the author of that teaching. There are places where the Talmud is concise and does not say "Gufa," as the *Tosafot* explained in the chapter "All Who Swear" regarding "They saw him hide his tools under his cloak," etc. See there.

### Type / Manner
<note>original: "Gavna"</note>
We find the term *Gavna* used for something that is most common. In the first chapter of *M—*, it is taught: "Others say in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, an egg may be eaten..." and we ask: "Is this not obvious?"

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Talmudic methodology and legal principles, specifically focusing on the interpretation of general rules and the burden of proof in civil disputes. It follows the previous page's analysis of legal definitions.</meta>

-># The Tablets of the Covenant<-

Therefore, wherever we analyze the Mishnah [and ask], "What does 'this is the general rule' come to include?" <note>original: "זה הכלל לאתויי מאי"</note> [it means] to include that which we divided [in the discussion], etc. As in the chapter "The One Who Robs" <note>the Talmudic chapter *Ha-Gozeil* in Tractate Bava Kamma</note>, "This is the general rule: all those who are robbed, etc." What does "this is the general rule" include? It includes the view of Rabbi Eliezer, "one should not question, etc." and similar cases. Rabbi Elazar does not explain the Mishnah explicitly, and we would not know the resolution of the general rule if not for Rabbi Eliezer. It is resolved for him through careful study, as in every place where we say "specifically this person came to teach us the Mishnah." Alternatively, he may state his words on the Mishnah and say, "this implies," <note>original: "זאת אומרת"</note> and similar phrasing. So wrote the author of *Halichot Olam* <note>a 15th-century manual on Talmudic methodology by Jeshua ben Joseph ha-Levi</note>: "I say regarding this that it is not a difficulty at all, for he only says it when the matter is somewhat explained in the Mishnah." Regarding the phrase "This is the general rule to include," it is not appropriate to say "this implies." See further that Rabbi Elazar stated this law based on logical reasoning <term>sevara<gloss>rational deduction rather than a direct scriptural or traditional source</gloss></term>, and afterward they agreed to use "this is the general rule to include." And so you say that when one says "the specific inference of the Mishnah comes to teach us," it means that originally this law was said from logical reasoning, and afterward it was supported by the inference of the Mishnah.

## Interpretation of the Beginning
The beginning of a dispute among the Tannaim <note>sages of the Mishnaic period</note> is whether "we interpret the beginning" <note>original: "דורשין תחילת"</note> or "we do not interpret the beginning." This means [interpreting] the first verse of a passage. Some say it is needed for its own context <note>original: "לענפא אצטריך"</note> and not for a midrashic derivation. For example, at the beginning of Tractate Sanhedrin: "and he who blasphemes the Name," "the house of one," "judges" <note>original: "אלהים" - *Elohim*, often used to mean judges</note>, "until the judges," "whom the judges shall condemn"—here are three mentions of "judges." There are those who interpret all of them there for the purpose of a numerical count <note>to determine the number of judges needed for a court</note>. It concludes that "we do not interpret beginnings," meaning the first verse, because it is needed for its own literal subject matter and not for a numerical derivation. This applies to all similar cases.
**After the fact** <term>Di'avad<gloss>a legal action that is accepted once it has already been performed, even if it was not the ideal way to do it</gloss></term>: This is composed of two words: *de-i-avid* <note>Aramaic for "that if he did [it]"</note>.

## The Letter He

# The burden of proof is on the claimant
<note>original: "המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה" - a fundamental principle of Jewish civil law</note>
This is commonly found in three [cases], except for the case of a "shortened egg" <note>referring to a specific legal debate in Tractate Bava Batra</note> where Rava said the law is that it does not acquire... and we do not say that it does not swallow, but if it swallows, he acquires it. And the sale was... for the latter version [of the law] he acquired it, and for the other version he did not acquire it. The Talmud decides the matter through the "row of the judges" <term>shura de-dayyani<gloss>a judicial compromise or a specific ruling where the court acts on its own discretion</gloss></term>, and it did not rule that "the burden of proof is on the claimant." Since we are in doubt whether the law follows this version or that version, it should be a case of "the burden of proof is on the claimant." Our finding is that the resolution is: when the Talmud says "the row of the judges," it is because we have a general rule that in every place where there is a dispute, one should strive to make the reasoning of the rule agree as much as possible and to minimize the conflict. Here, the Talmud labored to harmonize the two versions and say the versions do not disagree. But where it says that sometimes there is a version like this and sometimes like that, and we rejected it, it is a case of "the burden of proof is on the claimant," or "the seller sells with a generous eye," or "with a stingy eye," or "according to the local custom." And it will say the law is that he sells with a generous eye, and in such a case, one version says he acquired it; and if he sells with a stingy eye, the law says he did not acquire it, and in such a case, the other version says he did not acquire it—thus the two versions do not conflict.
It follows that when a dispute falls between two opinions, and there are two decisors, one exempting the defendant and one obligating him to pay the claimant, the claimant must bring clear proof that the matter is as he says, because a doubt has fallen upon the law due to the claim. Therefore, we find that the Talmud rules "they divide" <note>original: "חולקין" - splitting the disputed property</note> in a place where there is a doubt. For example, that which we say in the first chapter of Bava Kamma: "two brothers who divided [an inheritance], and a creditor came and took the portion of one of them." Rav says the division is void, and Shmuel says he has waived [his rights]. Rav Assi says he takes a quarter in land and a quarter in money. We say there: what do they disagree about? About the doubt of whether [the brothers] are like heirs or like purchasers. Therefore, they divide. Similarly, it says they divide in the chapter "There are those who inherit" and in the chapter "The Firstborn," regarding a firstborn who does not take a double portion in a loan because it is "potential" property <note>uncollected debts are not considered "held" property for the sake of the double portion</note. And from the language used there, we say "and they divide" because we are in doubt whether a loan and a lien on property are considered "collected" and "held" so that he should take a double portion or not; thus they divide due to doubt. So too in other places. The resolution is that this was an enactment of the Sages—that in these cases they divide, even though by strict law "the burden of proof is on the claimant" in a place of doubt. Do not err to rule "the row of the judges" in a place where they did not say "the row of the judges," nor "they divide" in a place where they did not say "they divide." But in a place not explicit in the Talmud, and where the law was not stated like this Master or that Master, and we are in doubt as to who the law follows, the ruling is "the burden of proof is on the claimant." If you hold by one of them, let it be given according to his words. For example, regarding the "tenants of the tithe," they said in the chapter "All those who swear": "Now that the law was not stated like this Master or like that Master, if one acted like this Master he has acted [validly], and if one acted like that Master he has acted [validly]." Sometimes the judge is in doubt regarding the subject matter itself, whether [the claimant] is telling the truth—for example, where there is one witness for this side and one witness for that side. They said: "Where the land stands, let it stand." There are many such cases in the Talmud where a doubt regarding money results in a lenient ruling <note>meaning the possessor keeps it</note> and "the burden of proof is on the claimant." And sometimes we find the law of "the burden of proof is on the claimant" when a doubt falls upon the law even though there is no doubt about the subject matter. For example, where litigants claim against each other regarding the law of "two who are holding..." <note>a reference to the opening of Tractate Bava Metzia</note>. In the chapter "The Borrower," regarding one who rented a bathhouse from his fellow for twelve gold dinars per year, at one gold dinar per month. The case came before Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish and before Rabbi Yochanan, and they said: "they divide the intercalated month" <note>a leap year month</note>. Shmuel establishes this as a case where the claimant comes in the middle of the month. In all such cases regarding the law of the entire month, if he [the landlord] has already seized the rent, it belongs to the seller/landlord. We are in doubt whether to follow the first expression—where he said "twelve for the year," implying the whole year even if it is a leap year—or the last expression—where he said "a dinar per month." So I found.

## And regarding
the matter where the Tosafot <note>medieval commentaries on the Talmud</note> disagree with the ruling of "dividing." He holds that according to the Tosafot in their commentary on page 38, [when the Talmud says] "this implies they divide," his colleagues disagree with him along with Summakhos <note>Symmachus, a sage who famously held that disputed money is always split</note> only in such a case. Summakhos argues that it is appropriate to be in doubt about the words [of the claim], such as the dispute over "the cow and the donkey" or "the clean and the aborted fetus." In all those, their claims are worthy of the court being in doubt. But in a place where the doubt is not based on their words, Summakhos does not disagree. For even according to the one who says Summakhos speaks even in a case where both are certain <note>original: "ברי וברי"</note>, would Summakhos say they divide if a person said to his fellow, "This garment you are wearing is mine"? And when two are holding a cloak, and each says "it is all mine," each takes an oath; even for Summakhos, they do not simply divide without an oath.

## Since
and afterward he stated the law. Behold, this rule is general. But in reality, it is like a doubt: do we say "since it was rejected, it remains rejected"? <note>original: "הואיל ונדחה ידחה"</note> Regarding the covering of the blood <note>the mitzvah of *kisuy hadam*</note>: if the wind covered the blood and it became uncovered again, one is obligated to return and cover it. We do not say "since the commandment of covering was rejected/fulfilled when the wind covered it, even though it was later uncovered, one is exempt." Rather, we say there is no "rejection" <term>dichuy<gloss>the principle that once an object is disqualified or a duty is temporarily suspended, it remains so</gloss></term> regarding commandments. The Talmud in Tractate Avodah Zarah, in the chapter "All the Images," is in doubt whether we say this both for stringency and for leniency—that there is no rejection regarding commandments—or specifically regarding the covering of blood to be stringent. In another matter where "rejection" would lead to a leniency, do we say there is rejection regarding commandments? For example, one who bows down to a palm tree [for idolatry] and later nullifies its worship: is the branch <note>Lulav</note> valid for the commandment? Now that it was used for idolatry, "rejection" has already passed over it, as it is forbidden to benefit from it or take a Lulav from it. Since it was rejected, perhaps even after the idolatry is nullified and the palm tree is no longer an idol, it remains forbidden to take a Lulav from it? This remains an unresolved query <term>teiku<gloss>an unresolved Talmudic dilemma</gloss></term>.

## This is well
This is composed of two words: *Ha niha* <note>Aramaic for "this is well"</note>. "So-and-so [ruled] the law for practical practice" <note>original: "הלכה למעשה"</note>: the explanation in *Halichot Olam* is that so-and-so instructed that the law should be performed as a deed. For you can find a law that is stated but not "instructed for practice," meaning one should not actually perform the deed because it might lead to a ruinous outcome. And so we say in Bava Batra in the chapter "There are those who inherit": "Rav Ashi said to Rabbi Yochanan: When the Master says the law [is such], is it to be performed as a deed? He said to him: Not until we say to you, 'the law is for practical practice.'"

## Instruction
A ruling <term>hora'ah<gloss>a formal legal instruction</gloss></term> is generally toward leniency. As we say in the first chapter of Ketubot: "When one says 'instruction,' it is to forbid." Rashi <note>the preeminent medieval commentator</note> explained that a prohibition is not called "instruction" because any person is permitted to be stringent upon himself, and a prohibition does not require formal authorization. Even if there is a doubt and the law does not follow that instruction, he comes to forbid it. But one who is lenient relies on a report or on his reasoning, and that is called an "instruction." And they were concerned there with a doubt where there is an instruction toward stringency, which disagrees with "the burden of proof is on the claimant." See there.

## Where
it is revealed, it is revealed; where it is not revealed, it is not revealed <note>original: "היכא דגלי גלי היכא דלא גלי לא גלי"</note>. This is found in many places in the Talmud. Yet, in many other places, we find the opposite, saying "since it is revealed [in one case], it is revealed for every place." I found that Rabbi Isaac Campanton <note>OCR: "קאפנשמ"ך" - referring to the 15th-century Spanish rabbi known as the "Gaon of Castile"</note> wrote the reason is: when we say "it was necessary to reveal," etc., it is when the scriptural revelation regarding the subject matter is a minor innovation, or regarding a subject where the reasoning is obvious to the ear. Then we certainly say the verse only came to limit the law and to say it applies specifically to this subject and not to its fellows, even if they are similar to it or more logical than it. For if you do not say so, let the verse remain silent! Or let it state the law regarding its fellow which has a greater innovation. This is the logic of why we say "specifically in this subject" when it is a minor innovation. But when we say "since it is revealed here, it is revealed for the whole Torah..."
