It also explores the concept of "rejection" in commandments and the distinction between theoretical law and practical legal instruction.</summary>

# Oral Torah

**And he sold** <note>original: *v'zavin*</note>—The term for a merchant. It is explained as a question: would a person sell a purchase at the same price they bought it for, simply to be called a "merchant"? For if a person works and eats but makes no profit, from where shall he eat? If he does not profit, you have no greater loss. This is how the Rashbam <note>Rabbi Samuel ben Meir, a 12th-century French commentator</note> explains it in the chapter "The One Who Sells the Ship." These are the words [of the Sages]: when the Gemara says "these are the words of So-and-so," it generally implies that the Gemara disagrees with him and does not hold like his view. So too wrote the Tosafot <note>medieval commentators on the Talmud</note> in the chapter "The Presumptive Ownership of Houses" on page 35, and these are their words: "these are the words of Symmachus" implies "only these," and the Sages do not agree with him. Although it is proven in the chapter "The House of a Kor" that sometimes the phrase is used even when the Sages agree, the general rule is that "these are the words" implies disagreement. This is also found in the eighth chapter of "These are the Maidens" on page 30: wherever it does not state explicitly "these are the words and he agrees with him," it implies disagreement.

-> Letter Chet <-

**A Chomer of Barley**—Know that a *chomer* is a measure also called a *kor*. A *kor* is equal to two *letech* measures. A *letech* is fifteen *seah*. Thus, a *chomer* consists of thirty *seahs*, which are ten *ephahs*, as an *ephah* is three *seahs*. The calculations following from the *ephah* were noted previously under the Letter Gimel. It is also known to us from the many teachings of our Rabbis that an area of fifty cubits by fifty cubits is a *Beit Seah* <note>literally "a house of a seah"</note>—meaning an area large enough to sow a *seah* of barley—which equals two thousand five hundred square cubits.

<margin>This one</margin>—He chooses one of them. How do we know that when the Talmud offers a resolution <term>peruka<gloss>a legal answer or settlement of a contradiction</gloss></term>, even if it could have offered a different resolution, it picks one and we draw our inferences based on it? This matter is explained in the chapter "The One Who Performs Levirate Marriage" <note>Tractate Yevamot</note> regarding the dispute between Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Akiva concerning those who keep slaves but do not circumcise them, etc. We say there: "Let Rabbi Akiva answer him regarding one who buys a slave at twilight." Let him answer this or that; he chose one of two reasons. Similarly, the *Sefer Ha-Keritut* <note>a 14th-century work on Talmudic methodology by Samson ben Isaac of Chinon</note> says that sometimes there are several resolutions, but the Talmud does not bother to mention more than one of them.

-> Letter Tet <-

**Good taste** and knowledge teach me <note>a reference to Psalm 119:66</note>. King David, peace be upon him, prayed for this, and his son [Solomon], whose soul is in Eden, said: "The tongue of the wise makes knowledge good." Therefore, know and believe that the language of the Mishnah and the Talmud is precise, shining like a luminary. If there is an extra word, a missing word, or a change in language, it is not an empty matter. "And if it is empty, it is from you" <note>a Rabbinic midrash on Deuteronomy 32:47, suggesting that if the Torah seems empty of meaning, it is due to the student's lack of understanding</note>. Whoever treats the language of the Sages as mundane will be distanced from wisdom; let his eyes be opened to see wonders from the Torah. One can learn many laws from these linguistic nuances. I will bring some examples: We learned at the beginning of Tractate Zevachim that "all animal sacrifices slaughtered not for their own sake are valid, but they do not count for the owners [to fulfill their obligation]." The Gemara asks: Why say "but they do not count" <note>original: *ela she-lo alu*</note>? It should have simply said "and they do not count" <note>original: *ve-lo alu*</note>. Rashi explains that a person is obligated to teach his students in a concise manner, yet this "redundancy" was used by the Gemara to derive a legal practical difference: that it is forbidden to sprinkle their blood or perform other services for a different purpose, because they still retain their original sanctity. Therefore, it used the word *ela* (but/rather) to say they do not have the status of being "rejected" sacrifices. Even greater than this, we find in the chapter "There are those who Inherit" on page 135 regarding a person on his deathbed <term>shechiv mera<gloss>a person facing imminent death whose verbal instructions carry legal weight</gloss></term> who said: "Give two hundred zuz to So-and-so, my creditor, as is fitting for him." He takes both the two hundred and his original debt. The Gemara asks: "Perhaps he meant the two hundred were *for* his debt?" Rabbi Akiva answers that he [the donor] is using redundant language. The Rashbam writes that even the Sages agree that we interpret redundant language, but in Rabbi Akiva's case, it is stated explicitly. I saw it written in the name of a Gaon <note>a high-ranking Babylonian communal leader and scholar</note> named Shotenz (?) who was precise: since the text says "they take" (*notlin*) rather than "they give to him" (*notnin lo*), it implies that even if the property was already in the hands of the orphans, we extract it from them. Thus you see that although the plain meaning of the language might suggest he meant the money to cover the debt—as the Gemara challenged—and although the property is in the possession of the orphans (and the rule is that the burden of proof is on the claimant), nevertheless, by the power of the redundant word, we say he takes the gift and also his debt. See how far redundancy reaches! From this and similar cases, the masters of legal rulings learned to derive laws from any redundancy. I will bring an example... in the chapter... since it says "we do not hold blood in a vessel," and did not say "there is no blood in a vessel," it implies that if we see them, we say they require salting like other meat... And in the book *Ha-Tashbetz* <note>a 14th-century work of legal responsa by Simeon ben Zemah Duran</note> he wrote: "From the Jerusalem Talmud in Megillah, we may hang books [scrolls] but not Tefillin or Mezuzot." This implies specifically that hanging is forbidden, but repairing the letters themselves is permitted. For if repairing letters were also forbidden, it should have said "one may hang books but not Tefillin," so why repeat "and one may not hang"? Even in the general conversation of our Rabbis, the law itself changes. Their "idle chatter" requires study. Consider the incident of the piece of metal with Rabbi Abahu: "He did not snatch, but a generation snatches." He asked, "Where did this law benefit?" The language here is redundant; why say "behold the path for the judges, how they should judge"? He should have said, "How shall we judge this case?" I settled the matter thus: in that incident, they ruled according to their own eyes, and Rabbi Abahu, who had prepared the case with them, knew where the truth lay. It is written that a judge who is a great expert may rule according to what is strong in his heart, as explained in the *Tur*, Choshen Mishpat, section 15. They were only saying that if the case came before ordinary judges who only have the Torah law to rely on, how would they judge? Therefore he said, "Where did this law benefit these judges?"

<margin>And we find</margin> in the chapter "The One Who Sleeps" <note>in Tractate Sukkah</note> a difficulty regarding the ointment of Rabbi [Judah the Prince]. We learned why it did not say "from his words," and from that slight change we derived that "the conversation of the Sages requires study." There are many such instances, beyond measure and number; let the wise understand.

-> Letter Yod <-

**He sat** <note>original: *yativ*</note>—So-and-so sat before So-and-so. The work *Halichot Olam* states that throughout the Talmud, when we say "So-and-so sat before So-and-so" and then "he sat and said," we only say this in a place where he disagrees with him or where he was the one speaking. But if he did not speak and did not disagree, we do not use this phrasing at all. So wrote the Rashba <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Aderet, 13th-century Spain</note> in his novellae on Tractate Yevamot. The Mahariq <note>Rabbi Joseph Colon, 15th-century Italy</note> wrote that this is not quite accurate, for if it says "he sat and said," then he is clearly the speaker, so what need is there for the Rashba's rule? However, the correct interpretation is like the Tosafot in Tractate Chullin, page 63: wherever it says "So-and-so sat before him," it mentions him thus because he taught them a novel law <term>chiddush<gloss>a new insight or legal innovation</gloss></term>. They wrote further: although in Tractate Avodah Zarah there is one instance of "he sat before him" where the person said nothing, Rabbenu Tam explains that this incident was connected to the one in Ketubot where Rabbi Hiyya spoke to him, and the Talmud brought the matters according to the order of the tractates.

-> Letter Kaf <-

**Every/All** <note>original: *kol*</note>—The way of every legal composition is to collect many details. Sometimes, however, we find that it collects only a single detail. The reason for using the word "all" for a single detail is not that the word refers only to that detail, but rather that it brings a general rule as a premise to derive a consequence for that specific case; search and you will find this. In the chapter "Presumptive Ownership," in the section "He pulled produce from him," we learned: "Rabbi Simeon says: In any case where the money is in his hand, his hand is on top [he has the advantage]." The seller can retract, but the buyer cannot. It is difficult: since the word "all" (*kol*) only includes the seller and not the buyer, why use "all"? One must say that he brings proof from generalities to generate a law for the seller in every subject: it is fitting that whoever holds the money has the advantage, therefore the seller, who holds it, can retract.

**Every**—Wherever the Mishnah teaches "all" (*ha-kol*), the Gemara asks: "What does 'all' come to include?" and brings an inclusion, as in the first discussion of Tractate Arachin and in many other places. But if...

# Tablets of the Covenant

## "And we learned in a Mishnah" and "And he taught"
<note>original: *ve-hatnan ve-hatni*</note>
This is a phrasing used to raise a difficulty; it comes to challenge a point. Occasionally, you will find the phrase "And he taught" <note>original: *ve-hatanya*</note> used as a support. The difference between them lies in the letter *vav* and the letter *aleph*. When used for a difficulty, it is written without an *aleph* <note>original: *ve-ha*</note> and we read it as a question. However, when it is used for support, it is written with an *aleph* <note>original: *ve-ha* as *ve-ha'a*</note>, as in: "and behold, we learned in a Mishnah" or "and behold, he taught," and we read it with a specific melody of support.

Similarly, "and behold he taught" <note>original: *ve-ha tanyia*</note> serves as support and assistance, as in "from that which was taught etc." At other times, you will find the term "we learned in a Mishnah" <note>original: *tnan*</note> without the letter *he* or *aleph*, functioning as a difficulty. This occurs specifically when one challenges one Mishnah using another Mishnah. You will find this in countless places.

**The one who reads it** <note>original: *de-ka'ari leh*</note>: Regarding the question "What is the meaning of 'the one who reads it'?", some explain that "the one who reads it" refers to the person who is currently studying this specific Mishnah in order to use it to answer a question in the Study Hall <note>term: *Bet Midrash* — the traditional house of Jewish study</note>. The question then asks: "Why did he bother to involve himself with this?" These are the words of the scholars.

However, in the *Aruch* <note>an 11th-century dictionary of the Talmud by Rabbi Nathan of Rome</note>, I found that "the one who reads it" <note>original: *ka'ari*</note> is a term for "mixing" or "intertwining." The letter *aleph* is substituted [for a *yud*]. The explanation is: "The one who intertwined this with that—what did he see that made him mix them?" In other words, "The one who compared this to that—what did he see that made him compare them to raise a difficulty from one to the other, when the distinction between them is already clear?"

**And how much?** <note>original: *ve-kama*</note>: For example, "So-and-so said etc." In the chapter "These Found Objects" <note>a chapter in Tractate Bava Metzia</note>, in the Mishnah where one finds scattered fruit, the Gemara asks "And how much?" Rabbi Isaac says: "A *kav* <note>a unit of volume</note> spread over four hundred [cubits]." The *Tosafot* <note>medieval commentators</note> wrote that this question "And how much?" belongs to the words of Rabbi Isaac himself. It cannot be said that the anonymous voice of the Talmud is asking it, for the Gemara says afterward that a measurement is not required at all. Therefore, it must be that these are the words of Rabbi Isaac, as if he said: "Rabbi Isaac said: 'And how much? A *kav* in four cubits.'" They wrote similarly there regarding finding a donkey or a cow running, where the Gemara asks [a question] and then Rabbi Judah says "three," and then it repeats "and in the first chapter of *Chagigah*..." and asks "From where do we derive the Hebrew?" <note>referring to a biblical source</note>. Rabbi Huna said "The verse says etc." and then asks "Why do I need a verse?" In the chapter "One May Not Dig," it says "Rabbi Isaac said etc. And in how much?" and you might say that the Gemara is currently asking "And how much?" while afterward in the chapter "And we learned in a Mishnah" regarding "four cubits," Rabbi Isaac himself asks "And how much?" and not the Talmud itself. So too in the second chapter of *Pesachim*, regarding "From where are these matters derived?" Rabbi Nachman bar Isaac said: "The verse says 'You shall give to him' and not to his light." Rabbi Nachman bar Isaac himself, who explained "To him and not to his light," is the one who asked "From where are these matters derived?"

**And even** <note>original: *ve-afilu*</note>: The *Rosh* <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, 13th-14th century</note> wrote at the beginning of the Laws of *Tzitzit* <note>ritual fringes</note> in the name of the Sages that in a place where the text should have said "even" but said "and even," the addition of the "and" <note>the letter *vav*</note> is meant to include more things. One should look closely at this.

**And further, and it says, and it is written** <note>original: *ve-od, ve-omer, u-khtiv*</note>: Wherever the Gemara says "and further," "and it says," or "and it is written," it is to strengthen the matter further. This is because the initial proof is not quite strong enough and needs further evidence, as the first proof could be refuted and contains a weakness. Therefore, the first [additional proof] is brought even if it is based on logic, or a verse is brought if the second verse is more persuasive than the first. For this reason, we ask in the Gemara: "What is the meaning of 'and further'? What is the meaning of 'and it says'? What is the meaning of 'and it is written'?" The answer is usually: "Lest you say etc." <note>meaning: "I might have misunderstood the first point, so the second point clarifies it."</note>. This implies there is a weakness in the first, so the second comes to teach us the truth. In this same way, "if you like, you can say" <note>original: *i nami*</note> functions like "and further." It is proper to learn this from the commentators, the *Tosafot*, and the *Nimukei Yosef*, for they follow the path of the Gemara. Everywhere, the Talmud is accustomed to asking "What is the meaning of 'and further' etc.?" and all the more so if the first proof is a biblical verse and the second is logic. This is explained in the first chapter of *Kiddushin* regarding the word "And they shall fear" <note>original: *ve-yira'u*</note>—"And further, a verse?" The commentators explain: "Does a verse need support?" On this, the *Tosafot* wrote that even though the second proof is logical, if it were the primary proof, we would ask why it was brought after the verse. It is only because the verse itself might be considered weak in that specific context <note>as we asked regarding 'And they shall fear'</note> that the logical proof was brought.

**And it is necessary** <note>original: *ve-tzarikh*</note>: Wherever we use the word "and it is necessary," it implies that this is the requirement *ab initio* <note>term: *le-khatchila* — the ideal way to perform a commandment</note>. This is seen in Tractate *Berakhot* in the chapter "One Who Recites," where it says: "And it is necessary that he makes his ear hear [his own recitation]." The commentators explain that "it is necessary" implies the ideal way, but if it was already done <note>term: *be-di'avad* — an action that is valid after the fact even if not performed ideally</note>, it is still valid. However, the Gemara gives it a meaning that even after the fact there is no remedy, for it says "it is necessary and there is no [alternative] etc." From this, we see that the term is more inclined to mean "ideally" unless specified otherwise.

---

# The Letter Zayin

**This implies** <note>original: *zot omeret*</note>: Whenever there is a Mishnah or a *Baraita* <note>term: *Baraita* — a tradition from the time of the Mishnah not included in the final Mishnah compilation</note> and the Talmud says "this implies" <note>zot omeret</note> about it, it means that were it not for this specific Mishnah or *Baraita*, we would not have known that specific law. For if that law were obvious on its own, why would we need to say "this implies"? Even if the law is simple, we only learn that the law is specifically so from this *Baraita* or Mishnah. See the chapter "One Who Sells a House" regarding the teaching of the Rabbis, Ben Levi, etc.

**This, and it goes without saying that... and the concept of "not only this, but also that"** <note>original: *zu ve-ein tzarikh lomar zu / lo zu af zu*</note>: Rabbeinu Shimshon <note>12th-century French scholar</note> wrote in the *Book of Principles* <note>Sefer Kritut</note> that the concept of "not only this but also that" occurs because the author of the Mishnah <note>term: *Tanna*</note> heard one version of a law and wrote it down, and then heard a second version and wrote it down because it seemed to contain a greater novelty. Even though, logically, he did not need to state the first one once he had the second, he did not want to remove it from his Mishnah.

In the case of "this, and it goes without saying that..." the author heard one version and wrote it, then heard a second version and wrote it even though it was entirely unnecessary, simply because he needed to record all the words of the earlier teachers that were before him. It is written in *She'erit Yosef*: "I heard that the intention of the Tanna was to say that we should not think the more novel division is simple just because we saw no one disagreeing with it; for certainly a dissenter would be found. Therefore, he records it to show it is a distinct law."

It appears that the phrase "it goes without saying" is used because these are "the words of the Living God" <note>a phrase meaning both opinions have divine validity</note>, as found in the first chapter of *Eruvin*: "Why were the words of the individual recorded alongside the majority when they are to be nullified? So that if a person says such words, they can say to him: 'You have heard them according to the opinion of So-and-so.'" Thus, the second version was written so that if a person sees a *Baraita* or hears from a scholar a certain ruling, they will know its source. They relied on the second version as recorded in Tractate *Eduyot*, stating that if a court sees fit, etc. Perhaps also in the case of "not only this but also that," he did not want to remove the first even though it was not strictly necessary.

The book *Halichot Olam* states: "This reasoning for 'this, and it goes without saying' does not seem right to me, and in my humble opinion, it is unnecessary. It is the style of the Tanna to say 'this, and it goes without saying,' as seen in the chapter 'One Who Recites,' regarding asking [after someone's welfare] out of respect and 'it goes without saying' that one responds." Sometimes the Tanna abbreviates and omits the phrase "this and it goes without saying."

*She'erit Yosef* <note>by Rabbi Joseph ibn Verga</note> wrote: "This does not seem right to me... if it isn't necessary, then it must be the opinion of a different Tanna, and the author brought it using the language of 'this, and it goes without saying.'" I further found in *She'erit Yosef* in the name of the *Shitta* <note>a collection of commentaries</note> of the Ramban <note>Nachmanides, 13th-century Spanish scholar</note>: "The Tanna, at the beginning of his analysis, saw two divisions—the first was a novelty and the second was even more of a novelty. To be cautious, he recorded the novel one first. Upon further reflection, he saw that legally the most novel one should also be written, so he wrote it after the first. He did not remove the first because it had already spread among the students. Thus, that section remained in the format of 'not only this but also that.'"

When the Gemara says "this, and it goes without saying this," it follows a similar path: the Tanna found a novel division and wrote it. After a second analysis, he understood another even more novel division and wrote it. But he did not write it after the first division <note>as in 'not only this...'</note>. Rather, because of its importance and extreme novelty, he gave it precedence and wrote it *before* the first one. Thus, the first one ended up last, creating the "this, and it goes without saying this" structure. He didn't do this for "not only this but also that" because the novelty was minor and he didn't feel the need to prioritize it. Proof for this is in the third chapter of *Yevamot* regarding three brothers, two of whom are married to two sisters, where there are two Mishnahs, the second of which is a logical consequence of the first. The Gemara answers: "The Tanna taught the first etc. and since it was dear to him, he prioritized it." This explains "this, and it goes without saying" in its place. The interpretation is that the Tanna taught the last Mishnah first, and it didn't occur to him to teach the second part, but as he went on, he taught it. There is a general principle here for every place that says "this, and it goes without saying this." This is also how the *Tosafot* explain it: "Since it was dear to him, he prioritized it." In other places, it isn't difficult to say this; we simply say "this and it goes without saying" is what he taught.

<header>Notes on the Oral Torah</header>

# It is not [otherwise] needed
<note>original: *Lo tzerikha* — a standard Talmudic resolution to a difficulty, meaning "This case is not needed except for a specific scenario."</note>
There are those who explain that every instance of "It is not needed" is a response to the question: "Is this not needed? Is this not obvious?" It resolves the difficulty by showing that the law is indeed necessary for a specific, non-obvious case. For example, we see the phrase "It is not needed, [except] for where one slaughtered two animals before us, etc." where the answer comes clearly, even though the Talmud uses concise language. However, the plain meaning is as if it says: "It is not needed **except** for etc." This is found in several places, such as the first chapter of the tractate *Avodah Zarah*, where Rabbi Elazar says: "If it is permitted when his master is present, it is obvious! <note>original: *pshita*</note> ... It is not needed except for the foreign worship itself, etc." 

There are also those who explain that the phrase should be divided when reading between the word "No" <note>original: *Lo*</note> and "It is needed" <note>original: *tzerikha*</note>. According to this, it means: "No, it is not as simple as you say; rather, it **is** needed to be stated." Thus, you have two ways to understand the resolution of an "It is obvious" challenge. Is "It is needed" synonymous with "It was only stated for this specific case" (despite the word "except" <note>original: *ela*</note> being missing), or is there a pause between the words, meaning "No, it is not obvious, rather it is necessary"? According to the latter explanation, there is a linguistic omission in the text.

## He Wrote
The scholar <note>likely Rabbi Samson of Chinon, author of a major work on Talmudic methodology</note> saw fit to be precise regarding this resolution of "It is not needed." This resolution works well when the Talmud asks a challenge of "It is obvious!" <note>original: *pshita*</note>. But at the beginning of a chapter, when the Talmud asks "Why?" and then resolves it with "It is not needed," how can a resolution intended for a challenge of "obviousness" answer a challenge of "why"? For if the questioner is asking why a person would act a certain way, answering that the case is necessary doesn't address the motive. I heard from my teacher, the Rabbi Isaac de Leon <note>a 15th-century Spanish rabbi and kabbalist</note>, of blessed memory, that one should pause in the reading between "No" and "It is needed," even when the challenge was "Why?". The meaning is: "No, it is not as you said; the case you described is not forced, but it is necessary to say this other case." In this context, "needed" <note>original: *tzerikha*</note> functions as a term of necessity <note>original: *hekhre'akh*</note>, similar to saying "A man **must** <note>original: *tzarikh*</note> recite the *Shema* prayer." Thus, when we resolve an "It is obvious" challenge, the word "needed" means it is not obvious; and if you wish to be precise for a "Why" challenge, the word "needed" immediately functions as a term of necessity.

## Let him split
<note>term: *Leflog* — "Let him make a distinction"</note>
**And let him teach within its own [context]**: This refers to when the Tanna <note>a sage of the Mishnaic period</note> seeks to find a distinction in a matter but can only find it by switching to a different subject. The challenge "Let him split and teach it in its own context" means: according to his logic, he could have made the distinction within the original case; why did he leave it for another? This is done to teach one matter from another, as in the chapter "What is Interest" regarding a runner. The Tosafists <note>medieval commentators on the Talmud</note>, of blessed memory, say that even if he had made the distinction in the original case, it wouldn't have taught us any new principle <note>original: *chiddush*</note>. Therefore, the challenge means: since what was taught now provides no new insight, he should have just stayed within the original context and made the distinction there.

## Let us say
**[it] supports him**: Our teacher Rabbi Joseph Colon <note>the *Maharik*, a 15th-century Italian scholar</note>, of blessed memory, said that when the Talmud says "Let us say it supports him" and then rejects it, it is treated as a major difficulty that the Talmud strives to remove. Others disagree, suggesting that "Let us say it supports him" is actually what the author of the statement himself would have thought: "Since this is already explicit in a Mishnah or Baraita, what is he coming to teach us?" The resolution then shows that from the source alone, one could have interpreted it differently; therefore, his statement was necessary. Alternatively, "Let us say it supports him" means the source is close to his view and rejects the opposing view. Do not find the first way difficult (where it seems like a support), for I say that the Talmud is concerned with the difficulty, as we find in the Jerusalem Talmud <note>original: *M.B.* likely referring to *Ma'aser Beheimah* or a specific tractate</note> regarding damaged produce. Rabbi Hisda said, "We also learned the same..." as per Rashi's explanation. It seems Rabbi Hisda's intent was to use the Mishnah as support. There are places where the only answer is the first way we mentioned—that the brought source proves no one disagrees with him, as in the chapter "Ten Lineages," where Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav: "This only applies to fit individuals... let us say this supports him." 

## No
<note>original: *Lao*</note>
This term is common in the Talmud, such as "is it not <note>original: *lao*</note> vacant?" Rashi explains it simply as "not." However, the *Aruch* <note>an 11th-century dictionary</note> explains that it consists of two words, *La* and *Yi*, meaning "not the people," for in the Greek language they call it so <note>note: This refers to the Greek word *laos*, meaning people</note>.

## Actually
**I will say to you**: It is the way of the Talmud to say "Actually, I will say to you" <note>original: *Le'olam eima lakh*</note> after a questioner has presented two sides of an argument and challenged them both. The respondent then clarifies that one of them is the "truthful" or "actual" position. When the questioner returns to challenge that position as well, the respondent says "Actually, I will say to you..." to reaffirm the original true position. Rabbi Shimshon de Leon <note>likely R. Samson of Chinon</note> asks: How can one say "Actually" <note>original: *Le'olam* — literally 'forever' or 'at all times'</note> if he hasn't already stated the position he is now defending? My teacher Rabbi Isaac de Leon, of blessed memory, answered that when the questioner presents two forced options, if there is no third option, the respondent's silence on one of them is considered an implicit acceptance. Therefore, even if he didn't explicitly state it, it is as if he had, allowing the Talmud to use the phrase "Actually, I will say to you what I had already implicitly affirmed."

## Scripture
**is expounded [based on what is] before it or before its predecessor**: This is a dispute in the chapter "With what [may we] light," regarding the sin of neglecting Torah study, for which children die. Others say it is for the sin of the Mezuzah. Their dispute centers on whether a verse is expounded based on what is immediately before it, or even the verse before that. The verse "So that your days and the days of your children may increase" (Deuteronomy 11:21) follows the verse about the Mezuzah (11:20), which itself follows the verse about teaching Torah to children (11:19). Those who say children die for the neglect of Torah study expound the verse (11:21) based on its predecessor (11:19), while those who say Mezuzah expound it based on the verse immediately before it (11:20). There are many opinions on whether a verse is expounded based on what follows it as well.

## They concede
**The Sages [concede] to the later Tanna**: When there is a dispute between Tannaim where one says "everyone is liable" and another says "everyone is exempt," and then a different subject is brought up saying "And the Sages concede..." it means they agree to the exemption (or liability) in that specific second case. This is true even if the concession only applies to a part of the case. See the Mishnah in "The one who sends his son to the shopkeeper," where it says "The Sages concede to Rabbi Yehuda." There, the concession only applies to the glass flask, but regarding the oil, they still disagree and hold him liable.

## Currency
**A Shekel is from the Torah**, and it is a **Sela** in the words of the Sages. A Sela is worth four **Dinars**. A Dinar's weight is 96 barleycorns. It is worth six **Ma'ahs**. A Ma'ah is 16 barleycorns. It is worth two **Pundions**. A Pundion is 8 barleycorns. It is worth two **Issars**. An Issar is four barleycorns. It is worth two **Masmasin**. A Masmas is two...

# Tablets of the Covenant
->104b<-

...as a **strong refutation** <note>original: "teyuvta"</note>. However, a refutation only occurs when one refutes based on the words of the Mishnah or a Baraita <note>external Tannaitic teaching</note>, but it is merely a "difficulty" when it comes from the words of later Sages <note>Amoraim</note>. But regarding a **legal query** <note>original: "ba'aya"</note> that was not resolved, even he <note>the author or the source cited</note> teaches that the matter remains suspended and standing, and a person is able to resolve it. Furthermore, even regarding this view of the Rashbam <note>Rabbi Samuel ben Meir</note>, we shall see it as he does, for the Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note> disagrees with him, as does the Ran <note>Rabbi Nissim of Gerona</note>, who are later authorities, and I will expand on this elsewhere. You should know that in the chapter "The Partners" <note>in Tractate Bava Batra</note>, the anonymous voice of the Talmud asks whether they disagree regarding a vow or a specific type of wall, and it remained unresolved. Yet, in the chapter "An Ox that Gored," we found that it was resolved, as I wrote later in Sign 54 regarding the case of "An ox that gored a cow." We find this several times in the Talmud: a query is not resolved in its original place, but we find it resolved elsewhere. Similarly, in the chapter "The Injurer" regarding one who shames a sleeping person (Sign 18), the Tosafists <note>medieval commentators</note> explain there that this is the way of the Talmud. This is also proven in this chapter regarding Rava's query: if pebbles <note>kicked by an animal</note> fly from its body and cause damage, does one pay full or half damages? It remains in a state of doubt, yet they are eventually resolved as the Ri"f <note>Rabbi Isaac Alfasi</note> wrote and as I explained above. The I"K wrote about all of these. But regarding the query of Rav Ashi in "if there is a change to a quarter-kab," and similar cases, the Sages said: **"Let it stand"** <note>original: "teiku" — an unresolved legal query</note>. Rather, any place where "Let it stand" is said, the matter is closed. But where "Let it stand" is not said, it is "suspended and standing," and it is possible that it was resolved. Even in a state of doubt, if a query is unresolved, one can say that **seizure of property** <note>original: "tefisah"</note> is effective; the one holding the property can say, "It is established for me <note>original: "kim li"</note> according to one side of the query that leans toward liability."

Know that nearby, regarding the case of "an animal wagging its tail," Maimonides explained that it was not resolved, yet the Rosh stood many years after him and wrote that it was indeed resolved. This shows that the Law depends on a person's logic and his decision-making power. If so, this person who has seized the property can decide the query in favor of the side of liability, even if his fellow does not agree to that decision. Even if he only has a slight reason and cannot fully present it before us, nevertheless, since an eminent scholar would have the right to resolve the query and deny the claim, even an unlearned person <note>original: "am ha-aretz"</note> can now say, "It is established for me according to one of the opinions." Although the Rosh wrote in the first chapter of Bava Metzia that seizure only works in a "clear" case of "Let it stand," he only meant to exclude a general doubt where seizure is ineffective. This is also implied by the language of the Rosh in the second chapter of Ketubot: "We only find that seizure is ineffective regarding a doubtful Firstborn," etc. If so, anything that is not comparable to a doubtful Firstborn <note>where the doubt is inherent</note>, seizure is effective. In our case, it is like a "certain" claim and not like a Priest who has no claim at all <note>regarding a firstborn animal</note>. But with the claim of "It is established for me according to one opinion," since it carries the power of a "certain" claim, it is treated like an actual certain claim. Know that this is the conclusion in the Mordechai <note>Rabbi Mordechai ben Hillel</note> in the chapter "The Young Girl," as follows: "Rabbi Samuel ben Baruch says that if the groom seizes the dowry, he can say: 'It is established for me according to Rashi's view that she sold from the marriage property,' even if it was not checked if she died... for the one who seeks to take from his fellow bears the burden of proof." Presumably, the Rashbam does not agree with the Tosafists that seizure is ineffective in such cases. The Mordechai also brought them as the final ruling in Ketubot without disagreement. Also here, the Mordechai did not bring any opinion that disagrees with the Rashbam regarding a groom's seizure—whether seizure is effective in a state of doubt. Rather, it must be that since it was not in the Rashbam's power to decide regarding the dowries of grooms, he ruled that seizure is effective based on the claim of "It is established for me according to Rashi," since it carries the power of a certain claim that even great authorities might decide upon. One might say to him: since the great authorities did not decide, shall those who come after them decide? Certainly, he can decide. These Gaonim <note>post-Talmudic leaders</note> are no greater than the Talmud itself, which leaves things "suspended and standing," as I explained above regarding a "difficulty."

Regarding an unresolved legal query: if there is a side to decide and prove one of the words, then any judge who knows can seize [the property] and say, "It is established for me according to Rashi," and his seizure is effective. It is not similar to a doubtful Firstborn. Similarly, in the case of a judge, even though the Rosh replied in a Responsum <note>legal letter</note> saying: "There are groom's dowries where the doubt of the Ri"f is such that he did not descend to the distinction I have made—between a male <note>argument</note> where it is possible to decide and a matter where it is impossible to decide, like a 'Let it stand'..." Nevertheless, according to what I have written, my distinction is something pleasant and decided in my eyes without any hesitation. So too ruled the Maharika <note>Rabbi Joseph Colon</note> in Root 161, that one who seizes based on these proofs [is supported]. Regarding what he wrote there—"Who can decide between these two world giants, Rashi and Rabbenu Tam? We are but orphans of orphans"—I do not agree with him in this. For "Jephthah in his generation is like Samuel in his generation," as I will mention with God's help in another chapter on civil laws. The Rosh also used to decide in matters of Torah law, and I too, with God's help, when I arrive there, will decide according to what is shown to me from Heaven. I only brought proof from Rabbi Samuel <note>the Rashbam</note> that even though he did not decide <note>between views</note>—for if he had decided, he wouldn't have needed to say that "if the groom seized, we do not take it from him," but rather even if he hadn't seized, we would take it from the other and give it to him since he decided like Rashi—but presumably, since it was not in his power to decide and the matter remained in doubt for him, he ruled that seizure is effective. The Maharika struggled pointlessly to bring proof that the Rashbam lacked the power to decide between the "great mountains" <note>famous scholars</note>, for presumably he simply chose not to decide by ruling that "if the groom seizes," as I explained. Also, what the Maharika ruled in Root 161—that seizure of an object designated as a "certain" collateral is effective even if it is not clear to us—the law is not with him. I will expand on this in the chapter "One who Leaves" (Sign 34). Therefore, in short, keep this rule in your hand for all matters of legal doubt: where it is the way of the judge to decide between a disagreement found in the Talmud or among the Gaonim, seizure is effective because he *could* have decided. But if the judge *does* decide—whether because the "mountains" are divided against an individual, or because it seems logical to the judge according to his own reasoning and clear proofs—even if many disagree with the individual, the one who seizes cannot say "It is established for me according to the other view"; rather, the judge removes it from his hand. And when we say "seizure is effective," it does not mean he can go and snatch the other's property, for if so, he would be a thief <note>original: "gazlan"</note>, and initially we would compel him to return the stolen item. Similarly, even if he lent him a vessel and the borrower then seizes the lender's vessel, even in this case seizure is not effective. For if he lent it to him for a fixed time, he must return it at that fixed time... and it is like the law of a "dishonest person." Similarly, if he lent it to him without specifying, it is for thirty days, which is like a fixed time. Even though we rule at the end of the first chapter of Bekhorot that a "certain" claim makes seizure effective, it is different there because they are seizing by right and with clarity because of a debt, they just cannot collect it through a court act; if so, he is "performing justice for himself" <note>original: "avid dina le-nafshei"</note> in a matter that is clear to all. Therefore, we wrote above that if a child seized once, the other cannot seize it back for this reason. But in our case, it would be a great extension of the law if one could seize anything; if so, he would be performing justice for himself in a matter that is *not* clear to us. Even everyone would agree that he cannot do this, as the Machaneh wrote in Sign 4. Rather, it is specifically in a case like the essence of the matter where the doubt fell, and this is called "seizure" throughout the Talmud. Similarly, regarding the dowry where the Rashbam wrote "if the groom seizes," this also refers to the essence of the matter where the disagreement and doubt occurred, but not from other money. The Maharika also made this distinction in Root 161. It seems to me that even in a loan, seizure is effective; for example, if Reuben owed money to Simeon, Reuben could effectively seize it to keep the money in his hand due to a legal doubt from another place... and he cannot remove him except with cash. Nevertheless, in a case of loss, we do not say this, as is found in the chapter "One who was Married" (Sign 11) and the chapter "At All Times"... and he must pay with cash and not cause him a loss where he cannot seize. Furthermore, there is a great distinction between a loan and a borrowing <note>original: "she'ilah"</note> or snatching something from his hand, which is like theft. For to steal from someone is forbidden, but to evade a loan <note>to offset it</note> is permitted for a person toward himself. This implies that evading a loan is a lighter matter; if so, where he withholds the loan because of seizure, this is not considered a stolen object where we would judge him to return it before the debt he owes him, but rather he has seized according to the law. And if the other party then returns and seizes from him the actual money over which the claim or loan fell, we also do not remove it from him. This concludes his words.

### Let us return to the matter of Halakhic rulings:
Between **Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua**, the law follows **Rabbi Joshua**.
Between **Rabbi Joshua and Rabban Gamliel**, the law follows **Rabban Gamliel**.
The law follows **Rabbi Akiva** over his fellow, but not over his fellows <note>i.e., when he is in the minority against a group</note>; so it is concluded in the chapter "He who was Taken Out."
The law follows **Rabbi Eliezer ben Jacob** in every place, for the teaching of Rabbi Eliezer ben Jacob is **"small in measure and clean"** <note>original: "kab ve-naki" — meaning few in number but highly authoritative/pure</note>. Rashi explained at the end of the chapter "One who Receives" that he did not teach much compared to his fellows, but what he said is "clean," meaning the law always follows him. The Rashbam wrote in the chapter "There are Those who Inherit" that even in a Baraita the law follows him. The Ran wrote in Shevuot that the law follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Jacob specifically against an individual. We say in the final chapter of Shevuot that where it is proven that the law is not like him, we do not rely on this rule of "small in measure and clean." The Rosh wrote in the chapter "He who was Taken Out" that even though we hold his teaching is "small and clean," in this case the law does not follow him because Rav Papa holds like the Sages, and perhaps this case is not counted among those meant by the rule. For Rabbeinu Chananel wrote based on tradition that we hold his words are law in a specific number of things and no more. In the third chapter of Nedarim, the Talmud asks if the law follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Jacob, and the Rosh wrote: even though he is "small and clean," these are words of the Sages <note>rabbinic decrees</note> which they strengthened. <summary>This page discusses the legal validity of seizing property ("tefisah") when a Rabbinic query remains unresolved, arguing that such seizure can be upheld by claiming "Kim Li" (I hold like this view). It also begins a list of standard principles for deciding between specific Talmudic Sages, such as the authority of Rabbi Eliezer ben Jacob.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author’s exploration of Talmudic logic and the methodology of legal decision-making. It transitions from discussing specific refutations to general rules for study and how to handle unresolved debates in the Oral Law.</meta>

<page-num>85</page-num>
<header>The Oral Torah</header>

# Always
Whenever you study any discourse or any matter, just as you make it your goal to understand that matter well, you should also seek ways to challenge it. You should stir up the "void of doubt" <note>original: "challat ha-sefika," referring to the intellectual space created by questioning</note> regarding that matter or that phrasing, and seek to know the potential responses and difficulties that could be raised. This will be the cause of establishing you upon the truth and understanding the matter clearly. For one who identifies the "illness" <note>the intellectual difficulty</note> will immediately find its cure. You must seek to investigate the appearance of the matter at the beginning of your study with an example, until you have searched and scrutinized it, for "a fool believes anything" (Proverbs 14:15). Be careful not to lead yourself down a difficult path by explaining one hidden thing with another equally hidden thing, or even with something revealed; the correct explanation is only that which clarifies the hidden through the revealed.

Know that the way of those who "give and take" <note>the Sages who debate in the Talmud</note> is that whenever they wish to raise a difficulty against a Mishnah, a Baraita <note>an external teaching from the era of the Mishnah</note>, or an Amoraic statement <note>a statement by later Sages</note>, they seek to know if it is necessary or not. Regarding the statement they are currently treating as doubtful, they hold all other statements to be true in order to challenge it. Later, they will return in another place and take those statements that they had previously assumed were true and treat *them* as doubtful, challenging them based on what was clarified here as being true. All of this is to clarify and "whiten" the law—to see if, by treating them as doubtful, they could still respond from one case to the other and clarify them.

Always, regarding any phrasing common in the Talmud that arises for you from a legal tradition: strive to know its nature and how it usually appears elsewhere as a positive assertion. See and observe if it follows that same path here as well; if it does not, you must understand why it changed.
<margin>Doubtful, etc.: One who does not know the custom and nature of a law should search for the ruling in the Talmud to see how it is handled; until here are his words.</margin>

<margin>
**To you**
**But**
</margin>
My sons (may God protect and grant them life), I have copied these matters even though they are expansive and contain simple things; nevertheless, they are correct for those who seek knowledge.

Know, my sons, that one needs knowledge and understanding to grasp the language of the Laws <note>original: "halakhot"</note> every day, so that one may stand intellectually upon the depth of the matters and understand each thing based on its foundation. One should "pepper" <note>debate sharply</note> the law with wisdom, for there is no comparison to such intellectual labor; it is the "glory of truth," and everyone will acknowledge them if the truth is with them. Their teachings will spread with the help of Heaven, which aids those who come to be purified. After clarifying the plain meaning of the law, one must review the law out loud and with joy.

<margin>
**And in the Zohar**
</margin>
In the Zohar, portion of *Bereshit* <note>Genesis</note>, they said: regarding what our Rabbis of blessed memory stated, "a word is worth a *sela* <note>a coin</note> but silence is worth two," this applies even to words of Torah. One should not be hasty to utter a word before God. The explanation is: when you stand before the Divine Presence—which is to say, when one is occupied with Torah—one should not hasten to bring words out of his mouth, but only that which is clear and proper. As our Rabbis said: "And you shall teach them diligently" <note>original: "ve-shinnantam"</note>—they should be sharp <note>original: "shenunim"</note> in your mouth. This "sharpening" is the preparation, and only afterward should he speak them aloud, as our Rabbis said: "They are life to those who find them" (Proverbs 4:22)—read as "to those who bring them forth" <note>original: "le-motzi'eihem"</note> with the mouth.

# A General Rule of Law
Regarding the matter found sometimes in the words of our Rabbis: "This is a law given to Moses at Sinai" <note>term: "Halakha Le-Moshe Mi-Sinai" — a law with no biblical source, believed to be an oral tradition from Sinai</note>. It could be said that every such law is indeed from Sinai. However, one might ask: was not the entire Torah, in its generalities, details, and minutiae, spoken at Sinai? Maimonides <note>original: "Rambam"</note>, in his introduction to the Order of *Zeraim* <note>Seeds</note>, clarified this matter.

These are his words: "But even though they are received traditions and there is no dispute regarding them, through the wisdom of the written Torah we are able to derive these explanations through the path of logic <note>original: "derekh Mordechai," likely a scribal error for "derekh madrash" or logical derivation</note>, supporting traditions, proofs, and hints found in the Scripture. When you see the Sages in the Talmud investigating and disagreeing with one another in the system of study, bringing proofs for one of these explanations or something similar—such as what was said regarding the verse 'The fruit of a majestic tree' <note>original: "pri etz hadar"</note>, whether these are hints or clarifications until it is clarified that it refers to the citron—one Sage says the taste of its wood and fruit are equal, another says it is a fruit that stays on its tree from year to year, and another says it is a fruit that grows by the water—these proofs were not brought because they were in doubt about the identity of the fruit until they knew it from these proofs. Rather, we have seen without doubt from the time of Joshua until now that they would take the citron with the Lulav every year, and there is no dispute about it. They were simply searching for the hint found in the Scripture for this explanation received from Sinai. You have surely also seen this regarding the laws of 'an eye for an eye' involving monetary compensation... and regarding the daughter of a priest... and everything similar that follows this principle. This is the meaning of 'its generalities, details, and minutiae'—meaning the matters we can derive through the 'particular and general' <note>hermeneutical rules</note> and the thirteen rules of interpretation, which were all received from the mouth of Moses at Sinai. And all of them, even though they were received from Moses, are not called 'a law given to Moses at Sinai.' For we do not say 'the majestic fruit is a citron' is a law given to Moses at Sinai... because it has been clarified to us that they are indeed from Moses but have hints in the Scripture or can be derived through logic. But regarding a matter that has no hint in the Scripture, and no connection to it, and it is impossible to derive through logic—regarding that alone is it said: 'a law given to Moses at Sinai.' Because of this, when we said that 'measurements' <note>e.g., the minimum size of an olive for certain laws</note> are a law given to Moses at Sinai, they challenged us and asked: 'Why do you say they are a law from Sinai when they are hinted at in the verse "A land of wheat and barley"?' The answer is that the measurements are indeed a law from Sinai; they have no logical basis to be derived and no hint in the entire Torah. That verse was only attached to the law as a sign <note>term: "asmakhta" — a scriptural support used as a memory aid rather than a source</note> so it would be preserved and remembered, but it is not the literal meaning of the text. This is what they meant by saying 'the verse is a mere support' <note>original: "kara asmakhta be-alma"</note> wherever it is mentioned." Until here are his words.
->A wise man kisses with graceful lips<-

# In Tractate Eruvin
In the chapter "He who was taken out," Rabbi Jacob bar Idi said in the name of Rabbi Johanan, etc.: Regarding Rabbi Judah, the law follows Rabbi Judah. Regarding Rabbi Yose, the law follows Rabbi Yose. It goes without saying that between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yose, the law follows Rabbi Yose; for if the law follows him even against Rabbi Judah, it certainly follows him against Rabbi Meir. <gloss>(Sefer Mitzvot Gadol at the end of the chapter on page 80 in Ketubot: the law follows Rabbi Meir in his decrees, specifically in his decrees and not in his fines)</gloss>. He said: We shall say that between Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Simeon, the law follows Rabbi Yose; for Rabbi Johanan said that between Rabbi Judah and Rabbi Simeon, the law follows Rabbi Judah. If in a place where Rabbi Judah stands, the law does not follow Rabbi Simeon, then in a place where Rabbi Yose stands, it certainly does not. The general rule of the matter: the law follows Rabbi Yose against a single colleague, but not against multiple colleagues. So wrote the author of *Halikhot Olam*. Even though in the chapter "One who vows," Rabbi Johanan disagrees regarding Rabbi Yose against multiple colleagues (as the Tosafists wrote), they wrote there that between Rabbi Judah and Rabbi Yose, the law follows Rabbi Yose even in a Baraita. Between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Simeon—this remains a "tie" <note>term: "teiku" — an unresolved legal query</note>. The author of *Halikhot Olam* wrote: Therefore, the law follows the one who is more stringent; until here are his words. The Maharika <note>Rabbi Joseph Colon</note> wrote on this in his *Rules of the Talmud*: These rules apply to the Baraitas, and they do not seem correct to me except in matters of Torah law; but in Rabbinic law, the law follows the one who is more lenient. Until here are his words.

# And Since
And since the matter of a "tie" <note>original: "teiku"</note> has come to our hand, I will write "excellent things" <note>original: "mili me'alyata"</note> written by the Gaon Maharshal <note>Rabbi Solomon Luria</note> of blessed memory in his books... regarding all matters of legal doubt, how to conduct oneself. These are his words: Regarding every "tie" stated in the Talmud: in matters of prohibition, one is stringent; in monetary matters, one is lenient <note>meaning the possessor keeps the money</note>.

Even though the author of the *Arukh* brought another explanation in the name of Rabbeinu Tam that he is in doubt if they disagree, nevertheless all the earlier and later Gaonim <note>Sages of the post-Talmudic era</note> hold that in monetary matters, it is lenient. So wrote the author of the *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol*... and it is not only a "tie," but even when a query is not resolved but remains standing. In that case too: monetary law is lenient and prohibitions are stringent. However, a dispute fell among the Gaonim—between the Rif <note>Rabbi Isaac Alfasi</note>, Rambam, and the *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol*—who ruled that even in a case of doubt, seizing property <note>term: "tefisa"</note> works. But Rabbeinu Isaac <note>Ri</note>, the author of the Tosafot, the Rosh, and most later authorities believe that seizing property never helps in a case of legal doubt. Even if the Talmud does not decide the matter, one may decide it. Certainly, the words of the Tosafists are the primary rule regarding a "tie" where the query was left open in the Talmud and not resolved. No Sage in the world has the authority to resolve it from another place, or from a Baraita, or from logic, for that would be like disagreeing with the Talmud, and with Ravina and Rav Ashi <note>the final editors of the Talmud</note>. Just as one cannot resolve a "strong refutation" <note>original: "teyuvta"</note> stated in the Talmud, so too with queries that were stated in the Talmud and not resolved—even if a scholar, even in our time, brings a proof to resolve it, he has the right to do so, and we do not follow him <note>as a final ruling</note>, for since the Talmud left it as a "tie," it remains in a state of doubt until its resolution is revealed to you.

A similar thing was written by Rabbeinu Chananel in "The Presumptive Ownership of Houses" regarding Samuel’s statement: "My father agrees with me that..." and his words resulted in a difficulty. Nevertheless, Rabbeinu Chananel ruled like him. The Rashbam brought this and these are his words: "We have a tradition from our Rabbis: regarding any 'strong refutation' in the Talmud... the words of the one who was refuted are void. But where a matter merely ended in a 'difficulty' like this one of Samuel... it remains suspended and standing." If so, even if the Talmudic logic is difficult, we still say the matter is suspended—how much more so when a query was simply not resolved. And even though Rashbam disagrees, it is because...

<summary>This page outlines critical methodologies for studying the Talmud, explaining that doubt and questioning are essential for reaching truth. It defines "Halakha Le-Moshe Mi-Sinai" as oral traditions that may or may not have scriptural hints, and provides rules for resolving legal ties and disputes between Sages.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Talmudic methodology, specifically focusing on the "rules of decision-making" (Halakhic priority) when two or more Sages disagree. It provides a reference guide for determining whose opinion becomes the final law.</meta>

<page-num>85</page-num>
<header>447 Oral Torah 85</header>

<margin>For all cases where Rav and Shmuel disagree, they both follow the order of the parchment <note>original: "sidrei klapha," likely referring to the physical arrangement of the scrolls or the tradition of their rulings</note>; since the majority are covered by them.</margin>

<margin>The Knasat HaGedolah <note>A 17th-century Halakhic work by Rabbi Chaim Benveniste</note> of blessed memory, in the chapter "Ownership of Houses," wrote that the law follows Rav Nachman in civil law against Rav Sheshet. However, in all other matters, it was written in the chapter "The Partners" that the law follows Rav Nachman in civil law and Shmuel in religious prohibitions. All the Tosafot <note>Medieval commentaries on the Talmud</note> wrote at the end of Tractate Arachin that the law follows Rav Nachman over Rav Sheshet.</margin>

His way was: between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yannai, the law follows Rabbi Yannai because he was [Yochanan’s] teacher. Similarly, between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Eliezer, the law follows Rabbi Yochanan. Between Rav Huna and Rav, the law follows Rav. Between Rav Huna and Rav Hisda, the law follows Rav Huna because he was the teacher of Hisda. Between Rav Assi and Rav Kahana, the law follows Rav Kahana. Between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman, the law follows Rav Nachman in civil law <note>original: "be-dinai"</note>, and Rav Huna in religious prohibitions <note>original: "be-issurei"</note>. Likewise, between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet, the law follows Rav Sheshet in ritual prohibitions and Rav Nachman in civil law. Between Shmuel and Rav Adda bar Ahava, the law follows Shmuel. Between Rav Ashi and Ravina, the law follows Rav Ashi.

Everywhere that Rav and Shmuel disagree, the law follows Rav in ritual prohibitions and Shmuel in civil law, except for three cases where the law follows Shmuel even in ritual prohibitions, as seen in the chapter "With What May One Light." It is proper for you to know that the rule "the law follows person X in civil law and person Y in ritual prohibitions" only applies specifically to their own disputes, such as Rav against Shmuel or Rav Nachman against Rav Huna; but if they disagree with someone else, this rule does not necessarily apply. Thus ends the words of Rabbi Yochanan. 

Regarding Rabbi Yochanan: the law follows Rabbi Yochanan except for three cases. The Tosafot wrote in the chapter "Ownership of Houses" that this applies when he speaks in his own name, but when he reports teachings in the name of others, the law follows him. See the chapter "Every Hour" regarding the Alfasi <note>Rabbi Isaac Alfasi, known as the Rif</note>. The Riv <note>Rabbi Isaac ben Melchizedek</note> wrote in "Ownership of Houses" that we established the law according to Resh Lakish even though Rabbi Yochanan wondered at him, as long as he did not actively disagree. This was also the ruling of the Rif and Maimonides. 

Between Rabbah and Rav Yosef, the law follows Rabbah except for three cases. The Tosafot wrote in the second chapter of Tractate Bava Metzia that some say in other places the law follows him [Rav Yosef]. They also wrote that throughout the Talmud, one can find proof for this. Rabbenu Yonah wrote: when we say the law follows Rabbah over Rav Yosef, it is specifically when they disagree based on their own reasoning, because we say "Sinai" <note>a sage with vast memorized knowledge</note> is Rav Yosef, but Rabbah is a "Uprooter of Mountains" <note>original: "oker harim," a sage with sharp, analytical logic</note>. However, when they disagree over the interpretation of a Mishnah, this rule does not apply. Thus ends his words, and the Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note> wrote similarly in the first chapter of Tractate Shabbat. The Rosh also wrote in the chapter "One May Not Stand" that the law follows Rav Assi over Rav Huna, and the Mordechai wrote that in several places Rav Huna speaks in the name of Rav Assi. The Tosafot and the Rosh wrote in the first chapter of Bava Metzia that between Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi, the law follows Rav Ashi. The Ritva <note>Rabbi Yom Tov Asevilli</note> wrote in the chapter "The One Who Dwells" that between Rav Yehuda and Rav Sheshet, the law follows Rav Sheshet except for the cases written in the "Order of the Tanaim."

# In the Legal Rulings and Writings

From our teacher Rabbi Israel [Isserlein], sign 101: The Rosh in the chapter "The Sinew that Displaced" regarding raw meat and eggs: Rav Achha and Ravina disagree throughout the entire Torah. Rav Achha is always for the strict view <note>original: "le-chumra"</note> and Ravina is for the lenient view <note>original: "le-kula"</note>. The law follows Ravina for leniency, except for those three cases where Rav Achha and Ravina were both strict, yet the law follows Rav Achha for leniency. You might ask: why not just say simply "the law follows the one who is lenient"? I do not know what difficulty you have; the Rosh simply used the language of the Talmud as it appears in the Gemara. The Talmud itself does not find it difficult why it wasn't stated more briefly. Rabbi Isaac explains that everywhere Rav Achha is strict and Ravina is lenient. This applies even in Tractate Shabbat where they disagree about "repulsive muktzah" <note>items set aside and forbidden to touch on the Sabbath due to being dirty or repulsive</note>, where Rav Achha and Ravina permit it. If we find any place where it is written that one of them thought the opposite, it would be a contradiction. Where it is said the law follows the lenient view, the Rosh wrote in the chapter "The Multiple" that this is only where other Sages do not disagree. 

The author of the *Terumot* <note>Rabbi Samuel Sardi</note> wrote: when they disagree on monetary matters, the "lenient" view is for the lender, because the borrower's property is pledged to the lender. He wrote similarly in the first chapter of Bava Metzia. Rabbi Isaac also wrote in "The Sinew that Displaced" that even in a place where an Amora <note>a Sage of the Talmudic era</note> acted against Rav, the law still follows Rav because he is the "master of the Talmudic book." Whether the law follows Rabbi Yose bar Hanina against Rabbi Yochanan is discussed by the Tosafot in the chapter "How Do We Bless."

# We Find the Law

As following Mar bar Rav Ashi throughout the entire Talmud, except for [the acronym] "MAPIK" <note>an acronym for specific legal cases: a certain oath, returning a ruling, and the "junction of the tendons"</note>: an oath in the chapter "The Oath of Judges," and returning a ruling in the chapter "The One Who Finds Difficulty" regarding the junction of the tendons. Your sign for this is "turned white" <note>original: "Hapach Lavan"</note>. This was the ruling of Rabbenu Chananel, the Rif, and the Rosh. It is brought in the rulings of "The One Who Finds Difficulty": *It was taught in a Baraita regarding the Sabbath that even if one praises his fellow who disagrees with him, the law does not necessarily follow the praised one.* Rabbi Ishmael said: "He who wishes to become wise should engage in monetary laws, for there is no greater profession in the Torah... let him serve Shimon ben Nannas." The Gemara says that even though Rabbi Ishmael praised Ben Nannas, the law follows Rabbi Ishmael. Similarly in the chapter of Gittin: even though Rabbi Yose praised Rabbi Shimon, the law follows Rabbi Meir. The Rosh wrote that the Jerusalem Talmud says they praised them for their *teaching* <note>for the logic</note> but not for the *final law*. We find a similar case regarding Amoraim in the chapter "How Do We Bless" where Rav Yehuda says one thing and Shmuel says another, and Shmuel said to Rav Yehuda: "Sharp one! Your reasoning is better than mine!" Yet the Gemara says that even though Shmuel praised Rav Yehuda, the law follows Shmuel.

# Of Blessed Memory

The *Halikhot Olam* <note>A manual on Talmudic methodology by Jeshua ben Joseph ha-Levi</note> says one should not be overly strict to extract a lenient ruling from a single Rabbinic doubt, but a "Double Doubt" <note>original: "Sfek Sfeika"</note> is lenient even in Torah law. I received from my teacher, the Sage, may his light shine: a "Double Doubt" is only called such if it is "reversible" from three sides. That is, however you start, you find two doubts. But if it cannot be reversed, it is not called a "Double Doubt." It is possible we treat it as a single, strong doubt. For example: "Perhaps he did not touch it, and if you say he did touch it, perhaps it was a dead creeping thing <note>original: "sheretz," which is impure</note> or perhaps it was a frog <note>which is pure</note>." This is a double doubt that is not reversible. If you say: "Perhaps he entered, and if you say he entered, perhaps he touched," but if you reverse it, there are not two doubts. If you start with "Perhaps he touched," and you conclude he did not, you cannot then ask "perhaps he entered." This is not a "Double Doubt." This is what Rabbi Isaac said in the name of the Tosafot.

# Everywhere in the Chapter

If a law is "loose in your hand" <note>you are unsure of the ruling</note>, go out and see what the people are doing <note>original: "puk chazi mah ama davar," a principle of following established custom</note>. This is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud. Rav Kahana and Rav Assi said to Rav: "The law is thus, now be silent." Rav was silent, and they brought proof from there that silence is like admission <note>original: "shituka ke-hoda'ah damya"</note>. The Rama wrote that this is a "Father of Buildings" <note>a primary principle</note> throughout the Talmud. In the chapter "One Who Sells a House," Rav Kahana and Rav Assi said to Rav to be silent, and the Tosafot wrote that we find many places where Rav was silent and the law follows them. We do not say he simply didn't care to answer, as we find later with Abbaye and Rabbah where one was silent but did not accept the other's words. Here, they were "student-colleagues" to Rav, so his silence must be acceptance. But Abbaye was a student, so Rabbah simply didn't care to answer him.

# There Are Those Who Say

The Tosafot wrote in many places that the opinion of the *Kuntres* <note>Rashi's commentary</note> is that wherever there are two versions of a debate, in Torah matters we follow the strict one, and in Rabbinic matters we follow the later version. Others say in Rabbinic matters we follow the lenient version. The Riva <note>Rabbi Isaac ben Asher</note> says the first version is always primary and the "There are those who say" is secondary. In *Halikhot Olam* it is written that the later version is the one Rav Ashi established as the final conclusion. However, the Rosh wrote in "Ownership of Houses" that the Geonim <note>Leaders of the Babylonian academies</note> ruled like the Riva.

# When Rav Ashi

Established the later version as the final word: The Rosh wrote that because Rav Ashi placed Rav Huna’s explanation last, it was an intentional confirmation. Even though the Alfasi usually follows the last version, that is only when the Gemara itself is analyzing the text. If the Sages are debating and the Gemara doesn't decide, we follow the first version as the primary one.

# No

Law is established by a student in the presence of his teacher. The Rosh wrote in the beginning of Tractate Sukkah: when a student disagrees with his teacher during the teacher's lifetime, since the teacher did not accept the student's words, the student's words are rejected. But if they disagree after the teacher's death, the law follows the later authority <note>original: "Halakha ke-Batrai"</note>, even though the later ones were students of the earlier ones. This rule of "no law follows a student over a teacher" only applied until the generation of Abbaye and Rava. From Abbaye and Rava onward, we have a tradition from the Geonim that the law follows the later authorities. The reason given by the Gaon is that before Abbaye, students only repeated what they received from their teachers (like the Baraitot of Rabbi Hiyya). But from Abbaye and Rava onward, they investigated all opinions and logic. Sometimes the teacher followed a path that was not the final law, and the later Sages clarified it. As it says in the *Hegyonot*: we repeat the law with "twelve faces" <note>referring to deep multifaceted analysis</note>, which was not done in the earlier days of the masters.

<summary>This page outlines specific rules of precedence for deciding the law when Talmudic Sages disagree, emphasizing that while teachers generally overrule students, later authorities (from Abbaye and Rava onward) are given weight due to their comprehensive analysis.</summary>
<keywords>Halakha, Tosafot, Rav Nachman, Rav Huna, Rav Ashi, Gemara, Jerusalem Talmud, Rav Achha, Ravina, Double Doubt, Law follows the later ones, Sinai vs. Uprooter of Mountains</keywords>
