<meta>This page continues the biographical and methodological guide to the Sages of the Mishnah and Talmud, specifically focusing on identifying anonymous mentions and the unique intellectual characteristics of the great masters.</meta>

# Every
**Rabbi Yehoshua** mentioned anonymously in the Mishnah refers to **Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah**. **Rabbi Eliezer** mentioned anonymously is **Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus**. **Rabbi Yehuda** <note>OCR reads "Yira/Yura," a common typo for Yehuda</note> mentioned anonymously is **Rabbi Yehuda ben Ilai**. **Rabbi Shimon** mentioned anonymously is **Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai**. **Yohanan the High Priest** refers to **Yohanan ben Mattathias**, who lived in the days of the Hasmoneans and similar figures. Regarding **Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha**, they wrote that he was the son of **Rabbi Akiva**, and was called "Korcha" <note>literally "the bald one"</note> because Rabbi Akiva was bald, as Ben Azzai said of him: "All the sages of Israel are like a garlic peel before me, except for this bald one." So it is written in *Halichot Olam*. However, in Tractate Shabbat, chapter *Ha-Shore* (page 107), the Tosafot <note>medieval French and German commentators</note> begin a discussion on this, but Rabbenu Tam refuted this identification as is appropriate; see there.

# In every place
where it says he would "illuminate and brighten the eyes of the Sages in the law," his name is **Nehemiah**, according to the *Baraitha* <note>external teaching not in the Mishnah</note> in the first chapter of *Eruvin*. Every **Rabbi Elazar** mentioned anonymously in the Talmud is **Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat**.

# In the chapter "Those Who Are Burned"
it is taught: The anonymous voice of the Mishnah follows **Rabbi Meir**; the anonymous voice of the Tosefta follows **Rabbi Nehemiah**; the anonymous voice of the Sifra follows **Rabbi Yehuda**; the anonymous voice of the Sifrei follows **Rabbi Ishmael**. All of these, however, follow the school of **Rabbi Akiva**, because they were all his students, and the anonymous tradition was established according to their views. However, there are times when the Talmud recognizes that certain Mishnahs were finalized according to the opinions of others, as we say in Tractate Megillah: "These are the words of Rabbi Menachem bar Yose the 'Collector of Traditions,'" and similar cases in other places.

Regarding those praised for their wisdom in the *Baraitha* in the chapter "He who says: Receive this Divorce": It was taught that **Isi ben Yehuda** used to enumerate the praises of the Sages:
**Rabbi Meir** was a sage and a scribe.
**Rabbi Yehuda** was a sage when he wished to be <note>Rashi explains: when he chose to debate, he would answer wisely; the Tosafot add that he was even wiser than Rabbi Meir, though Rabbi Meir was sharper in questioning</note>.
**Rabbi Tarfon** was a "heap of nuts" <note>Rashi explains via Avot de-Rabbi Natan: just as if you remove one nut from a pile, they all come tumbling down together, so too if a student asked Rabbi Tarfon a question, he would bring proof from Scripture, Midrash, Halacha, and Aggadah all at once</note>.
**Rabbi Ishmael** was a "spacious shop" <note>Rashi explains: like a shopkeeper who is always ready so a customer never has to wait, Rabbi Ishmael's learning was always prepared and organized for anyone who needed to learn from him. Tosafot suggest "spacious shop" refers to nourishment, while others read it as "shining/radiant"</note>.
**Rabbi Akiva** was a "full storehouse" <note>Rashi gives two explanations from Avot de-Rabbi Natan: Akiva was like a worker who gathers barley, wheat, and beans into his basket indiscriminately, and only upon returning home sorts them. Similarly, Akiva gathered Scripture, Law, Midrash, and Lore, and then organized them into distinct structures like the Sifra and Sifrei. My own view is that a "full storehouse" means he was partitioned and organized, like large chests used for precious vessels where different types of grain are kept separate</note>.
**Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri** was a "peddler's basket" <note>Rashi explains: like a peddler who enters a city and has everything—balsam, oil, cinnamon—Yohanan could answer from Scripture, Talmud, Midrash, or Lore. This differs from Akiva’s praise in that Akiva systematically organized everything first</note>.
**Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah** was also a "peddler's basket" <note>Rashi: specifically a basket of perfumes; like a peddler who is professional and has every variety tied in a bundle, ready for the asker</note>.
The Mishnah of **Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov** is "a *kav* and clean" <note>Rashi: he did not produce a large volume of teachings, but what he did say was "clean"—meaning the law always follows his opinion</note>.
**Rabbi Yose**: "His reasoning is with him" <note>Rashi: he always provided the underlying reason for his words, making them settled and logical</note>.
**Rabbi Shimon** "grinds much and produces little" and "what he produces is only bran" <note>Rashi explains this paradox: he studied much and taught a little of the essence, and what he "threw away" as bran were only the things where the law did not follow him; he never forgot anything essential</note>.
And so **Rabbi Tarfon** said to his students: "My children, be careful with these qualities, for they are the 'tithe of tithes' of the qualities of **Rabbi Akiva**" <note>Meaning: follow these teachings, for they are the choicest extracts of Akiva's wisdom</note>.

# We find in the Assembly
that a woman may argue with the Sages on a point of law, just as we find in the Tosefta at the beginning of *Kilayim*: **Rabbi Tarfon** would disqualify and the Sages would purify, and she said, "You have spoken clearly," etc., and the Sages said before him, "Rabbi Yehoshua says you have spoken well."
**The Holy Congregation**: This refers to **Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya** and **Rabbi Yose ben Meshullam**, who divided their day into thirds: one third for Torah, one third for prayer, and one third for work.
**Rabbi Yehuda the Prince** <note>OCR: Yura</note> is "Our Holy Rabbi" who redacted the Mishnah. There was another **Rabbi Yehuda the Prince** (II). Our masters of blessed memory wrote that the first Rabbi Yehuda taught the *Baraitha* in the second chapter of *Avodah Zarah* (page 36). He and his court were called "Our Rabbis," as mentioned at the start of *Ketubot* (page 2). Note that the second Rabbi Yehuda the Prince is mentioned at the end of the first chapter of *Rosh Hashanah* regarding his mother's mourning. Tosafot wrote: This is not the Rabbi Yehuda the Prince who permitted the use of gentile oil, for that one lived in the days of Rav and Samuel—he was the son of Rabban Gamliel, the son of the first Rabbi Yehuda the Prince.

# Rav
He was the greatest of this world. **Rabbi Yohanan** used to write to Rav, as long as he was alive, addressing him as "To our Rabbi in Babylon." When Rav died, he wrote to **Samuel**, "To our colleague." In the chapter *Elu Terefot*, it says: "Rabbi Yohanan is gone, Resh Lakish is gone; do you not remember who Rav was? I saw him before he went to Babylon, serving Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) and Rabbi Hiyya, and all those years I would serve standing while he sat." In the *Arukh*, it is written: Rav is counted among the Tannaim like **Bar Kappara**, **Rabban Shimon ben Rabbi**, and **Rabbi Hiyya**. If we find a *Baraitha* that contradicts Rav, it is treated as one Tanna disagreeing with another Tanna. Rashi wrote: Rav was the teacher of all the people of the Exile and the head of the academy for Israel, except for Samuel. It is inconceivable that Rav Hanan would disagree with him. Mahari Colon wrote that we challenge all Amoraim from the words of Rav, except for Samuel. His name was actually **Abba**, but they called him **Yehuda the Prince** <note>likely error for Rav's title/distinction</note>. In Babylon, they called him **Rav**, as Rashbam wrote. I have received a tradition that **Rabbi Abba the Tall** is Rav.

# Samuel
He was the colleague of Rav. Rav said of him: "No secret is hidden from him." Nevertheless, **Rav Assi** and **Rav Kahana**, who were "student-colleagues" of Rav, were greater than Samuel. In the chapter *Merubah* (page 80), it says Samuel would not enter a room before Rav Assi, and Rav Assi would not enter before Rav. Thus we must say Samuel was a student-colleague to Rav, as Rashbam wrote. Samuel was called "Arioch" <note>The Long/Tall One</note> because the law follows him in civil matters, for "the law of the kingdom is the law." Alternatively, it is because it is written "Arioch king of Ellasar"—meaning Samuel was like a king in all matters except for ritual prohibitions, where the law does not follow him. So it is written in *Halichot Olam*.

# Every
**Rav Yehuda** mentioned anonymously is **Rav Yehuda son of Rav Ezekiel**. Every **Rav Pappa** <note>or "Abaye"</note> mentioned anonymously is **Rav bar Nachmani**. <note>He was called "Nachmani" because his father's name was Rav Nachmani. Out of respect for his father, he did not use the name directly but used the nickname **Abaye**. Some say his father died and he was raised by Rabbah bar Nachmani, who gave him his father's name. This is alluded to in the verse "For in You the fatherless find mercy" (Yatom = Abaye in shorthand). Rashi says some used the name Nachmani as a slur, meaning he was merely a student of Rav Nachman</note>.

<insert>
Rashi in the chapter *Ha-Maniach* (end of page 30) wrote: "S.G.S." <note>Sages of the Great Synagogue?</note>... and Rashi on page 67...
</insert>

# And Rav
**Nachman** mentioned anonymously is **Rav Nachman bar Isaac** according to Rashi in *Gittin* (page 31). However, others hold he is **Rav Nachman bar Yaakov**; see the Tosafot there and in chapter "He who was taken out" (page 43) and in "Possession of Houses" (page 46).

<summary>This page provides a comprehensive guide to identifying anonymous figures in the Mishnah and Talmud and details the unique intellectual profiles of legendary sages like Akiva and Meir. It also clarifies the transition of authority from the Tannaim to the Babylonian masters, Rav and Samuel.</summary>

<header>The Oral Torah</header>

## The Small One
Rabbi Zeira was known as a sharp and diligent scholar. He was called "Katina" <note>original: קטינא; meaning "the small" or "short" one</note> because he used to test himself in a fiery furnace to see if the fire of Gehenna <note>the place of spiritual purification or "hell" in Jewish tradition</note> had any power over him. One day, the eyes of the Sages [were upon him and he was singed]. He was called "The Small One" because Rabbi Zeira was a man of short stature. This account appears in the Talmudic tractate *Bava Metzia*, in the chapter "He Who Hires Laborers."

## Those
These are the <term>Amoraim</term> <note>Sages of the Talmudic era, roughly 200–500 CE</note> who shared the same name. There were two named Rav Yitzchak bar Abumi: one was the teacher of Rav, and the other lived in the time of Rava, as noted in the *Tosafot* <note>medieval commentaries</note> at the beginning of... There were two named Rav Hamnuna, and two named Rav Ashi—one of whom was a colleague of Rav Kahana. There were also two named Rav Chanina, as appears in *Tosafot* in the first chapter of *Gittin*, page 91. There were two named Rav Chisda and two named Rav Yermiyah, one of whom lived in the days of Shmuel. There were two named Rav Huna: Rav Huna bar Chinana and Rav Huna bar Yehuda, as mentioned in *Tosafot* on page 21. There was also a Rabbi Shimon ben... who was a student of Rav, while another was a colleague of Rav Chisda, mentioned in the chapter *Hadar* on page 63. There were two named Rav Ada bar Ahavah: one was a colleague of Rav and Shmuel, and the other was a student of Rava, as written in... the chapter on the Order of Fasts. There were two named Rav Papa: one in the days of Rav Ashi and one in the days of Rav Chisda, according to *Tosafot* in *Yevamot*, page 21. There was a Rabbi Shimon ben... who was the teacher of Rabbi Yochanan. There were two named Rabina, as written by the *Rosh* <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note> in the chapter "These are Forbidden." There was also Rav Kahana the first, a student-colleague of Rav. Rav K... of Mishalshala was a student of Rava and lived in the time of Rav Ashi. The <term>Mahariq</term> <note>Rabbi Joseph Colon, a 15th-century scholar</note> wrote in his rules of the Talmud that when students mention their teacher's teacher in his presence, they do not say... "The teacher said such and such," but rather "Your colleagues said such and such," as found in the first chapter of *Rosh Hashanah*.

## General Rule of the Later Ones
The <term>Savoraim</term> <note>Sages who lived immediately after the Talmud was sealed, roughly 500–600 CE</note> are discussed in the book *Halichot Olam* <note>original: הליכות עולם; "The Ways of the World," a manual on Talmudic methodology</note>. After the Talmud was sealed, nothing may be added to it and nothing may be subtracted from it. However, the Savoraim who arose afterward added some small additions, as is accepted from the tradition of the <term>Geonim</term> <note>Leaders of the Babylonian academies, roughly 600–1000 CE</note>. For example, at the beginning of tractate *Kiddushin*... "his wife," this was from their tradition and logical reasoning. He also wrote in *Halichot Olam* regarding the explanation of Rav Ashi in the chapter "The One Who Withdraws" and Rabbi Abbahu in the chapter "One Does Not Place..." that the style of the language is not found elsewhere in the compositions of the Amoraim Rabina and Rav Ashi. Some say that these Rabbis—Rav Achai and Rabbi Abbahu—were not Amoraim but were among the Savoraim who added small additions to the Talmud at the beginning of *Kiddushin*.

## Everyone
"Everyone who reads it—why does he read it?" <note>original: כל דקארי לה מאי קארי לה; a common Talmudic question asking why a person would even suggest a certain difficult point</note> Some say this phrase is from the additions of the Savoraim. The meaning of this phrase is: what was on his mind to ask this difficulty? Did he not know or see that the difficulty is nothing? This is explained in tractate *Ketubot* and the chapter "These are Standing." The Mahariq discussed this in his rules of the Talmud but did not explain the literal meaning of these words. In the *Aruch* <note>an 11th-century Talmudic dictionary</note>, I found that the word for "read" <note>original: קארי; *kari*</note> is a language of mixing, and "to him" <note>original: לה; *leh*</note> is interchangeable with "eye." Therefore, the meaning is: now that he has mixed this with that, what did he see to mix them? That is to say, what connection do they have to one another that he saw fit to bind them and ask a difficulty from one to the other, when there is a clear distinction between them? Others say *kari* is like *ka’ari*, a term for pouring out.

## General Rule of Rashi
The Mahariq, in his rules of the Talmud, states: The path we follow in guarding the words of Rashi <note>the preeminent 11th-century commentator</note> is learned from the Talmud itself. For the Talmud often asks "It is obvious!" and answers "What you might have said is such and such, therefore it comes to teach us [this]." Then it asks again, "But why is it so?" and answers. Rashi's path is to always strive to provide the necessity and the distinction for everything explained. One should ask why he used a specific word or phrase. These words are meant to exclude the opinion of another, or to resolve some pressure or difficulty in the text. You must be careful to narrow down his language and interpret it in a way that no word remains redundant. If he could have stated his intention in three words, why would he say four? You should do the same with the language of the Mishnah and the Gemara <note>the two components of the Talmud</note>, meaning that one must be precise with their language so that nothing is redundant. They did not speak at length without purpose. Everything he wrote is based on the logic of the Sages, intended to be inclusive of many matters in few words, so that their words are "small in quantity but great in quality," and not even one letter is extra. As it is said: "A person should always teach his student in a concise way." He further wrote that it was Rashi’s custom and his school's way not to utter a single word for its own sake without necessity—meaning, when he speaks regarding the language of the Gemara because it is obscure or hidden in the depths of wisdom, or when you find a difficulty or a linguistic correction. My custom is to state the Mishnah, or the statement of the Gemara, or the *Braitā* <note>a tradition from the time of the Mishnah not included in the Mishnah itself</note>, and to explain the verse at the end, leaving the verses to correspond to... And to say "the Gemara asks," and it is also his way to sometimes state a premise upon which a *Braitā* is based... But in the end, it is nullified. Therefore, when Rashi says "it comes to teach us" or "you might have thought" <note>original: קס"ד; *ka-salka da'atakh*</note>, you must examine the necessity of this thought—if it was possible to say that statement and ask from it, or not. If it was nullified, why say "you might have thought"? In truth, that assumption or premise upon which the Mishnah questioned was correct according to the conclusion. But if it were possible to explain it as such, even if with effort... according to his opinion, he would not say "you might have thought." Keep this rule of his custom: he explains the matter first, and afterward returns to fix the language and settle it according to the context. Delve into this and you will find it.

## If
If you wish to truly understand Rashi, go and study the four teachers who explained Rashi's words on the Torah and clarified what he corrected with every word. In the Gemara, look to the *Tur HaMizrachi* <note>a commentary</note> to settle the words of those who disagree with Rashi, such as the Ramban <note>Nachmanides</note>. It is proper to do the same for Rashi in the Gemara—to settle the challenges the authors of the *Tosafot* raise against him. It is helpful for this to read the commentary of the Ran <note>Rabbi Nissim of Gerona</note>, the *Sefer HaMaor*, and the *Sefer Milchamot Hashem*. One who delves into the deep legal debates and other decisors will find Rashi's words clarified. A wise man will hear and increase his learning, becoming one who understands from his own knowledge; for the one who teaches a law, the law follows him.

## Now
Now I will write some rules regarding the expressions of Rashi that are commonly used, as cited by Rabbi Joseph Colon in Response 100. There is a difficulty regarding what we find in the chapter "Presumptive Ownership," where it discusses lashes, stoning, and burning based on <term>Chazakah</term> <note>legal presumption based on established status</note>. Why did the Gemara not combine them and say "Lashes, stoning, and burning are administered based on presumption"? The answer is that... burning does not deal with the same level of evidence; for lashes, which are not as severe, a minimal presumption is sufficient. But for capital laws, which are severe, we require a presumption that has... and a "stirring of the matter." The Rabbi [Mahariq] was alerted to this by what Rashi explained there: "Lashes are based on presumption—on something that we presume to be true and witnesses have seen." And regarding "burning, as he goes on to explain" <note>original: כדמפרש ואזיל; *ke-dimfaresh ve-azil*</note>. What did Rashi innovate here more than the Gemara itself? Especially since he himself explained the matter of presumption. Rather, he intended to say that for lashes, even if there is no testimony at all or a "stirring of the matter" <note>an action that corroborates the status</note>, it is sufficient. But for stoning and burning, that level of presumption is not effective, except "as he goes on to explain" in the Gemara—meaning a "stirring" like that which we say in the Gemara nearby regarding a boy and girl, or a man and woman, who grew up in a house under the presumption of being husband and wife... because of "coming upon his mother," etc. Thus we have learned from the words of Mahariq one rule in Rashi's words: when he says "as he goes on to explain." Furthermore, Rabbi Joseph wrote fifty ways regarding what he received from his teachers concerning Rashi's intention when he says "as he goes on to explain." This phrase in Rashi indicates that nothing new was innovated in that matter, but rather that the Amora or the author of the Gemara did not come to innovate, but since he mentioned it, he explains and proceeds in the way of expanding the explanation, not by way of innovation. And this is the language of... When it says in the Gemara "he explains as he goes on," the author of the <term>Okimta</term> <note>a contextual limitation or specific application of a law</note> himself is explaining. All this is when Rashi... the Okimta. But when he says "as he goes on to explain," it is the opposite: the author of the Okimta himself is explaining as he goes. All this is when Rashi mentioned the author of the Okimta or the author of the Gemara and was forced to say which of the two... The third path is that he wanted to say that in that whole Okimta, he had it in his mind at the end, and it was not innovated because of the difficulty that his opponent asked; rather, the custom is to be brief at first, and the author of the Okimta explains his original intention... because of a difficulty. For what occurred to the author of the Okimta at first that he did not see the difficulty standing against him?

## Further
I found in the aforementioned book: when Rashi says "and he explained" or "and he answered," several paths are stated. Some say they saw and... and wanted to say that there is... his method works well for the question the Gemara asks or the answer it gives. I was also forced to explain it this way, for according to the explanation of the Tosafot or an explanation you could provide from the outside, it is difficult... to the contrary. And what Rashi explained is as if he said, "even though I have a difficulty, this is possible," or "he answers and it can be settled such and such." Everything is according to the nature of the discussion and the matter. For the first path, there is support from the chapter "The Sinew that Displaced" on page 94, where we say in the Gemara...

<header>Ten Praises</header>

The proof is that "the end of the deed was first in thought" <note>original: סוף המעשה במחשבה תחלה; a philosophical maxim suggesting that the final result of an action is the original goal intended by the mind</note>. This is the general principle: build a house for Him and they shall call upon His Name, it shall rise. If only we knew! This is exactly what Rabbi Akiva meant by saying, "I am afraid," meaning: let not my own memory be the focus of this matter, but rather let it lead to merit. Why was the "Complete Name" <note>The combination of the names Y-H-V-H and Elohim</note> not mentioned in the Torah in the context of the peaceful oversight? These matters are forged in vessels of steel. According to those who explain the literal meaning, this is not merely a hint, but a proof of blessing regarding the secret of the Sanctification of the Name <note>term: Kiddush HaShem (Sanctification of the Name); the act of martyrdom or living ethically to bring honor to God</note>. 

Regarding Abraham and Daniel: Daniel was mentioned in the pit of lions <note>Daniel 6</note> as sanctifying the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, yet it was not written so of Abraham [regarding the furnace of Ur Kasdim]. This was so that future generations would not learn a specific order from Abraham and bring themselves into danger, for Abraham brought himself into that situation <note>According to Midrash, Abraham chose to be thrown into a furnace rather than worship idols</note>. It is forbidden for future generations to actively seek such a thing. However, Daniel was forced into the situation by others, and his story was recorded to teach that if such a thing happens to someone, they should indeed act to sanctify the Name. It is also asked: since Abraham’s act of circumcision was performed within his own initiative, why was it necessary? It was to publicize the true faith in the world among the created beings, for at that time, the Master of the Universe was not yet known or publicized.

## This is the language of

The *Pardes* <note>referring to *Pardes Rimmonim* (The Orchard of Pomegranates) by the 16th-century Kabbalist Rabbi Moshe Cordovero</note>, Gate 1, Chapter 9: In the verse "Hear O Israel," the existence of God is included, which is the letter *Yod*. Furthermore, He watches over His creation, and this is "Our God" (*Eloheinu*). Even individual providence <note>term: Hashgacha Pratit; the belief that God intervenes in the lives of specific individuals</note> is the meaning of "Our God," for He is the vitality of existence necessitated by the whole world. He was, He is, and He will be, and He brings all existences into being—this is the meaning of the Name of four letters <note>The Tetragrammaton, Y-H-V-H</note> as it is written. Though He is the Master of all worlds, upper and lower—which is the meaning of how we pronounce His Name as "Lord" (*Adonai*)—from this comes the necessity that His providence encompasses the entire world.

Nevertheless, "Our God" means He watches over us specifically. "The Lord is One" necessitates His unity, etc. (thus far his words). Therefore, I have arranged the writing of the first Name of God as "The One Who Exists." The writing regarding His unity and the removal of any physical form—for nothing in His Name is other than Truth—and that He is primordial and eternal, is hinted at in the Name of Being (*Havayah*), for He brings all into being and will exist after all. In the name *Eloheinu* (Our God), I have arranged Divine Providence. Because of this, it is proper to pray to Him alone, for He is the One who watches, blessed be He. From the greatness of this providence comes prophecy, particularly the prophecy of Moses our teacher, the "man of God," who gave the Torah of truth through his hand via the attribute of *Gevurah* <note>Strength or Judgment</note>, as it is said, "And God spoke all these words, saying." This represents eternity. In the second Name (Y-H-V-H) is the attribute of reward and punishment: "I am the Lord, faithful to pay reward," as Rashi explains on the portion *Va'era*. At the time of the redemption of the Messiah and the Resurrection of the Dead, delight and reward will be revealed.

# Wisdom, Knowledge, and Understanding in the Gate of Examination

**Examine** the wisdom of the Creator’s creation and your thoughts will rise to their meaning. "See who created these" <note>Isaiah 40:26</note>: the unfolding of the worlds and the levels—the Throne of Glory, the Seraphim, the *Chayot* <note>holy living creatures</note>, the *Ophanim* <note>angelic wheels</note>, the heavenly hosts, the elements, the inanimate, the plants, the animals, and the living human who shall praise Him forever. Contemplate the signs of wisdom seen in the human species. The speaker, who with the speech of his tongue rises above all else. Understand and prepare the totality of the structure, which stands by weight and measure; nothing of it changes. The Earth is in the center, and there the celestial sphere is joined. The waters surround the earth and the air is close to them, with fire placed above them all. And the great sea—though its waves roar and its winds rage—it does not cross its boundary by a single step.

Contemplate the earth, which is dead matter, yet through the rain it moves and performs wonders, arranged with the special properties of diverse herbs and plants, and fruits emerging from it. Observe the paths of the cattle, wild beasts, birds, swarming things, and fish, according to their kinds, their temperaments, their qualities, their wars, and their sustenance. Let us contemplate the wisdom, the crafts, and the actions which the Name, may He be blessed, prepared for man; happy is he who performs them and occupies himself with them. Let us understand the formation of man in his mother’s womb, his birth, his upbringing, the joining of his body and the powers of his soul, the light of the intellect and its order, and the differences in people in their deaths and their lives. Everything is beautiful in its time: cold and heat, life and what is most necessary—sustenance, air more than water, water more than food, etc. All that He has made and does is "very good," even if sometimes something appears bad in the eyes of men. My soul shall praise You as I realize that "how manifold are Your works, O Lord, in wisdom You have made them all," for "I see Your heavens, the work of Your fingers." Who can reach the point of recounting even one of a thousand thousand thousands and myriads of myriads of the greatness of Your levels and the height of the hiddenness of Your deeds? And who can reach the knowledge of one of a thousand thousand thousands of the hidden secrets concealed in Your creations? How much more so the inability to grasp even a tiny portion of the Holy One, blessed be He—one part in a thousand thousand thousands of Your emanations, for You are unique and there is no second to be unified with them, and they are as one with Your unity.

# Higher Than the High, Coming Through the Gate of Divine Service

**To serve** the holy service: serve the Lord by being humble before Him, running to His service and His commandments in all that He commanded. The definition of service to Him, may He be blessed, is to submit because of all the goodness of His existence, until the time his intellect is prepared by His great kindness, without any prior goodness [on the person's part]. If there is an obligation of service to a human being who does good—even if that goodness is accidental—how much more so to the Divine Presence <note>term: Shekhinah</note> who has done good, does good, and has rewarded and will reward him. Serve the Lord with joy by contemplating His great kindnesses—how He lifted us from the dunghills and brought us close to His service and His Torah, for He desires kindness for the Children of Israel. Concerning them, the Lord our God said: "Blessed be He who created us for His glory and separated us from those who stray, and gave us the Torah of truth, and planted eternal life within us." He chose us from all the nations, loved us, and found favor in us, and raised us above every tongue and sanctified us, and His great and holy Name He called upon us. "And you shall serve the Lord your God" with joy and a good heart when one serves the kindnesses of the Lord for all the good He has bestowed upon us. "The Lord your God you shall fear, and Him you shall serve" with the service of a faithful servant—by day and by night, at every time, every hour, and every moment. In action, in speech, and in thought; in the hidden places of the heart and its secrets. With awakening and a new *protanma* <note>note: Likely a transliteration of a technical term, perhaps related to 'prothymia' (Greek for readiness/zeal)</note>, with the flaming of the heart, and not like a person who is forced, but like a lion-hearted hero, desiring His commandments for their own sake. Even without action, merit rises when observing a prohibitive commandment; your soul should long to say: "I desire [to do this], but what can I do, for my Father in Heaven has decreed against me." For "the Merciful One desires the heart" <note>original: רחמנא לבא בעי; a famous Talmudic principle that God values sincere intention</note> and the Lord searches all hearts. "And you shall serve the Lord your God with all your heart." Pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord. Remove yourselves far from "commandments of men learned by rote" <note>Isaiah 29:13; referring to empty, habitual ritual</note> and from the vessels of a heart without understanding. Let every command and every warning be in your eyes as if it were commanded just now, today or yesterday.

**The path** of the righteous is to serve the Lord by increasing their submission and service in proportion to the goodness the Creator increases for them. The proof is from the actions of Shimon: if I possess ten, I set aside one; if I possess a hundred, I set aside ten. But if he has nine and a half, he shall be punished according to his ability and obligation. One who does not have the means is exempt from the obligation of [the wealth-based parts of] circumcision, the obligation of the Festival, and from the Torah—for the commandment depends on ability, and obligation follows ability. Therefore, we are obligated to contemplate the general goodness, the specific goodness of our nation, the specific goodness of our family, and the goodness of the individual person, to make known His love, His Torah, and His affection. We shall walk the King's Highway; we shall not turn right or left. We shall be His servants to praise the Lord for He is good, for we alone acknowledge Him, as Jacob our father said: "I am unworthy of all the mercies." Furthermore, "happy is the man who fears" <note>Psalm 112:1</note> when the goodness of the Most High emerges, so that he does not follow the way of the wicked, to whom He "repays his enemies to their face to destroy them," losing both this world and the World to Come. Serve for nothing—not for the sake of receiving a reward, and not out of fear of punishment. Accept both the good and the bad with either joy or trembling. The Creator who created you thinks of you and knows what is good for you; therefore, for every measure that He metes out to you, be thankful. Accept suffering with love and joy, and increase the beauty of your service. Once, people saw a pious man who was afflicted and they mocked him. He said to them: "I pity you for the [affliction] on your legs." They said to him: "I hold it as a goodness from my Creator that He did not put it in my eyes, and He gave me the Torah." "And you shall walk in His ways"—in all your ways, know Him. Let there be no movement of yours except for His glory: not seeing, not hearing, not walking, not standing, not sitting, not thinking, not acting, and not even a hint, except to serve Him. You shall desire nothing but His will, seek nothing but His desire, rejoice only in His service, and find no contentment without Him. The summary of the matter: do not move foot or hand, or move an eyelid, or open your mouth, or think thoughts, except for the Lord alone. My soul, sink to the dust and submit before

# Ten Praises
## Chapter
### Ten Praises with the help of the Cause of all Causes <note>original: עילת כל העילת; a philosophical term for God as the primary source of all existence</note> of the Worlds

## Is my hand too short? With the help of the Blessed Name.
->Holy books based on moral rebuke and the instruction of sinners in the way of God.<-
->Their words are like pearls strung together with additions; the majority of their structure and form<-
is from the paths of the pious Rabbi, the author of the *Duties of the Heart* <note>Rabbi Bahya ibn Paquda, an 11th-century philosopher</note>, may his memory be a blessing. I have arranged his "gates" <note>chapters</note> here: "This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it" <note>Psalm 118:20</note>. And "Who is the man who desires life" <note>Psalm 34:13</note> in these high days?
Let him meditate with heart and tongue on the First Gate day by day, and let him repeat it forever; then he will merit the "world that is entirely long" <note>term: the World to Come (Olam Ha-Ba); a state of eternal spiritual existence</note>, for remembrance leads to action.
May your God be with you in everything you do.

## The Gate of Unity: The Lord is our God, the Lord is One

**Unity** of the Name in heart, tongue, and knowledge: This is a demonstrative knowledge <note>logical proof</note> in addition to the tradition received from prophecy. Make Him King above and below and among all creatures. 
Extraneous thoughts should not be found or seen. The foundation of Unity hints at the union of the Ten Sefirot <note>term: Sefirot; the ten divine attributes or emanations in Kabbalah</note>, in which the purified thoughts roam.
Even the common person, who has never seen the spiritual lights, should at the very least keep the essentials of the faith—amounting to the number "One" <note>The Hebrew word for 'One' (Echad) has a numerical value of 13, corresponding to the 13 principles of faith listed below</note>—guarded in their intention.

**Existence** — "Hear O Israel, the Lord" is the Necessary Existence; He was, He is, and He will be.
**Unity** — One, individual, and unique; the True One. There is no image or likeness to His unity.
**Rejection of Corporeality** — He is not a body, nor a power within any body or physical form.
**Primordial and Eternal** — He is the first and the last of every living thing.
**Praying to Him Alone** — He hears the prayer of those who come to Him. All flesh shall come to serve Him and no other, even though the high angels of the Blessed Name act as intercessors for Him.
**Providence** — For He is our God and He watches over us; He does not withhold His influence.
**Prophecy** — Not only this, but He also bestows the heart of His prophecy for salvation.
**The Prophecy of Moses** — Moses, the servant of the Lord and man of God; none like him has arisen or will ever arise.
**Torah from Heaven** — The Torah of truth from the mouth of the Almighty. He gave it as an inheritance from the heavens to uphold good, upright, and pleasant judgments.
They are more desirable than gold and much fine gold, and they are sweet.
**Immutability** — Forever the God will not change or exchange His religion, for He is Truth and so is His Torah, which He gave to the people of His pasture.
**Do Not Add or Subtract** — It is a statute for His people Jacob, the lot of His inheritance.
**Reward and Punishment** — May His Name be faithful to pay reward to the righteous according to their righteousness, and to give the wicked evil according to their wickedness.
**Messiah** — May He hasten and speed our righteous Messiah in his time, and then he shall judge with the judgment of absolute truth.

## Resurrection of the Dead
The dead shall live, and many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awaken and sing together to the God who is Great, Mighty, and Awesome.
Listen and hear the voice of the *Shema* <note>The central Jewish prayer: "Hear O Israel..."</note> with all its wisdom, to separate between the joined letters and to be precise with its letters in awe, fear, trembling, and sweat. Remember the "Twenty-four" <note>The 24 books of the Bible, or perhaps the 24 words of the Shema paragraphs</note> in it.
One should repeat the *Shema* of the morning and evening to read it with intention. Look and see, let go of other things and "count the stars" <note>Genesis 15:5</note> to see if night has arrived to read it.
Complete the entire prayer, even the praises. It is good that the congregation delays, so that you may read the entire *Shema* before the sun rises <note>literally: before the dawn has gone up</note>. Do not rely on those two times <note>presumably the communal prayer times</note> when the members of the community read. "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you?" At the time of accepting the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven, you should be prepared to surrender your soul for the holiness of God.
And be willing to meditate on the word *Shema* <note>Hebrew: שמע</note> and *Echad* <note>Hebrew: אחד</note>. The acronym <note>The text suggests a mystical acronym linking letters of the Shema to biblical figures</note> refers to Mishael, Azaryah, Hananyah, and Daniel. This surrender is considered a sacrifice, like Isaac at his binding;
the ram was his substitute. This is on condition that you are not "flawed" at the time of your self-offering by any defect or blemish, for a blemish is not acceptable to Him. But everything written in the Book of the Torah
is found there, and then you shall find favor in the eyes of the Lord.

---

Chapter 103

The matter of "giving one's soul" <note>term: Mesirat Nefesh; the act of self-sacrifice or martyrdom</note> is as follows: one should meditate on the pain of the severe forms of death and resolve to suffer them for the sake of the Unique One of the world. One should think to oneself: "My nature
is ultimately physical"—meaning, think that in these moments, though his brain and body are torn, in the end, he prevails and suffers. At all times he should strengthen their hearts and subvert all physical matters
like stoning. He prevails like one who dips <unclear>before the sprinklings</unclear>. It is possible that this is what Rabbi Akiva meant in the Gemara <note>The Talmud, tractate Berakhot 61b</note>: "All my days I was troubled by this verse, and now that it has come to my hand, shall I not fulfill it?" That is to say: "All my days
I prepared my nature for this; I was prepared to suffer the pain of the body for my Beloved." He meant: "I will not merely fulfill it now, for I have already stripped away my physical nature." To this the verse also hints: "For
your sake we are killed all day long, we are considered as sheep for the slaughter" <note>Psalm 44:23</note>. Every single day we are ready to surrender ourselves, and we have merited to die and to suffer the pain of the severe deaths. <unclear>From me to the matter... it is written...</unclear>
The end of all our meditation is not merely our resolve, but to actually work to <unclear>strip away the physical nature...</unclear> and to fulfill the order of the heart...
nothing is missing from the matter of surrendering the soul. In the end, this is not something superficial... but from the depth of the heart... and this is the order of those who surrender their lives...
with me, and let it be so. That is to say, even if they were to throw <unclear>boiling water</unclear> upon him, or if he held a cup in his hand without spilling, or if they were to scrape his flesh with <unclear>iron combs</unclear>... he would be able to withstand it for the sake of the One...

# Ten Praises

**Give** <note>original: "הת'"—likely an abbreviation for 'Give' or 'Submit'</note> and humble yourself in His kingdom; fear always, lest you fall short in His service. Let your transgressions, iniquities, and sins be a memorial before you, and let them seem many in your eyes... compared to what is truly due to Him. Let your own deeds be despised in your sight compared to your obligations. Contemplate His greatness and give thanks in your constant smallness. Always set Him before you... so that you may gladden your Master, for He sees you. **Bless** the Lord and praise and laud Him always, day and night, with your mouth and your heart, in secret and in the open. Always [seek] Him... and to be written in the book of forgiveness and pardon. Pray always before Him that He may put it in your heart to understand, to hear, to learn, to teach, to keep, and to perform the [Torah]...

**Since** prayer is the "service of the heart," let us be awakened to the matter of the Gate of Heaven, which is the primary thing. Before you pray... consider His great [mercy] in how He conducts Himself with His creatures—that He does not despise the prayer of the community. Before you pour out your heart, ensure your heart is ready before the words leave your [mouth]... consider their meaning. When you mention the Divine Name, be filled with trembling, quaking, and terror.

**May the wise man hear** and increase his learning regarding the inner mystical intentions <note>original: "kavanot," referring to focused spiritual intent</note>, for from them a crown is made for the head of the Lord of Hosts. The pious and men of deed used to [meditate]... and focus their intentions in prayer until they reached a state of "divesting from physicality" <note>original: "hitpashtut hagashmiyut"—a meditative state where one loses awareness of the physical body</note> and the strengthening of the intellect, approaching the level of angels... speaking with clear speech. For even a single [error] could "destroy the world"; therefore, see that you do not fall into error. Be precise with every single word and move your lips... in speech so that you do not err, as if you were counting coins.

---

->From His place, He shall turn with mercy toward those who enter the Gate of Trust<-

**Happy** is the man who places his trust in the Lord. Cursed is the man who trusts in humans and makes flesh his strength, turning away from God. The cause of trust is that the Creator of all [has mercy]... over His creatures, knows their many needs, and always watches over the entire world in His goodness and wisdom. He [the believer] remains in tranquility and rest from our worries... even regarding the evil that reaches him, his heart is firm, for he [knows] his merits and that it comes from the kindness of God. But the one who lacks trust, who rules in the world [only by his own wit], does so because they do not sense... the Divine decree in its quantity, quality, time, or place. One cannot increase what has been decreed as small, nor diminish what has been decreed as great.

**If** so, why does a person receive what the Creator decreed for him with a sour and resentful face? Why let his mouth speak [against it]? I have been [diligent], I have left over the incense <note>a reference to meticulous ritual service</note>, yet I am deprived of reward... if he chooses an evil path, God will not grant him mastery over it. Is it possible that he would be conquered by his own guilt and surrender to the greatest of his enemies? [Instead], let him clothe himself in the straight path and weep to the Lord. Let him be [diligent] with his tasks... in his work according to his strength. Whatever work their hand finds to do, let them do it, but let them trust in [God]... the good which comes from Him, may He be blessed. Through the medium of work, one "wears" the means by which sustenance or healing is found; these are merely His messengers... Why then should a person flatter others? Let him realize that he is the one providing for others [through God's will], and he should not be haughty, nor shamed, nor embarrassed.

<margin>
One should trust [God] in matters of the body, sustenance, his end, the affairs of his wife and children, and their peace and welfare, for everything is from Him. Do not trust in your own good deeds alone; even the penitent and the convert who comes to be purified should trust that the Holy One, Blessed be He, will assist him.
</margin>
**Blessed** is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his trust. Those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good. He who trusts in the Lord, kindness shall surround him. In your conduct, ensure your mind is... free and strong to fulfill what the Creator has commanded you. For a strong [will] [overcomes] the hypocrite. As it is said: "Make His will your will, so that He may make your will His will."

<margin>
He is the Living God and His goodness never ends. He [created] the human inclination and it shall not be defeated. He who trusts in his wealth shall fall, for in the middle of his days it will leave him. In the end, he will trust in a spider's web... and the toil of his body. Why weary your eyes on [wealth] when it is gone? Trust in the Lord and do good, dwell in the land and cherish faithfulness in business, for this is [proper] for a man...
</margin>
**Blessed** be the Lord day by day. Let us be built up as a bundle [of life] and let us not say "What shall we eat tomorrow?" He who hoards <note>original: "Ba'al mashkonot"—literally 'master of pledges/mortgages,' referring to an obsessive accumulator</note>—detest him and utterly abhor him. Trust in the Lord, for He will not [fail you]...

<margin>
Do not wrong others; it is a good trait to be generous with money toward one's neighbor, going "beyond the letter of the law" so as not to enter into a quarrel quickly. Included in the faithfulness of deposits is that a person should not use his money except for [proper] returns, for money is a deposit given to us by Him, may He be blessed, and we have no permission... to use it more than what is needed for charity and kindness, God forbid.
</margin>
**Straight** shall your path be; pursue justice. Let your "yes" be just and your "no" be just. Do not be among those who lack faith. When you sell anything to your neighbor or buy from...

<margin>
And to give drink to the thirsty, to clothe the naked, to bring poor brides to the wedding canopy, and to lend to the poor in his time of distress. Welcoming guests and [hospitality]... is a great commandment above all. Tithe the tenth <note>The practice of Ma'aser (giving 10%)</note> from what comes into your hand, whether money or the equivalent of money—the first time from the principal, and thereafter from the profit. You shall become wealthy, and the Lord will bless you in your possessions. Say to yourself: "God gave me the strength to make this wealth," and you are His messenger to distribute it to His poor and His loved ones. Give to Him from His own, for you and yours are His.
</margin>
**Friend**, open your hand wide to spend [on charity]... for the poor, to give and to return and to give every single day with a pleasant countenance, according to the deficiency of what he lacks, to feed...

---

## We Shall Hear and We Shall Do: The Gate of Sincerity of Action

<margin>
"The hidden things belong to the Lord our God." He searches the heart and examines the kidneys <note>An idiom for the innermost thoughts and emotions</note>. His eyes are open to the ways of men. A hypocrite remains a hypocrite in his heart. The Lord seeks every inclination... the hypocrite is similar to an idol worshipper, for he serves his own ego (the "foreign god"). He is diminished in value; for the idol worshipper, his atonement is well-known, but the hypocrite is hidden and [full of] pains. Furthermore, the idol worshipper serves something that does not rebel against God, but the flatterer/hypocrite serves a rebel [himself] and is not [sincere]. Also, the idol worshipper serves one thing, but the hypocrite has no end to his masters and the darkness of the multitudes.
</margin>
**For to the Lord**—is this not [the goal]? To destroy hypocrisy. One who dedicates his deeds to God alone, without turning to the sight of people so that they might honor or praise him, or for any other reasons...

<margin>
Day and night, as the pious man said: when meeting people returning from a fierce war with spoils, he said to them: "You have returned from the 'Small War' [physical battle]; prepare yourselves for the 'Great War' [the internal struggle against the ego]." If you give the enemy a place even once, he will not leave you until he destroys you from this world and the world to come. He will make you a terror a hundred times over and lie in wait for you all your days. Therefore, do not trust in yourself until the day of your death. Go out and fight him always, and conduct the war with clever stratagem.
</margin>
**Who among the holy ones** shall turn before the Lord always? He shall fight the war of the Lord against the "foreign god"—the great enemy, the [Evil] Inclination, the king who rules over your external and internal self...

<margin>
He argues with false proofs, even doubting the creation of the world, making victories and ancient philosophies seem sweet and beautiful to you. If you seek counsel... he will try to distance this knowledge from you with "great and powerful proofs." When he despairs of this, he will make you doubt the Oral Torah, returning to your neighborhood and [misinterpreting] the scriptures. But "if a matter is hidden from you," do not deviate... for the Written Torah and the Oral Torah are twins.
</margin>
**And this is the impurity for you**: at first, he comes to make you doubt the questions of the soul, saying, "Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die," and he makes [the truth] seem false to you...

<margin>
If the spirit of [God] is pleased with you, strive also to be acceptable to His creatures, as the Sages said: "Anyone with whom the spirit of creatures is pleased, [the spirit of God is pleased]." If you ask, "What use is the favor of a weakling like me? I cannot even please the people of my generation!" Your proof from the Sages is not according to your [own] will; rather, it is as it says: "When the Lord desires a man's ways [He makes even his enemies at peace with him]." It is a sign: if creatures praise your character, it is because the Omnipresent loves you.
</margin>
**And you shall lack** even from them; or the hypocrite will strive for his sustenance and say, "I do not care for your faith or your spirit..."

### Preface

The copyist says: While I was in Spain, I discovered in a certain tower this book composed by the wise Rabbi Solomon ibn Gabirol <note>original: "שלמה בן גבירול"; an 11th-century Sephardic philosopher and poet, known in the Latin world as Avicebron.</note>, may his memory be a blessing. It was written entirely in Arabic. I made great efforts to acquire this precious volume so that it might serve as a guide <note>literally "as eyes"</note> for all who seek wisdom.

These are the names of the ten chapters concerning the <term>Middot<note>Hebrew for "measures" or "qualities," referring here to character traits or moral virtues and vices.</note></term>:
First: Pride and Lowliness; Second: Boldness and Shame; Third: Humility and Rebellion; Fourth: Joy and Anxiety; Fifth: Mercy and Cruelty. <note>The author lists five pairs of opposing traits, totaling the ten chapters mentioned.</note>

I have written concerning them various explanations, as well as some of what the sages of ethics have written regarding these qualities, so that they might be remembered by every person—to know the good and upright paths in which to walk, and the evil paths from which to distance oneself. All of this is introduced by verses from the Torah and the Holy Scriptures. This work is by Rabbi Solomon ibn Gabirol, may his memory be a blessing, who is called:

# Introduction by the Eminent Son of the Author, Pillar of the Torah

To determine their proper practice, I have seen and concluded that it is right for his memory to be set before us as a memorial. Regarding the matter of the "strong will" <note>This refers to a specific legal determination regarding the sequence of rituals</note> as the author explained. The Sage Rav Papa divided the practice for the house of Rav Huna; this is what we see regarding the oil and the spices. Rav Papa first blessed the oil for the sake of removing grease, and afterward, he prepared the spices. One said to him: "Does the Master not agree with the ruling of the House of Hillel in our teaching?" He replied: "This is what Rabbah said: the House of Hillel followed the House of Shammai in this case, and there was no need to search for additional stringencies." It is simple to understand that he acted and explained that "oil and spices at the end of a meal are for different purposes: the oil is to rub on the hands to remove the filth of the food, and the spices are for the scent." Since the scent and the enjoyment come together, they require a blessing. He did not follow Rabbah’s view to act like the House of Shammai except at the end, because he had erred and turned his mind away. Behold, Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair says one blesses over the oil and exempts the spices, whereas the Sages say one blesses over the spices and exempts the oil. Rabbi Yonah wrote that the blessing follows the teaching. And the Rif <term>Rabbi Isaac Alfasi, a major 11th-century legal authority</term> and the Rosh <term>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, a 13th-century German-Spanish scholar</term> both conclude that the blessings are not equal in status. The Rosh remained in doubt regarding the exact wording of the blessing at the end of the meal, but it seems logical that the House of Hillel's ruling stands. The Tosafot <term>medieval French and German commentators on the Talmud</term> in the chapter "He who was eating" (page 107) regarding the "third determination" write as follows: "That which was taught in the chapter 'How do we bless'—the House of Shammai says one blesses the oil and then the spices, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the House of Hillel decided the oil is for its scent and its use as an ointment." This was to explain the reasoning of each master. I have cleared away the difficulties to establish the words of the Rif correctly, so that the questions raised by the Rosh against him are resolved. However, we must add the Gemara from the chapter "These things" in Tractate Berakhot: Rav Huna said regarding spices of a certain type and oil used to remove filth, one does not bless over them. They answered: But wherever it is not made for scent, one does not bless! They challenged him regarding the spices used for a bride and a groom... and he answered that there, too, it is made for scent, like the scent used for clothes and vats. This is the language of Rabbeinu Yona there: oil intended to remove filth, which is brought at the end of the meal to wash the hands, is not blessed upon. And this is what is meant in "How do we bless"—that for an ointment of a certain kind, one does not bless in the presence of a group, but only when alone. This concludes his words. The essence of the matter is that you should follow this version: The House of Shammai says one blesses the oil and exempts the spices, and the House of Hillel says one blesses the spices and exempts the prepared oil. They do not actually disagree on the oil itself. If the House of Shammai said it exempts the spices, it is because for the House of Hillel, both require their own blessing. Thus we establish the position of the House of Shammai before us. You will find in the Midrash that it implies the water of the oil is what was given to the oil, and if so, their blessings are equal: "Who creates various kinds of spices," as Maimonides wrote in Chapter 2. One Master thinks the oil is the primary element, and the other Master thinks the spice is primary. Rabban Gamliel was precise in his determination: oil and spices used for scent and ointment require a blessing. But oil used merely to remove filth within a meal is different. If the House of Shammai says to bless the oil and exempt the spices, it is because the blessings are equal and the oil is superior. However, regarding the removal of filth at the end of a meal, the House of Hillel rules that one blesses over the spices but the oil does not require a blessing for scent, following Rav Huna's view. One should not ask why we don't bless "Who creates fragrant oil," as explained later, because even if the oil is brought to remove filth, it still smells good, and there is a concern that one's intention is also for the scent. Therefore, we bless "Who creates fragrant oil." This is not the case for an ointment used for a specific medical purpose where the intent is solely for the skin and not for the fragrance. In such a case, one must clarify in their heart that the blessing over the spices exempts it. This is the "path of the wise." Rabban Gamliel followed the House of Shammai to bless the oil and exempt the spices, because the oil is more significant. If it were during the meal, Rabban Gamliel would decide like the one who blesses over the spices and exempts the oil entirely, as I explained. Thus, one blesses the spices first and then blesses the oil.

<column-break/>

### Chapter Three

<margin>Let us speak</margin>
->Let us speak<- of the foundations of Torah study. It is written in the prayer, "And You have taught us..."
<margin>And now, Israel, hear the statutes and the judgments</margin>
* **"And now, Israel, hear the statutes and the judgments..."** <note>Deuteronomy 4:1</note> and do not let your uniqueness be forgotten, etc. The word "and now" is difficult according to the usual flow of the text. Furthermore, it is difficult when he says, "See, I have taught you..." Why is the language of "seeing" used here when the language of "hearing" would be more appropriate? And it says "our eyes have seen" elsewhere. Furthermore, it is difficult in the verse "which I have commanded you," where he mentions and begins "in the midst of the land." This is said to explain the matter of inheriting the land, but the meaning is not clear there, especially since he already said "so that you may live and come and inherit the land." Furthermore, it is difficult: "If you hold fast to the brightness of the split..." regarding our brothers, that he should turn his eyes and say, "And you shall not do..." what does this teach? It is a warning for different times. Furthermore, it is difficult: "For what great nation is there that has God so near to it?" This does not seem to fit the context of us repeating these words. In the third verse: "And what great nation is there that has statutes and judgments so righteous..." this refers back to what was said above, "I have taught you statutes and judgments." Why say "And what great nation..."? This is not the case in all other places. Similarly, it is difficult that the text repeats: "Only take heed to yourself, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget the things which your eyes have seen..." <note>Deuteronomy 4:9</note> which is already a warning about Torah study. Our Sages, of blessed memory, learned from this: "Anyone who forgets one thing from his studies is considered as if he is liable for his life." But we have not yet understood our errors here, as we have been small in the section of "Shema" and "Va'etchanan," where it says "And you shall teach them to your children," etc. It should have written there "Take heed to yourself and keep your soul." Furthermore, it is difficult to have a break between two sections that speak of the same matter. As it says, "The Lord spoke to you out of the midst of the fire..." and "from the place of the dwelling of the heavens..." and this is a difficulty. And between the verse "And you shall choose greatly for your souls, for you saw no image..." it interrupts with the verse "And the Lord was angry with me for your sakes..." What does this verse teach us here in the middle? Especially since he already mentions and repeats the matter of remembering what happened in the midst of the land, etc. The language "And now" and "Hear the statutes" is also difficult; it should have said "Hear the statutes." This can be explained according to the *Yalkut Shimoni* <term>a popular medieval collection of Midrash/homilies</term> on the book of Jeremiah (page 80, column 3): Rabbi Simon said in the name of Rabbi Simeon, "In this world, a person gathers grapes and no one tells him anything, but in the future, if he comes to gather on the Sabbath, the grape will cry out and say: It is the Sabbath!" In this world, a person goes to be with his wife and no one stops him, but in the future, the stone cries out and says: It is not the proper time! (Look there). It is written that the "end of the city" was like the description in the portion of *Chukat*: the entire congregation that was ready to enter the Land arrived. And behold, since they were prepared for the feast, they were afraid because they were like... as it says at that time... and there was not a single person who wanted to commit a transgression. This is the meaning of "And now, Israel, hear..." with a hearing of complete holiness and purity. "Hear *to* the statutes" and not "the statutes" that I teach you. That is to say: as I am teaching you the statutes and the judgments, let the statutes and judgments be done, and they will take you and remove you from sin. Therefore, it says "Hear *to* the statutes" and not "the statutes."

<column-break/>

After the House of Hillel ruled that when sitting at a meal, one blesses over the spices "Who creates various kinds of spices" and over the prepared oil "Who creates fragrant oil," the Sanhedrin <term>the supreme high court of ancient Israel</term> produced this ruling. If one was not using it for scent, the reason given is that when one rubs spices and oil during a meal, his intent is not for the fragrance but only for the preparation <note>likely for cleanliness</note>. The final law was decided according to the House of Hillel: when sitting during a meal, one blesses over the spices and exempts the prepared oil. This follows the Rif's ruling. There is no need for amazement, for this is a different matter. To observe the law according to the House of Hillel is one thing, and the way it is written in the books is another, following my explanation. In the afternoon prayer, Rabban Gamliel actually decided between the two views, not like the Rosh and not like the Tosafot. Regarding Rabban Gamliel's precision about oil—since its scent is enjoyed—he shows the foundation of his decision. Rashi <term>the preeminent 11th-century commentator</term> also explains that oil and spices at the end of a meal are as Rabban Gamliel decided. Therefore, the Rif's words are established and explained, and they are clear to us regarding oil and wine. This is what is written: the "moisture" of the wine is like the rest, and it will return to be taken in his days without removal, as I have written from "good days." When he covers it, it is exempted. As it is written, "Your olive oil shall be taken..." to remember in the Sanhedrin, the anger of the Lord is removed, and the crown of the letter *Yod* is to the right as well.

"What does it matter to me if they are children or children's children? It is accounted to him as if he received it from Mount Sinai."

Regarding the Rif and the Rosh, and what was written there: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: "Whoever teaches his son Torah... as if..." and I will not cite Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi as if he received it from Mount Sinai... "And you shall teach them to your children," and not your daughters, and not your children's children. And even though he assists your children and your children's children, to say "whoever teaches his son Torah it is as if..." is also permitted. And therefore, according to the version of the Rif and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi... if a person taught his son Torah, he is also obligated to teach his son's son Torah... but according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi... it was not mentioned... to learn... for he is not like one who teaches his son, who is obligated... for teaching one's son is as if receiving from Sinai.

As it is in the language of the Sages: "his son," and if his son's son... in the beginning, for the teaching is for his son... as it is in the Sifrei <term>a legal midrash on Numbers and Deuteronomy</term>... what is written there regarding "your children" and not "your children's children"... for everyone who teaches his son Torah... as it is written: "as if he received the Torah from Mount Sinai," for it says "to your children," and adjacent to it: "the day that you stood before the Lord your God in Horeb" <note>Deuteronomy 4:10</note>. And in the Gemara: "Why in the support of the Sages did they emphasize the verse 'And you shall teach them to your children'?" Which implies only his son. And I have another reason... on the verse "Everyone who teaches his sons"... in *Tractate Kiddushin page 30*... to ask... and "you shall make them known to your children..." etc. It seems the answer is... from the children's children... if so, "your children"... it is as if he stood at Mount Sinai... "And you shall make them known to your children and your children's children"... and to teach is written regarding children's children... and the verse emphasizes "to your children"... from where do we know... "And you shall teach them to your children"... therefore... and all the explanations... to say that here in the Gemara... there was a dispute among the Sages... Rabbi Yehoshua... the reason to learn until... and Rashi explained... what he read yesterday... and even more, etc.

It seems to me that based on this, we can distinguish between studying with one's son and studying with one's grandson. For with his son, he must study with him every day, but even on the second day, he must say with him what he read yesterday and add another verse... and he is obligated to build with him. This is the meaning of "to your children." And "to your children's children" means to review with him tomorrow what he learned yesterday and to add to it. And therefore, when he heard, he said "to your children's children." And he established the question... regarding the verse in *Parashat Ekev* <note>The Torah portion in Deuteronomy 7:12–11:25</note>... which is mentioned... "And you shall teach your children," for even regarding the adjacent verse "the day you stood at Horeb," it is said "in the sight of my eyes"... as it is known that the Torah was given first at Horeb and second in the plains of Moab. And it adjacent "the day you stood at Horeb" specifically to "your children's children." And from "your children's children" it is known regarding "your children"... and there it is adjacent to the idea that one who teaches his son is as if he taught his son and his son's son until the end of all generations. And the order of learning there "to your children's children" teaches the adjacency... to study with him a second year... and you shall sharpen them for your children and your children's children... and that day you stood at Horeb is to teach that studying with one's son each time is like one time... and it is not to build... but rather it shall be as if at Horeb. And the matter is according to the version of the Ramaz <note>Likely Rabbi Moshe Zacuto, a 17th-century kabbalist and commentator</note>, and it is settled.

<margin>
*Joshua’s Inheritance* <note>The title of another work by the author, *Nachlat Yehoshua*</note>

They supported me and told me of the story of his illness, as will be explained before us. They were happy to say: "Make your Torah study a fixed habit" <note>original: *aseh toratcha keva*, a famous maxim from Pirkei Avot 1:15</note>. The meaning of this word "fixed" is that the essence of your labor should be in the Torah and not in worldly work <note>original: *melacha*</note>. This matter is also an interpretation regarding his illness, as mentioned above, according to the sense of the scripture: "He who stands surety for a stranger will surely suffer harm," which is more fixed for those who receive converts and for the "guarantors of Zion" and for one who "fixes himself" <note>plunges himself deeply</note> into a matter of law <note>original: *halacha*</note>. This is what Rabbi Yose meant to say: anyone who learns only for himself and relies on others constantly diminishes until the Torah falls before him and his Torah becomes a personal matter. There is also the matter of what Rav Papa said: the verse says "You shall learn them and observe them to do them"—anything that is included in "doing" is included in "learning," etc. That is to say, one should be fixed in the "judgment of the judge," so that the law is before him and he has learned the *halacha* and is precise, so that our portion becomes an inheritance and gives him a heart and strength to serve the King, etc. And according to these interpretations for "fixing oneself" in a matter of law: recount and trade in all these matters of Torah, to learn and to learn in order to practice. The sign of one who "fixes himself" in a matter of law is that the judgment is before him and he comes to consult with his teacher. Through this, these three Mishnahs will be understood. They specified his "house of illness" to say: "Make your Torah study a fixed habit," and the meaning of this is that your business should be in Torah and not in worldly work.

The author saw that in our time, even during his illness, the "fixing" of Torah study was his strength, fixing himself in the law before him through the established structures of the Talmud <note>original: *Gematra*</note>. Each one comes with many portions and established arguments, fixing himself in the law to proceed with the judgment before him, having learned the law so as not to fall into a pit. A scribe's error—they transcribed everything, lest the listener err in thinking that the author only fixed himself in the order of judgment before him, for so it was said: "Engage yourself," etc. And with the power of the end, the arguments of the law were before him, and he began to teach the many with a heart of hearts. In the end, it is permitted to interpret "make your Torah fixed" as "fixing oneself in the law," meaning only to study Torah and not for the sake of action <note>practical application</note>. Because of this, his death was more than a mourning for his son, who said: "All my days I grew up..." etc., "and study is not the main thing, but rather the action" <note>quoting Pirkei Avot 1:17</note>. Through these principles, his interpretation of his illness will be understood: "Make your Torah fixed" and not in worldly work. And the author, whom I have relied upon in every trait, detailed his illness with the purpose of the language they "received" <note>the tradition</note>, for after they died and their teacher was gone, dispute <note>original: *machloket*</note> increased in Israel and the Torah became like "two Torahs," etc. In this, the wise Ben Pinto will see that he was careful not to warn "make your Torah fixed" solely because there would be dispute among them. Because of this, he relied on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, because his intention was not to diminish his father's house, heaven forbid, when there are students who maintain what is found—the truth and the peace. Because of this, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel assisted by saying in his own words: "The world stands on three things: on Truth, on Justice, and on Peace" <note>Pirkei Avot 1:18</note>. If so, we have fulfilled the attribute of Peace, and there was no dispute in Israel. Through this, his interpretation including the three Mishnahs will be understood. All of them are for the merit of the School of Shammai <note>original: *Beit Shammai*</note>, and he details their words with his intention, for which reason it is necessary to hand down the language they received, and that is right and correct.

### Introduction of the Eminent Sage, Son of the Author of "The Pillar of Worship"

->I have raised the fat of your sacrifices, O you who are weak in strength; I have raised it with knowledge, like one who is mute and astonished.<-
->The hidden things of the soul are for the weak of strength; our eyes look toward the Living God and exist before the Lord, and not before<-
->The powers of judgment <note>Hebrew: *Elohim*, often associated in mystical texts with strict justice</note>; and one should interpret the sacrifice as a word speaking of closeness <note>The Hebrew root for sacrifice, *K-R-B*, also means "to draw near"</note><-
->As they shall instruct me from the Heavens.<-

### **And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: When an ox, or a sheep, or a goat is born, etc. And He saw it as fit for an offering, etc. And an ox or a sheep, you shall not slaughter it and its young on the same day, etc. And when you sacrifice a thanksgiving offering to the Lord, etc. Until the end of the portion of "When a bull is born."**

<margin>And it should be said: The portion of the Sacrifice.</margin>
<margin>Behold, the secret of the Grain Offering that brings remembrance.</margin>
<margin>And see the portion of *Vayechi*.</margin>
Who can understand the doubts that arise in this portion? For it is difficult to understand why it was sufficient to mention "it and its young" alongside the laws of sacrifices. Furthermore, the phrase "And you shall keep My commandments and do them"—what does this have to do with this specific verse? For are we not commanded to keep all the commandments written in the Torah? Another difficulty: how are these three sections divided? And this sacrifice, following the section on the "Sanctity of the Name" <note>Kiddush HaShem</note>, what is the connection? Furthermore, twice the text mentions "for the Lord," referring to mercy. Rashi <note>A famous 11th-century commentator</note> explains regarding the goat: "Why do you pursue us?" Regarding the last part, the text says "I am the Lord," which is said for the purpose of paying a reward. But regarding the middle part, he explains nothing. And concerning the "Resident" <note>the *Tosafot*, a group of medieval commentators</note>, what Rashi explains there—what is the matter of the signs mentioned in this portion?

Rabbi Moshe <note>likely referring to Nachmanides or another major scholar</note> spoke on this portion. You should know the intention of the portion where it is written, "And you shall not profane My holy name." It is written in the Zohar <note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism</note>: Come and see, it is written, "And He descended and behold..." until the intention of "Take for yourself a goat... for the goats satisfy..." and what is the matter of the secrets of the grain offerings mentioned there? Furthermore, it is explained there in the Midrash Rabbah <note>A collection of ancient homiletic interpretations</note>: "And it shall be seven days under its mother." Why seven days? So that it does not appear as if they are entering the Sanctuary as a "blemished" animal if they have not yet seen the light of seven days. Rabbi Joshua of Siknin said in the name of Rabbi Levi: This is like a king who entered a province and decreed: "None of those who are to see me shall see my face until they have first seen the face of the Queen <note>Matrona</note>." So said the Holy One, blessed be He: "Do not bring me an offering until a Sabbath has passed over it," for there is no seven-day period without a Sabbath, as it is written, "Six days you shall work and the seventh is a Sabbath." Rabbi Isaac said: The judgment of a human and the judgment of an animal are equal. Just as a human child is circumcised on the eighth day, so too an animal is fit for sacrifice on the eighth day. That is to say, if it comes before Me as a sacrifice through the "will" and the "seven," then it is My sacrifice. And if it is brought through the <term>Leviathan</term> <note>symbolizing a deep spiritual process</note>, I will elevate your sacrifice before Me for every sin. And to warn the children of Israel and say to them: "My sacrifice, My bread," which is to say, do this for the sake of the Holy One, blessed be He, and with the "will" of my sacrifice, etc.

Furthermore, know what is held in the Zohar, Portion of Vayikra: Rabbi Judah opened with, "Serve the Lord with joy." But there, the person who sinned before his Master and transgressed His commandments... when he brings a sacrifice, it is accepted through the "broken spirit" and the "stormy spirit"... it is not accepted except through lowliness of voice and silence... behold he stands in the joy of the heavens, a building that was far from judgment. And thus, let him not be astonished by the joy and songs... for through the sacrifice, a perfect service to the Holy One, blessed be He, is found.

According to this, the matter of the Calf will be understood... for it is known and famous that Aaron did not intend to worship the Calf at all... but it was in his soul a small sin. Whereas the worshippers themselves were actually serving another god... Therefore, regarding the sacrifice of Aaron, he needed to be hidden in the secret of the silence.
