Moses said to him, "Why are you ashamed? For this you were chosen!" Rather, it was sufficient for him to take the calf with joy... but the name "calf" is a matter of commandment to atone for the deed of the Calf. This is not the case with the children of Israel, who actually worshipped the Calf... and therefore they needed atonement and to say over the sacrifice "the sins of our fathers"... and therefore we were required to bring a goat for a sin-offering. # Preface of the Eminent Author of "The Pillar of Worship"

The twentieth day of Sukkot and its night <note>The author likely refers to the festival of Sukkot to ground the discussion in a time of joy and sacrifice</note>, and even so, as it is written: "And you shall guard," that one should merit through the strength of the intention <term>kavanah: focused spiritual intention during a commandment</term> and the recognition of its prohibition. This means that the sages of the hidden wisdom <note>referring to Kabbalists</note> saw in these matters a clarification of the intention—not merely the intention regarding eating, but in order to inflame the soul, as it is written regarding me, etc. And one can be exempted by what is decided regarding the cutting of the skin, and so it is written, and he shall return to connect to the matters of the dwelling-place as in the beginning, specifically regarding eating, for the act of "desecration" <note>ma'ilah: misappropriation of sacred property</note> requires that everything be unified.

And regarding what I have clarified as to the verse concerning "it and its offspring" <note>Leviticus 22:28, the prohibition against slaughtering an animal and its young on the same day</note>, whether it be an ox or a sheep, and similarly "a sheep as his sacrifice" and "not to be profane," Rashi explains: "from your own will," which refers to consecrated animals. It also refers to "it and its offspring," about which the legal decisors wrote: "if we say the first is permitted to be slaughtered, and then he slaughters the second after it." The sages noted that the slaughter was not "fit" if it were for idolatry, etc. "You shall slaughter a sacrifice for the fifth"—in this, my letters <note>perhaps a reference to the divine names or the scribe's own notes</note> intended that his slaughter be a "sacrifice," a wide cutting, and not just any slaughter, but a "fit slaughter." Through this, the connection of the verses in this Torah portion is given, *to instruct us who is involved in the matter of the covering of the blood <term>kisuy ha-dam: the commandment to cover the blood of slaughtered birds or undomesticated animals</term>, and who are those disqualified from slaughtering.*

Regarding the prohibition of the "blessing that they joined" <note>likely referring to the blessing over slaughter</note>, since the sages saw that "all may slaughter and their slaughter is fit" <note>the opening line of Mishna Chullin</note>, even though a minor or one who is mentally incompetent might slaughter, their slaughter is only fit if an expert is supervising them. From this, we learn that for every common person, "all may slaughter," even for non-sacred meat <term>chullin: meat not intended for the Altar</term> that is to be eaten in a state of ritual purity. How so? It depends on his standing, the "signs" <note>the trachea and esophagus</note>, and the expertise of the person as discussed in the tractate of "Kiddushin" <note>Marriage/Consecration</note>. It was established according to the law, and his slaughter is fit. And we have written this together, etc. Rav Ashi was careful regarding the phrase "all may slaughter," and according to this, it is not just to exclude an idolater, who does not uphold the laws of slaughter. Rashi explains "those who are experts," and Rabbi Shmuel the Beloved said: whenever you find "all may slaughter," it means they may slaughter even if they are not certified experts <note>as long as the result is checked</note>.

All matters of profanation are hinted at in the verses regarding non-sacred meat, from which a second level of holiness branches out in all the verses. Therefore, even for a single thing, if one transgresses a verse as mentioned above, or regarding the non-sacred meat written in the portion, or regarding the entire Torah—his slaughter is disqualified. The explanation of the verses begins by saying: "When you slaughter a sacrifice... you shall slaughter it of your own will" [Leviticus 19:5], and Rashi explains: "from your own knowledge." From this, it is proven that the slaughter of a deaf-mute, an insane person, or a minor is disqualified because they are not "possessors of knowledge" <term>da'at: mature intellect and legal agency</term>. Therefore, it says "And you shall guard" regarding all the acts of slaughtering for their appointed time.

The explanation of these matters is that one must be careful with those who slaughter in this portion, as it says "haste and leniency" in his slaughtering, for these are found among all who speak. This is the reward for the investigation and the hint—the use of this service. "Stretching" refers to the drawing of the knife, and it is difficult because a teacher even draws during the teaching, but you wrote that it was not by will, not according to the desire of his master. In the chapter "All May Slaughter," it says all are experts, even the elderly. The heading says "in every slaughter," meaning all who are experts may slaughter. And this is the meaning: "And you shall slaughter..."—the slaughterer must be strengthened by it, needing to learn the method to merit the method of being an expert. One must be established so that he does not faint during his slaughter, as it is said "to do the service." Therefore, the verse says, "And you shall not profane My holy name" [Leviticus 22:32]. And when I entered, Rashi wrote: "Bequeath yourself and sanctify My name"—this language is included in the intention of slaughter. It is a strict matter, for those who are "summoned" <note>original: *mezumanin*</note> to explain the Lord's commandments are those who surrender themselves for the Sanctification of the Name <term>Kiddush Hashem: martyrdom or acting in a way that brings honor to God</term>, in accordance with "And when you sacrifice."

This is the explanation of the sage Bar Zalda, and even regarding "My name," the language is used in the Zohar, etc. This is the book of Maimonides <note>Rambam</note> in the laws of "Slaughtered Animals," where Rav Huna said regarding its prohibition: "it may be eaten," from what Rashi wrote regarding the fire, to teach that "the heat is from above." It was a difficult matter for him; he should have said "wide" regarding those who ascend. For my master Rabbi Ishmael said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: "I did not bring these people up from Egypt except so that My name would be sanctified through Israel." This is written in this portion where it says, "Who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God" [Leviticus 22:33]. This was done only so that you would not disqualify yourselves and that My name would be sanctified through you. Thus, "My holy things" will be remembered. This was written in the description of the "Exodus" in its entirety; search and you will find, and everything will be revealed correctly.

According to this, the Midrash will be clarified which is written in two places in the portion "speak to the children of Israel," etc. And "I have truly come on the way," for according to the health of the body, the Holy One, blessed be He, fills it. *In the chapter "All May Slaughter," it is proven that "all are included," etc.* From here they said: we are lenient with the sacrifices and the common people of Israel so that they will be careful in repentance, except for the apostate, etc. And the hidden meaning of what is written "My name is passed through the righteous," as the Guide <note>Maimonides' *Guide for the Perplexed*</note> says: "one who is an apostate regarding idolatry is an apostate regarding the entire Torah." He did not mention "the secret of the name," but in this portion, he mentioned "death to the apostates." Isaac explained that "that which is written for the teacher/judge" means until they verify that the lines are pure from the word that was written. His slaughter is disqualified, and with all precision, it is a "sacrifice" from him. An apostate regarding idolatry is mentioned first in the verse "and you shall not profane My holy name," referring to what is permitted in questioning. Only from the counsel of the wise—not just a hint—what he guarded for its weeping, or "his problem," etc. And I mentioned above in the Torah that he is like a Nazirite, or he increased because he returned to the general category of this name in the portion. Or he mentions "he shall give his money" and juxtaposes the two simple meanings to arrange in the Midrash "all that is lacking."
<sig>These</sig>

<column-break/>

These and those belong to the Holy One, blessed be He <note>original: *Ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu*</note>, who forgot the deeds and to lead all kindness with the beauty of days and the like, as we explained what is written, "and He rested" <term>va-yinafash: God resting on the seventh day</term>. It begins with the spreading of the Sabbath and the remembrance of its entirety. And in this way, it seems right to explain "the world and its fullness," and that He created and provided in His glory not only for the need of eating.

And in this way, it seems right to explain what they said: "it shall be seven days under its mother, and from the eighth day and onwards..." [Leviticus 22:27]. For this too reminds us of the Sabbath, so that the eating should not be in haste. For this reason, it is not said regarding sacrifices, "it is not said," and the verse is sufficient to clarify so as not to give an opening for the mouth to say "two seconds," God forbid, as Rashi explains: "one eats meat and this one wants it forbidden, and this one wants it in his pocket." Regarding the words of the Gemara <note>Talmud</note> in Shachat-la'i, it says: "the Emperor said to Rabban Gamliel: He who created the wind did not create the mountains," etc. Even from now, it will be clarified "And the Lord said," etc. And all these from now, "a drop on his face," etc. He said to him: "from the lip it was, all of them in their perception," etc. This is the secret in our own context regarding the "asking by way of the air," which is not comparable. This is for those who err by saying there are "two authorities" <term>shtei reshuyot: a dualistic heresy</term>—one who merits the bull and this one who wants the choice. This is not so; rather, "seven days under its mother" indicates unity. For when they are reconciled, they will be superior to the smoke. And this is a hint to all the powers prepared. What is the foundation of this matter? It is that which was forgiven, saying that "the forbidden becomes permitted" and "the slaughtered returns," wanting through this to merit the slaughter for the drawing near of the sacrifice, not to lack so that eight days shall pass over it. This is as found in the Midrash, that the angels were received, etc. The Holy One, blessed be He, brought the eighth, etc.

And I asked: why bring this verse? Whatever is disqualified as a sacrifice is like the verse that describes the disqualification of the "standing." Praise to the Lord for every general detail. "Garment for things," etc.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the laws and inner intentions (kavanah) of prayer, specifically the physical orientation of the body and the historical origins of the three daily services.</meta>

### Preface of the Illustrious Sage, the Son of the Author of "The Pillar of Service"

...below and his heart above, as a sign to follow, as it is said: "One should direct his heart toward heaven and then cast his eyes downward." For it is written in the holy Midrash <note>A genre of rabbinic literature that interprets biblical texts, often through homilies or parables.</note> regarding the instruction to "cast his eyes downward": this is toward the Land of Israel, which is the site of the Holy Temple. Our teacher, Rabbeinu Yonah <note>Rabbi Jonah of Gerona (c. 1200–1263), a famous Spanish scholar known for his works on ethics and prayer.</note>, sought to prioritize the heart over the eye, and in his wisdom, we must say there are three matters regarding prayer. For our teacher’s heart was drawn to explain the place toward which his eyes are lowered, as Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki (1040–1105), the preeminent commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note> explained: one who prays must direct themselves toward the Land of Israel, as written in the book *Ikkarim* <note>The "Book of Principles" by Joseph Albo, a 15th-century work on Jewish philosophy.</note> regarding the Land of Israel. One should fix a specific place for that spirit in which he prays, which is the Lord. If he were standing in the Diaspora, he should direct his heart toward the Land of Israel, for there his eyes are lowered to focus on the holiness that is there.

And because of this, he said that the posture of the body should be as if he is standing in the actual Holy Temple and praying there. Thus, there are three matters: first, that his eyes be downward to direct himself toward the Land of Israel which is opposite him. Second, he should fix a place for himself and compose his stature as if he were standing in the Temple. Third, after composing his stature, he should think as if he is standing in the Sanctuary and praying in the Holy Temple. This is according to the words of Rabbeinu Yonah in the *Massekhet HaKedushim*, where he said one who prays must direct his gaze downward toward the Land of Israel. This refers to the beginning of the matter of prayer. He then refined this further: "his heart above," in the explanation of Rabbeinu Yonah, means he should think as if he is standing in heaven, elevating his spirit above his material body. Afterward, he should think in his heart "downward," as if he is standing and praying within the Holy Temple.

Based on this, it is clear that one who prays must cast his eyes downward and his heart upward, encompassing everything in one vessel. If so, why must he also give his heart upward, just as he said he must cast his eyes downward? Is it not the same logic? One must understand what is "above" and what is "below." At first, he gives his heart above to contemplate the dwelling of the Name <note>A common Jewish way of referring to God (HaShem).</note> in His sanctuary, which is in heaven. But here, in a state of life, one searches and seeks for the Eye <note>The Divine watchfulness</note> in concealment. Afterward, he gives his heart to contemplate and humble himself. When it says one should give his heart above, it means that the one praying should not think there are only things "above," but also things "below."

According to this, the words of Rabbi Ishmael are resolved, who said in the name of the Sages that one who prays must cast his eyes downward, for the Temple was the place where His eyes and heart were set for all days. In this context, it implies even the heart must be directed downward toward the Temple. But since it is also said that it is like the Throne of Glory in heaven, the heart is directed upward. Therefore, the Sages said that the heart must be above, and why is this so? It is to fulfill both verses: the verse "My eyes and My heart shall be there perpetually" <note>1 Kings 9:3, referring to the Temple.</note> and the verse "Let us lift up our heart with our hands unto God in heaven" <note>Lamentations 3:41.</note>. Thus, the one praying casts his eyes downward to fix his place, then lifts his heart upward to transcend his physical form, and finally, he, his voice, and his heart are as one as if he were standing in the House of God and praying.

<margin>
It is found in the chapter "One Does Not Stand" <note>The fifth chapter of Tractate Berakhot in the Talmud.</note>: "One should only pray in a house that has windows," etc.
</margin>

<margin>
...in a house that has windows, etc.
</margin>

Through this, the matter is clarified. One must strip away the physical form from the soul. Along these lines, the end of the chapter "One Does Not Stand" is explained regarding the four types of individual prayer. One should only pray in a house with windows, as it is said [in the Book of Daniel]... and he would pray all day... three times a day, kneeling on his knees, "Evening, morning, and noon." He should let his voice be heard in his prayer... as it is written [of Hannah], "only her lips moved." One might think he can pray loudly, but he must pray as is explained regarding Moses, to hear the voice of the soul. The prayer is first the internal desire, and then the prayer itself...

<column-break/>

Evening. One might think he can include all three prayers in one reasoning. One might think he should read them all as if it were a song from the Torah. Rather, the process of the one who prays is thus: first, the three initial blessings, which are for praise. It is appropriate to ask: why is it mentioned at the end that he should not lengthen his prayer all day long? This is unlike the first view, which follows Rabbi Judah, who said the time for prayer is limited. Therefore, one might think he could pray all day, but it is not so. Regarding the first view of Rabbi Judah, the time of the [daily sacrifice] is what determines it.

In the chapter "The Morning Prayer" (*Tefillat HaShachar*), it is said: Rabbi Jose says in the name of Rabbi Chanina that the prayers were established by the Patriarchs <note>Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note>. Rabbi Joshua ben Levi says the prayers were established to correspond to the daily sacrifices (*Tamid*). We hold like Rabbi Joshua ben Levi... The morning prayer until midday corresponds to the morning sacrifice. The afternoon prayer (*Mincha*) corresponds to the afternoon sacrifice... and the evening prayer (*Arvit*) has no set limit, corresponding to the burning of the limbs and fats that remained from the day's sacrifices.

This is what was asked: since one could pray all day, and it is like a song from the Torah, why did the Sages set three prayers? They are to correspond to the three daily transitions of the sun and the sacrifices. From the Tractate *Berakhot*, it is clear they correspond to the sacrifices. Therefore, one should pray in every direction where the Presence resides. It was taught in a *Baraita* <note>A tradition from the time of the Mishnah not included in the main text.</note>: If one is standing in the Diaspora, he should direct his heart toward the Land of Israel. If he is in the Land of Israel, he should direct himself toward Jerusalem. If he is in Jerusalem, he should direct himself toward the Temple and the Holy of Holies.

Rabbeinu Yonah wrote: this is not specifically about the place, but about the focus on the site of the Temple. One might ask: why mention the Land of Israel, then Jerusalem, then the Temple? It is because the holiness increases in layers. Even if one is not in the Land of Israel, they are directed toward it. If one is in Jerusalem, they direct themselves toward the Holy of Holies... to direct the heart toward the Holy of Holies.

This is correct: he directs everything toward the Spirit and the Holy of Holies so that all the sacrifices are gathered there. Therefore, he directs his heart toward the place where the prayers ascend. We can explain our view: even though we said the prayers correspond to the Patriarchs, they also correspond to the daily sacrifices. Thus, for the additional prayer (*Musaf*), it is a distinct time. From Daniel's "Evening, morning, and noon," we have three times.

One might try to learn that the prayers were established solely based on the sacrifices. This explains why we pray at specific times: Morning, Afternoon, and Evening. For the morning sacrifice was offered until the fourth hour according to Rabbi Judah. The afternoon sacrifice lasted until evening. And the evening prayer can be said all night. Even though there are two views, the Sages brought evidence for both. For the morning prayer, it says "Abraham rose early in the morning to the place where he had stood" <note>Genesis 19:27.</note>, and standing refers to prayer. For the afternoon prayer, it says "Isaac went out to meditate in the field toward evening" <note>Genesis 24:63.</note>, and meditation refers to prayer. For the evening prayer, it says "And Jacob arrived ( *vayifga* ) at the place" <note>Genesis 28:11.</note>, and "hitting/arriving" refers to prayer.

However, regarding the daily sacrifices, the Bible explicitly says "evening and morning and noon," for they are called "continual" (*Tamid*). Therefore, the proof is stronger that the prayers correspond to the sacrifices. From this, we derive the rule that one should not raise his voice [too loudly] in prayer... like Hannah, of whom it is said "only her lips moved." This is because if prayer corresponds to sacrifices, just as the sacrifice is performed in silence and awe, so too the prayer should be. This is also the way of the Gemara in *Sotah*, asking why the Sages established the prayer in a whisper—so as not to embarrass transgressors who are confessing their sins. Rashi explains that a specific place was fixed for the hearing of the voice. One might think he should make his voice heard, but we learn from Hannah that it is better to pray in a whisper. If the prayers are in place of sacrifices, then the prayer must be...

<summary>This page discusses the proper physical and mental orientation during prayer, emphasizing that one should face the Holy of Holies with eyes lowered in humility and heart raised in spiritual focus. It also explores the dual origins of the three daily prayers—the Patriarchs and the Temple sacrifices—concluding that their timing and silent nature mirror the sacrificial service.</summary>

### Introduction of the Genius, the Son of the Author of the "Pillar of Worship"

<margin>The matter of the "Paths" and the expression "one who waits" <note>Hebrew: *hamamtin*</note> for the one praying (etc.). It seems even more strange to me to disregard all the books and erase the word "more." It seems correct to uphold the version before us. And what is written to assist according to the law of the Gemara <note>The Talmud</note> that "Worship" refers to "Prayer," this is because of why Moses desired to enter the Land of Israel, etc. It was forbidden and separate... but he only wanted to fulfill the commandments dependent on the Land. And so, he requested to enter the Land of Israel for the sake of fulfilling the commandments and the 613 laws <note>Hebrew: *Mitzvot*</note>. Regarding this he asked: to enter the Land to fulfill the commandments. from what was mentioned, and to say a parable, He said to him, "Do not speak further," etc., so as not to add, and He hinted at the explanation: for one must pray at all times. # Introduction of the <term>Gaon</term><note>A title of high honor for a preeminent rabbinic scholar.</note>, the Son of the Author, Page 58

<margin>
Acts of kindness [G.H.] at the beginning and end, and all acts of kindness. And <unclear>sects</unclear> of skin etc. and the matter of <term>Hashem</term><note>Literally "The Name," a common substitute for the Tetragrammaton.</note>.
</margin>
And from where do we learn that we should interpret the matters of <term>bringing in the bride</term><note>The act of assisting a bride and groom in their wedding needs.</note> and <term>accompanying the deceased</term><note>Attending a funeral and burial.</note> from the word "to walk" etc.? It is explained that this is as it says in the <term>Gemara</term><note>The part of the Talmud that contains rabbinical analysis and commentary.</note> in Sotah: <note>Original: "Torah techilata gemilut chasadim ve-sofah gemilut chasadim."</note> "The Torah's beginning is acts of loving-kindness and its end is acts of loving-kindness." Its beginning is acts of kindness, as it says, "And the Lord God made for Adam and his wife garments of skin" <note>Genesis 3:21</note>; and its end is acts of kindness, as it says, "And He buried him in the valley" <note>Deuteronomy 34:6, referring to God burying Moses</note>. And from this, a question returns: why specifically these? For in the Gemara, we also find that the Holy One, Blessed be He, visits the sick, as it says, "And the Lord appeared to him [Abraham] in the plains of Mamre" <note>Genesis 18:1</note> while he was recovering from his circumcision. If so, why did the Torah choose to hint at acts of kindness specifically at its beginning and its end?

<margin>
Gemara Avodah Zarah 17b: One who occupies himself with Torah but does not perform acts of kindness is like one who has no God.
</margin>
And it seems possible to answer this based on the Gemara in the tractate <term>Avodah Zarah</term><note>The Talmudic tractate dealing with laws concerning idolatry.</note>: "Rabbi Huna said: Anyone who occupies himself with Torah but does not perform acts of loving-kindness is like one who has no God." For it is written: "Now for a long season Israel was without the true God" <note>2 Chronicles 15:3</note>. This teaches that the person who occupies himself with Torah must also be a master of loving-kindness. Therefore, at the beginning of the Torah and at its end, the matter of acts of kindness was hinted to us, for the essence of the matter is in kindness. And as the <insert>Lord</insert> explained:

<margin>
The Lord [made garments for] Adam and his wife... and He buried... Why acts of kindness? Like one who has no God.
</margin>
Acts of kindness, as I have explained above, and Rashi explains: Just as acts of kindness are necessary, so too the "bringing in" and "escorting" [of people] are parts of the study of Torah. This is a great principle: just as God made clothes for them <gloss>as mentioned in the fourth chapter</gloss>, if so, one must also be humble. The Torah also needs to be approached with humility. This was hinted to us by what is written at the end of the Torah, where it says that the Holy One, Blessed be He, buried him [Moses]. And over there, my teacher and father <note>Refers to the author of the main work.</note> says that the verse states: "And He buried him in the valley... and no man knows his burial place" <note>Deuteronomy 34:6</note>.

<margin>
"And He buried him in the valley" — his burial place was hidden. A hint that one must act with humility. "No man knows his burial place."
</margin>
His burial place was a hint to us that one must perform kindness with humility. The Torah should not be made into a source of pride; rather, one should not speak of these acts. It is a hint that kindness must be done in secret, with humility, for the burial was hidden. This is why the Holy One, Blessed be He, kept the burial place secret. Why would He say this to the people? Because there is a reason the Holy One, Blessed be He, did this at the end; just as man's end in the world is more modest. And it was necessary to perform this kindness of the Torah with humility, as it says in Sotah regarding the words of the Torah: they require humility. This is what is meant by "walking humbly with your God" regarding bringing in the bride and accompanying the deceased, even though it is the rabbinic way to perform them publicly etc. This is what was hinted to us at the beginning and the end: the matter of acts of kindness. And to hint that it must be with humility, just as the Holy One, Blessed be He, did. It hints that we should also study Torah in its specific holiness, which is through humility. This is what people have always found difficult in Rashi: how does the word "to walk" hint at bringing in the bride and accompanying the deceased more than all other 613 commandments written in the Torah? But this will be settled correctly based on what I wrote.

In the book *Choice of Pearls* [Mivchar Hapeninim], in the "Gate of Humility," etc.

One makes his face pleasant, and the joy of the "bringing in" and "escorting" are joined. He participates with him in his blessing. Similarly, when one goes to a house of mourning, he participates with the mourner in the honor of the lamentations. This "bringing in" and "escorting" are the "walking" mentioned <note>Micah 6:8</note>. "To walk" is a hint to that "walking" mentioned in the verse: "It is better to go to a house of mourning than to go to a house of feasting" <note>Ecclesiastes 7:2</note>. From these matters, every understanding person learns the matter of submission and humility. These are the foundations of the qualities of a person: to be humble before God. This is what the Holy One, Blessed be He, seeks from us: "to walk humbly." These two things—bringing in the bride and accompanying the dead—bring a person to humility. However, we must clarify the matter of why "all things require humility."

One must make heard all the explanations of the scripture which mentions these three together in one verse.

The son of the Genius... just as He gave... clothes of skin...

# Introduction of the Gaon, the Son of the Author: The Pillar of Service

<margin>It is better to pray in a language one understands, even if it is not the Holy Tongue, rather than in the Holy Tongue without understanding.</margin>
The heart. Also, my uncle, the pious and God-fearing righteous man—may his memory be for a blessing—in his book, added much more to these words. I have taken the beloved words of the wise and complete scholar in his book regarding the "Pillar of Prayer," which are as powerful as water, drawing from all the rabbis who preceded and followed him. My companions served to sweeten every matter, particularly through his tender and wise heart. What more can I add to their words? I have only come to make known what is written in the *Sefer Hasidim* <note>The "Book of the Pious," a 12th-century foundational work of German-Jewish ethics and law.</note> in section 788: "It is better for a person to pray and recite the <term>Shema</term><note>The central declaration of Jewish faith: "Hear O Israel..."</note> and the blessings in a language he understands than to pray in the Holy Tongue <note>original: "Lashon HaKodesh" (Hebrew)</note> without understanding." For it is written of those who do not know the book, "Read this, please," and he says, "I do not know how to read," and the Lord says, "Because this people draw near with their mouth and honor Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me" <note>Isaiah 29:13</note>. Their fear of Me becomes like a "commandment of men learned by rote," for they pray and recite but do not understand what is coming out of their lips and mouth. It is also written, "To serve Him with all your heart" <note>Deuteronomy 11:13</note>. What is the "service of the heart"? This is prayer. If the heart does not know what it is saying before Him in its internal thoughts—even if it is in the Aramaic language—so that the heart understands its meaning, then the prayer is lacking. Therefore, one who does not understand should not pray [in Hebrew], because prayer depends on the heart; if the heart does not understand, the prayer and the blessing have left us. These are his words.

<margin>A great rectification for prayer for a person who prayed without intention: he should regret it, groan over it, and wipe away [the fault] etc.</margin>
Because of this matter, the wise men and the masters in the Holy Community of Frankfurt—may their souls be bound in the bond of life—established a great rectification for all the members of the <term>Chevra Kadisha</term><note>Literally "Holy Society," usually the group responsible for burial, but here referring to pious communal circles.</note> who are accustomed to adding <term>Selichot</term><note>Liturgical poems of repentance.</note>. They recite many penitential prayers at the end of the year and specific prayers for the festivals and months, so they will not be seized by sins or pray improperly. God forbid that they should finish the prayer without the Torah being upon them. Happy is the man who listens to my words and sees, understands, and hears the secret of the prayers that are in his mouth. God forbid that he should not understand his own actions! Let him consider that the Master of our world possesses the "merchandise" of these prayers and supplications, so that he knows how to direct the prayer to ascend through the <term>mazalot</term><note>Celestial constellations or spiritual channels.</note> to the world of eternity. How much more so should the simple maidservant aim for a precious intention.

<margin>If one writes to make a record in his ears, he has set his lips to its correction, as written in the *Yesod Avodah* regarding this matter.</margin>
It is known what they say: they should understand what they speak and direct their protection to the words coming out of their mouths. Regarding their intentions, the books of the Merciful One awaken them with the help of Heaven. There is no doubt that the lengthening of the voices—the voice of the destruction of the exile—is with the help of God. Happy is the man who accepts upon himself a set time for constant study, which is prepared before his eyes, and waits for three days to add the inner words of the pious. In any case, let them wait, God forbid, until they know and understand the principles of prayer. From here it follows that if the perfect man does not know what he is speaking, then the main thing—the "dwelling" and the claims of merit—is lost.

<margin>The two months of mercy, the Sabbaths of the firmaments, the emanations and the flow, and the conduct; not like the "smallness" of the pious, and it is not too much for one who merited it, for all intention is according to the secret, almost from the Throne of Glory and the secret of holiness...</margin>
There is a great level of prayer with the <term>Shekhinah</term><note>The Divine Presence, often viewed as the feminine aspect of God.</note> at the time one prays. See the *Zohar* <note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</note> on the portion *Vayechi* regarding "He was standing." It is taught: From the day that the eyes were darkened and aid was lost, charity was given to the poor... and for the heart, as the heart of the people is ready and fixed... for the foundation of the matter is the established standing. And even though for the "oven" of the merits, he shall be sanctified and cannot... he shall be in the aspect of the "Introductions to Jacob." Regarding those who pray with fitness and life in their prayer: In the explanation of the *Sefer Hasidim*, he brings in my books that he should have some heart and understanding of the verse, to have a precious intention. The verse says, "For the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping; the Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord will receive my prayer" <note>Psalm 6:9-10</note>. Why the "voice of my weeping"? Because through this I have chosen... through this introduction, several simple meanings were added to stir the grace of the heart. The *Sefer Hasidim* also wrote in section 772: A God-fearing person should take care that he does not connect his prayer with the prayer of any wicked man. If, during the time of his prayer, a wicked man is also praying, the "evil agents" and accusers are distanced from him. It is written, "The Lord is near to all who call upon Him" <note>Psalm 145:18</note>.

<margin>From the sins that are in it, let him see that he does not pray alongside a wicked man, for the prayer of the wicked is for all wicked men.</margin>
Keep distant, for the King will subdue them. It is written, "Even when you multiply prayer, I will not hear; your hands are full of blood" <note>Isaiah 1:15</note>. This implies that one who has fear should be careful and separate. When you spread your hands, I will hide My eyes from you. Therefore, the heart of a worthy person should be to direct a place for his prayer with every pure righteous person. I have gathered a little from your money with a desecrator, but the charity of a son of deeds who walks... Therefore, the heart of a worthy person should direct a place for his prayer with every righteous man. And regarding this is the intention of the verse: "He leads me in the paths of righteousness" <note>Psalm 23:3</note>, meaning in the paths of the righteous man.

<margin>God who is supported... and the light of holiness in prayer... Psalm... that we may merit the language of our prayer, for every wicked man in his prayer is [deprived of] grace.</margin>
That He may grant him merit and choose the greatness of the prayer, "A prayer of the afflicted when he is faint and pours out his complaint before the Lord" <note>Psalm 102:1</note>. See the *Zohar* on the portion *Vayishlach*, page 186: consider how much the prayer of a poor person is valued compared to the prayer of Moses our Teacher. Regarding the verse "A prayer of the afflicted," it is from the mouth of the King, and on page [unclear] the prayer of Moses and the prayer of the poor are weighed as equal. So too it is mentioned in the *Zohar*, portion *Terumah*, page 124, that the prayer of the poor is like a hidden gift. In chapter 82, one should have even more intention during the six hours of his prayer, for this voice is like the word of his portion and his destiny. To awaken the intention of prayer, I have mentioned what is written in the *Sefer Hasidim* in section 613: "In the *Sefer HaTemunah* <note>An early Kabbalistic work.</note> of our Rabbis, there are great secrets regarding seven things that prevent a person's prayer from being accepted even with intention." 1. If he was warned not to go before he gave [charity] to a poor person when he spread his palm. For when he stood before Him, it was said to him, "Let it be enough for you; do not speak to Me anymore..."

<column-break/>

on this matter. This hints that one who prays without the heart's intention, his prayer is not heard, as it is written: "They flattered Him with their mouth and lied to Him with their tongue; their heart was not firm with Him" <note>Psalm 78:36-37</note>. 2. The Fool: It is written of the pious man that he is wise in the words of the Torah, but the fool has no portion in their prayer and joy, as it is written: "The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination" <note>Proverbs 21:27</note>. 3. The Rejectionist: One who does not listen to the words of his neighbor and to the distress of the poor; just as he ignored the distress of the heart, so too he will call and not be answered. 4. The Oppressor: One who steals, robs, or withholds wages; his prayer is not heard, as it is written: "He hears the cry of the poor..." but He will not answer the oppressor. 5. The Unclean: One who prays without cleanliness and purity; his prayer is not heard, as it is written: "Even though you make many prayers, I will not hear; your hands are full of blood" <note>Isaiah 1:15</note>. 6. The Repentless: A person whose sins have overwhelmed him and who prays without the humility of repentance; his prayer is not heard, as it is written: "And his prayer shall be a sin." One who takes all these matters that hinder prayer to heart and then prays, his prayer will be desired and accepted before the Place, Blessed be He, as it is written: "You will prepare their heart; You will cause Your ear to hear" <note>Psalm 10:17</note>.

In Chapter 30, one who needs to enter the synagogue to call a child or a friend should first enter and recite a little bit of scripture or a tradition, and then call his friend, so that he does not enter in a state of panic for a mundane matter. If he forgets his study, let him return... the matter of listening and being nourished by the words of the synagogue. Let him add a little... for those who are occupied with difficulties in this... as our rabbis explained. From the words of the *Sefer Hasidim*, one should learn what Maimonides <note>The Rambam, a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> wrote regarding one who commits a sin in this place, for it is as if he is provoking the King in His own palace. It is fitting to sit and speak in the synagogue only about the prayer itself. See what is written in the *Zohar*. How much more so during the time of prayer or the reading of the Torah—one must not speak idle words <note>original: "devarim betelim"</note>. In our many sins, how long will this be a stumbling block for us? In every city and city, they cannot protest this. It is a great bitterness. Therefore, one should not speak a holy thing in a place where the King of the World is present... and he agreed to this. We have trusted in many mercies regarding all those who speak and cause damage to the public. Through this, the glory of the Lord is hidden in the land. May all the people give and be included, and may they no longer testify falsely...

Regarding those people who pray from within [the congregation] and have established the custom to buy a permanent place in the synagogue... for they are like those who dwell in the King's palace... and from what has changed in the world... to withdraw and answer from the depths of the heart to build blessings from within... one who does not remember this... let it be known to you that while he still has time to pray, he should do so, for the reward will be withheld if he delays past the fixed time. Sometimes the hour passes while he is occupied with his business. We have merited to see... that initially, one should not let the time of prayer pass because of a loss of money. It is proper to give... as I have seen in my notes. One should not err and say "on such and such a day I have to do this immediately in the morning," and then that day comes and he goes out and forgets his vow. If he did not do it, he might say "I still have time to do it," but there are those who say this is called a "debt," and some say it is not a debt. This is the essence of what is written in the *Shulchan Aruch* <note>The Code of Jewish Law.</note>. These are the "Pillars of Service" and prayer. With the joy of intention, may the Lord build for us the House of the Sanctuary, to be for us a name and a praise.

It is written "And the man was astonished at her," and they were standing by the well. Rashi explains that she hinted at the Ten Commandments. If so, in this giving, there was a hint to the receiving of the Torah. And he chose the trait of loving-kindness specifically because any Torah that does not have acts of kindness within it is like having no spirit. And as for the saying "great is acts of loving-kindness," it is greater than charity, for charity involves only one's money, but kindness involves both one's person and one's money, and it is for both the rich and the poor...

And you might wonder, "Does this apply to all types of rewards?" <note>The text is questioning if the reward is the same regardless of the recipient's worthiness.</note> Scripture says: "How precious is Your loving-kindness" and its entire explanation will follow, even if there are poor people, for Scripture says: "And the loving-kindness of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting." • **And Rashi explains** • that the statement about "all rewards being difficult" refers to charity being given impulsively, where "unworthy poor" <note>original: "עניים שאינם מהוגנים" (aniyim she-einam mehuganim); people who claim to be poor but are not, or who act wickedly.</note> happen to be the ones receiving it... and he concludes that a teacher said regarding marriage and its cover, etc., "Let them be overthrown before You; deal with them in the time of Your anger" <note>A quote from Jeremiah 18:23. The Talmud interprets this to mean that when God is angry, He causes people to give their charity to unworthy recipients so they receive no divine merit.</note> before the Holy One, Blessed be He. This is the will of the world: that they should be like people who are unworthy and will not receive a reward.

And this is what they relied upon because it is written: "And the loving-kindness of the Lord is from everlasting" upon those who love Him. Which "charity exalts a nation"? It is the good that ascends upward. But "kindness" <note>original: "חסד" (chesed)</note> when it is for the sake of heaven, it draws a "thread of kindness" upon him, as it is said: "And the loving-kindness of the Lord is from everlasting upon those who love Him." But for those who learn "sin," because there is no "fear of God in their hearts" and their thoughts are only evil—to mock their fellow—the Lord removes it from him. The Lord brings "unworthy poor" into the world so that they do not exhaust the reward, for there is no end to the commandment of giving charity to protect the nation.

And it fits well that the words of Rabbi Nehunia ben HaKanah explain all the views of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai: Why would charity be considered a "sin" in certain contexts, and why should they not receive a reward? Because they intend in their charity to cause "sin to the nations." <note>This refers to the interpretation that when non-Jewish nations perform acts of kindness, they sometimes do so only to boast or mock Israel.</note> On this, no reward is given, for it is "measure for measure" <note>original: "מדה כנגד מדה" (mida keneged mida)</note>—they praise us, but there is no fear of God in their loins. And they are also lacking in the world of our righteousness.

And so, Rabbi Nehunia ben HaKanah explains that the word "sin" <note>original: "חטאת" (chatat)</note> refers to the "sin-offering" sacrifice. Just as a sin-offering atones for Israel in this world, etc., the matter was that for all the views of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, and even according to his own words, there is a connection. Why did he examine the language at the end of the verse "the sin of the emptiness"? Regarding charity, the word "exalts" <note>original: "תרומם" (teromem)</note> is said for a "nation" [Israel], and at its end, the word "sin" <note>original: "חטאת" (chatat)</note> is for the "peoples." If so, it should have said "and kindness to the nations is a sin." Through the words of Rabbi Nehunia, the meaning he stated for himself can be understood. And this is what he wrote in his language: it was said thus to tell the nations that the word "kindness" <note>original: "חסד" (chesed)</note> is drawn upward. According to the words of Rabbi Nehunia, there is no room for the claims made regarding the word "kindness," for one who tastes it feels that this is the secret of the "pious one" <note>original: "חסיד" (chasid)</note> above.

And this is the explanation: "Charity exalts a nation," but "the kindness of the peoples" is like a "presents of emptiness" <note>referring to superficial or self-serving gifts</note> that does not ascend. And if one asks what the meaning is for the "sick peoples," the foundation of "kindness" and "sin" above will be good to the "taster" <note>the discerning reader</note>. To drag the word "sin" downward to assist Israel: it is an atonement like a "sin-offering" to remove the "stain of sin." And in its holiness, the Holy One atones for the world. This is the fulfillment of the word "for the peoples," so that "sin" is called "evil" upon the nations of the world and not upon Israel.

And "kindness" for him [Israel] is a "statement of kindness." If it were written that their reward is "paid out," it would follow this order: Charity would be similar to atonement like a sin-offering. And it is called "from all," which is a "drop" from above. And "charity in falsehood" is a "bad pair," a verse that does not prove anything. For sacrifices only atone for "unintentional sins," but charity atones even for "willful sins." Since sacrifices are like "sins" and the like, "exaltation" and "charity" among the nations are difficult. Charity in the world is as it is written. If so, charity has many more "good levels" than sacrifices. And according to the one who "tastes" <note>interprets</note>, it would imply that charity and sacrifices are equal. Therefore, the order is interrupted, placing "kindness" and "sin" within the word "peoples."

And it fits well that the first teacher explains that because there will be "added joy" to his words, they require our interpretation of "His kingdom." And to the peoples, "on the condition that my sons live," etc. <note>A reference to the Talmudic idea that if a person says "I give this charity so that my children may live," it is still considered a full act of righteousness for a Jew, but for a non-Jew, it is considered self-serving.</note>. For the sake of explanation, the fourth [sage] explains that they have no reward since they "mock their fellow." Another explains "kindness" as a "measure from above," and therefore the nations of the world have no reward. And all of them agreed with the words of Rabbi Nehunia, for according to his words, it is answered why it changed from "excision" <note>original: "כריתה" (keritah)</note>. And all the verses and interpretations will be correctly settled. Therefore, there is no desire in these words [for argument].

And regarding this matter, David [King David] hinted in his saying: "To You, Lord, belongs kindness, for You reward..." and "I will fulfill my vows to the Lord in the presence of all His people, in the courts of the house of the Lord, in the midst of Jerusalem." And it is difficult for me: at first, he speaks directly to God, saying "To You belongs kindness," but within the same speech, he says "vows to the Lord," speaking in the third person rather than saying "I will fulfill my vows *to You*." This will be understood by the phrase "in the presence of all His people." And it seems to me, based on the Gemara [Talmud] in Rosh Hashanah, that the rabbis taught: it is proven from this that there is a "positive commandment," etc., as they vowed a vow to the Lord to return these sin-offerings, guilt-offerings, burnt-offerings, and peace-offerings. Like the "vow of the poor," which are these "holy things for the maintenance of the Temple." Consider all these words in these verses. First, he mentions charity by saying "To You belongs kindness," and afterward the "vows" he accepted. And because of this, he mentions "kindness to the Lord," hinting at the perfection and the completeness of the "Prepared One" <note>God</note>... and it is difficult in our understanding also of this language. And there he mentions "in the courts of the Lord's house," which is the matter of the "holy things for Temple maintenance." And about everything, he said "in the presence of all His people," for he was their answer... not against the Lord to uphold charity, which is hinted at in this specifically, and what is in secret... and after

one who occupies himself with charity is as if he sits [with God], and despite all this, he stands and is obligated to give. It will be good for him to see with his eyes the "hand of protection" in goodness, and from goodness to merit for all the good, and to merit for refuge.

And it seems to me that they explained this: that anyone who gives to "scholars" <note>original: "לומדים" (lomedim)</note>, all of them go to the "Place" [God]. And each and every one sought to establish his reasoning regarding the "accident of kindness" to scholars. And it will be answered why each one takes the language of the verse as he says. And Rashi of blessed memory wrote that the dispute between the Rabbis and the Teacher, etc., and their intention was that one is obligated to support the "strength of the work" through him, etc. Blessed is He who enjoys this thing in the verses! For the verse at the end of the "Great Level" is "the end for you in the gift." They occupy themselves in order to fulfill the work, and by this merit "I have called by name," and "a king and his queen" <note>A mystical reference to the divine attributes</note> acquired this.

And afterward came Rabbi Joshua, and on the Sabbath his intention was to give a "reason for praise" to this, for there is a verse in Psalms saying: "Righteousness exalts a nation" with the word "nation" [Israel]. And he said thus: "And kindness to the scholars," mentioning the language of "scholars." And because of this, he returned and brought the beginning of the verse to decide the division between a nation and the "sinners." And this is the "voice of the bitter destruction" <note>referring to a spiritual plague or downfall</note>, adding to the words of Rabbi Eleazar to say: and the nations, in their giving of charity—even a full verse is missing—and "charity" and the word "sin," even without the purpose of protection... Why should they sin in the world? And in their language, they intend them for "kindness." Therefore, all their words are "strength and division" like the words whose intention is to draw and extend a "terrible kindness" to the "signs" <note>symbols or omens</note> between the "annulment" and the "obligation of the king" and his intention. For in the end, that he supports his kingdom alone will not help them from the "false kindness" whose horns are buried out in the open. Therefore, they are crowned with "jewelry," etc., for the king's obligation. And in his merit, so that they will be "subjugated," they support his kingdom. And "from then he shall write" it for good witnesses. Therefore, it is "kindness for them" to take the words of "compulsion" <note>performing commandments out of social pressure rather than devotion</note> on the condition of receiving a reward.

And he said thus against Rabban Gamliel, etc., any taking of the word "sin" that said "and the kindness of the peoples is a sin." Why mention the language of "sin" <note>original: "חטאת" (chatat)</note> and not the word "iniquity" or "transgression"? For in truth, the essence of the matter did not come to lighten the thing. For it is "his" to give as a gift that is not a gift; his voice is to "empty" it. Only this "seizing of the generation" is a seizing of the language from the "four." And in this manner, we understand in our Mishnah: "insolence" and "full of pennies," and "there is no Sela [coin]." And "Israel in four parts" <note>Refers to social categories or legal divisions in the Jewish community</note>. Thus they said to him: a standing at the end of the language, that there were in Jerusalem "actors" and "shepherds" and "grooms" who were "diminishing in destruction" on top of the key. Rabbi Jose says it was a "market of wool," etc. And in the body of the law, there is no disagreement; whether it was in this "market of actors" or in this "market of wool," only this one says it was in this place and that one says it was in that place.

And the intention of Rabban Gamliel was only to explain the word "sin" mentioned in the verse. And because of this, he returned to say that they only "strengthen to erase." Therefore, he seized the beginning of the verse: "Righteousness exalts a nation." And this is in the way the *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, author of a major code of Jewish law</note> wrote on the portion of *Bereshit* [Genesis]: without the "Name," this prayer will be good above and not descend below. And if they come to the "door" that a person wants, it is the one that stands in the measure below. And after everything, "charity" that he wrote—this is a "righteous man who is strengthened." And everyone who "seizes" falls into Gehinnom [Hell]. And because of this, he said "Righteousness exalts a nation"—they will strengthen their hands for them, and their "elevations" and "jewelry" will be above in this—this is a "righteous man who is strengthened." And "the kindness of the peoples" is equal to its opposite and will bring down to Gehinnom in the revelation of their nature. And in old age, it is called "sin" for the "transgressors." Regarding the "diminishing of sin," the verse accurately mentions "sin" to them.

And after Rabban Gamliel, they still needed the "Saviors," for it settled a great matter. But here we are speaking of one who learns not for its own sake [but] on the condition of being called "Rabbi," etc. And this is not Rabbi Eliezer the Modi'ite: "all the charity they do is to mock their fellow." And this is true in the study of Torah as well—its power is like "empty chaff." Therefore, it is for "some of them." And the main "purification" of the work is from the fact that the Holy One, Blessed be He, exalts and praises Israel, while they [the nations] are cast down in the eyes of the Place, as he brings "he who curses," etc. And the Lord will know when He examines, for "their sin is before Him." And in this matter, they are "mockers." And because of this, he brings the beginning of the verse: "Righteousness exalts a nation." And this "causes upward," while for the "scholars," the acceptance of the king's mouth—this "mocks his fellow."

# Preface of the Eminent Scholar <note>Hebrew: *Gaon* — a title for an exceptionally brilliant rabbinic leader</note>, the Author, of Blessed Memory

<margin>Bestowing kindness with one's physical person and one's reputation * and he shall have descendants who endure for his house and for his fellow. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: A person is permitted to say he will give a *kav* <note>A dry measure of volume, roughly 1.4 liters</note> to a poor person but in truth gives more, and this is pleasing to God because of it * and Rashi <note>The primary medieval commentator on the Talmud</note> of blessed memory explained "to do good for your house" as meaning he devoted the end of his days to kindness for his fellow. Furthermore, it is stated there that Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: Anyone who performs kindness for the children of Israel, three things are granted to him... a person should act beyond the letter of the law and not be overly exacting with his neighbor.</margin>

<margin>It is an obligation for a person to help his fellows in times of danger.</margin>

<margin>Charity is great, but the Sages said the performance of kindness is even greater; three things were said regarding its superiority.</margin>

<margin>It is good to practice these principles and to give charity in secret whenever possible.</margin>

* It is well known what the Sages said in the chapter *Elu Megalchin* <note>A chapter in the Talmudic tractate Moed Katan</note> regarding the commandment of performing kindness, as the Gemara concludes citing the School of Elijah: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav, etc. And Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: Anyone who performs kindness for his children and grandchildren merits to sustain everyone because of his kindness. This kindness is expressed in three ways: first, with one’s physical person <note>labor or presence</note>; second, with one’s money; and third, with one’s thought—when one thinks of the well-being of his fellow and seeks to find funds for him. This "kindness of thought" is powerful and a great deed, as we say: Rabbi Yohanan and Resh Lakish were traveling on the road, etc. And there they said that anyone who performs kindness for his fellow in thought, thinking well of him, the Holy One, Blessed be He, gives him a reward and establishes his deeds. Kindness with one’s money and person is well known, for they contain many benefits. Our Master, Yosef, wrote in *The Royal Throne* <note>referring to the work *Kisse Ha-Malkhut*</note>, chapter 4 on Charity, that performing kindness is greater than charity for several reasons. The first is that whoever prioritizes kindness and charity at the end of his days will not need to rely on other people. There is a secret regarding money... the scholar wrote that concerning this it is said, "the blessing of the wicked is a stumbling block"... it is proper for you to engage in the performance of kindness, even if it involves a loss of money. If this causes a loss of money, let him be satisfied with it, as is explained in the house of Joseph... regarding the law brought by the authorities... one should not be stingy or prevent the poor from making a mistake in their favor... and all this is good for the sake of God. Our Master Yosef also wrote in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud that one should even place oneself in a potential danger to save a life... and it is proper for every man to pursue kindness for his fellow with all his strength, whether in secret or in public. As the Sages of blessed memory expounded on the verse regarding the daughters of Laban... surely, if the world stands specifically on kindness, and if there is no kindness, Heaven forbid, the world would be destroyed... Charity is for the living, but kindness is for both the living and the dead. Charity is for the poor, but kindness is for both the poor and the rich. Charity is with money, but kindness is with both money and one’s physical person. Rabbi [the author] ruled: Why is the performance of kindness considered superior to charity? In all languages, if you search, you will find it is said "the performance of kindness is greater than charity." This is explained in three ways... because one merits to have children through it. It is mentioned in the book *Leket Yosher* regarding the people of Israel, that it is proper for this portion to atone for all who left Egypt. It is also beautifully stated in *The Book of the Pious* <note>*Sefer Hasidim*</note>, section 877, and from here they instituted that those who merit through charity should do good for those who have already died; it benefits the dead when the living pray for them and give charity on their behalf. Charity saves from death in this world and the world to come. Therefore, if the performance of kindness is greater than charity, one might ask: can charity also benefit the dead? Indeed, kindness is greater because it is performed for the dead themselves <note>e.g., burial</note>, whereas charity is not given *to* the dead, but rather given *on behalf of* the dead. Furthermore, charity is for the poor, while kindness is for both the poor and the rich—such as when a wealthy person travels from place to place and runs out of funds, becoming "poor" in that moment, and one helps him.

<column-break/>

As for what was said at the beginning—that charity is with money while kindness is with both money and one’s body—this is because Rashi explained in the chapter *Elu Megalchin* that when it says "Abraham believed in God and He counted it to him as righteousness <note>Hebrew: *Tzedakah*</note>," Rashi explains that He counted it as a merit. This "righteousness" mentioned regarding Abraham refers to his faith, which is a physical/spiritual act of the person. Even though it is called "kindness" in other places, it informs us that this is another explanation of the verse. God gave Abraham and Sarah children in the merit of the charity/kindness they performed... The Holy One, Blessed be He, gives a person righteous children because of the charity he performs with his money. Therefore, kindness is greater than charity because charity is only what one does with his money, while kindness involves the body. May a person remember and act, for this kindness done with intention is like charity. Sometimes one gives charity through struggle... and he who speaks kindly to the poor is blessed with kindness... Therefore, every person of heart should give charity with a generous face and perform kindness, removing all strife... It is proper to add charity to kindness and a tithe <note>Hebrew: *Ma'aser*</note> to kindness, for through the "tithe" one is tied to the Kingdom of the Holy One, Blessed be He, which is not the case with charity alone. From all this, one can learn... and those who hide their money are criticized... and why should I lengthen the discussion on the virtues of charity? Every wise-hearted person will find merit in the book of my lord and father, of blessed memory, in his work on the Megillah <note>The Scroll of Esther</note>, where he spoke much and expanded on the matters of charity and tithes... I also have labored on this pillar of the world. Although I have much to say, I have already preceded my words in my other writings... this is only to show a bit of our longing for the honor and glory of my lord, my father, may his light shine... and I add that I hope his salvation is near, and that I may grow old in virtue, and may it be

# Preface of the Eminent Scholar, Son of the Author, the Pillar of Law

<column-break/>

<margin>See the *Intent of the Additional Offerings* <note>original: "Kavanat ha-Musafin"</note> except regarding the Afternoon Prayer.</margin>
While he was occupied with the Torah and with merit, fulfilling the verse "And I will arise," etc. (Psalms 119:62), and taking what pertains to the matter of "relief and deliverance" (Esther 4:14). And we must truly ask: why did Jacob delay in his heart the command to "Arise and go up," until the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to him: "Arise, go up to Bethel," etc. (Genesis 35:1). It is even more difficult to understand why his honor did not bring him to arrive, as it is written: "And Jacob arrived whole <note>original: *shalem* — meaning complete, safe, or peaceful</note> at the city of Shechem," etc., "and he built an altar there" (Genesis 33:18-20). This was done with a blessing, and yet that which he had promised by moving his lips <note>i.e., his vow to return to Bethel</note> he did not fulfill. 

The matter will be explained according to the principle of "reward for all" in the third chapter of Mishnah Middot: Rabbi Meir said, "Whoever is whole <note>*shalem*</note> brings Peace Offerings <note><term>Shelamim</term>: A category of sacrifice where the meat is shared between the altar, the priests, and the owner; the name shares a root with "whole" and "peace."</note>, but one who is not whole does not bring Peace Offerings." I only know about Peace Offerings; from where do we know about an animal that is impure? From where is it exempt? From where is it a "treasure" <note>special property</note>, and from where for a firstborn, etc.? 

And regarding the Passover offering, from where do we include three, and the Guilt Offering, etc.? From where do we include birds and meal-offerings? It is written: "Peace offerings are his sacrifice" (Leviticus 3:1); as long as his kind is whole, he may bring a sacrifice. This concludes the citation. The scholar relied on this because Jacob, on his journey from the house of Laban to his father’s house, did not intend to offer a sacrifice, knowing the reasons why he might have sinned in his thoughts—perhaps because he transgressed the prohibition of delaying a vow. He should not have vowed meat <note>referring to a sacrifice</note> according to the words of Rabbi Meir, for it is written "always with meat," and he was not "whole," and it is not fitting to offer a sacrifice in a time of distress. 

However, after the wars with Esau at the house, "And Jacob arrived whole <note>*shalem*</note> at the city of Shechem." Rashi explains this as being whole in his Torah, his wealth, and his body. Therefore, he built an altar there with a blessing of the heart, because he was whole. He did not merely act out of fear, as another sage explained regarding the wilderness, where he thought that immediately a tithe would come upon him. He merited his daughter and his possessions, another tithe for his money, and Levi was hidden from me to bring him out, and I am in a state of prayer and danger and impurity, etc., and my house is different, etc. 

I intended the second reason for him not fulfilling his vow: a statement that he was not "whole," and it is not fitting to sacrifice. This is hinted at in the verse "And he shone for him," and even more so when God said: "Jacob, arise, go up to Bethel and dwell there." Why the word "dwell there"? Rather, the Holy One, Blessed be He, hinted to him: do not fear and do not dread regarding the tithe of his money, or regarding the character of Ishmael. But when one takes a man in jest, the anger of Joseph leaped upon him, for his brothers were adversarial and said: "Is it not enough for the righteous..." etc. When he is found "whole" in his blessing, he is permitted to offer sacrifices. 

But because he did not fulfill his vow, the Holy One, Blessed be He, hinted to him regarding a small "dwelling." If he asks how he blessed, it is because of my brother and what belongs to the garment. When a person is in a state of trembling and vows in a time of trouble, he must then fulfill the vow. And there it is precisely explained: in his business, in his pressure, and in his time of relief. Because in the vow he was more [distressed], therefore in the time of relief, "Jacob said to his household," etc. I place before you: from the power of the wilderness, in a time of trouble it was permitted for him to vow meat, and in a time of relief he returned to fulfill his vow. This is hinted at in these verses: "And they shall sacrifice peace offerings," for it is known that the word "Peace Offerings" <note>*Shelamim*</note> implies one who is whole <note>*Shalem*</note> and has no bitterness. "And they shall sacrifice peace offerings," for in the word "Peace Offerings" there is a hint that one should not offer a sacrifice unless in pressure, or when whole, or in life. If you say, "And they shall sacrifice peace offerings," his intention in the verse is to be whole at the time of the slaughter. But at the time of the vow, he does not fear being only "whole" in his completeness during the time of trouble; it is easy for him to vow his vow and merit. On this, the Tosafot <note>Medieval Talmudic commentators</note> ask: the verse says "not here," to forbid vowing meat. But in the wilderness it was permitted by way of the road, in a place of danger. Jacob’s vow was of his own mind, for he found in his soul "And they shall sacrifice peace offerings," that when you find a time of relief, you must be precise. From this, Hizkuni <note>13th-century French commentator</note> explained: he shall be whole and intend to avoid the stumbling block. Jacob fulfilled his vow because it was in a time of trouble. 

And this is what he said regarding the division of the Burnt Offering and the Sacrifice; he stated the foundation of the Burnt Offering and the Sacrifice, and if so, "at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting," etc. And it is written, and our Sages of blessed memory said, to say a Psalm in the name of... regarding the matter of the external dwellings.

<margin>See from this regarding a Burnt Offering or a Sacrifice.</margin>
* It seems to me this can be answered, but it is possible that in the Midrash on *Zevachim* <note>Sacrifices</note>, in the chapter "He who Slaughters and Offers Up," it includes two people who asked regarding a vow and offered it up—they are liable. And this is the intent: to inform us that two are liable, as it is written and as is adjacent. One who offers it for a commoner is not, and two are not diminished when they take what is forbidden. The Torah says, according to Rabbi Jochanan: "I say it is one and not two." If so, what does this teach us? It includes the "Torah in the language of men." And I have a difficulty with the opinion that says if two opened [the animal] and one offered it up, he is liable. If so, there is no difference between one who offers it or two who offer it. In truth, it mentioned by chance "whoever offers a burnt offering or sacrifice" in the singular, implying a single person who offers it. It should have said "they shall offer," implying even if two offer a single limb, they are liable.

<margin>See regarding "they shall offer a burnt offering or sacrifice."</margin>
And I can answer this, for we have an established Mishnah in the chapter of Rabbi Eliezer the Modi'ite: regarding a Synagogue... if two [performed the act] they are exempt; if one could not [do it alone] and two performed it, they are liable. And Rabbi S. exempts. Rashi explains that "two who performed it" refers to two engaged in the work... And we find that he exempts even on the Sabbath. Even if two opened a limb, they are liable, and do not wonder that he is liable because one could not have offered it up alone; if he was able to strengthen it and keep it alive and offer it alone...

<margin>See the intent of the Weeks <note>*Shavuot*</note> except regarding the Afternoon Prayer.</margin>
**T**he root of all the pious. And there is the group that is not in it—it is a living soul, and surrounding it is nothing but Isaac. Take and place a soul that hopes in the bones of Hillel, and its vitality is in the circuits of Kindness in the hidden worlds. He will forever provide refuge and rejoice and strengthen Kindness and its direction and preparation. And for this, he did not provide refuge in the wilderness... so that the Israelites would not grow weak and die. At the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, for the Divine Presence <note>Shekhinah</note> is whole, which was for the leading of every matter. Not like the "meat of desire" <note><term>Basar Ta'avah</term>: meat eaten for pleasure rather than for sacrificial purposes</note> that was accompanied only in the wilderness... as it says in the portion of *Vayikra* <note>Leviticus</note>: the souls of the wicked are harmful spirits to the world. But it is not so to give spirit, for in it is the soul... and besides this, for in the *Sefer ha-Yashar* it explains on "When a man brings an offering" (Leviticus 1:2), that an animal does not offer itself, only a man... This is exactly it: when the souls of the wicked are harmful spirits to the world, for the soul of the wicked is the soul of a beast. And behold, what is written... it is not difficult. 

And it seems to me to explain by way of a hint: that in the wilderness, "meat of desire" was forbidden, only Peace Offerings specifically. This is to show that it belongs to the Most High... and the word "property" <note>*nechas*</note> in this world is like a harm. Our Sages of blessed memory said: at the end of a person's life, his property is taken... and there is a hint in the verses: "When he shall sin further or in error," etc. "And to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting he did not bring it"—it does not say "to offer," but to suggest the verse's meaning regarding his portion. 

However, the first difficulties remain in their place to settle these exactings before you. And I have traveled to learn regarding the matter of a man... as it is written: "When you call to a Great One, it shall not be so," and it is written: "It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not fulfill" (Ecclesiastes 5:4). Regarding the Nazirite <note>one who takes a vow of abstinence</note>, Rabbi Meir says: "One should say 'it is better than this,'" and he speaks of the Nazir and offering it up, etc. And the Tosafot said... since it was offered in the wilderness... there is nothing better than being a Nazirite at all... Since the verse calls the Nazirite to be holy through a vow... this is even from home forever. And they can consecrate and turn away from it and bring about a stumbling block... according to Rabbi Meir, who says there is no "good" in a vow... even if he brings it in completeness... the Israelites ate Peace Offerings in the wilderness. And one can say that since they were in the wilderness, they were in need of every woman... and it is written: "And Jacob vowed a vow," and "That which I have vowed." And one can say regarding the souls of the wicked... "And Jacob vowed a vow" to say to future generations that they should be Nazirites in a time of trouble. 

And in this way, you shall choose the verses... Behold, the elder [says]... "To the entrance of the Tent of Meeting they did not bring it to offer a sacrifice." And one should be precise: why does it say "they did not bring a sacrifice"? Rather, it is to ask about vowing a vow... as the Hizkuni explains on the portion of *Vayikra*: "A male without blemish shall he offer" (Leviticus 1:3). A person should be afraid of the curse and the offering. "To the entrance of the Tent of Meeting they did not bring it to offer a sacrifice"—this does not refer to the sacrifice itself, but to the location, that they should not sacrifice it except at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting... so that he does not come to misuse sacred property <note><term>Me'ilah</term>: the sin of misappropriating sanctified items</note>... "So that they shall bring their sacrifices and bring them to the Lord at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting" (Leviticus 17:5). Now, the body of the tithe is as mentioned... and it does not say "until you sacrifice it at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting." The answer of the Tosafot... to bring Peace Offerings... the verse says "So that they shall bring their sacrifices," and "they shall sacrifice peace offerings," using a doubled language. There is a foundation for this doubling of "they shall sacrifice" and "sacrifices of peace offerings." And specifically regarding Jacob, this was the end of the Peace Offerings... after Jacob's vow...
