# Author’s Introduction to the Work "Pillar of Justice"

Even after He—may He be blessed—helped him, they are exempt just as in the case of the Sabbath. Therefore, he learned for the Festivals, for the 14th <note>The 14th of the month of Nisan, the eve of Passover</note>, and for the Passover concerning his exemption. For those who are lacking, he would conclude the law regarding unintentional sins through one between according to what is missing, and he shall not fear; they shall rejoice. And there it is written, "dread and fear shall fall upon them" <note>Exodus 15:16</note>. And it is said "a man, a man" <note>Hebrew: *Ish Ish*, a doubling often used in the Torah to include all categories of people</note> to include specific groups, vows, and donations among Israel. And these many of "a man, a man" stand by the power of the Holy One, Blessed be He; whereas the "thread of the captivity" <note>A reference to the exile or the collective fate of the people</note> depends entirely on Israel, as our Sages of blessed memory said. And they saw from His heights, as it is written in the teaching of "a man, a man," for if so, why the language of "a man, a man"? To teach that the responsibility for the matter falls upon the community—meaning upon Israel—not like those mentioned above where the increase of waters was difficult for the land. And according to Rabbi Joseph, who said that the Torah speaks in the language of human beings, the term "heights" is also part of the teaching, and the phrase "a man, a man" implies that the speech of "a man, a man" is directed to them as they speak in human language, just as all people do.

<margin>A correct reason regarding the one who interpreted "which you shall set before them" <note>Exodus 21:1</note> as "before them" and not before gentiles; and the one who said "before laypeople."</margin>

And let us return to our subject: after we wrote what our teacher wrote, "which you shall set before them"—before them and even before gentiles as a merit. And this is based on what was explained, meaning: why was the portion of the laws <term>Mishpatim; the civil and criminal laws of the Torah</term> placed after the laws of the Altar? But a person who sees the verse might mistakenly think that because they were placed next to the Altar, the Altar—what is the Altar? Just as the Altar atones for sons, so too these laws. Or perhaps to include thieves and those who measure dishonestly, etc. And if so, that the laws should apply to gentiles as well. Therefore, it says "these are the ordinances which you shall set before *them*" <note>Meaning the Israelites</note> and not before gentiles. And the one who says "before them" and not before laypeople <note>Unlearned or non-ordained judges</note> bases this on the fact that we find that the Sages were given authority over capital cases and from here they derived it, etc. And this is simple: that one does not use the terminology of "He will provide" <note>A common phrase in Talmudic logic</note>. According to my humble opinion, see in the commentary I wrote on the first fruits of Rabbi Yochanan, who said one does not write it for a specific time because of the Tractate Ketubot, etc. And I said in my explanations regarding the "juice of the wine," as written there, that it is proper to rely on the statement: "and you shall set aside from it a heave-offering for the Lord" to the priest. And the explanation of the lack of a priest was eternal, or because there is no one who decided, and not the language of the "juxtaposition of the Sanhedrin <term>the high court of 71 sages</term> to the Altar," the place where they build the stones there. And you shall further learn that after they approached the wine, they also approached the priest with the land. Thus, you are not permitted to appoint a judge who is not an expert. Therefore it said, "which you shall set before them"—before expert and ordained judges, and not before laypeople.

# Chapter Seventeen
->Introduction to the Writing: Pillar of Justice<-

<margin>And the matter of the juxtaposition: why the portion of the laws was placed next to the Altar to the House of Witnesses.</margin>

**The verse** "And these are the ordinances which you shall set before them" is difficult. Why were the ordinances mentioned here? Perhaps because the portion of the laws was placed next to the Altar. And from there, it was arranged. Perhaps a reason can be given why indeed the portion of the laws was joined to the Altar? "Before them" means that even these were given at Sinai. Why should they not be said at Sinai? For they are the "trousers of the Torah," as explained in the book of Joseph in the book *Keseh De-kharsya* <note>The Throne of the Chair</note>. Therefore, he said, starting the portion with the Hebrew slave <term>Eved Ivri; a Jewish man sold into service for debt or theft</term>, to include the laws mentioned in the portion. The matter of the juxtaposition to the Altar seems to follow what Maimonides <note>The Rambam, 12th-century scholar</note> wrote in Chapter 6 of the *Laws of Entering the Temple*: that the Great Sanhedrin was established in the Chamber of Hewn Stone <note>Lishkat HaGazit; the meeting place of the Sanhedrin in the Temple</note>, and the essence of their work was to clarify between the Shekhinah <term>the Divine Presence</term> and His light, and to clarify the priests regarding their lineage and blemishes. Every priest in whom a blemish of lineage was found would dress in black and wrap himself in black and depart. And anyone found to be valid would dress in white and wrap in white and enter with his brethren. And so we find in the Mishnah at the end of Tractate Middot. If so, the primary activity of the Sanhedrin was sitting for the sake of the priests to be near the Altar. On this, it points out the juxtaposition of the "ordinances" of the Sanhedrin to the Altar: there they would clarify and fix who is fit to offer sacrifices. Therefore they are joined. And as for the difficulty of why it opened with the Hebrew slave first, it is possible to answer according to what is written in the *Hagahot Maimoniot* <note>Citations on Maimonides' code</note> Chapter 2 of the *Laws of Sanhedrin*: "In the Jerusalem Talmud: Rav Mana was bothered by those who were appointed [as judges] because of money. He said: there is no law for your oxen. He said to him: 'A man, a man'—is there someone special for me? There is no law if they take a pledge from me." Meaning, he would not receive gifts. And there it is brought in the *Hasagot* of the Shulchan Aruch in the name of Section 8, the law that one who does not have money, or any judge who is appointed because of his money, is forbidden to serve as a judge. And why did it start with the Hebrew slave? Because the beginning of one who is appointed by force is this: "And these are the ordinances which you shall set before them." It is precise there: "before *them*" and not before gentiles, and not before laypeople. And it says "If you buy a Hebrew slave" to teach us this reason: that one who goes out to judgment is exempt from proof from the laws. If he has no slave, then let these two ordinances be before him, for who is fit for his appointment as a judge? And as for what is written there, "you shall not go up by steps" <note>Exodus 20:23</note>, and also the difficulty of "before them," it can be explained that the ordinances of the Lord are truth, they are righteous altogether. For it says that the ordinances the Lord spoke are truth, etc., in a known matter. Since they are divided into 76 <note>Possibly referring to the 70 nations or a numeric code</note>, lest one divide the reward to holiness, and these 76 said the lot falls on so-and-so for a severe death, and on so-and-so for a light death. But let it be in their custom to agree together on this, to punish the sinner for his crime according to their wisdom. This is not the case with the "ordinances of the Lord," which are true and righteous altogether, with correct reasons for every law and judgment.

<column-break/>

And the reason is that when a different master rules over him, and now according to the imagination that began after he sinned and trespassed, he was sent away. And further, I must introduce to you that which is missing from the "Covenant of the Brothers" <note>possibly a reference to Levirate marriage or a specific work</note>: Ben Azzai says it is said and stated from what is stated, "you shall not be," and what is the benefit of this? Like a master, just as the benefit with an animal in the book is no, even the master in his silence, if not so, then the master goes out. And is it because they relied on a redeemer... [the text here discusses specific legal derivations regarding animals and humans]. Behold, according to Ben Azzai, the reason is that through the commandments we learn the rules of logic <note>Hebrew: *middot*</note>, from the juxtaposition of the sorceress to the one who lies with an animal. And this is the intent of the verse "the ordinances of the Lord"—the ordinances and the laws that are explained explicitly in the Torah. But these [others] are the "judgments together," meaning the derivations and juxtapositions of the laws also come to teach one who claims from one who was joined to him... And this is the explanation of "which you shall set before them," meaning it shall be before them in the sense that the goal shall always be before your eyes, just as a person's goal is his sleep there... so that they will know that everything is with truth, justice, and action, and not in the "trousers" <note>External appearances or superficiality</note> of earthy thoughts, which confuse all knowledge of the Torah from everything written and not by error.

Indeed, one can answer the matter of the juxtaposition in the Torah: in the foundation of the portion of *Mishpatim*, three things were written where they were joined... and after it mentioned the exemption, "and these are the ordinances which you shall set before them" [is explained] by what I wrote here. And he wrote that the Torah should be 7 and 7. And the Lord, what are the merits of the daughter of the Lord? And he brought from the rest of the portions this benefit through the righteous one. And so, how much is this portion praised, and from it are the laws. And joined to this Midrash is another Midrash: Rabbi said in the name of the Sifrei: "Just as the Holy One, Blessed be He, warned about the laws, so He warned about the judges." And if so, the law of the sorceress... is in the matter. Because the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to the prophets as he said... from Sinai. The words regarding the Hebrew slave... "If you buy a Hebrew slave," the Holy One, Blessed be He, said: "Just as I sold myself to you, so he is mine..." and he stood for ten years... and it was difficult for him that you learned to follow this one. And three days... just as it is written in the city regarding the redemption and regarding the sacrifice of the law... why did he say in the name of the Sifrei? And here it seems that this Midrash is a commentary on the previous holy Midrash, just as it is said in Tractate Menachot... but I must introduce to you what the singer of the portion of Yitro wrote: "Do not murder, do not steal, do not bear false witness." In the case of one who returns a lost object by mistake... if they are to be exempted for themselves, it does not seem to me... for it implies that it is only for the one who small in crime in his standing, even though he transgressed the Torah. But when he is involved in the matter to say he is exempt, to mention... perhaps to the illness, the reason is because he is fit... to return it to him... and as long as the reason is decided... even if in the future, judges for others in roads and paths... for even the reason that he guides to write his mind... as I wrote... "Do not act wickedly until..." the reason is stated in the name of the Sifrei. And he admits to the Torah... for you did not decide... he transgressed the Torah already... and he made the fruits of the house of his friend... and now, etc. In all worldly matters, but in the Torah it is permitted to be; the Torah is free, its reasons are high... as the judge said... until the Midrash in what is proven in this portion, and all the laws are mentioned... for the covenant, for the time you will open by this... against what he said "when you cut," etc. And remember the Sabbath day, for in six days the Lord made, etc. And this is the change of the Sabbath... and why did he mention the commandments "I am the Lord your God who brought you out of the house of slaves" in order to speak about the law of the Hebrew slave... from there the Holy One, Blessed be He, created the world in days... what he completed in the ten commandments... and also the matter of the daughters... if he does not do these three things for her... and the rebuke... also from his place in the speech of the verse... "when a man sells his daughter as a slave"... and it is in his heart... and he went up in judgment in his light... to interpret with his mother-in-law, with his wife whom he took. And what is more, the five commandments from his place should be a brother... for the slave. And they explained it in the matter of "so he shall do for her." <header>Introduction of the Scholar, the Son of the Author, Pillar of Justice</header>

# Introduction of the Scholar, the Son of the Author, Pillar of Justice

<margin>See the *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "Sefer HaMoreh" by Maimonides</note>; and regarding the hidden path <note>Kabbalah</note>, see *Toldot Yitzhak*; see page 7, column 3, and in the commentary on the chapter "One Who Attains."</margin>
"You will surely wear out..." etc., "for the thing is too heavy for you; you cannot do it alone..." <note>Exodus 18:18</note>. It is difficult to understand why the word "now" is used here. Regarding the Blessed One, it says, "Be a representative for the people before God, and bring the matters before God" <note>Exodus 18:19</note>. And there were judgments before Him. Regarding "bringing the matters," Rashi <note>The preeminent 11th-century commentator</note> explains these are "matters of dispute." It is difficult to understand what distinction he makes between "judgments" and "matters of dispute." Furthermore, it is difficult to understand why it says again, "And you shall warn them..." etc., and "You shall make known to them the way they shall go and the work they shall do" <note>Exodus 18:20</note>. What does "make known" add? Could he not have included everything in "and you shall warn"? Why is the word "make known" necessary? It is also difficult to understand the phrase "which they shall go in." It is true that our Sages, of blessed memory, interpreted every single word as referring to acts of kindness, burial, and going beyond the letter of the law <note>term: <gloss>Lifnim mi-shurat ha-din</gloss>; the practice of acting more ethically or generously than the strict law requires</note>. All this was explained according to the plain meaning of the verses to resolve the phrase "and they shall go in it" according to the interpretation of the verse "and they went and they did." Rashi explains this means they received a reward for the walking as well as a reward for the actions. This hints that when he said "and you shall make known to them," there were two types of reward: the "way they shall go" refers to the walking, and the "work" refers to the actual deed. This explains the verse: the word "and you shall make known" is established.

<margin>See the *Book of Might* <note>original: "Sefer HaGevurah"</note>; and regarding the hidden path, see *Toldot Yitzhak*; see page 7, column 3, and in the commentary on the chapter "One Who Attains."</margin>
This will be explained according to the Talmud <note>original: "Gemara"</note> in the chapter "The Ship" <note>Baba Batra 73a</note>. According to the Rabbis, one does not make a decree after a decree, but rather they all stand as one. Furthermore, it is explained that his intention was to say "woe to me" because he said "woe is me" and did not say "woe to the master." The hints were clarified, and not every one of them was explained. These were disciples of the wise who were skilled in their handiwork. They said to him: "Keep God, do not say 'Samuel said to you,' Samuel bar Rav Hamnusa." From this we receive the hint that "the ways of the Lord are right; the righteous walk in them, but transgressors stumble in them" <note>Hosea 14:10</note>. Rashi explains that "the righteous walk in them" to keep the law, while "transgressors stumble" refers to those who neglect it. This is what the verse hinted to him: "and you shall make known to them the statutes," etc., to tell them "do this" and "do not do that." One who is God-fearing should not think that he is permitted to ignore any of them. They shall learn the hints from the beginning. Therefore it says "and you shall make known to them the way"—the general rule—and there you shall be prevented from violating it because of the hints. He said "they shall walk in it" to emphasize that from the start, the way of the righteous is to walk in it. He hinted that the righteous will walk in it...

<margin>An answer to the aforementioned difficulty; see the book *Nefesh HaChaim* at the end of page 66, column 3, and in the book *Meshivat Nefesh*, page 37, column 1.</margin>
...and he who wants to stumble shall stumble. This resolves the difficulties in the place where it was said to improve the matter, for it says "the ways of the Lord are right, they shall walk," etc. His entire intention was internal. For it begins in the plural "for [they] are right," and ends in the singular. This is like the Talmudic discussion of things said at once. This hints at the study of the law itself. Specifically, the beginning of the matter is difficult, and it concludes with the word "before her." It hints at the laws. It is proper to follow this, and so it was decided in the *Tur*, section 10 <note>The *Tur* is a foundational 14th-century code of Jewish law</note>. This is the meaning of "the thing is difficult." The phrase "and this" refers to the law that was already established. For in every place, the path is straightened between a man and his fellow, between the righteous and the wicked. The clarity of judgment should not be based on their own righteousness alone. This judgment is comparable to the "holy judgment" and says that the matter will be clarified. This is "and I have judged between a man and his fellow" <note>Exodus 18:16</note>. This means they will be vindicated in the judgment that clarifies the previous law, not through a simple exchange of words. Another explanation for this verse:

<margin>For more on the interpretation of the portion on this verse and in the commentary of Rabbi Isaiah di Trani, of blessed memory, see chapter 8, page 29, column 4.</margin>
This follows the Talmudic discussion brought in the *Beit Yosef* <note>A 16th-century legal commentary by Joseph Karo</note> in the section *Choshen Mishpat*, chapter 10. See there to correct the version of Rabbi Isai [di Trani]. We do not say that in this choice of judgment, the judge helps him. It does not say "they write for him" a reason to cover it, rather they write for him specifically where his merit is found through compromise. For in any place where the winner's merit is recognized, they write it for him. This hints at Moses when he said, "When they have a matter, it comes to me" <note>Exodus 18:16</note>, that they should not judge for themselves before seeking compromise. "And I make known to them the statutes of God and His laws"—meaning the reasons for the judgment will come through the law. This is an "argument from minor to major" <note>term: <gloss>Kal VaChomer</gloss>; a logical inference that if a rule applies in a less important case, it surely applies in a more important one</note>. Just as "I have judged between a man and his neighbor" through compromise, so too "I have made known to them the reasons of the law." Consider whether the hands of our ancestors were sufficient to resolve these difficulties correctly. Regarding the "deed before the law," it is written: "And Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, saw it, and rose up from the midst of the congregation, and took a spear in his hand" <note>Numbers 25:7</note>. He went after the man and stabbed him, etc. It is difficult to understand why Moses was holding the spear in his hand in the midst of the congregation with the people there...

<column-break/>

...from the midst of the congregation he took a spear from another place. This is explained according to the Talmud in the chapter "The Ship." "And Phinehas saw"—what did he see? He said to Moses, "O teacher Moses, [is this the law?]" etc. Moses said to him: "What did you see? Why did you hint to me? I saw in your way that which was sworn to be..." He said to him, "You have upheld the vow..." It is difficult to understand why he needed to look at it. What does the matter of offerings and the priest have to do with this? This is my judgment. Furthermore, it is difficult because many ask: "Thus you taught me in your way, that whoever is caught..." etc. Where did he learn this law from? Furthermore, why did he say it in the language of a question, "Did you not teach me thus?" instead of a language of obligation, "You taught me thus!"

<margin>In the name of the *Pikadon* and *Minuy* and our teacher Rabbi Isaac, portion 27, and especially regarding the way of the commandment, we have taken a hint from him through the "Rocks of the Commandment" and the Sages.</margin>
This is to resolve the matter mentioned above. The Talmud concludes there that "one who cohabits with a Midianite woman, the zealots strike him." This was handed down to Moses, and he said it was permitted. Do not say that the daughter of a Jew is forbidden to you. Rashi explains that before the giving of the Torah, Moses was in the status of a Noahide <note>term: <gloss>Ben Noach</gloss>; a non-Jew who follows the universal moral laws</note>, and when the Torah was given, they all entered the status of Israel and were included in the commandments, but she remained permitted to him. Why did he speak at length and say "In your way, let him be silent"? This is for the later scholars: Why did Moses fail with the daughter of Jethro? But one must know what was asked. They asked him if they were at peace with him or not. They treated him with the "old ones." It is a principle that a teacher precedes his student in the study of the law. "Judah was a master and he took it in his hand... and the master of a foreign god..." This refers to one who cohabits with a gentile woman. It is written, "The Lord will cut off the man who does this..." <note>Malachi 2:12</note>. This means he will have no witness among the scholars, and if he is a priest, he will have no son to bring an offering. Therefore, Phinehas hinted in his language so that the world would not think thoughts of judgment against Moses—asking why he took the daughter of Jethro. He said to him, "Did you not teach me this in your way?" hinting at Rashi's explanation that before the giving of the Torah, Moses was permitted. This was before he descended from Sinai. He still feared the "eyes of the visualists" <note>unclear: likely referring to those who judge by outward appearance</note> lest they disparage a great man like Moses our teacher, peace be upon him. In this world, they might think it was a sin for him to take Jethro's daughter. Therefore, he hinted to him from the tradition that whatever a man does that is good in his wisdom—and Moses our teacher established many disciples—the master has no rest. He said with a stout heart: "Did you not teach me, my master?" using a language of completion. That is to say, "Who is the one who would think to complain about the taking of Jethro's daughter? For did you not teach me?" meaning, "Have you not established many disciples, and they are like a city of strength?"

<margin>An answer to the difficulty of "My father-in-law, their father," etc. See *Atiyot* and similar works.</margin>
The matter of what he said—"my father-in-law, their father"—is an answer that will be explained according to the Talmud in the chapter "The Uncircumcised" <note>Yevamot 70</note> regarding the debate over who is a "Moabite" <note>referring to the prohibition of Moabites entering the assembly</note>. All those who answer ask what will be in the day that he is rewarded, who has the strength to bring to the house of the altar? It is written in the Torah that they should stand after many disciples of the wise. He said: "Anyone who does not hear this law and is precise in it, let him receive it from his house..." <margin>An answer from *Atiyot* and similar works.</margin> Fear of him stood, and they did not hear his teaching, and these were thoughts. We must check who the sign belongs to. A student of a wise man who teaches a law—is it before the deed that they asked him, or after the deed? It is understood that Rashi explains "we do not listen to him" lest, because of the actual event that happened, he inclines the law toward the transgression to permit it, and thus he would be lying. But we, the *Tosafot* <note>Medieval French/German commentators</note> there, say "before the deed," meaning specifically where he himself is personally involved in the matter. For example, if he needed to permit something for a person who was the daughter of Jethro, as it was said "a daughter of a son of one who died in the fields of the he-goats," etc. But if it is not his own survival, we should listen to him, for even though he brings a reason, it is within the law. The judgment of Phinehas was "after the deed," and despite that, we should listen to him. They hinted in their words the answer of Samuel that "this is not the established law." Therefore he said, "Did you not teach me thus in your way?" so that it would be the established law. And so that they would not say he is personally involved due to his closeness to Moses—"my father-in-law, their father"—he said it with a change of language. This is explained in the "Laws of Judgment," section 30, regarding the "language of the heart," because some say a witness in a language not his own is disqualified. However, our teacher Rabbi A. <note>likely Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note> in his responsa says it is only disqualified by Rabbinic decree, but by Torah law it is nothing. If so, why give it up? He said this law after the deed because Moses' judgment was established, and he should not be suspected of being personally involved, for the Torah is far-reaching.

<margin>An answer to the verse "And he took a spear from the midst of the assembly."</margin>
Now it will be explained why it is written "and he took a spear from the midst of the assembly." Why was he able to take the spear from the midst of the assembly? To show that the taking of the spear was not to forbid the verse "and he took from the sorcerers," but rather he did an act that spoke his way, etc. He said, "Anyone who does not hear this law shall be stabbed with a spear." So did Phinehas do; he took the spear from the midst of the assembly for the purpose of the deed, so that they would hear this law from him, or to stab him with the spear. If so, from all this we see a student of a wise man who comes to teach before the deed—we listen to him, etc. This was the debate regarding Jethro's instruction and Moses' rebuke. Moses said, "And I judged between a man and his neighbor, and I made known the statutes of God and His laws." Jethro understood from his words that Moses wanted to make known the reasons for the judgment after the deed. Therefore, Jethro said "his eyes" <note>unclear</note> against what Moses said. After he did the deed, Jethro said, "The thing you are doing is not good," that it should be through listening. Regarding this, he said, "You will surely wear out, for the thing is too heavy for you." He first sought to correct even that which he himself did, to give a reason, lest "now from me" <note>unclear</note>. Why? etc. Meaning, that which he asks is the reasons of the questioner to make known the reason that did not come in the judgment and the acceptance...

<catchword>and the acceptance</catchword>

It further connects this to Phinehas's zealotry, defending Moses' marriage to Zipporah and clarifying when a disciple may rule on a law if their teacher is silent or personally involved.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Introduction of the Scholar, the Son of the Author," focusing on the judicial ethics of the "Pillar of Justice" (Amud Ha-Din). The previous page discussed the burdens of leadership placed upon Moses; this page transitions into the legal qualifications of judges and the preference for compromise (Pesharah) over strict litigation.</meta>

->Introduction of the Great Scholar, Son of the Author, Pillar of Justice<-

<margin>Regarding the view of Maimonides <note>original: "Rambam"</note>, of blessed memory, on the ordination of judges, as explained previously in Chapter 3 of Tractate Sanhedrin...</margin>
Behold, a judge who acquits the guilty is considered as if he is mocking and honoring [falsehood]; in a place of Torah study <note>original: "Pithah Shel Torah," literally the 'opening of the Torah'</note>, he is like one who plants an Asherah <note>term: <gloss>Asherah</gloss>; a tree planted for idolatrous worship, strictly forbidden in Jewish Law</note>. It is written in the Gemara <note>The core text of the Talmud</note>, in the first chapter of Sanhedrin and in Tractate Avodah Zarah, Chapter "Rabbi Ishmael," that Resh Lakish said: "Anyone who appoints an unfit judge over the community is as if he planted an Asherah," as it says: "Judges and officers you shall appoint for yourself..." <note>Deuteronomy 16:18</note> and immediately following it is written: "You shall not plant for yourself an Asherah, any tree..." <note>Deuteronomy 16:21</note>. Furthermore, Rav Assi said: "In a place where there are Torah scholars, it is as if he planted an altar." One might wonder about Maimonides, who wrote that it is as if he erected a monument <note>original: "matzevah"</note>, as it says, "You shall not erect a monument," whereas the Talmud only brings the proof from "you shall not plant an Asherah." This implies a great disgrace in his eyes, but what is the underlying reason for this? These are his words [paraphrased] <note>original: "עכ"ל" - end of quote</note>. 

The resolution regarding this disgrace is as follows: there is a difference between a judge who possesses good character traits but is not an expert in Torah, and one who is not an expert in character. Maimonides explains that even if he has good traits, he is disqualified <note>as if he were a "monument," which was once beloved but later detested</note>. What is mentioned in the Gemara regarding an "unfit judge" being like an "Asherah" refers to one who might be learned but commits transgressions and lacks good character. He is compared to an Asherah tree, which appears beautiful on the outside but is spiritually repulsive. 

It seems to me that Maimonides’ view does not actually contradict the Gemara. It is known that in all places in the Talmud where one verse is linked to another, it is because of the proximity <note>term: <gloss>Semikhut</gloss>; the interpretive method of deriving meaning from the physical closeness of two verses in the Bible</note>. The Gemara asks: what is the connection between the appointment of judges and the prohibition of planting an Asherah? They answer with the teaching about the unfit judge. However, there was no need to ask about the connection to the verse "You shall not erect for yourself a monument," because that verse is naturally connected to the Asherah verse as they both deal with the practice of idolatry. Therefore, the primary question was only on the "Asherah" verse. Maimonides, however, seeks to teach us that the judge's unfitness is comparable to both. 

And in the Gemara, they brought the case of a judge who is not an expert, who is liable by law, yet a compromise was reached. Rav Safra, following the words of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, says that a judge should always aim for a compromise rather than a strict ruling. 

<margin>See at length the matters of the Ordination of Elders in the *Beit Yosef* <note>The 16th-century legal code by Yosef Karo</note> and in the responsa of Rabbi Akiva Eiger, section 72 at the end.</margin>
What is the connection between "You shall not plant an Asherah" and the portion regarding judges? There are those who explain the portion of Phinehas <note>The zealot from the Book of Numbers</note> as saying that a judge who allows the wicked to go free is as if he offered a blemished sacrifice. Therefore, the warning for judges is placed next to the laws of sacrifices and Asherah trees to teach us: if a judge acquits a person who deserved a death penalty, or errors in judgment, he is like one who offers a sacrifice that has a blemish. This is why the sections are adjacent. 

Furthermore, I have seen that the author of the *Tur* <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher</note> stated regarding "These are the Judgments" that a judge is obligated to seek a compromise <note>term: <gloss>Pesharah</gloss>; an equitable settlement or mediation that avoids the harshness of strict law</note> before he renders a formal judgment. See the hint to this in the *Tur*, Choshen Mishpat, section 12, where it says: "It is a mitzvah for the judge to ask the litigants: 'Do you want strict law or do you want a compromise?'" Even if the judge already knows which way the law leans, as long as the verdict has not been finalized by saying "So-and-so is innocent and so-and-so is guilty," he should pursue compromise. 

The Gemara in Sanhedrin (page 6) concludes that once the verdict is finalized, a compromise is no longer allowed. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: "The law follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who says that compromise is a mitzvah." 

<column-break/>

"Guilty," Rav Safra acted according to the words of Yehoshua ben Korcha. Rav Hisda and Rav Safra were students of Rav, and when they were about to issue a guilty verdict, Rav Safra would say to them: "Do we want strict law or do we want a compromise?" This was because Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha said it is a mitzvah to say to them: "Do you want strict law or do you want a compromise?" One might ask: why did the Gemara mention "judge" first? The reason is that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha holds that even if the judge knows which way the law is leaning, he should still favor compromise. 

Even if he knows the law, he should not say "I am certain the law is like this," but rather use language such as: "Do we want strict law?" even though he knows the law favors one side. This is to encourage the litigants to choose a path of peace. The *Tur* was very precise in his language when he said: "How much more do you want a compromise rather than strict law," or "even more so a compromise." This is only before the final verdict. As long as there is no final verdict, there is always a reason to seek a settlement. Even if the law would acquit a person, the judge should revisit the possibility of compromise again and again. 

We should not mention the word "strict law" too much, but rather emphasize "compromise" so that the litigants will return [to a state of peace] even in cases of financial loss. Even though the judge might say "Do we want strict law?" he should immediately emphasize, "or would you prefer a compromise?" In this way, they will naturally choose the compromise. Thus, this is not against the plain meaning of the text. Both in the *Tur* and in the Gemara, the priority is given to compromise because "the world is sustained by three things: truth, justice, and peace." 

This is the attribute of Phinehas. Initially, the world was created with the Attribute of Judgment <note>original: "Middat HaDin"</note>, but God saw that the world could not endure, so He combined it with the Attribute of Mercy <note>original: "Middat HaRakhamim"</note>. A judge must remember that while the law is a serious matter, the "Pillar of Justice" is strengthened when it leads to peace through compromise. Therefore, compromise is the primary goal. By choosing compromise, the judge ensures that even those who "pass through the law" choose the path of reconciliation. This is why the "Judgments" are linked to the concept of the judge's power to create a settlement before the law is finalized. If he does so, he fulfills what is written: "Judge truthfully, and execute the judgment of peace in your gates" <note>Zechariah 8:16</note>.

# Chapter Eighteen

## Explanation
Regarding the "Judgments" <note>Exodus 21:1, Parshat Mishpatim</note>. It was explained above on the verse: "And Moses sat to judge the people..." <note>Exodus 18:13</note>. It is written: "And Moses told his father-in-law [Jethro]..." Joseph [the author] of blessed memory writes: "Furthermore, it is difficult when he says 'Because the people come to me to seek God' <note>Exodus 18:15</note> and 'I make known the statutes of God and His laws.' This implies that Moses said, 'When the people come to me, I seek out the word of God for them.'" 

Yet Jethro says to him: "The thing you are doing is not good" <note>Exodus 18:17</note>. It seems difficult to understand—what was so "not good" about Moses teaching the people God's word directly?

<meta>The previous page introduced the legal qualifications of judges and the metaphor of the "unfit judge" as a prohibited idolatrous tree (Asherah). This page continues that theme, connecting the integrity of the judiciary to the very structure of the world's creation and King Solomon’s throne.</meta>

# **Introduction of the Great Sage, Son of the Author, the Pillar of Justice**

It is brought in the Midrash on the book of Judges <note>original: "Midrash Shofetim"</note>: "May our memory be upon you regarding the third level, etc." For it is known what Rashi <note>The preeminent medieval commentator, Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105)</note> explained in the Torah regarding the future of Israel: it is said concerning the inheritance that "every plant of yours is the Land," and you shall not set up a monument <note>original: "matzevah"</note> for the mention of judgments. The Gemara <note>The section of the Talmud containing rabbinic analysis</note> says that anyone who appoints a judge who is not fit is as if he set up a monument, and in a place of Torah scholars <note>original: "Talmidei Chachamim"</note>, it is as if he planted an Asherah <note>term: <gloss>Asherah</gloss>; a tree planted for pagan worship, forbidden near the Altar of God</note>. The *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* <note>term: <gloss>Smag</gloss>; a 13th-century legal code by Rabbi Moses of Coucy</note> wrote explicitly that one who appoints an unfit judge is as if he denies the divine judgment. Likewise, the great sage Maharal <note>Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague (1520–1609), famous for the legend of the Golem</note>, of blessed memory, in his book *Netivot Olam* <note>original: "Netivot," likely referring to the path of Justice</note> cites the Smag to say that the three prohibitions—"do not plant," "do not set up," and "do not sacrifice"—are general rules. I have explained this previously in the section on "Conduct" on this very page. Therefore, what was mentioned regarding the fourth level—that his memory should not be forgotten—is because the proclamation "you shall not do" regarding judgment itself refers to the fourth level. The intention is that if you do not perform justice, it is as if you have made for yourself an Asherah tree. They were very strict in this matter. Thus, these three Midrashic teachings follow a single theme. The purpose of separating the "throne of ethics" <note>original: "Kise Musar"</note> was to strengthen the general rules of "do not do," "do not set up," and "do not remember." These correspond to the three commands of a King. For the other two levels, the general rule applies to these three warnings: do not do, do not set up, do not sacrifice. He mentions these three "no's" regarding the last three levels (4, 5, and 6) to teach us that their essence is so deep: a judge who perverts justice is as if he plants an Asherah, etc. One should not ask why he did not make six levels and proclaim over each one individually as I explained; for it is possible that these three levels represent the totality of the six days of Creation, as stated in the Midrash. Nor should one ask why he did not make seven levels to correspond to the seven days of Creation (including the Sabbath). As the *Midrash Rabbah* concludes in the portion of "Vayechi," there are seven levels corresponding to the seven heavens. The logic of the Midrash is that the seventh heaven belongs to the Holy One, Blessed be He, and thus it is fitting to say that we only stand on the throne below the heaven of the Holy One. However, when we say the seven levels correspond to the days of Creation, the question remains: why did he not make seven levels?

<margin>The author of *Remez* <note>Rabbi Moses Zakut</note> wrote on the portion of "Ki Tisa" etc., regarding the sages of the Mishnah and the verses in the portion of "Naso" etc., and more.</margin>
The intention fits better with the seven days of Creation. This can be answered as follows: He made six levels to correspond to the six days of Creation <note>original: "Bereshit"</note>, for our Sages of blessed memory said: "Any judge who judges a true judgment according to its truth, it is as if he became a partner with the Holy One, Blessed be He, in the work of Creation." Because of this, the six levels are elevated, as it is fitting for a judge to sit [in judgment], and judgment does not cease for the Holy One except on the seven days. Therefore, he is called a "partner" specifically regarding the six levels, corresponding to the Six Orders of the Mishnah <note>term: <gloss>Shisha Sidrei Mishnah</gloss>; the foundational six volumes of the Oral Torah</note>. This hints that a judge should perform justice to illuminate what Rashi explained in the portion of "Yitro": "from the morning until the evening"—is it possible to think he sits all day? Rather, any judge who judges truly, the Holy One considers it as if he labored in the Torah all day long. Therefore, he made six levels against the Six Orders of the Mishnah to show that through the act of judging truly, it is as if he is occupied with the Torah all day. For this reason, he did not make seven levels. And since we have come to the *Midrash Rabbah* on the portion of "Naso"...

<margin>See what is mentioned regarding the days of Creation: why did they write "the heavens are one" and what the Midrash says in the portion of "Ki Tisa," etc.</margin>
Regarding the matter of the "six wagons" <note>original: "Agaltot," referring to the gifts of the tribal leaders in Numbers 7:3</note>, this is a significant thing. It says in the Midrash there that the six wagons correspond to the six levels of the throne, to the seven heavens, and to the six days of Creation. Why did they write "the heavens are one"? It would have been more correct for them to be written in proximity to the seven heavens on the throne, etc. The question is: what is the reason that it mentions "before the Lord"? For Rashi explained in the portion of "Leviticus" that "before the Lord" implies the placement of hands <note>term: <gloss>Semicha</gloss>; the ritual of leaning one's hands on a sacrifice</note>. And the placement of the wagons in the verses of the portion of "Naso" involves these two languages: "before the Lord" and "the sages of the Mishnah." Furthermore, it is difficult: he says "take them," but he should have said "take it." It seems to me that when the *Midrash Rabbah* concludes that the six wagons correspond to the six days of Creation, it clarifies what it says: "take them" literally until it says "that the prophecy was accepted" and he took them. The question is: why was he [Moses] prevented from accepting them until he was told so by the Mouth of the Almighty? From this, I saw there was a second reason. He said this: "Why was this prophecy needed concerning the throne?" Rather, the matter follows the *Midrash Rabbah* that the six wagons correspond to the six heavens, and not seven. Rabbi Abin said: "The son of the Queen brought 'timuqin' <note>gloss: a gift or tribute</note>." The *Aruch* <note>An 11th-century dictionary of the Talmud</note> explains that "timuqin" refers to the crown of the King, from the honor of the King's throne. This brings us back to the subject: the matter of the six wagons was so that everything would be established correctly. They brought six wagons "before the Lord," meaning they did not bring a seventh out of respect for the Name of God, may He be blessed. For the Sabbath is the fourth [commandment] and the seventh [day], and "before the Lord" means up to the heaven that is "before the Lord," which is the sixth heaven. Corresponding to the seventh heaven, they did not want to bring [a wagon] because the "Correct Foundation of the Lord" is prepared there, in the seventh heaven. "Before the Lord" is as if to say "out of the honor of the Lord." And behold, *Midrash Rabbah* on the portion of "Naso" says that they sent six wagons corresponding to the six days of Creation. Therefore, he [Moses] did not want to receive them without the permission of the Omnipresent, because of the lack of one day from the days of Creation, which is the Seventh Day, which is holy unto the Lord. It would have appeared as if a separation was being made between the days.

<column-break/>

And Moses our Teacher, peace be upon him, reckoned the Sabbath day as the world [itself], as written in the *Tur* in the section *Orach Chaim* <note>The standard code of Jewish law</note> regarding the prayer "Moses shall rejoice in the gift of his portion"—this refers to the Sabbath day. Because of this, it was said to him by the mouth of the Almighty: "Take them from them, that they may be used in the service of the Tent of Meeting" <note>Numbers 7:5</note>. If so, the Almighty hinted to him that the purpose of the wagons is to perform the service of the throne, the holy tasks, and the insights. If so, it is proven that the tribal princes acted correctly by not bringing a seventh wagon, for the main purpose is to perform labor. The Sabbath day is a holy day, a day of rest and tranquility from all work. Had they brought a seventh wagon, it would have been a contradiction in terms: the purpose of a wagon is for labor, while the Sabbath is a day of rest. Therefore, they did not bring a wagon corresponding to the Sabbath, for that day is a divine vessel, whereas the utility of a wagon is for work, and the Sabbath is a day of rest. As for why it says "Take from them" and not "Take it," it is possible according to what the Midrash concludes there: "For how long did those wagons exist?" There are three opinions: Rabbi Chama bar Hanina said they lasted until the sanctuary of Nob; others say until the Babylonian exile; and Rabbi Meir says even until now those wagons and oxen exist! They have not aged, they have not weakened, they have not become defective, and they have not been slaughtered. This is an "a fortiori" argument: if the wagons that were attached to the Tent of Meeting were granted eternal existence, how much more so Israel, who are attached to the Holy One, Blessed be He, as it is said: "And you who cling to the Lord your God are all alive today" <note>Deuteronomy 4:4</note>. This is the meaning of the verse "Take from them"—meaning, for the sake of showing their eternal nature. For the wagons and oxen exist without wear; they are "living" in their own right. This is the hint in the verse "and they brought them before the Lord"—meaning that the Chariots of Fire which are literally "before the Lord," since they are attached to Him, they have eternal life, just as Israel has life. This matter proves the progression of the "steps" on the throne that King Solomon made.

<margin>Why was he prevented [from taking them]? etc. And the answer... regarding the matter of the six wagons so that they would be established, etc.</margin>
*As it is said in the Midrash on the portion of "Peleh" <note>likely "Peleh" referring to a specific Midrashic collection or "Pinchas"</note>: The Torah said, "Master of the Universe, Solomon is uprooting me!" When a king seeks to uproot a single thing from the Torah, the whole Torah is undermined. Rabbi Joshua ben Levi said: "The letter *Yod* of the word *Yarbeh* <note>meaning 'he shall increase'</note> cried out." It was taught: Rabbi Simeon said: "The book of Deuteronomy <note>original: "Mishneh Torah"</note> ascended and prostrated before the Holy One, Blessed be He, and said: 'Master of the Universe, Solomon has uprooted me and made me a forgery! For a testament <note>original: "Diyatiki"</note> in which one part is void, the whole is void!'" And behold, he sought to uproot the *Yod* from me, for it is written "He shall not multiply (*Lo Yarbeh*) wives for himself," yet he multiplied them! "He shall not multiply (*Lo Yarbeh*) horses for himself," yet he multiplied them! For the Holy One, Blessed be He, said: "I am writing these things," and Solomon thought his wisdom would protect him. The Holy One said: "Solomon and a thousand like him shall pass away, but not one *Yod* shall be uprooted from the Torah!" Rabbi Yosef said in the name of Rabbi Assa: The *Yod* that the Holy One took from our mother Sarah <note>changing her name from Sarai to Sarah</note> was half given to Abraham and half to Sarah. Rabbi Joshua ben Korcha said: The *Yod* of Sarah was prostrating before the Holy One, saying: "Master of the Universe, You have uprooted me from the name of that righteous woman!" The Holy One said to her: "Do not be afraid; previously you were in a woman's name and at the end of the word; now I am writing you in the name of a male and at the beginning of the word," as it is written: "And Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun, Joshua (*Yehoshua*)" <note>Adding the *Yod* to the start of the name</note>. There is another Midrash in the portion of "Vayera" regarding the change to a male name. However, regarding Abraham, I have seen in other sermons that Solomon, before he sinned, asked why the Holy One wrote "He shall not multiply wives"? "Lest his heart turn away." Solomon said, "I will multiply and my heart will not turn away." Our Sages say that the *Yod* of *Yarbeh* went and prostrated before God and said, "Solomon is nullifying me!" God replied, "Solomon and a thousand like him will be nullified, but not one point of you shall be nullified." Since he strayed from the Torah and returned to the Torah, as it is said, "Let the name of the wicked rot," and regarding him Solomon said those words until the prophecy was accepted. The question is: who is more worthy to contemplate His attributes? It is said that God already informed Solomon that Pharaoh would not learn, and regarding the judgment he would complete, and he contemplated and said "Why have You done evil?" etc. Regarding these two Midrashim, one must be precise in what the Midrash said about Solomon and Moses... especially since Solomon was warned about it in deed. Furthermore, it is difficult: where does the Torah say he returned? What is the matter of the answer to reveal that the Holy One is the Master of souls and returns souls? Also, the language "they did regarding the speech" is not precise for prophecy. Moreover, why was the *Yod* of *Yarbeh* more distressed than the rest of the word? And why only the *Yod* of the word *Lo* <note>meaning 'Not'</note> that is written in "He shall not multiply"? Furthermore, what is the dispute between the sage who says the *Yod* was split between Abraham and Sarah, and the one who says it was given to Joshua? What is most wondrous is the answer given to the *Yod*: that she was at the end of a name and now she is at the beginning of a name—as if a judge doesn't just uproot but restores? Specifically, the story of Sarah precedes the story of Joshua in the Torah. Let us see the distinction between a female name and a male name.

# Introduction by the Eminent Son of the Author: The Pillar of Judgment

<margin>
What he brings in his book <note>The text refers to a work abbreviated as DMTK"U, likely *Divrei Pi Tizkak*</note> regarding the commandment "You shall surely stand," which is "good news" as mentioned in the books on this "Pillar." This refers to the diligence required for the 248 positive commandments through the commandment of "standing" etc.
</margin>
For death is ever before his eyes—may we be spared—and he wrote that a spiritual "blindness" fell upon him, to the astonishment of the heart. For in the "prison" <note>A metaphor for the physical body or perhaps a period of illness</note> he is designated, at any rate, one month of delay and eight days of fundamental lack. Just as in the association of a person—may we be spared—a month is required for a secondary study; therefore, even those who died on the eve of the New Year—may we be spared—their joy departed from them thirty days prior. And through the grace of mercies, the author of this book fled, for even though a "bubbling" <note>Likely referring to a fever or physical ailment</note> moved through his body, nevertheless, the palate of all was upon him, and it was as if his priesthood had ended and passed and he stumbled from the world. Therefore, there is no difficulty regarding those who died on the eve of the New Year, for their suffering—may we be spared—began thirty days prior to this. This is what is meant by saying that if all were removed at once, there would not be a full month of the "passing study." For this reason, the Palate <note>A metaphor for God's decree</note> extended it for him so long, for even in the month of the deposit he lived, and he wrote for him "Three Books are opened" etc. as we have explained. "He will swallow up death forever" <note>original: ובלע המות לנצח</note> and we shall be satisfied with life, and may He grant us long life, Amen. 

And from our place, we proceed as in the matter of the three books open before the Holy One, Blessed be He, when He sits upon the Throne of Judgment to clarify what I have written in the book *Dikduk"e* <note>Grammar/Details of the Law</note> on the portion of *Emor*. There it is written in the name of our Sages of blessed memory, that it is known that the New Year is the Day of Judgment for the entire world. Our Sages said: At the hour when God comes and sits upon the Throne of Judgment, the **Attribute of Strict Justice** stands at His left, and the **Attribute of Mercy** stands at His right, and they argue with one another. 

The **Attribute of Justice** says: "Shatter the world! He sits on the Throne of Judgment to act as an adversary against his creation." 
But the **Attribute of Mercy** says: "If You, Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?" <note>Psalm 130:3</note>
The **Attribute of Justice** says: "The wicked shall die in his iniquity!" 
The **Attribute of Justice** says: "For all this is the transgression of Jacob!" 
But the **Attribute of Mercy** says: "How then shall Jacob stand?" <note>Amos 7:5</note>
The **Attribute of Justice** says: "Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children." 
But the **Attribute of Mercy** says: "Fathers shall not be put to death for the children." <note>Deuteronomy 24:16</note>
The **Attribute of Justice** says: "I also will do this to you." 
But the **Attribute of Mercy** says: "For my sake, for my own sake, I will do it." 
The **Attribute of Justice** says: "For Tophet <note>A place of fire/Hell</note> has been ordained of old." 
But the **Attribute of Mercy** says: "In the evening, weeping may linger, but in the morning, there is joy." 
The **Attribute of Justice** says: "Therefore Sheol <note>The underworld</note> has enlarged its desire and opened its mouth without limit." 
But the **Attribute of Mercy** says: "It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it." 
The **Attribute of Justice** says: "For I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel." 
But the **Attribute of Mercy** says: "For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob." 
The **Attribute of Justice** says its argument, and the **Attribute of Mercy** says: "Who is a God like You..." <note>Micah 7:18</note> see there in the commentary for the full context. 

And it is difficult: since on the New Year there are memories and shofars <note>referring to the Zichronot and Shofrot prayers</note>, one side bringing merit and the other guilt, and each bringing a verse—if so, what do these verses say? Why does the Attribute of Mercy bring more than what the Attribute of Justice brings? This is a significant matter. More difficult still is what is the response that the Attribute of Mercy gave to the Attribute of Justice regarding the claim that "Sheol has enlarged its desire and opened its mouth etc."? The Attribute of Mercy answered, "It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it." What is the connection between one and the other? 

In order to settle this matter, we look toward the Heavenly Heights, Blessed be He. For there is, as it were, a place for the words of the Attribute of Mercy to find merit for Israel from within the very verse brought by the Attribute of Justice. Therefore, the Attribute of Justice agreed with the Attribute of Mercy. It begins with the first claim of Justice which says: "He sits on the Throne of Judgment," as found in the Midrash on Deuteronomy, section 20. The Attribute of Mercy returned a correct and necessary answer from within the words of the claim of Justice itself. I will uphold what is written in the *Pesikta* <note>A collection of homiletic teachings</note> and it is remembered in the portion of *Behaalotecha* regarding the verse "And it came to pass when the ark set forward" <note>Numbers 10:35</note>, that there are inverted *Nuns* <note>A scribal anomaly in the Torah</note> shaped like the letter *Khaf* (כ) or like the letter *Reish* (ר). So too are the surroundings, and it is proper to give another opening in the matter of the "AL"G" <note>likely a cipher or acronym</note> letters of the *Khaf* and the *Reish* of Rosh Hashanah to the right. 

The claim is that even if their deeds were not good, they are like those who flee from a schoolhouse. In every place, there is a hint to teach merit, as concluded in the Midrash: "She was like a widow." Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said: "She was like a widow, but not a real widow." So too, Justice did not fully strike their inheritance; they did not truly stray. For it is said, "And there were those of the people like murmurers"—it does not say "murmurers," but "*like* murmurers." Regarding the "shifters of boundaries," it does not say they were shifters, but "*like* shifters of boundaries." "Like a stubborn cow"—it does not say a stubborn cow, but "*like* a stubborn cow." Thus, Justice did not strike their inheritance; she was *like* a widow, but not actually widowed. There is a *Yod* (י) in the word "Like" <note>Hebrew: כ-י-אלמנה</note> and not a literal state. And it is already known from the chapter "The Builder" <note>Shabbat 104a</note> regarding the order of the Aleph-Bet: *Khaf, Lamed, Mem... Tzadi, Kof, Reish, Shin, Tav*... "Justice, Wickedness," etc. And this is the sign: the *Vav* (ו) indicates "Wickedness" (Rasha), but its time is against it like a *Khaf* (כ), to say he is *like* a wicked person but not a completely wicked one. He has wings for remembrance, such as the *Parashah* of the "Eye of Life." This is not the place for it, as it does not pertain to our current subject. This provided the Attribute of Mercy a place to dismantle the arguments of Justice and to advocate for Israel when it said "The wicked of the world," for the verse did not say "She opened her mouth for *them*," but from his sanctuary in the East, "His mouth did not strike their inheritance." Because of this, the language of "Like" was used in the world, and not a literal state. If so, the Attribute of Mercy answered the Attribute of Justice well.

<column-break/>

The response was not "If You, Lord, should mark iniquities," etc. For the iniquities are literally standing there, and they are before Him as sins. Therefore, one must focus and recognize that the world is held together by the Attribute of Mercy. 

The second claim of the Attribute of Justice is "The wicked shall die in his iniquity." This matter follows the Gemara of Rosh Hashanah: "A judgment that has been sealed cannot be torn up..." Behold, you see that a seal on a decree is not torn up, whether for the wicked or the intermediate. This verse, "The wicked shall die in his iniquity," is in Ezekiel chapter 33. The Attribute of Mercy replied toward the Heights that the explanation should follow what is written: "Say to them: As I live, says the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked..." <note>Ezekiel 33:11</note> This is the intent of Rashi's commentary on the portion: "As I live, I do not desire the seal." Therefore, the Attribute of Mercy claimed: "Behold, You Yourself said in Your writing that You do not desire the death of the wicked." If so, it is found that He does not desire the seal, for if He does not want the death of the wicked, then the seal of "The wicked shall die in his iniquity" is not spoken as a final seal. Thus, he can dismantle and delay it now and in the end. The Attribute of Mercy entered into the Attribute of Justice beautifully.

And so it is regarding the claim of the Attribute of Justice: "For all this is the transgression of Jacob," as stated in the chapter "All may slaughter." The Rabbis taught: Regarding the "Hidden Ones" <note>possibly referring to disqualified Levites</note> who are disqualified, and the Levites who are disqualified... what does the Scripture teach by saying "This"? It refers to the Levites who were disqualified because they were wicked. One might think blemishes disqualify them—this is a logical deduction: if the Priests, whose taste is not disqualified, are disqualified by blemishes, then the Levites, who were disqualified by years, should certainly be disqualified by blemishes! The Scripture says "This is for the Levites" <note>Numbers 8:24</note>—only this, and nothing else disqualifies a Levite. Furthermore, know what is juxtaposed: "A Psalm, a song for the Sabbath day," and "To give to those who sit between the lions." From what He did in justice, he made a "How much more so" (Kal Vachomer) argument... to pay back... and the accusers who sacrificed... and so it is in our case. For the verse "This" <note>Hebrew: *Zot*</note> is found because Jacob was struck for "All this." "Who gave Jacob for a spoil?" Not the apostates. "And who gave Judah for a spoil? It was Jerusalem!" And they said the guardians according to etc. until it reached the gate of Jerusalem. 

If so, the Attribute of Justice found a place to claim against Israel that they were causing the Holy One, Blessed be He, to dwell in a place of abandonment. As in the commentary on the portion *Bechukotai*: "I also will do this to you." This is to settle that you will not find your sustenance, for your altar shall be destroyed etc. Therefore, the Attribute of Justice claimed "For all this is the transgression of Jacob," knowing that Jerusalem and the Temple were destroyed. If so, you no longer need "This" <note>the service/altar</note>, so I will take "This" away from your deeds. Because of this, the Attribute of Mercy said, "How then shall Jacob stand?" after the persecution from within your sins, "The altar shall be established for Jacob." For this "This" is not for his harm, but for a "Good This," and on that day he will be established to destroy the "thick ones" <note>the enemies/husks</note> and to be built. Then, in the matter of the word "This" (*Zot*), it is said "In this I trust," a "How much more so" from the *Sotah* and in the matter of the claim of Justice "Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children." The response of Mercy "Fathers shall not be put to death for the children" needs no explanation, for it has already been reconciled in the Gemara: these two verses are reconciled by the distinction of whether the children "hold the deeds of their fathers in their hands" <note>continue their sins</note> or not. This is a fine reconciliation.

And so it is in the matter of the claim of Justice: "For Tophet <note>Gehenna/Hell</note> has been ordained of old." It is written in the chapter "The Builder" <note>Shabbat 104a</note> that the world was created with the letter *He* (ה). God said "If so, I will lead them to the Garden of Eden." Gehenna said before the Holy One: "What about me?" Rashi explains: "Wickedness is mine." The Holy One replied: "The seed of Isaac..." a "deposit" <note>Hebrew: *Pikaon*</note> in place of the nations of the world, I am giving to you. Rashi explains "Deposit": "Keep them and wait for them." It is a wonder: why does Gehenna need to wait? In those years, the wicked of the nations of the world will be there, and every day He can give to Gehenna according to what they did. (It seems to me to explain according to the *Ten Utterances*, page 80: "Furthermore, know that the Sages said: 'There is no Gehenna in the future to come,' meaning the light of the sun will punish the wicked. For the hollow of Gehenna, which was created before the world, is destined to be sanctified with the holiness of the Garden of Eden, and there the righteous will reside, and the Holy One will be seen among them...")

Thus, it is explained that the "sweetness" of Gehenna for the seed of Isaac was what the Holy One told it—to keep the seed of Isaac and wait for the future to come, when it is sanctified with the holiness of the Garden of Eden. Then I will give you the seed of Isaac in the holiness of the "Savor." For now, I have many groups of the nations of the world, and those I give to you immediately. This was the claim of Justice: "For Tophet has been ordained of old," for it was created for the children of Israel, as in the matter of "In the beginning" being for the sake of Israel who are called "Beginning." This is why it was created—the fire of Gehenna—to give it from the merit of their "stumbling." But the Attribute of Mercy replied: "In the evening, weeping may linger," meaning there is no Gehenna except with the seed of Isaac, because it was created before the world. It cannot be said it was created for Israel, for the creation of Heaven and Earth and the sun was for the sake of Israel. Then the Attribute of Justice replied to the Attribute of Mercy's response with the verse: "Therefore Sheol has enlarged its desire and opened its mouth without limit," and it is written...

<summary>This page presents a dramatic theological debate between the Attributes of Justice and Mercy regarding the fate of Israel during the High Holy Days. It utilizes wordplay and scriptural exegesis to show how Mercy finds potential for salvation even within the harsh decrees of Justice.</summary>
