# Introduction of the Eminent Son of the Author: The Pillar of Truth
# Chapter Twenty-Two
# The Pillar of Truth

<margin>
Remembered for good: regarding Chapter 8 [of Zechariah], as the Lord says: "I have returned to Zion and will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, and Jerusalem shall be called the City of Truth." <note>Original: "עיר האמת" (*Ir Ha-Emet*)</note> It was difficult for me to understand: why is Jerusalem specifically called the "City of Truth"?
</margin>
Why was the City of Truth specifically chosen as the name for the Assembly <note>Referring to the congregation of Israel or the city itself</note>, and not the "City of Peace" or the "City of Justice" or something similar? It seems that "Truth" here should be understood according to the path I have explained elsewhere. I interpreted this according to the "Mishnah of the Arabin," <note>Likely referring to a specific commentary on the Mishnah or a legal tradition</note> Chapter 9, Law 6: the "City of the Mighty" <note>Proverbs 21:22</note> was established in a place that was always strong. It is not written "Out of Zion shall come forth," but "In the midst of Jerusalem," as a way of connecting and joining the past. As it is said: "I remember the kindness of your youth," <note>Jeremiah 2:2</note> and this "kindness" refers to the initial preparations. Therefore, it is appropriate for the Assembly to sit before Him and place upon its heart the love of the union that existed from the beginning. Through this, Jerusalem and its inhabitants will merit [redemption]. Just as Jeremiah writes with truthfulness, we hold that a person is not always in Jerusalem <note>A metaphorical way of saying one is not always at a high spiritual level</note>; therefore, there is one who says in the Gemara <note>The Talmud</note> that they were in the "earthly" Jerusalem and this is not the "Holy" Jerusalem where the Temple was, but a Jerusalem that was in the Land of Israel. There is also a concept of an "inner wall," and these are its names: the Source, and it is called Jerusalem "in the midst" to exclude other Jerusalems in the Land of Israel that are not called by this name. It is possible that it mentions "clothing" to remove errors. These are the hints: the Holy City, Jerusalem, the City of Truth. Yet our minds have not yet calmed—why is Jerusalem called by the name "Truth" rather than any other name? To clarify this, I say: in the arrangement of the end of the blessings, and furthermore in Chapter 9 [of Daniel], verse 20: "And while I was speaking, and praying, and confessing... and Gabriel... talked with me and said, 'O Daniel, I have now come out to give you insight and understanding.'" <note>Daniel 9:20-22</note> It is difficult for me, for regarding all the prophets who prophesied to Israel, we do not find such a "discipline" used to tell them their very essence, as was said to Daniel. And the Blessed One said: "My people, My people," <note>a phrase of endearment</note> meaning: "In the gift of your understanding, go before." Why did He hang the understanding of this on the "Wall"? <note>A play on the word *Homat* (wall) and *Chokhmah* (wisdom/understanding)</note> This will be clarified according to what is mentioned in the Tosefta, first chapter of Menachot:

<margin>The Afternoon Prayer</margin>
In it, it says: "And it was at the time of the evening offering..." <note>1 Kings 18:36</note> What is the secret of the Holy One, blessed be He, returning to their "Table" according to these words? "And it was that he was looking upon the face of Isaac..." to the City of Truth. And if this was difficult in the eyes of Isaac regarding his son, or if it was the "Forbidden Path" of imagery... heaven forbid... this is the soul of the study of "returning to the water" <note>A metaphor for returning to Torah or repentance</note> as one who finds grace. It was said: "And in the evening he returned to the 'Table'..." 

<margin>Return to the waters</margin>
Regarding what was spoken, look into the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah</term> that rests upon the one who clarifies. As it says: "For He is a horse and we ride upon him," etc. Look there. Therefore, from our wandering, we find that the verse calls the Holy One by the name "He who has pity," through which the story of His anger is sweetened, and that which was in love is strengthened. And here we find in the "Silent Prayer" <term>Amidah</term> many times: "Return in mercy to Your city Jerusalem... and build it soon in our days." This is because, as stated, "And now hear our prayer," etc. The secret of the "Wall" comes from your thinking, that He should hear, etc. For regarding the many visions, she began to pray for the "Truth" of the Holy One, blessed be He, for we are His people, and regarding the dead, he spoke truthfully to return the understanding of the "waters." He said, "Return in mercy and build," etc. And it is difficult: from where did Daniel get the understanding to pray thus? This is only because this Source stood for his praise. If so, it seems our actions are in truth and in greatness, and he comes to the place of prayer, which is close to the mouth and below. And this matter is hinted at in the prophecy of the Afternoon Offering <note>The Minchah prayer</note> of your understanding. This is what was mentioned as a hint to the foundation of "Wall" and "Truth" regarding this. And Gabriel said: "I have come to give you insight, for you are greatly beloved," <note>Daniel 9:23</note> specifically because you went to the place of prayer from the verse that God told the people. But he said to him: "Because you are a man of delights." Through this, I sought to settle what we are accustomed to saying in the "Grace After Meals": "Favor us with Your will... and build the walls of Jerusalem." It is difficult: what difference does our prayer make regarding the "walls" of Jerusalem? For our whole aim is to build the Holy Temple and to bring the sacrifices, praying "and build it" to atone for all our sins. But these walls are not the ultimate goal! Rather, they are the "secret" entrusted to us in the building. For we find in the Zohar: regarding "the heavens were like a wall," do not read "wall" (*homat*) but "Truth" (*hemet*). One through our seeking of mercy and understanding. As it is said: "For upon Truth and upon My Truth was the city of Jerusalem." Therefore, the Holy One, blessed be He, gave this to his names and to the heavenly Mothers <note>A kabbalistic reference to the 'Mothers' or emanations</note> from the time of Truth, and we pray "and build the walls of Jerusalem" so that they may be a "Wall for Truth," which is what we seek: to bind the quality of Truth and Kindness. According to this, the verse "to Jerusalem... and she shall be called the City of Truth" is clarified. And the secret:

<sig>In the manner of</sig>

<column-break/>

<margin>
Regarding the taking [atoning] of sins through tithes.
</margin>
Specifically, every person of spirit should guard his soul regarding the Psalm [chapter...], how many times he says it, and the order of his prayer, etc. Heaven forbid that any blemish or insult should come to his soul from the taking of the strength of the commandments. For this is "Peace" in the eyes of God, and "Peace" on this day causes the "trembling of the lips" <note>prayer or speech</note> and shameful words among the common folk. I will inform you that I was with you in pleasantness.

**He said** at the time of the judgment of [37]... may his memory be for a blessing... from me to the hard lands. And he had proper reasons for this. One of them was because of his lowliness; he took "cut coins" <note>specific charity coins</note> as the portion for the "Good Luck" <term>Mazal Tov</term> from the Midrash of the simple folk, the officers, and the "Princes of my God." And on this day, they shall be exchanged for the upright. To speak a word: for at any rate, it is the duty of Israel to provide for their judges and their scholars and those who "kneel" [in prayer], as mentioned in the secret of the "Path of Life" [section 234], that we should follow in their footsteps so that the judges will be maintained and sustained with a clear life. Truly, my important friends, my princes, and those who inform me: I speak entirely according to the Rambam <note>Maimonides</note>, whose words are clear. And in the view of the perfect world, they are indeed the scholars who sit in the Chamber [of Hewn Stone] according to the measure of the Rabbis. I will clarify for myself the matter of "heart and bitter in soul," as it is understood from my visions regarding the tithes of sins and the widows of widows. This is the piyyut <note>liturgical poem</note> of "Peace," and my words are on my own behalf, for I merited through the thirteen [Attributes of Mercy] with their standing and their greatness to be accepted by the Great Rabbi over most of the provinces of Israel. And not through my own merit,

<margin>
Why the Psalms warn regarding the study of the Book of Psalms, and specifically those who occupy themselves with it.
</margin>
but only the merit of my fathers stands for me. I have only come to tell of the praises of the Lord among the assemblies of the nights—slaves and women upon horses—and those who fill the stars like servants upon the earth. Woe to them, for they were two students, slaves, and "princes" in their outbursts and blessings and evenings. And there is a "man of my hearing" in the language, and they are placed in corners and hidden spots, and there is no one who can understand them clearly. Our heart and their high positions are like hidden corners, far from their level in this world. And those "outer garments" <note>metaphor for superficiality</note> who are in the world with their poems—mere words—and the beauty of their songs are praising and magnifying. We know, and there are no days, and look at our prayers in their grace. And upon this, our prayers... our prayers are unto the Lord in the world of riddles. And their interpretations were refined—a soul in its loyalty and its dimensions, and those who cast anger and wrath upon the nations. They take "cut coins" and the "portion," and they shall be blotted out of the heavens for this. And regarding this secret, it is as if "Woe, they are perishing," and there is no judgment for the judges.

<margin>
Matters of the poor, orphans, widows, and the like.
</margin>
In my opinion, there are some remaining praises that enter the house, [asking] who among them... and they think to receive upon themselves the "Heart of the Eternal Truths." Benjamin [the author's name?] walked after the many commandments, and they were refined from good merits, as he said of me. And one does not write every "anger" from these nine "New Orders" <note>likely referring to new communal regulations</note>... "from the children of the poor, Torah shall come forth for Israel." <note>Talmud Nedarim 81a</note> Every intelligent person will understand and gain insight from the words of the great Genius, the R.L.M.S. <note>Rabbi Levi Maryash?</note>, regarding what was said: "He was among the wise men of Italy."

<margin>
The Rabbis, etc.
</margin>
The Rabbis, etc., as mentioned before, etc. And within his words, he wrote that he was found to be His servant. And even if one kindness is canceled from a thousand, we will still break out regarding the one who stands for the "service of the slaves," for we want everyone who walks in it, for in the world of holiness many and well-known "extensions" are produced. And my own opinion, the opinion of the humble, I will return one from all his arrangements, etc. For he was astonished that we should not be afraid to be gathered into the Hall of the "Arrogant Language," in the way of the Torah, a "service of slaves" to the Master of Deeds. And behold, those "Circles" <note>social circles or groups</note> who act treacherously, who gather in the blood of the poor, and the Lord of Hosts is like... as wrote the Rashba <note>Rabbi Shlomo ben Aderet</note>. And so there is an elder in the "City of the Sea" <note>possibly Venice or a port city</note> that even though they are called "those who draw near," they do not understand His kingship. And to the wise who descend into the depths of the law, they are not... and the desire for wisdom... they are boastful of honor and of their high standing, and they raise themselves and are astonished, and they put to shame the students who come before them, and they only receive full payment. And they are sent to seek all their days... they were like those who see signs, those who know the knowledge of the "princes." And these will be entered by whoever is worthy... from the "distorted standing." And their "Sabbaths" are in falsehood and in error. The insightful person will look into the tractate of the Rabbis... he forces him to listen to his voice, for his words are the words of the Living God. And so I say regarding this [manuscript] that was accepted: the "Gifts" were according to the awakening, not from the "species of their places," but the work of human hands. For we find that the lips provide the text of the "Altar," regarding this matter. And now, I have seen a sign in the "Great Assembly" in the provinces of Holy Poland, who were in those lands. They would perfect themselves in private and in public, and regarding the "Giver" and the "Hired One" by themselves. And the "Sent Ones" and the "Peace of our Sent Ones" are gathered there. Truly, they saw the works of the Lord, and the "Assembly of my Harvest," the Lord of Hosts. But in the holy world, its repair is its ruin, as you see from those who do not accept discipline and cross over in the "City of the Sea" against the widows and the "this" and the "curses" written in the book and from the "Vision of the Many." Therefore, this sign has come upon us in pure and clear generations, and there is no way that exempts us. But the "Portion" and the "Balance" [of the scale] go down and down through our hands—through the sins of our being. Therefore, you, the Glory of Israel, who pray uprightly and eat the "Way" and receive tithes: guard the holiness in the vision, to grasp the matter. It is close to the understanding and the insight to bridge the way and the song of their speed to remove the family. And may the prayer rise up, for he will act with the will [to establish] the foundation of the dwelling. And the Holy One, blessed be He, granted this to our fathers and our mothers... and he will speak here of our "Pleasantness"... and wine will go out in its kinds. And through the merit of our actions, He will make us hear. And the Holy One, blessed be He, is the source of Peace, the Helper and the Master of Wine. He will establish us at the time of Judgment, and for all who know knowledge and law: through the merit of our occupation with the Pillar of Judgment.

# Preface of the Genius, the Son of the Author of "The Pillar of Truth" [page] 33

The publication was expressed in a refined tongue <note>original: "leshon selila"</note> so that he would not retract any of his statements, even those quoted from the words of the Scribes <note>the Rabbis</note>. An explanation of this will be clarified, God willing. My father and teacher <note>the author</note> wrote in the month of Sivan, in the year 5422 <note>1662 CE</note>, regarding the ruling: "one should not knead [matzah dough] with lukewarm water." <note>original: "lo talush be-chamim"</note> He wrote there that from the language of the Sages, it implies that one should not knead with lukewarm water initially <note>le-chatchila</note>, but it does not say that if one *did* knead it, it is forbidden. If it had said "one may not knead with water that has been warmed," it would imply a total prohibition even after the fact <note>be-di'avad</note>. Therefore, the phrasing "do not knead with lukewarm water" suggests it is avoided at the start, but if done, it remains permissible. The same applies here, where the phrasing "the Sages have no intention other than..." was used. He derived from the language of the Baraita <note>an ancient oral tradition not included in the Mishnah</note> that there is no permission at all to retract, yet it is permitted to be lenient and add to it.

<margin>See my explanation on the Scripture, and specifically in the holy book *Etz Chaim* <note>Tree of Life</note>, for from the variations in the Scripture [we see] "Jerusalem, the City of Truth."</margin> This is the sign of the "Pillar of Truth": because of the power of the Sages of Truth, they would not retract their words even in a small amount. It is permitted for them to retract only when it concerns Rabbinic decrees. Nevertheless, they would be happy if they did not have to retract. It is known from Tractate Yevamot <note>a volume of the Talmud dealing with marriage laws</note> that a "second-degree" prohibition <note>a Rabbinic expansion of forbidden marriages</note> is sacred to the secular. The Gemara <note>Talmudic commentary</note> asks: why is it called a "second-degree prohibition" if it is merely a Rabbinic enactment? It is because the words of the Sages are treated with the weight of holiness. They protected their words so much that Jerusalem is called the City of Truth, for the words of the Sages are sustained there until they are called "holy."

Another explanation: why did the Sages have "no intention other than..."? This follows the path of what is said in the chapter "He Who Died" in Tractate Bava Batra, page 109, regarding the statement of Rava concerning the prohibition of robbery. Rava said: "Will our claims be finished?" This refers to the tithes and the legalities of the proselytes who converted, that they should not return to their former ways.

<margin>Another reason for this: it refers to the Intention, Constancy, Prayers, and Priests, etc., in the manner of "the greatness of acts of loving-kindness."</margin>

Regarding the sanctity of his birth and conception: if his conception and birth were both in holiness, he should not be required to return <note>to a lower status</note>. How does the Torah view a document written by a gentile? Rabbi Isaac bar Samuel explained that the Baraita does not teach this... but rather "there is no life but for you," etc. According to this, Rava and Hillel came to teach us that the Sages' intention was truth. Our Mishnah is established as true because the Sages' words are sustained.

<margin>Another reason why our reading of the Torah portions and the "Repairs" <note>Tikkunim</note> is called "upright": the greatness of acts of loving-kindness.</margin>

* Another matter: why is Jerusalem called the "City of Truth"? It requires clarification from the Gemara in the chapter "One Who Recites" <note>in Tractate Berakhot</note>. Rav Hisda said that Rabbi Yochanan said: "The law follows Rabbi Judah." He said: "One should not interrupt between 'Truth' <note>Emet</note> and 'And it is certain' <note>Ve-Yatziv</note>." He sat and did not interrupt. He was asked: "What is the reason according to Rabbi Judah?" It is because it is written: "The Lord God is Truth." <note>Jeremiah 10:10</note>. Therefore, we do not interrupt between "The Lord your God" and "Truth." The Gemara further discusses: Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: "He may repeat the word 'Truth'." But Rav Joseph said: "How excellent is this tradition!" When Rabbi Samuel bar Judah came, he said: "In the West <note>the Land of Israel</note>, they say in the evening: 'Speak to the Children of Israel and you shall say to them... I am the Lord your God, Truth.'" They asked: "Is this considered 'excellent'?" Rav Kahana said: "He should not start [the verse], but if he started, he must finish."

Rashi and Rashbam <note>medieval commentators</note> explain regarding the evening prayer: we do not normally recite the portion of *Tzitzit* <note>ritual fringes</note> because the commandment of fringes does not apply at night. However, if they start it, they finish it. They would skip and return to "The Lord your God is Truth." The scholars of the Land of Israel argued: does saying "And you shall say to them" count as a "beginning" of the obligation? This is surprising, for if saying "And you shall say to them" does not count as a beginning, why would it be considered "excellent" to finish it? It is more logical to say it is a beginning, especially since we are stringent regarding the portion of *Tzitzit*. This is like the difficulty raised by the Rashba <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Adret</note> in his novellae on Tractate Berakhot regarding Rav Papa’s view.

<column-break/>

However, after the word "Truth," it is permitted to interrupt. Therefore, when one says "True and Certain" <note>Emet ve-Yatziv</note>, it is not proper to stop, as it is the start of the subject. We find among the commentators regarding the "Red Heifer," they asked how one could be so precise at the very start of the matter? Just as our Sages requested in our context regarding "Make for yourselves fringes," one is obligated to start and say "True, and certain, and established..." and if so, there will be no lack there. This is "Truth." Thus, it is well explained why he repeats the word "Truth." This corresponds to the numerical value <note>Gematria</note> of the Holy Names. Or, even if he does not repeat it, since he interrupted, he should start with "firmness."

Let us clarify the two mentions of "remembrance" in the Torah portion where it says "And the Lord said to Moses, saying" and "Speak to the children of Israel and say to them." Why is the word "saying" <note>Lemor</note> used? The word "saying" implies that they should tell others. "Speak to the children of Israel"—this includes everyone. Even though we heard that Rabbi Shimon exempts women from the fringes because it is a "positive commandment caused by time" <note>a time-bound ritual</note>, it is not an "extra" obligation for women. It is a great principle in the Commandments that women are exempt from time-bound duties. However, the commandment of fringes applies to everyone.

It seems to me that we can answer this based on the Midrash Sifrei: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says, "Why is the blue thread called *Techelet*? Because the Egyptians were finished <note>kalu</note> through the firstborns." Another Rabbi says, "Why is it called *Tzitzit*? Because the Omnipresent peered <note>hetzitz</note> over the houses of our ancestors in Egypt." Now, these are the difficulties found in the Sifrei: they sought the Midrashic origin of these names. We find in Tractate Gittin (page 109): since only those who were in Egypt are subject to the law of *Techelet*, why are they obligated in *Tzitzit*? Now, back to what I wrote: if this is a time-bound positive commandment, women should be exempt.

It appears the reason for the custom is based on what is written in the *Shulchan Aruch* (Orach Chaim 470): we learn in Tractate Soferim that the firstborns fast on the eve of Passover. The reason is a "remembrance" of the miracle that they were saved from the Plague of the Firstborn. The *Agudah* <note>a legal work</note> writes that even female firstborns should fast because they were also saved. But the earlier authorities <note>Rishonim</note> disagree. In this same way, they asked: "Why is it called *Techelet* or *Tzitzit*?" To teach and remember why women might be obligated in fringes—because in the merit of the women, the Omnipresent protected our houses in Egypt. If so, it follows that women would be obligated in fringes. However, Rabbi Shimon disagrees; he holds that the Plague of the Firstborn does not apply to women in this context, and therefore he holds that women are exempt from time-bound positive commandments.

<margin>Another explanation: why "upright," as it is written concerning the melodies and the "Zikukin" <note>sparks/connections</note>, and in the manner written in the *Masoret* <note>Traditional notation</note>.</margin>

Or it can be explained in this way: the Gemara in the chapter "The Blue Thread" <note>Tractate Menachot</note> says that Rav Rabin sent a message: "Take heed of a gentile who is wearing fringes." For it says: "Speak to the children of Israel and tell them... and they shall make for themselves [fringes]." This implies the Children of Israel shall make them, but not gentiles. Rav Mordechai said: "If so, a gentile's fringes are invalid." But Rav Judah said: "Fringes made by a gentile are valid." This is also found in the portion of *Ekev*. It seems to me that the phrase "And you shall say to them" at the beginning of the portion is key. Does it mean "to them" <note>the Israelites</note> specifically? The word "to them" is extra, for it already said "Speak to the children of Israel." It comes to hint that you should not think a gentile's fringes are valid. The language "to them" implies: to them (the Israelites) they shall make fringes, and not to the gentiles.

The "and" in "And you shall say to them" <note>the 'Vav' in Ve-amarta</note> connects the thoughts, suggesting there might be a side where a gentile's fringes are valid, and this is where they argue. Through this, we clarify the dispute: those who say "And you shall say to them" is the start of the portion include women because the word "to them" is extra and serves to include women in the obligation of fringes. But those who say it is not the start of the portion rely on the general rule that women are exempt from time-bound commandments.

It is now possible to clarify the two mentions of remembrance, as well as the meaning of "How excellent is this tradition," as we questioned above. The reason why one authority holds that "And you shall say to them" is not the start of the fringes portion is because... it seems to me to answer according to the conclusion of the Gemara... the commandment of fringes is a great commandment. Moses said to the Holy One, Blessed be He: "Master of the Universe, You know that every day I wear Tefillin on my head and fringes on my garment..."

<sig>End of the page</sig>

# Preface of the Great Genius, the Author of the *Pillar of Truth*

->**In the order of the double opening of the firmament...**<-

In the order of the double opening of the firmament <note>original: "כפל פיתחא מרקיע"</note>, a gloss according to Rabbi Nehemiah: he was requested in the **Heavenly Academy** <note>original: "מתיבתא דרקיעא"</note> according to the sages, and our Rabbis went to engage with him all his life. They knew the place of wisdom was seen as the dust of his shoes. They fulfilled the statement of our Sages of blessed memory at the end of the tractate *Pesachim*: "three days and three nights," etc., see there. It is difficult to understand: why was the sign given specifically through birds?

The "Chosen of all Authors" wrote that one must scrutinize how it is possible to say that the entire Heavenly Academy would argue against **the Holy One, Blessed be He**, as it were? For if among those below on earth "you shall not testify against a superior," how much more so regarding the Supernal Treasure who gave us the **Torah** <term>Torah: The foundational legal and spiritual text of Judaism</term>. Furthermore, it is a great wonder that they would say, "Strengthen His mind," etc. Could it be that all my strength would lean upon the Sages, of blessed memory, to speak thus toward the One Above, Blessed be He?

And it is further difficult, as I have written in my words elsewhere: why do I need the word "exempt" <note>original: "פטור"</note> twice? I will explain this difficulty according to the plain meaning <note>original: "Peshat"</note>, following the chapter I wrote on pages 29 to 38. For regarding the matter of Judah, the son of Rav Hisda, he said that in a case of distress, the priority is the servant. Therefore, what is it? Also, regarding the gate, the priority is "exempt" in a case of doubt... <unclear>illegible legal shorthand</unclear>... and he thought perhaps he had erred...

Now, regarding the intent of the verse: what is the challenge? Perhaps it was a mistake? If he disagrees with the **First Teacher** <term>Tanna Kamma: The unnamed first authority quoted in a Mishnah</term>, he should have said so. This is also difficult regarding the plain meaning of the text, based on what **Rashi** <term>Rashi: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, the preeminent medieval commentator</term> explained on the portion of *Tazria* <note>original: "Leviticus 12-13, dealing with skin afflictions"</note>... and the matter of immersion and ritual impurity... and in the chapter concerning "And this shall be the law of the leper."

Behold, this was the intent of the questioner: "Perhaps he made a mistake?" For **Maimonides** <term>Rambam: Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon, the great 12th-century philosopher and legalist</term> explained that on the condition of a mistake... <unclear>text corrupted</unclear>... He could be exempt. The intent of the questioner was whether he erred in the reason for the impurity itself, similar to the laws of loving-kindness. And regarding the shaving and the sacrifice, see there: Rabbi Joshua holds that it is a distant matter, the opinion of the First Teacher being that they are literally defiled, but only impure enough to require immersion and a sacrifice. This is part of the work of their counting... and since it was written in the text, he said "exempt, exempt" twice. This refers to a complete exemption or an exemption based on the reasoning of his words. Whether it was this or that, the **Halakha** <term>Halakha: Jewish Law</term> remains in its place.

Even so, they do not disagree with the opinion of the Most High, may He be blessed, who gave us the Torah. For the end of His intention is to impart knowledge and teach the wise man understanding. Folly is only a hindrance to contemplation until the matter is clarified and we understand it with the Creator, blessed be He.

<margin>* And to clarify the matter as it was decided for me, it is proven in the language of the opening... for every scholar, Rav Yumi bar Kanina. See the **Maharsha** <note>Rabbi Shmuel Eliezer Edels</term> on the reason his name ascended to the voice of the Holy One, Blessed be He, who loves and engages in the "Opening of the Tomorrow." My son shall return to say the chapter of the "Yearling Heifer" <note>original: "עגלה בת שנתה," likely referring to the ritual of the Beheaded Heifer</note>... to say that the face of Moses our Teacher, peace be upon him, was before the Holy One... for by the power of the world, upper and lower beings are in his religion... and the Holy One, Blessed be He, did not say to him what the future holds... </margin>

<column-break/>

At this moment, kindness is present at all times that there is wisdom, similar to the **Sefirot** <term>Sefirot: The ten divine attributes or emanations in Kabbalah</term>. Everything exists and stands, and according to my aforementioned way, they are exalted above the heavens. Even though everything is for a moment, nevertheless it "stands," meaning it endures, as our Sages explained regarding two types of standing.

Furthermore, it is written: one does not speak in the presence of the deceased except for matters concerning the deceased, such as the ways of his burial and eulogy. But any other matter is forbidden. And the **Beit Yosef** <term>Beit Yosef: The commentary on the Tur by Rabbi Joseph Karo</term> wrote that the **Mordechai** <term>Mordechai: Rabbi Mordechai ben Hillel, a 13th-century German legal authority</term> wrote at the end of tractate *Moed Katan* that it is forbidden in any case...

And what is the reason? Because the entire order within four cubits <note>approx. 6-8 feet</note> is out of respect for the dead. But as for the law in the first house... and those who are meticulous... and everything they did for him at his death, namely his shroud and what was placed on his grave. The **Tosafot** <term>Tosafot: Medieval commentaries on the Talmud</term> wrote: even on his grave, one should not be within four cubits, for that would be **Mocking the Poor** <term>Lo’eg Larash: The prohibition against performing commandments in the presence of the dead, who can no longer perform them</term>. This was also written in *Mekor Yosef* in the name of the **Asherite** <term>The Rosh: Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</term>.

In my poverty, it seems to me that I can resolve the difficulty that the *Beit Yosef* had with the *Mordechai*. He challenged the *Mordechai* regarding the phrasing, so I will present to you the language of the *Mordechai*: "One does not say before the dead except matters of the dead." He wrote there: "And that which we do not say words of Torah is specifically within four cubits, as is found in the chapter *Mi Shemeto* <note>Talmud Berakhot, Chapter 3</note>... or in a cemetery."

He establishes it specifically within four cubits, meaning the dead occupies four cubits for the purpose of reciting the **Shema** <note>The central Jewish prayer</note>. But outside of four cubits, it is permitted. However, in the "First House," it is forbidden in that entire order of the dead.

On the surface, one might wonder: there in the Gemara at the beginning of the chapter *Mi Shemeto*, it says one is exempt from the Shema, from Prayer, and from **Tefillin** <term>Tefillin: Phylacteries worn during prayer</term>. The Gemara asks: is he exempt even if he is not carrying the body? No, it answers... unless he is in the cemetery with a Torah scroll in his arm, etc. And it establishes it within four cubits. If he is outside of four cubits, he is permitted. If so, why did the *Mordechai* say "in the presence of the dead"? It must be that "in the presence of the dead" refers to whoever is engaged in burying him. Because of his exemption, we only speak of matters of the dead. And the *Beit Yosef* wrote in the name of **Nachmanides** <term>Ramban: Rabbi Moshe ben Nachman</term>...

Now I have the idea to resolve the difficulty of the *Beit Yosef* regarding the language of the Gemara. Rabbi Shimi said in the name of Rabbi Joshua ben Levi: "One does not say in the presence of the dead anything but matters of the dead." Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said: "This was only said regarding words of Torah, but regarding worldly matters, we have no problem with it." Some are more stringent, saying: "This was only said regarding words of Torah, but all the more so regarding worldly matters [it is forbidden]."

Now, it is difficult to reconcile the *Mordechai* with the rule that one should not walk in a cemetery with a Torah scroll... Just as there, the rule depends on being within or outside of four cubits, it should be the same here. Why was the specific language "in the presence of the dead" used? It implies that if he is obligated to bury him, it is forbidden. In the presence of a grave or bones, the law is the same... The reason for "in the presence of the dead" is to show that while in a cemetery the reason is "Mocking the Poor," regarding worldly matters that would not apply. But when "in the presence of the dead" who is yet to be buried, the reason is so as not to neglect the burial.

Therefore, we must say that the language "in the presence of the dead" was used specifically to say that it is forbidden to speak words of Torah in his presence even *outside* of four cubits—for example, in a large room where one stands more than four cubits away. Even so, it is forbidden. This is different from a cemetery, where outside of four cubits it is permitted. This was the intent of the *Mordechai*...

As the Gemara concludes in the Heavenly Academy regarding the debate: "Is it a case of doubt? The Holy One, Blessed be He, says it is Pure, and the Academy says it is Impure." They said: "Who shall decide? **Rabba bar Nahmani**." For Rabba bar Nahmani said, "I am unique in the laws of skin afflictions and tent-impurity." They sent for him... and as he was dying, he said, "**Pure, Pure**" <note>original: "Tahor, Tahor"</note>. A **Heavenly Voice** <term>Bat Kol: A divine echo or voice</term> went forth and said, "Happy are you, Rabba bar Nahmani, for your body is pure and your soul departed in purity."

<margin>It is very good and beneficial to say every day... see the *Sefer HaLimmud* page 159a in the new insights... see the *Magen Avraham*... see what I wrote...</margin>

# Preface of the Great Genius, Son of the Author of the *Pillar of Truth*

<margin>Open your eyes to see what the Rambam <note>Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, known as Maimonides</note>, of blessed memory, wrote further regarding the secret of the donkey <note>original: "חמור" - here likely an allegorical reference to physical matter</note>, its measurements, and the necessity of its proof for life. It seems to me that they were awakened to know how much this is and upon what these righteous ones lean in the preface where Jacob went to settle in the land of his daughters and among the innocent people in their youth and zeal.</margin>

* The commandment of the donkey <note>The author uses "donkey" (hamor) as a pun on "matter" (homer) or "stringency" (humra)</note>, its measurements and its necessity as a proof for him. And regarding what was said to his division: we gathered with our colleagues. I saw fit to explain one matter which, by the grace of His will and assistance, they merited to bind in the land of his daughters and among the innocent people, through the power of our Rabbi <note>referring to the author's father</note>, peace be upon him—neither in his physical body nor in his labors. See in the commentary on the Torah portion *Vayechi* <note>Genesis 47:28–50:26</note>, there are claims according to the **Kabbalah** <term>Kabbalah: The Jewish mystical tradition</term>, and therefore we have no life except through the literal meaning <note>original: "Peshat"</note>. Only by way of the scribes, as it is written in the *Yalkut* <note>a collection of Midrashic teachings</note> on the portion *Va’etchanan*: "Enough for you" <note>original: "רב לך"</note>. The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moses: "Enough for you; you shall be placed among the generation of the wilderness, for there is a covenant between you, and they shall enter the Land." And what life is there in entering? Likewise, it adds and increases in the *Midrash Rabbah* on the portion *Phinehas* regarding the "donkey," another lack was added for life to repair, better than others. And if for a donkey, for Moses our Rabbi, peace be upon him, it shall be a merit; all the more so, it is an inference from minor to major <note>original: "Kal Vachomer"</note> that it is better than the rest of the desert generation who did not lose their merit.

And see what our Teacher said in the chapter *HaMapelet* <note>referring to Tractate Niddah</note>: Our Rabbis taught that there are **three partners in man**: the Holy One, Blessed be He, his father, and his mother. The father sows the "white," from which the brain, bones, nails, and membranes are formed. The mother sows the "red," from which the skin, flesh, and the black of the eye are formed. And the Holy One, Blessed be He, places within him the wind, the breath, and the **soul** <term>Soul: Neshamah, the divine spark in man</term>. And it settles well that Jacob was in the land of his daughters in flesh and bones, for his sons and brothers in their zeal for the choice parts of the body and the inclinations of the heart also entered there—but only in his body for burial in the Land of Israel. <margin>And some add, see also in the book *HaMapelet* chapter 13, page 75, side B, though it is not necessary for our matter.</margin> And this is the life, for Jacob—Jacob’s grace was like flesh in the land of his daughters, and his bones merited to receive the hint... in the portion *Vayechi*, the *Yalkut* says "Enough for you," and *Numbers Rabbah* on *Phinehas* answers my merit... to sustain one, and my opinion is that it is only upon me to remember, etc. <margin>And see in the book *HaMapelet* page 108, side B, that the pupil of the eye and the skin of the face are renewed; see further page 18, 26 in the second part.</margin> And I bind the grace of his will and assistance to life... and this I knew from the initiative to lack, he was buried alive and sick, a donkey... see the commentary of the **Ramban** <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nachman, Nachmanides</note>, of blessed memory, the pious one answered... the place for your placement upon the son of Joseph... the bones entered the Land... part of the village... did not enter the Land... to say what is life, from what they wept over him... the crown of the name... and therefore Moses our Rabbi, peace be upon him, did not merit burial in the Land of Israel, etc. From all flesh, grace and kindness, bones without flour... in the nullification of the reward of the body... and the sign... <margin>Open your eyes to see what the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote further in such-and-such a place and in the commentary, etc.</margin>

* The *Tur* <note>The Arba’ah Turim, a seminal code of Jewish law</note> wrote in *Yoreh De’ah* section 269: It is a great **mitzvah** <term>Mitzvah: A religious commandment</term> to eulogize the dead. Therefore, in his generation, there was a culmination of the grace of famous things, in order to increase weeping and lamentation and to mention his honor, so that after his rest, a voice would be placed before him. And if bound in flesh in the portion *Toldot* <note>Genesis 25:19–28:9</note>, Esau said, "Behold, I am going to die, etc." and even if all and many are destined to know the matter of death like a donkey, as it is said... what is the nature of this service? He said to him, what are these exemptions and sustainers, and before him as a beast from us... wine and crumbs of fish... Esau said, "Behold, I am going to die by your hand"... what desire have I for the birthright? They explained that Esau was wicked in his mind and thought in his heart that he would taste all pleasures, and their ending is bitterness and death in his wickedness... Jacob solved it by the power of his father... as our father King David, peace be upon him, answered regarding his donkey... my son, my son, they shall stumble... the days of your peaceful life... and therefore at the hour of eulogizing... to be for the service of the dead... and he has understanding... they thought in their hearts, alas... on the heart of burial... a donkey... for them a memorial of sin... see further... pious ones page 7 and 60... and enough for the wise. One who wrote thus... the body by the power of sin and guilt... when he was multiplied in his position... a heart for the world... after the nullification of the stench for the graveyard... and a heart in his mind... and he will remember and draw out in his mind the deaths... for death and fall... why should one mourn him since there is no honor... the Holy One, Blessed be He, granted me to die... he had a thought... let him not mourn for me... to ask from his paths... if it is not so in his heart, let him have thoughts... and Jacob bound... and I set him to be in his life... in all the days of his reincarnation and remembrance... the order of the matter of the eulogy and the dirges to honor the name... and death for his sin... * <margin>A connection to the verse "my son, my son," he opened with a bitter voice, a call was called above, etc.</margin> and it was marked, such as the matter of "you opened with a bitter voice," a call was called for the flesh of the skin... and he goes to me... and remember further... from his birth and it is finished... it was a call in the language... from his birth... our teacher, his memory for a blessing, was not eulogized... good seed, etc. The explanation of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, on the verse "I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel."

<column-break/>

## Preface of the Great Sage, Son of the Author of the *Pillar of Truth*

<margin>Look into the *Petihta* of the *Pesikta* <note>a collection of homiletic teachings</note>, and in the chapter of Rabbi Eliezer, and in the chapter of *Kiddushin* <note>Tractate on Betrothals</note>. He writes that the reason for their deaths is so that a person does not enter into a habit of arrogance. Also, look at the verse: "All His holy ones are in Your hand" (Deuteronomy 33:3), which follows the path of the explanation of the sages. This is the great intention of the verse "Even He who loves the nations," meaning He loves Israel from among the nations. Only from the House [of Israel] are His holy ones in Your hand... while the nations of the world were struck down. Therefore, it is explained in the chapter *Helek* <note>Sanhedrin 10th chapter</note>.</margin>

Just as it is possible to say of him, even on a Festival, that he did not fall into neglect regarding his holiness even at his death. And behold, **Rabbi Akiva** <note>One of the greatest sages of the Mishnaic period, martyred by the Romans</note> saw death as the end in this world and the entrance to the World to Come. Akiva said: "Have I lacked anything from the Torah?" And Rabbi Akiva saw fit to add that even if you have not lacked anything, if your days are lengthened further, you might come to sin. This is the language of the chapters: Akiva saw fit to add to it for you, for "there is no righteous man on earth who does good and sins not" (Ecclesiastes 7:20). He spoke in the future tense, not the past, for even if one is righteous now, he might sin if his days are prolonged. Therefore, he did not rejoice in long life. This explains the words they said to him: "Our Rabbi, you have taught us." Furthermore, I must examine what was said in *Rosh Hashanah* regarding a person: "Why do you laugh?" They said: "Look at the burning of our Rabbi," whereas Rabbi Akiva said to everyone: "Why are you weeping?" When they were at the House of God and saw a fox emerging from the Holy of Holies, **Rabban Gamliel** and the others wept, but Akiva laughed. <margin>* In the Midrash on the verse "And He saw that it was good," but regarding the time of suffering, it says: "Do not provoke me, Rabbi Hama bar Hanina."</margin> This is explained in the Midrash... but regarding the time of suffering, it says: "Do not provoke me." Rabbi Hama bar Hanina did not allow the nations of the world to have songs and laughter, so that they would not be waiting for Israel to say them. **Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai** <note>A 2nd-century sage and reputed author of the Zohar</note> said that the nations of the world were not worthy of receiving the Torah... so that they would not count against Israel, saying "You are the ones punished."

And many take issue with this statement... God forbid we explain the Midrash to say that the nations of the world are not worthy of being recipients of kindness. For did God not create all His creatures, even the animals and the plants? This is difficult. Would the Holy One, Blessed be He, perform an injustice in judgment just so they wouldn't taunt Israel? Rather, one Midrash explains another. In the portion of *Tazria* <note>Leviticus 12-13, dealing with plagues</note>, it explains that God does not strike the bodies of the righteous first. Rather, He strikes their houses. But regarding the *Terumah* <note>sanctified produce</note> which enters the King’s palace, the King says: "Do not fear," and he takes it into the house to eat and wait. When Israel acted [sinfully], He placed the plagues on their houses first. He said to them: "Do not fear these nations," but for you... This Midrash contradicts the Midrash in *Vayeshev* <note>Genesis 37-40</note> which says the nations are not worthy of being punished. 

Furthermore, it is difficult as it says: "With the death of a man..." How do we judge? By the plague of the body, the garment, and the house. This does not apply to them [the nations]... and the *Midrash Rabbah* brings this here. Through this, the language of the Midrash will be clarified where it says "the nations were not worthy to be masters of kindness." My father told me that the Midrashim should be explained according to the *Midrash Yelamdenu* on *Tazria*. The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Israel: "See what distinguishes you from the nations of the world. Regarding the nations, I strike their bodies first and then their houses, as it says: 'And the Lord plagued Pharaoh with great plagues, and his house' (Genesis 12:17). But for you, if you sin, I strike your houses first." Even in *Midrash Rabbah*, Rabbi Joshua ben Hanina says: "The Master of Mercy does not strike souls first." You learn this from the plagues of Egypt... first the staff, then the water, then the frogs... even regarding plagues (*Nega'im*), they come first on his house; if he does not repent, then on his garments; if he still does not repent, then on his body. One can distinguish this from Pharaoh, as he said: "I do not know the Lord," therefore he was judged in his body first, whereas for Israel, God goes with them from the light to the heavy.

Behold, the commentators are silent on this Midrash: "The Master of Mercy does not strike the body first." But go and read! Is it not written in the verse: "When a plague of leprosy is in a man" (Leviticus 13:9)? It says he shall be quarantined, and then in the portion of *Tazria* it speaks of the plague of the house. I settled this according to what I explained on the verse: "This shall be the law of the leper" (Leviticus 14:2). Why do I need the word "Law" (*Torat*)? In the Talmud, chapter *Hamavi* <note>Gittin 9a</note>, it concludes that "Law" comes to include a poor leper... Also, we find in chapter 27 of *Sorer U'Moreh* <note>Sanhedrin 71a</note> regarding the "Afflicted House": "It never was and never will be." Why then was it written? "Study it and receive reward." According to Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Shimon, a house never actually becomes impure until it is seen...

<column-break/>

## Preface of the Genius, Son of the Author of the *Pillar of Truth*

As the **Rambam** <note>Maimonides</note>, of blessed memory, indeed wrote. And one is exempt from being stringent upon yourself regarding the **graves of gentiles** <term>Graves of gentiles: According to Jewish law, there are debates about whether non-Jewish graves convey ritual impurity (tum'ah) in a "tent" (ohel)</term>. The reason is simple: my work is regarding the graves of Israel, and He knows the number of you all. A person should not casually go to the graves of gentiles. One should not question his explanation, for since the Rambam was stringent about not going to the graves of the nations of the world, why then is one exempt? And He knows the number of you all. This implies that death might bring ruin if one frequents the graves of the nations. One can answer this using the Rambam's response: it follows the dispute of our Rabbis whether the law follows **Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai** (Rashbi), who says they do not impart impurity in a tent, or Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who forbids it because of the "ruin of the world." Therefore, the Rambam, citing Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg, was only stringent *ab initio* <note>original: "Lechat'chila" - from the start/ideally</note> not to go to the graves of gentiles so that one does not become accustomed to also going to the graves of Israel. But for one who did go to the graves of the nations, after all, he did not desecrate anything... and it is permitted. 

He is stringent according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, for if one goes, it might lead to a lenient attitude. Therefore, he mentioned "He knows the number of you all" to inform us that regarding the graves of Israel, they definitely impart impurity, so one should not enter the "tent" of the corpse. This is not the case regarding the nations of the world; the impurity of a corpse does not apply to them after the fact, only as a stringency *ab initio*. As explained in the blessing "Who knows the number of you all," it was intended to explain that one should not go to the graves of Israel, and to the graves of the nations one should not go ideally, but after the fact, no impurity is attached. This is not like the view that they do impart impurity. The initial opinion of the Rambam was that it is permitted *ab initio* to go to the graves of the nations. If so, it is understood well. The Rambam was only stringent *ab initio*... for if according to the Rambam it were impure even after the fact, it would be forbidden. This settles the distant dispute... and "He knows the number of you all" does not mean he is stringent *ab initio* about the nations, but rather he should not go even *ab initio* because of the "ruin." All this is simple in the words of our Rabbi... see and contemplate.

In this way, I saw fit to explain in my books regarding the day of the portion *V'Zot HaBerachah* <note>Deuteronomy 33:1, the final portion of the Torah</note>:

<margin>The verse "Even He who loves the nations..." is difficult. Why use the word "Even" (*Af*)? It indicates anger... [alternative explanation]... The verse "All His holy ones are in Your hand" means they are placed there without a "carrier" <note>meaning they are directly under God's care</note>...</margin>

"Even He who loves the nations" — this teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He, did not distinguish in death between the nations of the world and Israel. This is difficult, for the word "Even" (*Af*) usually denotes anger. It should be explained that "Even" indicates that while Israel is beloved, they still suffer the "anger" of death. Some say that He loves Israel, and because of them, the nations are sustained, so that a person does not become arrogant. "All His holy ones are in Your hand" — this is like the explanation in the chapter *Hamanyan*. This is the meaning of the verse: "Even He who loves the nations," meaning He sustains Israel from the nations. "All His holy ones are in Your hand" means they are "resting" there, whereas the nations of the world are struck down by His foot. Therefore, "They sat at Your feet" (Deuteronomy 33:3) refers to the merit of Israel. This is what is said in the chapter *Helek*. 

Rabbi Eliezer, when he was dying, saw death coming upon the world... but Rabbi Akiva [rejoiced]. For as long as a person is alive, he is judged, therefore he is beloved. We do not have a "carrier" and we are not "placed" — this is from the Aramaic. What did Rabbi Akiva mean by "Even He who loves the nations"? He meant even in his life... he said to him: "Have I lacked anything from the Torah?" He said: "I have learned." It seems to me that our Rabbi meant that "there is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin." It is difficult for me... for the word is doubled. This teaches us that even if you are righteous, if you live long, you might stumble. This is the meaning of the verse: "For there is no righteous man on earth who does good" — meaning a person cannot remain perfectly righteous forever without eventually missing the mark. This is the intent of Ecclesiastes: "There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness" (Ecclesiastes 7:15). Why? It is revealed before God that this righteous man might eventually turn to evil, so God takes him from the world while he is still in his righteousness.

# Preface of the Great Sage, Son of the Author of the *Pillar of Truth*

<margin>

of Baruch Asher

As our sages explained, they did not seek, God forbid, to weep over the words of the Holy One, Blessed be He, as I have received. Rather, they sought to interpret for future generations the legal ruling <term>Psak Din<note>original: "פסק דין"; a final legal decision in Jewish law</term> issued by His hand. This serves as a commentary on His words. From what has arisen in the words of the Holy One, which is a double-folded note from the heavens <note>A metaphor for a divine decree or a complex legal tradition</note>, as I have explained. And if they saw a sign of exemption from the task, it would be understood from the beginning of our words. However, one must speak according to the names of the simple and well-known ones who lived in his time. For it is known that he was supported by the chain of tradition of the book *Kereitot* <note>A work on the methodology of the Talmud</note> by **Rabbah bar Nachmani** <note>A 3rd-century Babylonian Sage known for his expertise in the laws of ritual purity</note>. His eyes were darkened <note>A reference to his death while fleeing from government tax collectors</note>, and in the Midrash Rabbah on the portion of *Noach*, it adds that he was stirred by the verse "Darkness rose and it was dark."

The difficulty that was raised was that the verse says "He who has gifts written," meaning a world of light, etc. We must clarify the explanation of our Master <note>The author's father</note> on this word; on the contrary, his words were always "exempt." You will see that his explanation follows the path of the weight of our Sages, of blessed memory, in the Gemara <note>The part of the Talmud that contains rabbinic analysis</note>. They attributed the merit to those who were righteous. This is also found in the Midrash Rabbah: the explanation is that God filled the darkness, meaning the afflictions that brought about the darkness of the soul. There is a difficulty with the statement written there, for if the light was intended, it should not have said "it was not from us," but rather from a light closer to it, as it is written "from the brightness before Him." The explanation is: do not say "into the interior," but rather "from within it, before Him." And from there, the verse says "light rose," more than the light that was close to the Holy One. And that is the "Grace of Baruch," enough for him.

And he was stirred by the fact that it did not come from us, as is written regarding the day, that it was not from him. In truth, there is a reason for this in our logic: there is a reason for many or those close to nothing, in the way of birds of prey that are known. However, the righteous sleep, and the "Trustworthy Source" is for those who are not like birds of prey. From these things, it is known that it was "pure" <term>Tahor<note>original: "טהור"; ritually pure or clean</note></term> and it was said of Rabbah bar Nachmani, etc. His words on this matter are to say a ruling was established in his lifetime, "he is pure and precise." Regarding our discussion above, based on what is established in the verse "passing through the head of a man," that is the sages and their Torah. So there is a concern, since...

The blessing is found in the portion of "And This is the Blessing" <note>Deuteronomy 33</note>, so that people will say that "Baruch Asher" spoke. He shall be remembered for love according to the law, and you were happy according to the law. He stood to say and to revive you with wine. It is difficult to understand what the blessing meant to imply, for what is the reason for saying "KB"K" <note>An honorific acronym</note>? I have spoken of this as a form of the poem of the Name, that the Name was upon him, and he was proven right according to the law by the two, the daughter of the sun who was happy according to the law. It was written above regarding the **Resurrection of the Dead**, because of this he said: "and now the Holy One revives you according to the law through his explanation and through the salvation of the law," as stated above.

Therefore, one must say a word: through this examination, it concludes with the "Covenant of the Rabbinic Sages." They established the heavens in a directed way, and He knows the number of the stars according to the law. Always to bind and to revive you, Blessed be the Name. And the "Exempt" is light, as it was in the light of the sign... and he wrote on it "the sign of my hand." Know that in the Gemara it is brought: "The Sages taught: One who sees the graves of Israel... etc." A person must say, "Blessed be He... who knows the number of the stars." And the **Rif**, **Rosh**, and **Rashba** <note>Major medieval legal authorities: Rabbi Isaac Alfasi, Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, and Rabbi Solomon ben Adret</note> wrote "He knows the number of the stars." I do not know to whom the Rosh was referring there. His words certainly came to settle the law according to the opinion of the **Tur** <note>The *Arba'ah Turim*, a code of law</note>. This stands against the opinion of the **Rashba**, of blessed memory. This was written in the way of a "gift of the hands," as they said that when our hands are poor, we say this thing. These names are not waiting.

**Yohanan the High Priest** <note>A Hasmonean ruler and High Priest</note> would render things impure, and it is concluded there that he did so because he understood their impurity so that the tithe of his father and aunt would not be eaten. With this, it is also clarified that although it is simple that prayer belongs to the "Covenant of the Rabbinic Sages," one should not say "covers." Rather, the explanation is for your lineage. The Master, the son of the Rabbinic Sages, sought to give a reason for the holiness of Israel, who are present in the light and the walls of the world, for they are the ones who make things pure or impure. This was his intention, etc. Because of this, he adds to the story "He knows the number of the stars." This follows the explanation of **Rashi** <note>The premier medieval commentator</note> at the beginning of the book of Exodus: "Even though He counted them in their lifetime, He counted them again after their death to show His love for them, for they are compared to the stars, as it is said, 'He brings out their host by number' (Isaiah 40:26)." And so, through the Messiah, in their death, eye to eye, they will see the Unique Name. Therefore, he added "He knows the number of the stars," for through the counting, it will be seen who is missing. According to this, it is clear why Israel is more hidden than the nations of the world, for He loves them more. According to this explanation, it is well understood why the *Tur* placed this and added "the number of the stars." I must inform you of what is in the *Tur* regarding sign 322...

Regarding the graves of the nations of the world: **Maimonides** <note>The Rambam</note> wrote that they are impure and bring impurity through contact, etc. But the **Rashba**, of blessed memory, wrote in a response in the name of some dissenting rabbis. I saw that the **Maharil** <note>Rabbi Yaakov Moelin</note> of Rothenburg would warn women not to walk upon them, and may a blessing come upon him for being careful. These are his words. And this is the beauty of the poem "Pure is the Law" regarding "He knows the number of the stars." According to what I have written, "He knows the number of the stars" refers to them being pure and holy. But regarding the nations of the world, they do not bring impurity <note>in the same legal sense as Jewish graves</note>. If so, it is permitted to walk on the graves of the nations of the world in the courtyard...

<column-break/>

...to thousands of thousands and ten thousands, in the place of royalty, as seen by the Sage. You have seen this, and regarding this name, the law is learned from his mouth. In this way, the Holy One responded to him well and said to him: do not worry, I have heard the beginning of the gift as words, but the end you did not hear. For I rule the law according to the Sages, because you only heard from me **Rabbi Eliezer** <note>A 1st-century sage known for his strictness and traditionalism</note> saying "a calf in its year" <term>Eglah bat Shnatah<note>original: "עגלה בת שנתה"; a yearling calf used in specific rituals</term> at the beginning of the gift. After that, it says "And the Sages say, etc." They disagreed with him. This is the language of the Midrash regarding what Moses our teacher needed to understand. In the future, a righteous man will stand in the world and open the portion of the **Red Heifer** <note>Parashat Parah</note> saying: "Rabbi Eliezer says: a heifer of two years..." Who... why was it necessary to mention the words of Rabbi Eliezer? The words "etc." refer to the Sages.

Before this, it will be well understood why he said, "and now to open, etc." and there is no reason to delay. If so, one must look: why was it necessary only to mention the words of Rabbi Eliezer? For if his words were not the law, and the Sages say otherwise, why did Moses our teacher pray: "May it be Your will that he [Rabbi Eliezer] emerges from my loins"? Was it not for his benefit, that he be credited with a Torah scholar who studied his teachings? It seems to me the explanation is this: we find in our Mishnah <note>the core text of the Talmud</note> one righteous man, but only if he added more strength. And it is said: "The Sages say not according to his words." Regarding this matter, he was silent afterward. Why did they mention his words at all? It was for nothing! It was to teach for all generations that a person should not stand stubbornly by his words, for even the "Fathers of the World" <note>the great patriarchs or early sages</note> did not stand stubbornly by their words. This is the meaning of his language and the merit of the entire world.

After that, he said in our Mishnah: "Why did they mention the words of Rabbi Eliezer?" Meaning, among the many, even though the law is not like the individual, so that a court will not fear to weigh the words of the individual and stand upon them. For a court cannot nullify the words of another court unless it is greater in wisdom and in number. What Maimonides opened in his poem regarding years and generations and customs: everything that is strong in the body is "exempt." It seems to the court that they need to do this to destroy it, for it is contradictory. It is enough what was seen... as it is said: "to the judge who shall be in those days." Also, in our case, the matter will be thus: after the Holy One established the law like the Sages, why did He mention the words of Rabbi Eliezer among the many? For the Holy One concluded that one cannot contradict a court after the traditions and enactments. For the Holy One says that what is clear to the world is "pure." However, he himself had a first answer: to make known that he was a great man in Israel, so great that he was worthy, but he did not stand by his words when they disagreed with him. Therefore, Moses our teacher said a very great thing: "May it be Your will that he emerges from my loins."

And it is settled well. He said to return to opening with the prayer of Moses. For God forbid, a person might think his death is in the heavens and he will rise at the resurrection, etc. Everything I say to him is "living in Israel." The Holy One said "forbidden" to a man who says the words of the law are "pure," as understood. Only the one who is precise regarding impurity according to **Rabbi Joshua**. Therefore, they understood from the Heavenly Academy <term>Metivta de-Raki'a<note>original: "מתיבתא דרקיעא"; the celestial study hall where the souls of the righteous study</term> that the Holy One said "Pure." He did not rule the law as "pure," but rather sought to make peace. He only mentioned the words of Rabbi Joshua among the many "Pure," because a court cannot nullify another court's decision. He mentioned the words of Rabbi Joshua even though the law is not like him, for there could be a question of years, and if so, we would go from spring to spring and find the reason.

Is it possible that the Holy One would speak of enactments and customs that are not central to the law? A court can disagree with another. But this matter that the Holy One spoke of is the "Body of the Law" <term>Guf ha-Din<note>original: "גוף הדין"; the essential core of the legal statute</term>. If so, the logic and the question remain: the Holy One ruled the law like him—why not? It was to make known that even someone as great as him did not stand stubbornly by his words. Otherwise, it would be difficult: why were the words of the Sages also mentioned? And why was Rabbi Joshua's name chosen, specifically in the Mishnah, and specifically in the tractate of *Menachot*? For the Sages were prepared first. In *Menachot*, they said the ruling was according to the first opinion, and Rabbi Joshua says "Pure." This is similar to the matter of Rabbi Eliezer, for his words are in the beginning of *Menachot*, as explained.

If so, it is proven that the logic of the Holy One’s ruling is that the law follows Rabbi Joshua, which is "Pure." They agreed with his words—the words of the Living God—and there is no reason to doubt. Similarly, the "Heavenly Academy" understood it this way. Afterward, they understood the words of the Holy One. If so, why did they say "from the evidence"? Rather, they came to teach the ruling for generations. The Holy One will be in his glory to prove his words from the "evidence of man." Even the simple ones, as it were, do not need him in his logic in many places... as explained in the "Periphery" <note>likely a reference to a specific commentary or section of a book</note>. Certainly, against the order... to tell the judges, etc. Also, regarding the words of Eliezer in the gift, he did not redeem for generations so that there would not be any...

<margin>
...standing by his words. * See what was written in the response of **Rabbi Moshe Mintz**, of blessed memory, regarding what is found... that they have a gift of a legal ruling from his hand. And if so, he has permission afterward to make a commentary on the ruling. This was the reason for the act of the Holy One, who says "Pure" and writes in the "Heavens." After the Sages said it was sweet under his hand, he did not want to make a commentary, but only to leave the matter as it was.
</margin>
