# Preface to "The Building" by the Son of the Author: The Pillar of Peace

<margin>
Reasons for the [laws of] mourning
over the peace [of Jerusalem].
To clarify and fear,
and his intention is to interpret
to the person an established [place]
to the light, etc.
</margin>
...to us. The destruction of the First Holy Temple is a distant end for him, while the destruction of the Second Temple is close to us and the end [of the matter]. Rabbi Yochanan holds that the Prophet was establishing [his words] based on the end of the timeline; therefore, the Second Temple was closer to him. Consequently, he prioritized the word "peace," for it was closer to us, and afterwards "and I will heal him," referring to the destruction of the First Temple which is distant from us. 

However, Rabbi Pinchas explained that the order is based on what is more corrected regarding our current state—meaning the First Temple, which was [holier] compared to the Second, as I have prefaced. Therefore, he holds that he mentions the "distant" first, referring to the First Destruction which is chronologically distant from us, and afterwards "and I will heal our wounds," referring to the Second Temple destruction which is more recent. 

This is what Isaiah the prophet, peace be upon him, alluded to regarding how he established his hands to extend and point toward the distant and near destructions. He likewise sought "peace for the distant and for the near," meaning for the First and Second Sanctuaries. That is to say, it should be completed as it was in the first, which is recognizable compared to the Second Temple in terms of beauty and the removal of the bitter [exile], and it should be near to us in our days; may it be His will that it be rebuilt speedily in our days.

We have also learned that the fulfillment of the blessings is found in the prophecies of Zechariah. The Holy One said: "For the sake of the iniquity of his covetousness was I wroth," etc., since he sought this from the establishers of peace for the distant and the near. *Alternatively, one might say* that the mention of "peace for the distant" is according to what is said in Tractate Gittin (folio 7a). There, the Exilarch <note>The political head of the Jewish community in Babylonian exile</note> said to Rav Huna: "From where do we know that it is forbidden [to wear] crowns?" He replied: "By the authority of the Rabbis, for in the period of the war of Vespasian <note>The Roman general who besieged Jerusalem</note>, they decreed against the crowns of grooms and against the [bridal] canopies, etc." 

Then Rav Huna asked Rav Hisda: "A verse is written! 'Thus says the Lord: Remove the turban (mitznefet) and take off the crown; this shall not be this; exalt him that is low, and abase him that is high.'" [The Gemara asks:] What is the meaning of "Remove the turban and take off the crown"? At the time the turban is removed from the head of the High Priest, the crown is removed from the head of every person. This suggests that the turban on the head of the High Priest is linked to the crown on the head of every Israelite. From this, it would seem that the prohibition is from the Torah, yet you said it is only by Rabbinic authority? 

But "your people shall be whole," and from the foundation of your youth... <note>The text here enters a complex legalistic discussion regarding the source of the prohibition of wearing festive crowns after the Temple's destruction</note> in the response of the "Foundations of Yehuda" (page 147), he brings this discussion and asks why he needed to cite the verse... and "this shall not be this," for they derived a major teaching from it: "This is not this." They said that the turban of the High Priest was a source of atonement for Israel, and when it was removed, it caused a lack... <unclear>illegible</unclear>. 

As long as he stood in the Temple, etc., whereas in the sharp dialectic of Rav Hisda, the concept of "this is not this" does not apply there. There, they opened with the destruction of the [First] Temple times, and it is not similar here... as he said, "I have clarified from your hand," which implies he spoke well. And there, why did he say it was Rabbinic? The explanation of the matter is found in the *Tur* <note>A code of Jewish Law</note>, Orach Chaim, sign 560, who elaborated on this law. He wrote as follows: "The crowns of grooms are forbidden." This specifically refers to grooms, not to other people. However, during a time of great joy, he said every person is forbidden. 

And the Tosafot <note>Medieval commentators on the Talmud</note> in the chapter there explained the Talmudic discussion: because of the destruction, they enacted that there should be a memory of it always, like "blackening" a wall and leaving a square cubit unfinished in every house, etc. Similarly, they enacted that when one sets a table for guests, he should withhold something of its beauty and leave an empty space... and when a woman makes her silver and gold jewelry, she should omit one type of ornament so that the ornament is not complete. 

And similarly, they decreed against the crowns of grooms, including all types, as it is written: "Remove the turban and take off the crown." This specifically applies to the groom and bride, but for other men and women, they did not decree. Only the groom is prohibited because he is compared to a High Priest, as he is the "head" who establishes the family. Furthermore, the Rif and the Rosh <note>Major medieval legal authorities</note> wrote that a person should make his house... etc. And he mentioned the crown of the groom, and even though they did not write this specifically, it is possible... but if a person does not make his house [unfinished]... and it implies that even through a non-Jew it is forbidden to make paintings and carvings like the buildings of kings...

It will also be explained in the dialectic that Rav Huna holds the Mishnah's view that in the wisdom of the war of Vespasian they decreed, etc. And from where did Rav Hisda know to cite the verse "Remove the turban and take off the crown"? He understood that they are separate. He interpreted the language of "removal" in this verse, for the word "removal" in Scripture can mean "stripping," such as "And he saw the skin of his face shone" <note>Moses descending from Sinai</note> and similarly "He saw the king," and many such cases. We find that the language of "removal" is used. Because of this, in the laws of the Torah portion *Kol*, on the verse "He shall draw back from his hand," he also brings proof that it is a language of removal, like "raise up the portion" and "the daily sacrifice was removed." 

Therefore, Rav Hisda understood: do not say "Remove the turban" is a simple removal, but rather a language of "stripping" as mentioned. This was the removal of the crown. Rav Hisda understood that this was the intention of the phrase "this is not this," meaning that even though this is this, and this is all this, it is stripping. The interpretation is also a language of removal, similar to "Remove the turban." But then he asked: what is the connection between the turban and the crown? He understood the turban and the stripping of the crown entirely, as it is explained. And this is a language of removal. 

When Rav Huna came, he held that this was entirely a Torah prohibition. And afterwards, one should not include them together, the "removal of the turban" and the "crown." Initially, the measure of the turban implies stripping... and similarly in the dialectic found in the back of the tractate Chullin regarding the "speck of the sun," he knew not to return... and in any case, peace shall be with you.

<column-break/>

And behold, the term "omission" is also used for any hunter, because some of the spoils, such as his wisdom... the ancient language but to separate... as in the matter of "the city is small." This word "removal" (saros) has two interpretations: a language of "omission" and a language of "stripping." We find in this matter "the stripping of the devil." And Rashi <note>The primary medieval commentator</note> explains: "the word is derived from the inner offshoots," and his intention is the heritage of the son... the stripping of his inheritance. And similarly "and stripped from him his beast," which is a portion of the inheritance. 

[The scholar] said to him: therefore, the turban and the crown are not referred to by the language of "removal" for every man. If so, he should have included them in one category. See there, he could have interpreted it as "removal," but you hear two things from it: that which he leaves over, which is removal. And that is what he said: "there is a fundamental principle of removal on his head." This applies to every person. Therefore, he said regarding the people [the prohibition] is Rabbinic, but the "crowns of grooms" are forbidden even by a non-Jew, as stated. 

And that which he said, "every man is permitted by a non-Jew to leave [a space]," he who said it is interpreted as a language of removal is the one who said: "peace shall be with you and peace shall be with your youth." What you learned is that the word "saros" is a language of "omission," but "my thoughts are not like your thoughts." And similarly, Huna explained this teaching. 

And if the ruling was that the word "saros" meant "omission," it would be like "and he removed." However, it is not similar at all. On this, it says "this is not this," meaning: this is a language of "lack"—this and this and this. It is not a language of removal, but rather it resembles "omission" from all sides. In the end, it is an "omitted" omission. Thus all his questions are well settled. And regarding this, he said "Peace to the distant and the near." "Near" refers to the crown of every man which is near to you, and "distant" refers to the turban on the head of the High Priest.

The author concluded with a type of peace, saying "The Lord [said]... this matter to the wicked." Also, to clarify the language: there is no peace... as it concludes. Since this cessation is not in its [usual] place, "Peace to the stranger." For he seeks the Sanctuary and there was a desire... he said "Peace." The author concludes with another man, and Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: he did not intend to bless him, but rather it was his heart and his understanding... as is known, our difficulties are his... see there. And he was accustomed to sitting there... according to the mind of the people. And concerning the fact that a person does not have... unless they force peace upon him, therefore they force... etc. The near [temple] is a major difficulty, it needs... to settle the difficulty...

Regarding what Rashi found difficult: this was Rav Hisda's response against the question that the establishment was tripled... for you have written so. And they clarify their matters in the writings until they investigate them faithfully "for the sake of the ways of peace." And Rashi and his colleagues [noted] in their peace all day, even though he said it regarding the honor of Heaven... nevertheless, he thought they were the response of the Rambam <note>Maimonides</note>, meaning it is permitted to mention the Name of Heaven for his needs. 

And afterwards, it is difficult: why did Rashi say regarding peace that he "intended to bless him"? One cannot say Rashi's intention refers to the greeting of Rav Hisda, for that would be forced... The Rav <note>the author</note> approached the matter of being found many times... and see the *Yoreh Deah* code, sign 149, sub-section 1, regarding the "stripping of the head," as follows: "It is forbidden to greet him with 'Peace' before he [greets you]," for this is to prioritize peace for him so that they do not say... <unclear>illegible</unclear>. 

And it appears to my humble opinion that Rashi's intention is that it is forbidden to ask the name of "Peace" upon a non-Jew. And Rashi's words are not difficult, for he explains in the Mishnah of Avodah Zarah that "Peace" is the Name of the Holy One, Blessed be He. Thus, there is permission to say "Peace" to a non-Jew in a secular language (vernacular), meaning to be at peace with him. But to mention the word "Shalom" <note>Peace</note> which is in the Holy Tongue, this is [forbidden] because it is one of the Names of the Holy One. 

And this is what the Talmud meant in the Mishnah: "The non-Jew whose name is Peace..." etc. And according to the reason that "Peace" is a great thing and everyone... it is in the Holy Tongue, and the Name of the Holy One is applied to it. Therefore, it is forbidden to bless a non-Jew with "Peace" in the [Holy] language, but in the vernacular (foreign tongue), it is permitted. This is Rashi's intention: otherwise, it would be permitted to bless him. But one may not mention the name "Shalom" upon him in the Holy Tongue. 

And to force peace even in the vernacular is... and perhaps this is what is mentioned in the Gemara: Rav Sheshet said "Peace" to them... for the language they had was to put them close to the Holy Tongue. As is explained in Tractate Eruvin: Israel was not exiled to Babylon except because it was close to the language of the Torah. Therefore, the matter is clarified why he said "Peace," for they did not have another language or tongue. Therefore, Rashi's words are correct. 

Alternatively, it is "stealing the mind" <note>deception</note>... for it is in the Gemara in Gittin on the Mishnah "and they inquire after their peace for the sake of the ways of peace." He did not do it for their sake, but for the sake of Israel, so that there would be peace for us. And because peace brings... it is difficult because of the "peace." And this is to "steal the mind" of a non-Jew for the sake of peace. 

And regarding the matter of doubling the greeting of "Peace," the Gaon Rabbi Falk, of blessed memory, elaborated in his clarifications on the Talmud. He wrote that the doubling of "Peace" there is because of the "answer of the lie" of the one who gives peace. And just as our teacher answered "Peace, peace to you, and peace to your house," so too was the finding of David as written... "And David saw before him," etc. 

The Gemara concludes: Rav Huna and Rav Hisda... may He grant peace... he went in the "theft" [of the mind]... one to the other... he was supporting the hands of the... and he held: how could he be... they support the three... to support them. <header>Introduction of the Illustrious Son of the Author, The Pillar of Peace 41</header>

## Introduction of the Illustrious Son of the Author, The Pillar of Peace

It seemed to him that for this reason, the master of the book <note>Original: *Ba'al HaSefer*</note> accepted it. He wrote: I have seen fit to further explain a small measure of the grace found in the juxtaposition of the Priestly Blessing <note>Original: *Birkat Kohanim*, the "Aaronite" blessing from Numbers 6:24-26</note> and the subsequent section. It concludes with the phrase "they do not rise," and the Talmud <note>Original: *Gemara*</note> asks: What is the reason? It is because of Israel. It is so that Israel should not say that the Holy One, blessed be He, shows favoritism <note>Original: *panim*, literally "faces," referring to showing bias or partiality</note>. And yet they do not know that there is a reason for the "shining of the face" <note>favor</note> toward Israel, as we say in the tractate of *Berakhot*: "I said, 'You shall eat and be satisfied and bless...'" and there they are stringent upon themselves even for the size of an olive or an egg. And it is written in the *Sifrei* <note>An ancient legal commentary on Numbers and Deuteronomy</note>: On one hand it says, "[May He lift] His face toward you," and in another place it is written, "Who does not show favoritism" <note>Original: *lo yissa panim*, literally "does not lift a face"</note>. However, the simple meaning of the verse resolves this well, because in the Priestly Blessing it does not say "The Lord shall lift *Your* face," but rather "The Lord shall lift His face *to you*." Therefore, we are dealing with His face, and perhaps there is no room for error.

And he wrote: It seems to me, according to the explanation of the *Sifrei*, that they do not rise because of the matter of the curses. Regarding the Priestly Blessing, they do not rise because perhaps the verse "For He shall not show favoritism" was not meant for translation <note>In ancient times, certain sensitive verses were read in Hebrew but not translated into the local vernacular to avoid confusion</note>. As Rabbi Joshua ben Levi said, the reason they do not rise is not because of the curses; rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, acts because of the "face" <note>favor</note>, and they do not know that Israel is worthy of everything. Thus, there is no difficulty at all from our perspective, though for Rabbi Joshua it remains difficult.

To resolve this, we must look at the Midrash *Yalkut* <note>Yalkut Shimoni, a popular medieval compilation of Midrash</note> and its intent regarding the Torah portion of *Shemini*. There it says: Moses said, "This is the thing which the Lord commanded that you should do." Moses said to Israel: "Remove those evil inclinations <term>Yetzer HaRa: the internal impulse toward selfishness or sin</term> from your hearts, and let all of you be in one fear and one counsel to serve before the Place <note>A common Rabbinic name for God</note>. Just as He is unique in the world, so should your service be established before Him." This is the end of his quote. And why the phrase "the foreskin of your heart"? Because "the Lord your God..." etc. 

This Midrash says "I have sought" <note>an interpretive phrase</note> just as the Kabbalists did. What is the meaning of the Midrash saying "remove those evil inclinations"? It hints at the evil inclination known as the "four shells" <note>Original: *klipot*, kabbalistic terms for forces of spiritual impurity</note> which are the laborers of evil. See there, for "the Lord your God" represents the Sabbath of Knowledge, where a reason must be written. 

It appears that we say in the tractate of *Hagigah* in the name of Rabbi Judah bar Boani: "Do not hide from your kin," and "do not hide in the darkness." Someone might say to you: "The Holy One, blessed be He, pardons you, so do not hide it." Behold, the act of every offering is like atoning for iniquities and sins, as it is written, "and he shall bless him to atone for him." Similarly, the sacrifices <note>Original: *miluim*</note> atone for the sin of the Golden Calf; as our Sages of blessed memory said: "Let the elder of the herd come and atone for the deed of the Calf." Thus we find that just as the prophet Isaiah cried out and proclaimed that the Holy One, blessed be He, pardons all of Israel, the verse continues: "This is the thing which the Lord commanded," meaning that the evil inclination which was appointed to disrupt the conversation—do not turn to it and do not be hidden by it. Rather, let all of you be in fear before Him. And that same master <term>the evil inclination</term> who was appointed over you—God pardons you for the sins you removed from yourself. 

And why does the Holy One, blessed be He, pardon? Why would they not turn to Him? As it says in the Midrash: "For the Lord your God... He does not show favoritism." Your God is such that anyone who says the Holy One, blessed be He, is indulgent, his life shall be forfeited. According to this, the question of why the verse "For He shall not show favoritism" should be translated is resolved. For Israel, in their choice to merit the Name, must first remove the "foreskin of the heart" so that your neck shall no longer be stiff. One might ask: Why did he merit to see the Divine Presence <note>Original: *Shekhinah*</note>? Because "the Lord is God... Who does not show favoritism." And they did not rise... after the verse "circumcise the foreskin of your heart." And since he was compelled to translate this verse, it follows logically not to translate the Priestly Blessing to avoid the difficulty of the curses for the reader. One should not ask why he didn't also avoid translating the verse "circumcise the foreskin of your heart," because in the portion of *Ekev*, all the words are words of rebuke, as it is written: "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you..." and "circumcise the foreskin of your heart." There, they did not rise <note>to read or translate</note> so they would not enter into a situation of compulsion, for these rebukes are not like the Priestly Blessing. There <note>in the blessing</note> they do rise, so people will not say, "Heaven forbid, God wants to bless them." 

Now, the commentators have gone at length in explaining the verse "May the Lord lift His face to you," interpreting it as "He shall remove His anger from you." But this is difficult: is it not obvious that if there is peace, there is no anger? It appears that the Midrash emphasizes the greatness of peace; even the heavenly beings need peace. There is an "argument from minor to major" <term>Kal VaChomer: a logical inference</term>: if in the upper worlds, where there is no jealousy or hatred, they still need peace, how much more so the lower worlds where there is judgment and hatred—they certainly need peace. This is what is meant by "May the Lord lift His face to you and break His anger from you," for there is a place for anger to exist, and thus one must grant peace. This Midrash brings out the great level of peace from the verse itself. I would have liked to lengthen the discussion on the Priestly Blessing with hidden springs of wisdom, but this is not the place to be lengthy.

<column-break/>

To explain the Torah portion of *Naso*, as it is hinted at regarding these standing pillars, truly in my book and as brought in the *Yalkut* on *Naso*: We have learned that Simeon the Righteous was among the remnants of the Great Assembly. He used to say: On three things the world stands: on the Torah, on the Divine Service <note>temple offerings</note>, and on acts of loving-kindness. 

Rabbi Huna said in the name of Rabbi Aha: The world was saved by a measure of kindness; this is "acts of loving-kindness." The "dripping of the honeycomb" is the Torah. Yet the world was still shaking. When did it become firmly established? When they stood at Mount Sinai and offered sacrifices. Therefore, regarding some verses from the Song <note>at the Sea</note>, it says that the Torah was still... and he asked at the beginning of his words about the extra word "Then" <note>Hebrew: *Az*</note>, for the words seem contradictory. "Then" usually refers to that specific past moment, but the word implies the future as well, as our Sages explained: "Then Moses sang"—it does not say "sang" <note>past tense</note> but "will sing" <note>future tense</note>, implying the Resurrection of the Dead is hinted at in the Torah.

And further, we must ask: to whom did they say it? Everywhere else it says who they are speaking to. In kindness our faces were examined, as in the Talmud, tractate *Sukkah*: Rabbi Akiva sees and learns... Eleazar looked at the greatness of the honor... And if so, it is also upon us to clarify some more important questions. Let us look at one more difficulty and resolve it immediately: why does the text repeat the language "And Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore of the sea"? This was because of the "Face of the Lord," and "they believed in the Lord." And why does it say a second time, "And Israel saw the great hand which the Lord did in Egypt"? 

Furthermore, one cannot give a good reason for why faith was scattered. Rabbi said: In their greatness they showed us faith. We learn from these things... they are not just matters of plain meaning <note>Original: *Pshat*</note>. In the place where *Midrash Rabbah* explains the portion of *Naso*, it says: "Then" <note>Az</note> Moses sang. It is written: "They believed in His words; they sang His praise." This refers to what was written previously: "The people believed" in Egypt, but they did not truly believe <note>internally</note>, as it says: "Our fathers in Egypt did not contemplate Your wonders." But when they came to the sea and saw the might of the Holy One, blessed be He, how He performs judgment on the wicked, immediately "they believed in the Lord." The Divine Spirit rested upon them and they sang the Song. This is what is written: "Then sang Moses." "Then" <note>Az</note> is a language of "trust" <note>Amanah</note>, as it is said: "And he was the foster-father <note>Omen</note> of Hadassah." 

In the Midrash, we must look closely: only after Rabbi established his words on their plain meaning did he apply them to the verse. It is written, "And Israel saw... and they believed in the Lord." It is also difficult that in Egypt it is written "and the people rejoiced." Therefore, we must say that the verse "Then" refers to the returning of the hearts and the support of the song to bring about the greatness of faith. According to this, Rabbi's intent was the secret of "Then" according to what we heard. It is difficult: how many sections are there in the Torah where "and they believed in the Lord" is written? Was it not already written "And the people believed"? The resolution is that our fathers did not contemplate in Egypt, and their faith was shaky in their hands. Afterward, when they became wise at the sea, they returned to their former faith: "And they believed in the Lord and in Moses His servant." 

Furthermore, the commentators ask: regarding what was said, that the Divine Spirit rested on them because of their faith—why did they need to merit faith after they saw the miracles with their own eyes? When one sees God's judgment, is it not obvious they would believe? To explain this, I will bring another Midrash on *Naso*: "He brought me up from the desolate pit, out of the miry clay." The "desolate pit" is Egypt; the "miry clay" is the mortar and bricks. "And He set my feet upon a rock"—this was when they returned from crossing on dry land. Immediately, "He put a new song in my mouth." This Midrash also requires interpretation. What is the "Song"? Like His words... when Israel came to the dry land, it was a shore, and they sang the song. 

The matter is that the Midrash mentions "Then" as needing explanation. We find in *Midrash Rabbah* that it points to the verse "and their resting." Isaac, in the merit of the "resting" <note>tamimut/integrity</note> to receive, did not go after... rather, the merit of the "resting." Israel was only redeemed in the merit of the "resting," as it says, "And the people believed... and they bowed their heads." The Torah did not write "Then" in the merit of the "resting" that they looked from afar. Here it was not recorded in the merit of the "resting," as it says "and the people rejoiced in the Lord." In the exile, these merits of "resting" are hidden, as it says, "And it shall be on that day, a great shofar shall be blown and they shall come... to the Lord." The "Then" was not written there in the merit of the "resting," as it says "And they believed in the Lord our God and rejoiced in His holy word." It is fulfilled "And he saw" only in the merit of the "resting" mentioned by his Creator... in evil and in blessing... And if so, behold, everything that was done for Israel was only in the merit of the "resting." When they walked on the dry land, it was a shore; for this they did not kneel or bow before the Place, so that He would remind them of the merit of the "resting," to remember those testimonies. Rather, the Midrash shows us, like the words of David to the King.

<meta>This page continues the introduction by the author’s son, focusing on mystical interpretations of the Exodus and the Song of the Sea, transitioning from the previous page's discussion on divine peace to the specific mechanics of redemption.</meta>

# Introduction of the Sage, the Author’s Son, the Pillar of Peace

The *Zohar* <note>The primary foundational work of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</note> writes in the Portion of *Yitro* <note>Exodus 18:1–20:23</note> regarding the verse: *“Therefore say to the children of Israel...”* Rabbi Judah says: Come and see, when the Holy One, blessed be He, desired to bring Israel out of Egypt, He first bound the "husks" <note>original: "Kelipot"; spiritual forces of impurity that "enclosure" holiness.</note> and broke their power. He spoke to Moses and told him to say to Israel: "I will bring you out, I will deliver you, I will redeem you, and I will take you." These four expressions of redemption were necessary to release them from the powers of the "other side" <note>Sitra Achra, the demonic or impure realm.</note>. Rabbi Yose says: Why was it written, *“and I will take you to Me for a people, and I will be to you a God”*? This was so they would never return to their enslavement, for those who were tied to the lower crowns <note>Spiritual levels of Egyptian sorcery</note> could never leave their boundaries. Therefore, it is written about them that they were "bound," and the Holy One, blessed be He, had to first untie those knots. From this you can understand why the *Zohar* says that one should not descend under the *Kelipah* <term>Kelipah: Literally 'husk' or 'shell,' representing the external forces that conceal divine light</term>. 

And regarding this, the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: *“Therefore say to the children of Israel: I am the Lord, and I will bring you out... and I will deliver you... and I will redeem you... and I will take you.”* He explained His words by saying, *“And you shall know that I am the Lord your God who brings you out.”* From this, you should understand and be wise to how much I rejoiced with them, for I guarded your name for them and not for Me. Afterward, I "spoiled" and "stripped" <note>Referring to the despoiling of the Egyptians</note>, and *“you shall know that I am the Lord who brings you out.”* Through this, you will know that I chose you because of My causes, for you are most beloved to Me because you were saved from the power of the Egyptian attributes, which no other master could remove from there. When Pharaoh heard these three expressions, he did not know he was being stripped of his power, thinking God would simply say, *“and I will take you to Me for a people,”* but God did not do so until Moses spoke to the children of Israel, which teaches that he did not change his words.

And behold, in the Song <note>The Song of the Sea, Exodus 15</note>, the Kabbalists compared it by saying: *“The Lord is my strength and song, and He has become my salvation.”* When Pharaoh’s chariots and his army were cast into the sea, it was to remember first the judgment of the Holy One, blessed be He, and afterward the return to His Name. As it says: *“Pharaoh’s chariots and his host He cast into the sea,”* and the end is *“The Lord shall reign,”* as when He comes and reigns. <note>This refers to the transition from God's attribute of Judgment (Din) to His attribute of Mercy (Rachamim).</note> It is possible for the King to do two tasks at once. And here in the *Zohar*, Portion of *Bo*, you will understand: it is written *“And it was in the middle of the night,”* and the Egyptians were struck in their bodies, while Israel was saved. At that same hour, the Egyptians were surrounded by terror and trembling. 

And behold, I found in the prayer book of the Sage and Kabbalist, our teacher Rabbi Kasis, may his memory be a blessing, a question regarding the Torah's use of the **Atbash** <term>Atbash: A Hebrew cipher where the first letter (Aleph) is swapped with the last (Tav), the second (Bet) with the second-to-last (Shin), and so on.</term> system. In the Talmud, in the chapter "He who builds," it explains **Atbash** as a secret regarding the two books of the world: *“Aleph-Tav”* means "You shall love Me," and *“Bet-Shin”* means "He loathes My face." For the wicked, the attribute of **Atbash** is used for judgment, but for the righteous, it is used for blessing. If you do so, you will have a "Body of Blessing" and you will not tremble before the Accuser <note>The Satan</note>. This is the secret of why it mentions "He cast" (*Yarah*) in the Song. **Atbash** is used as a language of "solutions" to show the signs of the Lord, just as He pleads for the righteous, He Himself will judge the wicked.

Behold, the Attribute of Mercy pleads to be beautified when it approaches the Attribute of Judgment. The Holy One, blessed be He, as the Kabbalist Rabbi Isaac Luria <note>The Ari, the most influential Kabbalist of the 16th century.</note> wrote, first said "to stand" and then said "to cast." This means that when it was time for Him to sit upon the "Upper Chariots of Pharaoh," He removed the human form. For God made "this corresponding to that" <note>Ecclesiastes 7:14; a concept that for every holy force, there is a corresponding impure force.</note>. This is hinted at in the Name of 72 <note>The 72-letter name of God derived from Exodus 14:19-21</note>, which consists of three verses: *Vayisa* ("and he journeyed"), *Vayavo* ("and he came"), and *Vayet* ("and he stretched"). Each verse has 72 letters, and each word has 3 letters. This is hinted at in Pharaoh's chariots, which were set up "correspondingly," for they are names of "chariot" forces (*Rechev*). From the word *Rechev* (chariot), there is a secret arrangement. The Holy One, blessed be He, *“removed the wheels of their chariots”* <note>Exodus 14:25</note>, which refers to the "Upper Wheel of Pharaoh," a term for the celestial wheels (*Ophanim*). The wheel is found below, as it is written: *“And behold, one wheel was on the earth.”* And this is "Pharaoh’s chariots and his host He cast (*Yarah*) into the sea"—He cast them down, his chariot above and his officers drowned in the Reed Sea. By removing the "Wheel," their place was changed, for the holy "Living Creatures" (*Chayot*) were removed from them, and his chariot fell. On this, the **Atbash** explains the verse, hinting at what the Kabbalists wrote regarding the letters. The letters *Resh-Resh* hint at Mercy (*Rachamim*), while *Bet-Resh* hint at Kindness (*Chesed*). The Holy One, blessed be He, is called "Place" (*Makom*) because He is the place of the world.

<column-break/>

As mentioned above, you take from Him and it enters into the fear of Him. Concerning the matter of holiness, it is written: *“And it shall be a dwelling place for the Place,”* a place where the eyes of Kindness and Mercy are fixed. 

Afterward, it says: *“The enemy said, 'I will pursue, I will overtake...'”* This can be resolved according to the Midrash on the verse *“they drew near.”* Who said this? This was Pharaoh, as it says: *“The enemy said, 'I will pursue.'”* But there is a question: why does Rashi say regarding Amalek, *“who happened upon you on the way,”* <note>Deuteronomy 25:18</note> that he was the first to "cool" the boiling tub <note>A famous metaphor where the nations were afraid of Israel until Amalek jumped in, cooling the fear for others.</note>? Therefore, it is appropriate to say of him that "they drew near," but Pharaoh was first. 

It seems to me that the verse is difficult: *“The enemy said, I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil.”* This seems redundant; for surely, if he pursues, he intends to overtake and spoil. This is explained by the parable of an idolater who is led by an Israelite on a road. He keeps him to his right, etc. until he asks him, "What is the end of your journey?" Pharaoh's hint in saying "I will pursue" was that he believed he was acting of his own accord, but God was the one leading him. 

Alternatively, it is resolved according to the Midrash that Pharaoh took the lead himself and stood at the head of all his army. It was not seen that the great ones walk at the rear; therefore it says "they drew near," meaning Pharaoh brought himself near. In the *Mechilta* <note>A collection of ancient legal and homiletic interpretations of the Book of Exodus.</note>, the verse *“The enemy said, 'I will pursue'”* is at the beginning of the section. We say there is "no chronological order in the Torah" <note>A principle of biblical hermeneutics that the Torah is not always written in chronological order.</note>. However, one must always provide a reason and logic for the placement. 

The explanation is this: you must know what the Holy One, blessed be He, intended by the repetition of "pursue." It is because Pharaoh himself, and not just through a messenger, spoke against the Holy One, blessed be He. He said, *“Who is the Lord?”* Pharaoh in his greatness spoke, and immediately the response came through a messenger, as it says: *“By the hand of your messengers you have taunted.”* But for Pharaoh, it says: *“And the angel of the Lord moved.”* Israel in their Song turned to the Right Hand of the Lord, and they wrote the reason why it was done by the Holy One, blessed be He, in His own glory: because the "Enemy" said "I will pursue," using the singular voice, meaning he himself would do it and not through a messenger. Just as he spoke with his own mouth, so too the Holy One, blessed be He, acted Himself. This is why we say: *“Who is like You among the mighty, O Lord?”*—which is a response to Pharaoh asking *“Who is the Lord?”* 

Regarding the verse *“This is my God and I will glorify Him”* (*Ze Eli ve-Anvehu*): Rabbi Ishmael asks, is it possible for a human of flesh and blood to "beautify" his Creator? Rather, it means I will be like Him: just as He is merciful, you be merciful; just as He is gracious, you be gracious. However, our Rabbis interpreted this as a prayer. How can one exalt the Creator? Behold, the "Song of the Day" has 130 words, and the word *“And I will exalt Him”* (*Aromimenu*) is difficult. Is it possible for a human to exalt the Blessed Name? Rather, we must say the order of His exaltation and greatness is that He is "the Great One" at the end, and the "Greatness" belongs to Him in holiness.

Furthermore, know what is written in the *Mechilta* on Portion *Beshalach*: Rabbi Yose says, if Israel had said *“The Lord IS King,”* they would never have been exiled, for that is a language of the present. Instead, they said *“The Lord SHALL reign forever and ever”* (in the future). Israel says: *“Who is like You among the mighty, O Lord?”* and the Holy Spirit responds: *“Happy are you, O Israel, who is like you?”* Israel says: *“Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One,”* and the Holy Spirit responds: *“Who is like Your people Israel, one nation in the earth?”* Israel says: *“This is my God and I will glorify Him,”* and the Holy Spirit responds: *“This people I have formed for Me.”* 

The word *“And I will exalt Him”* (*Aromimenu*) implies the future as well. They did not speak only of the present, just as they said *“The Lord shall reign”* for the future. But for *“This is my God and I will glorify Him,”* that is something possible to do now, and there is no other way to explain it.

<meta>This page continues the introduction by the author’s son, transitioning from a general discussion of divine peace to a deep exploration of the "Song of the Sea" (Exodus 15) and the unique spiritual status of Israel compared to the angels. # Introduction of the Sage, the Author’s Son, the Pillar of Peace

I have toiled and labored to add to the words of our Sages of blessed memory <note>original: "רבותינו ז"ל" (Rabbeinu Zikhronam Livrakha)</note> regarding the gathering of the waters. It is like a glass vessel that reflects the light, revealing how every person who stands to press for the sake of Heaven must be precise. Rabbi Yose said: There is a beginning to a decree and an end to a decree. Therefore, at first, things were not truly attached in a complete union. This is hinted at in the earlier language: *“Let the waters be gathered to one place”* <note>Genesis 1:9</note>. The word *el-makom* <note>original: "אל מקום" (to a place)</note> indicates a greater sense of unity and attachment than the word *la-makom* <note>original: "למקום" (to the place)</note>, which does not indicate such attachment. It is similar to a soul that longs for its source. When the Holy One, blessed be He, first called things into being, what was written? *“Let the waters be gathered to one place.”* Why was it not written "to the place"? This teaches that they were not initially attached as one, for in the end they would be divided by a decree. In a simple sense, when the first light emerged at the beginning of creation, the "waters" were joined in a simple way. But then came the separation, and they were no longer one. This is the secret of our teacher <note>A reference to the author, his father</note> when he discussed the Midrash <term>Midrash: Ancient rabbinic commentary on the Hebrew Bible that uses parables and legal analysis to explain the text</term> on the verse *“Then sang Moses”* <note>Exodus 15:1; literally "Then he will sing"</note>. It does not say "He sang," but "He will sing," which hints at the future Resurrection of the Dead. It is fitting to settle the mind on what this "resurrection" of the waters means in this context.

Regarding the attribute of Mercy in *Midrash Rabbah* (Section *Beshalach*): When Israel sang the Song at the Sea, the Ministering Angels came to sing before the Holy One, blessed be He. But the Holy One, blessed be He, said to them, "Wait! Let My children sing first." As King David said: *“Let the inhabitants of the wilderness cry out”* <note>Isaiah 42:11</note>. The Holy One, blessed be He, chose the song of Israel over the song of the Priests or the Angels. Why did God say this to the angels? Because I am waiting for the song of these mortals. They say their song and then they die, but you [angels] live and exist forever. This is the matter of the "perfect blessings" when the God of Israel is praised among the angels. The angels mention the Divine Name after three words <note>original: "Holy, Holy, Holy"</note>, but Israel mentions it after only two words <note>original: "Hear, Israel, the Lord..."</note>. The angels do not say "Holy" above until Israel says it below, as it is said, *“When the morning stars sang together”* <note>Job 38:7</note>—this refers to the stars of the dawn, which we know refers to the human soul.

Now, concerning the song: they were fearful, seeing that the Holy One, blessed be He, does not allow the angels to sing until Israel sings first. But humans eventually die. Therefore, they compared this to the resurrection of the waters. He said to them: If Israel is to be "sons" to their Father in Heaven, then Israel will not be revealed until they fulfill the requirement of singing the song. This is not out of a fear of death, but rather a focus on the life of the world to come. They shall not fear anymore. This was the intention of the Lord, may He be blessed, and it is revealed here for His glory.

Regarding this, it seems right to explain *Midrash Rabbah* (Section *Bereishit*): Rabbi Shimon said that at the time the Holy One, blessed be He, created Adam, the Ministering Angels were divided into groups. Some said "Let him be created," and others said "Let him not be created." What did the King do? He hid the truth from them. Thus, when He created Adam, the angels saw his great form and wanted to say "Holy" before him, mistaking him for a divine being. What did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He cast a deep sleep upon Adam, so that everyone would know he was merely a mortal man. For the angels did not know the secret of his creation. They would have offered a sacrifice to him! How could it enter their minds to say "Holy" before a man?

Therefore, it appears to me that after they were created on the third and fourth days, they were arranged before the Holy One, blessed be He, before He created Adam. When He created the first man on the sixth day, the angels did not know the secret. This is why they wanted to sing the song before him—meaning, they thought man was a god who would live forever. The angels wanted to say "Holy" before Adam before he was made holy. What did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He cast a sleep on him to show the angels that the body of a man is subject to sleep and death. He told the angels: "Lest you continue to pursue him as a god, know that he is mortal." Therefore, it is fitting that they should not precede him in saying "Holy," for the earthly beings have this advantage over the angels—their souls are not just made of the spirit of the Lord, but they have the strength to give priority to the song over the angels. Look closely at the word *Veyishlach* <note>original: "וישלח" (And he sent)</note>, which is an extra word intended to show that Israel is more beloved to God than the angels, to say "Holy" and "Blessed."

After this, it says *“This is my God and I will glorify Him”* <note>Exodus 15:2</note>. Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, the preeminent medieval French commentator</note> explains: *“I will prepare for Him a beautiful habitation”* <note>original: "נוה" (Naveh)</note>. This refers to the building of the Temple. Others say it means *“I will declare His beauty and praise.”* For example, as David said, *“He is my God and I will praise Him.”* Rashi further explains: *“Even though I am first, the praise is already prepared and standing for me.”* These words require explanation. They will be clarified through what is cited in the *Mechilta* <note>A legalistic commentary on the Book of Exodus</note>: *“I raised my hand...”* and *“I performed...”* What is told to us from this? The explanation is that his greatness is before Him through the fulfillment of the commandments. You already know *Midrash Rabbah* (Section *Lech Lecha*) regarding the four things and the four expressions of redemption. This is what it says: "I raised my hand," which refers to the language of an oath.

<meta>catchword: of writing</meta>

<column-break/>

And this is the intention of Rashi, of blessed memory, according to the image of holiness. It does not mean that Moses spoke for himself, but rather for the Holy One, blessed be He. His "Holy One" and His "God" are my strength. From this, we can derive a great explanation: do not be surprised by the separation between "This is my God" and "the God of my father." The Holy One, blessed be He, performed wonders, and therefore they all sang together. There is a "writing" <note>original: "מכתב" (Mikhtav)</note> that says *“I raised my hand...”* What is written there? If I take hold of judgment... <note>Deuteronomy 32:41</note>. This refers to the four kingdoms and the Tefillin <term>Tefillin: Small black leather boxes containing scrolls of parchment inscribed with verses from the Torah, worn by Jewish men during prayer</term>. Regarding this, they decreed but did not explain the beauty of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it appears in the "writing" before Him in the wilderness of the exile.

We can explain Rashi's intention when he said "not from the question of the Holy One." This is what is cited in the Midrash: When the Holy One, blessed be He, came to give the Torah, He went to the children of Esau and asked, "Will you accept the Torah?" They asked, "What is written in it?" He said, "Thou shalt not murder." They replied, "That is the very blessing our father gave us (to live by the sword), we cannot accept it." He went to the children of Ammon and Moab and asked, "Will you accept the Torah?" They asked, "What is written in it?" He said, "Thou shalt not commit adultery." They replied, "Our entire origin is from adultery (Lot's daughters), we cannot accept it." He went to the children of Ishmael and asked, "What is written in it?" He said, "Thou shalt not steal." They replied, "Our father was a wild man whose hand was in everything, we cannot accept it." And so it was with all the nations.

But when He came to Israel, they said, "Everything the Lord says, we will do and we will hear" <note>Exodus 24:7</note>. Upon hearing this, it was fitting that they should receive it. In the merit of "We will do," before they even heard the content, they became worthy before the Holy One, blessed be He. Until we heard the commandments, we were like the other nations. But once we said "We will do," the decree of "Thou shalt not murder" was no longer a burden, for we had already accepted the life of the Torah. This is what it means: *“I raised my hand”*—this is the covenant of Joseph. And the commandments of the Sabbath and the like were already kept by the Patriarchs, as it is written that Abraham kept all the laws before they were given.

The intention of the explanation is that you should not act out of "life" <note>meaning, purely physical existence</note>, for the root of existence depends on all the inhabitants of the world. As it is said: "The Lord is a man of war." This is based on the idea that the glory of a mortal king is different from the glory of the Holy One, blessed be He. When a mortal king goes out to war, he wears the clothes of a commoner so as not to be recognized. But when he is at peace, he wears his royal robes. But the Holy One, blessed be He, is different. When He goes to war, He is recognized by His Name. As it is written: *“The Lord is a man of war, the Lord is His name”* <note>Exodus 15:3</note>.

It is well known from the Midrash that the Lord gives a gift to man through His names and His power. When He takes something from a person, He rules in His House of Judgment, which is hinted at in the name *Y-H-V-H* <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God</note>, which usually represents mercy, but here represents the merit of judgment. This is the secret of the verse: *“The Lord is a man of war.”* He threw Pharaoh's chariots and his army into the sea. This was for the sake of Israel, as indicated in the verse: *“Therefore say to the children of Israel: I am the Lord, and I will bring you out... and I will deliver you... and I will redeem you... and I will take you.”* These are the four expressions of redemption. And you shall know that I am the Lord who brings you out from under the burdens of Egypt.

The Midrash asks: why four expressions? It says they correspond to the four cups of wine we drink at the Passover Seder. Some say they correspond to the four exiles Israel would endure. Moses said to the Holy One, blessed be He: "Master of the Universe, it is enough for them to suffer in this exile!" But the Holy One, blessed be He, said: "No, I have written these four expressions to tell the children of Israel that I will be with them in every exile." Even though they did not yet know the full extent of the suffering they would face, God remembered His covenant for all the children of Israel.

A difficult question arises regarding the order of the verses: *“Therefore say to the children of Israel: I will bring you out... and I will deliver you... and I will redeem you... and I will take you.”* These are five things! And then it says *“And you shall know that I am the Lord your God who brings you out...”* This repeats the word "bring out" twice. It appears that...

# Indices
## This is the Book of the Generations of Adam

<margin>And the Lord showed me how to create signs so that every seeker of the Lord may find the proper way to act in his service,</margin>
<margin>balancing wisdom so that nothing is lacking.</margin>
**Behold**, those who look upon me have seen the precious splendor of the greatness of this monumental composition, the book *Two Tablets of the Covenant* <note>original: "Shenei Luchot HaBerit," a major 17th-century work of Jewish ethics and law by Rabbi Isaiah Horowitz</note>. It is a hidden treasure, containing the profound secrets of the world, the fear of the Lord, wisdom, and ethical instruction. By following its path, a person may live through them in the World to Come. If one looks at these references, they will find what their soul desires in abundance. Because the book is so vast, it is impossible for a person to recount all the matters contained within it, just as the moon is seen from afar through the Book of the Lord. Therefore, I have briefly outlined and ascended through the references where the original author wrote at length. Along the way, I have "gleaned between the sheaves" <note>A biblical idiom for gathering small, precious insights</note> of several sayings here and there—two or three "berries at the top of the branch"—and I have expressed my own thoughts therein. For the good Lord has answered me, and my strength and labor for the Lord were not in vain. However, I was afraid to approach the Holy or to mix my words with those of the Great Genius <note>A title of high honor for a preeminent rabbi</note>. Therefore, I have written my notes separately as a special pamphlet. If God decrees that I remain among the living, I shall bring them to light, that people of my standing may benefit from them. May the words of my mouth be acceptable before Him who provides my sustenance. Thus says the youngest of students, Jeremiah, son of my lord and father the Rabbi Jacob (of blessed memory), residing currently in the holy community of Berlin, in the state of Mark <note>Mark Brandenburg</note>, the metropolis. Written in the year "A Stream" <note>Hebrew: Nachal. A chronogram for the year 1678 or 1683 depending on the calculation</note> according to my words, in the sixth millennium.

<margin>Each and every reference is to the "Tower of Strength" built for many mouths—a hill toward which everyone turns. This is the name they shall call it: The Marble Tablet.</margin>
<margin>The words of Jeremiah.</margin>
<margin>The Mirror of Righteousness.</margin>
<margin>The custom of the scribes...</margin>
<margin>The scholar, son of...</margin>
**With** additions of sapphire and diamond, gleanings after gleanings, gathered with a rake. My discourse is southern <note>Likely referring to the "Darom" style of interpretation</note>, for four reasons. And this came out first: Is it not according to these names of the authors within it? Namely, Samuel, whose name is "Refining Silver" <note>A reference to Samuel b. Uri Shraga Phoebus</note> in the *Generations of Adam*; Solomon, whose name is "The Mirror of Righteousness" <note>Solomon b. Moses Chelm</note>. And should men quarrel and their hearts be troubled, saying: "Why did he despise it and not build the House of Israel?" The holy ones, the late Rabbi Israel Kahana and Mendel, who gathered and prepared the book *Mirror of Righteousness*, as seen in Solomon's introduction. Even after it was told to him according to the laws of "Opening," he spoke in secret from the beginning and called the book by his name, no longer mentioning the name of Israel. From now on, his name is also added to the second, and in secret, it is called the second Sukkot. This is modeled after the "Marble Tablet" <note>original: "Tabla shel Shayish"</note> that was in the Temple of the Lord, fifteen handbreadths high. For behold, the first author in the *Book of Generations*, and a third part as well, came to explain the word "Shayish" (Marble) with its three letters totaling 603 <note>Gematria: Shin (300) + Yud (10) + Shin (300) + 3 letters = 613, the number of commandments</note>. For all of them are included and explained in the holy book *Tablets of the Covenant*, both the revealed and the hidden. We were like dreamers with no interpreter. The reason for the scholars' turning and simplifying is that they weigh with scales of justice, the ancient weights and laws. Greatness has come from the mouth of the Great Genius; wherever a verse is difficult or there is a question, there he is. The worker searches through the textures under the foundations of the house. Each one checks for "leaks of water"—waters that have no end—reaching as far as his hand can go, saying, "My right hand spanned the heavens with fire and water." Truly, each one is a wonder, expanding without pause. For behold, the first author in the *Book of the Generations of Adam* only took a "small handful," and a small handful does not satisfy the lion, as he himself expressed in his wisdom. After him came the second, the "Refiner of Silver," desiring to add and refine one by one until the third "House of the Lord" came and sought to repair the breaches with the *Mirror of Righteousness*, to liken himself to the three upright ones. He wrote many words of truth and parables, like a clean cistern that does not lose a drop. He worked drop by drop, with no intention of publicizing his knowledge but only to quench the thirst of the parched. This was a support for the young student and for the reader, for it is never finished. For this reason, I call to them: let them stand together and say, "I read it in you!" There are four types of changes that entered the Orchard <note>original: "Pardes," referring to the four levels of Torah interpretation: Plain, Hint, Allegory, and Secret</note> and reached the place of pure marble stones. They emerged in peace and did not say "Water, water," for the river was full to its banks. Secrets of the Lord are for those who fear Him. May those who fear the Lord say: the heavens are for height and the earth for depth, but the heart of the author and his "L" <note>Likely referring to the "Lamed" or the depth of his heart</note> are unsearchable. No man can recount all that is found in the book. This is the logic of its structure, called the Marble Tablet—the wisdom of the Temple, a magnificent and beautiful building, like that built by the Hasmonean, of marble, blue, and white stones that look like the waves of the sea. The eye that gazes at them wanders, and the pleasant waves of the sea appear to move. And now, my brother, my dear friend the reader: take this beam from between your eyes, the hope of the crimson thread. It is a triple thread by the hand of the third person, woven with marble. Join the threads for me! If one thread exempts the entire reading, this is a great day. There are hints without number there, visions from the Holy of Holies. Its riddle is hidden in the north, tucked away like a consuming fire, like a flame bound to a coal. You shall heap coals upon your head. Your knowledge will diminish like the shadows on the throne. We have risen for this task with the strength of men of truth. It has legs—a throne of three legs. May your thirst be quenched by its Torah; may your poverty and lack be met like a man with a shield or a balm for sorrow. And if you say, "Blessed is the Merciful One who gave us the triple Torah," then we shall bless the final printer, who gathers all the camps with skill. Even if those who see him think it is mere labor and not wisdom, it is a significant matter, like the sounding of the Shofar or taking bread from the oven. Nevertheless, join your soul to his, and for his good work, say: "May his strength be firm." If my name is hidden from you, do not ask or test; only run quickly like a deer to the forest. There you will find flocks of hidden treasures, all of them glorifying their names. My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains. Here end the words of Agur son of Jakeh <note>A biblical pseudonym for King Solomon, often used to signal the end of a wise discourse</note>. May God guard you from pain and groaning. In the year "And let it be known to you as righteousness."

<margin>Ibid.</margin> On the ugly, and a fine parable concerning spoiled fruit.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> A beautiful custom to say "I have hoped for the Lord" <note>original: "Kiviti Hashem," from Psalm 130</note> when wrapping yourself in your garment.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> One should not uproot a plant or kill a living creature unless necessary, and one should choose for them a "beautiful" <note>meaning: merciful or painless</note> death.
<margin>Ibid. folio 66b</margin> Generosity: that there should be a surplus in money and one should spend it for the sake of a commandment.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Explanation of the Gemara <note>The Talmud</note>: "Beautifying a commandment" up to a third [extra cost] in the performance of a commandment.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> His business dealings should be in good faith; his "yes" should be a "yes," and he should not change his word.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> A bad trait in a person: one who chases after the "attribute of strict justice." It is said to the Lord: "Destruction comes before the judges." <note>A warning against excessive litigation or harsh judgment.</note>
<margin>Ibid. folio 66b</margin> A great commandment to sanctify the Name [of God] through money: to return [lost items] to a non-Jew so that they will say, "Blessed is the Lord God of Israel."
<margin>Ibid.</margin> A strong warning to beware of acting as a guarantor <note>specifically for loans</note>.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> To lend to the poor against collateral, and let no person return pushed away or ashamed.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> To buy books and lend them to those who have none.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> One who sells wine or oil should not be overly stingy with the measure.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> One especially needs to be generous-hearted with the wisdom of his Torah, to teach every person.
<margin>Folio 66a</margin> A person should be diligent in his actions and study with diligence; his study should be for Torah and for prayer.
<margin>Ibid. folio 66b</margin> A good friend that every person should have; for one is like the right hand and the friend is like the left—each is a "right hand" to the other.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Explanation of "my colleagues": they should tilt toward one another in Jewish Law, and the debate should be pleasant and not with a loud and bitter cry.
<margin>Folio 61a</margin> A person should join with the wise and pious, the poor and the sick who live in pain, and distance themselves from the opposite.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> To connect oneself with holy companions, such as through visiting the sick and [tending to] graves, so that I may have merits.
<margin>Ibid. folio 61b</margin> To guard oneself from all matters of impurity.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> The morning washing of hands and everything that requires ritual washing.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> That they should wash their hands after the *Selichot* <note>penitential prayers</note> during the days of *Selichot* when the day brightens.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> To accustom oneself to ritual immersion even when a nocturnal emission occurs.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Explanation: The ring [on a finger] should be clean and no dirt should stick to his clothing or his flesh, and he should have water during study.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> He should regularly have a knife and water, for this removes dirt most effectively.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> It is good to have special clothes for prayer; a story is told of a certain pious man.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Drinking vessels should be clean and made of metal or glass.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> A strong warning not to touch covered parts of the body during study or eating, and certainly during prayer.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> The "Good Inclination": many things regarding human passion and physical desire.
<margin>Folio 62a</margin> The matter of the Good and Evil Inclinations; the trait of the wicked regarding Jacob and Esau.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Explanation of the verse: "A small city and few men in it." <note>Ecclesiastes 9:14, often allegorized as the body and the soul.</note>
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Many reasons why it is called the "Good Inclination."
<margin>Ibid. folio 62b</margin> A reason regarding salvation: how the life of Boaz's emotions was saved [from sin].
<margin>Folio 63a</margin> A powerful question: How did the Holy One, blessed be He, create the "Evil Inclination"—a servant who rebels against his master?
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Explanation: "Teach us, we have strayed from Your commandments," etc. "And You are righteous."
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Explanation: "Truth is His seal" to make known that He is One.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Explanation on "Teach us": We have sinned before You through the Evil Inclination.
<margin>Ibid. folio 63b</margin> To judge every person favorably; one who is accustomed to this trait is also judged favorably in the Heavens.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> An average person should be judged favorably, but a completely wicked and famous person should be judged unfavorably—in the name of Rabbi Samuel.
<margin>Folio 64a</margin> A "good heart": that the mouth and the heart should be equal <note>meaning: one's words should match their true intentions</note>.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> "Anything that comes from the heart will enter the heart"; this is a great test for those who offer moral reproof.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> To nullify [distracting] thoughts, say many times: "Fire is engraved," etc., also "I hate vain thoughts," etc.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Be moderate in all actions. A sign for this: "In my haste I said, 'All men are liars'" <note>Psalm 116:11</note>—and the opposite: "In rest and quiet you shall be saved" <note>Isaiah 30:15</note>.
<margin>Ibid. folio 64b</margin> Even for the sake of a commandment [be moderate], despite what we say that "the diligent advance to perform a commandment."
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Regarding the "Fifth Grant": if one wants to do something that is pleasing to some people but displeasing to others, then do it skillfully/secretly.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> "Trustworthy of spirit" is a high virtue. A community leader, even if he is well-established, should give an account to the community.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Distance oneself from anger; whatever happens, accept it.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> The speed of contentment is like a precious stone. Our Sages explained: "No man dies with [even] half his desire in his hand," and the explanation of "Increasing possessions [increases worry]."
<margin>Folio 65a</margin> Great is the beauty of the trait of humility; through it, one will merit the Holy Spirit. One should be humble in his learning.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> A fine remark on the Gemara: "Those who are insulted but do not insult," etc., in the Haggadah <note>homiletic teachings</note> and this is it.

<margin>Ibid.</margin> Another comparison: quenching thirst with salt water. Rather, one should examine his deeds.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Everything that happens to him, he should believe it is from Him, blessed be He, and accept it with love.
<margin>Folio 61a</margin> To sacrifice oneself for the Sanctification of the Unique Name <note>Kiddush HaShem, or martyrdom/dedication</note>, and over which Sanctification of the Name one says a blessing.

<margin>Ibid.</margin> On the condition that he is a righteous person.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> In a gloss: Why do we bless over the Hanukkah candle "to kindle" and it cannot be done through an agent? Answered in the name of R.S.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Afterwards, to be refined with many ethical teachings and to remove hatred from the human heart.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> To be vigilant in a time of trouble for his fellow, with his money and his soul.
<margin>Folio 62a</margin> If he knows of a match <note>marriage partner</note> that is worthy for a daughter of Israel and he has no one to tell her.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> And certainly to guard her and warn her from a stumbling block, God forbid; "And you shall love your neighbor as yourself."
<margin>Ibid.</margin> A nice explanation: "You stir up a fight..." etc., and everything was caused by the writing of controversy.
<margin>Ibid. folio 62b</margin> A fine parable about those who abandon the Lord... indeed He examines [us].

<margin>Ibid.</margin> Proper conduct in all his speech; his words with many ethical sayings.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> One should eat what is beneficial, and even of that, do not fill the belly.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Not to eat except at a feast of a commandment <note>a celebratory meal for a religious milestone</note>.
<margin>Ibid. folio 63b</margin> A person should distance himself from all dangers and from bandits.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> To flee the "dots" <note>possibly a code for the plague or "spots" of disease</note> because of the danger of the Latins <note>original: "Belattin." This may refer to Latin-speaking authorities, a specific decree, or an era of persecution</note>.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Fix his hair and beard so he is not ugly.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Not to throw away an old account [bill] even if everything was paid; perhaps you will need it for evidence.

<margin>Ibid.</margin> They should not frighten an infant with an impure thing, saying "a cat" or "a dog" or "a non-Jew: take this child."
<margin>Ibid. folio 64b</margin> Not to cast excessive fear in his house, and be careful with the honor of his wife.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> The proper conduct of a woman toward her husband. And the matter of expenses for his children: he should not favor one son over the others.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Criticizing the fathers who give almost everything they have during their lifetime to their children.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> A person's conduct toward his fellow, from the saying of the Ramban <note>Nachmanides</note>: one should greet his fellow first.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Regarding himself, he should say "So-and-so and I" <note>putting the other person's name first</note>.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> He should not change his word in business dealings.
<margin>Folio 65a</margin> Explanation on the words of "DeKochi" in the portion of *Kedoshim* <note>Leviticus 19</note>, which is hidden in twenty ways.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> To praise in full for all the good things and for all He created, even if he sees a [bad] thing.

### Tractate Ta'anit
<margin>Ibid.</margin> It is a great commandment to mourn on the 9th of Av, involving many laws.
<margin>Ibid. verso</margin> Every individual should read the Book of Lamentations <note>original: *Megillat Eikhah*</note> the next day privately, and for an individual, the 9th of Av is like the tenth day; one should also read it then.

<margin>Ibid.</margin> Permission for a woman's ritual immersion on the night of the 9th of Av when it falls on a Saturday night.

<margin>Ibid.</margin> It is good to cease from all pleasure also during these days.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> When the 9th of Av falls on a Saturday night, one makes Havdalah in the prayer; women who do not know how to pray should not cook until they have made the Havdalah separation.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> During the eighth and tenth fasts, one should say the prayer of "Comfort" <note>original: *Nachem*</note> in all prayers.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Those passing by cemeteries should not go in large groups and should not speak idle words, but only words of mourning for the destruction of Jerusalem.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> To make a memorial for the Destruction: one should not make a complete square shape, but leave a cubit by a cubit unplastered.
<margin>Ibid. verso</margin> A complaint against women's jewelry, which violates rabbinic law and causes jealousy among the nations, causing the spiritual forces to withdraw.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> One should not fill their mouth with laughter or benefit from musical instruments even on a casual basis.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> Regarding the matter of "Blessing Fasts": it is said that anyone who sits in a fast is called a sinner, etc. <note>Discussing the debate over whether self-affliction is pious or sinful.</note>

<margin>Ibid.</margin> Inverting the verse "Go, eat with joy," etc.

<margin>Ibid.</margin> An individual may decree a fast upon themselves for their own troubles, and how they should behave.
<margin>Ibid.</margin> On a fast day, one should not indulge in pleasures and should guard oneself especially against anger.

<margin>Ibid.</margin> On a fast day, one should not speak of the evening meal at all if possible.
